At age 32, MRI revealed 32 new lesions, including two nonenhancing lesions in the right frontal centrum semiovale and a new left cerebellar white-matter lesion. Late that year, she presented with depression—anorexia, crying spells, and decreased energy—and was treated sequentially with sertraline and bupropion. Repeat MRI continued to show white-matter lesions, including in the cerebellar peduncles. She developed emotional instability treated with fluoxetine and took a leave of absence for cognitive decline. By age 33, no new lesions appeared on FLAIR imaging.

At 35, she developed frontal lobe symptoms and executive dysfunction and was hospitalized for a manic episode; she received a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis with bipolar disorder. Her symptoms included increased energy, emotional lability, grandiosity, impulsiveness, and reckless spending. Neuropsychological testing showed significant deficits across multiple cognitive domains. MRI at that time demonstrated progressive frontotemporal atrophy over the prior two years, and FDG-PET revealed hypometabolism in the frontotemporal lobes and cerebellum. Cerebrospinal fluid studies, EEG, and laboratory workup suggested possible autoimmune encephalitis, and she received intravenous immunoglobulin with only partial and temporary improvement. Over the next two years, repeat FDG-PET scans continued to show predominant frontotemporal hypometabolism, interpreted as favoring frontotemporal dementia.

At 37, she was admitted with catatonia, echolalia, and severe emotional distress; lumbar puncture showed disappearance of monoclonal bands. Trials of memantine, ramelteon, and trazodone had limited effect. At 38, she received valproic acid, paroxetine, and olanzapine for insomnia, compulsive and explosive behaviors, and agitation with hallucinations.

At 39, MRI and FDG-PET demonstrated interval increase in cerebellar atrophy and worsening cerebellar hypometabolism. Metabolic activity in the cerebellum was markedly lower than in the frontal lobes, suggesting that her executive dysfunction might be attributable to cerebellar rather than frontal pathology. A repeat neuropsychological evaluation showed overall stable cognition with improved fine motor speed, initial learning, and semantic memory but possible reduction in working memory and executive function. On examination, she exhibited notable cerebellar signs: impaired alternating hand movements, motor sequencing deficits (left greater than right), and a gait characterized by short tentative steps and balance instability.

A 60-year-old man presented with 2 months of lower abdominal discomfort. His history included chronic hepatitis C infection and cirrhosis. He denied abdominal trauma. On examination, the abdomen was soft and non-tender with no palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin, white blood cell count, platelet count, C-reactive protein, CEA (2.9 ng/mL), and CA19-9 (25 U/mL) all within normal limits. Dynamic CT of the abdomen revealed a 40-mm, well-defined, homogeneously enhancing solid mass anterior to the rectum without signs of invasion; the spleen was visualized in the left upper quadrant with mild splenomegaly. Pelvic MRI showed the mass measured 46×47×38 mm, with low T1 signal, slightly high T2 signal, and homogeneous contrast enhancement; a vascular pedicle extended to the ventral aspect of the mass, though its origin could not be identified on pelvic images. PET-CT demonstrated no abnormal radiotracer accumulation. Colonoscopy showed a normal rectal mucosa without extrinsic compression. Given the location and presumed mesenteric blood supply, a gastrointestinal stromal tumor or malignant lymphoma of the rectum was suspected preoperatively.

A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and a 10-year history of asymptomatic sarcoidosis (mediastinal lymph‐node biopsy) presented with one week of high-grade fever, fatigue, and intermittent confusion. Several days before the onset of fever, he had undergone an elective cystoscopy for incomplete bladder emptying; findings were unremarkable. He was a nonsmoker with no history of immunosuppressive therapy.  

On admission, temperature was 38.9 °C, blood pressure and heart rate were stable, and oxygen saturation was 95% on room air. He was intermittently confused. Lung auscultation revealed scattered rhonchi; there was no lymphadenopathy and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  

Initial head CT and lumbar puncture were normal. Chest and abdominal CT showed modest enlargement of mediastinal and retroperitoneal lymph nodes, consistent with known sarcoidosis. Laboratory studies revealed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (117 × 10^3/µL), and a normal total white-cell count, but peripheral smear showed 6–19% atypical lymphocytes during the first week. Renal and liver function tests were normal. Blood, urine, and respiratory bacterial cultures were negative, and tests for Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and HIV were all negative.

A 19-year-old man with no past medical history presented with a three-week history of persistent sharp precordial pain. The pain began acutely during an episode of gastroenteritis, and gastrointestinal symptoms resolved while the chest pain remained mild and worsened on inspiration. He also noted a sporadic clicking and popping sound on the left sternal edge that could be very loud and was audible without a stethoscope; he recorded it on his smartphone. He denied shortness of breath. 

On examination, his body mass index was 18.3 kg/m2. Vital signs were normal: blood pressure within normal limits, no fever, and an oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. Lung and heart auscultation were normal except for the intermittent clicking over the left sternal border. 

Laboratory studies, including arterial blood gas analysis, complete blood count, C-reactive protein, D-dimer level, and cardiac troponins, were all within normal limits. A chest radiograph was reported as normal. Electrocardiography showed a sinus rhythm at 78 bpm with a normal QRS duration and axis, without repolarization abnormalities.

A 64-year-old woman presented after acute visual deficits that resolved within 24 hours and were consistent with a transient ischemic attack. Her history was notable for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and migraines; she was taking aspirin 325 mg daily for stroke prophylaxis. On examination, blood pressure was 170/116 mmHg, heart rate 88 bpm and irregularly irregular, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiac auscultation revealed a soft midpeaking systolic murmur best heard at the right upper sternal border; there were no carotid bruits. 

Electrocardiography confirmed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 88 bpm and no ischemic changes. Laboratory evaluation was notable for a prothrombin time of 11.4 s, creatinine 0.5 mg/dL, HDL 71 mg/dL, LDL 105 mg/dL, and triglycerides 103 mg/dL. CT angiography of the head and neck showed only mild carotid bulb calcifications. Brain MRI revealed periventricular and subcortical white-matter changes consistent with prior ischemic events.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a round, echodense mass measuring 20 × 23 mm attached to the posterior mitral annulus, with smooth borders, mild mitral regurgitation, and preserved left ventricular size and function (LVEF 69%) without wall motion abnormalities. A subsequent transesophageal echocardiogram confirmed a well-circumscribed, echogenic, nonmobile mass measuring 19 × 23 mm at the posterior mitral annulus; the left atrial appendage was free of thrombus. 

To further characterize the lesion, a non–ECG-gated contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest was obtained, which showed a 17 × 18 mm round hyperdense mass along the inferior mitral valve annulus with a heterogeneous calcification pattern and a hypoattenuated central zone measuring 100 Hounsfield units.

A 69-year-old man with a history of cutaneous psoriasis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma in remission presented with a 3-week history of progressive oligoarticular joint pain affecting the right knee, right elbow, and right shoulder. He reported morning stiffness lasting 30 minutes and nocturnal pain. There was no history of trauma, upper respiratory infection, travel, risky sexual behavior, or animal exposures. 

On examination, he was afebrile. The right knee had a spontaneous flexum, a large effusion with positive Flot and Glaçon signs, and limited shoulder mobility bilaterally. A left prepectoral Port-a-cath was without erythema or swelling. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a CRP of 299 mg/dL and mild leukocytosis; serum chemistries and coagulation studies were normal. Arthroscopic drainage of the right knee yielded synovial fluid with 50,000 cells/mm3 (64% neutrophils) and no crystals. Empiric amoxicillin–clavulanate was started. Joint fluid and blood cultures remained sterile after 14 days.

Over the next week, the patient developed fever and sequential swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands and the right elbow. Physical examination now revealed signs of right-sided heart failure and a new grade 3/6 protosystolic murmur at the right second parasternal space. Bilateral pretibial edema was present; there were no peripheral embolic lesions or subcutaneous nodules, and the neurologic exam was normal. Repeat labs showed CRP 340 mg/dL, ESR 90 mm/h, normocytic anemia, thrombocytosis, hyperferritinemia, elevated liver enzymes, positive rheumatoid factor, and negative anti-CCP antibodies. Ultrasound of the small joints demonstrated synovitis in the tarsi, wrists, and elbows.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 16 × 9 mm mobile vegetation on the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve, protruding into the left ventricle without regurgitation, abscess, or left-ventricular dysfunction.

A 55-year-old Iranian man was admitted for evaluation of a 5-year history of left flank pain, dysuria, urinary frequency, and decreased urinary force and caliber. He reported recurrent febrile urinary tract infections treated medically. His medical history was notable only for these infections; he had no diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, malignancy, or drug abuse. 

On admission he appeared ill and had a temperature of 38.6 °C. Blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and pulse 83 beats/min. Lung, cardiovascular, genital, rectal, and neurologic examinations were normal. 

Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 8200/μL, hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, and platelet count 233,000/μL. Urinalysis and urine culture were negative. 

Renal ultrasonography revealed a 62×54 mm hypoechoic heterogeneous mass in the upper pole of the left kidney. The clinical impression was a renal tumor or xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis.

A 30-year-old right-handed woman presented to the emergency department with a knife wound at the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the left forearm, on the palmar surface. On initial examination she had no sensory or motor deficits and both radial and ulnar pulses were well palpated. Under regional anesthesia with a humeral tourniquet, exploration in the operating theatre on the day of injury revealed intact musculo-tendinous, nervous, and visible vascular structures, and the wound was closed with nonabsorbable sutures. Her postoperative course was uneventful, and by day 15 the wound had healed with only localized pain and no functional impairment. On postoperative day 20 she reported worsening pain; examination revealed a nonpulsatile, subcutaneous inflammatory mass opposite the scar. Needle aspiration yielded red blood. There was no dysesthesia of the fingers or signs of Raynaud phenomenon. Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated a pseudoaneurysm of a cutaneous perforating branch of the ulnar artery, which was confirmed by magnetic resonance angiography.

A 38-year-old woman with a history of anxiety, depression, hypertension, and alcohol use disorder presented with 6 weeks of nausea, vomiting, and bilateral upper‐quadrant abdominal pain, progressive abdominal swelling, 3 weeks of night sweats, and new jaundice. Over 2 weeks, she noted reduced stool and urine output and poor oral intake. On examination, she had severe scleral icterus, jaundice, and tenderness in the upper abdomen. Laboratory tests showed total bilirubin 23.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 18.9 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 7.6 mg/dL, AST 232 U/L, and ALT 102 U/L. 

Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed what was interpreted as an extensive malignant tumor in the liver, ascites, streaky changes in abdominal fat, and prominent submucosal fat in the colon; “peritoneal carcinomatosis could not be ruled out.” Radiology recommended a triple-phase liver CT. That study demonstrated hepatic steatosis, hepatomegaly, and multiple geographic and round hypodense areas—most notably an enlarged caudate lobe—and interpreted the findings as “fulminant hepatitis, with small hypodense lesions possibly representing developing fluid collections, such as abscesses,” with “no evidence of malignancy.” 

A biopsy of a peripheral right‐lobe lesion showed cirrhosis, macrovesicular steatosis, and severe reactive changes including feathery degeneration. MRCP then demonstrated moderate intraperitoneal fluid and a 10.3 × 5.7 cm porta hepatis mass “suspicious for cholangiocarcinoma, noncalcific gallstone, polyp, metastatic disease, or hepatocellular carcinoma.” Tumor markers were: AFP 2.8 ng/mL, CEA 1.89 ng/mL, CA 15-3 27.6 U/mL, CA 19-9 88 U/mL, CA 125 1012 U/mL, and hCG 2 mIU/mL.

A 4-month-old female infant, born at term after an unremarkable perinatal period, was brought to the clinic with five days of swelling of the left labia. There was no history of urinary tract infection, vulvar discharge, voiding disturbances, or trauma, and maternal prenatal course was normal. On examination, the infant appeared distressed but had normal vital signs. Local inspection revealed a tender, soft, fluctuant, and erythematous swelling measuring approximately 2 cm×1.5 cm in the lower half of the left labia minora, with deep lateral extension between the labia majora and labia minora. The clitoris and urethral meatus were unremarkable. Clinical assessment suggested an abscess. A sample of purulent discharge was sent for culture and grew Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Antibiotic-susceptibility testing indicated sensitivity to amoxicillin–clavulanate, ceftriaxone, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, and gentamicin.

A 28-year-old woman with an 18-month history of a 2 × 10 cm keloid scar on the upper anterior chest (secondary to acne) underwent treatment in the dermatology clinic. She received intralesional lidocaine, then triamcinolone acetonide injection, followed by two 40-second cycles of sprayed liquid nitrogen cryotherapy. Thirty minutes after the procedure, she noted acute swelling of the upper portion of the treated area. On examination, there was localized swelling with palpable cutaneous crepitus but no erythema, pain, or increased warmth. Vital signs were normal, and she had no fever or other systemic symptoms.

A previously healthy 3-year-old girl was admitted with generalized edema, abdominal distension, and abdominal pain. On examination she had puffy anasarca involving the face, limbs, and lumbar region, spastic cough, diminished breath sounds in the right lower lung field, and tense ascites. Vital signs were T 36.9°C, HR 115/min, BP 121/89 mmHg, RR 25/min, and SpO₂ 99% on room air. Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL; serum protein 3.3 g/dL with albumin 1.56 g/dL; total cholesterol 479 mg/dL; triglycerides 579 mg/dL; urea 59 mg/dL; uric acid 7.37 mg/dL; and nonselective proteinuria of 5 g/day. Thyroid testing revealed TSH 17.20 µIU/mL and free T₄ 2.42 ng/dL. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated marked ascites, and pleural ultrasonography revealed small bilateral pleural effusions. Viral hepatitis B and C, HIV serologies, and QuantiFERON test were negative, and complement levels, antinuclear, anti-thyroperoxidase, and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies were normal. She received a low-sodium, low-lipid, normal-protein diet, methylprednisolone, and albumin, with rapid resolution of edema and normalization of proteinuria by day 3. On day 4 she developed a focal seizure of the right face and extremities with impaired consciousness. An emergency brain CT with contrast was performed.

A 23-year-old man was admitted to a psychiatric unit at his parents’ request for evaluation of recurrent, prolonged sleep episodes. He was a farmer in a sub-rural area of India with an unremarkable developmental and family history and no history of substance use. Over the past 6 months, he had 2–3 episodes every 2 weeks, each lasting 15–17 days, during which he slept more than 20 hours per day and did not arise even for food or self-care. Each episode was followed by 4–7 days of apathy, irritability, disruptive behavior, and reduced environmental awareness. He described derealization, headaches, and sensitivity to light and noise during these periods. Depressive symptoms lasting 2–3 days often preceded or followed the sleep episodes. In later episodes, he would briefly awaken after about 14 hours of sleep for 15–20 minutes to eat and urinate, then return to prolonged sleep, with a similar post-sleep cognitive and behavioral disturbance. Between episodes, his behavior and cognition returned to baseline. He denied any hyperphagia or hypersexuality. Physical examination was normal. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, folate, vitamin B12, electrolytes, lactate, ammonia, urine metabolic screen, and copper studies, were all normal. Neuropsychological testing and electroencephalography showed no abnormalities. Initially, a provisional diagnosis of Kleine-Levin syndrome versus atypical depression was considered.

A 25‐year‐old Indian man presented with three months of fatigue, night sweats, fevers, a nonproductive cough, and 30 lb weight loss, plus ten days of worsening low back pain radiating to the thighs. He immigrated from India 2½ years earlier, with no known TB exposures. On admission he was febrile (103.1 °F), tachycardic (160 bpm), normotensive, and had an oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. Exam showed decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right middle and lower lung zones and mild digital clubbing; the remainder was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies revealed a mild normocytic anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, hyponatremia (127 mmol/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase (201 IU/L), and hypoalbuminemia. Chest imaging showed a large right loculated pleural effusion, right upper‐lobe density with compressive atelectasis, multiple bilateral subcentimeter pulmonary nodules, and a 1.5 cm right hepatic lesion. MRI of the lumbar spine identified multiple poorly defined enhancing lesions in the vertebral bodies and posterior elements, concerning for metastatic disease. Testicular ultrasound demonstrated bilateral intratesticular masses suspicious for metastases; serum α-fetoprotein and β-hCG were within normal limits. 

Thoracentesis yielded a lymphocyte‐predominant exudative effusion with normal adenosine deaminase; cultures were negative for acid-fast bacilli. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy showed necrotizing granulomas, with negative stains for mycobacteria and fungi; culture remained negative at six weeks. Subsequent pleural biopsy also grew no mycobacteria but revealed focal granulomatous inflammation.

A 53-year-old otherwise healthy man presented with a 4-day history of fever, headache, and arthralgia. Four days prior, he developed a fever of 37.5°C with chills that progressed to 39.1°C the next day despite negative rapid tests for influenza and coronavirus and a normal chest radiograph. Treatment with cefditoren pivoxil and acetaminophen yielded no improvement. Over the ensuing days, he experienced bilateral temporal and occipital headaches, arthralgia of both shoulders, and back pain, prompting referral.

On examination, he was febrile (39.5°C), tachycardic (110/min), blood pressure 121/76 mmHg, and fully alert; there were no murmurs, lymphadenopathy, rash, or meningeal signs. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed mild mediastinal and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and fatty liver. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 7000/μL with neutrophil predominance, platelet count 19,000/μL, aspartate aminotransferase 60 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 77 U/L, and C-reactive protein 6.56 mg/dL.

Empiric minocycline was initiated to cover tsutsugamushi disease. On the following day, the platelet count increased and inflammatory markers improved, leading to the conclusion that the transient improvement was spontaneous rather than antibiotic-mediated. Subsequently, his fever, headache, and arthralgia gradually resolved.

A 65-year-old Melanau woman with end-stage kidney disease secondary to diabetes started automated peritoneal dialysis two months ago. To prevent constipation, she was prescribed lactulose 15 mL three times daily and bisacodyl 10 mg at night. Initially, she had one bowel movement daily. Over the past four weeks, she developed increasingly frequent, watery diarrhea—initially 2–3 times per day, rising to more than 10 times per day in the week before presentation—associated with colicky abdominal pain, nausea, appetite loss, and a 10 kg weight loss. She denied fever, vomiting, or cloudy dialysis effluent. 

On examination, she appeared dehydrated but was alert, afebrile, with blood pressure 108/52 mmHg and pulse 85 bpm. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. Stool inspection revealed greenish, fluffy pieces with ragged edges and mushy consistency (Bristol stool type 6). Peritoneal dialysis effluent was clear, with zero cells and a negative culture. Stool cultures and blood cultures showed no growth. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, WBC 10.8×10^9/L, platelets 391×10^9/L; sodium 135 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, urea 10.0 mmol/L, creatinine 1031 μmol/L; albumin 24 g/L; C-reactive protein 34 mg/L; thyroid function tests and tumor markers were within normal limits. Abdominal radiograph and ultrasound were unremarkable.

An 83-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 1-week history of a palpable mass in the anteriomedial aspect of her left thigh. She reported no antecedent trauma. Her surgical history was notable for transverse colon cancer at age 73 and lung cancer at age 80. On examination, there was a tender, firm, nonmobile mass measuring 7 × 6 cm. Laboratory values, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, and white-cell count, were within normal limits. A plain radiograph of the thigh showed no abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a poorly defined 6 × 5 cm lesion within the left vastus medialis muscle that was isointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed marked enhancement after gadolinium administration, with surrounding muscle edema. A Tc-99m hydroxymethylenediphosphonate bone scan revealed intense uptake in the medial soft tissues of the left thigh. The possibility of a malignant neoplasm was raised, and a core-needle biopsy was performed.

An 8-year-old girl began to note progressive abdominal swelling and intermittent shortness of breath. She was managed empirically for abdominal tuberculosis without confirmed diagnosis. She has never traveled outside the Kano–Jigawa area, and there is no family history of similar illness. Both parents are health workers.

On examination at age 10, she was wasted (20 kg, 61% expected) without peripheral edema or cyanosis. Vital signs: heart rate 120 bpm, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg. Jugular venous pressure was 9 cm H₂O. The precordium was normoactive; the apex beat was poorly palpable, and heart sounds were distant. A grade 4/6 pansystolic murmur was heard at the left sternal border and at the apex, radiating to the axilla. Bilateral basal crepitations were present. Abdominal examination revealed massive ascites.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and unremarkable liver and renal function tests. Chest radiograph demonstrated a globular cardiac silhouette. Electrocardiography revealed low-voltage QRS complexes in lead V₁.

A 65-year-old previously healthy man was admitted for evaluation of hallucinations that began one day before admission. One week earlier he developed rhinorrhea, headache, malaise, and low-grade fever; a COVID-19 PCR test was negative. Three days before admission he received the second dose of the Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine, and 24 hours later he developed high-grade fever, hallucinations, and disorientation to time, place, and person. On admission he was not oriented to time, place, or person. Temperature was 38.0°C, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, pulse 80 bpm; cardiac, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were normal. Neurologic examination was notable only for disorientation. Laboratory studies showed sodium 122 mEq/L, white-cell count 10,200 per µL, hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, platelet count 352,000 per µL, normal liver function tests, and C-reactive protein 1 mg/L. Lumbar puncture revealed no white cells; antinuclear antibody, anti–double-stranded DNA, C3, C4, C-ANCA, and P-ANCA were all normal. Despite correction of sodium, the patient had a generalized seizure requiring intubation. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and cortisol levels were normal. Brain MRI demonstrated T2 and FLAIR hyperintense areas in the deep white matter and an increased signal with sulcal effacement in the right temporal lobe without contrast enhancement, findings suggestive of encephalitis. CSF herpes simplex PCR was negative.

A 37-year-old woman presented with nine months of pain and a slowly enlarging nodule in the perianal region. Initial antibiotic therapy was ineffective. Over the past two weeks, she noted worsening swelling and pain without purulent discharge. The discomfort did not fluctuate with her menstrual cycle, and she denied dysmenorrhea and changes in bowel habits. Her only surgical history was a full-term vaginal delivery with an episiotomy five years earlier.

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was a 1.5-cm, firm, tender swelling at the 11 o’clock position in the perianal area, with a nearby episiotomy scar. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. Viral hepatitis serologies and tests for immunocompromise were negative.

Anoscopic evaluation revealed mild internal hemorrhoids and otherwise normal rectal mucosa. Endoanal ultrasound showed no evidence of abscess or fistula. Transperineal ultrasound demonstrated a 1.5-cm irregular, mixed-echogenicity lesion in the perineal soft tissue, not involving the anal sphincters.

A 47-year-old woman presented with sudden-onset paraplegia that began 30 minutes earlier, accompanied by mild back pain. She was a smoker with no other significant medical history. On arrival, her blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg in both arms, heart rate 72 bpm, and pulses were palpable and symmetrical. Neurologic examination revealed flaccid paralysis of both lower limbs, abolition of deep tendon reflexes, and paresthesias in both feet. The remainder of the physical examination and the admission electrocardiogram were normal. Although pain was not a prominent feature, aortic dissection with neurologic symptoms was suspected. Contrast computed tomography of the chest and abdomen showed a Stanford Type B aortic dissection with partial thrombosis of the false lumen, extending from immediately distal to the left subclavian artery to the left iliac artery, without involvement of supra-aortic or abdominal branch vessels.

A 38-year-old woman (gravida 1, para 0) with a 20-year history of infertility and a prior hysteroscopic septum resection underwent her fourth intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) cycle. Two weeks after embryo transfer, her β-hCG level was >100 mIU/mL and rose to 1630 IU/mL four weeks later. At 6.5 weeks’ gestation, transvaginal ultrasound revealed a 5 mm embryo with cardiac activity implanted within the cervical canal; no intrauterine gestational sac was identified. Repeat ultrasound one week later confirmed a 7-week embryo with cardiac activity in the cervical canal. The patient was then referred for further management.

A 74-year-old man with a 17-year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (RA) maintained on methotrexate (12 mg/week), sulfasalazine, and bucillamine was transferred with acute respiratory failure. He was an ex-smoker (60 pack-years) and had no known environmental exposures. RA activity had been low according to composite indices. Eleven months earlier, chest CT had shown two solitary nodules in the right lower lobe and mild subpleural honeycombing.

He acutely developed dyspnea after a sore throat and fever to 39.0 °C. On admission, temperature was 39.6 °C, blood pressure 117/78 mmHg, heart rate 130 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on 6 L O₂ by reservoir mask. Pulmonary crackles were audible throughout both lung fields. Bilateral finger and wrist deformities were noted without swelling or tenderness.

Laboratory results included WBC 9 100/µL (84% neutrophils), hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, ESR 120 mm/hr, CRP 21.36 mg/dL, rheumatoid factor 60.0 IU/mL, and anti-CCP antibody 75.7 U/mL. Serum KL-6 was 930 U/mL and SP-D 33.0 ng/mL. β-D glucan was 12.9 pg/mL; aspergillus and cryptococcal antigens were negative. Blood and sputum cultures were negative, and PCR assays for tuberculosis, Mycobacterium avium complex, and Pneumocystis jirovecii were all negative.

Chest radiography showed diffuse ground-glass opacities. Chest CT revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities with a subpleural reticular pattern and honeycombing, along with multiple nodular lesions (15–45 mm) in both lung fields and the liver.

In February 2020, on a conventional piglet-producing farm in Styria, Austria, a fourth-parity sow farrowed 16 live piglets and one stillborn. Four live-born piglets were noted at birth to have multifocal pox-like skin lesions on the abdomen, inner surfaces of the legs, and ears; one of these piglets died on day 3 of life. During a farm visit by the herd veterinarian, two of the affected piglets exhibited lethargy and ceased suckling. Physical examination revealed erythematous macules, papules, and vesicles with serocellular crusts on the skin, as well as ulcerations of the oral mucosa including the tongue. The two piglets were euthanized for welfare reasons and for further diagnostics. Tissue samples (skin, lungs, heart, lymph nodes, liver, kidney, and intestine) were collected and submitted for histopathologic examination. Samples of the characteristic skin lesions were also sent for poxvirus PCR. Additionally, pooled organ samples were forwarded to the national surveillance program to exclude African and classical swine fever.

A 58-year-old woman presented with upper abdominal pain for more than 2 months. An endoscopic ultrasound showed an elevated and depressed area in the gastric body concerning for a submucosal tumor. Preoperative CT demonstrated a soft-tissue mass in the gastric body with uneven enhancement; no hepatic subcapsular lesions were seen. She underwent resection of the gastric mass. Histopathology revealed a high-risk gastric stromal tumor. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD117, CD34, DOG1, and vimentin; Ki-67 index was <5%. 

Three months after surgery, a routine abdominal CT showed a 1.1 × 0.8 cm lesion beneath the capsule of the left hepatic lobe with a fat attenuation of –70 HU, without other lesions.

A 46-year-old woman with fibromyalgia and controlled endometriosis presented 6 years after developing medial left knee osteoarthritis and undergoing an Oxford unicompartmental knee arthroplasty. Postoperatively she had persistent 4/10 medial knee pain at rest and “shooting” pain with activity. She denied fevers, chills, or systemic symptoms. On examination at 3 months, she had a small punctate wound over the medial joint line. Her white blood cell count was 7.0 × 10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 16 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein 0.9 mg/L. Knee aspiration yielded 998 nucleated cells/µL of thin, bloody fluid; cultures were negative. Radiographs showed a well-positioned implant with no lucencies. The wound healed with local care over 3 weeks. At 4 months and again at 1 year, she continued to have diffuse medial joint-line tenderness, range of motion of 0–120°, a normal gait, and no new wounds. She was using a fentanyl patch for pain. Physical therapy provided no relief. Because infection and instability were unlikely, she underwent a dermatology-performed patch allergy panel.

A 37-year-old man presented with 3 months of intermittent crampy abdominal pain, occasional abdominal distension, and intermittent vomiting of ingested matter, sometimes bilious. He reported constipation without failure to pass flatus or feces. He also noted easy fatigability, anorexia, and significant unquantified weight loss; these symptoms had been present on and off for 3 years but had worsened over the past 3 months. He denied diarrhea, cough, or significant past medical history.

On examination he appeared acutely ill. Vital signs: temperature afebrile to touch, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg. Conjunctivae were slightly pale. The abdomen was soft, moved with respiration, with no visible peristalsis or tenderness. Digital rectal examination was normal.

Laboratory studies: WBC 6.5×10^3/µL (73% granulocytes, 15% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, hematocrit 27.9%, platelets 295×10^3/µL. Electrolytes, renal and liver function tests were within normal limits. Chest radiograph was normal.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 4.5 cm × 2.2 cm segment of asymmetric small-bowel wall thickening (maximal thickness 1.2 cm) in the left upper quadrant, multiple adjacent mesenteric lymph nodes (largest 1.1 cm), proximal small-bowel dilatation to 5 cm, and collapsed distal bowel; the impression was short-segment small-bowel wall thickening with luminal stenosis, partial small-bowel obstruction, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy. Small-bowel carcinoma was considered as a differential diagnosis, and contrast-enhanced abdominal CT was recommended.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed multifocal short and long-segment symmetric wall thickening of small-bowel loops—most marked in the left lower quadrant—with luminal narrowing, proximal bowel dilatation with shouldering, multiple focal luminal constrictions, small mesenteric lymph nodes with adjacent fat stranding, and internal hypoattenuation suggestive of central necrosis.

A 65-year-old man presented with acute-onset atraumatic bilateral knee pain and swelling. Four weeks earlier he had undergone revision of a bicuspid aortic valve replacement, and 4 days before presentation he was diagnosed with a sternal surgical wound infection that was treated with oral clarithromycin. The wound appeared to be responding, but his left knee symptoms worsened, and 12 hours before presentation he developed acute right knee pain and swelling with generalized fatigue. In the emergency department, his temperature was 39°C and heart rate 100 beats per minute. Both knees were diffusely swollen, warm, and exquisitely tender, with no range of motion. Hip and ankle joints were normal, and there were no signs of cellulitis. Chest and urinary sources of infection were excluded. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 15.9×10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 288 mg/L. Knee radiographs revealed no bony abnormalities.

A 30-year-old pregnant woman (gravida 2, abortus 1) at 32 weeks’ gestation presented with hypertension and left thigh pain, reporting one week of inability to bear weight. A Doppler ultrasound ruled out deep vein thrombosis. Radiographs of the left femur showed an aggressive lytic lesion in the distal femur with periosteal reaction. Laboratory studies revealed a serum calcium level of 4.13 mmol/L (reference range, 2.10–2.60 mmol/L). An open biopsy of the lesion demonstrated numerous multinucleated giant cells, but the radiographic appearance was inconsistent with a giant cell tumor.

A 17-year-old Sardinian woman presented for a routine dental check. Examination revealed caries, a need for orthodontic evaluation, and atrophy of the filiform papillae with circinate erythematous ulcer-like lesions on the dorsum and lateral borders of the tongue. She reported that these tongue lesions had begun at age five, were intermittent, and had never been investigated. Neither she nor her parents reported any systemic disease or gastrointestinal symptoms. Her height was 145 cm, which was attributed to familial short stature. Given the finding of AG in a region with high celiac disease prevalence, laboratories were obtained. Hematologic tests showed a vitamin B12 concentration < 150 pg/mL (normal 193–982 pg/mL) and folic acid 1.65 ng/mL (normal 3–17 ng/mL). Immunologic tests were positive for antigliadin IgG, tissue transglutaminase IgA, and IgA-endomysial antibody, with negative antigliadin IgA.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of nonproductive, intermittent severe cough that began after excessive use of antiseptic solutions during the COVID-19 pandemic. The cough was aggravated by exposure to perfumes, strong odors, and spices, and failed to improve with various antitussives. Her medical history was notable only for allergic rhinitis; she had no history of gastroesophageal reflux, chronic sinusitis, tuberculosis, cardiopulmonary disease, or medication use. She was a nonsmoker with no occupational exposures. 

On examination, vital signs were normal and lung auscultation revealed no wheezes or rhonchi. The only abnormal finding was a reddish-purple discoloration on and around the eyelids.

Spirometry showed normal prebronchodilator values but “after using a bronchodilator, a substantial increase from baseline was noted in FEV1.” A methacholine challenge test and chest radiograph were normal. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated hyperinflation and tree-in-bud opacities. Sputum cultures, including for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, were negative. Laboratory tests revealed mild hypochromic microcytic anemia, negative cANCA and pANCA, mildly low vitamin D, and normal coagulation studies. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative.

A 34-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 5-year history of intermittent, self-limited palpitations presented with sudden onset of palpitations associated with chest pain and dyspnea. In the emergency department, he was found to be in supraventricular tachycardia at 220 beats per minute. The tachycardia terminated spontaneously, and echocardiography and other imaging showed no structural heart disease. He was referred for catheter ablation.

During electrophysiologic study, electrode catheters were positioned in the right atrium, right ventricle, His-bundle region, and coronary sinus. Baseline intervals were: sinus cycle length 680 ms, atrial–His 67 ms, His–ventricular 32 ms. Pacing the right ventricle at both apex and base revealed ventriculoatrial (VA) dissociation at cycle lengths of 350 to 650 ms. Programmed atrial stimulation showed no ventricular preexcitation or dual AV nodal physiology; the AV Wenckebach cycle length was 280 ms.

Tachycardia was readily induced by either rapid ventricular pacing or atrial extrastimuli. During tachycardia, the atrial activation sequence in the coronary sinus was distal to proximal. Pacing maneuvers were performed: premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) could terminate the tachycardia without atrial activation, and entrainment with right ventricular pacing produced a VAV response on pacing termination. Multiple tachycardia terminations followed immediately by ventricular burst pacing continued to demonstrate VA dissociation. After isoproterenol infusion, ventricular pacing produced only a concentric, decremental retrograde atrial conduction pattern, consistent with AV nodal conduction.

Incidentally, spontaneous PVCs during sinus rhythm occasionally conducted with an eccentric atrial activation pattern similar to that seen during tachycardia. Programmed PVCs during sinus rhythm replicated this eccentric retrograde activation within a critical coupling-interval window. Furthermore, pacing from the left ventricle near the mitral annulus also demonstrated eccentric VA conduction.

A 58-year-old woman with no pre-existing medical conditions presented to the emergency department with a slowly progressive reddish skin alteration in the right interdigital space. Eleven days earlier, while performing necropsies on 6-month-old geese in a veterinary laboratory, a sharp rib fragment penetrated her glove between digits II and III. The same day, four geese from a flock of 350 died suddenly without prior clinical signs. Cloacal swabs were tested with a rapid avian influenza and Newcastle disease antigen kit and were negative. Necropsy of two carcasses revealed dehydration, chronic ulcerative bilateral pododermatitis, multiple pericardial hemorrhages in one bird, congested livers and spleens, and a reticular pattern in the kidneys; parasitology was negative. Culture of heart, liver, and lung on sheep blood agar identified Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry (scores 2.02–2.15). 

From day 1 after the injury, the patient noted a localized erythematous maculopapular discoloration at the wound site. On day 11 she presented; she was afebrile and in good general condition and reported no systemic symptoms. Examination showed a strictly delimited erythematous maculopapular lesion between the right digits II and III without swelling or pain, accompanied by mild pruritus. Routine laboratory tests (hematology, clinical chemistry) were unremarkable, and blood cultures remained sterile.

A 94-year-old woman presented to the emergency department after sudden syncope and respiratory arrest immediately following a cervical epidural steroid injection at a pain clinic. EMS placed a supraglottic airway and delivered rescue breaths; no chest compressions were needed. On arrival she was awake, following commands, and the airway device was removed. She reported nausea, dizziness, and lightheadedness and had no recollection of the event. She denied shortness of breath or chest pain and had no other recent trauma or procedures.

Her medical history included atrial fibrillation, multiple myeloma on monthly bortezomib (VELCADE) infusions with dexamethasone, and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes. Medications were apixaban, metoprolol, tramadol, and dexamethasone. She did not smoke, used occasional alcohol, and had a family history of multiple myeloma.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits (SpO2 99%), and the physical exam was unremarkable. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with a first-degree AV block unchanged from prior tracings. Chest radiograph revealed no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality. Laboratory studies, including CBC, CMP, coagulation profile, troponin, arterial blood gas, and COVID test, were largely unremarkable except for a blood glucose of 138 mg/dL and troponin of 16 pg/mL.

Noncontrast CT of the head demonstrated approximately 5 mL of scattered intracranial gas, most prominently in the suprasellar region and left sylvian fissure, with partial effacement of the fourth ventricle and early downward cerebellar herniation. There was no evidence of skull fracture or disruption of air cells.

A 33-year-old African man with an 11-month history of continuous, blunt low back pain, worse with walking and radiating to the loins and thighs bilaterally, presented with a 9-kg weight loss. He had no significant past medical history and was a smoker. On examination, he was normotensive, with unremarkable cardiovascular and respiratory findings and palpable lower extremity pulses bilaterally. 

Lumbar-spine MRI showed T1- and T2-weighted isointense circumferential soft-tissue thickening around the infrarenal aorta without disk pathology. A CT aortic angiogram confirmed thickening of the anterior and lateral aspects of the infrarenal aorta without aneurysm or distal narrowing. A diagnosis of periaortitis was considered. 

Six months later, he returned with severe back pain and bilateral lower limb swelling. Repeat CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated extensive soft-tissue thickening concentrically surrounding the abdominal aorta, both iliac arteries, the inferior vena cava, and both ureters, with medial displacement of the ureters and bilateral hydronephrosis. His serum creatinine was elevated at 192 μmol/L. Bilateral Double-J stents were placed, and creatinine fell to 111 μmol/L. 

At this point, the differential diagnoses of retroperitoneal fibrosis, lymphoma, and retroperitoneal tumour/sarcoma were entertained.

A 58-year-old man with no known chronic illness was brought to the emergency department with one week of fatigue and progressive dyspnea. On arrival, he was tachypneic and hypotensive, and preliminary laboratories revealed: hemoglobin 21 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 154 fL, indeterminate platelet count, creatinine 219 μmol/L, and venous blood gas pH 7.19. He was intubated for respiratory distress and started on renal replacement therapy for acute kidney injury.  

His only medications were amlodipine and ezetimibe. He denied fevers, diarrheal illness, melena, or sick contacts. Physical examination showed jaundice but no petechiae, and a digital rectal examination was negative for blood.  

Initial investigations revealed:  
• A significant degree of red blood cell agglutination on peripheral blood film  
• A positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test for C3  
• Haptoglobin < 0.07 g/L  
• Indirect bilirubin 83.1 μmol/L  
• Lactate dehydrogenase 1776 U/L (normal < 225 U/L)  
• A cold agglutinin screen positive at a thermal amplitude of 37 °C

An 87‐year‐old postmenopausal woman presented for her annual gynecological follow‐up. Her history included bilateral breast in‐situ cancer treated by mastectomy, permanent atrial fibrillation, a transient ischemic attack, and placement of an aortic bioprosthesis. She denied pelvic pain, fever, vaginal bleeding, or weight loss. On examination, the uterus was enlarged. 

Pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated an intrauterine cystic mass measuring 82 mm in length, with homogeneous internal echoes, suggesting hematometra or pyometra; endometrial thickness was regular. Pelvic MRI confirmed a heterogeneous intrauterine collection of 105 mm, consistent with pyometra, with a normal myometrium, no enhancing tissue, no adnexal abnormalities, and no evidence of fistula. 

Hematological and biochemical studies, including hepatic and renal function and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits; tumor markers (CEA, CA 125, and CA 19-9) were also normal. During speculum examination, drainage was attempted but could not be performed because of complete cervical stenosis. In view of cervical stenosis and pyometra in an elderly woman, a clinical possibility of endocervical or endometrial carcinoma could not be ruled out.

A 10-year-old girl presented with patchy scalp hair loss for 1 year, noting rapid progression over the past 6 months. She had no preceding papules, pustules, or plaques; no other cutaneous or systemic illness; and no family history of alopecia. On examination, there was an irregular but well-defined confluent patch of alopecia over the vertex with minimal atrophy, wrinkling, shiny skin, absence of follicular ostia, and a few preserved hairs within the lesion. The lesions were asymptomatic; the hair pull test was positive without exclamation-mark hairs or leukotrichia. Remaining scalp and body hair, mucosae, and nails were normal. Potassium hydroxide preparation of adjacent hairs was negative. Trichoscopy demonstrated loss of follicular ostia, ivory-white macules, and focal pigmentation. A scalp biopsy was performed with lichen planopilaris and pseudopelade of Brocq as leading considerations.

A 75-year-old woman with a history of smoking, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and hypertension underwent an L1–S1 laminectomy and L2–L5 in situ fusion with iliac crest bone graft and bone morphogenic protein for severe multilevel lumbar stenosis and degenerative scoliosis. She had no history or symptoms of coronary artery disease or heart failure. Surgery was complicated by an incidental durotomy that was repaired without issue; estimated blood loss was 550 mL. She was extubated in the operating room and transferred to the postanesthesia care unit, where she required a brief trial of supplemental oxygen via Venturi mask but otherwise recovered uneventfully. The first two postoperative days were unremarkable.

On the evening of postoperative day three, she experienced a seven-hour episode of squeezing chest pain accompanied by shortness of breath. Initial cardiac biomarkers showed a peak troponin level of 1.3 ng/mL. Electrocardiography demonstrated diffuse T-wave inversions and T-wave flattening. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 30%–35%, a left ventricular end-diastolic diameter of 4.6 cm, a left atrial diameter of 5.0 cm, and akinesis of the anteroseptal, lateral, and apical walls.

A 27-month-old boy with a confirmed 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome), born at 32 weeks’ gestation, underwent repair of a type I ventricular septal defect and pulmonary atresia in infancy. Neonatal funduscopic examination showed no retinopathy of prematurity or retinovascular compromise. His history is notable for periventricular leukomalacia, cortical atrophy with epilepsy, severe encephalopathy with psychomotor delay, swallowing disorder, right ventricular failure, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and gastrostomy dependence.

In August 2020, he was referred for ophthalmic evaluation. Examination in the supine position revealed facial dysmorphism (lunar facies, hypertelorism, low-set ears), intermittent exotropia, and slow following of objects (left eye slower than right). Intraocular pressures were normal. Anterior segment examination showed persistent tunica vasculosa, clear media, and no evidence of inflammation. Cycloplegic refraction was −0.50 Sph −3.75 Cyl ×10° in the right eye and −1.00 Sph −3.50 Cyl ×150° in the left eye.

Dilated fundus examination revealed marked retinal vascular tortuosity with intraretinal hemorrhage in the right eye and a dysplastic optic nerve with peripapillary and vitreous hemorrhage in the left eye. B-scan ultrasonography of the left eye demonstrated an epipapillary structure connected to the area of vitreous hemorrhage.

A 57-month-old boy was brought for bruising and swelling of the legs and hands. One day earlier, he was seen for earache and cough and prescribed amoxicillin–clavulanate and gentamicin ear drops, which he had not yet taken. There was no recent vaccination or other drug use.

On examination, he was well-appearing with a temperature of 37.4 °C, heart rate 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, weight 18 kg (50th–75th percentile), and height 108 cm (25th–50th percentile). His arms and legs bore multiple palpable purpuric and ecchymotic plaques, 1–4 cm in diameter, with mild edema over the dorsum of the feet. Respiratory examination revealed prolonged expiration and bilateral crepitant rales; other systems were normal.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 18.2 × 10^3/mm^3 (72% neutrophils), hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, hematocrit 38%, platelets 452 × 10^3/mm^3, ESR 26 mm/h, CRP 7.03 mg/dL, aPTT 24.5 s, PT 12.4 s, and INR 1.2. Electrolytes, liver enzymes, renal function, urinalysis, ASO, C3, and C4 were within normal limits. Blood cultures were sterile.

Chest radiography showed paracardiac infiltrates.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of a persistent, progressive, non-postural headache. The headache was insidious in onset and was not associated with nausea, vomiting, altered consciousness, focal weakness, or numbness. Sixteen days earlier, she underwent a lower segment cesarean section under spinal anesthesia with a single dural puncture performed using a 25-gauge needle. She had no history of trauma, pre-eclampsia, connective tissue disorder, or coagulopathy, and her preoperative hematological, serological, and coagulation studies were normal. Neurological examination was unremarkable. A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed a 0.9-cm hypodense collection over the right fronto–parieto–temporal convexity with mass effect and a 0.6-cm leftward midline shift. Cerebral CT arteriography and venography were normal.

A 20-day-old male infant was admitted with a 17-day history of progressive abdominal distention and bilious vomiting. He had not passed stool in the first three days of life and thereafter only with rectal stimulation. His prenatal history was unremarkable, and there was no family history of intestinal obstruction. On examination, weight and height were at the 50th percentile, temperature 37°C, pulse 130/min, and blood pressure 60/45 mm Hg. The abdomen was distended but without tenderness or masses; other systems were normal. Laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, hematocrit 33.2%, leukocytes 10.2×10^3/µL, platelets 310×10^3/µL, and normal liver and renal function tests. Abdominal radiography revealed a distended bowel loop with air-fluid levels. A contrast enema was performed, showing a markedly dilated small-bowel segment with a normal-appearing colon. At laparotomy, a 15-cm ileal segment located 25 cm distal to the duodenum was found to be fivefold dilated with an abrupt transition to normal bowel; no intrinsic or extrinsic obstructing lesion was identified. Malrotation with Ladd bands and a left upper quadrant cecum were also noted; a Ladd procedure and appendectomy were performed, and the dilated ileal segment was resected with end-to-end anastomosis.

A 36-year-old woman presented six weeks after a cesarean delivery with a sudden episode of heavy vaginal bleeding. Ten years earlier, she had undergone a lower transverse cesarean section. In the current pregnancy, she was diagnosed with marginal placenta previa and at 28 weeks of gestation developed significant vaginal bleeding, premature rupture of membranes, and chorioamnionitis (white cell count 19,980/mm3; C-reactive protein 50.2 mg/L). She underwent a repeat lower transverse cesarean section, during which small adherent placental fragments were manually removed. Histologic examination of the placenta had shown chorionic villi implanted directly on the myometrium without intervening decidua and extravillous trophoblasts between villi and myometrial fibers. Her immediate postoperative course was unremarkable, and she was discharged on day five.

Over the next six weeks, she noted intermittent light vaginal spotting until the recent heavy bleeding. On clinical examination, the uterus was enlarged to approximately 12–13 cm with a soft consistency. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a homogeneous uterine body measuring 67 × 52 × 61 mm, with a 72 × 30 × 75 mm nonhomogeneous hyperechoic mass in the lower uterine cavity and upper cervical canal. Color Doppler demonstrated numerous intralesional vessels. Serum β-hCG was 15.5 IU/L. Pelvic MRI confirmed that the uterine mass consisted solely of placental tissue without involvement of the myometrium or adjacent organs.

A 71-year-old immunocompetent woman underwent uncomplicated phacoemulsification surgery in her right eye with immediate postoperative visual acuity of 20/20. One month later, anterior chamber cell was noted and she was treated with topical 0.1% preservative-free dexamethasone, given an allergy to 1% prednisolone acetate. Following a taper, she experienced rebound inflammation and was managed with twice-daily 0.05% difluprednate for three days before resuming twice-daily 0.1% dexamethasone for maintenance. At six months postoperatively, she underwent an uncomplicated YAG posterior capsulotomy. Sixteen months after surgery, her care was transferred, and dexamethasone drops were tapered off. One month later, she presented with acute-onset unilateral hypopyon uveitis, a visual acuity of 20/400 in the right eye, and was started on topical 0.05% difluprednate every 2 hours before referral. 

On examination, there was mild corneal edema, diffuse pigmented keratic precipitates, and 3+ anterior chamber cells. The vitreous was clear, and OCT showed no macular edema. Serologic testing for treponemal IgG, herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2 IgM, quantiferon gold, and Lyme ELISA were negative; chest radiography was normal. Empiric oral valacyclovir was initiated, and difluprednate was tapered. 

One month later, visual acuity improved to 20/60 and the anterior chamber was quiet, prompting a switch to a fluorometholone taper. Two months later, her exam was stable but she had two flares requiring difluprednate. She was started on oral prednisone and weekly methotrexate 15 mg, leading to transient improvement to 20/50. Two months after methotrexate initiation, vision declined to 20/150 with 1+ anterior chamber cells and 2+ vitreous cells, so methotrexate was increased to 25 mg weekly. One month later, vision improved to 20/70 but 2+ anterior chamber and vitreous cells persisted, and adalimumab 40 mg every other week was added.

Following adalimumab, vision deteriorated to count fingers. Slit-lamp examination revealed increased keratic precipitates and a hazy anterior and posterior chamber. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated hyperechoic vitreous opacities concerning for vitritis. Inflammation worsened despite immunosuppression, and a diagnostic vitrectomy was performed. PCR testing of aqueous for HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and CMV was negative. A vitreous biopsy and posterior capsule biopsy were sent for microbiologic culture, and she received 1 mg intravitreal vancomycin for suspected Propionibacterium acnes endophthalmitis.

A 76-year-old woman with stage IV esophageal carcinoma (ECOG performance status 3) underwent palliative feeding jejunostomy 2 months earlier, with an uncomplicated postoperative course and discharge on postoperative day 2. She presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of diffuse abdominal pain and inability to pass flatus or stool. She also reported regurgitation of feeding formula through the jejunostomy tube. 

On examination, the abdomen was distended, diffusely tender with guarding and rigidity, and tympanic to percussion. There was no external evidence of tube dislocation, and the insertion site appeared unremarkable. 

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen was performed.

A 25-year-old man presented with a 15–20–day history of an ulcer on the left side of his hard palate. Approximately 25 days earlier, he had begun root canal treatment of the upper left posterior teeth and noticed the ulcer expanding to its current size over 5–10 days. He had been prescribed multivitamins and antibiotics by his dentist without improvement. 

On examination, there was a well-demarcated, grayish-black necrotic area of palatal mucosa measuring about 3 cm in diameter, surrounded by an erythematous margin. Access cavities had been prepared in teeth 24 and 26. The patient reported that during the dental procedure, local anesthetic had been “forcefully injected” on the palatal side.

An orthopantomogram showed no bony abnormalities, and routine blood investigations were within normal limits.

A 36-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with 6–8 weeks of persistent right upper-arm pain that began after lifting a heavy piece of cast iron. Examination revealed swelling and tenderness over the midshaft of the right humerus.  
  
Plain radiographs showed a lytic, expansile, exophytic surface lesion on the humeral diaphysis with a thin rim of calcification. MRI demonstrated a 9-cm lesion with extension into the surrounding soft tissue and extensive intramedullary fluid signal. A bone scan revealed intense activity in the proximal humerus.  
  
An open biopsy of the surface lesion showed a giant-cell–rich lesion with prominent osteoid matrix formation. Histologic features favored an aneurysmal bone cyst, with a differential that also included subperiosteal hamartoma, periosteal chondroma, and giant cell tumor. However, the prominent soft-tissue involvement and extensive intramedullary signal abnormality on MRI were unusual for a classic ABC and raised concern for periosteal osteosarcoma or telangiectatic osteosarcoma.

A 45-year-old man presented with 2 months of progressive left hip pain and, over the preceding 2 weeks, increasing difficulty with mobilization. His general practitioner obtained a noncontrast CT of the pelvis, which revealed a cystic lesion within the left psoas muscle containing areas of coarse calcification; the findings were thought to be suspicious for a tumor, likely a teratoma. A contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed that the lesion in the left psoas muscle extended from a heavily calcified pancreas, coursing over the anterior aspects of the aorta and inferior vena cava before reaching the psoas muscle. Multiple other cystic areas were noted in the pancreatic parenchyma and peripancreatic tissues.

On examination in the emergency department, the patient lay supine with his left hip externally rotated and left knee moderately flexed. He had an antalgic gait and pain on weight bearing and active movement of the left hip, especially resisted hip flexion. There was no abdominal tenderness. 

Blood tests, including inflammatory markers and serum lipase, were within normal limits, with no evidence of acute pancreatitis. His medical history was notable for a single episode of alcohol-induced acute pancreatitis 10 years earlier and occasional mild postprandial epigastric pain. He consumed 6–8 standard drinks of alcohol per day.

A 17-year-old girl from western Nepal presented with fever for 17 days and altered sensorium for 4 days. The fever was insidious in onset and gradually progressive despite over-the-counter medications. She developed headache, vomiting, and confusion without photophobia, ear discharge, convulsions, or focal weakness. There was no significant past or family history. 

On arrival, temperature was 101.2°F, pulse 86/min, blood pressure 140/100 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. There was no rash, eschar, or lymphadenopathy. Lung and cardiovascular examinations were normal. Neurologically, she was drowsy (GCS 13), with normal motor and sensory examination and intact reflexes. Cranial nerve examination revealed bilateral lateral rectus palsy, dysphagia with food regurgitation on attempted feeding, dysarthria, and left-sided upper motor neuron facial palsy.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 6000/mm^3 (40% neutrophils, 50% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, platelets 320 000/μL, mild transaminase elevation (AST 63 IU/L; ALT 66 IU/L), and normal renal function. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Serologic tests for dengue IgM and NS1 antigen, herpes simplex IgM, and Japanese B encephalitis IgM were negative. Tests for malaria and leptospirosis were also negative.

A guarded lumbar puncture yielded CSF with 16 cells/μL (80% lymphocytes), protein 125 g/dL, glucose 82 mg/dL, and adenosine deaminase 2.5 IU/L. Gram stain, Ziehl-Neelsen stain, India ink, and CSF cultures were negative; PCR for herpes simplex virus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative. 

Brain MRI showed multiple mildly increased T2/FLAIR signals in the midbrain, pons, left middle cerebellar peduncle, insular lobe, and adjacent thalamus.

A 30-year-old white woman presented with an asymptomatic, brownish-to-blue grayish lesion on her right nipple of 4 years’ duration. The lesion measured 8 mm on its major axis and had an irregularly ovoid shape around the base of the nipple. Physical examination revealed no similar lesions elsewhere and was otherwise unremarkable. Her dermatologic history included a basal cell carcinoma on the lumbar region, which had been excised 5 years earlier. Dermoscopic examination of the nipple lesion showed multiple blue-gray globules and leaflike areas.

A 45-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of postprandial vomiting of ingested matter, occasionally mixed with blood. He also reported a 20-year history of burning epigastric pain relieved by meals and antacids, which worsened over the past month and failed to improve with a proton-pump inhibitor. He noted minimal weight loss (2 kg over one year), denied smoking, diabetes, or hypertension, and drank alcohol only occasionally.

On examination, vital signs were normal and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, serum electrolytes, liver and renal function tests, were within normal limits; serum albumin was slightly low at 3.62 g/dl (reference range 3.8–5.1 g/dl).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 5.4 cm length of gastric antral wall thickening with luminal narrowing, significant gastric dilatation, no lymphadenopathy or distant metastases, and an obscured fat plane between the distal stomach and pancreas but no clear pancreatic invasion, “concluding gastric outlet obstruction secondary to antral carcinoma, T3N0M0.” Chest radiography and ECG were normal.

Upper GI endoscopy showed inflammatory changes and an ulcer in the lower esophagus and a swollen, erythematous, ulcerated mass around the pylorus obstructing the pyloric orifice and preventing passage of the scope, “concluding gastric outlet obstruction secondary to prepyloric cancer.” 

Endoscopic biopsy of the pyloric lesion demonstrated bland non-atrophic, focally eroded gastric mucosa with overlying fibrino-purulent exudates, lymphocyte-predominant inflammation in the lamina propria, and Helicobacter pylori in glandular lumina, but “no dysplasia or malignancy seen; concluding prepyloric chronic active gastritis with superimposed acute erosive changes.”

A 38-year-old HIV-seropositive Bulgarian man presented with a several-month history of fever, chills, malaise, and multiple purulent skin lesions involving his face, scalp, and torso. He reported that the lesions initially appeared as “pimples” but evolved into pus-filled “bubbles.” He had been treated empirically in outpatient settings with oral acyclovir (5 × 800 mg daily for 7 days) and oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (3 × 1.0 g daily for 10 days) without improvement; after a brief remission, his symptoms recurred with greater intensity and persisted for 2 months.

On examination, he was febrile (up to 39 °C) with a heart rate of 123 beats/min and blood pressure of 130/100 mmHg. He had generalized lymphadenopathy and oropharyngeal candidiasis. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. Dermatologic examination showed extensive necrotic ulcerative lesions with abundant purulent discharge on the face, scalp, and lips, as well as scattered papular lesions on the torso. There were no lesions on the palms or soles.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 117 g/L, leukocyte count 18.8 G/L with 91% granulocytes, normal liver and renal function tests, and normal glucose and cholesterol levels. CD4 count was 208 cells/µL, CD8 count 845 cells/µL (CD4/CD8 ratio 0.20), and HIV viral load 745,000 copies/µL. Chest radiography was normal. Microbiologic cultures of throat, nasal swabs, sputum, urine, and blood grew no pathogenic organisms; sputum yielded non-significant Candida albicans. A skin biopsy showed non-specific inflammatory changes: a moderate perivascular mixed infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and polymorphonuclear cells in the dermis.

A 94-year-old Caucasian woman presented urgently with changes in her left vision. She had a history of neovascular age-related macular degeneration managed with OCT-guided anti-VEGF injections (last injection in the left eye in 2016) and dense asteroid hyalosis in both eyes. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, with systolic pressures in the 200s on presentation.  

The day before presentation, she noted a “shadow” over her left visual field, which progressed overnight to near-complete loss of vision except for a preserved inferior island. She denied headache or jaw claudication.  

On exam, visual acuity in the left eye was counting fingers, with a left afferent pupillary defect. Confrontational fields showed loss in all quadrants except the inferonasal quadrant. One month earlier, her left visual acuity had been 20/40.  

Given dense asteroid hyalosis obscuring the fundus view, multimodal imaging was undertaken. A B-scan ultrasonography ruled out retinal detachment. Optical coherence tomography of the macula revealed slight thickening and hyperreflectivity of the inner retinal layers, especially superiorly and inferiorly, suggestive of acute ischemia.

A 46-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus, prior left PCA stroke (with right homonymous hemianopia and sensory deficit), and coronary artery disease presented with a 6-day history of left lower extremity weakness, bilateral leg numbness, urinary retention, and constipation. Four months earlier, he had developed progressive back pain. One month before presentation, he noted intermittent left foot muscle stiffness, cramping, and numbness progressing to impaired dorsiflexion, along with new confusion about finances, changes in food preference, and irritability. Over the 6 days before admission, he experienced irregular bowel movements, urinary incontinence, loss of groin sensation, and a 12-lb weight loss despite increased intake.

On neurologic examination, he had subtle left proximal and distal lower-extremity weakness with spasticity; increased left patellar and ankle reflexes, crossed adductor response, and an extensor plantar response; loss of vibration and proprioception contralateral to the weakness; and ipsilateral reduction in pinprick and temperature sensation, consistent with a Brown-Séquard syndrome at the thoracic level.

MRI of the thoracic spine with gadolinium showed a 0.7 × 0.7 × 1.4 cm intramedullary lesion at T4 that was mildly T2 hyperintense and enhancing, without significant cord enlargement. Brain MRI demonstrated numerous nonspecific enhancing lesions.  

Lumbar puncture revealed elevated CSF glucose; flow cytometry showed scant cellularity without significant discrete lymphoid or progenitor cell populations.  

CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed bilateral adrenal masses, innumerable pulmonary nodules in the upper lobes, a wedge-shaped cortical irregularity of the left kidney, splenomegaly, an enlarged prostate gland, and bladder wall thickening. Oncology planned an IR-guided biopsy of an adrenal mass and continuation of corticosteroids.

A 59-year-old man with a 30–pack-year smoking history was evaluated for a 1-month history of productive cough. He had pulmonary tuberculosis 25 years earlier. He reported occasional dry cough yearly over the preceding 3 years. One month prior, at another institution, a provisional diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis was made despite negative sputum smear and culture for acid-fast bacilli. 

On examination, his respiratory rate was 21 breaths per minute; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 5.54×10^9/L, platelet count of 104×10^9/L, neutrophils 72.6%, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 21 mm/h, and elevated uric acid (937.9 μmol/L). Liver and renal function tests were otherwise normal. HIV and hepatitis B virus serologies were negative.

Chest CT demonstrated increased density in the lateral segment of the right middle lobe but was otherwise unremarkable. A methacholine bronchial provocation test was negative. Flexible bronchoscopy showed an uneven layer of inflamed mucosa. Histopathological examination of bronchial biopsies revealed mucosal inflammation with squamous metaplasia; serum bone morphogenetic protein 2 was negative. The patient was started on rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.

After 1 month of therapy, he returned with worsening cough and occasional blood-tinged sputum. Repeat CT revealed increased density in the cartilage ring surrounding the trachea. Bronchoscopy demonstrated tracheal stenosis with multiple white, hard spicules along the anterior and lateral walls.

A 36-year-old man presented with severe, continuous pain and swelling of the tongue for six weeks. He reported a 2 cm × 1 cm swelling on the posterior central tongue from which frank pus oozed. He had associated dysphagia, odynophagia, and speech difficulty but denied dyspnea, fever, or chills. He held his tongue fixed voluntarily because of pain.

He worked as a farmer, had poor dental hygiene, active dental caries, and a history of left upper molar extraction 10 years earlier. He denied tongue trauma, seizures, diabetes, hypertension, retroviral infection, smoking, or substance use other than occasional beer. 

Initially, he was diagnosed with tonsillitis at a health center and received amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for seven days plus paracetamol, with only transient improvement and subsequent worsening. A private clinic then prescribed amoxicillin–clavulanate 625 mg twice daily and tramadol 50 mg as needed, without relief.

Laboratory studies showed a random serum glucose level of 120 mg/dL, a normal complete blood count, negative HIV antibody test, normal liver and renal function tests, and negative results for VDRL, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C virus antibody.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of perineal pain and dyspareunia. She reported no palpable masses prior to examination. Vital signs were within normal limits. On genital inspection, the vulva appeared normal. Palpation of the vestibular gland region revealed bilateral, firm, fixed, non-tender masses. There was no vulvar discharge, no dysuria, and no sensitivity. 

Under regional anesthesia, a 1–2 cm incision was made at the most prominent point of each mass. Both lesions were completely excised and marsupialized. Grossly, the specimens were well-delineated, creamy-gray masses with an elastic consistency, measuring 4.0 × 3.0 × 2.5 cm and 4.5 × 1.7 × 1.7 cm. On cut section, each mass showed a homogeneous gray-white solid surface without necrosis or hemorrhage.

A middle-aged woman with a history of catatonia, hypothyroidism, and a long-standing but unclear psychotic disorder was admitted involuntarily after a suicide attempt by hanging. She had multiple past psychiatric hospitalizations over the prior decade, with diagnoses variably recorded as bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder with psychotic features, or schizophrenia. On presentation she was fearful, with significant psychomotor slowing, internal preoccupation, and emotional lability. Ligature marks were present around her neck. She described a complex delusion involving local authorities and her family, reported auditory hallucinations, and was reacting to internal stimuli. She remembered the attempt but had minimal recollection of events before and after. She was found wandering in a stupor before arriving at the emergency department. In the ED her urine drug screen and blood alcohol level were negative. During the interview she became mute and withdrawn. Most of her history was obtained from chart review and family report. Records indicated her first hospitalization occurred 10 years earlier after delirium from a urinary tract infection, during which she developed catatonia following physical restraints. Over the years she had episodic psychosis, catatonia, and variable treatment regimens, with progressive worsening. Family noted a history of irritability, sleep disturbances, episodic psychosis, hallucinations, and delusions. There was no documented psychiatric history before her first marriage, during which she was sexually abused by her husband, a member of local law enforcement, and both used crack cocaine, although she had not presented for substance-related care in over three decades.

A 30-year-old woman was referred with a 10-day history of multiple oral ulcers, a sore palate, and difficulty opening her mouth. The ulcers began on the buccal mucosa and palate and rapidly progressed to involve the entire oral cavity. She had no relief from pain medications and was subsisting on milk via straw. She habitually peeled scabs from her lips. Three days before admission she had fever without cough, rhinorrhea, or altered taste.

Three months prior she noted leg and abdominal swelling, polyarthralgias, hair loss, and photosensitive rash. She was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome and treated with furosemide, albumin, and methylprednisolone (32 mg daily), which she stopped after two weeks.

On examination, there were multiple hemorrhagic crusts and erosions on the bilateral frontal areas, zygomas, and nasal bridge, with irregular borders. The lips bore hemorrhagic crusts that bled easily. Intraorally, there was diffuse erythema of the mucosa and multiple irregular white plaques of varying size on the palate, which could be partially scraped off to reveal erythematous patches.

Based on history and clinical findings, the initial working diagnosis was oral lesions of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with acute pseudomembranous candidiasis. Pemphigus vulgaris, erythema multiforme, and Stevens–Johnson syndrome were also considered. An internal medicine team provisionally diagnosed SLE with mucocutaneous, musculoskeletal, renal, and serositis involvement; chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CCLE) and toxic epidermal necrolysis–like acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (TEN-like ACLE) were additional differentials.

Laboratory studies showed a reactive antinuclear antibody test (homogeneous pattern, titer 1:3200), rising leukocyte count (to 19.3×10^3/µL) with neutrophilia (84%) and lymphopenia (9%), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and hypoalbuminemia. The Mexican-SLEDAI score was 7. The internal medicine specialist confirmed SLE, and the oral medicine team diagnosed lupus cheilitis and a palatal erythematous ulcer.

A 71-year-old African American man with a history of liver cirrhosis (post–orthotopic liver transplant), end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, peripheral vascular disease (right above-knee amputation), and seizure disorder was brought from his nursing home with altered mental status. Three days earlier, he had developed a shingles rash and was started on valacyclovir. He missed his scheduled hemodialysis session on the day of presentation. There was no fever, headache, convulsions, illicit drug use, or new medications other than valacyclovir.

On examination, he was afebrile, blood pressure 176/85 mmHg, alert but disoriented, with no meningeal signs or focal neurologic deficits. Skin exam showed crusted vesicles on an erythematous base over the lower back in an S1 dermatomal distribution. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal exams were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL, white blood cell count 2,770/µL, platelets 201,000/µL; liver-function tests normal; blood urea nitrogen 37 mg/dL; creatinine 6.3 mg/dL; ammonia 30.8 µmol/L; no significant electrolyte abnormalities or metabolic acidosis. CT head and MRI brain showed no acute intracranial abnormalities. Medication review revealed valacyclovir 1 g three times daily, above the recommended 500 mg daily dose for patients with end-stage renal disease.
