An electroencephalogram demonstrated generalized slowing consistent with a toxic-metabolic insult.

A 59-year-old man presented in December with progressive headache, slowed speech, gait disturbance, and weakness. His temperature was 37.2 °C, blood pressure 140/80 mmHg, heart rate 84 bpm, and respiration 24 breaths/min. Neurological and fundoscopic examinations were normal. 
Cranial MRI showed bilateral cerebral and cerebellar millimetric gliotic lesions and leptomeningeal enhancement. 
Lumbar puncture revealed clear fluid with an opening pressure of 19 cmH₂O, 302 leukocytes/µL (5% polymorphonuclear, 95% lymphomononuclear), protein 113 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL (blood glucose 147 mg/dL). CSF studies for lymphoma, a paraneoplastic panel, Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, and India ink for Cryptococcus neoformans were all negative. Diffusion‐weighted imaging demonstrated acute ischemic lesions in the right caudate nucleus and left internal capsule; aspirin was started. His headache persisted despite slight overall improvement.
Approximately eight months later, he re-presented with worsened speech, somnolence, and weakness. Neurological examination now revealed dysarthria and inability to walk. Cardiac evaluation and large‐vessel imaging were normal; cerebral angiography showed hypoplastic left A1 and right P1 segments. A presumptive diagnosis of CNS vasculitis was made, and he received a 7-day steroid pulse plus one dose of cyclophosphamide. 
The following day he developed fever (38.1 °C) without meningeal signs. Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 23 cmH₂O, 193 leukocytes/µL (67% polymorphonuclear, 32% lymphomononuclear), protein 313 mg/dL, and glucose 11 mg/dL (blood glucose 101 mg/dL); therapeutic CSF drainage was performed.

A 16-year-old Punjabi Pakistani boy presented with a 2-month history of high-grade, continuous fever with morning and evening spikes, rigors, chills, a persistent productive cough with scanty whitish sputum, anorexia, and moderate weight loss. Two years earlier, he had been treated for a pyogenic liver abscess with antibiotics and drainage. Over the past year, he had multiple episodes of acute gastroenteritis, urinary tract infections, and respiratory infections. His parents were consanguineous; his brother and two cousins had similar histories and were edentulous.

On examination, temperature was 101 °F, pulse 116 /min, blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 20 /min. He appeared pale with poor oral hygiene and diffuse transgradient hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles. The spleen was just palpable; lung auscultation revealed coarse crepitations bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, total leukocyte count 11 400/µL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 68 mm/h; liver enzymes and alkaline phosphatase were mildly elevated. Three consecutive sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative. Stool examination, thick and thin blood smears for malaria, typhidot IgM/IgG, bone marrow examination, and serologies for HBsAg, anti-HCV, VDRL, and HIV were all negative. Blood cultures grew Pseudomonas. Chest radiography demonstrated soft-tissue opacities throughout both lung zones. A dental orthopantomogram showed marked alveolar bone atrophy.

A 45-year-old obese woman presented with a 3-week history of painful ulcers on the dorsal hands and fingers. She first observed small red macules that over 2 weeks progressed to painful swelling and ulceration. She denied trauma or new medications. Her history included laparoscopic gastric sleeve surgery and untreated mild diabetes. 
Initially diagnosed as a bacterial infection, she underwent wound cultures and was treated with oral trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole and topical mupirocin. She subsequently developed fever and malaise and was admitted for presumed sepsis, receiving intravenous vancomycin. 
A few days later, on re-evaluation, the dorsal aspects of the right index finger, left ring finger, and right third proximal metacarpophalangeal joint showed erythematous ulcerated nodules and plaques with violaceous borders and marked edema. Nonulcerated areas had fusiform swelling. Tender indurated erythematous plaques were also present on the right wrist dorsum. The remainder of the skin and mucosa were uninvolved. 
Given the progression despite antibiotics, a skin biopsy was performed to evaluate for atypical pyoderma gangrenosum, deep fungal or mycobacterial infection, or other etiologies.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of progressively worsening low back pain radiating to the left buttock and leg, accompanied by numbness and tingling below the knee. There was no history of trauma or constitutional symptoms. On examination, he had paravertebral tenderness in the lower lumbar spine and limited lumbar motion due to pain. Neurologic examination showed grade 3/5 dorsiflexion weakness in the left ankle and grade 4/5 weakness of the left extensor hallucis longus; other muscle strengths were normal. He had sensory loss in the left L4 dermatome and a positive straight-leg-raising test on the left at 45°. There was no bladder or bowel disturbance. His visual-analog pain scores were 4 for low back pain and 8 for leg pain.

Lumbar radiographs showed minimal degenerative changes. MRI demonstrated a disc extrusion at L3–4 and a large, spherical extradural lesion behind the L4 vertebral body that was low signal on T1-weighted images and high signal on T2-weighted images, compressing the thecal sac and left L4 nerve root. There was central L4–5 disc bulging with ligamentum flavum thickening and narrowing of the left L4–5 foramen. On contrasted imaging, the cystic mass enhanced uniformly and appeared connected by a stalk to the L3–4 intervertebral disc space. EMG/NCV confirmed left L4 radiculopathy. After several months of rest, NSAIDs, and an epidural steroid injection without improvement and with worsening neurologic findings, surgical decompression was planned.

A 36-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a two-month history of a vague lump below her left eye. She reported no pain, diplopia, or constitutional symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no prior autoimmune disease, sarcoidosis, malignancy, or trauma; she had stopped smoking four weeks earlier. Empiric systemic and topical antibiotics had been prescribed without improvement.

On examination, visual acuity was normal bilaterally. There was a nontender lump with mild swelling in the inferonasal quadrant of the left orbit, without proptosis or globe displacement. Extraocular movements were full, with no diplopia or discomfort. The ocular and fundus examinations were normal. Cardiorespiratory and skin examinations were unremarkable, and there was no lymphadenopathy.

Orbital CT revealed isolated, diffuse enlargement of the left inferior oblique muscle; the remainder of the orbits appeared normal. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and thyroid function tests, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, serum electrolytes, creatinine, creatine kinase, angiotensin-converting enzyme level, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, were all within normal limits.

A 29-year-old G6P3023 at 25 weeks’ gestation presented with chest and back pain and progressive shortness of breath. Her medical history included asthma, opioid use disorder, bipolar disorder, anxiety, seizures, anemia, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, and fibromyalgia. She was on buprenorphine, gabapentin, quetiapine, alprazolam, levetiracetam, and albuterol; she smoked one pack per day and had a remote history of heroin use. 

Initial chest radiography showed bilateral airspace infiltrates without hemidiaphragm elevation. She developed ARDS, was intubated, and required broad-spectrum antibiotics, stress-dose steroids, vasopressors, sedation, and initiation of single-lumen veno-venous ECMO. After 13 days of ECMO support, she was decannulated. A chest radiograph obtained the next day demonstrated elevation of the right hemidiaphragm.

She underwent tracheostomy and was weaned to 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula; after four days she maintained saturations on room air. A CT scan of the chest showed resolving pneumonia with persistent elevation of the right hemidiaphragm. She was transferred for methadone stabilization. Despite sedation weaning, she required 2 L/min of oxygen at rest. On hospital day 6 at the referral center, she desaturated to 75% on room air, requiring 3 L/min to maintain saturations above 95%. She reported dyspnea on exertion, and examination revealed decreased breath sounds in the right lower lung field. An echocardiogram was within normal limits, and a CT scan was negative for pulmonary embolism.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a 17-year history of symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis. In 2003 she noted the onset of multiple skin nodules symmetrically over the joints of her hands, ankles, shoulders, and elbows. Over the next 6 months she developed stiffness, joint deformities, contractures, and restricted mobility affecting bilateral elbows, wrists, knees, ankles, feet, MCP joints, PIP joints, and DIP and MTP joints. She also reported fever, decreased appetite, cough, and breathlessness. Her past surgical history was notable for subdiaphragmatic abscess resection and ovarian cyst removal.

On examination, there were numerous smooth, firm, freely mobile nodules 5–20 mm in diameter on the dorsal surfaces of both palms, the upper arms, MCP, PIP, and DIP joints, and the MTP joints. A large scar was present along the lateral margin of each upper arm. Flexion contractures of all fingers produced a claw-hand appearance. There was no Raynaud phenomenon, calcinosis, or palmoplantar thickening.

Laboratory studies showed positive rheumatoid factor and carcinoembryonic antigen, with all other routine and immunological tests—including anti-DNA antibodies, ANCA, CRP, ESR, ANA, anti-ENA, anti-CCP, anti-Jo-1, anti-SSA, and anti-SSB antibodies—either negative or within normal limits. Radiographs and CT scans of the hands and feet demonstrated progressive joint destruction in some PIP, DIP, and MCP joints, along with bilateral joint-space narrowing in MTP, MCP, and IP joints.

A 30-year-old male dairy farm worker presented with multiple painless nodules on the fingers of both hands for 1 month. Seven to ten days after the initial nodules appeared, he developed vesicles that ruptured and formed hemorrhagic crusts. He also noted discomfort and pain along the medial aspect of his right arm and forearm. He denied trauma or insect bites but reported that his cow had similar lesions on its teats.

On examination, 3–4 firm, non-tender nodules with central hemorrhagic crusts and surrounding erythema were present on the proximal phalanges of both hands. There was mild tenderness and increased warmth along the medial right arm and forearm.

Dermoscopy (10×) of one nodule showed an erythematous area with central ulceration and crust, yellow-white streaks, brown dots, a structureless whitish area partially surrounding the ulcer, an erythematous ring, and dot vessels.

A 70‐year‐old Iranian man presented with multiple pruritic blisters that had appeared all over his body 6 months earlier. He had a 25‐year history of psoriatic lesions treated with prednisolone tablets, clobetasol ointment, and a calcipotriol/betamethasone gel. On examination, there were erythematous, scaly plaques on the trunk, lower limbs, and elbows, along with numerous blisters on the upper limbs, lower limbs, and trunk. The patient also reported facial photosensitivity on sun exposure, joint pain in the knees, wrists, and ankles, and non‐scarring hair loss. Eight months before presentation, UVB treatment was initiated twice weekly for recurrent psoriasis, with the duration of irradiation gradually increased at each session. After the 15th irradiation session, multiple papules and vesicles emerged across the body, progressively increasing in number and size. He was treated with prednisolone (50 mg daily, tapered weekly) and clobetasol ointment, which led to partial improvement, but lesions recurred after 2 months. The same regimen was repeated, yet lesions resurfaced again after 2 months, prompting him to seek care at our clinic.

A 20-year-old man presented with mandibular deviation and crowding. He had no temporomandibular joint pain, sounds, or functional limitations. On extraoral examination, facial asymmetry was noted with the chin deviated 1 mm to the left. Intraorally, there was a Class I molar and Class III canine relationship on the right side, and a Class I molar and Class II canine relationship on the left. The lower dental midline was shifted 1 mm to the left, and the upper midline 3 mm to the right. Crossbites involved teeth #12, #15, #22, #24, #34, and #35. 

Cephalometric analysis showed a skeletal Class I relationship (ANB 2.5°) with bi-retrusion (SNA 76.1°, SNB 73.6°) and a hyperdivergent pattern (S-NA to Go-Me 40.3°). Wits appraisal was 3.6 mm. Incisor positions were within normal limits (U1–NA 8.8 mm, L1–NB 4.7 mm; interincisal angle 127.6°). Posterior–anterior cephalometry revealed good maxillary and mandibular widths (66.1 mm and 93.1 mm), an occlusal plane cant of 4.6°, and only slight mandibular lateral deviation. A panoramic radiograph showed all permanent teeth except #18 and #48.  

After radiographic and facial evaluation, the patient was diagnosed with a Class I malocclusion, presenting a dolichofacial, asymmetrical, and concave profile with bi-retrusion. The etiology of the asymmetry was deemed multifactorial, linked to a combination of skeletal and dental factors.

A 65-year-old man presented with a one-month history of a right-sided abdominal swelling that became painful and irreducible over the past day. He reported multiple episodes of vomiting and no passage of stool or flatus for several hours. He denied any history of trauma, surgery, or activities raising intra-abdominal pressure. His medical history was notable for right undescended testis diagnosed at age 6 without subsequent treatment and azoospermia noted on two occasions; no hormonal workup had been performed. He had no major comorbidities and was a non-smoker; his BMI was 26.4 kg/m2.  

On examination, there was a firm, tender, 7 × 7 cm swelling in the right lumbar region in the midclavicular line. The swelling was non-pulsatile, non-fluctuant, irreducible, and had no cough impulse; the overlying skin was normal. Palpation of the scrotum revealed an empty right hemiscrotum, with the left testis palpable and normal. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (12.6 × 109/L) with granulocytosis, elevated creatine phosphokinase (689 U/L), and elevated CK-MB (59 U/L). Abdominal radiography demonstrated distended small-bowel loops with multiple air–fluid levels, consistent with small-bowel obstruction. Ultrasonography revealed mild small-bowel dilation with increased peristalsis and confirmed an empty right scrotum; the right testis was visualized lateral to the rectus abdominis muscle. The imaging studies suggested a small abdominal wall hernia causing obstruction and ipsilateral cryptorchidism, but the precise location of the hernial defect was unclear.  

Given these findings, a right-sided hernia with cryptorchidism was suspected, and open hernial repair was planned.

A 73-year-old woman with hypertension presented with 30 minutes of severe, pressure-like substernal chest pain radiating to her left arm and jaw at rest, accompanied by nausea and acute dyspnea. She denied prior episodes, exertional dyspnea, trauma, new medications, sick contacts, or recent travel. Medical history included hypertension, generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, severe osteoarthritis, and an atypical polymyalgia rheumatica treated with a 6-month steroid taper. Family history was notable for a father who died suddenly from dilated cardiomyopathy. Home medications were buspirone, duloxetine, hydrochlorothiazide, valsartan, and meloxicam as needed.

On examination, she was normothermic, tachycardic (112 bpm), hypotensive (88/55 mmHg), and hypoxemic (SpO2 88% on 5 L nasal cannula). She was diaphoretic, in acute distress, with jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, a normal S1, diminished S2, and a holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Extremities were well perfused, with 1+ lower-extremity edema.

Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with diffuse ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V4–V6, and ST elevation in aVR. Initial labs revealed a lactate of 1.7 mg/dL and a troponin of 1.33 ng/dL. She received aspirin, ticagrelor, and a heparin infusion and was taken emergently for cardiac catheterization.

Coronary angiography demonstrated less than 30% obstruction in all vessels. Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure was elevated at 31 mmHg, and ventriculography showed severe (4+) mitral regurgitation with a dilated left atrium. In the cath lab, transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 65%, severe mitral regurgitation, a flail posterior mitral valve leaflet, and a flail head of the posterior papillary muscle. An intra-aortic balloon pump was placed, and she was intubated for severe hypoxemic respiratory failure. She was admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit, diuresed, and hemodynamically supported, with plans for surgical intervention on hospital day 3.

A 45-year-old man with a 20-year history of heavy alcohol use (approximately 250 mL of liquor daily for the past 2 weeks) and known liver cirrhosis of 5 years’ duration was brought with altered sensorium and generalized seizures. He appeared malnourished. On examination, he was confused and had poor motor coordination but no focal weakness.  
Electroencephalogram showed diffuse slow waves (5–8 Hz) without epileptiform discharges.  
Laboratory studies revealed serum osmolality 370 mmol/L (normal 290 mmol/L), creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (normal 0.5–1.2 mg/dL), blood urea nitrogen 40 mg/dL (normal 8–23 mg/dL), sodium 146 mmol/L, and potassium 4.3 mmol/L. Cerebrospinal fluid examination was unremarkable. Serum vitamin B12, folic acid, and albumin levels were low.  
Noncontrast cranial CT demonstrated diffuse hypodensity of the corpus callosum and bilateral periventricular white matter. On 1.5 T MRI, T2-weighted and FLAIR images showed diffuse hyperintensity in the corpus callosum and bilateral periventricular white matter with corresponding T1 hypointensity. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed restricted diffusion in the bilateral peritrigonal white matter and the middle layer of the splenium of the corpus callosum with a low apparent diffusion coefficient. There was no involvement of subcortical white matter and no postcontrast enhancement.

A 70-year-old woman was admitted for erythematous‐inflammatory lesions of the right side of the face with signs of secondary infection. History: In 2016, she had an ischemic stroke of the right cerebellar hemisphere and medulla oblongata, during which a nasogastric tube remained in place for 6 weeks. Shortly afterward, ulceration and destruction of the right nasal wing appeared. The first skin lesions developed in 2017 as small erythematous lesions and erosions with scabs on the right cheek and above the upper lip. The patient reported frequent touching and picking at the lesions due to sudden cold sensations and numbness. Over time, the affected area expanded to the entire right side of the face, the auricle, and adjacent scalp. She was treated repeatedly as having shingles, bacterial skin infection, or allergic eczema with acyclovir, antibiotics, topical antibacterial and anti‐inflammatory agents, and emollients without improvement; allergic prick tests were negative.  
Medical history: post-stroke right-sided cerebellar syndrome, Worster–Drought syndrome, hypertension, sick sinus syndrome, supraventricular arrhythmias, and frontal sinus osteoma; no personal or family history of skin or allergic diseases.  
On examination: well-demarcated erythematous lesions with numerous erosions covered by scabs and swelling on the right side of the face, auricle, and scalp; partial loss of the right nasal wing with superficial ulceration and scabs; right conjunctival congestion, swollen eyelids, and purulent discharge; enlarged submandibular lymph nodes.  
Laboratory tests: C-reactive protein 8.14 mg/dL (normal < 5), ESR 44 mm/h (normal < 10), normal glucose. Cultures from conjunctival sac and nasal ulcer grew MRSA. Ophthalmology: purulent conjunctivitis with corneal erosion. Neurology: right trigeminal neuropathy; distigmine bromide 2 × 5 mg prescribed. Topical detreomycin, benzocaine-menthol ointment, emollients, and ofloxacin drops were administered. After 1 month, inflammatory lesions and erosions had largely healed.  
The patient was advised about the mechanism of her skin lesions and to refrain from manipulating the area.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of pharyngeal discomfort and increased coughing. Contrast esophagography revealed a 3-cm diverticulum on the left side of the cervical esophagus but did not show a cricopharyngeal bar. Cervical computed tomography demonstrated an air-filled diverticulum measuring 1.6 × 1.8 × 3.2 cm arising posterior to the left thyroid lobe. Upper endoscopy showed the diverticulum filled with retained food residue just below the palisade vessels corresponding to the level of the upper esophageal sphincter. High-resolution manometry revealed no abnormalities other than an area of slightly elevated pressure in the cervical esophagus.

A 36-year-old woman presented with persistent severe pain on the left side of her face. Two months earlier, on the day after receiving her third dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, she experienced episodic sharp, electric-shock–like pain initially affecting the entire left hemiface. Within days, the pain localized to the V2 and V3 distributions of the left trigeminal nerve. Attacks lasted 4–5 seconds, were triggered by jaw movement during eating or tooth brushing, and reached 10/10 on a numeric pain scale. She reported allodynia to cold air and hypersensitivity to touch in the affected area. During attacks, she described distorted sensations in the V2 region, but sensory testing was otherwise normal. She had no other neurological deficits, no relevant past medical or family history, and prior doses of the same vaccine had been uneventful. Routine laboratory tests, including D-dimer, were normal. RT-qPCR for SARS-CoV-2 and other infections was negative. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the head showed no abnormalities.

A 47-year-old man was referred for marked elevation of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). He was a heavy smoker with a body-mass index of 23 kg/m2. Two months prior, he had begun a self-managed ketogenic diet, restricting carbohydrates to 30 g/day (≈5% of calories) and obtaining 42% of calories from protein and 53% from fat via mainly animal sources. He used a smartphone app to track intake and confirmed ketosis with urine test strips. Before the diet, his lipid profile was: total cholesterol 237 mg/dL, LDL-C 155 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol 30 mg/dL, and triglycerides 263 mg/dL. At the outpatient visit after 2 months on the ketogenic diet, his profile was: total cholesterol 322 mg/dL, LDL-C 274 mg/dL, HDL-C 30 mg/dL, and triglycerides 220 mg/dL. Physical examination was unremarkable, without tendon xanthomas, and he denied any personal or family history of cardiovascular disease.

A 33-year-old man with advanced AIDS (CD4 count 59 cells/mm3; HIV RNA, 308 000 copies/mL) and a history of disseminated histoplasmosis, disseminated MAC, PCP pneumonia, varicella-zoster, and a CMV gastric ulcer presented with two weeks of worsening cough, dyspnea, fevers, chills, and black, tarry stools. He admitted poor adherence to ART (emtricitabine/tenofovir, raltegravir) and prophylaxis (itraconazole, azithromycin, TMP/SMX, valganciclovir). On exam he was cachectic and distressed with tachycardia, mild tachypnea, facial molluscum lesions, right lateral tongue ulcerations, oropharyngeal thrush, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness, and hepatosplenomegaly. Labs showed leukocytes 2800/µL, hematocrit 20% (baseline 30%), platelets 28 000/µL; sodium 133 mmol/L; potassium 4.1 mmol/L; bicarbonate 22 mmol/L; creatinine 0.76 mg/dL; AST 113 U/L; ALT 25 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 450 U/L. That evening he spiked a fever to 39.5°C with worsening tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxemia requiring oxygen, IV fluids, and two units of packed red blood cells. Chest radiograph showed a diffuse miliary pattern. He was started empirically on vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, high-dose TMP/SMX, prednisone, ethambutol, azithromycin, and liposomal amphotericin B. Bronchoscopy with BAL was performed, and because of ongoing melena and a nadir hematocrit of 18% despite transfusions, an EGD was done, which revealed a well-healed scar on the gastric greater curvature from his prior CMV ulcer and new diffuse erosions in the second through fourth segments of the duodenum; multiple biopsies were taken.

A 44-year-old man presented with sudden onset atypical chest and jaw pain. He was otherwise healthy, a non-smoker, and had a normal CT coronary angiogram two years earlier. Over the preceding weeks he had fatigue, nasal congestion, and red eyes; imaging of his chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed pancreatic and pulmonary masses. A pulmonary biopsy demonstrated granulomata with acid-fast bacilli, and he was started on anti-tuberculous therapy.

On examination, he was febrile with a normal cardiac examination. Twelve-lead ECG showed widespread ST-segment elevation. High-sensitivity troponin T was 1089 ng/L (reference 0–14). Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal LV systolic function, no regional wall-motion abnormalities, but an echogenic antero-septal myocardium. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated multiple focal areas of high signal intensity on T2-weighted imaging with corresponding late gadolinium enhancement, consistent with acute myocarditis, and round infiltrative lesions with central necrosis in the basal and mid septum.

One week later, he developed recurrent left-sided chest pain with dynamic antero-lateral ST-segment elevation and runs of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. High-sensitivity troponin T rose to 24 786 ng/L, and C-reactive protein was 186 mg/L. Echocardiography now showed hypokinetic apical segments. Emergent coronary angiography revealed a 75% stenosis in the distal LAD artery and an occluded small posterior LV branch of the RCA, and a drug-eluting stent was placed in the LAD. Post-procedure echocardiography showed LVEF 45%, apical akinesia, and biventricular mural thrombi. Repeat cardiac MRI demonstrated transmural infarction of the apical septum.

A 70-year-old patient presented with a history of recurrent syncope that began in 2019. Over the first year, the patient experienced 11 syncopal episodes and up to 9 presyncopal episodes per day. The daytime events typically occurred while the patient was sitting quietly and were preceded by lightheadedness, nausea, warmth, and diaphoresis lasting several minutes. Episodes often culminated in loss of consciousness for up to 60 seconds upon standing, after which the patient regained consciousness pale and diaphoretic.

In April 2020, the patient described 3 additional spells that differed from the previous pattern: in 3 instances the patient fainted while sitting quietly, and in 1 instance the patient was supine in bed at night when a sudden sensation of warmth and presyncope was followed by syncope. These nocturnal events were witnessed and associated with disturbed breathing and brief unresponsiveness.

The patient’s medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, and prior smoking; the only medication was irbesartan 150 mg daily. On examination, blood pressure was 150/95 mm Hg; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. A baseline ECG, transthoracic echocardiogram, ambulatory blood pressure monitor, and 24-hour Holter monitor were all normal.

A 52-year-old man was referred for progressive right sensorineural hearing loss over 10 months. He had no history of otitis media. Otoscopic examination showed normal tympanic membranes. Pure-tone audiometry confirmed high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss predominantly on the right. To evaluate for an inner-ear or cerebellopontine‐angle lesion, MRI of the temporal bones was obtained. MRI showed an 18 × 26 mm lesion in the right mastoid that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and more hyperintense than cerebrospinal fluid on T1-weighted images, with sharp margins and no diffusion restriction on DWI. After gadolinium, there was a thin linear rim of enhancement. High-resolution CT of the temporal bone demonstrated expansion of the mastoid walls with areas of thickened, sclerotic bone and thinning of the posterior wall adjacent to the sigmoid sinus; the mastoid antrum and tympanic cavity were normally aerated.

A 14-year-old girl presented with sudden onset of severe right-sided lower abdominal pain and vomiting for 2 days. The pain was not associated with fever, chills, bowel or urinary symptoms, or abnormal vaginal discharge. She had a regular 35-day menstrual cycle since menarche 6 months earlier, with normal bleeding. She was sexually inactive and had no history of previous gynecological or abdominal surgery. 

On examination, her vital signs were: blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 98/min, temperature 98.3°F, and SpO₂ 99%. Secondary sexual characteristics were appropriate for age (Tanner stages 3–4). Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right iliac fossa without palpable masses, peritoneal signs, or organomegaly. Bowel sounds were normal.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL and a mild leukocytosis (11,300 cells/mm³). Urinalysis was normal and the pregnancy test was negative. All other parameters were within normal limits.

Transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a normal uterus and ovaries. A large tubular dilated cystic lesion (8.0 × 3.7 cm) was seen in the right adnexa with no flow on Doppler, separate from the right ovary which had flow, suggesting severe right hydrosalpinx. No free fluid was observed in the pouch of Douglas.

Pelvic MRI revealed a dilated, tubular, convoluted lesion in the right adnexa separate from the right ovary, with homogeneous fluid signal and no internal septations, consistent with an isolated large right hydrosalpinx.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a chief complaint of poor esthetics of her right maxillary teeth. Her medical history was unremarkable. Dental history included prior endodontic treatment of the right maxillary central incisor. On examination, she had an Angle Class I occlusion, a midline diastema, and an upper midline shifted to the left, with apparent asymmetry due to increased mesiodistal width of the right maxillary lateral incisor. All permanent teeth except the second and third molars were present. In the region of the right maxillary lateral incisor, two separate crowns were visible, and floss passed freely between them, demonstrating they were not fused coronally. A periapical radiograph was obtained but was inconclusive because of overlapping images in this two‐dimensional view.

A 16-year-old previously healthy Persian male presented with a 3-month history of right hip pain. The pain began during physical activity, became persistent, was moderate in intensity, and was associated with a limp and limited function.  
Plain radiographs of the right hip showed a proximal femoral lesion. MRI demonstrated signal changes in the same region.  
An initial percutaneous biopsy of the proximal femur revealed fibromuscular and bony tissue involved by a neoplasm composed of large cystically dilated vessels with thin walls, and was interpreted as a cavernous hemangioma of bone.  
Laboratory studies showed normal serum calcium, phosphate, albumin, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and alkaline phosphatase.  
Because of ongoing pain, absence of evidence for a primary bone sarcoma, and the extent of the lesion, prophylactic fixation with a cephalomedullary nail was performed.  
One month later, the patient returned with severe hip pain. Radiographs revealed a fracture and extensive bone destruction in the right trochanteric region and femoral neck. Curettage, structural fibula allograft, and repeat cephalomedullary nailing were performed. Cultures were negative for infection.  
At a follow-up 2½ months later, radiographs showed decreased bone density in the proximal femur and resorption of the allograft. A second incisional biopsy again demonstrated cavernous hemangioma and was negative for malignancy.  
Eighteen months after the initial biopsy, the patient was referred to our center. He remained wheelchair-bound with severe hip pain. Physical examination was notable only for painful limitation of hip motion. Repeat laboratory studies, including inflammatory and bone-metabolic markers, remained within normal limits.

A 35-year-old woman presented with the recent onset of numerous “floaters” and decreased vision. Her medical history was unremarkable. Examination revealed bilateral exudative retinal detachment and dilated episcleral veins.  
Lumbar puncture excluded Vogt-Koyanagi–Harada syndrome, and magnetic resonance angiography of the brain raised concern for a carotid–cavernous fistula, which was subsequently excluded by cerebral angiography. Laboratory studies were normal except for a mildly elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase (51 U/L [reference, 10–40]). She denied dyspnea but noted poor exercise tolerance. Vital signs showed a blood pressure of 126/79 mmHg, heart rate 75 bpm, and body mass index 26 kg/m²; physical examination revealed no jugular venous distension or peripheral edema.  
A full-body PET/CT scan performed to rule out a paraneoplastic phenomenon demonstrated hepatomegaly with ascites consistent with a nutmeg liver and a slightly thickened, calcified pericardium. CT pulmonary angiography showed no pulmonary embolism. Transthoracic echocardiography documented a dilated inferior vena cava with reduced respiratory collapsibility but no restrictive filling pattern, a normal mitral inflow pattern (E/A ratio 2, normal deceleration time, normal e′ velocities), and no direct or indirect signs of pulmonary hypertension; portal-vein Doppler demonstrated pulsatile flow.  
Because of evidence of systemic venous congestion and discordant non-invasive findings, the patient was referred for invasive hemodynamic assessment by right heart catheterization.

A 19-year-old obese (BMI 30.1) nonsmoking man with treatment-resistant schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, was admitted for worsening hallucinations, mania, and grandiose delusions despite compliance with olanzapine 15 mg daily, chlorpromazine 50 mg daily, and valproate 2500 mg daily. He had two prior brief trials of clozapine (150 mg over 17 days; 75 mg over 18 days) discontinued for myocarditis and sinus tachycardia, without any neutropenia (WCC 4.36–11.63×10⁹/L; ANC 2.38–9.22×10⁹/L). After cardiology clearance, clozapine was reinitiated on admission. Baseline labs showed WCC 3.7×10⁹/L and ANC 2.3×10⁹/L; echocardiogram and troponin T were normal. Clozapine was titrated to 200 mg by day 15 post-initiation, when routine PCR testing revealed asymptomatic COVID-19 infection. On day 19, WCC fell to 2.95×10⁹/L and ANC to 1.2×10⁹/L; CRP was 3.4 mg/L (reference <5 mg/L). Clozapine was immediately discontinued. Over the next 3 weeks (with no further evidence of COVID-19), WCC remained 2.90–3.32×10⁹/L and ANC 1.20–1.80×10⁹/L; lymphocytes and platelets remained stable.

A 13-year-old girl from a hilly region of Nepal presented with intermittent fever with chills and profuse sweating for 1 month. The fever was low grade, occurring at intervals, and associated with lassitude and dry cough. She had received courses of antibiotics and antipyretics without improvement. She had no travel history to leishmaniasis‐endemic areas. On examination, she appeared pale and ill; temperature was 99.4°F, respiratory rate was increased, and heart rate was elevated. Oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. There was no icterus, lymphadenopathy, cyanosis, clubbing, edema, or sternal tenderness. Abdominal examination revealed massive splenomegaly extending to the umbilical line and mild hepatomegaly, with the liver palpable two fingers below the right midclavicular line. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.2 g/dL, total leukocyte count 3150/µL, and absolute neutrophil count 1386/µL. Blood glucose and electrolytes were normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 46 mm/h, and C-reactive protein was reactive. Liver enzymes were elevated with ALT 130 U/L and AST 143 U/L. A chest radiograph and electrocardiogram were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed gross hepatosplenomegaly with a liver span of 16.2 cm and spleen span of 18.1 cm.

A 73‐year‐old man was evaluated for recurrent fatigue over the preceding year. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus (diagnosed 18 years earlier), stage 3 chronic kidney disease (diagnosed 4 years earlier), and osteoporosis (diagnosed 6 years earlier). His medications included a compound α-keto acid supplement (2520 mg three times daily, containing approximately 600 mg elemental calcium), Caltrate D (600 mg elemental calcium daily), and alfacalcidol (0.5 μg daily). One year earlier, he noted fatigue and was found to have a serum calcium level of 3.41 mmol/L; after discontinuation of calcium and vitamin D supplements, his serum calcium fluctuated between 2.24 and 2.93 mmol/L. Two months before admission, fatigue recurred and his serum calcium was 3.03 mmol/L. 

Laboratory evaluation revealed suppressed parathyroid hormone levels during periods of hypercalcemia (0.76–0.82 pmol/L; reference range not provided). Thyroid function tests, arterial blood gases, immunologic studies, protein electrophoresis, tumor markers, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and cortisol levels were within normal limits. Review of serial laboratory data showed that, as his serum calcium rose, 24-hour urinary calcium excretion was low (1.63–2.51 mmol; reference range 2.5–7.5 mmol/24 h). Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D, bone‐specific alkaline phosphatase, and C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen were all low. Bone mineral densitometry, chest and abdominal computed tomography, and bone scintigraphy showed no specific abnormalities.

A 65-year-old Nepalese woman with anti-synthetase syndrome (based on arthritis, interstitial lung disease, anti-Jo1 and anti‐Ro52 antibodies) and anti-CCP–positive rheumatoid arthritis received two cycles of rituximab, the last 6 months ago. In light of the COVID-19 pandemic, rituximab was withheld; azathioprine was initiated for 2 weeks, then switched to an escalating dose of mycophenolate because of headaches and dizziness.  
She was admitted with 5 days of fever, abdominal pain and headaches. On examination, temperature was 38.3 °C, blood pressure 109/70 mmHg, heart rate 94 bpm, and a maculopapular rash on her palms.  
Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 100 g/L [115–165], white-cell count 2.4 × 10^9/L [4–11], platelets 61 × 10^9/L [150–450]), neutrophils 1.75 × 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.50 × 10^9/L; ferritin >55 000 µg/L (15–300); triglycerides 4.3 mmol/L (≤1.8); lactate dehydrogenase 1200 IU/L (135–214); fibrinogen 2.8 g/L (normal); alanine aminotransferase 108 IU/L (<34); C-reactive protein 141 mg/L (0–6); erythrocyte sedimentation rate 24 mm/hr.  
A septic screen for common bacterial and viral pathogens, including parvovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HIV and hepatitis, was negative. Multiple COVID-19 swabs were negative.  
Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis showed no hepatosplenomegaly or evidence of malignancy.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of a slowly enlarging mass in the thenar eminence of his right hand. He denied trauma, systemic symptoms, or weight loss. His medical and social history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a 3.0 × 1.5 cm mobile, pulseless, ovular soft-tissue mass in the right thenar eminence; the overlying skin was normal, the mass was non-tender, and there were no sensory deficits or regional lymphadenopathy. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count, serum biochemistry, inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP), electrolytes, tumour markers, coagulation, liver and renal function, were all within normal limits.  
Ultrasound showed a well-defined, encapsulated, hypoechoic 2.8 × 0.8 cm lesion with intralesional calcifications and marked hypervascularity on color Doppler. The sonographer noted an intravascular tumour of equivocal interpretation, possibly a hemangiopericytoma.  
Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 2.7 × 1.7 × 0.9 cm encapsulated, ovular soft-tissue mass abutting but not invading adjacent muscles. On T1-weighted images, it was heterogeneous and nearly isointense to muscle with a central markedly hypointense area; on STIR and T2 sequences, it was heterogeneously hyperintense without fat and contained an internal low-signal septation consistent with calcification. The radiologist again favored hemangiopericytoma and recommended surgical removal.

A 49-year-old woman presented with intermittent visual disturbances over nearly four decades. Since age 10, she had episodes of scintillating scotomas several times per year, each resolving within 2 hours, often followed by mild nausea and increased photosensitivity. She also experienced mild photosensitivity daily without scotomas. She denied any headache associated with these visual events. Her medical history was notable for panic disorder, treated with anti-anxiety medication. On presentation, vital signs were within normal limits. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. Brain computed tomography showed no abnormalities. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were normal.

A 25-year-old woman presented with concerns of right-sided facial asymmetry and hyperpigmentation. She first noted a shallow depression over her right malar region at age 3, which progressively worsened over 20 years, then stabilized over the past 2 years. She denied pain, neurologic symptoms, or visual complaints. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, there was marked right hemifacial atrophy most prominent in the maxillary region, with hyperpigmentation of the overlying skin. Loss of underlying fat and muscle produced a sunken appearance. The right upper lip and nostril were smaller, and the mouth and nose were deviated to the right. Intraoral exam revealed reduction in size of the right upper dentition; no tongue atrophy or alopecia was noted. Neurologic and ophthalmologic exams were normal. Routine blood tests showed no abnormalities.

A noncontrast CT scan of the head demonstrated thinning of the subcutaneous fat and skin over the right malar region; atrophy of the right parotid and submandibular glands; and atrophy of the right masseter, temporalis, and pterygoid muscles. Bone-window images revealed atrophy of the right zygoma, greater wing of the sphenoid, right maxilla and mandible including the mandibular ramus and angle, and squamous part of the right temporal bone. There was reduction in size of the right upper premolar and molar teeth. The brain parenchyma appeared normal.

A 44-year-old woman presented with severe generalized abdominal pain for two days, accompanied by multiple episodes of non-bilious vomiting and diarrhea. She had two prior admissions in the past month for similar complaints treated conservatively as gastroenteritis. She reported six months of abdominal pain during menstruation that had increased in intensity over time; during the last two months, the pain was associated with diarrhea and tenesmus. She was not on contraceptive pills and had a history of cesarean delivery 10 years earlier.

On examination, she was hemodynamically stable. The abdomen was soft with diffuse tenderness; bowel sounds were present. An abdominal radiograph showed small-bowel obstruction with fecal loading in the ascending colon. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed concentric thickening of the distal ileum at the ileocecal junction, significant luminal narrowing with proximal small-bowel dilation, mild edematous thickening of bowel loops with prominent vasa recta, surrounding fat stranding, and small amounts of interbowel fluid. These findings suggested a subacute partial small-bowel obstruction, probably due to Crohn’s disease.

Colonoscopy disclosed a tight, short stricture just inside the ileocecal junction. Balloon dilation was attempted but the stricture recurred immediately upon withdrawal of the balloon. Three days later, a repeat colonoscopy with dilation to 15 mm produced submucosal hemorrhages and an ileocecal ulceration. A differential diagnosis of tuberculosis was also considered. Despite these interventions, her symptoms persisted, and she was scheduled for diagnostic laparoscopy.

A 59-year-old woman with hypertension was admitted after sudden deterioration to a semicomatous state. On examination, her pupils were pinpoint, she extended to painful stimuli, deep tendon reflexes were increased, and pathologic reflexes were present. Initial CT revealed an acute pontine hemorrhage. She received conservative management and was transferred to rehabilitation one month later, at which time she had quadriparesis, facial weakness, dysphagia requiring a feeding tube, and profound disequilibrium. Over the next several months, she regained alertness but continued to have diplopia, dysarthria, and paresthesia. 

Seven months after the hemorrhage, she was reassessed for worsened dysarthria and diplopia. Examination showed a low-amplitude, irregular, coarse tremor of the right upper extremity at rest and on posture, accentuated by action and absent during sleep. The tremor was a flexion-extension oscillation in the distal right arm at 2–4 Hz. She also had a bilateral palatal tremor and an irregular dystonic head tremor that worsened her horizontal diplopia. Upward and downward gaze were both markedly limited, and bilateral ptosis was present. Sitting unaided was difficult.

Brain MRI demonstrated residual hemosiderin in the pontine hemorrhage region and bilateral, symmetrical enlargement of the inferior olivary nuclei that were hyperintense on T2-weighted images, isointense on T1-weighted images, and showed no gadolinium enhancement.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of bilateral elbow swelling. Three years ago, she noticed a pea-sized, painful swelling over her right elbow; two months later, a similar swelling developed on her left side. Both swellings gradually increased to approximately 5 cm in diameter. The swellings were painless at presentation, with minimal restriction of elbow flexion. She reported no trauma, fever, discharging sinus, involvement of other joints, or history of renal stones. 

On examination, each elbow had a solitary, mobile, globular 5 cm × 5 cm, non–tender soft-to–firm mass over the posterior olecranon. There were no signs of inflammation, effusion, or instability. Elbow movements were painless except for the terminal 15° restriction of flexion. Examination of all other joints was unremarkable.

Investigations:
•  X-rays of both elbows (AP and lateral): erosion at the tip of the olecranon with otherwise normal joint space.  
•  Ultrasonography of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder: normal.  
•  Complete blood count: within normal limits.  
•  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 50 mm/hr.  
•  C-reactive protein: 0.4 mg/dL.  
•  Serum uric acid: 5.3 mg/dL.  
•  Rheumatoid factor: positive.  
•  ANA profile: SS-A and nucleosome positive.  
•  Serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium, alkaline phosphatase, and TSH: within normal limits.  
•  Bursal fluid analysis: 80% mononuclear cells with numerous intra- and extracellular positive birefringent crystals.

A 29-year-old black African woman presented with a 5-day history of headache and fever. Brain MRI was normal. Lumbar puncture revealed a cerebrospinal fluid white-cell count of 31 cells/mm3 (95% lymphocytes), elevated protein, and a borderline adenine deaminase level of 18.1 U/L. Ziehl–Neelsen stain, GeneXpert assay, and culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative. Blood tests were unremarkable. Her symptoms resolved with oral paracetamol, and she was discharged with a diagnosis of aseptic meningitis.

Two weeks later, she was readmitted with worsening neck pain and headache. Examination revealed significantly enlarged cervical lymph nodes. MRI of the neck showed features suggestive of tuberculous lymphadenitis. Repeat laboratory studies remained negative for tuberculosis. Epstein–Barr virus serology was positive for IgG but negative for IgM.

A cervical lymph node was excised. Histopathological examination showed necrotizing lymphadenitis without granulomas. On review at a referral center, the lymph node demonstrated marked architectural effacement with large areas of necrosis containing abundant apoptotic debris; adjacent viable areas contained numerous histiocytes, small lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and immunoblasts. Hematoxylin bodies were not identified. Immunohistochemical studies showed CD20/PAX5-positive B cells, CD68-positive histiocytes, CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and a Ki67 labeling index of 60%. “These findings were in keeping with a diagnosis of histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis likely secondary to either Kikuchi–Fujimoto disease or systemic lupus erythematosus.”

A 28-year-old woman in the final stages of orthodontic treatment presented with concerns about the aesthetics of her smile. She reported intermittent pain in the region of the upper right lateral incisor despite having undergone endodontic treatment on that tooth. 

Clinical examination revealed an enlarged clinical crown of the right maxillary lateral incisor (tooth 12) that appeared joined to an adjacent supernumerary segment. A periapical radiograph showed two crowns joined at the enamel level, only one root canal filled, and a periapical radiolucency at the root apex. 

To further characterize the lesion, a cone-beam CT scan with 0.5-mm slices was obtained. The scan demonstrated an extensive, well-defined, unilocular hypodense lesion surrounding the apices of the anomalous tooth.

A 40-year-old man of low socioeconomic status was referred from the ENT department for evaluation of a recurring pustule at the base of his right nostril that healed spontaneously over approximately 15 days only to recur. He had been treated for the past 6 months by a private practitioner with systemic antibiotics and intralesional steroids without improvement. He is a chronic heavy smoker (≥20 cigarettes per day for 15 years). He recalled trauma to his upper front teeth in his late 20s but denied any dental pain or swelling.

On extraoral examination, there was a pustular opening inferior to the right nostril. Intraoral examination revealed a discolored, attrited, noncarious right maxillary central incisor with prominent enamel cracks and generalized attrition; oral hygiene was poor. Pulp-vitality testing of the right maxillary central incisor with heated gutta-percha was negative. An intraoral periapical radiograph demonstrated a distinct periapical radiolucency and compromised periodontal status associated with the same tooth.

A 27-year-old man with ulcerative colitis, migraines, and childhood asthma presented with a 2-week history of severe vertigo, vomiting, bilateral hearing loss (left worse than right), and tinnitus. He was taking azathioprine 200 mg daily for ulcerative colitis but continued to have loose stools. On examination, he had left-beating nystagmus and catch-up saccades. An audiogram showed mild, symmetrical bilateral hearing loss. Initial blood tests were normal except for a slightly elevated neutrophil count. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and internal auditory meatus with and without contrast showed no mass lesion in the cerebellopontine angles or internal auditory canals, and no other cause for his symptoms was identified.

A 4-year-old girl with no significant past medical history was referred with a 2-month history of a right thoracic wall mass. She had no history of trauma and had been hospitalized one year earlier for pneumonia treated with intravenous antibiotics. She is currently asymptomatic, without fever or respiratory complaints. On examination, breath sounds were normal bilaterally. There was a 4×5 cm firm, tender swelling with overlying erythema in the right seventh intercostal space between the midclavicular and axillary lines; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count (with 35% neutrophils, 5% eosinophils, 48% basophils, 0.7% lymphocytes, and 11.3% monocytes), normal hemoglobin and platelet counts, and a negative C-reactive protein level. A chest radiograph demonstrated obliteration of the right costophrenic angle without lung or bone infiltration and soft-tissue swelling of the right chest wall. Given these findings, a panel of diagnoses was considered, including rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and tuberculous empyema necessitans. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest showed a 5×6 cm fluid collection eroding into the chest wall with visualization of a pleural fistula and no associated pleural effusion.

A 51-year-old man with a history of stage cT4a cN2c cM0 squamous cell carcinoma of the floor of the mouth was treated in 2018 with induction chemotherapy (docetaxel-cisplatin-fluorouracil), consolidation cetuximab, and radiotherapy (70 Gy to the tumor bed, 50 Gy to the neck), achieving complete remission. His medical history included mild untreated dyslipidemia and active smoking; there was no hypertension, diabetes, or prior stroke. In 2021, he presented with an 8-day history of intense tongue pain (glossodynia) and painful dysphagia, relying exclusively on a feeding tube. He denied fever, arthralgia, neurologic symptoms, weight loss, visual disturbances, jaw claudication, temporal tenderness, vasoconstrictor use, or history of syphilis or embolization. On examination, tongue movements were further restricted, with severe pain on light palpation and necrosis of the anterior third of the tongue bilaterally. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 2.51 mg/dL and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/hr; serologic studies for syphilis and other infections were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck demonstrated multiple areas of stenosis in both external carotid arteries and complete opacification of the lingual arteries. A biopsy from the margin of necrotic tissue revealed nonspecific inflammatory changes.

A 78-year-old Japanese man was brought to the emergency department for altered consciousness. Approximately 1 hour before arrival, he had been found sitting alone on a railway platform. Paramedics noted disorientation but were told he had been well 3 hours earlier. On arrival to the ED, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was E3V3M5.

Physical examination revealed systemic skin flushing and warmth without wheals, mucosal swelling, or pruritus. Vital signs were: heart rate 80 beats/min, blood pressure 64/33 mmHg, temperature 35.6°C, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

Venous blood gas analysis showed metabolic acidosis and elevated lactate (pH 7.289; bicarbonate 11.3 mmol/L; PvCO2 23.6 mmHg; lactate 9.3 mmol/L). Electrocardiogram and echocardiography were normal. A working diagnosis of distributive shock of unknown origin was made, and the patient received 2000 mL of lactated Ringer’s solution. Empirical piperacillin/tazobactam was started after two sets of blood cultures.

A whole‐body CT scan revealed no remarkable abnormalities, including no signs of infection or other causes of shock or altered consciousness. Laboratory studies showed serum osmolality 306 mOsm/kg, sodium 141 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL, and glucose 198 mg/dL, yielding an osmol gap of approximately 7.3 mOsm (estimated blood ethanol concentration ~33.6 mg/dL). Adrenal and thyroid hormone levels were within normal limits.

After initial resuscitation, his blood pressure improved to 118/75 mmHg and his GCS to E4V5M6. Although the patient denied alcohol ingestion…

A 45-year-old woman with metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix refractory to standard chemotherapy was enrolled in a clinical trial of daily cediranib and biweekly durvalumab. After four cycles she reported progressive dyspnea on exertion and fatigue over one month. On admission, temperature was 37 °C, heart rate 120 beats/min, blood pressure 90/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 93–97% on room air. Examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure, regular heart rhythm without a prominent P2, clear lung fields, and no peripheral edema.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelet count 159 k/μL, D-dimer 0.98 μg/mL, fibrinogen 517 mg/dL, pro-BNP 4541 pg/mL, and troponin-T 0.022 ng/mL. Chest radiography demonstrated hazy bibasilar interstitial markings. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed right ventricular dilation with TAPSE 8 mm (normal ≥17 mm) and estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 67 mmHg (new from baseline). Cardiac MRI confirmed a right ventricular ejection fraction of 27% with volume and pressure overload, without myocarditis. CT pulmonary angiography showed no pulmonary embolism, prominent interstitial markings, an enlarged main pulmonary artery, and severe right atrial and ventricular dilation. A ventilation-perfusion scan demonstrated mismatched perfusion defects along the pleural margins interpreted as high probability for pulmonary embolism; lower-extremity Doppler ultrasonography was negative for thrombosis, and anticoagulation was initiated.

Over the next 10 days, she developed syncope and resting hypoxemia. Right and left heart catheterization confirmed pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension with low cardiac output (mean pulmonary artery pressure 44 mmHg, pulmonary artery occlusion pressure 11 mmHg, cardiac index 1.5 L/min/m2, pulmonary vascular resistance 12.4 Wood units). Vasodilator challenge with inhaled nitric oxide and 100% oxygen paradoxically increased pulmonary artery pressures without pulmonary edema. Balloon-occlusion pulmonary venous sampling did not detect circulating tumor cells. Aggressive therapy was begun, including riociguat and intravenous epoprostenol, after which profound hypoxemia developed.

A 43-year-old man with diabetes mellitus and hypertension who recently recovered from COVID-19 infection presented with 2 months of progressive blurred vision in the left visual field followed by 3 months of retro-orbital pain. He denied diplopia, scalp tenderness, weight loss, and jaw claudication. Five months earlier, MRI of the brain and orbits had shown a mild T2-weighted hyperintense focus in the distal left optic nerve with post-contrast enhancement, leading to treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone for 3 days and an oral prednisolone taper; his symptoms recurred after steroids were discontinued. 

On examination, visual acuity was 6/36 in the left eye and 6/6 in the right eye; ocular motility showed impaired abduction and upward movement of the left eye. There was a relative afferent pupillary defect and blurred disc margin in the left eye; the retina was flat bilaterally. Laboratory tests showed a hematocrit of 42%, a white blood cell count of 14 500/μL (95% neutrophils), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 31 mm/h.

Repeat orbital MRI demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing intermediate-signal-intensity lesion in the left orbital apex encasing and compressing the optic nerve, contiguous with focal asymmetric enhancement in the left cavernous sinus but without abnormal signal or enhancement in the orbital fat. CT of the paranasal sinuses showed heterogeneously enhancing irregular soft tissue in the left orbital apex with widening of the orbital canal and mild extension into the sphenoid sinus. These findings were felt to represent likely infective pathology, with a differential diagnosis that included Tolosa-Hunt syndrome. The patient was scheduled for excision biopsy of the orbital apex lesion.

A healthy 16-year-old female student was referred with a 2-year history of a periodic nonpurulent bloody discharge from a tiny, nonhealing aperture located below the body of the left mandible. The lesion first appeared as a left submandibular swelling but was neither painful nor associated with fever, coryzal symptoms, or intraoral discomfort. She had received multiple courses of antibiotics and had undergone prior surgical excisions without resolution. Physical examination revealed a nontender, 1 × 1 cm hyperpigmented retracted lesion with a 3 mm central area of granulation tissue. Gentle pressure expressed scant nonpurulent discharge. Intraoral examination was unremarkable. The initial working diagnosis was a congenital fistula, and an MRI of the neck was obtained, which showed a 1.2 × 0.8 × 1.4 cm area of high T2/STIR and low T1 signal intensity in the left submandibular region along a 0.8 cm tract coursing superomedially, with no direct connection to any epithelialized structure.

A 62-year-old Italian-American man presented with new onset of bilateral pink nipple discharge and a history of long-standing retroareolar masses. He had undergone a left breast biopsy at an outside institution for a palpable mass, which the patient reported as benign. He denied trauma or prior infection. His medical history included type 2 diabetes managed with metformin and a 20–pack-year smoking history; there was no family history of breast cancer or gynecomastia.

On examination, he was well-groomed. Bilateral breasts were tender on palpation without overlying skin erythema or warmth; 2 × 2 cm retroareolar masses were noted on each side. A mammogram showed bilateral BIRADS-3 lesions. Same-day ultrasound demonstrated a 1.5 cm cystic lesion containing debris in the right breast and a 2.1 cm complex cystic and partially solid mass in the left breast.

Because of the nipple discharge and underlying masses, bilateral ultrasound-guided core biopsies were performed. Histologic examination revealed benign inflammatory tissue with granulation tissue, fibrosis, and multinucleated foreign-body–type giant cells, without evidence of malignancy. Microbiologic cultures of the biopsy samples grew Staphylococcus lugdunensis.

A 48-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of refractory “seizures” that began at age 22, four months after she sustained a traumatic head injury in a bus–motorcycle collision. She did not lose consciousness at the time of the accident but was hospitalized in the intensive care unit for several days. During her recovery she had difficulty walking and underwent an electromyogram, which was normal.

Four months after the accident, she began to experience paroxysmal behavioral and motor episodes occurring two to three times per week. Her episodes included transient lack of response (“absences”) and episodes compatible with dissociative fugue, during which she would become disoriented in public. She was diagnosed with posttraumatic epilepsy and treated sequentially with phenytoin, carbamazepine, and diazepam, without reduction in episode frequency. Concurrently, she underwent psychotherapy and received antidepressants for ten years with no change in her symptoms.

In July 2005, she was admitted for five days of video electroencephalographic (Video-EEG) monitoring. On admission, she was taking carbamazepine, phenytoin, and diazepam, which were tapered off. Neurologic examination was normal, and interictal brain MRI, SPECT, and EEG studies were unremarkable. During monitoring, three typical events were recorded. Each began with jerking of the trunk, progressed to bizarre movements, leg shaking, spitting, and crying, and lasted about one minute. She pointed to her head, stating that it hurt, remained aware throughout, and had no post-event confusion. There was no accompanying epileptiform activity on the EEG.

A 21-year-old male football player presented with several months of left popliteal fossa discomfort following minor trauma, aggravated by palpation and daily activities. On examination, there was no palpable mass or signs of inflammation in the popliteal fossa, but palpation of the anterior left knee elicited pain. There were no signs of peripheral arterial disease. Vital signs were normal, and chest and abdominal examinations, blood pressure measurement, chest radiography, oxygen saturation, and electrocardiography were unremarkable.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee without contrast showed a 4 × 2 cm oval formation with heterogeneous hyperintensity on T1- and T2-weighted sequences in the popliteal fossa adjacent to vascular structures, suggestive of a blood-containing lesion. Color-Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated a mixed echogenicity mass in the left popliteal fossa with no detectable arterial or venous flow.

A 38-year-old gravida 4 para 1021 with a dichorionic-diamniotic IVF twin gestation presented for routine prenatal care. Her medical and surgical histories were unremarkable, and her prior obstetrical history included one term vaginal delivery after IVF. At 9 weeks, her blood pressure was 122/65 mm Hg, prepregnancy weight was 172 lb, blood type O positive with a negative antibody screen, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, and hematocrit 35.9%. She declined aneuploidy screening.

At 17 weeks, a level II ultrasound confirmed normal anatomy in both fetuses. At 23 weeks, a growth scan showed twin A with adequate growth and twin B with severe hydrops: a 50% intertwin weight discordance, bilateral pleural effusions, pericardial effusion, and ascites, with a structurally normal heart. The differential diagnosis for fetal hydrops included intrauterine infection, congenital anatomic anomaly, or other causes. Isoimmunization was considered unlikely given a normal antibody screen and no ABO incompatibility (both parents were blood type O).

Workup included maternal serum TORCH titers and hemoglobin electrophoresis, diagnostic amniocentesis for karyotype, FISH, and PCR for HSV, CMV, parvovirus B19, and toxoplasmosis, and fetal echocardiography. Infectious and chromosomal causes were excluded, and fetal echocardiography revealed an atrioventricular canal malformation as the likely etiology of the hydrops. The patient declined selective fetal reduction.

At 24 weeks, she underwent therapeutic amniocentesis for worsening polyhydramnios and received betamethasone. Four days later, amniotic fluid normalized, but hydrops persisted. One week later (24 weeks 6 days), she presented with progressive abdominal distention, dyspnea, and new generalized edema. She had gained 10 lb over four weeks, and her blood pressure was 140/82 mm Hg. Laboratory evaluation showed a 24-hour urine protein of 360.4 mg, normal aminotransferases, serum creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, uric acid 5.3 mg/dL, LDH 250 U/L, hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, and hematocrit 30.1%. These findings raised concern for mirror syndrome.

A 53-year-old Japanese woman presented with sudden bilateral visual acuity decline 4 days after the onset of COVID-19 symptoms. She had tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by nasopharyngeal RT-PCR 15 days before presentation and reported resolution of fever at the time her vision worsened. Her past medical history included three doses of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, with the last dose administered approximately seven months prior.

On examination in the acute phase, best-corrected visual acuity was 0.5 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination revealed no inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber or anterior vitreous. Flare values averaged 2.4 photons/ms (right eye) and 2.1 photons/ms (left eye). Fundus photography and autofluorescence demonstrated bilateral atrophic changes of the retinal pigment epithelium along the inferior arcade vessels, extending from the optic disc to the midperipheral retina. Enhanced depth imaging optical coherence tomography showed outer retinal thinning and blurred outer retinal layers at the lesion sites in both eyes. Humphrey visual field testing revealed scotomas corresponding to these lesions. Fluorescein angiography disclosed diffuse punctate hyperfluorescence at areas of RPE loss without significant retinal vascular leakage or perfusion defects.

To exclude infectious retinitis or endophthalmitis, an aqueous humor sample from the left eye underwent comprehensive PCR testing, which was negative for human herpesviruses 1–8, bacterial 16S rRNA, fungal 28S rRNA, syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, and toxocariasis. The patient was managed conservatively without systemic treatment. At 15 weeks after presentation, visual acuity improved to 0.6 in the right eye and 0.8 in the left eye, with partial resolution of field defects and recovery of outer retinal architecture on OCT.

A 72-year-old man with kappa light chain–restricted multiple myeloma and high-risk cytogenetics (including TP53 deletion) presented with fever, confusion, and new-onset right upper- and lower-extremity weakness one week after receiving the first step‐up dose of teclistamab (0.06 mg/kg). His history included penta-refractory disease after multiple lines of therapy, prior spinal cord compression at T6 treated with laminectomy and radiotherapy, and ongoing maintenance immunosuppression. On presentation, his temperature was 100.4 °F, blood pressure and oxygen saturation were normal, and exam revealed disorientation and worsened right-sided weakness compared with his baseline. He tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 but had no respiratory symptoms and received a 3-day course of remdesivir.

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated multiple new regions of white matter hypoattenuation without infarction or hemorrhage. On hospital day 3, brain MRI showed extensive confluent multifocal T2/FLAIR hyperintense signal abnormalities predominantly in the bilateral frontal lobes and left parietal lobe with corresponding areas of restricted diffusion, and there was no contrast enhancement. By day 4, his motor weakness and sensory deficits (proprioception and vibration) in the lower extremities had progressed. 

On day 5, lumbar puncture revealed CSF glucose 54 mg/dL, protein 80 mg/dL, 1 RBC, 2 nucleated cells (68% lymphocytes, 32% monocytes), and negative Gram stain, fungal and mycobacterial cultures. CSF PCRs for Varicella-Zoster virus, HSV-1/2, HHV-6, and CMV were negative. CSF VDRL and cryptococcal antigen were negative, and PCR for BK virus in blood and CSF was negative. A routine EEG showed diffuse slowing without seizures or epileptiform discharges.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of low back pain and a vague swelling over the coccygeal area noticed when sitting. She denied bowel-related symptoms. One year earlier, a colonoscopy to investigate per rectal bleeding was normal to the cecum apart from grade I hemorrhoids. On lumbosacral MRI, there was a well-defined, bilobed cystic lesion (8.1 cm and 5.8 cm) in the presacral area anterior to the sacrococcygeal bones; the lesion bowed the levator ani, anal canal, and rectum anteriorly, and between the lobes lay a fibrous band-like structure in the plane of the levator ani. CT imaging showed no bony involvement. Examination under anesthesia revealed a soft, well-circumscribed mass in the retrorectal space with a freely mobile rectal wall over it. Following discussion at a multidisciplinary team conference, surgical excision of the lesion was planned given its symptoms and uncertain malignant potential.

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 5-month history of difficulty swallowing and breathing. She experienced dysphagia to both solids and liquids; the symptoms were nonprogressive and had been managed conservatively. She denied weight loss, fever, sore throat, cough, symptoms of connective-tissue disease, or features of hypothyroidism. On examination, a small, midline mass was palpable at the base of her tongue, and the thyroid gland was not palpable in the usual pretracheal location. Thyroid scintigraphy with technetium-99m showed isolated tracer uptake at the tongue base and no uptake in the thyroid bed. Laboratory studies revealed subclinical hypothyroidism with a TSH level of 12.1 μIU/mL (reference range, 0.3–4.5), total T4 of 6.8 μg/dL (4.5–12.5), and free T4 of 1.0 ng/dL (0.8–2.0). Levothyroxine at 25 μg daily was initiated.

A 27-year-old man was re-admitted with recurring right lower quadrant abdominal pain. He had a 3-year history of mild ulcerative colitis but had been asymptomatic without medications. On admission, vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a target sign in the ascending colon, and contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a target sign with dilatation of the cecum and terminal ileum, compatible with cecal intussusception. The patient had no previous abdominal surgery, and no intraabdominal masses or inflammatory changes were identified on imaging. The intussusception spontaneously reduced, and he was discharged. Six months later, his abdominal pain recurred. CT again showed cecal intussusception. An emergency colonoscopy was performed to reduce the intussusception; it revealed edematous colonic mucosa at the lead point but no neoplastic lesions in the colon or terminal ileum. The patient was thus diagnosed with recurrent cecal intussusception, and an elective laparoscopic surgery was planned.

A 36-year-old man with a 2-year history of right-sided lung adenocarcinoma with pleural metastases presented with intermittent lower back pain for approximately 6 months. The pain occurred 4 to 5 times per week, was rated 3/10 on a visual analog scale, worsened with bending or prolonged sitting, and improved with rest. He denied urinary symptoms or hematuria. His only notable allergy was to iodinated contrast media. He was a never-smoker, drank alcohol in moderation, and was receiving targeted therapy and immunotherapy for his lung cancer.

On examination, temperature was 36.6 °C, heart rate 71 beats/min, respiratory rate 17 breaths/min, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Abdominal and flank examinations were unremarkable, and there were no signs of renal dysfunction.

Non-contrast CT of the abdomen revealed a 3.8 × 2.4 cm soft tissue–density lesion in the right renal hilum and sinus, with a suggestion of connection to the right renal artery. Gray-scale ultrasound showed an ovoid cystic lesion measuring 68.3 × 30.6 × 46.3 mm in the right renal hilum with well-defined margins and a smooth contour. Color Doppler flow imaging demonstrated significant intralesional blood flow, and pulsed-wave Doppler analysis detected both arterial and venous flow but could not clarify the lesion’s relationship to the renal vessels.

A 37-year-old man in good health presented with a 2-month history of progressive left thigh pain that was severe even at rest. He denied fever, chills, or night sweats. On examination, there was no swelling of the thigh, but there was limitation of hip-joint range of motion. The white-blood-cell count was 4680/μL (reference, 3000–9000/μL) with a normal differential, and the C-reactive protein level was 1.82 mg/L (reference, 0.0–0.3 mg/L). Alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase levels were within normal limits. Plain radiographs and computed tomography of the left femur demonstrated a destructive osteolytic lesion in the lateral cortex of the greater trochanter with cortical erosion and an irregular periosteal reaction. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a diffuse abnormal marrow signal throughout the greater trochanter extending into the extramedullary space, and an osteolytic cortical lesion in the mid-shaft. Whole-body ^18F-fluorodeoxyglucose–PET revealed uptake in the left femur with a standardized uptake value of 13.37. Clinical differential diagnoses were osteomyelitis and benign or malignant bone tumors, and the patient underwent a pure bone biopsy for histopathological diagnosis.

A 62-year-old woman with a 7-year history of post-tuberculosis cystic bronchiectasis presented with a 7-day history of worsening cough and dyspnea. Her dyspnea progressed to MMRC grade 4 at rest. She used inhaled salmeterol–fluticasone and tiotropium. On admission, SpO2 was 86% on room air, 96% on 4 L O2; blood pressure was 90/50 mm Hg, and other vital signs were normal. Lung examination revealed bilateral coarse crepitations; cardiac examination was unremarkable. She was treated for an acute exacerbation of bronchiectasis.

On hospital day 2, she developed sudden central crushing chest pain without radiation. Only limb leads were obtained, showing ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, with ST depression in aVR. Initial troponin I was 0.1 ng/mL, rising to 3.36 ng/mL; CPK-MB rose from 6 U/L to 25 U/L. A provisional diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction was made.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated ballooning of the left ventricular mid- and apical segments, with akinesis of the apical and mid-anterior and mid-anteroseptal walls; the remaining mid-ventricular segments were hyperkinetic, and the basal segments were hyperkinetic. The left ventricular ejection fraction was 30–35%, and the outflow tract gradient was 8 mm Hg. Given her recent bronchiectasis exacerbation, these findings raised suspicion for Takotsubo syndrome; however, the regional wall motion abnormality was more pronounced in the LAD territory, creating diagnostic uncertainty.

A 20-month-old Kuwaiti girl was evaluated for a 6-month history of an enlarging mass in the left supraclavicular area. There was no preceding trauma or illness. She was born at term after an uncomplicated delivery; vaccinations were up to date, and there was no family history of malignancy. She appeared well systemically. Physical examination revealed a 5-cm, firm, non-tender mass in the left supraclavicular fossa, fixed to underlying tissue but not to overlying skin; there was no erythema. Laboratory tests showed a serum calcium concentration of 2.52 mmol/L (reference range 2.17–2.44 mmol/L), an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 34 mm/h (1–10 mm/h), a normal serum phosphate level, and normal results on full blood count and renal-function testing.  
  
Neck ultrasonography demonstrated a large, complex, densely calcified mass. A plain radiograph of the chest showed a 4-cm lobulated mass with heterogeneous calcification in the left supraclavicular region. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 4.6 × 4 cm mass in the left retroclavicular area that was low in signal on T1, T2, and short tau inversion-recovery sequences; diffusion‐weighted imaging showed minimal restriction, suggesting a benign process. Metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) I-123 SPECT–CT imaging demonstrated no uptake in the lesion. Although the mass abutted the brachial plexus, there was no evidence of bony destruction or invasion. Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy showed avid tracer uptake in the mass with normal uptake elsewhere in the skeleton.

A 3-month-old girl, born at term, presented with feeding challenges and colic. The evening before presentation, her father noted that she rolled off a couch and landed on her chin without observed bruising; she remained interactive.
