The following day, she refused breastfeeding and, when crying, tugged at her right ear. After a 24-hour period of limited intake, she was brought to the emergency department. No other symptoms were reported.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Oral inspection revealed a sublingual hematoma without lacerations or other mucosal injuries. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

A skeletal survey showed no abnormalities or evidence of anterior mandibular fractures. Head CT revealed bilateral high medial nondisplaced fractures of the mandibular condylar heads.

A 20-year-old woman presented with worsening dyspnea on exertion. Her medical history included hypertension since age 4, hyperlipidemia, bicuspid aortic valve with severe aortic insufficiency, aortic root dilation, and left ventricular dilation with preserved ejection fraction. She was born at 37 weeks in a pregnancy complicated by gestational hypertension and diagnosed with bicuspid aortic valve and aortic insufficiency at 3 months. At age 6, evaluation of her short stature and hypertension included karyotyping (46,XX), array CGH (negative), and skeletal survey revealing diffuse brachydactyly.

On examination, she was 58 inches tall, weighed 87 pounds (BMI 18.2), and had a blood pressure of 137/83 mm Hg. She had bilateral brachydactyly of the hands and feet without facial dysmorphism. Transesophageal echocardiography showed a bicuspid aortic valve, left ventricular ejection fraction 60%, severe aortic insufficiency with eccentric left ventricular dilation, mild aortic stenosis, and moderate mitral regurgitation. Cardiac MRI demonstrated an enlarged ascending aorta relative to body size. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy. A 29-gene aortopathy panel and an 82-gene cardiomyopathy panel were both negative.

An 79-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of gait disturbance, progressive weakness of all four limbs, and hand clumsiness. He denied weight loss, fever, cough, or bladder/bowel symptoms. He was apyrexial, alert, with intact cranial nerves. He was quadriparetic (motor power 2/5) with increased tone, brisk reflexes, bilateral Hoffmann’s signs, sustained clonus, and upgoing plantars. Brain MRI was normal. Cervical MRI showed a retro-odontoid mass that was isointense on T1, hypointense on T2, causing anterior subluxation of C2 on C1, severe spinal-cord compression, and focal cord signal change; postgadolinium images showed inhomogeneous enhancement with rim enhancement. Cervical CT confirmed a large retro-odontoid mass. A neuroradiology review proposed a differential diagnosis of pannus, metastasis, chordoma, myeloma, and lymphoma. There was no clinical evidence of rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, or gout. C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, serum calcium, and uric acid levels were normal. Rheumatoid factor and serum protein electrophoresis were negative, and Bence–Jones protein was absent. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no abnormalities.

A 59-year-old man with mild psoriasis, a long smoking history, obesity, and treated hepatitis C was followed for over 2 years for repeated hospitalizations due to erythroderma and a new 10/10 pruritic palmoplantar rash. Initial differential diagnoses included psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, and Bazex syndrome; a chest CT showed no malignancy. Two skin biopsies revealed mixed psoriatic and spongiotic dermatitis. He had transient improvement with cyclosporine but developed acute renal dysfunction each time; long-term prednisone led to a pathologic rib fracture. He failed multiple biologics (dupilumab for 2 months, adalimumab for 5 months, and guselkumab for 7 months) despite concurrent clobetasol and acitretin. Infliximab was then initiated, allowing prednisone tapering but with persistent rash. During a subsequent hospitalization, his eruption developed a sharply demarcated pattern on the dorsal feet corresponding to his footwear, raising concern for allergic contact dermatitis. He was referred for patch testing. On telephone screening, he was instructed to discontinue cyclosporine 2 weeks before testing; due to misunderstanding, he also stopped acitretin and nightly hydroxyzine.  
At the patch‐testing visit, he reported a new concern of “spiders” on and under his skin, pointing to inorganic debris on his clothing and legs.

A 32-year-old man and competitive rugby player reported a 2-year history of progressive swelling of his left calf. He noted intermittent aching and tightness in the calf and occasional tingling in the left foot. His medical history was notable for degenerative lumbar disk disease treated by microdiscectomy. On examination, the left calf was visibly larger than the right, without tenderness. Distal pulses were normal, and there was no sensory deficit. Because of concern for compartment syndrome, compartment pressure testing was performed and was normal. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging of the calves showed asymmetric enlargement of the musculature of the left calf with areas of high signal intensity on T1-weighted images consistent with fatty infiltration, most marked in the superficial posterior compartment.

A 62-year-old man with locally advanced cT4 squamous cell anal cancer involving adjacent structures and bilateral inguinal lymph nodes was treated with radical radiotherapy (IMRT) and concurrent chemotherapy (mitomycin and 5-FU). Radiotherapy delivered 45 Gy to the clinical target and 54 Gy to the gross tumor volume over 25 fractions; no special penile positioning or dose constraint was used, and the area where lesions later appeared received a maximum of 35 Gy. During his admission for the second chemotherapy cycle (cumulative radiotherapy dose 43.2 Gy), he reported a 1-day history of painful lumps on the midline of the anterior penile shaft, approximately 2 cm from the pubic symphysis. He denied hematuria, itching, dysuria, fever, trauma, recent sexual activity, masturbation, use of constrictor devices, or any history of sexually transmitted disease. Physical examination revealed two tender, rope-like lesions about 5 mm each in the midline anterior penile surface. Routine blood tests were normal. Doppler ultrasound of the penis showed a non-compressible superficial dorsal vein with absence of venous flow signals and surrounding soft-tissue hyperechogenicity.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of chronic, intermittent abdominal pain. He had a 20-year history of mild-to-moderate alcohol use but denied jaundice, fever, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal serum amylase, lipase, CA 19-9, and carcinoembryonic antigen. Unenhanced CT imaging revealed a poorly defined soft-tissue mass in the pancreaticoduodenal groove containing a hypodense cystic focus. On portal venous-phase contrast, the lesion enhanced minimally, and delayed images at 2–3 minutes demonstrated mild persistent enhancement consistent with fibrous scar, with adjacent mild thickening of the second-part duodenal wall and variable luminal narrowing. The common bile and pancreatic ducts and the remainder of the pancreas appeared normal. MRI confirmed a soft-tissue intensity lesion with intralesional cystic change in the groove merging imperceptibly with the pancreatic head and poorly defined fat planes with the duodenum. MR cholangiopancreatography showed smooth, regular tapering of the pancreatic and common bile ducts with normal duct calibers and a distended gallbladder.

A 41-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug abuse was admitted for diffuse abdominal pain and bloody stools. One year earlier, he had been diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C (genotype 1A) without cirrhosis. He reported intermittent, self‐limited episodes of abdominal pain and vomiting over the previous three months; his most recent cocaine use was the day before presentation. On examination, he was febrile (38.3 °C) and had tenderness in the right lower quadrant, maximal at McBurney’s point. Laboratory tests showed a C‐reactive protein level of 14 mg/dL and a white blood cell count of 14 500/µL.  
Abdominal ultrasound was performed to evaluate suspected appendicitis and demonstrated segmental, circumferential thickening of the ascending colon with preserved layers, limited hyperechoic mesenteric fat, and weak color Doppler signals in the affected segment. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen confirmed inflammation of the ascending colon and cecum, possibly extending into the terminal ileum.

A middle-aged man with no prior medical history presented with a 3-day history of intense throbbing headache (9/10), high fever up to 40.6 °C, and diffuse limb aches. He had no photophobia, phonophobia, vomiting, altered mental status, or meningeal signs. Neurologic and general physical examinations were unremarkable. He denied recent travel, animal exposures, gardening, or new medications.

Laboratory studies on admission showed leukocytes 7.7 × 10^3/µl, hemoglobin 15.9 g/dl, platelets 102 × 10^3/µl, creatinine 1.3 mg/dl, estimated GFR 70 ml/min/1.73 m^2, AST 60 U/l, γ-GT 60 U/l, and CRP 12.6 mg/dl. Urinalysis revealed proteinuria (urine albumin/creatinine ratio 1496 mg/g). Over the next days, platelets transiently increased above normal, creatinine peaked at 2.4 mg/dl, then improved.

Lumbar puncture on day 1 showed 11 cells/µl (9 lymphocytes), total protein 386 mg/l, normal glucose and lactate, an intact blood–brain barrier by Reiber diagram, negative PCR for CMV, EBV, HSV-1/2, VZV, HHV-6, and negative antigen tests for tick-borne encephalitis, Borrelia, Treponema, Leptospira, Legionella, and Pneumococcus.

Brain MRI on day 2 demonstrated a single ovoid lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum with diffusion-weighted hyperintensity and corresponding ADC reduction, without contrast enhancement. A follow-up MRI after 10 days showed marked resolution of the lesion, with only slight residual FLAIR hyperintensity.

An 83-year-old Caucasian woman presented with pain in the gingiva surrounding her mandibular dental implants. Her medical history was notable for chronic pulmonary embolism managed with rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) and a diagnosis of erosive oral lichen planus made more than 10 years earlier, for which she was not receiving active therapy. 

Intraoral examination revealed a maxillary complete denture and a mandibular bar overdenture retained by three implants (positions #43, #31, and #33) placed 30 years ago. The peri-implant mucosa exhibited gingival overgrowth and severe inflammation. Periodontal probing depths ranged from 5 to 11 mm around the implants, and bleeding on probing was present at 100% of sites. 

A periapical radiograph showed circumferential peri-implant bone loss of approximately one-third of the implant length at positions #43 and #33 and approximately one-half of the implant length at position #31.

A 63-year-old woman with a 15-year history of Crohn’s disease limited to the colon (on mesalamine) presented with 1 month of worsening dry cough and diarrhea. The cough was nonproductive with intermittent post-tussive vomiting. She reported up to 10 green, nonbloody, loose bowel movements per day associated with intermittent abdominal pain that was not relieved by defecation. She denied fevers, chills, rhinorrhea, headache, dysuria, ocular symptoms, sick contacts, new medications, antibiotic use, or recent travel. She noted mild dyspnea on exertion but had no history of lung disease or asthma. She was tolerating oral intake and denied appetite changes.

On admission, temperature was 100.4°F and heart rate 119 beats per minute. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 13.3 cells/mcL, hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 105 mm/hour. Empiric antibiotics were initiated but discontinued after 24 hours when a full infectious work-up was negative, without clinical improvement. Chest and abdominal CT scans revealed wall thickening of the colon from the proximal sigmoid to the cecum; no abnormalities were seen in the lung parenchyma or large airways. Symptomatic treatment with guaifenesin and codeine and inhaled ipratropium–albuterol provided mild relief. Colonoscopy with random biopsies confirmed moderately active colitis in the terminal ileum and the entire colon consistent with Crohn’s disease.

A 78-year-old woman presented with subacute, intractable left lower extremity neuropathic pain, back pain, and a two-week history of left foot drop. She had sustained a left acetabular fracture in a fall 20 years earlier, treated nonoperatively, and had intermittent left hip pain since. Over the past six months, she experienced increasing back pain, left-sided radicular discomfort, and excruciating pain over the left foot.

On examination, strength in the left lower extremity was 4/5 for hip flexion, 5/5 for knee extension, 0/5 for ankle dorsiflexion, 1/5 for great toe extension, and 4/5 for ankle plantarflexion. Hypersensitivity was present in the superficial peroneal, deep peroneal, sural, saphenous, and tibial nerve distributions. Distal perfusion was intact with brisk capillary refill and a palpable dorsalis pedis pulse.

A pelvic radiograph showed no acute fracture but significant hip arthrosis and sclerotic changes around the greater sciatic notch of the left innominate bone. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed post-traumatic changes in the left iliac bone with a 5.8 × 3.6 × 7 cm lytic lesion containing cystic or soft-tissue components, extending from the supra-acetabular region under the psoas, findings initially favored to represent tumor or infection. MRI with contrast demonstrated that the lesion had a nonaggressive appearance and was partially visualized on an examination performed in 2014.

A 43-year-old woman presented to the breast clinic with at least three new linear creases in her left breast that developed one week after receiving the first dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine in her left arm. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension managed with nifedipine. She had no history of SARS-CoV-2 infection, thromboembolic events, thrombophilia, malignancy, autoimmune disease, or hormone therapy; she was a nonsmoker and was not taking exogenous estrogens or contraceptives. Her body mass index was 39.7 kg/m². She reported no breast pain, nipple discharge, focal lump, trauma, or allergic reactions.

On examination, three linear indentations with overlying skin discoloration were seen in the left breast—one vertical laterally and two horizontal in the superior and inferior aspects. The creases were neither tender nor painful. The right breast was unremarkable. Bilateral diagnostic mammography (2D and digital tomosynthesis) showed fatty breasts without masses or calcifications. Targeted ultrasound of the left breast at the sites of the creases demonstrated mildly dilated superficial tubular structures with intraluminal echogenic material, absent flow on Doppler, and loss of compressibility. Ultrasound of the left axillary vein was normal, and no lymphadenopathy was seen. The findings were categorized as BI-RADS 2. 

In the emergency department, her vital signs were: blood pressure 140/97 mm Hg, heart rate 84 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 37.0°C, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. No laboratory tests were obtained, and she was discharged for outpatient follow-up.

A 45-year-old housewife presented with a 12-day history of multiple painful, reddish swellings on the right upper limb, beginning over the mid-forearm and extending linearly to the mid-arm. She had no history of trauma, thorn injury, insect bite, systemic symptoms, or immunosuppressive conditions, but she enjoyed gardening as a hobby. On examination, there were multiple well-defined, discrete, tender, warm, erythematous nodules, 1–2 cm in diameter, some with purulent, non-grainy discharge and a few with ulceration, extending in a linear (sporotrichoid) distribution from the flexor aspect of the mid-arm to the extensor mid-forearm. No sinuses were present. Tender axillary lymphadenopathy was noted. 

Initial clinical differential diagnoses included sporotrichosis, nocardiosis, mycetoma, atypical mycobacterial infection, cutaneous tuberculosis, leishmaniasis, and malignancy. 

Staining of purulent material revealed multiple gram-positive, branching filamentous bacilli with a “sunray appearance” in some fields, which were partially acid-fast on modified Kinyoun staining (1% sulfuric acid), and negative on 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount. On blood agar, multiple discrete, chalky white, wrinkled colonies appeared by day 3 of incubation; similar colonies appeared on Lowenstein–Jensen medium by day 9. No growth occurred on MacConkey or Sabouraud dextrose agar. Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization–time of flight (MALDI-TOF) analysis was inconclusive for species identification.

A 41-year-old previously healthy Persian man presented with a 7-day history of fever, myalgia, and malaise and a 2-day history of gastrointestinal bleeding manifested as coffee-ground vomitus and melena. Fourteen days before presentation, he had traveled to Karbala, Iraq. He was evaluated twice at other centers for presumed COVID-19 infection because of fever and myalgia but did not improve and had not developed GI bleeding at those times.

On examination at our hospital, he was alert. Blood pressure was 120/75 mmHg, pulse 100/min, respiratory rate 17/min, temperature 38.5 °C, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. The sclera were not icteric. There were no respiratory symptoms. Abdominal examination revealed mild right upper-quadrant tenderness without hepatosplenomegaly. Lung computed tomography and abdominopelvic sonography were normal.

Laboratory studies on admission showed: WBC 4,700/µl, hemoglobin 15.0 g/dl, platelets 45,000/µl, prothrombin time 14.2 sec, partial thromboplastin time 57.3 sec, INR 1.1, BUN 11 mg/dl, creatinine 1.0 mg/dl, AST 690 IU/L, ALT 700 IU/L, ALP 240 IU/L, LDH 1,276 IU/L, ESR 10 mm/h, CRP 22 mg/dl, albumin 3.6 g/dl, and D-dimer 1.2 µg/ml. Blood cultures were obtained. Serologic tests for IgM anti-HAV, IgM anti-CMV, IgM anti-HBc, HBsAg, and HCV antibody were all negative. Two sets of blood cultures were negative. A serum sample was sent for Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever testing.

A 47-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of headache, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, right leg claudication, diffuse musculoskeletal pains, progressive bilateral hearing loss, and decreased vision progressing to near-blindness. On admission, her blood pressure was 125/75 mmHg in the left arm and 120/70 mmHg in the right arm; pulse 85/min; respiration rate 18/min; temperature 37.1°C. Heart and lung examinations were unremarkable.

Ophthalmologic examination showed visual acuity of 0.1 in both eyes and intraocular pressure of 15 mmHg bilaterally. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy revealed bilateral ciliary hyperemia, cataract, and interstitial keratitis with marginal corneal infiltrates. Funduscopic evaluation showed mild optic-disc hyperemia with blurred margins but no vitreous or retinal inflammation.

Audiologic testing, including pure-tone audiometry and auditory brainstem responses, demonstrated bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 10,200/mm3, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelet count 340,000/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 65 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein 13.1 mg/dL.

Serologic tests were negative for autoimmune markers (anti-nuclear antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, rheumatoid factors, antiphospholipid antibodies, complements, and cryoglobulins) and for syphilis (VDRL, FTA-Abs). Cerebrospinal fluid and serum analyses were negative for antibodies (IgG and IgM) against Epstein-Barr virus, herpes zoster virus, herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, chlamydia, hepatitis B and C viruses, HIV, Toxoplasma gondii, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Brain MRI, chest and abdominal CT, colonoscopy, upper endoscopy, and minor salivary gland biopsy were all normal.

A 55-year-old man presented with a 1-day history of progressive abdominal distension and persistent colicky pain rated 6–7/10. He had passed feces and flatus but vomited twice. Three years earlier, he underwent a Hartmann procedure for gangrenous sigmoid volvulus; three months later the colostomy was reversed with a descending colorectal anastomosis. Since then he had recurrent constipation unresponsive to traditional medicines. He had no other comorbidities. On examination, he was afebrile, BP 100/65 mmHg, HR 101 bpm, RR 24/min. The abdomen was distended, hyper-tympanic with high-pitched bowel sounds and mild left upper quadrant tenderness without guarding or rebound. Digital rectal examination revealed loose stool without mass. Laboratory studies showed WBC 12 000/mm³, Hb 12.9 g/dL, platelets 266 000/mm³; renal function and electrolytes were normal. An erect abdominal radiograph demonstrated dilated large-bowel loops, multiple air-fluid levels, and a gasless pelvis. A provisional diagnosis of adhesive bowel obstruction was made; he was resuscitated with IV fluids and antibiotics, and a nasogastric tube was placed. Rectal tube decompression was attempted but failed, and radiographic findings suggested large-bowel obstruction possibly due to volvulus. Given the lack of improvement and concern for mechanical obstruction, emergency surgery was planned.

A 62-year-old Caucasian man presented with swelling and a sensation of fullness in the left posterior chest. He described mild chest-wall discomfort that had gradually worsened over the preceding 6 months and was aggravated by sitting or leaning against a wall. He maintained a full range of shoulder motion and performed activities of daily living without limitation. 

His medical history was notable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, sleep apnea, osteoarthritis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, chronic mild asthma, previous cervical spine surgery, and two motor-vehicle accidents resulting in a lower right-sided lumbar injury.  

On examination, he was morbidly obese. There was a non-tender, fluctuant mass on the left upper back, extending above and below the scapula and measuring approximately the size of a deflated football. No scars were present in the thoracic region, although an upper midline neck scar was noted.  

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest showed a large, purely cystic mass between the posterior thoracic ribs and the deep muscles of the left back and scapula, with no solid or enhancing components and no connection to the spinal canal or pleural space. An MRI confirmed a unilocular cyst extending from the lower neck to just above the diaphragm, measuring 11 cm transversely, 4.5 cm anteroposteriorly, and 23 cm craniocaudally.  

The primary care physician aspirated clear serous fluid under sterile conditions; cytologic analysis was unremarkable. Two weeks later, the mass had reaccumulated, and the patient was referred for further management.

A 15-year-old male track-and-field athlete presented with a one-month history of left lower–leg pain and discomfort, with a recurrence of similar pain during running 6 days before admission. The pain began insidiously, had no clear precipitant, worsened with activity, and had been partially relieved by outpatient treatments (antibiotics, circulation promotion, and analgesics) before relapsing during a running test. There was no history of fever, trauma, or systemic symptoms.

On examination, the left lower leg had slightly elevated skin temperature, normal color, no obvious tenderness, and normal ankle mobility; sensory, motor, and vascular examination of the limb were unremarkable.

Routine laboratory studies, including markers of infection and tumor markers, were within normal limits.

Outpatient radiography and CT of the left tibia and fibula showed increased density in the midshaft of the left tibial medullary cavity, a posterior cortical bone fracture, periosteal reaction around the fracture site, and adjacent soft-tissue swelling. “There is a high possibility of osteomyelitis in the tibia,” and the patient was admitted with a provisional diagnosis of osteomyelitis of the left tibia.

Magnetic resonance imaging of both lower limbs and whole-body bone scintigraphy demonstrated:
1. Increased metabolic activity in the proximal right femur and bilateral tibial cortical bones, indicating “a high possibility of benign lesions, possibly osteomyelitis.”
2. “The signal in the medullary cavity of the proximal femur and distal tibia on the right side appears abnormal, with discontinuous fractures observed in portions of the cortical bone and surrounding periosteal reactions, suggested the stress fractures cannot be ruled out.”
3. “No definite signs of tumor bone metastasis were identified upon examination of the whole-body bone scan.”

A 58-year-old Caucasian man was found dead by his wife, hanging from the ceiling in the basement where he lived; he had been dead for approximately 3 hours. He had a long history of severe depression, lived in seclusion, and had moved to the cellar years earlier. He took fluoxetine (60 mg daily) and had a previous suicide attempt 2 years earlier by taking alcohol with his antidepressants. His usual routine was gardening in the mornings and carpentry in the afternoons.

On initial inspection, the scene suggested suicide, but a large amount of blood and lacerations were noted on his sweater. Upon lifting the sweater, there was a wide incised wound with irregular edges in the umbilical area exposing muscle and adipose tissue. No other bloodstains were found except a small pool beneath the body. In the adjacent garden, police found a chainsaw with blood spatter on the blade and handle and fragments of fabric matching the sweater. The saw weighed 4.4 kg, had a 41 cm blade rotating up to 2400 rpm only while the throttle was depressed, and bore only the victim’s fingerprints. Wound examination (direction, orientation, depth) indicated it could only have been self-inflicted.

A post-mortem examination the following day revealed a ligature mark around the neck and a deep incised wound on the mesogastrium measuring 16 cm by 4.5 cm, with torn and grazed edges, surrounded by a 23 × 12 cm reddish abrasion. The neck skin was brownish-yellow and parchment-like, with hyperemia at the margins and subconjunctival petechiae. No other external injuries were present.

Internal examination showed hemorrhagic infiltration of the right omohyoid and sternocleidomastoid muscles, intact thyroid cartilage and hyoid bone, congestion of all organs, lacerated intestinal loops beneath the abdominal wound, and 100 ml of blood in the peritoneal cavity. Histology confirmed hemorrhagic infiltration in the skin and intestinal mucosa, and immunohistochemistry demonstrated vitality of both the abdominal wound and the ligature mark. Toxicology was negative for alcohol and other substances.

A 24-year-old man presented with multiple erythematous, itchy papules and plaques. He works in a lithium battery factory and sustained a chemical burn on his right wrist from lithium 2 weeks earlier. One week after the burn, a solitary erythematous papule appeared at the injury site and extended to his arms and thighs within a day. On examination, there were multiple erythematous to purple-red papules and plaques with central dark zones on the wrists, arms, and thighs; the oral and genital mucosa were uninvolved. He denied any history of herpes simplex infection or other recent illnesses. Laboratory studies were normal except for a white blood cell count of 11,750/µL. A punch biopsy of a wrist lesion showed scattered lymphocytic infiltration, vacuolar degeneration of basal cells, and necrotic keratinocytes.

A 30-year-old gravida 3 woman was referred at 19 weeks’ gestation for a fetal ultrasound. Transabdominal imaging revealed mild hydrops with moderate ascites. Both lungs were enlarged, bulky, and echogenic, resulting in increased chest circumference and eversion of the diaphragm. The fetal heart was small, centrally located, and structurally normal. The tracheobronchial tree was fluid-filled and dilated, and there was an abrupt transition in the fetal laryngeal lumen. No other congenital abnormalities were detected.

A 27-year-old man with no prior medical history presented in July 2020 with a 2-week history of daily fevers, sore throat, migrating polyarthralgias, and a macular rash on his forearms. Eight weeks earlier, he had been hospitalized for 10 days with symptomatic COVID-19 and subsequently recovered. On examination, his temperature was 39°C, and he had tenderness over the tracheal cartilage and nonpruritic macular rashes on both forearms. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 25.9 × 10^9/L with neutrophilia and normal lymphocytes, a C-reactive protein level of 187.8 mg/L, ferritin 17 500 ng/dL, and mildly elevated ALT (90 U/L) and AST (76 U/L). Nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 PCR and serum IgG were positive. Epstein-Barr viral antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and antinuclear antibodies were negative. Transthoracic echocardiography and CT of the chest and abdomen were unremarkable. He was admitted with possible COVID-19–associated cytokine storm versus postviral bacterial infection and received 5 days of intravenous antibiotics. His fever persisted intermittently, and blood cultures showed no growth.

A 26-year-old woman was referred for consultation on her right maxillary lateral incisor to complete previously initiated root canal therapy. Five months earlier, treatment had been started for coronal caries and spontaneous localized tooth pain. During the procedure she suddenly developed a progressive, painless swelling on the right side of her face, described as having a sandy sensation on palpation. She was diagnosed with an allergic reaction to local anesthetic and received 8 mg of intramuscular dexamethasone. Over the next few hours, the swelling extended to the left side of her face, and the allergy diagnosis was reconfirmed by an emergency specialist. The following morning, she awoke with worsening facial swelling, blurred vision, and severe throat and chest pain. A CT scan revealed pneumo-orbit and bilateral gas accumulation in the fascial planes and parapharyngeal spaces. Accordingly, she was diagnosed with necrotizing fasciitis, and emergency surgical debridement was planned.

An 83-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of progressive visual-acuity reduction and visual-field defects in both eyes. Initial intraocular pressures were 22 mm Hg OD and 29 mm Hg OS; tafluprost was started without IOP reduction and with gradual bilateral upper-eyelid swelling. Two months later, chest radiography at an annual check revealed a 5 cm mass in the left upper lung. On examination at our ophthalmology department, BCVA was 0.03 OD and 0.07 OS (previously 0.3 and 0.5 one month earlier). There was bilateral palpebral swelling, interpalpebral fissure of 2 mm, normal levator function, normal optic discs, IOP 16 mm Hg OD and 18 mm Hg OS, critical flicker frequencies 11.3 Hz OD and 20.8 Hz OS, and no afferent pupillary defect. Eye movements were full. Electroretinography was normal. OCT showed intact outer retinal layers. Goldmann perimetry revealed paracentral scotomas with peripheral constriction in both eyes and central absolute scotomas in the right eye. Labs showed CRP 1.1 mg/dL; thyroid hormones, TSH-receptor and other autoantibodies, IgG4, and soluble IL-2 receptor were within normal limits. MRI (STIR and contrast-enhanced T1) showed hyperintense, swollen bilateral extraocular muscles compressing both optic nerves at the orbital apex and enlarged lacrimal glands; there was muscle enhancement but no optic-nerve or sheath enhancement.

A 68-year-old man with essential thrombocythemia (ET) was referred after serial CT scans showed enlargement of a splenic lesion. He had a history of ET treated with aspirin due to resistance to hydroxycarbamide and acute heart failure induced by anagrelide. Surveillance imaging for possible renal cystic tumors was unremarkable. On admission he had no bleeding or thrombotic events. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 23.4 × 10^3/µL, platelet count of 854 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 15.9 g/dL, elevated lactate dehydrogenase 1431 IU/L, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 887 U/mL; other values were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 70 × 45 mm low-density mass in the spleen with heterogeneous hypoenhancement in the arterial phase and progressive homogeneous enhancement in the equilibrium phase; this lesion had grown from 45 × 30 mm over 6 months. MRI showed the lesion to be isointense on T1-weighted images, mottled hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and hypointense on diffusion-weighted imaging, with comparable enhancement on dynamic sequences. FDG-PET/CT showed moderate uptake (SUV max 4.9). Based on these findings, hemangioma or hamartoma were considered most likely, but malignancy could not be excluded. Splenectomy was planned for definitive diagnosis.

A 55-year-old woman with known gallstone disease presented with severe, constant upper abdominal pain of 5 days’ duration, non-radiating, worse after meals, associated with nausea and non-bilious vomiting. She denied alcohol use. On examination, vital signs were normal; abdominal tenderness was noted in the epigastrium and right hypochondrium without guarding. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers, a mildly elevated serum amylase of 140 U/L, and normal liver function tests. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed echogenic fluid between the second part of the duodenum and the head of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated edematous thickening and cystic changes in the duodenal wall, edematous changes with minimal enhancement in the pancreatic head and uncinate process, localized fluid and inflammatory strands in the paraduodenal/pancreatic head region, a normal main pancreatic duct, a normal biliary system, and no vascular encasement. Upper GI endoscopy was normal.

A 35-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of gradually progressive, bilateral diminution of vision. He worked as a silver-utensil polisher for 30 years, polishing at a bench 30–40 cm from his face for 8 hours daily.  
On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in both eyes; near vision was N-10 in the right eye and N-8 in the left. Intraocular pressure was 10 mm Hg bilaterally. Slit-lamp examination of both eyes revealed:  
  • Slate-gray pigmentation of the bulbar conjunctiva.  
  • Greenish-brown granular deposits at Bowman’s membrane, posterior stroma, and Descemet’s membrane.  
  • Nuclear sclerosis grade 2 with posterior subcapsular cataract displaying a polychromatic luster.  
Dilated fundus examination was limited by media haze.  
Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography demonstrated hyperreflective Bowman’s membrane and Descemet’s membrane in both eyes. Corneal confocal microscopy revealed scattered hyperreflective dots in the anterior to mid-stroma obscuring the endothelium. Scheimpflug imaging showed multiple hyperreflective areas in the cornea. Multifocal electroretinography showed a generalized decrease in P1-wave sensitivity with loss of the foveal peak (right eye more affected). Fundus fluorescein angiography demonstrated mild late-phase leaks from the optic disc and perifoveal areas in both eyes.

A 75-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted with a prosthetic hip infection 10 days after revision surgery. Her medical history included chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 130–150 μmol/L), hypertension, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and folate deficiency. Home medications included aspirin, bisoprolol, atorvastatin, furosemide, gliclazide, pantoprazole, folic acid, inhaled bronchodilators, and as-needed oxycodone. On admission she began intravenous vancomycin and acetaminophen for pain.

On hospital day 10 she developed drowsiness, confusion, disorientation, and hyperventilation. Examination showed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12. Temperature was 36.2°C, blood pressure 145/66 mmHg, pulse 80/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Cardiopulmonary and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
- Sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 3.5 mmol/L, chloride 118 mmol/L, bicarbonate 5 mmol/L  
- Blood urea nitrogen 8 mmol/L, creatinine 150 μmol/L (baseline)  
- Hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL, neutrophils 16.5×10^9/L, platelets 485×10^9/L  
- Albumin 17 g/L  
Arterial blood gas: pH 7.18, pCO2 1.7 kPa, pO2 16.7 kPa, bicarbonate 8.3 mmol/L, base excess –22.7 mmol/L. The corrected anion gap was 25 mmol/L.

Initial evaluations showed lactic acid 0.7 mmol/L, blood ketones <0.2 mmol/L, salicylate <0.4 mmol/L, and unchanged renal function insufficient to explain the degree of acidosis. Serum toxicology, including acetaminophen level, was unremarkable; the osmolar gap was mildly elevated at 21 mOsm/kg. Urine was sent for organic acid analysis.

A 44-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a one-week history of neck pain and odynophagia. He was afebrile with normal vital signs. Examination revealed mild erythema of the pharyngeal wall without exudate and no tonsillar enlargement. Laboratory studies were notable only for a mildly elevated C-reactive protein level of 26 mg/dl. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a moderate retropharyngeal effusion with adjacent prevertebral soft-tissue edema. Amorphous calcifications were noted in the superior fibers of the left longus colli tendon at the C1–C2 level. There was no peripheral enhancement around the effusion, and no cervical or retropharyngeal adenopathy or osseous destruction was identified.

A 46-year-old woman was evaluated for a right adrenal incidentaloma discovered at a routine health check. She had no significant medical history except a benign thyroid nodule and no signs of a functioning adrenal tumor on examination. Initial hormonal studies showed mildly elevated cortisol levels after an overnight 1-mg dexamethasone test, with plasma ACTH levels fluctuating at high values. To distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent cortisol secretion, she underwent a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test (2 mg orally every 6 hours for 2 days).

On the day after completing the test, she presented to the emergency department with rapidly progressive confusion and somnolence. There was no history of toxin or alcohol exposure. On neurologic examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 10. Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Serum ammonia, 289.5 μg/dL (normal, 18.7–54.5)  
• Alanine transaminase, 21 IU/L (≤33)  
• Creatinine, 0.6 mg/dL (0.6–1.1)  
• Blood urea nitrogen, 13 mg/dL (7–20)  

Brain MRI and head CT angiography were unremarkable. Electroencephalography demonstrated continuous generalized 2.5- to 3-Hz sharp-and-slow wave complexes with triphasic morphology.

A 41-year-old woman, gravida 6 at 32 weeks’ gestation, was admitted to the ICU with a 4-day history of recurrent vomiting that worsened over the prior 48 hours; the last two episodes were bloody. She denied fever, chills, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms and had no past medical or surgical history. She reported occasional alcohol use that continued during pregnancy. A urine toxicology screen was positive for cannabinoids. On examination, she was afebrile, appeared dehydrated, was tachycardic and tachypneic, and was normotensive. Initial laboratory studies showed: WBC 16,000/mm^3; arterial pH 7.162, PCO2 13 mm Hg, bicarbonate 5 mmol/L, anion gap 31; creatinine 1.4 mg/dL; lactate 1.4 mmol/L; urine positive for protein and acetone; serum acetone moderate; serum alcohol, salicylate, and acetaminophen levels undetectable; glucose 83 mg/dL; ammonia 49 mcg/dL; mild transaminitis; and normal CK. She developed worsening respiratory distress with Kussmaul breathing and mild hematemesis, requiring intubation. EGD revealed nonbleeding esophageal ulcerations. Blood and urine cultures and chest radiograph were negative for infection. She initially received normal saline, which was switched to 5% dextrose in lactated Ringer solution; thiamine and folic acid were administered. Fetal viability was confirmed by cardiotocography.

A patient was referred with a provisional diagnosis of primary eosinophilic enterocolitis. Initial evaluation revealed rectal bleeding and anemia. Colonoscopy showed terminal ileitis, and histology demonstrated active ileocolitis with eosinophilia. Enteric-release budesonide was started. Over the next six months, gastrointestinal symptoms worsened, and the patient developed widespread urticaria, anorectal itch, frequent nocturnal awakenings, and dyspnea. A follow-up colonoscopy again showed ileal and cecal erosions with a rich eosinophilic infiltrate. Laboratory studies revealed peripheral eosinophilia, elevated eosinophil cationic protein, and increased fecal calprotectin. “A coproparasitological examination on 3 samples and serology for Strongyloides stercoralis were negative.”

A 14-year-old Hispanic female presented with a two-week history of decreased vision, redness, and a central scotoma in her right eye. Two weeks before the onset of visual symptoms, she had fever, myalgias, headache, nuchal rigidity, nausea, and vomiting, which resolved two days after starting oseltamivir for presumed influenza. Her past medical and family history were noncontributory. 

On examination, visual acuity was 20/400 OD and 20/20 OS, with a 2+ relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye. Intraocular pressure, ocular motility, and confrontational visual fields were normal bilaterally. She identified 4/12 Hardy-Rand-Rittler color plates OD and 12/12 OS. Anterior segment examination showed bilateral trace anterior chamber cells and right conjunctival injection. Funduscopic exam of the right eye revealed a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.3 with hyperemia, subretinal edema, and 1+ vitreous cells; optical coherence tomography demonstrated subretinal fluid. The left eye had a 0.3 cup-to-disc ratio with hyperemia, macular striae, and 1+ vitreous cells. B-scan ultrasonography showed bilateral choroidal thickening (right > left) without a T-sign. Fluorescein angiography and indocyanine green chorioangiography revealed bilateral peripapillary hypofluorescence consistent with blocking and hyperfluorescence consistent with staining. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits was negative for optic nerve thickening or masses. Serologic studies showed a normal complete blood count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; negative tests for Borrelia burgdorferi, Bartonella henselae, Treponema pallidum, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, West Nile virus, HSV-1/HSV-2, HCMV, Cryptococcus neoformans, Neisseria meningitidis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Streptococcus species, Epstein-Barr virus, Listeria monocytogenes, HIV-1/2, and HLA-B27, HLA-A29, HLA-DR15; elevated Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM (1286) and IgG (777); and elevated C-reactive protein. Lumbar puncture revealed a normal opening pressure, no neutrophils, normal glucose, elevated protein (92 mg/dL), and CSF PCR was negative for Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

A 36-year-old Chinese woman with a history of atopic eczema presented with a 3-month history of skin blisters and scalp scaling that began 1 and 2 months, respectively, after she started an herbal medicine. Examination revealed pustular eruptions with peri-vesicular erythema and pustules over the trunk and proximal limbs, and pityriasis amiantacea–like scaling lesions over the midline scalp without alopecia. Anti–skin antibody serology was negative. A biopsy of a truncal blister showed predominantly subcorneal splitting, marked acantholysis, and a neutrophil-predominant infiltrate with occasional eosinophils; direct immunofluorescence was negative. The patient’s herbal medicine was discontinued, and she was treated with dapsone 50 mg daily, resulting in remission. Dapsone was tapered and stopped over 6 months, but 2 months later the vesicles and pustules recurred.

A 29-year-old Hispanic man with no prior medical history presented with 6 months of progressively worsening joint pain and swelling. On the day of presentation, he reported worsening left knee pain and swelling, new left elbow swelling, and purulent discharge from his right wrist, now accompanied by a scaly plaque-like lesion with skin breakdown over the wrist. He also noted scaly plaques over the left knee without breakdown. He had a 35 lb unintentional weight loss over 2 months. He denied recent travel but resided in Bakersfield, California, an area endemic for certain fungal infections.

Initial laboratory tests were notable for an erythrocyte sedimentation rate > 100 mm/h (consistent with prior value), C-reactive protein 19 mg/dL, hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, and platelet count 438 000/µL. Tests for HLA-B27, uric acid, rheumatoid factor, and anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide IgG were all within normal limits. Testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia by urine RNA was negative.

Radiographs of the left knee, left elbow, and right wrist demonstrated interval progression of osteopenia with erosive changes and sizeable joint effusions with soft-tissue swelling. Arthrocentesis of the left elbow yielded brown-colored synovial fluid with 520 000 total nucleated cells/mm³ (61% neutrophils) and no crystals; aspiration of the left knee produced orange-colored synovial fluid with 90 000 total nucleated cells/mm³ (93% neutrophils) and no crystals.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a one-day history of nausea, vomiting, seven episodes of diarrhoea with lower abdominal pain, and a two-week history of fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, and dry cough. She also noted paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, bilateral lower-limb and facial oedema, and subtle recent difficulties with concentration and memory. Her medical history was notable for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis treated with autologous stem cell transplantation three months earlier. 

On admission, temperature was 36.7 °C, blood pressure 160/95 mmHg, pulse 90 bpm, respiratory rate 24 bpm, and SpO2 97% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable except for mild non-pitting bilateral ankle oedema. 

Initial laboratory tests showed creatinine 142 µmol/L (baseline 80), eGFR 39 mL/min/1.73 m2, haemoglobin 90 g/L (baseline 103), platelet count 82×10^9/L (baseline 164), white cell count 6.5×10^9/L, normal liver-function and coagulation studies, and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 206.9 mg/mmol without dysmorphic erythrocytes or casts. High-resolution chest CT demonstrated multifocal consolidation in the right lower lobe. Extensive microbiological testing—including sputum, stool, blood cultures, CMV PCR, and bronchoalveolar lavage—was unrevealing.

By Day 4, haemoglobin had fallen to 70 g/L, platelets to 67×10^9/L, and the peripheral blood film showed fragmented erythrocytes. Haptoglobin was undetectable (< 0.08 g/L), LDH was elevated at 529 U/L, and the reticulocyte count was increased. On Day 13, a renal biopsy revealed mesangiolysis, glomerular and arteriolar fibrinoid necrosis, and capillary thrombi consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy.

A 52-year-old Chinese man presented with bilateral red eyes and itching for 1 year. The redness was constant with intermittent tearing, without pain, gritty sensation, photophobia, or discharge. He reported episodic blurred vision due to dry eye, relieved by lubricants. He denied diplopia. His medical history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia (all treated), and a chronic maculopapular rash on the chest and arms suggestive of atopy or eczema. He had no sinusitis, asthma, other autoimmune or dermatologic disorders, drug allergies, prior immunosuppression, ocular trauma or surgery, contact-lens wear, or family history of ocular or skin disease. He did not smoke.

On examination, vital signs were normal. He had a maculopapular rash over flexor and extensor surfaces of his elbows without excoriations. There were no rosacea-type or acneform facial lesions and no oral ulcers. Ocular examination showed bilateral moderate diffuse bulbar conjunctival hyperemia and grade 1 subtarsal papillary reaction. Each eye had an inferior symblepharon involving up to three clock hours and cicatrization of the caruncle. The inferior lacrimal punctum was scarred. There was no chemosis, scleral nodules, or ankyloblepharon.

Fluorescein staining revealed faint inferior punctate corneal staining in both eyes without epithelial defects, filaments, infiltrates, or edema. There were superficial inferonasal corneal scars in the right eye without thinning or vascularization. Corneal sensation was normal. Tear-breakup times were 4 seconds (right) and 5 seconds (left), and Schirmer I test values were 20 mm and 25 mm at 5 minutes, respectively. A few misdirected lower-eyelid lashes did not touch the cornea. Marx’s line showed mild advancement in the upper lids and borderline changes in the lower lids. Meibomian gland evaluation revealed no liquid meibum; manual expression yielded minimal viscous secretion from a single gland. Uncorrected visual acuity was 6/7.5 in each eye. Intraocular pressures were 17 mmHg (right) and 19 mmHg (left). Anterior chambers were deep and quiet, and the vitreous and posterior segments were unremarkable.

A clinical diagnosis of chronic cicatricial conjunctivitis was made.

A 40-year-old black man was referred for evaluation of a 6-month rise in plasma creatinine. Six months earlier, he had two emergency visits for severe abdominal and low back pain radiating to the hypogastrium, with nausea and vomiting. On the second visit, he also had gross hematuria. Urinary ultrasound showed bilateral nephrolithiasis with microcalculi in the right ureter and mild pelvicalyceal dilation; kidneys were normal in size but echogenic. A ureteral stone was passed spontaneously. He denied hypertension, diabetes, or known kidney disease.  
On referral, blood pressure was 160/110 mm Hg. Physical examination showed pallor, 4 cm hepatomegaly below the right costal margin, splenomegaly, and mild lower-limb edema; no peripheral lymphadenopathy. He reported polyuria, occasional fever, and 30 kg of unintentional weight loss over 6 months. He had taken NSAIDs chronically and underwent bilateral knee replacements 5 years earlier for a destructive arthropathy of unknown cause.  
Laboratory tests revealed elevated creatinine, severe hypercalcemia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated amylase, lipase, and alkaline phosphatase, plus urinalysis with nonnephrotic proteinuria, hematuria, leukocyturia, calcium oxalate crystals, and diuresis of 4–6 L/day. Serum PTH was low, calcidiol was normal, and there was marked hypercalciuria. Serum protein electrophoresis showed a polyclonal gamma-globulin peak; myelogram was normal.  
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated multiple retroperitoneal and iliac lymphadenopathy, heterogeneous hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, multiple nonobstructive renal microcalculi, and a normal pancreas.  
Given hypercalcemia with low PTH, lymphadenopathy, and systemic features, a neoplastic versus granulomatous process was considered.

MR is a male neonate born at 38 weeks’ gestation by elective cesarean delivery. Birth weight was 2350 g (5th–10th percentile), length 45 cm (5th percentile), head circumference 31 cm (<5th percentile). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes.  
Maternal history was notable only for immunity to rubella, negative toxoplasma serology, and a single CMV serology at 11 weeks (IgG positive, IgM negative). A maternal febrile episode occurred in the periconceptional period; there was no trauma, and no use of cocaine, warfarin, or anticonvulsants. No family history of bleeding disorders or stroke.  
Fetal ultrasound at 20 weeks suggested intracranial hemorrhage, confirmed by fetal MRI at 25 weeks, which showed a 2.3 cm porencephalic cyst in the right frontotemporal–insular region with ex vacuo enlargement of the right lateral ventricle, reduced right cerebral hemisphere volume, and abnormal micropolygyria of the right frontal cortex.  
At birth, examination revealed microcephaly, jaundice, micropurpura on the face and upper thorax, mild upper limb hypertonicity, and abnormal deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, assays of clotting factors (II, V, VII, IX, X, XI, XIII), protein C and S, von Willebrand factor, alpha-2 antiplasmin, antithrombin, APC resistance, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies, were all normal. Gene sequencing for MTHFR and factor V Leiden was wild type. Newborn metabolic screening was negative.  
Cranial ultrasound on day 1 showed a right porencephalic area with “ex vacuo” enlargement of the right lateral ventricle and a germinolytic cyst on the left; MRI confirmed these findings, with no vascular malformations or thrombosis.

A 30-year-old African American man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and end-stage renal disease due to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis underwent a 6-antigen–mismatched deceased‐donor kidney transplant 8 months ago. His baseline serum creatinine had been 1.8–1.9 mg/dL. Over the preceding week, he noted foul‐smelling, cloudy urine but denied dysuria, hematuria, fever, or chills. He self‐medicated with cranberry supplements, vitamin C, and over-the-counter phenazopyridine. His immunosuppression regimen consisted of extended‐release tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone; he admitted missing several doses of mycophenolate. 

On presentation, vital signs were stable. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed a serum creatinine of 9.86 mg/dL (baseline 1.8 mg/dL), blood urea nitrogen 125 mg/dL, potassium 3.5 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 19 mEq/L. The total leukocyte count was 9700 cells/μL. Urinalysis revealed cloudy urine, bacteriuria, leukocyturia, hematuria, proteinuria (50 mg/dL), nitrites, and leukocyte esterase. Prostate‐specific antigen was 0.06 ng/dL. 

Tacrolimus trough was slightly elevated at 11.3 ng/mL and the dose was adjusted. Donor‐specific antibodies were negative. BK virus PCR in plasma and blood cultures were negative. Ultrasound of the transplanted kidney showed no nephrolithiasis, hydronephrosis, or renal‐artery stenosis. Empiric ceftriaxone was initiated for presumed urinary tract infection. 

Despite three days of antibiotics, creatinine remained markedly elevated, prompting an allograft biopsy.

A healthy 33-year-old primiparous woman underwent an elective cesarean section at 37 weeks’ gestation under spinal anesthesia. A single dural puncture was performed at L3–L4 with a 25-gauge Quincke needle, and 8 mg of 0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine was injected intrathecally. The surgery was uneventful, with blood pressure between 90/58 and 140/70 mm Hg, pulse between 80 and 90 beats/min, and oxygen saturation of 98–100%. Forty-five minutes postoperatively, she complained of new-onset neck stiffness and a constant, tightening headache described as “heavy in her head.” The headache was nonpulsatile, unchanged by position, and unaccompanied by tinnitus, hearing loss, photophobia, nausea, or vomiting. Blood pressure fluctuated between 130/65 and 170/98 mm Hg. On postoperative day 1, she was diagnosed with postdural puncture headache and received a 15 ml epidural blood patch at the puncture site; a second patch was performed the following day. Her headache lessened but persisted, and she was discharged on postoperative day 6 with scheduled follow-up.

A previously healthy 27-year-old woman experienced a witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest while at work. Emergency medical services found her in ventricular fibrillation; after multiple defibrillations and infusions of amiodarone and epinephrine, return of spontaneous circulation was achieved 15 minutes later. On arrival at the hospital, the electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm at 100 beats per minute with short-coupled premature ventricular contractions. Laboratory studies revealed hypokalemia and lactic acidosis. Coronary angiography showed no obstructive disease. Shortly after transfer to the intensive care unit, she developed recurrent ventricular fibrillation that was refractory to magnesium, amiodarone, lidocaine, and esmolol. She was placed on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and therapeutic hypothermia was initiated at 33°C. Despite more than 20 unsuccessful cardioversion attempts over an 8-hour period, she remained in ventricular fibrillation.

A 24-year-old pregnant woman (G2P1) was referred at 8 weeks’ gestation for evaluation of bilateral pelvic cysts. Her history was notable for two prior open ovarian cystectomies, one for a mature cystic teratoma and one for a mucinous cystadenoma. Transvaginal ultrasound and pelvic MRI showed a unilocular left cyst measuring 9 cm and a multilocular right cyst measuring 5 cm. Serum tumor markers (CA-125, CA19-9, and CEA) were within normal limits for pregnancy. At 14 weeks, an attempt at cyst resection was converted to laparotomy because of dense adhesions around the cysts and posterior uterus; no metastatic lesions or lymphadenopathy were found, and peritoneal fluid cytology was negative for malignancy. At 32 weeks, repeat MRI demonstrated that the left cyst had enlarged to 27 cm and appeared to merge with the right cyst, forming a single large pelvic cyst without any solid components or papillary projections. Tumor markers remained normal. Given the remaining uncertainty about malignancy and the risks of preterm delivery with relaparotomy, the team elected to defer surgical intervention until term.

A 57-year-old man with a history of cocaine, phencyclidine, and opioid abuse; hepatitis C; and schizoaffective disorder was found down in a prone position in respiratory distress for an unknown duration. He was intubated on arrival and admitted with acute encephalopathy and acute hypoxic respiratory failure secondary to drug overdose, as well as multilobular aspiration pneumonia.  
One day after admission, dermatology was consulted for multiple fluid-filled lesions on the lower extremities that had been present on admission and were thought to be suspicious for Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis. On examination, there were well-defined, tense bullae with nonblanching stellate plaques and erosions on both knees. No other skin surfaces, including genital or mucosal areas, were affected, and the Nikolsky sign was negative.  
Laboratory studies showed a positive urine toxicology screen for opioids, cocaine, and phencyclidine; creatine phosphokinase 5598 mcg/L; creatinine 4.49 mg/dL; platelets 139 K/µL; and aspartate aminotransferase 202 IU/L.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A 61-year-old Norwegian man was referred for evaluation of presumed Parkinson’s disease. He first noted frequent leg fasciculations at age 48. Neurophysiology at that time showed a mild sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. At age 51, bilateral Babinski signs were present, and over the next decade he developed mild tetraspasticity, symmetrical hyperreflexia, muscle stiffness, gait difficulty, and unsteadiness, yet remained able to run and hike. At age 57, he developed asymmetric bradykinesia and rigidity. He had an excellent response to levodopa, returned to near-normal function, remained fully ambulatory, and worked full time. His father had levodopa-responsive Parkinson’s disease; there was no family history of myelopathy or adrenal disease. On examination, his Spastic Paraplegia Rating Scale score was 4/52 and his Expanded Disability Status Scale score was 3.0. 

Investigations at age 61 included:  
• CSF with normal cell count and protein, no oligoclonal bands  
• MRI of brain and spinal cord with no demyelination, Loes score 0  
• Brain DaTscan showing asymmetrically reduced basal ganglia uptake consistent with Parkinson’s disease  
• Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showing moderate predominantly axonal sensorimotor neuropathy of the lower extremities  
• Skin biopsy with reduced intraepidermal nerve-fiber density  
• Endocrine studies including cortisol and ACTH stimulation test within normal limits  
• Serum very long-chain fatty acids elevated (C26:0 1.02 mg/L; C26:0/C22:0 ratio 0.058)  
• ABCD1 gene sequencing demonstrating a previously unreported missense variant of uncertain significance

A 26-year-old woman with high myopia (spherical equivalent −10.0 diopters in both eyes) was referred for sudden onset of decreased vision and a central scotoma in the right eye. She denied recent trauma or a Valsalva maneuver. Her medical history was notable only for panic disorder treated with alprazolam and escitalopram; routine blood tests two months earlier were normal. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/100 OD and 20/20 OS.

Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a stellate intraretinal hemorrhage in the fovea with a petaloid pattern and feathery edges, suggesting localization within Henle’s fiber layer. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the right eye showed an elevated hyperreflective lesion in the outer retina with shadowing of the underlying retinal pigment epithelium and adjacent intraretinal fluid within the outer plexiform layer.

A 72-year-old man with a history of abdominal aortic aneurysm presented to the emergency department two days after endovascular aneurysm repair with a stent graft. He reported persistent right flank, right lower abdominal, and right testicular pain since surgery. He was discharged less than 24 hours earlier on a bowel regimen and pain medications. Despite regular bowel movements and analgesia, the pain continued. He denied fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, dysuria, hematuria, or diarrhea.

On examination, vital signs were normal. The right testicle was exquisitely tender on palpation, in normal vertical alignment, and had an intact cremasteric reflex bilaterally; testicular elevation did not relieve pain. The abdomen was mildly distended with diffuse tenderness worse on the right, without peritoneal signs or costovertebral angle tenderness. Femoral and dorsalis pedis pulses were present and symmetric.

Scrotal ultrasonography showed a mildly enlarged right testicle with decreased echogenicity and decreased blood flow compared to the left, raising concern for infarction; intermittent torsion was considered less likely. A computed tomographic angiogram of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated status post aortobi-iliac endograft without endoleak and no new aneurysm changes. On closer review, the right limb of the stent graft extended above the origin of the right hypogastric artery, although the hypogastric artery itself remained widely patent.

A 14-month-old infant presented with a 15-day history of seizures, asthenia, and hypotonia without fever. There was no history of delivery complications or neurodevelopmental disorders. On examination, there were no sensory or motor deficits, no cranial nerve involvement, and no signs of meningitis. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 17 mg/L (normal < 6 mg/L) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 22 mm/h (normal 3–13 mm/h). The infant had no respiratory symptoms; chest radiography was normal despite a paternal history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis. Brain MRI revealed multiple diffuse punctate lesions in the white and gray matter, predominating in the posterior cerebral fossa and brainstem. The lesions were hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, appeared as solid enhancing nodules surrounded by edema, contained central calcifications, and were associated with moderate hydrocephalus. There was no leptomeningeal enhancement.

A 40-year-old woman was evaluated for chronic, progressive ulcerations and disfigurement of her face. Her medical history included migraine with aura, celiac disease, cephalosporin intolerance, and nickel allergy. In 1996, she underwent a Le Fort I osteotomy with bilateral placement of metal “L” plates and wires for correction of malocclusion; her postoperative course was unremarkable. Over the subsequent years, she reported worsening migraines and photophobia. 

In 2004, she developed a painless but intensely pruritic rash on the right side of her face, involving the forehead, nose, and upper and lower jaw, accompanied by paresthesia in the trigeminal distribution. These lesions progressed to ulcerations that caused severe disfigurement on the right; similar but less severe ulcers appeared on the left. Notably, the tip of her nose remained intact. Dermatologic evaluation demonstrated allergy to nickel, and the plates and wires were removed in 2005. 

Instrumental studies, including skin biopsies, were negative for human herpes virus, autoimmune vascular and connective diseases, leprosy, granulomatosis, and skin cancer. Neurologic examination revealed no clinically evident deficits.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of left forefoot pain and swelling, initially diagnosed as Morton’s disease without improvement. She had no family history of rheumatoid arthritis. Three years after symptom onset, she was referred for progressive foot deformity, subcutaneous hemorrhage, and evidence of bone erosion on radiographs. On examination, there was pain and swelling over the fourth metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint; active range of motion was 0° of extension and 30° of flexion with pain on motion. Laboratory tests showed a negative C-reactive protein result, a rheumatoid factor of 29.3 IU/mL, and an anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody level of 496.6 IU/mL; she met classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis with a score of 6 points. Plain radiographs demonstrated bone erosion of the metatarsal head. MRI (axial T1-weighted fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced images) revealed synovial proliferation and fluid around the third and fourth metatarsals. Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs were not started due to diagnostic uncertainty; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs provided no relief. Given persistent pain from lateral dislocation of the proximal phalanx, synovectomy was planned for both diagnostic confirmation and symptom relief.

A 70-year-old woman reported a 3-year history of increasing salivation, slurred speech, dysphagia, macroglossia, and decreased taste. She described frequent choking with meals and food regurgitation. Over the same period, she noted progressive lower-extremity weakness without falls or gait instability. She denied other neurological, gastrointestinal, or sensory symptoms.

Her medical history included gastroesophageal reflux disease on omeprazole, breast adenocarcinoma treated by mastectomy and tamoxifen, and idiopathic right hemidiaphragmatic paralysis. Surgical history also included sacral colpopexy, hysterectomy, and right carpal tunnel release.

Initial evaluation elsewhere included brain MRI, which was negative for vascular abnormalities or ischemia. Myasthenia gravis was suspected; acetylcholine receptor–binding antibodies were negative, and she did not improve with pyridostigmine or intravenous immunoglobulin. Lumbar puncture yielded normal results.

On examination at our institution, her tongue was enlarged with moderate-to-severe weakness and rightward deviation. Neck flexor and extensor strength was normal. In the upper extremities, there was mild-to-moderate weakness of external rotators and pectoral muscles, mild deltoid and biceps weakness with spared triceps and brachioradialis, and slight interossei and hypothenar weakness. In the lower extremities, iliopsoas strength was moderately reduced, gluteus medius was moderately-severely weak (right more than left), and quadriceps, hamstrings, calves, and tibialis anterior were normal. She rose from a chair without support, walked with an asymmetric waddling gait, and could walk on her toes. Reflexes were +1 at the ankles and normal elsewhere. There was no myotonia.

Electromyography showed a myotonic myopathy with electrophysiological features supportive of inflammation, fiber splitting, vacuolization, and/or myonecrosis. Laboratory studies revealed normal blood counts, ferritin, folate, vitamin B₁₂, electrolytes, creatinine clearance, and liver function tests. Serum and urine electrophoresis with immunofixation and plasma cell immunophenotyping were negative for monoclonal disease. Creatine kinase was 242 U/L (38–176), lactate dehydrogenase 297 U/L (122–222), and aldolase 8.5 U/L (<7.7). Beta-2-microglobulin was normal.

CT and MRI of the head and neck demonstrated a soft-tissue nodule at the base of the tongue with diffuse fatty infiltration and age-related cerebral white matter atrophy. Pulmonary function tests showed mild-to-moderate restriction with reduced total lung capacity. Overnight pulse oximetry revealed gas exchange abnormalities and sleep-disordered breathing. Echocardiography showed normal left ventricular size, septal thickness, and an ejection fraction of 66%, with no evidence of cardiac amyloid.

After evaluation by hematology and otolaryngology, a tongue biopsy was planned to evaluate the macroglossia.

A 17-year-old girl with Down’s syndrome and hypothyroidism was referred for evaluation of refractory constipation. She had recurrent constipation since early childhood, managed intermittently with dietary measures, enemas, and laxatives. She passed stool every 2–3 days in early childhood, with intervals gradually increasing to 5–6 days, and in recent years required enemas or laxatives to stool. She did not pass stool for 9 days prior to referral. 

She weighed 35 kg and was 134 cm tall. Examination revealed typical features of Down’s syndrome. The abdomen was mildly distended and loaded with fecal matter. 

An abdominopelvic ultrasound showed no presacral mass or other abnormalities. A barium enema demonstrated a dilated colon and the lower end of the rectum ending in a high, beak-like narrowing.

A 60-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and sarcoidosis fell at home and lay immobilized on the floor for 2 days before being found. On arrival she was tachycardic and hypotensive. Laboratory studies showed a leukocytosis of 39.44 K/μL, lactate 3.4 mmol/L, creatinine 2.65 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 55 mmol/L, and creatine kinase 527 IU/L. She was treated empirically for sepsis with vancomycin and ceftriaxone, received copious IV fluids for presumed rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury, and blood and urine cultures remained negative. Over the next several days she developed generalized edema. Seven days after admission she noted superficial skin sloughing beginning on the lower extremities, which progressed to involve the trunk, upper extremities, and head and neck. Physical examination revealed superficial desquamation of nearly the entire body with one focal erosion on the forearm, sloughing of the facial skin and oral mucosa, and bilateral conjunctival injection. Nikolsky sign was negative, and the patient reported pain of the skin and mucosa.

A 47-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a non-painful swelling of the left cheek/preauricular region that developed over several weeks. She denied trauma, discharge, redness, or warmth. Her medical and family history were unremarkable. On examination, there was a firm mass causing facial asymmetry; intraoral inspection showed no dental pathology and salivary flow was normal. Because the site and origin of the lesion were uncertain, a CT scan was obtained. Imaging revealed a well-circumscribed lesion confined to the left mandibular condyle, measuring 32 × 23 × 29 mm, with partial lytic changes but no evidence of cortical breach or destructive effects on adjacent structures. The lesion had a benign appearance, but the diagnosis remained unclear. An incisional biopsy was then performed.

An eighteen-year-old previously healthy man was admitted with worsening chest pain, cough, and dyspnea. Chest CT showed bilateral cavitary lesions without mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy and no pleural effusion; there was no pulmonary artery or cardiac filling defect. Examination revealed no signs of jugular or subclavian vein thrombosis. Blood cultures grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, likely from a draining pilonidal cyst. Studies for bacterial endocarditis and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative. No other embolic or mass-like lesions were identified in the abdomen or brain. After twelve days of antibiotic therapy, repeat chest imaging demonstrated more diffuse cavitary lesions and a new left-sided loculated pleural effusion. Laboratory evaluation revealed worsening peripheral eosinophilia. Thoracentesis yielded approximately 300 mL of milky fluid mixed with blood. Pleural fluid analysis showed 81 111 red cells/µL, 444 white cells/µL with 65% neutrophils, pH 8.0, lactate dehydrogenase 659 IU/L, protein 6 g/dL, and glucose 28 mg/dL. The pleural fluid/serum LDH ratio was 4.2 and the fluid/serum protein ratio was 1.0, consistent with an exudative effusion. There was no microbiologic growth on pleural fluid culture.

A 40-year-old woman with prediabetes, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and a history of cluster headaches was seen 8 weeks after starting a ketogenic diet when she developed sudden severe abdominal pain and fevers. Laboratory tests at presentation showed total bilirubin 5.1 mg/dL, AST 462 IU/L, ALT 875 IU/L, and ALP 162 IU/L. A viral hepatitis panel and evaluations for Wilson’s disease and α₁-antitrypsin deficiency were negative. Serologic tests for ANA, ASMA, and AMA were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis and MRCP showed only mild periportal edema without biliary dilation or obstruction; the liver, spleen, gallbladder, and pancreas were unremarkable. A liver biopsy was performed, revealing two cores with mildly expanded portal tracts containing histiocytes, lymphocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils, and few plasma cells. Interlobular bile ducts showed epithelial disarray, nuclear hyperchromasia, and lymphocytic infiltration; some ducts were encased by vaguely formed granulomas. A few portal veins exhibited endotheliitis, and small poorly formed lobular granulomas were present. There was scattered hepatocyte ballooning, no fibrosis, and negative iron and copper stains. Given the combination of cholestatic liver chemistry, duct injury, and granulomas, autoimmune hepatitis–PBC overlap and AMA-negative PBC were considered, and histologically AMA-negative PBC was favored.

A 74-year-old woman with newly diagnosed hypertension presented with one day of left-sided body weakness and dizziness. She was conscious and denied speech slurring, abnormal movements, or incontinence. She had a transient right facial deviation earlier that resolved. She smoked 10 cigarettes daily for 50 years and drank locally made alcohol daily. She was on no medications.

On examination, blood pressure was 150/100 mm Hg. The right eye was down-and-out with ptosis, vertical nystagmus, and a mid-dilated nonreactive pupil; visual acuity was normal. The left eye was normal. There was no facial asymmetry. Neurologic examination revealed an extensor plantar response and reduced strength in the left limbs, with gait instability. On the second hospital day, a left-sided intention ataxia (impaired finger-to-nose) emerged; rapid alternating movements were normal. On the third day, a coarse resting tremor of the left hand was noted, which worsened with posture and action. Tone, bulk, higher mental status, and sensation were normal.

Electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, and routine blood tests were unremarkable except for elevated hemoglobin of 17.2 g/dL. Noncontrast head CT was normal. Brain MRI showed a 10×7 mm focus of restricted diffusion in the right paramedian midbrain (hyperintense on DWI, hypointense on ADC) involving the red nucleus and extending to the cerebral peduncle, and a separate late subacute infarct in the posteroinferior–medial right temporal lobe. Bilateral cerebellar white matter ischemic changes were also noted.

A 28‐year‐old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 2‐year history of left hip pain on walking, which had worsened over the past few months. She denied fever, chills, weight loss, or recent trauma. On examination, left hip range of motion was limited and painful, and there was a poorly defined, renitent, 4‐cm swelling in the left groin without overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13 g/dL, eosinophils 800/µL, and C‐reactive protein 56 mg/L. A pelvic radiograph revealed a mildly expansile lytic lesion in the periacetabular region of the left iliac bone with scalloped medial wing erosion and scattered hyperdense foci suggesting intrapelvic extension; the femoral head and neck were intact. Contrast‐enhanced pelvic CT confirmed a multiloculated, expansile lytic process of the left acetabulum and ilium with a honeycomb appearance, peripheral enhancement, calcifications, cortical destruction, periosteal reaction, adjacent muscle infiltration, and a communicating subcutaneous collection; the sacroiliac joint and femoral head were preserved. MRI demonstrated multiple small hyperintense T2‐weighted cystic areas in the iliac wing and supraacetabular soft tissues, heterogenous signal in the proximal femur without bone invasion, and no sacroiliac or sacral involvement.

A 75-year-old man presented 4 days after the sudden onset of a severe frontal headache. He reported no nausea, vomiting, or photophobia. His medical history included atrial fibrillation, bronchiectasis, lumbar stenosis, previous cerebral infarction, and ischemic heart disease; his medications included aspirin, ramipril, doxazosin, bisoprolol, simvastatin, and topical latanoprost.

On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15, temperature 38°C, and blood pressure 135/85 mmHg. He had mild neck stiffness; cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurological examinations were otherwise unremarkable. A provisional diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage was made.

A noncontrast CT scan of the brain showed a pituitary macroadenoma but was initially reported as showing no hemorrhage. Lumbar puncture revealed a CSF protein of 1.44 g/L (reference range 0.15–0.45), glucose 4.8 mmol/L (2.2–3.9), no organisms on gram stain, and xanthochromia; based on these findings, SAH was presumed.

The following morning, his Glasgow Coma Scale fell to 13 and blood pressure dropped to 66/46 mmHg. Laboratory tests showed a sodium of 131 mmol/L and a normal potassium. Review of the CT scan by a neuroradiologist identified hemorrhage within the pituitary macroadenoma, and the patient was treated with intravenous hydrocortisone for presumed adrenal insufficiency.

CT angiography was then performed, confirming the pituitary macroadenoma but showing no intracranial aneurysm.

A 13-year-old girl was referred for dental evaluation at a specialized pediatric dentistry clinic, accompanied by her mother. On examination, she had a small face with a prominent brow, exophthalmos, micrognathia, and cranial hyperostosis. Musculoskeletal findings included short upper limbs, pronounced bowing of the long bones (humerus and tibias), metaphyseal thickening, genu valgum, shortening of the distal phalanges, a narrow pelvis and shoulders, tapering and irregular ribs, elongation of the vertebral bodies, and kyphoscoliosis.

Intraorally, she exhibited poor tooth alignment with maxillary crowding and an anterior deep bite.
