A panoramic radiograph showed hypoplastic coronoid processes of the mandible, ossification of the left stylohyoid ligament, agenesis of the second maxillary right premolar (tooth 15), retention of primary teeth 65 and 85, and impaction of teeth 33, 37, 43, and 46 with semi-impaction of tooth 36. Cephalometric analysis demonstrated disproportion between the effective lengths of the maxilla and mandible, with the mandible being underdeveloped relative to the maxilla.

A 75-year-old Caucasian man with a five-year history of tophaceous gout and recurrent arthritis presented with a large, painful, ulcerated nodule over the first metatarsophalangeal joint of the left foot. Four months earlier he had stopped allopurinol therapy; he denied recent diet changes, alcohol use, or diuretics. Five days before admission the lesion became red, swollen, and painful; NSAIDs provided no relief. Ten hours before presentation the nodule burst, discharging viscous, chalky material. On exam, temperature was 37.8 °C. A greyish, ulcerated, voluminous nodule containing chalky material was seen at the first metatarsophalangeal joint of the left foot. Multiple other firm nodules were noted over metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints of both hands, wrists, elbows, ankles, and heels; two smaller ulcerated nodules were present on the left thumb tip and right first interphalangeal joint. Many joints were deformed, and the left great toe was nonfunctional.  
Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis of 14 524/mm3, C-reactive protein 7.21 mg/dl, and serum uric acid 14 mg/dl. Radiographs of the foot revealed soft-tissue swelling and total destruction of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Cultures of material from the ulcerated tophus were negative.

A 56-year-old woman presented with intermittent hemoptysis. Examination was notable only for mild hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 90 mm/h; all other tests were unremarkable. Chest radiography and CT revealed a spiculated 2.5 cm lesion in the left lower lobe. Ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy of the lung mass demonstrated moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. Contrast-free thoracic CT also showed a few necrotic mediastinal lymph nodes without calcification and mild hepatomegaly without focal lesions. For staging, 18F-FDG PET/CT showed intense uptake in the lung lesion and mediastinal lymph nodes; the enlarged liver exhibited markedly increased FDG uptake with suppression of normal background activity (“hot liver”), while renal and cerebral uptake were relatively less intense. Given the known lung primary and PET findings, concern was raised for stage IV disease with hepatic metastases, and an ultrasound-guided biopsy of a heterogeneous area in the right hepatic lobe was performed.

A previously healthy five-month-old male twin presented with sudden-onset respiratory distress. On arrival: heart rate 150/min, blood pressure 80/47 mm Hg, respiratory rate 50/min, oxygen saturation 70% on room air, temperature 36 °C. He appeared cyanotic, lethargic, and dehydrated with dry mucous membranes. Respiratory exam revealed tachypnea with subcostal retractions and faint expiratory wheezing. Cardiac auscultation revealed no audible murmurs. He was initially suspected to have acute respiratory failure due to severe bronchiolitis in the setting of the early COVID-19 pandemic. Oxygen was administered via a non-rebreather mask, and broad-spectrum antibiotics and intravenous fluids were given for presumed sepsis. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 10.6×10^3/mm^3 with lymphocytic predominance, hemoglobin 20.4 g/dL, creatinine 0.4 mg/dL, and lactate 12.5 mmol/L; a COVID-19 PCR test was negative. Chest radiography was technically limited but demonstrated diffuse prominent interstitial markings concerning for viral pneumonia. After initial resuscitation the patient’s responsiveness improved but he remained hypoxic (SpO2 76%) with ongoing respiratory distress despite high-flow nasal cannula (9 L/min at 70% FiO2). Given persistent hypoxia and cyanosis, cardiac point-of-care ultrasound was performed and was notable for right ventricular hypertrophy raising suspicion for right ventricular outflow tract obstruction suggestive of congenital heart disease.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of painless swelling of her right middle finger, left middle finger, and right second toe. She denied fevers, weight loss, skin rashes, joint pain, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, the affected digits were diffusely swollen with a “sausage” appearance, and there was no erythema or warmth. Radiographs of the hands and right foot showed bilateral, symmetric, multilocular lytic lesions of the middle phalanges of the third fingers and the proximal phalanx of the right second toe. The lesions exhibited thickened trabeculae forming a lace-like (honeycomb) pattern, a geode-like cystic area in the right middle phalanx, radial-side cortical scalloping, and adjacent soft-tissue swelling.

An 18-year-old Japanese man presented with a 4-day history of fever, neck pain, and painful swallowing. He had a history of incomplete Kawasaki disease at 20 months of age (persistent fever, polymorphous exanthema, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and fingertip desquamation), for which he received neither aspirin nor intravenous immunoglobulin. Follow-up coronary CT angiography at age 14 was normal, and pediatric care was discontinued.

On admission: temperature 40.2℃, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 116/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination showed oral and pharyngeal mucositis and bilateral erythematous cervical lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies revealed: white blood cell count 16,000/μL (89.6% neutrophils), C-reactive protein 26.36 mg/dL, procalcitonin 1.52 ng/mL, soluble interleukin-2 receptor 1,286 U/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 66 mm/h; blood chemistries were otherwise unremarkable. Serologic tests for adenovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, rubella, measles, HIV, and parvovirus B19 were negative. Antistreptolysin O titer and rapid group A streptococcal antigen were negative, and two sets of blood cultures showed no growth.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated multiple cervical lymphadenopathy and a low-density area without ring enhancement in the retropharyngeal space. Intravenous antibiotics were administered without clinical improvement.

A 62-year-old man was evaluated for a 1-month history of a nonhealing ulcer on his lower lip. He reported that the lesion began as an inflammatory papule and gradually transformed into an ulcer with elevated borders and serous exudate. Outpatient treatment with cephalexin and acyclovir yielded no improvement. He denied any history of physical or chemical injury. His medical history was notable only for a psychiatric disorder treated with sertraline; he did not smoke or use illicit drugs.

On examination, he had a painless, indurated, oval ulcer on the central lower lip measuring 2.0 × 1.2 cm, with elevated borders, a fibrinous base, and adjacent desquamation of the vermilion border. Oral hygiene was poor, but there was no lymphadenopathy.

Routine laboratory results were within normal limits. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays for HSV-1 and HSV-2 and a rapid plasma reagin test for syphilis were negative.

A 36-year-old Ghanaian woman (BMI 32 kg/m2, G1P0) conceived via IVF presented with 6 hours of sudden-onset severe lower abdominal pain and one episode of vomiting. Six weeks earlier she had undergone transfer of two blastocysts; a scan 2 weeks ago confirmed a singleton intrauterine gestational sac. She had a 5-year history of infertility, PCOS, one failed IUI, one prior failed IVF, and no history of ectopic pregnancy, PID, or IUD use.

On examination she appeared moderately pale and distressed. Pulse was 96 beats/minute, blood pressure 103/73 mmHg. The abdomen was distended with left lower-quadrant tenderness and guarding. Bowel sounds were normal. An initial diagnosis of possible left ovarian torsion was made. Intravenous access was obtained and blood was drawn for complete blood count and serum β-hCG; crystalloid infusion was started.

Bedside transabdominal ultrasound revealed a slightly bulky uterus with a 15.6 mm empty intrauterine gestational sac (no fetal pole), approximately 130 mL of organized hematoma in the pouch of Douglas, and about 190 mL of free fluid in the right paracolic gutter. Over the next 10 minutes the patient became lethargic, tachycardic at 108 beats/minute, and hypotensive with an unrecordable blood pressure. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL, platelet count of 89 × 10^9/L, and β-hCG of 58 121 mIU/mL.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 7-day history of watery diarrhea, fever, and myalgia, followed by acute-onset bilateral ptosis, diplopia, slurred speech, and difficulty swallowing. He noted an unpleasant tongue sensation, impaired lateral tongue movement, loss of bitter and sour taste, and absent gag reflex. On examination, he had bilateral internal strabismus with vertical diplopia, symmetrical facial weakness, marked impairment of mastication and deglutition, palatal palsy, aphonia, and diminished hearing. Strength of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles was reduced, but gait was normal and tendon reflexes were preserved. There was no limb weakness, spasticity, sensory loss, ataxia, or autonomic dysfunction. He was alert and cognitively intact. Brain magnetic resonance imaging was normal.

A 44-year-old man with a 20-year history of paranoid schizophrenia was admitted under crisis due to relapse after poor compliance with oral and injectable antipsychotics. His cardiac, metabolic, and renal baselines were normal. He was started on clozapine 12.5 mg once daily, with planned up-titration by 25 mg per day beginning on day 3.  

On day 2 (25 mg total), he developed dizziness, hypotension, and tachycardia. Over the next week he became more withdrawn, thought-disordered, and drooling. He remained intermittently tachycardic, with other vital signs normal and temperature consistently <38 °C.  

By day 10 (175 mg total), he exhibited mild truncal rigidity, diaphoresis, worsened mental status, and a heart rate up to 135 beats/min. He suffered facial bruises after running into a door in confusion. Clozapine was discontinued; an initial CK level was 651 U/L and attributed to trauma. After transfer back to psychiatry, clozapine was restarted at 25 mg daily. A repeat CK on the same evening was 1757 U/L. A multidisciplinary team permanently stopped clozapine and transferred him to medicine for intravenous fluid hydration.  

Investigations on transfer included:  
• CT of the head: normal  
• White-cell count: normal  
• Troponin: normal  
• Chest examination and chest X-ray: normal  
• Abdominal examination: normal  
• ECG: sinus tachycardia, QTc 432 msec  
• Lactate: normal  
• Renal function: normal  
• Blood cultures: no growth  
• Lumbar puncture: normal

A 24-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with 6 months of fatigue and exertional palpitations and 8 days of chest pain. On examination, peripheral pulses were bounding and collapsing, and prominent carotid pulsations (Corrigan’s sign) were noted. Blood pressure was 110/40 mmHg in both arms. The cardiac apex was displaced laterally and hyperdynamic. A palpable diastolic thrill was present in the left parasternal area, and a high-pitched, loud pan-diastolic murmur was heard best at the left parasternal border when sitting and leaning forward.  
Electrocardiography showed left bundle branch block, left-axis deviation, left ventricular enlargement, and Q waves in the lateral leads, consistent with volume overload. A chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly with a left ventricular-type apex.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated left ventricle with severe systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction 20%) and global hypokinesia. In the parasternal long-axis view with color Doppler, there was a diastolic jet arising from the aortic root that dissected into a tract within the interventricular septum and entered the left ventricle. The parasternal short-axis view showed a multilobulated aneurysmal sac impinging on the lateral wall of the left ventricle and opening into its cavity. Continuous-wave Doppler measured a diastolic regurgitant jet from the aorta to the left ventricle with a pressure half-time of 179 ms, indicating severe aortic regurgitation.

A 25-year-old never-smoking office worker with known severe eosinophilic asthma presented with 2 days of progressive coryzal symptoms, dry cough, and dyspnea. He experienced acute pleuritic chest and neck pain immediately following an episode of coughing. He reported no recent trauma, procedures, recreational drug use, or occupational inhalant exposures. His asthma regimen consisted of twice-daily high-dose inhaled corticosteroid–long-acting β₂-agonist therapy and monthly mepolizumab, with good compliance; he used salbutamol about five times daily but had not needed oral corticosteroids in the preceding year. He had never required invasive ventilation, and his most recent outpatient spirometry and TLCO were normal.

On presentation, he was tachycardic and tachypneic and required 2 L of supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula to maintain an oxygen saturation of 96%. Physical examination revealed a widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze and palpable subcutaneous emphysema over the chest wall; he was afebrile and had no neurological deficits. Initial blood tests (drawn after prehospital intravenous dexamethasone) showed mild neutrophilia, an eosinophil count of 0.0 ×10^9/L, and a C-reactive protein level of 23.9 mg/L. A venous blood gas demonstrated mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis with a lactate level of 1.9 mmol/L. Nasal swab PCR was positive for rhinovirus/enterovirus and negative for SARS-CoV-2. 

A chest radiograph revealed extensive pneumomediastinum and chest wall and neck subcutaneous emphysema. To assess for possible esophageal rupture, contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and neck was performed and confirmed large-volume pneumomediastinum extending throughout the soft tissues of the neck and upper chest wall and demonstrated air within the lower cervical spinal canal. No injury to the oesophagus or throat was identified, and there was no pneumothorax.

A 30-year-old man suddenly collapsed at mile 17 of a marathon. Bystanders initiated CPR for approximately 10 minutes until emergency medical services arrived; he regained spontaneous circulation and was intubated due to a Glasgow Coma Scale of 4. On admission, he had generalized tonic–clonic seizures that resolved with benzodiazepine.  

He had a history of anxiety-related palpitations since childhood and recurrent left shoulder dislocations but no prior chest pain, cardiac disease, or family history of sudden death. He trained 5 days per week, up to 19 miles, and had one episode of dizziness without syncope at 12 miles a month earlier. He denied smoking or drug use.  

Initial investigations included:  
- Cranial and cervical CT scans, CT angiography of cerebral arteries, spine radiographs, and brain MRI: no acute structural lesions.  
- Toxicology: negative.  
- ECG: sinus rhythm at 69 bpm, no ST–T changes.  
- Cardiac biomarkers: high-sensitivity troponin T 0.115 ng/mL (normal <0.014), CK 328 U/L (24–204), myoglobin 212 μg/L (28–72).  
- Electrolytes and metabolic panel: normal.  
- Transthoracic echocardiogram: normal systolic and diastolic function, normal chambers, no valvular or pericardial abnormalities.  

He was extubated on day 2. Continuous telemetry showed no arrhythmias. An EEG demonstrated normal baseline activity without epileptic discharges. A repeat head CT on day 10 remained normal.

A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes was referred for evaluation of non-resolving pneumonia. Over three weeks he had received amoxicillin–clavulanate plus azithromycin followed by piperacillin–tazobactam without improvement. High-resolution CT of the thorax showed bilateral lower-lobe consolidation and a small pleural collection. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed bilateral pleural effusions, minimal lower-lobe infiltrates, and a paraoesophageal fluid collection with thickened oesophageal wall. On further questioning, he admitted to progressive dysphagia to solids for two months. PET-CT showed diffuse fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the oesophageal wall and at the gastro-oesophageal junction. A working diagnosis of oesophageal carcinoma with possible tracheo-oesophageal fistula was made. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrated multiple mucosal sinus tracts 3–7 mm in diameter with overlying plaques but no mass lesion or evidence of fistula.

A 30-year-old Caucasian man with a history of end-stage renal disease from childhood meningococcal septicaemia received a live-donor kidney transplant 2 years ago. Four months after transplantation, a rise in creatinine prompted treatment intensification for presumed mild rejection. His current medications were tacrolimus, mycophenolate, low-dose prednisolone, omeprazole, folic acid, and bumetanide.  

He presented to nephrology with a 3-week history of dyspnoea and sinus tachycardia on minimal exertion. He denied fever but had mild bilateral ankle oedema and a 6-month history of progressive skin eruptions. Vital signs: pulse 95 bpm at rest, rising to 120 bpm on walking; blood pressure 120/80 mmHg; SpO2 98% on room air; afebrile.  

Laboratory studies showed lymphopenia, normocytic anaemia (Hb 11.0 g/dL), stable creatinine (120 µmol/L, eGFR 64 mL/min/1.73 m^2), mild CRP and ESR elevation, and markedly raised beta-D-glucan (>523 pg/mL). Serologies for toxoplasma and leishmania, an autoimmune screen, and PCR tests for herpesviruses, BK virus, COVID-19, and other respiratory viruses were negative. Chest radiograph, ECG, and echocardiogram were unremarkable.  

A few days later, he reported sudden onset of painless, rapidly progressive bilateral blurring of vision. Visual acuity was 6/36 in the right eye and 6/60 in the left, with reactive pupils and no afferent defect. Anterior segments and intraocular pressures were normal. Dilated fundus examination revealed mild nasal blurring of disc margins, multiple perivascular patches of retinal pallor, cotton wool spots, and intraretinal haemorrhages in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography showed bilateral hyperreflective inner nuclear layer patches consistent with paracentral acute middle maculopathy. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated an enlarged foveal avascular zone and early patchy hyperfluorescence.

A 52-year-old man with a 10-year history of recurrent palpitations was referred for evaluation of incessant ventricular arrhythmia. Transthoracic echocardiography showed global hypokinesia and an ejection fraction of 41%. Coronary angiography excluded ischemic cardiomyopathy. A 12-lead electrocardiogram during tachycardia demonstrated a wide complex rhythm at 120 bpm with alternating right bundle branch block morphologies. An electrophysiologic study recorded sinus atrial activity. For one QRS complex with RBBB pattern, a His-to-proximal RBB potential was present (A-RBB, 180 ms; RBB-V, 44 ms); for the next QRS complex with a different RBBB morphology, the His-proximal RBB signal was absent.

A 16‐year‐old girl with recently diagnosed Crohn’s disease presented with perianal pain and purulent discharge one month after diagnosis. Imaging showed a complex intersphincteric fistula with abscesses. She received 500 mg oral metronidazole three times daily for 25 days, 500 mg rectal metronidazole twice daily for 15 days, and 500 mg intravenous metronidazole on the day of surgical fistula repair, then resumed 500 mg oral metronidazole three times daily postoperatively. On postoperative day 2, she developed swallowing difficulty. Neurologic examination showed an unstable gait, slow, slurred, scanning speech, positive finger–nose dysmetria, and generalized muscle weakness; the remainder of the examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed a mildly elevated CRP (1.48 mg/dL); liver enzymes, serum sodium, and potassium were normal. Electroencephalography was normal. Head CT was unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated symmetric increased T2/TIRM signal in the corpus callosum and cerebellar white matter and dentate nuclei, with diffusion‐weighted high signal in the splenium of the corpus callosum and corresponding reduced ADC values.

A 42-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea, chest pain, and fatigue over 2–3 months. He was a heavy smoker with no other notable medical history. On examination, he was alert; heart rate 98 bpm; blood pressure 180/90 mmHg; oxygen saturation 98% on room air; cardiovascular and respiratory findings were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, electrolytes, and lipid panel; hyperglycemia (glucose 182 mg/dL); and low serum TSH (0.33 mU/L). Tumor markers including CEA, AFP, CA 19-9, ferritin, β-hCG, and PSA were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 9 × 6 cm heterogeneous anterior mediastinal mass with contrast enhancement, initially thought to represent an enlarged lymph node, and a 5 × 3 cm mass in the right adrenal gland, which was further evaluated by abdominal MRI. Imaging also showed a 9 mm nodule in the inferior left thyroid lobe and stage II fatty liver. Scintigraphy of the thyroid with Tc-99m pertechnetate demonstrated normally positioned but slightly enlarged lobes with reduced fixation and cold nodules; uptake at 20 minutes was 0.2%. These findings were attributed to recent asymptomatic thyroiditis, and a teratoma of the anterior mediastinum was suspected.

A 50-year-old woman presented with acute left-sided abdominal pain 9 days after an uncomplicated laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (BMI 41). Her post-operative course had been uneventful; she received standard DVT prophylaxis including calf compressors, graduated compression stockings for 3 days, and enoxaparin 40 mg daily. On day 9, while walking on a treadmill, she developed sudden left flank and epigastric pain. 

Vital signs: BP 140/80 mmHg; HR 68 bpm; RR 17/min; SpO2 98% on room air; T 36.0 °C. Physical examination revealed localized tenderness in the left upper quadrant and epigastrium without peritoneal signs.

Laboratory studies: WBC 5.5 × 10^9/L; Hb 130 g/L; CRP 6 mg/L; normal liver and renal function tests.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed an anterior-inferior left renal wedge infarction and incidental bilateral renal and hepatic cysts. Renal Doppler ultrasound demonstrated normal arterial and venous flow without evidence of renal thrombus. 

Cardiac rhythm evaluation: ECG showed sinus rhythm; 24-h Holter monitoring revealed sinus rhythm with rare ventricular ectopic beats. 

A thrombophilia screen, including protein C, protein S, antithrombin III, and antiphospholipid antibodies, was normal. Bilateral upper and lower limb Doppler ultrasound showed patent veins without thromboembolism.

A 3-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of a whitish, clouded left cornea and vision loss for 1 week. There was no history of trauma, pain, systemic infection, or known genetic disorder. His development and systemic examination were unremarkable. The parents, of Turkish origin, were consanguineous. Under general anesthesia the sclera in both eyes appeared blue. Intraocular pressures were 8 mmHg (left) and 10 mmHg (right). B-scan ultrasonography showed a normal posterior segment without retinal detachment. Axial lengths were 22.1 mm (left) and 21.7 mm (right). Cycloplegic retinoscopy of the right eye disclosed –4.0 diopters of myopia and –4.5 diopters of astigmatism at 168 degrees; retinoscopy of the left eye was not possible. The left cornea exhibited full-thickness stromal edema with bullous epithelial changes; central pachymetry was 745 μm and peripheral was 550 μm. The right cornea was abnormally thin (central, 212 μm; peripheral, 308 μm) with topographic astigmatism (–4.5 D at 169 degrees) and an inferoparacentral stromal scar. Funduscopic views were normal. The combination of decreased central thickness with stromal scarring in one eye and acute corneal edema in the other suggested bilateral keratoconus with acute hydrops on the left, and raised suspicion for an underlying connective-tissue disorder.

A 29-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman at 16 weeks’ gestation was transferred with one day of nausea, vomiting, and inability to tolerate oral intake. Her pregnancy had been complicated by hyperemesis gravidarum and chronic hypertension.  
On examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft with mild suprapubic tenderness and no guarding or rebound.  
Initial laboratory studies showed WBC 18.6×10^3/µL, potassium 2.7 mmol/L, AST 94 U/L, ALT 189 U/L, amylase 129 U/L, and ketonuria.  
She was admitted for presumed hyperemesis gravidarum and received IV fluids, potassium repletion, and antiemetics. By hospital day 2, vomiting improved, abdominal pain resolved, and labs showed amylase 179 U/L and lipase 1,324 U/L; AST and ALT had decreased.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed biliary sludge without cholelithiasis or cholecystitis. Conservative management with bowel rest was recommended due to concern for pancreatitis.  
On hospital day 8, her nausea had resolved, and she was advanced to a clear liquid diet. Despite clinical improvement, serum lipase rose to a peak of 2,739 U/L. Repeat ultrasound again showed no cholelithiasis or pancreatic abnormalities.

A 5-year-old girl was referred with a 3-month history of raised lesions on her right upper eyelid and persistent redness and watering of the right eye. She had been evaluated by three different ophthalmologists and treated for 2 months with topical ofloxacin, olopatadine, and dexamethasone without improvement. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes; intraocular pressure was 12 mmHg bilaterally. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed two small pitted papules on the upper eyelid margin (2 mm from the lash line) and a similar lesion on the lateral lid, along with conjunctival hyperemia and an intense follicular reaction in the lower fornix. Complete blood count and immunoglobulin levels were within normal limits.

A 35-year-old woman presented with sudden-onset chest pain and dyspnea for two hours, with severe pain in the back of her neck and left arm worsened by inhalation. She denied fever, cough, leg pain, or swelling. Her medical history included three-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting, coronary artery disease, uncontrolled type 2 diabetes, obesity, deep vein thrombosis, dyslipidemia, gastroesophageal reflux, headaches, and hypertension. She was a former smoker and denied alcohol or recreational drug use.

On arrival she was tachycardic (126 bpm), tachypneic (18 breaths/min with labored effort), normothermic, hypertensive (140/90 mmHg), and 97% saturated on 2 L/min oxygen. Examination showed increased work of breathing without adventitious lung sounds, regular heart rhythm without murmurs, and no lower extremity edema.

Treatment included aspirin, hydromorphone, ondansetron, diphenhydramine, intravenous fluids, and supplemental oxygen. Initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia with nonspecific T-wave changes similar to prior tracings. Chest radiograph was unchanged from two years earlier, demonstrating hyperlucent lungs, sternotomy wires, and vascular clips, with no pneumothorax, consolidation, redistribution, or pleural fluid. Laboratory tests revealed a normal complete blood count, procalcitonin, creatine kinase, and troponin; glucose was 667 mg/dL with pseudohyponatremia; D-dimer was mildly elevated.

A CT angiogram of the chest was obtained to exclude pulmonary embolism. During the study she desaturated to 83% and was escalated to 12 L/min high-flow oxygen, but remained at 90% saturation. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.42, PaCO2 36 mmHg, PaO2 50 mmHg, HCO3 23 mEq/L, methemoglobin 0.4%, carboxyhemoglobin 1.1%, and lactate 2.4 mmol/L. BIPAP was initiated but her respiratory effort worsened, necessitating endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.

A broader exposure history elicited that she used two refill containers of open-system ENDS vaporizer liquid daily (25 mg/mL nicotine), with three devices at home. She and her husband denied trauma, fever, “huffing” paint, methamphetamine use or production, bonfires, or other smoke exposures.

A 34-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of painful, progressive diminution of vision in both eyes, accompanied by redness and whitish corneal opacities. He had been applying topical antibiotics for 3 days. He reported a 10-year history of heavy alcohol use and multiple prior episodes of hemoptysis. On examination, he appeared severely malnourished and had multiple oral ulcers with difficulty in swallowing. Visual acuity in both eyes was light perception with accurate projection of rays in all quadrants. The eyelids and adnexa were normal. There was diffuse conjunctival congestion and mild chemosis. Corneal examination showed total corneal melt with fluorescein uptake, peripheral thinning, and adjacent limbitis in both eyes, without neovascularization. Details of the anterior chamber and fundus were obscured. B-scan ultrasonography of both eyes was unremarkable. Corneal scrapings were sent for Gram and KOH stains, as well as bacterial and fungal cultures, and tear PCR for herpes simplex virus. Blood tests, including a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide, cytoplasmic and perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, serum calcium, and ACE level; peripheral blood smear; stool examination; Mantoux test; chest radiography; and serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis were all inconclusive for a causative etiology.

A 34-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of progressive facial changes and worsening wrinkles, to the point that she no longer recognized her own face. She also noted increased adipose tissue in the abdomen and lower limbs and loss of adipose tissue in the chest and upper limbs. Over the same period, she developed palpable lumps under both axillae along the milk line, from which a white, milk-like fluid was intermittently discharged. She had no significant past medical history and took no medications.

On examination, she had prominent cheekbones, hollowing around the eyes, and hypertrophy of the zygomatic and oral tubercle muscles. Hematological studies revealed hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL (normal 12.0–15.5 g/dL), complement C3 15 mg/dL (normal 90–180 mg/dL), creatinine 0.56 mg/dL (normal 0.6–1.2 mg/dL), and HDL cholesterol 30 mg/dL (normal >40 mg/dL). Further evaluation of the axillary lumps demonstrated glandular tissue consistent with accessory breast tissue bilaterally. An abdominal ultrasound showed no abnormalities.

A 64-year-old woman presented with a mass involving her mid back. She had sustained a fall 7 years earlier, after which she noted persistent swelling in that area. One month before presentation, the mass enlarged and became painful. On initial examination, there was an ill-defined subcutaneous nodule with overlying erythema. One month later, the lesion had evolved into an exophytic nodule with elevated borders, central ulceration and crust, and surrounding erythema; it was extremely tender to palpation. The initial differential diagnosis included a malignant neoplasm or a calcified hematoma with secondary infection. She was treated with oral antibiotics, which improved her pain but did not change the size of the lesion. A punch biopsy specimen revealed changes suggestive of an inflammatory reaction to follicular rupture. Because of the clinicopathologic disparity, excisional biopsy was planned. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging showed a 3.8 × 2.6-cm round collection within the subcutaneous tissue at the L1–L2 level with internal fat density and associated calcifications, and an area of discontinuity along its superior aspect with a small fat collection and surrounding inflammation.

A 17-year-old male presented with 3 months of progressive generalized weakness, fatigue, palpitations, and exertional dyspnea. One month earlier, he had been diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia and treated with oral iron supplements, with initial improvement followed by recurrence of symptoms. He denied jaundice, pica, blood transfusions, or a family history of anemia. On examination, he appeared pale with scleral icterus; vital signs included a heart rate of 120 beats/min and a respiratory rate of 32 breaths/min on exertion. Cardiac examination revealed a grade II/VI systolic ejection murmur. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.9 g/dl, red-cell count 5.35×10^12/L, mean corpuscular volume 72.1 fl, and serum ferritin 9 ng/ml. The peripheral smear demonstrated hypochromia, microcytosis, anisocytosis, and poikilocytosis. Hemoglobin electrophoresis showed an Hb A2 of 2.9%. High-performance liquid chromatography revealed peaks of Hb A and an unknown band at a retention time of 3.93 minutes.

A 4-year-old boy presented with 10 days of persistent fever, vomiting, and diarrhea following an 8-week family visit to Bangladesh. Three weeks into the trip he received 3 days of oral ciprofloxacin for an initial self-limited gastroenteritis, after which gastrointestinal symptoms resolved but fevers persisted intermittently at up to 38 °C. In the last 10 days of travel, fevers became daily spikes to 40 °C. There was reduced oral intake and constipation without vomiting. The family denied street-food consumption or tap-water exposure. His vaccinations were up to date; he had not received typhoid vaccine or malaria prophylaxis. His medical history was notable only for mild asthma.

On arrival he appeared unwell and moderately dehydrated. Temperature was 39.8 °C, heart rate 160 beats/min, respiratory rate 32 breaths/min, and blood pressure was normal. He had no rash, petechiae, or bruising. Cardiorespiratory examination was unremarkable. His abdomen was soft, mildly tender, and distended without organomegaly or ascites. Neurologic examination was normal.

Initial blood tests showed hemoglobin 102 g/L, white cell count 4.3×10^9/L (neutrophils 2.6×10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.9×10^9/L), and platelets 97×10^9/L. Renal function was normal except for mild hyponatremia. Liver tests revealed hypoalbuminemia and mild transaminitis with normal bilirubin. C-reactive protein was 92 mg/L.

Based on his presentation and travel history, the differential diagnosis included typhoid fever, malaria, and dengue. Blood cultures were sent, thick and thin films for malaria parasites were prepared, and dengue serologies (IgM, IgG) plus NS1 antigen testing were ordered. Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone was started, and he was admitted for further management.

A 17-year-old female presented with a 2-week history of periumbilical pain. She had a remote tonsillectomy and was taking pantoprazole for intermittent epigastric discomfort. She denied dysuria, hematuria, or other urinary symptoms. 

On examination, her vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal palpation revealed a tender, well-circumscribed mass approximately 5 cm in diameter just posterior to the umbilicus. No peritoneal signs were present. 

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. 

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a 41×39 mm cystic mass posterior to the umbilicus, extending toward the left. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed a well-defined, unilocular fluid-filled structure in the same location without evidence of adjacent organ inflammation or solid components.

A 39-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, well controlled on metformin and gliclazide, presented with a 3-day history of fever and sudden-onset pain and swelling of both hands and wrists. He also noted pain and swelling of his left knee for 1 week. He denied back pain, ankle swelling, rashes, weight loss, chronic cough, dysuria, urethral discharge, or sexual risk factors. He had no family history of rheumatologic disease or malignancy and no history of smoking or alcohol use.

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was tender pitting edema over the dorsum of both hands. The wrists, bilateral metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and the left knee were warm, tender, and swollen, with restricted movement. There was no ankle edema, lymphadenopathy, sacroiliac or lower back tenderness, or enthesitis; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 67 mm/h and a C-reactive protein level of 55.1 mg/L. Rheumatoid factor, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, anti–nuclear antibodies, anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, VDRL, and HIV tests were negative. Tuberculosis screening (three sputum smears, chest radiograph, and tuberculin skin test) was negative.

Ultrasonography of both hands and wrists revealed tenosynovitis with soft-tissue edema and joint effusion. Radiographs of the hands showed no erosions; radiographs of the lumbosacral spine and sacroiliac joints were normal. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography showed no lymphadenopathy or mass lesions.

An 11-year-old girl presented with a 4-month history of left hip pain that was most pronounced in the morning but did not initially limit her activities. She had no fever. On examination, the left hip was held in mild flexion and adduction, with pain on passive movement and apparent pseudo-paralysis. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 14 900 per μL, hemoglobin of 13.7 g/dL, a C-reactive protein level <0.2 mg/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 16 mm/h. Plain radiographs of the hip were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left hip demonstrated increased joint fluid and a thickened, inflamed synovium. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded synovial fluid with 18 000 leukocytes per μL (63% neutrophils), a sterile Gram stain, and no bacterial growth after three days.

A 28-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis B was admitted with 1 week of fever (39.4 °C), headache, vomiting, and cough. Chest CT was normal. Brain MRI showed bilateral cortical and subcortical T2 FLAIR hyperintensities without abnormal enhancement or hydrocephalus. CSF analysis revealed glucose 2.52 mmol/L, protein 1.76 g/L, and white blood cells 300 × 10^6/L (80% mononuclear cells); acid-fast stain, India Ink preparation, and bacterial culture were negative. She had one seizure and received ganciclovir for 3 days. A diagnosis of possible tuberculous meningitis was made, and oral rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol were started; isoniazid and dexamethasone were administered intrathecally for 1 month. Six serial CSF samples showed persistent pleocytosis (80–394 × 10^6/L, 80–90% mononuclear cells). Ethambutol was withdrawn for blurred vision and replaced with levofloxacin. Fever and headaches improved but she developed bilateral hand tremor.

Three months later she developed back pain, leg weakness, memory loss, irritability, and confusion, progressing to inability to walk independently. Cervical MRI demonstrated patchy T2 hyperintensities from C2 to C7. Brain MRI showed linear and radial gadolinium enhancement perpendicular to the lateral ventricles. CSF analysis showed glucose 2.32 mmol/L, protein 1.09 g/L, and white blood cells 52 × 10^6/L (90% mononuclear cells). CSF Xpert MTB/RIF and culture were both negative. Anti-tuberculosis therapy was adjusted to moxifloxacin, amikacin, isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide. Intravenous immunoglobulin (25 g/day for 5 days) led to symptom improvement. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days, then 500 mg/day for 3 days) produced no further benefit.

A 16-year-old girl presented with tingling pain in her left leg and continuous involuntary movements of her left great toe for one month. These movements—extension and flexion of the great toe—occurred when she was awake and in early sleep and could not be suppressed voluntarily. Walking, sitting, or straining did not exacerbate the pain.

At birth, she had a sacral dimple at the S2–3 level. Four years earlier, she had voiding difficulty and underwent untethering surgery for a lipomeningomyelocele at the S2 level of the conus medullaris. A nerve conduction velocity study showed polyradiculopathy at the left L5 level and below with axonal involvement. A needle electromyogram revealed abnormal spontaneous activities in the left gastrocnemius medial head, abductor hallucis, and tibialis anterior and posterior. She did not report any movement symptoms at that time. She also underwent plantar fasciotomy for equinovarus deformity of both feet.

Five months later, voiding difficulty recurred, and she underwent a second untethering surgery. Postoperatively, she developed fever and meningeal irritation. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a red blood cell count of 60,000/mm3, a white blood cell count of 150/mm3 (69% polymorphonucleocytes), a protein level of 274 mg/dL, and a glucose level of 39 mg/dL. No organisms were cultured. Her fever and meningeal signs resolved after intravenous teicoplanin, which was later discontinued due to neutropenia.

One month after surgery, the left leg pain and involuntary movements of the left great toe began. On examination, deep tendon reflexes were increased at both knees, and the Babinski sign was negative. Brain computed tomography and electroencephalography showed no pathologic findings. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine revealed reactive inflammatory changes in the operative scar and decreased reactive meningeal enhancement compared to the previous study. Repeat nerve conduction studies showed no significant change, and needle electromyography again demonstrated abnormal spontaneous activities in the same left lower-extremity muscles with no interval change.

A 40-year-old woman with a history of severe alcoholic hepatitis complicated by grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy was readmitted less than 24 hours after discharge following a witnessed tonic–clonic seizure. She had no prior history of seizures and reported strict abstinence from alcohol and nonprescription drugs since her last hospitalization, with documented compliance with lactulose and rifaximin. 

On arrival, her temperature was 97.2°F, pulse 95/min, respiratory rate 8/min, and blood pressure 114/78 mmHg. Off sedation, she had no focal neurologic deficits. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL, INR 1.79, creatinine 0.3 mg/dL, total bilirubin 10.8 mg/dL, ALT 54 IU/L, AST 112 IU/L, bicarbonate 15.5 mmol/L, anion gap 21 mEq/L, unchanged from prior discharge. Urine toxicology was negative, and blood alcohol level was undetectable.

A brain MRI performed while the patient remained postictal showed high signal intensity in the subcortical and periventricular white matter of the bilateral temporal and parietal lobes on FLAIR images, similar in distribution to a limited prior study. A 60-minute EEG revealed high focal epileptogenic potential in the same temporal-parietal regions.

A 55-year-old right-handed man with no significant medical history presented with two days of worsening “heaviness” in his right arm. He denied gait difficulty, pain, sensory changes, or cranial symptoms. He had an upper respiratory illness three weeks earlier and denied diarrhea or recent vaccinations. On arrival, blood pressure was 220/139 mm Hg; he was afebrile and alert. Examination showed uniform weakness of the right upper extremity (motor strength 3/5) with 1+ reflexes; left upper extremity and bilateral lower extremities had strength 5/5 with 2+ reflexes. Sensation was intact, cranial nerves were normal, and he walked unassisted. Urine toxicology, head CT, brain MRI with diffusion‐weighted imaging, and cervical‐spine imaging were all unremarkable. He was admitted for observation. On hospital day 2, lumbar puncture showed 1 white blood cell, no red blood cells, and protein 33 mg/dL. Serum assay for botulinum toxin was negative. On hospital day 3, right arm strength declined to 2/5, and new left arm weakness (4/5) appeared; repeat MRI remained normal. On hospital day 4, he was unable to walk unassisted, had complete flaccid paralysis of the right arm, left arm strength 3/5, and areflexia throughout all extremities.

A 12-year-old girl from a Himalayan district of Nepal presented with a 6-month history of headache and fatigue. She was born at term at home, with no family history of thyroid or autoimmune disorders. She denied menarche, visual changes, hair loss, constipation, or medication use. On examination, her height was 129 cm (<3rd percentile), weight 54 kg (>75th percentile), and BMI 32.4 kg/m^2. Blood pressure was 104/72 mm Hg, heart rate 63 beats/min, and respiratory rate 15 breaths/min. She had coarse, dry skin and looked short and obese for her age. Neurological and visual-field examinations were normal. The thyroid was markedly enlarged bilaterally. She was Tanner Stage I for breast and pubic hair development.

Initial laboratory studies revealed:
• TSH 149.6 µIU/mL (0.4–6.1 µIU/mL)  
• T4 0.2 µg/dL (4–11 µg/dL)  
• T3 11 ng/dL (69–202 ng/dL)  
• Prolactin 59.2 ng/mL (1.2–15.5 ng/mL)  
• GH 4.7 ng/mL (<10 ng/mL)  
• LH 0.26 mIU/mL; FSH 0.78 mIU/mL  
• Cortisol and ACTH within normal limits  
• Hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL; random glucose 80 mg/dL  
• LDL-C 156 mg/dL; triglycerides 193 mg/dL  
• Urinary iodine 12 µg/L (100–299 µg/L)  
• Thyroid autoantibodies negative

Noncontrast and contrast CT of the head demonstrated a 9 mm, round, symmetrically enlarged, homogeneously enhancing, hyperdense mass in the widened pituitary fossa.

A 50-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus presented with a 1-month history of left hip and back pain accompanied by intermittent low-grade fevers, generalized malaise, and anorexia. On examination, he was afebrile, with mild tenderness over the left groin and pain on extension of the left hip; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16 × 10^3/µL, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 110 mm in the first hour, and a C-reactive protein level of 180 mg/L. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed an 8 × 5 × 5.5 cm left psoas abscess and multiple abscesses in the liver and spleen. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed a multiloculated left psoas abscess extending from T11 to L5 (measuring 4.6 × 7.6 × 14.3 cm) and multiple well-defined, round, hypodense lesions without ring enhancement in both the liver and spleen.

A 6-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of severe global developmental delay, hypotonia, and recurrent intractable seizures. According to her parents, she never achieved age-appropriate milestones, including sitting or babbling. Her history since infancy was notable for generalized hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and abnormal movements consistent with seizures. Family history was unremarkable.

On examination, she had microcephaly, poor head control, and lack of purposeful hand movements. Neurologic findings included severe hypotonia, bilateral nystagmus, and increased deep tendon reflexes. Routine metabolic panel, urine analysis, and complete blood count were normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated thickened cortex in the high frontoparietal regions bilaterally, predominantly anteriorly, with a micro-lobulated, multi-nodular surface described as a “pebbly/cobblestone complex,” sparse cortical sulci, and prominent lateral, third, and fourth ventricles. There were also asymmetrical FLAIR hyperintensities in the periventricular and deep white matter suggestive of ischemic microangiopathy.

A 44-year-old man had obstructive hydrocephalus due to idiopathic midbrain aqueduct stenosis and underwent a right ventriculoperitoneal shunt in September 2016, with complete symptom relief. On February 15, 2021, he developed a stiff facial expression. Two weeks later, he had progressive bradykinesia and body stiffness. His family noted depression after a conflict, and he was diagnosed with catatonic syndrome and treated with paroxetine and mirtazapine. One month later, he worsened, with limitation of vertical gaze, cogwheel rigidity and tremor, limb bradykinesia, difficulty turning in bed, a slow soft voice, mutism, and memory loss. He was treated empirically for parkinsonism, autoimmune encephalitis, and depressive stupor with duloxetine, clonazepam, donepezil, amantadine, ganciclovir, and methylprednisolone without improvement. Two months after symptom onset, he became bedridden, drowsy, required nasogastric feeding, and was intubated. On neurologic examination, he had increased muscle tone, bilateral pyramidal signs, and hyperactive deep-tendon reflexes. Cerebrospinal fluid examination was normal. Brain MRI and CT showed fluctuations in lateral ventricular size, with periods of enlargement and return to normal dimensions.

An 18-year-old man presented with 20 days of pain and swelling around his right scapula, which had been gradually increasing in size, and 2 days of fever. He had been receiving anti-tubercular therapy for presumed pulmonary tuberculosis for 6 months; the diagnosis had been based on cough, chest radiograph findings, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with negative sputum studies. Despite continued therapy, 3 days before presentation he developed swelling and pain of the left ankle with difficulty walking. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 73 mm/h and a positive C-reactive protein level of 96 mg/L. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder and left ankle demonstrated findings consistent with osteomyelitis involving the scapula and the distal tibia. An aspiration of the scapular swelling was performed, and specimens were sent for culture, sensitivity testing, and histopathologic examination for possible multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a 6-year history of progressive abdominal swelling that had worsened over the past year, accompanied by cough, night sweats, easy fatigability, and unquantified weight loss. He had been treated empirically for tuberculosis at another hospital with no improvement. There was no family history of a similar illness. On examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was grossly distended; the liver edge was palpable 10 cm below the right costal margin (total span 15 cm), and the spleen measured 18 cm. Neurologic examination was normal. Anthropometric measurements showed weight 24 kg, height 109 cm (length-for-age < –3 z score), and BMI 20.2 kg/m2. Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (WBC 3360/µL, hemoglobin 9 g/dL, platelets 92 000/µL) and elevated liver enzymes (AST 200 U/L, ALT 116 U/L, ALP 124 U/L). Two GeneXpert tests for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and HIV testing were negative. Abdominal ultrasound and contrast CT showed massive hepatosplenomegaly with a wedge-shaped splenic infarct. High-resolution chest CT demonstrated diffuse interlobular septal thickening and ground-glass opacities without lymphadenopathy, indicating interstitial lung disease. Based on these imaging findings, a radiologic diagnosis of Gaucher’s disease was suggested.

A 58-year-old man presented with intermittent high-grade fever up to 40 °C, sore throat, anosmia, ageusia, myalgia, fatigue, and weakness. On illness day 3, he noted pruritic, erythematous, blanching maculopapular rashes over the trunk, neck, and extremities, sparing the face, palms, and soles. He then developed a nonproductive cough, nausea, and four daily episodes of watery, nonbloody, nonmucoid diarrhea without vomiting, abdominal pain, or dehydration. By day 10, the fever, sore throat, and rash had resolved; myalgia improved by day 14; ageusia by day 32; and anosmia, cough, and coryza by day 36.

His medical history included urolithiasis and gouty arthritis, with no current medications. He had no high-risk drug exposures during the illness. He occasionally drank alcohol and smoked (19.5 pack-year history). Family history was notable for hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and asthma.

Physical examination was conducted via teleconsultation under isolation precautions. The skin was dry with generalized, erythematous, blanching maculopapular lesions on the trunk and extremities without excoriations, crusting, or scaling.

No biopsy or additional assays were performed at that time.

A 37-year-old Caucasian man presented for hyperopic eyeglass evaluation and reported intermittent bilateral eye pain, halos, blurry vision, and dull headaches after ≥1 h of reading that resolved with accommodative rest. He had longstanding high hyperopia, astigmatism, and intermittent esotropia; no personal or family history of glaucoma or zonular disorders. His medical history included childhood ALL in remission, migraine with aura, hypertension (lisinopril), and depression (sertraline).

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OU. IOP measured 24 mmHg OD and 41 mmHg OS. Pupils, extraocular movements, slit-lamp exam (normal anterior chamber depth; clear lenses), and fundus (cup-to-disc ratio 0.55 OD, 0.80 OS) were unremarkable. Dorzolamide-timolol lowered pressures to 13 mmHg OD and 11 mmHg OS. Manifest refraction was +4.75 D OU.

During a follow-up, serial tonometry during sustained accommodation (using a device) showed IOP rising from 14 mmHg OD and 9 mmHg OS at baseline to 32 mmHg OD and 37 mmHg OS after 145 minutes, with onset of his characteristic symptoms; topical agents returned pressures to baseline.

Optic disc OCT showed average RNFL thickness of 118 μm OD and 111 μm OS, with cup-to-disc ratios of 0.64 and 0.72. Automated perimetry revealed nonspecific defects with a possible inferior nasal step OS. Gonioscopy demonstrated narrow angles (ATM and PTM visible in various quadrants) with a 20° angle recess bilaterally and normal iris configuration. UBM during accommodation revealed narrow angles without anterior rotation of the ciliary body or iridociliary contact. Optical biometry showed axial lengths of 21.61 mm OD and 21.68 mm OS; anterior chamber depths of 2.96 mm OD and 2.95 mm OS; and lens thicknesses of 3.83 mm OD and 3.94 mm OS.

A 19-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a one-day history of rapidly progressive right eye pain, redness, and vision loss. On initial emergency evaluation, afferent pupillary function was intact; however, by the following morning he had no light perception in the right eye. Intraocular pressure was elevated, and concern arose for central retinal artery occlusion; an attempted anterior chamber paracentesis was performed. On transfer, examination revealed a hyperemic right eye with intraocular pressure of 45 mmHg and pan-uveitis. Fundus examination showed vitreous haze, optic nerve edema, exudative macular detachment, and diffuse retinal hemorrhages along the major arcades (“blood and thunder” appearance). Peripheral retina demonstrated large discrete patches of whitening concerning for necrotizing retinitis. Optical coherence tomography of the macula revealed inner retinal hyperreflectivity and large subretinal fluid. Intravenous fluorescein angiography demonstrated extinguished central retinal artery and vein flow with inflammatory leakage around a cilioretinal artery and areas of blocked choroidal fluorescence underlying hemorrhages and exudate. The left eye showed early optic neuritis and minimal inferior arcade vasculitis. Based on the presumed diagnosis of acute retinal necrosis, the patient was admitted and treated with intravenous acyclovir, topical antihypertensives, atropine, prednisolone, and intravitreal foscarnet for fellow eye involvement.

A 71-year-old woman presented with vision loss in the left eye two weeks after uncomplicated cataract extraction with posterior chamber intraocular lens implantation; she had undergone the same procedure in the right eye one day earlier. During both surgeries, a compounded intracameral formulation containing vancomycin, moxifloxacin, and triamcinolone was injected for endophthalmitis prophylaxis. On examination, Snellen visual acuity was 20/25 without correction (pinholing to 20/20) in the right eye and 20/60 (PH 20/30) in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 16 mmHg OD and 18 mmHg OS. Slit-lamp evaluation showed 1+ cell and 2+ flare in the right anterior chamber and 1+ cell in the left. Posterior-segment examination revealed disc hemorrhages, mild disc edema, venous dilation, and mild tortuosity in both eyes (worse OS). The right vitreous contained visible triamcinolone; the left had a sub-hyaloid hemorrhage nasal to the optic nerve. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated minimal retinal thickening and preserved foveal contour bilaterally. Fluorescein angiography showed mild vascular leakage in both eyes and a small area of peripheral capillary nonperfusion in the superotemporal periphery of the left eye.

A 44-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 2-week history of crops of red-brown papulovesicles on his trunk and upper extremities. He denied involvement of the palms or soles, pruritus, fevers, chills, purulent drainage, or other systemic symptoms. He also denied a history of genital ulcers or new sexual partners. His medical history was notable for hypertension and hyperlipidemia, treated with amlodipine, gemfibrozil, hydrochlorothiazide, and simvastatin.

Punch biopsies of lesions from the epigastrium and left ventral forearm showed a dense superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal dermal infiltrate composed predominantly of small lymphocytes, some medium-sized lymphocytes, and a few plasma cells and histiocytes. Immunoperoxidase analysis demonstrated predominantly CD20/CD79a+ B cells with a background of CD3+ T cells and a normal CD4:CD8 ratio; there was variable bcl-2 reactivity, while bcl-6 and cyclin D1 were negative, and CD30 staining was also negative. In situ hybridization for kappa and lambda light chains showed a polyclonal pattern.

T-cell and B-cell gene-rearrangement studies revealed that the epigastric specimen was positive for T-cell receptor β and γ gene rearrangements; the forearm specimen was negative for T-cell receptor β but positive for γ rearrangement matching the epigastric clone. B-cell clonality studies were negative. These molecular findings raised concern for a T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder, although a reactive clonal expansion could not be completely ruled out.

A 39‐year‐old man with a history of resection of a left cerebellar hemangioblastoma 8 weeks earlier presented with a 10‐day history of fever (up to 38.7°C), fatigue, and dizziness. His white blood cell count and C‐reactive protein level were normal. Noncontrast and contrast‐enhanced CT of the brain showed no fluid collection. Lumbar puncture revealed 253 leukocytes/µL (65% polymorphonuclear) without organism growth; blood cultures were sterile. He was treated empirically with vancomycin, cefotaxime, and metronidazole, but fevers persisted despite broad‐spectrum coverage. On hospital day 14, with persistent fevers and a suspicion that his bone flap was infected, he underwent reopening of the posterior fossa craniotomy wound and removal of the bone flap. The procedure was confined to the extradural compartment, although there was intraoperative CSF loss. Bone‐flap cultures and PCR were negative for infection. After surgery, he developed bilateral lower‐motor‐neuron facial weakness (House–Brackmann grade 4 bilaterally), mild slurred speech, and a left abducens nerve palsy. Limb strength, reflexes, and sensation were normal; gait was moderately ataxic. MRI of the brain on postoperative day 2 showed a FLAIR hyperintensity within the floor of the fourth ventricle at the dorsal pons, involving the facial colliculus.

A 50-year-old Chinese woman presented with a 4-year history of recurrent high-spiking fevers, an evanescent maculopapular rash, and arthralgias. Ten months before admission, she noted painless nodules on both eyelids. On examination, she had a salmon-pink maculopapular eruption on the hands, arms, neck, and back, and enlarged superficial lymph nodes in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions. Distinct, palpable nodules were present on both upper eyelids. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14,020/mm3 with 92.3% neutrophils, a C-reactive protein level of 19.8 mg/L, and negative tests for rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies. Visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye. The anterior segments and fundi were unremarkable. Orbital magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated thickened soft tissue around both orbits with heterogeneous enhancement and enlargement of the lacrimal glands.

An 83-year-old man was admitted with a one-week history of postprandial vomiting and left upper-quadrant abdominal pain. He denied dysphagia or weight loss and had experienced a similar self-limited episode one year earlier. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no abdominal succussion splash. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, liver function tests, and renal profile, were normal. A chest radiograph showed no free air under the diaphragm. A plain abdominal film revealed no aerobilia or gallstones. A nasogastric tube was placed for decompression. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a large, smooth mass occupying the entire lumen of the first part of the duodenum, with ulceration of the adjacent mucosa; the mass could not be retrieved endoscopically. 

Abdominal computed tomography demonstrated a large calcified mass in the first part of the duodenum.

A 60-year-old Korean woman presented with right ankle pain that worsened on dorsiflexion. Twenty years earlier, she had first noticed a nodular mass on the medial side of her right knee that moved up and down slowly; she had not sought medical attention at that time. Three months before admission, she noted reappearance of the mass near her right ankle, which began to cause pain. 

On examination, there was an oval, rubbery, soft, non-tender, 3-cm mass just proximal to the lateral malleolus of the right foot, and a second mass over the anterior ankle that produced discomfort with dorsiflexion. Vital signs were within normal limits. Routine laboratory tests were unremarkable, and there was no eosinophilia.

A plain radiograph of the right leg showed multiple calcifications extending from the medial knee to the calf, with no abnormalities around the ankle joint. MR imaging of the right leg demonstrated heterogeneous signal intensity in the mass near the lateral malleolus. Based on these findings, an epidermoid cyst or dermatomyositis was suspected.

A 68-year-old Caucasian woman was referred in May 2017 for blurred vision in her left eye. Her medical history was notable for essential hypertension and hypothyroidism, both well controlled with medication. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures and anterior segments were normal bilaterally. 

Fundus examination of the left eye revealed an isolated unilateral perifoveal round lesion and a small cluster of hard exudates inferotemporal to the fovea, without any other retinal vascular abnormalities. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (OCT) B-scan of the left eye demonstrated a 216 μm round lesion with hyperreflective walls, adjacent intraretinal cystic spaces, minimal hard exudates, and localized retinal thickening. 

Indocyanine green angiography of the left eye showed a well-defined aneurysmal lesion in the early phases connected to an arterial vessel, with no late leakage. OCT angiography (6 × 6 mm scan, manually segmented) localized the lesion to the deep capillary plexus, revealing a high-flow, well-circumscribed round structure without evidence of neovascularization. No abnormalities were seen in the right eye.

The patient denied any history of diabetes, blood dyscrasia, inflammatory disease, or retinal vascular occlusion. Her hypertension remained medically controlled, and there were no signs of hypertensive retinopathy.

A 22-year-old woman with asthma was brought to the emergency department for lethargy, confusion, hematuria, and severe right arm pain. Nine days earlier she had noted pain and a rash over her right mid-humerus after what she suspected was an insect bite; she reported her home was infested with spiders. One week before this admission, she had presented for abdominal symptoms and right arm pain; laboratory tests were normal and she was treated symptomatically. 

On arrival, she was lethargic, diaphoretic, and writhing in pain; examination of the right arm showed an erythematous lesion without fluctuant collection. Initial laboratory results were notable for:  
• White-cell count 103.5 × 10^3/µL  
• Hemoglobin 3.3 g/dL  
• Platelets 194 × 10^3/µL  
• INR 1.35, D-dimer 2.22 mg/L  
• AST 3335 U/L, ALT 860 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 9.8 mg/dL  
• Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL  
• LDH 3260 U/L, haptoglobin <10 mg/dL  
• Lactic acid 20 mmol/L  
• Direct Coombs’ test positive for IgG and complement  
• Creatine kinase 1200 U/L  
• Urinalysis: red-brown urine, 2+ blood, no red cells  

CT of the right humerus demonstrated cellulitis without abscess or osteomyelitis. She was admitted to the intensive care unit with a possible diagnosis of acute leukemia with leukostasis and was started on hydroxyurea, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and blood-product transfusions.

A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented with an 11-day history of a pruritic, painful, blistering rash on her trunk, face, and extremities, without mucosal involvement. She had started naltrexone for alcohol use disorder 3 days before rash onset and denied any other new medications or supplements. Initially, she was admitted elsewhere for fever and a perioral rash and treated with antibiotics and steroids for one week. Two days after discharge, she developed a vesiculobullous eruption that progressed to her trunk and extremities, prompting transfer for further evaluation.

On examination, she was afebrile and tachycardic. The skin showed diffuse erythema with bullae and pustules forming dependent pus lakes, hyperpigmented scaly plaques on the face extending to the scalp, multiple erythematous papules coalescing into semiannular plaques, and pronounced desquamation on the extremities. Nikolsky and Asboe-Hansen signs were negative. There was no palmoplantar or mucosal involvement. Estimated body-surface-area involvement was 40%, with 6% of areas denuded.

Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (26.78 × 10^3/mcL) with neutrophilia (24.14 × 10^3/mcL), eosinophilia (0.89 × 10^3/mcL), and a negative antinuclear antibody titer. A 4-mm punch biopsy demonstrated neutrophilic dermatitis with subcorneal pustules and a superficial and mid-dermal perivascular and interstitial infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, eosinophils, and scattered neutrophils. There was no evidence of epidermal necrosis or fungal elements, and direct immunofluorescence was negative.

A 68-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol use presented after a syncopal fall. He denied abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dysphagia, odynophagia, melena, hematochezia, changes in bowel habits, or weight loss. He had no family history of colorectal cancer. On examination, vital signs were stable and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 5.1 g/dL (baseline 10 g/dL), and fecal occult blood testing was positive. Abdominal CT scan showed chronic pancreatitis and diffuse fatty infiltration of the liver but no evidence of retroperitoneal hematoma. After transfusion of packed red blood cells, his hemoglobin rose to 10 g/dL. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed multiple, large, linear strips of superficial, white sloughing mucosa throughout the esophagus; the sloughed tissue was easily removed with biopsy forceps, revealing normal-appearing underlying mucosa with no bleeding. The stomach showed mild erythema of the body and antrum, and the duodenum had nonbleeding erosions. Colonoscopy demonstrated nonbleeding diverticulosis and two small polyps, which were removed without complication.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a nine-month history of right eye swelling and protrusion. Initial computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits revealed isolated enlargement of the right lacrimal gland without other orbital abnormalities. A course of oral steroids produced no improvement, and a lacrimal gland biopsy demonstrated a mild chronic inflammatory infiltrate composed of plasma cells without evidence of malignancy. Laboratory testing showed normal thyroid‐stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and antinuclear antibody levels. On examination, visual acuity was 20/25 in both eyes; there was right upper eyelid fullness with 4 mm of proptosis. Ocular motility testing demonstrated a mild elevation deficit of the right eye and a 4 prism‐diopter right hypotropia. The remainder of the eye examination was unremarkable.

A 36‐year‐old man presented to the emergency department with multiple fluid‐filled blisters over his body for more than one month. The first blister appeared in his mouth, causing dysphagia, and subsequently the lesions spread extensively to his scalp, face, neck, chest, arms (including axillae), back, groin, genitals, and lower limbs. He reported a 4–5‐year history of persistent silvery, scaly, pruritic lesions on his scalp, which he treated as dandruff without improvement. On examination, he appeared cachectic; vital signs were within normal limits. Most blisters were ruptured, some were bleeding or had a putrid pustular discharge, and many were smeared with a foul‐smelling greenish‐brown paste. Unruptured blisters exhibited a positive Nikolsky's sign. The patient admitted applying cow dung, urine, and local herbs to his wounds for nine days. Laboratory testing showed a moderately elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and mild anemia; total leukocyte count, PT/INR, liver and renal function tests, and blood glucose were within normal ranges. The patient declined skin biopsy.

A 32-year-old unemployed Yemeni man with a 10-year history of schizophrenia characterized by auditory hallucinations and passivity phenomena had been stable for 6 years on clozapine (400 mg daily) and olanzapine (10 mg daily). In March 2014, he developed anxiety, tremor, dizziness, and slowing of movements, and all antipsychotic medications were stopped. Four weeks later he presented to the emergency department with a sudden decline in consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale score, 5) and generalized fast-rhythm tremors of all four limbs. He was intubated and admitted to the intensive care unit. Status epilepticus with possible herpes encephalitis and neuroleptic malignant syndrome were considered. He underwent electroencephalography, lumbar puncture, and brain MRI, all of which were within normal limits. He received antiepileptic therapy and empirical antiviral therapy and was discharged on levetiracetam. Over the following months, he had multiple brief hospital admissions with recurrent altered mental status, fast-rhythm limb tremors, perseverative and echolalic speech, and odd staring. Each time, comprehensive medical evaluations including neurologic and toxicologic studies were unremarkable. On the most recent admission, a prolonged video EEG showed no ictal changes during the tremor-like movements and no interictal epileptiform discharges.

A 3-year-old Hispanic boy in Arizona with a baseline right facial palsy presented with 5 days of fatigue, abdominal pain, and right cheek pain. Outpatient treatment for presumed otitis and sinusitis with ear drops and penicillin yielded no improvement. He then developed intermittent fevers, speech changes, gait instability, and difficulty sitting up. A rapid Group A Streptococcus test was positive, and penicillin was changed to cephalexin. The next day, he had seizure-like activity unresponsive to voice and received midazolam en route to the Emergency Department. On arrival he was febrile, had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8, and altered mental status. He experienced a generalized tonic–clonic seizure treated with lorazepam and levetiracetam. Noncontrast head CT showed hypoattenuation consistent with edema in the right frontal and left frontoparietal lobes. He was started on ceftriaxone and vancomycin. Admission laboratory studies showed a normal metabolic panel, WBC 10.1 K/μL, hemoglobin 14.4 g/dL, and platelets 321 K/μL. CSF obtained by lumbar puncture demonstrated 75 WBC/μL, 5 RBC/μL, glucose 53 mg/dL, and protein 85 mg/dL. A multiplex CSF PCR panel was negative for bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens. Pending studies included CSF oligoclonal bands, serum aquaporin-4 receptor antibody, and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody. Empirical dexamethasone and IV immunoglobulin were begun. After transfer to the PICU, he was intubated without sedation and lacked brainstem reflexes. EEG showed diffuse slowing consistent with moderate encephalopathy. MRI four days after admission revealed extensive bilateral supratentorial and infratentorial diffusion restriction, T2 hyperintensity, necrosis, subarachnoid and parenchymal enhancement, and patchy frontal-lobe involvement. A follow-up MRI three days later showed marked progression of diffusion restriction and T2 FLAIR hyperintensity with increased involvement of the periventricular regions, cerebellum, basal nuclei, thalami, brainstem, leptomeninges, and petechial hemorrhages.

A full‐term male neonate was referred at age 20 days with a swelling in the sublingual region present since birth. The mass had progressively enlarged, causing difficulty in feeding, noisy breathing, and failure to thrive. On examination, there was a firm, nonpulsatile, midline cystic swelling of the floor of the mouth elevating the tongue. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. A CT scan and MRI scan revealed a well‐defined, unilocular cystic lesion measuring 2.65 × 1.7 × 2.21 cm, located in the midline of the floor of the mouth above the level of the mylohyoid muscle.  
What is your leading diagnosis, and how would you distinguish among the possible entities?

A 19-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of insidious, gradually progressive weakness of both lower limbs, beginning in the right leg and extending to the left within one month. He also noted urinary frequency for the past 5 months but denied fever, low backache, or radicular pain. He had no upper-limb weakness. The patient was a resident of Uttar Pradesh, India, an endemic region for Taenia solium infection.

On examination, cranial nerves and higher mental functions were normal. The lower extremities had increased tone, Medical Research Council grade 4/5 strength at all major joints, brisk deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral Babinski signs. Sensory testing revealed decreased pain and touch sensation below the L2–L3 level, with preserved vibration and joint position sense. Upper limbs were normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracolumbar spine showed an intramedullary mass lesion extending from T11 to L1, causing focal cord bulging and mass effect. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited mild peripheral contrast enhancement.

A 53-year-old Afro-Caribbean man presented with a two-day history of vomiting, hiccups, and abdominal pain. He was initially treated for presumed gastroenteritis and discharged, but four days later he reported continued epigastric and lower abdominal pain, ongoing vomiting, and no bowel movements or urine output for four days. His history was notable only for hypercholesterolemia; he smoked ten cigarettes per day and denied alcohol or recent travel. 

On examination he was apyrexial and clinically dehydrated, with a pulse of 108 beats per minute and blood pressure of 145/82 mm Hg. The abdomen was tender but soft, without peritoneal signs. A urethral catheter was inserted; urine dipstick was strongly positive for blood and protein, and positive for glucose and leukocytes. 

Laboratory studies showed:  
- Sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 6.7 mmol/L  
- Urea 45.2 mmol/L, creatinine 1885 µmol/L  
- C-reactive protein 421 mg/L, neutrophils 25.9 × 10^9/L, ESR 100 mm/h  
- Arterial blood gas on 28% O₂: pH 7.19, HCO₃⁻ 14.5 mmol/L, base deficit –12.9, anion gap 28 mmol/L  

Renal ultrasound demonstrated normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis and an empty bladder. He was started on continuous veno-venous hemodiafiltration and empirical ciprofloxacin. A CT scan of the abdomen showed bilateral perinephric stranding suggestive of pyelonephritis but was otherwise unremarkable. Investigations for underlying causes of acute renal failure, including autoantibodies, complement levels, and protein electrophoresis, were all within normal limits.

A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman at 26 weeks +3 days of gestation presented with a 1-day history of severe, persistent occipital headache, blurred vision, and 1 week of generalized edema. Her antenatal course had been unremarkable, with no early anatomic scan performed. She denied any family history of hereditary or chromosomal disorders. 

On examination, her blood pressure was 180/120 mmHg, pulse 84/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and she was afebrile. She had a non‐tender 24-week–sized gravid uterus with a positive fetal heart rate, no vaginal bleeding, and 2+ pretibial edema. Neurologic examination was normal. After two doses of intravenous hydralazine, her blood pressure stabilized.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 7300/µL, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, platelets 169,000/µL, and urine protein 2+. Liver enzymes were elevated (SGPT 89 IU/L, SGOT 102 IU/L, ALP 229 IU/L, LDH 288 IU/L). Renal function and oral glucose tolerance were normal.

Obstetric ultrasound demonstrated a single, live intrauterine fetus consistent with 26 weeks of gestation in breech presentation, an amniotic fluid index of 13.4 cm, and an anterior placenta. The cerebral imaging showed a single large ventricle with partially formed midline structures, absent cavum septi pellucidi, and partial falx cerebri formation. The four-chamber heart view and outflow tracts appeared normal.

A 16-year-old boy with known HIV infection presented with a one-month history of skin lesions. He first noticed thickened, hyperkeratotic plaques on the scalp and forehead, which rapidly spread over his entire body without associated pruritus. On admission, there were extensive, generalized, thick, hyperkeratotic, crusting, yellowish papular lesions covering the face (including ear lobes), shoulder blades, trunk, limbs, and back.

He was afebrile (98.8°F) with a pulse rate of 80 beats per minute. He had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis treated with anti-tuberculosis therapy for three years, with poor adherence. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL (normal 12–17)  
• ESR 20 mm/h (normal 0–14)  
• Platelets 144 × 10^9/L (normal 137–367)  
• Leukocytes 18.2 × 10^9/L (normal 3.9–9.4)  
• Lymphocytes 3.7 × 10^9/L (normal 1.2–3.4)  
• CD4 T-cell count 342 cells/μL (normal 350–1411), CD4% 8%  
• ALT 28 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.1 mg/dL  
• Urine creatinine 0.5 mg/dL, blood urea 11 mg/dL
