The initial differential diagnosis included adverse drug reaction, atopic dermatitis, dermatitis herpetiformis, psoriasis, ichthyosis, seborrheic dermatitis, erythroderma, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

A 24-year-old unmarried day laborer presented with a 4-year history of spontaneous episodes of fearfulness, palpitations, shortness of breath, choking sensation, and fear of impending death lasting 10–20 minutes, occurring two to five times per week. One month before presentation, symptom frequency increased and interfered with daily activities. He had no prior psychiatric consultations and no personal or family history of psychiatric illness. He was diagnosed with panic disorder and started on sertraline 25 mg/day for 4 days, then 50 mg/day for 3 weeks. With partial improvement, the dose was increased to 75 mg/day over 2 weeks and then to 100 mg/day. Five days after reaching 100 mg/day, he reported new blackish discoloration over his face. 

Baseline blood tests, thyroid function, and echocardiogram were all normal. He denied any allergy to foods or drugs, recent fever, use of other medications, change in residence or job, or excessive sun exposure. On examination, there was symmetric hyperpigmentation over the malar regions, temples, and nasal ridge. There was no pruritus, macules, papules, discharge, erosion, or ulceration, and no hyperpigmentation elsewhere. Vital signs and the rest of the general physical and systemic examinations were normal. The possibility of a sertraline-related skin reaction was raised, and the patient was referred to dermatology and rheumatology for further evaluation.

A 33-year-old man presented with multiple, edematous, erythematous to greenish, sharply demarcated, indurated plaques with violaceous borders ranging from 3 to 30 cm in diameter on the back, trunk, and upper limbs, recurring over 6 months. He also reported a 1-year history of bronchial asthma. Laboratory studies showed peripheral eosinophilia of 10.5 g/L (normal <0.4 g/L) and an elevated eosinophilic cationic protein level of 297 µg/L (normal <11.3 µg/L). Total IgE was minimally elevated; specific IgE to common allergens and serologic tests for parasitic infections were negative. Tests for antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Molecular studies revealed no JAK2 V617F mutation, no FIP1L1–PDGFRA translocation, and no T-cell–receptor rearrangements in peripheral blood. Pulmonary-function testing showed an obstructive pattern, and chest CT was normal. A lesional skin biopsy demonstrated superficial and deep perivascular as well as diffuse interstitial infiltrates composed predominantly of eosinophils, lymphocytes, and histiocytes, with prominent flame figures surrounding collagen bundles.

A 53-year-old woman underwent a chest CT during a routine health examination. She was asymptomatic, a lifelong non-smoker, and had no history of connective tissue or lymphoproliferative disease. Basic serologic tests were negative. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. 

The initial CT scan showed multiple irregularly shaped part-solid nodules and pure ground-glass nodules predominantly in the subpleural areas of both lower lobes. Part-solid nodules measured up to 12.7 mm, and pure ground-glass nodules measured up to 6.2 mm. 

At 6-month follow-up, the multifocal subsolid nodules persisted, and the largest part-solid nodule in the left lower lobe increased from 10 mm to 15 mm. The differential diagnosis at that time included early lung cancer, organizing pneumonia, and lymphoproliferative disease such as MALT lymphoma. 

An 18F-FDG PET/CT scan demonstrated mild uptake in the largest left lower lobe lesion (maximum SUV 1.8). For diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, the patient underwent a wedge resection of the left lower lobe.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of left-sided throat pain, dysphagia, and odynophagia that she believed followed swallowing a fish bone. The pain, tender to palpation, radiated to her left jaw. She had no prior thyroid symptoms and no significant medical history. On examination, her vital signs were normal. The neck was supple with a full range of motion. There was pinpoint tenderness medial to the left sternocleidomastoid and tender left supraclavicular lymph nodes without enlargement or crepitus. Laboratory studies were notable only for a leukocytosis of 13,100 μL. A CT scan of the neck demonstrated a 2.9 cm × 0.02 cm radiopaque linear structure in the anterior wall of the cervical esophagus at C6–T1, with surrounding air, and an enlarged lymph node adjacent to the left thyroid lobe. Initial esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed slight left-lateral esophageal bulging but no foreign body. A repeat neonatal-scope EGD identified an umbilicated lesion 3 cm proximal to the upper esophageal sphincter; again, no foreign body was found. At this point, the differential diagnosis included a periesophageal abscess from esophageal perforation, an embedded fish bone, inflamed ectopic thyroid tissue, or malignancy.

An 82-year-old man was referred for evaluation of gallbladder wall thickening discovered on abdominal ultrasonography performed for abnormal liver-function tests. He had no abdominal pain or other symptoms. His medical history included hyperlipidemia and a prior right thyroid lobectomy for follicular carcinoma. On examination, vital signs were normal and the abdominal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal liver enzymes, no elevation in inflammatory markers, and normal tumor markers (CEA 1.2 ng/mL, CA 19-9 9.0 U/mL).

Dynamic contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated localized thickening of the gallbladder wall from the body to the fundus with early enhancement and a prolonged contrast effect; there was no pancreatic enlargement, bile duct dilatation, or retroperitoneal fibrosis. MRI showed gallbladder wall thickening on T2-weighted images, high signal on diffusion-weighted images, and early enhancement without intramural cyst-like structures. MRCP revealed no dilatation, stenosis, or irregularity of the bile ducts or pancreatic duct. Endoscopic ultrasonography revealed a smooth, localized thickening of the gallbladder wall (maximum thickness 6 mm) with preservation of the outer hyperechoic layer and laminar internal architecture.

A 38-year-old Afro-Trinidadian woman with known endometriosis, intermittently adherent to oral contraceptive pills, presented with 2 days of acute dyspnea. Her blood pressure was 142/?, heart rate 112/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. On examination, jugular venous pressure was mildly elevated to 10 cm H2O; the right chest was stony dull to percussion; there was no peripheral edema; and she was actively menstruating. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia with an incomplete right bundle branch block, right ventricular hypertrophy, and subtle secondary ST-T changes. Chest radiography revealed a large right pleural effusion with mild perihilar vascular congestion. Laboratory studies showed a D-dimer of 208 ng/dL (normal ≤500), pro–BNP 323 pg/mL (normal ≤300), troponin I 0.08 ng/mL (normal 0.0–0.15), and arterial blood gas consistent with mild hypoxia and an alveolar–arterial gradient of 14 mm Hg on 24% FiO2. CT-guided thoracentesis yielded a hemorrhagic exudative effusion that recurred within 48 hours. Video-assisted thoracoscopic pleural biopsy revealed endometrial tissue, consistent with catamenial pleural effusions. The patient reported dyspnea that often coincided with her menses. During hospitalization, she developed persistent shortness of breath and an episode of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Transthoracic echocardiography showed preserved left ventricular function with moderate right heart enlargement, septal flattening, and an estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 45 mm Hg. Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated an intact interatrial septum with an agitated saline “bubble” study but incompletely visualized pulmonary veins.

A 77-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of sharp right-sided groin pain, decreased urine output, and a new right-sided groin lump. He noted that the swelling and pain were more prominent when standing and that the lump receded spontaneously when lying down. He reported one week of diarrhea without vomiting and denied fever. His medical history included chronic kidney disease and a recent episode of cystitis treated 4 weeks earlier. One year before presentation, he underwent transurethral resection of the prostate for benign prostatic hyperplasia, complicated postoperatively by urinary retention requiring insertion of a permanent suprapubic catheter. On examination, the right inguinal region was swollen and tender; the mass was reducible and had a pronounced cough impulse both when the patient stood upright and lay down. There was no scrotal or perineal swelling, erythema, or discrete scrotal mass. Laboratory studies showed serum sodium 129 mmol/L, serum creatinine 168 μmol/L (baseline 104 μmol/L), and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 33 ml/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis was positive for leukocytes and blood. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed an incarcerated right indirect inguinal hernia containing omental fat and a portion of the urinary bladder passing into the scrotum.

A 37-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with continuous chest pain for two hours. She denied dyspnea, syncope, or prior similar episodes. There was no personal or family history of cardiovascular or thromboembolic disease. Vital signs were: pulse 110/min, blood pressure 100/65 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 37 °C, oxygen saturation 95% on room air (99% on 2 L/min nasal cannula). Cardiac auscultation was normal, and neck veins were not distended. Initial ECG showed sinus rhythm with 2 mm of ST-segment elevation in leads V2 and V3. She was given aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous heparin and taken to the catheterization laboratory. Twenty minutes later, a second ECG showed a new right bundle branch block and resolution of the precordial ST-segment elevations. Forty-five minutes after presentation, coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries without stenosis. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated right ventricular dilatation and an estimated pulmonary arterial pressure of 60 mmHg.

A 4-month-old female infant was referred to the otolaryngology service with bilateral nasal stents in place, which had been inserted at another center for relief of nasal airway obstruction. On examination, silastic stents protruded from both nares, and there was partial absence of the nasal septum on anterior inspection. Previous CT images of the nasal cavity and brain were obtained and reviewed. Axial CT of the nasal cavity showed a narrowed pyriform aperture measuring 5.4 mm, with mild medial angulation of the nasal processes of the maxilla. A single central mega-incisor was also noted. CT of the brain demonstrated no intracranial abnormalities.

An 84-year-old overweight woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and osteoporosis was taking levothyroxine, metformin, linagliptin, losartan, indapamide, pregabalin, calcitriol, and denosumab. One month before admission, her sodium level was normal. She presented with anginal chest pain and two epileptic seizures. On exam, blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, heart rate 85 bpm, jugular venous pressure was normal, there was no peripheral oedema, and heart sounds were normal. Laboratory tests showed a serum sodium of 119 mmol/L, NT-proBNP 53 175 pg/mL, and high-sensitivity troponin I 1657 ng/L; complete blood count, liver and renal function, thyroid function, and cortisol were normal. The initial ECG showed sinus rhythm without ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities. Cranial CT was unremarkable. She received 60 mL of 20% saline in 500 mL of 0.9% saline at 1 mL/kg/h, with gradual correction of sodium to >130 mmol/L over 48 hours. Approximately 48 hours after admission, repeat ECG showed anatomically heterogeneous ST–T wave changes, including ST-segment elevations in the anterolateral and inferior leads (Wellens Type B). She was transferred to the coronary care unit, and urgent coronary angiography showed no significant coronary artery stenosis.

A 53-year-old Sri Lankan man with a 14-year history of diabetes and hypertension presented with a 7-month history of progressive swelling of his left (non-dominant) hand. The swelling involved both volar and dorsal aspects of the wrist and carpal region, was associated with mild pain and restriction of movement, and was not preceded by trauma. He denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, cough, or prior tuberculosis exposure. His appetite and weight were unchanged.

On examination, there was a non-warm, mildly tender swelling around the left wrist; flexion, extension, and circumduction were reduced. Distal neurovascular status was intact. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 98 mm/hr; complete blood count and other biochemistry were normal. A chest radiograph was unremarkable.

Plain radiographs of the left hand revealed destructive lytic lesions in the carpal bones and the bases of the second through fifth metacarpals, with sparing of the radiocarpal and distal radioulnar joints. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated multiple destructive lesions in the carpal bones, surrounding focal fluid collections, and narrowing of the intercarpal and carpometacarpal joints; the flexor muscle tendons were intact.

Upon initial assessment with these basic investigations and imaging, a conclusive diagnosis was not achieved.

An 18-year-old man from Gorgora, Ethiopia, with no prior medical history presented with one week of progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, palpitations, bilateral leg swelling, a cough producing blood-tinged sputum, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. One week before these symptoms, he had developed left knee swelling with high-grade fever. Three days before admission, he noted decreased urine output with reddish discoloration. Two months earlier he had a self-healed penetrating foot injury. He denied intravenous drug use and any recent dental, genitourinary, or gastrointestinal procedures.

On examination he was febrile, in cardiopulmonary distress, and hypoxemic. Respiratory findings included bronchial breath sounds and signs of right pleural effusion. Cardiovascular findings were elevated jugular venous pressure, a displaced apical impulse, and a tricuspid regurgitation murmur. He had tender hepatomegaly and a spleen palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. Musculoskeletal exam revealed a swollen, tender right knee. Additional findings included palmar pallor, dark patches on the lateral left foot, clubbing, and peripheral edema. He was diagnosed with acute decompensated heart failure and severe multilobar pneumonia and admitted to the ICU for diuretics and intravenous antibiotics.

Chest radiography showed a homogeneous opacity in the right hemithorax. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 32 200/µL, hemoglobin of 5 g/dL, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 159 mm/hr, blood urea nitrogen of 190 mg/dL, creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL, and microscopic hematuria on urinalysis. A rapid HIV test was negative.

A 64‐year‐old man presented with several days of right iliac fossa pain. He denied vomiting, constipation, or weight loss. His surgical history included a laparotomy for abdominal trauma in 1987; no operative records were available. On examination, he was febrile, and a midline laparotomy scar was noted. The abdomen was diffusely tender, most pronounced in the right iliac fossa, with no palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed an inflammatory syndrome. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed signs of appendicular peritonitis and a bulky, well‐defined tumoral lesion in the right upper quadrant, with heterogeneous density and enhancement, located adjacent to the liver and the abdominal wall, without any apparent communication with hollow organs.

A 53-year-old man presented with low back pain and bilateral radicular leg pain worsening over the past month. He had no respiratory symptoms and his general condition was good. His medical history was significant for osseous hydatosis since age 30, with three prior surgical interventions for the disease. On examination, there was tenderness over the lumbar spine and a slightly warm, painful, tumor-like mass in the right hemipelvis without erythema. Straight leg–raising was positive bilaterally. He had motor and sensory deficits, muscle atrophy, and gait disturbance. 

Plain radiographs of the right femur showed advanced lytic bone destruction centered in the proximal two thirds of the femur, with evidence of intramedullary nailing from prior surgery. A pelvic radiograph revealed marked mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions in the right hemipelvis. Whole-body bone scintigraphy demonstrated multiple foci of increased radiotracer uptake in the lower lumbar spine, left sacroiliac region, and right knee, along with soft-tissue bulging in the right hemipelvis and a displaced, deformed right femur. A chest radiograph was normal.

A 50-year-old man presented with a progressively enlarging, tender swelling over the right scapular area for 2 months. He had no history of trauma. Four months earlier, he had a similar anterior shoulder swelling that spontaneously drained, forming a sinus that later healed; on presentation he had a new axillary sinus draining pus. There was marked wasting of shoulder musculature and decreased range of motion. He reported evening fevers, weight loss, and anorexia; he had no known tuberculosis exposure. Initial laboratory tests showed elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and white-cell count. Radiographs of the right shoulder revealed destruction of the humeral head with sequestrum formation and generalized osteopenia. Ultrasound demonstrated a 10.0×4.4×8.8 cm hypoechoic collection with multiple internal foci overlying the infraspinatus muscle, and a separate 1.7×1.4×1.2 cm hypoechoic collection in the right axilla tracking to the skin. MRI confirmed a moderate-sized subcutaneous abscess over the infraspinatus communicating with the glenohumeral joint, complete destruction of the humeral head, marked osteolysis, and marrow edema, consistent with infective arthritis of the shoulder and associated abscess formation.

A 59-year-old Haitian woman with biopsy-confirmed dermatomyositis on prednisone 30 mg daily for six months presented with a two-month history of a painful, non-healing tongue ulcer and a four-month history of progressive right shoulder pain. Four months earlier, a shoulder radiograph was unremarkable; a recent outpatient MRI was “suspicious for septic arthritis of the right acromioclavicular joint,” prompting admission. The tongue lesion began after a bite, expanded over two months despite full courses of acyclovir and famciclovir, and was foul-smelling with white exudate. She had traveled to Haiti one year ago and denied fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, cough, or other systemic symptoms.  
On exam: T 100.3 °F, HR 120 bpm, BP 135/65 mmHg, RR 18, SpO₂ 98% on room air; heliotrope rash, shawl sign, Gottron’s papules; a tender 3×3 cm fungating ulcer with indurated borders on the left lateral tongue; a 1 cm mobile left anterior cervical lymph node; clear lungs; painful, mildly effused right shoulder with limited motion.  
Labs: WBC 7.0×10³/µL (86% neutrophils, 10% lymphocytes), normal chemistries, HbA₁c 11.1%, HIV negative.  
A tongue biopsy showed extensive ulceration with granulation tissue and noncaseating granulomas. AFB stain of the tissue was positive for mycobacteria; Periodic acid-Schiff stain was negative for other microorganisms. A routine chest radiograph then revealed diffuse micronodular densities.

A 54-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a seven-month history of progressive headache and episodic memory deficits. In the days before admission, he developed abnormal speech, episodes of disorientation, right-sided weakness, and an unstable gait. On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 13; he was slightly disoriented and had right hemiparesis, anomia, and motor aphasia. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a lesion suggestive of a mass in the left parietal lobe, involving periventricular white matter and the semioval center, with extension into the right temporal and ipsilateral occipital lobes and left cerebellar parenchyma; there was leptomeningeal enhancement and bilateral hemorrhagic areas, predominantly in the left hemisphere. MR angiography showed multiple segmental areas of thinning in the middle cerebral artery and anterior cerebral artery, compatible with a vasculitic process.

Laboratory studies demonstrated a normal complement (C3 148 mg/dL, C4 39.5 mg/dL), C-reactive protein 1.91 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 2 mm/h. Tests for carcinoembryonic antigen, syphilis serology, and HIV were negative. IgG and IgM anticardiolipin antibodies; p- and c-ANCA; antinuclear antibodies; anti–La; anti–Ro; anti-Sm; anti-RNP; and anti-DNA antibodies were all negative. Chest radiography, abdominal ultrasonography, and abdominal CT were unremarkable.

A 36-year-old gravida 1, para 1 woman presented with a 1-day history of acute lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Her menstrual cycles were regular; the last menstrual period was 5 weeks earlier. On examination, she was pale but hemodynamically stable (BP 110/60 mm Hg; pulse 64 /min; T 37.1 °C); the abdomen was tender in the lower quadrants with mild peritoneal signs, and speculum exam showed a small amount of vaginal bleeding. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 10.1 g/dl, hematocrit 29.0%, a positive urine pregnancy test, and serum hCG 1149 mIU/ml. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a large amount of complex free fluid and echogenic debris in the pelvis, without a visible intrauterine gestational sac; the ovaries were not well visualized. During hospitalization, she developed dizziness, pallor, hypotension (BP 80/50 mm Hg), tachycardia (pulse 110 /min), and worsening peritoneal signs. She underwent emergency laparoscopy, which revealed approximately 1800 ml of hemoperitoneum. After suctioning, active bleeding was identified from the peritoneal surface of the pouch of Douglas; the uterus, both ovaries, and fallopian tubes appeared grossly normal without adhesions. Bleeding was controlled by excisional biopsy and electrocoagulation.

A 50-year-old man with no previous medical history was admitted after being found unresponsive at home. On arrival, he was confused (GCS 11), hypotensive, mottled in the legs, and hypoperfused. Initial labs showed extreme hyperglycaemia (unrecordable), ketones 3.6 mmol/L, lactic acidosis, acute kidney injury (urea 41.3 mmol/L, creatinine 277 µmol/L, eGFR 21 mL/min), hypernatraemia (Na 172 mmol/L), elevated CRP rising from 53 to 374 mg/L over 5 days, and a normal white cell count. He tested positive for SARS-CoV-2, developed respiratory failure requiring intubation and haemofiltration, and had findings of pulmonary aspergillosis treated with voriconazole.

One month after admission, he developed acute chest pain. ECG showed anterior ST-segment elevation. Emergency coronary angiography revealed an acute occlusion of the left anterior descending artery and moderate bystander atheroma elsewhere. He underwent primary PCI with a drug-eluting stent and restored TIMI 3 flow. During the procedure he developed acute pulmonary oedema poorly responsive to IV furosemide.  
Bedside transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated moderately impaired left ventricular systolic function with relatively preserved basal segment contraction and an echogenic mass attached to the hypokinetic anteroseptal wall.

A 74-year-old Japanese man underwent carotid ultrasound that incidentally revealed a right thyroid lobe mass. He had a history of cerebral infarction 8 years earlier and no family history of thyroid or immune disorders. Initial fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the mass showed clusters of large atypical cells of varying size, raising suspicion for poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma. On admission, he had no rapid tumor growth, dysphagia, hoarseness, or compressive symptoms. Physical examination revealed diffuse swelling of the right thyroid lobe with a smooth surface and normal consistency, without tenderness, skin changes, or palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, chemistry, and thyroid function, and serum calcitonin, carcinoembryonic antigen, and thyroglobulin levels were within normal limits. Ultrasonography demonstrated several irregular, well-demarcated, lobular low-echoic lesions up to 21 mm in the right lobe, each containing short linear high-echoic spots. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed an irregular mass in the right lobe without mediastinal or pulmonary nodules and noted reactive lymph nodes along the right jugular chain. Repeat FNA revealed normal thyroid follicular cells with abundant lymphocytes and no evidence of malignancy. Given ongoing concern for lymphoma or poorly differentiated carcinoma, right lobectomy was planned.

A 39-year-old parous woman presented with a 6-month history of an umbilical nodule. She reported monthly cyclical pain and bleeding from the site. Three years earlier, she had undergone a laparoscopy-assisted vaginal hysterectomy for symptomatic fibroid uterus; operative notes were unavailable, and both ovaries had been preserved. On examination, there was a 2 × 2 cm purplish nodule at the umbilicus; it was nontender and showed no signs of infection. Transvaginal sonography was normal, with no evidence of ovarian endometriosis.

A 20-year-old previously healthy man presented with a one-week history of a nonpruritic erythematous maculopapular rash that began on the face and spread to the trunk, arms, legs, palms, and soles. He reported headaches, photosensitivity, and intermittent fevers at onset. Initial evaluation, including workup for viral meningitis, was negative, and the rash partially resolved without treatment.  

One month later, he returned with worsening of the same nonpruritic rash, accompanied by neck pain, photophobia, headache, low-back pain, fatigue, anorexia, and fevers up to 102°F. On examination, there were well-defined, nonblanching, confluent targetoid papules and plaques resembling erythema multiforme in various stages of healing, distributed over the torso, back, arms, legs, palms, soles, and lips. New lesions were erythematous; older lesions were darker. Fine scaling was noted on lesions of the forearms and face. There was no mucosal involvement.  

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL  
• Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 75 mm/h, C-reactive protein 11.05 mg/L  
• ANA titer >1:1280 with a speckled pattern  
• Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB titers >8.0  
• Rheumatoid factor 34 IU/mL  
• Lupus anticoagulant positive (>44.4 sec), low-positive anticardiolipin IgM (>13 U/mL), negative β2-glycoprotein antibody  
• Negative anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, anti-Jo-1, anti-centromere, and anti-Scl-70 antibodies  
• Normal serum chemistry and urinalysis  
• Negative serologies for HBV, HCV, HSV-1/2, mycoplasma, EBV, HIV, and parvovirus B19  

A left arm skin biopsy demonstrated vacuolar interface dermatitis and dermal mucin deposition.

A 36-year-old woman with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma presented on day 17 of her sixth cycle of CHOP chemotherapy with a 2-day history of fever (maximum 38.1°C) and nonproductive cough. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed an absolute neutrophil count of 0.6×10^9/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 50 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein level of 12.3 mg/L. A chest radiograph was normal. Initial septic workup was negative, including sputum bacterial culture, sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and culture, bacterial and fungal blood cultures, and urine acid-fast bacilli studies. Because fever persisted, a noncontrast thoracic CT was performed, which showed bilateral patchy ground-glass opacities without zonal predominance.

A 64-year-old man presented with a 6-year history of a chronic, pruritic, occasionally tender rash affecting both ears. Six years earlier, he was diagnosed with eczematous dermatitis and treated with clobetasol 0.05% cream; three years later, he received triamcinolone 0.025% cream for a similar diagnosis. He noted mild relief of itching with topical steroids but recurrent flares within two weeks of discontinuation. He denied contact with irritants or allergens, worsening of symptoms at night, immunosuppression, or systemic symptoms. Personal and family histories were negative for connective tissue disorders, including relapsing polychondritis. 

On examination, there was confluent erythema, fine white scaling, and scattered pustules on the helices and antihelices of both ears, with relative sparing of the lobules and no involvement of the scalp or face. Dermoscopic evaluation of the right antihelix revealed background telangiectasias and follicular, cone-shaped, fine, translucent white scales.

A 48-year-old woman, 1 month after orthotopic liver transplantation for secondary biliary cirrhosis, was taken for exploratory laparotomy due to fever and CT evidence of pneumoperitoneum; no perforation was found, but purulent fluid was cultured. During the procedure, she developed a maculopapular rash and numerous tense bullae across her chest and torso. Her temperature reached 103°F. Laboratory studies showed new pancytopenia: her white-cell count fell from 10.1×10^3/µL to 0.3×10^3/µL and her platelet count from 237×10^3/µL to 47×10^3/µL. A punch biopsy of affected skin showed interface dermatitis with vacuolar changes, necrotic keratinocytes, and an inflammatory infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and scattered eosinophils—a finding noted to be nonspecific for Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis, acute graft-versus-host disease, and bullous erythema multiforme.

A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 10-year history of vulvar pruritus, burning, soreness, stinging, vaginal dryness, and introital dyspareunia. She had been repeatedly treated for presumed vulvar mycosis with topical antifungals without relief. Her medical history included arterial hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and two pregnancies delivered with episiotomy. On examination, the vulvar mucosa was pale and atrophic, with a glistening, u-shaped erythematous halo of the introitus extending from the lower right labia minora to the lower left labia minora, almost encircling the urethral meatus. There was no bleeding, fissuring, excoriation, exudation, or regional lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and urinalysis, were within normal limits. Clinical differential diagnoses included erosive lichen planus, genital psoriasis, lichen sclerosus et atrophicus, and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (Vulvar Intraepithelial Neoplasia III). A skin biopsy was obtained from the erythematous area for histopathological evaluation.

A 56-year-old man presented to the emergency department with sudden severe abdominal pain of 4 hours’ duration. He had no history of abdominal surgery, chronic disease, or regular medications; his only prior operation was on his left shoulder. He did report intermittent bouts of abdominal pain lasting 2–3 days every few months since age 20. On examination, his vital signs were normal. The abdomen was flat, with severe tenderness to palpation, peritoneal signs, and absent bowel sounds. Laboratory tests revealed a leukocyte count of 16.62 × 10^3/µL; other values were within normal limits. A plain abdominal radiograph showed a single dilated loop of small intestine in the lower abdomen. Because of intense pain, a contrast-enhanced CT scan was obtained, demonstrating a 40 mm-diameter fluid-filled small-bowel loop in the lower abdomen that abruptly narrowed at the level of the sacral promontory, transitioning to another 123 mm loop in the left iliac fossa. The mesenteric fat and adjacent bowel wall appeared obliterated, with a small amount of perienteric fluid and findings suggestive of possible ischemia. The patient was taken for surgical intervention.

A 17-year-old male presented with a 3-month history of generalized pruritic eruptions. The lesions began on the neck and then progressed to involve the forehead, scalp, postauricular and preauricular regions, external ears, nasolabial folds, anterior chest, and scapular area. On examination, there were firm, grayish, warty, greasy papules and plaques scattered over these seborrheic regions. Additionally, small flat-topped warty papules were noted on the dorsum of both hands and feet. The oral mucosa appeared normal. The patient denied any family history of similar illness. Routine laboratory investigations were within normal limits. Skin punch biopsies were obtained from a papule on the neck and a papule on the dorsum of the left hand for histopathological examination.

A male neonate was born at 30 weeks’ gestation by urgent cesarean delivery because of an abnormal nonstress test, oligohydramnios, and cerebral blood flow redistribution. The 25-year-old mother had developed severe anemia (hemoglobin 5.0 g/dL) from multiple episodes of vaginal bleeding beginning at 24 weeks’ gestation; she received eight red‐cell transfusions in total. Maternal screening for TORCH infections, parvovirus B19, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis was negative, and the indirect Coombs test was negative. Placental histology showed terminal villous hypotrophy, infarction, and intervillous fibrinoid deposition, consistent with chronic hypoxia.

At birth (weight 1530 g; Apgar scores 1 at 1 minute, improving to 8 by 20 minutes), the neonate required full ventilatory support (FiO₂ 100%). Umbilical pH was 6.97 with a base excess of –12.2 mmol/L. Physical examination revealed a red-violaceous, nonblanching macular rash on the head, neck, and trunk. During the first 24 hours, he developed multiorgan dysfunction (brain, heart, liver, kidneys, lungs) with disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Laboratory tests on day 1 showed platelet count 38×10⁹/L, markedly elevated leukocyte count with 270 nucleated red blood cells (NRBC) per 100 WBC, absolute NRBC 63 558/mm³, reticulocyte count 519×10⁹/L, prolonged prothrombin time (>2 minutes), and elevated D-dimer 9419 ng/mL. C-reactive protein, TORCH and viral serologies, and thrombophilia screening were all negative. Echocardiography demonstrated right ventricular distension, hypokinesis, tricuspid insufficiency, and a bidirectional patent ductus arteriosus. Brain ultrasound revealed edema, periventricular hyperechogenicities, and bilateral porencephalic lesions in the posterior temporal regions.

By day 4, respiratory support was weaned from mechanical ventilation to CPAP, with improving organ function and normalized platelets and coagulation parameters. The cutaneous rash began to fade and had completely resolved by day 7. Serial brain ultrasounds showed persistent porencephalic areas; MRI on day 10 confirmed bilateral parietal, temporal, and occipital porencephalic cysts. The infant was discharged on day 41 in good condition, with mild transient hypotonia and normal growth.

A 61-year-old man with a history of left lingual resection and left anterior cervical lymph node dissection followed by chemoradiotherapy for tongue cancer, and no prior syncope, was transferred two months after surgery for loss of consciousness.  
On admission:  
• Head MRI showed no cerebral infarction or metastatic tumour.  
• Electroencephalography was normal, ruling out epilepsy.  
• Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no structural heart disease.  
While hospitalized, after walking and after urination, he experienced sudden loss of consciousness lasting ∼30 minutes without prodromal symptoms. Continuous monitoring showed sinus arrest with junctional escape beats, followed by sustained sinus bradycardia for ∼20 minutes and concurrent hypotension, with recovery of consciousness as heart rate and blood pressure normalized.  
Orthostatic blood pressure testing (Shellong test) was normal. He was not taking any medications known to cause bradycardia.  
Given his surgical history, three reflex-syncope mechanisms were considered: carotid sinus syndrome, glossopharyngeal neuralgia syndrome, and parapharyngeal space lesions syncope syndrome. Carotid artery massage and cervical rotation–extension examinations revealed no abnormalities, and glossopharyngeal neuralgia was not observed. Therefore, parapharyngeal space lesions syncope syndrome was suspected.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a tender, palpable right breast lump that she first noticed 4 months earlier. She denied fevers, night sweats, cough, recent vaccinations, animal bites, or trauma. On breast examination, there was a firm, tender, mobile 3-cm mass at the 9:00 position, 8 cm from the nipple, without overlying skin changes. Exam of both axillae revealed a single tender node in the right axillary tail; other nodes in both axillae were not enlarged. A diagnostic ultrasound of the breast mass demonstrated an enlarged intramammary lymph node measuring 2.9 cm with cortical thickening up to 7.5 mm, preserved fatty hilum, and maintained oval shape. A second enlarged lymph node with cortical thickening was identified in the right axillary tail. Other imaging of the contralateral axilla was unremarkable. An ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the intramammary node was performed.

An 86-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a history of pulmonary tuberculosis treated in the 1950s, and localized prostate cancer presented with a 3-day history of productive cough, dyspnea, and wheezing. He denied fever, chills, chest pain, night sweats, or weight loss. He had a 40-pack-year smoking history, having quit more than 40 years ago.

On examination, he was afebrile, with normal blood pressure and heart rate but was tachypneic. A large, nonmobile, globular mass was visible under the skin in the left supraclavicular area. Lung auscultation revealed diffuse expiratory wheezing, bilateral basilar crackles, and diminished breath sounds over the left upper lobe. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 20.6×10^3/μL with a left shift and a hemoglobin level of 9.2 g/dL.

A chest radiograph showed a large, partially calcified mass projecting over the left lung apex, measuring approximately 16.5×10.0 cm. Chest CT demonstrated a peripherally calcified soft-tissue mass in the left upper chest wall measuring 9.4×11.8×14.7 cm, with destruction of the first through third ribs.

Differential diagnoses included osteosarcoma, metastatic prostate cancer, mesothelioma, and other mass lesions. A tissue biopsy was deemed necessary to establish a diagnosis.

A 46-year-old Indo-Trinidadian male agriculturist presented with two main complaints: pain in the region of tooth 1.1 and progressive enamel loss on multiple teeth that began three years earlier. He works as a budder and grafter in a citrus nursery and frequently embeds his anterior teeth into oranges and grapefruits to assess flavor. He also regularly consumes a local pickled green fruit (“chow”). He reports intermittent heartburn, self-medicates with omeprazole (20–40 mg daily as needed), and drinks Pilsner beer socially on weekends, with occasional vomiting.

On examination, tooth 1.1 was tender to vertical percussion and to palpation at the root apex, and a fistula was present on the attached mucosa at its apex. A periapical radiograph demonstrated a periradicular radiolucency consistent with pulp necrosis and chronic periradicular periodontitis. Teeth 3.6, 4.6, and 3.8 had been previously extracted. Bitewing radiographs revealed proximal caries on multiple posterior teeth. Generalized supra- and subgingival calculus deposits were noted, and multiple mandibular tori were present.

Intraoral inspection showed moderate to severe loss of enamel and dentin on all remaining teeth except the upper left molars and premolars. Cupped-out occlusal lesions were seen on molars and premolars, especially on the right. The palatal surfaces of maxillary incisors exhibited erosion. The facial surfaces of the upper anterior teeth had erosive lesions from the cervical to middle thirds, with fractured incisal edges and horizontal striations. The lower incisors showed incisal cupping. There were no occlusal contacts in the anterior sextants and right quadrants, resulting in increased interocclusal space.

A 13-month-old boy with a small ventricular septal defect was brought to the emergency department for acute onset of respiratory distress after suspected foreign-body aspiration. He had grabbed a granola bar containing nuts and began choking while walking and laughing. Back blows by family members did not dislodge any nuts. EMS arrived within minutes; the patient was cyanotic but breathing spontaneously, with no visible foreign body in the oropharynx. Bag-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen was initiated en route.

On arrival in the ED, he was in moderate respiratory distress: respiratory rate 52/min, heart rate 171/min, and oxygen saturation 90% on a non-rebreather mask with 100% oxygen. He had noisy breathing but could phonate intermittently with a weak cry. His skin was pale and mottled with cold extremities. Auscultation revealed decreased air entry in both lung fields without wheezes or crackles. Direct laryngoscopy did not reveal a foreign body. Because of worsening distress and desaturation, he was intubated with a 4.0-mm uncuffed endotracheal tube. Intravenous and intraosseous lines were placed, and a normal saline bolus was started.

Initial chest radiograph showed a patchy opacity in the right middle lobe. A repeat radiograph to confirm endotracheal-tube position, obtained 45 minutes later, demonstrated bilateral, diffuse, hazy ground-glass opacities suggestive of pulmonary edema.

A 27-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 0, at 34 weeks and 4 days of gestation presented to the emergency obstetrical department with sudden-onset headache and visual disturbances. The headache was pulsating, beginning occipitally and spreading to the forehead; visual symptoms were described as repetitive flashes of light.  

Her medical history included two prior miscarriages, a laparoscopic ovarian cyst removal, and a laparoscopic appendectomy. During this pregnancy she had insulin-dependent gestational diabetes managed with 22 IU of long-acting insulin (Lantus), with fasting blood glucose of 6.2 mmol/L and a postprandial value of 14.6 mmol/L. First-trimester thyroid screening was normal.

On examination, her blood pressure was elevated; the remainder of her neurological examination was normal. Fetal cardiotocography indicated fetal well-being. Laboratory evaluation ruled out pre-eclampsia, and she was discharged home.  

Over the next two weeks, she returned several times with persistent headaches and ongoing hypertension. At that point, a cranial MRI was ordered to further evaluate her symptoms.

A 15-month-old Caucasian boy was brought with a 6-week history of progressive abdominal distension. He had no renal or gastrointestinal symptoms, and his antenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks was normal. On examination, he appeared unwell, with a pulse of 150 beats per minute and blood pressure of 108/82 mm Hg. His abdomen was distended and tense, with general discomfort on palpation but no peritoneal signs; an ill-defined cystic mass was palpable on the right. Routine hematology, coagulation, biochemistry, C-reactive protein, liver function tests, urinary electrolytes, alpha-fetoprotein, and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin levels were all within normal limits.  
An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large, multiseptated cystic mass containing a small solid nodule, suspected of malignancy; its origin was unclear. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 14.7 × 13.6 × 15.2 cm complex septated cystic mass arising from the peritoneum, with enhancing septae and solid nodules. The right kidney was mildly hydronephrotic, displaced superolaterally, and appeared separate from the mass; the left kidney was normal. No intra-thoracic or abdominal lymphadenopathy was noted. The overall impression was of a teratoma, with a differential diagnosis of mesenchymal hamartoma or a complicated mesenteric cyst.

A 73-year-old woman was referred for mild breathlessness on exertion. She denied chest pain, fluid retention, orthopnoea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Her past history was significant for infra-renal abdominal aortic aneurysm repair 15 years earlier. On examination, she was in atrial fibrillation at 64 bpm, normotensive, and without pedal edema. Cardiovascular examination revealed a significantly elevated jugular venous pressure with systolic V waves, a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge, and a systolic flow murmur in the pulmonary area. Lung fields were clear. A continuous loud bruit was auscultated over the lower abdomen. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anaemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL) with normal liver and renal function tests. The electrocardiogram confirmed rate-controlled atrial fibrillation without ischaemic changes. A chest radiograph demonstrated massive cardiomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left ventricular systolic and diastolic function, severe biatrial and biventricular dilatation, moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation, mild pulmonary hypertension, and no evidence of intracardiac shunting. The cardiac output was 9.8 L/min with a cardiac index of 6.0 L/min/m2.

A 63-year-old man with no prior ophthalmologic history presented with a 3-day history of bilateral foreign-body sensation, redness, and purulent discharge. On examination, visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye. Slit-lamp evaluation showed intense conjunctival hyperemia, a follicular tarsal reaction in both eyes, and significant corneal involvement: in the right eye, a 7×5-mm central epithelial defect with a ring-shaped stromal infiltrate and a grade 2+ anterior chamber reaction; in the left eye, a 2×4-mm epithelial defect with an inferior marginal infiltrate and a grade 1+ anterior chamber reaction. Corneal edema and Descemet’s membrane folds were noted bilaterally; there was no limbal ischemia or visible foreign bodies. Intraocular pressure and fundus examinations were unremarkable. High-resolution anterior segment OCT demonstrated stromal hyperreflectivity and Descemet’s membrane folds without stromal thinning in both eyes. Cultures for bacteria, fungi, and Acanthamoeba were obtained, and empirical therapy was started with hourly fortified vancomycin and ceftazidime drops, daily dexamethasone–chloramphenicol ointment, and oral doxycycline. The following day, the patient’s vision and exam were unchanged. He then reported that 6 days prior he had removed a zoanthid coral from his home aquarium without gloves and had rubbed his eyes afterward; he had no systemic symptoms.

A 60-year-old man with a 9-year history of severe tophaceous gout affecting multiple joints, maintained on colchicine and febuxostat, presented after a syncopal episode and ground-level fall with direct trauma to his right forearm and knee. He was unable to bear weight on the right leg due to knee pain. On admission, hemoglobin was 9.8 g/dL, creatinine 1.29 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase 247 U/L; other blood tests were unremarkable. Radiographs of the right knee showed a lateral tibial plateau fracture through a round radiolucent lesion. A noncontrast CT scan demonstrated an intra-articular fracture extending to both intercondylar spines and a 29 × 27 × 26 mm focal lytic lesion with non-sclerotic “map-like” margins, cortical thinning posteriorly, no periosteal reaction or trabecular edema, and a solid matrix (50–90 HU) without calcifications; severe osteoporosis, diffuse popliteal vascular calcifications, and joint effusion were also noted. Bedside ultrasound revealed diffuse periarticular microcrystalline deposits on the patellar cartilage and menisci without active synovitis. To exclude malignancy, a contrast-enhanced total-body CT showed no macroscopic tumor lesions, and tumor markers with serum free chains and Bence-Jones protein assays were negative. A CT-guided biopsy was scheduled to determine the nature of the lesion.

A 36-year-old South Asian woman with systemic lupus erythematosus complicated by class IV lupus nephritis and hypertension, in clinical remission on prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, hydroxychloroquine, and antihypertensives, received her first dose of intravenous rituximab (375 mg/m2). Ten days later, she presented with one day of spontaneous oral and nasal bleeding and new patchy ecchymoses on her trunk and extremities. She had no other complaints.  
On examination, she had oozing blood from the gums, two blood-filled blisters on the hard palate, blood on the alar nares without crusting, and multiple ecchymotic patches. The spleen tip was palpable. The rest of the examination was unremarkable.  
Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• Platelet count 5 × 10^9/L (150–450)  
• Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL (11–15)  
• White-cell count 6.8 × 10^9/L (4–11)  
• Serum creatinine 98 μmol/L (44–97)  
• Serum albumin 4.03 g/dL  
• INR 0.92 (<1.0)  
• C-reactive protein 0.6 mg/dL (<5.0)  
• Direct Coombs test negative  
Blood smear confirmed severe thrombocytopenia without schistocytes or abnormal cells.

A 43-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 9-day history of a pruritic skin eruption, fever, myalgia, arthralgia, and malaise. Four days before onset, she received her first dose of an inactivated COVID-19 vaccine (CoronaVac). The eruption began as a single pruritic patch on the chest and then became generalized over 9 days, with randomly distributed blanchable erythematous macules, patches, and excoriated papules and plaques on the trunk and extremities, some with reticulate erythema. She also reported fever (38.1 °C), severe myalgia and arthralgia, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. She denied any recent infections, new medications, other vaccinations, or blood transfusions.

Laboratory data revealed leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance and marked elevations of inflammatory markers: ESR 42 mm/hr (normal 4–20), CRP 165.7 mg/L (0–5), ferritin 3210 ng/mL (15–150), and LDH 336 U/L (125–220). Chest radiograph, urinalysis, and serum creatinine were normal. Serologic studies showed an inactive hepatitis B carrier state and absent hepatitis C infection. Blood cultures, SARS-CoV-2 PCR, antinuclear antibodies, and rheumatoid factor were negative. Complement levels (C3c and C4) and anti–C1q antibodies were normal/negative.

A biopsy of a lesional skin site showed superficial perivascular and interstitial inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes, neutrophils, nuclear debris, and erythrocyte extravasation. No fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls was present.

A 72-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of anorexia, asthenia, intermittent abdominal pain, general weakness, and a 10-kg weight loss. Her weight was 45 kg. On examination, there was a 15-cm, mildly tender, hard, immobile mass in the upper abdomen without muscular defense or rebound. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 8490/mm^3 with neutrophilia, hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, and C-reactive protein 12.26 mg/L; alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and CA 19-9 were normal. Serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and syphilis were negative; CMV and EBV IgG were positive with negative IgM. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy disclosed a hiatal hernia; colonoscopy revealed an infiltrative-appearing lesion at the hepatic flexure and proximal transverse colon, resembling neoplasia, and diverticula in the left colon. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 17.5 × 12 × 6 cm heterogeneously enhancing solid mass involving the colonic hepatic angle and proximal transverse colon with effaced margins and invasion of the abdominal wall musculature; no regional lymphadenopathy or distant lesions were seen. Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy revealed well-differentiated adipocytes, spindle cells with slight atypia, rare mitoses, and no necrosis. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse Vimentin expression, S100 positivity in adipocytes, and nuclear MDM2 positivity in spindle cells and some adipocytes, leading to a diagnosis of well-differentiated liposarcoma. Six weeks later, she developed a palpable, erythematous periumbilical skin lesion, and MRI confirmed the known mass with extension into the anterior abdominal wall and overlying skin involvement.

A previously healthy 9-year-old boy fell from a second-story balcony and sustained multiple injuries. On arrival in the emergency department, he was tachycardic, hypertensive, and had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6. Head CT demonstrated a 9-mm right subdural hematoma with subfalcine and impending transtentorial herniation and displaced skull fractures through the occipital, bilateral parietal, and right temporal bones. CT of the thorax revealed bilateral pulmonary consolidations consistent with aspiration and a left clavicular fracture. 

Within 30 minutes of arrival, a CBC with differential showed a WBC count of 32.3×10^9/L (reference 4.5–11×10^9/L), an absolute neutrophil count of 18.8×10^9/L, an absolute lymphocyte count of 10.0×10^9/L (age-specific lymphocytosis cutoff 6.5×10^9/L), a monocyte count of 2.9×10^9/L, an eosinophil count of 0.5×10^9/L, and a basophil count of 0.2×10^9/L. 

Peripheral-blood smear review showed predominantly small lymphocytes and neutrophilia; large granular lymphocytes were present but not increased. Flow cytometric immunophenotyping demonstrated that lymphocytes comprised 36% of white cells, with 18% CD19+ B cells, 41% CD3+ T cells (CD4:CD8 ratio 1.8), and 27% CD3– CD56+ and/or CD57+ natural killer cells. No monoclonal B-cell or immunophenotypically abnormal T-cell population was identified.

A 17-year-old boy of Congolese origin presented with a 6-month history of progressive upper-limb tremors on action—such as lifting a glass, bringing his hand to his mouth, and during writing—and difficulty with distance vision. He is the second of three siblings from a dizygotic twin pregnancy; his twin sister is in apparent good health. There was no perinatal illness or early childhood history, and no known consanguinity. Parents noted growth arrest in weight and height since age 10–11, unlike his twin. 

On examination, his weight was 30 kg, height 143 cm, head circumference 52 cm (BMI 14.6), with secondary sexual characteristics at Tanner stage P5/G5 and slight bilateral ptosis. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed visual acuity 2/10 in both eyes and left macular degeneration. Neurologically, he was alert and oriented, with no resting tremor, but had an action tremor on finger–nose testing and during writing causing dysgraphia. Gait was normal, and there was no dysdiadochokinesia or nystagmus.

Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced helical CT of the brain revealed bilateral calcifications of the caudate heads, putamen, and globus pallidi; symmetric hypodensities of subcortical white matter adjacent to the occipital horns bridging the splenium and extending through the midbrain and pons into the cerebellar hemispheres; and moderate bulbar–pontine atrophy with enlarged basal cisterns. Laboratory studies showed normal serum calcium (9.1 mg/dL) and phosphate (4.8 mg/dL), negative VDRL, Toxoplasma IgG 2.2 and IgM 0.5, weakly positive antinuclear antibodies, and normal thyroid hormones and cortisol. 

In view of the failure to thrive, progressive cerebellar syndrome, and intracerebral calcifications, a diagnosis of Rajab-type cerebral calcification was considered pending genetic testing.

A 34-year-old man was referred for incessant, narrow-QRS tachycardia and symptoms of congestive heart failure; echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25%. He had intermittent episodes over several years that were resistant to verapamil, flecainide, propafenone, and sotalol; adenosine did not terminate the tachycardia. A 12-lead ECG showed a rate of 200 beats/min, atrioventricular dissociation, and onset after two normally conducted sinus beats, with subtle QRS changes (lower R-wave in V1, loss of Q waves in V5–V6, slight leftward axis shift) consistent with right-to-left septal activation.

An electrophysiological study used multipolar catheters in the coronary sinus, His-bundle region, right ventricular septum, and apex. In sinus rhythm, AH and HV intervals were 65 ms and 55 ms, respectively; during tachycardia (cycle length, 310 ms), the HV interval was 50 ms, and His electrograms preceded each QRS. His activation was proximal-to-distal in sinus rhythm but simultaneous on proximal and distal electrodes during tachycardia. Atrial activation was dissociated. Tachycardia could not be initiated by atrial stimulation but was incessant and was repeatedly terminated by premature ventricular beats (PVBs) or overdrive ventricular pacing.

To differentiate narrow-QRS tachycardias with ventriculoatrial dissociation, single PVBs were delivered from the right ventricular apex and septum during tachycardia. Late-coupled PVBs introduced when the His bundle was refractory advanced the next His electrogram and reset the tachycardia. Progressive shortening of the PVB coupling interval produced reset with progressive fusion on surface ECG, demonstrating ventricular involvement in the circuit. Overdrive pacing from the right ventricular apex entrained the tachycardia with progressive fusion and postpacing intervals < tachycardia cycle length + 115 ms. Programmed stimulation from the anterosuperior right ventricular septum showed that premature beats from the para-Hisian area captured the His bundle and reset the tachycardia with a QRS similar to sinus rhythm, whereas very late coupled PVBs delivered distally after right bundle branch activation reset the tachycardia with concealed fusion on the surface ECG.

A 2-year-old neutered male Boxer (32 kg) was referred for evaluation of a recent change in a known heart murmur, fever, and lethargy. He had a history of a mild (2/6) left basilar systolic murmur due to subaortic stenosis (SAS) without progression on serial echocardiograms. Five days before referral, he developed lethargy and fever and was presumptively treated for immune-mediated thrombocytopenia with prednisolone and vincristine. Three days into immunosuppressive therapy, his condition worsened and the murmur changed.

On presentation, he was depressed and febrile (39.8 °C). Cardiac auscultation revealed a loud (4/6) left basilar to-and-fro murmur. Heart rate was 56 beats/min with regular rhythm and bounding femoral pulses. The rest of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed severe leukocytosis (55 × 10^9/L) with neutrophilia (45 × 10^9/L) and a left shift.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild left atrial and ventricular enlargement with hyperdynamic systolic function. Multiple fluttering vegetative lesions were seen on all aortic valve cusps (largest 5.5 × 10 mm). Color Doppler showed turbulent antegrade systolic flow across the aortic valve (peak 6 m/s) and mild diastolic aortic insufficiency. A large (23 × 35 mm), hyperechoic periannular mass extended toward the right heart, involving the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve, which was thickened and irregular. Within the mass was a tangled fistulous tract. Color Doppler demonstrated a turbulent jet from the aortic root into the right ventricle through two openings with a high-velocity (3.7 m/s), diastolic, left-to-right shunt. Concurrent ECG monitoring revealed third-degree atrioventricular block with nonconducted P waves and mild mitral and tricuspid regurgitation.

A 15-year-old female with no prior medical history presented with a 1-day history of substernal, pleuritic chest pain. She awoke with chest discomfort and shortness of breath, then developed fever, chills, diaphoresis, and transient facial and ankle swelling. She denied sore throat, rash, vomiting, or diarrhea. In the ED her blood pressure was 180/70 mm Hg; other vital signs were normal. Examination showed clear lungs, no murmurs, normal peripheral pulses, no hepatosplenomegaly, and no edema. There was mild erythema of the tonsillar pillars without exudate. Initial labs demonstrated a high-sensitivity troponin-T of 16 ng/L (normal < 11 ng/L), a BNP of 5901 pg/mL (normal < 125 pg/mL), and urinalysis with >50 RBC/hpf and 30 mg/dL protein. A rapid strep swab was positive. On admission her blood pressure normalized to 125/72 mm Hg. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. Chest radiograph revealed trace pleural effusions and bilateral interstitial opacities concerning for pulmonary edema. Cardiology performed an echocardiogram showing significant bilateral pleural effusions with a structurally normal heart. Initial differential considerations included viral myocarditis, pericarditis, and atypical nephritic syndrome.

A 73-year-old woman from the northeast of Brazil was brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset chest and neck pain accompanied by a decreased level of consciousness. She reported a 6-month history of anorexia and a 15-kg weight loss. Her medical history included systemic hypertension, severe mitral insufficiency, pulmonary hypertension (pulmonary artery systolic pressure, 60 mmHg on echocardiography 5 months earlier), and congestive heart failure. She was a former smoker with exposure to wood-burning–stove smoke. Home medications were furosemide, carvedilol, losartan, aspirin, hydralazine, isosorbide mononitrate, and simvastatin. She denied fever.  
On examination, she was torpid (Glasgow coma scale score, 9), dyspneic, and pale. Vital signs were blood pressure 60/40 mmHg, heart rate 130 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and delayed capillary refill. Cardiovascular examination revealed a systolic thrill and a pansystolic murmur at the mitral area. Pulmonary auscultation disclosed rhonchi and wheezing. Neurologic examination showed no focal deficits. Abdominal and extremity examinations were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL, hematocrit 23%, platelet count 96,000/mm3, C-reactive protein 131 mg/L, lactate 18.2 mEq/L, troponin I 0.21 ng/mL, and CK-MB 0.18 ng/mL. Urinalysis revealed 220,000 leukocytes/mm3, >1,000,000 red blood cells/mm3, proteinuria, and no casts or crystals.  
Chest radiography demonstrated a normal cardiac silhouette, signs of pulmonary congestion, and a possible focus of pulmonary infection. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm, left atrial overload, a QRS axis of 0°, and ST-segment depression with T-wave inversion in leads V4–V6, DI, and aVL.  
The patient was treated empirically with ceftriaxone and clarithromycin. She remained hypotensive despite saline infusion and increasing doses of norepinephrine and died on hospital day 1.

A 44-year-old previously healthy man presented to the emergency department with a 7-day history of fever, myalgias, dry cough, and mild odynophagia. He had self-medicated with acetaminophen, brompheniramine, caffeine with ascorbic acid, and levodropropizine. On day 4, he developed a pruritic rash on the trunk and groin, which transiently improved after intramuscular clemastine; he was discharged on oral hydroxyzine. 

Three days later, he returned with worsening symptoms, including severe odynophagia, a generalized pruritic rash, hoarseness, fever, dyspnea, and persistent dry cough. On examination, he was anxious and febrile (38 °C), hemodynamically stable, and had a peripheral oxygen saturation of 100% on room air. There was no tonsillar hypertrophy or pharyngeal inflammation, and no cervical lymphadenopathy. A hypersensitivity reaction was suspected, and he received intramuscular clemastine, intravenous hydrocortisone, and lysine acetylsalicylate. Two hours later, dyspnea and rash persisted, and fever remained. 

Laboratory studies showed neutrophilia without eosinophilia and a C-reactive protein level of 8.55 mg/dL (normal < 0.50 mg/dL). A chest radiograph was normal. He was diagnosed with a viral infection with bacterial over-infection and an associated hypersensitivity reaction and was discharged on azithromycin, paracetamol, and prednisolone.

A 6-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of worsening dry cough, episodes of nonbloody vomiting, and intermittent abdominal pain, particularly at night. Over the previous 6 months, he had received serial packed-cell transfusions for anemia, with transient improvement in hemoglobin. He had been asymptomatic until earlier that year. There was no family history of similar illness. 

On examination, temperature was 37.2 °C, pulse 88 beats/min, blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. He appeared pale. Findings included mesomelia of the arms, low-set ears, multiple hyperpigmented macules on the trunk, microcephaly, microphthalmos, and hypoplastic thumbs bilaterally; both testicles were undescended. The abdomen was soft and nontender. Developmental milestones were normal for age.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL, red-cell count 2.87 million/µL, hematocrit 21.8%, red-cell distribution width 20%, total leukocyte count 4930 cells/mm^3, and platelet count 86,000/µL. Serum alanine aminotransferase was 71.7 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 66.6 IU/L, and C-reactive protein 17.2 mg/L; electrolytes and renal function were normal. Urinalysis revealed glycosuria, aminoaciduria, and low bicarbonate.

Renal ultrasonography demonstrated a dilated right calyceal system and absence of the left kidney consistent with congenital agenesis. A radiograph of the forearms showed bilateral radial hypoplasia.

A previously healthy 13-year-old girl was referred to the emergency department with altered consciousness, drowsiness, and generalized seizures. Ten days earlier she had an upper respiratory infection accompanied by fever and headache. She was intubated for airway protection and placed on mechanical ventilation due to persistent altered mental status and seizure activity. On examination she opened her eyes to painful stimuli, had symmetric and reactive pupils, brisk deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar responses.

Arterial blood gas and serum chemistry were notable for pH 7.45, PCO2 26 mmHg, HCO3– 18.7 mmol/L, Na 142 meq/L, K 4.2 meq/L, Cl 115 meq/L, Mg 2 mg/dL, glucose 110 mg/dL, WBC 15 380/µL (70% neutrophils), Hb 11 g/dL, platelets 188×10³/µL, ESR 60 mm/h, and CRP 3 mg/dL. Oxygen saturation was 99% on ventilator settings.

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed protein 40 mg/100 mL, glucose 65 mg/100 mL, and WBC count 3/µL. CSF cultures were negative, and PCR for herpes simplex virus was negative.

Noncontrast head CT on admission was unremarkable. Forty-eight hours later, CT revealed widespread symmetric hypodense areas in the bilateral frontal, temporal, and occipital lobes, involving both cortex and subcortical white matter, without evidence of hemorrhage.

For seizure control, phenytoin and levetiracetam were administered. Empiric ceftriaxone and acyclovir were started for presumed herpetic meningoencephalopathy. Episodes of elevated intracranial pressure—manifested by bradycardia, hypertension, and pupillary dilation—were treated with increased sedation and 3% sodium chloride. After two weeks of this management, there was no improvement in her neurologic status.

A 53-year-old woman was treated for a urinary tract infection with nitrofurantoin, 100 mg twice daily. Two doses after starting the antibiotic, she noted redness and irritation over her left breast. She denied any sun exposure to the area or changes in other medications.  

Her only known allergy is hives to dye contrast. On examination, her vital signs were stable. There was a sharply demarcated erythematous and excoriated rash confined to the left breast.  

Her oncologic history is significant for poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the left breast diagnosed in December 2010. She underwent neoadjuvant carboplatin, paclitaxel, and anthracycline chemotherapy, followed by lumpectomy with axillary-node dissection in May 2011, and adjuvant whole-breast radiation totaling 6040 cGy in 33 fractions over 6 weeks. She tolerated the radiation well, with only mild erythema at the time.

A 36-year-old man with a 20–pack-year smoking history presented with a 6-month history of chronic cough, intermittent shortness of breath, generalized body aches, and sore throat. He denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, sinusitis, epistaxis, ocular symptoms, ulcers, haematuria, or urinary changes. Multiple courses of oral antibiotics over this period had provided no lasting improvement. A chest radiograph showed bilateral patchy lung opacities and he was treated as atypical pneumonia with oral piperacillin/tazobactam, but his symptoms worsened.

He returned with new-onset haemoptysis, a non-pruritic petechial rash over the lower extremities, and migratory joint pains of the wrists and interphalangeal joints with swelling but no redness or morning stiffness. On examination, he was afebrile, appeared pale, and was continuously coughing but not dyspnoeic at rest. Oxygen saturation was 94% on room air. There was a non-blanching petechial rash on both lower limbs and mild pitting oedema. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral decreased air entry and basal crackles; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed microcytic anaemia (haemoglobin 10 g/dL), normal leukocyte count, and normal renal and liver function. Inflammatory markers were elevated (ESR 120 mm/hour, CRP 251.0 mg/dL). Rheumatoid factor was 648 IU/mL. Cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) was 139.3 U/mL; perinuclear ANCA (p-ANCA) was negative. Antinuclear antibodies were negative. Urinalysis revealed microscopic haematuria without proteinuria or casts.

Chest CT demonstrated bilateral multifocal areas of consolidation with surrounding ground-glass opacities and scattered pulmonary nodules, some of which were cavitated. Bronchoscopy revealed inflamed, nodular-appearing mucosa with blood-streaked secretions and active bleeding on bronchoalveolar lavage from the right upper and middle lobes; cultures were negative. A lung biopsy was not obtained due to ongoing bleeding.

A 39-year-old Indian man presented with 2 weeks of epigastric pressure, pruritus, acholic stools, diarrhea, and jaundice. He denied fevers or chills and had no tobacco or alcohol use or family history of pancreatic cancer. Medications included only a multivitamin and chamomile tea. On examination, he had scleral icterus. Laboratory studies showed AST 191 U/L, ALT 550 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 444 U/L, total bilirubin 12.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 11.3 mg/dL, lipase 351 U/L, and a normal CA 19-9 level. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic lobular mass in the head of the pancreas measuring 6.7 × 4.0 × 3.7 cm, a 10-mm common bile duct, and a distended gallbladder. Contrast-enhanced MRI with MRCP demonstrated enlargement of the pancreatic head and uncinate process (5.0 × 4.1 cm) with occlusion and tapering of the common bile duct within the pancreatic head and obstruction of the pancreatic duct. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a diffusely enlarged pancreas, especially in the head and neck region, with a normal, non-dilated pancreatic duct measuring 1.6 mm and no focal mass lesion.

A 50-year-old man presented with acute anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. In the emergency department, his complete blood count, including a platelet count of 265 × 10^9/L, was normal. He had no history of bleeding disorders, hematologic or renal disease, or prior heparin exposure. He received 300 mg of aspirin, 600 mg of clopidogrel, and 10 000 IU of unfractionated heparin, then underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention. Coronary angiography revealed a totally occluded left anterior descending artery with a large, fresh thrombus after predilatation. Tirofiban was administered intracoronarily at 10 μg/kg, followed by an intravenous infusion at 0.15 μg/kg/min, and a 4.5 × 18 mm bare-metal stent was placed. He was maintained on aspirin, clopidogrel, enoxaparin, and tirofiban infusion. Approximately 4 hours after PCI, petechiae and ecchymoses appeared around the sternum and on both legs. His platelet count was 5 × 10^9/L. Peripheral-blood smear showed an extensive lack of platelets without evidence of platelet clumping. All antiplatelet agents, including tirofiban, were immediately discontinued.

A previously healthy 10-year-old girl presented with progressive pain of the left knee of eight weeks’ duration. Three weeks after sustaining a superficial skin abrasion to the left knee while trampoline jumping, she walked 35 km over three days; thereafter she had moderate, mainly nocturnal knee pain without swelling, redness, or fever. Initial radiographs were reported as normal, and she was treated with NSAIDs with minimal relief. Eight weeks after symptom onset, examination revealed pain on active extension of the leg without other abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 8.75×10^3/μL (normal 5.5–13.5), an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 19 mm/h (normal 1–10), and an antistreptolysin-O titer of 352 IU/mL (<200). Repeat radiographs and MRI demonstrated a 1.5-cm osteolytic lesion of the patella with central necrosis. Five days later, she returned with increased pain and new prepatellar swelling and warmth; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate had risen to 61 mm/h and the C-reactive protein to 9.3 mg/dL (normal <1.1). A CT scan showed a 2.0×1.1×1.0 cm osteolytic lesion of the patella with ventral cortical destruction. She was then referred for further evaluation.

A 21-year-old woman with no significant medical history except childhood mumps presented with six days of fever up to 38 °C, loss of appetite, headache, and acute confusion. On arrival she was febrile (39.9 °C), tachycardic (128 bpm), tachypneic (24 breaths/min), and hypertensive (130/81 mmHg), with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of E3V1M1. She had no neck stiffness or focal neurologic deficits, but tonic-clonic seizures lasting several minutes were observed.  

Laboratory studies showed WBC count 11 530/µl with 23% atypical lymphocytes, CRP 3.34 mg/L, AST 116 IU/L, ALT 183 IU/L, and IL-6 10.3 pg/ml. SARS-CoV-2 RNA and influenza A/B antigen tests were negative. Abdominal contrast CT revealed hepatosplenomegaly without masses.  

CSF analysis showed 186 cells/mm³ (180 mononuclear, 6 polymorphonuclear), protein 41 mg/dL, and glucose 96 mg/dL (serum 140 mg/dL). Brain MRI FLAIR images demonstrated high-intensity lesions in the left medial temporal lobe, bilateral caudate nuclei, and left lentiform nucleus.  

Empiric therapy for meningoencephalitis was initiated with intravenous acyclovir, ceftriaxone, high-dose methylprednisolone pulse therapy for three days, and fosphenytoin for seizure control.

A 47-year-old woman, gravida 3, presented with a 2-day history of progressive lower abdominal pain and a palpable mass. She denied any menstrual abnormalities. On admission, vital signs were stable: temperature 36.6 °C, heart rate 70 beats/min, blood pressure 120/75 mmHg, oxygen saturation 100%. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness in the lower abdomen without rebound or guarding. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, red blood cell count 4.17 × 10^6/μL, platelets 226 × 10^3/μL, white blood cell count 12.2 × 10^3/μL, AST 13 U/L, ALT 11 U/L, and a negative urine β-human chorionic gonadotropin test. Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 15.7 × 12 cm solid mass near the posterior aspect of the uterus with peripheral vascularization and a modest amount of anechoic free fluid in the pelvis, perisplenic, and perihepatic spaces; both ovaries appeared normal. During hospitalization, her abdominal pain worsened. Repeat ultrasound showed hyperechoic fluid filling most of the abdomen, suggestive of large-volume hemorrhagic fluid. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed a large intraperitoneal hemorrhage with active extravasation of contrast, although the precise bleeding site could not be identified; vessels in the pelvic cavity were considered potential sources.

A 56-year-old multigravida postmenopausal woman presented with persistent nausea, nonbloody nonbilious vomiting, and sharp left-sided abdominal pain (10/10) for 1 day, and constipation for 4 days. She denied fever, chest pain, urinary symptoms, or diaphoresis. Her history was notable for diabetes, asthma, anxiety, chronic back pain, and multiple abdominal surgeries including cholecystectomy, appendectomy, hysterectomy, and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. She was a chronic smoker with allergies to morphine, promethazine, and sulfa drugs.

On examination, she was afebrile, tachycardic (HR 108 beats/min), hypertensive (206/106 mmHg), RR 22 breaths/min, and SpO₂ 93% on room air. The abdomen was distended with hypoactive bowel sounds and tenderness in the left upper quadrant without guarding or rebound. Neurologic, cardiovascular, and respiratory exams were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 16,000/mm³, hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, hematocrit 42%, platelets 196,000/mm³, and mild hyponatremia (Na 134 mmol/L). Other chemistry and liver-function tests were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed dilation of the jejunum and proximal ileum with multiple air-fluid levels, collapsed distal small-bowel loops, and a tight stricture in the proximal ileum associated with a small irregular soft-tissue mass adjacent to the narrowing and acute angulation of the ileal loop.

After 24 hours of nasogastric decompression without improvement, an exploratory laparotomy was performed. Intraoperatively, 500 cc of clear ascites was evacuated. The proximal two-thirds of the small bowel were markedly dilated. A tight adhesive band caused a stricture in the proximal ileum with near-complete obstruction. Approximately 15 cm proximal to the terminal ileum, a firm nodular lesion was identified in the small-bowel mesentery. The adhesive band, mesenteric nodule, and obstructed bowel segment were resected, and a functional end-to-end anastomosis was performed.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of intermittent acute epigastric pain radiating to the back and associated with abdominal fullness. She also reported fevers up to 101.2°F for 2 days. She had a history of cervical spine surgery 10 years earlier and a lower-segment cesarean section followed by copper-T insertion 2 years ago. She denied alcohol use, smoking, substance abuse, diabetes, viral infections, abdominal trauma, and use of steroids, estrogens, or other potential pancreatitis-inducing medications. Her family history was negative for pancreatitis, dyslipidemia, gallstones, or autoimmune disease.

On examination, she was tachycardic (116 bpm) with normal blood pressure; BMI was 32. Abdominal examination showed distention, epigastric tenderness, and sluggish bowel sounds. Laboratory tests revealed serum amylase 451 U/L, lipase 603 U/L, calcium 8.1 mg/dL, and triglycerides 579 mg/dL; liver enzymes, bilirubin, and renal function were unremarkable except for mildly elevated creatinine. ANA testing was negative. 

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated hepatomegaly with grade III fatty infiltration, significant free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, an enlarged pancreas with peripancreatic fluid, and no cholelithiasis.
