Non-contrast CT of the abdomen showed a diffusely enlarged pancreas with marked stranding and peripancreatic fluid, consistent with acute pancreatitis, and minimal bilateral pleural effusions.

A 29-year-old woman, G1P0, with no relevant medical or family history underwent routine prenatal evaluation. At 13 0/7 weeks’ gestation, fetal ultrasound revealed a markedly distended bladder measuring 9 mm × 9 mm, an enlarged stomach, and an omphalocele measuring 9.8 mm × 6 mm. Chorionic villus sampling at 13 4/7 weeks showed a normal female comparative genomic hybridization array. A follow-up ultrasound at 19 4/7 weeks demonstrated a persistently enlarged bladder now measuring 38 mm × 31 mm, gastric distension (19 mm × 11 mm), dilated bowel loops, hyperechogenic kidneys, and bilateral hydronephrosis. Fetal biometries were appropriate for gestational age.

A 40-year-old man with no significant medical history was brought to the trauma center after a motor vehicle collision. He had severe right thigh pain, swelling, bruising, and deformity. He was hemodynamically stable, and vital signs were within normal limits. Radiographs confirmed a displaced right femoral shaft fracture. He underwent successful open reduction and internal fixation under general anesthesia and was transferred to recovery in stable condition.

Twelve hours postoperatively, he developed a heart rate of 130 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute, acute respiratory distress consistent with ARDS, and a fever of 38.5 °C. His Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15 without neurological deficits. Laboratory tests revealed a drop in hemoglobin from 13.2 g/dL postoperatively to 7.4 g/dL and a rise in blood urea nitrogen from 42 mg/dL to 63 mg/dL; other laboratories, including white-cell and platelet counts, were normal. Oxygen therapy by mask maintained an SpO2 of 96%. Emergency CT angiography of the lungs showed no evidence of pulmonary thromboembolism. He received enoxaparin and a single unit of packed red blood cells. Twelve hours later, he developed petechial lesions and purpura on the neck, chest, and right lower limb. Specific tests for Henoch–Schönlein purpura or other vasculitides—including urinalysis, serum IgA, ANCA, complement levels, and coagulation tests—were within normal limits.

A 62-year-old man with a history of heart failure with recovered ejection fraction and persistent atrial fibrillation presented for evaluation of new anemia. A routine transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a 12 mm × 4 mm mobile echodensity on the noncoronary cusp of the aortic valve, suspicious for vegetation. He reported 2 months of progressive dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, anorexia, and a 16 kg unintentional weight loss, but denied fevers, night sweats, chills, chest pain, or palpitations. He had two ischemic strokes in the prior 2 months attributed to embolic atrial fibrillation; no echocardiogram had been obtained at that time. On admission he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, with an unremarkable physical examination. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.9 g/dL (MCV 90 fL), normal leukocyte and platelet counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate <1 mm/h, normal B12, folate, iron studies, haptoglobin 269 mg/dL, and normal coagulation parameters. Antiphospholipid and lupus serologies were negative. Blood cultures were drawn before empiric antibiotics and ultimately showed no growth. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated diffuse right adrenal thickening with a hypoattenuating focus, peritoneal carcinomatosis, multiple small hepatic hypodense lesions, and a splenic infarct, but no lung masses or intrathoracic adenopathy. A PET–CT scan showed hypermetabolic activity in the right adrenal gland and peritoneum without an identifiable primary lesion. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed small-to-medium–sized mobile echodensities on all three cusps of the aortic valve.

A 42-year-old woman presented with several weeks of right facial pain and deformity. She had no history of endocrinopathy, peptic ulcer disease, renal stones, fractures, or radiation exposure, and she did not use tobacco or alcohol. On examination, she appeared well; vital signs were unremarkable. Head and neck examination was normal; there were no palpable lymph nodes or masses. Laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 39.8%, a white-cell count of 6800/µL with a normal differential, normal platelet count, and normal coagulation studies.

Computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses revealed a round, osteolytic, radiolucent, bone-expanding lesion in the anterior right maxillary sinus, with erosion of the orbital floor and extension into the ethmoids and nasal cavity. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a 2-cm submucosal mass originating from the orbital floor. Rigid nasal endoscopy showed medialization of the right lateral nasal wall without mucosal change.

Under general anesthesia, an excisional biopsy via a Caldwell-Luc approach was performed. The mass measured approximately 2 cm in diameter, had an intact overlying mucosa, and was associated with erosion of the orbital floor and prolapse of periorbital fat, which was repaired.

Histopathological examination demonstrated regions of discrete bone resorption with osteoclast activity, newly formed bone, a loose fibrillar matrix containing hemosiderin deposits, and numerous multinucleated giant cells. A giant cell lesion was diagnosed, with a brown tumor among the leading considerations.

A 5-month-old male infant was admitted with anxiety, persistent crying, and a tender right testicle. Doppler ultrasonography of the scrotum revealed normal testicular vascularization. During surgical exploration, there was no torsion but evidence of epididymitis; he was treated with antibiotics. Two months later, he presented again with recurrent right epididymitis.  
On ultrasound examination, the right kidney was dysplastic (single system, 18 mm in longitudinal diameter) with a dilated right ureter (up to 9 mm in diameter) and a normal left kidney. Renal scintigraphy using 99mTc-ethylenedicysteine showed extremely diminished function of the right kidney (0% versus 100% of the left). Voiding cystourethrography suggested reflux into an ectopic right ureteral orifice.

A 76‐year‐old man presented with a 24‐hour history of sudden onset, progressively worsening abdominal pain. He reported fever to 101.4 °F at home, nausea, multiple episodes of vomiting, and inability to pass flatus. His medical history included atrial fibrillation (on apixaban), polymyalgia rheumatica, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and other comorbidities. On arrival, blood pressure was 128/73 mmHg, pulse 76 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and temperature 99.3 °F. The patient appeared mildly distressed. His abdomen was distended and diffusely tender with slight guarding and signs of peritonitis. Laboratory studies showed WBC count 18.59 × 10^3/µL (4.5–11), absolute neutrophils 16.45 × 10^3/µL (2.5–7), CRP 158.96 mg/L (<3), total bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL (0.1–1.2), direct bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL (<0.3), PT 22.1 s (11.0–12.5), and INR 1.9 (≤1.1); creatinine, lactate, and BUN were normal. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a closed‐loop small bowel obstruction in the mid‐abdomen with a decompressed loop of small intestine, dilated small bowel with fecalization, and a contained perforation accompanied by phlegmon, extraluminal fecal content, and free air posterior to the small intestine.

An 18-year-old man with a history of oxycodone use presented with a 1-week history of progressive left-sided weakness after falling while attempting to jump over a gate. He was able to walk immediately after the fall but noted worsening weakness on awakening the next day, accompanied by slurred speech and decreased sensation on the left. He denied recent viral illnesses, sick contacts, or vaccinations. 

On arrival, vital signs were: temperature 98.0°F, blood pressure 138/93 mm Hg, heart rate 80/min, respiratory rate 19/min, BMI 18.4. Examination revealed left facial asymmetry with an asymmetrical nasolabial fold, left lower-extremity strength 3/5, ataxic gait veering to the right, and left-sided dysarthria; right-sided strength was 5/5, and no sensory deficits were noted elsewhere.

Noncontrast brain MRI demonstrated multiple areas of prolonged T2 signal intensity in both supratentorial and infratentorial regions, primarily in the deep white matter, with scattered subcortical gray-matter and right thalamic foci. MRA of the brain showed a hypoplastic right A1 segment. Noncontrast CT scans of the brain and cervical spine revealed no acute intracranial or vertebral abnormalities. Laboratory studies—including CBC, basic metabolic panel, lipid profile, hemoglobin A1C, ANA, ESR, and HCV PCR—were all within normal limits.

A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented for a routine follow-up. He was asymptomatic. Vital signs were within normal limits: blood pressure 124/72 mm Hg, heart rate 78 bpm, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, temperature 98.3°F. He denied any supplemental calcium or vitamin D intake and was not taking proton pump inhibitors or H2‐receptor antagonists. He reported no palpitations, fatigue, abdominal pain, polyuria, constipation, or other systemic symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable, and there was no evidence of dehydration.  
Laboratory studies drawn the previous day showed:  
• Calcium 11.1 mg/dL  
• Albumin 4.7 g/dL  
• Blood urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL  
• Creatinine 0.91 mg/dL  
• Chloride 101 mmol/L  
On further questioning, he recalled that the evening before the blood draw he had sudden-onset epigastric burning and took six chewable tablets of Tums (200 mg calcium [500 mg] per tablet). He denied regular use of antacids. He was advised to stop taking Tums and to increase oral hydration. Given the mild hypercalcemia and absence of cardiac symptoms, an electrocardiogram was not performed.

A 90-year-old man was evaluated for a one-month history of progressive fatigue and abdominal and lower extremity edema. His medical history was notable for ischemic cardiomyopathy (left ventricular ejection fraction, 15%) with a dual-chamber pacemaker for resynchronization, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and frequent ventricular ectopy treated with amiodarone (200 mcg/day) initiated six months earlier, and stage IV chronic kidney disease (not on dialysis). He reported full compliance with his heart failure medications and denied dietary indiscretion, alcohol use, or anginal symptoms.

On examination, his weight had increased by 4.6 kg; the heart rate was 60 beats/minute, with jugular venous distension and a positive hepatojugular reflex. Inspiratory crackles were heard at the lung bases, and there was pitting edema to the mid-thigh level. The skin appeared dry, and the thyroid examination was unremarkable.

A chest radiograph showed pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly. Electrocardiography revealed a paced rhythm at 62 beats/minute, and cardiac biomarkers showed no evidence of myocardial infarction. Laboratory studies revealed an N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide level of 10,644 pg/mL and a serum creatinine level of 3.7 mg/dL (baseline, 2.3 mg/dL). Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 12% with global hypokinesis, a right ventricular systolic pressure of 44 mmHg, and a moderate-sized concentric pericardial effusion.

He was treated with cautious intravenous furosemide, resulting in improved pulmonary, abdominal, and peripheral edema and a decrease in serum creatinine to 3.2 mg/dL; however, he remained severely fatigued.

A 74-year-old woman was referred by her endocrinologist for evaluation of persistent hyperandrogenic symptoms. Over the preceding three years, her total testosterone levels had ranged from 134 to 177 ng/dL. She reported male-pattern alopecia, worsening seborrheic dermatitis, increased central adiposity with a firm protuberant abdomen, and mood changes including increased anger and aggression. Treatment with finasteride and spironolactone had not improved her symptoms.

Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, polycystic ovarian syndrome, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, Sjögren’s syndrome, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, basal cell carcinoma, and a nonspecific mitochondrial metabolism disorder. She had menarche at age 12, regular menses until menopause at age 54, and no family history of cancer.

On examination, she had moderate alopecia and an unremarkable pelvic examination with no palpable masses. Laboratory studies confirmed elevated total testosterone; other hormone levels were within normal limits, including 17-α-hydroxyprogesterone, dehydroepiandrosterone-sulfate, prolactin, sex hormone–binding globulin, insulin-like growth factor I, and aldosterone, and she had a normal dexamethasone suppression test. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland, ovaries, and adrenal glands showed no abnormalities. Given the absence of an extra-ovarian source, she was counseled that her symptoms likely originated from the ovaries.

A 29-year-old man presented with sudden-onset epigastric pain radiating to the left iliac fossa for several hours, accompanied by nausea but no vomiting or anorexia. He reported 7 loose bowel movements in 24 hours. His medical history was notable for allergic bronchitis since childhood and chronic sinusitis. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Digital clubbing was noted. Pulmonary auscultation was unremarkable, but heart sounds and the point of maximal impulse were detected on the right side of the chest. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the left iliac fossa without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 19,000/mm3 with 5% band forms, 28,000 leukocytes/mL in the urine, and a C-reactive protein level of 8.90 mg/dL. Chest and abdominal radiographs demonstrated dextrocardia. CT scans of the thorax and abdomen confirmed situs inversus totalis with transposition of thoracic and abdominal organs, bronchiectasis with bronchial wall thickening and mucoid impaction, and focal wall thickening of the colon with mucosal edema and haziness of the adjacent fat in the left iliac fossa.

An 82-year-old Asian man presented with a two-month history of swelling of both hands. The swelling was symmetric, localized to the dorsum of both hands, and associated with pitting edema. He denied dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, weight loss, or jaundice. He had been taking furosemide 40 mg daily without improvement. 

On examination, vital signs were stable. There was pitting edema of the dorsum of both hands and tenderness with limited motion of the proximal interphalangeal joints bilaterally. Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 8.9 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dL, platelets of 292 × 10^3/µL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 118 mm/hour, C-reactive protein of 6.58 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen of 13.6 mg/dL, creatinine of 0.91 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase of 19 U/L, alanine aminotransferase of 17 U/L, and glucose of 131 mg/dL. Rheumatoid factor and anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody were negative.

Plain radiographs of both hands showed soft-tissue swelling without joint-space narrowing or bone erosions.

A 73-year-old male farmer presented with a 2-year history of an ulcer in the right inguinal–scrotal region associated with hemorrhagic points at the scrotal–inguinal junction, which eventually progressed to the contralateral side. He also reported a 9-kg weight loss over 6 months but denied fever, cough, dyspnea, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a 1 × 10 cm ulcerated lesion with a granulomatous base and hemorrhagic points at the transition between the scrotum and the right inguinal area, extending slightly to the opposite side. 

An incisional biopsy was performed. Histopathological analysis showed non-specific chronic dermatitis with intraepidermal microabscesses, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, and numerous yeast cells of varying sizes amidst scattered giant cells. Fungal culture and direct microscopic examination of the tissue specimen were negative.

Chest computed tomography revealed a confluent ground-glass opacity in the right middle lobe without mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Serologic tests for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. Sputum studies for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and fungal elements were also negative.

A 60-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, nephrolithiasis, and COVID-19 infection 4 months earlier presented 6 days after her second dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine with 3 days of substernal chest pain radiating to her back and both shoulders. She denied shortness of breath, cough, fever, or dyspnea on exertion. On evaluation, her ECG showed T-wave inversions in leads III and aVF. Cardiac troponin levels were normal, and a CT angiogram of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis as well as a nuclear stress test were unremarkable. She was discharged the following day but noted that her chest pain persisted at home. Over the next several days, she also developed pain, erythema, edema, and warmth in her left arm but continued working and performing daily activities. She re-presented to care 6 days after discharge. On examination, the left biceps circumference was 31 cm compared with 28 cm on the right.

A 43‐year‐old woman presented with a 6‐month history of left upper–quadrant abdominal pain. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no palpable abdominal masses. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 7900/mm3 with eosinophils comprising 35% of leukocytes; other routine biochemical studies were normal. Serologic testing for hydatid disease was strongly positive (indirect hemagglutination test titer, 1:1280). Chest radiography was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a 15 × 11 cm cystic lesion extending from the left lobe of the liver to the transverse colon. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 17 × 11 cm cystic mass with a thick, smooth wall located between the left hepatic lobe, diaphragm, spleen, tail of the pancreas, and transverse colon, with apparent invasion of the splenic hilum; no other intraabdominal abnormalities were seen.

A 60-year-old woman underwent routine screening mammography, which revealed an abnormality in the left breast. She had no breast symptoms, history of trauma, or skin changes aside from minimal skin retraction overlying the lesion. On examination, there was a non-tender, relatively well-circumscribed nodule in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast without erythema or warmth.

Diagnostic imaging was performed:
- Mammography showed a 1.5 cm ill-defined, high-density mass in the left outer breast without calcifications.
- Ultrasound demonstrated an irregular, ill-defined, homogeneous hypoechoic mass with an echogenic halo.
- Color Doppler imaging revealed moderate vascularity in the peripheral halo of the lesion.

Given these findings, the lesion was classified as BI-RADS category 4c (moderate suspicion for malignancy, estimated probability 50–95%).

A 51-year-old man was brought to the emergency department by police after he had not been seen or heard from in 3 weeks. His stepfather had raised the alarm. On forced entry, police found the apartment in extreme domestic squalor, with piles of rubbish, rotting food, faeces stored in small bags, maggots, cobwebs, overgrown garden, and rats. The man was found naked under a rug on a heap of debris and was breathing.  

On admission to the psychiatric ward, vital signs were stable. Physical examination and routine blood tests were unremarkable except for onychogryphotic toenails and cerumen impaction causing partial deafness.  

Initial psychiatric evaluation included a sleep chart, mood chart, the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS), Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II), and Clinical Outcomes in Routine Evaluation (CORE-10). Results indicated:  
• BDI-II score 38 (severe depression)  
• BPRS showed moderate anxiety and conceptual disorganization, moderately severe depressive mood, and severe guilty feelings  
• CORE-10 clinical score 13 (mild psychological distress)  

Mental-status examination revealed a flat mood, vacant expression, poor appetite, low sociability, suicidal ideation without intent, and no evidence of hallucinations, delusions, or thought disorder. The patient reported long-standing social withdrawal, occasional dissociative episodes, and fears that others could “take advantage” of him, leading him to block all contacts on his phone. He had difficulty reading, often needing to reread pages.  

Screening with the Autism Spectrum Quotient short form (AQ-10) yielded a score of 7 (cut-off ≥6), suggestive of some ASD traits. Further ASD assessment did not meet criteria for autism spectrum disorder. A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed mild generalized cerebral atrophy consistent with age. Scores on the Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination-III (ACE-III) and Frontal Assessment Battery (FAB) were within normal limits and not indicative of cognitive impairment or dementia.

A 28-year-old previously healthy Caucasian man presented one day after a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection with a purpuric rash on both flanks, symmetrical polyarthralgias, and multiple painful oral aphthous ulcers. He reported a similar transient rash after his second dose of the BNT162b2 vaccine three months earlier. One week prior, he had undergone CT of the abdomen for right upper-quadrant pain and arthralgias, which showed only nonspecific right-sided abdominal wall fat stranding; he was discharged. On presentation to our center, vital signs were stable. Examination confirmed a purpuric rash on the flanks and tender joints; there was no abdominal tenderness. Initial labs showed a leukocyte count of 15.1×10^9/L and C-reactive protein of 75 mg/L. On hospital day 2, he developed severe haematochezia with hemodynamic instability requiring transfusion. CT angiography demonstrated an arterial blush in the distal ileum consistent with active bleeding. Angioembolization was attempted twice without localization of bleeding. Ongoing hemorrhage prompted exploratory laparotomy three days later. Intraoperatively, the small bowel showed frequent patchy vasculitic lesions most pronounced in the terminal ileum, which appeared nonviable, leading to resection and end ileostomy.

A previously healthy 5-month-old boy was brought for 6 hours of refusal to move his left leg and increased irritability. There was no history of trauma, fever, or recent illness. He is exclusively breastfed without vitamin D supplementation. Born full term at home, newborn screening was normal; he is unimmunized. On exam, temperature was 101°F and the left lower extremity was held flexed without erythema or swelling but was tender on palpation. The rest of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 9.9 K/μL with 53% neutrophils, hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, calcium 5.9 mg/dL (normal 8.7–10.5), CRP 22.8 mg/L, and ESR 30 mm/hr. Radiographs of the lower extremities demonstrated widening, cupping, and fraying of metaphyses without fracture, consistent with rickets. Further testing revealed 25-hydroxyvitamin D 9.2 ng/mL, parathyroid hormone 466 pg/mL, and phosphorus 3.1 mg/dL. He was started on calcium, vitamin D, and supportive care.

A 69-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted with 3 days of throat and right neck pain and progressive dysphagia. The day before admission she noted a small neck hematoma that rapidly spread. She denied dyspnea. Her history included two internal carotid artery (ICA) aneurysms diagnosed in 2002, one coiled on the right and one managed conservatively on the left, with angiographic features of fibromuscular dysplasia noted in the left ICA, and later stenting of a dissecting left ICA aneurysm. Medications: aspirin 100 mg daily and amiodarone 100 mg daily for atrial fibrillation. 

On admission, vital signs were normal and she was afebrile. Examination revealed a large subcutaneous hematoma from the thyroid region to the right chest wall, tenderness over the right lateral neck above the cricoid, and slight tracheal deviation to the left. There were no signs of airway compromise. Fiber-optic laryngoscopy showed a normal glottis and no laryngeal compression. 

Laboratory studies, including a coagulation profile, were within normal limits. A blood calcium level to evaluate for parathyroid adenoma was 8.2 mg/dL (normal 8.4–10.2). Neck ultrasound showed a large hematoma displacing the right thyroid lobe anteriorly. Contrast CT angiography revealed a large right neck hematoma with anterior displacement of the right thyroid lobe and tracheal deviation to the left but no active bleeding; the aortic arch and both ICAs were intact.

A 4-year-old boy with no known medical conditions was referred for evaluation of left foot swelling and diarrhea. The swelling was first noted at 4 months of age, attributed at that time to a local infection, and persisted with a waxing and waning course; it was later labeled as hemihypertrophy by a physician. Over the past year, he experienced intermittent watery to semi-formed stools 3–6 times per day, aggravated by fatty foods and occasionally difficult to flush. He appeared undernourished, despite a body weight on the 90th percentile. Family history was negative for lymphedema or genetic disorders.

On examination, vital signs were stable. He had mild ascites but no organomegaly. The right foot was normal. The left foot had significant edema of the dorsum and toes up to the ankle, which was minimally pitting, and the Stemmer’s sign was positive. Cardiac and respiratory exams were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed: albumin 2.0 g/dL (normal 3.5–5.5), total protein 2.9 g/dL (6–8), IgG 147 mg/dL (565–1765), IgM 16 mg/dL (55–375), IgA 30 mg/dL (85–385). Urine protein was negative; liver enzymes and tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody were normal or negative.

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed the duodenal mucosa diffusely studded with white spots representing dilated lacteals. Colonoscopy revealed lymphoid nodular hyperplasia; otherwise the colon was unremarkable.

A 45-year-old previously healthy man presented with paroxysmal, stereotyped involuntary movements of the face and dystonic posturing of the right upper arm lasting 3–5 seconds, occurring 20–30 times per day. There was no tongue biting, incontinence, or impaired awareness. On examination he was alert, oriented, and exhibited no cognitive deficit, extrapyramidal signs, or cerebellar findings. Routine blood tests, including electrolytes, liver and renal function, were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was within normal limits. Brain MRI showed diffuse cortical atrophy, and 24-hour EEG monitoring revealed no epileptiform discharges. Serum antibody against LGI1 was positive. He received intravenous immunoglobulin and methylprednisolone, with complete resolution of the facio-brachial dystonic seizures within three days. He remained well on oral steroids for two months without neurologic symptoms.

In the third month, he developed a two-week history of stiffness in all four limbs, difficulty walking, reduced verbal output, and cognitive decline. On examination he was conscious but hypophonic; Mini-Mental State Examination score was 19/30, with impairment in delayed recall, naming, visuospatial function, verbal comprehension, reading, and writing. There was rigidity and generalized bradykinesia with brisk reflexes, a positive Myerson’s sign, and prominent gait and truncal ataxia. Routine laboratory studies and repeat CSF analysis were normal. Brain MRI showed marked cortical atrophy and T2-FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral thalami. Serum autoimmune and paraneoplastic panels were negative, and anti-LGI1 antibodies were no longer detected. Thyroid function tests, including anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody, were normal. FDG-PET revealed diffuse hypermetabolism in the basal ganglia, thalami, and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres. He was treated again with IVIG and methylprednisolone, and discharge planning included a course of oral steroids and consideration of rituximab infusion.

A 72-year-old woman was first noted to have mild pancytopenia (white blood cell count 2600/μL; hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL; platelets 105 000/μL) three years before admission. Bone marrow evaluation showed no dysplasia in the three lineages, no chromosomal abnormalities, and no increase in blasts. Serum studies at that time revealed microcytic hypochromic anemia and elevated ferritin; serum copper was low (30 μg/dL) despite copper supplementation.

Over three years her activity declined, and mild cognitive impairment, slowed speech, and bradykinesia were noted. On readmission, she had progressive pancytopenia (white blood cells 800/μL; hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL; platelets 48 000/μL), continued microcytic hypochromic indices, high ferritin (1165 ng/mL), impaired glucose tolerance, and elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor. Trace-element studies showed low serum copper and low urinary copper excretion.

Bone marrow smear now demonstrated dysplastic changes, including binuclear myelocytes, giant platelets and neutrophils, and vacuolation in the myeloid lineage, with a normal blast fraction and normal karyotype. Whole-body CT revealed abdominal lymphadenopathy with increased FDG uptake; needle biopsy showed preserved lymphoid follicles and hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Susceptibility-weighted brain MRI demonstrated a diffuse low signal over the cortical surface, and abdominal MRI showed hepatosplenomegaly with low T1 and T2 signals consistent with iron deposition. Upper and lower endoscopy were unremarkable.

A 14-year-old girl presented with 2 months of progressive proximal muscle weakness. She initially noted difficulty combing her hair and rising from a chair; over weeks she became wheelchair-bound. She also reported morning stiffness of both small hand joints lasting about 30 minutes, dysphagia for solids and liquids, and poor appetite, without fever or weight loss.

Her medical history was notable for thyroiditis in 2015 that resolved without long-term therapy. Family history included a younger sister with Prader–Willi syndrome. She was up to date on vaccinations.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic testing showed symmetric muscle strength of 4/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs, with brisk reflexes more pronounced on the left. She could not stand from the wheelchair unaided. In the left hand, she was unable to make a fist or tuck the fingers; there was tenderness at the fourth and fifth proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (WBC 2.96 × 10^3/µL), microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL), elevated C-reactive protein (18.8 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (109.2 mm/hr), and normal creatine kinase (39 U/L). Thyroid function tests showed suppressed TSH (0.017 µIU/mL), elevated free T4 (20.9 pmol/L), normal free T3 (4.53 pmol/L), and markedly elevated anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (3410 IU/mL). Antinuclear antibody titer was 27 (reference <20); rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and ANCA were negative. Viral serologies, renal and liver tests, and other hormonal assays were normal.

Hyperkalemic paralysis was ruled out. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a multinodular goiter consistent with thyroiditis. MRI of the brain and lumbosacral spine was normal; cervical spine MRI showed a small C6–C7 disc herniation. Incidentally, the lumbosacral spine MRI revealed bilateral sacroiliitis. Dedicated MRI of the sacroiliac joints confirmed bilateral sacroiliitis; HLA-B27 was negative. MRI of the hips and pelvis showed bilateral thigh intramuscular edema with enhancement. Although myositis was suspected, electromyography and repeat creatine kinase were normal.

A 47-year-old woman with a history of actinic keratosis, seborrheic dermatitis, anxiety, deep vein thrombosis, and depression presented with 4 days of progressive shortness of breath, nasal congestion, fevers, chills, cough, lower-extremity swelling, and body aches. She denied sick contacts, tuberculosis exposure, or recent travel. Her home medications included alprazolam, amlodipine, buspirone, clonazepam, dicyclomine, losartan, ondansetron, warfarin, escitalopram, ibuprofen, methadone, and topical tretinoin. 

In the emergency department, she became hypoxemic and required endotracheal intubation. Auscultation revealed bilateral crackles and rhonchi. She was treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics and, later, steroids and azathioprine without improvement. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 9.97 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, hematocrit 35.8%, and platelets 266 × 10^3/µL. Blood cultures showed no growth. Influenza A and B antigens and cryptococcal antigen were negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage culture showed no growth, and Gram stain was negative. Serologic testing for rheumatoid factor was normal, and histoplasma antigen was not detected. Electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine were within normal limits. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 81–90 mmHg, confirmed as pulmonary hypertension on right-heart catheterization. 

Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated bilateral diffuse ground-glass attenuation with scattered alveolar opacities. Nine days later, a noncontrast chest CT showed multifocal bilateral consolidation that had worsened, with small pleural effusions and no pneumothorax. Five days after that, a pulmonary embolism CT angiogram revealed no significant pulmonary embolus, a small partial occlusive thrombus in the right internal jugular vein, and extensive worsening multifocal airspace opacities, predominantly in the upper lobes.

A 60-year-old woman was referred with a 3-month history of bilateral lower-limb and abdominal swelling and exertional dyspnea. She had no significant family history. On examination, there were multiple tender, wart-like papules over the skin. The abdomen was distended, and both the spleen and liver were palpably enlarged. Oral examination revealed painful, necrotic ulcers covered by a pseudomembrane on the labial mucosa, dorsal tongue, and hard and soft palate. Bilateral submandibular lymphadenopathy was present. Extraorally, there were multiple firm, tender nodules on the chin, face, lips, forearms, and thighs, with overlying warmth. 

Laboratory studies showed a random blood sugar of 130 mg/dl, serum creatinine 1 mg/dl, urea 30 mg/dl, albumin 3.2 g/dl, triglycerides 189 mg/dl, VLDL 38 mg/dl, hemoglobin 7.9 g/dl, and platelet count 100 × 10^3/ml. Levels of urea, creatinine, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and cortisol were within normal limits. Urinalysis revealed proteinuria and 2–4 red and white blood cells per high-power field. 

Chest and paranasal sinus radiographs and abdominal ultrasonography were unremarkable. Peripheral blood smear was negative for malarial parasites. Febrile agglutination tests for typhoid, brucellosis, and infectious mononucleosis were negative. HIV antibody testing was negative.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of chronic productive cough with greenish sputum and intermittent fever. He denied dyspnea or hemoptysis. He worked in construction for 20 years, had no significant medical history, no tobacco use, and no family history of lung disease or malignancy. He had received multiple courses of antibiotics without improvement. Examination was unremarkable, with normal systemic and chest findings and no lymphadenopathy. A chest radiograph showed right middle zone consolidation. CT of the thorax revealed right middle lobe subsegmental collapse with bronchiectasis and nodular calcified excrescences protruding into the lumen of the trachea and main bronchi; there was no contrast-enhancing lung mass or pleural effusion. Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated a patent but narrowed airway with numerous whitish granular nodules along the anterolateral walls of the trachea and main bronchi, sparing the posterior wall.

A 51-year-old Indian woman presented with a sudden-onset, severe bilateral occipital headache that began three days earlier without prodrome or visual aura. The continuous pain was exacerbated by coughing, relieved when recumbent, and radiated over the vertex to the temporal regions; it was also associated with nausea and mild photophobia. She had no prior headaches, no significant medical history, and no regular medications. There was no family history of headache or sudden death. On examination, she was alert with normal vital signs. The neurologic examination was unremarkable: Kernig’s sign was negative, there was no neck stiffness or rash, and fundoscopy showed no papilledema. Initial labs showed mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia; erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were normal. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture revealed no red cells, an opening pressure of 11 cm H2O, and no xanthochromia. A magnetic resonance angiogram of the head was normal. With symptomatic improvement on bed rest and weak opioid analgesia, she was given a tentative diagnosis of migraine and discharged.

A Swiss man in his 50s was hospitalized after a fall at home caused by recurrent short-lived episodes of generalized weakness, which over 8 years had increased to three or four times weekly and led to pelvic-ring fractures. He denied loss of consciousness, memory gaps, post-event confusion, tongue biting, or incontinence; there were no chest pain, dyspnea, or palpitations. His medical history included an orthotopic heart transplantation in 1991 for idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated), chronic immunosuppression with cyclosporin and mycophenolate mofetil, chronic kidney disease on dialysis, and a right pneumonectomy in 2006 for pulmonary carcinoma.  
Laboratory studies showed creatinine 513 μmol/L, urea 8.6 mmol/L, and hemoglobin 86 g/L; electrolytes, thyroid function, and inflammatory markers were normal. Protein electrophoresis and immunofixation were unremarkable. Radiographs revealed nondisplaced fractures of the right ischiopubic and iliopubic rami and left sacral ala. The patient’s prior cardiac follow-up—including multiple coronary angiograms, 72-hour Holter monitoring, and echocardiography—had shown only a high burden of atrial fibrillation and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 50%. On admission, the ECG was normal, and extended Holter monitoring was pending. An orthostatic challenge could not be performed because of the fractures.

A 67-year-old man with history of noninvasive papillary urothelial carcinoma, atrial fibrillation on warfarin, surgically corrected aortic stenosis with bioprosthetic valve, CAD status post CABG, and severe emphysematous COPD presented in mid-March 2021 with 3 weeks of malaise and poor oral intake. Over several days he noted dysgeusia, anorexia, generalized fatigue, myalgias, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and oliguria (no urine for 3 days). He denied fever, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, or edema. Three months earlier he had been hospitalized for valve replacement and CABG complicated by shock, COPD exacerbation, and malnutrition; he had returned home a few weeks before this presentation. He had quit smoking 9 years ago; no alcohol or substance use; and had received one dose of mRNA-1273 COVID-19 vaccine one month earlier.

On arrival: temperature 97.6 °F, blood pressure 86/44 mmHg, heart rate 73 bpm, oxygen saturation 92% on room air. He appeared chronically ill; oral mucosa was dry. Cardiac exam: grade III/VI systolic murmur at left upper sternal border. Lungs: bilaterally diminished breath sounds. Abdomen: severe right lower quadrant and suprapubic tenderness. Thighs: severe bilateral tenderness. No focal neurologic deficits. A Foley catheter produced 200 cc of urine.

Laboratory studies: SARS-CoV-2 PCR positive. Serum sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, chloride 95 mmol/L, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L (anion gap 20). Creatinine 9.55 mg/dL (baseline 1.04 mg/dL 2 months earlier), BUN 57 mg/dL, eGFR 6 mL/min/1.73 m2, creatine kinase 521 U/L, albumin 2.1 g/dL, total protein 5.8 g/dL. WBC 15.4 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, platelets 584 × 10^3/µL, AST 78 U/L, ALT 34 U/L, ALP 200 U/L, CRP 114.6 mg/L.

Urinalysis: turbid orange urine, pH 6, specific gravity 1.019, 2+ protein, 1+ blood, positive leukocyte esterase, negative nitrite. Microscopy: 0–3 hyaline casts, many WBCs, 0–2 RBCs, many bacteria. Urine chemistry: sodium 118 mmol/L, creatinine 62 mg/dL, random protein 9.39 g/L, albumin/creatinine ratio 6130.6 mg/g, osmolality 298 mOsm/kg.

Chest radiograph: no acute pathology. CT abdomen/pelvis: wall thickening of descending and rectosigmoid colon (suggestive of colitis), horseshoe kidney, and an irregular spiculated right lower lobe lung lesion.

He received 3.5 L normal saline and empiric antibiotics for presumed colitis and UTI, later tailored to cephalexin for E. coli in urine. Nephrology consultation: initial impression of pre-renal AKI from volume depletion. Lisinopril and rosuvastatin were held. There was no evidence of obstruction. On hospital day 3, his creatinine rose to 11.5 mg/dL, BUN to 72 mg/dL, eGFR fell to 4 mL/min/1.73 m2 with anuria and worsening acidosis, and he was started on intermittent hemodialysis. HIV, hepatitis B and C serologies were negative; serum light chains were elevated without monoclonal spike.

A 24-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging mass in his left eye and a longstanding history of severe itching in both eyes. Visual acuity was 20/20 OU, and intraocular pressures were 16 mm Hg OD and 18 mm Hg OS. Examination of the right eye showed upper-lid papillae without limbal involvement. In the left eye, eversion of the upper lid revealed intense papillary reaction with several 1.5–2 mm cobblestone papillae and ropy discharge. At the temporal limbus of the left eye there was a reddish, sessile papillary mass from 2 to 4 o’clock. The surface exhibited multiple capillary fronds appearing as red dots, with focal keratinization on its inferior border. The mass was freely movable, and the temporal edge was associated with engorged conjunctival vessels. The rest of the anterior and posterior segment examination was unremarkable. The surface of the limbal mass stained significantly with rose bengal. Clinically, the patient was diagnosed with bilateral palpebral vernal keratoconjunctivitis (left eye more severely affected) and a unilateral temporal limbal mass. The leading clinical considerations for the mass were epithelial hyperplasia versus ocular surface squamous neoplasia.

A 13-year-old girl presented with primary amenorrhea and a 6-month history of cyclical lower abdominal pain, constipation, and an episode of acute urinary retention that was temporarily relieved by catheterization. She had no prior surgeries and was self-medicating with anti-helminthics. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Secondary sexual characteristics were appropriate for age. Abdominal palpation disclosed a mobile, slightly tender midline mass extending nearly to the umbilicus. External genital examination revealed normal labia and a completely intact, bulging hymenal membrane without any canalization. On rectal examination, a mobile central pelvic mass was palpable anterior to the rectum.  
A repeat abdominal ultrasonogram showed a single ovoid, sonolucent mass in the mid-pelvis extending from the upper vaginal area to just below the umbilicus; the bladder was decompressed, and no separate uterine structures were identified.

A 75-year-old woman, previously well, transferred her care to a new general practitioner in June 2022. She reported a presumed stroke in April 2020 with slurred speech, imbalance, and confusion lasting 48 hours; at that time, brain MRI showed chronic periventricular white matter changes without acute ischemic lesions, and CT angiography demonstrated carotid tortuosity with stenosis from myointimal plaques. Her medications included barnidipine 20 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

Since 2020, she experienced recurrent dizzying attacks characterized by sudden subjective vertigo, absence of nausea or vomiting, and unsteadiness with a wide-based gait requiring support; episodes lasted days to weeks and gradually resolved. Symptomatic treatments for dizziness were ineffective. Over months, attacks increased in frequency and duration until dizziness became constant, leading to loss of autonomy.

At the first visit, general and neurologic examinations were normal, and she reported a low mood. Days later, a severe attack prevented her from getting out of bed, prompting a home visit. Vital signs were normal; she was alert, oriented, and cooperative with normal speech. She described severe dizziness worsened by any movement or position change, without nausea or vomiting. With assistance, she sat on the bed with difficulty maintaining trunk control. When upright, she adopted a wide-based stance, was unsteady, and required external supports to walk. Romberg’s test was positive, with marked unsteadiness on eye closure. Strength and sensation were intact, reflexes were normal, and cranial nerves were intact. The finger–nose test was weakly positive on the right. The HINTS examination was negative.

A diagnostic algorithm for dizziness suggested a low probability of central or peripheral vestibular origin. Review of the CTA suggested that carotid stenosis had been overestimated due to marked vessel tortuosity. Transcranial Doppler confirmed tortuosity and plaques but demonstrated normal hemodynamics of the cerebro-afferent vessels. Repeat brain MRI showed no signs of recent vascular lesions.

A 22-year-old man presented with 4 days of fever, myalgia, arthralgia, and sore throat, and 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea. He had no past medical history, did not smoke or use recreational drugs, and had no notable family history. On examination, temperature was 38.4°C, pulse 89/min, blood pressure 77/34 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He had cool peripheries, normal heart sounds without murmurs or rub, and no signs of fluid overload.
Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis (22.9×10^9/L) with neutrophilia, monocytosis, and lymphopenia; mild thrombocytopenia; creatinine 333 µmol/L; urea 22.2 mmol/L; AST 123 U/L; ALT 46 U/L; high-sensitivity troponin T 4550 ng/L; NT-proBNP 1485 pmol/L; C-reactive protein 415 mg/L; lactate 3.6 mmol/L; and sodium 129 mmol/L. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, right-axis deviation, and diffuse ST-segment elevation. Chest radiograph was unremarkable.
He was admitted to the intensive care unit for presumed septic shock with myocarditis and acute kidney injury. He received broad-spectrum antibiotics, vasopressor support (noradrenaline then dobutamine), and high-dose intravenous dexamethasone (10 mg four times daily). Transthoracic echocardiography showed severe global left ventricular systolic impairment (ejection fraction 35%) and moderate right ventricular impairment, with no pericardial effusion or significant valvular disease. Endomyocardial biopsy demonstrated interstitial lymphocytes and edema without myonecrosis. Cardiac MRI on hospital day 4 revealed myocardial edema and extensive subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement, consistent with acute myocarditis.
Two attempts to transition to oral steroids on hospital days 10 and 14 were followed within 12 hours by hypotension, fever, chest pain, and rising inflammatory markers, all of which promptly resolved when intravenous steroids were reinstated.

A 42-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted for fluctuating diplopia, ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria, and fatigable chewing at the end of meals or at the end of the day. Her medical history included antiphospholipid syndrome, with three spontaneous abortions, and transient hypothyroidism. She took aspirin 81 mg daily. On examination, she had dysarthria and weakness of the facial muscles, tongue, and neck, and displayed progressive fatigability in upward gaze during the Simpson test. Repetitive ulnar nerve stimulation showed an abnormal (>10%) decrement. Tests for antibodies against AChR, MuSK, and titin were negative. A thoracic computed tomography scan was normal. Thromboplastin time and activated partial thromboplastin time were elevated; anticardiolipin and anti–β2-glycoprotein-I antibodies were elevated, consistent with her antiphospholipid syndrome.

A 20-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with 10 days of undocumented fevers, productive cough with green–yellow sputum, one episode of small-volume hemoptysis, night sweats, a 12-lb weight loss, pleuritic chest pain, and mild dyspnea at rest. He lives in Georgia, works as a gutter installer without a face mask, has daily nicotine vaping for 4 years, and owns four dogs. In the ED his temperature was 101.8°F, pulse 108/min, respiratory rate 23/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on 3 L/min of oxygen. Lung examination revealed crackles in the right lower lobe; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 25,400 cells/mm3 and a C-reactive protein level of 6.83 IU/L. A chest radiograph demonstrated right upper-lobe consolidation. A CT scan of the chest showed a small right pleural effusion and patchy alveolar opacities throughout the right lower lobe. He was started on IV vancomycin, piperacillin–tazobactam, and azithromycin for presumed community-acquired pneumonia. On hospital day 5, a contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed right upper-lobe consolidative opacities with cavitation and ground-glass consolidation in the right lower lobe, without lymphadenopathy. Despite broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, he continued to spike fevers and his white-cell count rose to 35,500 and then to 41,800 cells/mm3.

A 67-year-old woman presented with two months of burning epigastric pain that was intermittent, nonradiating, and associated with nausea and vomiting. She reported unintentional weight loss of approximately 30 pounds over three months but denied diarrhea, hematemesis, or melena. Her medical history was notable for bilateral silicone breast implants, exploratory laparotomy with partial bowel resection after a gunshot wound, Billroth I gastrectomy for peptic ulcer disease, and partial thyroidectomy for a follicular adenoma. 

On examination, she appeared pale and severely dehydrated. Vital signs were: heart rate 141 beats/min, blood pressure 143/72 mm Hg, temperature 97.4°F, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. Her weight was 44 kg (BMI 18.3 kg/m2). A firm right-sided thyroid lump with regular margins moved with swallowing. Both breast implants felt rock hard, with loss of the distinct margin over the lower part of the right implant. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. The abdomen was soft with multiple surgical scars and mild epigastric tenderness without guarding or rebound. Stool guaiac was weakly positive. Multiple fixed, hard, nontender masses were palpated over the arms and thighs. The patient disclosed a right breast implant rupture diagnosed several years earlier.

Admission laboratory studies showed a serum calcium of 18.4 mg/dL (normal 8.6–10.2 mg/dL) and phosphorus of 6.8 mg/dL (normal 2.5–4.5 mg/dL). She denied antacid use but reported taking vitamin D 5000 U twice daily for five years. Parathyroid hormone level was 13 pg/mL (normal 15–65 pg/mL), parathyroid hormone–related peptide was <2 pmol/L (normal 0.0–3.4 pmol/L), and 25-hydroxy vitamin D was 40 ng/mL (normal 30–100 ng/mL). Serum and urine protein electrophoreses were normal.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed moderate chronic gastritis without Helicobacter pylori or intestinal metaplasia. CT of the chest and abdomen showed no evidence of malignancy but revealed extensive soft tissue calcifications in the upper thighs. X-rays of the arms and thighs confirmed extensive soft tissue calcifications. Biopsy of the thyroid mass showed benign follicular cells. Colonoscopy revealed a hyperplastic polyp and melanosis coli without malignancy. Serum 1,25-hydroxy vitamin D level was 290.7 pg/mL (normal 19.9–79.3 pg/mL) and angiotensin-converting enzyme was 137 U/L (normal 9–67 U/L). A biopsy of a soft tissue mass was discussed but the patient declined. She was managed symptomatically and discharged.

A 3-week-old female infant was referred for evaluation of an annular rash on her face and trunk that was initially thought to be tinea corporis. The lesions first appeared at 2 weeks of age and increased in size over the following week. She was feeding well and gaining weight appropriately. The baby was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy to a 26-year-old healthy mother (gravida 2, para 1) with a history of one previous spontaneous abortion. Prenatal laboratory studies and fetal ultrasonography were normal. Delivery was spontaneous vaginal; birth weight was 3060 g, length 50 cm, and Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. In the nursery, she received antibiotics for a presumed nonspecific neonatal infection and was discharged on day 5 with mild thrombocytopenia deemed transient.

On examination at 3 weeks, the infant appeared well but was pale. Multiple discrete and confluent annular lesions measuring 1–3 cm with central hypopigmentation were present on the face, anterior chest, and abdomen. There was no erythema, scale, or discharge. Heart rate was 150 beats/min with a regular rhythm and no murmurs. The abdomen was soft without hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 90 g/L, red-cell count 2.88 × 10^12/L, platelet count 58 × 10^9/L, aspartate aminotransferase 216 U/L (normal 15–59), and alanine aminotransferase 136 U/L (normal 9–72). Serum electrolytes, proteins, albumin, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine were within normal limits.

A 39-year-old woman presented with 2 years of infertility and chronic pelvic pain. The pain was noncyclical, spasmodic, and of sudden onset. She reported dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia. Her medical history was notable for recurrent herpes infections managed with as-needed acyclovir; she had no drug allergies. She smoked 1–2 cigarettes per day, consumed about 20 units of alcohol weekly, and had a body-mass index of 31.8. Obstetric history included a mid-trimester surgical dilation and curettage at 20 weeks’ gestation 20 years earlier. 

On transvaginal ultrasonography, there was heterogeneous echotexture in the anterior fundal wall with an 8-mm cystic area. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a small fundal cystic structure. Semen analysis of her partner was normal, and tests for chlamydia and cervical cytology were negative. Hysterosalpingography was attempted but cervical cannulation was unsuccessful. 

Eighteen months later, she returned with persistent left-sided pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, and menorrhagia. A repeat transvaginal ultrasound showed a linear, highly reflective foreign body measuring 18 × 3 mm within the endometrial cavity adjacent to the cervix; there was also evidence of adenomyosis, and the endometrium appeared otherwise normal.

A 19-year-old man was evaluated for involuntary palatal movements and unsteady gait. Five months earlier, he had sustained a pontomesencephalic hemorrhage. On examination, he had rhythmic palatal myoclonus synchronous with a gaze-evoked nystagmus, dysarthria, and cerebellar findings including finger-nose dysmetria. Brain MRI showed a heterogeneous T2-hyperintense lesion in the left central tegmental tract consistent with a chronic hemorrhagic cavernoma, extending to the superior and middle cerebellar peduncles and the inferior colliculus. In addition, there was bilateral enlargement and T2 hyperintensity of the inferior olivary nuclei (more pronounced on the left) without gadolinium enhancement, and mild cerebellar cortical atrophy.

A 71-year-old man with hypertension and coronary artery disease status post permanent pacemaker implantation 3 years earlier presented to the Emergency Department with a presyncopal episode while sitting. He reported lightheadedness, profuse sweating, and blurred vision. In the ED, his blood pressure was 115/75 mm Hg, heart rate 75 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Pacemaker interrogation showed normal functioning, regular parameters, and no arrhythmias. A nasopharyngeal swab for SARS-CoV-2 was performed and returned positive. A chest radiograph was unremarkable.

A 63-year-old African American man with a history of tongue cancer status post surgery and radiation therapy 5 years ago presented with 4 days of worsening right eye pain, upper-lid swelling, ptosis, significant chemosis, and mucous discharge. He noted chronic bilateral eye swelling and discharge for a “long time,” but the right-side pain and swelling acutely worsened until the eye was swollen shut. He denied trauma, fevers, or chills. 

On examination, he had pain with extraocular movements, decreased vision in the right eye, normal pupillary reactions, and no neurologic deficits. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed ALT 39 U/L, AST 100 U/L, total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL, INR 1.0, platelet count 150 × 10^3/µL; WBC 4.2 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, hematocrit 31.1%.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits demonstrated enlargement and inflammation of both lacrimal glands and surrounding tissues, right greater than left. An extensive autoimmune and rheumatic serologic panel—including ANA, SSA, SSB, ANCA, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and thyroid antibodies—was negative. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Screening for Treponema pallidum, HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis A, and Epstein–Barr virus was negative. Hepatitis C antibody was positive; HCV viral load was approximately 600,000 IU/mL, genotype 1A.

A 73-year-old man presented with progressive dysphagia and a history of melena. He had been taking nonsteroidal analgesics for several weeks for back pain but was not on antacids. Laboratory tests revealed microcytic anemia (red blood cell count, 2.04×10^6/μL; hemoglobin, 5.4 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume, 88.2 fL). Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a semi-pedunculated, 50-mm submucosal mass in the gastric fundus that appeared to originate from the oral side of the esophagogastric junction and prolapsed into the stomach; the surface was eroded but without active bleeding. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a low-enhancement lesion in the same location. Endoscopic ultrasonography revealed a homogeneous, hypoechoic, well-vascularized tumor in the second and third layers of the gastric wall, although its exact layer of origin was obscured by prolapse. Two attempts at EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded insufficient tissue; the samples were negative for c-kit, DOG1, and desmin, and the lesion was therefore suspected to be a benign tumor such as leiomyoma.

A 32-year-old woman with obesity presented with postprandial nausea and spasmodic upper abdominal pain. She had no jaundice, pruritus, or bleeding tendency. On examination she was afebrile, not jaundiced, and had unremarkable abdominal findings. Laboratory studies showed aspartate aminotransferase 98 U/L (normal 8–33), alanine aminotransferase 129 U/L (4–36), alkaline phosphatase 229 IU/L (44–147), and normal albumin and coagulation studies. Viral markers for hepatitis A, B, and C; autoimmune markers; and tests for Wilson’s disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency, and hemochromatosis were all negative. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated gross erosive gastritis, and biopsies showed reactive gastritis. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed adenomyomatosis and possible gallbladder polyps or adherent stones; the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts were not dilated. Because her symptoms persisted without a clear diagnosis, she underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy with a liver biopsy. Intraoperatively, the liver appeared soft, normal in size, and without surface abnormalities; blood loss was minimal.

A 48-year-old man of Persian ethnicity presented multiple times over 3 months to the surgical emergency department with colicky abdominal pain in the left upper and lower quadrants that worsened after meals, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and obstipation. He had no prior abdominal surgeries and no significant medical history other than occasional acid reflux. He denied medication use, alcohol, and allergies. 

On four separate visits, vital signs were stable. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the left upper and lower quadrants with normal bowel sounds. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. An abdominal radiograph suggested obstipation without signs of obstruction. He was treated with an osmotic laxative, a proton-pump inhibitor, analgesics, and a spasmolytic, with symptomatic relief.

Outpatient evaluation included gastroscopy, which showed erythematous gastric mucosa and fluid retention in small-bowel loops; colonoscopy, which was normal; and abdominal ultrasound, which suggested a small-bowel subileus. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed proximal small-bowel loops dilated to 3.5 cm, distal loops of normal caliber arranged in a “sac-like” configuration with mesenteric fat stranding, a small amount of free fluid, no free air, and no lymphadenopathy. The radiologist reported findings suggestive of duodenojejunal flexure stenosis due to an internal mesenteric hernia.

Because of these clinical and radiologic findings, the patient was scheduled for exploratory laparoscopy.

A girl was born at 34 weeks’ gestation (twin pregnancy) with a birth weight of 2.3 kg. Her twin brother had normal development. Since birth she had giant melanocytic nevi covering both legs and extensive smaller nevi over her trunk and limbs. 

At age 7 years she returned for evaluation of short stature and progressive limb deformities. Orthopedic examination showed bilateral genu valgum (30°), hip valgus (right 20°, left 15°), and thoracolumbar scoliosis. She had a positive Gowers sign. 

Neurologic evaluation revealed normal serum creatine kinase, aspartate transaminase, and aldolase levels; intact cranial nerves; normal strength in the arms; but decreased muscle bulk and proximal weakness in the legs, hypotonia, hyperreflexia, and an exhaustible Achilles clonus. Gait was notable for mild claudication, lower-extremity dragging, and increased lumbar lordosis, consistent with paraparesis and pyramidal signs. 

Spine MRI showed diffuse loss of vertebral body height from T3 to T11 and at L2 and L4 without intradural abnormalities. Radiographs demonstrated impaired bone mineralization. 

At age 7 years 7 months, endocrinology evaluation revealed serum phosphate 1.7 mg/dL (normal 3.3–5.2), calcium 9.7 mg/dL (8.8–10.7), PTH 70 pg/mL (10–65), alkaline phosphatase 4590 U/L (<280), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 12.6 ng/mL (30–60). Height was below the 3rd percentile (Z score –4.96). She began oral calcitriol and phosphate. 

Given the hypophosphatemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and bone deformities, the team suspected hypophosphatemic rickets (including X-linked hypophosphatemia, vitamin D deficiency, or tumor-induced osteomalacia). 

At age 8 years, repeat radiographs showed persistent rickets. Serum FGF23 was elevated at 185 kRU/L (26–110). Fractional tubular reabsorption of phosphate was 73% and TmP/GFR was 1.60 mg/dL (2.9–6.5).

A 64-year-old woman with significant mental and physical disability residing in a nursing facility was brought to the emergency department with a 4-month history of chronic intermittent constipation. She had required multiple treatments for severe constipation and fecal impaction without sustained relief. On examination, she was malnourished, bedbound, and noncommunicative. An aggressive bowel regimen was initiated without significant improvement. A plain abdominal radiograph revealed a massive stool burden filling the rectum, with distension extending cephalad to the diaphragm and anterior peritoneal displacement occupying much of the abdominal cavity. A computed tomography scan of the abdomen confirmed a large volume of stool in the rectosigmoid colon without evidence of an obstructing lesion. Colonoscopy performed within the preceding 2 years showed no polyps or malignant process.

A 30-year-old woman was admitted for recurrent biliary colic with suspected acute calculous cholecystitis. Initial laboratory tests showed mildly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. She was started on analgesics, spasmolytics, and antibiotics. Three days later, she developed fever to >38.5 °C, a maculopapular rash on the arms and torso, a malar rash, and dyspnea. N-terminal pro–b-type natriuretic peptide was 9373 ng/L (normal <208 ng/L), and high-sensitivity troponin I was 293 ng/L (normal <39 ng/L). ECGs showed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Laboratory markers of inflammation included low albumin, elevated fibrinogen, and normal ferritin.  
Abdominal ultrasound showed no signs of acute cholecystitis. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed hypocontractility of the basal anterior, septal, and lateral walls with preserved wall thickness and left ventricular (LV) diameter, mildly reduced ejection fraction (45%), reduced global longitudinal peak strain (–15.1%), moderate mitral regurgitation, grade 3 diastolic dysfunction, and a small (2–3 mm) pericardial effusion. Concern for an allergic reaction led to low-dose corticosteroids and antihistamines while guideline-directed heart failure therapy was initiated.  
Blood and urine cultures and viral panels for cardiotropic agents were negative. Tumor markers and an interferon-γ release assay for latent tuberculosis were within normal limits. Coronary angiography showed no obstructive disease. The patient received diuretics, a β-blocker, an aldosterone antagonist, sacubitril/valsartan, and ibuprofen for pericarditis.  
A few days later, repeat echocardiography showed markedly increased LV wall thickness with an ejection fraction of 57%, global longitudinal peak strain of –19%, mild mitral regurgitation, grade 1 diastolic dysfunction, and a pericardial effusion of 10 mm. Depressed strain persisted in basal anterior, septal, and lateral segments, raising suspicion for myocarditis.

A 23-year-old woman presented to the emergency department in serious condition, reporting six episodes of emesis and intense, diffuse abdominal pain over the past 24 hours. She had fever up to 38.5 °C the previous day but denied headache, sore throat, or cough. Two days earlier she began feeling unwell; over the preceding three months she noted intense thirst with increased fluid intake, polyuria—especially nocturia—and an unintended 5 kg weight loss. She had no known medical issues, did not take medications, and was unvaccinated against SARS-CoV-2.  
On examination she appeared thin (BMI 16 kg/m2), tachypneic at 32 breaths/min but with SpO2 99% on room air; heart rate was 119 beats/min, blood pressure 115/57 mm Hg, and temperature 37.1 °C. Lung and heart auscultation were unremarkable; the abdomen was diffusely tender without rebound. She was alert and cooperative.  
A rapid SARS-CoV-2 antigen test was positive. Point-of-care glucose was 580 mg/dL. Laboratory tests showed: C-reactive protein 31.4 mg/L, ferritin 400.7 ng/mL, HbA1c 14%. Arterial blood gases (room air) revealed pH 7.06, PaCO2 10.7 mm Hg, HCO3– 3.1 mmol/L, anion gap 32.5 mmol/L. Urinalysis showed glycosuria (+4), proteinuria (+1), and ketonuria (+2). Blood and urine cultures were sterile.  
A chest X-ray was normal.

A 16-year-old girl was brought to the emergency department with an inability to walk and near-total mutism of several days’ duration, following months of progressive fatigue, loss of appetite, and social withdrawal.  
History of Present Illness: Over the preceding 3–4 months, she became increasingly fatigued, isolating herself, and eating less. In March she was assessed at a child and adolescent psychiatry emergency department for mild depressive symptoms; neurological examination and blood chemistry were normal and fluoxetine was initiated. In April she stopped walking, became almost entirely mute, and required her mother to feed her.  
Past Medical and Developmental History: She is a cautious, conscientious, withdrawn only child, independent from an early age, with idiosyncratic language. She has excellent academic performance, extreme auditory memory, and was suspected to have autism, although no formal evaluation was completed.  
Family and Social History: The intact but strained family environment includes a father with an undiagnosed neurological condition leading to posttraumatic stress symptoms. She recently transferred to a more demanding high school program, skipping a grade, and reported feeling “different.”  
Medications: Fluoxetine, titrated up over 3 months.  
Physical Examination: Vital signs stable. Neurological exam normal apart from refusal to cooperate with gait and speech testing. She communicates only by tapping for yes/no and displays agitated outbursts when prompted to move or speak. She accepts nasogastric tube feeding but refuses oral intake.  
Initial Investigations: Complete blood count, metabolic panel, inflammatory markers, and imaging studies were unremarkable.  
A Bush–Francis Catatonia Rating Scale was applied, yielding a total score of 5, not indicative of catatonia.

A 32-year-old man from Pakistan presented with a 2–3-month history of painless bilateral retroauricular masses and progressively worsening edema of the lower limbs and scrotum. He had no significant past medical or family history. On examination, he had 3.0 × 1.5 cm and 2.5 × 1.3 cm retroauricular masses and pitting edema of the lower limbs and scrotum. 

Laboratory studies showed:
  • Serum albumin 1.2 g/dL and creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (MDRD 37 mL/min/1.73 m2)  
  • Eosinophil count 2.65 × 103/µL (normal WBC count)  
  • Total cholesterol 322 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 266 mg/dL  
  • C-reactive protein 1.2 mg/dL; liver function tests and coagulation normal  
  • Negative screening for parasitic, fungal, and viral infections  
  • Serum IgE 19 000 U/mL  
  • Urinalysis: specific gravity 1.026, 4+ proteinuria, 80 RBCs/µL; 24-h proteinuria 19 g  

A total-body CT scan was unremarkable. To exclude lymphoma or metastatic disease, an excisional biopsy of a retroauricular mass was performed.

An 82-year-old woman with hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic constipation, and insomnia presented with three days of intermittent abdominal pain and vomiting. The pain began in the right lower quadrant and became generalized on the day before admission. On arrival, vital signs were normal. Examination showed dry mucous membranes, a soft but distended abdomen with hyperactive bowel sounds, and tenderness in the right lower quadrant without peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 9400/μL, blood urea nitrogen of 50.9 mg/dL, and creatinine of 1.07 mg/dL. A plain abdominal CT scan demonstrated obstruction at the rectosigmoid colon, proximal colonic dilation with stool, and a cecal diameter of 95 mm. Colonoscopy on hospital day 2 showed a large amount of stool but no mechanical obstruction; abdominal distension and pain improved after decompression. Ogilvie syndrome was diagnosed, oral intake was withheld, parenteral nutrition was started, and subcutaneous neostigmine was administered. Following endoscopic decompression, the patient developed watery diarrhea. On hospital day 3, the diarrhea ceased and she became hypotensive and oliguric, unresponsive to crystalloid infusion, with recurrent abdominal distension and diffuse mild tenderness without peritoneal signs. Repeat CT scan showed massive pneumatosis intestinalis in the small bowel and ascending colon, with superior mesenteric venous gas and hepatic portal venous gas. Her serum lactate level was 6.7 mmol/L.

A 70-year-old Japanese man with a 9-year history of well-controlled rheumatoid arthritis (on iguratimod, low-dose prednisolone, and methotrexate) presented with a 3-month history of nonresolving cough. Two months earlier he had been treated for presumed community-acquired pneumonia with amoxicillin-clavulanate without improvement; repeat chest CT showed worsening infiltrates.

On examination, T 36.3 °C, BP 156/76 mm Hg, pulse 92/min, RR 16/min, SpO₂ 95% on room air; chest auscultation was clear. Laboratory studies revealed WBC 9000/mm³ with marked eosinophilia (3825/mm³), CRP 0.34 mg/dL, total IgE 233 IU/mL, negative anti-GLP core IgA, negative IGRA, positive Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG. 

Chest radiograph demonstrated consolidations in the right upper and lower fields. Chest CT revealed a nodular shadow in the right upper lobe, central bronchiectasis, centrilobular nodules in the right lower lobe, and mucus-filled bronchi with high attenuation mucus (density ≥ paraspinal muscle).

A 45-year-old woman was admitted with a 3-day history of right facial weakness and progressive vision loss in her right eye. She noticed facial asymmetry and an inability to close her right eyelid on awakening, accompanied by drooping of the right angle of her mouth, diplopia, and blurring of vision in the right eye. She also reported episodic, self-resolving vertigo but denied headache, fever, infection, nasal congestion, discharge, or sinus pain. There was no history of trauma. Baseline laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and serum electrolytes, were within normal limits; C-reactive protein was 1.25 mg/dL (reference < 1 mg/dL) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 30 mm/h (reference < 20 mm/h). On examination, she was alert and oriented but had House-Brackmann grade IV right facial palsy with loss of forehead movement, orbicularis oculi function, and nasolabial fold. There was no light perception in the right eye, and funduscopic examination showed optic atrophy. Right eye movement was limited in all directions, suggesting involvement of cranial nerves III, IV, and VI. Pupillary reflexes were poorly preserved on the right. Urgent imaging was obtained. Noncontrast CT of the brain and paranasal sinuses revealed a space-occupying lesion in the sphenoid sinus extending into the sellar region with compression of the right optic nerve and bony erosion, without intracranial extension. A CT angiogram was normal, excluding a vascular neoplasm. MRI demonstrated an invasive mass with marked pressure on the optic nerve and encroachment on adjacent cranial nerves. Pituitary hormone assays, including prolactin, growth hormone, cortisol, ACTH, TSH, free T4, LH, and FSH, were all within normal limits.

A 68-year-old Caucasian woman with acute myelogenous leukemia on idarubicin and cytarabine presented with new-onset, intense, sharp right-sided headaches 15 days into her admission. She had a strong history of migraines and experienced some relief with a migraine cocktail. A lumbar puncture was deferred for thrombocytopenia, and a contrasted MRI was initially not performed. Over the next five days, she continued to have severe headaches and was noted to have mild right-sided ptosis and very subtle periorbital edema. An MRI of the brain and a CT angiogram of the head and neck were unremarkable except for mucosal thickening of the sphenoid and ethmoid sinuses. Her headaches and ptosis persisted for two more days; examination by a community ophthalmologist showed only mild ptosis, and a stroke specialist noted right-sided ptosis with tenderness over the right eye. A repeat CT angiogram showed no stroke but increased sinus mucosal thickening and opacification. Angiography to rule out a carotid cavernous fistula, a CT venogram, and a lumbar puncture were all negative. She was discharged with ongoing headaches and right-sided ptosis. Two weeks later, she presented to a retina clinic with light-perception vision in the right eye, a cranial nerve III and VI palsy on the right, and subtle proptosis.

A 19-year-old woman with aplastic anemia underwent an 8/8 HLA-matched unrelated-donor allogeneic HSCT (with a single HLA-DQB1 mismatch and sex mismatch). Conditioning included cyclophosphamide, fludarabine, rabbit antithymocyte globulin, and total body irradiation. GVHD prophylaxis was tacrolimus and methotrexate. She had no personal or family history of atopic dermatitis.

On day 152 post-transplant, she developed diffuse pruritus without rash and was started on prednisone (0.5 mg/kg) for presumed GVHD, with continuation of tacrolimus. Several weeks later, she developed nummular eczematous patches on the trunk. Despite topical clobetasol and tacrolimus ointments and addition of ruxolitinib, her rash progressed to lichenified, crusted nummular patches on the trunk and extremities, including flexural areas, with 10/10 pruritus. She had no extracutaneous GVHD involvement. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count with normal eosinophil count, and she had no new environmental or food allergies.

By day 239 post-transplant, she had approximately 10% body surface area involvement, pruritus 10/10, and an investigator’s global assessment score of 3 for atopic dermatitis. A punch biopsy of an arm lesion showed subacute spongiotic dermatitis with a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate and eosinophils; “typical features of GVHD such as an interface component, satellitosis, lichenoid inflammation, and sclerosis were not seen.”

A 54-year-old farmer presented with a 2-year history of a left parotid swelling. On examination, there was a firm, mobile, painless, well-circumscribed mass measuring 3 cm in the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland; the overlying skin was normal, and there was no cervical adenopathy or facial nerve palsy. Cervical ultrasonography revealed a 3 cm cystic lesion in the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 33 mm cystic mass with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, no diffusion restriction, and no enhancement of the cyst wall after gadolinium administration. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion yielded clear fluid containing occasional epithelial cells.

A 30-year-old G3P1011 woman presented at 20 weeks of gestation for routine fetal anomaly screening. Her past medical history was unremarkable, and there was no family history of congenital anomalies. 

Ultrasonographic examination revealed:
- Bilateral popliteal webbing extending from the posterior thighs to the heels, with knee extension limited to ≤90°
- Bilateral talipes equinovarus
- Syndactyly and ectrodactyly of the toes
- Ambiguous external genitalia: a penis-like phallus, poorly developed scrotum, and suspected hypospadias
- Suspicion of cleft lip

Fetal biometry, placental appearance, and amniotic fluid volume were all normal. Both upper limbs appeared structurally normal with normal movement. No additional anomalies were identified. 

Fetal cord blood and parental blood samples were obtained for genetic analysis.

A 10-week-old male domestic pig (Sus scrofa domestica) weighing 35 kg was examined before an experimental study. Physical examination findings were unremarkable, and there was no history of ocular injury, head trauma, or systemic disease.
