Ophthalmic examination of the right eye showed normal anterior segment findings on slit-lamp biomicroscopy and clear vitreous. Indirect ophthalmoscopy revealed a white, tumor-like mass protruding from the optic nerve head into the vitreous cavity, composed of multiple pedunculated nodules with a smooth surface temporally and an irregular, rough surface superonasally. Surrounding the optic disk, there was local retinal folding and neuroepithelial detachment most pronounced along the inferior margin. The vitreous was clear, with no signs of inflammation, hemorrhage, vascular congestion, or vitreous haze. Despite some distortion of retinal vessel branching by the lesion, vessel caliber and appearance were otherwise normal. The right pupil was mildly dilated with a relative afferent pupillary defect. The left eye examination was normal. Intraocular pressures measured 15.8 mm Hg in the right eye and 15.4 mm Hg in the left eye.

A 53-year-old man presented with 3 days of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools. His medical history was unremarkable. On exam he was icteric, with mild right upper quadrant tenderness and no stigmata of chronic liver disease.  
Laboratory studies showed:  
• Normal complete blood count, lactate dehydrogenase, albumin, prothrombin time, and thromboplastin time (INR 1.0).  
• Total bilirubin 19.91 mg/dL, AST 418 U/L, ALT 695 U/L.  
Serologic testing for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and Epstein-Barr virus were negative. A peripheral blood smear and comprehensive autoimmune panel were normal. Acetaminophen toxicity was ruled out on history and initial evaluation.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 24 × 29 × 33 mm interpolar solid exophytic mass in the right kidney (RENAL nephrometry score 9) and hepatosplenomegaly, with no evidence of choledocholithiasis, pancreatic mass, or metastases. Chest CT was unremarkable. MR cholangiopancreatography and portal‐vein Doppler ultrasound revealed no structural biliary or hepatic vascular abnormalities.

A 6-year-old, 22-kg girl with suspected Down syndrome and a history of recurrent otitis media and pneumonia was scheduled for strabismus surgery under general anesthesia. Her prior surgical and family histories were unremarkable. Anesthesia was induced with fentanyl 44 μg, propofol 66 mg, and suxamethonium 22 mg, followed by orotracheal intubation; anesthesia was maintained with halothane 1–2%. Approximately 90 minutes after surgery, her pulse rose from 126 to 166 beats/min, and her temperature from 37 °C to 42 °C. She developed generalized muscular rigidity and a generalized tonic–clonic seizure, followed by bradycardia and cardiac arrest.

A 35-year-old homeless woman was brought to the psychiatric emergency in a disheveled state after being found roaming by the roadside. She exhibited unkempt hair with patches of hair loss and multiple crusted lesions on the scalp, face, and extremities. She demonstrated poor personal hygiene and severe pallor on examination.  

On mental status examination, her speech was increased in flow and volume, psychomotor activity was elevated, and she was markedly uncooperative and irritable. She experienced third-person auditory hallucinations, occasional inappropriate smiling, and predominantly irrelevant speech; her judgment and insight were impaired. Observation in the ward revealed disorganized, disruptive, and hallucinatory behavior, disturbed sleep, poor self-care, and socially disinhibited behavior.  

She frequently scratched her genitals and was diagnosed with bacterial vaginitis and treated with ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. Dermatology was consulted for itchy, crusted, verrucous, scaly lesions over the chest, trunk, and upper extremities. There were no signs of inflammation, no discharge or induration, and no disruption of the skin surface.  

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL with a hypochromic, microcytic red-cell picture (low MCV and MCHC). HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and VDRL tests were negative.

A 34-year-old man presented with a 5- to 6-month history of bleeding and swollen gums in the upper and lower front teeth. He was in fair general health, denied any personal or family history of systemic illness, abnormal bleeding, surgeries, or drug allergies, and had stopped a 10-year tobacco-chewing habit 3 months earlier.

Examination revealed heavy extrinsic stains, plaque, calculus, severe generalized attrition with sharp incisal edges, and an anterior deep bite. There was generalized gingival overgrowth involving marginal, attached, and interdental gingiva—red and edematous in the papillary region, pale pink and fibrotic on the attached gingiva—with traumatic impressions of the maxillary incisors on the enlarged mandibular gingiva. Bleeding on probing was noted. Probing depths measured 6–8 mm anteriorly (true and pseudo pockets) and averaged 5 mm posteriorly. Panoramic radiography showed horizontal bone loss in the mandibular anterior region.

Routine blood tests—including hemoglobin, bleeding time, and clotting time—were within normal limits. Phase I periodontal therapy was completed without bleeding complications. An incisional biopsy confirmed inflammatory gingival hyperplasia. Four weeks later, nonsurgical therapy had reduced inflammation but residual 5–6 mm pockets persisted in the mandibular anterior sextant. A full-thickness periodontal flap procedure was performed under local anesthesia; hemostasis was achieved intraoperatively, and the flap was sutured with periodontal dressing applied. Postoperative instructions included ibuprofen, amoxicillin, cold fomentation, and chlorhexidine rinses.

On postoperative day 1, the patient returned with continuous oozing and a blood clot extruding beneath the dressing. Manual pressure with plain gauze failed to control the bleeding, but a tranexamic acid–soaked pack achieved hemostasis. Advanced coagulation studies then showed an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time of 55 seconds, with all other parameters in the normal range.

A 71-year-old man with a 1-year history of rheumatoid arthritis treated with prednisone (6 mg/day) and salazosulfapyridine (1000 mg/day) was admitted for evaluation of elevated liver enzymes. He denied alcohol use, recent travel, sexual contacts, and had no new medications. On examination, he was icteric and had mild pruritus; vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound, CT, and MRCP showed no biliary obstruction or mass lesions. Laboratory studies revealed: total bilirubin 3.76 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.12 mg/dL, AST 167 IU/L, ALT 435 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 2539 IU/L, γ-GTP 590 IU/L; IgG 1322 mg/dL, IgM 705 mg/dL; ANA titer ×40; AMA titer ×20; AMA-M2 antibody 34.1 (normal <6); anti-gp210 antibody 0.2 U/mL (normal <6); anti-centromere antibody 55.6 U/mL (normal <9.9). A liver biopsy on hospital day 4 showed marked inflammatory cell infiltration surrounding and destroying the interlobular bile ducts in the portal area without granulomas or evidence of chronic nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis.

A 68-year-old woman presented with moderate bilateral temporomandibular joint (TMJ) pain and impaired mouth opening. Ten years earlier she had a mandibular injury in a car accident, with a chin laceration and swelling; shortly afterward she experienced severe bilateral TMJ pain and restricted jaw movement for five weeks, resolving with NSAIDs. Her general health was otherwise good. On examination, the interincisal opening was 25 mm, lateral and protrusive movements were limited by pain, there was dental loss and malocclusion, and an enlargement of a distal interphalangeal joint (Heberden’s node) was noted. There was no family history of arthrosis. Laboratory studies (CBC, ESR, RF, ANA) were within normal limits. CT of the TMJs showed bilateral condylar articular-surface erosion, roughened condylar contours, joint-space narrowing, subchondral bone thickening with sclerosis, subchondral cysts, and osteophyte formation.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of right shoulder pain, notably worse at night, accompanied by stiffness and weakness. She had no history of trauma or athletic activity. On examination, there was a painful, reduced arc of motion of the right shoulder and mild weakness on resisted external rotation and abduction. General examination and laboratory studies were normal.

Noncontrast CT of the shoulder demonstrated a large semilunar calcification within the infraspinatus tendon adjacent to an area of increased bone density in the greater tuberosity of the humerus, with a thin cortical discontinuity. A second small rounded calcification was also noted.

MRI showed that the sclerotic area in the greater tuberosity was hypointense on T1- and T2-weighted sequences, with marked surrounding bone marrow edema visible on STIR images.

Initial differential diagnoses included osteoblastoma, osteoid osteoma, osteochondritis, and an infective process.

A 52-year-old Kurdish woman first noted lesions on her toes 20 years ago, which gradually involved the interphalangeal joints of both feet, both hands, both wrists, both knees, and both hips. She had no family history of similar disease. At age 32, surgical excision of a lesion on the second toe of her right foot led to necrosis and amputation of its distal phalanx. Over the next decade, she developed progressively worsening pain and limitation of motion in the affected joints.  
On examination, there was severe restriction of movement in the fingers, toes, wrists, knees, and hips bilaterally. Biochemical laboratory tests showed normal serum levels of calcium, phosphorus, creatinine, uric acid, and alkaline phosphatase. Urinalysis was negative for protein, glucose, ketone, bilirubin, and urobilinogen.  
Plain radiographs demonstrated extensive interphalangeal and wrist joint ossification, periarticular ossification around the knee joints, and interarticular and periarticular ossifications in the hip joints.

A 69-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of progressive dyspnea on exertion and 2 weeks of swelling over the dorsum of his right foot. He had no significant past medical or family history, had smoked 30 cigarettes per day for 50 years, and had no occupational dust exposures. On examination, fine crackles were audible bilaterally over the posterior lung fields and there was edema of the right foot dorsum. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 30,402/μL with a left shift (2% myeloblasts, 1% promyelocytes, 3% myelocytes, 2% metamyelocytes, 9% band forms, 68% mature granulocytes, 7% lymphocytes, 1% basophils, 7% monocytes), hemoglobin 15.6 g/dL, platelets 195,000/μL, lactate dehydrogenase 430 IU/L, carcinoembryonic antigen 15.8 ng/mL, KL-6 38,090 U/mL, surfactant protein D 185.9 ng/mL, and otherwise unremarkable chemistries and serologies. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral alveolar opacities in the mid- and lower lung zones, and high-resolution computed tomography revealed diffuse ground-glass opacities with interlobular septal thickening (“crazy-paving”). Pulmonary-function testing showed a diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide of 11.39 mL/min/mmHg (80.8% predicted). Bone marrow biopsy revealed hypercellularity with granulocytic hyperplasia, a modest increase in megakaryocytes without dysplasia, and mild reticulin fibrosis. Cytogenetic analysis was 46,XY[20/20] and fluorescence in situ hybridization for BCR-ABL was 0%. There was no splenomegaly, leukoerythroblastosis, anemia, polycythemia, thrombocythemia, eosinophilia, or marrow dysplasia. By exclusion of chronic myelogenous leukemia, primary myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, chronic eosinophilic leukemia, myelodysplastic syndromes, atypical CML, and chronic neutrophilic leukemia, a diagnosis of myeloproliferative neoplasm, unclassifiable (MPN-U) was made.

A 7-year-old right-hand–dominant girl presented with 2 months of dull, constant pain and gradually progressive swelling of the right fourth metacarpal. There was no history of trauma or infection. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was a solitary, diffuse, bony hard swelling over the right fourth metacarpal that was tender without erythema or warmth. Range of motion at the fourth metacarpophalangeal joint was terminally restricted by pain in all directions. Neurovascular examination of the hand was normal. Plain radiographs showed an expansile lytic lesion in the metaphyseal–diaphyseal region of the fourth metacarpal with a pathologic fracture. MRI demonstrated a cystic lesion with internal loculations and fluid–fluid levels and minimal soft-tissue extension. Routine laboratory, coagulation, and metabolic profiles were normal; serum alkaline phosphatase was mildly elevated. Needle biopsy yielded serosanguinous fluid with a hemorrhagic tinge.

A 74-year-old man with hypertension, coronary artery disease, and peripheral vascular disease presented with a 3-month history of ataxia, diplopia, and generalized fatigue. On examination, he had a wide-based gait with postural instability and horizontal nystagmus; reflexes, motor strength, sensation, and cranial nerve function otherwise were normal. Brain MRI with contrast showed numerous 1–2 mm intraaxial FLAIR-hyperintense lesions scattered predominantly throughout the central brain, with several periventricular and subcortical lesions concerning for possible central nervous system lymphoma, metastatic cancer, or an atypical granulomatous, inflammatory, or infectious etiology. Lumbar puncture revealed mildly elevated protein (64 mg/dL) without oligoclonal bands or malignant cells. Serum studies including ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-ssDNA, antimitochondrial antibody, and ACE were unremarkable. Infectious studies for Coccidioides, toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcus, Q fever, Rickettsia typhi, Borrelia burgdorferi, syphilis, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, CMV, EBV, and HIV were negative. Chest CT revealed a spiculated right upper lobe lung mass; biopsy demonstrated primary squamous-cell carcinoma. PET/CT showed intense FDG uptake in the lung mass without nodal or distant metastases. A dedicated brain-stealth MRI with contrast revealed angiocentric enhancement predominantly in the brainstem and cerebellum, with involvement of the basal ganglia, thalami, and supratentorial white matter, raising suspicion for CLIPPERS; however, the differential diagnosis also included neurosarcoidosis, lymphomatoid granulomatosis, angiocentric lymphoma, vasculitis, cerebral amyloid disease, and leptomeningeal carcinomatosis.

A 16-year-old girl presented with a 3-year history of a progressively enlarging, painless swelling in the left posterior cheek overlying the masseter region, causing facial asymmetry that was more pronounced when she clenched her teeth. She denied bruxism, gum chewing, facial trauma, dental problems, or psychiatric illness. On examination, the swelling was homogeneous, soft to firm, non-tender, and there were no signs of local inflammation or occlusal abnormalities. 

The initial differential diagnosis included salivary gland pathology, lymphatic or arteriovenous malformation, muscle tumor, and lipoma. Multidisciplinary consultations (psychological, neurosurgical, dentoalveolar and maxillofacial surgery, ophthalmologic) and laboratory tests were all within normal limits.

Ultrasound of the left masseter region showed uniformly enlarged muscle fibers measuring 13 × 48 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed that the left masseter muscle was approximately twice the size of the right, with normal morphology and signal characteristics and no abnormal contrast enhancement. No intracranial abnormalities or mandibular bone changes were identified.

A 76-year-old man with no history of immunosuppression or known malignancy presented with 3–4 weeks of lethargy, reduced exercise tolerance, anorexia, and a 4-kg weight loss. He was an ex-smoker (50 pack-years) and consumed 50–70 g of alcohol daily. His brother had pancreatic cancer. He denied fever, and examination showed no jaundice, stigmata of chronic liver disease, organomegaly, or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests revealed mild transaminase elevations, normal bilirubin, low albumin, normal APTT, and an INR of 1.4. To screen for occult malignancy, contrast-enhanced CT of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis was performed. The head and chest were unremarkable. Abdominal images showed: 
- A 7.5 × 6.3 × 8.0 cm ill-defined, heterogeneous low-density mass in hepatic segments 5 and 6 extending toward the hilum  
- A wedge-shaped heterogeneous low-density lesion in segment 8  
- Marked intrahepatic biliary duct dilatation without extrahepatic dilatation  
- Thrombi in both right and left portal veins  
- Mild to moderate ascites  
- No pathologically enlarged lymph nodes or extrahepatic malignancy  
Tumor markers showed normal alpha-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen, with a mildly elevated CA 19-9 of 51 IU/mL (reference < 37).

A 52-year-old African American man with a history of alcohol abuse presented with four days of an intensely pruritic rash that began on his trunk and extremities. He denied fevers, night sweats, chills, weight loss, respiratory, gastrointestinal, or urinary symptoms, though he noted dark urine. He drank two to three beers daily, had not seen a physician in two years, and had no tobacco or illicit drug use. He recently traveled in the northeastern United States.

On examination, temperature was 98.9°F, heart rate 113–117/min, respiratory rate 16/min, blood pressure 160/80 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Skin examination showed nonblanching purpura on the anterior calves, pruritic nonblanching macules and papules on the chest, back, arms, abdomen, and petechiae on the palms and soles. Oral mucosa was clear except for mild bleeding on the lower lip. Scleral icterus and cervical lymphadenopathy were present. Abdominal examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly and moderate bilateral pitting edema.

Laboratory studies showed thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis with a left shift, normocytic anemia, hyponatremia, elevated total bilirubin, and prolonged INR. Urinalysis revealed proteinuria, moderate bilirubin, >182 red blood cells, and 13 white blood cells; urine sediment had many RBCs without casts. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia with left axis deviation; chest radiograph was unremarkable.

Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed multiple hypodense hypovascular lesions throughout the liver with contour deformity and small periportal, periaortic, splenic, and periesophageal lymph nodes; the spleen had linear and rounded hypodensities suggesting infarcts, abscess, or malignancy. On hospital day 2, he developed fever to 101°F, acute kidney injury, hepatic dysfunction, and worsening coagulopathy, and he was transferred to the ICU. Noncontrast chest CT demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities, possibly pulmonary hemorrhage or effusions. All blood cultures, urine cultures, and infectious studies returned negative.

A female infant was delivered by cesarean section after an uncomplicated full-term pregnancy, weighing 3500 g, with Apgar scores of 8 and 9. The antenatal course was uneventful, with no maternal medication use or radiation exposure. On examination, there was a malformed accessory extremity resembling a tiny arm attached to the midline of the upper back. The appendage was nonmovable and without an arterial pulse. The remainder of the neurologic and systemic examination was normal.

Cranial ultrasonography showed no abnormality. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spinal cord was normal except for a 2 cm lipoma at the level of the accessory limb; there was no meningocele or myelocele. Abdominal ultrasonography was normal. Thoracic computed tomography revealed spina bifida from the fifth cervical to the seventh thoracic vertebrae and demonstrated that the accessory limb contained two hypoplastic metacarpal bones and three phalanges without a humerus, radius, or ulna. MRI further showed that the spinal cord terminated between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae, and that the ectopic arm originated from subcutaneous soft tissues, ending at the interspinous ligament without extension into neural elements. Routine blood tests, urine analysis, and echocardiography were all within normal limits.

A 38-year-old Indian man with a history of recurrent low-grade fevers and newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus treated with metformin presented with 10 days of right-sided chest and right upper abdominal pain and dyspnea. He described sharp, tearing, localized pain (7/10), worsened by movement and deep inspiration, without cough or hemoptysis. He denied gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, sick contacts, recent travel, or asbestos exposure. He reported past extramarital sexual relationships. On admission: temperature 37.2°C; heart rate 110 bpm; blood pressure 130/80 mmHg; respiratory rate 40 breaths/min. Examination revealed a patchy, macular hyperpigmented rash on both shins and dorsum of the feet, and decreased breath sounds and vocal fremitus at the right lower chest. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count 12.3 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 15 g/dL, platelets 219 × 10^3/µL; blood urea nitrogen 4.3 mmol/L; creatinine 69 µmol/L. Chest radiograph demonstrated patchy infiltrates in the right lower zone and obliteration of the right costophrenic angle. Thoracentesis yielded pale yellow fluid with 1260 WBCs/µL (87% neutrophils), 1590 RBCs/µL, pH 7.237; a rare giant cell was seen; cultures were negative. Pleural biopsy showed empyema without granulomas; Quantiferon and acid-fast bacilli studies were negative. CT chest revealed multiple encysted pleural effusions in the right lung. Transesophageal echocardiography showed no thrombi or intracardiac masses. A comprehensive respiratory viral and atypical pathogen panel was negative. The patient was treated sequentially with piperacillin/tazobactam and then meropenem, with gradual resolution of fever and clinical improvement; a chest tube and thoracotomy were performed to drain the effusion.

A 36‐year‐old woman with diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with a one‐month history of abdominal pain and fatigue. She denied vomiting, diarrhea, fever, chills, rashes, hematuria, cough, weight loss, chest pain, or dyspnea. Vital signs were stable, and physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a total serum calcium level of 13.2 mg/dL (corrected to 14.4 mg/dL), an intact parathyroid hormone level of 6.8 pg/mL, and a serum creatinine level of 2.4 mg/dL. She was not taking calcium supplements. The 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D level was 37.6 ng/mL and the 25‐hydroxyvitamin D level was 9.9 ng/mL. Workup for multiple myeloma, thyrotoxicosis, and tumor markers was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed increased liver echotexture and normal kidneys. She was treated with intravenous fluids, diuretics, and calcitonin, yet hypercalcemia and renal impairment persisted. Whole‐body 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated areas of increased metabolic activity in the liver, spleen, and left internal iliac, left external iliac, and right internal iliac lymph nodes.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a 3-year history of right thigh pain and a limp. He was afebrile and in good general health, without redness, swelling, or draining sinuses over the thigh. Plain radiographs of the right femur demonstrated pan-femoral diaphyseal involvement with widening of the bone compared with the opposite side, marked cortical thickening, and patchy intramedullary lucencies. MRI of the right femur revealed diffuse T2-weighted hyperintensity along the entire diaphysis without cortical breach.

A 59-year-old woman presented with recurrent episodes of erythema, swelling, pain, and pruritus localized to her feet and lower extremities. She described each episode as beginning with an itchy blister on the foot, which then expanded to involve surrounding skin. Her medical history included atopic dermatitis, autoimmune thyroiditis, hypertension, and colitis. On initial examination, there was minimal erythema with scale on the plantar surface of her feet, and a clinical diagnosis of tinea pedis was made and treated with topical clotrimazole. Several weeks later, she developed acute erythema, edema, and pain of the left foot and was admitted for intravenous antibiotics after failing oral therapy; she improved and was discharged. Several weeks after that, the same area developed an erythematous, nonpurulent bulla with associated pruritus, prompting hospital evaluation.

Laboratory studies revealed negative blood cultures and Lyme serologies, and a normal complete blood count. Wound cultures from the interdigital spaces grew normal skin flora, Klebsiella oxytoca, and Enterococcus faecalis, which were considered nonpathogenic colonizers. A punch biopsy of the left medial fifth toe was performed. Histopathologic examination showed papillary and reticular perivascular dermatitis with numerous eosinophils and a subepidermal blister. In the deeper dermis and subcutis, there were numerous degranulating eosinophils admixed with lymphocytes and histiocytes. Periodic acid–Schiff stain was negative for fungal elements, and direct immunofluorescence testing was negative. The histologic differential diagnosis included a bullous arthropod reaction.

A 77-year-old man presented with a 6-day history of progressive left-sided abdominal pain. The pain began suddenly, was constant, rated 8/10 on a numerical scale, radiated to the back, and had no clear exacerbating or relieving factors, worsening markedly over the preceding 3 days. He was independent with a WHO performance status of 0. His medical history included hypertension, a prior pulmonary embolism, chronic work-related back pain, and a suprapubic catheter placed for multiple urethral strictures after green light prostatectomy. He initially attributed his new pain to his chronic back condition.

On examination, he appeared comfortable at rest. Blood pressure was 220/90 mmHg in the left arm and 224/89 mmHg in the right arm. A suprapubic catheter was in situ without signs of local infection. The abdomen was soft but tender in the suprapubic region; there was no costovertebral angle tenderness, and bowel sounds were normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal function, and serum electrolytes, were all within normal limits. Given his hypertension and acute abdominal pain, a CT angiogram was performed to evaluate for aortic dissection or ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. The CT angiogram demonstrated intra-abdominal free fluid on the left side.

A 24-year-old man presented with acute global aphasia and right-sided hemiplegia. Four months earlier he had intermittent headaches. One month after headache onset he developed evening fevers and abdominal pain; abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly with multiple granulomas, and CT of the abdomen revealed periportal, para-aortic, and aortic caval lymphadenitis-like features. He was treated presumptively for mycobacterial tuberculosis. Ten days later he developed new speech difficulty and right-sided weakness; brain MRI at that time showed a thin left frontal subdural collection (2×3×2 mm) and a rim of thin epidural collection, and anti-tubercular therapy was continued. One month into therapy he presented with worsening aphasia and hemiplegia. On examination his Glasgow Coma Scale score was E3 V A M5, and he had dense right-sided hemiplegia. Repeat MRI of the brain showed on T1 an isointense rim with a hypointense left frontal collection, on T2 a fluid-fluid level, and on FLAIR a hyperintense extra-axial/subdural collection; contrast images demonstrated conglomerate peripheral ring-enhancing intraparenchymal lesions in the left frontal lobe with moderate to significant perilesional edema causing mass effect; diffusion-weighted imaging revealed diffusion restriction in the lesion wall and contents; and MR spectroscopy showed large lipid-lactate peaks. These findings were interpreted as suggestive of an infective etiology with cerebral abscess, subdural empyema, dural thickening with an intradural abscess in the left frontal region, and frontal cortical vein thrombosis.

A 51-year-old man with multiple hereditary exostoses, allergic rhinitis, and recent nasal repair for a fracture presented with sinus pain, pressure, low back pain, and fevers up to 100.8°F, predominantly at night. Postoperatively he received cyclobenzaprine and amoxicillin–clavulanate for presumed sinusitis, but fevers persisted and he was admitted for presumed sepsis. On admission, his qSOFA score was 0; laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (WBC 16.8→19.4 K/μl), elevated glucose, and mild AST elevation. CT of the sinuses demonstrated opacification of the frontal and ethmoid sinuses with polypoid soft-tissue densities. MRI of the lumbar spine revealed slight enhancement of the cauda equina, consistent with arachnoiditis. Venous duplex imaging was negative. Flexible nasolaryngoscopy revealed hemorrhagic sinus drainage; the fluid was sent for culture. A broad microbial cell-free DNA panel was negative, but gram stain of the sinus fluid showed budding yeast, and micafungin was started. Point-of-care ultrasound of the right lung base showed a small pleural effusion. PET-CT of the skull base demonstrated no significant FDG uptake. Autoimmune evaluation revealed a positive ANA titer (1:40 speckled) but negative dsDNA and anti–Smith antibodies; rheumatology favored an infectious etiology given the acute postoperative onset, elevated WBC count, and improvement with antimicrobial therapy.

A 62-year-old previously healthy man presented with several hours of right lateral foot pain, swelling, and difficulty moving the right great toe after an inversion‐type injury. He had no prior foot pain. An initial radiograph obtained at an outside clinic was interpreted as showing an avulsion fracture at the base of the right fifth metatarsal and an undisplaced fracture of the distal phalanx of the right hallux. On examination, there was tenderness over the proximal phalanx of the right hallux and the lateral side of the right foot at the base of the fifth metatarsal, with a small palpable bony prominence at that site. Plantar flexion and inversion reproduced his pain; the ankle joint was stable and neurovascular exam was normal. A foot and ankle disability index (FADI) score was 66. A set of anteroposterior, lateral, and oblique radiographs of the right foot in our hospital demonstrated an oval, bean‐shaped bony fragment adjacent to the base of the fifth metatarsal, which was reported as possible avulsion of the tuberosity.

A 66-year-old man was referred for evaluation of progressive intermittent fevers, night sweats, and new exertional dyspnea. He had a 5-month history of fluctuating upper airway symptoms consistent with rhinosinusitis and had received multiple courses of oral antibiotics with minimal relief. Two weeks before admission, he noted increasing shortness of breath on exertion.

On examination he was afebrile. Cardiovascular exam revealed a soft pansystolic murmur at the mitral area; a cardiac resynchronization therapy-defibrillator (CRT-D) pocket was clean and non-tender. There were no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. Lung, abdominal, and skin examinations were unremarkable.

His history included dilated cardiomyopathy diagnosed 2 years earlier after cardiac arrest, for which a CRT-D was placed; he also had mitral regurgitation, hypertension, congestive heart failure, and gout. He lived at home with his wife and had no history of alcohol excess, smoking, ischemic heart disease, or familial cardiac disease.

Three sets of blood cultures drawn on admission grew Staphylococcus aureus (two of the three sets were positive). No antibiotics had been started at that time. A CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrated segmental pulmonary emboli with a small pulmonary infarction. Transthoracic echocardiography did not identify any new pathology. On day 2, a working diagnosis of sub-acute bacterial endocarditis was made, and transesophageal echocardiography was planned.

A 16-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of persistent electrolyte imbalances. Three days earlier she had been admitted for viral illness–related labs showing serum sodium 130 mEq/L and potassium 2.9 mEq/L; potassium normalized but hyponatremia recurred (128 mEq/L). At our center she appeared well, vital signs stable, with weight 6.4 kg (–5.4 SD) and length 68 cm (–3.35 SD). Developmental milestones were age‐appropriate except walking at 14 months. Physical examination was unremarkable. The mother reported that the child drank several bottles of water daily, seemed distressed until given water, refused milk and solid food, and used >8 heavy wet diapers per day.

Baseline studies showed serum sodium 132 mEq/L, potassium 3.8 mEq/L, serum osmolality 262 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality 56 mOsm/kg. A 24-hour urine collection yielded 2350 mL (15 mL/kg/h). Renal ultrasound revealed mild dilation of the left lower calyces; abdominal and chest CT scans were unremarkable. During a 3-hour water deprivation test, serum sodium rose to 143 mEq/L, and urine osmolality increased to 234 mOsm/kg; 24-hour urine output fell to 900 mL (5.8 mL/kg/h).

A 43-day-old male infant, born at 31 weeks of gestation (birth weight 2250 g), presented with 10 days of bilateral lower-limb swelling and 8 days of skin peeling on the lower limbs and buttocks. He was born after an uncomplicated antenatal course, exclusively breastfed, but failed to gain weight and had dropped to 1700 g. Initially evaluated for sepsis at a local hospital, he had a positive septic screen, dilated bowel loops on abdominal radiography, hemoglobin of 5.9 g/dL (transfused twice), and was treated with meropenem and vancomycin for presumed necrotizing enterocolitis with late-onset sepsis before transfer.

On arrival, he was afebrile. The lower limbs showed ichthyotic, desquamative skin changes with mild swelling. The liver edge was palpated 2 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory testing revealed hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, white-cell count 40,000/mm3 with neutrophil predominance, platelets 70,000/mm3, corrected reticulocyte count 8%, and a positive direct Coombs test. Peripheral smear showed anisocytosis with normocytic normochromic and hypochromic red cells. Liver enzymes were elevated. An x-ray of both lower limbs demonstrated diffuse periostitis of the femora, tarsals, and metatarsals.

Given prematurity, failure to thrive, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and periosteal changes, TORCH infection was suspected, and TORCH IgM/IgG ELISA tests plus a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) screen were sent.

A 26-year-old Hispanic man presented with jaundice. For 10 days, he noted yellowing of his eyes and skin, dark urine for 2–3 weeks, and pale stools for 5–7 days. He also reported nausea, fatigue, and malaise but denied abdominal pain, fever, or pruritus. On examination, he was afebrile, vital signs were normal, and he had diffuse jaundice and tender hepatomegaly without stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory tests on admission showed total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 272 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 2112 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 1055 IU/L, a normal complete blood count, and normal INR. Serologic evaluation for viral and autoimmune hepatitis and metabolic liver disease was negative. Ultrasound and MRCP showed no biliary obstruction. A liver biopsy revealed portal and lobular inflammation with sinusoidal lymphocytosis, centrilobular hepatocytic injury, mild fibrosis, and “spotty necrosis,” with negative immunostains for viruses. He was treated with prednisone and ursodiol, with gradual improvement and discharge. At follow-up (Day 142), laboratory monitoring disclosed a new severe pancytopenia, and he was admitted for evaluation. All viral etiologies of acute pancytopenia were ruled out by serologic analysis.

A 37-year-old previously healthy man presents with acute chest pain. Three days earlier he had been diagnosed with group A streptococcal pharyngitis and started on penicillin. He reports sudden-onset substernal chest pain radiating to his left shoulder, accompanied by mild shortness of breath. 

On examination, his pulse is 96 beats/min, blood pressure 128/96 mm Hg, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Cardiovascular and pulmonary examinations are unremarkable; there are no signs of heart failure or rash.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF and slight reciprocal ST-segment depression in leads I and aVL. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates akinesis of the inferior wall with otherwise normal left ventricular function. 

Urgent coronary angiography reveals normal coronary arteries without stenosis. Serial laboratory studies reveal troponin T 1.5 ng/mL (normal <0.04), creatine kinase 1129 U/L (normal 26–192), C-reactive protein 19.6 mg% (normal <0.5), hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 14 × 10^9/L with 87% neutrophils and 0.1 × 10^9/L eosinophils, platelets 142 × 10^9/L, INR 1.1. Antistreptolysin O titer is positive. Antinuclear antibodies, anticardiolipin antibodies (IgM and IgG), and complement levels (C3, C4) are all normal or negative. Viral serology for parvovirus B19 is negative.

A 45-year-old obese man, 7 days after a Bentall procedure for Stanford A aortic dissection, experienced sudden shortness of breath while straining, with right chest pain (VAS 5–7) and cold sweats. He remained hypotensive (81/51 mmHg) and tachypneic (24 breaths/min) despite fluid support and vasoconstrictors. ECG was normal. Laboratory tests showed a small drop in hemoglobin (from 13.1 to 11.1 g/dL over 2 days), elevated troponin-T (341 pg/mL), a hypercoagulable state, and acute kidney injury (eGFR 65.9 mL/min/1.73 m2). Transthoracic echocardiography revealed middle right ventricular free-wall hypokinesis with apical sparing. Chest X-ray demonstrated right lung oligaemia and abrupt tapering of the pulmonary artery. Based on these findings, he was started on heparin for presumed pulmonary embolism.

A 74-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus for 13 years and a history of coronary artery bypass grafting and recent percutaneous coronary intervention presented with a one-week history of fever, vomiting, and dyspnea. His temperature was 38.0°C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Auscultation revealed coarse inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. Chest radiography showed patchy bilateral lung consolidation and a pleural effusion. Influenza type B was confirmed, and aspiration pneumonia was diagnosed. Esophagogastroscopy demonstrated chronic gastritis and an esophageal ulcer. A percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube was placed for recurrent vomiting, but vomiting and aspiration persisted. He also complained of neck pain when he positioned his head up.

A 5-year-old boy was brought to the emergency department for right lower abdominal pain followed by right scrotal pain over several hours. He had a low-grade fever. His surgical history was notable for right scrotal orchiopexy five months earlier for a hydrocele. On examination, the right hemiscrotum was firm, erythematous, and tender; the testes could be palpated bilaterally. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 11.0×10^9 per L with a neutrophil predominance. Scrotal and inguinal ultrasonography demonstrated a dilated right inguinal canal (11 mm), herniation of the tip of the appendix into the canal, increased appendiceal wall thickness, and increased periappendicular fat echogenicity suggestive of gangrene and scrotal abscess. Both testes appeared morphologically normal, although the right testis was edematous.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of pain in the upper jaw region. Fourteen months earlier, he had dengue fever complicated by leukopenia and thrombocytopenia; serology was positive for NS1 antibodies. Two months after the dengue episode, he noted gum swelling followed by recession, exposing the underlying bone. He denied prolonged medication use, drug allergies, or prior dental procedures. 

On examination, there was complete gingival recession with irregular exposure of alveolar and part of basal bone in both maxillary quadrants, extending from the lateral incisors to the first molars; retained root fragments were present. Oral hygiene was poor. 

Orthopantomography showed irregular radiolucency of the alveolar and basal bone in both maxillary quadrants from the lateral incisor to the second molar. Cone-beam computed tomography and contrast-enhanced CT revealed bone destruction in the anterior hard palate. A provisional diagnosis of osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ) was made. 

Microbiologic studies, including Gram staining and culture, were non-specific; Ziehl–Neelsen staining showed no acid-fast bacilli. Incisional biopsy of bone demonstrated necrotic bone with empty lacunae and necrotic marrow; soft tissue showed focal inflammatory cells, plump endothelial cells, and blood-vessel occlusion. Periodic acid–Schiff staining showed no fungal hyphae. Blood glucose, renal and liver function tests, and HIV screening were all normal. No clear etiology could be identified.

A 62-year-old man was admitted on June 25, 2021, with a 20-day history of episodic slurred speech that had worsened over the previous 9 days. Initially, episodes lasted about 10 minutes without loss of consciousness, headache, dizziness, diplopia, dysphagia, or limb weakness; by presentation, they occurred 2–3 times daily lasting about 30 minutes. His medical history included hypertension (>20 years), diabetes mellitus (8 years), and coronary heart disease (8 years); he was blind bilaterally after retinal detachment in adolescence. He denied smoking and alcohol use. On examination, temperature was 36.5°C, heart rate 70/min, respiratory rate 17/min, and blood pressure 144/86 mmHg. Cranial nerve exam showed dysarthria and midline tongue extension; limb strength was 5/5 with normal tone; Babinski and other reflexes were normal; he had no light perception with irregular pupils and absent light reflexes. Routine blood tests, coagulation studies, rheumatologic panels, thyroid function, tumor markers, liver and kidney function, and electrolytes were all normal. Brain MRI and susceptibility-weighted imaging were unremarkable; MRA showed mild cerebral arteriosclerosis; carotid MRA showed carotid arteriosclerosis with limited stenosis of the intracranial left vertebral artery; transcranial Doppler was normal. The initial diagnosis was transient ischemic attack of the vertebrobasilar system. On review, symptoms did not improve with rest; a fatigue test and a neostigmine test were both negative.

An 87-year-old woman with known aortic valvulopathy and atrial fibrillation (complicated by an ischemic stroke 2 years earlier) presented with an 8-month history of dysuria, a burning sensation on urination, and intermittent gross hematuria with occasional clots. Her medications included calcium channel blockers, antiplatelets, and anticoagulants; she was a non-smoker. Initial outpatient treatment with antibiotics for presumed cystitis failed to relieve her symptoms, which progressively worsened. She was admitted urgently for clotting hematuria and an estimated hemoglobin drop of 9 g/dL. Bedside ultrasound showed a reduced-capacity bladder with a small irregular tissue mass on the left lateral and posterior bladder wall and a mobile echogenic structure consistent with a blood clot. For uncontrolled hematuria despite continuous bladder irrigation, she underwent bipolar transurethral resection of the bladder for hemostasis. Cystoscopy revealed an inflamed bladder mucosa with multiple submucosal granulations in the trigone and lateral walls, generalized patchy bleeding, and an enormous blood clot. The clot was removed, the bladder wall lesions were resected, and the tissue specimens were sent for histopathological examination.

A 37-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus and Sjögren’s syndrome was diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis and scheduled for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy before starting prednisolone. She had never received acid-secretion inhibitors, including proton pump inhibitors or vonoprazan. Vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable. 

Endoscopic findings:
- Antrum: normal appearance.
- Gastric corpus: normal coloration with a regular arrangement of collecting venules; red streaks and slight mucosal swelling on the lesser curvature of the angle.
- Magnified narrow-band imaging of the corpus: regular round pit patterns.

Biopsy sites: greater curvature of the prepyloric area and lesser and greater curvatures of the gastric corpus.

Histologic findings (lesser curvature of corpus):
- Three defined layers: first (foveolar epithelium) showed foveolar hyperplasia; second (parietal cells) was shortened with mild degeneration; third (chief cells) preserved.
- Layer contours slightly disorganized with mild lymphocytic infiltration.
- H+/K+-ATPase staining: heterogeneously reduced.
- Pepsinogen I: uneven staining.
- MUC6: positive throughout the region.
- Chromogranin A: slight enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia.

Laboratory tests after endoscopy:
- Anti-parietal cell antibody: <1:10 (negative)
- Anti-intrinsic factor antibody: negative
- Serum gastrin: 150 pg/mL (normal 37–172)
- Vitamin B12: 870 pg/mL (normal 233–914)
- Anti-H. pylori IgG: <3 U/mL (negative)

A 66-year-old woman with morbid obesity status post–Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in 2003 and revision with partial gastrectomy and gastrojejunostomy in 2017 presented with 2 weeks of worsening abdominal pain, fevers, chills, and anorexia. On examination, her temperature was 101.1°F, blood pressure 101/55 mmHg, and heart rate 69 bpm after IV fluids and analgesia. Laboratory tests showed a WBC count of 11.5×10^9/L with 80% neutrophils, alkaline phosphatase 280 U/L, ALT 83 U/L, and AST 208 U/L. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed an 11-cm extrahepatic collection between the liver and diaphragm and an adjacent right pleural effusion. CT-guided drainage returned 150 mL of purulent fluid; subsequent cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae and Citrobacter freundii. Given the recurrent nature of her perihepatic abscesses since her revision surgery, the differential diagnosis was expanded to include enteric fistula, biliary leak, or retained surgical product. An upper endoscopy demonstrated Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy anatomy with healthy mucosa and a normal jejunum. A HIDA scan was grossly normal, with no abnormal tracer accumulation in the right upper quadrant. An initial CT fistulogram identified the known perihepatic collection but did not demonstrate a new fistulous tract. A repeat CT fistulogram showed a fistulous communication to the biliopancreatic limb.

A 37-year-old Japanese man presented with a two-week history of nonproductive cough without fever or dyspnea. His medical history included right hemiparesis, intellectual disability, and epilepsy related to a remote intracerebral hemorrhage; he denied smoking or alcohol use.

On examination, his temperature was 36.5°C, blood pressure 105/55 mm Hg, pulse 70/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. There was no lymphadenopathy; lung fields were clear to auscultation; cardiovascular, abdominal, and neurological examinations were unremarkable. No rash or petechiae were noted.

A chest radiograph showed bilateral diffuse infiltrates. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral airspace consolidation and ground-glass opacities. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 8850/mm3 with a left shift, lactate dehydrogenase 425 U/L, C-reactive protein 9.18 mg/dL, total protein 5.3 g/dL, albumin 2.1 g/dL, KL-6 2940 U/mL, surfactant protein D 173.0 ng/mL, and surfactant protein A 115.0 ng/mL. Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies were negative; immunoglobulin levels were normal.

Sputum cultures and acid-fast stains were negative. Blood cultures were sterile. Bronchoscopy revealed a normal tracheobronchial tree. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid analysis showed 87% histiocytes, 6% neutrophils, 4% lymphocytes, and 3% eosinophils; cultures were negative. Transbronchial biopsy showed alveolar septal thickening with chronic inflammation and collagenous fibrosis.

A presumptive diagnosis of acute interstitial pneumonia was made, and the patient received intravenous levofloxacin plus high-dose methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone. On hospital day 5, his respiratory status deteriorated, requiring noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation, and cyclophosphamide was administered.

A 37-year-old active man presented with a 1-week history of painful, erythematous swelling of his right elbow and arm. He denied fever or rash. He is an engineer who also tutors judo; he had no relevant past medical history, no family history of thrombosis, no recent surgery, and no regular medications. After a routine judo session, he noted acute onset of redness, swelling, and pain in his right arm. His general practitioner diagnosed cellulitis with possible trauma-related injury and started analgesics and antibiotics. One week later, with no improvement, he was referred to the hospital.

On admission: T 37.3 °C, BP 124/74 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, RR 16 breaths/min, O₂ saturation 96 % on room air. Physical examination showed swelling and redness from the right elbow to the shoulder with mild tenderness; there were no superficial chest-wall veins visible and no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies were unremarkable except for a C-reactive protein of 26 mg/L (normal < 5 mg/L). The working differential included olecranon bursitis, cellulitis, and DVT. He was started on parenteral antibiotics and low-molecular-weight heparin.

Plain radiographs of the right elbow, arm, and chest were normal. Venous Doppler ultrasonography revealed thrombosis of the right axillary vein extending into the cephalic and brachial veins.

A 17-year-old Nigerian male presented with a 6-day history of jerking movements and inability to move his lower limbs. He was previously healthy until an episode of high-grade fever treated with paracetamol, followed by additional medications at a local clinic and passage of dark-brown urine. Five days later, he began limping on the right, then developed insidious, progressively worsening jerking of both legs that spread to involve his whole body, rendering him unable to walk.

On admission, he was febrile, developed hypertension, and received antihypertensives, antibiotics, corticosteroids, and muscle relaxants. Three days into admission, he was conscious and oriented but in distress from intermittent severe lower-limb spasms. Vital signs were blood pressure 140/90 mmHg, pulse 84/min, respiratory rate 30/min, and temperature 38°C.

Neurologic examination:
• Upper limbs: normal strength, tone, and reflexes  
• Lower limbs: increased muscle tone, frequent spasms, and spasticity; reduced active and passive range of motion; fixed plantar flexion of the left ankle with Achilles’ tendon tightness  
• Reflexes: exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs with clonus  
• Sensation: a shocking sensation elicited from the T12 level downward  
• Muscle strength (Oxford scale): bilateral weakness (right 3/5, left 1/5)

A brain MRI was normal. Spinal MRI showed no signs of inflammation, no disc herniation, stenosis, tumor, or epidural/subdural hematoma.

Differential diagnoses included transverse myelitis, Guillain–Barré syndrome, disc herniation, spinal stenosis, spinal epidural/subdural hematoma, and spinal tumor.

A 22‐year‐old woman with end‐stage kidney disease on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis for 1 year presented after two generalized tonic–clonic seizures 2 weeks apart. She had chronic kidney disease since age 6, presumed due to chronic glomerulonephritis, and no prior history of seizures. Each event lasted approximately 5 minutes, involved tongue biting without sphincter loss, and had no preceding fever, headache, or trauma. Between seizures, she had no focal neurologic symptoms and no family history of seizures or renal disease.

On examination, she was alert (GCS 15); vital signs were HR 92 bpm, BP 160/100 mm Hg, RR 18/min, and temperature 37.1 °C. Neurologic examination was normal except for decreased visual acuity in the left eye; chest auscultation revealed mildly decreased air entry at both lung bases. Abdominal ultrasound showed bilaterally small kidneys, mild ascites, and bilateral pleural effusions. Brain MRI and EEG were normal.

Laboratory studies revealed blood urea nitrogen 128 mg/dL, serum creatinine 13.1 mg/dL, sodium 125 mmol/L, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, calcium 5.72 mg/dL, magnesium 2.1 mg/dL, parathyroid hormone level 281 pg/mL (reference 10–55 pg/mL), phosphate 2.6 mg/dL (2.8–4.5 mg/dL), and 25‐OH vitamin D 6 ng/mL (20–40 ng/mL).

An 18-year-old previously healthy man was admitted with an 8-day history of nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting, epigastric pain, intermittent hiccups, anorexia, and weight loss. He had been evaluated multiple times and treated empirically for a presumed viral illness with ondansetron and metoclopramide. A CT scan of the abdomen showed gas and fluid levels in the small bowel and colon without evidence of obstruction or pancreaticobiliary pathology. On admission, he was hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies showed hypokalemia (3.1 mEq/L), hypochloremia (94 mEq/L), normal lipase, normal inflammatory markers, and a monocytosis (14.8%) on CBC. Urinalysis revealed 1+ ketones, 1+ bilirubin, and 4+ urobilinogen; toxicology, streptococcal antigen, monospot, and COVID-19 PCR were negative. An abdominal radiograph and ECG were normal. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no abdominal tenderness or focal neurologic deficits. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy performed the next day showed severe distal esophagitis, and biopsy demonstrated acute ulcerative esophagitis; infectious studies on tissue were negative. He was started on high-dose IV proton-pump inhibitors and sucralfate, after which his nausea and vomiting improved, but his hiccups became persistent. Abdominal ultrasound and upper GI series were unremarkable. Treatment with metoclopramide, cyproheptadine, and baclofen led to no improvement in the hiccups.

A 33-year-old Caucasian man presented with three weeks of feeling unwell, a nonproductive cough, and constant upper abdominal discomfort, all beginning after a tooth extraction. He denied any changes in bowel or bladder habits. His medical history included only a subarachnoid aneurysm clipping seven years earlier. 

On examination, his pulse was 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation and temperature were normal. Auscultation revealed bronchial breathing at the left lung base, and his abdomen was tender in the epigastrium without rebound or guarding. 

Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 14,000/µl and a C-reactive protein level of 88 mg/dl; other blood tests were normal. A chest radiograph demonstrated an opacity at the left lung base. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen revealed cavitating nodules in the left lower lobe and a small infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm.

A 23-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 1-month history of constant fever (up to 40 °C), fatigue, abdominal pain, and bilateral elbow swelling. Two weeks earlier, he had been treated in primary care with amoxicillin–clavulanate for 7 days, oral paracetamol, a high-potency topical corticosteroid, and topical fusidic acid without improvement. On admission, vital signs were notable for temperature 40 °C; other vital signs were normal.

Physical examination revealed widespread scaly, crusted, hyperpigmented papules coalescing into plaques, with multiple necrotic ulcers on the trunk and all extremities. A few days after admission, he developed new-onset dyspnea and dry cough; oxygen saturation fell to 68% on a non-rebreather mask, blood pressure was 98/46 mm Hg, and heart rate was 190 beats/min. Laboratory studies showed normocytic normochromic anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, and mild transaminase elevations. Tests for infectious and rheumatologic diseases were negative.

Computed tomography of the neck showed multiple prominent bilateral deep cervical lymph nodes. Pulmonary CT angiography revealed no embolism but bilateral lower-lobe honeycombing, adjacent ground-glass and nodular opacities, lung reticulation, prominent bilateral hilar lymph nodes, and a left pleural effusion. Abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated multiple enlarged lymph nodes and mild free fluid.

A skin punch biopsy was obtained from the edge of a trunk ulcer, and the patient was empirically started on intravenous methylprednisolone, vancomycin, and meropenem. Despite intensive care support for worsening hypoxemia, tachycardia, hypotension, and radiographic progression of bilateral patchy infiltrates, no clinical improvement occurred.

A 50-year-old healthy man, a lifelong gardener, sustained a blow to his left zygomatic region from a projected object while using a grass trimmer eight years ago. He noted a small skin lesion, mild burning pain, and ipsilateral rhinorrhea with minimal bleeding but did not seek care. In September 2010, a dental examination revealed a metal‐appearing opacity in the left facial skeleton and “absence of areas of apical/radicular osteolysis affecting the teeth,” despite no history of dental implants or surgery. He was advised to see an otolaryngologist but declined until 2015, when he developed left facial pain. Fiberoptic nasolaryngoscopy was normal except for a deviated nasal septum. A noncontrast CT scan of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated “the presence of a metal foreign body with thread-like shape located in the region of the left maxillary sinus, which determined intense inflammatory reaction of the sinonasal mucosa interesting the same maxillary sinus. Additionally, the ipsilateral anterior ethmoidal air cells were partially involved. Radiological findings of minor importance were the presence of left concha bullosa and nasal septum deviation, while the other paranasal sinuses were within normal limits.”

A 74-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department because of severe lethargy at home. Four days earlier, she had started duloxetine 20 mg daily for chronic musculoskeletal pain. Her long-standing medications included telmisartan 40 mg/day and benidipine hydrochloride 8 mg/day for hypertension. She denied use of diuretics or other new medications. 

On arrival, she reported headache and nausea without vomiting. Vital signs were: blood pressure 143/79 mmHg; heart rate 66 bpm; respiratory rate 18/min; oxygen saturation 99% on room air; temperature 36.5°C. Physical examination showed no conjunctival pallor, no edema or dehydration, and no thyroid enlargement. Lung and heart sounds were normal. Neurologic examination was unremarkable aside from profound lethargy that prevented her from walking unaided.

Laboratory studies revealed: serum sodium 110 mEq/L, potassium 3.8 mEq/L, chloride 73 mEq/L, BUN 11.4 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL; plasma osmolality 230 mOsm/kg·H₂O; urine osmolality 493 mOsm/kg·H₂O; urine sodium 59 mEq/L; plasma antidiuretic hormone 2.1 pg/mL. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, free T₃, and free T₄ levels were normal. Computed tomography of the brain and chest showed no abnormalities.

An 8-month-old preterm female infant known to have Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome was referred for evaluation of a left bicolored iris that had been noted by her parents since birth and remained unchanged. She had a history of neonatal hypoglycemia requiring NICU monitoring. She was born by cesarean delivery at a birth weight of 2205 grams, with Apgar scores of 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. 

On general examination, she had macroglossia, a nevus flammeus over her forehead, and epicanthic folds but no lateralized overgrowth. The right iris was dark brown, and the left iris showed an area of hypopigmentation. 

Ophthalmic examination revealed visual acuity of central, steady, and maintained in both eyes. Both pupils were reactive to light, intraocular pressures were 15 mmHg in each eye, and extraocular movements were full. Slit-lamp examination showed a sharply demarcated hypochromic sector occupying almost half of the left lateral iris. Dilated fundus examination was normal in both eyes. Cycloplegic refraction demonstrated mild astigmatism without any other significant refractive error.

A 26-year-old man presented with severe headache, persistent high fever, chills, and nausea beginning 3 days after a hiking trip to Baiguzha Mountain. On day –3, he developed sudden headache, fever to 39.5ºC, chills, sweating, and nausea. A self-performed CRP was 13.7 mg/L. He self-treated with loxoprofen sodium, moxifloxacin, and oseltamivir without relief. On day 0, he continued to have fevers up to 40.4ºC and intractable headache. Initial laboratory tests on day 2 post-admission showed mildly elevated AST and direct and indirect bilirubin levels, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and elevated lactate. High-resolution chest CT and viral tests for influenza and SARS-CoV-2 were negative. Despite intravenous fluids and electrolyte correction, fevers fluctuated between 38.6ºC and 40.4ºC, headache persisted, body weight decreased by 3 kg, and liver enzymes rose further. On examination, he had conjunctival edema. He reported sleeping under an air conditioner before symptom onset and noted two small lesions with a 4 mm erythematous mark on his right hand. He recalled brushing off a small insect during his hike, later identified as a tick. Tick-borne infection was considered, and metagenomic and targeted next-generation sequencing were ordered.

A 62-year-old man with a history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (diagnosed in 1998), refractory to multiple lines of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, began treatment with alemtuzumab and dexamethasone in December 2011. Three weeks after alemtuzumab initiation, he was hospitalized for invasive aspergillosis involving lung, eye, and brain, treated with voriconazole. Six weeks after the first alemtuzumab dose, he developed profuse, watery diarrhea persisting intermittently for over 12 weeks. There was no blood or mucus in the stools, no abdominal pain, vomiting, or systemic myalgia. He had no travel history, no known exposure to outbreaks, and no family members with similar symptoms. All medications known to cause diarrhea, including voriconazole and alemtuzumab, were discontinued without improvement. Empiric antibiotics (ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, piperacillin/tazobactam) were administered sequentially but yielded no benefit. Repeated stool cultures for Clostridium difficile, Campylobacter, Salmonella, and Yersinia, as well as assays for protozoans (Microsporidium, Cryptosporidium, Isospora, Giardia lamblia), were negative. Serum PCRs for cytomegalovirus and adenovirus were negative, and stool PCRs for rotavirus and adenovirus were also negative. Colonoscopy revealed no ulcerations, and colonic biopsies showed no cytopathic effects. There was no evidence of gastrointestinal involvement by aspergillosis.

A 31-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of generalized itching and dark-colored urine. He denied abdominal pain, gastrointestinal symptoms, fevers, or chills. He reported social alcohol use (approximately one drink per week), no illicit drug use, no recent travel, and no prior liver disease. Three weeks before presentation, he began taking an over-the-counter muscle-building supplement containing enobosarm; symptoms began after 2 weeks of use. 

On examination, his vital signs were normal. Body mass index was 33.9 kg/m2. He appeared well without jaundice or scleral icterus. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, without hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• ALT 346 U/L, AST 110 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 123 U/L, total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL  
• Albumin 4.9 g/dL, INR 1.0  
• Complete blood count and remaining metabolic panel normal  
• Viral hepatitis A and C antibodies negative; hepatitis B serologies consistent with vaccination

A right upper quadrant ultrasound with Doppler demonstrated an enlarged fatty liver (length 199 mm), normal hepatic and portal venous flow, and no lesions, gallstones, or bile duct dilation.

A 69-year-old woman underwent radical cystectomy with orthotopic ileal neobladder reconstruction in August 2020 for T3bN0 grade I squamous-cell carcinoma of the bladder. Postoperatively, she developed a left ureteric stricture managed with a ureteric stent and bilateral percutaneous nephrostomies (PCNs). In January 2021, she had an extensive right lower-limb deep venous thrombosis treated with anticoagulation. That same month, the left PCN slipped, and the ureteric stent protruded through the urethra while its upper coil remained in the renal hilum; the stent was pushed back into the pouch but the patient then defaulted on follow-up for three years.

In March 2024, she presented with a firm right subcostal anterior abdominal wall mass. Ultrasound showed a well-defined hypoechoic solid lesion (10.3 × 4 cm) within the right rectus muscle, with internal vascularity, calcific foci, and cystic areas, suggesting a desmoid tumor or a secondary deposit from her bladder cancer. Ultrasound-guided biopsy revealed a bland spindle-cell proliferation, suggestive of a desmoid tumor. Noncontrast CT confirmed a well-defined soft-tissue mass (7 × 4.5 cm) in the right anterior abdominal wall without intra-abdominal extension. She was scheduled for wide local excision and abdominal wall reconstruction.

During preoperative catheterization, a stony hard object was identified within the vaginal cavity.

A 40‐year‐old man underwent high inguinal orchiectomy for a 15-cm right testicular tumor, which was diagnosed as seminoma, pT1. Postoperative imaging showed no metastasis, and he chose surveillance. One month later, pelvic lymph nodes were enlarged, prompting a diagnosis of nodal metastasis (International Germ Cell Consensus Classification: good prognosis). Three cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin (BEP) were initiated.

During the first cycle:
• Day 4: The patient experienced nausea and constipation without vomiting or loss of consciousness.  
• Day 8: Serum sodium was 126 mEq/L; gastrointestinal symptoms were stable.  
• Day 9: The patient developed vomiting (CTCAE Grade 2) and disorientation (Grade 1). Serum sodium had fallen to 110 mEq/L; urinary osmolality was 740 mOsm/L and plasma osmolality was 231 mOsm/L. Plasma ADH was elevated at 10.1 pg/mL (normal ~4.2 pg/mL). Renal, thyroid, and adrenal dysfunctions were excluded.

A 72-year-old man with no prior medical history underwent dual-chamber pacemaker implantation in the left prepectoral area for 2:1 atrioventricular block. The procedure was uneventful, and he was discharged the next day. On postoperative day 4, he presented with fever (38.1°C) and an inflamed, infiltrating, necrotic lesion over the implant site. Laboratory studies revealed an elevated inflammatory syndrome; blood cultures were obtained and antibiotics (amoxicillin–clavulanate, 1 g three times daily) were started empirically. A swab of the lesion grew Staphylococcus epidermidis. By day 7, despite antibiotic therapy, the lesion had darkened and enlarged, and blood cultures remained negative.

A 55-year-old Saudi woman presented with a 10-year history of bilateral flank pain. The pain was mild, colicky, nonradiating, and associated with mild dysuria but without hematuria, fever, weight loss, or abdominal distension. She had no history of hypertension, diabetes, or significant family medical history. 

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in both lumbar regions without rebound, guarding, or organomegaly. 

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 11.6 g/dL and a random blood sugar of 6.78 mmol/L. Renal and liver function tests, complete urine examination, and other routine tests were unremarkable.

Renal ultrasonography demonstrated normal kidney size, outline, and parenchymal echotexture, with bilateral dilatation of the pelvicalyceal systems and no stones or masses in the ureters or bladder.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed both kidneys of normal size, shape, and position with preserved corticomedullary differentiation. In the early phase, there were bilateral hypodense filling defects in the renal pelves with attenuation values between –3 and +7.25 HU. In the drainage phase, the pelvicalyceal systems appeared compressed with mild dilatation of the proximal ureter; the middle and distal ureters and the bladder were normal.

A 69-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease secondary to IgA nephropathy had been receiving monthly subcutaneous continuous erythropoietin receptor activator (CERA) for renal anemia. His hemoglobin concentration rose from approximately 10 g/dL to 12 g/dL over the initial months. Seven months after starting CERA, he experienced a sudden drop in hemoglobin to 6.7 g/dL and noted dizziness on standing, prompting hospital admission.

Laboratory studies on admission revealed:  
• Hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL; hematocrit 19.6%  
• White blood cell count 5,100/μL with normal differential  
• Platelet count 94×10^3/μL (baseline ~116×10^3/μL)  
• Reticulocyte count 2,170/μL (0.1%)  
• Serum erythropoietin level below the detection limit  
• Normal liver and renal function consistent with CKD; CRP 0.01 mg/dL

Gastrointestinal endoscopy showed no bleeding source, and the fecal occult blood test was negative. Bone marrow aspiration demonstrated an absence of erythroblasts with normal myeloid cells and megakaryocytes. Serologic tests for parvovirus B19 IgM, cytomegalovirus IgM, Epstein–Barr virus capsid antigen IgM, and antinuclear antibodies were negative. Systemic CT imaging revealed no thymoma, lymphoma, or other malignancy. Discontinuation of his routine medications for three weeks did not improve the anemia.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of painless, progressively enlarging neck swelling and 1 week of altered sensorium. Eight months earlier, he had been diagnosed with miliary tuberculosis and started on empirical anti-tubercular therapy; three months later, he developed sub-acute meningitis confirmed by positive CSF TB PCR and completed treatment for tubercular meningitis while remaining on therapy.

On examination, his pulse was 88/min, blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg, and Glasgow Coma Scale score 9/15. He had a 10×8 cm non-tender, fluctuant right thyroid swelling without erythema or warmth. Neurologic examination showed bilateral papilloedema; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed communicating hydrocephalus and multiple ring-enhancing lesions. CSF analysis showed 3 white cells/mm³, protein 40.6 mg/dL, and glucose 64 mg/dL; CSF TB PCR was negative, and cytospin preparation was negative for malignant cells. Laboratory studies demonstrated euthyroidism (TSH 1.662 μIU/mL, T4 7.1 mg/dL, T3 90.6 ng/dL, free T4 0.98 ng/dL) and negative anti-thyroglobulin and anti-microsomal antibodies. HIV testing was negative. Hematological and biochemical parameters, as well as chest radiography, were unremarkable.

Neck ultrasonography showed a large, heterogeneous nodule in the right thyroid lobe measuring 8.6×5.9×8.3 cm, with a predominant cystic component, fine internal floating echoes, and dependent internal debris.

A 32-year-old gravida 6, para 3 woman at 31 weeks of gestation presented with irregular uterine contractions and right-sided abdominal pain that was worsened by movement, palpation, and coughing. She denied recent trauma or coughing spells. Her previous obstetric and surgical history included three vaginal deliveries and one cesarean; two prior spontaneous abortions were unexplained. 

On examination, she was hemodynamically stable. The uterus was appropriately enlarged for gestational age. There was moderate rigidity and tenderness of the right abdominal wall, with blue discoloration over the lateral abdomen and flank. No masses were palpable. Vaginal examination showed a closed cervix and no vaginal bleeding. Fetal heart rate was 140 beats per minute without uterine contractions.

Laboratory studies revealed hematocrit 25.2%, hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelet count 132 000/mm3, INR 1.01, and APTT 30 s. Leukocyte count and urine protein were normal. Obstetric ultrasound showed a posterior placenta without retroplacental hematoma and normal fetal growth; Doppler studies were unremarkable. An initial abdominal ultrasound was normal.

Twenty-four hours after admission, her abdominal pain markedly worsened, and positional changes were intolerable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen revealed a large suprafascial mass on the right anterior abdominal wall measuring approximately 11 × 6 × 20 cm.

A 76-year-old man with a 10-year history of HIV-1 infection (most recent CD4 count 668 cells/mm3 and viral load <50 copies/mL) presented with several days of fever (38–39.5 °C) and new disorientation. His medical history included treated pulmonary tuberculosis, hypertension, and hyperthyroidism; medications were zidovudine, lamivudine, efavirenz, tiamazol, and captopril. On examination, he was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, moderately dehydrated, and pale; neurologic examination showed disorientation in time and space with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14, with no focal deficits. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis with a left shift and otherwise normal values. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the brain showed a single low-attenuation lesion with uniform ring enhancement in the left temporal region. Empiric treatment for cerebral toxoplasmosis was initiated with parenteral trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (5/25 mg/kg twice daily).

A 23‐year‐old woman presented with intermittent, sudden right‐sided facial twitching and persistent right‐sided hearing loss of 1 year’s duration. She had had three prior episodes of right facial palsy, each diagnosed and treated as Bell’s palsy with full recovery, but her current facial asymmetry had persisted for 6 months despite corticosteroid therapy. On otoscopic examination, a whitish mass was visible in the anterior superior and posterior superior quadrants behind an intact right tympanic membrane. Neurologic examination confirmed House–Brackmann grade III right facial paralysis. High-resolution CT of the right temporal bone showed a soft‐tissue density filling the anterior epitympanum medial to the malleus head and incus body, causing ossicular disarticulation and appearing centered around the geniculate ganglion and labyrinthine segment of the facial nerve. MRI of the temporal bone demonstrated the epitympanic mass as hypointense on T1‐weighted images, hyperintense on T2‐weighted images, with minimal circumferential enhancement post-gadolinium; diffusion-weighted imaging showed no evident diffusion restriction.

A 61-year-old woman presented with right thigh pain that began after she stepped on something. She had no history of cancer. 

Radiographs of both femurs showed multiple osteolytic bone lesions and cortical thinning in the proximal right femur. A computed tomography scan from the chest to the lower extremities confirmed multiple osteolytic lesions in the ribs, pelvis, tibia, and first metatarsal bone, with no findings suggestive of a primary tumor. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right femoral lesion demonstrated low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and peripheral but no internal enhancement on contrast-enhanced sequences. Consequently, metastatic tumors or multiple myeloma was suspected.

Initial blood tests revealed a calcium level of 15.2 mg/dL (normal 8.8–10.1), an alkaline phosphatase level of 2082 U/L (normal 38–113), and a phosphate level of 2.2 mg/dL (normal 2.7–4.6). Tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA19-9, CA125, SCC antigen, IL-2 receptor) and Bence-Jones protein were all within normal limits. 

To establish a diagnosis, an incisional biopsy of the first metatarsal lesion was performed. Histology revealed hemosiderin deposition, mild fibrosis, a few osteoclasts in the trabeculae, and no neoplastic changes.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of skin-colored, flat-topped papules confined to the black portions of a tattoo on his right forearm and arm. The tattoos had been applied by a professional artist 20 years earlier, with no prior eruptions in those areas. The asymptomatic papules appeared suddenly and progressively increased in number to several hundred. His only medical history was occasional atopic dermatitis treated with topical corticosteroids. He denied tobacco use, intravenous drug use, or systemic symptoms. On examination, the papules were present only within the tattooed regions; the remainder of his skin was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including tests for HIV and hepatitis B and C, were all within normal limits. Initial differential diagnoses included lichen nitidus, papular eczema, papular sarcoidosis, lichen planus, and verrucae planae.

A 70-year-old woman presented with mild left axillary pain. Six years earlier, she had reactive axillary lymphadenopathy. She reported no personal or family history of breast disease. On examination, there was a soft, elastic, egg-sized, smooth-surfaced mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast with mild tenderness, and multiple bean-sized nodes in the left axilla. 

Mammography showed asymmetric breast tissue, classified as BI-RADS 3 on the left, with no obvious calcifications or discrete mass. Ultrasonography of the left upper-outer breast revealed a poorly echoic, irregularly shaped area extending widely, with poor Doppler flow signal; axillary nodes were thickened with low cortical echoes and internal heterogeneity but retained their hilum. 

Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated numerous punctate areas of rapid enhancement with dynamic washout throughout the left breast, without pectoral muscle, chest wall, or skin invasion.

A 46-year-old woman presented to dermatology with a 3-month history of nonpruritic, nontender, hyperkeratotic papules and plaques on her upper and lower extremities. Her medical history was notable for de novo metastatic hormone receptor–positive breast cancer (involving the brain, liver, bones, and lymph nodes) and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. She was being treated with dexamethasone, whole-brain radiation, tamoxifen, leuprolide, and insulin, with good control of her cancer and glycemia. She was referred by her oncologist to rule out disseminated zoster because of significant lymphopenia from prolonged steroid use. On examination, there were discrete, erythematous, umbilicated papules and plaques with central adherent hyperkeratotic cores measuring 1 to 2 cm on the extensor surfaces of her arms and legs; Koebnerization was noted on the forearms. Laboratory studies showed a creatinine level of 0.48 mg/dL, a glucose level of 217 mg/dL, and a hemoglobin A1c of 11.5%.

An 86‐year‐old woman was transferred to the intensive care unit for evaluation of thrombotic microangiopathy and acute renal failure. One week earlier, she had acute onset abdominal pain with bright red blood per rectum and some breathing difficulty.
