Abdominal CT scan showed nonspecific colitis, and she was started on levofloxacin and metronidazole. Urine studies were negative for infection. She became confused with word‐finding difficulty and slurred speech, without focal neurologic deficits, and was electively intubated for altered mental status and oxygen support. At the outside hospital, a diagnosis of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) with suspected thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) was made, and she was transferred for higher‐level care. 

Her medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism. There was no known autoimmune or hematologic disorder. On examination she was intubated, with scattered purpura and ecchymoses on the skin and coarse breath sounds bilaterally. Laboratory tests on admission showed hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, platelet count 57 × 10^3/µL, lactate dehydrogenase 4576 U/L, undetectable haptoglobin, creatinine 6.8 mg/dL, and blood urea nitrogen 112 mg/dL. Serum ferritin, cobalamin, and folate levels were within normal limits. Peripheral blood smear demonstrated marked schistocytosis, reticulocytosis, and occasional spherocytes. 

Given ongoing MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, plasma exchange and methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg twice daily were initiated, and hemodialysis was started, while ADAMTS13 activity and Shiga‐toxin assays were pending.

An 8-year-old girl presented with a 3-day history of fever, diffuse abdominal pain, and coffee-ground emesis.  
On arrival she was afebrile, tachycardic, hypotensive, and had a rigid abdomen with features of septic shock.  
Laboratory studies showed venous pH 7.08, PCO₂ 47 mm Hg, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L, lactate 3.9 mmol/L; WBC 3.7×10⁹/L (ANC 0.96×10⁹/L); CRP 389 mg/L; INR 1.7; PTT 36 s; fibrinogen 5 g/L; creatinine 100 µmol/L; urea 10 mmol/L.  
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a starry-sky appearance of the liver and moderate right-upper-quadrant free fluid.  
She was not fluid-responsive, so was started on an epinephrine infusion, ceftriaxone, and vancomycin, and transferred to a tertiary center.  
During transport, she developed right calf erythema with severe pain on palpation and dorsiflexion out of proportion to clinical findings; her CK was 10 000 U/L.  
CT of the right leg revealed extensive soft-tissue gas and myonecrosis.  
Abdominal CT showed loculated fluid, free air in the right lower quadrant, and proximal small-bowel dilation.  
Broadening antibiotics to piperacillin–tazobactam, vancomycin, and clindamycin, she underwent fasciotomy and debridement of the right leg, followed by diagnostic laparoscopy, which revealed ischemia of the terminal ileum, cecum, and ascending colon; an ileocolic resection with end ileostomy was performed.

A 25-year-old graduate student presented with 1 week of fever, sore throat, fatigue, nausea, and “dizziness.” She denied vertigo, trauma, migraine history, drug or alcohol use, and tick exposure. Initial rapid strep and monospot tests were negative, and she was treated supportively. Over the next 4 days, she developed worsening nausea with emesis, vertigo, tension headache, mental fatigue, gait unsteadiness, and increased sleep requirement.  
On examination at a second clinic visit, she was afebrile with no rash. Findings included bilateral horizontal nystagmus, cervical lymphadenopathy, exudative pharyngitis, dysarthria, a positive Romberg sign, and a broad-based ataxic gait. Neurologic examination was otherwise normal.  
Laboratory studies showed atypical lymphocytosis (55%), transaminitis (AST 31 U/L, ALT 59 U/L), and IgG polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia on protein electrophoresis. EBV serology was positive for viral capsid antigen IgM and negative for IgG. Heterophile antibody and repeat rapid strep tests remained negative.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed no abnormal signal intensity or mass effect.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of gradually progressive swelling, pain, and stiffness in her left lower leg. She reported pain at rest and denied fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, hemoptysis, or syncope. Her medical history was notable for three prior abortions, recurrent microcytic anemia treated with iron supplementation, and two prior dilation and curettage procedures. She had no personal history of DVT and no family history of thromboembolic disease.

On examination, her temperature was afebrile, heart rate 85 bpm, blood pressure 125/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. The left lower leg was tender, swollen, warm, and erythematous. Bilateral dorsalis pedis pulses were palpable, and sensation was intact without ischemic changes.

Laboratory studies showed normal renal function, electrolytes, C3, C4, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time; hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL with an MCV of 63 fL; C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (normal); and ESR 40 mm/hr (elevated). ECG and chest radiograph were normal. Doppler ultrasonography of the left lower extremity demonstrated extensive deep vein thrombosis. A porto-venous phase CT scan revealed compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery with a filling defect in the dilated, nonenhancing left common iliac vein. Given her obstetric history, tests for anti-beta-2-glycoprotein antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, and antiphospholipid antibodies were sent, all of which returned negative.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a 7-month history of blue discoloration of his sweat. His dermatologic history was notable for atopic dermatitis treated with dupilumab injections every 14 days for 3 months, keratosis pilaris, pincer nail deformity, and chronic paronychia. He also had food and environmental allergies and asthma. After approximately 3 months of dupilumab therapy, he noticed that alcohol swabs used to clean his injection sites turned blue. He denied consumption of artificially colored foods, dark or blue clothing, or use of dyes or paints. Other medications included inhaled albuterol and fluticasone, topical mupirocin, and sertraline. One month before presentation, he discontinued dupilumab because of injection-site pain. On examination, cleaning his arms, hands, and axillae with alcohol swabs produced blue discoloration. No fluorescence was observed under Wood’s lamp examination. A bacterial swab was obtained from the affected skin.

A 37-year-old man presented with severe pain and deformity of the left ankle half an hour after slipping and falling while playing soccer; his left foot was plantarflexed and inverted on impact. He was unable to bear weight. His medical history was unremarkable, with no prior ankle sprains or ligamentous laxity. On examination, the left foot was medially displaced, and the talar head was prominent dorsolaterally beneath a tense overlying skin; there was swelling and bruising. Plantarflexion and dorsiflexion were markedly limited, and any attempt to correct the plantarflexed position increased pain. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were palpable, but sensation to light touch in the foot was diminished. Routine blood tests, a chest radiograph, and arterial blood gases were normal. Plain anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the left foot showed dislocation of both the talocalcaneal and talonavicular joints with medial displacement of the calcaneus and the talar head directed upward and forward; the tibiotalar joint appeared undisturbed.

A 32-year-old man was referred for right critical limb ischemia. He had a 3-month history of bilateral intermittent claudication and chronic alcoholism. He had smoked approximately 10 cigarettes daily since age 10 and 10 cannabis joints daily since age 12; he reported no other cardiovascular risk factors or superficial thrombophlebitis. On examination, the right leg was extremely painful and pale, with absent pedal pulses bilaterally and mild sensory loss on the right. Allen’s test of the upper extremities was negative.  
An echo Doppler study suggested bilateral common iliac occlusion and a three-vessel occlusion of the right lower leg. CT angiography showed an intraluminal aortic and iliac clot and bilateral distal tibial vessel occlusions. The patient was anticoagulated with intravenous heparin. A transthoracic echocardiogram did not detect any proximal source of emboli.  
He underwent a right iliofemoral embolectomy with selective right popliteal, tibial, and peroneal embolectomy and intraoperative intraarterial thrombolysis. No thrombus was found in the infrapopliteal vessels, but intraoperative arteriography showed diffuse narrowing and total occlusion at the ankle with typical “corkscrew” collateral arteries suggestive of a chronic vasculitis.

An 81-year-old man presented with bilateral hearing loss that had progressively worsened over three years. He denied otorrhea, otalgia, tinnitus, vertigo, or headaches, and he had no history of ear surgery, trauma, or significant noise exposure. On examination, both auricles were normal, and the external auditory canals were patent. Otoscopy of the right ear revealed a diffusely thickened tympanic membrane and a white, spherical mass involving the pars flaccida and proximal malleus manubrium; palpation showed the mass to be firm but compressible. The left tympanic membrane was normal, and both middle ears were aerated. Audiometry demonstrated mixed hearing loss bilaterally, slightly worse on the right. High-resolution CT of the temporal bones showed a 3–4 mm lesion on the upper drum and proximal malleus with an otherwise aerated middle ear and epitympanum and no evidence of bone erosion.

A male infant was born at 36 weeks 6 days’ gestation via elective cesarean delivery. At birth, he had extensive purpuric erosions over the back (in an “X”-shaped configuration), buttocks, anterior chest, arms, neck, and scalp; the oral mucosa, hair, and nails were normal. He was born flat and dusky, required positive-pressure ventilation for 3 minutes, and remained hemodynamically stable thereafter.  
His mother is a 33-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed at age 17, maintained on prednisolone, hydroxychloroquine, and aspirin throughout pregnancy. There was one prior miscarriage; this pregnancy was via in vitro fertilization. Antenatal scans were normal.  
On day 2 of life, surface swabs of the skin lesions and oral cavity were positive for HSV-1 by PCR, and HSV total antibody was 1:128. However, PCR for HSV from cerebrospinal fluid, blood, and conjunctiva and serum HSV IgM (days 2 and 11) were negative. The mother’s HSV IgG was 1:128, and she had no history of herpes lesions. Skin lesions were negative for cytomegalovirus PCR, varicella-zoster PCR, and Toxoplasma gondii PCR. The infant received parenteral acyclovir for 2 weeks, then oral acyclovir.  
On day 1 of life, serologic testing showed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:320 (homogeneous pattern) and anti–double-stranded DNA antibody of 219.35 IU (reference <25 IU); extractable nuclear antigens were negative. Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram were normal. Complete blood count and liver-function tests were within normal limits. Further evaluation for antiphospholipid syndrome, including anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, anti–β2 glycoprotein 1 antibodies, renal-vessel Doppler ultrasound, and cranial ultrasound, was unremarkable.

A 26-year-old primigravida at 28 weeks’ gestation was referred after a peripheral centre performed an exploratory laparotomy that revealed gangrenous small bowel. Two days before presentation, she developed sudden sharp supra-umbilical pain, rapidly progressive abdominal distension, constipation, and two episodes of nonbilious vomiting. She denied hematemesis, melaena, fever, or urinary symptoms and had no history of abdominal surgery, trauma, or hernias. Her pregnancy had been uneventful.

On arrival she appeared acutely ill and pale. Vital signs were: temperature 36.8 °C, pulse 160/min, blood pressure 97/61 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Chest examination was normal. Abdominal examination revealed distension, a midline laparotomy scar closed with nylon sutures, and generalized tenderness worst in the left hypochondrial, left lumbar, and umbilical regions; bowel sounds were absent. Pelvic examination showed a posterior, firm cervix 3 cm long with a closed os and no vaginal discharge. Fetal heart tones were absent. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable.

She was diagnosed with an acute abdomen with suspected gangrenous bowel and intrauterine fetal demise. Management included nasogastric decompression (bilious effluent), urinary catheterization, nil by mouth, intravenous fluids, antibiotics, analgesics, and transfusion of two units of whole blood. Initial laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, packed cell volume 29%, white-cell count 44.1×10^9/L (74% neutrophils), platelets 286×10^9/L, serum sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, urea 4.1 mmol/L, and creatinine 216 μmol/L. Obstetric ultrasound confirmed intrauterine fetal death. After 36 hours, vital signs stabilized (pulse 130/min, blood pressure 121/74 mmHg) and repeat labs showed white-cell count 19.3×10^9/L, platelets 142×10^9/L, urea 12.9 mmol/L, and creatinine 319 μmol/L. She was then scheduled for exploratory laparotomy.

A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and hypothyroidism presented with acute-onset nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. He denied fevers or chills and had no prior gastrointestinal procedures. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the right upper and lower quadrants without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated no evidence of bowel obstruction, ischemia, or abscess; however, there was an extensive amount of gas in the portal venous system. Given his stable presentation and lack of alarming findings, he was managed conservatively with intravenous fluids and bowel rest.

A 12-year-old girl presents with a 6-month history of gradually enlarging gum swelling in the maxillary right quadrant, provoked bleeding, and multiple painful oral ulcers in the vestibular mucosa, causing difficulty with mastication. Her medical history is notable for vaginoplasty, urethroplasty, esophageal dilatation, and a transfusion for immune thrombocytopenic purpura. She is the product of a consanguineous union. She is small for her age (height 100 cm, weight 25 kg). On examination, there are multiple hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules with prominent poikilodermatous changes, xerosis, and diffuse skin atrophy; hair is sparse and thin. The sclera appear icteric. The dorsum of her hands and feet show cigarette paper–like wrinkling. She is alert and oriented.

A 58-year-old Chinese woman presented with a 3-week history of dysgeusia. Over the next 2 months, she developed nonbloody vomiting, loose stools, numbness in her hands and feet, and a 6-kg weight loss. She noted increased pigmentation and thickening of the skin around her eyes, hands, and feet, along with hair loss. Examination revealed xerosis, onycholysis, periorbital hyperpigmentation, and alopecia.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15.5 g/dL, C-reactive protein 31.9 mg/L, albumin 29 g/L, zinc 832 μg/L, and fecal calprotectin 765 µg/g. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed diffuse gastric mucosal hyperemia, edema, and nodular changes; biopsies demonstrated hyperplastic polyps. Helicobacter pylori testing was negative. Colonoscopy showed confluent circumferential nodular colitis throughout the colon and a single 1-cm sessile polyp in the transverse colon; colonic biopsies exhibited dense inflammatory-cell infiltrates with crypt architectural distortion, cryptitis, and crypt abscesses, and the polyp was interpreted as an inflammatory pseudopolyp.

In view of her dysgeusia, diarrhea, ectodermal findings, and atypical endoscopic features of colitis in the absence of classical polyposis, the case was discussed at a multidisciplinary meeting.

An 85-year-old woman presented with an enlarging right axillary mass. Eight years earlier, she had undergone revision of cosmetic bilateral breast augmentation, with exchange of implants to textured silicone devices and an open periprosthetic capsulectomy. Four weeks before presentation, she noted significant enlargement of a previously small palpable lump in the right axilla, accompanied by a change in the shape of her right breast. She had had a negative screening mammogram one month earlier and no history of breast biopsies or surgeries other than augmentation.

Given the concern for implant complications, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breasts with and without contrast was performed, including T2-weighted water-suppressed sequences and dynamic T1 fat-suppressed postcontrast sequences. MRI demonstrated an enlarged internal mammary chain lymph node and a large T2-hyperintense mass in the right axilla, both suggestive of silicone. Both breast implants appeared intact, and there was no suspicious enhancement in either breast or peri-implant fluid collection. The study was assigned a BI-RADS category 4 (“suspicious”), and MRI-directed ultrasound was recommended.

Ultrasound of the right axilla revealed multiple areas of “snowstorm” artifact without identifiable normal or abnormal lymph nodes, a finding suggestive of free silicone granulomas. Despite these findings, the surgical team remained concerned for breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma, metastatic disease, granulomatous infection, or squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck, and ultrasound-guided tissue sampling was requested.

A 3.5-year-old spayed female Maine Coon cat was evaluated in mid-July for lethargy and anorexia of 3 days’ duration. The owner reported that the cat had been hiding, developed ocular discharge, and had not eaten, drank, urinated, or defecated since the onset of symptoms. The cat had just returned from a summer cottage in southeastern Finland, where it was often kept outdoors on a leash. The owner noted two ticks attached to the skin one day before presentation.

On examination, the cat was febrile (39.5 °C) and tachypneic, with bilaterally increased lung sounds. The cranial abdomen was slightly painful to palpation, and there was purulent discharge in both eyes. Four healed skin lesions were noted; one live Ixodes ricinus tick was attached.

Thoracic and abdominal radiographs showed a minimal bronchial pattern in the lungs but were otherwise unremarkable. A venous blood sample revealed lymphopenia (0.4 × 10^9/L; reference, 1.3–7.5) and mild hyperglycemia (7.7 mmol/L; reference, 3.5–5.7). Examination of a May-Grünwald-Giemsa–stained peripheral blood smear demonstrated intracytoplasmic morulae in neutrophils.

An 82-year-old man presented with progressively generalized skin lesions since adolescence. He first noted hyperpigmented macules on his face, which gradually spread to the neck, axillae, groin, trunk, and limbs, accompanied by pruritus. He was born of a non-consanguineous marriage, and all of his offspring had similar lesions. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Skin examination revealed:
• Symmetrical reticulate hyperpigmentation of the lower face, major flexures, back, and legs  
• Scattered reticulate hypopigmented macules on the legs  
• Multiple 1–3 mm pits and open comedo-like lesions over the cheeks, perioral area, neck, and back  
• No palmar or plantar ridge breaks; mucosa, nails, teeth, and hair were normal  

Complete blood count, serum chemistry, and liver and renal function tests were all within normal limits.

A 13-year-old girl, three days after an appendectomy, presented with fever and loss of appetite. On examination she was dehydrated, tachycardic, tachypneic, and febrile (38.8 °C); blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were normal. The abdomen was diffusely tender with rebound pain, normal bowel sounds, and a hyperemic surgical scar.  
An abdominal ultrasound showed a pericolic abscess that was surgically drained. Cultures grew multisensitive Escherichia coli and group G β-hemolytic Streptococcus; she was treated with ceftriaxone and metronidazole. On postoperative day 3 she continued to have abdominal pain and fever; antibiotics were changed to vancomycin, ceftazidime, and amikacin, but fever persisted. An abdominal CT scan showed no surgical complication; fluconazole was added.  
On postoperative day 12 (from the second surgery) she became hypotensive, tachycardic, and febrile to 39.4 °C and was transferred to the ICU for vasoactive support. Laboratory tests on ICU admission showed:  
• Hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL; hematocrit 24.6%  
• Leukocytes 7.2 × 10^3/mm^3 (bands 14%, neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 8%)  
• Platelets 26.9 × 10^3/mm^3  
• INR 4.66; fibrinogen 98 mg/dL  
• Total bilirubin 7.6 mg/dL  
• ALT 16 556 IU/L; AST 6126 IU/L; AP 926 IU/L; γGT 202 IU/L  
• Triglycerides 105 mg/dL; ferritin 1287 ng/mL  
Repeat abdominal CT ruled out abscess. Serologic studies revealed HIV negative; hepatitis B surface antibody positive, antigen negative; hepatitis C negative; anti-CMV IgG positive/IgM negative; anti-EBV IgG positive/IgM negative; other viral IgM studies negative. Blood, urine, catheter, and abdominal fluid cultures remained negative.  
On postoperative day 20 laboratory evaluation confirmed worsening thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, prolonged prothrombin time, and marked transaminase elevations.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of an asymptomatic enlarging nodule on the left mandible and progressive alopecia of the scalp. He had been diagnosed previously with cutaneous sarcoidosis on the basis of a scalp biopsy performed at another institution and was treated with methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, and hydroxychloroquine without clinical improvement. On examination, there was a skin-colored papillomatous alopecic plaque on the right temporal scalp, a smooth, skin-colored, mobile nodule on the left mandible, and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. A review of systems was otherwise unremarkable. A 4-mm punch biopsy of the scalp demonstrated a diffuse dermal histiocytic infiltrate admixed with intense lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and effacement of adnexal structures. Immunostains for S100 and CD1a were negative. Stains for acid-fast bacilli, Fite, and Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver were also negative.

A 65-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on thrice-weekly hemodialysis since 2013 presented with a 2-month history of an increasingly painful ulcer at the tip of his penis. Four months earlier, he had undergone a transmetatarsal amputation of his right foot for ischemia, and over the preceding year he had suffered painful, infected lower-limb ulcers. Initially managed with local dressings and antibiotics, the penile lesion failed to heal, and within 2 weeks it spread to involve the entire glans. The patient described agonizing pain, and over the next month a hard, black eschar developed over the glans, with dry skin changes on the shaft and oozing, infected margins.

On examination, there was a circumferential black eschar covering the entire glans penis that was extremely hard and tender, with surrounding dry, infected-appearing skin.

Laboratory studies showed: albumin 2.0 g/dL; C-reactive protein 58.9 mg/L; hemoglobin 5.13 g/dL; white-cell count 6.8 × 10^3/µL; serum creatinine 4.9 mg/dL; phosphorus 5.15 mg/dL; calcium 8.8 mg/dL; parathyroid hormone 26.45 pg/mL.

A pelvic radiograph demonstrated extensive vascular calcifications in the pelvic and penile vasculature.

An 18-year-old Japanese woman with known myopia, otherwise healthy and without systemic disease, presented with floaters in her left eye. She had received her second dose of the Pfizer mRNA COVID-19 vaccine one day before symptom onset; her first vaccination had been uneventful. She noticed worsening floaters over the next week and was referred 10 days after vaccination.  
On examination, blood pressure was 103/56 mmHg and pulse 76 beats/min. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes; intraocular pressures were 15 mmHg bilaterally. Critical flicker fusion frequency was 37.0 Hz in the left eye. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect and no signs of intraocular inflammation.  
Fundus photography of the left eye revealed hemorrhage around the optic disc with disc swelling; the right eye was normal. Optical coherence tomography angiography showed no abnormal vessels. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated hemorrhage extending from the subretinal to the preretinal spaces in the left eye. Kinetic perimetry of the left eye showed a relative scotoma in the temporal lower quadrant; the right field was normal.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of recurrent oral and genital ulcers. The lesions initially occurred every 2–3 months and resolved spontaneously. Three years earlier, during pregnancy, the ulcers became more numerous and larger, involving the gums, palate, and tongue, leading to painful swallowing and a brief hospital admission; a biopsy of a genital lesion at that time revealed a granulomatous lesion, and she subsequently experienced a miscarriage at 7 months’ gestation. Since then, she has had monthly recurrences of oral and genital ulcers, with exacerbations during her menstrual periods. She also reports acne-like eruptions on the face, neck, chest, buttocks, and back, intermittent throat pain, low backache, abdominal distension, difficulty passing stool, and, for the past month, bilateral eye pain with blurred vision and itchiness. She denies fever, joint pain, neurological, cardiopulmonary, or renal symptoms. 

On examination, multiple 0.5 × 0.5 cm aphthous ulcers with white centers and erythematous borders were noted on the tongue and buccal mucosa. In the vulvar area, there were several 1–2 cm ulcers with thick purulent discharge, tender to palpation. Erythematous papules and nodules were present on the temporal face, acneiform eruptions on the forehead, and papulopustular lesions on the chest, back, and axillae.

Laboratory studies revealed normal complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and random blood sugar. Serologic tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, HIV I and II, Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay, and VDRL were all negative. Antinuclear antibody testing was negative. Inflammatory markers were elevated (ESR 37 mm/h, CRP 77 mg/L). A pathergy test performed on both forearms with a 20-gauge needle produced an erythematous papule at 48 hours.

A 43-year-old woman with a history of migraines presented with acute bilateral central vision loss. One week earlier, she had severe headaches, vomiting, and diarrhea; during that visit she tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by PCR, received IV fluids and antiemetic, and was discharged. The following morning she awoke with central vision loss in both eyes. She denied any trauma; review of systems was otherwise unremarkable.

On examination, blood pressure was 154/62 mm Hg. Visual acuity was hand motion in the right eye and count fingers in the left eye, with no afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressures were 14 mm Hg OD and 12 mm Hg OS. Dilated fundus examination showed diffuse peripapillary cotton-wool spots extending into the macula in both eyes, without optic disc edema. There was a flame hemorrhage along the inferior arcade in the right eye and pinpoint hemorrhages along the superior arcade in the left eye.

Neurovascular imaging—including non-contrast CT of the head, CT angiography of the head and neck, MRI of the head, and carotid ultrasound—showed no abnormalities. Serum amylase and lipase were normal. A broad inflammatory, infectious, autoimmune, and hypercoagulability workup was negative except for a mildly elevated LDH (209 U/L; normal 100–190). Optical coherence tomography revealed subretinal fluid, inner retinal thickening, hyperreflectivity, and disruption of normal architecture corresponding to areas of cotton-wool spots. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated early blockage and late leakage in the areas of cotton-wool spots and retinal hemorrhages.

A 48-year-old Chinese man with chronic hepatitis B and multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma beyond standard criteria underwent a deceased-donor liver transplant abroad. He was discharged on tacrolimus 1 mg twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 750 mg twice daily, and prednisolone 20 mg daily. Three weeks later he returned with deep jaundice. Laboratory studies showed a mixed cholestatic–hepatitic pattern (elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and transaminases).  
Serologic and PCR testing of blood were positive for Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) and hepatitis E virus (HEV) genotype 3; liver tissue was also EBV PCR–positive; tests were negative for cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, parvovirus, and human herpesvirus 6; no viral inclusions were seen in liver tissue.  
He was treated with intravenous acyclovir, and the EBV viral load decreased. Doppler ultrasound showed patent graft vessels. MRI of the biliary tree suggested an anastomotic biliary stricture, and an endoscopic stent was placed with interval changes every 3 months; despite good bile flow, liver tests remained abnormal.  
In December, a liver biopsy demonstrated moderate acute cellular rejection (rejection activity index, 5), which was treated with pulse methylprednisolone. A repeat biopsy 2 weeks later confirmed histological resolution of rejection, yet liver function tests did not improve.  
In February, a third biopsy showed lymphocytic portal and lobular hepatitis with marked cholestasis, without features of acute or chronic graft rejection; the Metavir fibrosis score was 1/4, with no atypical mononuclear infiltrates or evidence of lymphoproliferative disease.

A 40-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with six months of rapid palpitations accompanied by dizziness. Treatment with atenolol and verapamil did not relieve his symptoms. On examination, his heart rate was irregular at 105 bpm; otherwise the physical exam was unremarkable. A 24-hour Holter recording documented multiple episodes of narrow complex tachycardia with a peak heart rate of 240 bpm. At rest, a 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 60 bpm with a normal PR interval and QRS width. However, alternating QRS complexes with a left anterior fascicular block pattern—sometimes combined with complete or incomplete right bundle branch block morphology—occurred in a bigeminal pattern, resulting in an overall rate of 120 bpm. Transthoracic echocardiography and cardiac MRI demonstrated a dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesia and an ejection fraction of 42%, with no delayed enhancement. During exercise testing, the ECG initially showed sinus tachycardia at 110 bpm (P waves positive in leads II, III, and aVF; negative in aVR; P-P interval 560 ± 10 ms), then abruptly the ventricular rate doubled to 220 bpm while preserving the group-beating pattern and alternating narrow QRS morphologies. Before the tachycardia, the PR interval was 520 ± 10 ms; during tachycardia, each P wave was followed by two QRS complexes with a P-to-second-R interval of 520 ± 10 ms. These findings recurred at different sinus rates.

A 35-year-old multiparous Nigerian woman presented at 35 weeks’ gestation with premature rupture of membranes and suspected abruptio placentae. She began antenatal care at 6 weeks; booking investigations were normal. There was no history of consanguinity, diabetes, teratogen exposure, or irradiation. Her first three pregnancies were unremarkable; a fourth was terminated at 20 weeks for anencephaly. A routine ultrasound at 24 weeks showed tetraphocomelia, which had been missed on earlier scans. The mother elected to continue the pregnancy.

An emergency cesarean delivered a live female infant weighing 1.1 kg (<3rd percentile) with Apgar scores of 5 at 1 and 5 minutes. The neonate required intranasal oxygen but died 10 minutes after NICU admission. Examination revealed microbrachycephaly (OFC 24 cm), length 34 cm, oligodactyly with thumb aplasia, micrognathia, malar hypoplasia, down-slanting palpebral fissures, ocular hypertelorism, broad nose, dysplastic low-set ears, and absence of all four limbs (tetraphocomelia). Additional findings included minor omphalocele, imperforate anus, absence of external genitalia, and hemangiomas on the forehead and back. Heart sounds were faint; renal and cardiac structures could not be assessed. Autopsy and radiographs were declined, and cytogenetic testing was unavailable.

A 30-year-old uneducated woman from a rural area presented with a 5-year history of episodes of intense anxiety and a feeling of impending doom. Initially these episodes occurred once every 2–3 months and lasted 15–30 minutes; over the past year they increased to 2–3 episodes per month. She also reported 4–5 years of decreased energy, loss of interest in work, and easy fatigability. She had consulted multiple traditional healers, alternative-medicine practitioners, and general medical practitioners without benefit; medical investigations were all normal. On mental status examination, she had an anxious affect and excessive somatic concern. On further confidential questioning, she reported a 15-year history of unrelenting passage of a mucoid per-vaginal whitish discharge that she called “Dhat,” which she believed caused all her physical and psychological symptoms. The discharge stained her undergarments and had persisted before and after her marriage at age 18 and two subsequent pregnancies. Traditional healers had told her it was harmful and prescribed various herbal remedies without relief.

A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was transferred at 31 weeks 5 days’ gestation. Dichorionicity had been confirmed on first-trimester ultrasound. Pregnancy complications included early-onset growth restriction in twin 2 and new-onset preeclampsia at 30 weeks. At 16 weeks, ultrasound showed twin 1 with normal growth and normal amniotic fluid; twin 2 had estimated fetal weight <5th percentile, anhydramnios, and an absent bladder. Confirmatory ultrasound at 19 weeks revealed Tetralogy of Fallot in twin 2. By 21 weeks, twin 2’s amniotic fluid improved from anhydramnios to oligohydramnios (maximum vertical pocket 1.9 cm), and later normalized in both twins. Invasive testing was declined initially; at 31 weeks, chorionic villus sampling of twin 2 showed a normal chromosomal microarray.  
At 32 weeks, ultrasound at the tertiary center demonstrated:  
• Twin 1: estimated fetal weight 1904 g (62nd centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) 26 cm/s (0.56 multiples of the mean).  
• Twin 2: estimated fetal weight 1128 g (<5th centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and MCA-PSV 50.9 cm/s (1.3 MoM).  
Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

A 70-year-old man presented with swelling and pain in the left upper thigh that began 8 days earlier after he fell from a bicycle and struck his left groin on the handlebars. He had smoked three to four cigarettes per day for 10 years but had quit 3 months earlier. On examination, there was a fluctuant nonpulsating mass of about 8 cm in diameter in the upper medial left thigh. The left groin pulse was brisk, but the popliteal and foot pulses on the affected side were absent; pulses were palpable on the contralateral side. The left foot was moderately swollen and painful, with numbness, decreased skin temperature, and limited movement of the toes. Duplex ultrasound of the groin showed a complex cystic lesion measuring 7.6 × 6.5 cm, with both the femoral vein and artery seen within the lesion, displaying increased viscosity and slow flow.

An 81-year-old woman presented with 2 days of fever, dizziness, and weakness following a finger dog-bite three days earlier. She also noted nausea and vomiting. Her medical history included coronary artery disease on prasugrel, hypertension on amlodipine, ramipril, and metoprolol, and a peritonsillar abscess 6 months prior.  

On arrival: temperature 39.9°C, blood pressure 107/57 mmHg, pulse 110/min, respiratory rate 29/min, oxygen saturation 90% on 12 L by reservoir mask. Examination revealed a livid fingertip wound on the right third digit and marked mottling of both legs to the groin. Heart and lung sounds were normal.  

Laboratory studies showed CRP 186.2 mg/L, creatinine 1.41 mg/dL, platelets 114 × 10^9/L, and arterial lactate 6.5 mmol/L. Chest radiograph demonstrated basal atelectasis. She was diagnosed with sepsis, received fluids and piperacillin–tazobactam, and was transferred to the ICU.  

Over the next 48 hours she became anuric and required vasopressors. Repeat labs revealed hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 24 × 10^9/L, leukocytes 21.1 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 3.3 mg/dL, and haptoglobin 74 mg/dL. Twelve hours later platelets fell to 14 × 10^9/L and haptoglobin 37 mg/dL. On hospital day 3, platelets were 39 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.28 mg/dL, haptoglobin <5 mg/dL, LDH 1083 U/L, and peripheral smear showed 20‰ schistocytes.

An 82‐year‐old man with cryptogenic hepatic cirrhosis complicated by portal venous thrombosis and multiple prior paracenteses presented for management of a right‐sided pleural effusion. Eleven days earlier, he had sought care for shortness of breath; CT angiography of the chest had shown a large right pleural effusion with complete collapse of the right lower lobe and no signs of malignancy. A follow‐up chest radiograph confirmed a large right effusion with overlying atelectasis. 

On admission, he reported only mild baseline dyspnea and denied fever, cough, chest pain, abdominal pain, or distension. Vital signs were stable. Examination revealed decreased breath sounds on the right, 1+ bilateral lower‐extremity edema, and no abdominal distension or ascites. 

Thoracentesis yielded 1.5 L of turbid yellow fluid. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL; normal leukocyte and platelet counts; persistent hypoalbuminemia and slight elevations in alkaline phosphatase, aspartate aminotransferase, and total bilirubin; an unremarkable BNP; and a negative SARS-CoV-2 test. Abdominal ultrasound three months earlier had shown no ascites.

Pleural fluid analysis revealed a transudative effusion with triglycerides of 175 mg/dL. Fluid culture showed no growth, gram stain was negative for organisms, and cytology was negative for malignancy.

A 72-year-old woman presented with a 12-month history of tenderness on the left side of the oropharynx and progressively painful swallowing, especially with solids. She was unable to lie flat due to severe pain. Her general practitioner diagnosed gastroesophageal reflux and prescribed esomeprazole, with no improvement. Her history was notable for left-sided tonsillar carcinoma treated years earlier with surgery and radiotherapy. 

On oral examination, she was edentulous. There was an irregular red lesion on the left soft palate, overlying a bony hard, slender mass protruding into the oral cavity, covered by mucosa. There was no ulceration or induration and no other oral lesions. Extraoral examination was normal, with no cervical lymphadenopathy. 

An orthopantomogram showed elongation of the left styloid process.

A 38-year-old right-handed woman presented with a 10-month history of progressive pain and swelling in her right first dorsal web space. The constant pain was worsened by repetitive tasks such as writing (Numeric Rating Scale [NRS] score 10) and partially improved with rest (NRS score 5). She denied sensory changes, had no history of trauma, and did not engage in hand-intensive exercise or use musical instruments. Her medical history was unremarkable.

On examination, there was visible enlargement in the right first dorsal web space without erythema or skin changes. Palpation revealed a firm, tender, non-mobile mass without warmth or fluctuance. Hand movements were limited by pain, and grip strength was reduced on the right compared with the left. Sensation and neurologic examination were normal.

Laboratory studies were within normal limits. A hand radiograph was unremarkable. Ultrasonography demonstrated enlargement of the first dorsal interosseous muscle. Magnetic resonance imaging of the hands showed mild hypertrophy of the right first dorsal interosseous muscle with preserved architecture and regular signal intensity; no tumor, abnormal structure, or vascular lesion was identified. Nerve conduction studies were normal, and electromyography showed normal motor unit recruitment and morphology without denervation.

An 84-year-old man presented to the emergency department with an 8-hour history of wet cough that had gradually worsened. He denied sore throat, nasal discharge, or chest pain. His medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) managed with vilanterol, fluticasone, glycopyrronium, l-carbocisteine, and home oxygen (2.5 L/min), as well as lung cancer infiltrating the left vagal nerve under supportive care. He had no known allergies. 

On arrival: temperature 36.2 °C, heart rate 93 beats/min, blood pressure 171/65 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on 3 L/min nasal-cannula oxygen. Physical examination revealed wheezing. The white blood cell count was 9,100 cells/mcL (neutrophils 72.9%, lymphocytes 20.2%). Chest radiography showed only his known left lung tumor without new abnormalities.

He was initially treated for an acute exacerbation of COPD with inhaled procaterol and parenteral methylprednisolone (40 mg). Because his response was limited, and given his history of untreated lung cancer with no new chest radiographic changes, central airway obstruction (CAO) was suspected. Non-contrast lung CT demonstrated a 1 cm round nodule partially obstructing the right intermediate bronchus that had not been present 2 months earlier, raising concern for tumor progression.

An 84-year-old man underwent CT of the thorax and abdomen to stage a newly diagnosed prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason 7 [3 + 4]). The CT showed suspicious retroperitoneal lymph nodes but no metastases and incidentally revealed a left-sided perirenal mass with mild dilatation of the left renal pelvis. Without any history of trauma, this was tentatively diagnosed as a perirenal hematoma. 

His surgical history included a prostate enucleation 10 years earlier and transurethral resection of a bladder polyp 9 years earlier, which was a noninvasive low-grade papillary transitional cell carcinoma. Urinary laboratory values were normal. A 68Ga-PSMA PET scan showed that the lymph nodes were not PSMA-avid; the prostate cancer was staged as T2-3N0M0 and treated with combined hormonal therapy (decapeptyl) and local radiotherapy.

One year later, CT urography showed persistence of the left perirenal soft tissue mass (density 40 HU on noncontrast images), with extension into the left psoas muscle and caudally toward the pelvis. The left renal pelvis and calyces remained mildly dilated; there was no ureteral abnormality and no evidence of active bleeding. The right upper urinary tract was normal.

Three weeks later, MRI of the kidneys demonstrated mild anterior displacement of the left kidney by a discrete T2-hyperintense infiltrating cuff in the left perirenal space, encasing the renal vessels and proximal ureter and extending toward the aorta, with caudal extension along the iliopsoas muscle. On T1-weighted images the lesion was hypointense. After IV contrast, it showed vivid enhancement in the portal venous phase and faint homogeneous enhancement in the renal parenchymal phase. The lesion also exhibited diffusion restriction with a low apparent diffusion coefficient.

A 65-year-old man presented following a 2-week history of frequent syncopal events. The episodes occurred at night when lying in bed and were provoked by rightward neck rotation. After he was found unresponsive on the bathroom floor without seizure or incontinence, he presented to our hospital. He also noted a gradually enlarging right neck mass in addition to new taste changes and right lower facial numbness. He denied orthostatic, exercise-induced, or daytime syncope and was not taking any medications. During this presentation, he had unintentional weight loss but denied fever, night sweats, exertional chest pain, or shortness of breath. His smoking history was significant for 3 packs per day for the last 40 years. On physical examination, there was a right suprahyoid, firm neck mass from the level of the right earlobe to the middle of the neck without overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Heart and lung sounds were normal.

His 12-lead electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm and was otherwise unremarkable. Orthostatic blood-pressure measurements were normal, initial blood tests did not show any electrolyte abnormalities, and serial troponin levels were not detectable. He was admitted for close observation, and during this time, he had a witnessed episode of syncope with documented hypotension while supine; telemetry demonstrated sinus pauses. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left ventricular systolic function (55 to 60 %) without outflow-tract obstruction or valvular disease. Computed tomography of the neck demonstrated a 4.7- × 4.1- × 7.9-cm vascular mass in the right suprahyoid neck adjacent to the carotid artery bifurcation.

A 70-year-old man presented three weeks after coronary artery bypass grafting with fatigue, fever, decreased oral intake, and dyspnea on exertion. His postoperative course had included multiple blood transfusions for intraoperative losses. He denied chest pain, cough, gastrointestinal, urinary, or night‐sweats symptoms. Medical history included hepatic sarcoidosis, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. 

On admission, temperature was 39.6 °C, heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 122/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, and SpO2 96% on room air. Examination revealed normal heart sounds, minimal crepitations at the left lung base, a soft non-tender abdomen without organomegaly, and an alert, oriented patient. 

Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia and worsening liver function tests. Chest radiography demonstrated his recent sternotomy without consolidation. Blood and urine cultures were obtained, and he was started on IV piperacillin–tazobactam for presumed pneumonia. Over two weeks, he clinically and biochemically deteriorated. CT of the thorax revealed small bilateral pleural effusions and a small pericardial effusion without hemodynamic compromise on echocardiography. Cultures remained sterile. 

He developed jaundice, fluctuating consciousness, episodic hypoxemia, and hypotension. Abdominal ultrasound showed no biliary obstruction or focal liver lesions. CT of the abdomen revealed widespread reactive-appearing lymphadenopathy. Serologies for hepatitis B and C and HIV were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis showed no monoclonal bands. Alpha-1 antitrypsin and ceruloplasmin levels were normal. Antinuclear, neutrophil cytoplasmic, smooth muscle, mitochondrial, and liver–kidney microsomal antibodies were all negative. Iron studies revealed normal serum iron, low total iron binding capacity, elevated transferrin saturation, and ferritin >30,000 µg/L. Serum triglycerides were 3.22 mmol/L, and fibrinogen was 1.2 g/L. EBV DNA was detected by PCR, and EBV nuclear antigen IgG was positive.

A 20-year-old right-handed male soccer goalkeeper presented after a forceful collision with a ball, complaining of acute pain and deformity of the left third finger. On examination, the proximal interphalangeal joint of the third digit was swollen and deformed with dorsal displacement of the middle phalanx, tender to palpation, and showed no active movement due to severe pain. Radiographs demonstrated a comminuted fracture-dislocation of the proximal interphalangeal joint with a volar fragment comprising approximately 50% of the articular surface, corresponding to a Grade 3 injury by the Hastings and Carroll classification.

A 28-year-old woman presented with multiple asymptomatic hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules on the skin since age 3. The lesions began on both legs, spread to the thighs, then to the hands and elbows, and later appeared on the buttocks and trunk. There was no history of photosensitivity, chemical exposure, or significant drug intake. She reported that her father and sister had similar but milder lesions. Mental status examination revealed depression. 

Physical examination showed numerous generalized 0.5–1 cm hyperpigmented macules interspersed with spotty hypopigmented macules, densely distributed on the limbs and trunk, with sparing of the palms and soles and mild facial involvement. There was no atrophy, erythema, or telangiectasia. Hair, nails, teeth, and mucosae were normal. Systemic examination was unremarkable. 

Routine laboratory investigations and chest radiography were normal. Tests for syphilis and HIV were negative. 

Skin biopsies from hyperpigmented and hypopigmented lesions showed a mildly atrophic epidermis with hyperkeratosis, mild vacuolar change in the basal layer, papillary dermal melanin incontinence, and dilated dermal vessels. The hyperpigmented lesion exhibited increased pigment extending into the stratum spinosum; the hypopigmented lesion showed decreased pigment. The dermis in both samples had a mild perivascular and periadnexal lymphomononuclear infiltrate.

A 57-year-old woman presented 4 hours after the onset of left hemibody weakness and slurred speech. Her level of consciousness fluctuated. Neurologic examination revealed a mild left-sided motor deficit and limited left lateral gaze (NIHSS score of 5). She denied any history of neck trauma and had no cardiovascular or family history of connective tissue disease. Routine blood tests were normal. Noncontrast head CT performed 4 hours after symptom onset was unremarkable. MRI performed 11 hours after symptom onset showed multiple ischemic areas involving the bilateral posterior thalami, bilateral occipital lobes, the left side of the pons, and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres; no hemorrhage was detected.

A 79-year-old woman with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, and arterial hypertension underwent successful transcatheter mitral valve repair with one MitraClip. Transthoracic echocardiography immediately and 1 day after the procedure showed no pericardial effusion. On post-procedural Day 3, she reported fatigue, malaise, and non-specific epigastric pain. Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 70 mg/L (normal <5), white blood cell count 9/nL, and procalcitonin 0.16 ng/mL (normal <0.5). Chest X-ray revealed new bilateral pleural effusions without congestion or infiltrate. Electrocardiogram was unchanged, and blood cultures remained sterile. On Day 5, TTE demonstrated a mild circular pericardial effusion (8 mm); by Day 7, this progressed to 13 mm without hemodynamic compromise. Cardiac CT showed pericardial and pleural effusions of similar low density (~10 HU), suggesting serous fluid.

A 53-year-old man presented with progressive right knee pain for 1 year without fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Examination showed a swollen right knee with range of motion 0–100° and pain on lateral compression of the femoral condyle. Arthrocentesis on two occasions yielded clear fluid. Chest and knee radiographs were normal. Laboratory studies revealed WBC 11.38 G/L, CRP 5.0 mg/dL, ESR 34/71 mm/h, and rheumatoid factor 18.6 IU/mL. MRI of the right knee demonstrated multiple 5–8 mm intra-articular bodies on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences.

A 30-year-old woman with a 14-year history of anorexia nervosa (restricting type) and a BMI of 9.2 presented with a 1-week history of productive cough, fever, dyspnea, chest pain, and hemoptysis. She had experienced recurrent respiratory infections over 3 years and had previously refused hospitalization. On admission her heart rate was 110 bpm, blood pressure 80/40 mmHg, temperature normal, and she was fully alert. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 54.6 mg/L, serum albumin 24.85 mg/L (normal 35–40 mg/L), blood glucose 55.2 mg/dL, and arterial pH 7.49. A chest radiograph revealed multifocal, ill-defined consolidations predominantly in the right lung. Blood and sputum cultures, bronchoalveolar lavage samples, and tuberculosis and fungal panels were negative. Tests for cystic fibrosis (CFTR gene panel, two occasions) were negative. A chest CT scan demonstrated massive cylindrical and saccular bronchiectasis in multiple lung segments, some bronchi filled with fluid, and diffuse ground-glass opacities bilaterally.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of progressive exertional dyspnea and a non-purulent cough. She denied fever, hemoptysis, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and exposure to tuberculosis. Her medical history included hyperlipidemia (on atorvastatin) and hypothyroidism (on levothyroxine); she had no known drug or seasonal allergies. She was a lifelong housewife, never smoked, and reported no specific occupational exposures. 

On examination, her BMI was 35.5 kg/m2. Vital signs were within normal limits except for an oxygen saturation of 78% on room air. Auscultation revealed inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 10,900/mm3, hemoglobin 18.6 g/dL, hematocrit 58.9%, and mild anisocytosis; other cell counts were unremarkable. Arterial blood gas analysis confirmed hypoxemia. 

Pulmonary function tests demonstrated a severe restrictive pattern (FVC 1.0 L, 47% predicted; TLC 2.97 L, 76% predicted) with a reduction in DLCO to 73.9% of predicted. After bronchodilator administration, FVC increased by 21% and FEV1 by 17.7%. 

A PPD test was negative. Echocardiography revealed a pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 40 mmHg with normal left and right ventricular function. 

Chest radiography showed a new reticulo-nodular pattern in the lower lung fields. HRCT of the chest demonstrated diffuse ground-glass opacities, focal areas of emphysema, patchy lobular air trapping on expiratory views with mosaic perfusion, a dilated main pulmonary artery, and cardiomegaly.

A 12-year-old Vietnamese-American boy with a history of recurrent oral aphthous and genital ulcers, fevers several times per year, and failure to thrive was admitted one month earlier for fever, oral and perirectal mucositis, and poor oral intake. Initial treatment with amoxicillin, nystatin, and IV acyclovir produced little improvement. Several days later, due to concern for an underlying systemic process, he received three doses of IV methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day) followed by oral prednisone, which improved his mucosal ulcers and fevers. One week after admission, he noted decreased vision in both eyes and was found to have anterior uveitis bilaterally, for which topical prednisolone was prescribed. 

On ophthalmologic examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 in each eye. Intraocular pressures were normal. Pupils were reactive without afferent defect. Anterior chambers showed 0.5+ cells and 1.5+ flare bilaterally. Posterior examination revealed pale optic nerves, sclerosis of superior nasal retinal arteries, peripheral vascular sheathing, and collateral vessels in both eyes. Spectral-domain OCT of the macula demonstrated subretinal and intraretinal deposits, disruption of the ellipsoid zone, and reduced foveal thickness in the right eye, and subretinal fluid with hyperreflective material in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography showed optic disc and vascular leakage and widespread retinal nonperfusion in both eyes. 

Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 19.3 × 10^3/μL and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 105 mm/hr. A complete chemistry panel, urinalysis, HLA-B51 typing, antinuclear antibody testing, antiphospholipid antibody panel, C-reactive protein, QuantiFERON-TB Gold, HSV testing, syphilis serology, brain MRI, and chest radiograph were all normal or nonreactive.

A 54-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 2-day history of epigastric pain and melena. On examination, his vital signs were stable. Laboratory testing revealed a hemoglobin level of 5.3 g/dL, and he received packed red-cell transfusions. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a large, submucosal, noncircumferential mass in the gastric cardia without active bleeding; biopsies were inconclusive. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a complex gastric mass with a greater than 6-cm component extending posteriorly from the distal gastric body toward the tail of the pancreas and a greater than 10-cm component extending anteriorly toward the splenic flexure of the colon; there were no signs of liver cirrhosis.

A 51-year-old man with nonischemic cardiomyopathy on a left ventricular assist device was admitted for heart transplant evaluation. Because of a family history of colorectal cancer, he underwent an elective screening colonoscopy under propofol sedation following standard bowel preparation. The nocturnal procedure was completed without difficulty, although brief external abdominal pressure was required to navigate the splenic flexure. Findings included sigmoid and descending colon diverticula and two small sessile polyps removed with cold forceps. He was asymptomatic immediately postprocedure and tolerated oral intake that night and the next morning. Approximately 12–14 hours later, he developed midmorning epigastric abdominal pain and had one episode of nonbloody, nonbilious emesis. On examination, he was afebrile, blood pressure 104/89 mm Hg, heart rate 68/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. The abdomen was mildly distended, with moderate epigastric tenderness and decreased bowel sounds, without guarding or rebound. Laboratory tests showed a lipase of 2275 U/L and amylase of 1141 U/L, as well as elevations in aspartate aminotransferase (105 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (94 U/L), and total bilirubin (1.4 μmol/L). An abdominal X-ray revealed no free air or obstruction. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated diffuse edematous changes of the pancreas with surrounding inflammatory stranding extending superiorly to the perihepatic region and into the pelvis.

A 2-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of suspected intestinal malrotation. He was born at 35 weeks +4 days’ gestation, weighing 2560 g, with Apgar scores of 9 and 9 and a negative prenatal workup. The mother was a heavy smoker, and both maternal and neonatal serologic studies were negative. On examination, the infant had a distended, tender abdomen, poor feeding, and intermittent vomiting. A water-soluble contrast enema demonstrated filling of the colon lumen up to three narrowed segments, beyond which the contrast could not pass even under high pressure.

A 17-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 3 hours of hemoptysis. She had expectorated about 10 mL of bright-red blood without preceding cough, sputum production, chest tightness, or dyspnea. She had no past medical history. On arrival, her temperature was normal, heart rate 105 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, blood pressure 90/59 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 90% on 29% FiO2. Physical examination showed decreased breath sounds in the right lung without adventitious sounds.

Chest CT showed patchy, high-density opacities in both lungs, predominantly in the right lung, with indistinct borders. The initial differential diagnosis included hemoptysis of unknown origin, suspected alveolar hemorrhage in the right lower lobe, and possible pulmonary infection. A complete blood count, coagulation profile with D-dimer, rheumatologic panel, antinuclear antibodies, anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies, and pulmonary tumor markers were all within normal limits. Two days later, bronchial artery CT angiography showed no abnormalities in the right bronchial artery; the left bronchial artery was poorly visualized. The patient declined bronchial artery angiography and bronchoscopy. She was treated with piperacillin, etamsylate, and tranexamic acid, her condition improved, and she was discharged.

Six days later, she had a second episode of hemoptysis, expectorating approximately 100 mL of blood. Given the recurrent hemoptysis, a bronchial arteriovenous malformation or submucosal vascular anomaly was suspected, and she underwent bronchial artery embolization three days later.

A 3-year-old boy was evaluated for high-grade intermittent fever of 1-week duration and cough for 3 days. He had four to five nonbilious, nonprojectile vomiting episodes per day and decreased activity over the past day. His oral intake was reduced. He had a history of recurrent febrile illnesses requiring previous admissions. He was born to consanguineous parents. 

On examination, he appeared pale and dehydrated, with dysmorphic facies including frontal bossing, a depressed nasal bridge, and large ears. His temperature was 100°F, pulse and respiratory rate were normal, and oxygen saturation was adequate on room air. Chest auscultation revealed decreased air entry on the left; cardiac and abdominal examinations were otherwise unremarkable, with no organomegaly. Neurologic and spine examinations were normal.

Initial laboratory tests showed: hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL, red cells 1.79 million/mm3, platelets 2,205,000/mm3, white cells 59,890/mm3 (neutrophils 52%, lymphocytes 45%); C-reactive protein 25 mg/L, ESR 70 mm/h; LDH 17,910 μ/L; AST 348 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 395 IU/L; total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL. 

Abdominal ultrasonography suggested a small left liver lobe and absent spleen; CT confirmed asplenia. During hospitalization, he developed hypertension and a generalized seizure; MRI brain, MR venogram, and EEG were normal. Renal Doppler ultrasound and endocrine workup were unrevealing. 

Persistent fever spikes, elevated ferritin, LDH, liver enzymes, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, asplenia, and dysmorphic facies prompted further evaluation. Hemoglobin electrophoresis was normal, and testing for JAK2 mutations was negative. Bone marrow aspiration showed erythroid hyperplasia with normoblastic and megaloblastic maturation. The low bilirubin level despite ongoing hemolysis raised suspicion of a defect in the heme metabolic pathway.

A 40-year-old woman presented with one month of progressive weakness in both lower limbs and two days of bladder and anal sphincter dysfunction. On examination, she had spastic paraparesis with motor strength 3/5 in both lower limbs, impaired sensation below the T4 dermatome, brisk tendon reflexes, and bilateral Babinski signs. MRI of the thoracic spine showed two well-defined round intramedullary cystic lesions at the T4 and T5 levels, which were homogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with slight peripheral edema causing narrowing of the subarachnoid space at those levels. There were no other spinal or brain abnormalities. A diagnosis of intramedullary mass lesion was made.

An 84-year-old woman presented with a several-day history of seeing people who were not present and hearing singing voices, phenomena she recognized as unreal. She had no previous neurologic or psychiatric disorders. Her medical history included ankylosing spondylitis, hypertension, atrial fibrillation treated with rivaroxaban, chronic heart failure, coronary artery disease, right-eye glaucoma surgery, and bioprosthetic aortic-valve replacement. On examination, she appeared in good overall condition; the only neurologic finding was right-sided anisocoria. Routine blood and urine tests revealed only mild anemia. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Electroencephalography showed discontinuous slowing in both parietal regions without epileptiform discharges. Neuropsychological testing (CERAD battery, MMSE, Brief Test of Attention) demonstrated normal cognition without signs of dementia or schizophrenia, although concentration fluctuated. An ophthalmologic evaluation was noncontributory. Lumbar puncture produced xanthochromic CSF with 8 leukocytes/µl (normal <5), protein 0.754 g/l (normal <0.45), and ferritin 129 ng/ml (normal <15); CSF microbiologic and virologic studies and antineuronal-antibody testing were negative. CT angiography did not identify a source of subarachnoid hemorrhage.

A 45-day-old male infant was admitted to the intensive care unit with a 2-day history of dry cough, progressive difficulty in breathing, and reduced feeding. The mother’s pregnancy was uncomplicated except for rhinitis and a cough without fever at 32 weeks’ gestation; no SARS-CoV-2 testing was performed at that time. The infant was delivered by cesarean section at 38 weeks’ gestation, was exclusively breastfed, and had no prior hospitalizations or known allergies.

On admission, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination showed good bilateral air entry with wheezing, nasal flaring, subcostal retractions, and audible grunting; the Silverman score was 4, indicating moderate respiratory distress.

On hospital day 3, nasopharyngeal testing for respiratory syncytial virus and SARS-CoV-2 by PCR was negative, but SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies were positive. A chest radiograph revealed hilar congestion, thickened bronchial walls, and infiltrates in the right upper lobe, suggestive of bacterial pneumonia. The patient was started on amoxicillin–clavulanate.

By day 6, the infant’s respiratory distress worsened (Silverman score 8), and he required endotracheal intubation. A repeat chest radiograph showed a thin-walled, air-filled cavity in the right middle lobe complicated by a moderate right-sided pneumothorax. A chest tube was placed, and broad-spectrum antibiotics including vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and clarithromycin were initiated.

A 2½-year-old male Rottweiler was evaluated for an 8-week history of progressive ataxia. The dog had been ataxic on presentation to a shelter 8 weeks earlier, and the ataxia worsened despite general supportive care. No pedigree information was available. Prior to referral, complete blood count, serum biochemical analyses, thoracic and abdominal radiographs, and echocardiography were unremarkable. On physical examination, there was excessive wearing of all toenails. Neurological examination revealed severe, generalized ataxia with marked hypermetria and prolonged protraction of the thoracic limbs, intermittent crossing of the thoracic limbs, and a wide-based stance of all limbs. Postural reactions (wheelbarrowing, hopping, proprioceptive positioning) were delayed in all limbs, worse in the thoracic limbs. Spinal reflexes were normal, and cranial nerve function, including vision, was intact except for an inconsistent menace response. There were no signs of pain on palpation of the spine or neck. Findings localized to a cervical (C1–C5) myelopathy involving the spinocerebellar tracts. Differential diagnoses included cervical spondylomyelopathy, arachnoid diverticula, inflammatory myelitis, neoplasia, and inherited neurodegenerative disorders such as neuronal vacuolation and spinocerebellar degeneration, neuroaxonal dystrophy, and leukoencephalomyelopathy. A repeat laboratory examination showed mild eosinophilia; serum biochemistry was normal. MRI of the brain was normal. MRI of the cervical spine showed bilateral, symmetrical, well-demarcated, ovoid hyperintensities in the lateral funiculi extending from C1 to C6 on T2-weighted images; lesions were isointense on T1-weighted images with no contrast enhancement. CSF analysis (cisterna magna) revealed 0 leukocytes/μl, 4 erythrocytes/μl, normal protein, and normal lactate. Electromyography and motor nerve conduction studies were within reference ranges.

A 14-year-old Iranian girl presented with 7 months of vague, progressive left upper-quadrant abdominal pain. One month before evaluation she also noted left shoulder pain, a sense of fullness, early satiety, and shortness of breath. Initially, she awoke with acute severe left shoulder pain, followed three days later by hypochondrial pain; primary workup then revealed only microcytic anemia (hemoglobin, 10.3 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume, 63.6 fL), and she received analgesics and folic acid. After three more monthly visits with worsening pain and no additional diagnostics, she sought reevaluation.

She denied nausea, vomiting, jaundice, fever, or bowel or urinary symptoms. She lived in the countryside and reported ingestion of unwashed fruit. On examination, her abdomen was asymmetrically distended with a large, nontender mass in the left hypochondrium; vital signs were normal. There was no past medical history. A basic metabolic panel was within normal limits.

Ultrasonography showed a huge irregular-walled cystic lesion below the left hemidiaphragm measuring about 220 mm × 150 mm × 160 mm with a few septa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed splenomegaly (241 mm) and an intraparenchymal cystic lesion measuring 205 mm × 180 mm × 150 mm with thin septations and fine wall calcifications, suggestive of hydatid cyst versus epidermoid cyst. The lesion displaced the left kidney downward and shifted the stomach, duodenum, and pancreas to the right. The liver, biliary tract, right kidney, and adrenal glands appeared normal.

A 41-year-old man presented with two swellings on the left chest—one anterosuperior (15 × 12 cm) and one posteroinferior (18 × 12 cm)—that had been enlarging over two months. He reported intermittent fever and night sweats but denied cough, chest pain, or tightness. He had been diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis by sputum AFB five months earlier and was on anti-TB therapy with only slight improvement. On examination, he appeared ill and wasted but was afebrile and alert. Vital signs: blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, pulse 102 bpm, respiratory rate 28 bpm, temperature 36.5 °C, oxygen saturation 95% on room air. The chest wall swellings were warm, tender, hyperemic, and fluctuant without fistula formation. The trachea was shifted to the right. On the left hemithorax percussion was dull with absent air entry; the right side was resonant with good air entry. Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts and chemistries; HIV serology was negative. A chest radiograph showed complete homogeneous opacification of the left hemithorax with rightward tracheal and mediastinal shift and no rib abnormalities.

A 54-year-old woman was admitted with worsening dyspnea, now NYHA class II. Her blood pressure was 130/60 mm Hg, heart rate 85 beats/min, and body mass index 38 kg/m2. Physical examination revealed a holodiastolic murmur and mild basal lung crackles. She was taking a direct oral anticoagulant and furosemide. Laboratory tests showed a normal white blood cell count, mild anemia, normal renal and liver function, and a negative C-reactive protein level. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, normal atrioventricular conduction, and a narrow QRS complex.  

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed trivial mitral regurgitation with a mean gradient of 4.75 mm Hg, a severely enlarged left atrium, preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, and severe aortic regurgitation. There was moderate tricuspid regurgitation, preserved right ventricular function, elevated pulmonary pressure, and no pericardial effusion.  

Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed severe regurgitation through a tricuspid aortic valve, with the regurgitant jet originating from the commissure between the noncoronary and left coronary cusps. The valve leaflets appeared normal, but the noncoronary cusp was mildly pinched.

A 26-year-old Hispanic G2P1001 woman at 38 1/7 weeks’ gestation with obesity (BMI 41) and gestational diabetes presented with 8 hours of progressive shortness of breath. On arrival, temperature was 102.2 °F, blood pressure 119/73 mm Hg, heart rate 144 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air; fetal heart rate was 211 bpm. Cervical examination showed 1 cm dilatation, 0% effacement, intact membranes, and a posterior, long, vertex fetus. A urine toxicology screen was negative. Intravenous hydration and broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin/tazobactam and vancomycin) were initiated for presumed sepsis.  

Because of a nonreactive fetal tracing with tachycardia and minimal variability (category 2), a stat primary low transverse cesarean delivery was performed under general anesthesia with rapid-sequence intubation. Induction agents included propofol 200 mg and succinylcholine 100 mg; the endotracheal tube was placed atraumatically, and bilateral breath sounds and end-tidal CO₂ confirmed placement. A healthy infant was delivered (Apgars 9 and 9) with meconium-stained fluid.  

Immediately after delivery, before placental extraction, the patient’s heart rate remained 140 bpm, but oxygen saturation dropped to 72%, blood pressure fell to 72/48 mm Hg, and end-tidal CO₂ fell from 32 to 0 mm Hg. Anesthesia equipment was checked, and phenylephrine boluses (total 1800 µg) were administered without sustained effect. The obstetrics team found no hysterotomy extensions, lacerations, or uncontrolled bleeding. Within one minute of symptom onset, the anesthesia team administered atropine 0.2 mg, ondansetron 8 mg, and ketorolac 15 mg intravenously. Over the next 2–3 minutes, the patient’s oxygen saturation rose to 97%, blood pressure to 138/68 mm Hg, and end-tidal CO₂ to 32 mm Hg, although tachycardia persisted at 140 bpm. She received additional intravenous fluids, uterotonics, and blood products, had an estimated blood loss of 2000 ml, and was transported intubated to the ICU for further monitoring.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 1.5-year history of abdominal pain and three loose, watery stools daily. He had gastroesophageal reflux disease and hereditary hemochromatosis (grade 3 iron overload, mild portal fibrosis, C282Y homozygosity). He denied rectal bleeding, fever, or weight loss. Vital signs were normal, and physical examination was unremarkable. 
 
Laboratory evaluation showed negative ova and parasites, bacterial culture, fecal leukocytes, and Clostridium difficile NAAT. Histoplasma antigen, anti-transglutaminase, and anti-endomysial antibodies were negative. Rapid plasma reagin and Tropheryma whipplei testing were also negative. 
 
Colonoscopy revealed erythematous mucosa in the transverse colon and rectum and congestion in the terminal ileum. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed diffuse gastric erythema with erosions and duodenitis. Biopsies from the stomach, duodenum, terminal ileum, colon, and rectum all demonstrated non-caseating microgranulomas; acid-fast bacilli and fungal stains were negative, and no Helicobacter pylori organisms were identified. 
 
CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed hepatosplenomegaly; a prior liver biopsy showed no granulomas. Chest CT was unremarkable. Angiotensin-converting enzyme level was elevated at 77 U/L.

A 69-year-old woman presented with a 9-year history of low back pain that had progressed over the past 2 years and radiated to the left hip and leg. There was no weakness, sensory loss, or bowel or bladder dysfunction. Her medical and surgical histories were unremarkable. Neurological examination revealed normal strength, sensation, deep tendon reflexes, and plantar responses in the lower extremities.

Conventional spinal MRI showed a well-defined intradural extramedullary serpiginous tubular lesion from T12 to L3 displacing the cauda equina. The lesion was isointense to the spinal cord on T1-weighted images, exhibited peripheral hypointensity with central hyperintensity on T2-weighted images (the “doughnut” sign), and enhanced intensely and homogeneously on delayed post-contrast T1-weighted images. There was no spinal cord edema or perimedullary flow voids.

At 6-month follow-up, repeat conventional sequences showed a stable lesion. First-pass arterial-phase MR angiography demonstrated no arterial shunting. Blood-pool phase MR angiography revealed avid enhancement of the lesion with areas of relatively reduced central enhancement. Conventional digital subtraction angiography (lumbar aortogram, selective angiograms of thoracic intercostal and lumbar arteries, and bilateral internal iliac angiograms) showed normal arterial and venous phases without evidence of an arteriovenous shunt.

A 49-year-old Jamaican woman with no significant past medical history presented with 4 weeks of progressive dyspnea. On examination, she had marked jugular venous distension, bilateral basal crackles, a distended tender abdomen with positive fluid shift and hepatojugular reflux, and bilateral 2+ lower-leg pitting edema. Laboratory studies showed anemia, elevated troponin level, markedly increased N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide, elevated transaminases, mildly elevated TSH, and increased C-reactive protein. An ECG showed atrial flutter with a ventricular rate of 126 beats/min. A chest radiograph demonstrated a markedly enlarged cardiac silhouette with a water-bottle appearance. Transthoracic echocardiography on hospital day 1 revealed a severely dilated right ventricle, severe tricuspid regurgitation, moderate mitral regurgitation without structural abnormalities, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30–40%, and a large pericardial effusion. CT of the chest with a pulmonary-artery protocol showed no evidence of pulmonary embolism. The clinical diagnosis was dilated cardiomyopathy with right-sided heart failure, and treatment with a beta-blocker and diuretics led to clinical improvement. An etiologic workup revealed negative toxicology and infectious disease markers; a viral panel returned unremarkable; and a search for underlying malignancy was negative. Left-heart catheterization showed normal coronary arteries. Right-heart catheterization demonstrated severe mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, moderate pulmonary regurgitation, and only mildly increased pulmonary artery pressure, supporting decompensated heart failure secondary to dilated cardiomyopathy.

A 16-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with dizziness, syncope, weakness, and fatigue. He was febrile (37.7 °C), with a blood pressure of 100/60 mm Hg, a pulse rate of 20 bpm, and an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. He was drowsy but had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15, and systemic examination was unremarkable. 

An urgent ECG showed complete atrioventricular dissociation with ST-segment depressions in leads I, II, and aVL. He received 1 mg of IV atropine and an infusion of normal saline without improvement. A temporary transvenous pacemaker was placed, achieving a paced rhythm at 75 bpm with a left bundle–branch–block morphology.

Further history revealed that 6 days earlier he had a high-grade fever, severe myalgias, and an episode of epistaxis; dengue serology at that time was positive, and he was managed as an outpatient with antipyretics, antibiotics, and fluids. 

On admission, laboratory studies showed:
– Platelets 46 × 10^3/µL  
– Sodium 128 mmol/L; potassium 4.0 mmol/L  
– Troponin I 21 ng/mL; CK-MB 73 U/L  
– ESR 38 mm/h; CRP 5.1 mg/dL; LDH 580 IU/L
