– Thyroid‐stimulating hormone, total T3, and total T4 within normal limits  

Dengue PCR confirmed DENV-2 serotype. Blood cultures and tests for malaria, typhoid, influenza, COVID-19, and diphtheria were negative. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a normal ejection fraction, normal systolic function, and no structural cardiac abnormalities.

A 35-year-old amateur dancer presented with a 5-year history of gradual, progressive, painless restriction of movement of her right hip. She had no history of surgery, bleeding disorder, or systemic illness. On examination, there was fullness in the right femoral triangle without a discrete palpable mass, no distal neurovascular deficit, and significant limitation of hip flexion and internal rotation; there was no muscle wasting. Plain radiographs of the pelvis demonstrated bilateral ossified masses lying anterior to the hip joints, extending from the anterior superior margin of the acetabulum to the lesser trochanter. A three-dimensional CT scan confirmed well-defined bilateral ossified masses measuring approximately 10 cm on the right and 5 cm on the left. A three-phase bone scintigraphy was obtained to assess the maturity of the lesions.

A 61-year-old man with a history of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (35%), pulmonary sarcoid, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, prior cerebrovascular accident, and active crack-cocaine use presented with 3 days of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea and vomiting. He denied chest pain, cough, dyspnea, fever, or chills. He was a former 8-pack-year smoker with remote alcohol use. He reported regular intranasal crack-cocaine use, most recently 3 days before presentation. His medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, and metoprolol tartrate; he denied any new medications or recent steroid use.

Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, he had tenderness to palpation in the epigastrium, normal breath sounds, and no peripheral edema. Laboratory testing revealed lipase 2300 IU/dL (reference 11–82), total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, AST 30 IU/L, ALT 16 IU/L, white blood cell count 5700 cells/mL, triglycerides 90 mg/dL, calcium 9.3 mg/dL, and IgG4 18 mg/dL (reference 1–123). A urine toxicology screen was positive for cocaine only. Electrocardiography showed more pronounced T-wave inversions in the inferolateral leads compared with a prior study. Chest radiography demonstrated lung base scarring and mild central pulmonary vascular congestion.

Abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneously hypoechoic pancreas consistent with pancreatitis, a normal-sized common bile duct, and a distended gallbladder without gallstones. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed edematous enlargement of the pancreas, peripancreatic fat stranding and free fluid, and subcentimeter peripancreatic lymphadenopathy, consistent with acute pancreatitis.

A 20-year-old healthy woman was brought to the emergency department after colliding with a snowgun while skiing. She sustained a closed right femoral shaft fracture and underwent reaming of the femoral canal followed by intramedullary nailing under general anesthesia; the procedure lasted 32 minutes without intraoperative complications. Fourteen hours after surgery, she developed sudden bilateral visual impairment: she could no longer read text messages on her phone and felt dizzy and weak. Blood pressure was 80/40 mmHg, rising to 100/50 mmHg after infusion of 250 mL of HES solution and 500 mL of Ringer’s lactate; visual symptoms persisted. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 18.3 × 10^3/µL (normal 4.3–10.0) and LDH 245 U/L (normal 120–240). A neurologic examination and brain MRI were both normal. On ophthalmologic assessment, uncorrected and best‐corrected visual acuities were 0.25 decimal in each eye. Pupils were equal, round, reactive, and there was no relative afferent pupillary defect. Slit‐lamp examination of the anterior segment was unremarkable. Funduscopy revealed multiple cotton‐wool spots and polygonal areas of whitening in the posterior pole of both eyes, along with a small intraretinal hemorrhage in the periphery. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated hyperintense lesions within the retinal nerve fiber layer consistent with microinfarctions.

A 47-year-old white woman presented with a 7-year history of recurrent episodes of severe vulvar swelling associated with itching, prominent hyperemia, white vaginal discharge, low-grade fever (up to 38.5°C), heaviness in the genital area, and dyspareunia. Each flare began with itching, followed within hours by edema and erythema of the vulva and perianal region, and then fever. Initially flares recurred every 6 months but later shortened to 2–3 months despite local and systemic antibiotics and glucocorticoids. Between flares she noted persistent mild hypertrophy and induration of the labia majora and minora. Past gynecologic history included recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, bacterial vaginosis, uterine leiomyomas, and endometrial polyp.

On examination, there was bilateral asymmetric enlargement and indurative edema of the labia majora (right > left) with fissures exuding clear fluid, crusted in places. The labia minora were dense, hypertrophic, protruding beyond the majora, with papilliform vegetations. In the perianal area there were cone-shaped vegetations resembling condylomata. Bimanual and pelvic examinations were otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normal total IgE, elevated antistreptolysin O (562 IU/mL; reference <200), C-reactive protein 2.4 mg/L (reference <5 mg/L), positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA titer 4.0 ++, SS-A positive), and slightly elevated anti–Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA 21.31 rel μ/mL; reference <20 rel μ/mL). Tests for Treponema pallidum, HIV, hepatitis B and C viruses, and protozoan infections were negative. Annual cervical and vaginal swabs for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma, Ureaplasma, Trichomonas vaginalis, Gardnerella vaginalis, Candida albicans, HPV, HSV, and CMV by microscopy, culture, and PCR were consistently negative. Molecular assays for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Candida spp., and Actinomyces DNA from the lesion were negative.

Colonoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed no significant structural or endoscopic pathology. Abdominal and pelvic CT scans showed no fistulas, abscesses, or masses.

A 68-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and right shoulder, with associated nausea but no vomiting or antecedent trauma. Her medical history included poorly controlled hypertension on four antihypertensive agents and daily aspirin; she had a remote total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral oophorectomy. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable without fever; the abdomen was soft with right upper-quadrant tenderness and no palpable mass.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 10.3 × 10^9/L, normal lipase, lactate, liver and renal function tests, and a coagulation profile within normal limits, but a hemoglobin decrease from 144 g/L five months earlier to 103 g/L. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a normal gallbladder and pancreas, chronic hepatic hemangiomas, and a small amount of nonspecific perinephric and subhepatic fluid.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated extensive edema and induration surrounding the duodenum with complex hyperdense fluid tracking into the paracolic gutters and pelvis; these changes raised concern for paraduodenal hemorrhage from a ruptured duodenal ulcer or hemoperitoneum but were not typical of perforation or vessel erosion, and an infiltrating fibrotic or lymphoproliferative mass was considered unlikely to account for the fluid. MRI of the abdomen confirmed an acute periduodenal collection surrounding the second and third portions of the duodenum, characterized by T2-hypointense, T1 iso–hyperintense material without enhancement, in keeping with hemorrhage, and showed no evidence of a bowel wall lesion or vascular abnormality.

A 29-year-old Tunisian construction laborer with no prior medical or surgical history presented with a 2-week history of progressively worsening left flank pain and urticarial skin lesions. He denied trauma, nausea, or vomiting. On examination, he was afebrile, and there was localized tenderness in the left flank without palpable mass. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, leukocyte count 13 430/mm3 with eosinophils 640/mm3, and C-reactive protein 140 mg/L. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large cystic lesion in the left iliac fossa. Contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated a 12 × 7 × 21 cm multiseptated cystic mass in the retroperitoneal space adjacent to the psoas muscle, with a detached membrane and evidence of intraperitoneal rupture. There were no other cystic lesions in the liver, lungs, or elsewhere.

An 80-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of progressive left thigh pain without trauma. She denied anorexia, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. She had undergone total left hip arthroplasty 15 years earlier, after which she noted an asymptomatic anterolateral thigh swelling. On examination, she was afebrile. There was edema and flushing of the anterolateral left thigh and lateral hip without fistula or wound. The area was warm and tender; range of motion of the hip was normal. Laboratory tests showed a normal white-cell count and a C-reactive protein level of 13.67 mg/dL. A pelvic radiograph showed soft-tissue shadowing in the proximal left femur region and a well-positioned hip prosthesis without osteolysis or component loosening.

A 64-year-old right-handed neurosurgeon with hypertension and hyperlipidemia received his second dose of the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine in his left deltoid without significant immediate side effects other than transient malaise. Two weeks later, he developed intense, unremitting left shoulder girdle pain with muscle tenderness that did not improve with stretching, heat, or ibuprofen. One week after onset of pain, he noted decreased strength and dexterity in his left hand, including difficulty opening bottle caps and manipulating small instruments. Within days, he developed paresthesia and hypoesthesia in the left fourth and fifth digits and the ulnar aspect of the forearm. 

On neurologic examination, strength was 4+/5 in the left finger extensors—particularly digits four and five—and in the thenar eminence. Deep-tendon reflexes were normal. Sensation to light touch was impaired distally in the left fourth and fifth digits and to a lesser extent in the third digit. Brachial plexitis was suspected, and he was started on a prednisone taper.

Three weeks after symptom onset, electrodiagnostic testing was performed. The right median and radial sensory nerve action potentials had low amplitude but were attributed to prior trauma. On the left, median sensory and motor studies were normal. The left ulnar sensory nerve action potential and ulnar–abductor digiti minimi compound motor action potential had borderline low amplitude. The left median and ulnar F waves were unremarkable. Needle EMG showed a reduced recruitment pattern in the left extensor indicis and left flexor digitorum profundus to digit IV, with increased spontaneous activity in the left first dorsal interosseus. “These findings were felt to reflect a mild, patchy, and acute-to-subacute lower trunk brachial plexopathy.”

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left brachial plexus demonstrated “increased short-TI inversion recovery (STIR) signal and increased T2-weighted signal, with mild T1 postcontrast enhancement of the medial left scalene muscles along the inferior brachial plexus consistent with inflammatory changes and intramuscular edema.”

A 36-year-old woman presented with occasional dull pain below the xiphoid. Her medical history was notable for resection of a symptomatic ovarian teratoma 10 years earlier. She had no family history of thyroid or hepatic disease. Physical examination was unremarkable. Liver function tests and serum tumor markers were within normal limits.

Abdominal CT revealed:
• A lobulated 1.2 × 2.9 × 2.8 cm lesion in the hemidiaphragm (60–70 HU on noncontrast imaging) with heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast images.  
• A 4.2 × 3.9 × 3.9 cm solid lesion in segment VI of the liver (60–70 HU on noncontrast imaging) showing heterogeneous enhancement post-contrast.

MRI demonstrated that the lesions were slightly low signal on T1-weighted imaging, equal signal on T2-weighted imaging, and showed a diffusion-weighted signal increase (b = 800) without restricted diffusion. There was no uptake of hepatobiliary-specific contrast on delayed imaging.

Based on these examinations, a working diagnosis of a benign hepatic adenoma with hemorrhage was made.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a chief complaint of progressively enlarged gums, early loss of a lower first molar, and pus discharge from multiple oral sites. She reported that gingival enlargement and pus discharge began at age 15 following mobility of her teeth. She had left school at age 17 due to difficulty keeping up academically and was described as slightly sluggish, with a notable lack of desire to eat because of mobile teeth and gum pain. 

On general examination, she appeared pale and slightly younger than her stated age. Psychiatric assessment using the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale diagnosed borderline depression, for which only cognitive behavioral therapy was recommended. Full-body radiographs, including right hand–wrist and multiple joint films, were normal.

Laboratory evaluation revealed a reduced hemoglobin level. Peripheral smear showed mild anisocytosis, normocytes, microcytes, pencil cells, hypochromia, occasional polychromatic macrocytes, and neutrophilia, consistent with dimorphic anemia. 

Oral examination demonstrated diffuse gingival enlargement with superimposed inflammation and multiple periodontal abscesses around the upper canines and lower molars. Probing depths were increased, and moderate-to-severe clinical attachment loss with vertical bone defects was noted at various sites. The amount of microbial deposits appeared inconsistent with the severity of tissue destruction. Pathological mesial migration of the mandibular left second molar and several carious teeth were also observed. An orthopantomogram confirmed extensive bone loss at sites beyond the first molars and incisors. Microbiological testing revealed elevated proportions of Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, with normal antibody titers.

A 28-year-old man with no chronic illnesses presented with 3 days of bilateral testicular and inguinal pain and swelling. One month earlier, he had left testicular pain and left inguinal swelling that was diagnosed elsewhere as an inguinal hernia without imaging; manual reduction failed and the pain partially resolved over several days, but the swelling persisted. Recently, he developed right testicular pain that worsened with movement and improved with ice packs. He denied fever, urinary symptoms, urethral discharge, or risky sexual contact. He is a heavy smoker, married, and has two children.

On examination, he was afebrile and vitals were normal. His abdomen was soft with mild inguinal and suprapubic tenderness; bilateral inguinal swellings were tender with a positive cough impulse and no peritonitis. The scrotum appeared small; both testes were retracted to the scrotal neck. The left testis was mildly enlarged with a small firm nontender intratesticular mass; the right testis was normal. The vas deferens were engorged and mildly tender.

Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 14.1×10^3/µL with otherwise normal hemoglobin, lactic acid, and creatinine; urine culture showed no growth. 

Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated a thickened and enlarged right spermatic cord with hyperemia suggestive of an infectious or inflammatory process. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed bilateral enlargement and congestion of the spermatic cords without any anterior abdominal wall defects and with adjacent fat stranding.

A 29‐year‐old man with HIV, end‐stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and hypertension presented with a 2‐day history of generalized, nonthrobbing headache and blurred vision. He reported compliance with antiretroviral and antihypertensive medications and denied tobacco, alcohol, or drug use. On examination, he was afebrile, alert, and oriented; blood pressure was 245/141 mm Hg; visual acuity was 20/80 in both eyes without scotomas or field deficits; cranial nerves II–XII were intact; muscle strength and sensation were normal; reflexes were 2+; and there were no cerebellar findings. CBC was within normal limits. His CD4 count was 325 cells/mm3 and HIV‐1 RNA was 5100 copies/mL. Noncontrast CT of the head was negative. Lumbar puncture showed normal opening pressure and clear cerebrospinal fluid with a white cell count of 2 cells/μL and protein of 39 mg/dL; CSF studies (Indian Ink, cocci, cryptococcus, HSV, VDRL) were all negative. Urine toxicology screening was negative.

A 14-year-old girl presented with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. She was initially treated for presumed viral gastroenteritis but found to have hyperglycemia (500 mg/dL) and ketonuria. On transfer, she was lethargic and dehydrated (GCS 14), tachycardic (124/min), tachypneic (40/min), and hypothermic (35°C). Venous blood gas showed metabolic acidosis (pH 6.92, HCO3 5.6 mmol/L). Serum chemistry: glucose 569 mg/dL, corrected sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, calcium 8.5 mg/dL, phosphate 2.1 mg/dL, BUN 25.9 mg/dL, creatinine 0.57 mg/dL. Endocrine studies confirmed type 1 diabetes (low C-peptide, positive GAD antibody). She received 0.45% saline and insulin infusion per DKA protocol. 

Four hours after admission, she had a generalized tonic seizure followed by bradycardia and cardiopulmonary arrest; spontaneous circulation returned after 6 minutes of CPR. Post-resuscitation labs showed pH 7.05, HCO3 6.7 mmol/L, glucose 517 mg/dL, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, phosphate 1.2 mg/dL. A head CT showed no edema. She received initial phosphate supplementation. In the intensive care unit, she remained drowsy. 

Sixteen hours after starting therapy, she became stuporous (GCS 9) with shallow, weak respiration and was intubated. Arterial blood gas revealed respiratory acidosis (pH 6.80, PCO2 92.9 mmHg) and severe hypophosphatemia (phosphate 0.4 mg/dL).

A 17-year-old woman presented with progressive exertional dyspnea, worsening fatigue, and bilateral pedal edema over several months. She denied chest pain or syncope. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable (blood pressure 136/75 mm Hg), in atrial fibrillation with an average ventricular rate of 68 bpm, and had elevated jugular venous pressure. Auscultation revealed a variably split first heart sound and normal inspiratory splitting of S2; there were no murmurs. Laboratory evaluation, including a thrombophilia panel, was unremarkable. Lower-limb venous Doppler ultrasonography showed no deep vein thrombosis. A 12-lead electrocardiogram confirmed atrial fibrillation at a rate of 81 bpm. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 0.70) with right atrial enlargement. Transthoracic echocardiography disclosed a massively dilated right atrium, an “atrialized” right ventricle with small functional chamber, apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet by 2.3 cm, an elongated anterior leaflet with restricted motion, slow transvalvular flow (approximately 0.5–1 cm/s), dense spontaneous echo contrast, and a large free-floating thrombus measuring 5.2 × 3.5 cm in the right atrium. Left ventricular systolic function was preserved. Agitated-saline contrast imaging revealed an intact interatrial septum without evidence of a patent foramen ovale. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed these findings and demonstrated a patent pulmonary valve and pulmonary artery.

A 43-year-old Hispanic man from Peru with remote travel in the Peruvian and Brazilian jungles two decades prior was diagnosed with Bell’s palsy three weeks earlier and started on prednisone 50 mg twice daily without follow-up. He presented with a three-week history of diarrhea, a 10-kg weight loss, intermittent fevers, and three days of hematochezia. On examination he was pale and tachycardic, had mild abdominal tenderness, and blood on rectal examination; the remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 16 000 cells/mm^3 (82% neutrophils, 2% eosinophils, 7% bands), hemoglobin 8 g/dL, and platelets 700 000/mm^3. He was presumed to have diverticulitis and was started on intravenous ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. One week after admission, he became drowsy with bradylalia and bradypsychia, developed nuchal rigidity with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, fever, right lower‐lobe crackles, abdominal distension, and constipation. A lumbar puncture yielded cloudy fluid with a protein of 179 mg/dL, glucose of 5 mg/dL, 2070 leukocytes/mm^3 (92% neutrophils), and Gram‐negative rods on Gram stain. Repeat blood count showed 25 000 leukocytes/mm^3 (84% neutrophils, 0% eosinophils, 7% bands). A CT scan of the abdomen revealed a dilated ascending colon.

An 86-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of intermittent right lower-quadrant abdominal swelling, occasional erythema, and mild discomfort. He reported infrequent nonbloody, nonbilious emesis followed by loose stools, poor appetite with early satiety, and a 16-pound weight loss. He denied fevers, night sweats, or recent travel. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, and a laparoscopic cholecystectomy with endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography for acute cholecystitis and choledocholithiasis over 15 years earlier. 

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable. There was a 9×7-cm slightly fluctuant mass on the right lateral abdominal wall with overlying erythema but no warmth or drainage; the rest of the abdomen was soft and nondistended. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (15.2 k/µL) with 80% neutrophils, mild normocytic anemia, pseudohyponatremia, and an elevated lactate that normalized with fluids. Blood cultures were drawn.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large fluid collection in the right upper quadrant lateral to the liver with an irregular, thickened wall measuring 12×6×9 cm, and a second thick-walled, loculated fluid collection measuring 6×4 cm in the right paracolic gutter containing a small focal calcification, without gas. Right upper-quadrant ultrasound demonstrated a 10.6×7×16 cm cystic mass with echogenic debris adjacent to the anterior segment of the right hepatic lobe. 

An ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded 300 mL of purulent fluid. Initial cultures were negative. Two weeks later, symptoms recurred and a drainage catheter was placed; cultures grew scant Klebsiella pneumoniae, and oral ciprofloxacin was initiated. One month later, CT showed resolution and the catheter was removed. Ten days after removal, the abscess recurred; a new catheter was placed, and ciprofloxacin was resumed. 

Magnetic resonance imaging two weeks later showed marked improvement of the perihepatic abscess, residual peritoneal thickening with muscular enhancement, and a punctate T2 hyperintense focus in the abdominal wall musculature, suggestive of calcification.

An 18-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 1.5×1.2 cm oval nodule on her right lower eyelid that she first noticed 2 months earlier. The lesion had been diagnosed as an abscess by ophthalmology, and under general anesthesia it was removed via lateral canthotomy and a lateral conjunctival incision without biopsy; she then received a course of antibiotics. Despite treatment, the periorbital mass enlarged and the overlying skin became erythematous and tender. She also developed right cervical lymphadenopathy. On examination, visual acuity was normal, and there was no proptosis, diplopia, or ophthalmoplegia. Her systemic examination was otherwise unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits showed chronic inflammatory changes and a small abscess cavity on the lower eyelid, without involvement of the orbital bones.

A 53-year-old woman was admitted with a 6-month history of 6–10 daily episodes of bulky, watery, nonbloody diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and progressive asthenia, accompanied by a 20% involuntary weight loss. She denied abdominal pain, fever, recent travel, sick contacts, dietary changes, or recent medication changes. Her only medication was olmesartan, 40 mg daily, for hypertension, which she had taken for six years. Previous outpatient treatments—including probiotics, an opioid agonist, a gluten- and lactose-free diet, and a trial of oral antibiotics—had failed to improve her symptoms. 

On examination, she appeared pale with muscle wasting. Vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed mild microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 11 g/dL), leukopenia (3.8 × 10^9/L), thrombocytopenia (130 × 10^9/L), and hypokalemia (2.8 mmol/L). Tests for inflammatory markers, liver and kidney function, total protein, albumin, immunoglobulins, vitamin B12, folate, thyroid-stimulating hormone, anti–tissue transglutaminase antibodies, HIV, and cytomegalovirus were all within normal limits or negative. Stool cultures and PCR for Clostridium difficile toxins were negative.

Abdominopelvic CT scan showed no pancreatic abnormalities or lesions suggestive of malignancy. Colonoscopy with terminal ileoscopy and random biopsies revealed normal mucosa without evidence of inflammatory bowel disease or microscopic colitis. Upper endoscopy demonstrated attenuation of duodenal folds. Duodenal biopsies showed partial villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytosis and no granulomas, microorganisms, or malignancy.

A 41-year-old man from eastern Sudan presented with a 7-year history of a skin lesion on the ventral aspect of his left foot. It began as a small asymptomatic nodule that gradually enlarged, became painful and pruritic, and developed a sinus discharging foul-smelling pus. He denied fever, cough, or prior tuberculosis. On examination he appeared well, afebrile, and without pallor, jaundice, or cyanosis; vital signs and systemic examination were normal. Local inspection revealed a single sinus tract on the plantar midfoot with purulent discharge; the contralateral foot and the rest of the skin were unremarkable. A chest radiograph was normal. A swab of the discharge grew Staphylococcus aureus. Foot radiographs showed no bone involvement. Tests for HIV and hepatitis B and C were negative. Liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. Complete blood count revealed leukocytosis (12.0 × 10^3/µL), hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, and platelets 397 × 10^3/µL. The lesion was surgically excised under the assumption of mycetoma, and tissue was sent for histopathologic analysis.

A 14-year-old previously healthy boy presented with a 2-hour history of acute posterior neck pain that began while singing karaoke. The pain radiated to his right shoulder and did not improve. He then developed progressive right-sided weakness and was unable to stand without support. He denied trauma, anticoagulant use, bleeding disorders, or other systemic symptoms.  
On arrival he was alert and hemodynamically stable. Pain in the posterior neck was 7/10 on the visual analog scale. Neurological examination showed right hemiparesis with muscle strength of 3/5 in the right extremities and normal strength on the left, without sensory deficits or bladder-bowel dysfunction.  
Laboratory studies, including a coagulation profile, were within normal limits. Urgent brain and spine MRI were obtained. On brain MRI there was no evidence of infarction, hematoma, or dissection. On cervical spine MRI there was a right posterolateral epidural lesion extending from C4 to C7 that was isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, causing anterior displacement of the spinal cord to the left.

A 43-year-old woman woke with left-sided neck discomfort 10 days before presentation. The pain radiated to the trapezius and scapular region and worsened with neck movement. Four days after the pain began, she noted difficulty abducting her left arm. She denied sensory changes, headache, or other neurologic symptoms. She recalled mild cervical discomfort when rotating her head while reversing her car about 4 days before the onset of weakness.

On examination, strength was 4/5 in the left deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and biceps muscles, with 4+/5 strength in forearm pronation and supination. The left biceps reflex was absent, and the left brachioradialis reflex was reduced. Sensation in the left upper limb was intact, and cranial nerve examination was normal. The remainder of the neurologic examination was unremarkable.

Cervical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and MR angiography (MRA) were performed to evaluate the cause of her symptoms.

An 11-year-old boy with known homozygous sickle cell disease presented with a 1-week history of bilateral eyelid swelling and progressive proptosis, more marked on the left, and a reduction in vision. He also had fever and severe headache but no trauma, neck pain, convulsions, or loss of consciousness. He reported bilateral lower limb pain without joint swelling. He was on daily folic acid and monthly sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine and had received two units of whole blood at a peripheral hospital prior to transfer.

On examination, he appeared ill, with mild pallor and icterus. Vital signs: temperature 38.0°C, pulse 100/min, respiratory rate 32/min, blood pressure 112/66 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The left eye was protruding and hyperemic with purulent discharge, tearing, and eyelid edema; there were no elicitable pupillary reflexes. The right eye was mildly swollen and hyperemic without discharge; the pupil was small and reacted poorly to light. There was a firm tender 2×3 cm swelling over the right parietal scalp. The spleen was palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Both lower legs were tender below the knees without swelling.

A pretransfusion CBC showed WBC 18.9×10^9/L, hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, MCV 75 fL, MCHC 30.0 g/dL, RDW 18.5%, and platelets 194×10^3/µL. Electrolytes revealed Na+ 131.3 mmol/L, K+ 4.12 mmol/L, Cl– 100.9 mmol/L; creatinine and urea were normal. Malaria smear was negative.

Contrast-enhanced axial CT of the head demonstrated multiple extra‐axial hypodense biconvex collections in the right frontal (2.13×3.6 cm) and left temporal regions suggestive of epidural hematomas. Similar hypodense lesions were seen in the extra‐conical superolateral aspects of both orbits, more pronounced on the left, with left proptosis; the adjacent bones appeared normal. The sinuses were opacified in the left frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid regions. There were no other intracranial space‐occupying lesions.

Ophthalmologic evaluation of the left eye revealed proptosis, chemosis, hyperemia, and a mild punctate epithelial defect; the lens was normal, the anterior chamber was deep and quiet, visual acuity was 6/60, and intraocular pressure was 11 mmHg. The right eye was otherwise normal, with visual acuity 6/24 and intraocular pressure 16 mmHg.

A 31-year-old man presented with a 6-day history of systemic symptoms and skin lesions. He had returned from vacation in Miami, Florida, when he developed fatigue and fever. Two days after symptom onset, he noticed blisters covering his body and was seen at an urgent care clinic, where lesion swabs were sent for PCR testing. He received no isolation instructions and continued normal activities, including social events. Four days later, he sought dermatologic evaluation. 

The patient had no significant past medical history and identified as gay. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Skin findings included approximately 20 pink, umbilicated papules 2 to 8 mm in diameter—all in the same stage of development with surrounding erythema—distributed on the face, trunk, arms, and legs. In addition, there were five to six 5–6 mm pink, deep-seated vesicles with erosions on the palms and soles. Bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy was present. There were no lesions in the oral or genital mucosa.

A 15-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of long-standing developmental delay and neurological impairment. He was born at term after an unremarkable pregnancy and perinatal period. At 3 months of age, bilateral congenital cataracts were identified, and he underwent lens extraction at 4 months of age. Early in infancy he developed central hypotonia and global psychomotor delay: he gained head control at 6 months, sat unsupported at 12 months, and never achieved independent walking, using a wheelchair for transfers. Language was delayed but social communication appeared preserved.

On examination at age 15 years, he had moderate intellectual disability and severe thoracolumbar scoliosis. There were no dysmorphic features. Ocular findings included divergent strabismus and multidirectional nystagmus. He had axial and lower‐limb hypotonia, normal upper‐extremity reflexes, absent lower‐extremity reflexes, leg wasting, and active movements against gravity in all four limbs. No cerebellar signs were observed.

Brain MRI showed diffuse supratentorial white-matter hyperintensity on T2-weighted images and corresponding hypo- to isointensity on T1-weighted images, with enlargement of the ventricles and subarachnoid spaces and thinning of the corpus callosum; the cerebellum appeared spared. Spinal MRI was normal. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies demonstrated a chronic sensorimotor demyelinating polyneuropathy with secondary axonal loss. Electroencephalogram and cardiac evaluation were normal.

A 26-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of right ankle contracture, calf muscle pain, and gait disturbance. His initial symptom was myalgia in the right calf, which worsened after acupuncture 4 weeks before presentation. He had no history of trauma, systemic disease, or family illness. On examination, right ankle dorsiflexion was limited to –5°, with no muscle weakness or sensory deficits in either leg. Calf circumferences were symmetric, and there were no palpable masses, skin changes, or differences in pedal pulses. Laboratory evaluation showed a C-reactive protein level of 7.05 pg/mL (normal, 0.00–3.00), with normal leukocyte count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, muscle enzymes, and viral markers. Plain radiographs of the tibia and fibula were unremarkable. A three-phase bone scan revealed increased uptake in the right calf. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated diffuse high signal intensity on T2-weighted images in the right gastrocnemius, flexor digitorum longus, and tibialis anterior muscles, and T1-weighted images showed soft-tissue edema suggestive of ischemia or myositis. Computed tomography angiography of the lower extremities showed no vascular abnormalities. Nerve conduction studies were normal, and needle electromyography of the affected muscles revealed spontaneous activity and small-amplitude motor unit potentials.

A 50-year-old woman with a 17-year episodic psychiatric history presented with an 8-month acute-onset illness. Initially, over 10–14 days, she had increased talkativeness, decreased need for sleep, increased vigor in household tasks, unplanned market shopping, anger outbursts, and abusive behavior. She was started on lithium 600 mg/day, quetiapine up to 200 mg/day, and lorazepam 2 mg/day. Within days, her speech output markedly decreased; she stared for prolonged periods and withdrew from chores. Over 1 month, medications were increased to lithium 900 mg/day and quetiapine 350 mg/day, but she deteriorated with reduced appetite, declining self-care, urinary incontinence, and talk of deceased relatives. She was admitted for further management.

On admission, she had mild pallor, a BMI of 19 kg/m2, and low hemoglobin; thyroid, renal, liver functions, folic acid, and vitamin B12 were normal. In the first 6 weeks, she showed mutism, reduced activity, intermittent crying spells, night-time wakefulness, disorientation to time/place/person, restricted affect, and no clear psychotic symptoms. She misidentified family members, drank water from a toilet pot, and exhibited disinhibited behavior. Her sleep–wake cycle was reversed. Mini–Mental State Examination scores were 9–11 repeatedly. Consultations were obtained from medicine, gynecology, and neurology. Serum electrolytes, creatine phosphokinase, brain MRI, and EEG were normal. An ultrasound revealed an incidental benign ovarian mass.

A 14‐year‐old Caucasian male presented for a routine orthodontic assessment. On panoramic radiography, there was a well‐defined, homogeneous radiopaque spherical mass measuring 1.5 × 1 cm at the apex of the right maxillary permanent canine. A lateral cephalometric radiograph localized the lesion superior to the canine fossa and anterior to the anterior wall of the maxillary sinus. Review of an orthopantomogram taken at age 10 showed no such lesion. The patient reported a history of facial acne vulgaris since age 12, successfully treated by dermatology. On extraoral examination the overlying skin was intact and acne‐free; the mass was palpable and mobile but not visible. Facial profile and contour were normal. Orthodontic evaluation revealed a Class III incisor relationship on a Class III skeletal base with maxillary crowding. No other abnormalities were noted.

A 73-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus and autoimmune hemolytic anemia, for which he had been on oral corticosteroids for one year, presented with a one-month history of memory impairment and gait disturbance. Examination revealed a right inferior quadrantanopia and grade 4/5 strength in the right upper and lower limbs. Brain MRI with contrast demonstrated multiple large, predominantly cystic lesions in the left parieto-occipital region, with significant surrounding edema and local mass effect. The cyst contents showed restricted diffusion, and most lesions enhanced with smooth rings after contrast administration. Some peripheral lesions were associated with dural thickening and enhancement. Susceptibility-weighted imaging revealed small foci of low signal consistent with hemorrhage. A diagnosis of a multiloculated brain abscess was made, and a high-grade glioma was included in the differential diagnosis.

A 28-year-old Italian woman was referred for decreased visual acuity in the left eye of 4 months’ duration. Four to five months before presentation, she had developed persistent low-grade fever (37.5 °C) for approximately 1 month, with intermittent urticaria-like eruptions on her trunk and limbs that were diagnosed as contact dermatitis. Two weeks after the onset of systemic symptoms, she noted a sudden drop in vision in her left eye. She was initially diagnosed elsewhere with myopia-related choroidal neovascularization and received two intravitreal ranibizumab injections, 1 month apart, without improvement.

On examination, she had mild myopia (–1.5 diopters) and best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 0.2 in the left eye. The anterior segment was unremarkable, with no cataract, and fundus examination of the left eye showed a partially pigmented, yellowish, ameboid lesion in the macula and multiple small, round, cream-colored spots in the perimacular area. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg in both eyes. The right eye had BCVA of 1.0 (–2 diopters) and normal anterior and posterior segments.

Fluorescein angiography of the left eye demonstrated active choroidal macular neovascularization and hyperfluorescent perimacular spots, while the right eye showed peripheral vascular leakage. Indocyanine green angiography revealed hypocyanescent annular rims around the perimacular lesions with mild central hypercyanescence in the left eye and normal findings in the right eye.

Given the mild myopia, contralateral subclinical retinal vasculitis, and chorioretinal lesions, an infectious etiology was suspected. A comprehensive uveitis workup was performed, including Mantoux skin test, QuantiFERON-TB Gold test, VDRL and TPHA serologies, anti–Toxoplasma and anti–Toxocara antibodies, antiviral serologies (HSV-1, HSV-2, EBV, CMV, VZV), anti–Brucella, anti–Bartonella, and anti–Rickettsia antibodies; complete blood count; erythrocyte sedimentation rate; C-reactive protein; liver and kidney function tests; and both IgM and IgG antibodies against West Nile virus.

A 42-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presented with a 1½-year history of intermittent high-grade fevers, each episode lasting 7–10 days with 2–3-month symptom-free intervals, and a 15- to 20-kg unintentional weight loss. He described daily fevers up to 102°F with rigors, chills, and night sweats unresponsive to oral antipyretics. He denied rashes, arthralgia, myalgia, or other systemic complaints, reporting only intermittent constipation, a mild cough, left shoulder pain, and nonspecific headaches. He had multiple prior hospitalizations; a prior EEG and neurologic evaluation were unremarkable. Medications included metformin PRN, glargine insulin, clonazepam at bedtime, and a recent 14-day course of meropenem. He had a ceftriaxone allergy with prior rash. He used naswar and smoked 2–3 cigarettes daily. 

On examination the temperature was 102°F. A single 1×1-cm firm, nontender, fixed lymph node was palpable in the occipital region. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies showed mild anemia (Hb 11.6 g/dL), leukopenia (3.6×10^3/µL), normal platelets, renal and liver function, and electrolytes. Inflammatory markers were elevated (ESR 62 mm/hr; CRP 4.79 mg/L). Hemoglobin A1c was 8.5%. Malaria, dengue, and other infectious serologies were negative. Autoimmune markers (ANA, anti-dsDNA, ENA) were negative. Echocardiogram, abdominal ultrasound, and CT imaging showed no abnormalities. An ultrasound of the occipital region revealed bilateral hypoechoic lymph nodes with benign features.

Persistent fever prompted an excisional biopsy of an occipital lymph node and a bone marrow biopsy to rule out hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

A 75-year-old man with a 10-year history of bipolar disorder managed on duloxetine, quetiapine, and lorazepam and started on sodium valproate one month earlier presented to the emergency department after a transient episode of confusion. He had transient inability to speak, an open mouth with simple vocalizations, and reached toward his wife’s face as if to cover it. The episode lasted a few minutes, after which he described a foreign-body sensation in his throat accompanied by agitation, fear, and disgust. He was treated with intravenous lorazepam for a presumed panic attack and discharged.

A few hours later, a similar event occurred, and he was admitted. He had stopped sodium valproate four days earlier. On admission he was alert, oriented, and communicative; neurologic examination was normal; routine blood tests, including liver function, thyroid studies, and viral and syphilis serologies, were unremarkable. During the first hospital day, he had 5–7 stereotyped episodes in which he moved his hands as if extracting something from his mouth and simultaneously covered bystanders’ eyes. He remained awake but unresponsive to verbal questions, with episodes lasting minutes and followed by brief confusion with anxiety and stuttering that resolved completely afterward. He then reported that, during each event, he saw a multicolored, snake-like animal emerging from his throat, preventing him from speaking, and felt intense disgust and fear while trying to hide the vision by covering others’ eyes. A psychiatric consultation diagnosed a psychotic disorder complicating depression and recommended increasing quetiapine to 150 mg/day.

A 58-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease presented to an outside hospital with acute inferior‐wall myocardial infarction and cardiogenic shock. Emergent cardiac catheterization revealed right coronary artery occlusion, and a bare‐metal stent was placed. An intra‐aortic balloon pump was inserted for hemodynamic support, and an Impella 2.5 device was also placed via the femoral artery. A transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated severely dilated ventricles with severe biventricular systolic dysfunction. The patient was transferred to our tertiary center for further management. 

Upon arrival, he continued to require hemodynamic support, so the IABP and Impella were removed and venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) was initiated via the femoral vessels. Eight days after the myocardial infarction, persistent cardiac decompensation prompted conversion to surgical biventricular assist devices (BIVADs); cannulas were placed in the right ventricle and pulmonary artery for right ventricular support and from the left ventricular apex to the ascending aorta for left ventricular support. 

Three days after BIVAD placement (eleven days post–myocardial infarction), the patient developed acute hypotension accompanied by approximately 2 L of bleeding through his chest tubes. With concern for device malfunction, he was emergently taken to the operating room with a provisional diagnosis of cannula dislodgement.

A 67-year-old man visiting from New Delhi presented with a 3-day history of fever, confusion, non-productive cough, anorexia, and inability to mobilize independently. Over the previous 3 weeks he had gastrointestinal upset and over 6 months had unintentional weight loss and lethargy. His medical history included poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus (non-compliant with metformin), past alcohol excess (abstinent 6 months), and a 20 pack-year smoking history. Family history was notable for an uncle with tuberculosis. 

On examination he was febrile to 38.4°C, hypotensive, tachycardic, tachypnoeic, and had an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. He appeared cachectic and dehydrated, with oral hyperpigmentation, dry mucous membranes, and reduced skin turgor. 

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 12×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 37 mg/L, creatinine 159 µmol/L, urea 9 mmol/L, deranged liver-function tests, and venous blood gas with pH 7.30, bicarbonate 18.6 mmol/L, lactate 2.23 mmol/L, ketones 3.8 mmol/L, and blood glucose 3.6 mmol/L. Viral screens, including SARS-CoV-2, were negative. 

A random cortisol level was 31 nmol/L (normal 166–507) with an adrenocorticotropic hormone level of 112 pg/mL (normal 7–63), and the patient improved with intravenous hydrocortisone.  

Imaging of the chest showed extensive bilateral reticulonodular opacities, most prominent in the lung apices. Abdominal cross-sectional imaging revealed cirrhotic morphology with portal hypertension and bilateral adrenal masses that were non-adenomatous. Magnetic resonance imaging of the adrenals demonstrated granulomatous involvement of both glands. The patient was hypercalcaemic.  

At this point—given his recent travel from India, a febrile illness with bilateral pulmonary nodularity, and bilateral granulomatous adrenal enlargement with hypercalcaemia—what infectious diagnosis must be considered and how would you investigate further?

A 16-year-old female with well-controlled HIV infection, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, menorrhagia, anemia, thyroid disease, and a complicated right tympanomastoidectomy two days earlier presented with 8 hours of severe right-sided abdominal pain and non-bilious, non-bloody vomiting. She endorsed constipation but was passing flatus and denied fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, diarrhea, bleeding, urinary symptoms, or headaches. Medications included eltrombopag, abacavir–lamivudine, dolutegravir, levothyroxine, cephalexin, and ferrous sulfate. She denied sexual activity and substance use.  
Vital signs: T 97.8 °F; HR 87 bpm; RR 18 bpm; BP 112/78 mm Hg; SpO₂ 100% on room air. She was in moderate distress, with right upper and lower quadrant tenderness and guarding but no rebound, masses, or costovertebral angle tenderness. The remainder of her cardiopulmonary, neurologic, and skin exams was unremarkable. While in the ED, she had two episodes of gross hematuria.  
Laboratory studies showed WBC 21.8 K/μL (94% neutrophils), hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, platelets 98 K/μL; electrolytes, renal and liver function, and coagulation tests were normal. Urinalysis demonstrated proteinuria, ketonuria, hemoglobinuria, urobilinogen, and small leukocyte esterase.  
Given a broad differential that included biliary tract disease, appendicitis, ovarian pathology, ureterolithiasis, urinary tract infection, and small bowel obstruction, she received IV fluids and analgesia, and a point-of-care renal ultrasound was performed.  
Ultrasound findings: mild right hydronephrosis; an enlarged right kidney with surrounding free fluid; and a diffusely hyperechoic cortex with decreased corticomedullary differentiation.

A 27-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 3, presented with lower abdominal pain of 2 days’ duration. Two days earlier, she had inserted a straw into her vagina at night. Shortly afterward, she experienced transient lower abdominal pain and light vaginal bleeding but denied fever, nausea, vomiting, or other symptoms. She had no history of surgery, alcohol use, or drug misuse.

On speculum examination, there was blood in the vaginal vault without clots, discharge, or visible lacerations; the cervix was closed. Bimanual examination revealed slight uterine tenderness without cervical motion tenderness. Transvaginal ultrasound showed minimal intrauterine fluid and interruption of the uterine serosa at the uterine fundus, suggesting perforation. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a tubular, echogenic structure in the right upper abdominal cavity. A diagnosis of an abdominal foreign body was made, and differential considerations included pelvic inflammatory disease, appendicitis, and bowel perforation.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 5.78 × 10^9 cells/l (52% neutrophils), a C-reactive protein level of 18.98 mg/l, and normal coagulation, liver, and kidney function tests. Abdominal radiography was unremarkable.

A 14-year-old boy presented after a fall while playing cricket with forced hyperextension and axial loading of his dominant right thumb. He immediately noted severe pain and was unable to move the thumb. He also observed an abnormal bony prominence at the base of the thumb.

On examination, there was prominent, tender bony swelling over the dorsal aspects of both the carpometacarpal (CMC) and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, with diffuse swelling of the entire thumb. The joints were locked in a dislocated position, and any movement caused extreme pain. A palpable step was noted on the palmar aspect of the MCP joint. The anatomical snuff box was obscured by the dorsal prominence of the first metacarpal base. Sensation and capillary refill in the thumb were normal, and there were no signs of neurovascular compromise or injury to other hand joints.

Plain radiographs of the right hand showed dorsal dislocation of both the MCP and CMC joints of the first metacarpal without any fractures or evidence of volar plate avulsion.

An 82-year-old Greek woman presented with a 3-month history of progressive bilateral upper-extremity weakness, burning pain, and significant walking difficulties. She reported longstanding cervical pain with transient episodes of upper-extremity numbness, but her current symptoms were more intense and persistent. Her medical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, hypothyroidism, ischemic heart disease, depression, and osteoporosis. Surgical history was notable for bilateral carpal-tunnel release and unilateral knee and hip arthroplasties.

On neurological examination, motor strength was diffusely decreased: deltoid, biceps, and triceps strength was 3/5 on the left and 4/5 on the right; quadriceps and adductor strength was 3/5 on the left and 4/5 on the right. Burning pain and hypoesthesia were present in the C4 and C5 dermatomes, more pronounced on the left. Light touch deficits were limited to those dermatomes; proprioception and temperature sensation were intact. Deep tendon reflexes were decreased bilaterally in the biceps and triceps, and the right patellar reflex was less brisk than the left. The patient’s gait was markedly impaired.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine demonstrated a large, well-demarcated cystic lesion on the dorsal aspect of the spinal cord at the C3–C4 level, causing significant cord compression and abutting the ligamentum flavum and the left C3 lamina. The lesion measured 1.4 cm in its greatest diameter and showed no enhancement after intravenous contrast. Multilevel degenerative changes, including decreased disc height, dehydration, and facet hypertrophy, were also noted. Routine laboratory studies were unremarkable.

An infant was referred by an emergency nurse practitioner to the regional plastic surgery center for possible infection of the right middle finger. On presentation, the child was crying, and the affected digit was noted to be swollen and pale. The infant appeared well-groomed and interacted appropriately with the mother. The parents reported that the child had become increasingly irritable since the day before and was now inconsolable. They also noted that the infant was using the hand with the affected finger less often, despite that hand being dominant. There were no recent infections, no concerning past medical history, and no known congenital issues, and the parents thought that blunt trauma was very unlikely. Physical examination revealed swelling and pallor of the right middle finger without obvious erythema, abrasions, or signs of laceration. Hair-thread tourniquet syndrome was considered, but a constricting thread was not visible. A magnifying glass and depilatory cream were unavailable, so the clinician used 3× loupes and a pen torch to examine all digits for any subtle annular constriction.

A 33‐year‐old man with a history of heavy alcohol use presented with 24 hours of epigastric pain and progressive abdominal distention. He reported drinking 3 L of cane alcohol daily over the past week and had six prior hospitalizations for alcohol‐related acute pancreatitis in the past two years. He noted steatorrhea, worsening ascites, and a 10-kg weight loss over the past year. On examination, he was tender throughout the abdomen, had tense ascites, and was oliguric. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 16 g/dL, white blood cell count 11 × 10^9/L, platelets 262 × 10^9/L, INR 1.4, AST 42 IU/L, ALT 19 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 111 U/L, lipase 1270 U/L, amylase 442 U/L, triglycerides 140 mg/dL, creatinine 6 mg/dL, and albumin 2 g/dL. Hepatitis and HIV serologies were negative. Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed pancreatic necrosis with atrophy, no biliary tract abnormality, and free intraperitoneal fluid. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded 4.4 L of opaque black fluid. Ascitic fluid analysis showed 2–3 red cells/μL, 30 white cells/μL, total protein 3.3 g/dL, amylase 2769 U/L, and albumin 1.6 g/dL; the serum–ascites albumin gradient was 0.4. Fluid cytology was negative for malignant cells, tests for tuberculosis were negative, and bacterial and fungal cultures showed no growth.

A 22-year-old gravida-1 nulliparous woman with an unremarkable medical history underwent a routine second-trimester anatomy ultrasound that demonstrated ventriculomegaly and possible agenesis of the corpus callosum. A fetal MRI was obtained at 21 weeks 5 days’ gestation and showed:
• Severe lateral and third ventriculomegaly (atrial diameters up to 15 mm bilaterally).  
• A dysplastic, Z-shaped brainstem.  
• Poor visualization of the cerebral aqueduct; a normal fourth ventricle.  
• Hypoplastic cerebellar vermis (5 mm craniocaudal), with normal cisterna magna and transverse cerebellar diameter for gestational age.  
• Subjectively decreased supratentorial brain parenchymal volume without definite cortical malformations.  
No additional anomalies were identified. A detailed family history revealed no birth defects or known genetic disorders.

A 36-year-old woman presented as a new outpatient with a history of symptomatic thrombocytopenia causing mucosal bleeding and easy bruising. She had a prior diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) based on isolated low platelet counts. She reported heavy menstrual bleeding requiring 9–11 pads per day, bleeding gums with tooth brushing, and occasional painless bruises; she denied hematuria, hematemesis, hematochezia, and had no family history of blood disorders or cancer.

Laboratory studies showed:
• Platelet count 9 × 10^3/µL  
• Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, hematocrit 31%, mean corpuscular volume 76 fL, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration 33.9 g/dL, ferritin 101 mg/L  
• Negative platelet-bound and free anti-GP IIb/IIIa and anti-GPIb/IX autoantibodies  
• Negative hepatitis and HIV panels  
• Peripheral smear with hypochromic microcytosis but normal platelet and leukocyte morphology; no abnormal cells  

She was started on oral iron for iron-deficiency anemia. A review of her prior medical records revealed fluctuations in platelet counts, with nadirs around 10 × 10^3/µL and peaks around 400 × 10^3/µL.  

Treatment and response:
• Pulse oral dexamethasone 40 mg for 4 days: platelet count remained at 8–9 × 10^3/µL over three cycles  
• Rituximab 375 mg/m^2 weekly for 4 weeks: platelets 11, 230, 130, then 15 × 10^3/µL  
• Eltrombopag 50 mg orally for 2 weeks: platelet count 17 × 10^3/µL  
• Splenectomy: platelet counts continued to fall to 10–50 × 10^3/µL  
• Bone marrow biopsy: normal, without evidence of myelodysplasia  
• Two additional doses of rituximab were given before transfer of care

A 70-year-old man with prostate carcinoma was scheduled for radical retropubic prostatectomy. His medical history included HIV infection, an ischemic cerebellar stroke one year earlier, mild bronchiectasis, hypertension, and early dementia; he denied dyspnea or cardiovascular symptoms. Preanesthetic examination, laboratory results, and ECG were normal; preoperative peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) was 95%. 

After induction of balanced general anesthesia, SpO2 fell from 100% to 86–90% on several occasions, coinciding with a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 60 mmHg. Desaturation did not improve with increased inspired oxygen fraction or recruitment maneuvers but resolved after phenylephrine boluses that raised MAP to 90 mmHg. The 60-minute operation was completed with 700 mL blood loss and 0.5 mg total phenylephrine. Recovery and transfer to the postanesthesia care unit (PACU) were uneventful.

In the PACU, despite minimal dyspnea, the patient developed severe hypoxemia (PaO2 5.48 kPa; SpO2 73.4%) on a Venturi mask delivering 15 L/min of oxygen. He received intravenous hydrocortisone, aminophylline, and inhaled ipratropium/salbutamol with minimal benefit. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Computed tomographic angiography revealed peripheral subsegmental pulmonary emboli that did not fully explain the degree of hypoxemia. Notably, SpO2 rose to 94–96% when the patient lay supine and dropped to the low 90s when he sat up.

A 32-year-old woman noted a thyroid swelling of 9 months’ duration. Physical examination revealed a multinodular goiter without symptoms of hypo- or hyperthyroidism. Thyroid function tests were normal. Neck ultrasound showed an oval, 0.7 × 0.5 cm solid nodule with mostly isoechogenic echotexture and a hypoechoic focus in the left upper pole. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology performed elsewhere revealed papillae lined by epithelial cells with enlarged nuclei and occasional grooves (Bethesda category V). The patient underwent a left hemithyroidectomy. On gross examination, the specimen contained a well-circumscribed encapsulated gray-tan nodule with a focal whitish solid area. Histologically, the nodule was circumscribed by a thin fibrous capsule and composed predominantly of thyroid follicles. A focal area showed papillary architecture lined by follicular cells with enlarged nuclei and rare nuclear grooves.

A 34-year-old woman with Fitzpatrick skin type V presented with a 4-month history of pruritic patches of hair loss on the occipital scalp. She denied systemic symptoms. Examination showed large, irregular, sharply demarcated areas of alopecia on the posterior crown and occiput. Dermatoscopy of an affected patch revealed patchy erythema, numerous brown dots, and some obliterated ostia. Laboratory evaluation included a nonreactive rapid plasma reagin test, negative antinuclear antibodies, and normal iron studies, adrenal and sex hormones, complement levels, rheumatoid factor, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and calcium. She was mildly anemic (hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL, hematocrit 34.5%). A punch biopsy of an involved area showed a normal interfollicular epidermis with a normal total hair count; almost all follicles were greatly miniaturized, and most were in the catagen or telogen phase. Lymphocytic inflammation surrounded, infiltrated, and damaged follicular bulbs and suprabulbar zones. Some follicular units were replaced by well-formed granulomas with multinucleated giant cells, and several eosinophils were present. The upper portions of most follicles were spared, and small granulomatous foci were also seen around damaged infundibula.

A 73-year-old woman was referred to the pulmonary clinic for evaluation of cystic lung disease. Her history is significant for left breast adenocarcinoma treated in 2010 with lumpectomy, chest radiation, and letrozole, and metastatic endometrial adenocarcinoma diagnosed in 2017. For the endometrial carcinoma, she underwent total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, pelvic radiation, and five cycles of carboplatin, paclitaxel, and bevacizumab.

Three years after her endometrial cancer diagnosis, surveillance CT of the chest revealed numerous solid masses and nodules of variable size and shape throughout both lungs, the largest measuring 4.9 × 3.8 cm in the right lower lobe. A CT-guided biopsy of a left upper lobe lesion confirmed metastatic endometrial adenocarcinoma. She completed five cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin, paclitaxel, and bevacizumab.

Follow-up CT imaging after chemotherapy showed resolution of the solid masses and nodules and the development of bilateral, asymmetrical, air-filled cystic lesions with thin walls, anatomically corresponding to the prior metastatic sites. Serial CT scans over the next two years demonstrated stable cystic lung disease without new solid lesions.

A 67-year-old African-American man with type 2 diabetes (hemoglobin A1c 6.6%) and a remote history of treated prostate cancer presented with fever, chills, and weight loss. One month earlier, a liver mass was discovered on ultrasound, and he had just completed a 7-day course of ciprofloxacin for presumed urinary tract infection. Over the week before admission, he experienced shaking chills, fevers to 39.5 °C, anorexia, nausea, and a 4.5 kg weight loss. He had not traveled outside the United States since Vietnam. On examination, he was febrile (39.5 °C) and tachycardic (115 beats/min) but appeared well; the abdomen was nontender without organomegaly. Liver function tests were normal; hepatitis B and C serologies were negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a multiloculated cystic mass in the liver, multiple smaller low-density hepatic lesions, a nonocclusive portal vein thrombus, a mildly prominent right infrahilar lymph node (1 cm), and bilateral renal cysts. MRI of the liver did not narrow the differential diagnoses, which included primary and metastatic cancer, hepatic abscess, and parasite infection.

Three days after admission, fever recurred to 39.2 °C despite resolving initial fever. Sputum culture grew Escherichia coli; blood and urine cultures were negative. Chest radiography showed expansion of the liver mass into the right lower lung field. On hospital day 6, CT-guided biopsy of the cystic portion of the lesion was performed. An aspirate of the cystic components did not show any sign of infection or malignancy on cytology. A PET scan did not help narrow the differential diagnosis.

A 45‐year‐old man presented with a three-week history of right testicular pain and swelling. The pain was acute in onset and gradually increased over time. He had no history of diabetes, hypertension, genitourinary trauma, pulmonary tuberculosis, TB exposure, weight loss, night sweats, or fever. On examination, vital signs were normal, and he appeared well. Genital examination revealed a right, round, erythematous, movable scrotal mass measuring 5–8 cm in diameter, with no discharging sinus or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and biochemistry profile. Hepatitis B and C serologies, syphilis serology, and HIV ELISA were negative. However, serum adenosine deaminase and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were elevated, while serum alpha-fetoprotein, β-hCG, and LDH levels were within normal limits. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous right intratesticular mass with avascular necrotic areas and septated fluid collections in the tunica vaginalis, features suggestive of a testicular tumor. The patient underwent a right orchiectomy through a transinguinal approach.

An 87-year-old man presented with severe, atypical recurrent chest pain of one month's duration. He had no history of diabetes, hypertension, or smoking and was not taking any medications. On examination, blood pressure was 125/80 mm Hg, pulse 60 beats/min, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, and temperature 37 °C; the cardiac and pulmonary examinations were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography was unremarkable, with an ejection fraction of 55%. The admission electrocardiogram demonstrated a right bundle branch block and mild ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads without dynamic changes. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function, and lipid profile; troponin was negative. Inflammatory and autoimmune markers revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 32 mm/h, C-reactive protein negative, antinuclear antibody negative, anti–double-stranded DNA negative, and VDRL negative. A spiral chest computed tomography scan demonstrated normal pulmonary parenchyma and mediastinal structures.

A 37-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 9-day history of headache and vomiting. Ten days before admission he developed fever (peak, 40 °C), diarrhea, and headache; after antipyretics, the fever persisted at 38 – 39 °C for several days and then normalized three days before admission. Two days before admission he had acute urinary retention requiring transurethral catheterization, which was continued on presentation. 

On examination, his temperature was normal. Neurologic findings included nuchal rigidity. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 10.99 × 10^9/L, a C-reactive protein level of 9.41 mg/L, and serum sodium of 131.8 mmol/L. Routine immunologic screening and tumor markers were negative. 

Lumbar puncture disclosed an opening pressure of 190 mmH₂O; cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed 97 leukocytes/μL and a protein concentration of 124 mg/dL, with negative infectious studies, normal oligoclonal bands, IgG index, and myelin basic protein levels, and negative paraneoplastic antibodies. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain on hospital day 2 demonstrated a midline splenial lesion characterized by T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted hyperintensity, decreased apparent diffusion coefficient, isointensity on T1-weighted images, and no contrast enhancement. Spinal-cord MRI was unremarkable.

A previously healthy 6-year-old boy presented with a one-week history of diffuse colicky abdominal pain, recurrent vomiting, pain and swelling of the hands and feet, and limitation of movement in both knees and ankles following an upper respiratory infection two weeks earlier. On examination he had non-pitting edema, tenderness, and restricted mobility of the wrists, ankles, feet, and knees. Initial laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, serum urea, creatinine, electrolytes, albumin, acid–base status, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria and non-nephrotic proteinuria (urine albumin/creatinine, 150 mg/mmol), and stool testing was positive for occult blood. His gastrointestinal symptoms, edema, and arthritis resolved with supportive care, and he was discharged. Two weeks later he returned with dark “cola-colored” urine, oliguria, periorbital edema, hypertension (149/95 mm Hg), pallor, pitting edema of the extremities, and moderate ascites. Laboratory evaluation revealed hemoglobin 7.0 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 87 fl, corrected reticulocyte count 1.5%, white-cell count 11.4×10^9/L, platelets 401×10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 87 mm/hr, blood urea nitrogen 45 mmol/L, creatinine 198 mmol/L, nephrotic-range proteinuria (urine protein/creatinine, 5436 mg/mmol), and more than 100 red cells per high-power field in the urine. Serum electrolytes were notable for sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 94 mmol/L, bicarbonate 14.2 mmol/L; complement C3 was normal, cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (c-ANCA) was positive, and antinuclear antibody was negative; stool occult blood remained positive. Renal ultrasonography showed bilaterally enlarged, slightly echogenic kidneys.

A 54-year-old man was referred after two brief episodes of memory loss over the past year. During both episodes, he abruptly became unable to orient himself to the time and date and could not retain new information. The first episode occurred at home while working at his computer; he wandered about searching for the date, which he could not remember, and gradually recovered after approximately three hours. The second episode occurred while he was alone in his office, lasted about 20 minutes, and was witnessed by coworkers, who reported that he repeatedly asked the same questions about the time and date. During both episodes, he remained fully alert, with no staring spells, automatisms, or focal neurologic deficits. He experienced a mild headache in the week preceding the second episode. His medical history was notable for well-controlled hypertension treated with metoprolol and prior surgery for obstructive sleep apnea. Neurologic examination between episodes was normal. A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed no abnormalities, and cardiac evaluation, including assessment for arrhythmia, was unremarkable.

A 25-year-old right-handed woman with no prior medical history presented with one week of right lower extremity numbness from toes to hip and three days of progressive left lower extremity weakness, resulting in use of crutches. She reported a minor fall onto an air mattress three days before the onset of weakness but denied significant trauma or other injuries. She had no fevers, chills, upper extremity symptoms, facial or visual changes, speech or swallowing difficulties.
On examination, she was alert and afebrile with normal cranial nerve function. Upper extremity strength and sensation were intact. In the lower extremities, left hip flexion was 3/5, knee extension 4/5, foot dorsiflexion 3/5, and plantarflexion 5/5; right lower extremity strength was 5/5 throughout. Sensory testing showed decreased pinprick and temperature on the right up to the T11–T12 dermatomes, and reduced proprioception and vibration in the left from mid-shin downward. Left patellar clonus was present with 6–7 beats; ankle jerks were symmetric, and Babinski and Hoffman signs were equivocal.
MRI of the spine demonstrated multifocal T2‐hyperintense lesions with contrast enhancement, suspicious for an inflammatory or demyelinating process, without space-occupying lesions. Brain MRI showed periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial gadolinium-enhancing lesions. An axial T2‐weighted image at L1 revealed a high-signal lesion hemisecting the spinal cord.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of progressively worsening abdominal pain. She had no significant past medical history. On examination, her temperature was 37.7 °C, blood pressure 113/72 mmHg, and pulse 97/min. Abdominal examination revealed intermittent epigastric colicky pain without peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, hematocrit 39.2%, white cell count 10 870/mm3 (74.6% neutrophils), and C-reactive protein 0.07 mg/dL. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a large intraluminal mass in the transverse colon with imaging signs of intussusception but no evidence of intestinal ischemia or necrosis. Given the absence of peritonitis or ischemia, colonoscopic reduction was attempted. Endoscopy revealed an oval, 4-cm pedunculated mass near the ileocecal valve, consistent with ileocecal-type intussusception. The lesion moved freely with air insufflation, and the clinical impression was a non-epithelial tumor such as a gastrointestinal stromal tumor.

A 36-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with a 2-year history of intermittent, stabbing pain in the left lumbar region associated with a palpable swelling that increased in size with the Valsalva maneuver. She denied any history of trauma. On examination, there was a 7 × 5 cm soft, reducible swelling in the left posterolateral lumbar area, just below the twelfth rib, with no overlying skin changes. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan demonstrated an aponeurotic defect in the left lumbar region at the Grynfeltt–Lesshaft triangle measuring 69 × 51 mm, with retroperitoneal fat protruding through the defect.

A 47-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and fever of 24 hours’ duration. She had localized tenderness and rebound at McBurney’s point, along with a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa. Vital signs were notable for low-grade fever. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 14.0×10^9/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 90 mm in the first hour. She was managed conservatively for one day without improvement. Abdominal ultrasonography was inconclusive. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a large soft-tissue mass in the right lateral pelvis with adherent loops of bowel, thickened intestinal walls, and three enlarged regional lymph nodes. A radiological differential diagnosis of inflammatory versus neoplastic mass was made, and the patient was taken for exploratory laparotomy.

A 9‐year‐old boy was referred for bilateral leukocoria. He was born at term, had no history of prematurity or oxygen supplementation, and had no family history of ocular disease; both parents’ ophthalmologic exams were normal. On exam, he could fix and follow with each eye but had reduced direct and consensual pupillary responses and nystagmus without a null point. Best‐corrected visual acuity was 1.3 logMAR in each eye. Horizontal corneal diameters measured 11.8 mm OD and 11.9 mm OS. The lenses were clear except for localized posterior capsular opacifications. Fundus examination showed bilateral fibrovascular stalks connecting the optic disc to the posterior lens capsule and dragging of retinal vessels. Under anesthesia, RetCam imaging confirmed fibrovascular stalks: in the right eye the stalk ran temporally from the optic disc to the posterior lens, causing opacification; in the left eye it ran inferotemporally, stretching the capsule peripherally. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated patent vessels along the stalks branching on the posterior lens capsule, fine capillary arborization with bridging fibrous material, inclusion and stretching of the macula within the folds, absence of a foveal avascular zone, patchy perivascular hyperfluorescence, ischemic areas in the vascularized retina, and peripheral nonperfusion without exudation. OCT showed diffuse internal limiting membrane hyperreflectivity, no foveal depression, and abrupt interruption of retinal layers with cone‐shaped fibrous tissue arising from the optic nerve head.

A 63-year-old woman presented with an 8-day history of fever and cough, followed by palpitations and dyspnea. She had no significant medical, surgical, or gynecologic history, and no tobacco or alcohol use. On admission: temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 139/87 mmHg, pulse 120 beats/min, SpO2 92% on room air. Examination showed absent breath sounds over the right hemithorax; the abdomen was soft and non-tender.

Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 6.16 mg/dL and CA-125 of 114 U/mL. Liver and renal function were normal; various autoantibodies were negative. Chest radiography showed a large right pleural effusion with mediastinal shift. Contrast-enhanced chest CT confirmed complete collapse of the right lung due to pleural fluid; abdominal CT incidentally noted an 18 mm right ovarian nodule.

A right-sided thoracentesis yielded yellow, turbid exudative fluid: specific gravity 1.036; cells 3383/µL (95% lymphocytes); LDH 214 U/L; total protein 5.0 g/dL; albumin 2.8 g/dL; ADA 13.8 IU/L; hyaluronic acid 7400 ng/mL; CEA 0.5 ng/mL; SCC 32.8 ng/mL; other tumor markers unremarkable. Cytology showed lymphocytes and mesothelial cells without malignancy.

Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 20 mm mono-cystic lesion in the right adnexa with high T1 signal, slightly low T2 signal, and high diffusion signal; uterine leiomyomas were also noted. A chest drain removed 1200 mL initially and 180 mL/day thereafter.

On hospital day 4, medical thoracoscopy showed mild pleural redness and yellowish ridging, without endometriotic implants, diaphragmatic defects, or metastatic nodules. Random pleural biopsies revealed hyperplasia of pleural tissue and mesothelial cells with mild lymphocytic infiltration, without atypia; immunostaining was negative for PgR, ER, and CD10, consistent with nonspecific pleurisy.

A 50-year-old Romanian woman with a history of intravenous drug use and active smoking was receiving a 48-week course of interferon alfa-2a plus ribavirin for hepatitis C. Thirty weeks into therapy, she presented with a 3-week history of progressive shortness of breath and hemoptysis.  
On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed enlarged hilar lymph nodes and diffuse nodules throughout both lungs. A positron emission tomography–CT scan showed increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the hilar lymph nodes and lung parenchyma.

A 76-year-old Syrian man presented with a 6-hour history of urinary frequency, dysuria, and gross hematuria. His medical history included hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On examination, vital signs were stable, and findings were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 20,000/μL, hemoglobin 11 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 82 fl, platelets 254,000/μL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, and urea 130 mg/dL. Renal ultrasonography demonstrated severe right-sided and mild left-sided hydronephrosis without stones, and a bladder-wall thickness of 1.5 cm. Cystoscopic biopsy of the bladder revealed denuded cystitis, low-grade dysplasia, and severe interstitial cystitis without invasive tumor. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed right hydronephrosis with a nonenhancing hypodense filling defect in the renal pelvis and inferior calyces.
