Chest CT revealed band-like opacities in the right upper lobe. On the basis of these findings, a primary diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma was made, and the patient underwent an open right radical nephrectomy and ureterectomy.

A 49-year-old Asian woman with a history of stage IIB right upper lobe lung adenocarcinoma underwent video-assisted thoracic surgery, followed by adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy complicated by neutropenia and dysesthesia. Ten weeks after completing platinum-based chemotherapy, she began adjuvant atezolizumab. There was no personal or family history of cardiac disease; baseline cardiac function was normal.

She was observed inpatient during the first cycle of atezolizumab (day 1–8) without issues. On day 9 she developed persistent fever (to 38 °C) and by day 13 she presented with a temperature of 40.3 °C, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, pulse 116 bpm, WBC 4300/µL (lymphocytes 18.5%), AST 23 U/L, ALT 27 U/L, and CRP 4.76 mg/dL. Chest radiography was normal. CT of the neck showed an enlarged, tender right cervical lymph node, and subacute necrotizing lymphadenitis was diagnosed.

On day 16 she developed dyspnea on exertion, progressing to dyspnea at rest on day 17. Chest radiograph then demonstrated pulmonary congestion. Systolic blood pressure fell below 90 mmHg, consistent with shock, and she was admitted to the ICU. Laboratory tests showed AST 86 U/L, ALT 53 U/L, LDH 566 U/L, and troponin I 538.8 pg/mL. Electrocardiography revealed a sinus tachycardia at 125 bpm. Transthoracic echocardiography showed circumferential wall hypokinesia and pericardial effusion. Right‐ and left‐sided cardiac catheterization revealed a cardiac index of 2.05 L/min/m2 and right ventricular pressure of 35 mmHg. Coronary angiography was performed.

A 77-year-old woman with JAK2V617F-positive post–essential thrombocythemia myelofibrosis treated with ruxolitinib for 5 years, Hashimoto thyroiditis, hypertension, depression, and osteoarthritis presented with redness and swelling of her nose. On examination, there was an erythematous papule on the nasal dorsum. 

A shave biopsy revealed a moderate-to-dense dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and a few plasma cells extending from the reticular dermis to the base of the specimen, with one focal area of caseation necrosis. Periodic acid–Schiff stain was negative for organisms. Six months later, multiple pink papules coalesced into a plaque on the nasal dorsum. A second shave biopsy showed a dermal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate surrounding a ruptured hair follicle. Gomori methenamine-silver nitrate and Fite stains were negative for organisms. Immunoperoxidase studies on paraffin sections showed predominantly CD3+ T cells (75% CD4+, 25% CD8+) with preserved CD2 and CD5 and mildly decreased CD7 expression; CD68 highlighted histiocytes; immunophenotyping did not suggest a primary lymphoproliferative disorder.

A working diagnosis of granulomatous rosacea was made, and the patient received oral doxycycline and a sulfur-containing cleanser for 3 months. Despite therapy, the nasal lesions progressed into a disfiguring red-brown crusted plaque encompassing the entire nose. A third shave biopsy grew only coagulase-negative staphylococci (likely skin flora); acid-fast bacterial and fungal stains and cultures were negative. Laboratory studies revealed mild anemia and mildly elevated inflammatory markers; white blood cell count, platelet count, metabolic panel, serum calcium, protein electrophoreses, lactate dehydrogenase, antinuclear antibodies, anti-Ro, anti-La, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and Quantiferon-TB Gold were all within normal limits. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Rheumatologic and ophthalmologic evaluations found no evidence of inflammatory arthritis, connective tissue disease, or ocular sarcoidosis. Over the next 6 months, topical ivermectin, adapalene gel, intralesional triamcinolone, oral minocycline, oral prednisone, oral isotretinoin, and a Jessner’s-trichloroacetic acid peel were tried without benefit.

A 46-year-old North-African man with well-controlled hypertension and hereditary spherocytosis presented after 12 days of fever, cough, and progressive dyspnea when he developed visual loss in his left eye. He was admitted to the ICU for respiratory failure and unilateral visual impairment. Chest radiograph showed bilateral peripheral airspace opacities, and SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by RT-PCR; bacterial co-infection was excluded. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL, normal platelet and leukocyte counts, total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL (mostly indirect), lactate dehydrogenase 690 U/L (normal 230–460), and haptoglobin 244 mg/dL (normal 34–200). Peripheral blood smear demonstrated erythrocyte agglutinates (confirmed with direct antiglobulin test), spherocytes, polychromasia, and circulating erythroblasts; G6PD levels were normal. Ophthalmic evaluation showed visual acuity 20/20 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left. Fundus examination revealed bilateral retinal hemorrhages with right parafoveal and left foveal involvement. Anterior segment examination, pupillary responses, and intraocular pressure were normal. Optical coherence tomography identified hemorrhages beneath the internal limiting membrane in both eyes, obliterating the foveal depression in the left eye. Fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography demonstrated bilateral blockage corresponding to areas of hemorrhage in the context of normal retinal and choroidal circulation, excluding vascular occlusion, hypertensive retinopathy, and vasculitis.

A 64-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease (inferolateral MI in 2008 with left‐circumflex stent), well‐controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea, and tobacco use presented with 2 weeks of shortness of breath, 20 lb weight gain, lower extremity oedema, and hyperglycaemia. He had preserved left ventricular ejection fraction and no prior congestive heart failure. On examination, blood pressure was 189/101 mmHg; jugular venous distention, bilateral rales, and pitting oedema were noted. Transthoracic echocardiography showed new global hypokinesia with an ejection fraction of 30–35%, mildly increased wall thickness (interventricular septum 1.1 cm, posterior wall 1.1 cm), normal cavity size (end-diastolic diameter 5.7 cm; volume 135 mL; indexed 61.6 mL/m2), normal relative wall thickness (0.39), and normal LV mass index (96.2 g/m2). Biplane ejection fraction was 31%, and global longitudinal strain was reduced at –11.4%. Diastolic parameters (E‐wave 87.9 cm/s, E/A 1.6, e′ 7.6 cm/s, E/e′ 11.6, LAVI 36 mL/m2, pulmonary vein S/D < 1) were consistent with grade II diastolic dysfunction. Coronary angiography revealed patent stents, non‐obstructive CAD, and an elevated LV end‐diastolic pressure of 30 mmHg. Hospital course was notable for refractory hypokalaemia (serum K⁺ 2.7 mmol/L) despite aggressive replacement. The differential for resistant hypokalaemia included hypercortisolism, hyperaldosteronism, diuretic or laxative use, renal tubular acidosis, and increased insulin availability. Additional studies showed BNP 277 pg/mL, HbA1C 10.9%, normal cardiac enzymes, and urine potassium 39 mmol/L. Renin activity and aldosterone were both normal. Thyroid‐stimulating hormone, ferritin, and iron studies were normal. Serum cortisol was 59.9 μg/dL (reference 7–23 μg/dL); 24-hour urine free cortisol was 8790 μg/day (reference ≤ 60 μg/day); ACTH was 224 pg/mL (reference 7–69 pg/mL). His cortisol levels were not suppressed with high-dose dexamethasone.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of progressive pain and swelling in his right thigh. The pain was dull, moderate in intensity, increased gradually, and was worse with walking. Thirteen years earlier, he had undergone open reduction and K-nail fixation for a malunited femoral fracture, with an uneventful postoperative course.

On examination, the overlying skin was normal. There was a 10 × 10 cm oval, nonfluctuant swelling on the posteromedial aspect of the right thigh, deep to the medial muscle group. The mass was soft and tender on deep palpation, with ill-defined margins. Hip and knee range of motion were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count and differential, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/hr. Radiographs of the right femur revealed increased soft-tissue density over the posteromedial upper third of the femur with excavation of the posteromedial cortex; the healed malunion was also visible. These findings suggested a destructive soft-tissue lesion.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded serosanguineous fluid, which was cultured and examined cytologically. The culture was sterile and no malignant cells were identified. CT angiography of the lower limbs demonstrated normal blood flow in both femoral arteries and no evidence of a vascular mass. MRI was not performed due to financial constraints.

With a provisional diagnosis of either chronic infection or low-grade malignancy, a surgical biopsy was planned to establish a definitive diagnosis.

A 22-year-old female medical student presented with a 4-day history of pain on swallowing. It began as burning epigastric pain and intense heartburn treated empirically with omeprazole and domperidone without relief. After 12 hours the pain became constrictive, intermittent, and located retrosternally. She developed asthenia, malaise, anorexia, and daily afternoon fevers up to 38.5 °C. She reported a 5 kg weight loss over one week, nausea, and progressive odynophagia for solids, pastes, and liquids, initially limited to the distal esophagus and later involving the entire esophagus.

On examination she appeared well, with mild oropharyngeal hyperemia but normal mucous membranes, was afebrile, hydrated, and had normal respiratory, cardiovascular, and abdominal findings without lymphadenopathy. Serologic testing for herpes simplex virus IgM and IgG was negative.

Upper digestive endoscopy revealed numerous yellow-whitish, pleomorphic, isolated circular plaques with central erosions and depressed hyperemic bases throughout the esophagus, most prominently in the distal third, suggestive of infectious esophagitis.

A 79-year-old woman was referred to otolaryngology for an incidental finding on a head CT scan obtained for holocranial headache. She had no sinonasal symptoms. Her medical history included hypertension and well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. Physical examination, routine blood tests, and oral examination (with good hygiene and regular dental follow-up after implant placement 3 years earlier) were unremarkable. 

CT of the head demonstrated right fronto-ethmoid-maxillary sinus opacification with partial penetration of a dental implant into the maxillary sinus. Within the isodense sinus opacity, there were hyperdense floccular bodies. Nasal endoscopy showed a congested middle osteomeatal complex with marked medialization of the uncinate process. 

Based on these findings, a diagnosis of paranasal sinus fungus ball was made. A functional endoscopic sinus surgery procedure was planned, and a head MRI without contrast was prescribed both to confirm the diagnosis and to exclude a neoplastic process prior to surgery.

A 61-year-old man with a 12-year history of myasthenia gravis presented with a 1-week history of acute, deep, right knee pain (NPRS 8/10) located on the anterior and medial aspect. Pain worsened during prolonged sitting (7/10), walking (8/10), and descending stairs (9/10). He also noted hypoesthesia in the same area and intermittent bilateral leg weakness with quadriceps fatigue. There was no antecedent trauma. He took ibuprofen with only partial relief. His past history included myasthenia gravis treated with pyridostigmine, HIV on antiretroviral therapy, benign prostatic hyperplasia on anticholinergic medication, and a sedentary lifestyle. 

On examination, there were no signs of inflammation around the knee. Superficial sensitivity testing with von Frey monofilament revealed slight hypoesthesia (0.1 kg/Pa vs. 0.07 kg/Pa contralaterally). Pressure pain threshold over the anteromedial tibia was decreased (1.22 kg/Pa vs. 2.17 kg/Pa left). Active knee flexion and extension under axial load reproduced pain, dysesthesia, and fatigue, especially during single-leg squats. Accessory joint mobilizations did not alter symptoms. Palpation of the vastus medialis trigger point elicited pain (9/10) and dysesthesia, and quadriceps strength was mildly reduced on the right (20.98 kg vs. 22.34 kg). Patellar reflexes were normal.

A prone knee-bending neural tension test reproduced the patient’s pain (9/10) and diffuse medial knee dysesthesia. Ultrasound examination of the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve (IBSN) with axial transducer compression elicited all the patient’s symptoms, although no sonographic space-occupying lesion was seen.

A 56-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 1, presented with a 1-week history of lower abdominal pain and fever. She had a prior laparoscopic myomectomy but denied pelvic inflammatory disease, antibiotic treatment, or intrauterine device use. On examination, there was a palpable nontender mass in the lower abdomen. Laboratory tests showed C-reactive protein 181 mg/L (0–3), leukocytes 13.8 × 10^3/μL (3.3–8.6 × 10^3), and hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL (12.1–14.5). Serum CA-125 and CA19-9 were within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a left adnexal hypoechoic mass. Pelvic MRI revealed a 7-cm left adnexal mass extending to the uterus and rectum, with high T2 and low T1 signal. On diffusion-weighted imaging, the central component was hyperintense with an ADC of 0.46 × 10^-3 mm^2/s, and the peripheral component was hypointense with an ADC of 1.68 × 10^-3 mm^2/s. On contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images, the central component showed no enhancement, whereas the peripheral component enhanced intensely. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed an ill-defined left adnexal mass with a nonenhancing central area. The initial imaging diagnosis was tubo-ovarian abscess; differential diagnoses included adnexal malignancy and pelvic actinomycosis. After antibiotic therapy, inflammatory markers improved and the abscess cavity collapsed on MRI, but the enhancing peripheral component remained unchanged and continued to extend to adjacent organs. The patient was taken for exploratory laparotomy.

A 56-year-old woman with a history of schizophrenia was admitted 2 months earlier for perforated diverticulitis requiring sigmoid resection. Her hospitalization was complicated by an anastomotic leak, defunctioning ileostomy for high-output losses, feculent peritonitis, wound dehiscence, multiple laparotomies, percutaneous drainage, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and wound debridements. She remained malnourished despite a high-protein/calorie diet. For pain, she received acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours from admission (total dose 78 g over the first several weeks), which was increased over 3 weeks to 650 mg every 4 hours (3.9 g/d).

On transfer to the intensive care unit for hypovolemic shock attributed to gastrointestinal losses and poor oral intake, she was found to have new abdominal collections, acute kidney injury, and a severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Laboratory testing on ICU day 0 showed:  
  • Serum sodium 143 mmol/L, chloride 110 mmol/L, total CO₂ 5 mmol/L, anion gap 28 mmol/L  
  • Creatinine 181 µmol/L (baseline 84 µmol/L), albumin 24 g/L  
  • Arterial blood gas: pH 6.92, PaCO₂ 18 mm Hg, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L  
  • Serum osmolality 319 mOsm/kg (calculated gap 19 mOsm/kg)  
  • Urine anion gap 51 mmol/L, urine osmolality 308 mOsm/kg  
  • Whole-blood lactate 0.6 mmol/L  

Initial investigations revealed a negative screen for ethanol, methanol, isopropanol, and ethylene glycol; normal liver function tests; a negative salicylate level; and a mildly elevated β-hydroxybutyrate level of 0.56 mmol/L (reference <0.27 mmol/L). Although acute kidney injury and ketosis could partially explain the anion-gap elevation, the gap was disproportionately high. Serum osmolal gap was elevated (19 mOsm/kg), probably in the setting of acute kidney injury.

A 54-year-old female farm worker from rural India presented with a 6-month history of a painless, gradually enlarging mass in her left iliac fossa. She had no prior surgeries or hospitalizations. On examination, there was a smooth, bilobed, well-defined cystic mass measuring approximately 16 × 8 cm, located diagonally across the suprapubic region and left iliac fossa. The swelling did not change with position, was nonreducible, noncompressible, and fixed to the pubic crest in the parietal plane. The patient’s complete blood count was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a cystic lesion in the parietal wall; the liver and remaining abdominal organs appeared normal. A chest radiograph was unremarkable.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of chronic back pain that began after epidural anesthesia for a cesarean delivery. The pain was constant, progressive, worse with sitting and walking, and temporarily relieved by analgesics. She denied fever or weight loss. Because of severe pain and progression, she became unable to walk or bear weight. Initial treatment with antibiotics and muscle relaxants provided no improvement. She also developed a perianal abscess related to constipation due to limited mobility.

On examination, there was tenderness over the thoracolumbar spine, most pronounced at T12–L2, and paraspinal muscle spasm. Neurologic examination was normal, with intact motor and sensory function of the lower extremities and preserved sphincter control.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed multiple endplate changes in the thoracic (especially T11–T12) and lumbar regions. Laboratory studies, including CBC, C-reactive protein, and ESR, were obtained to evaluate for septic or infective spondylodiscitis. Cultures, sensitivity testing, and gene Xpert of the lesion were negative for tuberculosis or any other infection. Serum vitamin D level was normal. A bone biopsy demonstrated inflammatory infiltrates without granuloma or malignancy.

A 27-year-old woman at 33 weeks’ gestation was diagnosed with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy after presenting with proteinuria and elevated blood pressure (maximum 172/112 mmHg). Despite intravenous nicardipine and labor induction, her hypertension remained uncontrolled and laboratory tests revealed disseminated intravascular coagulation (platelets 24,000/μL; PT-INR 1.44; fibrinogen 65 mg/dL; FDP 15.8 μg/mL). She underwent an emergency cesarean delivery at 36 weeks. Twelve hours postpartum, she noted changes in color vision and metamorphopsia. On day 5 after delivery, she was treated with oral amlodipine (5 mg) and referred for ophthalmic evaluation. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 1.2 in both eyes, intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg, and she denied meningismus, tinnitus, alopecia, vitiligo, or other systemic symptoms. Slit-lamp and funduscopic examination showed subconjunctival hemorrhage in the right eye but no anterior-chamber or vitreous inflammation; funduscopy revealed serous retinal detachment in the posterior pole of the right eye, with no active lesions in the left eye.  
On day 8 postpartum, fluorescein angiography demonstrated granular leakages above the optic disc in the right eye and around the disc in the left eye during the early to mid phase. Indocyanine green angiography revealed focal choroidal filling delay in the early phase with mottled hyperfluorescent lesions in the mid phase at corresponding sites. Spectral-domain OCT showed macular serous detachment in the right eye and peripapillary flat detachment in the left eye. Enhanced-depth imaging OCT measured subfoveal choroidal thickness of 501 μm in both eyes and revealed retinal pigment epithelium irregularity with shallow detachment over the optic disc in the right eye.

A 23-year-old woman with skin phototype IV presented with pruritic lesions in her armpits and bikini area that began shortly after she completed five sessions of 755–805 nm Alex/Diode laser hair removal in those regions. She did not develop lesions in other laser‐treated areas (face and lower extremities). She reported no other medical history and no family history of similar lesions. The pruritus worsened with heat and sweating, although her sweating pattern was otherwise unchanged. On examination, there were multiple bilateral, skin-colored, perifollicular papules on both axillae and in the pubic area.

A 28-year-old unmarried woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive shortness of breath and cough with occasional scant sputum. Over the past 2 weeks, her dyspnea worsened to the point that she required supplemental oxygen to maintain saturation. She denied chest pain, hemoptysis, palpitations, limb swelling, fever, or weight loss, and had no known exposures to environmental dusts or toxins. 

On examination, she was alert. Heart rate was 96 bpm, respiratory rate 36/min, and SpO₂ was 62% on room air, improving to 89% with 15 L/min of oxygen (FiO₂ 60%) via Venturi mask. Chest auscultation revealed diffuse bilateral crackles; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14 g/dL, white-cell count 8000/µL, and platelets 250 ×10³/µL. Peripheral smear, liver and renal function tests were normal. Antinuclear antibody and HIV tests were negative. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed PaO₂ 44 mmHg and an alveolar–arterial gradient of 458 mmHg.

A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral interstitial and alveolar opacities, predominant in the mid and lower lung zones. Sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli and Xpert MTB/RIF assay were negative. Transthoracic echocardiography was normal. High‐resolution CT of the chest showed diffuse areas of consolidation and ground-glass opacities with smooth interlobular septal thickening, producing a “crazy‐paving” pattern.

A 49-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of left low back pain. He described unilateral lower lumbar and buttock pain below the L5 spinous process that worsened with sitting, especially on a chair without back support. On examination, neurological findings were normal; there was tenderness over the left posterior iliac spine, and Patrick’s test, Gaenslen’s test, and the SIJ shear test were all positive on the left.  
Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine and pelvis and MRI of the lumbar spine were unremarkable. Blood chemistry studies were within normal limits. A left SIJ block under fluoroscopic guidance provided no relief. The patient was treated with NSAIDs and observed.  

Two weeks later, MRI of the pelvis demonstrated diffuse bone marrow edema in the left SIJ characterized by low T1 signal and high T2 signal. A subsequent CT scan of the pelvis showed no evidence of tumors or fractures. The patient was advised local rest and continued NSAIDs, and his symptoms resolved over the next 3 months.  

Two months after resolution, he returned with right low back pain. Examination findings mirrored those of the initial presentation. MRI revealed new diffuse bone marrow edema in the right SIJ, with resolution of the left SIJ changes. Repeat conservative management with rest and NSAIDs led to symptom resolution and normalization of MRI findings by 5 months. There was no recurrence over 2 years of follow-up.

A 60-year-old man was referred for progressive blurred vision in both eyes over the past 2 years. Three years earlier, he had undergone liver transplantation for hepatitis C–related liver failure. Post-transplant, he developed chronic arterial hypertension and mild renal insufficiency but had no episodes of graft rejection. His current medications were aspirin, amlodipine, furosemide, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil; he had received oral corticosteroids (5–10 mg daily) for 6 months immediately after transplantation.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in each eye. Pupillary responses were normal, and biomicroscopy of the anterior segment was unremarkable. Fundoscopy showed mild hypertensive retinopathy and mottled pigmentary changes in the posterior pole. Spectral-domain OCT demonstrated a serous macular detachment with protein-enriched subretinal fluid and no RPE detachment. Enhanced-depth imaging revealed subfoveal choroidal thickening (450 μm) with hyperreflective dots. Fluorescein angiography showed multiple small (100 μm) round hypofluorescent dots and diffuse pooling around the fovea without any focal leakage points. Fundus autofluorescence revealed round granular hyperautofluorescent lesions corresponding to the hypofluorescent areas on angiography, set against a granular hypoautofluorescent posterior pole. Indocyanine green angiography demonstrated multifocal choroidal vascular hyperpermeability without focal leakage.

A 65-year-old Caucasian woman, lifelong non-smoker with no prior medical history, presented with a 10-month history of progressive breathlessness, dry cough, fatigue, arthralgias, and mild weight loss. On examination, she was afebrile, with palpable bilateral axillary lymph nodes and otherwise normal cardiopulmonary findings. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 4.7×10^3/μL, lymphocytes 0.8×10^3/μL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 42 mm/h; autoantibodies, C-reactive protein, and angiotensin-converting enzyme were within normal limits or negative. Pulmonary-function tests revealed an obstructive pattern (FEV1 66.8% of predicted, FVC 83.4% of predicted) with a mildly reduced DLco (69.7% of predicted). A Mantoux test was negative.

High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated a soft-tissue–density mass at the right hilum extending into the right upper lobe, causing narrowing of the lower trachea, right main bronchus, and lobar branches, and encasing the right pulmonary artery. There were bilateral nodules up to 1 cm with a perivascular distribution in the upper and mid lung zones, enlarged paratracheal, aortopulmonary, mediastinal, and axillary lymph nodes, and a moderate pericardial effusion. These findings were described as consistent with bronchogenic carcinoma.

Bronchoscopy revealed submucosal infiltration and narrowing of the right upper bronchus. Cultures, stains, and cytologic analysis of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid were negative. Endobronchial biopsy specimens unexpectedly showed non-caseating granulomas.

A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented after his fourth generalized tonic-clonic seizure in 2 months. He had been started on levetiracetam after his second seizure but experienced two more breakthrough events. Vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination revealed weakness of the right lower extremity. His family has ties to Western Africa; he last traveled to Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire 2 years earlier. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed a 1.8-cm cortical/subcortical enhancing mass in the left precuneus with significant adjacent vasogenic edema. The lesion demonstrated areas of intrinsic T1 shortening and susceptibility hypointensity with both negative and positive phase shifts, suggesting mineralization and intralesional blood products. Differential diagnoses included cortically based neoplasms (such as oligodendroglioma, pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, and ganglioglioma) and infectious or inflammatory etiologies.

A 61-year-old woman with stage IV cervical cancer metastatic to the liver, peritoneum, pleura, lungs, and adnexa, and a history of hypertension and extensive venous thrombosis, presented to the emergency department with chest pain. Two hours after completing her third cycle of carboplatin and paclitaxel chemotherapy, she developed oppressive chest pain at rest, rated 8/10 on the VAS, radiating to the neck and jaw. On arrival she was tachycardic but hemodynamically stable. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. An ECG showed ST-segment elevation in leads V2 through V6 and inverted T waves. Laboratory studies revealed a troponin level of 0.824 ng/mL (reference 0–0.014 ng/mL) and normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10 g/dL, MCV 77 fL).

A 16-year-old male with a history of moyamoya disease and intellectual disability presented with progressive exertional dyspnea since age 10. His father died of heart failure; his brother had a cerebral infarction at age 18. At 13, an ECG showed elevated R waves in lead V1 and inverted T waves in leads V1–V4, suggestive of right ventricular hypertrophy; mild pulmonary hypertension was suspected on echocardiography. At 16, chest radiography revealed protrusions of the right and left second cardiac arches and a cardiothoracic ratio of 47%. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm at 60 beats/min, an axis of +120°, elevated R waves in V1, and inverted T waves in V1–V4. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed dilation of the main pulmonary artery trunk, right atrial and ventricular enlargement, right ventricular wall thickening, and mosaic attenuation of the lung parenchyma; no pulmonary arterial thrombi were seen. A ventilation–perfusion scan revealed segmental perfusion defects with preserved ventilation. Right heart catheterization measured a mean pulmonary arterial pressure of 63 mmHg, pulmonary artery wedge pressure of 10 mmHg, cardiac output of 3.99 L/min, cardiac index of 2.48 L·min⁻¹·m⁻², and pulmonary vascular resistance of 13.3 Wood units. Pulmonary angiography demonstrated a pouching in the right A₂ segment and abrupt narrowing with poststenotic dilatation of bilateral segmental pulmonary arteries.

A 10-year-old boy sustained a glass laceration to his left proximal forearm with resulting posterior interosseous nerve palsy. Two years later, he underwent tendon transfers (flexor carpi radialis to extensor digitorum and palmaris longus to extensor pollicis longus). Dyed 3-0 polypropylene sutures were used for tendon repair, and polyglactin sutures were used for skin closure. He recovered full finger and thumb extension in neutral wrist position.

Five months after surgery, he noted a slowly enlarging mass at the dorsal wrist over the tendon repair site. Two months later, examination revealed a 3 × 5 cm granulomatous lesion without erythema, warmth, fluctuance, tenderness, fever, or lymphadenopathy. The tendon transfers remained fully functional. Laboratory evaluation showed normal complete blood count, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. To assess for a possible hypersensitivity reaction, two 4-0 polypropylene sutures (one dyed and one undyed) were implanted intradermally in his arm; the test sites remained negative for reaction.

An 87-year-old Japanese man was evaluated after a paraspinal mass was detected on MRI during workup for lumbago. He had undergone surgery for lumbar canal stenosis 19 years earlier. At presentation, his temperature was 37.1 °C. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 8700/μL (normal range, 4000–8000/μL) and a C-reactive protein level of 0.9 mg/dL (normal range, 0–0.2 mg/dL). The neurologic examination was normal.  
Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a soft-tissue mass at the L3–4 level that was hypointense relative to the spinal cord on T1-weighted images and had heterogeneous signal intensity on T2-weighted images.  
Plain computed tomography of the lumbar spine showed a well-circumscribed mass posterior to the lamina of L3 with osteolytic change.

A 76-year-old man presented to dermatology with an 8-month history of diffuse, edematous, red-to-violaceous papules and plaques. A skin punch biopsy from the chest showed minimal spongiosis with a superficial to deep dermal perivascular, periadnexal, and interstitial lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with admixed neutrophils and eosinophils. Laboratory studies revealed peripheral eosinophilia of 24% (normal <5%). He discontinued hydrochlorothiazide and simvastatin out of concern for a drug-induced reaction and was started on prednisone, 60 mg daily.

Over the next weeks, he developed periodic night sweats and new-onset inflammatory arthritis. Peripheral eosinophilia peaked at 32% (absolute count 1.88 × 10^9/L; normal <0.9) and C-reactive protein was 57 mg/L (normal 1–8). Tryptase levels were normal. Peripheral flow cytometry showed a low-count monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis. Two additional punch biopsies demonstrated mild spongiosis with a superficial to mid-dermal perivascular, periadnexal, and interstitial lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with frequent eosinophils and neutrophils, most consistent with a hypersensitivity reaction with an interstitial granuloma annulare–like background. Direct immunofluorescence was negative. A positron emission tomography scan showed mildly avid mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes. He was treated with hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate (up to 25 mg weekly), and intermittent prednisone with improvement in his joint pain.

Four months after initial presentation, he continued to have persistent edematous plaques. A punch biopsy revealed mild spongiosis, focal papillary dermal edema, and a mixed lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with numerous neutrophils and eosinophils; a palisaded neutrophilic granulomatous dermatitis was raised in the differential. Dapsone was added to methotrexate.

Six months after initial presentation, he remained with a diffuse, edematous rash with plaques and studded pustules on his trunk and extremities, with similar findings on biopsy.

A 30-year-old woman underwent wide local excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy for a 15-mm, grade 2 invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast. She received adjuvant chemotherapy with three cycles of fluorouracil (600 mg/m2), epirubicin (75 mg/m2), and cyclophosphamide (600 mg/m2) every 21 days, followed by three cycles of single-agent docetaxel (100 mg/m2 every 21 days). Pegfilgrastim was given 24 hours after each cycle. 

The first two cycles of docetaxel were tolerated with grade 2 fatigue, grade 1–2 nausea, and grade 1 neuropathy. After the fifth total cycle (second docetaxel cycle), she sustained a low-risk needlestick injury from her HIV-positive partner. She had tested HIV-negative three months earlier and was started on post-exposure prophylaxis with Combivir (lamivudine/zidovudine) and Kaletra (lopinavir/ritonavir) one week before her third cycle of docetaxel. Standard dexamethasone prophylaxis was given.

Pre-treatment blood tests were normal. On day 6 after docetaxel, she was admitted with fever, grade 2 mucositis, grade 2 arthralgia, and myalgia. White-cell count was 1.3 × 10^9/L with a neutrophil count of 0.6 × 10^9/L, dropping to 0.005 × 10^9/L the next day. Renal and hepatic function remained normal. She was started on piperacillin-tazobactam, gentamicin, and fluconazole. Blood cultures grew a sensitive Cellulosimicrobium species, then cleared.

Over the next days, mucositis progressed to grade 4, fevers persisted, and neutropenia continued despite teicoplanin, meropenem, gentamicin, increased fluconazole, and daily GCSF. Neutrophils recovered to 2.1 × 10^9/L on day 7, but she then developed diarrhea followed by facial swelling and erythema on day 10. She stopped antiretrovirals herself and a florid desquamating rash appeared on her hands and feet. Fluconazole was changed to caspofungin, and CT thorax was negative for fungal infection. Topical treatments were applied.

Two weeks after admission, her condition failed to improve.

A 48-year-old woman was found to have a mass in the left retroperitoneum during a routine follow-up examination. She reported no abdominal pain, weight loss, or other symptoms. Her history was notable only for brain surgery 6 months earlier for a ruptured intracranial aneurysm and a 6-year history of well-controlled hypertension treated with amlodipine. On examination, she was afebrile, with a blood pressure of 124/86 mmHg, and her abdominal and costovertebral–angle examinations were unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests showed a mildly low plasma albumin level; all other results, including complete blood count, serum electrolytes, and tumor markers, were normal. Endocrine evaluation—24-hour urinary cortisol and catecholamines, plasma potassium, and serum adrenocortical hormones—was within normal limits, as were serum amylase and lipase. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-circumscribed, oval cystic mass measuring 54×40 mm adjacent to the left adrenal gland, with homogeneous attenuation of 85 HU and no enhancement.

A 30-year-old primigravid woman with a 12-year history of chronic pulmonary disease presented for routine antenatal care. At age 8, she had been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis and had chest tube drainage for empyema. Since that time, she reported recurrent episodes of fever, cough, and dyspnea. 

On examination, the trachea was deviated to the right. Auscultation revealed diffuse crackles over the right lung field. Spirometry showed moderate obstructive impairment (FEV1/FVC, 69%). 

A chest radiograph demonstrated cicatricial collapse and hyperlucency of the right lung. Computed tomography of the thorax revealed markedly decreased attenuation of the right lung and of the basal segment of the left lung, diminished right hilar vessels, and bronchiectasis.

An elderly man with diabetes, ischemic heart disease, and peripheral vascular disease had sudden cardiovascular collapse after several episodes of hematemesis. He underwent 20 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation with defibrillation and inotropic support, regained circulation, and was admitted to the intensive care unit intubated and ventilated. Upper endoscopy showed marked luminal narrowing of the esophagus due to diffuse submucosal swelling and bluish mucosal discoloration without evidence of perforation, suggesting a submucosal hematoma. Contrast-enhanced CT aortography demonstrated a diffusely swollen esophagus and a small focus of contrast extravasation in the distal esophageal wall on arterial-phase images with progressive pooling on delayed-phase images, indicating active hemorrhage.

A 46-year-old man presented with a slow-growing nodule behind his left ear, present for 30 years. He denied pain, discharge, or systemic symptoms, and had no significant medical history aside from a childhood bump injury to the area. On examination, there was a 3 cm, soft, slightly tender, subcutaneous nodule with unremarkable overlying skin on the left temporal scalp. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were within normal limits. Two-view skull radiographs showed no abnormality. The mass was then completely excised under local anesthesia, revealing an elliptical capsule adherent to the periosteum of the temporal bone.

A previously healthy 12-year-old boy presented with 1 day of progressive right lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever to 40°C. Three days before admission, he had vomiting and persistent fever of 38°C treated with antipyretics and antibiotics by a pharmacist. He was taken to surgery without prior imaging or laboratory studies and underwent an open appendectomy; the appendix appeared normal macroscopically.

Two days after surgery, a COVID-19 RT-PCR test was negative. On postoperative day 5, because of unremitting fever and new conjunctivitis, wound and blood cultures were obtained, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were started; the wound culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and blood cultures were negative. On postoperative day 10, he developed diffuse abdominal pain. An abdominopelvic CT scan with contrast showed a few enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, minimal free fluid in the right iliac fossa, and a liver edge enlarged to 15 cm. A rapid SARS-CoV-2 test was positive for IgG antibodies and negative for IgM antibodies.

Fever persisted for 2 weeks after appendectomy. He then developed orthopnea, bilateral lower extremity pitting edema, and bilateral basal fine crepitations. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. Cardiac troponin I was elevated; total CK and CK-MB were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal coronary arteries, normal left ventricular dimensions, ejection fraction of 76%, mild tricuspid regurgitation with right ventricular systolic pressure of 30 mm Hg, mild mitral regurgitation, congested inferior vena cava, and no pericardial effusion.

Chest CT without contrast revealed bilateral mild pleural effusions and was classified as CO-RADS category 1, indicating a very low level of suspicion for pulmonary COVID-19 involvement. Laboratory investigations revealed markedly elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, D-dimer, ferritin), neutrophilia, hypoalbuminemia, and thrombocytosis.

A male newborn, born at 38 weeks’ gestation by cesarean section (birth weight, 3.6 kg), had an uneventful prenatal and perinatal course. Beginning on day 1 of life, he had nonbilious vomiting after each feed, which progressed to bilious vomiting and jaundice on day 3 without fever or diarrhea. On day 6, his parents noted an abdominal swelling in the epigastric area and brought him to the hospital.

On examination, he was in good general condition but mildly dehydrated, with visible jaundice; heart rate was 120 beats per minute. The abdomen was soft, and there was a palpable, mobile mass in the epigastrium and right hypochondrium without skin changes or fixation to the anterior abdominal wall. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 11.8 g/dL, a white-cell count of 9000 /mm3, a platelet count of 763 000 /mm3, and a total bilirubin level of 15 mg/dL.

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 4.5 × 3.8 cm cystic structure in the epigastric region that was not adherent to the liver or kidneys, with an undetermined origin. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen identified a 5 × 5 cm cystic mass with dense fluid content located between the liver and the right kidney, with its posterior border abutting the right kidney.

A 27-year-old woman was evaluated for a 3-year history of hirsutism, acne, menstrual irregularities, and mood changes. On examination, she had skin thinning, a dorsocervical fat pad, moon facies, proximal muscle weakness, and blood pressure of 145/90 mm Hg. Laboratory studies showed an elevated morning cortisol level of 702 nmol/L (reference range, 130–690), suppressed ACTH of 3.2 pg/mL (9–52), a 24-hour urinary free cortisol of 221 μg (20–90), loss of diurnal cortisol rhythm (16:00, 693 nmol/L; 00:00, 694 nmol/L), and failure to suppress cortisol (800 nmol/L) after a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test. Adrenal CT demonstrated a 2 cm mass in the left adrenal gland, while the right gland appeared normal.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a 10-year history of intermittent pricking and burning pain in the left soft palate, radiating to the left ear and associated with difficulty swallowing. She described the pain as triggered by touching the region with her tongue or finger. There was no history of trauma. Over the past year, she had been treated at otorhinolaryngology clinics with antibiotics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for otic pain and a sensation of ear fullness; her symptoms recurred whenever the medications were discontinued. One year earlier, local corticosteroid injection near the hamular region produced symptom relief for 1 year. On oral examination, a firm, palpable mass was noted in the left soft palate just medial and posterior to the maxillary tuberosity; the overlying mucosa was normal. Palpation of the mass elicited burning pain in the hard and soft palate. Orthopantomography was unremarkable. Computed tomography revealed that the left pterygoid hamulus protruded more medially than the right side.

A 41-year-old Hispanic woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 4-week history of fatigue, malaise, spontaneous ecchymoses, bleeding gums, and subjective fevers. She had no personal or family history of autoimmune, hematologic, or oncologic disease. On examination, she had bilateral upper-extremity ecchymoses, pale conjunctivae, mucosal pallor, and scattered petechiae.

Laboratory studies on admission revealed:
  • CBC: WBC 1.2 × 10^3/µL, RBC 1.22 × 10^6/µL, hemoglobin 4.6 g/dL, hematocrit 13.4%, MCV 110.3 fL, platelets 13 × 10^3/µL, neutrophils 0.3 × 10^3/µL, lymphocytes 0.9 × 10^3/µL.  
  • Coagulation: PT 15.2 s (reference 12.5–14.2), INR 1.22, PTT 25.2 s.  
  • Peripheral smear: circulating blasts.

Bone marrow aspirate (day 2) showed ~70% immature myeloid blasts; flow cytometry revealed strong CD117 and dim HLA-DR expression. Cytogenetic analysis demonstrated 47,X,t(X;8)(q13;q24.1),+8 in 6 of 20 metaphases. Molecular studies were positive for CEBPA, IDH1, U2FA1, and JAK2 and negative for P53, FLT3, NPM1, and RUNX1.

She received induction chemotherapy with daunorubicin (60 mg/m^2/day on days 1–3) and cytarabine (100 mg/m^2/day on days 4–10). Eleven days after completing the first cycle, her PT rose to 18.7 s with an INR of 1.61, despite a PT of 14.7 s while receiving induction chemotherapy.

A 54-year-old woman was referred for transthoracic echocardiography before general anesthesia for cataract surgery. She had a history of left-sided invasive ductal breast carcinoma treated 8 years earlier with mastectomy, chemotherapy, trastuzumab, and radiotherapy. She was asymptomatic and afebrile. On examination, a systolic murmur was heard at the mitral area. Blood tests, including CA 125, were within normal limits; there was no hyperleukocytosis or elevated C-reactive protein. The electrocardiogram was unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a soft-tissue–appearing mass with central echolucencies on the posterior mitral annulus, impeding posterior-leaflet motion and resulting in mitral regurgitation. There was no acoustic shadowing and no flow on color Doppler. The patient declined transesophageal echocardiography. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed a low-signal mass at the posterior mitral annulus on cine images, blocking the posterior leaflet and causing regurgitation, with extension into adjacent myocardium. The lesion was high signal on T1-weighted black-blood images, low signal on STIR sequences, and demonstrated peripheral intense enhancement on late gadolinium–enhanced images.

An 84-year-old man underwent right-eye phacoemulsification for cataract; the procedure was complicated by a posterior capsule rent, and an anterior-chamber intraocular lens was placed. One week later, he presented with lacrimation, corneal edema with keratic precipitates, anterior-chamber and vitreous haze, and absence of a retinal red reflex on indirect ophthalmoscopy. A vitreous tap was performed, and intravitreal vancomycin (1 mg) and ceftazidime (2 mg) were administered. The following day, lid edema, conjunctival hyperemia, corneal striae, and worsened anterior-chamber inflammation were noted. Vitreous cultures at 48 hours showed no growth. On postoperative day 11, corneal decompensation worsened; intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime were repeated, subconjunctival methylprednisolone was given, and a bandage contact lens was placed. On day 14, with no improvement, intravitreal amphotericin B and oral fluconazole were administered for presumed fungal endophthalmitis. On day 16, three-port pars plana vitrectomy was performed with repeat intravitreal vancomycin and sampling for microbiology; the next day, new grayish flocculent material reappeared in the vitreous and anterior chamber, and amphotericin B plus ceftazidime were again given without clinical improvement. On day 20, a second vitrectomy with intravitreal amikacin was performed. Vitreous cultures again showed no growth; samples were reserved for potassium hydroxide preparation and Gram stain.

An 18-year-old otherwise healthy female presented with a 4-month history of a growth on her tongue that was painful on mastication, as well as recent onset of stomach cramps and nausea. She also noted lesions in her anal and vaginal areas. She smokes two cigarettes per day and self-medicated with ibuprofen, paracetamol, and a topical agent. She reported being sexually active.  
On examination, there was right submandibular lymphadenopathy. A panoramic radiograph showed missing teeth 18, 36, and 37; a root remnant at tooth 46 with periapical radiolucency; impacted teeth 23, 28, and 48; a retained tooth 53; and over-eruption of teeth 26 and 27.  
Intraorally, there were multiple ulcerations over the soft palate and mucous patches on the hard palate, uvula, and right retromolar area. The tongue had multiple indurated papillary nodules on the tip, anterior lateral, mid-lateral, and ventral surfaces.  
Based on the history and clinical presentation, the differential diagnosis included bacterial infections (such as tuberculosis and syphilis), deep fungal infections (such as mucormycosis and blastomycosis), and metabolic disease (such as Crohn’s disease). Special investigations including serologic tests and incisional biopsy were performed with patient consent.

A 69‐year‐old man with a 35–pack‐year smoking history and recurrent infective exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease requiring multiple hospitalizations over 2 years presented with fever, shortness of breath, cough, hemoptysis, and a 6‐month history of progressive weight loss (admission weight 39 kg; BMI 12 kg/m2). His father had COPD; there was no family history of lung cancer or connective tissue disorders. He denied occupational exposures.

On examination, he appeared cachectic and diaphoretic and was in moderate respiratory distress. Vital signs were: temperature 37.9 °C, pulse 96/min, respiratory rate 38/min, blood pressure 146/94 mm Hg. Chest examination revealed hyperinflation, bronchial breathing over the left upper chest, and scattered wheezes.

A chest radiograph showed upper‐zone emphysema, irregular pleural thickening, and a rounded mass‐like density in the left apex, raising a differential of aspergilloma versus pleural mass. Chest CT demonstrated marked widening of the trachea and main bronchi (sagittal diameter 38 mm; transverse 27 mm) along with cavitary lesions containing internal masses in the left upper lobe. A serum galactomannan assay was positive on two occasions.

A 40-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with a 3-day history of nasal discharge and sore throat, and 1 day of fever. Her husband had similar symptoms, and several of his colleagues had been diagnosed with COVID-19. On presentation, her temperature was 40.0°C, SpO₂ was 92% on room air, and she was alert. Examination revealed lymphatic follicles on the posterior pharyngeal wall but no cervical lymphadenopathy; lung auscultation was clear. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13,200/µL (90.1% neutrophils, 3.9% lymphocytes) and a C-reactive protein level of 3.06 mg/dL; liver and renal function studies were within normal limits. Chest radiography showed ground-glass opacity in the right lower lung field, and chest CT demonstrated pan-lobular ground-glass opacities in both lower lobes. A nasopharyngeal swab RT-LAMP test for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. The patient was admitted and placed in isolation.

An 18-year-old man was evaluated for short stature, delayed puberty, and a one-year history of exertional dyspnea and dizziness. He had a history of small-bowel resection in the neonatal period—from 50 cm below the ligament of Treitz to 5 cm above the ileocecal valve—resulting in short-bowel syndrome. Total parenteral nutrition had been gradually replaced by enteral feeding, but he was lost to follow-up after age 4. He denied substance use and was not sexually active.

On examination, he appeared chronically ill and pale. Vital signs were: blood pressure 113/77 mmHg, pulse 95 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, temperature 36.1 °C. Height was 137.7 cm (below the 3rd percentile) and weight 28.9 kg (below the 3rd percentile). Pubic hair and genital development were Tanner stage I (testis volume <4 mL). Other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 3.3 g/dL, hematocrit 12.5%, mean corpuscular volume 86.2 fl, mean corpuscular hemoglobin 22.8 pg, red cell distribution width 22.2%, and reticulocyte count 0.59% (reticulocyte production index, 0.16). White blood cell count was 4,900/mm3 and platelet count 182,000/mm3. Iron studies revealed serum iron 23 µg/dL (normal 50–170), total iron-binding capacity 534 µg/dL (normal 280–400), and ferritin 2.5 ng/mL (normal 20–320). Serum vitamin B12 was 60 pg/mL (normal 211–911) and serum folic acid 11.3 ng/mL (normal >5.4). Peripheral smear showed normocytic, hypochromic red cells with marked anisocytosis, mild poikilocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils, and mild thrombocytopenia.

A man in his twenties with no significant medical history presented with an erythematous rash tracking proximally up his left arm, accompanied by numbness and paresthesias, developing two weeks after trauma to his left hand. He was admitted for presumed cellulitis with acute lymphangitic spread.  
During admission, he reported a second skin lesion on the medial aspect of his left plantar foot that appeared one month earlier. This lesion was erythematous, serpiginous, intensely pruritic, and frequently changed location overnight. Topical antibiotic ointment and hydrogen peroxide produced no improvement.  
He lived with dogs and stray cats and worked as a roofer, frequently handling sand and soil, and occasionally wore flip-flop sandals but denied barefoot walking outside, beach visits, water-spring exposure, or recent travel. He denied fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting, dyspnea, headaches, or vision changes.  
On examination, both hands had multiple traumatic lesions with pustules and bullae; the left wrist showed a large blood-filled blister with surrounding erythema tracking toward the arm. The left plantar foot had an erythematous, tortuous serpiginous lesion with a migrating track adjacent to a 4 cm patch of erythema with a central scab and bullae. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies on admission revealed a white-cell count of 15.3×10^9/L (4.0–10×10^9/L), C-reactive protein of 22.69 mg/dL (0–5 mg/L), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 32 mm/h (0–10 mm/h). The absolute eosinophil count was 0.14×10^9/L (0.03–0.46×10^9/L), comprising 15% of total leukocytes.

A 90-year-old Japanese man was admitted for lethargy of 3 days’ duration. He had been working as a general practitioner until 3 days before admission. His past history included hypertension and prostatic hypertrophy; there was no psychiatric history. Two days before admission he began repeating inconsistent stories and talking to unseen persons. He was drowsy but intermittent cheerfulness was noted. 

On examination, blood pressure was 160/100 mmHg, pulse 60 beats/minute, and temperature 36.3 °C. There was no dry skin, hoarseness, nonpitting edema, or other obvious hypothyroid signs. He was somnolent, disoriented to place and date, and carried on a one-sided monologue. Neurologic findings included hearing loss, gait disturbance with small steps and hesitation, and asymmetry of limb strength; there was no sensory deficit.

Laboratory studies showed a thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 105.87 mIU/ml (normal 0.54–4.26) and a free thyroxine level of 0.34 ng/dl (normal 0.71–1.52). Thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin antibodies were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a normal cell count and mildly elevated protein (58.5 mg/dl).

Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen demonstrated left pleural effusion and moderate ascites. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head showed crescent-shaped T2 hyperintense foci beneath the dura, interpreted as slight effusion, and generalized brain atrophy. Electroencephalography revealed slow α- and θ-waves. N-isopropyl-p-(iodine-123)-iodoamphetamine SPECT showed decreased cerebral blood flow in both frontal lobes.

A 50-year-old woman was referred for treatment of limited mouth opening. She reported onset of jaw immobility at age 12 after a fall; details were unclear. She also had a history of right-sided otitis media more than 20 years ago. On examination, facial asymmetry was noted and maximal interincisal opening was 2 mm. Panoramic radiograph showed bony fusion of the right temporomandibular joint with a prominent right antegonial notch, deviation of the mandible to the right, multiple dental caries, retained roots, and generalized alveolar bone loss; the left condyle had a well-defined outline. CT imaging revealed a large bony mass obliterating the right TMJ space, loss of air cells in the temporal squama and mastoid, and a thickened right zygomatic arch; the left TMJ maintained a normal articular space. MRI demonstrated a fused bone mass with normal marrow signal in the right TMJ and, in the left TMJ, flattening of the condyle, a thin disk, and irregular cortical bone of the articular fossa and condyle. A 3D rapid-prototyping model confirmed fusion of the right condyle to the zygomatic arch and abnormal bone formation around the joint, and a narrowed articular space in the left TMJ. Radiographically, the differential diagnosis for the right TMJ mass included benign bone tumors such as osteochondroma, osteoma, chondroma, chondroblastoma, osteoblastoma, fibro-osteoma, fibrous dysplasia, myxoma, and giant cell tumor.

A 63-year-old woman with a 5-year history of sarcoidosis involving the eyes and skin presented with progressive dyspnea and palpitations on minimal exertion. An ECG showed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia and frequent ventricular extrasystoles. Her NT-proBNP level was 729 pg/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an elevated right atrial–right ventricular pressure gradient; no thrombus was seen in the left atrium, left ventricle, or atrial appendage. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed no thrombus in the pulmonary arteries or major veins. FDG-PET did not show myocardial uptake, excluding cardiac sarcoidosis. Right heart catheterization showed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 44 mm Hg, a pulmonary artery wedge pressure of 5 mm Hg, and a cardiac index of 2.2 L/min/m2. Holter monitoring revealed sinus rhythm without atrial fibrillation. She was diagnosed with pulmonary arterial hypertension related to sarcoidosis and was started on warfarin and selexipag. A few days after discharge, she developed sudden left-sided hemiplegia.  

Head CT showed no intracranial hemorrhage. Diffusion-weighted MRI of the brain revealed acute infarctions in the left frontal and parietal lobes.

A 32-year-old university-educated man and smoker with treatment-resistant schizophrenia was started on clozapine 450 mg daily. After 9 months, trifluoperazine 20 mg daily was added because of a partial response. Weekly hematological monitoring was performed for 5 months, then monthly for the next 26 months, during which he remained stable.

Thirty-five months after starting clozapine, he developed sudden high-grade fever without focal symptoms. A complete blood count showed a total leukocyte count of 1100/mm3 with an absolute neutrophil count of zero; the differential count was 98% lymphocytes, 1% monocytes, and 1% eosinophils. Hemoglobin was 13.5 g/dL, and the platelet count was 1.5/μL. He had no history of antibiotics, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or antiepileptic use.

On examination, there was a small ulcer on the prepuce and a tender right axillary swelling. Evaluation for hematological malignancies; autoimmune disorders (systemic lupus erythematosus, Crohn’s disease, rheumatoid arthritis); and infections (bacterial, tubercular, and viral, including HIV, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and hepatitis) included serum electrolytes; renal and liver function tests; chest radiography; urine analysis and culture; blood cultures for bacteria and fungi; electrocardiography; and echocardiography—all of which were unremarkable. Additional testing (EBV IgM antibody, Widal test, dengue IgM antibody, malaria smear, abdominal ultrasound, and VDRL) did not reveal any abnormality. Fine-needle aspiration of the axillary mass grew Proteus mirabilis sensitive to piperacillin–tazobactam, and his fever improved with antibiotic therapy.

An 18-year-old man presented with one week of continuous high-grade fever without chills or rigors, accompanied by vomiting and one day of altered sensorium progressing to delirium and unconsciousness. On examination, he was unconscious; pulse 82/min, respiratory rate 14/min, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg; heart sounds were normal, lungs were clear, and there was right hypochondrial tenderness without organomegaly. He was diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum cerebral malaria (ring forms 1/1000 RBCs) and severe thrombocytopenia, with evidence of DIC (prolonged PT, APTT, fibrinogen 64 mg/dL) and elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin. He required mechanical ventilation and received multiple blood components, including platelets and fresh frozen plasma.

Immediately after several platelet transfusions, he developed diffuse rash, bronchospasm, endotracheal secretions, hypoxemia, tachycardia, and acute breathlessness. A clerical check excluded misidentification. Postreaction sample showed no hemolysis on inspection. Initial blood group was O Rh-positive with negative antibody screen; on day five direct antiglobulin test was positive but indirect Coombs and antibody screening by three-cell panel were negative. Blood cultures of components and patient sample were sterile. Gel column hemagglutination showed IgG antibodies and no IgA. Serum immunoglobulin measurement revealed elevated IgE levels.

A 14-year-old Indian girl with acute promyelocytic leukemia was started on induction therapy with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide. She developed sudden-onset shortness of breath and a chest radiograph showed bilateral middle and lower zone alveolar infiltrates with relative sparing of the upper zones. On admission, laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 6.5 g/dL, a total leukocyte count of 6.7 × 10^9/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 62 mm/h, and a platelet count of 1.85 × 10^9/L. Shortly after initiation of therapy, she developed worsening respiratory distress with increasing oxygen dependence and was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit. The differentiation agents were discontinued, and dexamethasone and bilevel positive airway pressure were initiated. A computed tomography scan of the chest demonstrated multiple bilateral pulmonary parenchymal nodules with surrounding ground-glass opacity predominantly in the lower lobes, with relative sparing of the upper lobes. The differential diagnosis based on imaging included infective causes (bacterial, viral, fungal), leukemic infiltrates, acute respiratory distress syndrome, leukostasis, drug toxicity, pulmonary edema, and pulmonary hemorrhage.

A 22-year-old previously healthy white man presented with sudden onset of lower abdominal pain for 2 days. The pain began centrally and then localized to the right lower quadrant and was associated with anorexia, nausea, and two episodes of nonbilious vomiting. He had no urinary symptoms or prior similar episodes. His review of systems was otherwise unremarkable, and his past medical history was insignificant. 

On examination, he appeared uncomfortable but was afebrile. His pulse was 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/80 mm Hg, and body mass index 27.8. Abdominal palpation revealed focal guarding and tenderness in the right iliac fossa; the remainder of the examination was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14 100 /μL with 81% neutrophils and a C-reactive protein level of 44 mg/dL. Urinalysis was normal. 

He was admitted for observation and received intravenous fluids and analgesia. After 8 hours, his pain intensified. With an Alvarado score of 9 out of 10 indicating a high likelihood of acute appendicitis, the team proceeded to diagnostic laparoscopy with planned appendectomy without preoperative imaging.

A female infant was born at 35 weeks’ gestation by uncomplicated caesarian section to a G2P2 mother, weight 2460 g. Prenatal ultrasound had repeatedly shown a markedly distended bladder, which was drained in utero on three occasions. After birth, the patient exhibited abdominal distension, a palpable enlarged bladder, massive hematuria, failure to pass meconium, and feeding intolerance. On day 2 of life, she was referred for surgical evaluation for presumed Prune Belly Syndrome. Abdominal ultrasound showed a distended urinary bladder with bilateral uretero-hydronephrosis. Voiding cystography demonstrated a markedly enlarged bladder without vesicoureteral reflux. Initial labs were notable for hemoglobin 12 g/dL and white blood cell count 9800/mm3. A rectal tube was placed and bladder instillations with saline, antibiotics, and hemostatic agents were recommended twice daily. On day 4, the neonate developed bilious vomiting and marked abdominal distension. A thoraco-abdominal radiograph revealed pneumoperitoneum, and contrast studies confirmed perforations of the stomach and distal colon. Repeat labs showed a white blood cell count of 23 000/mm3 and C-reactive protein of 12.6 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 49 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.10 mg/dL.

An 11-month-old black Limousin-cross heifer was referred for investigation of an 8-month history of episodic seizures and a 3-month history of skin lesions. Neurologic signs began at 3 months of age with intermittent lateral recumbency and paddling of all limbs; postictal ataxia and altered mentation were noted. Initial treatment with intravenous dexamethasone and multivitamins produced only temporary improvement. At 8 months, shortly after turnout to pasture, the heifer developed a large erosive, exudative alopecic area (15×10 cm) in the lumbosacral region, crusting and alopecia on the lateral thigh distal to the stifle, and crusting of the elbows. Ocular changes included ulceration of the right lower palpebra, crusting of the upper palpebra, thickening and depigmentation of the left lower lid, and bilateral epiphora.

On presentation the animal was bright and alert, with a body condition score of 2.75/5 and stature below that of cohort heifers. Neurologic examination was normal except for bilateral facial and nasal hypalgesia. Heart rate, respiratory rate, and rectal temperature were within normal limits. Videos supplied by the farmer showed forelimb hypermetria, stiffness, and ataxia following seizure episodes.

Initial differential diagnoses for the dermatologic lesions included Type-1, Type-2, or Type-3 photosensitisation and immune-mediated dermatoses. Neurologic differentials included cerebrocortical necrosis, brain abscessation, meningitis, lead poisoning, epilepsy, and neurologic signs associated with certain photosensitisation syndromes. 

Haematology was within normal limits. Serum biochemistry revealed a Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase of 80 U/L (reference 0–36 U/L), Glutamate Dehydrogenase of 91 U/L (0–19 U/L), and albumin of 26.3 g/L (29–39 g/L). A faecal sample was negative for Fasciola hepatica eggs.

A 53-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 9 years, treated with methotrexate and leflunomide, presented with 2 weeks of pain and swelling in the right calf. She denied fever, cough, skin erythema, or prolonged immobility. Two years earlier, she had two similar episodes in the same calf, each treated with incision and drainage—yielding 1 liter of pus—and parenteral antibiotics, with poor recovery. On examination, her right calf was swollen and tender, the overlying skin was warm but not erythematous, and a scar from prior incision was present. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 8200/μL with 75% neutrophils, an ESR of 114 mm/hr, a CRP of 33.4 mg/L, and normal procalcitonin. Blood, urine, and pus cultures (aerobic, anaerobic, fungal, and mycobacterial) were sterile; Gram and Ziehl–Neelsen stains were negative. Ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic, loculated collection in the medial gastrocnemius muscle with no Doppler uptake and no thrombosis. MRI of the right leg demonstrated a 4 × 4 × 1.5 cm loculated collection in the medial head of the gastrocnemius, mild to moderate knee effusion, synovial thickening, and patchy marrow edema in the lateral femoral condyle.

A 26-year-old Mexican man presented with sudden-onset dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. He denied recent respiratory infections or chest trauma. His history included two prior spontaneous pneumothoraces: a right pneumothorax in 2010 requiring chest-tube drainage and a left pneumothorax in 2014 managed with supplemental oxygen. A prior CT had shown a pulmonary parenchymal abnormality of uncertain etiology. His father was diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis at age 30 on routine imaging but remained asymptomatic and declined biopsy. The patient had no history of smoking, drug use, occupational, or environmental exposures.

On examination, blood pressure was 123/71 mmHg, pulse 88/min, respirations 16/min, temperature 36.6°C, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Respiratory and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, negative autoantibodies and rheumatological markers, normal serum calcium levels, and normal liver function tests. Cardiac evaluation was unremarkable.

A chest radiograph showed subtle bibasilar reticular opacities without a clear pneumothorax. A thoracic CT scan demonstrated a small right-sided pneumothorax and background subpleural and peribronchovascular opacities in posterior dependent regions, with dense, partly calcified linear reticulations most consistent with dendriform pulmonary ossification.

A young primigravid woman with no past medical history underwent an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery of a healthy female newborn at full term. Four hours after delivery, she reported noticing bilateral swelling of her face and neck. Vital signs were within normal limits and she was afebrile. On examination, widespread crepitus was palpable across the right side of the neck radiating toward the jaw. Respiratory examination revealed clear lungs on auscultation, equal bilateral air entry, and no tracheal deviation. A chest X-ray showed extensive bilateral subcutaneous emphysema throughout the thorax and base of the neck with no visible pneumothorax or pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and cervical region demonstrated a moderate pneumomediastinum and extensive subcutaneous emphysema in the neck, supraclavicular fossae, axillae, and upper chest wall, with no overt evidence of esophageal injury.

A 29-year-old manual labourer presented with a 4-day history of fever, myalgia, and oliguria. He had no chronic illnesses but was addicted to heroin. On admission, he was febrile (102 °F), icteric, and complained of severe myalgia. Vital signs: HR 110 b/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, SpO₂ 96% on room air. Laboratory studies showed WBC 13.1 × 10⁹/L with neutrophilia, platelets 31 × 10⁹/L, CRP 234 mg/L, and creatinine 189 µmol/L. ECG revealed anterior T-wave inversions and a troponin I of 3 ng/mL. He was treated as severe leptospirosis with IV cefotaxime. On day 2, he developed hypotension, hemoptysis, and worsening renal failure (creatinine 245 µmol/L) requiring ICU transfer. In the ICU, HR 115 b/min, BP 90/40 mmHg, mild LV dysfunction on echo, RR 32 breaths/min, bilateral alveolar shadows on chest X-ray, and normal coagulation. He received fluids, noradrenaline, plasma exchange, methylprednisolone, and dialysis. Leptospira microagglutination was positive. He improved over 5 days and was weaned off vasopressors and oxygen. On ICU day 6, he became confused, agitated, and developed refractory generalized tonic-clonic seizures with BP rising to 160/120 mmHg, requiring intubation. He was sedated with midazolam and started on levetiracetam. Noncontrast head CT showed hypodense lesions in both occipital regions.

A 59-year-old woman presented with insidious onset of right leg radicular pain without numbness, tingling, weakness, or bladder/bowel symptoms. Physical examination showed a positive right straight-leg–raise test at 45° (left at 70°). Lumbosacral MRI demonstrated a right L4–L5 lateral disc herniation with extrusion. After partial relief with conservative management, she underwent right L4–L5 hemilaminotomy and removal of extruded disc material, with immediate postoperative pain relief.

Two weeks after discharge, she experienced new, constant burning pain in the left pelvic region, with sharp, shooting pain in the left leg radiating in multiple trajectories without a specific dermatomal distribution. The pain worsened while sitting and was not aggravated by coughing or sneezing. On examination, there was no infection or dehiscence of the lumbar surgical scar. She had an antalgic, waddling gait and a significant Tinel sign over the left gluteal region at the sciatic nerve. The straight-leg–raise test was negative in supine, sitting, and prone positions. Spinal range of motion was full without pain; muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes were normal. The piriformis stretch test was significantly positive and reproduced her pain. Repeat lumbosacral MRI showed only postoperative changes without disc herniation.

Over the next weeks, she underwent a multimodality pain regimen (antiepileptic and antidepressant medications, muscle relaxant, short-acting narcotics, and physical therapy) without significant relief. A diagnostic ultrasound-guided injection of 5 cc 1% lidocaine into the left piriformis muscle produced immediate pain relief, and a second injection provided again only a short course of relief.

A female infant, born at 38 weeks’ gestation by cesarean delivery for cephalopelvic disproportion, weighed 2810 g (10th–25th percentile). On day 1 she was tachypneic and had one episode of mild hypoglycemia (blood glucose 27 mg/dL). An elevated C-reactive protein and chest radiograph suggesting pneumonia prompted empiric piperacillin and netilmicin; blood cultures remained negative after five days and antibiotics were discontinued. Newborn screening thyrotropin (TSH) was undetectable (0 μU/mL; reference range 0–15 μU/mL). Over the next two weeks she developed progressive feeding difficulties, muscular hypotonia, somnolence, and jaundice (peak bilirubin 15.8 mg/dL). On day 19, serum free thyroxine was 0.8 pmol/L (normal 12–22 pmol/L), free triiodothyronine was 0.4 pmol/L (normal 3.0–8.4 pmol/L), and TSH was 0.05 μU/mL (normal 0.27–4.2 μU/mL).

A 48-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of dry cough and occasional dyspnea on exertion, unintentional weight loss of 10 kg, fatigue, and lack of energy. He also reported occasional left flank and lower back pain over the preceding weeks and a 2-week history of fever about 6 weeks earlier. He denied night sweats, hemoptysis, or sick contacts and had stopped smoking 2 months prior. He had no significant medical history and took no regular medications.

On examination, he appeared mildly pale and ill, coughing continuously. Vital signs were within normal limits. Cardiovascular exam was unremarkable. Respiratory examination revealed decreased air entry in the left lower lung lobe. Abdominal exam showed tenderness in the left hypochondriac region without palpable masses.

Laboratory studies showed mild hypochromic microcytic anemia, C-reactive protein 139 mg/L, ferritin 149 ng/mL, and adrenocorticotropic hormone 67.9 pg/mL. Cortisol and aldosterone levels were normal. Electrolytes, liver, and renal function tests were normal. A Quantiferon test was negative, and stool occult blood testing was negative.

Chest radiographs demonstrated elevation of the left hemidiaphragm with visible bowel loops on both anterior–posterior and lateral views. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed a well-defined cystic lesion measuring 14.2 × 13.5 × 13.1 cm in the left suprarenal region, with a thin wall, areas of rim calcification, and proteinaceous/hemorrhagic contents. The left adrenal gland was not visualized separately. There was eventration of the left diaphragmatic dome and atelectasis of the left lower lung lobe. No lymphadenopathy or pleural/pericardial effusions were seen.

A 13-year-old previously healthy girl presented with a 4-day history of perioral swelling, necrotic black ulcerations around the mouth, and a tender right-sided neck swelling. She also reported fever, fatigue, and progressive decline in her general condition. On examination, there was severe lip edema with necrotic lesions, surrounding erythema, warmth, and exudate in the submental and perioral regions, along with violaceous ecchymoses on the skin. A right cervical mass was tender, and oropharyngeal examination revealed tonsillar hypertrophy with peritonsillar swelling suggestive of an abscess.

Laboratory studies showed lymphocytosis (12 500 cells/mm³), a C-reactive protein level of 230 mg/L, and a procalcitonin level of 2 g/L. Contrast-enhanced cervical CT demonstrated a peritonsillar abscess with mild narrowing of the pharyngeal lumen; the cervical bones and adjacent soft tissues appeared normal.

A 54-year-old woman with recently diagnosed early-stage invasive ductal breast carcinoma (ER+, PR+, HER2+) started adjuvant chemotherapy with docetaxel, carboplatin, trastuzumab, and pertuzumab every 3 weeks (TCHP), with dexamethasone premedication and granulocyte colony–stimulating factor support. Seven days after her first infusion she developed persistent diarrhea, and five days later she had melenic diarrhea and dizziness without vomiting, fever, chills, or abdominal pain. She had no history of peptic ulcer disease or alcohol abuse but had been taking ibuprofen intermittently (≈400 mg/day). On admission she was afebrile, normotensive, and had no abdominal tenderness. Her hemoglobin fell from 11.7 to 8.4 g/dL over 18 hours; her white blood cell count was 17.5×10^3/mcL with neutrophilic predominance. She was started on IV PPI therapy. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a nonbleeding post-bulbar duodenal ulcer; biopsies were negative for H. pylori. Melena resolved, and she was discharged on oral PPI.  

Less than 24 hours after her second TCHP infusion, she had several episodes of black, initially formed, stools that became loose, with dizziness and palpitations, but no abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. She was compliant with PPI therapy. On exam she had conjunctival pallor, frank melena on rectal exam, and no abdominal tenderness. Hemoglobin was 6.5 g/dL (down from 8.2 g/dL despite 2 units of packed red cells the day before); white blood cell count was 19.9×10^3/mcL with normal differential. Urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed scattered gastric erosions, the previously noted clean-based post-bulbar ulcer, and multiple oozing linear superficial mucosal breaks circumferentially involving the majority of the second portion of the duodenum. Biopsies were obtained from all three sites.

A 78-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of a slow-onset, moderate-intensity, stabbing pain in the right inguinal area and an associated bulge without overlying skin changes. Her medical history was notable for a 15-year history of insulin-treated type 2 diabetes and a 7-year history of hypertension managed with amlodipine. On examination, a right groin bulge was palpable and tender to touch. There were no systemic signs of sepsis. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Clinical suspicion was for an incarcerated inguinal hernia, and the patient was referred for ultrasonographic evaluation.
