Ultrasonography of the right groin using a 9 MHz linear transducer demonstrated a well-defined cystic mass containing a central tubular structure terminating in a blind end on longitudinal imaging and a target appearance on cross-sectional imaging. The tubular structure measured 0.63 mm in one axis and 0.72 mm in the perpendicular axis, with focal hypoechoic thickening of the mucosal layer. Color Doppler imaging showed increased flow at the tip and in adjacent soft tissues. The patient experienced focal tenderness when the transducer was pressed over the lesion, and the surrounding fat exhibited increased echogenicity consistent with inflammation. The preoperative surgical diagnosis was a strangulated inguinofemoral hernia.

An 82-year-old Japanese woman with stage 4 breast cancer and known multiple bone metastases diagnosed 4 years earlier presented with left shin pain. Since her diagnosis, she had been treated with an aromatase inhibitor and monthly intravenous denosumab (120 mg) for 4 years; she had no history of bisphosphonate or glucocorticoid use. She reported no history of trauma; pain began one day while walking.  
Initial plain radiographs of the left tibia showed focal endosteal thickening of the medial cortex in the proximal third (“beaking sign”). Because the lesion was non-displaced, she continued full weight bearing at home. Over the next month, pain persisted and ambulation became difficult. Repeat X-rays demonstrated a non-displaced transverse fracture of the proximal diaphysis of the left tibia.  
Given her known bone metastases, CT and MRI of the left tibia were obtained; they did not show definitive evidence of metastatic bone tumor but could not entirely exclude it. Laboratory studies at the time of fracture showed 25-hydroxyvitamin D 32 ng/mL, total calcium 10.3 mg/dL, TRACP-5b 192 mU/dL, CEA 66.3 ng/mL, and CA 15-3 109.7 U/mL.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of a gradually enlarging midline neck swelling and 1 year of progressive dysphagia for solids. She denied hoarseness, dyspnea, weight change, heat or cold intolerance, or constitutional symptoms. Her medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable. Examination revealed a smooth, firm, nontender enlargement of both thyroid lobes and isthmus (8×4 cm), moving with deglutition, without nodularity or cervical lymphadenopathy. Respiratory, cardiovascular, abdominal, and musculoskeletal examinations were normal. Routine blood counts, liver, renal, and thyroid function tests were within normal limits; urinalysis showed no proteinuria; chest radiograph was normal. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a bulky gland with multiple hypoechoic nodules (largest 9.3×9.0 mm in the left lower pole), with a TIRADS score of TR2. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was Bethesda category II, showing follicular cells in clusters and occasional macrophages in a hemorrhagic background. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was normal.

A 10-year-old boy presented with nocturia, thirst, and polyuria exceeding 5000 mL per day. He reported no headache or visual disturbance. Height was 136 cm (–0.7 SD) and weight was 28.4 kg (–1.0 SD). Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a plasma sodium level of 144 mEq/L, plasma osmolality of 289 mOsm/L, urine osmolality of 76 mOsm/L, and urine specific gravity <1.005. Plasma arginine vasopressin level was 0.4 pg/mL. A T1-weighted pituitary MRI demonstrated absence of the posterior pituitary bright spot and diffuse enlargement of the pituitary stalk measuring up to 6.9 mm. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed uniform enhancement of the anterior pituitary and stalk without a discrete mass lesion. Serum alpha-fetoprotein and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin were negative. Tuberculin skin test, gallium scintigraphy, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and IgG4 levels were all within normal limits. Ophthalmologic and dermatologic examinations showed no evidence of sarcoidosis or Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Anti-pituitary and other autoantibodies were negative. Desmopressin therapy was started, and prednisolone (1 mg/kg/d) was initiated on day 10.

A 38-year-old man experienced severe central chest pain shortly after taking sildenafil. His medical history included intellectual disability and unexplained abdominal pain managed with amitriptyline, metoclopramide, and lansoprazole. He smoked five cigarettes daily and frequently consumed caffeinated energy drinks. He had no known COVID-19 infection. The chest pain lasted about 10 minutes and recurred throughout the day without associated sexual activity.

Six hours after symptom onset, his brother noted slurred speech and called emergency services. A prehospital ECG showed inferolateral ST-segment elevation. On arrival at the Emergency Department, he was pain-free but hypertensive (166/115 mmHg). Neurologic examination revealed dysarthria and a right homonymous hemianopia (NIHSS score 3); there were equal peripheral pulses, no murmurs, and no cardiac failure. Respiratory and abdominal exams were unremarkable. A repeat ECG again demonstrated persistent inferolateral ST-segment elevation. Transthoracic echocardiography showed inferoseptal hypokinesis with preserved ejection fraction (56%) and no other abnormalities.  

Computed tomography of the brain revealed acute left occipital and right superior cerebellar infarcts. Given the combination of myocardial infarction and stroke, primary PCI was deferred pending urgent further imaging.

A 36-year-old Pakistani woman living in Italy for 10 years presented with chest pain and dyspnea of recent onset. She also reported subtle vertigo, headache, and apathy; the neurologic examination was otherwise nonfocal. Two prior fine-needle aspirations of a submandibular lymph node (2 years and 1 month earlier) had shown only small monomorphic lymphocytes and macrophages, and no chest radiograph had been obtained until this admission. A chest radiograph showed mild interstitial infiltrates, focal multiple opacities with a miliary distribution, and right basal consolidation; high-resolution CT confirmed these findings. Bronchoalveolar lavage with nucleic acid amplification was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis susceptible to first-line drugs. Four-drug antitubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) was initiated. Because of the patient’s subtle neurologic symptoms, a brain MRI was obtained, which demonstrated numerous small contrast-enhancing lesions in both supratentorial and infratentorial regions, nodular enhancement of the prechiasmatic optic nerve sheaths bilaterally, and focal leptomeningeal enhancement in the right sylvian fissure.

A 43-year-old woman was admitted for recurrent falls and confusion. Her history was notable for congenital bicuspid aortic valve disease, for which she underwent mechanical aortic valve replacement and tricuspid annuloplasty in 2011. In April 2021, she had a second aortic valve replacement with an On-X valve, complicated intraoperatively by the development of an aorto–right ventricular fistula and severe tricuspid regurgitation. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. She was obese and had slowed mentation with slurred speech. Cardiac examination revealed a regular rate and rhythm, a III/VI holosystolic murmur at the upper right sternal border radiating to the carotids, a mechanical S2 with near-obliteration of S1, and no jugular venous distension. Neurologic exam showed bilateral asterixis. There was no peripheral edema, organomegaly, or labored breathing. Laboratory evaluation revealed an elevated serum ammonia level of 122 µmol/L (normal 13–40), an alkaline phosphatase of 411 U/L (35–104), an AST of 40 U/L (10–35), and an ALT of 22 U/L (10–35). A liver ultrasound demonstrated dilated hepatic veins and bidirectional flow in the main portal vein. Contrast CT of the abdomen showed hepatomegaly, hepatic steatosis, and features consistent with congestive hepatopathy.

A 57-year-old man with a 7-year history of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis presented with 2 months of progressive shortness of breath and productive cough. He denied chest pain. He had smoked for 25 years but quit 2 years ago and had no history of hypertension, diabetes, or known coronary disease.  
On arrival, blood pressure was 114/71 mm Hg, and electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed moderately severe pulmonary hypertension, mild right atrial dilation, and normal left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction >55%) without regional wall-motion abnormalities.  
As part of pre–lung transplantation evaluation, he underwent coronary angiography, which showed branching of the proximal right coronary artery into multiple thin channels that converged distally into a normal-caliber vessel with TIMI III flow. The left anterior descending and left circumflex arteries exhibited mild ectasia but otherwise demonstrated TIMI III flow.  
Optical coherence tomography of the right coronary artery demonstrated a braid-like configuration with multiple channels within the vessel lumen.

A 31-year-old woman presented with a five-year history of left lateral hip pain. She had been diagnosed elsewhere with trochanteric bursitis and received a non–X-ray-guided steroid injection, which worsened her pain. She described the pain as dull, 4/10 in intensity, alleviated by rest and aggravated by movement, and denied joint swelling or erythema. On examination, gait and station were normal, and there was full range of movement of the left hip without joint swelling, tenderness, or erythema. Point tenderness was elicited over the left lateral thigh. Laboratory studies revealed normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP). Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the hips were unremarkable. Musculoskeletal ultrasound of the left lateral and posterior hip showed a normal gluteus minimus; however, the gluteus medius had dense hypoechogenicity with loss of normal echotexture, and posteriorly there were hyperechoic areas with several anechoic foci correlating with tenderness. The right lateral hip had similar but less prominent findings. Further history revealed that the patient had undergone silicone injections abroad in the past. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with contrast demonstrated innumerable small low-signal foci throughout the gluteus maximus and overlying subcutaneous fat bilaterally, consistent with injectable material, possibly silicone.

A 6‐week‐old male, born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery with an uncomplicated nursery course, presented with progressive jaundice, pallor, difficulty feeding, and decreased urine output. On the day of presentation he developed respiratory distress and, in the pediatric emergency department, was noted to be pale, lethargic, and hypotonic. Vital signs were: temperature 34.8 °C, pulse 152 beats/min, respiratory rate 44 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. A venous blood gas showed pH 7.06, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, and lactate 18 mmol/L. Hemoglobin was 3.0 g/dL.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Hemoglobin 3.0 g/dL, hematocrit 10%, MCV 107 fL, WBC 35.5 × 10^3/mcL, platelets 971 × 10^3/mcL  
• Total bilirubin 4.55 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL, bicarbonate <5 mmol/L  
• Reticulocyte count 7.6% (ref 0.5–1.8%), haptoglobin <8 mg/dL (ref 7–221 mg/dL), LDH 616 U/L (ref 163–452 U/L)  
A head ultrasound and plain radiographs showed no evidence of hemorrhage or trauma. Empiric intravenous antibiotics were started, and type O negative blood was ordered emergently. Peripheral smear showed few schistocytes or helmet cells, normal central pallor, anisocytosis, and marked polychromasia. There was no family history of hematologic disease. Type and screen demonstrated blood type A positive with a positive antibody screen; the direct antiglobulin test was positive with a panagglutinin, showing no complement on red cells but 4+ IgG bound to the patient’s erythrocytes.

A 52-year-old woman presented with headache and progressive alteration of consciousness. Five days earlier, she had developed fever and cough and tested positive for influenza B by nasal swab; she received a single inhalation of laninamivir. On admission she was stuporous (Glasgow Coma Scale E2V4M6) without focal neurologic deficits or meningeal signs. Laboratory tests showed iron-deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 7.8 g/dl, MCV 63.2 fl, iron 11 mg/dl), mild thrombocytosis (434×10^3/μl), an elevated D-dimer (3.9 μg/ml), and an IL-6 level of 43.9 pg/ml. Renal, hepatic and electrolyte panels were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) had an opening pressure of 300 mmH2O, xanthochromia with 1820 red cells/μl, protein 622.2 mg/dl, and 4 white cells/μl; cultures were negative, and PCR assays for herpes simplex virus, varicella–zoster virus, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus were all negative. Brain MRI revealed bilateral thalamic and caudate-nucleus lesions with left internal capsule involvement; on T2*-weighted images, there was diminished signal and enlargement of the deep cerebral veins.

A 71-year-old male farmer with a 3-year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis and diabetes mellitus (on metformin) presented with painful ulcers on his lips, oral mucosa, and around the corona of the penis for 2 weeks, associated with intermittent fevers and chills and difficulty swallowing. Two weeks earlier, after diagnosis at an Indian tertiary care hospital, he had been prescribed methotrexate 10 mg once weekly, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg at night, and folic acid 5 mg daily. On return home, he inadvertently took methotrexate 10 mg daily for 2 weeks (cumulative 70 mg/week). 

On examination: temperature 99°F; pulse 72 /min; blood pressure 99/60 mmHg; respiratory rate 20 /min; SpO2 99% on room air. Ulcers were noted on the lower lip, floor of mouth, and circumferentially around the penile corona. There was no pallor or lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed WBC 1210 cells/cmm with an absolute neutrophil count of 206/μL, hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, platelet count 32 × 10^3/cmm, normal renal function, AST/ALT within twice the upper limit of normal, CRP 7.73 mg/dL, rheumatoid factor >100 IU/mL, anti-CCP >200 U/mL. Peripheral blood smear showed microcytic hypochromic red cells with spherocytes; white cells and platelets were decreased in number with normal morphology. 

Blood and urine cultures showed no growth. Dengue NS1, IgM, IgG were negative; Plasmodium vivax and falciparum films were negative; scrub typhus IgM was negative. ECG and chest radiograph were normal.

A 71-year-old woman underwent debridement and posterior fixation (D6–D7 to D10–D11 with fusion at D8–D9) for D8–9 spondylodiscitis. On postoperative day 3, she developed progressive dyspnea.  
  • Temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure were within normal limits.  
  • Chest radiograph showed complete opacification of the left lung.  
  • Chest ultrasound demonstrated a massive left pleural effusion with multiple mobile echoes (the “plankton sign”).  
  • An 8-French pigtail catheter was placed, draining 2.5 L of cloudy, milky fluid over 24 hours.  
  • Pleural-fluid analysis: triglyceride 800 mg/dL (10.1 mmol/L), total protein 36.8 g/L, total cholesterol 180 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 154 μ/L, adenosine deaminase 1.5 U/L.  
  • White-cell count in blood was 11,000/mm³; hemoglobin 11 g/dL; platelets 230,000/mm³; serum total protein 7 g/dL; serum creatinine 1 mg/dL; serum urea 15 mg/dL.

A 27-year-old Caucasian man presented with the acute onset of severe, sharp chest and abdominal pain radiating to his shoulder blades and testicles. The pain began five hours earlier, waking him from sleep, and was worse when supine. He reported associated nausea, a single episode of emesis in the emergency department (ED), and generalized weakness. 

On arrival, his blood pressure was 80/60 mm Hg with a thready heart rate of 60 beats/minute; respiratory rate was 26 breaths/minute and he was afebrile. After fluid resuscitation, his blood pressure stabilized at 110/60 mm Hg. Abdominal examination revealed guarding and rebound tenderness with normal bowel sounds; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

His past medical history and review of systems were unremarkable; he took ranitidine intermittently for heartburn. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 115 g/L and a white blood cell count of 13.8 × 10^9/L; liver enzymes, electrolytes, renal function, and amylase were normal. An electrocardiogram was unremarkable. Erect and supine abdominal and chest radiographs were normal, with no rib fractures and a normal left hemidiaphragm. The point-of-care ultrasound was unavailable.

Despite administration of 20 mg morphine, 50 mg dimenhydrinate, and 20 mg hyoscine, his intense pain persisted. He was sent for a contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.

A 32-year-old man with a history of renal cell carcinoma presented with acute right-sided abdominal pain. Six years earlier, he had undergone nephrectomy for localized disease; recent staging revealed supraclavicular and abdominal lymph node metastases. He was started on high-dose interleukin-2 therapy (600,000 IU/kg IV per dose daily for 10–14 days per cycle). After eight of the planned 14 doses in the first cycle, he developed severe right upper-quadrant pain and was admitted.  
On examination, his temperature was 37.8 °C, pulse 102/min, blood pressure 114/68 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 18/min. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 15.6 K/µL (normal, 4.0–10.9 K/µL), total bilirubin 0.90 mg/dL (normal, 0.00–1.20 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 234 U/L (normal, 40–130 U/L), AST 28 U/L (normal, 10–50 U/L), and ALT 39 U/L (normal, 0–41 U/L).  
A right upper-quadrant ultrasound demonstrated uniform gallbladder wall thickening up to 16 mm with heterogeneous echotexture and trace pericholecystic fluid. No echogenic gallstones were definitively identified. The common bile duct was 6 mm in diameter. A computed tomography scan obtained one month prior to IL-2 therapy had shown a normal gallbladder wall thickness of 2 mm without gallbladder hypermetabolism.

A 33-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of chest tightness and dyspnea at rest. He had no history of pulmonary infection or asthma in childhood or adulthood and a 5-pack-year smoking history. On examination, his respiratory rate was 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Pulmonary auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds over the left lung. Complete blood count, urinalysis, D-dimer, and blood chemistry results were within normal limits. Pulmonary function tests showed an obstructive pattern with a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 2.76 L (64% predicted) and a forced vital capacity of 4.93 L (110.8% predicted). 

Chest radiography demonstrated unilateral hyperlucency of the left lower lung with a small hilar shadow and reduced bronchovascular markings. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a hyperlucent left lung without anteroposterior gradient attenuation, hypoplasia or absence of the left pulmonary artery and peripheral vascular bed, and overall reduction in the left inspiratory lung volume; there was no mass or evidence of pulmonary embolism, and no abnormalities in the right lung. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction showed reduced airway branching and cylindrical and cystic bronchiectasis scattered throughout the left lung, most prominently in the left lower lobe. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed no bronchial stenosis.

A 19-year-old previously healthy man reported a 4-month history of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting beginning 2 weeks after his second dose of an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine. He had no prior medical history. He presented on three occasions to outpatient and emergency settings for these symptoms and was treated with antacids and antiemetics. Outpatient right upper quadrant ultrasound showed cholelithiasis, ascites, and a right pleural effusion. Laboratory tests revealed a total bilirubin of 3.9 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 22 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 7.8 mg/dL. A chest radiograph demonstrated a borderline enlarged cardiac silhouette. Over the next weeks, his symptoms progressed to include diarrhea, shortness of breath, and pleuritic chest pain. On examination, he was tachypneic (26 breaths/min) and tachycardic (123 beats/min) without jugular venous distension, pericardial rub, or peripheral edema. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with low-voltage QRS complexes. CT angiography of the chest demonstrated pericardial thickening and effusion with moderate bilateral pleural effusions. A technically limited transthoracic echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%, mild right ventricular dilation, a moderate “jelly-like” pericardial effusion, an E/A ratio of 2.33, and a mild septal bounce. Infectious workup was notable for positive histoplasmosis complement fixation with negative antigen, positive Mycoplasma IgM with negative PCR, and low-grade Epstein–Barr virus viremia, later felt to represent reactivation. Left thoracentesis yielded transudative fluid negative for malignancy and acid-fast bacteria. Colonoscopy and endoscopy with duodenal biopsy were unremarkable.

A 70-year-old woman with hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia presented with a 1-day history of fever, left-sided chest pain, cough, mild dyspnoea, fatigue, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhoea. She was normotensive, with normal oxygen saturation on room air, and had a mildly distended but non-peritonitic abdomen. 

Admission studies showed:  
• Chest radiograph with bilateral mid- and lower-zone patchy airspace consolidation.  
• Positive RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2.  
• Lymphopenia of 0.7×10^9/L (normal 1.5–4×10^9/L).  
• C-reactive protein 38 mg/L (normal 0–5 mg/L).  
• Normal liver function tests.  
• Progressive hyponatraemia, nadir 112 mmol/L (normal 133–146 mmol/L); urinary sodium 46 mmol/L.  
• Normal serum potassium, random plasma cortisol, and ACTH levels.

On hospital day 2, an abdominal X-ray demonstrated a mildly distended colon with right-sided faecal loading but no free intraperitoneal air. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis in the portal venous phase showed bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands that were diffusely hypoattenuating with poor enhancement, ill-defined contours, and significant surrounding retroperitoneal fat stranding, with no evidence of haemorrhage. The remainder of the abdominal viscera appeared normal.

A 9-year-old Mongolian girl was referred with a 2-week history of frequent adherence of a small amount of blood to her underwear. Her past medical and birth history were unremarkable. On examination, there was a sessile, smooth-margined, clearly demarcated, elastic, soft red tumor encircling the urethral meatus. The lesion was hemorrhagic but the patient reported no pain and had no difficulty with urination. There were no other abnormalities on physical examination. Complete blood count and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Given her age, urethral prolapse was suspected and she was treated with topical steroid ointment for 3 weeks without clinical response. To exclude malignancy, enhanced computed tomography of the pelvis was obtained, which showed no invasion of the muscle layer and no evidence of distant metastases.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a one-day history of periorbital swelling, a papular rash, pruritus, and low-grade fever. One day before symptom onset, he received mebendazole 300 mg in the morning and evening as an anti-helminthic. The following morning, peri-orbital and facial swelling appeared, accompanied by a pruritic rash on the face, trunk, and upper limbs; the upper body seemed “bigger than normal.” There was no preceding insect bite, ingestion of a new food, or latex exposure, and no family history of similar swelling. He had also taken oral cotrimoxazole, vitamin C, and bitter leaf extracts before presentation.

On examination, he had peri-orbital edema with submental fullness and a papular rash limited to the face, trunk, and upper limbs. He was not dyspneic (respiratory rate 16/min), with a heart rate of 80 beats/min, blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, and normal heart sounds. No other abnormalities were noted.

Laboratory studies, including urinalysis, blood electrolytes, urea, full blood count, and fasting lipid profile, were all within normal ranges.

A 42-year-old Laotian woman with adult-onset immunodeficiency due to anti–interferon γ autoantibodies, on a 2-month antibiotic regimen for disseminated Mycobacterium hassiacum, presented with 2 days of fever, headache, diffuse myalgia, dark urine, and anorexia. Family members had similar symptoms. She was febrile to 102.9 °F and tachycardic. Laboratory studies showed AST 1281 U/L, ALT 511 U/L, ALP 265 U/L, normal bilirubin and ammonia, and INR 1.60. A respiratory viral panel was positive for human rhinovirus. Viral hepatitis serologies (A, B, C, HIV), autoimmune hepatitis antibodies (antismooth muscle, ANA, antimitochondrial), and abdominal Doppler ultrasound were unrevealing. Antibiotics were held for presumed drug-induced liver injury. The patient remained intermittently febrile, developed a generalized tonic–clonic seizure, and underwent lumbar puncture with empiric meningitis treatment. A comprehensive rheumatologic and infectious workup remained negative. Subsequent laboratories revealed ferritin 62,225 ng/mL, triglycerides 343 mg/dL, WBC 12.6 × 10^3/μL, hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelet count 27 × 10^3/μL, and soluble IL-2 receptor α level 6477 pg/mL.

A 75-year-old man presented with a 7-day history of worsening abdominal pain, distension, and constipation. He reported similar self-limited episodes of abdominal pain, distension, and constipation lasting 2–3 days over the past 8–10 years, managed at home with acetaminophen and laxatives. He denied chronic use of NSAIDs or other medications, bleeding per rectum, weight loss, anorexia, or systemic symptoms. His medical and surgical history was unremarkable.

On examination, he was tachycardic (109/min) and tachypneic (22/min) with a blood pressure of 108/72 mmHg. The abdomen was distended without surgical scars or hernias. Mild, diffuse tenderness was present, with hyperactive bowel sounds. Digital rectal examination revealed an empty rectum. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11 g/dL) and neutrophilic leukocytosis; renal, liver, and thyroid functions and blood glucose were normal. A chest radiograph was normal; an erect abdominal film showed multiple air–fluid levels and centrally located dilated loops. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed multiple strictures in the jejunum and ileum without mass lesions, fistula, or collections.

A 19-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with an 8-day history of a burning, itchy rash that began as small red dots on his arms and legs and subsequently involved his trunk, face, and scalp. Shortly after rash onset, he developed fever, a frequent cough, and swelling of the face, hands, elbows, and ankles. He also endorsed transient abdominal pain and joint stiffness. The patient denied recent travel outside Missouri, tick or insect bites, sick contacts, and any prior skin rashes. 

On examination, he was afebrile, normotensive, and in no acute distress. There was mild edema of the right side of the face and left periorbital region. Lungs were clear bilaterally. Skin examination revealed:
- Erythematous, dusky, targetoid papules on the posterior scalp, back, glabella, and abdomen  
- Violaceous to red-brown ecchymoses on the left upper eyelid and antecubital fossae  
- Scattered violaceous papules on the legs, some with hemorrhagic crust, scale, vesicles, and bullae  
- Pinpoint violaceous nonblanching macules on the feet  

Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis (WBC 14.62 × 10^9/l), normal renal function, normal urinalysis, an ESR of 20 mm/hr (0–15), and a CRP of 3.2 mg/dl (0.00–0.50). Lyme serology was positive. Two sets of blood cultures, RPR, CT/NG urine test, HIV antigen–antibody assay, and ANCA panel were all negative; complement levels were normal. Chest x-ray revealed subtle right middle lobe opacities, and chest CT demonstrated right lower lobe opacities with ground-glass nodules. CT of the orbits showed left periorbital soft-tissue edema.

A 56-year-old Caucasian man with no significant medical history presented with a four-day history of flashes and floaters in his right eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/40 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed a horseshoe tear with vitreous hemorrhage and subretinal fluid; laser retinopexy was performed. Examination of the left eye incidentally showed a chronic inferior rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RD) extending from 4 to 8 o’clock with proliferative vitreoretinopathy and an epiretinal membrane. The patient was lost to follow-up and returned two years later with new floaters in the left eye. Visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/200 OS, and fundus examination OS revealed vitreous hemorrhage. B-scan ultrasonography showed a bullous superior RD with posterior attachment and an inferotemporal mass-like lesion associated with diffuse hyperechoic material in the vitreous, preretinal, and subretinal spaces. The patient underwent scleral buckle placement and pars plana vitrectomy; intraoperatively there was combined rhegmatogenous and exudative RD with extensive hemorrhage that precluded full evaluation of an underlying lesion. Vitreous fluid cytology was negative for malignant cells. One week later, the patient developed a hyphema and elevated intraocular pressure; B-scan and ultrasound biomicroscopy showed an attached retina with residual gas bubble and an inferior retinal lesion with high internal reflectivity but no anterior segment mass. Two weeks postoperatively, B-scan revealed a peripheral shallow RD under residual gas and an enlarging inferior solid lesion measuring 14.1 mm × 6.3 mm. Given lesion growth, ocular oncology consultation was obtained.

A 28-year-old previously healthy Chinese woman at 4 months’ gestation underwent water-sac induced abortion. Two days later she developed high fever, chills, and continuous vaginal bleeding. She was treated with intravenous ceftazidime but progressed to shock (BP 70/30 mmHg) and required emergency evacuation of retained fetal tissue. During surgery she sustained a vaginal injury, became comatose, and was transferred to the surgical ICU.

On arrival:  
– Temperature: hypothermia (on ventilator-assisted ventilation)  
– Blood pressure: not detectable off vasopressors  
– Neurologic: coma  
– Skin: cyanosis of the shins  
– Genitourinary: ongoing vaginal bleeding, anuria

Initial laboratory studies:  
– Hemoglobin: 7.0 g/dl  
– Platelet count: 6 × 10^9/l  
– White blood cell count: 22 360/µl (87.8% segmented neutrophils)  
– INR 1.99, APTT 51 s  
– Procalcitonin: 50 ng/ml  
– Lactate: 8.4 mmol/l, HCO3– 12.8 mmol/l  
– Creatinine: 200 µmol/l

Treatments included fluid resuscitation; transfusions of plasma, platelets, and red cells; meropenem; intravenous immunoglobulin; ventilatory support; continuous venovenous hemofiltration; and high-dose norepinephrine. By hospital day 2, she remained comatose with persistent bleeding, her hemoglobin fell to 3.4 g/dl, and lactate rose to 12.4 mmol/l. On day 3, she underwent an emergency hysterectomy.

After surgery, she improved clinically (bleeding stopped, regained consciousness, milrinone weaned, BP stabilized at 110/60 mmHg on norepinephrine 1 µg/kg/min, lactate 4.1 mmol/l, increasing urine output). However, over the next days her white-cell count rose to 78 000/µl, and her platelet count fluctuated between 3 and 28 × 10^9/l despite intermittent platelet transfusions.

A 25-year-old woman with no prior medical or surgical history presented with a 2-month history of a progressively enlarging abdominal-pelvic mass and diffuse abdominal pain. On examination, there was a large, nonpulsatile, tender abdominal mass occupying nearly the entire abdomen, with mild guarding. Laboratory studies, including routine blood counts and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large cystic mass extending into the pelvis, displacing the bladder and uterus to the left without evidence of peritoneal fluid. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 214×195×130 mm lobulated, nonenhancing, fluid-attenuation mass (18 HU) with few thin internal septations; the mass abutted but did not infiltrate adjacent organs (rectum, sigmoid, bladder, uterus), insinuated between the gluteal muscles, compressed both ureteropelvic junctions causing bilateral hydronephrosis, and encompassed the right iliac vessels which remained patent. 

MRI of the abdomen and pelvis showed the lesion to be hypointense on T1-weighted images, markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and to contain thin T2-hypointense septations with mild T1 hyperintensity.

A 22‐year‐old man underwent a noncontrast CT scan of the chest after a motor vehicle accident. He was asymptomatic, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed a mild lymphocytosis that had been present for 8 years. He had no history of recent illness, systemic stress, or other medical problems.

CT imaging demonstrated a large (76 × 148 × 123 mm), well‐circumscribed anterior mediastinal mass composed of both fat attenuation and soft‐tissue attenuation. The mass abutted the visceral pleura, pericardium, great vessels, and diaphragm but showed no evidence of invasion. Because of the bulk fat content and absence of aggressive features, the lesion was radiologically favored to be a thymolipoma. Given the patient’s age, preference, and the presumed benign nature of the lesion, a video‐assisted thoracoscopic surgical (VATS) resection was performed without prior biopsy. The mass was dissected from adherent structures and removed intact via a subxiphoid incision. The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day 2.

A 38-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of central sharp chest pain radiating to the shoulder, associated with breathlessness, fever, and chills. He had undergone an elective laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy 5 days earlier. He denied abdominal pain, vomiting, or obstructive symptoms. His medical history included obesity, diet-controlled type II diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, gout, and childhood asthma. He also reported a remote upper abdominal stab wound ∼20 years earlier. 

On examination, he was tachycardic (heart rate 118 bpm), blood pressure 103/62 mmHg, temperature 37.9°C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. There was no jugular venous distension. Heart sounds were dual and soft, without murmurs or pericardial rub. Lung auscultation revealed reduced air entry and bilateral basal crepitations. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no distension or signs of obstruction; surgical wounds appeared unremarkable, and no old scars were noted. There was no peripheral oedema.

Electrocardiography showed ST-segment elevation in the inferolateral leads and PR-segment depression, consistent with pericarditis. Chest radiography revealed a widened cardiothoracic ratio with bibasal atelectasis and a small right pleural effusion. Laboratory tests demonstrated a leukocytosis (white cell count 25.8 × 10^9/L) and elevated C-reactive protein (409 mg/L); renal function was normal, no troponin was requested, and serial blood cultures were negative.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large amount of echogenic material in the pericardial space, with evidence of interventricular dependence and constrictive physiology. A computed tomography pulmonary angiogram excluded a pulmonary embolism but revealed a 9 mm defect in the central tendon of the diaphragm and a large amount of herniated omental fat with fat stranding within the pericardial space.

A 28-year-old nulliparous woman, who had migrated from India 1 year earlier, presented with a 6-month history of persistent right breast pain and ipsilateral nipple discharge. Three months earlier, she was diagnosed with a right breast abscess, treated with incision and drainage and 1 week of oral cefpodoxime, with initial resolution. She then noted a new, gradually enlarging, tender lump measuring approximately 4 cm × 4 cm in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, associated with peri-areolar nipple discharge at the prior incision site. She denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, cough, or known tuberculosis exposure.  
Vital signs were normal. Examination confirmed a firm, tender mass in the right upper outer quadrant without skin changes or axillary lymphadenopathy; the left breast was normal.  
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, renal function, blood glucose, HIV, HBsAg, and HCV serologies, were all within normal limits or negative.  
Breast ultrasonography revealed a 21 × 0.9 mm rounded, iso- to hyper-echoic lesion in the right upper outer quadrant; the left breast was normal and there were no calcifications.  
Fine-needle aspiration yielded thick, pus-like material with numerous polymorphonuclear neutrophils and necrotic debris; no malignant cells were seen. During repeat incision and drainage, multiple grayish-yellow fragments were noted; microscopy showed acute inflammatory cells and peripheral fibrosis but no granulomas.  
Owing to her recent migration from a high-tuberculosis-burden country, prolonged discharge, lack of immunosuppression, and absence of pulmonary findings on chest radiograph, a provisional diagnosis of primary breast tuberculosis was considered.

A 58-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 1-year history of progressive gait difficulty and bladder incontinence. On examination, he had spasmodic paraparesis with exaggerated lower-limb reflexes, marked spasticity, and proprioceptive sensory disturbances; there were no thermoalgesic impairments, no defined sensory level, and no upper-limb abnormalities. A standard spinal X-ray showed no static skeletal abnormalities. Sagittal and axial spinal MRI revealed a well-defined, 2-cm intramedullary lesion at the T1 level that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed no enhancement after gadolinium administration; the cord and canal at that level were expanded.

An 18-year-old Asian man presented with primary hyperparathyroidism. His parathyroid hormone level was 335.4 pmol/L (normal, 2.3–9.3), and his serum calcium was 4.11 mmol/L (normal, 2.10–2.57), despite treatment with bisphosphonates, aggressive hydration, and calcitonin. Neck ultrasound revealed a large heterogeneous hypoechoic nodule in the expected location of the right parathyroid gland. Tc-99m sestamibi scintigraphy showed intense uptake with differential washout in the right thyroid bed, and SPECT/CT localized a hypodense nodular mass posterior to the right thyroid lobe without other foci of uptake. The patient underwent parathyroidectomy, and a 3.5-cm mass weighing 10.27 g was removed; histology confirmed a giant parathyroid adenoma.

Two weeks later, he reported bone pain in the right arm and both thighs. A skeletal survey including X-ray, CT, and MRI showed multiple lytic bone lesions, a right humeral fracture, and bilateral femoral fractures. Laboratory studies revealed a serum calcium of 2.01 mmol/L (normal, 2.10–2.57), phosphate of 0.4 mmol/L (normal, 0.8–1.6), magnesium of 0.59 mmol/L (normal, 0.70–0.91), an alkaline phosphatase level of 1784 IU/L (normal, 52–171), and a 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D level of 12 nmol/L (normal, 50–220).

A 63-year-old man of Surinamese descent presented with acute onset of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. He denied hematochezia, melena, fever, or diarrhea. His medical history included herpes zoster ophthalmica and renal failure from benign prostatic obstruction treated with transurethral resection 6 months earlier; he also noted an unexplained 6-month weight loss. On examination, he was tachycardic (112 beats/min), febrile (39.5 °C), and normotensive (134/81 mmHg). The abdomen was distended, hypertympanic, and diffusely tender; there was a large, non-incarcerated right inguinal hernia. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 6.1 mmol/L, white-cell count 8.2×10^9/L, and C-reactive protein 56 mg/L. CT of the thorax and abdomen revealed intra-abdominal free air and fluid consistent with perforation, plus pulmonary nodules described as suggestive of sarcoidosis and hilar and mesenteric lymphadenopathy. Emergency laparoscopy disclosed fecal peritonitis and numerous diffuse white studs on the peritoneum, small intestine, and mesentery, raising the suspicion of peritoneal carcinomatosis. Two small-bowel perforations associated with these lesions were resected, and stapled side-to-side enteroenterostomies were performed. Peritoneal fluid and tissue specimens were sent for pathologic examination.

A 17-year-old African male with homozygous sickle cell disease presented with persistent left knee pain for 6 months following a fall. He had been treated by his family physician with pain medications and a plaster cast but never fully recovered and remained unable to bear weight on the left leg. He had no prior history of joint injections or infections.

On examination, hip range of motion was full and painless bilaterally. Active movement of the left knee was very painful and limited, with tenderness on palpation. He was afebrile. Laboratory studies before referral included routine blood counts and inflammatory markers (results not available). Bilateral knee arthrocentesis and culture of synovial fluid were performed; cultures were negative. A plain radiograph of the left knee demonstrated a Salter–Harris I fracture of the distal femoral physis with radiographic features of mechanical non-union.

He underwent percutaneous crossed-pin fixation of the distal femur and was started on intravenous cefazolin, followed by two weeks of oral cephalexin upon discharge. Four weeks later, he returned with fever and worsening left knee pain not controlled by NSAIDs.

A 14-year-old girl with no prior medical history presented to the emergency department with paresthesias of the right foot that gradually ascended to involve her entire right hemibody. During evaluation she developed deviation of the labial commissure, aphasia and an acute confusional state accompanied by an intense pulsatile headache localized to the left side of her head. She was hemodynamically stable and denied fever or recent infection. Two days earlier she had experienced a 45-minute episode of paresthesias and migraine-like headache that resolved completely, similar to a migraine with aura. Her family history was notable for migraine in her mother and aunt. 

On neurologic examination during the acute event she did not obey commands, could not name objects or repeat sentences, and spoke fluently but incoherently. Both plantar reflexes were extensor. All neurologic deficits resolved spontaneously within 5 hours, and she was admitted for further evaluation.

A lumbar puncture revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid with an opening pressure of 260 mmH₂O. CSF analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (114 cells/mm³, 99% mononuclear), with normal glucose (68 mg/dL) and protein (37 mg/dL). Empiric acyclovir was initiated. Serologic tests for Lyme disease, neurosyphilis and neurobrucellosis were negative. CSF PCR for varicella-zoster virus, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, enterovirus and Epstein–Barr virus were negative. Immunologic studies, including antineuronal, anticytoplasm and antinuclease antibodies, were negative; anti-NMDA receptor antibodies were also negative. A gynecological evaluation to exclude an ovarian teratoma was normal. 

Urgent noncontrast head CT and CT angiography were unremarkable. An electroencephalogram during hyperventilation showed paroxysmal epileptiform discharges in the left frontal and left temporal regions. Five days after admission, she experienced a third similar episode of right-sided hemiparesthesia and headache. A repeat lumbar puncture 3 days later showed 148 cells/mm³ (lymphocytic), with normal glucose and protein. A sleep-deprivation EEG showed no significant abnormalities. Brain MRI demonstrated no ischemic, hemorrhagic or space-occupying lesions, no diffusion restriction, no leptomeningeal enhancement and no gray-matter edema.

A 58-year-old woman with stage IIA invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast (ER−, PgR+, HER2−; pT2N0M0) underwent left mastectomy followed by dose-dense paclitaxel (175 mg/m2 biweekly). Two days after the first cycle, she received prophylactic pegfilgrastim (3.6 mg). Eight days later, she developed fever to 38 °C and self-administered levofloxacin without improvement. On day 11 after pegfilgrastim, she presented to the emergency clinic.  
On examination, she remained febrile. Laboratory studies showed WBC 22,600/μL (neutrophils 93%) and CRP 13.7 mg/dL. Blood, urine, and sputum cultures were obtained. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated wall thickening and periarterial soft-tissue infiltration of the right subclavian artery; there were also poorly contrasted areas in the renal cortex.

A 26-year-old African American woman with morbid obesity, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented after an incidental finding of elevated serum creatinine (2.2 mg/dL) and proteinuria discovered during evaluation of foot pain. Her hypertension had been well controlled on metoprolol and amlodipine. She denied a personal or family history of kidney disease or autoimmune disorders and took ibuprofen monthly for shoulder pain. On examination, her blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg; she had obesity and moderate lower-extremity edema. A 24-hour urine collection showed 11 g of protein and hematuria, and her serum albumin was 1.8 g/dL. Renal ultrasonography revealed normal-sized kidneys. 

A kidney biopsy revealed severe noncaseating epithelioid granulomatous necrotizing interstitial nephritis, a necrotizing vascular lesion, and cellular crescent formation. Immunofluorescence studies were negative for immunoglobulin A, immunoglobulin M, kappa, lambda, C1q, C3, and fibrinogen, but showed mild diffuse linear glomerular capillary staining for immunoglobulin G, consistent with pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis. Electron microscopy demonstrated no immune complex deposits. Mycobacterium tuberculosis studies were negative.

A 58-year-old woman with a 30-year history of HIV infection presented with a 3-month history of a mildly pruritic, widespread rash accompanied by fevers, night sweats, headaches, cough, and dyspnea. Originally from Zimbabwe, she immigrated to Canada 7 years earlier and had since discontinued antiretroviral therapy. Over the preceding year, she and her family noted weight loss and progressive functional and cognitive decline. 

On admission, her CD4+ cell count was 1 cell/μL, and her HIV viral load was 5.28 log10 copies/mL. Dermatologic examination revealed diffusely infiltrated, scaly, verrucous, hyperpigmented thick plaques on the face producing a leonine facies. On the torso and extremities, there were non-blanching, violaceous-to-brown papules and plaques of varying sizes, each surrounded by a blanchable, erythematous halo.

A computed tomography scan of the chest showed calcified granulomata in both upper lobes and bulky mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain identified a small lesion in the right parietal lobe.

A lesional skin biopsy, stained with hematoxylin and eosin, demonstrated a dermal infiltrate of histiocytes containing numerous ovoid, yeast-like organisms. These organisms were more clearly defined using periodic acid–Schiff and Grocott’s methenamine silver stains, supporting a fungal etiology.

A 58-year-old woman presented with sudden onset central chest pain. She had no recent viral symptoms, no family history of ischaemic heart disease or cardiomyopathy, and no significant past medical history. On examination, she was euvolemic, with normal heart sounds and clear lung fields. A 12-lead ECG showed widespread ST-segment elevation. Serum high-sensitivity troponin I was 1998 ng/L (reference <37 ng/L); white cell count and C-reactive protein were normal. Urgent coronary angiography revealed unobstructed coronary arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated globally mild hypokinesia and mildly impaired left ventricular systolic function. Nine days after presentation, a 1.5-Tesla CMR scan showed a non-dilated left ventricle with preserved ejection fraction (67%). The apical segments appeared hypertrophied (maximal thickness 14 mm) and subtly hypokinetic. On T2-weighted imaging, the signal intensity ratio of apical myocardium to skeletal muscle was 2.8 (1.8 at the base), suggesting active inflammation. Late gadolinium enhancement imaging demonstrated diffuse mid-wall hyperenhancement in the apical segments. At this stage, differential diagnoses included acute coronary syndrome with bystander apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, acute myocarditis, and Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

A 37-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a two-year history of a palpable lump in her right groin that became more painful during the menstrual period. She had no prior surgeries and an otherwise unremarkable medical history. On examination, there was a 15 mm, tender, tense mass near the right pubic arch; the left groin was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging showed an oval lesion measuring approximately 21 × 17 mm; its superficial portion was partly cystic, and the deeper portion was finely corpuscular with small hemorrhagic foci. During surgical resection by a gynecologic surgeon, the subcutaneous tissue near the inguinal ligament appeared dense and fibrotic with a small nodule; upon incision, dark, “chocolate-colored” material leaked from the lesion.

A 68-year-old woman presented six years after implantation of a cemented endoprosthetic hinge total knee arthroplasty for conversion of a long-standing knee fusion. For the past five months she noted mild distal thigh and knee pain while walking. On examination, the knee was cool, stable, with a range of motion of 0–80° of flexion and no extensor lag. Radiographs of the femur showed a radiolucent line in the distal diaphyseal cement mantle, a periosteal erosion, and an adjacent soft-tissue mass surrounding the distal femoral diaphysis. A CT scan demonstrated an eccentric lytic lesion of the medial cortex of the distal femoral diaphysis with an adjacent soft-tissue mass measuring approximately 7 cm in length and 2–3 cm in breadth, with septations and a peripheral calcific border. Knee aspiration yielded 259 white cells (71% neutrophils) and was negative for bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast cultures; alpha-defensin and Synovasure tests were negative. Serum C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were normal. Evaluation for metastatic disease was negative.

A 36-year-old G5P2+2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries and two first-trimester miscarriages was referred at 6 weeks of amenorrhea for evaluation of a pregnancy of unknown location. Her serum quantitative β-hCG was 16,124 mIU/mL. A transabdominal ultrasound at presentation did not locate an intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy. A copper intrauterine device had been removed 2 months before her last menstrual period. She had used one cycle of clomiphene. She had no chronic illnesses, did not smoke or drink, and was not on medications.

On examination, blood pressure was 113/70 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. Abdominal, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 13 mm gestational sac with irregular margins and a yolk sac in the anterior isthmic portion of the uterus, raising suspicion for a cesarean-section scar ectopic pregnancy. Doppler was declined. Serial β-hCG measurements rose by 33% over 48 hours (21,521 mIU/mL). The patient missed follow-up and returned 1 week later with 5 days of worsening pelvic pain.

Repeat transvaginal scan revealed a fetal pole with cardiac activity (crown–rump length 0.9 cm) in a sac traversing the full width of the anterior myometrium, extending exophytically toward the serosa, with trophoblastic flow on Doppler; there was no endometrial fluid or free pelvic fluid. She was taken to laparoscopy and hysteroscopy: the bladder was densely adherent to the anterior uterine wall, the ectopic was not visualized, and extensive intrauterine adhesions obscured the view; there was no intracavitary bleeding. Postoperatively, she became hypotensive (systolic 82–95 mmHg) without vaginal bleeding. This prompted an urgent MRI to map the location of the pregnancy.

An 82-year-old woman with hypertension presented with fever, cough, and dyspnea over several days. She was a non-smoker. On admission, her peripheral oxygen saturation was 84% on room air and her respiratory rate was 22 breaths per minute. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed type 1 respiratory failure with a PaO₂ of 41 mm Hg and a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio <200. Laboratory studies showed an elevated C-reactive protein level of 7.8 mg/dL and lymphopenia (470 cells/mm³). Lung ultrasound and chest CT demonstrated moderate-to-severe interstitial involvement, more pronounced at the lung bases (lung ultrasound score 18/36; CT severity score 11/20).

She was treated with CPAP (initial PEEP 7 cm H₂O, titrated to 9 cm H₂O) in a semi-sitting supine position, alternating with high-flow nasal oxygen, along with prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin and dexamethasone (6 mg/day). There was no significant improvement over the first two days.

On hospital day 3, she developed sudden hypoxia (SpO₂ <80%) and tachypnea (RR >35/min) despite escalating oxygen supplementation and conversion to pressure-support ventilation with increasing pressures. Bedside lung ultrasound revealed no pneumothorax or pleural effusion, and echocardiography showed no hypokinesia or right heart overload. The PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio dropped to around 46, with stable hemodynamics. Orotracheal intubation was planned, and she was placed supine for preparation. Soon after, there was a rapid and spontaneous improvement in peripheral oxygenation, with SpO₂ rising by more than 30% and the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio improving to 150 on a Venturi mask (FiO₂ 40%). This allowed deferral and ultimate avoidance of intubation and continuation of noninvasive respiratory support in the supine position.

A 67-year-old man was evaluated for a progressive 13-kg weight loss over 6 years. He denied gastrointestinal symptoms, arthralgias, or neurologic complaints. A PET-CT scan revealed a hypermetabolic right paracoeliac lymph node. To exclude lymphoma or inflammatory disease, gastroscopy and colonoscopy were performed. Endoscopic findings included two small polyps (5 mm) in the gastric fundus and right colon. Histologic examination identified a fundic gland polyp in the stomach and a low-grade dysplastic tubular adenoma in the colon. The duodenal mucosa appeared normal on endoscopy, and four random biopsies of duodenal mucosa and submucosa showed no abnormalities. Ileal biopsies taken from endoscopically normal mucosa included submucosal lymphoid tissue containing Peyer’s patches. On routine hematoxylin and eosin staining, several foamy macrophages were observed within lymphoid follicles, and periodic acid–Schiff staining highlighted numerous PAS-positive macrophages in these follicles.

A 32-year-old white woman presented with 24 hours of diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, and frequent bilious vomiting without changes in bowel habits. Her history included hypertension diagnosed 3 months earlier after preeclampsia and cesarean delivery. She had been taking metoprolol 250 mg twice daily for 1 month and perindopril 4 mg daily for 1 month. She had no known allergies or family history of disease.

On admission she was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Abdominal examination showed diffuse tenderness with guarding and rebound in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 16.46 × 10^3/µl with 14.00 × 10^3/µl neutrophils, normal urea and creatinine, and a C-reactive protein level of 0.69 mg/dl.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated moderate ascites and segmental jejunal wall thickening with submucosal hypoattenuation and mucosal and muscularis enhancement (“target sign”). No lymphadenopathy, free air, or vascular compromise was seen; mesenteric vessels were patent and solid organs were normal.

Because of severe pain resembling an acute abdomen, an emergency diagnostic laparoscopy was performed, revealing only serous intra-abdominal fluid and mild erythema and edema of the small bowel. The fluid was aspirated, a prophylactic appendectomy performed, and cultures of peritoneal fluid were negative. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 3.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a one-week history of acute low back pain radiating to the left leg. The pain worsened despite conservative therapy and was not associated with trauma. She had no significant past medical history and denied anticoagulant use. On examination, vital signs were normal. There was no motor weakness (grade V) or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities; deep-tendon reflexes were intact. Spinal range of motion revealed painful limitation of rotation on the left side. Lumbar spine MRI demonstrated generalized degenerative spondyloarthropathy and a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous extradural mass adjacent to the left L2–L3 facet joint. The lesion measured approximately 2.8 × 2.5 × 0.5 cm, caused narrowing of the spinal canal, and compressed the dural sac and the left L3 nerve root.

A 28-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 14 weeks of amenorrhea, presented to the emergency department with acute-onset, 6-hour history of right lateropelvic pain described as torsion-like. She had no prior medical or surgical history and regular menstrual cycles. On examination, she was alert (GCS 15), reported pain at 10/10 (VAS), and was hemodynamically stable: BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 19 breaths/min, T 37.2 °C. Abdominal exam revealed a soft abdomen with normal respiration and focal right latero-uterine tenderness. Speculum examination showed a normal-appearing cervix without endocervical bleeding. Bimanual examination confirmed an enlarged uterus (3 TDD above the pubic symphysis) with right latero-uterine tenderness.  
Transabdominal and endovaginal ultrasound demonstrated an intrauterine embryo sac with positive cardiac activity (CRL corresponding to 13 weeks) and, in the right adnexal region, a 7.92 × 3.99 cm slightly heterogeneous echogenic mass with anechoic areas and absent Doppler flow, suggesting a large twisted ovary.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a several-month history of chronic constipation, difficulty in defecation, and episodic passages of bloody and yellowish stools. He denied use of mechanical methods or enemas to relieve his constipation. On digital rectal examination, a polypoid mass was palpated in the rectum. Laboratory evaluation revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 13.6 g/dL. A barium enema study was unremarkable. Colonoscopy demonstrated a circumferential polypoid lesion protruding into and occupying the entire mid to lower rectal lumen; the surface showed tortuous and dilated small blood vessels. The remainder of the colon appeared normal.

A 9-year-old Indian boy was evaluated for chronic, recurrent skin lesions present since the first year of life. He had been treated for presumed atopic dermatitis with topical corticosteroids without improvement. His history was negative for growth failure, gastrointestinal symptoms, malabsorption, infections, autoimmune or chronic diseases; family history was unremarkable. On examination, he had diffuse, nonpruritic, annular erythematous lesions with scaly borders and central clearing on the trunk, abdomen, neck, and extremities. Thyroid function tests, autoimmune screening, and serum immunoglobulins were normal. Complete blood count showed a moderate iron‐deficiency anemia (Hb 9 g/dl; transferrin saturation 4%). Screening for celiac disease revealed elevated tissue transglutaminase antibodies (156 UI/ml) and positive anti‐endomysial antibodies. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsies showed villous atrophy consistent with Marsh III celiac disease. A skin biopsy demonstrated a superficial perivascular dermal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, hyperkeratosis, and focal epidermal spongiosis, and direct immunofluorescence revealed no IgA deposits.

A 28-year-old Hispanic American woman visiting from out of state was brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset stiffness and weakness of her upper and lower extremities, involving wrists, ankles, fingers, and toes. Symptoms began acutely while waiting outdoors in direct sunlight. She reported a rapid heart rate, shortness of breath with minimal exertion, diaphoresis, anxiety, numbness, and transient loss of mobility in her right leg. She denied fever, headache, musculoskeletal pain, carbohydrate binge, diarrhea, vomiting, laxative use, tobacco, recreational drugs, or chemical exposures. Her past medical history was significant only for Hashimoto’s hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. She described two similar, self-limited episodes in the past (one 7 months earlier affecting only her arms and one 2 weeks earlier lasting 2 hours and resolving with rest and hydration).

On examination, she was alert and oriented. Vital signs showed a heart rate of 150/min, blood pressure 133/89 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and temperature 98.4 °F. She had dry mucous membranes, no focal neurologic deficits, normal sensation, speech, and coordination.

Initial laboratory studies revealed:
• Potassium 2.3 mmol/L  
• Magnesium 1.2 mg/dL  
• Chloride 81 mg/dL  
• Sodium 139 mmol/L, calcium 8.8 mg/dL  
• Lactate 12.93 mmol/L, anion gap 31 mmol/L  
• Arterial pH 7.48, PCO2 36.6 mmHg, HCO3–27.3 mmol/L  
• Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (baseline ~0.5), GFR 68 mL/min  
• TSH 17 U/L, free T4 1.25 ng/dL  
• AST 113 U/L, ALT 53 U/L  
• MCV 107 fL, normal leukocyte and platelet counts  
• Urinalysis: hazy, 3+ bacteria, 3+ leukocyte esterase; negative troponin and CK  
• ECG: sinus tachycardia  

She received adenosine for possible SVT, intravenous fluids, and potassium/magnesium supplementation. Four hours later, magnesium normalized to 2 mg/dL, but potassium fell further to 1.8 mmol/L. Calcium decreased to 7.3 mg/dL and phosphorus to 2.2 mg/dL. She was transferred to the ICU for telemetry and ongoing electrolyte repletion; empiric ceftriaxone was started for urinary findings. After 28 hours, her electrolytes normalized, yet the cause of her profound electrolyte and acid–base disturbances remained unclear.

A 7½-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of balance disturbances, incoordination of extraocular muscles during walking, dysfunctional gag reflex and swallowing, vocal tremor, monotone speech, and weakness of the masticatory muscles. His motor development had been delayed. There was no family history of laryngeal dystonia; his grandfather had late-life Parkinson’s disease. He had no history of birth asphyxia or cyanosis, and psychological evaluation revealed normal cognition.

Routine laboratory tests, including serum electrolytes, blood glucose, liver function, and kidney function, were normal. Urine and blood chromatography showed no abnormal bands or amino acid elevations. Plasma copper (90 μg/dl) and lactate (9.6 mg/dl) levels were within normal limits, with no evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction.

On examination, he was alert with normal language comprehension, naming, and repetition. Cranial nerves were intact: pupils, visual fields, and funduscopic exam were normal; Kayser–Fleischer rings were absent. He had extraocular incoordination during walking. Facial sensation and movements were normal. The palate and uvula elevated symmetrically; tongue protruded midline. Deep tendon reflexes were hyperactive with bilateral Babinski signs and persistence of a biting reflex. Cerebellar testing was normal. Masticatory muscles were weak, and the gag reflex was hypersensitive.

Brain MRI showed bilateral signal abnormalities in the globus pallidus: axial FLAIR images demonstrated hypointensity with central hyperintensity, and sagittal T2-weighted images confirmed a hyperintense medial portion. The remainder of the brain, ventricular system, brainstem, and cervical cord appeared normal. CT head showed normal gray–white matter differentiation and no lesions. Brainstem auditory evoked potentials, somatosensory evoked potentials, and flash visual evoked potentials all had normal wave morphology, amplitudes, and latencies.

Audio recording and perceptual assessment of a 10-minute speech sample revealed breathiness, roughness, vocal tremor, monotone pitch, and breathy breaks. Maximum phonation time averaged 5 seconds.

A 60-year-old man was referred for implant placement in the right mandible to restore missing first and second molars. He reported no history of jaw trauma, pain, or swelling. Physical examination revealed no facial asymmetry or lymphadenopathy; the right third mandibular molar was absent. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a well-limited unilocular radiolucent area with a smooth, sclerotic border located below the right mandibular canal. At this stage, several diagnoses were possible, including traumatic bone cyst, residual cyst, dentigerous cyst, odontogenic keratocyst, focal osteoporotic bone marrow defect, and Stafne’s bone defect. For further evaluation and to establish a definitive diagnosis, cone-beam computed tomography was recommended.

A 56-year-old Caucasian man who works as a farmer presented with a pricking pain in the lower lip and an unhealed wound present for approximately six years. His medical history was notable for hypertension and diabetes; he denied tobacco and alcohol use and reported daily sun exposure without UV protection. 

On examination, there was a 3-cm ulcerated and crusted area on the lower lip; the upper lip and intraoral mucosa were unremarkable. Based on the clinical appearance and his occupational sun exposure, a provisional diagnosis of lip squamous cell carcinoma or actinic cheilitis was made. 

An initial incisional biopsy was deferred because of markedly elevated blood pressure (200/120 mmHg), and the patient was prescribed topical 0.1% triamcinolone acetonide cream. Seven days later, he returned with significant clinical improvement, and an incisional biopsy was performed. 

Histopathological examination revealed a parakeratotic stratum corneum with ulceration and, in the lamina propria, a dense sheet-like infiltrate composed predominantly of mature plasma cells, along with some lymphocytes, few eosinophils, and sparse Russell bodies. The plasma cells extended through the connective tissue into the minor salivary glands. There was no cellular atypia, pleomorphism, or mitotic activity. Immunohistochemistry for kappa and lambda light chains demonstrated a polyclonal plasma cell population with lambda predominance. 

Serological testing for syphilis was negative. Thirty-five days after the biopsy, with continued use of lip balm and sunscreen, the lesion had completely regressed, and there was no recurrence at six months.

A 1-day-old Black Bantu African female infant was born at preterm gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 32-year-old gravida 3, para 2 mother. The pregnancy was complicated by abruptio placentae, severe oligohydramnios noted on third-trimester ultrasound, and late antenatal care (first visit at 28 weeks). The mother denied diabetes (random blood glucose 5.1 mmol/L at delivery) and did not receive folic acid supplementation.

At admission, the baby weighed 1000 g, measured 40 cm in length, and had an occipitofrontal circumference of 30 cm (<10th percentile). She was alert but exhibited mild respiratory distress. Physical examination revealed:
- Microcephaly  
- Prominent occiput  
- Low-set ears  
- Right unilateral cleft lip and palate  
- Micrognathia  
- Bilateral elbow contractures  
- Disproportionately short lower limbs  

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, C-reactive protein, renal function, and electrolytes, were within normal limits. Cranial ultrasound was unremarkable. Chest radiography showed rib flattening. Skeletal X-rays demonstrated right femoral aplasia and left femoral hypoplasia. Echocardiography identified a small patent ductus arteriosus.

A 30-year-old man presented with right-knee pain, recurrent swelling, a sense of instability, clicking sounds, and occasional locking episodes for 6 months, all beginning after a twisting injury sustained while playing kabaddi. He applied bandages and received massage from a bonesetter at the time of injury. He denied any prior joint symptoms elsewhere.

On examination, there was medial joint-line tenderness and minimal effusion. Varus and valgus stress testing showed no laxity. The anterior-drawer, Lachman, and pivot-shift tests were positive. The McMurray test reproduced pain medially. There was noticeable quadriceps wasting, and range of motion was terminally painful and restricted. His Lysholm Knee Score was 31.

Plain radiographs of the knee showed minimal arthritic changes with marginal osteophyte formation and a well-maintained joint space (Kellgren–Lawrence grade II). Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a complete anterior cruciate ligament tear, a bucket-handle tear of the posterior and body segments of the medial meniscus (double PCL sign), and a hyperintense area in the posteromedial femoral condyle suggesting cartilage injury.

The working diagnosis was a complete ACL tear with a medial-meniscal bucket-handle tear and early osteoarthritic changes. Arthroscopic surgery was planned. Intraoperatively, the ACL was completely torn, and a bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus was confirmed, along with a 3 cm × 3 cm cartilage defect on the medial femoral condyle. Debridement and microfracture were performed. Additionally, an extensive and unusual amount of synovitis was noted; this tissue was debrided and sent for histopathology and culture sensitivity. ACL reconstruction was completed with a quadrupled hamstring graft and titanium screw fixation.

A 22-year-old man was brought to the ICU after being found on the street with fluctuating consciousness—initially agitated, then somnolent. On arrival he was hypotensive, tachycardic, and breathing labored; his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 6, necessitating endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation under sedation with fentanyl, midazolam, and etomidate. He was hemodynamically unstable (shock index, 2), had mild muscle rigidity, and a core temperature of 42.0°C. No medical history was available. Antipyretic drugs had no effect. Laboratory studies showed marked rhabdomyolysis (creatine kinase elevated), lactate dehydrogenase 2020 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 785 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 157 U/L, pH 7.27, lactate 5.8 mmol/L, hemoglobin 18.7 g/dL, glucose 6.9 mg/dL, sodium 148 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, and central venous oxygen saturation 59%. Toxicology screening detected only a cannabis metabolite and the benzodiazepine used for sedation. A noncontrast head CT scan and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were unremarkable. Due to acute renal failure from rhabdomyolysis, continuous hemodialysis was initiated. Despite cessation of the cooling device, antipyretic therapy remained ineffective.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive pain and swelling over the left thenar eminence and proximal thumb. She denied any preceding trauma, constitutional symptoms (no fever, weight loss, or night sweats), or history of tuberculosis exposure. On examination, there was a tender, firm swelling over the first carpometacarpal area with painful thumb movement; she was afebrile and otherwise hemodynamically stable.

A plain radiograph of the hand demonstrated a lytic lesion at the base of the first metacarpal with a pathological fracture and surrounding soft-tissue haziness. Ultrasound confirmed a fluid collection consistent with an abscess. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a large heterogeneous lesion at the first carpometacarpal joint space with joint widening, findings interpreted as most consistent with an infectious abscess and less likely a neoplastic process. 

Based on these findings, the initial differential diagnoses included pyogenic osteomyelitis, tuberculous osteomyelitis, soft-tissue swelling (eg, post-traumatic), and malignancy.

A 52-year-old man with a history of congestive heart failure, hypertension, alcohol abuse, and endovascular abdominal aortic aneurysm repair 4 years earlier initially presented to an outside hospital with abdominal pain and diarrhea. CT of the abdomen showed an expanding abdominal aortic aneurysm with a type II endoleak, and coil embolization of the inferior mesenteric artery was performed with thrombosis of the leak. He was discharged home but returned 1 month later with persistent abdominal pain. A follow-up CT scan showed further expansion of the aneurysm and a few gas bubbles around the endovascular graft. His white blood cell count was 14,000/mm3 (normal 4,000–10,000/mm3). He was transferred to our center, where two sets of blood cultures were drawn, and he was started on intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin. Vascular surgery recommended explantation of the endovascular graft with surgical bypass reconstruction.

A 21-year-old woman with autism spectrum disorder (on risperidone) and intellectual disability was brought to the hospital after a witnessed collapse. She had no prior history of syncope, cardiac arrest, or known cardiovascular disease, and her family denied any illicit drug or alcohol use. While at a noisy auto mechanic shop, she became pale and lost consciousness; bystander ECG showed ventricular fibrillation. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after two defibrillations. On arrival, her blood pressure was 93/70 mmHg, pulse 86 bpm, and oxygen saturation 100% (bag–valve–mask). An intravenous amiodarone infusion (1 mg/min) and oral amiodarone 400 mg were administered. On examination she was comatose (GCS 3), with agonal respirations; cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. In the intensive care unit, her differential diagnosis included channelopathies, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and metabolic abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed normal chemistry panel and electrolytes. Initial electrocardiogram revealed sinus rhythm with interpolated premature ventricular complexes and a QTc of 380 ms, without any evidence of infarction, pre-excitation, or Brugada pattern. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 45–50%, normal wall thickness, and no valvular abnormalities.

A 33-year-old gravida 1 at 23 weeks gestation presented with fatigue and persistent fever. Ten days earlier she had been hospitalized elsewhere for gastroenteritis and nephrolithiasis, treated with oral second-generation cephalosporin, and discharged the day before with intermittent fevers. She denied dysuria, diarrhea, sore throat, cough, nausea, or rupture of membranes. Fetal ultrasound showed a healthy 23-week fetus. At home her temperature reached 39.8 °C; on arrival it was 37 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. Examination revealed clear lungs except for shallow sounds on the right, a nontender abdomen, and normal cervical exam. Initial laboratory tests—including complete blood count, urine analysis, and stool analysis—were normal, except for an elevated C-reactive protein level of 19.96 mg/dL. 

A few hours later she developed sudden tachycardia (210 beats/min), tachypnea (30 breaths/min), and fever (39.6 °C). Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild tricuspid regurgitation, first-degree pulmonary hypertension, and normal systolic function. Chest radiograph was normal. Blood, urine, stool, and cervical cultures were obtained, and intravenous meropenem was started. In the ICU her blood pressure fell to 70/40 mm Hg and pulse rose to 140 beats/min. One hour later she developed dyspnea and chest pain; her D-dimer was >100 000 ng/mL, white blood cell count 25 000/mm³, platelet count 77 000/mm³, PaO₂ 77 mm Hg, PaCO₂ 20 mm Hg, and pH 7.47. Low-molecular-weight heparin was administered for possible pulmonary embolism or disseminated intravascular coagulation. Venous ultrasound was normal but incidentally noted a 6 cm calcific echogenic mass in the liver.

A 66-year-old man with end-stage renal disease from diabetic nephropathy, on thrice-weekly hemodialysis for 20 years, was evaluated for right carpal tunnel syndrome due to nocturnal numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Physical examination revealed positive Tinel’s sign and Phalen’s test. Nerve conduction studies showed a median distal motor latency of 10.86 ms and absent sensory conduction in the right hand. Conservative measures failed, and surgical release was scheduled immediately after dialysis.

Before admission, hemodialysis sessions (4 hours, three times weekly) used an Asahi Kasei ABH-21F hemodiafilter with heparin anticoagulation. On the first scheduled surgery day, he developed fever (~38°C) during dialysis; surgery was postponed. One week later, during a second preoperative dialysis session, he again developed fever (~38°C), chills, shivering, hypotension (80–90 mmHg systolic), and tachycardia (108/min). Laboratory tests met DIC criteria (systemic inflammatory response, thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT ratio, elevated fibrin degradation products). Whole-body CT and echocardiography were unremarkable, and blood cultures were negative. Sepsis was suspected; he received meropenem and vancomycin, and symptoms resolved within hours. Inflammatory markers normalized over 17 days.

One month after completing antibiotics, surgery was rescheduled. During the third preoperative dialysis session, he again developed fever (~38°C), nausea, and vomiting during dialysis; surgery was postponed and all symptoms subsided within a few hours of completing dialysis.

A 35-year-old woman, gravida 5, para 3, abortus 2, was referred for continuous vaginal bleeding for 2 months after an uncomplicated first-trimester curettage at 12 weeks 4 days for a missed abortion. Her obstetric history included two prior low-transverse cesarean deliveries and two prior curettages without complication. The pathology report after the curettage showed decidual tissue. 

On presentation, her vital signs were stable. Physical examination was unremarkable. Gynecologic examination revealed a normal vulva and vagina, a closed cervix, and a retroverted uterus enlarged to approximately 10–12 weeks’ size; mild bleeding was noted. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, a normal urinalysis, β-hCG 112 mIU/mL, and normal coagulation, hepatic, renal, and electrolyte panels.

Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated a retroverted uterus with an endometrial thickness of 2.6 mm and a hypoechoic 8-cm mass in the lower uterine segment with necrotic changes and increased vascularity with low resistance. Total abdominal ultrasound and chest radiography were normal.
