Differential diagnosis included invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, and uterine tumors, including degenerating myoma.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a 5–7-day history of abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and absence of gas and fecal discharge. She reported a one-year history of chronic constipation and had undergone surgery for a left femoral neck fracture. On examination, she had mild abdominal tenderness and distension without signs of peritonitis; digital rectal examination revealed stool in the rectal vault. Her white-cell count was 12 450/mL. Supine and left lateral decubitus abdominal radiographs showed abundant fecal material throughout the colon. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated extensive rectosigmoid dilatation containing large, dense fecal material, with maximal transverse diameters of 8 cm in the sigmoid colon and 12 cm in the rectum. Focal mural thickening of up to 7.2 mm and subtle pericolic fat stranding were seen in the distended rectosigmoid. Mild free fluid was present in the abdominal and pelvic cavities, but no extraluminal free air was detected.

A 5-year-old girl was admitted with a 2-month history of intermittent fever, cough, and shortness of breath. She had experienced recurrent lower respiratory tract infections since infancy. There was no family history of primary immunodeficiency or consanguinity. On examination, she was tachypneic with audible stridor and moist rales over both lung fields; there was no rash, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly.  

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• WBC 18.6×10^9/L, neutrophils 13.02×10^9/L, CRP 11.2 mg/L  
• Serum IgG 4.56 g/L (normal 5.0–10.6), IgA 0.11 g/L (0.34–1.38), IgM 0.16 g/L (0.44–1.44), IgE 5 IU/mL (0–60)  
• HIV antibody test and viral load negative  
• Normal counts of CD4+ (1223 cells/µL), CD8+ (382 cells/µL), CD19+ (309 cells/µL), and NK cells (286 cells/µL); normal NBT test  

High-resolution CT of the chest showed multifocal small-airway obstruction with bilateral diffuse infiltrates and areas of bronchiectasis. Electronic bronchoscopy revealed heavy yellow-white purulent secretions throughout the airways, and bronchoalveolar lavage was performed.

A 66-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive shortness of breath. She had no significant medical history and took no medications. Born and raised in a shrine, she initially sought care for sudden right shoulder pain. Chest radiography and high-resolution CT revealed a right pneumothorax and interstitial shadows in both lower lung fields. After chest-tube drainage resolved the pneumothorax, the interstitial changes persisted, and she was referred for further evaluation of interstitial lung disease.

At initial examination: respiratory rate 14 breaths/min; blood pressure 100/50 mmHg; temperature 36.8 °C; oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Auscultation revealed inspiratory fine crackles in the right lower lung field; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, C-reactive protein level, and blood chemistry; serum KL-6 was elevated at 1116 IU/L, and arterial PaO2 was 67.4 mmHg. Repeat chest radiography and CT scans demonstrated ground-glass attenuation predominantly in the right lower lobe.

A 59-year-old Japanese woman with no history of smoking or medical issues was referred for evaluation of an abnormal chest radiograph noted on an annual health check. The radiograph revealed a nodular shadow with irregular and indistinct margins in the left lower lung field. Chest computed tomography showed a 1.2 cm irregularly margined solid nodule in the superior lingular segment with surrounding multilocular cystic air spaces; the lesion was subpleural without direct visceral pleural contact, devoid of ground-glass opacity, and showed no enhancement or calcification. Serum tumor markers, fungal antigens, and antibody to Mycobacterium avium complex were all negative. A transbronchial biopsy was inconclusive, and the nodule remained unchanged on follow-up CT 2 months later. Because of suspicion for primary lung cancer arising in the cystic lesion and the risk of pleural dissemination with percutaneous biopsy, video-assisted thoracic surgery was planned for diagnosis.

A 45-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to obstructive nephropathy presented with 2 months of swelling of the left side of his neck, face, and left upper limb. He denied recent trauma, fever, or chills. His medications included amlodipine, pantoprazole, carvedilol, calcium carbonate, and calcitriol. He had been on hemodialysis for 1½ years via a left internal jugular catheter. After failure of a left radiocephalic arteriovenous fistula, a left brachiocephalic fistula was created, after which he developed severe venous hypertension of the left arm.

He denied chest pain, night sweats, or weight loss. On examination, he was afebrile with a blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg. There was diffuse edema over the left face, neck, chest, and left upper limb. The arteriovenous fistula showed no signs of infection. There was no thyroid enlargement or lymphadenopathy. Jugular veins were not distended, cardiac auscultation was normal, and lung fields were clear.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, white-cell count 8400 cells/mm3, normal liver function tests, and normal bleeding and clotting times. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, T3, and T4 levels were within normal limits.

A chest radiograph demonstrated increased density and soft-tissue swelling over the left neck, chest, and arm, with a massive left-sided pleural effusion. Doppler ultrasonography of the neck revealed decreased flow in the left subclavian vein. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal biventricular function with an ejection fraction of 62%. Computed tomography of the thorax confirmed a large left pleural effusion without evidence of malignancy or lymphadenopathy. A conventional angiogram revealed total occlusion of the left innominate vein. Percutaneous angioplasty of the left innominate vein was performed, after which his facial and upper-limb swelling markedly improved.

A 26-year-old woman with a history of congenital disorder of glycosylation type 1 diagnosed in infancy, who had been lost to metabolic follow-up, presented with acute-onset dyspnea. She denied chest pain, palpitations, or wheezing but reported upper respiratory symptoms for 2 weeks. On arrival, she was lethargic, hypotensive (78/60 mmHg), tachycardic (127 b.p.m.), tachypneic (32 breaths/min), and febrile (38.8°C). Lung auscultation revealed bilateral crepitations; cardiovascular examination was otherwise unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies showed type 1 respiratory failure, markedly elevated inflammatory markers, a troponin level of 21 ng/L (normal <15 ng/L), and an NT-proBNP level of 7511 ng/L (normal <150 ng/L). Chest radiography demonstrated globular cardiomegaly and patchy consolidations in the right middle and both lower lung zones. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia without arrhythmias. She was diagnosed with severe multilobar pneumonia and septic shock, and was intubated, ventilated, and started on broad-spectrum antibiotics and an intravenous noradrenaline infusion.

Further history revealed that she required partial assistance with activities of daily living due to cognitive impairment, had no known cardiac disease, and had three siblings, one of whom also had CDG. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a dilated left ventricle with severe global systolic dysfunction and a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion without tamponade.

A 54-year-old man presented in April 2018 with a 2-month history of fever and persistent cough. He had a 17-year history of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and a 360-pack-year smoking history. Physical examination was unremarkable, and vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests showed a fasting blood glucose of 15.5 mmol/L with normal liver and renal function, normal C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, and serum tumor markers. Sputum culture, sputum smear for acid-fast bacillus, and T-SPOT® TB were negative. Immunoglobulin levels, T cell subsets, and autoantibody screens were within normal limits; HIV serology was negative. Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography revealed enlarged mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes and a mass-like lesion in the left hilum causing stenosis of the proximal left upper bronchus. Bronchoscopy showed reddening and thickening of the bronchial mucosa with stenosis of the left main bronchus. Bronchial membrane biopsy specimens were obtained, and endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration of stations 7 and 11L lymph nodes was performed.

A 47-year-old Yemeni woman with systemic lupus erythematosus/systemic sclerosis overlap, usual interstitial pneumonia, and pulmonary hypertension presented with 5 days of fever, productive cough, and dyspnea. Her home medications included hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisolone, sildenafil, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis. On admission, temperature was 39.1 °C, blood pressure 107/68 mmHg, pulse 118/min, respiratory rate 30/min, and oxygen saturation 90% on 60 L/min high-flow nasal cannula (FiO2 0.95). Chest examination revealed diffuse coarse crackles. Chest radiograph showed extensive bilateral consolidations. Laboratory tests were notable for lymphopenia and mild transaminase elevations. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive. She was treated with dexamethasone and antiviral therapy, improved by hospital day 14, and was weaned to low-flow nasal cannula; prednisolone was increased to 15 mg daily. 

On day 21, she developed worsening dyspnea. Temperature was 37.2 °C, blood pressure 110/71 mmHg, pulse 101/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on 4 L/min nasal cannula. Chest radiograph showed worsening bilateral infiltrates. Laboratory studies revealed a drop in white cell count from 13,000 to 3,900 × 10^9/L, platelets from 640,000 to 131,000 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 51 mg/L, alanine aminotransferase 138 U/L, and aspartate aminotransferase 43 U/L. Repeat SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. Computed tomography of the chest demonstrated new bilateral ground-glass opacities and progression of fibrotic changes. Tests for Pneumocystis jirovecii (microscopy and β-D-glucan), tuberculosis (sputum acid-fast smear and PCR), Aspergillus (serum galactomannan), varicella, herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus were sent.

A 5-year-old boy with a history of preterm birth and a relatively large right forearm since birth presented with progressive swelling of the right second and third fingers 2 months after an insect bite. On examination, there was marked swelling, erythema, skin erosions, and crusts of those fingers. He was admitted and treated with antibiotics for suspected infection without improvement. Because of progressive swelling and poor wound healing, contrast-enhanced CT of the right upper limb was obtained, showing enlarged serpiginous vascular structures on the radial side of the forearm and extensive soft-tissue edema in the hand. Contrast-enhanced MR angiography revealed an enlarged, mildly tortuous vessel presumed to be the radial artery, draining into many indistinct collateral veins in the early arterial phase, findings that were initially interpreted as an arteriovenous malformation fed by the radial artery. The patient had no signs of high-output heart failure. Interventional radiology was consulted for catheter angiography and management.

A 67-year-old man presented with bright red rectal bleeding and copious mucus discharge. He reported a lifelong history of constipation, excessive straining, and a sensation of incomplete evacuation that had worsened over the past 12 years, recently accompanied by perineal pain. He had undergone evaluation for iron deficiency anaemia in 2012, including colonoscopy (revealing only hemorrhoids), gastroscopy, and small-bowel MRI, all of which were normal. He had no other comorbidities. 

On examination, the abdomen was soft and non-tender. A large polypoidal growth was seen protruding from the anal canal, surrounded by circumferential hemorrhoids; digital rectal examination was limited by pain and partial luminal obstruction. 

Under anaesthesia, rigid sigmoidoscopy to 15 cm showed normal rectal mucosa. A pedunculated polyp measuring 25 × 20 mm arising posterolaterally at the anorectal junction and protruding 50 mm externally was identified along with grade III hemorrhoids. The polyp was excised down to the muscle layer and sent for histologic evaluation.

A 26-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus complicated by aseptic meningitis and multiple small strokes 2 weeks earlier presented with sudden, painless decreased vision and a right visual-field deficit in her left eye (OS) of 12 days’ duration, without improvement. Visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye (OD) and count fingers at 1 foot OS. Pupils were equal and reactive, with a left afferent pupillary defect. Brightness and color vision were reduced OS. Anterior segments and intraocular pressures were normal in both eyes. Dilated fundus examination showed mild disc edema and a cotton-wool spot along the superior arcade OD, and severe disc edema with peripapillary hemorrhage, a cherry-red spot in the macula, sclerosed and sheathed vessels, diffuse retinal ischemia, and peripheral retinal hemorrhages OS. Optical coherence tomography revealed nerve-fiber-layer thickening. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated complete capillary nonperfusion extending from the macula OS and normal perfusion OD. Laboratory studies revealed positive antinuclear antibodies (1:160, speckled), anti-Smith (>8), anti-RNP (>8), SSA (3.1), and anti-cardiolipin (26), with low complement levels (C3, 39; C4, 8.3). Hypercoagulability testing and extensive infectious studies were unrevealing. Brain MRI showed a punctate lacunar infarct; MRA was normal. She was treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, then prednisone, cyclophosphamide, hydroxychloroquine, and warfarin for presumed antiphospholipid syndrome. Visual acuity OS was 2 ft/200 at discharge.  

Two months later, she returned with recurrent fevers up to 102°F. Repeat infectious workup was negative. PET–CT revealed hypermetabolic cervical lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration and core-needle biopsy of cervical lymph nodes were nondiagnostic.

A 58-year-old man was referred to the ENT outpatient clinic on an urgent two-week-wait pathway with a history of intermittent exertional stridor, dysphonia, and dysphagia. His symptoms had recurred over multiple emergency department visits, and an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was normal. He had undergone a partial thyroidectomy for multinodular goitre in 2006 and a revision right hemithyroidectomy in 2017 for compressive symptoms. He was prescribed thyroxine and calcium supplements but admitted to poor adherence with calcium.

On examination, there were well-healed thyroidectomy scars. Flexible nasendoscopy revealed tongue-base fullness with symmetrical vocal-cord mobility and no mucosal lesions. A CT scan of the neck and thorax showed a small mucous-retention cyst at the tongue base and residual thyroid tissue bilaterally but no evidence of malignancy.

He was scheduled for panendoscopy under general anaesthesia, and routine pre-operative blood tests were obtained.

A 42-year-old man presented with nonpainful edema of the right leg of subacute onset. He had no history of trauma, malignancy, or hypercoagulability. On examination, the right leg was edematous but neither tense nor hyperemic; there was no lymphadenopathy or palpable mass. Doppler ultrasound of the right lower extremity demonstrated significant stenosis of the external iliac vein caused by an anechoic lesion. Computed tomography angiography confirmed a 3-cm oval mass on the medial side of the right external iliac vein, between the inguinal ligament and pubic bone, containing homogeneous fluid and producing focal reduction of the vessel lumen.

A 63-year-old man presented with months of hypogastric abdominal pain and bowel disturbance. He had a positive fecal occult blood test on screening. Colonoscopy was incomplete because of a sigmoid stricture; numerous small diverticula were noted in that segment. Routine blood tests showed a mild microcytic hypochromic anemia. 

Abdominal radiographs (upright and supine) demonstrated a large, well-defined oval air-filled structure in the lower abdomen; the remainder of the bowel gas pattern was unremarkable, with no free intraperitoneal air. 

Given the incomplete colonoscopy and positive occult blood, a CT colonography was performed. Axial, coronal, and sagittal images revealed a thick-walled, 7 cm cystic mass arising from the sigmoid colon, with surrounding inflammatory fat stranding and multiple small diverticula. Communication between the mass and sigmoid lumen was seen, and the sigmoid colon wall showed circumferential thickening consistent with severe diverticular disease. Three-dimensional reconstructions confirmed a thin connection (neck) between the cystic mass and the bowel lumen. 

Two days later, a contrast-enhanced CT scan showed weak delayed enhancement of the cyst wall.

A 21-year-old woman from southern Thailand presented with a 5-day history of high-grade fever, polyarthralgia, and polymyalgia, with an erythematous rash appearing one day before admission. She had no chronic illnesses, no photosensitivity, oral ulcers, or recent travel outside Bangkok, and denied animal or floodwater exposures. On examination, temperature was 38.6°C; blood pressure 105/60 mmHg; pulse 98 /min; respiratory rate 24 /min. She had mild dehydration, bilateral conjunctival injection, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, and pain in her calves and multiple joints; cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurologic, and abdominal examinations were otherwise unremarkable. 

Initial laboratory studies on day 0 showed leukocytosis without thrombocytopenia, mild elevation of transaminases, normal renal function, and an unremarkable urinalysis. She was started on ceftriaxone for presumed leptospirosis. On hospital day 2, she developed worsening joint and muscle pain with puffy hands and feet and proximal muscle weakness; repeat blood counts remained notable for leukocytosis. Serologic tests for chikungunya (IgM rapid test and HAI IgG), scrub typhus, murine typhus, and leptospiral antibodies were negative. By day 5, she had progressive edema, a generalized erythematous rash, painful symmetric arthritis of the hands and feet, an ESR of 83 mm/hr, and elevated muscle enzymes; urinalysis remained normal.

A 14-year-old boy from a rural region of Ethiopia presented with an 8-month history of a painless, reddish-pink, fleshy mass on the left eye, associated with foreign-body sensation and intermittent discomfort. He denied any trauma or similar lesions elsewhere. Vital signs were within normal limits. On ocular examination, there was a 20×4 mm pinkish, pedunculated, fleshy mass on the left palpebral conjunctiva, studded with multiple yellowish and white nodules on its surface; visual acuity was normal. With a clinical impression of pyogenic granuloma, the lesion was excised at its base under local anesthesia, and hemostasis was achieved. A formalin-fixed tissue fragment was submitted for histopathologic evaluation.

A 21-year-old woman was admitted in 1978 with acute pulmonary edema, circulatory collapse, headache, vomiting, and dyspnea with frothy, blood-tinged sputum. Neurologic examination showed right central facial palsy, left facial hyperesthesia, nystagmus, anisocoria, asymmetric palate elevation, tongue deviation to the left, dysphagia, and nasal speech. Brain MRI and lumbar puncture were normal. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, hyperglycemia, and elevated transaminases; immunologic tests for collagen and viral diseases were within normal limits. She was treated with diuretics, bronchodilators, cardiotonics, corticosteroids, and antibiotics, with partial neurologic recovery but persistent mild left facial hyperesthesia, palate paresis, bladder incoordination, and speech difficulties.

In 1979 she experienced a recurrence of neurologic symptoms. MRI now showed demyelinating changes; systemic collagen diseases were excluded, and multiple sclerosis was diagnosed. High-dose corticosteroids resulted in partial improvement.

From 1979 to 1984 she was stable. Two years after pregnancy, she developed painful eye movements and acute bilateral vision loss. In April 1984 visual acuity declined to 0.7 in the right eye and 0.9 in the left. Bilateral retrobulbar neuritis was diagnosed and treated with intravenous methylprednisolone. Six months later she developed total uveitis with anterior chamber proteins and cells, vitreous inflammation, retinal vasculitis (predominantly venous), papillitis, and macular edema. Therapy included systemic and local corticosteroids.

In 1989 she was rehospitalized for transient speech disturbance, right-hand weakness, and urinary incontinence. MRI revealed diffuse, high-intensity bilateral periventricular, subcortical, and deep white matter lesions consistent with multiple sclerosis. Ophthalmologic findings included recurrent bilateral uveitis, macular edema, and optic disc atrophy. She received repeated pulse corticosteroids.

In 2003 she had speech impairment, paresthesias, ataxia, visual impairment, and urinary incontinence. ANA was positive; other collagen and viral tests were negative. Progression of uveitis led to bilateral complicated cataracts.

In 2004 chest radiography demonstrated fibrotic, bilateral pulmonary changes. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme was elevated at 68 U/L (normal 8–52). Brain MRI showed diffuse multifocal white matter lesions with global atrophy; CSF analysis was negative. A secondary CNS demyelinating vasculitis was suspected, and corticosteroid therapy was continued.

In 2009 chest CT showed intense consolidation of the right upper lobe with a mixed reticular/nodular pattern, peribronchial fibrosis, and necrotic mediastinal lymph nodes. Serum ACE levels were 86 U/L and 65 U/L.

A 43-year-old man presented with bilateral worsening of visual acuity and photophobia over several years. His medical history was unremarkable, with no systemic or metabolic diseases, no medications, no contact-lens use, and a negative family history for ocular disease. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 0.63 in both eyes. Slit-lamp evaluation revealed bilateral diffuse yellowish deposits confined to the corneal stroma. Central corneal thickness measured 543 μm OD and 542 μm OS, intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg bilaterally, and the retinas appeared normal. Over the next three years, vision declined to 0.25 OD and 0.16 OS. Genetic testing for TGFBI and DCN mutations was negative. In vivo confocal laser-scanning microscopy showed rarefied keratocytes and decreased transparency in the anterior stroma; loss of keratocytes with “coral”-like hyperreflective structures in the mid stroma; and homogeneous hyperreflection with obscured details in the posterior stroma in both eyes. Non–HLA-matched penetrating keratoplasty was performed OS and HLA-matched keratoplasty OD, both with uneventful postoperative courses. Two years after surgery, fine stromal deposits recurred, and vision was 0.63 OD and 0.8 OS. Three years postoperatively, vision declined to 0.32 OD and 0.5 OS, slit-lamp appearance was identical to preoperative findings, anterior segment OCT showed homogeneous stromal hyperreflectivity, and CLSM again revealed rarefied keratocytes anteriorly, “coral”-like mid-stromal hyperreflective structures, and posterior stromal hyperreflection.

A 38-year-old man sustained a high-pressure nitrogen gas blast to the chest at 30 cm while attempting to dismantle a cylinder. He presented with chest pain and dyspnea. Initial vital signs were normal. A chest radiograph demonstrated a large left pneumothorax, and a chest tube was placed. On post-injury day 3, the tube drained 1500 mL of foul-smelling, cloudy fluid; cultures grew anaerobes and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and the white-blood-cell count was elevated. On day 7, he underwent a left anterolateral thoracotomy with decortication and placement of two new chest tubes. Postoperatively, he continued to accumulate large amounts of milky pleural effusion, and chylothorax was suspected.

A 27-year-old woman presented with an eight-year history of a slowly growing mass in the anterior nasal cavity, associated with persistent bilateral nasal obstruction, recurrent mucoid discharge, intermittent epistaxis, diffuse facial pain, and chronic headaches. Three years earlier, she underwent local resection of submucosal tissue and partial septal cartilage under suspicion of obstructive pathology; biopsy at that time showed fibrous tissue with hyaline degeneration. Two years ago her nasal obstruction recurred and progressively worsened. Examination revealed a broad nasal bridge and firm, submucosal thickening of the anterior septum palpable on both sides. There were no cutaneous lesions on the nose or face. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated a perforation of the anterior septal mucosa, likely from prior surgery.

Noncontrast CT of the paranasal sinuses showed homogeneous soft-tissue thickening of the anterior septum and adjacent lateral nasal walls that was isoattenuating to cerebral gray matter, with focal thinning of the frontal process of the maxilla and a 1.3 × 1.0 cm septal perforation. MRI demonstrated an anterior septal and bilateral anterior inferior turbinate lesion that was isointense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images, without involvement of the lacrimal sac or nasolacrimal duct. Chest radiograph was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed a slight neutropenia; hemoglobin, hematocrit, platelets, ESR, and biochemistry profiles were normal. Serum IgA was mildly elevated; antinuclear and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies were negative. Anti–proteinase 3 (c-ANCA) and anti–myeloperoxidase (p-ANCA) antibodies were below detection. Skin-prick testing was positive to dandelion and dust mites, and total serum IgE was elevated.

A 30-year-old woman with no past medical history received a third dose of the mRNA-1273 COVID-19 vaccine 5 days before presentation. Two days after vaccination, she noted a pruritic, erythematous macular rash on the back of her neck and volar forearms, accompanied by a mild dry cough. She tested positive for COVID-19 antigen and began outpatient antihistamines. On day 4 of symptoms, she presented to the emergency department with progression of the pruritic rash to the neck, face, arms, trunk, and legs, along with mild fever (37.9°C) and dyspepsia, but no respiratory distress or abdominal pain. She denied new food, medication, herbal, or insect exposures; no history of similar rashes or allergic conditions; and no family history of dermatologic disease.

On examination, temperature 37.9°C, blood pressure 114/72 mmHg, heart rate 85/min, respiratory rate 20/min, O₂ saturation 99% on room air. Widespread raised, erythematous, pruritic lesions were noted on the face, trunk, and all extremities. The remainder of the examination, including the respiratory system, was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed white cell count 12×10^9 cells/L (4–10), C-reactive protein 129 mg/L (<8), interleukin-6 74 pg/mL (<7), ferritin 308 μg/L (12–160), alanine aminotransferase 63 U/L (0–33), aspartate aminotransferase 71 U/L (0–32), normal renal function, and normal electrolytes. COVID-19 PCR was positive. Chest radiograph was unremarkable; electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia.

A term male neonate (birth weight 2.5 kg) was discharged home on day 2 of life after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. On day 3, he was treated with intensive phototherapy for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 20.6 mg/dL). By day 5, his bilirubin had decreased to 9.6 mg/dL and he was discharged. On day 9 of life, he presented with a 6-hour history of poor feeding, lethargy, and reduced activity, along with yellow discoloration of the hands and feet for 2 days. 

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable: heart rate 120 beats/min, warm extremities, capillary refill <3 s, and temperature 36.6 °C. Random blood glucose was 98 mg/dL. Icterus was noted up to knees and elbows without any signs of bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction. Neurologic examination revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9 (eye opening to pain, withdraws to pain, cries to pain), equal reactive pupils, a level anterior fontanelle, normal cry, generalized hypotonia, hypoactive deep tendon reflexes, and poor respiratory effort. There were no seizures, neck retractions, or cranial-nerve deficits.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15.8 g/dL, white-cell count 7300 cells/mm³ (63% neutrophils), platelets 290 000/mm³, C-reactive protein 0.5 mg/L, total bilirubin 12 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.8 mEq/L, total protein 5.5 g/dL, albumin 3.5 g/dL, AST 50 U/L, ALT 36 U/L, and a normal random blood sugar. 

The patient was admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit for further evaluation.

A 55-year-old man with a history of HIV/AIDS presented with several weeks of malaise, unintentional weight loss, abdominal distension, nausea, and decreased urine output. His HIV had been well controlled on HAART for several years; 6 months earlier he had completed 1.5 years of clarithromycin, ethambutol, and moxifloxacin for disseminated MAC, with full resolution and negative testing before antibiotic discontinuation.

On examination, he was cachectic with marked abdominal distension and a fluid wave. Laboratory studies showed a CD4 count of 520 cells/mm3 and undetectable HIV viral load. Liver tests revealed an AST of 38 U/L, ALT of 29 U/L, bilirubin of 1.1 mg/dL, and an alkaline phosphatase of 491 U/L; platelet count and INR were normal. Diagnostic paracentesis demonstrated a serum–ascites albumin gradient of 1.6 (serum albumin 2.6 g/dL; ascites albumin 1.0 g/dL).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a markedly attenuated portal vein with cavernous transformation and a 4.0 × 2.9 cm infiltrating mass in the periportal/portacaval region along the posterior margin of the attenuated portal vein, causing complete occlusion of the main portal vein. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed extrinsic compression in the duodenal bulb with mucosal edema and superficial erosions. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated extensive celiac, peripancreatic, and periportal lymphadenopathy (nodes >1 cm, round to oval, well-demarcated, hypoechoic) and a 4.0 × 3.0 cm hypoechoic, heterogeneous, calcified, irregularly shaped solid mass in the porta hepatis abutting—but not arising from—the pancreatic head.

A 60-year-old woman with hypertension presented with headache and dizziness. On examination, her heart rate was 82 bpm, blood pressure 157/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 100%. A grade 4/6 ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid arteries was auscultated.  
Preoperative evaluation:  
• Chest radiograph: clear lung fields, cardiothoracic ratio 50%  
• ECG: sinus rhythm at 90 bpm, left ventricular hypertrophy  
• Transthoracic echocardiography: tricuspid aortic valve thickened and heavily calcified, peak-to-peak gradient 113/71 mmHg, ejection fraction 73%, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, mild mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, aortic annulus 17 mm  
She was scheduled for elective aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve and possible aortic root enlargement due to the small annulus.  
Intraoperatively, the ascending aorta appeared calcified with unusual green–black discoloration of the adventitia. Transesophageal echocardiography showed no evidence of aortic dissection. On aortotomy, the intimal surface exhibited dark green–black pigmentation extending to the coronary ostia, the aortic valve leaflets, and the base of the anterior mitral leaflet.

A 20-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks of gestation was admitted after a generalized tonic–clonic seizure. She received intravenous magnesium sulfate and underwent an emergency cesarean delivery of a healthy 2.5 kg male infant; the amniotic fluid was clear. Six hours after surgery, she became drowsy, her blood pressure fell to 70/38 mm Hg, and urine output decreased to 20 ml over 2 hours. Dopamine infusion was initiated, and 36 hours postoperatively she was transferred to our tertiary care center.

On arrival, she had a second generalized seizure treated with lorazepam and fosphenytoin. She was intubated for airway protection and placed on mechanical ventilation. Her blood pressure was 100/74 mm Hg on dopamine (12 μg/kg/min) and norepinephrine (15 μg/min). She had been anuric for 6 hours and developed a distended, tense abdomen with blood-stained vaginal discharge. There was no history of hypertension or proteinuria during her antenatal visits.

Arterial blood gas analysis showed severe metabolic acidosis. A peripheral smear demonstrated 3+ fragmented red blood cells, and the reticulocyte count was 3.4%. Direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative. Laboratory tests revealed thrombocytopenia and elevated liver enzymes. Abdominal ultrasonography showed free fluid and possible bleeding from the anterior uterine wall suture.

A diagnosis of severe preeclampsia–eclampsia with a differential of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura versus HELLP syndrome was made.

A 44-year-old previously healthy Japanese man presented with a 2-hour history of rapidly progressive difficulty breathing. He denied throat pain, diarrhea, or ingestions but noted a 2-year history of rash and itchiness in cold temperatures. His child had a mild cough 1 week earlier. He had no known allergies or medications; vaccination history was unclear.

On arrival: temperature 39.0 °C; blood pressure 178/114 mmHg; respiratory rate 30/min; SpO₂ 100% on 10 L/min oxygen; Glasgow Coma Scale 15. He had marked stridor, could not speak or lie flat, and no oral pseudomembrane. Bronchoscopic intubation revealed severe pharyngeal and laryngeal edema. CT showed severe right-dominant swelling of the pharynx and larynx with near-complete airway obstruction; there was no abscess, mass, or pneumonia.

Laboratory studies on admission showed white cells 10.5×10⁹/L (neutrophils 9.3×10⁹/L; lymphocytes 0.84×10⁹/L), eosinophils 0.021×10⁹/L, and C-reactive protein 0.17 mg/dL. SARS-CoV-2 antigen and PCR tests were negative. A Mycoplasma pneumoniae rapid antigen test was positive, and the PA titer was 1:640 (it was 1:40 on day 11); PCR for M. pneumoniae on tracheal aspirate was negative. Two sets of blood cultures were negative, and tracheal aspirate culture grew normal oral flora.

He received methylprednisolone, antibiotics, and bronchodilators. The swelling improved, and he was extubated on day 7. On day 8, laryngeal swelling recurred, prompting reintubation; tracheostomy was performed on day 11. Throat pain persisted, and serum pancreatic amylase rose to 451 U/L (day 13) without radiographic evidence of pancreatitis. On day 13, fever, leukocytosis, and epiglottic swelling recurred and resolved by day 15. On day 18, he developed generalized erythema; all medications were stopped, and he received fexofenadine and topical glucocorticoid. He was transferred on day 20 for further evaluation. Biopsy of the right oropharynx (day 25) showed low-grade dysplasia without malignancy. Rash recurred on day 34 but improved over 10 days. No further laryngeal swelling occurred; tracheostomy was closed on day 41. He was discharged on day 49 and remained relapse-free for 12 months; mild lingual tonsil swelling gradually resolved.

Immunologic and allergic evaluation included C4 23.8 mg/dL (ref. 11–31), C1 inhibitor 147% (ref. 70–130), nonspecific IgE 173 U/mL (ref. <250), RAST positive for house dust mite (Class IV). Drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation tests for meropenem and clindamycin were negative. Immunoglobulins (IgA 259 mg/dL; IgG 924 mg/dL; IgM 112.7 mg/dL) and HIV screening were unremarkable. EBV VCA IgM was negative; VCA IgG and EBNA were positive.

A 67-year-old Japanese woman with no history of smoking or atopic disease repaired ceramics using urushiol with turpentine oil. She stopped work after a few minutes due to a strong odor, and the urushiol container remained unopened. Two days later, she developed fever and dry cough.

At her primary care office, chest radiography showed consolidation in the right upper lung field, and she was treated with tazobactam/piperacillin for 3 days; however, her fever persisted and the pulmonary opacity enlarged. She was referred to our hospital.

On presentation, temperature was 38.6 °C, blood pressure 134/83 mmHg, pulse 93/min, respiratory rate 13/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Examination was notable only for diminished breath sounds at the right posterior lung. No rash or lymphadenopathy was present.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 4840/μL (eosinophils 2.6%), CRP 11.8 mg/dL, normal HDL and LDL cholesterol, normal IgE, and negative autoimmune antibodies. Chest CT revealed consolidation with ground-glass opacity in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe, patchy ground-glass opacity in segment 6, and small right pleural effusion.

Bronchoalveolar lavage from the right B2 bronchus yielded 4.39 × 10^6 cells/mL: 2% neutrophils, 45% lymphocytes, and 29% eosinophils. Macrophages with intracellular lipid droplets were observed. Gram stain and cultures for bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, and viral pathogens were negative.

A 12-month-old boy was referred for a 4-month history of a recalcitrant diaper-area eruption. He was exclusively breastfed for 6 months, after which solid foods were introduced; his development and growth were otherwise normal. Since age 6 months, his stools had been loose but not watery. His parents used nondisposable cloth diapers and had treated the rash with topical zinc oxide, multiple courses of topical antifungals, topical antimicrobials, and fluorinated steroid creams—alone or in combination—with minimal improvement. There was no history of seborrheic dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, or use of powder preparations on the diaper area. 

On examination, there were numerous erythematous, round-to-oval, nontender papules and nodules in the perianal and bilateral gluteal regions; some lesions were friable and eroded. The remainder of the skin and systemic examination was unremarkable, with no acral or periorificial dermatitis and no alopecia. 

A skin-swab culture from a lesion was negative for bacteria. Microscopic examination of skin scrapings in 10% potassium hydroxide was negative for fungal elements. Histologic examination of a representative lesion demonstrated acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and spongiosis with overlying crust, along with a dense dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes, neutrophils, plasma cells, histiocytes, and scattered eosinophils; periodic acid–Schiff staining showed no fungal elements.

A 51-year-old man presented with a ten-month history of progressive left shoulder pain and a recent firm swelling. He reported no trauma. The swelling increased over three weeks, then stabilized. Pain was elicited by shoulder elevation and abduction but not by rotation. He had no relevant medical or family history.

On examination, there was a firm, localized, mildly tender swelling in the anterosuperior left shoulder with overlying skin redness. He had nearly full range of motion, with mild pain on abduction and internal rotation. The impingement and Hawkins tests were positive; tests for biceps tendonitis, rotator cuff tear, acromioclavicular arthritis, and instability were negative.

Plain radiographs showed calcifications around the greater tuberosity and subacromial space, and hyperostotic lesions in the scapular blade. CT demonstrated extensive, well-defined ossification within the proximal deltoid muscle and hyperostotic masses dribbling from the scapular blade. MRI revealed numerous low-signal-intensity calcific foci within and beneath the deltoid muscle, without intra-articular involvement or extension into the proximal humerus, and multiple areas of cortical thickening of the scapula; all other structures appeared normal. A Tc-99m MDP bone scan showed increased uptake in the left shoulder lesions, indicating high-grade osteoblastic activity, with no other abnormal tracer activity.

A 25-year-old woman presented 21 days after an uneventful delivery with severe headache and progressive fatigue. An ophthalmologic examination detected bitemporal hemianopsia. On admission she was alert; blood pressure 94/55 mm Hg; pulse 85/min; temperature 37.2 ℃; height 150 cm; weight 39.5 kg (BMI 17.6 kg/m2). MRI of the sellar region showed symmetrical enlargement of the pituitary gland and stalk with homogeneous gadolinium enhancement, compressing the optic chiasm. Laboratory evaluation revealed a white blood cell count of 6,200/µL with 13.8% eosinophils; dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate 3 µg/dL (low); serum IgG4 55.7 mg/dL (normal). Basal pituitary hormones were uniformly decreased (ACTH <5 pg/mL; cortisol <2.0 µg/dL; TSH 0.074 µIU/mL; free T3 2.85 pg/mL; free T4 0.81 ng/dL; LH 0.42 mIU/mL; FSH 5.80 mIU/mL; estradiol <10 pg/mL; GH 1.69 ng/mL; IGF-1 57 ng/mL; prolactin 2.48 pg/dL). Dynamic testing showed no cortisol response to CRH or insulin‐induced hypoglycemia despite an ACTH rise, low TSH response to TRH, and delayed responses of other pituitary hormones. A water‐restriction test revealed inability to concentrate urine (urine osmolality <234 mOsm/kg) with improvement after vasopressin. These findings supported a diagnosis of panhypopituitarism with adrenal insufficiency and central diabetes insipidus.

A 60-year-old man presented with a two-month history of a lump on the tongue that was painless but bled easily when he ate acidic foods or drank acidic beverages. Over the same period, he experienced abdominal discomfort, difficulty with defecation, weight loss, and decreased appetite; he subsisted on porridge and had poor fluid intake. On examination he appeared weak and pale; vital signs were within normal limits. Extraoral findings included pale conjunctiva and icteric sclera. Intraoral examination revealed:  
• Multiple branching fissures on the median dorsum of the tongue.  
• Multiple depapillated areas scattered over the anterior third of the tongue dorsum, resembling islands with hyperkeratotic edges.  
• A blackish-red, irregular lesion on the posterior third of the tongue dorsum that did not blanch on diascopy.  

Initial diagnostic considerations included fissured tongue, geographic tongue, syphilitic ulcer, oral squamous cell carcinoma, and oral hematoma. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL (13.2–17.3) L  
• Hematocrit 21.4% (40–52) L  
• Red cells 3.08 ×10^6/µL (4.4–5.9) L  
• MCV 69.5 fL (80–100) L  
• MCH 21.8 pg (26–34) L  
• MCHC 31.3 g/dL (32–36) L  
• Platelets 382 ×10^3/µL (150–440)  
• Leukocytes 12.0 ×10^3/µL (3.8–10.6)  

Serologic tests were nonreactive for VDRL/RPR and TPHA; total Ig-E was 14.7 KIU/L (reference <150).

A 7-year-old girl was admitted with a 1-month history of low-grade fever and intermittent abdominal pain. She is the first child of consanguineous parents, with normal developmental milestones and no significant past medical history. She was born with light-brown scalp hair and gray eyelashes. On examination, she appeared ill and had hepatomegaly (liver span 136 mm) and splenomegaly (spleen 142 mm). Initial vital signs were within normal limits.

Laboratory studies revealed:
– Pancytopenia on complete blood count: WBC 2700/μl (neutrophils 42%, lymphocytes 53%), Hb 8.1 g/dL, platelets 57,000/μl.  
– Elevated liver enzymes: AST 128 U/L, ALT 99 U/L, ALP 528 U/L.  
– Mild hyponatremia (Na 128 mmol/L) and elevated LDH (160 U/L).  
– Coagulation studies: PT 13.3 s, PTT 60 s, INR 1.2.  
– Other labs: BUN 24 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, uric acid 1.84 mmol/L, total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, CRP +1.

Abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. Oncology consultation for suspected malignancy or leukemia prompted peripheral blood smears and bone marrow aspiration, which demonstrated hemophagocytosis. Tests for hepatitis B and C, HIV, adenovirus, and tuberculosis were negative. Echocardiography was normal, excluding Kawasaki disease and endocarditis. Empiric antibiotics, FFP, and IVIG were administered, with normalization of counts and discharge after two weeks.

Ten days later, she re-presented with fever, epistaxis, diffuse abdominal pain, weakness, anorexia, altered mental status, and dyspnea. On admission, her GCS was 11/15; she had periorbital edema, oral mucosal inflammation, respiratory distress, and marked hepatosplenomegaly. Chest radiograph and brain CT were normal.

Repeat laboratory results showed:
– Worsening pancytopenia: WBC 1800/μl, Hb 7.0 g/dL, platelets 17,000/μl.  
– AST 1132 U/L, ALT 319 U/L, ALP 187 U/L.  
– Triglycerides 310 mg/dL, ferritin 600 ng/mL.  
– Hypoalbuminemia (2.7 g/dL), hyperbilirubinemia (2.2 mg/dL), prolonged PT 27 s, PTT 150 s, INR 4.1.  
– Hyponatremia (Na 128 mmol/L).

At this point, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) in the context of Griscelli syndrome and Chediak‐Higashi syndrome was suggested.

A 42-year-old man with a prior penetrating injury to his left eye presented for a corneal amniotic membrane graft. His medical history included hypertension and diabetes mellitus managed with metoprolol, lisinopril, and metformin. On admission, his fasting blood sugar was 223 mg/dL. In the holding area, standard monitors were applied; blood pressure was 122/83 mmHg, pulse 90/min, and SpO2 99% on nasal oxygen. After sedation with midazolam (2 mg) and fentanyl (100 μg), a left inferotemporal transconjunctival eye block was performed with a 27-gauge, 31-mm needle in neutral gaze, injecting 9 mL of a mixture of 2% lidocaine, 1% ropivacaine, and Hylenex 7.5 IU/mL. Ten minutes later, he developed paroxysmal tachycardia to 140/min and acute hypertension to 240/140 mmHg, treated with intravenous nicardipine (200 μg) and labetalol (10 mg). He became somnolent but responded to verbal commands and had mild left facial weakness. Within five minutes, vital signs normalized and SpO2 remained ≥98%. He was transferred to the operating room; on re-monitoring, he was unresponsive to verbal command but opened his eyes to stimulation and reported that he could not hear. His vital signs remained stable, and SpO2 was ≥98%. Neurologic examination revealed deafness, left facial weakness, slurred speech, and inability to protrude the tongue. The right pupil was dilated, but the light reflex and extraocular movements were intact. A repeat blood glucose was 271 mg/dL. At this stage, the differential diagnosis included brainstem anesthesia and cerebrovascular accident secondary to hypertensive crisis, and an urgent CT scan was arranged.

A 22-year-old woman with no history of autoimmune disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or malignancy presented 5 days after cosmetic bilateral augmentation mastopexy with 150-mL smooth gel implants and suction-assisted lipectomy of the trunk and thighs. She received perioperative first-generation cephalosporin prophylaxis. On postoperative day 3, she developed well-demarcated erythema of both breasts (right worse than left), which progressed from the lower poles toward the nipples and was accompanied by wound dehiscence, necrosis, and bloody, purulent drainage. She also had fever (up to 40.5°C), headache, elevated C-reactive protein, thrombocytosis, and a left-shift leukocytosis. Serologic tests for antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and rheumatoid factor were negative; thyroid function and serum glucose were normal. Emergency surgery was performed to remove both implants, debride necrotic tissue, irrigate with antibiotic solution, and place drains. Intraoperative cultures were collected. The working diagnosis was severe cellulitis and acute breast implant infection. Despite treatment with vancomycin, daptomycin, clindamycin, cefepime, and micafungin, progressive skin necrosis continued with persistent fever (40°C–40.6°C). Initial wound cultures were negative for bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, and fungi. A second debridement and irrigation were performed, new cultures were obtained, and histopathology revealed acute and chronic inflammation with neutrophils, fat necrosis, and stromal fibrosis. The patient’s condition continued to deteriorate despite broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgery.

A 33-year-old unmarried man presented with a 5-year history of a single, asymptomatic, skin-colored swelling on the glans penis. He reported no trauma, local medication use, or high-risk sexual behavior. On examination, there was a solitary, 7 × 5 mm, flesh-colored, nontender, smooth swelling just proximal to the urethral meatus on the ventral surface of the glans. The lesion was neither compressible nor transilluminable. Aspiration with a 20-gauge needle yielded a viscous, nonmalodorous fluid; the smear showed multiple flat epithelial cells resembling transitional and squamous cell epithelium, and cultures were sterile. High-frequency sonography revealed a well-defined, hypoechoic lesion measuring 6 × 5 × 3 mm, spanning the epidermis and dermis of the glans, with no deeper cystic or solid extension.

An 8-month-old Caucasian boy with heterotaxy syndrome was admitted from clinic with fever, cyanosis, and oxyhemoglobin saturations as low as 70% on room air. His past history included dextrocardia, polysplenia, interrupted inferior vena cava, biliary atresia status post-Kasai procedure, and malrotation status post-Ladd’s procedure. On admission he was febrile and started on oxygen via nasal cannula. A chest radiograph showed a patchy right lower lobe opacity, and he was started on antibiotics for presumed pneumonia. He was transferred to the PICU for refractory hypoxemia requiring high-flow oxygen (up to 9 L/min and FiO₂ of 1.0) and developed increased work of breathing necessitating bilevel positive airway pressure. A repeat radiograph revealed pulmonary edema, and his brain natriuretic peptide was elevated at 1130 pg/mL. He improved with diuresis and returned to standard nasal cannula but required a brief dopamine infusion for blood pressure support. Multiple echocardiograms showed no cardiac lesion explaining his hypoxemia. A chest CT angiogram demonstrated diffuse dilatation of the pulmonary vasculature bilaterally without parenchymal abnormalities; right ventricular pressures were less than half of systemic pressures. Given his history of biliary atresia and this constellation of findings, a vascular shunt syndrome was considered.

A 38-year-old woman presented with 4 months of progressively worsening symmetric pain in the small joints of her hands, wrists, knees, and ankles. She reported early morning stiffness lasting 2 hours daily and severe fatigue throughout the day. One month before presentation, she had a mild COVID-19 infection confirmed by SARS-CoV-2 PCR; symptoms were limited to fever, chills, and a non-oxygen-requiring cough. She had not been vaccinated against COVID-19 at that time. She denied fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, rash, or appetite changes since recovering. There were no recent genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections and no history of psoriasis or uveitis. She is a non-smoker, does not drink alcohol, and has no recreational drug use. Family history is notable for a maternal aunt with rheumatoid arthritis.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 13 mm/hour and a C-reactive protein of 4.3 mg/L (both within normal limits). Immunologic testing revealed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:640, negative extractable nuclear antigen and double-stranded DNA antibodies, a rheumatoid factor of 62.29 IU/mL (normal <20 IU/mL), and an anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody of 237.39 units (normal <20 units). Hepatitis B and C serologies were negative.

Radiographs of the hands, knees, ankles, and feet were unremarkable. Hand ultrasound showed no joint erosion. MRI of the hands demonstrated synovitis of the bilateral distal radioulnar joints and the left second metacarpophalangeal joint, with tenosynovitis around the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon; no osseous destruction was identified.

A 51-year-old man was admitted with a one-week history of sudden right-sided extremity weakness followed by the development of diplopia. Five months earlier, he had been diagnosed with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, with a relapse one month before presentation. On neurologic examination, he had left facial nerve palsy, right extremity weakness, and right-sided gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus. Unenhanced head CT showed no acute intracranial process. Brain MRI revealed numerous punctate enhancing lesions involving the pons, middle cerebellar peduncles, medial cerebellar lobes, middle frontal gyrus, cingulate gyrus, and corona radiata. Laboratory testing showed a normal blood count and biochemical profile. Serum analysis was negative for multiple infections, including toxoplasmosis, herpes simplex virus, Epstein-Barr virus, West Nile virus, cytomegalovirus, Histoplasma, and varicella-zoster virus, and angiotensin converting enzyme was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid obtained by lumbar puncture was negative for any significant abnormality.

A 63-year-old man with osteoarthritis of the left knee underwent a posterior-cruciate–retaining total knee arthroplasty without a patellar component. The postoperative course was uneventful. Three weeks later, he noted sudden swelling and discomfort of the operative knee. On examination there was medial joint-line tenderness and a moderate effusion. Radiographs showed a well-aligned prosthesis. Over the next months all symptoms except the effusion gradually improved.

Two years after surgery, he developed increasing pain and a sensation of “catching” in the knee. Physical examination showed a stable joint, range of motion 0 to 130°, no extension deficit, moderate swelling, and medial joint-line tenderness. Standard radiographs remained unchanged, with no evidence of loosening or polyethylene wear. Laboratory studies including complete blood count with differential, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and knee aspiration for cell count and culture excluded infection. A triple-phase technetium-99m diphosphonate bone scan demonstrated increased perfusion in the early phase and increased uptake in the static phase at the medial aspects of the femoral and tibial components and in the patella.

A 69-year-old man presented with fever and chills one week after discharge for Haemophilus influenzae bacteremia, having completed a two-week course of cefuroxime. During the prior admission, transthoracic echocardiography had shown an ejection fraction of 55%, mild aortic stenosis, and moderate aortic insufficiency, which was not further investigated despite bacteremia. Additional prior studies included a normal chest radiograph, CT of the chest demonstrating minimal tree-in-bud opacities, and MRI of the ankle showing synovitis.

On this presentation, he reported one day of achy, nonradiating, nonreproducible chest pain. Vital signs were temperature 101.0 °F, heart rate 127 bpm, blood pressure 67/39 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Physical examination revealed a grade 3 systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border without radiation to the carotids and no Janeway lesions or Osler nodes.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis and a troponin level of 20.6 ng/mL. Electrocardiography demonstrated diffuse ST-segment depressions. Chest radiography revealed bibasilar patchy airspace disease. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography showed anterior wall hypokinesis and an ejection fraction of 25–30%. Blood cultures drawn on admission grew beta-lactamase–negative H. influenzae serotype F. Coronary angiography revealed severe distal left main disease extending into the proximal left anterior descending and circumflex arteries but with TIMI 3 flow throughout. Right heart catheterization showed a cardiac index of 2.1 L/min/m2, a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 23 mm Hg, a right atrial pressure of 15 mm Hg, and a systemic vascular resistance of 900 dyn·sec·cm−5.

A 22-year-old woman presented with progressive weakness and numbness of the hands. Two years earlier, she noted difficulty moving her right hand; a brain MRI then showed a T2 hyperintensity along the left corticospinal tract, and her symptoms partially improved without treatment. At age 22, she developed bilateral hand numbness that spread to both upper extremities and weakness of the left hand. Neurologic examination revealed atrophy of the hands and feet, decreased muscle tone, loss of tendon reflexes in all extremities, and sensory loss on the right side of the body and face. Nerve conduction studies showed reduced conduction velocities in the upper extremities (motor 25.7 m/s; sensory 19.3 m/s) and a low compound muscle action potential in the right median nerve (10.8 mV). Brain fluid-attenuated inversion recovery MRI showed hyperintensities along bilateral corticospinal tracts. Cervical spine MRI with short tau inversion-recovery sequences demonstrated bilateral enlargement of the brachial plexus.

An 83-year-old man presented with a lesion on his central forehead that had been present for 5 years. There was no preceding trauma, and the lesion was mostly asymptomatic but of cosmetic concern. He underwent two surgical excisions by plastic surgery, after which the plaque recurred and developed a spontaneous, very tender central ulcer. He was otherwise well and took no medications.

On examination, he was a well-appearing man with Fitzpatrick type III skin. In the glabellar region there was a solitary, 7 cm × 5 cm, brown-purple, shiny, bossellated, annular, firm plaque with prominent telangiectasias. A 1-cm deep ulcer occupied the center of the plaque. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count and differential. Tissue cultures for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial infection were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis showed a monoclonal IgG kappa gammopathy consistent with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. The serum IgG4 level was normal. Serum creatinine and alanine transaminase concentrations were within normal limits.

A 44-year-old woman was referred for progressive abdominal pain and weight loss due to worsening chronic constipation. Her history included temporal epilepsy treated with lamotrigine for three years. Three years earlier, she developed progressive muscle pain and stiffness in her legs and lumbar region associated with chronic constipation, abdominal bloating, occasional nausea, and vomiting. Previous gastroenterology and neurology evaluations—including endoscopic examinations—revealed no abnormalities, and a diagnosis of functional idiopathic constipation was made.

On admission, vital signs were normal. Physical examination showed marked lumbar hyperlordosis and paraspinal muscle contractures, a swaying gait, asymmetrical diffuse polykinetic patellar hyperreflexia more pronounced on the right, abdominal distension with high-pitched bowel sounds, and signs of subocclusive digestive syndrome. No skin changes or joint inflammation were observed. Routine blood tests—including haematology, electrolytes, calcium, vitamins, lipase, lipids, muscle enzymes, iron studies, renal function, thyroid function, blood glucose, and inflammatory markers—were within normal limits. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (20 g/L). Liver tests revealed mild elevations of gamma-glutamyl transferase, alkaline phosphatase, and conjugated bilirubin (1–2× upper limit of normal). Extensive infectious serologies (HIV, HTLV-1/2, hepatitis B, C, and E) were negative. Autoantibody testing (including ANA, ANCA, mitochondrial, LKM, ASCA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, anti-smooth-muscle, and various paraneoplastic antibodies) was negative except for anti-GAD65 antibodies (serum 52 U/mL, CSF 68 U/mL; normal <5 mU/mL). Cerebrospinal fluid otherwise showed normal cell count and chemistry without clonal lymphoid populations. Abdominal ultrasound and CT scan revealed abundant stercoral stasis without mechanical obstruction. Brain and spinal MRI and electromyography were unremarkable, and repetitive nerve stimulation showed no evidence of myasthenia gravis or Lambert–Eaton syndrome. MR cholangiography demonstrated marked common bile duct dilatation with mild focal stenoses and multiple small intrahepatic stones.

A 6-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of gingival overgrowth that had been present since his first tooth erupted at 6 months of age. The painless gingival enlargement progressed slowly without discomfort until age 6, when its esthetic appearance became intolerable. He had no other complaints and was systemically healthy. He was the only child of two healthy non-consanguineous parents, and there was no family history of similar findings.

Oral examination showed severe gingival enlargement involving both mandibular and maxillary arches, most prominent in the anterior regions. The gingivae had slight redness, mild edema, and absence of normal stippling. Oral hygiene was poor, with pseudopockets containing abundant dental plaque and minimal calculus; marginal gingiva was slightly inflamed. No other mucosal lesions were observed. Radiographs revealed no periodontal bone destruction.

Routine hematological and biochemical tests were unremarkable. Initial phase therapy to control gingival inflammation did not alleviate the overgrowth. A gingivectomy was performed, and healing was uneventful. Histopathological examination of gingival specimens stained with hematoxylin–eosin revealed hyperplastic epithelium, mild inflammatory cell infiltration, proliferation of the capillary layer, and increased fibrous tissue. One week after the gingivectomy, recurrence of gingival enlargement occurred.

A 65-year-old man with a history of hypothyroidism and hyperlipidemia presented with two months of recurrent lightheadedness and dizziness at rest. He denied chest pain, palpitations, diaphoresis, dyspnea, focal neurologic symptoms, exertional or positional triggers, medication use including AV-nodal blockers, or recent illness. There was no family history of heart disease or sudden death. In the emergency department, his blood pressure was 70/50 mm Hg and heart rate 30–50 beats/minute. ECG showed sinus bradycardia at 47 beats/minute, an incomplete right bundle-branch block pattern, and a PR interval of 200 ms. He remained hypotensive despite fluid resuscitation and required a dopamine infusion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 60%, mild left ventricular hypertrophy, and normal right ventricular size and function. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies were notable for sodium 121 mEq/L, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 89 fL, ferritin 856 ng/mL, TSH 5.33 mIU/L, and total T4 5.39 μg/dL. Evaluation of hyponatremia showed serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 346 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium 66 mEq/L, findings consistent with either adrenal insufficiency or SIADH. Endocrinology was consulted and a cosyntropin stimulation test was performed.

A 41-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presented with a 3-month history of left cervical lymph node enlargement. She had been treated twice with antibiotics, each time with partial response followed by recurrence. She denied smoking, alcohol use, fever, weight loss, night sweats, or systemic symptoms. 

On examination, multiple small, tender lymph nodes were palpable in the left posterior cervical triangle; no hepatosplenomegaly was noted. 

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Hematocrit 36%, total leukocyte count 4600/µL, absolute neutrophil count 1450/µL, absolute lymphocyte count 2610/µL  
• Mild neutropenia and MCH 26.3 pg  
• ESR 22 mm/hr  
• Negative serologic screens for HIV-1/2, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C  

A neck ultrasound showed bilateral small cervical adenopathy; the largest node in the left posterior triangle had loss of the fatty hilum. An excisional lymph node biopsy suggested a lymphoproliferative disorder based on loss of nodal architecture with infiltration by small lymphocytes and large areas of necrosis. 

Further evaluation included a chest radiograph, which revealed bilateral bronchitic changes and mild cardiomegaly. Sputum samples were negative for acid-fast bacilli, and the Mantoux test was nonreactive. A screening mammogram showed no significant findings.

A 39-year-old Caucasian multigravida at 42 weeks’ gestation was admitted for induction of labor. She had five previous uncomplicated vaginal deliveries, was a non‐smoker, and had no history of chest disease. After artificial rupture of membranes, meconium-stained liquor was noted, and cardiotocography showed repetitive late decelerations with diminished beat‐to‐beat variability. An emergency cesarean section was performed under general anesthesia.

Preoperatively, she was oriented; pulse 115 beats/min, respiratory rate 12/min, blood pressure 160/90 mmHg. Airway assessment was Mallampati class III. Chest examination revealed normal vesicular breath sounds without added sounds. A very junior medical officer performed rapid‐sequence induction; intubation was difficult and completed on the second attempt with a stylet and an 8.0 low‐volume, high‐pressure endotracheal tube. General anesthesia was maintained with isoflurane in oxygen and nitrous oxide.

The operation was uneventful. Soon after extubation, she developed respiratory distress and persistent hypoxia. Within 3 minutes, oxygen saturation fell to 65% on 100% oxygen, blood pressure to 65/40 mmHg, and pulse rose to 158 beats/min. She was reintubated and transferred to our hospital intubated and ventilated.

On arrival, Glasgow Coma Scale score was E2 M3 V3; blood pressure 70/40 mmHg; pulse 145 beats/min; oxygen saturation 65%. Breath sounds were absent over the left hemithorax. There was extensive subcutaneous emphysema over the left thorax and neck. Diagnostic pleural puncture at the left apex yielded air. A 28‐French chest tube was placed in the left 5th intercostal space. Chest radiography showed left pneumothorax, minimal right pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, and subcutaneous emphysema. Mediastinal enlargement was evident. Chest CT confirmed extensive air in cervical soft tissue, mediastinum, and pleural spaces.

On hospital day 2, her oxygenation worsened, and a right pneumothorax was seen on chest radiograph. A second chest tube was placed. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy demonstrated diffuse tracheal hemorrhage and a thrombotic plug nearly occluding the left main bronchus, which was removed. Over the next days, pneumothoraces resolved and both chest tubes were removed on day 5. The patient was extubated when her oxygen saturation remained >97% on room air. Nutrition was provided via nasogastric tube until day 5, then clear liquids orally.

She then complained of severe throat pain and coughing during swallowing.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of palpitations, dyspnoea on exertion, and peripheral oedema. His medical history included hypertensive heart disease with previously normal left ventricular ejection fraction, well-controlled blood pressure, type 2 diabetes mellitus, ascending aortic ectasia, and a history of tobacco use. Medications were perindopril/amlodipine, carvedilol, and metformin.  
On examination, blood pressure was 144/118 mmHg, heart rate 159 b.p.m., and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Bibasilar crackles and moderate bilateral lower-extremity oedema were present; heart sounds were regular and tachycardic without jugular venous distension.  
Electrocardiogram showed a regular narrow-complex tachycardia consistent with typical atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15% with diffuse hypokinesia and no significant ventricular hypertrophy or dilatation (left ventricular end-diastolic diameter 53 mm).  
To evaluate for cardioversion, transoesophageal echocardiography was performed and demonstrated a thrombus in the left atrial appendage.  
Laboratory tests showed normal electrolytes and haemoglobin, a serum creatinine of 110 µmol/L, and an NT-proBNP level of 2400 pg/mL.

A 29-year-old Brazilian woman was referred for evaluation of hepatomegaly detected on imaging. She reported progressive weakness, skin hyperpigmentation, and joint pain in the shoulders and hands, as well as secondary amenorrhea since age 25. Her father died before age 50 of nonalcoholic cirrhosis and diabetes; one brother died at age 31 of similar diseases, and two brothers are healthy. On examination, hepatomegaly and diffuse skin hyperpigmentation were noted. Laboratory studies showed serum ferritin 5696 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 85%, hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, INR 1.3, AST 91 U/L, ALT 69 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 288 U/L, GGT 84 U/L, glucose 72 mg/dL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, and albumin 4.3 g/dL. Echocardiography was normal. Secondary causes of iron overload, including hepatitis, chronic hemolysis, oral or parenteral iron overload, metabolic syndrome, and alcohol abuse, were excluded. Genetic analysis for HFE mutations (p.C282Y, p.H63D, p.S65C) revealed heterozygosity for p.H63D. Taking into account her age and the absence of a causative HFE mutation, the HJV (exons 1–4) and HAMP (exons 1–3) genes were sequenced.

A 55-year-old Turkish woman on maintenance haemodialysis for end-stage renal failure of unknown etiology (initiated 4 months ago) presented with a 5-day history of fever, chills, malaise, headache, and mild left-sided chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration. She reported left iliac fossa pain without bowel changes. Her past history included hypertension, carpal tunnel release, steroid epidural injections, and recurrent self-limited episodes of fever, abdominal pain, arthralgia, and headache over the past 5 years. Four months earlier, she was treated with corticosteroids for presumed autoimmune pericarditis after MRI and echocardiography showed a pericardial effusion and blood cultures were negative. On this admission, temperature was elevated; physical examination was notable only for mild lower abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed CRP 285 mg/L, leukocyte count 18.6 × 10^9/L, and hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL. Abdominal CT revealed focal rectal wall thickening with perirectal fat stranding. She underwent a left colonoscopy with blind biopsies, which were normal. Multiple blood cultures remained negative, yet empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics produced no improvement. Repeat echocardiography demonstrated a small pericardial effusion without hemodynamic compromise; cardiac MRI confirmed mild pericardial thickening and small effusion. An ^18F-FDG PET-CT scan showed increased uptake in the pericardium, pleura, synovia of large joints, spleen, bone marrow, and multiple lymph node stations (axillary, mediastinal, retroperitoneal, and para-iliac).

A 46-year-old previously healthy Caucasian man presented with sudden-onset headache, nausea, vomiting, and collapse, followed by a witnessed tonic–clonic seizure lasting about one minute. Upon awakening, he was disoriented, had retrograde amnesia and mild motor aphasia. He was afebrile with normal vital signs; neck stiffness was noted on examination. After admission, orientation normalized but he displayed tactlessness and facetiousness. Laboratory tests showed mild monocytosis (850 cells/µL) with normal C-reactive protein and procalcitonin. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a hypodense area in the left temporal lobe white matter and a smaller hypodense focus in the left frontal lobe. Brain MRI demonstrated a 50×55×56 mm T2/FLAIR-hyperintense, contrast-enhancing lesion in the left temporal lobe extending to the insula and frontal lobe, a mild T2/FLAIR signal increase in the right ventral temporal lobe, and cortical hemosiderin in the left frontal region. Lumbar puncture showed CSF pleocytosis (80 mononuclear cells/µL, 12 polymorphonuclear cells/µL), elevated protein (1235 mg/L), elevated albumin (441 mg/L), elevated IgG (840 mg/L), and an IgG index of 5.53; glucose and lactate were normal. CSF PCR for HSV-1 and HSV-2 was negative. A point-of-care CSF CXCL13 assay was highly positive. Empiric intravenous acyclovir and ceftriaxone were initiated.

A 24-year-old man underwent open reduction and internal fixation of a right intra-articular distal radius fracture with a locking plate 2 days after a road-traffic accident. Six months postoperatively, he noted a painless swelling on the lateral aspect of his right forearm. He was treated with oral antibiotics without improvement, and 1 month after plate removal he developed a new, firm, ill-defined swelling on the medial aspect of the right forearm.

On examination, he was afebrile with no weight loss. There was a non-tender, firm swelling on the medial forearm; the overlying skin was normal, and the mass was mobile over deeper tissues. Regional lymph nodes were not enlarged. Routine blood tests were normal except for a mildly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

A forearm radiograph showed a malunited distal radius fracture with screw holes from the previous implant and a soft-tissue shadow adjacent to the ulna without bone erosion or periosteal reaction. Contrast MRI revealed an 8.3 × 1.6 × 10 cm calcified soft-tissue mass along the medial lower third of the ulna, isointense on T1-weighted images, hyper- to hetero-intense on T2-weighted images, with peripheral rim enhancement on post-contrast imaging.

An ultrasound-guided core biopsy yielded a dry tap with no diagnostic tissue.

A 79-year-old man with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and atrial fibrillation presented with a 2-month history of intermittent left nocturnal otalgia, dull in character, 5/10 in severity, without ear discharge, hearing loss, facial nerve dysfunction, or nasal symptoms. He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Examination of the left ear revealed a patent but erythematous canal without granulation tissue and a bulging tympanic membrane; the right ear was normal. He was prescribed oral moxifloxacin and ciprofloxacin, but discontinued therapy after pain improved. Soon thereafter he noted sudden left-sided hearing loss. Otoscopic examination then showed a normal canal and a dull tympanic membrane on the left. Tympanometry revealed type B on the left and normal type A on the right. Pure-tone audiometry demonstrated conductive hearing loss on the left with a normal right ear. Laboratory evaluation revealed WBC 12.6×10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, hemoglobin below normal, C-reactive protein 38.2 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 120 mm/hr. A left myringotomy with grommet insertion was performed; one week later the grommet was in place and the patient was doing well. One month later he returned with two weeks of left ear pain and intermittent yellow discharge, without tinnitus, dizziness, or facial palsy. Examination showed an inflamed canal with yellowish discharge and a dull tympanic membrane. Ear-swab culture grew no organisms. A bone scan showed increased radionuclide uptake in the left middle-ear ossicles extending to the mastoid air cells and sphenoid bone, suggestive of active bone infection and a necrotizing process originating from the ear.

A 21-year-old woman presented with intermittent right-sided epistaxis and occasional headaches for 6 months. Vital signs were normal. Anterior rhinoscopy revealed a hard white mass surrounded by granulation tissue on the floor of the right nasal cavity. Dental examination showed complete intraoral occlusion with no missing or displaced teeth. An orthopantomogram demonstrated a radiopaque mass within the right nasal cavity. A noncontrast CT scan of the paranasal sinuses (bone window) showed a conical-shaped mass tapering to a point, oriented in an anteroposterior direction along the right nasal floor.

A 24-year-old woman presented with sudden onset of right-sided chest pain for 1 week. She denied breathlessness, cough, or fever prior to presentation but was noted to be dyspnoeic on arrival; oxygen saturation was maintained on room air. On examination, air entry was decreased over the right hemithorax. A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed a right-sided pneumothorax and a dense opacity overlying the right hilar region. Because secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due to pulmonary tuberculosis was suspected, sputum was sent for acid-fast bacilli by immunofluorescence and for CBNAAT; both were negative. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed patchy areas of consolidation, centrilobular nodules, bronchiectatic changes, finger-in-glove opacities, high-attenuation mucus in dilated bronchi, and a small right-sided pneumothorax. The patient had never been diagnosed with asthma.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of diffuse, moderate abdominal pain of gradual onset. Three days before admission he noted abdominal distension, but his bowel movements remained normal. One day before presentation he developed non-bilious vomiting and subjective fever. He had a history of chronic moderate to severe alcohol intake. There was no recent trauma, diabetes, or hypertension; he was HIV negative.

On examination, he appeared ill and in pain. Vital signs were: blood pressure 95/62 mmHg, pulse 98/min, temperature 38.2 °C, and respiratory rate 27/min. The abdomen was distended, moved minimally with respiration, and was diffusely tender with guarding, rigidity, and rebound tenderness; there was no shifting dullness or palpable masses, and bowel sounds were present. Hernia orifices were normal. Lung and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (WBC 16,100/mm3), hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, ESR 38 mm/hr, CRP 154 mg/L, and γ-glutamyltransferase 51 U/L; renal function and urinalysis were normal. Serum lipase was 67 U/L (0–160 U/L).

A 47-year-old woman with no significant past medical or family history presented with acute onset of right ankle pain and swelling of 1 day’s duration. Three months earlier, she had tripped and hyper-plantarflexed the right ankle and had intermittent mild pain at the base of her toes, for which an ankle radiograph showed incidental calcium deposits near the talonavicular region. After attending a Pilates class and using ankle weights for the first time, she woke the next morning with progressive swelling and severe pain in the dorsoanterior aspect of the right ankle. She was unable to bear weight. She denied fevers, chills, rashes, or a history of rheumatologic disorders. On examination, there was noticeable anterior swelling without erythema or warmth. Dorsalis pedis pulses were intact; strength was 4/5 in all muscle groups. Tenderness was focal over the talonavicular region and the common extensor tendons; other tendons were non-tender. Sensation was intact, and range of motion was severely limited by pain. A repeat ankle radiograph demonstrated no fracture or osteochondral lesion but again showed a soft-tissue calcification along the dorsal aspect of the talonavicular region, distinct from an ossicle or osteophyte and suggestive of acute calcific periarthritis. An MRI of the ankle was obtained.
