A 36-year-old woman with a 2-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus (class II lupus nephritis) who was not receiving immunosuppressive therapy presented with a 5-day history of severe right-sided pleuritic chest pain (10/10), fever, dyspnea, and nonproductive cough. She also reported a 2-month history of polyarthralgias and a facial and upper-extremity rash. On examination, temperature was 39.1 °C, blood pressure 114/61 mmHg, heart rate 102 beats/minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths/minute, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She had a malar rash, an erythematous rash over both upper extremities, and rhonchi over the right upper chest. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 3.7 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, platelets 145 × 10^9/L, creatinine 2.37 mg/dL (baseline 1.00 mg/dL), blood urea nitrogen 35 mg/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL, total protein 8.5 g/dL, normal electrolytes and liver enzymes, TSH 1.91 mIU/L, ESR > 120 mm/h, and CRP 30.6 mg/dL. 

Chest radiograph revealed a right upper lobe opacity and pleural effusion. CT angiography of the chest demonstrated a new 5-cm cavitary lesion in the right hilum without evidence of pulmonary embolism. A CT chest one month earlier (done for a 2-week cough) showed no cavitary lesion. The patient was started on vancomycin, piperacillin–tazobactam, levofloxacin, and fluconazole. Blood and sputum cultures were negative, and serum screening for cytomegalovirus, coccidioides, cryptococcus, histoplasma, and aspergillus was negative. Quantiferon-TB Gold was indeterminate, and subsequent acid-fast sputum cultures were negative. Cytology of bronchoalveolar lavage and pleural fluid was negative. 

Serologic studies revealed positive dsDNA, Smith, and RNP antibodies, an ANA titer of 1:640 with a speckled pattern, low C3 and C4 levels, and nephrotic-range proteinuria. A renal biopsy confirmed class IV lupus nephritis.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of painless gingival overgrowth in the left maxillary posterior region that had progressively enlarged, involving multiple teeth and impairing aesthetics and mastication. She had no cardiovascular, endocrine, respiratory, immune, or musculoskeletal complaints. Her elder brother had sporadic epileptic episodes since childhood treated irregularly with antiseizure medications. On extraoral examination, nodular lesions were noted around the nasal and perinasal area. Intraorally, there was a localized diffuse overgrowth of the marginal, papillary, and attached labial gingiva from the left maxillary canine to the left maxillary premolar; the gingiva was pink, nonerythematous, semifirm, with loss of stippling. Multiple small enamel pits were observed on the vestibular surfaces of the upper anterior teeth, and the patient reported delayed eruption of her permanent teeth. She also had a long-standing history of tobacco chewing. Based on the clinical presentation and history of antiseizure drug use, a provisional diagnosis of drug-induced gingival overgrowth was made, and phase I periodontal therapy with oral hygiene instructions was initiated.

A 50-year-old woman presented with 2–3 days of severe right upper-quadrant colicky pain and biliary vomiting. She reported a history of intense dieting and minimal water intake. On arrival, she was afebrile, normotensive (120/80 mmHg), with a heart rate of 90 beats/min, respiratory rate of 16/min, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. She was conscious but not fully oriented. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the right hypochondrium without pallor, icterus, cyanosis, or edema. Laboratory studies showed:  
• CBC: Hb 11 g/dL, WBC 6600/mm3, platelets 171 000/mm3  
• LFTs and alkaline phosphatase: within normal limits  
• Serum creatinine: 0.8 mg/dL  
• Serum amylase: 60 U/L; lipase: 17 U/L  
• Viral hepatitis markers: nonreactive  

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple gallbladder calculi, a distended gallbladder with a 12-mm calculus at the neck, and a mildly fusiformly dilated common bile duct measuring 11–12 mm with prominent hepatic ducts; no ductal stones were visualized. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography confirmed multiple gallstones, persistent common bile duct dilation (11 mm), and ruled out choledocholithiasis.

An 11-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of fractures and abnormal bone density. She was born at 38 weeks’ gestation, with low birth weight but normal length. At 5 months, head CT for rapidly increasing head circumference showed prominent ventricles and sulci without mass lesion. At 7 months, a radiograph for arm trauma revealed metaphyseal sclerosis attributed to rickets. From birth to 8 months, she had recurrent ear and skin infections; between 8 and 11 months, limb pain episodes were attributed to dislocations. At 11 months, psychomotor development and tooth eruption were normal. She fractured her left femur at 20 months and had delayed healing; at 30, 36, and 44 months, she sustained additional fractures of long bones with slow union. She reported daily morning stiffness in her lower limbs and chronic nasal stuffiness.

On examination at 11 months, she had frontal bossing, a high forehead, small midface, blue sclerae, a flattened nasal bridge, downturned mouth, a narrow high-arched palate, and nine normal-appearing teeth. Growth in length declined from the 30th percentile at 11 months to below –2 SD by 35 months, with disproportionate short limbs; head circumference remained elevated.

Biochemical studies showed intermittent low serum alkaline phosphatase and consistently low markers of bone formation (bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, osteocalcin) and bone resorption (TRACP-5b).

Radiographs from ages 7 to 33 months revealed:
- Skull: diffuse sclerosis of the skull base and periorbital regions, large neurocranium with frontal bossing, and small midface.
- Spine: ovoid, sclerotic, flattened vertebral bodies with anterior wedging and widened disk spaces.
- Pelvis: “bone-in-bone” appearance of iliac wings and sclerotic pubic and ischial bones.
- Appendicular skeleton: Erlenmeyer flask–shaped metaphyseal expansion with sharply demarcated osteosclerosis in long bones, thin cortices in diaphyses, and evidence of delayed fracture healing.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a burning sensation and occasional bleeding on the right side of her mouth. She had no systemic medications, no tobacco or betel-quid use, no recent changes in oral care products, and no dental restorations or prostheses.

On examination, halitosis and extensive dental calculus were noted. Diffuse erosive areas were present along the line of occlusion on the right buccal mucosa and the right lateral border of the tongue. Fine white striae consistent with Wickham’s striae bordered the lingual lesions. Erosive involvement of the gingiva and labial mucosa was seen predominantly on the right side, in close proximity to dental calculus. Examination of the skin, nails, esophagus, genitals, and eyes was unremarkable. The patient was in good general health, denied significant psychosocial stressors, and displayed no anxiety during the visit.

Laboratory studies were normal except for a hemoglobin level of 8.3 mg/dL. Given the topographic relationship between the lesions and dental calculus, dental scaling was advised, and no topical corticosteroids were prescribed at that time.

A 63‐year‐old woman farmer presented with a 4‐month history of a slowly enlarging mass in her upper jaw associated with discomfort while eating but no pain or sensory loss. She denied trauma. Her past medical history included chronic nephritis, bilateral submandibular lymphadenectomy, and weight loss; there was no relevant family history. On examination, there was a red, intact mass involving nearly the entire soft palate with bilateral symmetry. Oral hygiene was poor, with multiple missing teeth. Laboratory studies revealed peripheral eosinophilia with an absolute eosinophil count of 2.94 × 10^9/L (39.5%); renal function was normal. MRI of the upper jaw demonstrated a 5 cm × 2 cm bilaterally symmetric soft‐palate mass with high contrast retention, grade III palatine tonsillar swelling, soft‐tissue infiltration without bone destruction, and multiple 1–2 cm enlarged but nonmetastatic cervical lymph nodes; these findings were reported as consistent with malignant lymphoma or sarcoma. Contrast‐enhanced CT showed a hypodense, nonenhancing lesion without vascular invasion or distant metastases, again suggesting sarcoma or lymphoma.

A 69-year-old woman presented with a several-month history of increasing shortness of breath (Hugh–Jones degree 3). Three years earlier, she had been diagnosed with otitis media–associated ANCA vasculitis (OMAAV) on the basis of refractory bilateral otitis media and an elevated MPO-ANCA level. Induction therapy with prednisolone led to recovery of her mixed hearing loss; maintenance therapy with methylprednisolone and azathioprine was attempted but azathioprine was discontinued because of hepatotoxicity. Methylprednisolone was tapered to 10 mg/day.

On admission, she had no otitis media but did have a saddle nose deformity. Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 7.6 mg/dL, brain natriuretic peptide 135 pg/mL, normal MPO-ANCA and PR3-ANCA levels, and serum creatinine 0.43 mg/dL with red blood cell sediment on urinalysis. An ECG showed signs of right ventricular strain. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a markedly enlarged right ventricle with mid‐ventricular systolic ballooning, a tricuspid regurgitation pressure gradient of 38 mmHg, and a small pericardial effusion.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated circumferential bronchial wall thickening at the tracheal carina, right main bronchus, and right segmental bronchi, as well as mass‐like lesions in the mediastinum compressing the right pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, and superior vena cava, with associated stenoses. Bronchoscopy revealed swollen mucosa of the trachea and right bronchi with airway narrowing. A biopsy of the right upper lobe bronchus ostium showed neither granulomatous inflammation nor malignant cells. Bronchial lavage fluid cultures were negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and other bacteria.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A female infant was born at 35 weeks 4 days’ gestation, weighing 2152 g. She was one of monochorionic diamniotic twins; her identical twin died in utero at 24 weeks. Fetal ultrasound had shown microcephaly and ventricular enlargement. Postnatal MRI of the head revealed microcephaly, marked enlargement of both lateral ventricles without signs of elevated intracranial pressure, and severe thinning of the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes; the temporal lobes, basal ganglia, thalamus, brain stem, and cerebellum were preserved. No intracranial hematoma or neoplastic lesions were seen. Family history was noncontributory. 

At 1 week of age, examination of the eyes showed very weak light reflexes bilaterally. The anterior chambers were slightly shallow, but there were no pupillary abnormalities, cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus, or ptosis. Funduscopic examination revealed mild optic nerve pallor with suspected peripapillary double-ring sign. The fundus had a faint reddish tone; retinal vessels appeared normal in caliber and reached the periphery. No chorioretinal dysplasia was noted.

A 33-year-old healthy, nonsmoking man underwent horizontal ridge augmentation of the maxillary right central incisor (#11) with an autogenous block graft harvested from the right mandibular ramus (including extraction of an impacted third molar). Ultrasonic osteotomy was used to prepare both donor and recipient sites; the graft was fixed with a titanium screw, gaps were filled with bone powder, and a resorbable collagen membrane was placed. The wounds were closed without tension. Postoperatively, he received amoxicillin (1000 mg three times daily for 7 days), dexamethasone (2 mg for 3 days), and analgesics as needed, and was advised to avoid actions that increase intraoral pressure. 

Three days after surgery, he reported pain and swelling that began on postoperative day 2. On examination, his right cheek and lips were swollen, he had mild trismus, and palpable crepitus was noted in the affected areas. There was no wound dehiscence or signs of infection at either the donor or recipient site, and he had no breathing difficulty, dysphagia, or dysphonia.

A 60-year-old man from a low socioeconomic background presented with left flank pain and unintentional weight loss. He had no flank tenderness on examination but had several enlarged cervical and inguinal lymph nodes.  
Laboratory studies showed albuminuria (2+), numerous leukocytes on urine dipstick, and 227 RBCs/hpf, 314 WBCs/hpf, and 239 bacteria/hpf on urine microscopy; bacterial cultures exhibited no growth, indicating sterile pyuria. A diagnosis of renal tuberculosis was considered with a differential diagnosis of chronic pyelonephritis.  
Plain CT of the abdomen revealed disproportionately dilated upper pole calyces, urothelial thickening with narrowing of the renal pelvis, papillary calcifications in the lower pole, and marked perinephric and periureteric fat stranding with locoregional lymphadenopathy.  
CT urogram demonstrated multiple filling defects within the calyceal system, papillary cavities in the upper and lower poles, calyceal distortion, infundibular-pelvic stenosis, and thickened, enhancing ureteric walls.

A 28-year-old Caucasian man, a career firefighter, was brought to the emergency department by his wife and parents after holding an unloaded gun to his head. He had no prior psychiatric history except for a six-month history of depressed mood, anxiety, blunted affect, and reduced vocalization in the setting of family and work stress. He reported episodic nightmares every few months since witnessing scenes of death at work, including a suicide by hanging and a violent motor-vehicle accident. Three months earlier, after witnessing the car wreck, he began having thoughts about killing himself, which were worsened by seeing firearms or sharp objects. He denied any family history of psychiatric illness and denied substance use except for moderate alcohol intake. All medical and substance-related causes were ruled out, and he was admitted on suicide precautions. The initial differential diagnosis included major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, and cyclothymia. He was discharged on olanzapine, divalproex, prazosin, and clonazepam. Two days later, he was readmitted with persistent suicidal thoughts he could not control. During the interview, he described sudden-onset, recurrent (5–6 times daily), brief (a few minutes), anxiety-provoking, unwanted thoughts of suicide for the past three months. He found them distressing, reported good insight (he did not want to die and believed his family would suffer if he did), and denied any compulsive rituals. To cope, he attempted to distract himself, redirect his thoughts, or sought reassurance from his family. His social and occupational functioning had deteriorated due to fear of triggering these thoughts.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of polydipsia, polyuria, headache, menstrual disorder, and fatigue. Laboratory studies showed a urine osmolality of 63 mOsm/kg (plasma osmolality 307 mOsm/kg) and serum sodium of 148 mmol/L. Endocrine evaluation revealed deficiencies of adrenocorticotropic hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and gonadotropins. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the sellar region demonstrated homogeneous signal within an 18.6 × 8.2 × 9.9 mm pituitary lesion and thickening of the pituitary stalk to 5.1 × 1.7 mm. FDG PET (SUVmax 5.5 in both pituitary and stalk at 40 min) showed increased uptake in these areas. Subsequent FDS PET demonstrated uptake in both lesions (SUVmax 1.1 at 30 min, T/N ratio 7.3; SUVmax 0.73 at 120 min, T/N ratio 9.1), with no extracranial abnormalities. The findings raised concern for either autoimmune or infectious pituitary inflammation.

A 62-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to chronic glomerulonephritis received a deceased-donor kidney transplant in September 2013. Induction therapy included thymoglobulin and methylprednisolone pulses, followed by maintenance tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. The serum creatinine nadir was 2.24 mg/dL. Two months posttransplant, tacrolimus was withdrawn for nephrotoxicity and replaced with everolimus, which was subsequently stopped due to lymphocele and proteinuria. In February 2014, belatacept was initiated at 5 mg/kg monthly, with continuation of mycophenolate mofetil and tapering of prednisone to 10 mg daily.

Shortly after starting mycophenolate mofetil, he developed anorexia and nonbloody diarrhea. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy in March 2014 showed no mucosal abnormalities; duodenal biopsies were normal. In October 2015, stool cultures grew Campylobacter jejuni; antibiotics provided minimal relief, and diarrhea persisted.

In February 2016, he was hospitalized with bloody diarrhea, anemia, and abdominal pain requiring transfusion. Colonoscopy revealed large, round, deep ulcers with normal surrounding mucosa in the cecum, transverse colon, left colon, and sigmoid colon; the terminal ileum and rectum appeared normal. Biopsies showed acute colitis with ulcerations, crypt abscesses, and mixed lymphocyte and neutrophil infiltration; there was no crypt dystrophy or granuloma. Wireless capsule endoscopy showed no small-bowel mucosal lesions.

A female infant was born at 38 weeks’ gestation by uncomplicated vaginal delivery. The Apgar scores were 7 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively; birthweight was 2540 g (10th percentile). Prenatal history included treated maternal hypothyroidism and daily folic acid supplementation; there was no family history of congenital anomalies.

On initial examination, the infant appeared well. Examination of the skull revealed a 3×3 cm, well-circumscribed mass over the occipital scalp. The overlying skin was intact and of normal color; palpation revealed a soft, smooth, nonfluctuant, nonreducible lesion. There were no signs of neck rigidity or neurologic deficits.

Differential consideration included caput succedaneum, subgaleal hemorrhage, and cephalohematoma. A cranial ultrasound showed no intracranial abnormalities. On day 2, phototherapy was administered for hyperbilirubinemia attributed to the presumed cephalohematoma. Over the next 5 days of hospitalization, the occipital swelling remained unchanged in size, and the infant was discharged with plans for outpatient observation.

At follow-up visits at 15 days and 1 month of age, the occipital mass persisted unchanged in size and consistency. The infant continued to grow and develop normally. The persistence and midline occipital location of the lesion prompted consideration of an alternative diagnosis, and brain magnetic resonance imaging was planned.

A 16-year-old girl with ulcerative colitis on infliximab presented with two weeks of abdominal pain, hematochezia, and diarrhea. Laboratory evaluation revealed a fecal calprotectin level of 210 mg/kg (normal <50 mg/kg), a positive Clostridium difficile toxin PCR assay with a negative enzyme immunoassay, and otherwise unremarkable results. She failed to improve after seven days of outpatient oral vancomycin for presumed C. difficile infection and oral corticosteroids for a presumed IBD flare. Magnetic resonance enterography performed for persistent symptoms showed a normal terminal ileum and a markedly dilated proximal colon, raising concern for toxic megacolon versus a distal colonic stricture. At the time of imaging she had no abdominal distension, pain, or vomiting and was passing flatus but no stools. On admission, she was kept nil per os, received nasogastric decompression and intravenous corticosteroids, and underwent serial abdominal examinations. A kidney–ureter–bladder radiograph demonstrated dilation of the large bowel in the left upper quadrant with a maximum diameter of 8.3 cm. On hospital day 3, she became obstipated, and repeat radiography showed a transverse colon diameter of 10.2 cm.

A 59-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia treated with tamsulosin presented to the emergency department with a rash on his left nasolacrimal area and forehead, confined to the ophthalmic (V1) dermatome. Two days earlier, he had received the first dose of the recombinant zoster vaccine. He reported pain and tingling on the left side of his face but denied any vision changes or systemic symptoms. At an outside hospital on day 2 after vaccination, he had been prescribed amoxicillin, valacyclovir 1 g twice daily orally, and topical eyedrops. By day 9, the vesicles were fully developed and his symptoms had not improved, prompting this presentation. Examination revealed clustered vesicles and erythema limited to the left V1 dermatome; no other skin lesions or systemic signs were observed. Mupirocin 2% three times daily was prescribed to prevent secondary infection, and he was referred for ophthalmology consultation. During the ED visit, a sample was taken from the vesicles and sent for polymerase-chain-reaction testing for herpes simplex virus (HSV) 1 and 2 and varicella-zoster virus (VZV); an HIV antigen/antibody test was also ordered.

A 52-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of whitish lesions on both buccal mucosae and crusting of the lips. He initially noted oral dryness and discomfort that worsened on hot, sunny days, followed by crusting and fissuring of the lips with tenderness at the outer margin. The condition gradually progressed over time. His medical history included type 2 diabetes (on antidiabetic medications) and gastric ulcers. He worked as a clerk, was a smoker, a social drinker, and wore dentures. There was no family history of similar lesions. On examination, there were no cutaneous abnormalities. Intraoral examination revealed multiple asymptomatic, coalesced papules with a rough texture along the vermilion border; the lips appeared dry and crusted. A biopsy of the lip margin was performed. Histopathologic examination showed suprabasal splits in the epithelium with acantholytic and dyskeratotic cells observed as round and granular corpuscles.

A 56-year-old Japanese man was referred for evaluation of tarry stools. His medical history included gastritis, hypertension, and anxiety disorder, treated with lansoprazole, irsogladine, metoprolol, flutoprazepam, and ethyl loflazepate. He had no history of dyslipidemia or diabetes mellitus. On examination, his abdomen was soft and nontender, and there were no cutaneous xanthomas. Laboratory tests, including serum cholesterol, triglyceride, and plasma glucose levels, were within normal limits. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed erosive, atrophic gastritis. 

During colonoscopy, multiple yellowish spots, each measuring approximately 3 to 5 mm, were observed in the rectum, along with hemorrhoids. Magnification with narrow-band imaging showed that the pits of the rectal mucosa over the lesions were intact. Application of indigo-carmine dye accentuated the lesions’ whitish to yellowish color.

An 81-year-old Asian man with erectile dysfunction, CKD stage 3a (baseline creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, eGFR 47 mL/min/1.73 m2), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, gout on long-term allopurinol, and osteoarthritis presented with one month of generalized edema and a 9.1 kg weight gain. Two weeks before admission his creatinine rose to 1.9 mg/dL with nephrotic-range proteinuria (14.7 mg/mg). He noted an acute increase in peripheral and facial edema four days after a single sildenafil dose. His only new medication was sildenafil; he denied recent NSAID use.  

On admission: BP 144/70 mmHg, exam notable for diffuse bilateral lower extremity edema; cardiac and lung exams unremarkable. Chest radiograph showed small bilateral pleural effusions. Renal ultrasound was normal without hydronephrosis. Echocardiogram: EF 68% with normal structure.  

Laboratory studies: WBC 5.4 × 10^9/L with 5.6% eosinophils; serum BUN 48 mg/dL; creatinine 3.7 mg/dL; albumin 2.6 g/dL. Urinalysis: specific gravity 1.020, 4+ blood, 4+ protein. Sediment: 0–2 granular casts/high-power field, 0–5 RBCs/hpf, 0–1 WBC/hpf.

A 25-year-old previously healthy man presented with 1 day of worsening tachypnea and dyspnea. He reported intermittent fevers, myalgia, and headache for 1 week after returning from a 2-week trip to Costa Rica, with initial symptoms beginning 1 day before his return flight. On examination in the emergency department, his temperature was 38.6 °C, blood pressure 125/75 mmHg, heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 35 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 82% on room air. He was alert (GCS 15) but in respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Chest radiograph showed bilateral pulmonary opacities. He was intubated after failing to improve on 100% nonrebreather. Arterial blood gas on 100% FiO₂ showed PaO₂ 65 mmHg. Basic blood tests, including electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, and coagulation studies, were normal.

In the ICU, he met Berlin criteria for ARDS with a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 110, bilateral infiltrates, and no evidence of cardiac dysfunction. Ventilation followed a low–tidal volume strategy (5 mL/kg ideal body weight, target pH >7.25) with PEEP up to 10 cm H₂O. Blood, urine, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cultures were sent. Bronchoscopy revealed no pulmonary hemorrhage or purulent secretions. Chest CT confirmed bilateral edema without focal consolidation. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated normal biventricular function and no valvular abnormalities. Empiric piperacillin–tazobactam, azithromycin, and vancomycin were started. Initial blood, urine, and BAL cultures were negative. Malaria thick and thin smears were repeatedly negative. Dengue serology, HIV, and hepatitis A, B, and C tests were all negative. Despite broad-spectrum antimicrobials, his respiratory status worsened, necessitating prone ventilation.

A 56-year-old Japanese woman with no smoking history presented in May 2022 with dyspnea on exertion and a severe wet cough. Since November 2021 she had been treated for suspected bronchial asthma with high-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting β2-agonist and a leukotriene receptor antagonist; clarithromycin was added in March 2022 without improvement. Her medical history included Graves’ disease in remission, and she had no relevant family history or pet exposure. On admission her oxygen saturation was 93% on room air and lung fields were clear without wheezing. Laboratory studies showed a peripheral eosinophil count of 3010/μL and a fractional exhaled nitric oxide level of 80 ppb; total IgE was 120 IU/mL and specific IgE against Aspergillus was negative; MPO-ANCA and PR3-ANCA were negative. Chest radiography revealed diffuse granular shadows bilaterally. High-resolution CT showed diffuse centrilobular nodules and bronchial wall thickening. Pulmonary function tests demonstrated an FEV1 of 1.29 L (51% predicted), FVC of 2.10 L (67.1% predicted), DLCO of 44.2%, and no bronchodilator reversibility after salbutamol. Nasopharyngeal endoscopic examination and head CT showed no evidence of sinusitis.

A 17-year-old female with obesity, prediabetes, and marijuana use presented with a 1-month history of left frontotemporal and retro-orbital headaches accompanied by photophobia, nausea, vomiting, and localized numbness over the left temple. The headaches, which often awakened her from sleep, became constant over the 3 weeks before presentation. Over the preceding 2 weeks she developed persistent binocular diplopia progressing to complete ophthalmoplegia. She also reported 1 week of intermittent left mandibular pain and new sensory changes over the maxillary (V2) division of the left trigeminal nerve.

On examination, she was afebrile with a blood pressure of 156/83 mmHg and otherwise normal vital signs. She appeared mildly ill. Pupils were 5 mm and briskly reactive to direct light, with sluggish left‐eye consensual response. Funduscopic examination was normal. Extraocular movements of the left eye revealed near‐complete ophthalmoplegia with minimal upward and downward gaze, and marked ptosis consistent with severe oculomotor and abducens nerve palsies. Visual fields were full bilaterally, and there was no facial asymmetry. Trigeminal sensory testing showed left‐sided hyperesthesia in the V1 and V2 distributions.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel (glucose 170 mg/dL), hemoglobin A1c 6.1%, angiotensin‐converting enzyme 14 U/L (reference, 16–85), and negative autoimmune serologies (ANA, CCP, anti-SSA/Ro, anti-SSB/La, Sm, RNP, Scl-70, Jo-1, RF, MPO, PR3). Lactate dehydrogenase and uric acid were normal; serum electrophoresis showed no monoclonal proteins. Infectious workup was negative for Borrelia burgdorferi, syphilis IgG, CSF VDRL, and QuantiFERON-TB Gold; bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures and acid-fast smear were negative. Lumbar puncture revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid except for lymphocytosis (92%); CSF ACE, IgG index, albumin, and flow cytometry were unremarkable.

MRI of the brain and orbits demonstrated an extra-axial enhancing, ill-defined lesion centered in the left cavernous sinus, with extension into Meckel’s cave, superior orbital fissure, orbital apex, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, and the middle cranial fossa, and mild narrowing of the patent right cavernous internal carotid artery.

A 65-year-old man presented with 3 weeks of mid-dorsal back pain and low-grade fevers. The pain was mechanical, worsened by movement and coughing, nonradiating, and unassociated with neurologic symptoms. He reported a 40-lb weight loss over several months. His history included hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and type II diabetes. Examination showed tenderness at T8–9 without deformity or neurologic deficits. Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 45 mm/hr and C-reactive protein of 2.1 mg/dL. He had traveled to Mexico a year earlier to work in a slaughterhouse and regularly consumed unpasteurized cheeses.

MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated increased T1 signal at T8–9 involving the disc, with endplate and soft-tissue enhancement after contrast. CT of the thoracic spine revealed destruction at the anterosuperior corner of T9 accompanied by osteosclerosis and osteophyte formation.

A 50-year-old African-American veteran with a 9-year history of PTSD and severe recurrent major depressive disorder presented to the psychiatric emergency room with suicidal ideation and worsening flashbacks of dismembered body parts from his service in the first Gulf War. His PTSD symptoms included flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance of reminders, insomnia, and hyperstartle. His depressive symptoms—present since before military service—consisted of depressed mood, anhedonia, worthlessness, psychomotor retardation, and intermittent suicidal thoughts without prior attempts.  
He also reported waxing and waning headaches that began 3 years before this admission, during which his PTSD symptoms worsened. He denied any history of traumatic brain injury, concussive blasts, or head trauma. Outpatient headache treatments (acetaminophen, gabapentin) had provided no relief and were discontinued on admission. He was switched to ibuprofen 800 mg as needed, but over the first week of hospitalization he continued to have daily headaches that were worsened by light and noise and minimally relieved by ibuprofen. Ibuprofen was tapered off because of concern for rebound headache. The patient was then given sumatriptan, but “showed no relief with sumatriptan.” Further questioning revealed that his headaches had been “constant for greater than eight months,” were “localized to the left side, and associated with left-sided rhinorrhea and lacrimation.”

An elderly man presented with a 6-week history of dysphagia for both solids and liquids and a 4-day history of a sensation of tongue swelling. He had been seen by his general practitioner, who diagnosed anaphylaxis and administered epinephrine without improvement. On hospital assessment, he had dysphonia with a marked nasal quality on prolonged speech and reported tongue weakness and fatigability, which left him unable to elevate his tongue by the end of meals. There was no objective swelling of the tongue or lips. His medical history included renal cell carcinoma treated by nephrectomy, insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus, and uncomplicated hypertension. His vital signs were stable, and no other focal neurologic deficits were noted. Initial blood tests showed neutrophilia, and a chest radiograph demonstrated a left basal pneumonia. A CT scan of the brain revealed global cortical atrophy and enlarged ventricles consistent with age-related change but no acute infarction or metastasis. At this point, differential diagnoses included amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, cerebrovascular accident, central nervous system metastasis or paraneoplastic disease, and cranial polyneuropathy. Following review by a consultant neurologist, testing for neuromuscular junction disease was pursued.

A 5-month-old entire male domestic shorthair kitten was referred for investigation of a month-long history of stranguria, pollakiuria, and urinary incontinence. One month earlier, the kitten had presented with stranguria and pollakiuria; examination revealed a large, firm bladder that could not be expressed, and urethral catheterisation was achieved easily without evidence of a plug, sediment, or urolith. Penile conformation and the urethral opening were normal. In-house urine sediment examination revealed bacteriuria, and urine culture was negative. The kitten received meloxicam, prazosin, and potentiated amoxicillin–clavulanate, which prevented further obstructive episodes but did not resolve stranguria, pollakiuria, or incontinence, and excessive perineal grooming was observed. On referral, clinical examination was unremarkable, with a small soft bladder. Haematology was unremarkable. Biochemistry showed a moderate increase in creatine kinase (794 IU/l [RI 33–168]), borderline high urea (10.9 mmol/l [RI 5.4–10.7]), and age-related elevations in phosphate (2.56 mmol/l [RI 0.9–2.1]) and alkaline phosphatase (135 IU/l [RI 10–93]). Abdominal radiographs revealed a normally positioned, full bladder with a smooth, rounded border. Abdominal ultrasound showed a thickened bladder wall (0.37 cm) with a hyperechoic mucosal layer and slightly irregular luminal border; no other abnormalities were noted. Cystocentesis yielded inadequately concentrated urine (specific gravity 1.010), bacteriuria, and proteinuria; culture grew sparse pure Escherichia coli resistant to cephalexin. The kitten was anesthetized for a retrograde urethrocystogram, which revealed an outpouching of the intrapelvic urethra.

A 60-year-old woman with a history of simultaneous pancreas–kidney transplantation for diabetic nephropathy two years earlier presented with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and minimal urine output. She noted an interval weight gain; her body-mass index was 31.8, up from 26.6 four months earlier. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Laboratory evaluation revealed acute renal failure with a serum creatinine level of 9.9 mg/dL. Noncontrast computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed an enlarged renal allograft in the left iliac fossa with moderate hydronephrosis and trace pelvic free fluid. Comparison with prior imaging demonstrated that the graft hilum, previously directed anteromedially, was now oriented laterally. Subsequent ultrasound revealed an enlarged, hyperechoic allograft with moderate collecting-system dilatation. On color Doppler examination, only a short segment of the proximal renal artery was seen; the distal renal artery and renal vein were not visualized, and no blood flow was detected within the graft. These findings were concerning for renal artery thrombosis and impending infarction.

A 50-year-old woman with a 30-year history of poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus presented with one day of fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. She described cramping left-sided pain (6/10) relieved by lying down. She denied pruritus, jaundice, fever, or bleeding. Six months earlier, she was admitted with similar symptoms and underwent an appendectomy; at that time, she had elevated liver enzymes. Her medications included insulin glargine and lispro (which she had omitted for 2 days), amlodipine, metoprolol, aspirin, gabapentin, oxycodone, and low-dose pravastatin. She denied alcohol, tobacco, and recreational drugs. Family history was notable for type 1 diabetes in an aunt and fatty liver disease in both parents and her aunt.

On examination, she was obese and afebrile (BP 147/94 mmHg; pulse 80/min; BMI 31.4 kg/m2). The abdomen was soft with mild left-lower-quadrant tenderness; the liver was palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin (span 13 cm) with a smooth edge; there were no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Initial labs showed blood glucose 610 mg/dL, anion gap 13, pH 7.35, and 1+ urine ketones; she was treated for mild diabetic ketoacidosis. Liver tests revealed AST 1460 U/L, ALT 682 U/L, ALP 569 U/L, GGT 436 U/L, LDH 823 U/L, total bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL, albumin 3.7 g/dL. Electrolytes and renal function were unremarkable. Hemoglobin A1c was 11.4%. WBC count, platelets, INR, B12, folate, and thyroid-stimulating hormone were within normal limits. Iron studies (iron 76 µg/dL, TIBC 384 µg/dL, ferritin 165 µg/L) were normal.

Serologies were negative for hepatitis B and C, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus. Autoimmune markers (AMA, ASMA, ANA) were negative. Ceruloplasmin, urinary copper, and ophthalmologic exam were normal. Alpha-1 antitrypsin level was normal. Acetaminophen, salicylate levels, and urine toxicology were negative.

CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrated diffuse colonic wall thickening suggestive of colitis and no focal hepatic lesions; there was mild intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary dilation without obstruction. Doppler ultrasound of the liver showed no fatty infiltration and normal echogenicity. MRCP confirmed mild ductal dilation without choledocholithiasis or parenchymal signal abnormalities. 

During the first three hospital days, transaminase levels decreased sharply (AST and ALT fell to the mid-300–400 U/L range) with strict glycemic control and holding potentially hepatotoxic medications.

A 33‐year‐old G2P1 woman at 19 weeks’ gestation presented with several days of dyspnea on exertion. She denied alcohol, tobacco, and drug use. Examination was notable only for mild jaundice; blood pressure and other vital signs were within normal limits for pregnancy.

Laboratory studies on admission:
- WBC 86.5 k/µL (82% blasts), hemoglobin 5.5 g/dL, platelets 18 k/µL  
- ALT 33 U/L, AST 21 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 215 U/L, INR 1.1  

Bone marrow biopsy confirmed AML with inv(16). She received hydroxyurea for cytoreduction and then induction chemotherapy with cytarabine (100 mg/m2 days 1–7) and daunorubicin (60 mg/m2 days 1–3).

On cycle 1 day 5, total bilirubin rose to 2.7 mg/dL (direct 1.0 mg/dL) while AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, and INR remained normal. By day 15, total bilirubin peaked at 13.4 mg/dL (direct 8.5 mg/dL) without transaminase elevations. There was no clinical or laboratory evidence of hemolysis.

Imaging and serologic studies:
- RUQ ultrasound on day 5: cholelithiasis without ductal dilation or cholecystitis  
- MRCP without contrast: no biliary ductal dilation  
- Hepatitis A, B, and C serologies and CMV and EBV PCR: undetectable  
- Autoimmune hepatitis panel (ANA, AMA, ASMA, total Ig): negative

A 29-year-old man was referred for left ptosis and diplopia. Six months earlier, his car had crashed into a roadside tree, after which he developed orthostatic headaches and malaise. He noted an increasing difficulty opening his eyes and an out-of-focus feeling that worsened after waking and improved after lying down. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 1.5 in both eyes, and the pupillary light reflexes were normal. There was no limitation of extraocular movements, but alternate prism cover testing revealed 8 prism diopters of left exotropia and 4 prism diopters of right exotropia at distance. Slit-lamp and fundus examinations were unremarkable. Routine blood tests were normal, and both the anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody and the edrophonium tests were negative.

A 50‐year‐old man of Indian ancestry with a 3‐year history of multiple myeloma presented with progressive abdominal and lower‐extremity edema and dyspnea. He reported a 15‐lb weight gain over 2 weeks. His only other chronic condition was mild hypertension. His myeloma had advanced despite corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, etoposide, cisplatin, stem‐cell transplant, thalidomide, and bortezomib.

On examination, he was afebrile, heart rate 100/min, blood pressure 97/50 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 96% on 3 L/min nasal oxygen. He had bilateral basal crackles, jugular venous distension to 12 cm, a 2/6 systolic flow murmur at the left upper sternal border, distended abdomen with shifting dullness, a liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin, warm extremities, and 3+ bilateral pitting edema with scrotal swelling.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, platelets 10,000/µL, blood urea nitrogen 55 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, albumin 3.6 g/dL, and calcium 13 mg/dL. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with normal voltage and diffuse T‐wave flattening. Chest radiograph revealed mild cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema. Echocardiography demonstrated a hyperdynamic left ventricle with normal wall thickness, no regional wall motion or valvular abnormalities, and normal diastolic function.

He received aggressive intravenous furosemide for 10 days without improvement in volume status. On hospital day 11, right‐ and left‐sided cardiac catheterization was performed.

An 8-year-old girl presented with a 10-day history of wounds on the upper and lower lips, 7 days of gum redness and swelling, and inability to eat for 5 days. Two weeks earlier she had a fever, followed by the appearance of a small lip wound that progressed to involve the entire vermillion borders of both lips. The lesions were severely painful, especially with eating. There was no significant past medical, family, or drug history. The patient was alert with stable vital signs.

Extraoral examination revealed sparse ruptured vesicles with crusted margins on the upper lip and chin, and tender, soft-to-firm submandibular and submental lymphadenopathy bilaterally. After topical debridement, intraoral examination showed irregular erythematous areas with crustations on both upper and lower lips, bilateral commissures, and labial mucosa. The gingiva around teeth 11, 21, 52, and 62 was erythematous and swollen. Multiple ulcers with irregular margins and an erythematous halo were present on the hard and soft palate, the largest measuring approximately 2×1 cm distal to teeth 16 and 26.

Laboratory studies showed a monocyte count of 12%, sodium 131 mmol/L, normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, noncontributory blood cultures, and negative serologic tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and HIV.

A 61-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease underwent bilateral lung transplantation. His immunosuppressive regimen included prednisone, tacrolimus, and azathioprine. On posttransplant day (PTD) 28, he developed leukopenia, leading to discontinuation of azathioprine and a switch from trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole to pentamidine.

On PTD 113, he had fever, worsening oral erosions, and an erythematous, targetoid papular rash on the dorsal hands and forearms. Laboratory studies showed anemia (hematocrit 25.3%) and leukopenia (1.6 × 10^3/uL) with normal liver function tests. Punch biopsy of the rash revealed vacuolar interface dermatitis with basal vacuolar degeneration, dyskeratotic keratinocytes, and a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction. He was diagnosed with erythema multiforme and, after clinical improvement, discharged on PTD 117 with prednisone, tacrolimus, and azathioprine.

On PTD 122, he returned with fever, weakness, new oral erosions, and a generalized morbilliform eruption with rare atypical targetoid papules. His back was Nikolsky-positive; mucosal surfaces were initially reported as spared. Repeat laboratory studies again showed anemia and leukopenia with normal liver function tests. Skin biopsy demonstrated vacuolar interface dermatitis with dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis. Mycoplasma IgM was minimally reactive, and IgG was negative. He was transferred to the intensive care unit for fever, tachycardia, progressive desquamation, and new mucous membrane involvement and received intravenous immunoglobulin for suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome, possibly from piperacillin–tazobactam. Given ongoing progression, molecular chimerism studies from peripheral blood and bone marrow were submitted and returned negative for donor DNA.

A 31-year-old nulliparous woman was referred for primary infertility of five years. She reported oligomenorrhea with prolonged, irregular menstrual cycles but denied acne, hirsutism, weight gain, hot flashes, or night sweats. She had no history of diabetes, thyroid disease, or immunological disorders. Development was normal in childhood, with no intellectual or behavioral problems, and there was no family history of a similar condition. On examination, her BMI was 23.7 kg/m2; height 170 cm; arm span 173 cm. Nevi were noted on the outer aspect of the left hand; dental and foot examinations were unremarkable. Thyroid examination was normal. Cardiac auscultation revealed a loud mid-diastolic murmur. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, platelet count 276 ×109/L, prolactin 10.4 ng/mL, follicle-stimulating hormone 18 IU/L (repeated 26.72 IU/L), luteinizing hormone 14.8 IU/L, estradiol 229 pmol/L, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 38.7 nmol/L, TSH 2.035 mIU/L, free T4 12.1 pmol/L, and free T3 3.8 pmol/L. Pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated a normal uterus with a 3-mm endometrium; right and left ovarian volumes were 0.33 mL and 1.15 mL respectively, with an antral follicle count of zero in both ovaries. Diagnostic laparoscopy showed a normal-sized uterus, bilateral streak ovaries, and patent fallopian tubes.

A 59-year-old woman was admitted with a one-year history of asthenia on minimal exertion, dyspnea, stable angina, blurred vision, nausea, hair loss, and a sensation of heavy legs. She had multiple prior hospitalizations for similar symptoms. Her medical history included megaloblastic anemia, refractory cytopenias with multilineage dysplasia (myelodysplastic syndrome), hypothyroidism (on levothyroxine 50 µg/day), stable angina (on a statin and nitrates), untreated pulmonary emphysema (37 pack-year smoking history), hysterectomy at age 32, and a left ileocolectomy six months earlier for an inflammatory colonic mass.

On admission, her vital signs were normal. She was anicteric, acyanotic, eupneic at rest, and markedly pale (3+/4+). Cardiac examination revealed a regular rhythm with an S3 and thready peripheral pulses. Laboratory studies including a complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, coagulation profile, inflammatory markers, electrolytes, hemolysis markers, and blood gases were obtained (Table 1). She received two units of red blood cells, inhaled corticosteroids with a long-acting β₂-agonist, nitrates, a statin, and aspirin and initially improved.

On hospital day 3, she developed a pustular, erythematous, and painful lesion at her right cubital venous puncture site. She then became febrile, tachycardic, tachypneic, and her overall status worsened. Empiric intravenous vancomycin (1 g every 12 h) and piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g every 6 h) were started without clinical improvement.

By hospital day 12, the lesion had progressed to an infiltrated erythematous plaque with a hemorrhagic center, then to an erythematous-violet ulcer with peripheral vesicles. Lesional material was sent for bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal stains and cultures, all of which were negative. A skin biopsy for histopathology showed epidermal necrosis with a predominantly neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. The lesion worsened at the biopsy site.

A 25-year-old man from rural Nepal presented with a 10-year history of insidious, progressive pain and swelling of both hands and feet, worsened by prolonged standing or dangling. He reported profuse sweating of the extremities, progressive enlargement of his hands and feet, easy fatigability, heat intolerance and skin changes including acne, scalp dandruff and thickened eyelids. There was no family history of similar symptoms.

On examination, the patient was moderately built. He had marked thickening of forehead skin folds, bilateral ankle joint swelling and grade IV clubbing of all fingers and toes. Other systemic examinations were normal.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Normal serum insulin-like growth factor-1 level  
• Normal thyroid function tests  
• Normal complete blood count, liver and renal function tests  
• Negative rheumatoid factor and anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody tests

Radiographs demonstrated:  
• Ankles: symmetric, shaggy subperiosteal new bone formation and cortical thickening of the tibia and fibula, with periarticular osteopenia and preserved joint spaces  
• Feet: hyperostosis of metatarsal bones  
• Hands: periosteal new bone formation of metacarpals and phalanges, with increased soft-tissue shadow ("sausage-finger" appearance)  
• Skull: “hair-on-end” appearance of the parietal bones, hyperostosis of calvarial bones and a normal sella turcica

A 6-year-old boy presented with his mother for evaluation of painful, bleeding gingiva of seven months’ duration. The onset was gradual, without mechanical, thermal, or chemical trauma; dietary changes; use of new dental‐hygiene products; or exposure to cinnamon‐containing products. He had no fever, malaise, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Two weeks earlier, a complete blood count and metabolic panel were normal. One week earlier, dental prophylaxis produced no improvement.

His medical history was significant only for asthma treated with daily mometasone inhaler and as‐needed albuterol; he rinsed his mouth after inhaler use. Review of systems and family history were otherwise unremarkable.

Intraoral examination revealed:  
• Subtle erythema of gingiva buccal to the right primary maxillary molar, canine, and lateral incisor  
• Well-defined erythema of alveolar mucosa facial to the left primary maxillary incisors and canine  
• Multiple mucosal-colored swellings and ulcerations on gingiva facial to the right permanent mandibular incisors and primary canine  
• Mild tenderness on palpation; rest of oral mucosa normal  
Panoramic radiograph showed no bone loss.

A biopsy of the affected mandibular gingiva showed spongiotic stratified squamous epithelium with mild exocytosis, underlying fibrous connective tissue with lymphocytes and plasma cells, and well-formed noncaseating granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes and lymphocytes. PAS, GMS, and AFB stains were negative for fungi and mycobacteria. Polarized light microscopy revealed no foreign material. A diagnosis of granulomatous inflammation was rendered with a comment regarding possible etiologies, including Crohn’s disease, orofacial granulomatosis, and sarcoidosis.

A 37-year-old man with no past medical history presented to the emergency department eight days after receiving yellow fever 17D-204, hepatitis A, and meningococcal A/C/Y/W-135 vaccines. Four days postvaccination, he developed fevers to 40 °C with chills. Three days later, he noted a nonproductive cough, dyspnea, malaise, sore throat, nonbloody diarrhea, and a morbilliform rash on the chest.

On arrival: temperature 39.3 °C, blood pressure 106/73 mmHg, pulse 103/min, respiratory rate 25/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Examination revealed a thoracoabdominal maculopapular rash without purpura, conjunctival injection, pharyngitis, right upper-quadrant tenderness, and a “strawberry tongue.” Chest radiograph was normal.

Initial laboratory values:  
• Platelets 46 G/L (150–450)  
• Lymphocytes 0.41 G/L (1–4)  
• WBC 4.62 G/L (4–10)  
• AST 428 U/L (13–40), ALT 309 U/L (7–40)  
• Total bilirubin 42 µmol/L (5–21)  
• Creatinine 99 µmol/L (64–104), sodium 131 mmol/L (136–146)  
• CRP 179.9 mg/L (< 5), lactate 2.1 mmol/L (< 1.6)

He was admitted to the ICU. On day 9, he had hepatomegaly, inguinal and axillary lymphadenopathy, extension of the rash to lower limbs, and occipital headache. Repeat labs showed AST 621 U/L, ALT 506 U/L, bilirubin 54 µmol/L, lymphocytes 0.11 G/L, normal WBC and renal function, and prothrombin time 91%.

A 51-year-old postmenopausal Asian woman presented with a 3-cm lump in her left breast and several palpable axillary nodes. She had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and no family history of malignancy. Breast ultrasonography revealed an indistinct hypoechoic mass measuring 3 cm in the lower outer quadrant of the left breast and several swollen lymph nodes in the left axilla and subclavian fossa. CT of the chest confirmed left axillary and infraclavicular lymphadenopathy without evidence of distant metastasis. Core biopsy of the breast mass showed grade 2 infiltrating ductal carcinoma that was estrogen receptor–negative, progesterone receptor–negative, and HER2-positive (3+ by immunohistochemistry). The clinical stage was cT2N3M0. She received four cycles of doxorubicin plus cyclophosphamide followed by four cycles of docetaxel with trastuzumab and pertuzumab. After completion of neoadjuvant therapy, mammography and ultrasonography demonstrated reduction of the breast tumor to 1.5 cm, and MRI showed a 9 mm enhancing lesion. However, the infraclavicular and axillary lymph nodes remained enlarged. A multidisciplinary tumor board recommended mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection.

A 40‐year‐old Caucasian woman was found in her apartment by the fire department after her carbon monoxide detector had been beeping intermittently. She woke at 3 a.m. with a severe frontal headache, deep orbital pain, blurred vision, light‐headedness, and stabbing chest pain. On arrival, her blood pressure was 150/100 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and temperature 97.6°F. The fire department measured indoor CO levels of 60 ppm, and her carboxyhemoglobin concentration was 3.9%. She was given 100% oxygen by non‐rebreather mask during transport, after which her vital signs normalized and her mental status improved. She was discharged later that day. The following morning, she noted that the distal margins of all her fingernail beds—most prominently on the first and second fingers—were eroded with a bite‐like border. There was no separation between nail plate and nail bed, no other surface deformities, and the nail beds were pink, with redder and bluish areas at the top border. She denied any history of trauma to her nails or extremities.

A 72-year-old man with Fitzpatrick skin type I, a history of scalp actinic keratoses, and no prior bullous disease was prescribed imiquimod cream 3.5% for scalp lesions. He applied it nightly for 2 weeks, took a 2-week break, then began a second 2-week course. During the first course, he developed expected painful crusting on the scalp but no other symptoms. A few days into the second course, he noted pruritic, painful blisters on the scalp that rapidly appeared on the hands, thighs, abdomen, and inside the mouth. He was initially treated with permethrin cream for suspected bullous scabies without improvement and was referred to dermatology. His medications included amlodipine, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and escitalopram, all unchanged for over a year. 

On examination, there were hemorrhagic crusted plaques on the bald scalp consistent with prior imiquimod reaction, as well as tense bullae on erythematous bases on the palms, dorsal hands, thighs, and abdomen. Some lesions had a targetoid appearance. Several ulcers were present on the labial and buccal mucosa. A diagnosis of erythema multiforme was considered, with bullous pemphigoid as a differential, and skin‐directed biopsies were performed.

A 6-year-old intact male Russian Tsvetnaya Bolonka weighing 6 kg was referred for a 4½-month history of progressive weakness. Clinical signs began with tail weakness and reduced general condition, then progressed to dysphonia, muscle pain, and right-sided pelvic limb lameness. Two months before referral, lumbar MRI and CT showed asymmetrical atrophy of the right iliopsoas and quadriceps muscles. The dog had a past diagnosis of hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine; he had never traveled outside Norway.

On examination, he was afebrile (38.8 °C) and had reduced muscle mass of the right proximal pelvic limb. Neurologically, he was ambulatory but paraparetic—worse on the right—showing hip hypoflexion, a “bunny-hopping” pelvic gait, and a paretic tail. Cranial nerves were normal except for dysphonia. Postural reactions were decreased in both pelvic limbs, and right pelvic spinal reflexes were reduced. Neuroanatomic localization was the neuromuscular system.

CBC and serum biochemistry revealed a mildly increased creatine phosphokinase; otherwise unremarkable. Toxoplasma gondii–specific IgM titer was borderline at 1:32 with negative IgG and follow-up IgM. Neospora caninum antibody titers were negative. Serum total thyroxine was within the reference range.

Two weeks later, signs had progressed to general paresis of all four limbs. Laryngeal inspection under light anesthesia showed bilateral arytenoid and vocal cord immobility, consistent with laryngeal paresis. Under general anesthesia, a whole-body pre- and post-contrast CT scan demonstrated bilateral muscle atrophy with fat infiltration affecting limb, back, and head muscles—most severe on the right. Electromyography revealed spontaneous activity in multiple muscle groups, and motor nerve conduction velocity in the ulnar nerve was reduced to 40.5 m/s (normal 60 ± 1.1 m/s).

A 30-year-old man presented with several months of pain, tenderness, and swelling on the left side of his palate. On examination, the left palatine mucosa was diffusely swollen—most pronounced in the molar region—with poorly defined borders and increased pain on palpation. T2-weighted MRI demonstrated a high-signal-intensity lesion in that area. Panoramic radiography and CT scans of the maxilla and sinuses were unremarkable, and all left maxillary teeth appeared healthy. His medical and family histories were unremarkable, and he denied any history of trauma or inflammation in the head or neck. Empiric treatment with oral antibiotics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for 7 days produced no improvement. Based on the clinical and radiographic findings, a soft-tissue tumor was suspected, and an incisional biopsy was performed.

A 27-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 3-month history of a swelling in his left upper lip that had grown rapidly over the past month. He denied trauma, pain, bleeding, ulceration, or color change. On examination, the lesion was a 6.0 cm × 2.5 cm soft, pulsatile, immobile mass with well-defined borders; it was nonreducible and noncompressible, and there were no signs of inflammation (no erythema, heat, or discharge). Initial considerations included abscess and vascular tumors.  
 
Magnetic resonance imaging (axial T2-weighted) showed diffuse linear-tubular signal‐void areas in the soft tissue of the upper lip. MR angiography (coronal maximum-intensity-projection) demonstrated a vascularized mass in the upper lip with arterial supply from distal branches of the external carotid artery. MR venography (axial maximum-intensity-projection) revealed the mass draining into the venous system.

A 47-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for sub-acute paresis of her left leg, accompanied by a dull sensation in her inner thigh, knee, and lower leg. The weakness had progressed over 1½ weeks, and she was unable to walk without bilateral walking aids. Eight months earlier, she had undergone left total hip replacement; in the initial weeks postoperatively she experienced left buttock pain due to a hematoma that was treated surgically. Two months later, pain recurred and was attributed to loosening of the acetabular component; she underwent a second operation three months after the first, with an uncomplicated recovery and steady improvement in leg strength without pain.

Two weeks before presentation, she noted sudden weakness in left hip flexion and, to a lesser degree, knee extension. A neurologist documented paresis of the left iliopsoas and quadriceps femoris muscles, diminished left patellar reflex, and sensory loss in the femoral nerve distribution. MRI performed at that time showed an increased amount of fluid within the left ileopectineal bursa, and left-sided bursitis was diagnosed without explanation for the nerve dysfunction.

On examination, she reported left inguinal pain but had no palpable swelling or mass. Motor testing revealed 3/5 strength for left hip flexion and 4/5 for left knee extension; all other muscle groups were normal. The left patellar reflex was decreased; other reflexes were symmetric and normal. Sensory testing showed paresthesia and hypoesthesia of the left inner thigh, knee, and medial lower leg. Laboratory studies revealed normal C-reactive protein and white blood cell count. Neurography showed increased distal motor latency of the left femoral nerve, with normal tibial and sural responses. Electromyography demonstrated acute denervation with reduced maximal innervation of the left iliopsoas. The findings were summarized as an acute femoral nerve palsy.

A 37-year-old woman with hypertension and biopsy-confirmed metastatic clear cell renal carcinoma (lung and liver metastases) started on pembrolizumab-axitinib 8 days ago presents with fatigue and palpitations.  
Vital signs: blood pressure 98/70 mmHg, pulse 118 bpm, respiratory rate 22/min, temperature 98.6°F.  
Physical examination: nonobese female in acute distress, tachycardic, with mild abdominal tenderness.  
Laboratory studies show:  
 • Potassium 6.5 mmol/L (baseline 4.2)  
 • Uric acid 11.2 mg/dL (baseline 6.3)  
 • Calcium 8.8 mg/dL (baseline 10.0)  
 • Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL (baseline 0.9)  
EKG demonstrates sinus tachycardia with peaked T waves. Chest radiograph is normal.  
She is admitted to the intensive care unit and started on intravenous fluids, calcium gluconate, allopurinol, and an insulin drip.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of abdominal pain. The pain began suddenly in the upper abdomen, increased in severity, and became localized to the epigastrium and right upper quadrant. It was constant, associated with nausea, vomiting, and radiated to the back. Her medical history was notable for type II diabetes mellitus, ischemic heart disease, and chronic hypertension. On examination, blood pressure was 160/95 mmHg; other vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed generalized guarding and tenderness, with maximal severity and rebound tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Bowel sounds were hypoactive, and there was no abdominal distension. A tender, ill-defined fullness was palpable in the upper abdomen. The total white blood cell count was 9500/mm3. An abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous echogenic mass in the upper abdomen; no cecal or appendiceal abnormality was identified, and the kidneys and hepatobiliary system appeared normal. Because her tenderness persisted, a computed tomography scan was performed the next day, demonstrating a 12 × 7 cm amorphous solid mass at the site of maximal tenderness in the upper abdomen, adherent to the anterior abdominal wall at the midline. There was no evidence of pancreatic disease.

An 80-year-old woman presented with severe abdominal pain and vomiting. She reported a two-month history of persistent, constant, nonradiating periumbilical and hypogastric pain that acutely worsened three days ago and localized to the left lower quadrant and hypogastric regions. She also had nonbloody, nonbilious nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. On examination, her temperature was 38.2 °C; blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg; heart rate 82 beats/min; and oxygen saturation 95 % on room air. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness, rebound tenderness, and peritonism predominantly in the lower abdomen. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14 000/mm^3, hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL, normal renal and liver function tests, and normal electrolytes and coagulation parameters. An upright chest radiograph demonstrated free air under the diaphragm. Upright and supine abdominal radiographs revealed a radio-opaque structure in the lower abdomen. The patient denied swallowing foreign objects, enemas, or recent procedures.

A 45-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and a 25-pack-year smoking history was evaluated for 3 months of progressive exertional dyspnea, malaise, and a productive cough with pink-tinged sputum. She also reported a 100-lb weight loss over the past year. She lived in southeastern Minnesota, had no recent travel or animal exposures, and was not taking immunosuppressive medications. On examination she appeared cachectic and tachypneic; vital signs were temperature 37.0 °C, heart rate 134 bpm, respiratory rate 32 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 78% on room air. Lung auscultation revealed diffusely reduced breath sounds with faint inspiratory crackles. Laboratory studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, hypokalemia, low creatinine, and hypoalbuminemia. An arterial blood gas on 2 L/min oxygen demonstrated pH 7.38, PaCO2 24 mmHg, PaO2 71 mmHg, and bicarbonate 14 mmol/L. HIV testing was negative, serum immunoglobulins were normal, and rheumatologic serologies were unremarkable. Chest radiography revealed diffuse bilateral interstitial and airspace opacities, slightly more pronounced in the upper lobes. High-resolution CT of the chest showed extensive bilateral interstitial thickening with ground-glass opacities, cavitation, and parenchymal destruction most pronounced in the upper lobes. A CT scan from 9 months earlier had been essentially normal except for subtle upper-lobe emphysema. The patient underwent bronchoalveolar lavage, and specimens were sent for microbiologic and cytologic studies. She was empirically started on vancomycin, cefepime, levofloxacin, and amphotericin B.

A 23-year-old G0 woman presented with 3–4 months of increasingly heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding and 2 months of metrorrhagia. She denied pain, had no contraception, and was sexually active without a history of STIs. She had no significant past medical or surgical history. Family history was notable for various cancers, including maternal cervical cancer. She had not traveled internationally in the past 2 years.

On exam, she had abdominal distention; otherwise the physical examination was normal. A urine pregnancy test was negative. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an anteverted uterus with a 1.9 mm endometrial stripe and a large amount of ascites; the ovaries were heterogeneous with irregular borders. Serum CA125 was 432 U/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated large-volume ascites, extensive omental cake formation extending to the left upper quadrant near the spleen, and a 5.3 cm paraovarian process concerning for a mass; no lymphadenopathy was seen. 

Paracentesis yielded 3900 mL of serous fluid; cytology showed T cells and polytypic B cells without acute inflammatory cells, and aerobic/anaerobic cultures were negative at 5 days. Germ cell tumor markers (AFP, LDH, Inhibin A, Inhibin B) and CEA were within normal limits. 

Diagnostic laparoscopy revealed dense adhesions (uterus to bladder, tubes to peritoneum), extensive thick inflammatory exudates over the abdomen and pelvis, and no discrete masses; the ovaries were not visualized. Intraoperative frozen-section biopsy was reported as “granulomatous inflammation.” Final pathology showed “diffuse granulomatous inflammation with reactive mesothelial cell hyperplasia, lymphocytosis, histiocytosis, and multinucleated giant cells.” Grocott’s methenamine silver and acid-fast stains were negative for fungal and acid-fast organisms, and aerobic and anaerobic cultures remained negative.

A 20‐year‐old Hispanic man with no past medical history presented with 4 weeks of generalized weakness, 3 weeks of progressive cough productive of yellow sputum, and persistent shortness of breath; he also reported intermittent fever and chills for the preceding 3–5 days. He denied smoking, alcohol use, and illicit drugs. He was monogamous, with two lifetime sexual partners, and had not traveled outside the United States in 12 years. On examination, he appeared cachectic and tachypneic, with bilateral diffuse crackles and rhonchi. Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits. Chest CT revealed diffuse tree‐in‐bud nodularity, bronchiectasis, thick‐walled cavities in the upper lobes, and a moderate right pleural effusion. An HIV rapid ELISA was reactive. Acid‐fast bacilli were seen on sputum smear, and he was started on combination anti-tuberculosis therapy. Over the next 3 days, his symptoms improved. HIV Western blot was negative, and HIV viral load was undetectable. His CD4+ T-cell count was 124 cells/mm3, CD8+ T-cell count was 185 cells/mm3 (CD4:CD8 ratio, 0.7). Further workup, including immunoglobulin A, immunoglobulin G, and immunoglobulin M levels, urine protein electrophoresis, and serum protein electrophoresis, was unremarkable.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of a painful ulcerative lesion on the left lateral tongue. Initially the lesion was the size of a sorghum grain and ulcerated after 2 weeks; it subsequently enlarged steadily to about 2 cm. He had tried oral anti-inflammatory agents, topical sprays, and mouthwash without improvement. He reported no weight loss, chills, night sweats, or cough. His medical history was unremarkable; he had smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 30 years and consumed alcohol regularly.

On examination, there was a 2.0 cm round mass on the left tongue margin with a central ulcer, firm consistency, ill-defined borders, and tenderness. The tongue could be extended centrally without deviation. Palpable left submandibular lymph nodes measured up to 1.5 × 1.0 cm, were moderately mobile, and slightly tender.

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; three standard infectious disease screenings were negative. Chest CT revealed diffuse patchy and nodular opacities in both lungs with areas of coalescence, visible bronchograms, and punctate calcifications in the right upper lobe, suggesting pulmonary tuberculosis.

A 38-year-old man was referred for evaluation of reduced vision in his left eye that began shortly after dental treatment 5 days earlier. He had received local infiltration anesthesia (articaine with epinephrine 1:100,000) near the upper left canine, with negative aspiration, and shortly thereafter experienced a headache and gradual visual decline. He noted occasional flashing stars in the left visual field but no nausea or phonophobia. His medical history was unremarkable; he had undergone similar anesthesia on the right side without complication and had no prior ophthalmic problems.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OS and 20/20 OD. Intraocular pressure was 11 mm Hg bilaterally. A relative afferent pupillary defect was present on the left. Ocular motility was normal. Color-plate testing was slightly abnormal OS. Automated perimetry revealed a relative paracentral scotoma in the left eye; the right visual field was full.

Fundoscopy of the left eye showed optic disc swelling, cotton wool spots, and hard exudates in the papillomacular bundle; the right eye was normal. Optical coherence tomography angiography demonstrated hypoperfusion in both the superficial and deep retinal capillary plexuses in the affected region. There was no history or signs of cardiovascular disease or embolic sources. Initial laboratory studies, including complete blood count, C-reactive protein, glucose, liver function tests, cholesterol, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were within normal limits.

A 59-year-old man was referred for a 3-day history of painless visual loss in the right eye. He also reported 3 months of asthenia and occasional vomiting. He had a 45 pack-year smoking history and otherwise no relevant medical history.  
On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/63 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. A subtle right relative afferent pupillary defect was present. Visual field testing showed a severe diffuse defect in the right eye; the left visual field was normal. Slit-lamp examination revealed only an edematous right optic disc. Neurologic examination demonstrated diminished reflexes and mild gait instability, prompting hospital admission.

Laboratory studies showed normal C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Serologic tests for Treponema pallidum, HIV, hepatitis B and C viruses, Borrelia burgdorferi, Bartonella henselae, Coxiella burnetti, and Toxoplasma gondii were negative. CMV, EBV, and VZV serologies were IgG-positive but IgM-negative. QuantiFERON-TB Gold and blood cultures were negative. Visual evoked potentials revealed increased latency in the right eye. MRI of the brain and orbits was unremarkable. The patient was discharged without a definitive diagnosis.

On follow-up, visual acuity worsened to hand motion in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. A right afferent pupillary defect persisted, and bilateral optic disc edema was noted. Neurologic signs progressed to instability and dysmetria of all limbs, confirmed by sensory evoked potentials and electromyography. He was readmitted. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 170 mm H₂O, protein 137.5 mg/dL, 94% lymphocytes, and negative cytology and cultures. A chest radiograph was abnormal, and thoracic CT revealed mixed emphysema with a right hilar adenopathy of malignant appearance.

While awaiting PET-CT, visual acuity declined to 20/40 in the left eye. Slit-lamp exam showed no anterior chamber cells or flare. Fundoscopy revealed vitreous haze (RE +3, LE +2) and creamy-yellow deep retinal lesions: a perifoveal circular pattern in the right eye and a placoid parafoveal lesion in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated papillitis and peripapillary phlebitis. SD-OCT of the right eye showed severe disorganization of outer retinal layers with focal granular hyperreflectivity in Henle’s fiber layer and outer nuclear layer coalescing into wedge-shaped and band-like lesions at the fovea; the RPE and ellipsoid segment layers were granular, with atrophy and a hyperreflective deposit at the fovea. Vitreous hyperreflective dots were present. SD-OCT of the left eye showed vitreous hyperreflective dots and a single hyperreflective tangential band at the fovea with granular disorganization of outer retinal layers.

A 33-year-old Caucasian man presented with sudden onset of severe pleuritic chest pain and haemoptysis. He reported progressive dyspnoea and malaise for one month, unresponsive to three courses of antibiotics prescribed for a presumed chest infection. His medical history was notable only for a pyloromyotomy in infancy; he had an 18 pack-year smoking history and no other cardiovascular risk factors or drug use.

On examination, heart rate was 120 bpm, respiratory rate 36 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 90% on room air, and blood pressure was normal. The physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, troponin-I <0.04 ng/mL, creatine kinase 17 U/L, and D-dimer 800 ng/mL. Electrocardiogram demonstrated right ventricular strain. Chest radiograph revealed ill-defined patchy shadowing in the left mid-zone.

Given the clinical history, raised D-dimer, and ECG findings, a computed tomography pulmonary angiogram was performed, showing bilateral pulmonary emboli with parenchymal infarction in the left upper and lower lobes. A mass was also noted in the right ventricle, thought to represent either thrombus or tumor. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a mass attached to the base of the lateral wall of a mildly dilated right ventricle with preserved systolic function; features were suggestive of a thrombus. The patient was started on intravenous heparin; thrombolysis was considered but withheld due to stability and concerns about thrombus fragmentation.

After one week, repeat echocardiography showed no change in the mass. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was then performed, revealing a hypokinetic inferior wall of the right ventricle, a mildly reduced right ventricular ejection fraction, and a mural thrombus attached to the inferior wall. There was evidence of recent subendocardial infarction of the right ventricle.

A 43-year-old man with no significant medical history was found unconscious outdoors after an evening of heavy alcohol consumption. Emergency Medical Services performed CPR and intubated him on scene because of decreased respiratory effort and a low Glasgow Coma Scale score. On arrival at the hospital he remained mechanically ventilated, unresponsive, and hemodynamically stable.

Initial noncontrast head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormality. Echocardiography was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed normal cell counts without xanthochromia. Electroencephalography demonstrated paroxysmal epileptiform activity, and repeat studies documented ongoing epileptiform discharges despite anticonvulsant therapy.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain on hospital day 1, including T2, FLAIR, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) sequences, showed no abnormalities.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, electrolytes (sodium 144 mmol/L), renal function, and C-reactive protein level, were noncontributory. Arterial lactate was 1.7 mmol/L and pH was 7.35. Liver tests were mildly elevated (ALT 153 IU/L, AST 122 IU/L, GGT 305 IU/L). Viral hepatitis serologies were negative. Troponin was 0.31 μg/mL without ECG evidence of myocardial infarction. Toxicology screening revealed a blood alcohol level of 48.8 mmol/L and benzodiazepines; opiates and amphetamines were negative.

On hospital day 6, repeat MRI of the brain demonstrated new areas of increased signal on DWI with corresponding low signal on ADC mapping, symmetrically involving the white matter of the centrum semiovale and posterior parietal regions. Conventional T2 and FLAIR sequences remained normal.

A 45-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus presented with palpitations and shortness of breath for 2 weeks. Her history included rheumatic mitral valve disease treated with mechanical mitral valve replacement and tricuspid annuloplasty 6 years earlier, and a transient ischaemic attack 2 weeks ago. Current medications were hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day (cumulative dose 2774 g), warfarin, prednisone, amiodarone, colchicine, and azathioprine. 

On examination, prosthetic valve sounds were normal and bilateral lung crackles were present. A chest radiograph showed pulmonary congestion.
