Laboratory tests revealed an N-terminal pro–brain natriuretic peptide peak of 16 040 pg/mL, high-sensitivity troponin I 597 ng/L (ULN < 54 ng/L), INR 2.7, and C-reactive protein 4.9 mg/L (ULN < 5.0 mg/L); biomarkers of lupus activity were normal. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and right bundle branch block. She was diagnosed with acute heart failure and received high-dose furosemide.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed severe concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, mildly reduced LVEF at 51% with global hypokinesia, and severe right ventricular hypertrophy with systolic dysfunction. Two years earlier, she had only mild LV hypertrophy and normal systolic function.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging on a 3 T scanner revealed a non-dilated LV with concentric hypertrophy (mass 81 g/m2, septum 16 mm), LVEF 46%, global hypokinesia, a non-dilated RV with marked hypertrophy and RVEF 38%, no valvular insufficiency or pericardial effusion, significantly elevated native T1 times (max 1332 ms; ULN 1212 ms), uniformly elevated T2 values (42–43 ms; ULN 40 ms), extensive mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement in basal and lateral LV segments with nodular apical foci, diffuse RV enhancement, and an extracellular volume of 33%.

These CMR findings suggested myocardial inflammation but did not allow differentiation between lupus myocarditis and hydroxychloroquine-induced injury.

A 4-month-old female infant was brought for evaluation of an upper-lip mass noted since birth. On examination, the lesion measured approximately 2×2 cm, was smooth, nonpulsatile, and mobile, occupied the midline and left upper lip with slight extension to the right, and caused deformation of the columella with superior displacement of the left alar. There was no respiratory distress. The mass did not transilluminate and did not change in size with crying. The remainder of the head, neck, and systemic examinations was unremarkable. Ultrasonography with color Doppler revealed a solid lesion without evidence of increased vascularity. Magnetic resonance imaging was planned to assess for an intracranial connection.

A 60-year-old woman with a history of treated pleural tuberculosis and no tobacco or other toxic exposures presented with progressive dyspnea. She was afebrile, had a performance status of 0, and reported no weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count and renal function, were within normal limits.  
A chest radiograph showed a peripheral, well-defined, rounded opacity in the right lung. Chest CT confirmed a solitary pulmonary nodule in the right middle lobe without spiculations or lymphadenopathy. Flexible bronchoscopy revealed no endobronchial lesions. Concerned about a possible malignancy, the team proceeded with a CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of the nodule.

An 8-year-old girl was seen for an upper respiratory infection (fever, cough, rhinorrhea, pharyngodynia). Her history included a prior admission for dehydration and fatigue. Her 14-year-old sister has uninvestigated primary amenorrhea and lack of secondary sexual characteristics. On examination, her weight was 28 kg (69th percentile), height 130 cm (62nd percentile), and blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg (>99th percentile). Tanner staging showed breast bud (stage I) and no pubic hair (stage I); external genitalia appeared normally female.

Laboratory studies revealed sodium 142.8 mmol/L, potassium 2.6 mmol/L, arterial blood gas pH 7.49, PaCO₂ 22 mm Hg, PaO₂ 96 mm Hg. Hormonal assays showed morning cortisol 3.09 µg/dL (normal 6.2–19.4), ACTH 198.3 pg/mL (normal 5–60), standing aldosterone 335.9 pg/mL (normal supine 10–160, standing 35–300), erect plasma renin activity 0.61 ng/mL/h (normal erect 0.98–4.18), FSH 31.65 mIU/mL (normal 0.3–11), normal thyroid function, 24-h urine metanephrine 0.79 µg/24 h (normal ≤1), DHEA-S 2.47 µg/dL (normal females 6–9 y 13–114), 17-OH progesterone 0.411 ng/mL (normal prepubertal 0.07–1.53). 

Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound showed no ovarian or uterine structures. Renal artery Doppler was normal bilaterally. Chromosome analysis revealed a 46,XY karyotype.

A 75‐year‐old man presented with a 3-month history of vague upper abdominal discomfort described as a stretching sensation and a palpable intra-abdominal mass that he estimated to be the size of his fist and growing over the last 2 months. On examination, there was a mobile, smooth 6 × 7 × 5 cm mass above the umbilicus that was slightly tender on deep palpation. Routine blood tests, including hepatic and renal function, were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a heterogeneous soft-tissue mesenteric mass with calcifications at the root of the mesentery, encasing the superior mesenteric vessels, associated mesenteric fibrosis with tethering of small-bowel loops, and small mesenteric lymph nodes. The radiologist reported a high suspicion of a bowel carcinoid tumor, with fibrosing mesenteritis as an alternative, and a diagnostic laparoscopy was planned.

A 52-year-old perimenopausal multiparous woman (G4P4) presented with a 4-hour history of “something coming out of her vagina” after lifting a light weight, accompanied by lower abdominal pain. Her last menstrual period was 18 days ago; cycles had become irregular and lengthened over the past 1.5 years, and a Pap smear 4 months earlier was negative for intraepithelial lesions or malignancy. She had no urinary or bowel symptoms, chronic cough, constipation, prior cervical surgery, or family history of malignancy. On examination, vital signs were normal, the abdomen was soft and nontender, and pelvic examination showed second-degree cervical prolapse with a firm-to-soft, slightly reducible mass protruding through the introitus. The uterus was mobile, parous in size, firm, and mildly tender; fornices were free. Serum CA-125, CA 19-9, and CEA levels were within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a 9.5 cm × 8.0 cm multicystic mass arising from the posterior lip of the cervix and protruding into the vaginal canal. The preliminary differential diagnosis was nabothian cyst versus cervical leiomyoma with multicystic degeneration causing uterine prolapse.

An 18-month-old girl was referred with a three-day history of worsening stridor and difficulty breathing. Over the preceding week, she had low-grade fever and mild flu-like symptoms, along with progressive difficulty swallowing and drooling of saliva. There was no history of trauma, foreign-body ingestion, anticoagulation use, bleeding from any orifice, or known allergies. She had received antibiotics, steroids, and paracetamol with minimal improvement. On examination, she was afebrile, well-nourished, and in moderate respiratory distress with inspiratory stridor; oxygen saturations were 92–95%. She preferred sitting, had minimal neck movement, and a soft, non-tender, fluctuant swelling (3×3×4 cm) in the left level II neck. There were no palpable lymph nodes. Oropharyngeal examination revealed a normal tongue, non-erythematous grade 1 tonsils, and a prominent posterior pharyngeal bulge. Flexible laryngoscopy showed a large posterior bulge obscuring the vocal cords, though the epiglottis tip was visible. Chest examination was normal, and there were no stigmata of bleeding. A working diagnosis of retropharyngeal abscess with parapharyngeal extension was made. A lateral neck radiograph demonstrated thickening of the retropharyngeal soft tissues from the skull base to the hypopharynx. The institutional CT scanner was not functional. A COVID-19 antigen test was negative. Complete blood count values were within normal limits (hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, WBC 9.5×10^3/mL, platelets 446×10^3/mL).

A 59-year-old man with chronic back pain presented with a 5-day history of central chest pain and several weeks of malaise, dry cough, and breathlessness. He was pale and clammy, with a blood pressure of 147/76 mm Hg, heart rate 59 b.p.m., oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and no fever. Cardiac examination revealed a regular rhythm and normal heart sounds, and lung auscultation was normal.  
Electrocardiogram showed complete atrioventricular block with inferior Q-waves and a ventricular rate of 58 b.p.m. He had transient loss of consciousness with hypotension, and telemetry confirmed intermittent long pauses due to atrioventricular block.  
Coronary angiography showed atheromatous changes but no obstructive lesions. A temporary transvenous pacemaker was inserted via the right femoral vein and programmed to VVI 60. Prophylactic cloxacillin was started.  
Troponin-T was 17 ng/L on admission (ULN < 15 ng/L) and peaked at 49 ng/L; CK-MB and myoglobin were normal. BNP peaked at 1078 ng/L (ULN < 100 ng/L). Renal function and inflammatory markers were normal.  
Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a moderately dilated left ventricle (EF 30%) and mildly reduced right ventricular function. He developed left heart failure requiring intravenous loop diuretics, a 48-hour infusion of levosimendan, and low-dose noradrenaline. His underlying rhythm remained complete atrioventricular block.  
With a working differential of myocardial infarction, systemic inflammatory disease, and myocarditis, cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging was indicated but initially contraindicated by the temporary pacing system.  
On hospital day 1, an active‐fixation right ventricular lead (Medtronic CapSureFix Novus MRI-conditional 4076-58 cm) was placed via the right subclavian vein and connected to an external MRI-conditional pulse generator. The lead and generator were secured to the skin, and sensing, impedance, and pacing thresholds were adequate.

A 37-year-old woman with two prior lower-segment cesarean deliveries presented with an absence of menstrual periods for 3 years. She reported cyclical episodes of gross hematuria coinciding with her expected menses and associated breast tenderness, but she had no vaginal bleeding or watery vaginal discharge at any time. Three years earlier, during her second cesarean section, she sustained a bladder injury that was repaired at that time. Her medical and family histories were otherwise unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were normal, and the physical and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a normal-sized retroflexed uterus with homogeneous myometrium, an endometrial thickness of 11 mm without intrauterine fluid, and normal bilateral ovaries. A tubular hyperechoic tract, measuring 8 mm in diameter, was seen between the posterior bladder wall and the lower uterine segment. A hysterosalpingogram demonstrated uniform filling of contrast material in the bladder and no opacification of the uterine cavity or fallopian tubes.

A 27-year-old woman with adult-onset Still’s disease, maintained on chronic prednisone and recently started on anakinra, presented with palpitations, tachycardia and hemoptysis. One week earlier she had been hospitalized for arthralgia and cough attributed to a disease flare; arthralgia resolved at home, but she developed worsening bilateral leg swelling over the week.  

On arrival she was drowsy and anxious. Temperature was 38.8 °C, blood pressure 170/110 mm Hg, pulse 160 beats/min, and respiratory rate 40 breaths/min. Jugular venous pressure was elevated; she had severe peripheral edema and bilateral crackles. Cardiac and abdominal examinations were normal.  

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, leukocytes 9.9 × 10^3/μL, creatinine 92 μmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 13.8 mmol/L, albumin 26 g/L, C-reactive protein 46 mg/L, antinuclear antibodies 1:160, anti–native DNA 92 IE/mL, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies 1:160, complement C3 0.32 g/L, C4 0.07 g/L, and elevated free κ- and λ-light chains. Serologies for HIV and hepatitis B and C were negative.  

Legionella pneumophila was identified by sputum PCR and urine antigen assay. Chest radiograph showed a right upper-lobe infiltrate and small pleural effusion. She was started on levofloxacin, and her respiratory status improved over two days.  

Despite this, her leg edema worsened; her weight increased from 63.4 to 68.4 kg, creatinine rose to 121 μmol/L, and albumin fell to 18 g/L. Repeat urinalysis revealed dysmorphic erythrocytes, hyaline and granular casts, proteinuria of 6.76 g per 24 h, and albuminuria of 3112.4 μg/min.

A Japanese boy, born at 38 weeks to nonconsanguineous parents without a family history of renal disease, was noted in early infancy to have renal dysfunction and polyuria with a urinary concentration defect. Ultrasonography and MRI showed multiple renal cysts of various sizes, several small liver cysts, and dilated bile ducts; the kidneys were normal in size. By 3 months of age, he had three episodes of bacterial cholangitis but no hypertension. At 15 months, he was admitted for chronic renal failure. On exam his height was 67.4 cm (–4.1 SD), weight 7.16 kg (–2.9 SD). Laboratory studies showed a serum creatinine level of 0.68 mg/dL, 24-h creatinine clearance of 40.9 mL/min/1.73 m2, no hematuria, proteinuria of 240 mg/day (spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, 1–2 g/gCr), and urine β2-microglobulin 14 468 μg/L. He received ursodeoxycholic acid and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis; after admission he had one further cholangitis episode. At 2 years of age, MRI again demonstrated bilateral multiple renal cysts extending from the cortical surface to the medulla in normal-sized kidneys. Over the next several years, his renal dysfunction slowly progressed, and his spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio rose to 5–6 g/gCr without hypoalbuminemia.

A 4-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of intermittent, colicky abdominal pain associated with crying episodes and significant discomfort. She had no prior medical problems. On examination, she had tenderness on superficial palpation of the right hypochondrium without fever, jaundice, or pruritus. Laboratory tests showed normal liver function studies and a white-cell count of 11 000/μL. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a gallbladder divided by multiple fine septations with evidence of sludge but no gallstones or pericholecystic fluid. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen confirmed a gallbladder with multiple internal septa and showed no biliary or pancreatic anomalies.

A 9-year-old Chinese girl presented with a one-month history of recurrent fevers (38–39 °C) and cough. She had been treated for presumed upper respiratory infection without improvement. Over the last 4 days, her caregivers noted a palpable mass in the right upper abdomen and right lower chest. There was no significant past medical history or known exposures.

On examination, she was febrile and appeared pale. A large tender mass involved the right lower chest and right upper abdomen. Breath sounds were diminished on the right side.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 24.5 × 10^9/L (82% neutrophils), hemoglobin 70 g/L, hematocrit 24.6%, CRP 177 mg/L, normal liver enzymes, and albumin 29.6 g/L. Tumor markers revealed CA-125 45.5 U/mL; other markers, including CEA, CA-199, AFP, were within normal limits. Stool microscopy was negative for amoebae. Serologies for hepatitis A–E and HIV were negative.

Chest CT demonstrated a patchy, ill-defined area of uneven density in the right lower lung, pleural thickening, and soft-tissue swelling of the chest wall. Abdominal CT with contrast revealed a 5.2 × 7.2 × 5.5 cm hypodense, nonhomogeneous lesion in the right hepatic lobe with central arterial enhancement and a surrounding low-density rim.

Because of imaging features suggesting invasion and the elevated CA-125 level, a bone marrow aspiration was performed to exclude malignancy; results were negative. An ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy of the hepatic lesion was obtained, and the patient began intravenous cefoperazone-sulbactam. Over the subsequent two weeks, her fever resolved, the abdominal mass became less tender, and both WBC count and CRP declined markedly.

A 69‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of macular degeneration. Her visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes, intraocular pressure was normal, and blood pressure was 132/72 mm Hg. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable. Funduscopic evaluation revealed intermediate drusen and pigment mottling in the macula of both eyes. During acquisition of spectral‐domain OCT images, dramatic choroidal pulsations in the macula of the right eye were noted on the B‐scan, corresponding to the patient’s heartbeat and dampening with gentle pressure on the eye. SD‐OCT revealed greater subfoveal choroidal thickness in the right eye during systole that thinned during diastole. Fluorescein angiography was unremarkable, while indocyanine green angiography revealed engorgement of the choroidal vasculature of the right eye. Investigational OCT angiography showed subtle tortuosity of the superficial vascular complex and engorgement of the deep vascular complex in the right eye compared to the left. B‐scan ultrasonography demonstrated subtle orbital pulsations of the right orbit without a detectable mass. The patient denied any history of trauma or orbital surgery. Magnetic resonance imaging, venography, and angiography of the orbits were unrevealing apart from slight enhancement of the right orbital soft tissue and symmetric, normal caliber of the superior ophthalmic veins.

A 69-year-old man presented four days after receiving his third dose of the Spikevax vaccine (mRNA-1273) with a 4-cm area of redness and swelling over the hypothenar eminence of his left hand, the same side as the injection. The swelling was painless, with only mild discomfort on pressure, and had a firm, rope-like consistency. He denied any trauma or repetitive pressure to the hand. Musculoskeletal ultrasound revealed a 30-mm thrombus in the arcuate branch of the ulnar artery. 

Vital signs were blood pressure 133/82 mm Hg, heart rate 70 beats/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air; BMI was 23.4 kg/m2. Examination showed normal distal perfusion and pulses, without signs of ischemia. His history was notable for hypothyroidism (post–thyroidectomy) and benign prostatic hyperplasia; medications included levothyroxine and tamsulosin. In September 2021, routine blood tests—including complete blood count, glucose, creatinine, liver enzymes, PSA, and TSH—were within normal limits. A lipid panel showed LDL cholesterol 109.8 mg/dL, total cholesterol 188 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol 50 mg/dL, and triglycerides 141 mg/dL. He was a lifelong nonsmoker and took no herbal or alternative remedies.

A 12-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, diagnosed over two years ago, presented with 3 days of blurred vision in his right eye. He is in the maintenance phase of therapy on oral methotrexate and mercaptopurine and has never undergone stem-cell transplantation. His most recent complete blood count showed a white-cell count of 3200/µL and a neutrophil count of 1600/µL. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination revealed a 3+ anterior chamber cellular reaction in the right eye and was normal in the left eye. Funduscopic examination of the right eye showed cream-colored lesions with hemorrhages and perivascular cuffing in the peripheral retina; the left fundus was normal.

A 33-year-old man with a history of massive small-bowel and ileocecal resection 12 years earlier (leaving 40 cm of small intestine) was maintained on a normal diet after bowel rehabilitation. One month before admission, he developed diarrhea and a 7-kg weight loss with progressive weakness, anorexia, dizziness, and cachexia. On admission his weight was 36 kg (BMI 12.2 kg/m^2), heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 70/50 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18 bpm. He was alert and oriented. Physical examination showed pitting edema of the lower extremities, thin skin, a scaphoid abdomen, and no ascites. Chest radiography revealed a dense nodule outside the right upper lung field (thought to be rib calcification). Lower-limb radiographs and renal ultrasonography were normal; gallbladder ultrasonography showed atrophy. ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with T-wave flattening/inversion in leads II, III, aVF, and V4–V6, and an incomplete right bundle-branch block. Initial laboratory values included: phosphate 1.10 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 144 mmol/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.60 mmol/L, calcium 1.7 mmol/L, albumin 27.7 g/L, prealbumin 100 mg/dL, hemoglobin 48 g/L, hematocrit 14.0%, BUN 5.0 mmol/L, and creatinine 86 mg/dL. He was diagnosed with severe malnutrition and received blood transfusion; parenteral nutrition (500 kcal/day); fluids; electrolyte, trace-element, and multivitamin supplementation (including daily thiamine 100 mg IV). Over 24 hours his strength and edema improved. Then he acutely developed profound fatigue and flaccid weakness of all four limbs. His heart rate was 98 bpm, respiratory rate was unchanged, and repeat labs showed a phosphate level of 0.05 mmol/L.

A 21-year-old Caucasian man with a 2-year history of biopsy-proven Goodpasture’s disease and end-stage renal failure on peritoneal dialysis was admitted after two generalized tonic–clonic seizures preceded by decreased alertness and slowed executive function. On arrival, he was somnolent and hypertensive (180/90 mmHg) when he had a third seizure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation for 3 days.  

Past treatment included three intermittent cycles of cyclophosphamide; maintenance immunosuppression had not been consistently continued. Peritoneal dialysis was ongoing, and there was no history of recent medication errors.  

On examination after extubation, he had mild cognitive slowing, memory deficits, and a left Babinski sign; otherwise the neurologic examination was normal.  

Laboratory studies showed creatinine 1107 μmol/L (normal 72–127), urea 16.4 mmol/L (3.0–9.2), and normal blood cell count, electrolytes, liver enzymes, and blood gas analysis. Chest radiography indicated aspiration pneumonia. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple T2- and FLAIR-hyperintense lesions in the subcortical posterior dorsal and lateral white matter and cerebellar white matter, without contrast enhancement; time-of-flight angiography showed normal vessel calibers without stenosis.  

Serum anti–glomerular basement membrane antibody titer was 200 U/mL (normal <10).

An 8-year-old girl presented with five days of worsening abdominal pain. She had no significant past medical history. Family history was notable for endometriosis in her mother, chronic myelogenous leukemia in her maternal grandfather, and heart disease in her paternal grandmother. On examination, her temperature was 38.9 °C, heart rate 142 beats/min, and she had abdominal distention with tenderness over the right hemi-abdomen. The pain began five days earlier without an inciting event and progressed from non-bilious, non-bloody emesis to bilious vomiting by day four, accompanied by subjective fevers. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14.4 × 10^9/L (rr 4–11.8), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 56 mm/h (rr 0–20), and C-reactive protein 13.6 mg/dL (rr 0–0.8). Tumor markers revealed CA-125 43.6 U/mL (rr 0–35), lactate dehydrogenase 75 U/L (rr 120–260), and normal human chorionic gonadotropin and alpha-fetoprotein. A comprehensive metabolic panel, uric acid, and lipase were within normal limits. Abdominal radiography demonstrated contrast opacification without evidence of bowel obstruction and dilatation of the left renal collecting system, likely from distal ureteral compression by an abdominal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 10.5 × 8.7 × 7 cm large cystic mass involving the entire abdomen, possibly of ovarian origin.

A 55-year-old man with hypertension had an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest while at rest watching television. He had no preceding symptoms or family history of sudden cardiac death. His wife began CPR immediately. Emergency responders found ventricular fibrillation, delivered two shocks, and achieved return of circulation; he was intubated and transferred to our centre. On arrival his physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed a potassium of 3.1 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.3), which was corrected, and troponin I levels of 573 and 303 ng/L (<21). Noncontrast head CT was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild left ventricular hypertrophy with normal systolic function, no regional wall motion abnormalities, and no pericardial or valvular pathology. His initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia, a QTc of 490 ms, 1 mm ST depression in leads II, III, aVF, and V6, and subtle, variable <0.5 mm ST‐elevation in lead aVR. One hour later, inferolateral ST changes and QTc prolongation had resolved, and new subtle down‐sloping 1 mm ST‐elevation appeared in lead V1. Coronary angiography demonstrated unobstructed coronary arteries but revealed an anomalous right coronary artery originating from the left coronary sinus. Cardiac MRI showed borderline left ventricular hypertrophy, normal systolic function, and no late gadolinium enhancement. CT coronary angiography confirmed the anomalous artery had an acute takeoff, an intramural segment, and an interarterial course. Exercise stress echocardiography produced no symptoms, ECG changes, arrhythmias, or regional wall motion abnormalities, and QT analysis was also normal.

A 63-year-old man with a history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes presented from eastern India with a one-month history of high-grade fevers with chills and rigors, unintentional weight loss, and anorexia. He denied cough, dyspnea, chest pain, abdominal pain, or diarrhea. On examination, he was pale and had moderate, non-tender splenomegaly; there were no other remarkable findings.

Laboratory studies revealed:
• Pancytopenia: hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, leukocytes 3,200 cells/µL, platelets 109,000/µL  
• Markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 90 mm/hr  
• Peripheral smear: normocytic, normochromic, no abnormal cells  
• Liver and renal function tests within normal limits  
• Glycemic control: fasting glucose 123 mg/dL, postprandial 189 mg/dL, HbA1c 7.4%

Chest radiograph was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed gross splenomegaly without focal lesions. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen confirmed isolated splenomegaly with no additional abnormalities. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Serologic tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative.

Given persistent fever, splenomegaly, and pancytopenia, visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-Azar) was suspected. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showed no Leishmania bodies and no abnormal cells apart from occasional hemophagocytes. An anti–K39 antibody test was negative. Markers for connective‐tissue disorders (ANA, ENA profile, c-ANCA, p-ANCA) were also negative. Empiric antifungal therapy was initiated for persistent fever despite broad-spectrum antibiotics.

A 17-year-old male high-school athlete presented with a one-year history of bilateral, symmetrical swelling of the second, third, and fourth proximal interphalangeal joints. He first noticed painless nodules three months before evaluation. He denied pain, redness, or limitation of his usual activities, including sports. Physical examination showed non-tender, symmetric swelling of the PIP joints with preserved active and passive range of motion. Laboratory evaluation, including serologic testing for inflammatory and connective-tissue diseases, was negative. Plain radiographs of both hands demonstrated soft-tissue swelling around the PIP joints with normal bone and joint architecture. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed no evidence of inflammation in the synovium, ligaments, tendons, or subcutaneous tissues and no osseous or soft-tissue mass.

A 51-year-old woman with no prior comorbidities presented with a 1-year history of persistent, left-sided, non-pleuritic chest pain and gradually progressive dyspnoea. Eight months earlier she had two syncopal episodes and was found to have complete heart block, for which a permanent pacemaker was implanted. She was also diagnosed with pericardial effusion and was treated empirically with anti-tuberculosis therapy for 8 months without improvement. 

On examination, she was afebrile; blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg without pulsus paradoxus; heart rate 78 beats/min; respiratory rate 18 breaths/min; oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiovascular examination revealed muffled heart sounds without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; other systems were unremarkable.

Chest radiography showed cardiomegaly with a pacemaker in situ. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large pericardial effusion (maximum 27 mm posteriorly), global left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction 41.3%), global hypokinesia, mild mitral regurgitation, and a “sparkling” appearance of the septal myocardium. 

Laboratory investigations revealed: haemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; WBC 5600/mm3; platelets 182,000/mm3; ESR 10 mm/h; CRP <3.16 mg/L; HIV, HBV, HCV serologies negative; TSH 4.6 μIU/mL; cortisol 9.1 μg%; sodium 136 mmol/L; potassium 4.1 mmol/L; creatinine 0.61 mg/dL; ANA and RF negative; ACE 7 U/L; pericardial fluid: WBC 310/mm3 (92% lymphocytes), protein 4.9 g/dL, glucose 88 mg/dL, ADA 5 U/L, no malignant cells.

Contrast CT of the thorax and abdomen confirmed cardiomegaly and pericardial effusion without other abnormalities. Autoimmune workup and serum ACE levels were normal. 

Differential diagnoses considered included infections (tuberculosis, post-viral), connective tissue disorders (systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma), infiltrative disorders (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, histiocytic diseases), malignancy (primary or secondary pericardial involvement), and IgG4-related disease.

A 72-year-old Asian woman presented with a 1-day history of abdominal pain, vomiting, and acute onset of respiratory distress. She had a history of hypertension and asthma, managed with inhalers for the past 5 years, and bilateral knee replacements for osteoarthritis. She reported no history of chest or abdominal trauma, abdominal surgery, or similar prior complaints. On examination, she was alert and oriented; heart rate 106 beats/min, blood pressure 160/94 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min. Abdominal examination revealed distension with mild epigastric tenderness and hypoactive bowel sounds; digital rectal examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph demonstrated bowel shadows beneath the right hemidiaphragm, suggestive of Chilaiditi syndrome. An abdominal radiograph showed multiple dilated small-bowel loops and absence of air in the rectum. Baseline laboratory studies were notable for a blood urea nitrogen level of 8 mg/dL and creatinine 0.7 mg/dL.

A 33-year-old previously healthy woman presented to ophthalmology 42 days after an uneventful vaginal delivery. On postpartum day 3 she developed mastitis treated with cabergoline, then fever unresponsive to oral cefixime. By day 15, laboratory studies revealed an elevated neutrophil percentage and CRP; chest radiograph, urine exam, and CBC were otherwise unremarkable. She received intramuscular gentamycin for 7 days. On day 36 she noted floaters and decreased vision in both eyes. Work-up showed toxoplasma IgG positive and IgM negative; chest radiograph normal; angiotensin-converting enzyme normal; HLA-B27 negative; HLA-B5 positive; and ANA 1:400. 

At presentation on day 42, visual acuity was 20/150 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were low bilaterally. Slit-lamp examination revealed keratic precipitates and anterior chamber inflammation in both eyes (1+ cells OD; 2+ cells OS), trace flare OD and 1+ flare OS, posterior synechiae OS, and vitritis with haze OU. Fundus examination showed foveal exudates OD and optic nerve exudates OS.

A 68-year-old Chinese woman was admitted with severe, persistent, colicky abdominal pain of 6 hours’ duration that began after physical labor. She adopted a knee–chest position for relief. She reported significant weight loss over the preceding 12 months. Her only surgical history was a left inguinal hernia repair 11 years earlier. On examination, she had tenderness in the lower abdomen without marked muscular rigidity.  
Abdominal CT showed a whirl sign consistent with mesenteric volvulus and small-bowel obstruction, with mesenteric edema, twisting of the mesenteric vessels around the superior mesenteric artery and vein, ascites, and decreased enhancement of the intestinal wall suggestive of exudation and necrosis. A mixed-density mass with high-density calcification was noted in the right mesentery, raising concern for a mesenteric tumor.  
Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 19.9×10^9/L with 86.7% neutrophils, hemoglobin 130 g/L, lactate 1.7 mmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 236.4 U/L, creatine kinase 77.5 U/L, carcinoembryonic antigen 0.89 ng/mL, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 6.2 U/mL.

A 17-year-old male presented with a 2-day history of nausea and right lower quadrant abdominal pain. He denied fever, vomiting, dehydration, or anorexia. He had a similar self-limited episode of pain 3 weeks earlier. His diet was high in carbohydrates (75–80% of intake). He had no other medical history except childhood treatment for a hearing problem; his mother has diabetes mellitus.  
On examination, his vital signs were normal and findings were consistent with acute appendicitis. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 14.9×10^3/µL (reference 4–10), neutrophils 74% (50–70), lymphocytes 17.8% (20–40), C-reactive protein 148.6 mg/L (0–5), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 99 mm/hr (0–20). Other blood counts and chemistries were normal.  
Abdominal ultrasonography did not visualize the appendix separately but identified a 40×35 mm septated abscess in the right lower quadrant with surrounding mesenteric and intestinal inflammation, suggesting a retrocecal location.  
Emergency laparoscopy revealed an appendix firmly adherent to the cecum cranially, without omental wrapping. The borders between appendix and cecum were distinguishable. The appendix appeared inflamed but lacked the typical hyperemia and increased vascularity of acute bacterial appendicitis. The surrounding fluid resembled lymphatic extravasation, and the appendix measured 1.5–2 cm in thickness without a discrete phlegmon. Difficulty in mobilization prompted conversion to laparotomy.  
At open surgery, the appendix showed intense fibrotic adhesions to the cecum and was excised with difficulty. The ileum, cecum, and ascending colon appeared normal. A Penrose drain was placed, and the patient was discharged after 1 week of broad-spectrum antibiotics with an uneventful recovery.

A 59-year-old Southeast Asian man with gastroesophageal reflux disease, hiatal hernia, and hyperlipidemia presented with a 4-week history of low-grade fevers, generalized weakness, anorexia, and a 5-kg weight loss. He then noted dark urine but denied abdominal pain, alcohol use, or significant medication history. Vital signs were notable only for a temperature of 37.8°C. Examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed elevated alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, amylase, and lipase. An ultrasound and contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 3 × 4 cm hypoechoic mass in the pancreatic head, dilatation of the common bile duct and pancreatic duct, and multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the porta hepatis, peripancreatic, and perigastric regions. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the pancreatic lesion showed reactive epithelial atypia without malignant cells, and cytology of a celiac lymph node revealed atypical cells with noncaseating granulomas.

A 49-year-old woman presented with low back pain radiating down her right leg following three weeks of intractable cough productive of green sputum. She denied chest pain, shortness of breath, fevers, neurologic symptoms, or urinary or bowel complaints. She had completed a course of oral cephalexin prescribed by her general practitioner. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension and chronic low back pain. She smoked 20 cigarettes per day (15 pack-year history). 

On examination, she was afebrile, with normal vital signs and no respiratory distress. Lung auscultation revealed bronchial breath sounds and coarse crepitations in the right mid- to lower zones. Her abdomen was soft and non-tender. Neurologic examination of the lower limbs was normal. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 19.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophilia. A chest radiograph demonstrated obscuration of the right heart border, consistent with right middle lobe consolidation. 

She was diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia and started on benzyl penicillin, doxycycline, and analgesics. On the second hospital day, she became presyncopal and hypotensive, reporting new epigastric and chest pain in addition to her back pain. She appeared pale; heart rate was 78 bpm and blood pressure 66/38 mmHg. Her chest and abdominal examinations remained unchanged. Her hemoglobin fell from 115 g/L to 77 g/L over three hours, and she was identified as being in haemorrhagic shock. 

An initial differential diagnosis included aortic dissection, rupture of an aortic aneurysm, haemorrhage from a peptic ulcer, sepsis secondary to pneumonia, and obstructive shock from pulmonary embolism. She received large-bore intravenous access, fluid resuscitation, and red-cell transfusion, and was given intravenous ceftriaxone. After surgical review, she remained haemodynamically responsive, and an urgent contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and abdomen was ordered.

A 42-year-old woman was evaluated for a slowly enlarging left parotid swelling of several months’ duration. She reported no pain, fever, or weight loss. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, 3-cm nodule in the left parotid region without overlying skin changes. An orthopantomogram was unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed peripheral eosinophilia and elevated serum IgE levels. An initial biopsy of the gland yielded only adipose tissue. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck demonstrated a well-circumscribed mass within the left parotid gland without obvious invasion of adjacent structures.

A 59-year-old man was evaluated for recurrent upper gastrointestinal bleeding leading to refractory iron-deficiency anemia. His father had died of gastrointestinal bleeding at age 63. On examination, there were multiple, round-to-oval, well-demarcated, brown-to-black macules on the lips, buccal mucosa, palms, and genitalia, as well as multiple small, pinpoint, reddish papules on the tongue and lower labial mucosa. He denied any other family members with similar cutaneous findings. From this constellation of signs, PTEN-hamartoma tumor syndrome (Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcalba syndrome) was initially suspected, and the differential diagnoses also included hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, capillary malformation–arteriovenous malformation syndrome, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and Bandler syndrome. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed an arteriovenous malformation of the duodenum.

A 10-month-old girl was brought with four episodes of bloody vomiting and melena. She also had fever and clinical dehydration.  
Her neonatal history included sepsis at 3 days of life treated with exchange transfusions via an umbilical catheter, meningitis, and bouts of abdominal distention requiring incubator care before switching to bottle feeding. Parents are consanguineous; there is no known family history of bleeding or clotting disorders.  
On examination, temperature was 39 °C; she had sunken eyes, mild jaundice, abdominal distention with a navel bulge, bilateral inguinal hernias, and a spleen palpable 4–5 cm below the left costal margin without hepatomegaly.  
Laboratory studies showed WBC 41 300/mm3, CRP 16.5 mg/l, platelets 37 × 10³/µl, hemoglobin 6.8 g/dl, albumin 2.7 g/dl, BUN 74 mg/dl, and potassium 3.1 mEq/l.  
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed multiple esophageal ulcers causing constriction, grade IV esophageal varices, and congestive gastritis.  
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated approximately 3 L of ascites, homogeneous splenomegaly, and absence of a visible portal vein in the hepatic hilum.  
Doppler ultrasonography showed prior splenic vein thrombosis, varices in the gastric antrum and splenic hilum, fibrosis, and impaired blood flow in the portal vein.

A 5-year-old boy born to second-degree consanguineous parents from Turkey was evaluated for mild muscle weakness. Pregnancy and development had been normal. Physical examination revealed predominantly proximal weakness with preserved deep tendon reflexes, no contractures, and a normal gait, though he had mild difficulty climbing stairs and running. Pulmonary function tests were normal. His serum creatine phosphokinase level was 9000–15000 U/L (normal <250 U/L), and electromyography showed myopathic changes. A muscle biopsy of the left gastrocnemius muscle was obtained for histopathologic examination, immunohistochemical analysis, and molecular genetic testing.

An 86-year-old woman with a history of right hip replacement was found by her granddaughter to have altered mental status after 2 days of feeling unwell. She had no known medication use, alcohol, smoking, or recreational drug history. There was no history of neurologic symptoms or prior similar episodes. In the emergency department, she was intubated for respiratory distress and altered mental status. Vital signs: temperature not documented, pulse 110 bpm, blood pressure 148/100 mm Hg, respiratory rate 32 per min, O₂ saturation 80% on 6 L by mask. Examination revealed dehydration, rapid shallow respirations with wheezing, mild pedal edema, and no trauma. 

Initial laboratory studies showed: WBC 6.5 × 10^3/µL; hemoglobin 3.2 g/dL; hematocrit 9.6%; MCV 127 fL; platelets 59 × 10^3/µL; reticulocyte count 7.5% (corrected 1.6%); LDH 7077 IU/L; haptoglobin 14 mg/dL. Electrolytes were normal. Arterial blood gas revealed severe metabolic acidosis (anion gap 29). BUN 34 mg/dL; creatinine 1.9 mg/dL; lactic acid 20.3 mmol/L. Coagulation studies: INR 2.48; PT 29 s; aPTT 24 s; fibrinogen 185 mg/dL; D-dimer 5170 ng/mL. Toxicology was negative. Chest radiograph showed mild cardiomegaly; CT scans of the head, abdomen, and chest (PE protocol) were negative.

She was admitted to the ICU, received intravenous antibiotics and three units of red blood cells, with rapid normalization of lactic acid, improvement in renal function and mental status, and extubation in 2 days. Fecal occult blood tests were negative. Iron studies were within normal limits. Peripheral blood smear demonstrated large red cells, hypersegmented neutrophils (6–7 lobes), 1% schistocytes, poikilocytes, and anisocytosis. Anemia work-up was noted to show a mixed picture of megaloblastic anemia and hemolytic anemia.

A 2-month-old boy presented with persistent jaundice since day 1 of life. At age 1 month, laboratory tests showed total bilirubin 202 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 86.4 µmol/L, ALT 33 U/L, AST 119 U/L, γ-GT 341 U/L, and total bile acids 73.1 µmol/L. On transfer at age 2 months, his temperature was 36.9 °C, pulse 135 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, and blood pressure 80/50 mmHg. Physical examination revealed scleral icterus and a liver edge palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin; the spleen was not palpable. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 145.6 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 118.3 µmol/L, indirect bilirubin 27.3 µmol/L, ALT 67 U/L, AST 148 U/L, and γ-GT 492 U/L. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated poor gallbladder filling, an irregular gallbladder wall, absence of the common bile duct, and multiple enlarged lymph nodes at the porta hepatis. 

Laparoscopic exploration and cholangiography revealed no visualization of the common hepatic duct or intrahepatic biliary radicles, and a Kasai portoenterostomy was performed. During the procedure, a 0.8 cm × 0.5 cm × 0.4 cm fibrous plaque was excised from the hepatic hilum. On hematoxylin and eosin staining, the plaque contained fibers, blood vessels, nerves, and scattered follicle-like structures filled with colloid and mixed lymphocytes.

A 46-year-old Indian man presented with a 5-month history of fever and weight loss, 2 months of multiple reddish papules, and 1 month of dry cough. He sold tea under a tree for 15 years and had chronic exposure to bird droppings. The fever was sudden in onset, high-grade, and unresponsive to chloroquine prescribed for presumed malaria. One month after fever onset, he noticed multiple 0.5–1 cm skin-colored to erythematous papules over the nape of his neck, then spreading to his face, oral mucosa, scalp, upper limbs, abdomen, back, and lower limbs. These papules coalesced into plaques with skin thickening, pus discharge, and crusting. He also had hoarseness of voice, nasal stuffiness, difficulty breathing, and dysphagia.

On examination, there was mild hepatomegaly and bilateral subcentimetric inguinal lymphadenopathy; no cervical or axillary lymph nodes were palpable. A chest radiograph showed no significant abnormality. HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C serologic tests were negative. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 10.5 mg/dL, a total leukocyte count of 15,500 mm^3 with reactive lymphocytosis on peripheral smear, platelet count 400,000/µL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 32 mm in the first hour, and C-reactive protein 150 mg/dL. Liver function tests showed serum bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, SGOT 90 IU/L, SGPT 39 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 197 IU/L. Renal function and electrolytes were within normal limits. Antinuclear antibody testing was negative. He had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or other significant medical or surgical conditions.

A 71-year-old man with a 10-year history of rheumatoid arthritis maintained on prednisolone (10 mg/day) and immunosuppressive agents developed stage IB large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the lung, treated by lobectomy in December 201X. In July 201X + 1, his cancer relapsed and he began cisplatin and etoposide chemotherapy in September 201X + 1. He was also receiving antituberculosis therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol).

Clinical Course A:
- Pegfilgrastim was administered on day 4 of chemotherapy.
- Day 9: grade 1 fever prompted initiation of meropenem.
- Day 14: grade 3 fever; maximum temperature 40.3 °C on day 20.
- C-reactive protein paralleled the fever; blood and urine cultures remained negative.
- Day 21: pyrazinamide was discontinued for suspected drug fever; fever resolved by day 28.

Clinical Course B:
- Second chemotherapy course administered in November 201X + 1 with pegfilgrastim on day 4.
- Day 10: grade 2 fever with remittent pattern; peak 39.2 °C on day 15.
- Contrast-enhanced CT on day 14 demonstrated wall thickening of the aorta and left subclavian artery with surrounding soft-tissue changes.
- No skin lesions or other organ symptoms.
- Blood tests were negative for MPO-ANCA, PR3-ANCA, and antinuclear antibody.

A woman in her 30s with no significant medical history presented with a 2-day history of a red “bump” and surrounding swelling on her back and a rash in her left axilla associated with an ipsilateral swollen lymph node. She was started on cephalexin for presumed cellulitis, but within 24 hours she noted progression to larger, warm, more painful bumps on her back with increased swelling, prompting presentation to the emergency department. She described weeping and crusting of the bumps with the worst pain in the center of a target-shaped lesion. 

She had gone hiking in the Northeastern United States a few days before symptom onset but denied seeing any ticks or exposure to poison ivy or other irritants. She reported mild cough, bilateral hip pain, and headache but no fever at home. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was a 2-cm soft, tender, mobile lymph node in the left anterior axillary fold. Skin examination revealed a large, circular, well-demarcated erythematous plaque on the back with a central cluster of herpetiform vesicles, bullae, and purple necrotic puncta, as well as scattered erythematous patches on the anterior chest and left lateral breast.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 25 mm/hr and a C-reactive protein level of 174 mg/L; the complete blood count was unremarkable. Bacterial wound cultures and blood cultures yielded no growth. Polymerase chain reactions for herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, and Ehrlichia/Anaplasma were negative. Giemsa-stained blood smears showed no evidence of malaria or babesiosis. Lyme disease serologic testing (IgM and IgG) was negative.

A 7-year-old boy with T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma was receiving induction chemotherapy with the MCP-841 protocol, including prednisolone, vincristine, and intrathecal methotrexate; L-asparaginase was discontinued after a hypersensitivity reaction to the first dose. On day 6 of induction, he had a generalized tonic–clonic seizure preceded by blurred vision and followed by altered sensorium. On examination his blood pressure was 130/100 mm Hg, and funduscopic examination revealed grade II hypertensive retinopathy. Laboratory studies showed a normal hemogram, biochemistry, and electrolytes. Workup for secondary hypertension—including cardiac echocardiography, abdominal ultrasonography, renal Doppler studies, and urinalysis—was unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral frontal and parietal hypodense areas suggestive of vasogenic edema. He was started on antihypertensive and antiepileptic therapy.

A 45-year-old South Asian woman presented with multiple generalized tonic–clonic seizures characterized by eye‐rolling, tongue biting, and frothing at the mouth. She had a history of bacterial meningitis at age 1, complicated by febrile seizures treated with carbamazepine for two years, after which she was seizure-free until five years ago when she had another brief course of carbamazepine. She remained well until the current episode. 

On examination, she was fully alert (GCS 15), with intact sensation. Motor strength was 4/5 in the right upper and lower limbs, which also showed mild atrophy and hyperreflexia. A right upper motor neuron facial palsy was present. Laboratory studies, including serum electrolytes, were within normal limits. Electroencephalography did not reveal any active seizure focus.

Brain MRI with 3D-TOF MRA demonstrated diffuse atrophy of the left cerebral hemisphere, including deep gray structures, with ex vacuo dilatation of the left lateral ventricle and widening of left sulci. There was unilateral calvarial thickening on the left, hypertrophy of the left frontal sinus and mastoid air cells, and elevation of the left petrous ridge. Atrophy of the left cerebral peduncle and pons was consistent with Wallerian degeneration; diffusion‐weighted and FLAIR sequences showed no abnormal signals. Crossed cerebellar diaschisis was noted in the right cerebellar hemisphere. Magnetic resonance angiography showed normal cerebral vessels.

A 35-year-old Chinese woman noted an asymptomatic black, threadlike line on her left lower abdomen 3 years ago. Three days before presentation, she observed that the lesion had advanced toward her iliac crest and lay very superficially; attempts at self-removal had failed. On examination, there was a fine, very superficial, black line about 6.5 cm in length visible through the skin, with no surrounding erythema, although a small area of broken epidermis was present from prior self-manipulation. Dermoscopic inspection revealed a straight black line and a Z-shaped angle in the middle of the lesion, without any inflammatory signs.

A 66-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a right pararectal mass that had been incidentally noted 14 years earlier and was followed with serial CT scans. The lesion grew from 19 mm to 34 mm and appeared hypervascular on the most recent CT. She was asymptomatic until recently developing mild right groin pain. Her medical history was notable only for a dysplastic rectal polyp resected 2 years earlier; there was no history of malignancy. 

On examination, vital signs were normal, and the physical exam was unremarkable. A right extraluminal mass was barely palpable on digital rectal examination. A recent 18F-FDG PET scan showed no hypermetabolic activity in the mass. Initial imaging led to the suspicion of a gastrointestinal stromal tumor or a neuroendocrine tumor. A Gallium-68 Dotatate PET scan demonstrated high somatostatin receptor expression. Pelvic MRI revealed an isodense, slightly heterogeneous lesion on T1-weighted images, with persistent T2 hyperintensity and restricted diffusion, infiltrating the right lateral mesorectum without direct contact with the rectal wall. Colonoscopy showed no endoluminal lesion. Two ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspirations were inconclusive and complicated by osteodiscitis. Finally, a transgluteal CT-guided biopsy revealed the presence of thyroid tissue. 

Listed diagnostic considerations at that point included teratoma, tailgut cyst, or, less likely, thyroid carcinoma.

A 78-year-old woman with hypertension presented with a 6-day history of insidious colicky right lower abdominal pain and 5 days of recurrent nonprojectile bilious vomiting. She had not opened her bowels for 5 days and noted progressive abdominal distension and anorexia but denied weight loss or jaundice. She reported a recent high intake of vegetables. On examination, her respiratory rate was 28/min, pulse 100/min, blood pressure 157/100 mmHg, and SpO₂ 98% on room air. The chest was clear. The abdomen was distended with right lower quadrant tenderness without guarding or rebound; bowel sounds were hyperactive. Rectal examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts and renal function, with a serum potassium of 3.0 mmol/L. Abdominal CT scan revealed grossly dilated edematous small bowel loops and stomach with fluid distension.

A previously healthy 9-year-old boy presented with 2 days of left-sided groin and thigh pain, inability to bear weight, and general malaise that began after a rugby match. There was no history of trauma or recent infection. On examination, his temperature was 38.6°C. He had a limp on weight-bearing, tenderness in the groin, and signs of an irritable hip, but the overlying skin was neither warm nor erythematous. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16.5×10^9/L (neutrophils 14.3×10^9/L) and a C-reactive protein level of 97 mg/L; other tests were unremarkable. Blood cultures grew Gram-positive cocci later identified as methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Pelvic and lumbar-spine radiographs were unremarkable. Ultrasound of the left hip demonstrated free fluid in the pelvis and a small hip-joint effusion. A presumptive diagnosis of septic arthritis of the hip was made, and before proceeding to surgical washout, an MRI without sedation was organized to confirm the diagnosis.

A 30-year-old primigravida was referred at 37 weeks’ gestation for evaluation of a fetal scrotal mass detected on ultrasound. Prior scans at 12, 21, and 30 weeks were unremarkable. Fetal biometry and amniotic fluid were normal. Sonographic examination of the scrotum revealed on the right side a 50 × 46 mm echogenic mass with mixed echostructure, regular walls, and a few small echo-free cystic areas; the left side showed a simple hydrocele. No intestinal peristalsis was observed within the mass, and there was no evidence of bowel obstruction or meconium peritonitis. Color Doppler demonstrated regular vessels in the testicular sac. A pediatric surgeon was consulted and recommended postnatal clinical evaluation with emergency surgery if complications arose.

A male infant, birth weight 4.4 kg, was delivered at 39 5/7 weeks to a 25-year-old G2P0 mother complicated by shoulder dystocia requiring forceps assistance. Thick meconium was noted at delivery. At birth, the infant had hypotonia, heart rate <50 bpm, and required positive‐pressure ventilation; APGAR scores were 1, 6, and 8 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes. He was intubated within 15 minutes for poor respiratory effort, then extubated on day one but remained hypoxic and tachypneic, initially attributed to meconium aspiration. He also held his left arm in adduction and internal rotation with weakness in wrist and finger extension, consistent with Erb’s palsy; the right arm was normal. Over the next three weeks, left arm strength improved with therapy, but he continued to require high‐flow nasal cannula oxygen. Serial chest radiographs showed progressive clearing of lung fields but persistent elevation of the right hemidiaphragm. Diaphragm ultrasonography demonstrated decreased motion of the right hemidiaphragm with normal left hemidiaphragm excursion. Thoracic MRI was performed to evaluate for soft-tissue injury or intrathoracic mass compressing cervical nerve roots or the phrenic nerve but was unremarkable except for findings related to his known left brachial plexopathy.

A 58-year-old obese woman was brought to the emergency department with a 2–3-day history of abdominal pain, fever, decreased oral intake, and oliguria. She had a history of hypertension managed with medication. On arrival she was confused, tachypneic, and tachycardic. Several minutes later, she developed pulseless electrical activity and underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation according to ACLS protocols. Peripheral vascular access was difficult despite multiple attempts; resuscitation included adrenaline, endotracheal intubation, and chest compressions.  

Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, an elevated C-reactive protein level, and marked hyperglycemia in a patient without a prior diagnosis of diabetes. A working diagnosis of septic shock was made, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were started and then tailored to culture sensitivities. A femoral arterial line was placed for monitoring and infusions. She required invasive mechanical ventilation and was admitted to the intensive care unit.  

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed an impacted proximal right ureteric stone with hydronephrosis; there was also bilateral basal lung consolidation. Urology placed a JJ stent and drained pus, confirming urosepsis as the source of shock. Her urine output improved, but she remained febrile with a declining yet persistently elevated leukocyte count and CRP. On hospital day 6 she was awake, extubated, and was transferred out of the ICU.  

Shortly after transfer, she again developed high-grade fevers and persistent leukocytosis and CRP elevation. She began to complain of left shoulder pain and left upper-limb weakness. Examination suggested mild shoulder effusion, and arthrocentesis yielded turbid, blood-stained fluid. Plain radiographs of the shoulder were notable only for degenerative changes. MRI of the left shoulder demonstrated a large joint effusion with surrounding soft-tissue edema, bone marrow edema, and gas formation in the proximal humerus. MRI suggested the differential diagnoses of septic arthritis with proximal humerus osteomyelitis, gas gangrene, and sequelae of proximal humeral intraosseous line.

A 33-year-old woman from Cuba, living in Italy for 10 years, was admitted with a one-month history of fever up to 40°C and maculopapular lesions on the face and trunk. Four months earlier, she had spent one month in Cuba. She had no known past medical history but reported prior unprotected sexual encounters. On admission, HIV serology was positive; HIV-RNA was 2,150,000 copies/mL, CD4+ count was 2 cells/μL (1%), and the CD4+/CD8+ ratio was zero. Empirical piperacillin–tazobactam was started.  
Chest CT revealed ground-glass opacities in the lung parenchyma, multiple bilateral micronodules, and mediastinal, supraclavicular, and lateral cervical lymphadenopathy. She was transferred for presumed Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.  
On examination, temperature was 40°C, heart rate 113 bpm, respiratory rate 40 breaths/min; blood gas on room air showed pH 7.49, pO2 70 mmHg, pCO2 29 mmHg. Maculopapular lesions were present on the face, trunk, and limbs. Hepatosplenomegaly, lateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and fine crackles at both lung bases were noted.  
Laboratory studies demonstrated pancytopenia (WBC 1×10^3/μL, platelets 137×10^3/μL, hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL), ALT 67 IU/L, AST 446 IU/L, GGT 147 IU/L, ALP 500 IU/L, LDH 6752 IU/L, γ-globulins 21%, CRP 24 mg/dL, ferritin >7500 ng/mL, and triglycerides 247 mg/dL. Routine blood and urine cultures; serology for syphilis, toxoplasma, and Leishmania; latex agglutination for Cryptococcus neoformans; and a malaria smear were negative. Plasma CMV-DNA was 83,087 copies/mL and CMV p65 antigen was positive in 3 cells. The QuantiFERON-TB test was indeterminate; the tuberculin skin test was nonreactive.  
Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for bacteria and fungi, including Pneumocystis jirovecii. Despite empirical sulfamethoxazole–trimethoprim, ceftriaxone (later switched to tigecycline), and foscarnet, she remained febrile without clinical improvement.

A previously healthy 20-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of worsening symptoms. Three weeks earlier he had an episode of acute pharyngitis while camping. One week later he developed painful, swollen knees that impaired weight bearing, along with crusting skin lesions on his lower limbs. Two weeks after the pharyngitis, he experienced fever, anorexia, and a progressively enlarging, painful right-sided neck mass. He denied other medical conditions or substance use.

On examination, his temperature was 38.0 °C and he had an antalgic gait. There was a large tender mass lateral to the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. Both knees were tender and swollen, and multiple small eschar-like lesions were present on the lower limbs. There were no signs of conjunctivitis, urethritis, rheumatic fever, or infective endocarditis.

Initial investigations showed a normal urine dipstick, chest radiograph, and renal function. Liver enzymes were elevated (ALT 213 U/L, AST 200 U/L, ALP 280 U/L, GGT 204 U/L) and C-reactive protein was 287 mg/L. Rickettsia IgG and IgM, leptospira IgM, viral hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody were all negative. Anti-streptolysin O titre was 2900 IU/mL and anti-DNase B was 1210 IU/mL. Streptococcus pyogenes grew in blood culture and was susceptible to penicillin and ampicillin. Synovial fluid from the right knee showed a polymorphonuclear cell predominance but no bacterial growth. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a right internal jugular vein thrombus and a small low-density collection in the right sternocleidomastoid muscle, with no deep neck space infection.

A 78-year-old man with a history of type II diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and coronary artery disease was evaluated for two months of malaise. Laboratory studies showed normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL), hyperglobulinemia, hypercalcemia (corrected calcium 12.1 mg/dL), and elevated creatinine (1.88 mg/dL). Serum protein electrophoresis revealed a monoclonal IgM spike; immunofixation confirmed IgM kappa, and the serum IgM concentration exceeded 58.5 g/L. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated 20–25% infiltration by a small B-cell neoplasm with plasma cell differentiation, consistent with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, establishing the diagnosis of Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

Four days before presentation, he developed an asymptomatic, progressive erythematous rash on the abdomen and thighs. He had no symptoms of hyperviscosity and was untreated for his macroglobulinemia when the rash appeared. Examination revealed multiple linear and serpiginous nonblanchable erythematous patches on the abdomen and both thighs, consistent with purpura following vascular territories.

Skin biopsy of an abdominal lesion showed dense superficial perivascular infiltration with lymphocytes, neutrophils, nuclear dust, and extravasated red blood cells, along with superficial vascular lumen occlusions. Periodic acid–Schiff staining demonstrated eosinophilic homogeneous material in vascular lumens and walls; Congo red staining was negative. Immunohistochemical staining highlighted IgM deposition in the vessel lumens and walls, with negative staining for IgG, IgA, and IgD. Direct immunofluorescence revealed homogeneous deposition in vessel lumens of IgM, IgA, and C3; C3 also showed homogeneous deposition in vessel walls and granular perivascular staining.

Further evaluation for secondary vasculitis—including hepatitis B and C serologies, cryoglobulin testing, antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (C-ANCA and P-ANCA), and HIV—was negative. The blood sample for cryoglobulins was processed at 37 °C and then stored at 4 °C without precipitate formation. The patient denied any use of medications known to cause purpura.

A 68‐year‐old man who heated his home by burning wood or coal was found 16 days earlier unconscious in his room, with vomit and incontinence; the stove had gone out. He regained alertness and complained of left‐sided weakness; a local hospital brain CT was reportedly unremarkable and he was treated with antiplatelet agents and a statin for presumed cerebral infarction. Two days before transfer, he became slow to respond and refused to eat, and he was admitted to our hospital. His history included untreated prostatic hyperplasia and a 40‐year history of heavy alcohol use. On admission, blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg. He was apathetic with memory loss; his left nasolabial fold was shallow, but there were no other focal neurologic signs. On hospital day 3 he developed worsening cognitive impairment, including language, memory, and spatial‐orientation deficits; his tongue deviated slightly to the right, and right lower‐extremity strength was proximally grade 4+, distally grade 3. Emergency brain CT and electrocardiography remained normal. Comprehensive laboratory evaluation, including arterial carboxyhemoglobin, metabolic panels, infectious and autoimmune studies, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis, was unremarkable except for mildly elevated thyroid‐stimulating hormone and prostate‐specific antigen. Brain MRI demonstrated an abnormal symmetrical signal in the bilateral basal ganglia and, notably, abnormal symmetrical signals in the bilateral cerebral peduncles on diffusion-weighted imaging with corresponding low‐signal areas on ADC sequences.

A 39-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 2-year history of left-sided nasal obstruction and anterior rhinorrhea. He had a confirmed history of grass and birch pollen allergy and no prior nasal surgery. Fiberoptic examination revealed complete obstruction of the left nasal cavity and nasopharynx by multiple polyps occupying the middle and superior meatus. Noncontrast CT of the sinuses showed complete filling of the left nasal cavity extending into the nasopharynx and left posterior ethmoidal cells, with central clustered radiodensities and no evidence of bone erosion. A course of systemic and topical corticosteroids produced no improvement in his symptoms.

A 23-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of epigastric pain, nausea, postprandial vomiting, anorexia, generalized malaise, and an 11-kg weight loss. He had no prior gastrointestinal disease, abdominal surgeries, or hospitalizations, and was not on medications. On examination, vital signs were stable, and abdominal examination revealed only mild epigastric tenderness without organomegaly or peritoneal signs.

Laboratory tests showed normal hemoglobin, hematocrit, white-cell count, and liver and kidney function. HIV serology was negative. Syphilis serologies were positive (VDRL and Treponema pallidum reagents). 

Upper endoscopy revealed diminished gastric expandability and diffuse mucosal lesions from the cardia to the pylorus. The gastric mucosa appeared thickened, friable, nodular, and had multiple ulcerations. Gastric biopsies demonstrated a dense inflammatory infiltrate rich in plasma cells.

A 44-year-old Asian woman presented with a 6-year history of right postauricular swelling and a 1-year history of left postauricular swelling. Both swellings were itchy and had slowly enlarged. She had pulmonary tuberculosis 17 years earlier and a family history of tuberculosis but denied fever, weight loss, or chronic cough.

On examination, the right postauricular mass was a 4.5 cm × 4 cm matted, nontender lymph node extending to the mastoid; the left was a 2 cm × 1 cm superficial, nontender lymph node. No other lymphadenopathy or organomegaly was present.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, white-cell count 10.47 × 10^9/L with 15% eosinophils, and normal platelets. Blood urea and creatinine were normal; ESR was 22 mm/h. Sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative. Tests for HBsAg and anti-HCV antibody were negative. Chest radiography showed an old healed focus of tuberculosis.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology, performed three times on both swellings at two laboratories, showed reactive lymphadenitis with histiocytes having prominent nucleoli, plus eosinophils and plasma cells.

A 44-year-old Japanese man was referred for ophthalmologic follow-up. He had gray hair and hair loss since his 30s, skin hardening and intractable ulcers of the ankle and Achilles region since his 40s, soft‐tissue calcification, Achilles‐tendon calcification, a bird‐like facial appearance, a high‐pitched hoarse voice, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, osteoporosis, and hypothyroidism. At age 38 he underwent bilateral cataract extraction with intraocular‐lens implantation and began treatment with tafluprost, timolol, and brimonidine for glaucoma.  

On examination, best‐corrected visual acuity was 1.2 in each eye. Refraction was –1.00 DS / –0.50 DC × 125° OD and –0.50 DS / –0.50 DC × 120° OS. Axial lengths were 23.68 mm OD and 23.60 mm OS. Intraocular pressures were 6 mmHg in both eyes on medical therapy.  

Spectral‐domain OCT (enhanced‐depth imaging) revealed average circumpapillary RNFL thicknesses of 93 µm OD and 81 µm OS, with inferior‐macular GCC thinning OU (97 µm superior and 76 µm inferior OD; 92 µm superior and 59 µm inferior OS). Central choroidal thickness was 222 µm OD and 189 µm OS. Humphrey 30-2 visual‐field mean deviations were –0.19 dB OD and –5.14 dB OS.

A 54-year-old woman with alcohol abuse, intravenous drug use, depression, and untreated hypertension presented after a witnessed generalized tonic–clonic seizure. Earlier that morning she had complained of nausea and vision changes. She was postictal on arrival to the emergency department. Her blood pressure was 170/103 mmHg and heart rate was 104 beats/min; other vital signs were normal. Outpatient records showed chronically elevated pressures of 150–180 s/80–90 s mmHg without antihypertensive therapy. Laboratory tests revealed AST 5,359 IU/L, ALT 2,359 IU/L, total bilirubin 3.0 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 81 IU/L, lactate 18.1 mmol/L, venous pH 7.11, anion gap 31 mmol/L, and WBC 17,800/μL. A urine drug screen and serum alcohol level were negative. ECG showed sinus tachycardia without ischemia. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Noncontrast head CT showed a small left parietal scalp swelling without fracture. Right upper-quadrant ultrasound demonstrated a normal liver and gallbladder. Lumbar puncture was unremarkable. The patient was admitted, and the initial differential diagnosis included alcohol withdrawal, hepatic encephalopathy, infection, or posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.  
By hospital day 1 her mentation normalized, lactate fell to 5.5 mmol/L, pH rose to 7.44, and AST/ALT began to decline. She never exhibited signs of alcohol withdrawal. Additional hepatic studies showed ferritin 16,368 ng/mL, iron 289 µg/dL, transferrin saturation 98%, and negative markers for hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and EBV. Tests for hemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease, and autoimmune hepatitis were negative. Neurology and hepatology were consulted; neurology recommended a brain MRI, and hepatology suggested ischemic hepatopathy secondary to seizure activity.

A 39-year-old man, previously in good health, presented four weeks after his third (booster) dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine with epistaxis, petechiae, and intermittent hematuria. An initial evaluation resulted in a diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), as investigations did not reveal any other causes for his thrombocytopenia. He had no additional cytopenias or signs of hemolysis. 

On examination, he had widespread petechiae on his arms and legs but no palpable lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. 

Laboratory studies on admission showed:  
• White blood cells 16.94 × 10^3/μL, hemoglobin 15 g/dL, platelets 2 × 10^3/μL  
• AST 19 U/L, ALT 34 U/L, LDH 302 U/L  
• BUN 4.6 mmol/L, creatinine 67 μmol/L  
• Total bilirubin 12 μmol/L, albumin 40 g/L  
• HBsAg, HBsAb, HBcAb, HCV Ab, and HIV tests negative  
• Helicobacter pylori antigen positive  
• Lupus anticoagulant ratio 1.28, ANA titer 1:80 (mildly positive)  
• Blood film: isolated thrombocytopenia without schistocytes  

A CT scan of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis did not reveal any lymphadenopathy or other abnormalities, although prior steroid treatment might have reduced sensitivity. Bone marrow biopsy showed active marrow with abundant megakaryocytes, suggesting peripheral destruction of platelets.

A 13-year-old girl from rural Morocco, born to nonconsanguineous parents with no relevant family history, presented with lifelong growth failure and chronic diarrhea. She was exclusively breastfed for 6 months, introduced to solids at age 2, and at 6 months of age developed two months of watery, sometimes fatty diarrhea with failure to thrive and moderate ascites. CT imaging and upper endoscopy at that time led to a diagnosis of celiac disease; a gluten-free diet was pursued for 18 months without improvement. Lymphoedema of the left upper limb appeared at age 1, contributing to limb deformity and worsening growth delay. Lost to follow-up for several years, she re-presented at age 11 with severe oedemato-ascitic syndrome, including marked abdominal distension (umbilical perimeter 100 cm), pleural effusion, and pitting edema of the lower limbs. Examination revealed an asthenic girl with height at –4 and weight at –3 standard deviations, left upper-limb lymphoedema with sausage digits and clubbed nails, genu valgum, and multiple molluscum contagiosum warts on the lips, perioral region, and fingers. Laboratory studies showed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 8.5 g/L; mean corpuscular volume 70 fL; mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration 22 pg), low ferritin (3.02 mg/L), severe hypoalbuminemia (12 g/L), total protein 35 g/L, hypocalcemia (58 mg/L), hypophosphatemia (33 mg/L), elevated parathyroid hormone (140.7 pg/mL), vitamin D deficiency (4.8 ng/mL), hypolipidemia (cholesterol 1.05 g/L; HDL 0.21 g/L; LDL 0.67 g/L), and hypogammaglobulinemia (γ-globulins 4.8 g/L; IgG 2.79 g/L). Serum α1-antitrypsin was 1.32 g/L, fecal α1-antitrypsin 0.51 g/L, with fecal clearance elevated at 224 mL/24 h. Abdominal ultrasound showed large-volume ascites and small-bowel wall thickening; CT imaging demonstrated abundant ascites, diffuse digestive wall thickening, and sclerolipomatosis without lymphatic obstruction. Ascitic fluid was milky and rich in triglycerides. Upper endoscopy revealed congestive gastritis without villous atrophy, and duodenal biopsies were normal. Echocardiography showed no evidence of heart failure, pericarditis, or thrombosis. Tuberculosis workup and stool studies were unremarkable, and HIV and CMV serologies were negative. Radiographs of the lower limbs demonstrated changes of osteomalacia.

A 65-year-old man from southern Ontario, with dyslipidemia on a statin, presented with new neurologic findings after travel. Approximately four weeks earlier he had spent 12 days in urban and rural Ecuador and the Galapagos Islands. He felt unwell on arrival and attributed it to altitude. One week into the trip he noted three isolated, erythematous lesions (~1 cm in diameter) on his right lateral chin and left lower back/upper buttock; the chin lesion was tender, and the others were nonpainful and resolved rapidly. He returned to Canada and continued to experience fatigue, lower extremity myalgias, and one febrile episode. Eight days after return, he developed a 6–8 cm nonpainful, nonpruritic, uniformly erythematous “bull’s-eye” rash on the left lower back. He was started on doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for two weeks. Five days into therapy, he developed a right-sided facial droop and noted a non-tender, reducible right lower quadrant abdominal mass.  
In the Emergency Department, abdominal ultrasound showed no hernia or fluid collection. He was advised to finish doxycycline. Two days later, in specialist clinic assessment, he was afebrile. Neurologic exam revealed right-sided cranial nerve VII palsy involving the forehead and a mild left-deviating cranial nerve XII palsy; there were no meningeal signs. Abdominal exam confirmed a soft, reducible 10 cm × 5 cm right lower quadrant mass. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable, and the erythema migrans rash had resolved.  
Laboratory studies showed a normal CBC and electrolytes, with mildly elevated but down-trending liver enzymes (ALT 42 U/L; AST 40 U/L; ALP 271 U/L). A broad infectious workup—including blood and urine cultures, respiratory virus PCR, malaria smears and rapid test, and serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, E, Dengue virus, Chikungunya virus, West Nile virus, Yellow Fever, Rickettsia (spotted fever and typhi), and Trypanosoma cruzi—was negative. Heterophile antibody testing was positive, and possible Epstein–Barr virus reactivation was suspected. Borrelia burgdorferi serology had been sent and was pending. Given his cranial nerve deficits and vascular risk factors, a noncontrast CT scan of the brain was performed, which showed no evidence of stroke or other intracranial abnormality. An MRI brain was arranged for further evaluation.

A 61-year-old woman with known Marfan syndrome presented with a 3-day history of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and absence of bowel movements. Her medical history was significant for three previous type A aortic dissections and recent replacement of the aortic root, ascending aorta, and bioprosthetic aortic valve. She was an ex-smoker and lived independently. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Laboratory studies showed a lactate dehydrogenase level of 309 IU/L and a C-reactive protein level of 101 mg/L; other results were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed a diffusely tender, distended abdomen without signs of peritonism. An erect chest radiograph demonstrated a left pleural effusion and an unfolded, dilated aortic arch. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis was then performed.  
Findings included a dilated cecum measuring 8.8 cm, twisting of the cecum consistent with a volvulus, and upstream small-bowel dilatation with air–fluid levels; a chronic aortic dissection extending from the ascending thoracic aorta to the common iliac arteries was also noted.

A 24-year-old right-handed man presented with 2 days of severe headache and incoherent speech. Two weeks earlier he had a cold with cough and fever that resolved one week before admission. He had no significant past medical or family history and took no medications.
