Vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination showed cognitive impairment, neck rigidity, and a positive Kernig’s sign; Brudzinski’s signs were negative.  
Laboratory tests revealed normal blood counts, liver and renal function, electrolytes, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Autoimmune antibodies and serologies for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B and C were negative.  
CSF analysis showed an opening pressure of 250 mmH₂O (normal <180), protein of 51 mg/dl (normal <40), normal cell counts, glucose, and chloride; Gram stain and bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures were negative; the IgG index was normal without oligoclonal bands.  
An EEG showed diffuse intermittent slow waves over the left temporal area; visual and brainstem auditory evoked potentials were normal.  
Brain MRI revealed a 5-cm irregular mass in the left basal ganglia with T1 hypointensity, T2 hyperintensity, heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement, and surrounding edema. Proton MR spectroscopy demonstrated an elevated choline peak and a suppressed N-acetylaspartate peak. Spinal MRI was unremarkable.  
He was treated with IV dexamethasone (10 mg/day) and IV acyclovir (500 mg every 8 hours) for 1 week, but his headache and cognitive impairment worsened.

A 66-year-old man residing in a nursing home was brought to the emergency department after an episode of profuse per-rectum bleeding, estimated at 1 L. He had advanced Parkinson’s disease and schizophrenia, with very limited communication and mobility, and was fed via a percutaneous gastrostomy tube. Nursing-home staff reported a longstanding history of chronic constipation. 

On arrival, he was cachectic, pale, and drowsy, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 11. He had cold extremities, a blood pressure of 67/46 mmHg, a pulse rate of 94 beats/min, and a respiratory rate of 26 breaths/min. Laboratory tests showed a haemoglobin concentration of 90 g/L, platelet count of 153 × 10^9/L, serum creatinine of 177 µmol/L, and urea of 41.6 mmol/L. 

He received immediate resuscitation including one unit of O negative packed red cells. On examination, ongoing fresh PR bleeding was noted, and a large, hard central abdominal mass was palpated. The discharge was mostly fresh red blood rather than melaena, suggesting a lower gastrointestinal source. 

Given the palpable mass, a large colonic tumour was initially suspected. Other possible aetiologies such as diverticular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, arteriovenous malformations, or benign anorectal diseases were considered less likely. Because of the massive blood loss, a fistula between the colon and an abdominal aortic aneurysm was also raised. An urgent CT angiogram of the abdomen and pelvis was requested.

A 73-year-old woman with a 1-year history of polymyalgia rheumatica presented with a 1-month history of progressive right hip pain, stiffness, and right thigh myalgia. She also reported intermittent diarrhea for 4 weeks without blood or mucus. Three weeks earlier, her general practitioner had increased her prednisolone to 20 mg daily for a presumed PMR flare, but her symptoms worsened. Her medical history included hypertension, and her only regular medications were prednisolone 20 mg daily and bendrofluazide 2.5 mg daily. 

On admission she was afebrile. Examination showed reduced power (4/5) of the right hip and knee. Laboratory results revealed a white-cell count of 22.6×10^9/L with neutrophils 18.36×10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 279 mg/L; body-mass index was 27 kg/m^2. Plain radiographs of the hip, pelvis, chest, and abdomen and an abdominal and pelvic ultrasound were unremarkable. Stool cultures were negative. Sigmoidoscopy showed mild active proctitis and diverticulosis.

Her corticosteroid dose was increased to 40 mg daily, and she was started on intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam and gentamicin for presumed infection. Despite these measures, her limb weakness and hip pain worsened and inflammatory markers continued to rise.

A 34-year-old woman was referred by her endocrinologist. Her older sister had been diagnosed with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome at age 17. The patient had a female phenotype with normal external genitalia and breast development, but very little axillary and pubic hair. On digital vaginal examination, her vagina was short, tight, and blind-ending. A pelvic ultrasound performed elsewhere suggested the presence of gonadal tissue in the pelvis. A magnetic resonance imaging study showed two soft-tissue structures suggestive of gonadal tissue in the right obturator canal and along the left external iliac artery, each with an adjacent pericentimetric cyst; no Müllerian duct structures were identified apart from the short vagina.

A 26-year-old white woman presented with a 2-week history of fever, fatigue, migratory arthralgias, and four enlarging left posterior cervical lymph nodes. Initial laboratory evaluation revealed a white blood cell count of 2.0×10^3/mm^3 (lymphocytes 900/μL, granulocytes 1000/μL), hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, mean cell volume 91.5 fL, and platelet count 100,000/μL. HIV-1 and ‑2 screening tests were non-reactive; anti–double-stranded DNA and anti-nuclear antibodies were negative. Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus serologies were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed normal cytogenetics (46,XX) without evidence of malignancy. Chest imaging demonstrated bibasilar infiltrates that resolved with antibiotics. Abdominal CT without contrast revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly and portal venous dilation. PET/CT showed hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy in bilateral cervical and left supraclavicular regions (SUV max 3.7–9.8) with no other sites of uptake.

A 5-year-old girl with a history of mackerel allergy, atopic dermatitis, and chronic constipation presented with a 3-month history of epigastric pain and vomiting recurring every two weeks. Physical examination during an asymptomatic interval was unremarkable, but on referral she had a small palpable upper-abdominal mass. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10,100/μl, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dl, C-reactive protein 0.66 mg/dl, and normal liver enzymes. Abdominal ultrasonography with color Doppler imaging revealed an 11.8×13.6 mm nonvascular lesion of mixed echogenicity near the round ligament of the liver. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 14×16×20 mm low-attenuation mass surrounded by a hyperdense line with disproportionate fat stranding on the right side of the round ligament; there was no ascites or hemorrhage. These findings suggested an abscess of the round ligament of the liver, and oral antibiotics were prescribed with plans for elective laparoscopic exploration and resection.

A 44-year-old woman with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease, depression, insomnia, and cervical cancer in remission presented with epigastric burning pain since the prior evening, wrapping to her back, associated with diaphoresis, nausea, and vomiting. She denied fevers, hematemesis, dysuria, or vaginal discharge. Home treatment with antacids provided no relief. She drinks one alcoholic beverage daily and has a maternal history of premature myocardial infarction.

On arrival: heart rate 77/min, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate 15/min, temperature 36.8º C, and O₂ saturation 98% on room air. Pain was 9/10 epigastrically. An ECG showed deep T-wave inversions across leads V1–4. Examination revealed marked right upper quadrant and epigastric tenderness with a positive Murphy’s sign. Initial laboratories: sodium 133 mg/dL, leukocyte count 18.6 × 10^3/µL, troponin-I 0.18 ng/mL (ref <0.03–0.39).

A stat bedside transthoracic echocardiogram showed septal wall motion abnormalities, possible apical hypokinesis, and an estimated left ventricular ejection fraction of 45–50%. A repeat ECG demonstrated a new left bundle branch block. The patient was treated for presumed acute coronary syndrome with aspirin, heparin, and ticagrelor and taken emergently for coronary angiography, which revealed no significant coronary artery disease.

A 27-year-old African American man presented with 4 weeks of bilateral flank and diffuse lower abdominal pain described as a constant ache associated with early satiety. He denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, melena, hematochezia, weight loss, or urinary symptoms. His medical history was notable for unprovoked recurrent right lower extremity deep vein thrombosis and bilateral testicular hydrocele. He took apixaban and diphenhydramine as needed. He did not smoke or use alcohol or recreational drugs.

On examination, temperature was 37.1°C, blood pressure 121/69 mmHg, pulse 96/min, and respiratory rate 16/min. Lungs and heart were unremarkable. Abdominal palpation revealed mild tenderness in the lower half without rebound or guarding. There was mild right costovertebral angle tenderness and trace bilateral pedal edema. Genital examination was normal.

Laboratory testing showed sodium 133 mEq/L, potassium 5.0 mEq/L, chloride 98 mEq/L, bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 57 mg/dL, creatinine 12.6 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL one month earlier), and estimated glomerular filtration rate 6 mL/min/1.73 m2. Calcium was 8.6 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed specific gravity 1.014, pH 8.0, no red or white blood cells, 100 mg/dL protein, and no glucose or blood. The urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 0.5 g/g and the albumin-to-creatinine ratio was 0.293 g/g.

Renal ultrasonography and noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed mild bilateral hydroureteronephrosis with nonspecific inflammatory changes.

A 15-year-old boy was evaluated for a deformity of the right third toe noted 6 months earlier and gradually increasing in size, causing difficulty wearing shoes. Six years prior, his father first observed that the patient's right foot was larger than the left. The patient reported no pain and no history of trauma. His medical history was unremarkable, and there was no known family history of similar foot problems; however, two maternal uncles died young from an unknown kidney disease.

On examination, there was a flexion contracture of the right third toe with dislocation of the proximal interphalangeal joint, limited extension of the second and fourth toes, and mild skin thickening over the first metatarsophalangeal joint. On the plantar aspect of the right foot, there was a non-tender, firm pseudotumor without overlying skin changes. 

Laboratory studies showed:  
- ESR 9 mm/h  
- CRP 3 mg/dL  
- LDH 276 U/L  
- Uric acid 3.3 mg/dL  
- Creatinine 0.7 mg/dL  
- Calcium 10 mg/dL  

Plain radiographs of the foot demonstrated inferior dislocation of the PIP joint of the third digit without evidence of bone lesions or fractures. Ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous enlargement of the Flexor Digitorum Brevis muscle. MRI of the right foot showed a heterogeneous hyperenhancing lesion with irregular margins confined to the Flexor Digitorum Brevis muscle on T1- and T2-weighted sequences before and after gadolinium administration.

An 86-year-old woman presented with 3 days of watery diarrhea that became progressively dark and occasionally bloody. She denied abdominal pain, fever, or vomiting. This was her second similar episode in one month. Her history included hypertension and three ischemic strokes; she has been bedridden for 2 years. Medications were hydralazine, captopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and aspirin. On examination she was lethargic with slurred speech, dehydrated, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, pulse 96 bpm. Neurologic exam showed complete left hemiplegia and central facial palsy. Laboratory tests revealed normal electrolytes and renal function; hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL with normal MCV and RDW; leukocytes and platelets were normal. Upper endoscopy performed for suspected GI bleeding showed an esophageal hernia, Los Angeles grade A esophagitis, enanthematous gastritis, and non-bleeding gastric angiodysplasia. The duodenal mucosa appeared lightly pale with multiple small black spots throughout the distal bulb and second portion. Duodenal biopsies were obtained. Histologic examination showed multiple foci of brown-black granular pigment mostly inside macrophages at the tips of the duodenal villi.

A 61-year-old woman was admitted after experiencing multiple brief episodes of mutism and hand spasms one day following an acute stressor. Psychiatric evaluation revealed mutism, marked negativism, and resistance to suggestions, and a diagnosis of catatonia and possible brief psychotic disorder was made. Neurologic consultation, EEG, brain CT, and routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. She was started on diazepam, alprazolam, and escitalopram. On hospital day 2, haloperidol (0.5 mg twice daily) was added, later increased to 5 mg intramuscularly with biperiden for agitation. On day 4, oral haloperidol and injectable diazepam were discontinued and perphenazine was initiated. Electroconvulsive therapy was declined. Brain MRI and CSF PCR for herpes simplex virus were negative. By day 10, perphenazine was stopped because of dysphagia and an elevation in serum creatine phosphokinase to 1500 U/L. On day 12, she was transferred to a psychosomatic medicine ward. There, she exhibited recurrent catatonic signs including echolalia, echopraxia, negativism, posturing, verbal stereotypes, muscle rigidity, tremors, mutism, and excessive sweating. Laboratory studies showed elevated ESR, CRP, CPK, and LDH. A repeat brain MRI was unremarkable, and CSF analysis—including studies for infection factors and autoantibodies—was negative.

A 46‐year‐old man presented with palpitations. He had no significant medical history and no family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden cardiac death. An electrocardiogram showed T-wave inversion in leads V1–V3. Both transthoracic echocardiography and single-photon emission computed tomography were interpreted as normal. A 24-hour Holter monitor revealed episodes of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia with left bundle‐branch-block morphology and a superior axis, and a premature ventricular contraction burden of 1.3%. 

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a normal left ventricular size and function but a dilated right ventricle (114 mL/m2) with normal ejection fraction. Dyskinesia was noted in the mid segment of the right ventricular free wall along with extensive late gadolinium enhancement. Genetic testing for a panel of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia genes was negative. He was started on bisoprolol and referred for further evaluation. 

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable and physical findings were unremarkable. A stress test showed rare premature ventricular contractions of the same morphology. On review of the MRI, the late gadolinium enhancement in the right ventricle appeared more prominent than typically seen in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, prompting evaluation for right ventricular myocardial infarction and cardiac sarcoidosis. A cardiac CT scan ruled out obstructive coronary artery disease but revealed calcified mediastinal lymph nodes.

A 38-year-old woman was evaluated for a 5-year history of secondary amenorrhoea and infertility.  
Past medical history:  
• Beta-thalassaemia major since childhood on periodic blood transfusions.  
• Restrictive cardiomyopathy (diagnosed at age 10; on digoxin), liver fibrosis with siderosis, and pancreatic fibrosis.  
• Allogeneic HLA-identical brother bone marrow transplantation at age 19 after 15 days of conditioning (fludarabine, busulfan, cyclophosphamide).  
Menstrual history: Menarche at 13 with regular cycles until age 15; cycles ceased at age 33. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea was suspected; eating disorders, excessive exercise, and stress were ruled out.  
Laboratory studies:  
• FSH 1.06 IU/L, LH <0.3 IU/L, estradiol >18.4 pmol/L, AMH <0.007 pmol/L  
• GnRH stimulation: baseline FSH 1.03 IU/L & LH <0.3 IU/L; 30-min FSH 1.15 IU/L & LH 0.57 IU/L (subnormal pituitary response)  
• Human menopausal gonadotropin stimulation: no detectable response  
• Insulin tolerance test: peak GH 11.6 ng/mL; cortisol 26.3 μg/dL  
Pituitary MRI: decreased signal intensity on T2-weighted images and reduced gland size

A 67-year-old woman presented with one week of increasing painful swelling and erythema over the right parotid region. She had been on oral amoxicillin–clavulanate for seven days without improvement. On admission she had malaise, fever, and elevated inflammatory markers. Examination revealed mild weakness of the right marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve and trismus. Intraorally she was edentulous and wore upper and lower dentures. Ultrasonography showed a fluid collection with signs of abscess formation in the right parotid area. The patient reported two prior similar episodes that had been treated successfully as parotid sialadenitis with short courses of antibiotics. She received intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanate and underwent submandibular incision and drainage under general anesthesia. Swelling and pus recurred, prompting a second drainage three days later, after which the wound initially healed and she was discharged eight days later in good condition. A few days after discharge an exuding fistula developed at the incision site and persisted for four months despite multiple antibiotic regimens and an unsuccessful attempt at surgical closure. Magnetic resonance imaging with sialography did not reveal a cause for the persistent fistula, and sialendoscopy showed no abnormalities.

A 47-year-old Caucasian woman with a 23-year history of presumed multiple sclerosis—characterized by four episodes of optic neuritis since 1989, a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis in 1995, persistently negative cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) oligoclonal bands, and unremarkable brain MRI scans—was treated with monthly intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and interferon-β. In January 2012, she presented with subacute onset of expressive aphasia and right-sided hemiparesis. On examination, she was alert with expressive language impairment and 3/5 strength in the right arm and leg; vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies demonstrated a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel. Brain MRI showed a large T2-hyperintense, tumefactive lesion in the left prefrontal white matter and smaller T2 lesions on the right without clear evidence of a disturbed blood–brain barrier. MR spectroscopy revealed an unchanged choline peak. CSF analysis was unremarkable, with no evidence of intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis, no oligoclonal bands, and a normal cell count. Time-of-flight MR angiography showed no signs of vasculitis, and laboratory work-up revealed no clinical or serological evidence for connective tissue diseases. Serum aquaporin-4 antibody titre was 1:1000 by cell-based assay.

A 35-year-old woman presented with 6 weeks of severe upper abdominal pain, anorexia, subjective fevers, and constipation. Her surgical history included cholecystectomy complicated by a bile leak and placement of a common bile duct stent via ERCP 6 years earlier that was never removed; she also had a cesarean section, hysterectomy, and gastric sleeve. Laboratory evaluation showed a white-blood-cell count of 12,000/mm3, platelets 549,000/mm3, ESR 56 mm/hr, CRP 58 mg/L, albumin 4.0 g/dL, GGT 73 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, ALT 14 U/L, AST 16 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 159 U/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated migration of the stent to the superior aspect of the common bile duct and a 5.6 × 4.2 cm hepatic lesion with heterogeneous enhancement, washout in the postarterial phase, and apparent involvement of the anterior branch of the right portal vein. An ERCP removed an occluded stent and revealed mild narrowing of the lower third of the common bile duct. Abdominal ultrasound then showed a focal area of marked bile-duct attenuation with mild peripheral ductal dilation, concerning for cholangiocarcinoma. Serum tumor markers including α-fetoprotein, CEA, CA 19-9, and CA 125 were all within normal limits.

A 42-year-old woman presented to a community hospital with a 2-year history of recurrent nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. On examination she was hemodynamically stable with abdominal distention and tenderness. A small-bowel follow-through showed multiple dilated segments of small bowel, and contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed small-bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right lower quadrant and a possible second transition point in the mid pelvis. Initial management with bowel rest and intravenous fluids provided symptomatic relief. Given the recurrent nature of her symptoms, outpatient colonoscopy was performed; there was no evidence of Crohn’s disease, but a stricture with definitive narrowing was identified in the terminal ileum.

Her medical history was notable for Hashimoto’s disease. Surgical history included a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 15 years earlier and a dilation and curettage 11 years earlier that was complicated by uterine perforation, after which she developed secondary amenorrhea and infertility. 

Prior to diagnostic laparoscopy, top differentials included adhesions from her prior cholecystectomy, gallstone leakage, and Crohn’s disease; endometriosis was considered unlikely.

A 60-year-old white woman was referred to nephrology for an unexplained rise in serum creatinine from a baseline of 0.9 mg/dL to 1.4 mg/dL. Her history was notable for POEMS syndrome diagnosed 1 year earlier—manifested by sciatica, hypothyroidism, monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), and onychomycosis—with regular hematology follow-up. Serum protein electrophoresis performed 2 years earlier showed an M spike of 1.0 g/dL with monoclonal IgG kappa; bone marrow biopsy confirmed 5%–7% plasma cells with kappa predominance.  
She had a 3-year history of hypertension that had been well controlled on losartan, hydrochlorothiazide, and metoprolol. Other medications included allopurinol, aspirin, levothyroxine, and prednisone 20 mg daily. She denied active smoking but reported heavy passive exposure at home and during 30 years as a bartender. She denied long-term NSAID use.  
On examination, blood pressure was 97/64 mm Hg, pulse 59/min, and body-mass index 19.3 kg/m2; there was no rash. She was not diabetic (HbA1c 5.4%). Initial nephrology evaluation confirmed chronic kidney disease stage 3B (eGFR 43 mL/min/1.73 m2), with a further rise in creatinine to 1.8 mg/dL one week later and persistence at that level one month later.  
Urinalysis one month after referral showed nephritic-range proteinuria (UPCR 2.4 g/g), hematuria (50 RBCs/HPF), pyuria (15 WBCs/HPF), and moderate bacteriuria without symptoms; nitrites were negative. Autoimmune and infectious serologies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, SSA/SSB, SCL-70, Jo-1, anti-centromere, C-ANCA, P-ANCA, hepatitis B) were negative. Kidney ultrasound was unremarkable.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a three-year history of left flank and left upper quadrant abdominal pain that increased with exertion. She had no significant past medical, allergic, or medication history. On examination, there was a firm, mildly tender mass measuring 15 cm × 14.5 cm in the left upper quadrant extending into the left flank; it was dull to percussion. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, total leukocyte count 8000/mm3 with a differential of 64% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes, 5% eosinophils, 1% monocytes, and no basophils; liver and kidney function tests were normal.  
Ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined large cystic lesion in the left upper quadrant closely attached to the inferior pole of the left kidney, with minimal hydronephrosis and hydroureter. Other abdominal organs, including liver, pancreas, and spleen, appeared normal. Intravenous urography revealed a large cyst involving the lower pole of the left kidney with displacement of the collecting system and mild hydronephrosis.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-defined, low-attenuating, thick-walled cystic lesion in the left upper quadrant that was inseparable from both the lower pole of the left kidney and the pancreatic tail, producing moderate dilatation of the left pelvi-calyceal system. The initial imaging hypothesis was an infected hydatid cyst; a mesenteric cyst was also considered.

A 43-year-old asymptomatic woman with Lynch syndrome but no personal history of cancer underwent surveillance colonoscopy. Colonoscopic examination revealed a 5-mm transverse colon polyp and, at the appendiceal orifice, a protuberant polypoid lesion suggestive of a submucosal mass. Narrow-band imaging of this lesion showed a tubular pit pattern with a 2-mm area of neoplastic appearance on its surface. Cold forceps were used to resect the focal lesion on the appendiceal orifice. After resection, a pale mass was visualized within the appendix and eventually extruded through the appendiceal orifice into the colonic lumen.

A 51-year-old woman (BMI 52.3) presented with persistent left knee pain three years after a Smith & Nephew OXINIUM™-coated total knee arthroplasty. Six months postoperatively there was a slight tilt of the prosthesis but no pain until two years after surgery, when pain gradually worsened and limited activities of daily living. Over the following year, extensive testing for aseptic loosening, infection, and metallosis was essentially unremarkable. On examination, active range of motion was 0–100° with increased anterior–posterior translocation, and a metal-on-metal grinding sensation was noted at approximately 90° of flexion. Plain radiographs demonstrated a cloudy density within the soft tissues around the joint, consistent with a “cloud sign.”

A 60-year-old Caucasian woman presented after a motor-vehicle collision in which she sustained blunt trauma to the chest. She was a nonsmoker with a history of type II diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and New York Heart Association class III heart failure. On arrival she was hemodynamically stable and well perfused. Pulmonary auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds over the right hemithorax, and she had pain with right shoulder motion. Laboratory evaluation showed a white-blood-cell count of 15.6×10^3/μL and mild elevations in serum transaminase, creatine phosphokinase, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. 
A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral pulmonary contusions, fractures of the right fifth and sixth ribs, and a cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level in the basal segment of the right lower lobe. The patient was admitted for observation. On a computed tomography scan performed 24 hours later, there was a small right pneumothorax and a thin-walled air cavity in the anterior segment of the right lower lobe adjacent to the interlobar fissure. In addition, there was an extensive contusion in the posterior and lateral segments of the right lower lobe with air within the contused parenchyma, suggesting the early formation of a second cavitation.

A 50-year-old right-handed man with no known chronic illnesses presented with acute‐onset weakness of the right limbs 2 days earlier. His mother had an ischemic stroke at age 87. He smokes one pack per day for 30 years and drinks two units of alcohol daily. There was no head trauma or allergies.

On examination he was alert, afebrile, BMI 21 kg/m2, blood pressure 234/146 mm Hg, heart rate 104 bpm. Neurologically, he had right hemiparesis (MRC 4/5), a right extensor plantar response, and central right facial palsy. Extrapyramidal signs included slowness, left upper‐limb rigidity, hypomimia, and low‐volume monotonous speech. MMSE was 27/30; MOCA was 25/30 with deficits in visuospatial/executive tasks, short‐term memory, and calculation.

Noncontrast head CT showed a small hypodense lesion with ill-defined borders in the posterior limb of the left internal capsule, consistent with an acute lacunar stroke. There were diffuse, symmetric hypodense white matter changes in the periventricular regions, centrum semiovale, internal capsules, brainstem, cerebellar peduncles, and cerebellum, with sparing of the juxtacortical arcuate fibers.

Brain MRI confirmed a 10×19 mm hyperintense lesion on DWI, FLAIR, and T2WI in the left posterior limb of the internal capsule extending to the lenticular nucleus, and diffuse hyperintense white matter areas in the same supratentorial and infratentorial regions without restricted diffusion. SWI sequences showed hypointense conglomerates in the pons and centrum semiovale consistent with old hemosiderin deposits.

Laboratory studies revealed normal hematology, liver and kidney function, coagulation parameters, and no inflammatory markers. ECG was normal. Carotid Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated bilateral nonstenotic atheromatous plaques with irregular surfaces and thicknesses of 2.7 mm on the left and 4.2 mm on the right.

A 42-year-old Asian man presents with longstanding nyctalopia and metamorphopsia in both eyes and recent difficulty adapting to bright light. He was diagnosed with macular degeneration 20 years ago. He has no significant medical history and denies exposure to pentosan polysulfate or hydroxychloroquine. His father has macular degeneration. Best-corrected visual acuity is 20/20 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. Anterior segment examination is normal with no corneal limbus crystals. 

Dilated fundus examination reveals multiple punctate, drusen-like, refractile deposits in the posterior pole and midperiphery, with prominent choroidal vessels in areas of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy. Fundus autofluorescence shows patchy hypoautofluorescent RPE atrophy extending from the posterior pole to the midperiphery. Spectral-domain OCT demonstrates patchy areas of complete RPE and outer retinal atrophy, diffuse choroidal thinning, and hyperreflective dots predominantly in the outer retina and RPE. En face OCT localizes hyperreflective crystalline deposits at various retinal levels, some of which were not evident on clinical examination or fundus photography. Full-field electroretinography shows approximately 50% reduction in rod and cone amplitudes bilaterally.

A 26-year-old woman was admitted with a 12-day history of fever (maximum, 39.5 °C), asthenia, nausea, myalgia, arthralgia, and an itchy maculopapular rash. Thirty days before the onset of fever, she had begun lamotrigine for bipolar disorder; the drug was discontinued after 4 days of fever. Initial outpatient treatment included cefixime, followed by a one-day course of betamethasone and antihistamine, then a 3-day course of azithromycin, without improvement.

On admission, examination showed a diffuse maculopapular rash on the face, neck, trunk, and extremities; hard, tender 2–3 cm lymph nodes in retronuchal, laterocervical, axillary, and inguinal regions; and hepatomegaly.

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 31,770 /mm3 with 18% eosinophils, elevated CD4 and CD8 counts (3,674/mm3 and 5,759/mm3), alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase levels 19-fold and 14-fold above normal, respectively; bilirubin, 2.84 mg/dL; and prothrombin activity, 39%. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses were negative. Serologies for herpesviruses I and II, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and multiple other viral and bacterial pathogens were negative, and cultures of blood, pharynx, urine, and feces showed no growth. Antinuclear antibodies and thyroid-function tests were normal.

Pathological examination of a right axillary lymph node showed no malignancy, an increase in mature T cells and dendritic cells, scarce B-cell zones, some eosinophils, and foam and hydropic cells. Bone marrow examination was unremarkable. Computed tomography revealed hepatomegaly without other abnormalities.

On hospital day 2, she was given intravenous betamethasone and acyclovir, with mild initial improvement. After 5 days, steroids were tapered from 8 mg to 3 mg daily, resulting in relapse of fever and rises in aminotransferase levels and eosinophil count.

Differential diagnosis included lymphoproliferative diseases, autoimmune diseases/vasculitis, infectious diseases, and allergic reactions to drug.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a five-day history of worsening abdominal pain, distension, and vomiting. On examination she was peritonitic, tachycardic, hypotensive, tachypneic, and required 4 L of supplemental oxygen. Three months earlier she had been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma with brain metastases and treated with craniotomy, CyberKnife radiotherapy, and a tapering course of oral dexamethasone (reduced to 2 mg three times daily at presentation). She was not on Pneumocystis prophylaxis.

Abdominal CT demonstrated perforation of the large bowel secondary to diverticulitis, and chest CT showed bilateral, patchy ground-glass opacities in both central and peripheral lung fields. She underwent emergency subtotal colectomy and ileostomy formation. Postoperatively, she was managed as COVID-19 pneumonia. However, five RT-PCR tests for SARS-CoV-2 (nose and throat swabs on days 1 and 10, bronchoalveolar-lavage samples on days 2 and 4, and endotracheal secretions on day 13) were negative. Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics, she remained febrile with persistently elevated inflammatory markers, progressive bilateral ground-glass opacities on repeat CT, and failure to wean from mechanical ventilation. On postoperative day 13, an alternative diagnosis was sought.

A term male neonate was born via uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 45-year-old mother with inadequate antenatal care. His birth weight was 3 kg. He was admitted for neonatal jaundice and sepsis. Seventy-two hours after birth, a painless left hemiscrotal swelling was noted. There was no bleeding from any orifice and no bruising over the groin. Abdominal examination was normal. External genital examination revealed scrotal asymmetry with a fluctuant, non-tender left hemiscrotal swelling; the left testis could not be palpated separately. The swelling did not transilluminate, and one could get above it. There was no evidence of trauma. An initial diagnosis of acute scrotum was made.

Emergency scrotal ultrasonography showed both testes to be normal in position, size, and outline. The left tunica vaginalis contained a fluid collection with high-level echoes. The testicular parenchyma echo pattern was normal, and color Doppler interrogation demonstrated normal blood flow; the testicular arteries were preserved. Abdominal ultrasonography was normal. The packed cell volume was 42.6%; coagulation studies and platelet count were within normal limits. A direct Coombs test was negative.

A 34-year-old man, a laborer of lower socioeconomic status, presented with a 2-month history of dull aching pain and a swelling over the right lower chest wall, accompanied by low-grade evening fevers and unintentional weight loss. He denied trauma or joint symptoms. His father had pulmonary tuberculosis 20 years earlier. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. There was a 5×3 cm tender, soft, noncompressible swelling on the lateral aspect of the right lower chest wall without cough impulse; there was no lymphadenopathy or spinal or other joint abnormality. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 90 mm/h, and a reactive C-reactive protein; liver and renal function tests were normal, and HIV testing was negative. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the chest showed a lytic lesion in the right ninth rib with a superficial cold abscess characterized by a thin, peripherally enhancing rim; the spine, lungs, and pleura appeared normal.

A 77-year-old man with low-grade prostate cancer, hypertension, and known diverticulosis presented with three episodes of rectal bleeding—initially dark, then bright red—as well as a syncopal event accompanied by eye-rolling and generalized shaking but no incontinence or tongue biting. He had no prior GI bleeding, no NSAID use, and no history of radiation. He is a former heavy smoker and drinks minimally. Family history was notable for gallbladder and throat cancer.

On arrival: blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg; heart rate 90/min; respiratory rate 18/min; temperature 98.6°F. Examination showed mild left lower-quadrant tenderness without peritonitis, melena on digital rectal examination, pale skin, and slightly dry mucous membranes. Neurologic exam was nonfocal. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, hematocrit 30%, normal BUN, electrolytes, and coagulation profile.

A colonoscopy demonstrated pan-colonic diverticulosis with evidence of bleeding throughout the colon. Computed tomography angiography showed numerous colonic diverticula, no focal inflammatory changes, and no active bleeding. A tagged red blood cell scan then localized an active hemorrhage to the distal descending colon/sigmoid region.

A 42-year-old woman with a history of endometriosis and prior hysterectomy presented with a 3-day history of nausea and vomiting. 
Initial abdominal CT showed obstruction of the distal ileum, and she underwent emergent exploratory laparotomy with adhesiolysis and decompression. 
During her postoperative recovery, she developed watery diarrhea and persistent sinus tachycardia despite intravenous fluids and electrolyte repletion. 
On postoperative day 13, an ST-elevation “MI code” was called when a 12-lead ECG demonstrated inferolateral ST-segment elevations. The patient reported epigastric discomfort and shortness of breath but denied chest pain. 
A bedside transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular systolic function with inferior wall hypokinesis. 
Subsequent cardiac catheterization revealed angiographically normal coronary arteries and normal left ventricular contractility on ventriculography. 
Serial cardiac enzyme levels were within normal limits.

A 12-year-old boy (36 kg) with cerebral palsy, epilepsy (on divalproex), hydrocephalus (multiple VP shunts), cortical blindness, and neuromuscular atrophy was scheduled for posterior spinal fusion. Examination was unremarkable. Anesthesia was induced with sevoflurane in N₂O/O₂, followed by uncomplicated intubation and placement of peripheral, central, and arterial lines. After prone positioning (with efforts to avoid abdominal compression), TIVA was started with propofol 180 mcg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ and remifentanil 2 mcg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ to facilitate combined motor and somatosensory evoked-potential monitoring without muscle relaxants. Two hours later, mean arterial pressure fell to 46–50 mmHg; propofol and remifentanil were reduced to 150/1 mcg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, phenylephrine 50 mcg and calcium gluconate 100 mg IV were given, and one unit of PRBCs was transfused. Over the next six hours, dopamine at 5 mcg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ was added; propofol/remifentanil were further decreased to 75/0.075 mcg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; and phenylephrine (7000 mcg), calcium gluconate (1200 mg), calcium chloride (600 mg), sodium bicarbonate (100 mEq), 5200 mL normal saline, three units of PRBCs, and 840 mL cell-saver blood were administered. Two hours later, he again became unstable (BP 48–65/18–38 mmHg, HR 122–135 bpm) with worsening metabolic acidosis. The propofol infusion was stopped; dopamine was increased to 7 mcg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; phenylephrine infusion (5 mcg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹), sodium bicarbonate (100 mEq), and hydrocortisone (100 mg) were administered; TIVA was discontinued in favor of sevoflurane 1%; phenylephrine was stopped, and a vasopressin infusion was initiated along with one more unit of PRBCs.

A 76-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a four-week history of cough productive of mucous-purulent sputum and progressive dyspnea. She was a lifelong nonsmoker, had no recent travel or animal exposures, and no known contact with substances associated with lipoid pneumonia. Her medical history included atrial fibrillation treated with amiodarone (200 mg daily) for 30 years, hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism.

On examination, her vital signs were normal (pulse 69 /min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, SpO2 95% on room air). Lung auscultation revealed bibasal crackles; there was no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. Routine blood tests were within normal limits.

Pulmonary function testing showed a moderate restrictive defect (FVC 90% predicted, FEV1 65% predicted, FEV1/FVC 96%) and a marked reduction in diffusing capacity (DLCO 55% predicted). There was no bronchodilator response.

Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral infiltrates, prompting high-resolution CT, which revealed ground-glass opacities and air-space consolidations predominant in both lower lobes. 

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage yielded 287 500 cells/mL (macrophages 64%, lymphocytes 31%, neutrophils 3%, eosinophils 2%). Smears and cultures for bacteria, fungi, and acid-fast bacilli were negative, and cytology showed no malignant cells.

A 59-year-old man with hypertension, well-controlled diabetes, and osteoarthritis presented with a 5-day history of neck stiffness. He first saw his physician and was given methocarbamol without relief. Two days later he went to the ED reporting involuntary contractions of the neck muscles holding his head to the left. He denied headache, photophobia, fever, nausea, vomiting, upper-extremity weakness or numbness, stridor, dysphagia, drooling, odynophagia, or respiratory symptoms. He had no history of trauma. 

Vital signs were temperature 36.4°C, heart rate 70/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and blood pressure 131/81 mm Hg. He was alert, oriented, and in mild discomfort. Neurologic examination showed clear speech, normal cranial nerves, and pinpoint pupils with poor light reaction but no photophobia. HEENT examination revealed normal tympanic membranes, no otitis, no nasal discharge, no pharyngeal erythema, and no tonsillar inflammation. His head was held in left rotation. Neck examination revealed no midline vertebral tenderness, left paraspinal tenderness, and decreased range of motion due to pain. Extremity examination showed full strength and intact reflexes; lower-extremity range of motion was limited by osteoarthritis; a right lower-extremity ulcer was dressed.

He received ketorolac 60 mg IM and underwent CT scans. CT of the head showed “normal aerated sinuses, no sign of mass effect or shift, no acute bleed, minimal atrophy.” CT of the neck showed “degenerative changes but no sign of a discrete fracture; the prevertebral soft tissues appeared intact; there is some straightening; a significant compression was not seen.” He reported significant relief and was discharged with Tylenol #3 and primary-care follow-up.

Four days later he returned with persistent neck pain. He was afebrile, examination was unchanged, and he was treated with ketorolac and discharged with acetaminophen/hydrocodone, cyclobenzaprine, and ibuprofen.

Six days after that (day 15) he presented after a near-syncopal episode. He reported dizziness upon standing and attributed it to cyclobenzaprine. He again denied headache, fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting. Examination showed a heart rate of 120/min and was otherwise unchanged. An ECG was normal. Admission laboratory testing revealed a white-cell count of 34,500 per mm³ with 92% neutrophils.

A 9-year-old girl from a rural area presented with a 2-week history of severe itching over a reddish, granular polypoidal lesion on the left palpebral conjunctiva. The lesion measured 5 mm × 5 mm and tended to bleed on touch. She had normal vision and no systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL, a white-cell count of 9000 cells/mm3 with 65% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes, and 5% eosinophils. A stool examination was negative for ova or parasites. She reported regular bathing in village ponds. Clinically, a differential diagnosis of conjunctival papilloma, foreign-body granuloma, and oculosporidiosis was considered. The lesion was completely excised with electrocautery and sent for histopathologic examination.

A 32-year-old man from northern Ethiopia presented with intermittent rectal bleeding for 40 days, associated cough and fever. He noted a painless mass over the anus for five years without prior treatment. He was under evaluation for suspected colorectal carcinoma. On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed splenomegaly (5 cm below the left costal margin) and hepatomegaly (2 cm below the right costal margin). There was a 5×5 cm erythematous, nontender plaque over the inner right buttock and perianal area. Digital rectal examination showed a firm, circumferential rectal swelling 4 cm from the anal verge. Abdominal CT scan demonstrated a 2.5 cm–thick circumferential rectal mass with mesorectal extension, thickening of the mesorectal fascia suggestive of rectal cancer, mesorectal lymphadenopathy (stage III), and hepatosplenomegaly. Chest radiograph was normal.

A 47-year-old woman noted a painless “bump” over her left sternoclavicular joint for 4 months, which had gradually increased in size. She denied trauma, fevers, weight loss, or family history of cancer.  
On examination, there was a non‐tender prominence over the left medial clavicle without erythema or warmth; range of motion of the shoulder was normal.  
Plain radiographs showed a lytic lesion of the medial left clavicle. Noncontrast CT of the left clavicle revealed a lytic lesion of the medial metaphysis and epiphysis extending through the cortex with a small area of periosteal reaction.  
MRI of the clavicle with and without contrast confirmed an erosive, lytic lesion of the medial clavicle with surrounding edema.  
Laboratory tests showed a CRP of 1.28 mg/L (normal 0.0–0.5), an ESR of 24 mm/hr (normal 0–15), and a normal white blood cell count.  
Biopsy of the clavicular lesion demonstrated fibrous tissue with acute and chronic inflammation, predominantly lymphocytes, scattered plasma cells, and aggregates of neutrophils forming abscesses, consistent with acute and chronic osteomyelitis. Immunophenotyping revealed “no significant lymphoid immunophenotypic abnormalities detected. There was no evidence of lymphoma, plasma cell neoplasm, or metastatic carcinoma.”  
Despite 5 days of culture incubations, no organisms grew. The patient underwent irrigation, debridement, and partial medial clavicle excision, with pathology again showing acute and chronic inflammation with multinucleated cells; cultures remained negative.  
Three and a half months after initial presentation, she developed left knee pain. Radiographs demonstrated a well‐marginated osteolytic lesion in the fibular head without sclerosis. A three‐phase bone scan showed persistent uptake in the left medial clavicle and positive uptake in the left fibular head and right clavicle, suggestive of chronic osteomyelitis.

A 37-year-old gravida 4, para 4 woman with chronic kidney disease on dialysis, awaiting renal transplantation, was found on preoperative examination to have a significant left adnexal mass. She reported lower abdominal fullness, pain, and irregular menstrual cycles. On abdominal palpation, a mass equivalent to a 20-week uterine size was noted. A vaginal examination was limited by discomfort as the mass in the pouch of Douglas abutted the vagina and rectum. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.0 g/dl, leukocyte count 14,000/mm3, total bilirubin 1.22 mg/dl, GGT 178 U/l, ALP 424 U/l, low albumin and total proteins, creatinine 2.45 mg/dl, urea 45 mg/dl, normal lipid profile, negative tuberculosis screening, and CA-125 elevated at 98 units/dl with other tumor markers within normal limits. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed a midline thick-walled adnexal cyst measuring 11 × 10 cm with internal septation and an unvisualized contralateral ovary; the uterus was normal in size. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a large left adnexal multiloculated, thick-walled mass measuring 12 × 10 × 11 cm, with incomplete septations, suggestive of a tubo-ovarian abscess or neoplastic lesion.

A 26-year-old man with a history of asthma treated with montelukast presented with recurrent respiratory tract infections and multiple episodes of haemoptysis. Physical examination was unremarkable. Flexible bronchoscopy revealed only a small depression in the tracheal mucosa without an obvious communicating tract. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest demonstrated a 15 mm, well-defined, air-filled cavity immediately above the thoracic inlet on the right side, closely abutting the posterior tracheal wall at the level of C6; there was no fluid within the cavity and no surrounding inflammatory changes.

A 12-year-old boy of Tunisian descent, born to first-cousin parents, was referred for evaluation of severe limitation of mouth opening. Two siblings have a similar appearance, and two brothers in the family died of acute heart failure. The patient had no perinatal abnormalities and normal psychomotor and cognitive development. 

On examination:
• Craniofacial dysmorphia: mandibular hypoplasia with anterior dental crowding, labial incompetence, prominent zygomatic bones and orbital arches, a beak-shaped nose, prominent eyes, and a small mouth opening (maximum interincisal distance, 18 mm).  
• Trunk: decreased biacromial distance attributable to clavicular hypoplasia.  
• Extremities: contractures and flexion deformities of the interphalangeal joints; mottled cutaneous pigmentation over the body (sparing face and palms/soles).  
• Endocrine: growth hormone deficiency; otherwise unremarkable.  

Initial radiographs of the skull showed delayed closure of the metopic and lambdoid sutures, slight mandibular hypoplasia with antegonial depression, and dental crowding. A panoramic radiograph confirmed flattened mandibular condyles and antegonial notching. 

To further assess the temporomandibular joints, CT images demonstrated bilateral condylar head flattening with subchondral microgeodes, cortical erosions, and joint-space narrowing, more pronounced on the left.

Chief complaint: Evaluation of progressive abdominal distention.

History of present illness: A 52-year-old woman with a 20-year history of anorexia nervosa, binge–purge subtype, characterized by self-induced vomiting and laxative abuse (>200 tablets/day), presents with several months of increasing abdominal swelling. She has a history of multiple psychiatric admissions for supportive psychotherapy and symptomatic treatment of her eating disorder.

Physical examination: Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg; heart rate 82 bpm; temperature 36.5 °C. Notable findings include a distended abdomen with shifting dullness, prominent epigastric vein dilation, and striae cutis distensae.

Laboratory studies:  
– Albumin 1.8 g/dL (4.1–5.1)  
– AST 79 U/L (13–30), ALT 62 U/L (7–23)  
– ALP 591 U/L (106–322), γ-GTP 115 U/L (9–32)  
– Creatinine 1.62 mg/dL (0.46–0.79)  
– Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.6–4.8)  
– Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL  
– Platelet count 324,000/µL  
– Prothrombin time 81.6% (70–140)

Imaging:  
– Abdominal ultrasound: Irregular liver surface, dull margins, heterogeneous parenchyma, suggesting chronic hepatitis.  
– CT abdomen: Gastro-renal shunt present; no definite esophageal or gastric varices.

Clinical course: Findings of ascites and collateral circulation raised suspicion for portal hypertension due to cirrhosis, and a liver biopsy was performed.

An 8-month-old boy of Turkish origin was referred to pediatric dentistry for unexplained early loss of his primary lower central incisors. He was the first child of healthy second-degree consanguineous parents; his younger sister was unaffected. On examination he had multiple facial, bodily, and intraoral injuries from self-mutilation. He was born with bilateral foot deformities managed by an orthopedic appliance. By age 6 years he sustained a metatarsal fracture leading to bone necrosis and hardware placement, and he used a wheelchair for long distances. He also suffered severe burns from boiling water without reporting pain. At 8 months, his mandibular central incisors exfoliated three months after eruption; the left lateral incisor was mobile (grade 2) and the mandibular left second primary molar showed enamel hypoplasia. He experienced no pain during dental procedures. One year later he had lost ten more primary teeth. Because of the premature tooth loss and self-mutilation behaviors, he was referred to the Department of Human Genetics for evaluation.

A 64-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of bilateral foot pain, erythema, and redness that was more prominent on the right. The pain was excruciating (10/10), burning in quality, and worsened with ambulation and when her feet were in a dependent position. 

Her medical history included hypertension, myelodysplastic syndrome in remission, and a stroke 2 years earlier for which she had been taking aspirin. Two weeks before presentation, she was found to have a right iliac artery thrombosis and was started on warfarin with discontinuation of aspirin. One week earlier, she had been treated elsewhere for presumed cellulitis with antibiotics, without improvement. She denied any trauma. Other medications were gabapentin, omeprazole, and atenolol.

On examination, she was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Distal pulses in the lower extremities were intact. There was blanchable erythema of both feet, worsening when the legs were moved from a supine to a dependent position. She reported increased pain and redness when wearing socks or under a blanket, and noted partial relief with a cooling fan or by pouring cold water over her feet. Sensation to light touch and pinprick was intact, and monofilament testing was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count, normal platelet count, and an elevated international normalized ratio (INR).

A 68-year-old man was evaluated for a 6-month history of frequent, urgent, and painful urination without fever. He had end-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy and underwent a living-donor kidney transplant in January 2001. His immunosuppressive regimen included mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus (switched from cyclosporine after treatment for acute T-cell–mediated rejection in December 2021), and prednisone. Serum creatinine had been stable at 140–165 μmol/L.  
On initial evaluation in June 2022, urine protein was 0.15 g/L, urinary white blood cells were 64.6/μL, and serum creatinine was 165 μmol/L. Empiric levofloxacin failed to improve his symptoms. On admission, physical examination showed pitting edema of both lower limbs. Urine cultures grew Enterobacter cloacae, and meropenem was started.  
Renal ultrasound demonstrated multiple heterogeneous echo foci in the transplanted kidney (largest 2.3 × 2.0 cm) with poor blood perfusion. Chest CT revealed masses in the upper and middle lobes of the right lung and multiple pulmonary nodules bilaterally, initially raising concern for malignancy or metastases. Abdominal CT showed enlargement of the transplanted kidney with multiple low-density lesions, peripancreatic exudation, and enlarged retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymph nodes.  
18F-FDG PET/CT revealed hypermetabolic lesions in the right lung, transplanted kidney, sigmoid colon, and multiple lymph nodes in the abdomen and left iliac fossa, leading to consideration of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.

A 3-year-old Caucasian girl was referred for evaluation of splenomegaly. Six months earlier she had a febrile illness with cough, mouth sores, and cervical lymphadenopathy; empiric antibiotics resolved the fever and malaise, but her spleen remained enlarged. Over time she developed abdominal distention, pain, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Initial evaluations for HIV, CMV, and EBV were negative, and gastrointestinal and metabolic causes were excluded. Abdominal ultrasonography and MRI showed a mildly prominent liver with diffuse multiple hypoechoic lesions and a markedly enlarged spleen with non-enhancing structures at the splenic hilum. On presentation she was playful and afebrile. Examination revealed a distended abdomen, splenomegaly extending to the superior iliac crest, and an umbilical hernia. Outside evaluation excluded hemolytic anemia (normal hemolytic anemia panel, hemoglobin electrophoresis, red blood cell enzymes, and osmotic fragility tests). Malignant infiltration was excluded by bone marrow aspirate/biopsy and brain/spine MRI. Metabolic disorders were excluded by normal karyotype, urine/serum organic acids, serum amino acids, plasma acylcarnitine profile, arylsulfatase B activity, and a normal lysosomal disease panel. Immune deficiency disorders and infections such as Toxocara, Brucella, Bartonella, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were excluded. Doppler abdominal ultrasound showed patent portal and splenic veins and confirmed splenomegaly with diffuse hypoechoic foci.

A 34-year-old woman with major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, bulimia nervosa, posttraumatic stress disorder, and a history of self-harm and suicide attempts has been receiving maintenance electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) for refractory mood symptoms and recurrent catatonic episodes. She is taking duloxetine 120 mg daily, buspirone 30 mg three times daily, and clonazepam 0.5 mg three times daily; lamotrigine was discontinued prior to ECT. She tolerated three inpatient ECT sessions, then continued outpatient treatments. Two weeks after hospital discharge, she underwent her eighth ECT session. Approximately one hour after the treatment, she became acutely confused, was non–command responsive, and repeatedly said “yes.” Her temperature was 38.0 °C; she was diaphoretic, and her pupils were equal, dilated, and reactive. Neurologic examination revealed hyperreflexia and psychomotor agitation with restless lower extremity movements. She received 1 mg IV midazolam with minimal improvement. A head CT scan showed no acute intracranial process.

A 12-month-old girl from Nakornsawan province presented with a painless, progressively enlarging round mass at the right costal margin. She had no fever, maintained a good appetite, but showed poor weight gain; her height and weight were both below the fifth percentile. There was no known tuberculosis contact, although her mother had completed treatment for tuberculous lymphadenitis more than ten years earlier. Natal history was unremarkable. Her immunizations included the national schedule plus pneumococcal, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and intradermal tuberculosis vaccine at birth; a BCG scar was noted on the right upper leg.

On examination, there was a 2 cm fixed, firm, round mass at the right anterior lower chest wall; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph demonstrated a moth-eaten osteolytic lesion of the right anterior eighth rib. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 12 790/mcL (20.4% neutrophils, 73.1% lymphocytes), platelets 339 000/mcL, alkaline phosphatase 201 U/L, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein 20.98 mg/L. Chest magnetic resonance imaging was obtained, confirming a mass at the right eighth rib.

The presumptive diagnosis was probable Ewing’s sarcoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and resection of the mass was arranged.

A 21-year-old woman was evaluated for a 6-month history of progressive weight loss, poor appetite, and profound weakness. Over the preceding 8 years, she had noticed gradually increasing patchy pigmentation of the skin and marked hair loss. She had never experienced menarche. She denied fever, diarrhea, sexual exposure, polyuria, or palpitations. 

On examination, she was 140 cm tall and weighed 20 kg (BMI, 10.8 kg/m2), with an emaciated appearance and moderate pallor. Her pulse was regular, and blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg without orthostatic drop. Secondary sexual characteristics were infantile. There was no edema, clubbing, icterus, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly. 

Dermatologic examination showed reticulate hyperpigmentation, telangiectasia, and scattered depigmented macules on the neck, chest, and flexural surfaces. The oral mucosa exhibited swollen gums and white patches over the tongue, hard palate, and buccal mucosa. She had diffuse scalp alopecia. The fingernails were brittle with vertical ridges. 

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL, white-cell count 3500/mm3, and platelet count 100,000/mm3. Electrolytes and serum albumin were within normal limits. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed a hypoplastic uterus and infantile ovaries. Antinuclear antibody testing was negative, and HIV serology was nonreactive. A cosyntropin stimulation test yielded a normal one-hour serum cortisol level. Thyroid‐function tests were normal. Serum luteinizing hormone, follicle‐stimulating hormone, estrogen, and progesterone levels were all low, consistent with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. A skin biopsy specimen was obtained for further evaluation.

A 27-year-old Hispanic woman with a history of nasal-type natural killer/T-cell lymphoma treated 12 years earlier with 8 cycles of CHOP chemotherapy (cumulative doxorubicin dose 320 mg/m2) and mediastinal radiation therapy presented with a 2–3-month history of fever, cough, shortness of breath, and a 20-lb weight loss. She denied chest pain, palpitations, edema, or claudication. Physical examination was unremarkable: blood pressure 108/57 mm Hg, pulse 86 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 100% on room air, normal jugular venous pressure, clear lungs, no murmurs or gallops, and no peripheral edema. Initial laboratory tests, including cardiac enzymes, B-type natriuretic peptide, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and iron studies, were within normal limits. Chest imaging revealed moderate bilateral pleural effusions. Thoracentesis with flow cytometry confirmed lymphoma relapse. A pre-treatment transthoracic echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 37%, confirmed by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging.

A 33-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 2 months of worsening neck pain and stiffness accompanied by intermittent bilateral hand tingling. He had sustained a whiplash injury in a motor vehicle accident 5 months earlier and had experienced minimal relief with topical diclofenac gel and physical therapy. On examination, there were no neurologic deficits. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Noncontrast CT of the cervical spine showed patchy sclerosing hyperostosis involving the base of the dens and the right lateral masses of C1 and C2, resulting in fusion of the odontoid process with the right C1 lateral mass and ossific remodeling reminiscent of "dripping candle wax."

An 80‐year‐old woman with hypertension (never smoked) presented with acute dyspnea. At 7:40 am she suddenly developed fecal incontinence, left hemiplegia, dextroversion, dysarthria, and vomiting; she was last seen well by family at 1 pm the previous day. At 8:20 am she arrived by ambulance with impaired consciousness (Japan Coma Scale II-10). Head CT showed right thalamic and putamen hemorrhage. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 12. Vital signs: blood pressure 91/– mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO₂ 86% on 4 L/min by nasal cannula. Oral hygiene was poor. Pulmonary exam revealed diminished left breath sounds and coarse crackles on the right. Despite 10 L/min by reservoir mask, SpO₂ could not be maintained above 90%, so she was intubated and mechanically ventilated. Chest CT showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and she was admitted to the ICU for severe pneumonia. Laboratory findings: WBC 1900/μL, CRP 3.6 mg/dL, PaO₂ 64 mmHg on 4 L/min O₂; normal liver and renal function. Chest radiograph demonstrated extensive infiltrates in the entire left lung and right lower zone. A-DROP score indicated severe pneumonia. Rapid antigen test for SARS-CoV-2 was negative.

A 59-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. On scene, he was in respiratory distress with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7 and was intubated. Breath sounds were absent on the right side, prompting needle decompression and placement of a right intercostal chest drain, which yielded minimal bloody output. On arrival, he was hypotensive and tachycardic. Pelvic X-ray showed an unstable anteroposterior compression fracture. A chest X-ray was interpreted as consistent with pulmonary contusion, and a focused assessment with sonography for trauma scan was negative. While receiving blood products, he was taken to a hybrid operating room for iliac angiography, which demonstrated a proximal cutoff of the left and right internal iliac arteries; both were embolized, resulting in temporary improvement in his hemodynamic status.

A 56-year-old Iranian woman presented with a one-month history of low-grade fever, generalized malaise, weight loss, anorexia, and palpable neck glands. She denied cough, sore throat, ear discharge, gastrointestinal symptoms, a history of tuberculosis, or high-risk exposures. Her past medical history was notable for hypertension and dyslipidemia. One month earlier, she had bilateral knee arthritis; laboratory studies then showed an isolated thrombocytopenia of 109×10^9/L (150–400×10^9/L) with normal leukocytes and hemoglobin, and tests for ANA, rheumatoid factor, and anti-CCP were negative.  

On examination, she was febrile but had no pallor or jaundice. There were firm, tender, discrete lymph nodes in the right upper cervical region, the largest measuring 2 cm; the cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Ultrasound of the neck revealed multiple cervical lymph nodes, the largest measuring 24 mm in the right submandibular area, and additional lymphadenopathy in the right axilla.  

Laboratory studies showed persistent thrombocytopenia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and elevated ferritin levels. She received a 7-day course of co-amoxiclav and metronidazole without clinical improvement and developed a generalized urticarial rash. She was then referred for an excisional biopsy of a cervical lymph node.

A 64-year-old Afro-Caribbean man with locally advanced prostate adenocarcinoma (T4 N0 M0, Gleason 4+5) was randomized to the transdermal estrogen arm of a clinical trial. Four weeks after starting three patches (100 µg/24 h, changed twice weekly), he noted tender lesions on his shins with painful swelling of his ankles, wrists, and left shoulder, followed by progressive fatigue. On oncologic review, swollen ankles and fatigue raised concerns for heart failure. His testosterone level had fallen to castrate levels, and the patch frequency was reduced per protocol. Seven days later, his general practitioner found bilateral subconjunctival hematomas and tender shin nodules. He was treated with oral diclofenac and misoprostol, oral cephalexin, and chloramphenicol eye drops without improvement. One week later, estrogen patches were discontinued and replaced with a luteinizing hormone–releasing hormone analog. Two weeks after the switch, he was admitted with worsening fatigue and arthralgia. Examination revealed sinus tachycardia (115 beats/min) with a normal electrocardiogram. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein of 122 mg/L (normal < 8 mg/L) and an alkaline phosphatase of 265 U/L (normal 30–130 U/L). A chest radiograph was unremarkable; tests for tuberculosis were negative, and streptococcal infection was excluded.

A 78-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe left thigh pain and spasms. Three days earlier, while squatting in his garden, he had sustained a small superficial scratch on his left thigh. The pain first appeared, lasted about one hour, then resolved without intervention before returning and becoming progressively worse and spasmodic. He described the pain as sharp, localized to the left thigh, with no radiation, no other symptoms, and no alleviating or aggravating factors.

On examination, his temperature was 37.3°C, pulse 119 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, blood pressure 159/104 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. A superficial scratch was noted on the left thigh with no other suspicious wounds. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 24.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophilia (21.8 × 10^9/L), creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, lactate 3.8 mmol/L, creatine kinase 980 units/L, and C-reactive protein 23 mg/L.

Initial differential diagnoses included aortic dissection, myositis, or skeletal injury, and a CT scan of the aorta showed no abnormalities. While in the ED, he experienced an episode of severe respiratory distress with inability to open his mouth and limited air movement, which resolved spontaneously. Shortly thereafter, he developed another episode of self-resolving trismus with oxygen desaturation to 85% on room air requiring 15 L/min via mask. He also developed a stiff neck.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of a progressively enlarging swelling of the left nasal ala. She noted difficulty breathing over the past 3 months and intermittent pain in the nasolabial fold for the past year. She had no history of facial trauma and no significant past medical history. On examination, there was a smooth, fluctuant mass over the left nasal ala and a palpable, floating tumefaction in the nasolabial sulcus. Intraorally, there was a bulge of the buccoalveolar sulcus on the left. All associated teeth were vital on electrical testing. Facial asymmetry was evident due to the left-sided swelling. A panoramic radiograph showed bone destruction in the region. CT imaging confirmed bony erosion and revealed a well-circumscribed cystic lesion adjacent to the left nasal ala. Ultrasonography demonstrated a 1.5 cm, well-defined cystic structure beneath the skin in the left nasolabial fold.

A 45-year-old man with a history of primary antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) presented for evaluation of sudden neurologic deficits. Eighteen months earlier, he had developed right-sided neck swelling, resting dyspnea, and small-volume hemoptysis. CT pulmonary angiography revealed pulmonary emboli in bilateral lower-lobe branches, and ultrasound showed right internal jugular vein thrombosis. Laboratory testing at that time showed antiphospholipid IgG 237 GPL (normal <10 GPL), lupus anticoagulant 164 s (normal 24–36 s), and factor V Leiden 49% (normal 78–152%). Secondary causes of APS were excluded, and he was treated with apixaban.

Over the following year, he remained on follow-up with occasional dyspnea until he developed dull, moderate left upper quadrant pain for three weeks. Abdominal CT showed splenomegaly with two hypodense lesions consistent with splenic infarctions. He was admitted and started on IV heparin, warfarin, and prednisolone 40 mg daily. Rheumatologic testing revealed positive extractable nuclear antigen, antiphospholipid antibodies, perinuclear ANCA, and anti-dsDNA >200 IU/mL; ANA and c-ANCA were negative. INR was 2.2, and PTT was 70 s (normal 25–35 s).

A few days later, he acutely developed right-sided weakness, dysarthria, vomiting, and diaphoresis. On examination, he was alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15; cranial nerves and sensation were intact. He had right upper and lower extremity weakness with an upgoing right Babinski sign. Brain CT was unremarkable. MRI of the brain showed acute ischemic infarction in the right brainstem, a lacunar infarct in the left occipital lobe, subacute cortical infarction with laminar necrosis, and an old superior sagittal sinus thrombus. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular thrombus with an ejection fraction of 55%.

To evaluate for other thrombotic microangiopathies, a peripheral blood smear was obtained and showed slightly reduced red cells with no nucleated or helmet cells and neutrophilia.

A 24-year-old previously healthy Afro-asiatic man presented with a 3-month history of headache and one generalized tonic–clonic seizure. He had no other symptoms. On examination he was afebrile, alert (GCS 15), and oriented. Neurologically, power was 4+ in the right upper and lower limbs; tone and reflexes were normal. General physical and systemic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including stool and urine tests, were normal. 
Noncontrast head CT showed a focal area of high density in the left parietal region. MRI of the brain revealed a fairly well-defined 1.8 × 1.0 cm lobulated, cortical-based intra-axial lesion in the left posterior parietal region with homogeneous enhancement, moderate perilesional vasogenic edema, and mild localized mass effect; no other lesions were identified. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrated a choline peak suggestive of cell membrane turnover seen in conditions such as neoplasms, demyelination, inflammation, and gliosis; given the patient’s age and history, an inflammatory lesion was thought to be more likely. 
A preliminary differential diagnosis included granulomatous lesion, lymphoma, primary glial neoplasm, and less likely meningioma.

An 89-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus presented with one week of swelling of the left hallux toenail. He had been seen by a podiatrist for a right foot injury when an incidental nodule was noted on the nail bed of the left hallux. On examination, there was a 0.7 cm × 0.8 cm pink, irregular, tender nodule over the distal nail bed of the left hallux, with onycholysis and destruction of the overlying nail plate. Dermoscopic examination under polarized light showed shiny white lines on a pink-orange background.

A 60-year-old man presented with headache following tympanic membrane surgery. He had no visual disturbances or focal neurologic deficits. On examination, he was alert and oriented; visual fields and formal ophthalmologic assessment were normal. Laboratory evaluation revealed mild central hypothyroidism not requiring hormone replacement. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the sellar region showed a 17 × 15 × 12 mm cystic lesion in the sella turcica with a thin peripheral enhancing rim on the left side. The lesion was isointense to brain on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images; no intracystic nodule was seen, and there was no displacement or compression of the optic apparatus. CT of the head demonstrated slight sellar enlargement without calcifications. Based on these findings, the differential diagnosis included Rathke’s cleft cyst and, less likely, craniopharyngioma or cystic pituitary adenoma. Given the absence of visual or neurologic compromise and the low probability of reversing mild hypopituitarism surgically, conservative management with close clinical, ophthalmologic, and radiologic follow-up was elected.

A 61-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented to the emergency department six days after discharge from a hospitalization for severe COVID-19 pneumonia. He had two days of worsening cough productive of blood-tinged sputum, dyspnea, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, and poor oral intake. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable but tachypneic with an oxygen saturation of 84% on room air; coarse bilateral crackles were heard on lung auscultation. He required 15 L of supplemental oxygen via nonrebreather mask to maintain oxygenation. Chest radiograph showed a marked bilateral interval increase in interstitial and airspace opacities with near-complete consolidation at the lingula compared to prior imaging. An initial nasopharyngeal RT-PCR test for SARS-CoV-2 was negative but was repeated the next day and returned positive. Laboratory studies showed a ferritin level of 2010 mcg/L (prior admission peak 4157 mcg/L), a C-reactive protein of 31 mg/L (prior peak 193.1 mg/L), an interleukin-6 of 7.2 pg/mL (prior peak 67.0 pg/mL), and a serum SARS-CoV-2 IgG index of 3.58.

A 41-year-old multigravida woman, unaware of her pregnancy, presented with one week of bilateral visual loss. Several days earlier, she had been treated for presumed pyelonephritis after low-grade fever and back pain. On exam, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/67 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye; intraocular pressures were 17 mm Hg and 15 mm Hg, respectively. Slit-lamp examination was unremarkable. Funduscopy revealed bilateral papilledema and severe macular edema with retinal hemorrhages and fibrin deposits. Her blood pressure was 230/168 mm Hg, and fluorescein angiography was aborted due to her poor condition. Spectral-domain OCT showed bilateral extensive serous retinal detachment with sensory retinal swelling, multiple intraretinal cysts, irregular retinal pigment epithelium undulations, outer-plexiform-layer delamination, and hyperreflective subretinal dots. Enhanced-depth imaging OCT demonstrated extreme choroidal thickening (>500 µm), an indistinct choroid–sclera border, barely identifiable lumens in Sattler and Haller layers, and an overall “ground glass” appearance. Ocular findings and systemic presentation suggested malignant hypertension or Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease.

A 75-year-old man with diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with a 6-month history of intense left flank pain. On examination, vital signs were stable and physical findings were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a left renal mass. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 7.3 × 5 cm eccentric parietal thickening of the descending colon with a cavitated center, displacing the left kidney anteriorly and with loss of cleavage planes involving the inferior third of the kidney, the psoas-iliac muscle, and the lateral abdominal wall; no distant metastases were observed. Laboratory studies revealed a serum creatinine level of 2.0 mg/dL, a glycosylated hemoglobin level of 8.8%, and a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 2.8 ng/mL; urine culture grew Escherichia coli.

A 21-year-old Thai woman presented with a 1-month history of blistering eruptions on the lips, hard palate, scalp, trunk, and extremities, accompanied by desquamation of the palms and soles. She also reported non-scarring alopecia and arthralgia.

On examination, there were multiple tense vesicles on the lips, hard palate, and scalp; tense bullae on an erythematous base over the trunk and extremities; and erythematous desquamated plaques on the palms and soles.

Laboratory studies showed hemolytic anemia with a positive direct Coombs’ test, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and positive antinuclear antibodies with a fine speckled pattern (titer 1:320) and a nucleolar pattern (titer 1:80).

A skin biopsy revealed focal interface dermatitis. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrated mixed linear and granular deposition of IgG, IgA, and C3, along with granular IgM deposition at the dermoepidermal junction and superficial blood vessels, and perifollicular deposition of C3. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay detected circulating antibodies to type VII collagen (>200 RU/mL).

A 62-year-old woman with well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a 2-day history of burning sensation and numbness in both hands and feet. The symptoms were exacerbated by standing and weight-bearing during walking and by warm stimulation such as bathing. She denied fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, or other complaints. On examination, temperature was 36.7℃, pulse 78/min, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air; she was alert and oriented. Her hands and feet were diffusely reddened; sensation was intact, and assessment of muscle strength was limited by pain on movement.
