Notably, her husband developed similar symptoms on the same day, raising concern for a contagious process.

A 29-year-old man presented with acute midsternal, sharp, severe chest pain radiating to the back that worsened when supine and improved by leaning forward. He also reported palpitations, shortness of breath, and cough. Vital signs were: temperature 37°C, heart rate 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 35 breaths/min, blood pressure 118/90 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air (on oxygen supplementation thereafter). On examination, lung fields were clear. Cardiac auscultation revealed normal heart sounds and a grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the left sternal border; there was no jugular venous distension, peripheral edema, or clubbing. 

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 8.11 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, negative high-sensitivity troponin, and a respiratory alkalosis on arterial blood gas. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus rhythm with a right bundle branch block. A chest radiograph revealed an enlarged cardiac silhouette and widened superior mediastinum without infiltrates. CT angiography of the chest identified a large pericardial effusion and a dilated superior vena cava with no pulmonary embolism. Noncontrast chest CT then showed a large atrial septal defect and total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, with pulmonary veins failing to drain into the small left atrium.

Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a large circumferential pericardial effusion without tamponade and severely dilated right atrium and ventricle. Emergent pericardiocentesis drained 900 mL of hemorrhagic fluid, but a repeat echocardiogram demonstrated reaccumulation, prompting a second pericardiocentesis that removed 520 mL of hemorrhagic fluid. Follow-up echocardiography revealed a large bidirectional atrial shunt and a small to moderate pericardial effusion. Given the unusual pulmonary venous anatomy and recurring hemorrhagic effusion, he was transferred to a tertiary center for further evaluation.

A 70-year-old woman presented with right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain without jaundice. She had a history of eosinophilic esophagitis treated with prednisolone (2.5–7.5 mg/d) for one year. On examination, she was tender in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6,800/µL with 6.9% eosinophils, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, hematocrit 38.3%, and platelet count 254,000/µL. Liver-function tests revealed AST 159 U/L, ALT 400 U/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 732 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 996 U/L, and total bilirubin 1.9 mg/dL. Hepatitis serologies, carcinoembryonic antigen, antinuclear antibody, antimitochondrial antibody, and serum IgG4 level were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated diffuse wall thickening and contrast enhancement of the common bile duct and gallbladder without radio-opaque stones. MRCP showed no common bile duct stricture. On hospital day 2, her abdominal pain worsened, and ultrasonography revealed gallbladder swelling and wall thickening with debris. Percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder aspiration relieved her pain but not her liver-function abnormalities. Endoscopic ultrasound showed diffuse thickening of the gallbladder and common bile duct walls. ERCP revealed no biliary strictures, and intraductal ultrasound confirmed diffuse common bile duct wall thickening.

A 4-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of slight intermittent leakage of clear fluid from a cutaneous pit that had been noted near the left sternoclavicular joint since infancy. On physical examination, there was a 1 mm diameter dermal pit situated just superior to the left sternoclavicular joint. 

Transverse and longitudinal grayscale sonography performed without sedation demonstrated a hypoechoic fistulous tract extending caudally from the dermal pit toward the left sternoclavicular joint.  

Magnetic resonance imaging performed without sedation revealed a well-circumscribed subcutaneous mass adjacent to the left sternoclavicular joint that was hyperintense on diffusion-weighted and T2-weighted sequences and hypointense on T1-weighted images.

A 2-year-7-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of microcephaly and marked growth retardation.  
History of Present Illness:  
– First year of life unremarkable. In year 2, he developed recurrent viral and bacterial infections (respiratory and urinary), including repeated CMV in urine and chronic norovirus diarrhea with persistent bloody stools. He had multiple hospitalizations and received eight courses of antibiotics in 1 year.  
– Failure to thrive and mild hepatomegaly noted.  

Examination:  
– Weight 10.3 kg (<3rd percentile), length 83 cm (<3rd percentile), head circumference 44 cm (<3rd percentile).  
– Skin scaly, dry, pale; hair dry, brittle, sparse. No focal neurologic deficits.  

Laboratory Studies:  
– CBC: WBC 2900/μl, Hb 6.8 g/dl, platelets 168 000/μl.  
– Lymphocyte subset analysis: total lymphocytes 484/μl, CD3+ 282/μl, CD4+ 214/μl, CD8+ 34/μl, CD19+ 1/μl, CD16/56+ 81/μl.  
– Immunoglobulins: IgG 924 mg/dl, IgA 112 mg/dl, IgM 63 mg/dl. IgG subclasses: IgG1 705 mg/dl, IgG2 43 mg/dl, IgG3 24 mg/dl, IgG4 <7 mg/dl. He lacked protective antibody titers after standard vaccinations.  

Additional Workup:  
– Cystic fibrosis, coeliac disease, other gastrointestinal disorders, and hepatitis were ruled out.  
– Genetic sequencing for RAG-1/2, Artemis, XLF, and TCF3 revealed no abnormalities.  
– Chromosomal analysis showed a balanced translocation 46,XY,t(1;19)(q21;p13), inherited from his healthy father.  

He was started on antibiotic, antiviral, and antifungal prophylaxis plus intravenous immunoglobulins. Genetic analysis for other causes of combined immunodeficiency was undertaken.

A 55-year-old man presented with 3 months of progressive exertional dyspnea, generalized weakness, and productive cough with brown sputum. One month earlier he had been evaluated elsewhere, treated with levofloxacin and prednisolone, and discharged on home oxygen without improvement. Medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and a 40-pack-year smoking history. Two months before presentation he had dry cough and dyspnea attributed to COVID-19; PCR was negative at this admission, but chest imaging showed diffuse bilateral infiltrates with ground-glass opacities and crazy-paving predominantly in the lower lobes. He was treated for presumed post-COVID fibrosis with superimposed infection, discharged on oxygen, antibiotics, and steroids, but returned 2 weeks later with worsened dyspnea, occasional dry cough, weakness, and fever to 38.6 °C. On exam his SpO2 was in the 70s on room air, with decreased air entry at both lung bases and minimal crackles. Laboratory studies showed WBC 14.7×10^3/mm^3 (86% neutrophils), CRP 78 mg/L, ESR 60 mm/hr. Arterial blood gas on 100% FiO2 via non-rebreather mask revealed PaO2 58 mmHg. Repeat chest X-ray and CT scan demonstrated worsening diffuse ground-glass opacities and crazy-paving without pulmonary embolism. Blood and sputum cultures and a COVID-19 PCR were negative. Over the next 5 weeks he deteriorated on high-flow oxygen and finally agreed to diagnostic bronchoscopy.

A 12-year-old girl with Turner syndrome (45,X), short stature, aortic stenosis, and partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage was evaluated for microcytic anemia. Diagnosed prenatally, she received recombinant human growth hormone from ages 4 to 15 years. At age 11, she presented with severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin, 5.3 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume, 56 fL) and a positive fecal occult blood test. Iron supplementation produced only transient improvement. Thyroid function was normal, and celiac disease was excluded. Laboratory studies showed red-cell anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, and hypochromia, with low serum iron despite normal absorption. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Gastroscopy and scintigraphy for Meckel’s diverticulum showed no abnormalities. Capsule endoscopy and full colonoscopy were then performed, revealing widened venous vessels just beneath an otherwise normal mucosa throughout the colon and in the terminal ileum.

A 71-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis and stress incontinence presented with worsening lower extremity spasms and new visual hallucinations. Routine laboratory tests revealed a serum creatinine of 8.18 mg/dL (baseline normal 3 months earlier). She received intravenous fluids without improvement and was transferred for nephrology evaluation. She denied fever, chills, rash, urinary symptoms, or decreased urine output. Medications included long-term amantadine and nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily, which she had continued for over 3 months after cancellation of an elective urologic procedure. On examination, she was lethargic with altered mental status; vital signs were normal and lungs were clear. Laboratory studies showed creatinine 7.6 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 60 mg/dL, bland urine microscopy (no cells or protein), negative urine cultures, urine protein/creatinine ratio 0.20 mg/mg, and an absolute eosinophil count of 1.8 × 10^3/µL. Liver tests, albumin, and complete blood count were otherwise unremarkable. Renal ultrasound showed no stones or hydronephrosis. Vasculitic screening, autoimmune panel, serum immunoglobulins, protein electrophoresis, complement levels, hepatitis B and C serologies, and parathyroid hormone level were all within normal limits.

A 48-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and psoriasis presented with a 2-day history of acute diffuse abdominal pain. On arrival, she was tachycardic (heart rate 130/min), hypotensive (blood pressure 78/45 mm Hg), afebrile, and fully oriented. She received intravenous fluids with improvement in blood pressure and heart rate. Initial laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 8.3 × 10^3/µL, arterial pH of 7.29, and lactate of 3.5 mmol/L. An acute abdominal radiograph demonstrated free air beneath the right hemidiaphragm. Examination of the abdomen showed distension, tenderness, guarding, and signs of peritonitis. Because her vital signs stabilized after resuscitation, a contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan was obtained to localize the source of the pneumoperitoneum.

An 87-year-old bedridden woman with Alzheimer’s dementia and no family support, living in a nursing home, developed fever and vomiting and was admitted to a local hospital. A diagnosis of intestinal obstruction was made, and nasogastric decompression and conservative treatment led to symptomatic improvement, but abdominal radiography continued to show persistent intestinal gas. She was transferred to another hospital, where noncontrast CT showed a high-intensity shadow in the upper small intestine with a change in caliber, and was referred for suspected small-bowel tumor.

On admission to our hospital, her temperature was 37.8°C, heart rate 90/min, and blood pressure 130/75 mm Hg. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 8.3×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 59.1 mg/L, hypoproteinemia from prolonged fasting, aspartate aminotransferase 48 U/L, and otherwise normal liver and biliary enzymes. Plain abdominal radiography demonstrated dilated small-bowel loops. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed biliary emphysema and a large intraluminal mass in the small intestine with Hounsfield units ranging from 31 to 134; the mass had migrated distally compared with the prior CT. Abdominal ultrasonography identified a mobile echogenic mass with an acoustic shadow within the small bowel.

We considered an enterolith, gallstone, or bezoar as the cause of obstruction and placed an ileus tube under endoscopic guidance. Small-bowel series with amidotrizoate via the ileus tube showed no diverticula, and duodenal series showed no biliary-enteric fistula. Multiple gastric stones containing hair suggested a bezoar. We recommended surgical removal, but the patient declined invasive treatment.

A term female neonate was delivered vaginally to a 25-year-old G2P1 mother. Apgar scores were 6 and 7 at 1 and 5 minutes. The parents left before NICU admission and returned 14 hours later with the baby due to inability to suck and progressive respiratory distress. The mother had routine antenatal care; a third-trimester ultrasound noted polyhydramnios without fetal anomalies. No family history of congenital malformations was reported.

On examination, the neonate was in severe respiratory distress with chest-wall retractions, nasal flaring, tachypnea, and central cyanosis. Dysmorphic features included macrocephaly, frontal bossing, sutural diastasis, depressed nasal bridge, low-set ears, extreme shortening of the upper and lower limbs with multiple circumferential skin folds, brachydactyly, a narrow chest, and protuberant abdomen. The head was not trilobed. Anthropometric measurements were: weight 2.5 kg; length 38 cm (upper segment 27 cm, lower segment 11 cm; US:LS ratio 2.45); occipitofrontal circumference 40 cm; chest circumference 27 cm (OFC:CC ratio 1.5).

Plain radiographs showed macrocephaly with craniofacial disproportion, a narrow thorax with flattened ribs, poorly aerated lung fields, shortening of the long bones with a telephone-handle configuration of the humeri and femora bilaterally, and flattening (platyspondyly) of the vertebral bodies.

A previously healthy 2½-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of a 2-week history of fever, left knee pain, and a mild cough. He had a history of consuming unpasteurized milk. On examination, the left knee was swollen, warm, and painful with limited range of motion, and mild pain was noted on flexion of both hips. Laboratory testing showed a white-cell count of 15,300/mm3 (65% neutrophils), hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, platelets 456,000/mm3, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 25 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein level of 40 mg/dL. Diagnostic arthrocentesis of the knee yielded fluid with 15,000 white cells/mm3 (85% neutrophils), 2,000 red cells/mm3, glucose 62 mg/dL, and protein 4 g/dL; Gram stain and cultures of synovial fluid were negative. A tuberculin skin test and blood cultures were negative. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were normal. Chest radiography and abdominopelvic ultrasonography were unremarkable. However, a spiral chest computed tomography scan showed multiple bilateral parenchymal nodules up to 4 mm.

An 84-year-old man was referred after an unsuccessful elective colostomy reversal. He had undergone a Hartmann procedure for sigmoid volvulus 3 months earlier. His medical history included 8 years of hypertension managed with amiloride and benign prostatic hyperplasia treated with tamsulosin. He appeared non-toxic; vital signs were within normal limits. Postoperatively he had not passed stool. On examination his abdomen was soft, without tenderness or rebound; other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed:
- WBC 13.3×10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL (13–16)
- Platelets 331×10^3/µL (150–450)
- Urea 35 mg/dL (11–55), Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (0.6–1.3)
- AST 28 U/L (≤37), ALT 11 U/L (≤41), ALP 139 U/L (100–360)
- Total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL (0.3–1.2), Direct bilirubin 0.1 mg/dL
- PT 12.9 s (12–14), PTT 28 s (25–45), INR 1.03
- Blood glucose 122 mg/dL (<140)
- Electrolytes normal, amylase 71 U/L (<100), lipase 16 U/L (<60), troponin negative

A preoperative abdominal radiograph showed irregular high-opacity shadows in the adipose and muscular planes near the colostomy site. At laparotomy, there were dense retroperitoneal adhesions, and a firm, bone-like structure was found in the abdominal wall adjacent to the surgical scar. The colostomy was reversed and the hard tissue was resected and sent for histopathologic examination.

A 28-year-old man presented with progressive painless facial swelling over the last seven months and a change in his voice.  
His medical history was notable for end-stage renal disease of undetermined etiology for nine years, currently on hemodialysis three times per week, severe uncontrolled secondary hyperparathyroidism, and hypertension. He denied vision impairment, hearing loss, dyspnea, or dysphagia.  
On arrival, his blood pressure was 161/101 mmHg; other vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed a hard, bony craniofacial protrusion most pronounced along the maxilla, without tenderness.  
Laboratory studies showed:  
• Urea 13.4 mmol/L (4.2–7.2)  
• Creatinine 920 µmol/L (64–115)  
• Estimated GFR 6 mL/min/1.73 m2  
• Phosphate 1.65 mmol/L (0.80–1.45)  
• Alkaline phosphatase 1714.3 U/L (50–116)  
• Calcium 2.080 mmol/L (2.100–2.550)  
• Parathyroid hormone 3012 ng/L (15–65)  
Noncontrast CT of the facial bones was performed:  
– Scout film demonstrated overgrowth of the jaws, particularly the maxilla, with multiple tiny lucencies in the calvaria (“salt-and-pepper” appearance).  
– Axial, coronal, and sagittal images showed significant jaw overgrowth with internal serpiginous tunneling or channeling and loss of corticomedullary differentiation.  
– Sagittal images revealed sclerosis of the vertebral endplates (“rugger-jersey spine”).

A 71-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of constant, progressive right shoulder pain and stiffness, accompanied by numbness along the arm. She had a 10-year history of diabetes mellitus and no known tuberculosis exposure.  
On examination, she was afebrile. The right hand was mildly swollen, and two firm, mobile right axillary lymph nodes (largest 1.5 cm) were palpable.  
Laboratory tests showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level, with normal white-cell count and differential. The interferon-gamma release assay was positive. Chest radiograph was normal.  
Right shoulder radiograph showed lytic and sclerotic lesions in the humeral head, preserved joint space, and a blurred soft-tissue shadow in the subdeltoid bursa without calcification.  
Ultrasound of the right shoulder revealed diffuse subdeltoid bursa wall thickening, moderate hypoechoic fluid, numerous well-defined hyperechoic oval lesions without acoustic shadowing, and rotator cuff tendinitis. Sonography of the right axilla showed multiple lymph nodes with thickened cortex and preserved hilum.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder demonstrated multiple lesions in the humeral head that were hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on proton-density fat-saturated sequences, and showed thick rim enhancement postgadolinium. There was diffuse synovial and bursal thickening with vivid enhancement, an 11-mm joint effusion, and numerous free intra-articular and bursal nodules (approximately 7 mm) that were hypointense on all sequences without contrast enhancement. Several mildly enlarged axillary lymph nodes were also noted.

A 65-year-old man with known myelodysplastic syndrome, not yet on therapy, presented to the emergency department with acute epigastric pain radiating to his back, associated with dyspnea, nausea, and vomiting. He denied any trauma, fever, hematuria, or urinary symptoms. His blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg. Laboratory studies showed a platelet count of 82 000/mm3, prolonged INR and aPTT, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and anemia; serum lipase and amylase levels were normal. A contrast-enhanced multislice CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed bilaterally and symmetrically enlarged adrenal glands that were round and demonstrated hyperdense areas on precontrast images (mean attenuation, 55 Hounsfield units), mild peripheral heterogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase, stranding of the periadrenal fat, and small pleural effusions. The patient received blood transfusions and prompt glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement therapy.

A 74-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease presented with a five-year history of right ureteral obstruction treated with ureteral stents every six months. She had documented chronic infection with Extended-Spectrum Beta-Lactamase–producing Klebsiella pneumoniae. Recent imaging revealed obstruction at the right renal pelvis with pyohydronephrosis. On ureteroscopy, the renal pelvis had a cobblestone appearance; the bladder was unremarkable, and the left kidney showed compensatory changes but was otherwise normal. Her medical history included diabetes mellitus and well-controlled hypertension; there was no history of urinary reflux, exstrophy, or paralysis. A right nephroureterectomy was performed.

A 16-year-old girl presented with one week of progressively worsening shortness of breath. Over the preceding two months, she had a nonproductive cough, nocturnal fevers, 10 kg weight loss, migratory joint pains, and fatigue. Two months earlier, she had been HIV-tested (negative) for her cough and fever, but no further follow-up occurred.

On admission she was tachypneic (RR 40/min), tachycardic (HR 148/min), febrile (37.8 °C), and required 6 L/min of oxygen by face mask to maintain SpO₂ 100%. Blood pressure was 123/85 mmHg. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral crepitations; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory testing showed microcytic anemia (Hb 7.6 g/dL, MCV 76 fL) and leukocytosis (WBC 15.4 × 10⁹/L); renal function and electrolytes were normal. Chest radiography revealed innumerable small “miliary” nodules in both lungs. Chest CT confirmed diffuse miliary nodules without mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy.

Differential diagnoses included pneumocystis pneumonia, viral or fungal pneumonia, miliary tuberculosis, and metastatic disease. She was reviewed by infectious diseases, placed in isolation, and another rapid HIV test was negative. A QuantiFERON assay was sent, and empiric therapy with levofloxacin, fluconazole, and acyclovir was started.

On hospital day 2 she deteriorated (SpO₂ 70% on 15 L nonrebreather), was intubated for moderate ARDS (PF ratio 130), and treated with lung-protective ventilation (tidal volume 6 mL/kg, PEEP 10 cm H₂O). Neuromuscular blockade with cisatracurium was initiated for worsening oxygenation (PF ratio 113). Further history from her parents revealed contact with a relative who had a prolonged nonproductive cough.

On day 3 she became hypotensive (MAP < 60 mmHg) and febrile. Multiple fluid boluses and a norepinephrine infusion (up to 50 µg/min) failed to restore hemodynamics and her condition continued to deteriorate.

A 32-year-old man with a 12-day history of ulcerative colitis treated with mesalazine (1.5 g twice daily) presented with a 24-hour history of severe (8/10) central chest pain radiating to the left shoulder and back. He also reported mild dyspnea and generalized weakness but denied cough, fever, or other flu-like symptoms. On examination, he was afebrile, normotensive, and had a normal heart rate and oxygen saturation; cardiovascular and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed clear lung fields and a normal cardiothoracic ratio. A 12-lead ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with concave ST-segment elevation in leads I, II, and V4-6. Laboratory studies revealed a troponin-I level of 6.53 ng/mL (normal < 0.5), CK-MB of 65 IU/L (normal < 25), and a C-reactive protein of 105 mg/dL (normal < 5); leukocyte and eosinophil counts were within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a normal‐size left ventricle with preserved systolic function (ejection fraction 55–60%), normal global longitudinal strain, no pericardial effusion, and no significant valvular disease.

A 73-year-old woman with gastroesophageal reflux disease presented with a 3-day history of severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the right shoulder, back, and flank. The pain worsened after meals and when she lay flat or on her right side, but was otherwise constant. She reported passing a small amount of flatus the day before and had nausea and difficulty taking a deep breath due to the pain. She denied fever, vomiting, changes in bowel habits, hematochezia, and dysuria. She had no prior abdominal surgeries and no history of smoking or alcohol abuse.

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Lying flat provoked severe pain. There was tenderness in the right upper quadrant and epigastrium, but Murphy’s sign was negative. There were no peritoneal signs, jaundice, or costovertebral angle tenderness. Laboratory studies showed normal liver function tests, normal lipase and lactate levels, and no pyuria. Right upper quadrant ultrasound was negative for cholecystitis or gallstones. A computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a gaseous-distended distal ileum interposed between the liver and the right upper anterior abdominal wall, without wall thickening or adjacent fat stranding.

An 89-year-old man, previously healthy and living independently, was evaluated for a 6-month history of difficulty walking on uneven ground and a 1-month history of intermittent episodes of disorientation and amnesia accompanied by moderate balance impairment. He had known obstructive asthma, bilateral hearing loss, cataracts, and eczema; he was a former smoker.

On initial evaluation, neurologic examination and noncontrast head CT were unremarkable. Mini–Mental State Examination (MMSE) was 30/30; clock drawing was normal. Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer’s Disease (CERAD) testing revealed only decreased verbal fluency (8 points) and delayed word recall (62%).

Two months later, he was admitted with severe balance and cognitive impairments and urinary and fecal incontinence. MMSE was 15/30; CERAD testing was abnormal in 8 of 10 categories. Brain MRI without gadolinium showed bilateral hippocampal atrophy (2/4) without other temporomedial atrophy. On examination, he was alert but disoriented to time and place, spoke in a low voice, had slight upward gaze restriction, static tremor of the upper extremities, a pronounced startle response with eyes closed, brisk tendon reflexes, and a slow, wide-based gait. No myoclonus was observed. EEG showed only slight generalized disturbance.

Laboratory evaluation revealed an elevated serum anti-thyroglobulin antibody titer with normal thyroid function tests and negative onconeuronal antibodies. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated a slight lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and a positive protein 14-3-3 assay. Infectious studies and bacterial cultures of CSF were negative.

A 55-year-old man presented with a 6-year history of dysesthesia described as sensations of movement beneath the skin, accompanied by pruritus, erythema, burning, and pain. He believed “flies and worms” were emerging from his skin and attributed his symptoms to a parasitic infection, noting prior camping and travel—including South Carolina, South Florida, the Bahamas, Kansas, Louisiana, Texas, New York, Colorado, and Nevada—in which he felt he might have been exposed. His medical history was notable for a primary immunodeficiency of unknown etiology diagnosed 5 years earlier and treated with immunoglobulin; there was no history of diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency.

Over the course of his illness, he remained afebrile and received multiple courses of antiparasitic agents (ivermectin, albendazole, permethrin, and praziquantel), antibacterial agents (doxycycline and ciprofloxacin), and antifungal therapy without improvement. He subsequently developed nodules, erosions, and ulcers on his extremities, including a persistent ulcer on his left second finger from scratching and attempts to extract the presumed pathogen. 

Multiple skin biopsies revealed chronic spongiotic dermatitis, acute and chronic folliculitis, and panniculitis. Bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures were repeatedly negative, and serologic studies showed no evidence of infection. A duplex ultrasound of the upper extremities ruled out vascular disease. Although many lesions healed, the ulcer on the left second digit progressed to cellulitis and osteomyelitis, necessitating surgical amputation.

He presented to the dermatology clinic carrying his amputated left second finger in a glass container and requested evaluation to identify the causative organism. On examination, he had erythematous, eczematous patches on the face, chest, abdomen, back, and arms, along with excoriated papules and generalized xerosis. His left second digit showed a healing stump.

A 44-year-old lactating woman with no breast complaints underwent a screening breast ultrasound that revealed multiple small (≤7 mm), hypoechoic, non-parallel lesions with irregular margins and peripheral vascularity in the outer quadrants of both breasts. These foci were soft on shear-wave elastography (Emax < 20 kPa), without calcifications, enhancement, or acoustic shadowing. Ultrasonography of both axillae showed enlarged hypoechoic lymph nodes up to 21 mm in length with a 4 mm-thick hypoechoic cortex and preserved hilar vascularization. Mammography demonstrated a predominantly glandular pattern without architectural distortion or microcalcifications. 

Given the numerous BIRADS-4 breast lesions, a 14-gauge core-needle biopsy of the dominant breast lesion was performed, yielding three specimens. Histopathology revealed no malignant tumour cells and multiple non-necrotizing granulomas with multinucleated giant cells. A diagnosis of granulomatous lobular mastitis (GLM) was initially considered, and testing for Corynebacterium spp. in the biopsy material was negative. 

To extend the work-up, a 14-gauge core-needle biopsy of an enlarged axillary lymph node (three cores) was performed; histology showed clusters of epithelioid cells with sparse multinucleated giant cells and no necrosis. These findings led to the suspicion of sarcoidosis and referral for pulmonary evaluation.

A 29‐year‐old woman presented with a two‐month history of progressively worsening mucosal ulcerations. She reported an initial small ulcer on the lateral tongue, which she self-treated with an alcohol‐containing “Natural Green Tea” mouthwash; this was followed by widespread oral ulcerations and severe lip swelling with hemorrhagic crusts that bled easily. She had a history of recurrent mouth ulcers but had never experienced lesions of this severity. She denied fever or known allergies.

On examination, there was marked edema of the upper and lower lips with hemorrhagic crusts. Intraorally, the labial mucosae were macerated with multiple shallow ulcers surrounded by erythematous rims. Additional irregular ulcers were present on the buccal mucosa on both sides, the ventral and lateral tongue surfaces, and the floor of the mouth. The gingiva of teeth 21–24 showed painless erythema with diffuse borders.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL (low), WBC 9.4×10^3/µL, differential within normal limits.  
• Total IgE 612 IU/mL (reference <100).  
• Anti–HSV-1 IgG 5.73 U/mL (nonreactive <9).

A 14-year-old male high-school quarterback presents two days after injuring his right buttock playing football. He bent awkwardly to retrieve a loose ball behind him and was tackled, immediately feeling a sharp, constant deep pain in the right buttock that radiated to the hip. He was unable to continue playing and now ambulates with a significant limp. He denies numbness or weakness. There is no bruising or swelling.

On examination, vital signs are normal. He is 175 cm tall and weighs 58 kg (BMI 18.9 kg/m2). Hip range of motion is limited chiefly by pain: forward flexion to mid-thigh, normal extension, and a straight-leg raise to about 30° on the right. He is tender medial to the right ischial tuberosity without edema or ecchymosis. The neurovascular examination is unremarkable.

Plain radiographs of the pelvis and right hip are unremarkable.

A 59-year-old man presented to the emergency department with dyspnea at rest and right loin pain eight weeks after augmentation of an ileal neobladder. His past medical history included polycystic kidney disease, and he was receiving oral antibiotics for a presumed urinary tract infection. He had undergone radical cystoprostatectomy and Studer pouch reconstruction one year earlier and neobladder augmentation cystoplasty three months before presentation.

On examination, he appeared cachectic with dry mucous membranes. His respiratory rate was 26 breaths per minute, heart rate 108 beats per minute, and blood pressure 92/64 mmHg. Cardiorespiratory and abdominal examinations were otherwise unremarkable, and his surgical incision was well healed.

Initial blood tests showed a leukocyte count of 14.1 × 10^3/μL and a C-reactive protein of 23.3 mg/dL. Biochemistry revealed a potassium of 3.3 mmol/L, creatinine of 304 μmol/L (baseline 98 μmol/L), and urea of 33.1 mmol/L; all other electrolytes were within normal limits. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated an uncompensated metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap of 12.1 mEq/L. Urinalysis showed microscopic hematuria and sterile pyuria. The ECG revealed sinus tachycardia and the chest radiograph was normal.

The patient was admitted with a presumed diagnosis of severe urosepsis and acute kidney injury and was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, urinary catheterization, and crystalloid resuscitation. Over the next 48 hours, he became increasingly confused and dyspneic. A repeat arterial blood gas showed a worsening hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

A 34-year-old man with no significant medical history reported an 18-month history of swelling and pain in the floor of his mouth, especially during meals. He also noted mild dry mouth and episodes of spontaneous pus discharge beneath his tongue. On examination, there was bilateral submandibular region swelling with palpable tender lymph nodes. Milking of the right submandibular gland produced purulent discharge at the sublingual caruncle, and overall salivary flow was slightly reduced. Intraoral palpation of the floor of the mouth revealed two firm structures, one on each side, without overlying mucosal erythema. A computed tomography scan of the submandibular regions demonstrated two well-defined, radiopaque structures, each approximately 10 mm in diameter, localized near the hila of both submandibular glands.

A 73-year-old woman with a history of gout, rheumatoid arthritis, right carpal tunnel release, and right hip and left knee arthroplasties presented with a slowly enlarging mass over her left shoulder that had been present for several years. She denied any history of trauma. The mass was associated with significant pain. On examination, there was a palpable, soft, mobile mass approximately 5 cm in diameter over the acromioclavicular area; it was extremely tender to palpation. She had full range of motion of the elbow, wrist, and hand, intact distal sensation, and no signs or laboratory evidence of infection. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the shoulder revealed a 10.5 cm × 3.4 cm × 4.4 cm cystic-appearing mass arising from the acromioclavicular joint and extending into the superior fibers of the trapezius muscle, with peripheral and septal enhancement. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and contained septations. MRI also demonstrated diffuse rotator cuff tendinopathy, superior migration of the humeral head, a focus of avascular necrosis of the glenohumeral head with partial collapse, multiple intra-articular bodies, and glenohumeral and acromioclavicular osteoarthritis.

A 55-year-old woman with no prior surgeries or trauma presented with a 5-year history of left-sided neck swelling. On examination, there was an 8 × 5 cm elastic, soft, painless subcutaneous mass on the left side of the neck without skin adhesion. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed an indistinct lesion with signal intensity equal to fat on T1-weighted imaging and high signal on fat-suppressed T2-weighted imaging; the left external jugular vein coursed through the lesion, which extended from the internal jugular vein to the posterior surface of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Ultrasonography revealed a subcutaneous mass with echoluminance comparable to fat. Considering the possibility of angiolipoma or venous malformation, an incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia, during which milky white fluid flowed from the lesion.

A 25-year-old active duty male presented with a 5-month history of bilateral calf pain (left worse than right) triggered by running, described as tenseness, cramping, and numbness in the feet that resolved after 20–30 minutes of rest. Initial radiographs and bone scan were negative. Postexercise compartment pressures in the left leg rose markedly, with the deep posterior compartment increasing from 34 mmHg preexercise to 66 mmHg postexercise. He underwent an elective left leg fasciotomy, but symptoms persisted and worsened over two years, now occurring with lower-intensity activity. On examination, the posterior tibial pulse was diminished and became impalpable during ankle dorsiflexion, and weight-bearing plantarflexion immediately reproduced his symptoms. MRI of the left leg showed no anatomic abnormality of the medial head of the gastrocnemius.

A 48-year-old non-smoking man presented with progressive dyspnea and left chest pain three months after a blunt chest trauma. Initial chest radiography showed a left pleural effusion, and a chest tube drained serosanguinous, exudative fluid; cytology was negative for malignancy and all other laboratory tests were within normal limits. After removal of the tube and discharge, dyspnea and chest pain recurred days later. CT of the chest revealed a left pleural effusion, left lung collapse and soft-tissue edema. Thoracoscopy was converted to a limited thoracotomy for decortication; multiple biopsies were non-diagnostic. The patient was discharged with a presumed diagnosis of hemothorax secondary to trauma.

Three months later, he returned with left chest pain and an area of softening and excavation over the anterior left hemithorax. Chest CT demonstrated mild left pleural effusion, nodular pleural thickening, destruction of the left anterior ribs and suspected masses. CT-guided biopsy was non-diagnostic, so an anterolateral thoracotomy was performed; intraoperatively there was pleural thickening, diffuse soft-tissue inflammation and complete destruction of anterior ribs. Multiple biopsies again yielded non-specific findings.

Twelve days after discharge, he presented with swelling of the left chest wall and flank. CT showed reaccumulation of fluid and collapse of the left lower lobe and lingula. A chest tube drained 800–1500 mL daily; the fluid appeared milky and laboratory tests confirmed it was chylous. Because the diagnosis remained unclear, a repeat thoracotomy was performed, revealing complete destruction of ribs two through six and multiple small nodules on the internal rib surfaces. Portions of ribs, adjacent soft tissue and lung were resected and sent for histologic examination.

A 17-year-old previously healthy male presented with recurrent severe right pharyngeal pain. He described intense paroxysmal electric shock–like pain lasting seconds to minutes in a well-defined unilateral area from the right tongue root to the pharynx, occurring about 10 times per day and triggered by tongue movement or deglutition. There were no bradycardia or syncopal episodes. He rated the pain 8/10. 

Magnetic resonance imaging with CISS sequence demonstrated compression of the right glossopharyngeal nerve by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. Examination by otorhinolaryngology and other cranial nerves was normal, and there were no signs of Eagle’s syndrome. A diagnosis of glossopharyngeal neuralgia was made. High-dose carbamazepine, up to 800 mg daily, initially provided relief but only transiently; baclofen 5 mg daily was ineffective. Two years later, owing to refractory pain and imaging evidence of nerve compression, he underwent microvascular decompression with postoperative cerebral venous sinus thrombosis that resolved without sequelae. 

One year after surgery, he developed new severe lancinating pain in the right preauricular region radiating to the mandible, worsened by lying down or chewing, with a maximum pain score of 8–10/10. These features were consistent with trigeminal neuralgia. Carbamazepine, increased to 800 mg daily, provided initial relief but then lost efficacy over several months. His quality of life was significantly impaired—he could not brush his teeth, chew solid food, or sleep. Trials of pregabalin (up to 450 mg), duloxetine (60 mg), and tramadol (300 mg) yielded no improvement.

An 8-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder presented with a several-month history of limping and recurrent left knee pain localized chiefly to the back of the knee, worsened by activity and partially relieved by rest. Clinical examination was limited by the patient's cooperation; there was no swelling or joint-line tenderness. Range of motion of the left knee was slightly limited in extension compared with the right side, and flexion was painful and mildly restricted. McMurray, Lachman, and varus/valgus stress tests were negative. Plain radiographs of the knee were normal. Because of the patient’s difficulty remaining still, an MRI was performed under general anesthesia. Scans revealed a 29 mm × 16 mm × 17 mm well-defined septated cyst in the intercondylar notch between the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, abutting primarily the posterior cruciate ligament. On proton density–weighted and turbo spin echo images, the mass was homogeneous and low in signal intensity, slightly hyperintense relative to muscle, and on turbo inversion recovery magnitude images it was hyperintense.

A 46-year-old woman presented with recurrent, intermittent, painless hematuria over the past six years. Two years ago she was diagnosed with systemic hypertension and has been taking irbesartan 150 mg daily, along with various herbal remedies for her hematuria. 

On examination, her vital signs were within normal limits, and systemic examination was unremarkable. Urinalysis showed 3+ blood and 5.1 red blood cells per high-power field; phase-contrast microscopy revealed 70% dysmorphic red cells. Serum electrolytes and renal function tests were normal. An abdominal ultrasonogram demonstrated a fatty liver and multiple small (“sand-like”) stones in the left kidney. 

To further evaluate her hematuria, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen was performed.

A 30-year-old Japanese man presented with a 4-month history of right leg discomfort, swelling, and intermittent serosanguinous drainage. His medical history was significant for osteomyelitis of the right leg at age 4, treated with intravenous antibiotics; thereafter he experienced mild, self-resolving “flare-ups” every few months during adolescence, which responded to rest and NSAIDs. He reported that the current episode did not resolve with rest or NSAIDs and that drainage had persisted for 2 weeks from a central punctum. He denied fever, chills, sharp pain, sensory changes, or restriction of active or passive range of motion.

Plain radiographs of the right knee showed no evidence of acute osteomyelitis or fracture. MRI of the right thigh demonstrated a 6.8 × 5.3 × 8.5 cm septated fluid collection extending from the subcutaneous adipose tissue along the lateral thigh through a fascial perforation posterior to the vastus lateralis, with diffuse soft-tissue edema but no periosteal or marrow edema. Orthopedic consultation determined that no acute intervention was required and recommended outpatient follow-up. Initial culture and biopsy of the lesion revealed granulation tissue with skin flora. Concern for a cold abscess versus malignancy prompted transfer of care to orthopedic oncology for surgical exploration.

A 76-year-old German Caucasian woman with a history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis in remission for more than 30 years, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, and heavy cigarette smoking presented with increased glare and a sudden decrease in visual acuity in both eyes over a few days. Her ophthalmic history included left-eye amblyopia, retrobulbar optic neuritis in the left eye in 1986 and in the right eye in 1987 (diagnosed as MS and treated with azathioprine), and bilateral cataract surgery with intraocular lens implantation in 2012. Six months before presentation, she experienced decreased vision in the right eye diagnosed elsewhere as anterior uveitis and vitreous hemorrhage, but she did not follow up.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was counting fingers in the right eye and 0.32 in the left eye without improvement with refraction. Intraocular pressures were 19 mmHg (right) and 22 mmHg (left). Slit-lamp examination of both eyes showed 3+ anterior chamber cells, granulomatous endothelial precipitates, vitreous turbidity with cells and snowballs, mild sheathing of retinal vessels, and adjacent retinal hemorrhages. In the left eye, there were posterior synechiae and precipitates on the IOL surface.

Macular optical coherence tomography in the right eye revealed inflammatory cells in the vitreous, an epiretinal membrane, preserved foveal architecture, and parafoveal thickening without cysts or detachment; the left eye showed inflammatory cells, an epiretinal membrane without traction, and preserved foveal architecture without cysts or detachment. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated in the right eye blockage of choroidal fluorescence from vitreous opacities, ischemic areas in the inferotemporal arcade, collateral vessel formation, and leakage near the optic nerve head and along retinal veins; the left eye showed similar blockage, macular leakage, and periphlebitis.

Neurologic examination was normal with intact cranial nerves, no motor deficits, no pyramidal signs, and normal reflexes. MRI of the orbits showed no optic neuritis, and brain MRI revealed no acute inflammatory lesions. Paraclinical testing showed: normal serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and unremarkable chest x-ray; negative ANA and ANCA; HbA1c 5.2%; no cardiac arrhythmias; negative serologies for syphilis, Bartonella, and Lyme disease; carotid Doppler without plaques, dissection, or stenosis; and vitreous biopsy from the right eye showing no malignant lymphocytes with negative PCR for Herpes simplex, Varicella Zoster, Cytomegalovirus, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A 37-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 1-week history of dry cough and dyspnea on exertion. She denied fever or chills but reported a 20-lb weight loss and anorexia over 2 months. She immigrated from Nigeria 2 years earlier, is a lifelong nonsmoker, and takes no medications. 

On examination she was in mild respiratory distress. Temperature was 99 °F, pulse 152 beats/min, blood pressure 116/83 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. She had hepatomegaly; the remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, platelets 94 000/µL, AST 664 U/L, ALT 1703 U/L, LDH 3462 U/L, and CPK 2742 U/L. A rapid HIV test was positive; CD4 count was 8 cells/µL and HIV viral load exceeded 10 million copies/mL. Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody were positive, with a viral load >17 million IU/L.

Chest radiography revealed bilateral homogeneous ground-glass opacities. Chest CT showed lower-lobe predominant bilateral ground-glass opacities and atelectasis.

Differential diagnosis included Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, atypical bacterial pneumonia, and viral infections. The patient was started empirically on intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (220 mg trimethoprim component every 6 hours) plus oral prednisone 40 mg daily for presumed PJP, and on ceftriaxone with azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia. 

Over the next 48 hours her respiratory distress worsened, and she required endotracheal intubation. Arterial blood gas analysis on 100% FiO2 showed a PaO2 of 157 mm Hg with an alveolar–arterial gradient of 506 mm Hg. She subsequently underwent flexible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial lung biopsy because of poor response to standard therapy.

A 10-year-old girl was referred for fever and painful genital ulcers. Three days before admission, she had fever, sore throat, and mild dry cough; a rapid group A streptococcal antigen test was negative. On day 3 of fever, she developed intense pain and burning in the genital area. At admission, she remained febrile with cough but had no abdominal pain or diarrhea. Examination showed painful ulcers of variable depth and diameter with elevated violaceous borders inside the labia majora; there were no oral ulcers or lymphadenopathy. She was not sexually active and had no prior history of similar lesions. She was treated with intravenous antibiotics and local antiseptic care. Cultures from the lesions were negative for bacteria, and PCR of tissue for herpes simplex virus was negative. Serologic tests for HSV-1 and HSV-2 antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase) were all negative. Four days later, the genital lesions had significantly improved, but fever and cough persisted. Chest radiography revealed a right-sided pneumonia, and oral azithromycin was added.

A 37-year-old nulliparous woman presented to the emergency department with continuous dull lower abdominal pain. One week earlier she had a positive urine pregnancy test; her last menstrual period corresponded to 5 weeks 5 days of gestation. Her medical and surgical history were unremarkable, and she had not undergone any fertility treatments or had known risk factors for ectopic pregnancy.

On examination, she was hemodynamically stable. Abdominal palpation revealed mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant without peritoneal signs. Pelvic examination elicited pain in the right adnexa; there was no vaginal bleeding.

Laboratory studies were within normal limits except for a serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin concentration of 5436 mIU/mL.

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple subserosal uterine fibroids (largest diameter 41 mm) and a single intrauterine gestational sac measuring 7.3 mm, with a fetal pole of 1.7 mm and visible cardiac activity. In the right fallopian tube, there was a 64 × 32 × 29 mm hypoechoic mass with minimal blood flow on Doppler. The pouch of Douglas was free of fluid, and both ovaries appeared normal.

Differential diagnosis included hydrosalpinx, hematosalpinx, ovarian torsion, and heterotopic pregnancy.

A male neonate was born at 38 + 5 weeks’ gestation by cesarean delivery to a 33-year-old G4P2+1 mother. Prenatal findings included mild polyhydramnios, chorioamniotic membrane separation, and an enlarged fetal gastric bubble. At birth (weight 2800 g; Apgar scores 9, 10, 10), he was tachypneic (respiratory rate 55/min). Examination revealed sharply demarcated absence of skin along Blaschko’s lines over the anteromedial lower legs extending to the feet, and skin absence on the nasal tip, ears, right neck, and right hip; mucosal absence was noted in the oral cavity. These defects covered about 17% of the body surface and were accompanied by scattered blisters, with adjacent skin appearing normal but showing a strongly positive Nikolsky sign. Both external ears were dysplastic.  
He was placed in a temperature-controlled incubator (34 °C, 55% humidity), received total parenteral nutrition, antibiotics, wound care with alternate-day dressings, analgesia, and oxygen.  
A plain abdominal radiograph demonstrated a single gas bubble in a distended stomach with no gas in the distal bowel.

A 47-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of dysarthria and dysphagia. He denied frank swallowing difficulty but noted subtle tongue‐movement impairment and frequent inadvertent tongue biting. His medical history was notable for multiple cerebral aneurysms, with cerebral angiography performed 6 months earlier. He drank alcohol occasionally and denied tobacco use. On neurologic examination, he had an isolated left hypoglossal nerve palsy without involvement of other cranial nerves. High-resolution MRI with CISS sequences showed a dilated, tortuous left vertebral artery with atherosclerotic changes compressing the V4 segment of the left hypoglossal nerve, which consisted of two thin bundles coursing along the artery into the hypoglossal canal. The contralateral hypoglossal nerve appeared linear and unremarkable. Intracranial vessels were overall dilated and tortuous, and additional findings included a partially thrombosed large left MCA saccular aneurysm and a fusiform left PICA aneurysm.

A 56-year-old man, 7 months after live-donor renal transplantation (induced with basiliximab; maintained on prednisolone, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil), presented with a progressively enlarging lesion on the plantar surface of his right foot. Four months post-transplant, he noted a pea-sized nodule that evolved into an ulcero-proliferative, cauliflower-like mass. He denied trauma or travel to endemic regions. His course was complicated by new-onset diabetes mellitus (HbA1c, 11.4%) and a rise in serum creatinine from 1.2 to 2.8 mg/dL.

Examination revealed a 6.0×3.2 cm fungating lesion with necrotic granulation tissue, indurated margins, and occasional foul discharge; there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy, and systemic examination was unremarkable. Complete blood count, metabolic panel, and chest radiograph were normal. Urinalysis was unremarkable; VDRL and HIV tests were negative. Doppler ultrasonography of the lower limbs was normal, and imaging showed no bony involvement. The lesion was completely excised and sent for histopathologic examination.

A 26-year-old woman was brought to the hospital on postpartum day 3 because of sudden onset of bilateral lower-extremity weakness and numbness. She had an uncomplicated first pregnancy and a normal vaginal delivery, during which an epidural was placed at L2–L3 without use of heparin or other anticoagulants. One and a half hours after delivery, she noted inability to move her legs and numbness from the waist down, along with difficulty voiding and constipation. 

Her vital signs were normal. On neurological examination, mental status and cranial nerves were intact. She had flaccid paraparesis (MRC score for iliopsoas 2/5 on the right, 1/5 on the left), absent knee and ankle reflexes bilaterally, and a right Babinski sign. Pain and temperature sensation were lost below L1, whereas vibration and proprioception were preserved. 

CT angiography of the artery of Adamkiewicz revealed tandem narrowing most pronounced at T10–T11. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the thoracolumbar spine showed bilateral “owl’s eyes” hyperintensities at T10–T11 without evidence of cord compression or stenosis. 

On admission, platelet count was 222 × 10^9/L (previously 250 × 10^9/L three days earlier), D-dimer 5213 ng/mL (reference <500), and fibrinogen 3.21 mg/mL. On subsequent testing, fibrinogen levels ranged from 2.14 to 3.51 mg/mL. Anti–human heparin platelet factor 4 (anti-PF4) antibody was 58.89 ng/mL (reference <50) in the absence of heparin exposure.

A 54-year-old recreational male trail runner (∼5 hours per week) presented with several months of palpitations at rest and during exercise. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, dizziness, syncope, stimulant use (including caffeine), illicit drugs, supplements, or recent infection. His medical history was unremarkable; he had no hypertension, diabetes, or smoking history. Family history included a mother who died suddenly at 72 (no autopsy) and a father who died at 60 of chronic illness. 

On examination, blood pressure was 124/81 mm Hg, heart rate 66 beats/min; cardiac and pulmonary exams were normal. Laboratory tests were within normal limits, with no elevation of creatine kinase or troponin. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm, normal atrioventricular and intraventricular conduction, and low QRS voltage (<0.5 mV in limb leads). 

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated nondilated ventricles and atria, preserved systolic and diastolic function, and no valvular disease. On exercise stress testing (Bruce protocol), he achieved 107% of maximum predicted heart rate, with isolated infrequent polymorphic PVCs suggesting both LV and RV origins, three ventricular couplets, and one monomorphic triplet; no PVCs occurred during recovery. 

A 24-hour Holter monitor recorded frequent PVCs (419 total, 0.5% of all beats), frequent couplets, and one 5-beat run of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia; the predominant PVC morphology was negative in both leads, with other morphologies also noted.

A 30-year-old Chinese woman presented with a 6-year history of painless swelling in the left submandibular region that, over the last 3 months, had begun to extend to the root of the neck. On examination, there was an approximately 12 cm × 6 cm soft, fluctuant, non-tender mass in the left anterior cervical region, with no swelling visible in the floor of the mouth. Color Doppler ultrasound showed a well-defined, anechoic, loculated fluid collection in the left superficial anterior cervical region—extending from the mandibular angle to the suprasternal fossa—measuring about 10.98 cm × 1.49 cm × 4.92 cm, with poor internal sound transmission, visible soft-tissue separations, and no obvious blood-flow signal on color-flow Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a non-enhancing cystic lesion extending from the submandibular region to the supraclavicular region. Fine-needle aspiration in clinic yielded an egg white–like liquid discharge.

A 50-year-old woman was transferred at 23:00 for acute-onset, severe, retrosternal squeezing chest pain and dyspnea. She had a history of bilateral peroneal neuropathy of unknown origin and a cerebral hemorrhage 6 years earlier (decompressive craniotomy). She had well-controlled hypertension on long-term diltiazem and no diabetes, dyslipidemia, smoking, or family history of coronary artery disease.

An ECG from the referring hospital showed ST-segment elevation in the inferior, anterolateral, and posterior leads, and dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus ticagrelor) was started. On admission, vital signs were stable and the cardiovascular exam was unremarkable. A repeat ECG showed persistent ST-segment elevation in the same leads. Laboratory tests revealed troponin T 50 ng/l and myoglobin 89 ng/l. Complete blood count, liver and renal function, lipid profile, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were normal or negative. Echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 64% with segmental wall-motion abnormalities in the inferior and posterior walls.

The patient was diagnosed with acute inferior myocardial infarction. Emergency coronary angiography revealed nonobstructive coronary arteries; intracoronary nitrates relieved her chest pain. Continuous nicorandil infusion and antiplatelet therapy were continued and troponin I levels decreased.

Three days later, she developed recurrent chest pain progressing to cardiogenic shock with troponin T >2000 ng/l. She required intubation, mechanical ventilation, and vasopressor support. PET-CT demonstrated diffuse elevated myocardial metabolism in the interventricular septum, lateral wall, and inferoapical regions, with patchy mild uptake in the right ventricular epicardium and increased metabolism in segments of the right coronary and left circumflex arteries. Myocardial perfusion scintigraphy showed a perfusion-metabolism mismatch in the apical and mid-inferior walls.

Since admission, she had worsening right lower limb pain. Electromyography confirmed bilateral peroneal nerve damage. Serologic testing revealed negative antinuclear antibodies and positive anti–proteinase-3 ANCA.

A female infant was delivered at 39 4/7 weeks’ gestation by cesarean section for suspected fetal distress. At birth she was hypotonic and cyanotic, with a faint cry, bradycardia, and irregular respirations; Apgar scores were 3, 5, and 8, and birth weight was 3220 g. A chest radiograph showed bilateral homogeneous opacification consistent with voluminous pleural effusions. In the delivery room, she underwent orotracheal intubation, bilateral thoracocentesis, and paracentesis due to anasarca and respiratory failure.

The mother was 30 years old, gravida 2 para 1, with four prenatal visits. Her blood type was A, Rh-positive; tests for irregular anti-erythrocyte antibodies were negative. Serologies for HIV, syphilis, and parvovirus were negative; she was immune to rubella and cytomegalovirus and susceptible to toxoplasmosis. A fetal ultrasound at 40 weeks showed hydramnios (amniotic fluid index, 31.4 cm) and signs of fetal hydrops (pleural effusion and ascites), not previously detected.

On physical examination, the newborn had a flattened nose, low-set ears, a short neck, and a nuchal fold. She had relapsing non-chylous pleural effusions, predominantly on the right, requiring thoracic drainage. Abdominal ultrasound showed moderate ascites with thin septa. Echocardiography revealed no structural cardiac malformations, and the karyotype was 46,XX.

A 72-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, treated with methotrexate for 1 year, was admitted initially for acute pancreatitis of unknown etiology. She denied alcohol, recreational drugs, or supplements. There was no family history of liver disease. Admission liver chemistries were: total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL, AST 125 U/L, ALT 94 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 468 U/L, and INR 1.3. Despite treatment for pancreatitis, her liver function progressively deteriorated, prompting concern for drug-induced liver injury and initiation of intravenous methylprednisone and N-acetylcysteine. She then underwent transjugular liver biopsy, which revealed steatohepatitis, minimal fibrosis (1a/4), cholestasis, and anisonucleosis, described as “consistent with methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity vs Wilson disease.” Transferred to our center with worsening hepatocellular injury, she developed hemolytic anemia, acute renal failure, depressed mental status, and worsening jaundice. Evaluation for Wilson disease included ophthalmologic assessment of Kayser-Fleischer rings, which was equivocal, and laboratory testing showing serum copper 79 μg/dL, 24-hour urinary copper excretion 31 μg/24 hr (GFR 34 mL/min/1.73 m²), ceruloplasmin 14 mg/dL, and nonceruloplasmin bound copper 37 μg/dL.

67-year-old woman with 33 years of intermittent wheezing and cough, and 7 years of exertional dyspnea. Symptoms began after colds, recurred every 1–2 years, and most recently worsened 22 days earlier with fever (38.2°C); treated as an asthma exacerbation with IV methylprednisolone and moxifloxacin with slight improvement. No hemoptysis, night sweats, rash, or joint pain. History of allergic rhinitis; no smoking or TB history. Physical examination notable for diffuse inspiratory and expiratory wheezes.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 11.7×10^9/L (82.5% neutrophils, 0% eosinophils); total serum IgE 444 KU/L with Artemisia argyi IgE 100 KU/L.  
Pulmonary function tests: FEV1/FVC 55.7%, FEV1 61.5% predicted, negative bronchodilator response.  
Chest radiograph: atelectasis of right middle and lower lobes and linear opacities in the left lung.  
Chest CT: irregular high-attenuation thickening of the tracheal wall, main bronchi, lobar and proximal segmental bronchi, with luminal stenosis and right middle/lower lobe atelectasis.  
Bronchoscopy: diffuse, circumferential mucosal thickening of the trachea and bilateral main bronchi with multiple nodular protuberances and narrowed lumens.

A 12-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a 2-month history of right wrist pain, swelling, and overlying skin redness without fever, rash, diarrhea, or preceding infections. At 1.5 years of age, he had recurrent right knee swelling every 5–6 months with fever spikes that resolved with NSAIDs. He was misdiagnosed with juvenile idiopathic arthritis and treated with prednisolone and methotrexate until age 5, after which therapy was stopped during a remission. Subsequently, he developed two aseptic abscesses of the right chest wall (surgically drained) and another non-responding right ankle abscess complicated by osteomyelitis on MRI; cultures remained sterile. 

On examination, he was afebrile and normotensive, with two surgical scars on the right chest wall and two on the right ankle. There was localized tenderness, swelling, and erythema over the right wrist radial side with limited range of motion; adjacent joints were normal.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 6.9×10^9/L, hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, ESR 19 mm/h, CRP 4.6 mg/L, normal immunoglobulin levels, normal liver and kidney tests, negative virology screens, and negative interferon-gamma release assays. Wrist swab cultures yielded no growth. CT of the wrist showed normal bone alignment and density. A bone biopsy demonstrated no evidence of a bone infection or malignancy.

A 60-year-old woman presented to the emergency department after a syncopal episode during which she struck her head. She reported the syncope was associated with acute central abdominal pain radiating to her back. On arrival she was initially hemodynamically stable but had a transient drop in blood pressure to 75/60 mmHg that responded to intravenous fluids. Her heart rate was 70 bpm in sinus rhythm, and all other vital signs were within normal limits. She had no significant medical history or cardiovascular risk factors.  

On examination, her abdomen was soft with central tenderness but no signs of peritonism. No abdominal masses were palpable, and the abdominal aorta was not palpable. Initial laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 7.8 g/dL and an international normalized ratio of 1.3; all other laboratory values were unremarkable.  

The initial working diagnoses included aortic dissection, perforated viscus, and severe pancreatitis. A contrast-enhanced CT angiogram of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a 6-mm pseudoaneurysm arising from a branch vessel approximately 3 cm distal to the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, accompanied by a large mesenteric hematoma measuring 4.5 × 8.0 × 13 cm and a high-volume hemoperitoneum. There was no active contrast extravasation.

A 12-year-old boy from southern Ethiopia presented with 3 days of severe colicky right upper quadrant pain lasting 10 minutes per episode, with no clear aggravating or relieving factors. The pain was associated with nausea and non-bilious vomiting. One month prior, he had passed an Ascaris worm and was treated with oral albendazole. He had no other significant history.

On examination, vital signs were normal. He had slightly icteric sclera and mild tenderness over the liver, which spanned 11 cm. Initial laboratory tests showed a normal complete blood count and ova of Ascaris lumbricoides on stool examination. Liver enzymes were elevated (AST 86 U/L; ALT 141 U/L), and total and direct bilirubin levels were 1.84 mg/dL and 1.31 mg/dL, respectively.

Abdominal ultrasound performed the same day showed two adjacent, well-defined, tubular, hyperechoic structures with a central lucency on subcostal axial view within the common bile duct and right intrahepatic duct. The common bile duct was dilated to 1 cm, and the proximal intrahepatic ducts were mildly dilated.

An 87-year-old Cantonese-speaking man with Alzheimer’s dementia, hypertension, stroke, hyperlipidaemia, gout, peptic ulcer, and chronic kidney disease presented with one week of increasing left leg pain and weakness, impaired mobility, and a single episode of urinary incontinence. He also reported anorexia and a 12% body-weight loss over six months.  
On examination, his blood pressure was 88/45 mmHg (responsive to IV fluids), heart rate 96/min, temperature 36.4 °C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He weighed 51 kg (BMI 19 kg/m2). Cardiac and chest examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination was normal. Neurologic examination showed 4/5 strength in left hip and knee flexors and extensors; the rest of the exam was normal.  
Initial laboratory results demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 76 mg/L, WCC 11.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.5 × 10^9/L) and pre-renal acute-on-chronic kidney injury.  
An initial differential of cauda equina syndrome or epidural abscess prompted an urgent MRI of the lumbar spine, which showed mild foraminal narrowing at L5–S1 but no central canal stenosis or abscess. He was admitted for possible sepsis; chest X-ray, atypical pneumonia serology, and urine microscopy and culture were all unremarkable. A plain X-ray of the left hip showed no fracture.  
Despite analgesia, his left hip pain worsened, strength declined to 2/5 at the hip and 3/5 at the knee, and CRP and ESR continued to rise. A left hip ultrasound revealed a small anterior joint effusion. Normal tumour markers, MRI of the hip, and an isotope bone scan argued against malignancy. Attempts at hip aspiration were unsuccessful. Colchicine was started for presumed crystal arthropathy and atorvastatin was discontinued for possible myopathy, but creatine kinase was normal, and symptoms persisted.  
An MRI of the hips and pelvis then demonstrated bilateral iliacus and iliopsoas muscle oedema with enhancement and a left-sided insertional tendinopathy, with no evidence of trochanteric bursitis.

A 29-year-old Indonesian woman, gravida 2 para 1 at 39 weeks’ gestation, presented with a 5-day history of COVID-19 confirmed by PCR, accompanied by gross hematuria, dry cough, fever, dyspnea, nausea, anosmia, and fatigue. She had no prior medical history and no family history of hematologic disorders. On examination, she was fully conscious, blood pressure 109/77 mmHg, heart rate 89/min, respiratory rate 28/min, temperature 37.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 100% on 2 L/min nasal cannula. Fetal heart rate was 142/min, and estimated fetal weight was 4 kg without signs of distress.  
Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral bronchopneumonia. Laboratory studies on admission showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.8×10^9/L (neutrophil–lymphocyte ratio 11), lymphocytes 696/µL, platelet count 2×10^9/L, PaO2/FiO2 ratio 200, C-reactive protein 7.77 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.35 ng/mL, prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time 54.9 s, d-dimer 1400 ng/mL, fibrinogen 333 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed 2+ proteinuria, gross hematuria, and pyuria. Renal, electrolyte, and liver functions were normal. Peripheral blood smear revealed spherocytes. Serologies for HIV, cytomegalovirus, and hepatitis B and C were negative.

A 14-year-old boy with severe developmental delay, dysmorphic facial features, cranial nerve dysfunction, and a known hindbrain malformation presented with progressive difficulty walking. He had a history of failure to thrive as an infant and underwent cardiac evaluation shortly after birth for multiple murmurs.

On examination, his head was normal in size with plagiocephaly; he had a high, broad forehead; long, narrow face; flat midface; small mouth; hypertelorism; bilateral ptosis; and short palpebral fissures. Facial scars and a notched nose from self-mutilation were noted. He had mild pectus excavatum, long fingers, and a positive thumb-and-wrist sign. Neurologically, he had bilateral facial paresis, generalized hypotonia, was nonverbal, and nonambulatory, though he could bear weight and cruise.

Cardiac MRI demonstrated an enlarged aortic root with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 48% (under anesthesia) and a normal right ventricular ejection fraction of 54%. Genetic testing for Marfan syndrome was negative.

MRI of the brain and cervical-thoracic-lumbar spine showed hypoplasia of the cerebellar peduncles and vermis, with an abnormal bulge of the pontine tegmentum into the fourth ventricle. There was dextroconvex thoracolumbar scoliosis due to multilevel vertebral segmentation anomalies, including a right T3 hemivertebra, a butterfly vertebra at T6, and hypoplastic ribs at L1.

A 66-year-old Caucasian French man presented with a 2-day history of incoherent, pressured speech. Six days earlier he had developed dysuria; urine culture grew Klebsiella pneumoniae at 10^5 CFU/ml with leukocyturia and he was started on levofloxacin 500 mg daily. After 5 days, levofloxacin was replaced with sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim (800/160 mg twice daily) per antibiogram. On the evening of the first day of the new regimen, following the morning and evening dose, he exhibited a sudden onset of incoherent logorrhea. Two days later, levofloxacin was resumed, but 48 hours passed without improvement, and he was brought to the emergency department.

On examination he was hemodynamically stable, afebrile, and alert, with prominent incoherent, rapid speech; burning micturition persisted. His medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, hypertensive heart disease, obesity (BMI 35), insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes, placement of a pacemaker, and sleep apnea. He had a prior urinary tract infection in 2020 attributable to benign prostatic hypertrophy. There was no immunosuppression, no known neurological disease, and no recent changes in medications other than antibiotics.

Laboratory studies showed creatinine 120 µmol/L (reference 59–104) with clearance 54 ml/min/1.73 m^2 (normal >90), serum sodium 132 mmol/L, and normal potassium, chloride, and bicarbonate. C-reactive protein was <5 mg/L; liver tests, complete blood count, hemostasis panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, albumin, and glucose were normal. Blood alcohol and toxicology screens were negative. Urinalysis revealed 17 leukocytes/mm^3, 11 red cells/mm^3, no organisms on microscopy, and a final culture with coagulase-negative staphylococci at 10^3 CFU/ml, suggesting contamination. Brain CT revealed no abnormalities; abdominopelvic CT showed no obstructive uropathy but a distended bladder. Catheterization evacuated 400 ml of urine without any change in his neurocognitive state.

He was admitted for further evaluation and antimicrobial therapy was adjusted: levofloxacin was stopped and ceftriaxone 2 g daily was begun to complete a 14-day course. Repeat blood tests were unchanged. Additional studies showed 08:00 a.m. cortisol 603 nmol/L, ammonemia 23 µmol/L, creatine kinase 51 IU/L; blood cultures were sterile. Lumbar puncture at 48 hours yielded acellular fluid with normal biochemistry; Alzheimer’s markers, S-100, and neuron-specific enolase were normal. Renal function normalized (creatinine 74 µmol/L, clearance >90 ml/min/1.73 m^2) and the urinary infection resolved, but his incoherent pressured speech persisted.

A 14-year-old white girl was referred to nephrology in November 2018 for evaluation of right-eye inflammation and abnormal urinalysis. She had a history of obesity, impaired glucose tolerance, hyperlipidemia, and borderline hypertension managed with lifestyle modifications. Family history was positive for hypertension but negative for metabolic syndrome. She denied any recent drug exposures, allergies, infections, or systemic symptoms.

One week before presentation, she developed redness, pain, tearing, and decreased vision in the right eye. Ophthalmologic examination led to a diagnosis of acute anterior uveitis, treated with topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics, with symptomatic improvement.

On admission, her pulse was 100 beats/min, blood pressure 126/81 mmHg, and temperature 36.5 °C. Review of systems was otherwise unremarkable, and right-eye symptoms were improving.

Investigations:
- Renal ultrasound: normal  
- Chest radiograph: normal  
- Laboratory results: ESR 98 mm/hour; CRP 13 mg/L; hemoglobin 113 g/L; serum creatinine 80 µmol/L; proteinuria 0.38 g/day; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 58 mg/g; urine α1-microglobulin-to-creatinine ratio 3.24 mg/g; glycosuria (1+).  
- Complement and serologies: C3 2.01 g/L; negative ANA, ENA, anti-DNA, and ANCA.

Borderline blood pressure readings and persistent abnormalities in ESR, renal function, and urinalysis prompted a renal biopsy.

A 45-year-old Caucasian woman with a 10-year history of diabetes mellitus (on NPH insulin) and hypertension (on enalapril) presented with fatigue and painful, erythematous nodules on the posterior and medial aspects of both lower legs. She was afebrile (35.7 °C). Examination showed subcutaneous nodules measuring 2–3 cm in diameter with overlying marked erythema. 

A biopsy of one lesion revealed caseous necrotic granulomatous panniculitis. Immunohistochemical staining for BCG antigen was positive. A tuberculin skin test showed 15 mm of induration. Serologic tests for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B were negative. Extensive evaluation for active tuberculosis—including chest radiography, CT of the chest and abdomen, three urine cultures, three sputum Ziehl–Neelsen stains, and gastric fluid studies—was unrevealing.

She was started on rifampicin, isoniazid, and pyrazinamide. Ten days later, she developed marked asthenia, depressive mood, and dizziness on standing without documented orthostatic hypotension. Sertraline was initiated and uptitrated to 300 mg/day with no improvement. She was hospitalized three times for heart failure and hyponatremia (serum sodium, 125 mg/dL). During the last hospitalization, insulin was discontinued because of good glycemic control.

Six months after starting anti-tuberculosis therapy, she developed facial hyperpigmentation. A skin biopsy showed only a nonspecific increase in melanin. Because of the combination of hyponatremia, improved glucose control, ongoing asthenia, low blood pressure, and facial hyperpigmentation, a serum cortisol level was ordered.

A 59-year-old Brazilian man with a history of presumed rheumatoid arthritis presented with several months of severe occipital headache and neck pain radiating to the left arm. He had been diagnosed 10 years earlier with polyarthritis of large and small joints, morning stiffness, subcutaneous nodules on extensor surfaces, and hand and foot deformities, and was maintained on methotrexate and low-dose prednisone. He also had hypertension treated with captopril, propranolol, and hydrochlorothiazide. 

On examination, blood pressure was 130/80 mm Hg. He had swan-neck deformities of the fingers, camel-back deformities of the wrists, fixed deformities of the feet and knees with severely limited range of motion, and multiple subcutaneous nodules over the elbows. Neurologic examination revealed mild (4/5) left brachial paresis, shoulder muscle hypertrophy, and hyperreflexia (3/4) in the upper limbs, with preserved sensation but signs of autonomic dysfunction. 

Laboratory studies showed a serum uric acid of 8.6 mg/dL, triglycerides elevated, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, and negative rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies. Cervical MRI demonstrated a destructive lesion of the odontoid process, and CT of the upper cervical spine showed hyperdense foci within C1 suggestive of microcrystal deposition. Radiographs of the knees, feet, ankles, and hands revealed periarticular soft-tissue swelling, extensive bone erosions, joint-space narrowing, and normal bone density.

A 22-year-old man presented with a lifelong history of poor dentition and a chief complaint of wanting evaluation and treatment for his jaw. He denied pain, numbness, facial asymmetry, or drainage. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, with no relevant family history. On intraoral examination, a condyloma acuminatum was noted on the lower lip. A panoramic radiograph showed mixed radiopaque lesions in both the maxilla and mandible, as well as multiple impacted and malformed teeth. Subsequent cone-beam CT revealed:

• Generalized multilocular mixed radiopaque and radiolucent trabecular pattern in the tooth-bearing regions of both jaws
