• Absence of enamel in multiple maxillary and mandibular teeth  
• Enlarged pulp chambers, apically positioned furcations, and shortened roots in tooth #19 and right molars, consistent with taurodontism  
• Multiple large radiolucent areas within the bone  
• Focal enlargement of the maxilla and mandible, most pronounced on the left side  
• Thinning of the buccal cortical plate and disruption of the lingual cortical plate on the left mandible

A 44-year-old woman with a 4-year history of treated depressive episodes presented with 5–6 months of intermittent stiffness of all four limbs, progressive decrease in activity, oral intake, and interpersonal interaction, and 1 month of limb posturing with involuntary movements. There was no fever or family history of neurologic disease. On admission, she was alert and oriented; vitals were normal and she was afebrile. Examination showed decreased muscle bulk, increased tone with rigidity in all limbs, power 4/5, brisk deep tendon reflexes, mute plantar responses, and resting and action tremors. Routine blood tests—including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, ESR, CRP, serum ammonia, and blood gases—were unremarkable. Autoimmune and infectious markers were negative, and cerebrospinal fluid studies for bacterial and viral pathogens were normal. Brain MRI showed no intracranial abnormality, and the MR Parkinsonism index was 11.3 (within normal limits). Two days into hospitalization, she became disoriented, mute to verbal and superficial pain stimuli, retained response to deep pain, exhibited prolonged staring, and maintained fixed postures. Funduscopic exam was normal, and a head CT was unrevealing. A lorazepam challenge (2 mg IV) produced initial hypotension but no reduction in rigidity or improved interaction; ongoing lorazepam worsened sedation without neurologic benefit, and was discontinued when she developed jaw rigidity, sialorrhea, and hypothermia (95 °F). Arterial blood gas analysis remained normal. She was then evaluated for autoimmune causes of her presentation, especially myxedema coma or autoimmune thyroiditis.

A three-month-old, sexually intact female Suri alpaca was evaluated for her two-week history of anorexia, delayed growth, and poor body condition. On admission she had a dull hair coat and a body condition score of 2/9. Serum chemistry and urinalysis were unremarkable except for mild hypoproteinemia (total serum protein 53 g/L; reference range 55–70 g/L). Serial fecal flotations and bovine herpesvirus type 1 serology were negative, and abdominal ultrasound was normal. A presumptive diagnosis of protein–energy malnutrition was made, and a high-energy diet was instituted.

Three days later, despite no reported ocular trauma, extensive superficial corneal ulcerations with mild corneal edema were noted in both eyes. Topical neomycin–polymyxin B ointment was started every 8 hours OU. On the second day of therapy, both eyes developed marked melting keratitis with malacic corneal material in the ulcer beds. Treatment was changed to a fortified gentamicin solution every 4 hours OU and subcutaneous flunixin meglumine once daily.

Three days after initiating the revised therapy, ophthalmic examination revealed absent menace responses bilaterally with preserved palpebral and dazzle reflexes. Pupillary light reflexes could not be assessed because of severe corneal opacification. There was marked blepharospasm and purulent ocular discharge OU. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy showed pronounced conjunctival hyperemia and diffuse stromal edema with a central 8-mm-diameter bulla involving the anterior half of the corneal stroma in both eyes. The surrounding stroma was malacic with multiple yellow infiltrative areas, and fluorescein staining was positive on the bullae. Intraocular pressures were not measured due to corneal fragility, and a mild hypopyon was noted in the left eye.

A 35-year-old woman presented with intermittent low back pain of 5–6 years’ duration, occasionally radiating to the right leg with associated numbness and tingling. Physical examination revealed no focal tenderness over the lumbar spine, normal motor strength and sensory function in both lower limbs, a negative straight-leg raise test, and no bladder or bowel dysfunction. Routine blood and urine studies were normal.

An initial anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis demonstrated a subtle vertical curvilinear radiolucency in the midportion of the S1 vertebral body. Subsequent MRI of the lumbosacral spine showed a low-signal vertical cleft in a slight right paramedian location of the S1 vertebral body; the cleft was filled with tissue that was isointense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted and STIR sequences. Adjacent L5–S1 intervertebral disk height and signal intensity were normal. Cervical-spine and chest radiographs showed no other vertebral anomalies.

A male infant, born at 35 weeks’ gestation to healthy nonconsanguineous parents after an uneventful pregnancy, was admitted at 4 hours of age with respiratory distress and generalized exfoliative erythroderma involving the face, trunk, and limbs, along with excessive scalp scaling. No blisters or pustules were noted. Eyelids and glans penis were swollen; mucous membranes were spared. Nikolsky and Darier signs were negative.

On day 2, he developed severe hypernatremia (peak sodium 180 mmol/L on day 3) and a 17% weight loss by day 4 attributed to transepidermal water loss. Laboratory evaluation revealed hypokalemia, mild metabolic alkalosis, elevated aldosterone (392 ng/dL; normal 19–141), and normal renin activity. During hospitalization, he experienced sepsis due to Klebsiella pneumoniae (day 9), Candida parapsilosis (day 12), and Staphylococcus haemolyticus (day 27). Immunologic studies showed normal IgE (8.6 IU/mL), immunoglobulin levels, and complement components. TORCH screen and metabolic workup were negative.

A skin biopsy demonstrated mild acanthosis and hyperkeratosis with loss of the granular layer, consistent with nonbullous ichthyosiform erythroderma. Light microscopy of hairs from the scalp and eyebrows revealed invagination of the distal hair shaft into the proximal shaft (trichorrhexis invaginata).

A 46-year-old woman was referred to dermatology for evaluation of a 2-month history of a persistent rash on her abdomen. Her medical history included cataplexy, narcolepsy, Hashimoto thyroiditis (stable on levothyroxine), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, polycystic ovarian syndrome, restless leg syndrome, herpes labialis, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She denied new medications or products. 

The primary care physician had suspected a fungal infection and treated her with over-the-counter antifungal cream, ketoconazole 2% cream, and triamcinolone 0.1% ointment, with slight improvement but no resolution. On examination, there was a solitary, well-demarcated, 5-cm erythematous plaque with a trailing scale on the mid-abdomen. No lymphadenopathy was noted.

To clarify the diagnosis, a potassium hydroxide preparation, skin scraping for fungal PCR, and a punch biopsy were performed. Meanwhile, the patient was given samples of crisaborole cream to assess for response, and she was instructed to continue her topical therapies.

A 58-year-old man presented with 8 hours of left lower quadrant abdominal pain. He had experienced intermittent chronic abdominal pain over the preceding 2 years that resolved spontaneously and denied nausea or vomiting. His medical history included nonvalvular atrial fibrillation managed with warfarin; he had no prior abdominal surgery. On examination, he was afebrile; the abdomen showed tenderness and guarding in the left lower quadrant with a firm, 5 × 8 cm palpable mass. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 11 000 per μL and a C-reactive protein level of 175 mg/dL, with other values within normal limits. Upright and supine abdominal radiographs were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed diffuse thickening and enhancement of the peritoneum encasing small-bowel loops with ascites between loops; there was no bowel dilation or signs of obstruction.

A 63-year-old man with G2 pT1c high-grade papillary bladder transitional cell carcinoma, treated by transurethral resection followed by six weekly intravesical BCG instillations, presented 3 weeks after a booster BCG dose with general malaise, fevers, night sweats, reduced appetite, and headaches. He denied respiratory or urinary symptoms. On examination he was apyrexial and appeared well. Laboratory studies revealed acute kidney injury (creatinine 176 µmol/L), mild transaminitis (ALT 99 U/L, AST 85 U/L), pancytopenia (neutrophils 1.5 × 10^9/L, platelets 54 × 10^9/L), and a C-reactive protein of 111 mg/L. A chest radiograph was normal. Blood and urine cultures, a viral gargle, and sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli were negative. Abdominal ultrasound and CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed right-sided hydronephrosis and mild splenomegaly.

A 65-year-old man fell approximately four meters from a coconut tree and was found unconscious for about 10 minutes. He had lacerations on the right elbow and right knee, and abrasions on the chin and right side of the face. On arrival 8½ hours later, his vital signs were: temperature normal, pulse 92/min, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28/min. He was alert (GCS 15), with slurred speech; pupils were equal, central, and reactive; sphincter function was intact. He complained of headache and had right scalp tenderness without open wounds. There was reduced movement of the right limbs. He had no past history of hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, seizures, or prior neurologic events; he was a smoker. Radiographs of the right limbs and chest showed no fractures. A noncontrast CT scan of the head and cervical spine demonstrated an intracerebral hemorrhage in the left thalamic region without evidence of traumatic injury. On detailed neurologic examination, the right side showed increased muscle tone, reduced muscle power, exaggerated tendon reflexes, and a positive Babinski sign.

A 62-year-old Romanian man with hypertension, a history of ischemic stroke, chronic renal failure (GFR 59.5 mL/min), alcohol use, and occasional smoking presented with sudden onset of inflammatory neck pain without radiation and left ankle pain for 3 days. He denied fever, chills, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms, and there were no signs of infection in the ears, throat, respiratory or urinary tracts. On examination, occiput-to-wall distance was 3 cm, chin-to-chest distance was 7 cm, and there was multidirectional cervical stiffness. The left ankle was warm, slightly swollen, and had limited range of motion. Arthrocentesis of the left ankle yielded 10 mL of cloudy fluid. Examination of other spinal segments, skin, mucous membranes, and cardiovascular and respiratory systems was normal, and no lymphadenopathy was present. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9530/mm3, C-reactive protein of 232 mg/L, and serum uric acid of 689 µmol/L. Analysis of the ankle fluid revealed 20,000 white cells/mm3 (85% neutrophils), the presence of sodium urate microcrystals, and an absence of germs on direct examination and culture. Blood cultures were negative, and urine cultures were sterile. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated inflammatory edema of the C4–C5 and C5–C6 vertebral endplates with epidural contrast enhancement, suggestive of spondylodiscitis with epiduritis.

A 13-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a giant pelvic mass initially suspected to be malignant. She had 1 year of daily metrorrhagia without cyclic menstruation and was diagnosed with anovulatory cycles. Over that time she developed progressive hirsutism (modified Ferriman–Gallwey score 23), a deepened voice, and severe nodular-cystic acne treated with retinoids. Her pediatrician palpated a soft, painless abdominal mass extending from the pubic symphysis to the supraumbilical region, and the family noted mild progressive abdominal distension. 

On examination, she had moderate hirsutism and virilization. Transabdominal ultrasound and pelvic MRI revealed a 21×17×9 cm multicystic mass with thin septa and a 1 cm nodular-papillary projection with contrast enhancement occupying most of the abdomen and arising from the left ovary; it compressed the inferior vena cava and caused grade II right hydronephrosis. The right ovary measured 7 cm and appeared multicystic. 

Laboratory studies showed negative serum tumor markers (CA-125, AFP, β-hCG, and neuron-specific enolase), elevated total testosterone of 2.73 ng/mL, an LH/FSH ratio of 29.9, a HOMA-IR of 8.4, and hyperinsulinemia (27.4 mU/L). Although these findings were consistent with PCOS, the presence of a giant multicystic lesion with solid components prompted exclusion of androgen-secreting neoplasms, and an exploratory laparoscopy was planned.

An 86-year-old woman was admitted to a geriatric inpatient unit for frequent episodes of involuntary, uncontrolled outbursts of crying and, less frequently, episodes of laughing, which were disturbing and disproportionate to the situation. She also had nighttime wandering. Her husband was no longer able to manage her behavior at home. 

Her medical history included hypertension, osteoporosis, gait abnormality, nocturnal urinary incontinence, and Alzheimer’s disease with related behavioral problems. Current medications were amlodipine, venlafaxine, quetiapine, and calcium with vitamin D. On examination, parkinsonism was present. 

Initial laboratory investigations, including biochemical, inflammatory, hormonal, and toxicology tests, were all within normal limits. A brain CT scan performed four years earlier had shown mild cerebral atrophy and leukoaraiosis. An electromyogram was negative for motoneuron disease. Brain MRI showed nonspecific subcortical white-matter signal abnormalities with ischemic changes and a left-sided cerebellar lacuna. Brain FDG-PET demonstrated an altered metabolic pattern suggestive of Alzheimer’s disease dementia or dementia with Lewy bodies. 

She was seen by a psychiatrist, who diagnosed dysregulation of affective expression without evidence of significant depressive or anxious symptoms. She was evaluated by a neurologist for further assessment.

A 58-year-old woman presented with left-sided chest pain worsened by exertion, accompanied by shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, and diaphoresis. Her history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, prior myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation on warfarin, heart failure, and stage 4 chronic kidney disease. On arrival, blood pressure was 207/140 mmHg, and she had clinical signs of decompensated heart failure. Electrocardiography showed ST depression and T-wave inversion in the lateral leads. Chest radiography confirmed pulmonary edema. Bedside echocardiography demonstrated moderate to severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, left ventricular hypertrophy, and a calcific but unobstructive aortic valve. High-sensitivity troponin I was elevated, confirming an acute coronary syndrome. She was treated with aspirin, clopidogrel, fondaparinux, a high-dose statin, intravenous glyceryl trinitrate, and diuretics, and amlodipine was added for persistent hypertension. Coronary angiography was planned the next morning. 

On the following morning, she was noted to have a fine, petechial, non‐blanching rash over the dorsum of her left hand and forearm and, to a lesser extent, over her right hand and forearm. There was no rash on her face, trunk, or lower limbs, and no features of meningism. Blood pressure had been measured at 15-minute intervals overnight, initially on the left arm, then switched to the right arm at the patient’s request because of local discomfort.

An 89-year-old man with second-degree Mobitz II and intermittent third-degree AV block had a left-sided dual-chamber pacemaker implanted for syncope. He developed an abrupt rise in right ventricular lead impedance and high capture thresholds, consistent with impending lead fracture. Left innominate vein occlusion precluded lead extraction, so the left device was abandoned and a new right-sided dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted and programmed to DDD 60–130 ppm, with paced and sensed AV delays of 220 msec and 165 msec, respectively. Because he was pacemaker-dependent, the abandoned left device was programmed to VVI 40 ppm as a backup.  
One month later, interrogation revealed that the abandoned left device was pacing approximately 75% of the time. An intracardiac electrogram from the new right-sided pacemaker showed that every fourth ventricular complex was a paced beat by the new device, while the intervening beats formed a regular nontracking rhythm at approximately 75 ppm.  
Why might this be? Possibilities include rate response phenomenon, pacing behavior resulting from End of Life mode, interference or cross-talk from the other device, and a manufacturer-specific pacing algorithm, such as rate smoothing.

A 16-year-old girl with a 1.5-year history of polyuria, polydipsia, and polyphagia presented with 1 week of vomiting and fatigue. On examination, she was alert; heart rate 120/min; respiratory rate 20/min; blood pressure 100/70 mmHg. Laboratory evaluation showed a random blood glucose of 560 mg/dL, pH 7.12, and urine ketones 3+, consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis. She was treated with IV fluids and insulin infusion, then transitioned to subcutaneous regular insulin (12 U–16 U–12 U before meals) and glargine insulin (10 U at 9 PM). Baseline HbA1c was 17.4%, C-peptide 0.05 ng/mL, and glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody was positive; screening for retinopathy, nephropathy, and thyroid function was negative. She was discharged with home blood sugars of 150–200 mg/dL.

Five weeks later, she reported 10 days of burning pain in both feet and soles, causing inability to walk and sleep disturbance. Vitals were notable for blood pressure 100/70 mmHg. Neurologic examination showed normal lower limb reflexes and intact pain, temperature, vibration, and position sense. There were no motor deficits. Laboratory tests revealed vitamin D insufficiency (15.7 ng/mL) and a normal vitamin B12 level (240 pg/mL). Two weeks of outpatient treatment with NSAIDs, vitamin B12, and cholecalciferol provided no relief, and she was admitted for further evaluation.

On admission, blood pressure was 150/100 mmHg and heart rate 122/min. Motor reflexes remained normal. Sensory examination revealed reduced fine touch in the feet and soles with other modalities intact. Hypertension work-up showed normal serum electrolytes, normal creatinine, and no microalbuminuria. A CT angiogram of the renal vessels, echocardiogram, vanillylmandelic acid, and metanephrine levels were normal. A vasculitis panel (ANA, dsDNA, ANCA) was negative. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated preserved motor action potentials with significant reduction in sensory nerve action potentials and mildly slowed conduction in the superficial peroneal and sural nerves, consistent with severe axonal sensory polyneuropathy. Upper limb studies were normal. Ophthalmologic examination revealed diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy with capillary nonperfusion, macular ischemia, and cystoid macular edema on fluorescein angiography. She was started on amitriptyline, pregabalin, and gabapentin for her neuropathic pain.

A 30-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with sudden-onset right-sided chest pain, shortness of breath, and wheezing. On examination, breath sounds were reduced on the right, and generalized rhonchi were heard. Vital signs were within normal limits except for mild tachypnea. Chest radiography showed a right-sided pneumothorax, which was treated with chest-tube insertion and resolved symptomatically. Seventeen days later, she experienced a second right-sided pneumothorax. A CT scan of the thorax demonstrated a non-enhancing, non-radiopaque filling defect within the right main bronchus, causing obstruction of the upper and descending bronchi in association with the recurrent pneumothorax.

A 65-year-old woman with a history of left-sided infiltrating ductal carcinoma of the breast (diagnosed 2012; treated with modified radical mastectomy, prophylactic contralateral mastectomy, adjuvant chemoradiation, and ongoing anastrozole) had surveillance imaging in late 2019 that revealed a pulmonary nodule and bilateral adrenal hyperactivity. Biopsy of the right adrenal gland confirmed metastatic breast adenocarcinoma. During summer 2019, she underwent stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) to the left lung (50 Gy in 5 fractions), right adrenal (45 Gy in 5 fractions), and left adrenal (40 Gy in 5 fractions). 

In the fall of 2019, she presented to the emergency department with intractable nausea and vomiting that she attributed to her recent adrenal radiation. Admission laboratory studies showed:  
- Sodium 130 mmol/L (137–147)  
- Potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.1)  
- Glucose 235 mg/dL (70–100)  
- Random cortisol 0.9 µg/dL (5–20)  

An adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) level drawn before steroid administration was 2 pg/mL (7–63), low. Thyroid function tests revealed TSH 0.85 mIU/mL (0.35–5.00) with free T4 0.3 ng/dL (0.6–1.6). Gonadotropin levels were low (FSH 0.9 mIU/mL [27–153], LH < 0.2 mIU/mL [11–64]), indicating pituitary insufficiency.

A 28-year-old woman with well-controlled polycystic ovary syndrome presented with a 7-month history of hair loss following a tick bite on her vertex scalp. Initially, she noted alopecia confined to the attachment site, but 1 month later the hair loss spread rapidly to involve the entire scalp. Treatments tried elsewhere included over-the-counter vitamins and intralesional corticosteroids without improvement.

On examination, there was diffuse patchy scalp hair loss with a Severity of Alopecia Tool score of 52. Trichoscopy revealed yellow dots, black dots, and exclamation point hairs scattered throughout the scalp. The tick‐bite site showed postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and scar‐like alopecia. There was no loss of eyebrows, eyelashes, or other body hair. A hair pull test was not performed.

A 4-mm punch biopsy included the attachment site and adjacent scalp. Histology showed a predominance of vellus hairs (terminal/vellus ratio 0.7), with 42% of follicles in catagen or telogen. There were mildly atrophic sebaceous glands, a mild to moderate superficial and deep perivascular, interstitial, and focally perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with scattered eosinophils, and mild perifollicular fibrosis.

A 40-year-old man presented to the emergency department with swelling and pain in the left hemiscrotum of acute onset without a history of trauma or surgery. He had no significant medical or family history, smoked one pack-year, and did not consume alcohol. On examination, the left hemiscrotum was tender and swollen, consistent with acute epididymitis. Incidentally, a non-tender mass was palpated in the right hemiscrotum; his parents had first noted this mass when he was two years old, and it had been misdiagnosed as a hydrocele at that time. Scrotal ultrasound showed a normal left testis, an enlarged hypoechoic left epididymis with increased Doppler flow, and an oval right scrotal lump with echotexture and blood flow similar to the ipsilateral testis. Serum α-fetoprotein (1.44 IU/mL) and β-hCG (0.5 mIU/mL) levels were within reference limits.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive dyspnea on exertion, abdominal swelling, and lower extremity edema. Three months earlier, she had been treated for presumed liver disease with furosemide, but her swelling and functional limitation worsened, and she developed orthopnea. She had no prior medical history. On examination, blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg, pulse 100 beats/min and irregular, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. She appeared pale but not cyanotic. Jugular venous distention extended to the mandibular angle, and hepatojugular reflux was positive. The liver was palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin, and there was bilateral pitting edema to the knees (+++/++++). Cardiac auscultation revealed an irregular rhythm with normal S1 and S2; lung bases had diminished breath sounds and crackles. Laboratory tests, including cardiac enzymes, were normal; brain natriuretic peptide was 140 pg/mL (reference 0–125 pg/mL). Chest radiography showed an oblique linear calcification within the cardiac silhouette. Electrocardiography demonstrated atrial fibrillation and diffuse nonspecific T-wave inversions. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed biatrial enlargement, normal left ventricular size and systolic function, restrictive transmitral inflow velocities, normal mitral annular tissue Doppler velocities (10 cm/sec), and a dilated inferior vena cava (25 mm) with <50% respiratory variation.

A 5-year-old Turkish boy presented with a 3-year history of nasal obstruction without fever, cough, discharge, or epistaxis. On examination, a pink mass filled the right nasal cavity, causing leftward septal deviation and mild external nasal enlargement. Needle aspiration of the mass yielded clear fluid with shrinkage of the lesion. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 11.5×10^3/mm^3, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, platelets 361×10^9/L, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 9 mm/hour. High-resolution computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses revealed a well-defined soft tissue density lesion originating from the middle concha, with no evidence of intracranial or orbital extension.

A well-appearing 6-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department for two days of excessive crying without fever, feeding difficulties, or changes in activity. He had no prior medical history. Vital signs were normal. Examination of the right foot revealed a mild swelling and a visible groove at the middle phalanx of the middle toe. Skin perfusion was intact with a capillary refill of less than three seconds, and there was no erythema or discoloration. Examination of the other toes, genitalia, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Although no constricting material was seen on initial inspection, a hair tourniquet was suspected.

A 62-year-old man with recently diagnosed squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue and hypopharynx presented after a 1-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. He had a longstanding seizure disorder well controlled for 7 years on levetiracetam and had received his first cycle of carboplatin, abraxane, and pembrolizumab 18 days earlier. His medical history also included gastroesophageal reflux disease treated with oral pantoprazole.

On examination, he was drowsy but oriented, able to follow simple commands, with impaired attention and recall. He had generalized weakness (3/5 strength in all extremities) with preserved reflexes and no focal sensory or motor deficits. He was afebrile, and other vital signs were within normal limits. After an initial postictal confusion, his mental status deteriorated over the next 48 hours, with persistent agitation and confusion but no new focal findings.

Laboratory studies on presentation revealed: hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, WBC 3.4 K/μL, platelets 43 K/μL, lactate 5.9 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, anion gap 19, calcium 6.1 mg/dL (corrected 6.8 mg/dL), potassium 3.5 mmol/L, and magnesium 0.7 mEq/L. Renal function and liver tests were unremarkable. Fractional excretion of magnesium was 24.9%. CT and MRI of the head were normal. A 24-hour video EEG showed mild-to-moderate diffuse cerebral dysfunction “nonspecific in etiology, but may be seen in the context of toxic-metabolic encephalopathies.”

A 6-year-old Middle-Eastern girl presented to dermatology with two skin lesions on the dorsum of her right foot, scaling of her soles, erythematous pruritic rashes over her palms and fingers, patchy hypopigmented facial lesions, and areas of patchy alopecia on her scalp. Her past medical and family history was noncontributory. The mother first noted eczematous-appearing lesions on the soles, which over a few days spread to the palms and ventral fingers. Shortly afterward, she developed facial skin hypopigmentation and patchy hair loss. On examination, there were well-defined patches of noninflammatory alopecia on the parietal scalp with trichoscopic “exclamation marks.” Both palms and soles showed multiple erythematous, pruritic lesions—some painful or ulcerated—with white scaling and hyperlinearity. The face had symmetrical hypopigmented patches over the buccal areas with fine scaling. In addition, two distinct red-to-pink nodules were noted on the dorsal aspect of the right foot.

A 51-year-old man presented initially with a 4-day history of shortness of breath, dry cough, and weakness. A lateral flow test was positive for SARS-CoV-2; chest x-ray showed bilateral patchy opacification. His oxygen saturation remained above 94% on room air, and he was discharged home with a pulse oximeter. 

Twelve days after symptom onset, he re-presented with oxygen saturation of 78% and chest x-ray–documented progression of pneumonitis. He was treated with oxygen, dexamethasone, doxycycline, and amoxicillin; the antibiotics were stopped when procalcitonin was < 0.25 μg/L and he remained afebrile. A CTPA ruled out pulmonary embolism. After 3 days, he maintained saturation on room air with improved inflammatory markers and was discharged to complete a 10-day course of dexamethasone.

Twenty-three days after symptom onset (8 days post-discharge), he experienced 48 hours of progressively worsening shortness of breath. In the emergency department, examination revealed reduced breath sounds and reduced chest expansion on the right. He required 4 L/min of oxygen, was alert, tachypnoeic at 40 breaths/minute, tachycardic at 129 beats/minute, and normotensive at 116/94 mmHg. Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.53, PaO2 8.3 kPa, PaCO2 3.6 kPa, and HCO3– 22.6 mmol/L. The absence of hemodynamic instability, tracheal deviation, or raised jugular venous pressure prompted investigation with chest x-ray rather than immediate needle decompression.

A 50-year-old female receptionist first noted progressive loss of energy and exhaustion in early 2011 without identifiable stressors. By year’s end she developed impaired concentration, slowed thinking, disturbed memory, low mood, decreased activity, sleep disturbance, social withdrawal, and an inability to work. Adynamia and cognitive impairment were her most debilitating symptoms, and a diagnosis of major depression was made. Treatment with venlafaxine (up to 112.5 mg daily), agomelatine (25 mg daily), and cognitive-behavioral therapy yielded no significant improvement. In autumn 2012 an attempt at part-time work was aborted due to cognitive and physical exhaustion; she continued to experience forgetfulness, difficulty with complex tasks, prolonged reaction times, and depressed mood.

In January 2014 she was admitted for further evaluation. Medical history was notable only for hypertension treated with telmisartan (80 mg) and a remitted lumbar disc prolapse. Thyroxine 75 μg daily had been started in early 2012 after detection of elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO) and thyroglobulin (TG) antibodies in an outpatient setting; thyroid hormone levels had remained normal. There was no prior psychiatric history and no family history of psychiatric, neurologic, or autoimmune disease.

On examination, vital signs and general and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Serum studies showed TPO antibodies 804 IU/mL (normal <34), TG antibodies 661.4 IU/mL (normal <115), and normal thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies; triiodothyronine, thyroxine, and TSH were within reference ranges. Tests for intracellular onconeural (Yo, Hu, CV2/CRMP5, Ri, Ma1/2, SOX1) and synaptic (GAD, amphiphysin) antigens were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed protein 678 mg/L (reference <450), albumin quotient 7.7 × 10⁻³ (age-related reference <7.3 × 10⁻³), white cells 1/μL, no intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis or oligoclonal bands, and no antibodies against NMDAR, AMPA-R, GABA-B-R, or VGKC-complex. Brain MRI showed nonspecific supratentorial white-matter lesions and frontal-accentuated atrophy. Electroencephalography was normal. In formal testing of attentional performance, her response times were markedly prolonged and measures of alertness and processing speed were below average.

A 53-year-old woman with no prior neurologic history underwent primary cytoreductive surgery (including bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, hysterectomy, omentectomy, and lymph node dissection) for high-grade serous ovarian cancer (FIGO stage IC). Two days after an uncomplicated surgery, she noted short-term memory loss that did not interfere with daily activities; she was discharged on postoperative day 10 when her deficits appeared stable.

Fourteen days after surgery, she was admitted with acute confusion, disorientation, speech dysfunction, agitation, and visual hallucinations. On examination, she had deficits in short-term memory, disorientation, and difficulty with serial counting. Chest and abdominal CT scans were unremarkable except for mild pneumonia. Brain MRI showed bilateral hippocampal volume loss on T2-FLAIR images, and MR spectroscopy demonstrated diminished N-acetylaspartate/(choline + creatine) ratios in both hippocampi. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a pleocytosis of 309 × 10^6 cells/L and elevated protein of 0.688 g/L.

A 44-year-old Chinese man presented to the emergency department with gross hematuria and passage of blood clots, first noted immediately after a routine morning run. He had a history of hypertension but no personal or familial bleeding disorders, nephrolithiasis, or trauma. He was a nonsmoker and exercised regularly. On examination, vital signs were stable and the physical exam was unremarkable. Bladder ultrasonography demonstrated a large volume of clots without hydronephrosis. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 16.1 g/dL, hematocrit 47.3%, creatinine 83 µmol/L, urea 4.2 mmol/L, activated partial thromboplastin time 31.4 seconds, and prothrombin time 10 seconds; there was no evidence of anemia, infection, coagulopathy, or renal impairment. 

Computed tomographic urography (plain, nephrographic, and pyelographic phases) revealed left perinephric fluid, delayed enhancement and excretion of the left kidney, and dependent material in the collecting system consistent with blood, but no mass or urinary calculus. Flexible cystoscopy showed no bladder lesions and no active bleeding from the ureteral orifices. A working diagnosis of recent stone passage with acute pyelovenous leakage was made. 

He was managed with bladder catheterization, manual clot evacuation, continuous bladder irrigation, and intravenous antibiotics. On hospital day 2, he complained of left flank pain and experienced intermittent mild hematuria. On day 6, he had a recurrent episode of gross hematuria with acute bladder clot retention; his hemoglobin fell to 8.9 g/dL, and he received 1 L of packed red-cell transfusion.

A 39-year-old man was admitted with 6 hours of severe chest pain. He has a 14-year history of amphetamine and cannabis abuse and is prescribed lisdexamfetamine 70 mg daily for ADHD. He is a non-smoker, with no diabetes or hypertension, and a BMI of 33 kg/m2. On admission, heart rate was 65 bpm and blood pressure 123/78 mmHg. ECG showed minor ST-segment elevations in the anterior leads. Initial cardiac troponin T was 319 ng/L (normal < 16 ng/L), rising to 1148 ng/L at 4 hours and peaking at 2035 ng/L the next day before declining to 19 ng/L at discharge. Pro-BNP was 420 ng/L on admission, peaked at 2648 ng/L the following day, and fell to 992 ng/L before discharge.

Urgent coronary angiography revealed normal epicardial coronary arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (48%) with hypokinesis of the apex and distal lateral and inferior walls; global longitudinal strain was reduced in these segments. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging performed the next day demonstrated multiple focal areas of late gadolinium enhancement in the mid- and subepicardial myocardium of the anterior, lateral, and inferior walls, suggestive of chronic fibrosis; left ventricular ejection fraction was 46% with inferolateral hypokinesis. There was no evidence of myocardial edema on T2-weighted imaging. Cardiotropic viral panels, including SARS-CoV-2, were negative. Endomyocardial biopsy showed no evidence of viral or autoimmune myocarditis.

A 77-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with sitagliptin was found unconscious in her apartment (GCS 10: E3/V2/M4). On arrival she was tachypneic, tachycardic, hypothermic, hypotonic, and had dilated, sluggish pupils. Initial labs showed serum glucose 44 mmol/L, HbA1c 15.9%, positive serum and urine ketones, osmolality 368 mOsm/kg (osmol gap 18), anion gap 39 mmol/L, β-hydroxybutyrate 11 395 µmol/L, arterial pH 6.8, pCO₂ 17 mmHg, base excess –27.1 mmol/L, lactate 3.4 mmol/L, and acute kidney injury. Insulin, fluid resuscitation, bicarbonate, and thiamine were started. Nonenhanced head CT revealed a right acute subdural hematoma (max 8 mm) and a left chronic subdural hematoma (max 3 mm) without parenchymal edema or infarction. CT angiography showed patent extra- and intracranial vessels. CT perfusion demonstrated global cortical hypoperfusion with prolonged mean transit time and normal cerebral blood volume.

A 26-day-old male neonate weighing 2.9 kg presented with a 4-day history of increasing abdominal distention. He was born at term without complications. On examination, he was alert and active, with marked abdominal distention and palpable masses in both upper quadrants. Laboratory studies, including clotting tests, renal function, and urinalysis, were within normal limits. Urinary vanilmandelic acid, homovanillic acid, and catecholamine levels were normal.  
Gray-scale ultrasonography of the abdomen showed bilateral suprarenal cystic masses containing internal echoes and debris, measuring 7.9 × 4.3 cm on the right and 4.4 × 4.6 cm on the left. Color and power Doppler imaging confirmed that the masses were avascular. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated well-defined bilateral suprarenal cystic lesions that were hypointense on T1-weighted images and markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted images.

A 46-year-old man with stage IV EGFR-mutated lung adenocarcinoma (bilateral lung and brain metastases) treated sequentially with erlotinib, osimertinib, multiple chemotherapy regimens, and most recently two cycles of nivolumab, presented to the emergency department with 3–4 days of temporospatial disorientation, dizziness, and increased dyspnea without cough or fever. He reported drinking 9 L of water daily with intense thirst and marked polyuria. His medications included metformin and tapering methylprednisolone.

On examination, he was alert but slightly disoriented, normoperfused, and tachypneic (28 breaths/min). Heart sounds were normal; scattered wheezes were heard in the lungs. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. Neurologic exam showed slow speech, bradypsychia, and dysarthria; cranial nerves and pupils were normal; no nystagmus or gait abnormality; Glasgow score 15/15.

Laboratory studies revealed:
• Serum sodium 111 mmol/L, plasma osmolarity 219 mOsm/kg  
• Urine sodium 6 mmol/L, urine osmolarity 89 mOsm/kg  
• Free T4 1.75 ng/dL (0.93–1.71), TSH 0.553 µU/mL (0.27–4.2)  
• Prolactin 30.7 ng/mL (4.04–15.2), ACTH <10 pg/mL  

Chest X-ray showed multiple nodular opacities consistent with known pulmonary metastases. Noncontrast cranial CT demonstrated no acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass effect, or midline shift.

A 2-year-8-month-old girl was seen with 3 days of fever (to 38.8 °C), vomiting, and refusal to eat. Parents estimated her oral intake at approximately 500 mL over that period. On presentation, she appeared pale and slightly dehydrated. Her weight, height, and head circumference were all below the 3rd percentile. Vital signs were: temperature 37.6 °C, blood pressure 97/65 mmHg, and heart rate 102 beats/min. 

Her medical history was notable for grade III intraventricular hemorrhage as a neonate, hydrocephalus, recurrent neonatal hypernatremia, pituitary hypoplasia with central hypothyroidism and growth hormone deficiency on replacement therapy, motor delay, and a prolonged seizure at 18 months.

Laboratory studies on admission showed serum sodium 187 mmol/L, chloride 148 mmol/L, normal pH and base excess, and calculated osmolality 362 mmol/kg. She was started on isotonic glucose–electrolyte infusion (Na+ 140 mmol/L, 5% glucose), with KCl supplementation; serum sodium decreased at an average rate of 0.5 mmol/L per hour to a nadir of 143 mmol/L. Initial blood glucose was 11.1 mmol/L and normalized with fluids. Urine output was 2.4 mL/kg/h on day 1 and 4 mL/kg/h on day 2. Urine osmolality was 876 mosmol/kg, ADH 23.7 ng/L, copeptin 4.4 pmol/L, aldosterone 7.0 ng/dL, and cortisol 32.7 µg/dL. Thyroid and growth hormone supplementation continued.

On hospital day 4, she developed tremor when standing, a general reduction in movement, slight bilateral arm rigidity, and ataxia. A 10/20 EEG was normal. Brain MRI demonstrated vague, non-ischemic diffusion restriction in the basal ganglia, corpus callosum, and subcortical white matter bilaterally, with only discrete T2-FLAIR signal changes. The pons appeared unremarkable, and lateral ventricles were mildly dilated without active hydrocephalus.

A 39-year-old man with acute B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation 6 weeks earlier. He presented with a 1-week history of nonproductive cough and fevers. Vital signs were stable, with an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Pulmonary examination revealed faint crackles at the right lung apex. Laboratory studies showed a normal white-blood-cell count and differential. A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral airspace opacities. Chest CT revealed widespread, multifocal patchy opacities most prominent in the apices and scattered bibasilar opacities. On hospital day 2, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (right upper lobe) yielded 605 WBC/mL (76% histiocytes, 19% neutrophils, 6% lymphocytes); cultures for bacteria, fungi, viruses, and acid-fast bacilli were negative. Transbronchial biopsy of the right lower lobe was nondiagnostic. The patient was treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungals, but over the next week he had worsening cough, progressive dyspnea, and hypoxemia.

A 48-year-old Hispanic man with a history of chronic cavitary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis nonadherent with therapy and uncontrolled diabetes presented with 8 days of fever, dry cough, and myalgias. He was initially treated for bronchitis with azithromycin. Two days later he reported persistent fever, progressive cough, weakness, and body aches to the emergency department. His vital signs were stable, with an oxygen saturation of 99% on room air, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 1000 cells/µL), hyperglycemia (glucose 317 mg/dL), hypoalbuminemia (albumin 2.6 g/dL), and total protein 8.3 g/dL. Blood cultures were negative, and rapid antigen tests for influenza A and B were negative. Chest radiography showed an increase in the right upper lobe cavitary lesion compared with prior films. Chest computed tomography demonstrated multiple new bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities that were absent on previous scans.

A 22-year-old man with non–transfusion-dependent sickle cell disease, maintained on hydroxyurea, presented with a 3-day history of fever, sore throat, mild nonproductive cough, generalized body aches, chest pain, fatigue, and decreased appetite. He reported close contact with a confirmed COVID-19 case but no recent travel. His medical history was significant for recurrent vaso-occlusive crises, most managed at home, and avascular necrosis of the hip. 

Investigations:
Chest radiograph: small ill-defined patchy opacity in the right lower lung zone periphery; clear costophrenic angles; normal cardiothoracic ratio.  
ECG: corrected QT 379 ms; no ischemic changes.  
Laboratory studies: blood type B+; hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL; RBC count 4.0×10^6/μL; WBC 3.2×10^3/μL (ANC 1.76×10^3/μL; lymphocytes 1.03×10^3/μL); platelets 77×10^3/μL; reticulocyte count 1.1%; ferritin 608 μg/L (prior 49); IL-6 9 pg/mL; CRP 9.5 mg/L; D-dimer 0.41 μg/L; LDH 199 U/L; renal and liver function tests within normal limits; G6PD normal; hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbS 70.1%, HbF 26.9%.  
SARS-CoV-2 PCR: positive.

At this point, the differential diagnosis was acute chest syndrome triggered by COVID-19 infection versus viral pneumonitis.

A 65-year-old man participating in a 13.1-mile half marathon in San Diego developed progressive, asymptomatic swelling of both hands and all fingers beginning approximately 1 hour into the race. Ambient temperature rose from 47°F at the start to 60°F at finish, a total race time of 3 hours 46 minutes. He denied pruritus, pain, hives, angioedema, or swelling elsewhere. Immediately post-race, examination revealed diffuse uniform swelling of the dorsal and palmar aspects of both hands and digits, and he was unable to clench his fingers into his palms (positive fist sign). Neither mucosal involvement nor urticaria was present. Without any intervention, the swelling completely resolved within 2 hours of stopping ambulation, and he regained full ability to make a fist.

A 55-year-old man presented with sudden-onset diplopia, headache, weight loss of approximately 10% over one month, and chronic back pain. His history was notable for right colon cancer treated 20 years earlier and pulmonary tuberculosis treated 4 years earlier; he had been lost to follow-up after initial therapy. On examination, he was underweight and had ophthalmoplegia but was otherwise unremarkable. 
Laboratory testing included a lumbar puncture, which was nondiagnostic; cerebrospinal fluid was negative for malignant cells and microorganisms. Serologies for HIV and toxoplasmosis were negative. Chest radiography was normal. 
Brain CT revealed multiple contrast-enhancing lesions with peri-lesional edema. Brain MRI confirmed four space-occupying lesions with central necrosis, irregular peripheral enhancement, and moderate edema. Thoracic and abdominal CT showed small mediastinal lymph nodes, bilateral pulmonary micronodules, a small right middle-lobe consolidation, and a lytic lesion at the T8–rib junction. Bronchoscopy demonstrated anthracotic plates; bronchial washings showed no malignant cells and were negative on direct mycobacterial examination. Upper and lower endoscopies were unremarkable. PET imaging revealed increased uptake in multiple lung foci, mediastinal and abdominal lymph nodes, bone lesions (ribs and iliac wing), both adrenals, and the brain. 
A CT‐guided biopsy of the lytic rib lesion showed epithelioid granulomas.

A 16-year-old female presented to the ENT clinic with a long-standing history of right-sided nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea. She denied facial pain, anosmia, epistaxis, or headache. Her medical, surgical, family, and social histories were unremarkable. 

On anterior rhinoscopy, there was a right-sided deviated nasal septum with mucopurulent discharge. Nasal endoscopy of the right nostril revealed a white, solid mass arising from the floor of the right nasal cavity, covered in secretions; the left side and the nasopharynx were normal. Examination of the throat and neck was also unremarkable.

A noncontrast CT scan of the paranasal sinuses showed an enveloped focal soft-tissue density insinuated between the medial surface of the right inferior turbinate and the bony nasal septum.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of progressive decreased vision in her left eye, which began shortly after a flu-like illness. She had no other systemic symptoms or past medical history. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/400 in the left eye and 20/20 in the right. Anterior-segment examination was normal bilaterally. Fundus examination of the left eye showed cystoid macular edema, a serous (neurosensory) detachment at the macula, flame-shaped retinal hemorrhages inferior to the fovea, hard exudates at the margins of the detachment, and two juxtafoveal yellowish lesions located nasal and temporal to the fovea. The peripheral retina was unremarkable. The right fundus was normal. Fluorescein angiography of the left eye revealed early blockage of background fluorescence by the superficial hemorrhages with patchy mild hyperfluorescence, and in the late and very late phases, diffuse leakage at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium under the hemorrhages with pooling of dye in the subretinal space. Optical coherence tomography of the left macula demonstrated cystoid macular edema with multilayered cystic spaces, neurosensory detachment, and two hyperreflective juxtafoveal globular lesions in the outer retina; there was no evidence of choroidal neovascularization. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, tuberculin skin test, angiotensin-converting enzyme level, rapid plasma reagin, antinuclear antibodies, and IgM antibodies against Bartonella and Toxoplasma, were all negative.

A 45-year-old previously healthy Asian woman presented with bilateral visual loss of one week’s duration. One week earlier she had been discharged after an undiagnosed febrile illness with temperatures above 38°C and an erythematous, tender, painful rash composed of small papules, pustules, and nodules coalescing into swollen plaques on her upper and lower limbs; there was minimal involvement of the torso and no oral or genital ulceration or joint pain. Skin biopsy was pending. Laboratory studies showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein level, leukocytosis with more than 70% neutrophils, and negative blood, urine, fecal, and throat cultures; serologic tests for hepatitis B and C, HIV, and syphilis; HSV and VZV PCR of skin swabs; and a normal chest radiograph. She received empirical intravenous cefuroxime and oral aciclovir.

On ophthalmologic examination, her rash appeared to be resolving. Best corrected visual acuity was hand motions in the right eye and 20/120 in the left eye; intraocular pressures were within normal limits. Conjunctival injection was present without lesions. Slit‐lamp examination revealed severe non‐granulomatous bilateral panuveitis with 3+ anterior chamber cells and flare, posterior synechiae, and 3 to 4+ vitreous flare. Fundoscopic examination showed bilateral hemorrhagic occlusive retinal vasculitis, retinitis, and macular edema without optic disc involvement. A right vitreous tap was performed, and she received bilateral intravitreal ganciclovir injections, intravenous aciclovir, and prednisolone eye drops. Vitreous aspirate results were pending.

A 70-year-old man was brought by his family for psychiatric evaluation because he was restless at home with a false belief that police would arrest his family. His vital signs and neurological examination were normal. One month earlier, after retiring because of hearing problems, he began complaining of memory loss. On examination he was perplexed and oriented only to person; he could recall coming to the hospital the day before but not how he arrived or returned home, repeatedly stating, “I have lost my memory.” He repeatedly asked for the time, saying that time seemed to pass very fast or to stop. He could not state the day of the week or current year and appeared disoriented. He also questioned the real value of a yen and said, “I feel as if I didn’t wash my body,” despite having showered. Routine blood tests were normal. Electroencephalography, brain MRI, and cerebrospinal fluid studies (cell count, glucose, LDH, osmotic pressure, and color) were all normal. Quetiapine, 50 mg at bedtime, was prescribed without change in his complaints. During the first week of admission, he walked the corridors, was occasionally confused, sometimes grinned, and refused baths. On day 11 he covered his ears as if responding to voices and then stamped his foot, declaring nihilistic delusions: “I am dead,” “I have become a stone,” “my heart has stopped,” “I have destroyed all mankind,” and “loans have accumulated to an astronomically large amount.” He denied depressed mood. Sequential trials of risperidone, olanzapine, and quetiapine had no effect. Clomipramine was administered intravenously, but his condition remained unchanged.

An 86-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 6-month history of a darkly pigmented, irregular patch on her vulva. She denied pruritus, burning, or pain. On examination, there was a well-demarcated brownish to blackish macule measuring 3 × 2 cm at the vestibule and over the clitoral frenulum, and a 0.5 cm indistinct satellite papule on the left labium minus; both lesions were nonpalpable. No other vulvar or cutaneous lesions were present. She had a history of urinary incontinence. Because melanoma could not be clinically excluded, three punch biopsies were taken: two from the main patch and one from the satellite lesion. The patient had received no prior local treatment.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of lower abdominal pain. He had no significant past medical or surgical history, aside from intermittent abdominal discomfort over several years. On examination, his temperature was normal, blood pressure and pulse were within normal limits, and there was tenderness to palpation of the lower abdomen without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 11.2×10^3/μL and a C-reactive protein level of 30.7 mg/dL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 7.5-cm irregular polycystic mass in the lower abdomen that was contiguous with the small intestine. Based on these findings, the leading preoperative considerations were a large Meckel’s diverticulum or a small intestinal tumor. We elected to proceed with laparoscopic-assisted surgery.

A 20-year-old primigravida was transferred 4 days after delivering a nonviable fetus at 24 weeks’ gestation because of progressive respiratory distress. On arrival she was intubated. There was no past medical history and no pregnancy complications such as preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, or infection. The temperature was 101°F, pulse 122/min, blood pressure 118/78 mm Hg, and Glasgow Coma Scale score E4M6Vt. No rash was observed. Bilateral lung crepitations were present. Chest radiograph showed bilateral infiltrates. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed poor left ventricular systolic function without right‐side dilatation. She was treated for pneumonia, sepsis, acute kidney injury, and peripartum cardiomyopathy; her hemodynamic, pulmonary, and renal parameters improved but she continued to have high-grade fevers. On hospital day 5, she was noted to have gross symmetric weakness of the proximal muscles of all four limbs and dark-colored urine. Laboratory studies showed positive urine myoglobin, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 47 mm/hr, a creatine phosphokinase level of 109 200 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase of 460 U/L. Thyroid function tests were normal. Testing for systemic lupus erythematosus (antinuclear antibody and anti–double-stranded DNA) was negative. Despite supportive care and hemodialysis, there was no major recovery of muscle strength or enzyme levels.

A woman in her late seventies with a prior infrarenal endovascular aortic repair seven years earlier was electively admitted for embolization of a type II endoleak in September 2019. Superselective embolization of the iliolumbar branches supplying the nidus was performed using Onyx® under fluoroscopic guidance, with complete exclusion of the nidus from both sides. Five hours after the procedure, she noted acute bilateral lower‐limb weakness and numbness, right more than left.

On examination, there was a lower‐motor‐neuron pattern of weakness in both lower limbs, worse on the right (Table 1). Sensation to light touch and pinprick was normal on the left but impaired from L2 to S1 dermatomes on the right. Proprioception at the bilateral great toes was intact. Deep‐tendon reflexes were absent in both lower limbs.

A 60-year-old Thai woman presented with a 4-month history of episodic, painful, horizontal binocular diplopia that was consistently triggered by prolonged eccentric gaze. She denied any oscillopsia. Her medical history was notable for nasopharyngeal carcinoma treated with chemotherapy and external-beam radiotherapy (total dose, 7000 cGy), with the most recent treatment 13 years earlier and no evidence of recurrence. 

On general neurologic examination, findings were unremarkable. Neuro-ophthalmic examination showed normal visual acuity, visual fields, pupillary responses, and fundi. Alternate cover testing demonstrated orthotropia and orthophoria at distance and near. Ocular motility was normal in all directions, including full adduction of both eyes. There were no signs of orbicularis oculi weakness, fatigable ptosis, or Cogan’s lid twitch.

Provocative testing was then performed. After 30 seconds of sustained right gaze, the patient developed an involuntary contraction of the left medial rectus, resulting in a left esotropia when both eyes returned to the primary position; the esotropia persisted for approximately 2 minutes before resolving spontaneously. Similarly, after 30 seconds of sustained left gaze, she developed an involuntary contraction of the right medial rectus with resultant right esotropia in primary gaze, lasting about 2 minutes. During these episodes, the esodeviation was steady and non-variable, and both pupils and eyelid positions remained normal. Sustained vertical eccentric gaze did not provoke any misalignment.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, including the brain stem and parasellar regions, showed no parenchymal lesions or tumor recurrence.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of recurrent lower abdominal pain. Her past medical history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and a total abdominal hysterectomy one year earlier. The pain was initially thought to be due to a urinary tract infection, but did not resolve with treatment. She complained of acute worsening of suprapubic pain over the 4–6 hours prior to presentation; it became generalized, constant, and worsened with sitting up or leg extension. She also reported bilious vomiting but denied fever, obstipation, or overt rectal bleeding. She noted constipation and a change in stool caliber over the past 6 months, along with night sweats and weight loss. She had never undergone colonoscopic screening.  

On examination, vital signs were normal. She was obese, with a midline surgical scar and a small umbilical hernia. The abdomen was tender with voluntary guarding in the lower quadrants; bowel sounds and rectal examination were unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies revealed a lactate level of 6.0 mmol/L (reference 0.5–1.0) and a white-cell count of 15.0×10^9/L (reference 4.0–11.0); other parameters were within normal limits.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed high-grade small-bowel obstruction with hypoattenuating bowel wall consistent with ischemia. On axial and coronal images, mesenteric vessels and loops of dilated ileum were seen passing beneath a tented sigmoid colon to the contralateral side, forming a closed-loop configuration. The sigmoid colon appeared collapsed and draped (“Omega sign”), and there was steamy mesenteric change and moderate free intraperitoneal fluid.

A man in his sixties with type 2 diabetes, COPD (no home oxygen), hypertension, and hypothyroidism was brought in after being found unresponsive at home. He reported one day of dizziness, cough, fatigue, and balance loss but denied dyspnea, myalgia, gastrointestinal symptoms, travel, sick contacts, and chest pain. On admission he was afebrile initially, then had a temperature of 101°F, blood pressure 137/82 mmHg, heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on 6 L nasal cannula. Exam showed dry, pale skin and bilateral lower-lung rales. Lab tests revealed creatine kinase >5,000 U/L, mild AST/ALT elevations, normal lactate and leukocyte count with no bands, and a negative rapid flu test. Chest radiograph showed no new acute changes compared with prior imaging. He was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin for presumed pneumonia versus bronchitis leading to a COPD exacerbation. Over the first 48 hours, he remained stable. Fifty-two hours after admission, he spiked a fever of 101.7°F, his oxygen saturation fell to 88% on room air (92% on 6 L), and new bilateral wheezing was noted on exam.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a several-day history of a pruritic rash. It began on the dorsal aspects of her hands and subsequently appeared on the dorsal aspects of her feet. She was afebrile with unremarkable vital signs. In the emergency department, she was treated with triamcinolone 0.1% cream twice daily without improvement. Two days later, her primary care physician prescribed fluocinonide 0.05% ointment twice daily; pruritus improved but the rash spread to her left thigh. Ten days after rash onset, she was evaluated in dermatology. She reported a positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR result six weeks before the rash, having recovered at home without supportive care.  
On examination, she had violaceous smooth papules coalescing into plaques on the dorsal hands and feet and fewer lesions on the anterior left thigh. Petechial macules were noted on the fingertips and shins. There was no mucosal, palmar, or plantar involvement.  
A 3-mm punch biopsy from the left dorsal hand showed focal epidermal spongiosis, papillary dermal edema with extravasated erythrocytes, and a lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate in the superficial dermis.  
Parvovirus B19 serologies were positive for IgG and negative for IgM. Complete blood count with differential and comprehensive metabolic panel were unremarkable.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 29-year-old gravida 1, para 0 woman at 22 weeks of gestation presented for a scheduled induced abortion via dilation and evacuation. Her pregnancy was complicated by a fetus with trisomy 22 and multiple anomalies. Her pre-procedure hemoglobin was 12.1 g/dL and platelet count was 134 × 10^3/µL; blood pressures ranged from 80s to 100s mmHg. Cervical dilators were placed the day before. On the day of the procedure, monitored anesthesia care was administered, dilators were removed, and a paracervical block was performed. Ultrasound-guided dilation and evacuation was completed without immediate complications and with an estimated blood loss of 100 mL. In the post-anesthesia care unit 15 minutes post-operatively, vaginal bleeding of approximately 200 mL was noted; methylergonovine and a crystalloid bolus were given. Forty-five minutes after the procedure, an additional 200 mL of bleeding occurred; transabdominal ultrasound showed a thin endometrial stripe without free fluid, and firm uterine tone was confirmed; rectal misoprostol was administered. Seventy-five minutes post-operatively, the patient became acutely hypotensive (54/42 mmHg). She was returned to the operating room. On examination, a 1 × 2 cm clot was removed from the endometrial canal, firm uterine tone was maintained, and no cervical lacerations or retained products were found; hemostatic agents were applied to minor oozing at the external os. Estimated total blood loss was 750 mL. Intra-operative laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 10.4 g/dL, platelet count of 84 × 10^3/µL, an international normalized ratio of 1.7, and an activated partial thromboplastin time of 84 seconds.

A 45-year-old man with no significant medical or surgical history presented with an asymptomatic, slowly growing, palpable right inguinal mass. On examination, there was a hard, multinodular, mobile mass along the right spermatic cord near the upper pole of the testis, and the testis itself appeared uninvolved. Scrotal ultrasound showed normal testicles and a 3.5 cm paratesticular heterogeneous hyperechoic lesion along the right spermatic cord, cranial to the testicle, without tunica albuginea involvement. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a diffuse-proliferated nodular mass with iso- and low-intensity signal on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and minimal contrast enhancement. Laboratory investigations revealed negative lactate dehydrogenase, alpha-fetoprotein, and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin. The patient underwent inguinal surgical exploration; intraoperative frozen-section assessment was reported as benign, and a testis-sparing enucleation of the mass was performed.

A 15-year-old previously healthy girl underwent contrast-enhanced pelvic MRI with a gadolinium-based agent for evaluation of persistent pelvic pain. A few minutes after receiving gadolinium, she developed shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting, and presented to the emergency department. On arrival, she had a transient loss of consciousness. Vital signs were: blood pressure 84/40 mmHg, heart rate 122/min, respiratory rate 30/min, temperature 36.4 °C, and oxygen saturation 78% on room air. On pulmonary auscultation, bilateral rales were present; there was no rash or lip/tongue swelling. She spoke in full sentences and was placed on 10 L/min oxygen via non-rebreather mask.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 18.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 15,360/mm3, C-reactive protein 41.8 mg/L, lactate dehydrogenase 176 U/L, and D-dimer 1.7 mg/mL. B-type natriuretic peptide and troponin levels were low. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal. Chest computed tomography performed about 1 hour after gadolinium administration showed bilateral confluent consolidations predominantly in the posterior lower lobes, ground-glass opacities in the upper lobes, and interlobular septal thickening. CT pulmonary angiography was negative for pulmonary embolism. A SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal swab was negative.

A 25-year-old G2P1 woman presented with sharp, constant lower abdominal pain and no initial vaginal bleeding. Her history included PCOS and a cesarean delivery 2 years earlier; she was presumed to be at 16 weeks’ gestation. Vital signs were stable. That evening she developed vaginal spotting that progressed to heavy bleeding with clots and severe cramping radiating to the back. An urgent obstetric ultrasound showed a single live intrauterine pregnancy at 16 weeks, but the internal cervical os could not be traced into the uterine cavity. Transvaginal scanning was performed, and the radiologist recommended repeating the ultrasound at 20 weeks. The patient was discharged.

Two weeks later, she returned with generalized abdominal pain, chest and back pain, which later localized to the right lower quadrant with nausea and vomiting. Emergent ultrasound documented an age-appropriate live fetus at 17 weeks without distress and a mild to moderate amount of echogenic free fluid in the pelvis and right lower quadrant. On transabdominal imaging, a uterus-like structure with a thin endometrial stripe was noted in the right adnexa. Transvaginal scanning confirmed an empty left lateral endometrial cavity and communication between the cervix and uterine cavity, and further pockets of free fluid were seen in the hepatorenal and splenorenal recesses. Despite these findings, the radiologist’s report listed differential diagnoses including hemorrhagic neoplasm, heterotopic pregnancy, red degeneration of a fibroid, dermoid cyst, decidualized endometrioma, and ovarian torsion. The patient was again discharged after blood tests.

A 71-year-old man reported a subtle onset of severe neck flexion over several months, which progressively worsened. He also noted mild dysphagia and dysphonia. His medical history included type II diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, arterial hypertension, and mild cervical spondylosis. His father had Parkinson’s disease; the patient himself did not smoke or drink and took no medications. 

On neurologic examination, he had hypomimia, mild bradykinesia, asymmetric rigidity, and a shuffling gait. There was no ptosis or diplopia. Strength testing revealed 2/5 power in the neck extensors and 5/5 power in all other muscle groups; cognition was intact. 

Brain and cervical spine MRI scans showed no structural abnormalities. Repetitive nerve stimulation of the neck extensors revealed a reduction in the amplitude and area of compound muscle action potentials between the first and fourth stimuli. Needle electromyography did not show any myopathic or neuropathic features. Laboratory testing demonstrated high‐titer acetylcholine receptor–binding antibodies (8 nmol/L; normal <0.40 nmol/L), whereas muscle‐specific kinase antibodies and other markers, including creatine kinase, aldolase, and thyroid‐stimulating hormone, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed no thymoma.

A 35-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2 at 34 weeks 5 days’ gestation with gestational diabetes mellitus treated with 6 units of insulin detemir daily, presented with a 1-week history of dyspnea, myalgia, headache, tachycardia, fatigue, and productive cough causing chest pain. Symptoms worsened over the preceding 2 days despite outpatient IV fluids.  
Her history included papillary thyroid carcinoma diagnosed by fine-needle aspiration in early pregnancy, for which surgery was deferred postpartum; she was taking levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. She had mild gestational diabetes since 20 weeks’ gestation and pre-pregnancy propranolol therapy that was stopped for pregnancy.  
On admission, blood glucose was 70 mg/dL; blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg; heart rate 120 bpm; respiratory rate 35 breaths/min; oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She reported household exposure to COVID-19; SARS-CoV-2 PCR returned positive the next day.  
Chest CT demonstrated 40% bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltration with subpleural and ground-glass opacities. Platelet count was 70,000/µL with no schistocytes on smear.  
Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.33, PCO₂ 16.7 kPa, bicarbonate 8.2 mmol/L, with an anion gap of 21 mmol/L.  
Urinalysis revealed 3+ ketones and no glucosuria.

A 55-year-old man with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus presented with acute hypoxic respiratory failure. He was afebrile, blood pressure 84/45 mm Hg, heart rate 67 bpm, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. Examination revealed 1+ pitting edema in the lower extremities, fine bibasilar crackles, and a 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex. A CT angiogram with PE protocol showed pulmonary edema, severe coronary atherosclerotic disease, and calcification in the right ventricle. Cardiac troponin T was elevated at 2245 ng/L (normal ≤22 ng/L), and the ECG demonstrated ST elevations in the anterolateral leads with poor R-wave progression.

Transthoracic echocardiography estimated an LVEF of 45% with inferior and inferolateral wall hypokinesis and revealed an immobile cystic mass in the right ventricular apex and interventricular septum. Coronary catheterization showed marked aneurysmal dilation of the left main and left anterior descending arteries without focal coronary artery disease. His dyspnea worsened, requiring BiPAP, and he developed fascicular ventricular tachycardia, which was controlled with amiodarone. He was transferred to our center, where re-catheterization demonstrated 100% stenosis of the left circumflex artery, likely embolic from aneurysmal segments. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed the transthoracic findings.

Cardiac MRI showed a severely reduced LVEF of 26% with transmural scar and superimposed thrombus in the inferior and inferolateral walls and a 3.4 × 2.9 cm mass involving the mid-inferoseptum protruding into the right ventricle. Differential diagnoses included cardiac tumor vs sarcoidosis, and a biopsy was initially planned.

A 22-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive memory loss, visual disturbances, and intermittent generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurring weekly and lasting 5–10 minutes, followed by eye rolling and severe headache. She denied fever, cough, night sweats, or weight loss. Her medical history was unremarkable; she took no medications and had no known immunosuppression or tuberculosis exposure. On examination, she appeared ill but had no focal neurologic deficits.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/hr, a negative HIV test, mild thrombocytosis (329 000/µL), normal liver and renal function, negative sputum cultures for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Xpert MTB/RIF), and a normal serum adenosine deaminase level.

Contrast-enhanced brain MRI demonstrated multiple ring-enhancing lesions clustered in the left parietal lobe (largest 2.1 cm) and a smaller lesion in the right occipital lobe. The lesion cores were heterogeneous on T2-weighted images, isointense on FLAIR, without blooming on susceptibility-weighted imaging and without diffusion restriction on DWI. There was extensive surrounding vasogenic edema on T2/FLAIR sequences, and no leptomeningeal enhancement was seen.

A 43-year-old man presented with a 12-hour history of high-grade fever, cough, and left-sided chest pain. He had no history of trauma. On examination, his temperature was elevated; auscultation revealed reduced air entry over the left upper and mid lung zones. A chest radiograph showed a triangular opacity in the left upper and mid zones laterally. The finding was interpreted as possible lung consolidation, and the patient was treated medically. Two follow-up chest radiographs, each obtained at two-week intervals, showed no change in the left-mid-zone opacity, although he was asymptomatic. Review of the radiographs also noted depression of the left third rib. To further evaluate the persistent opacity and rib abnormality, a helical CT scan of the chest with multiplanar and 3D reconstructions was obtained.

A 56-year-old man who works as a gym instructor and trains five times per week was evaluated for one month of gradually worsening neck pain with a feeling of heaviness in the head. The pain began during weightlifting (bench press, shoulder press, squats) and treadmill use, was aggravated by lower-body training, and reached a worst intensity of 8/10 on a numeric rating scale. He noted stiffness and limited rotation of the neck bilaterally, worse with cold exposure, and morning stiffness that improved over hours but left persistent head heaviness. He had no history of trauma, night pain, or dizziness, and he self-treated with foam rolling. Medical history included adolescent-onset hyperreflexia and dysmetria of the left arm, testicular torsion repair in 1982, and left shoulder arthroplasty in 2018. Both he and his brother had lifelong thrombocytopenia and leukopenia; his father had hypertension.  

On examination, there was bilateral trapezius spasm, painful restricted neck rotation (8/10), and neck extension that increased head heaviness. Temperature was normal. Oxygen saturation was 99%, resting heart rate 68 bpm, and resting blood pressure averaging 130/80 mmHg. To assess exercise response, BP, heart rate, and rate of perceived exertion were measured every 3 minutes during treadmill walking at 5 km/h with a 2% incline, with the left arm relaxed. At minute 3, BP was 145/85 mmHg (HR 91 bpm, RPE 0); at minute 6, BP 160/95 mmHg (HR 96 bpm, RPE 5) with recurrence of his usual neck pain; at minute 9, BP 190/100 mmHg (RPE 8) with sharp worsening of neck pain and an unsteady gait, prompting test termination. After exercise, left blepharoptosis was noted.

A 51-year-old man was referred for evaluation of recent-onset bilateral knee pain and progressive deformity just below the knee joints. He had chronic pancreatitis secondary to long-term alcohol use, insulin-dependent type II diabetes for 4 years, and chronic diarrhea with 7–8 bowel movements per day for 3 years. He denied steroid use. Knee pain first appeared on the right after activity and, one month later, on the left. He noted swelling and worsening deformity but relatively little pain. 

On examination, both knees had large effusions, flexion from 5° to 120°, and marked mediolateral instability at the proximal tibia, especially when weight bearing. Gait and clinical tests were relatively painless, and he required crutches. Neurologic examination revealed stocking-glove paresthesia with decreased sensitivity to pain, temperature, and pressure in both lower limbs, decreased patellar and Achilles reflexes, and an old scar from a diabetic ulcer on the left leg. Pulses in the femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis arteries were 3+ bilaterally.

Radiographs showed progressive insufficiency fractures of the medial tibial plateaus, worse on the right. CT and MRI of both knees demonstrated bilateral medial tibial plateau fractures with dense bone marrow edema, soft-tissue edema, joint effusion, and hypointense marrow signal in the distal femurs on all sequences. White blood cell count and C-reactive protein were normal, and MRI did not suggest osteomyelitis. DEXA scanning revealed generalized osteopenia. Electromyography showed high-degree sensorimotor polyneuropathy consistent with diabetic neuropathy. Thyroid and parathyroid evaluations were normal.

A 57-year-old woman presented in 1995 with a six-week history of acute-onset polyarthralgia. She also reported Raynaud’s phenomenon, dry eyes, dyspepsia, intermittent night sweats, brittle nails, intermittent hair loss, mouth ulcers, and fatigue. A provisional diagnosis of mild connective tissue disease (Sjögren’s syndrome or lupus) was made based on these symptoms and a single positive double-stranded DNA result. Her medical history included Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and osteoarthritis. 

In 2007, she acquired a sheep bot fly infection in Morocco and underwent removal of larvae from her left maxillary sinus and right eye. 

In 2010, she re-presented with intermittent left-sided facial pain and swelling, associated with hearing loss in her left ear, gradually worsening epiphora, blepharospasm, and left eye swelling. An extensive autoimmune screen was negative (anti-Ro, anti-La, ANCA, ANA); the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 6 mm/h (normal 1–20), and immunoglobulin G and A levels were mildly elevated. Schirmer’s test was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the sinuses, skull base, and parotid glands showed only mild sinus thickening. A tympanogram demonstrated low-tone hearing loss with negative middle-ear pressure. Ultrasound of the left face was non-diagnostic, and flexible nasoendoscopy was normal. She was treated with carbamazepine and botulinum toxin injections to her facial muscles with minimal symptomatic improvement. A second MRI scan was performed and reviewed by a neuroradiologist.

A 36-year-old woman with gastroesophageal reflux disease, obesity, hypertension, and polycystic ovary syndrome presented with one month of postprandial right upper quadrant pain without jaundice or acholic stools. Her physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including a hepatic function panel and complete blood count, were within normal limits.
