Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a large calculous gallbladder with wall thickening and a single pericentimeter low-attenuation focus in segment four of the liver, which was thought to reflect focal fat infiltration. A right upper quadrant ultrasound was ordered but not completed. She was diagnosed with symptomatic cholelithiasis and underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Upon entry, numerous diffuse subcentimeter flat white lesions were noted scattered throughout both lobes of the liver. Three excisional biopsies of these nodules were performed and sent for permanent pathology and microbiology. The cholecystectomy proceeded without complication.

A 7-year-old male intact indoor/outdoor domestic shorthair cat (4.5 kg) was referred in winter for non-pruritic facial skin lesions and bilateral ceruminous otitis externa. Over the past year, the cat received multiple intramuscular methylprednisolone acetate injections for stomatitis. Eleven days before referral, the cat was diagnosed with uncomplicated diabetes mellitus after a complete work-up, which revealed marked hyperglycemia (blood glucose 489 mg/dl; RI 66–150), elevated fructosamine (412 µmol/l; RI 190–340), mild ALP elevation (139 U/l; RI 15–125), glucosuria without ketonuria, negative urine culture, and positive FIV serology. The diabetes was controlled with glargine insulin (0.25 IU/kg q12h SC) and a diabetic diet.

On dermatological examination, there was erythema, hypotrichosis, crusts, and a brownish oily exudate over the dorsal nasal region. Both ear canals contained a brown ceruminous exudate, and the haircoat was dry and dull. Initial dermatological differential diagnoses included dermatophytosis, demodicosis, and solar (actinic) dermatitis.

A 6-month-old boy was brought to the vascular surgery clinic with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging swelling on the hypothenar eminence of his left hand. The parents noted no unusual crying or signs of pain. On examination, the mass measured approximately 4×2 cm, was pulsatile on palpation, and had no overlying skin changes. There were no motor deficits in the left hand, both radial and ulnar pulses were palpable, and capillary refill was normal. Further history revealed that the infant habitually banged his left hand against hard surfaces while feeding. Given the location and pulsatile character of the swelling, an aneurysm arising from the ulnar artery or superficial palmar arch was suspected. An arterial duplex ultrasound confirmed the presence of an aneurysmal sac; detailed vascular anatomy could not be delineated due to the patient’s age, and no additional imaging studies were obtained.

A 69-year-old man presented with a 1-day history of chest pain. He was diagnosed with a non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction on the basis of elevated high-sensitivity troponin T levels and was referred for urgent invasive coronary angiography via a right transradial approach. Significant tortuosity of the subclavian artery necessitated use of a hydrophilic guidewire to advance the catheter into the aortic root, and a heavily calcified ostial obtuse marginal lesion was successfully stented.

Immediately postprocedure, he developed marked hypotension (70/20 mm Hg in the right arm; 95/40 mm Hg in the left arm), tachycardia to 120 beats/min, diaphoresis, and dull central chest discomfort. He remained alert and oriented. Despite 2,000 mL of intravenous 0.9% saline, hypotension persisted, although vasopressors were not administered.

His preprocedure hemoglobin was 102 g/L, which fell to 81 g/L postprocedure. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia with normal QRS voltages and no ST-T-segment changes. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated no pericardial effusion, left ventricular dysfunction, or ascending aortic dissection. A portable chest radiograph revealed a new widening of the mediastinal contour.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of right shoulder pain and a progressively enlarging “dumbbell-shaped” swelling developing over 4 months. He denied trauma, fever, or night sweats. His history was notable for treated pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years earlier. On examination there was a large, soft, fluctuant swelling around the right shoulder with tense overlying skin, no sinus or discharge, normal local temperature, and tenderness of the shoulder capsule and axilla. Active and passive shoulder movements were painful and severely limited; axillary lymph nodes were enlarged; distal neurovascular examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, white cells 11,000/mm3 (48% lymphocytes), and an ESR of 60 mm/hr. Plain radiography of the right shoulder revealed erosion of the glenoid cavity and humeral head, joint-space narrowing, obliteration of adjacent fat planes, and soft-tissue shadowing without dislocation. Chest radiograph showed diffuse small nodular opacities throughout both lungs. MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated cortical erosions of the humeral head and glenoid, moderate joint effusion, synovial thickening, rotator cuff atrophy, enlarged axillary nodes, and a large (14×6 cm) loculated periarticular fluid collection extending into the supraspinatus fossa and deltoid region.

A 32‐year‐old woman with a 4‐year history of antiphospholipid syndrome—confirmed by triple‐positive antiphospholipid antibodies on two occasions 12 weeks apart, prior deep vein thrombosis, and two miscarriages—presented with 4 weeks of nocturnal fevers (peak 38.4°C) with chills and a 3‐month history of persistent anemia. Her medications included prednisolone and hydroxychloroquine. On presentation, blood pressure was 115/80 mmHg, pulse 140/min, temperature 39°C, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Cardiac exam revealed a third heart sound and a III/VI pansystolic murmur at the mitral and tricuspid areas with tachycardia; pulmonary exam showed fine crackles. Laboratory tests demonstrated elevated ESR (77 mm/h) and CRP (14.5 mg/dL), hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, and normal white cell and platelet counts. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed severe posterior‐directed mitral regurgitation with partially flail mitral leaflets, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, a 30 × 5 mm mass on the posterior mitral valve leaflet extending into the left atrium, and a 26 × 12 mm multilobulated calcified mass on the anterior mitral valve leaflet extending into the left ventricle.

A female neonate weighing 3.970 kg (94th percentile; +1.52 SDS), length at the 87th percentile, and head circumference at the 57th percentile was referred on day 1 for hypoglycemia (2.11 mmol/L) and congenital inability to feed due to fused jaws. She was the first child of healthy, nonconsanguineous parents; prenatal history was unremarkable except for shoulder dystocia and a nuchal cord. The mother’s oral glucose tolerance test was normal, and there were no placental or amniotic fluid anomalies. Apgar scores were 8 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes.

On examination, the infant had macrosomia, overfolded superior helix ear malformation, broad nasal bridge, thin lips, mild retrognathia, multiple fibrous bands between the maxillary and mandibular gingiva, and tongue-to-palate fusion. There were no clefts visible externally, and the lips were normal. Additional findings included clitoral hypertrophy, hypoplasia of the labia majora, bilateral cutaneous syndactyly of the second and third toes, cutaneous syndactyly of the fourth and fifth right toes, and pyramidal skinfolds over both halluces.

Total parenteral nutrition was initiated. Awake nasopharyngoscopy showed palatal hypermobility suggestive of submucosal cleft palate, with a normal laryngeal air column. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction of the face revealed a cleft palate, underdeveloped mandibular condyles, reduced temporomandibular joint spaces with flattening of bony components, and a supernumerary deciduous maxillary premolar; no bony fusion was identified. Cardiac and cranial ultrasonography and fundoscopy were normal.

A female infant was born at 34 weeks and 2 days of gestation by secondary cesarean section to a 38-year-old mother with a positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR result five days before delivery and mild COVID-19 symptoms; she was unvaccinated. Maternal gestational diabetes was diet-controlled. The cesarean section was performed under epidural anesthesia for preterm labor, and maternal vital signs remained stable. 

The infant’s Apgar scores were 7, 8, and 9 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes, respectively. Umbilical arterial pH was 7.40 with a base excess of +0.9 mmol/L. In the delivery room, the baby required suctioning for airway obstruction, five sustained inflations, and intermittent mask ventilation (FiO₂ up to 0.5) for 5 minutes. Heart rate and oxygen saturation subsequently normalized, but mild respiratory distress prompted transfer to the neonatal intensive care unit, where she received continuous positive airway pressure (FiO₂ 0.21) for 10 hours. A chest radiograph showed mild diffuse granular opacification consistent with respiratory distress syndrome. Vital signs remained stable throughout.

A peripheral venous catheter was placed, and empiric antibiotics were given for 2 days until blood cultures, gastric aspirate cultures, and infection parameters were repeatedly negative. Complete blood counts and differential results were within normal limits. Nasopharyngeal swabs on days 1, 4, and 8 of life were negative for SARS-CoV-2. On day 5, routine cranial ultrasonography demonstrated increased echogenicity in the left subependymal area and basal ganglia; repeat sonography on day 10 showed clear demarcation of this lesion.

A 20-year-old man presented 5 hours after his abdomen was struck by a tractor and impacted against a felled tree stump. He reported sudden onset, constant, severe abdominal pain and progressive swelling at the impact site. He had no history of hernias or chronic illness. On examination, he had slight abdominal distention and a 10×10 cm tender swelling above the umbilicus with bruises and abrasions on the left side; the mass was partially reducible, and subcutaneous emphysema extended to the left flank and hypochondrium. The remainder of the abdomen was very tender, with board-like rigidity and rebound tenderness. His pulse was 104 beats/min and blood pressure 150/90 mmHg. Complete blood count results were unremarkable. An erect chest radiograph demonstrated free air under the diaphragm. Abdominal ultrasound showed free intraperitoneal fluid. A CT scan was not performed due to financial constraints. Given these findings, an emergency exploratory laparotomy was planned.

A 6-year-old girl was admitted with a 5-day history of left-sided neck swelling, fever, and mild dysphagia. One day before admission she developed bilateral conjunctival injection despite 5 days of cefoperazone–sulbactam and metronidazole. Her medical, family, and social histories were unremarkable. 

On examination, she had low-grade fever, mild posterior pharyngeal wall congestion, grade II tonsillar enlargement, and a tender, erythematous swelling below the left earlobe extending anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Multiple thumb-sized lymph nodes were palpable in the left supraclavicular fossa. Conjunctival injection with scleral edema and scattered dry rales were also noted.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 35.3×10^9/L (83.4% neutrophils), HGB 124 g/L, PLT 441×10^9/L, CRP 30.2 mg/L, PCT 0.14 ng/mL, and urinalysis WBC 85.6/µL. Liver and kidney function and cardiac enzymes were normal.

Neck CT revealed an irregular soft-tissue density with partial cystic components deep to the left parotid gland and sternocleidomastoid muscle (13×25 mm), with mild rim enhancement but no enhancement of cystic areas. Chest CT was normal.

She was diagnosed with acute cervical lymphadenitis, left parapharyngeal abscess, and acute conjunctivitis. She received intravenous cefoperazone–sulbactam and underwent surgical resection of the left parapharyngeal mass with lymph node excision. 

Histopathology of the tissue showed proliferative lymphoid changes with abundant nuclear fragments in necrotic foci, suggestive of acute necrotizing lymphadenitis. Pathogen gene sequencing of the tissue did not identify any specific pathogens. 

On postoperative day 2, WBC was 22.5×10^9/L, neutrophils 67.8%, PLT 651×10^9/L, and CRP 28.3 mg/L. Despite surgery, her temperature continued to fluctuate and conjunctival injection persisted. MRI on day 3 demonstrated multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral carotid sheaths, submandibular, and submental regions (largest 10 mm) and an oval T2-hyperintense lesion (31×19×23 mm) adjacent to the left carotid sheath, with poorly defined borders and increased signal in the left anterior cervical fascia.

A 42-year-old man presented after stubbing his right ring finger on a wall while falling. He reported pain in the finger. He was healthy, worked as a hairdresser, and was a social smoker. On examination, there was minimal tenderness at the radial aspect of the distal phalanx of the right ring finger, with swelling, clubbing, and redness; the skin was intact. He had a full range of motion and no neurovascular deficits. Initial radiographs showed a lytic and expansile lesion originating proximally at the subchondral base of the distal phalanx with loss of radial cortex and a transverse fracture. Serial radiographs demonstrated no fracture union and suggested enlargement of the lesion. A preoperative MRI demonstrated a 9.5 × 11.5 × 9.6 mm well-defined mass lesion with expansion through the radial cortex, and T2 fat-suppressed sequences showed foci of hyperintensity thought to represent internal calcifications; these features were felt to be in keeping with an enchondroma.

A 10-month-old boy from Pakistan, the product of a first-cousin marriage, was referred for evaluation of progressively protruding eye globes with a watery discharge over the past 6 months. The parents reported that he was irritable, had disrupted sleep, poor coordination of movements, and diminished alertness and concentration. 

His mother, in her third pregnancy, did not take folic acid or antenatal vitamins, underwent no prenatal imaging, and experienced no fevers, convulsions, or bleeding during gestation. He was born at term via uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery, with a birth weight of 2.5 kg (2.9th percentile) and a head circumference of 32.1 cm (11.5th percentile). 

On examination, the child had bilateral enlargement and protrusion of the globes without a history of trauma. Neurologic examination confirmed uncoordinated movements but was otherwise nonfocal. No other systemic abnormalities were noted.

A 68-year-old Caucasian woman presented with an ulceration on the anterior surface of her left leg. Thirty years earlier, during an exacerbation of rheumatoid arthritis, she had been treated for a similar ulcer on her left forearm, diagnosed as pyoderma gangrenosum. Since that episode, her rheumatoid arthritis had been quiescent and had not required any therapy; at admission there were no signs of arthritis recurrence. 

On examination, there was an ulcerated lesion on the lower quadrants of the left breast. The patient reported that a breast lump had first appeared four years earlier and had enlarged rapidly over the past month. Clinical staging was T4aN1M0. A core-needle biopsy of the breast lesion revealed invasive ductal carcinoma with estrogen receptor expression in 90% of tumor cells and no expression of progesterone receptor or HER2.

A skin biopsy from the edge of the leg ulcer showed an intensive mixed inflammatory infiltrate composed predominantly of neutrophils, with destruction of vessels and necrosis of the overlying epithelium, consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum.

A 12-year-old girl with no history of menarche and no prior medical problems presented to the emergency department with severe acute pelvic pain of sudden onset. She had no vomiting, diarrhea, or fever. On examination, she had tenderness in the lower abdomen and right flank. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed a slight leukocytosis with mild neutrophilia and a slight decrease in hematocrit; liver and kidney function and inflammatory markers were within normal limits. Given her primary amenorrhea and acute pelvic pain, ovarian torsion was initially suspected. A suprapubic abdominal ultrasound was performed. The ovaries had normal echotexture and size, but there was marked distension of the cervix and upper vagina by an ovoid collection with heterogeneous, layered echogenicity consistent with hemorrhage in various stages. No free fluid was seen in the pouch of Douglas.

A 66-year-old woman was evaluated for dull, nonradiating retrosternal chest pain that began on the second day after an otherwise uneventful radiofrequency ablation of frequent, symptomatic premature ventricular complexes originating in the right ventricular outflow tract. Her medical history included well-controlled hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and class-1 obesity. Two days after ablation, her blood pressure was 125/80 mm Hg, heart rate 75 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Cardiac auscultation revealed muffled heart sounds without a pericardial friction rub; the second heart sound was accentuated at the aortic area. Lung examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed biphasic T waves in leads V1–V4. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated no pericardial effusion or regional wall-motion abnormalities. Complete blood count was normal, and the high-sensitivity C-reactive protein level was 3.38 mg/L (reference range 1–3 mg/L). Measurement of cardiac troponin was not performed due to expected post-ablation biomarker elevation.

A 60-year-old woman with no prior medical history was evaluated for 3 weeks of new psychiatric symptoms, including unreasonable irritability, anxiety, and fear. One week after symptom onset, she developed short-term memory loss, repetitive movements, and reduced verbal output. One week later, she had intermittent myoclonic jerks of her right hand and bilateral eyelids.

On neurologic examination, she was alert but disoriented to time and place, with slowed responses and intermittent stimulus-sensitive myoclonus. Vital signs were normal. 

Laboratory studies showed normal inflammatory markers, normal liver and kidney function, and no metabolic derangements.  
CSF analysis revealed very few cells, normal protein, and a negative bacterial culture.  
An electroencephalogram demonstrated generalized slowing with periodic triphasic sharp-wave complexes.  
Brain MRI showed diffuse, asymmetric cortical hyperintensity in bilateral frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes and cingulate gyri, as well as involvement of the right insula, right caudate, globus pallidus, and bilateral dorsomedial thalamus. The lesions were hyperintense on FLAIR, exhibited restricted diffusion on DWI/ADC, and showed no contrast enhancement or mass effect.

A 73-year-old woman with no personal or family history of bleeding disorders presented with a two-month history of difficult-to-control bleeding. She initially developed a large ecchymosis after a fall onto her left hip. Over the following month, she had spontaneous bruising on her arms, thigh, and ankle; petechiae; and hemarthroses of the right knee and left ankle, leading to limited joint motion. Several days before transfer, she noted dyspnea on exertion and new right-thigh and tongue swelling.

Her medical history included hypothyroidism, vitiligo, Raynaud phenomenon, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and a recently removed rectal polyp. She had no prior bleeding complications with surgeries. She was a former heavy drinker and a 50-pack-year smoker.

On arrival, her vital signs were stable. Physical examination revealed extensive ecchymoses over the trunk and extremities and swelling of the right knee and left ankle.

Laboratory studies showed:
- Prothrombin time, fibrinogen, and platelet count within normal limits
- aPTT elevated at 50–60 seconds
- Coombs test negative; serum protein electrophoresis normal
- Factor VIII activity 16%
- All other factor activities normal (FII 138%, FV 192%, FVII 1212%, FIX 137%, FX 190%, FXI 90%, FXII 60%)
- 4:1 mixing study aPTT 34.3 seconds initially and 39.7 seconds after 2 hours of incubation
- Dilute Russell viper venom time normal at 37 seconds
- Heparinase test did not shorten the aPTT
- von Willebrand factor antigen and ristocetin cofactor activity within normal limits

A 32-year-old man with HIV diagnosed in January 2021 (CD4 <100 cells/mm3) was started on tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz, later switched to raltegravir. He developed bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy (largest 11×10 mm) and retroperitoneal adenopathy (largest 35×20 mm). In March 2021, he had abdominal pain with fever and night sweats. Cervical lymph-node and bone biopsies showed no malignancy, fungal infection, or tuberculosis. A PET scan in May 2021 revealed hypermetabolic intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy (SUV 17.6), raising suspicion for lymphoma; CA 19-9 was normal.

In June 2021 he presented with acute band-like abdominal pain radiating to the back, asthenia, adynamia, night fever, and diaphoresis. On exam his abdomen was soft, non-tender, with no palpable masses or organomegaly. Laboratory tests showed an amylase of 700 U/L and lipase of 1400 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an enlarged pancreatic head (53×50×55 mm) with poorly defined borders and heterogeneous echogenicity. Contrast CT confirmed a mass in the head of the pancreas with intra- and extrahepatic bile duct dilation and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a hypoechoic lesion with a predominance of blue-green elastography, suggestive of an inflammatory process.

Serial sputum AFB smears, a PPD skin test (0 mm), and Xpert MTB/RIF were negative; a chest CT showed a diffuse micronodular centrilobular pattern without consolidation. Bronchoscopy and an initial EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration of the pancreatic mass showed no microorganisms or malignancy. A repeat EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy of the pancreatic head lesion was then performed.

A 4-year-old girl presented with 2 days of fever and emesis and was initially treated with amoxicillin for presumed strep throat. Fever persisted, and on day 5 she developed a rash, hand puffiness, and bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis and received a 3-day course of corticosteroids with transient defervescence. Fever recurred 10 days after onset. On admission, laboratory tests showed ESR 53 mm/hr, CRP 3.9 mg/dL, WBC 23.4 × 10^3 cells/µL, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 393 × 10^3 cells/µL, sodium 132 mEq/L, and multiple negative SARS-CoV-2 antibody and PCR tests. Echocardiography was normal. On day 11 she was treated with IVIG (2 g/kg) and high-dose aspirin for presumed incomplete Kawasaki disease and defervesced. She was discharged on day 13 but had low-grade fevers and elevated inflammatory markers 3 days later, prompting readmission; a second IVIG dose was given with persistence of fever, so oral corticosteroids were started. On day 17 echocardiography revealed a new small saccular aneurysm of the left anterior descending coronary artery (max diameter 2.9 mm, z-score 3.27). She met incomplete Kawasaki disease criteria and received a second IVIG dose, but fever persisted and steroids were continued. Outpatient follow-up showed progressive enlargement of the left anterior descending aneurysm to 4.5 mm (z-score 9.0) and a right coronary artery aneurysm of 3.5 mm (z-score 4.2). Steroids were weaned over 3 weeks but she developed recurrent fever and elevated CRP on day 37, with mild systemic hypertension. Echocardiogram and CT on day 38 demonstrated further enlargement of the coronary aneurysms, and she was treated with cyclophosphamide and steroids for presumed refractory Kawasaki disease. Given her prolonged and atypical course of presumed Kawasaki disease with relapsing inflammation on steroid taper, alternative forms of vasculitis were considered.

A 10‐year‐old neutered male domestic longhair cat was evaluated for a 4‐day history of acute lethargy, hiding, reduced appetite, and right pelvic limb lameness. The cat was indoor, occasionally supervised in the garden. Initial radiographs by the referring veterinarian were unremarkable, and a trial of oral meloxicam yielded no improvement. On presentation, the cat weighed 4.5 kg (BCS 6/9). General physical examination was normal. Neurologic examination revealed grade 2/5 right pelvic limb lameness with reduced stifle extension; cranial nerves, segmental spinal reflexes, proprioception, and spinal palpation were normal. Orthopaedic examination confirmed right pelvic limb lameness and discomfort on right hip extension. L4–L6 femoral nerve lesion was suspected. Haematology and biochemistry showed moderate hyperglycaemia (19.9 mmol/l; RI 3.8–7.6) with normal fructosamine (226 µmol/l) and negative infectious disease titers. Under anaesthesia, radiographs of the pelvis, right stifle, and hock revealed narrowing of the L5–L6 intervertebral disc space; the disc at L5–L6 was mineralised and slightly dorsally displaced. The hips had adequate acetabular coverage bilaterally; a smoothly marginated bony spur was noted at the lateral malleolus, and periarticular new bone was seen at the tarsometatarsal joint. The stifle was normal.

A 92-year-old Caucasian woman presented with sudden-onset epigastric and right upper quadrant pain that awoke her from sleep. The pain was constant, radiated to her back, and was immediately followed by profuse vomiting. She denied fever, rigors, urinary or bowel symptoms and had no prior similar episodes. Her medical history included hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, a previous transient ischaemic attack with left carotid endarterectomy, peripheral vascular disease, an L2 vertebral crush fracture, and a remote open appendicectomy. 

On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with diffuse right-sided tenderness and a palpable gallbladder in the right iliac fossa. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 13.2×10^9/L; electrolytes, renal function, and liver-function tests were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a distended gallbladder with prominent wall thickening and mild adjacent inflammatory change, most consistent with cholecystitis. Ultrasound revealed a gallstone, minor gallbladder wall thickening, and no biliary ductal dilatation. She was started on intravenous antibiotics for presumed acute cholecystitis and admitted for surgical review.

The following morning, she had worsening pain despite analgesia, was tachycardic, tachypnoeic, and diaphoretic, and had developed a peritonitic abdomen. The white-cell count had risen to 17.6×10^9/L, C-reactive protein was 198 mg/L, and liver-function tests remained normal. A repeat contrast-enhanced CT was reported as showing “cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis with intra and extra bile duct dilatation as well as marked gallbladder distension and pericholecystic fluid.”

A 56-year-old woman of Surinamese descent with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus and prior splenectomy was admitted after collapse and fever. Her last visit to Suriname was in 2008. She was on mycophenolate mofetil 1250 mg twice daily and prednisone 20 mg daily, both recently increased for a flare of SLE nephritis with nephrotic syndrome. On admission, temperature was 39.1 °C. She had polyarthritis with swelling and warmth of the left knee and right-hand interphalangeal joints. Laboratory tests showed WBC 7.9 × 10^9 L^−1 (neutrophils 7.50 × 10^9 L^−1, lymphocytes 0.24 × 10^9 L^−1), hemoglobin 7.5 mmol L^−1, platelets 419 × 10^9 L^−1, and CRP 210 mg L^−1. Urinalysis revealed nitrite positivity. Intravenous ceftriaxone was started for suspected complicated urinary tract infection. Within one week, she developed respiratory insufficiency requiring mechanical ventilation and was transferred to the ICU. CT of the chest showed segmental pulmonary embolism, diffuse ground-glass opacities, and bilateral upper-lobe consolidations. She also developed liver failure (bilirubin 35 µmol L^−1; ALP 950 U L^−1; GGT 6335 U L^−1; AST 116 U L^−1; ALT 273 U L^−1) without an abdominal CT correlate. Initial bronchoalveolar lavage cultures were negative, and PCR assays for Legionella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and genus, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Chlamydia psittaci, Pneumocystis jiroveci, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and respiratory viruses were negative. Clinical deterioration was attributed to an SLE exacerbation, and methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily was given for three days. She improved and was extubated, but three days later became somnolent, re-developed respiratory failure, and required reintubation. Repeat chest CT showed progression of the ground-glass opacities. Histoplasmosis was considered, but fungal cultures remained negative and no antifungal therapy was initiated.

A 10-year-old girl presented with a 1-month history of right-sided epistaxis, nasal obstruction, proptosis, and epiphora. She denied pain, headache, neurologic symptoms, diplopia, visual disturbance, trauma, or prior sinonasal surgery. On examination, a large, partially reddish, smooth-surfaced mass was visible in the right nasal cavity, displacing the septum leftward and causing complete obstruction of the left nasal passage. The mass slightly displaced the right globe laterally, with mild exophthalmos. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Routine hematological and biochemical tests, including serum calcium, alkaline phosphatase, phosphorus, renal function, and parathyroid hormone, were within normal limits. Paranasal sinus CT and MRI demonstrated a large, multiseptated cystic expansile lesion with peripheral enhancement in the right sinonasal cavity, extending into the orbit, ethmoid sinus, and anterior cranial fossa. The radiologist’s initial impression was an infected mucocele. Endoscopic biopsy revealed a smooth, rubbery surface and a cystic interior filled with loose connective tissue and hematoma-like material. Histopathological evaluation of the biopsy specimens was inconclusive, described as “ulcerative and necrotic tissue” or “granulation tissue proliferation,” with the possibility of pyogenic granuloma. Considering these findings, the lesion was thought to be inflammatory with granulomatous features combined with mucocele.

A 44-year-old man with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis was referred for evaluation of bilateral lower limb edema that appeared two days after his most recent rituximab infusion. He also reported headache, generalized arthralgia, and increasing somnolence. He was not febrile, and vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination showed bilateral symmetric pitting edema of the lower limbs without skin lesions. Laboratory tests revealed: serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL; alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L (normal 6–45); aspartate aminotransferase 64 U/L (8–40); C-reactive protein 57 mg/dL (normal <10); hemoglobin 13.6 mg/dL; hematocrit 44%; white-cell count 5,600×10^9/L; platelets 123,000/μL.

His neurologic history began in 2001 with right optic neuritis, followed a year later by ataxia and diplopia when MRI showed hyperintense cervical spinal cord lesions and interferon-beta 1a was initiated. Five years later he developed bilateral lower limb paresis, and three years after that a severe quadriparesis, prompting a switch to fingolimod. In 2018, fingolimod was replaced with rituximab (1 g IV). Following the first infusion, he experienced erythema and urticarial lesions, and two days later developed bilateral edema and somnolence, which improved with antihistamines and corticosteroids. Six months later, after a second rituximab infusion (1 g IV), he again developed similar edema, headache, arthralgia, and somnolence. An infectious disease consultation was obtained to exclude infection or sepsis.

A 19-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a painful swelling on the buccal aspect of the gingiva of the mandibular left first molar. He first noticed the swelling 2 days earlier, which was accompanied by white, pinhead-sized ulcers. He had no systemic symptoms (no lymphadenitis, malaise, fever, or skin lesions). His medical history was unremarkable. He had recently undergone initial preparations for orthodontic treatment for crowding, including placement of elastic separators between teeth. On examination, there was a tender gingival swelling adjacent to the mesial aspect of the left mandibular first molar. A periapical radiograph taken at a non-orthoradial angle showed a small, ill-defined radio-opaque area at the interproximal alveolar crest (mesial to the first molar). A subsequent orthoradial radiograph demonstrated a rectangular-shaped radio-opaque mass in the interproximal area, along with evidence of subgingival calculus.

A 31-year-old woman presented with acute urinary retention for 1 day and a 2-month history of gradual, intermittent lower abdominal pain radiating to her back and lower limbs. She also noted intermittent bleeding during micturition over the same period. She had no history of trauma, instrumentation, dysuria, bowel complaints, or cyclical dysmenorrhea. Menarche occurred at age 14 with regular menses; her last menstrual period was 20 days ago. She was G2P2, both deliveries by Cesarean section, and had been informed of a didelphys uterus after her first delivery.

On examination, she was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and alert. Chest, cardiac, and neurologic exams were normal. Abdominal exam revealed a soft, tender suprapubic bulge without guarding or rigidity. Speculum examination showed a large, smooth cystic mass in the anterior vaginal wall obscuring the cervical os. Bimanual examination confirmed a large cystic mass filling the vagina. A Foley catheter was placed, relieving the urinary retention.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were normal. Urine pregnancy test was negative.  
Pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated nonvisualization of the right kidney, two separate uterine horns, and a cystic collection posterior to the uterine horns containing low-level echoes. Intravenous pyelogram confirmed absence of the right kidney with normal left renal excretion.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis revealed two widely separated uterine horns with preserved zonal anatomy, two distinct cervices, and a patent left vaginal canal. A 7.8×7.4×4.9 cm cystic collection inferior to the cervix showed intermediate T1 signal intensity and hyperintense T2 signal with fluid-fluid levels; it communicated with the right cervical canal. MRI of the abdomen confirmed right renal agenesis.

A 63-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, atrial fibrillation on warfarin for 12 years, and congestive heart failure presented with a 2-month history of progressively painful, non-healing, necrotic ulcers and brown discoloration on her right lower extremity. The lesions were tender, swollen, and refractory to local wound care. A computed tomography scan of the right lower extremity showed no evidence of osteomyelitis. Laboratory evaluation revealed a parathyroid hormone level of 82.5 pg/mL (reference 15–65), serum phosphorus 4.0 mg/dL, calcium 9.2 mg/dL, and magnesium 1.8 mg/dL. An anticoagulation panel showed an international normalized ratio of 3.54, protein C activity 56%, and protein S activity 58%. Her baseline serum creatinine was 1.7 mg/dL (CrCl ≈48 mL/min), rising to 2.25 mg/dL (CrCl ≈36 mL/min) on admission, with an associated serum potassium of 5.8 mg/dL.

A 3-year-old Saudi girl was admitted with a 2-day history of fever, cough, and intermittent tonic-clonic seizures associated with up-rolling of the eyes. She had two prior admissions for febrile convulsions and had been treated for asthma and bronchopneumonia. Her parents noted generalized darkening of the skin beginning at 18 months of age. There was parental consanguinity and a brother with early-onset adrenal insufficiency treated with hydrocortisone, but no genetic testing.

On examination: temperature 38.3 °C, heart rate 130 bpm, respiratory rate 40 per min, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg. There was diffuse hyperpigmentation, most pronounced on the elbows, hands, knees, and buccal mucosa; hypotonia and hyporeflexia were noted. Lacrimation was normal and there were no signs of achalasia.

Laboratory studies showed a random blood glucose of 30 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.24, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, PaCO₂ 45 mmHg; serum sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, phosphorus, and magnesium were normal. Liver and renal function tests, HbA₁c, free T₃, free T₄, TSH, insulin, and C-peptide were within normal limits. The 17-hydroxyprogesterone level was normal. A critical sample during hypoglycemia revealed plasma ACTH >2000 pg/mL and serum cortisol 53 nmol/L (reference 140–690 nmol/L). Serum androgens were 0.65 nmol/L (reference 0.5–2.4 nmol/L) and aldosterone was 50 pg/mL (reference 2–200 pg/mL). 

Ultrasound showed bilaterally small adrenal glands (right 5 × 6 mm, left 5 × 7.5 mm). A noncontrast CT scan of the brain was normal.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 9-month history of right groin pain and a 1-month history of right labial swelling. The pain was insidious, dull, mild to moderate in intensity, worsened by exertion, and relieved by rest and analgesics. She denied fever, weight loss, or constitutional symptoms and had no history of tuberculosis exposure, trauma, surgery, or gynecologic procedures.

On examination, there was an ill-defined, fluctuant, tender swelling over the right labium with erythema and warmth; no inguinal lymphadenopathy was noted, and hip range of motion was normal. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 22 mm in the first hour and a CRP of 36 mg/dL. A Mantoux test showed 38 × 45 mm of induration.

Plain radiography of the pelvis demonstrated a destructive lesion of the right pubis extending into the superior pubic rami with periosteal reaction, suggestive of chronic osteomyelitis. MRI of the pelvis revealed an oblong, multiloculated, thick-walled collection measuring 11.5 × 5.0 × 5.1 cm involving the right adductor longus, brevis, and obturator externus muscles, with focal bony destruction of the right superior pubic rami; one loculus extended into the subcutaneous tissue anterior to the pubic symphysis, and there was a small right hip joint effusion.

Under aseptic precautions, the labial swelling was aspirated with a 16-gauge needle, yielding frank pus, which was sent for Gram stain, AFB stain, aerobic culture, Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture, and GeneXpert testing.

A 34-year-old right-handed man from Eritrea, employed as a goldsmith, presented with a 6-month history of progressive bilateral hand tremor, associated with distal limb weakness and difficulty walking, more pronounced in the lower limbs. Two weeks before presentation, he had topical exposure to an expired ammonia solution. He described a long-standing gait abnormality for several years, with forefoot dragging and difficulty climbing stairs, which had not impacted daily activities. He also reported lifelong nasal congestion since age 7, treated surgically for a nasal mass, with persistent symptoms and snoring. He denied diabetes, hypertension, cardiac, renal, liver, or psychiatric illness, and had no known family history of neurologic disease.

Vital signs were normal. General examination revealed a left nasal polypoid mass. Neurologic examination showed intact cognition (MMSE 30/30), grossly intact cranial nerves, mildly decreased vibratory sensation distally, and otherwise normal light touch, pain, temperature, and proprioception. Motor examination disclosed bilateral high-arched feet with foot drop, muscle strength 5/5 proximally and 4+/5 distally in the arms, and 5/5 proximally and 3/5 distally in the legs. Muscle tone was normal; reflexes were 2+ in the upper limbs and absent at the ankles; plantar responses were downgoing. Gait was a stomping gait with difficulty on tandem walking, tiptoeing, and heel walking. There was a symmetrical 4–6 Hz low-amplitude tremor of both hands on posture, attenuating in neutral position; there was no rigidity or bradykinesia.

Laboratory studies including CBC, renal and liver function, fasting glucose, TSH, vitamin B12, ESR, VDRL, and HIV testing were unremarkable. Cervical spine MRI showed diffuse disc bulges; brain MRI demonstrated a nasopharyngeal polyp; chest radiograph was normal. Biopsy of the nasal polyp revealed non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas.

A 51-year-old woman with a 2-year history of acute severe ulcerative pancolitis refractory to steroids underwent subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy in February 2015, followed by an ileal pouch–anal anastomosis (IPAA) with a proximal neo-ileostomy in January 2016. One month after IPAA, her 24-hour ileostomy output gradually increased to 1.5–2 L, and she noted oliguria. In early May 2016, she presented with episodes of unconsciousness over 10 days.  

On examination, her blood pressure was 74/50 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm, and she appeared malnourished (height 160 cm; weight 39 kg). Bowel sounds were active, 7–9 per minute. Laboratory tests showed serum creatinine 183 μmol/L. She received fluid resuscitation and noradrenaline, with recovery of renal function, but high‐output diarrhoea persisted. She developed fever and vomiting.  

Stool analysis from the diverted ileostomy showed many leukocytes; repeated stool cultures and tests for Clostridium difficile toxins were negative. Tests for CMV-DNA, CMV-pp65, and EBV-DNA were all negative. She was not taking any medications, including NSAIDs. Empirical antibiotics (ceftazidime, metronidazole, oral vancomycin) produced no improvement. Intravenous hydrocortisone (50 mg q6 h) reduced her stool volume to <500 mL/day, allowing discontinuation of vasopressors.  

Pouchoscopy revealed oedematous, inflamed mucosa with patchy superficial ulcers in the diverted pouch. Upper endoscopy and endoscopy through the stoma showed a grossly normal stomach, duodenum, and pre-stomal ileum.  
Histologic examination of biopsies from the descending duodenum and pre-stomal ileum demonstrated moderate villous atrophy, cryptitis, decreased goblet cells, and severe active inflammation with neutrophil infiltration in the lamina propria; intraepithelial lymphocytosis was absent.

A 24-year-old Asian man presented with a 2-week history of pain and swelling in the left distal leg following a blunt injury to the ankle. He also reported a low-grade fever for 1 month and a 6-kg weight loss over 3 months. His past medical history was unremarkable, and he had received BCG vaccination without known tuberculosis contacts. On examination, the left distal tibia was tender, warm, and swollen; he was afebrile. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 12 mm/hr, a C-reactive protein level of 18 mg/L, and a normal white-cell count. Plain radiographs demonstrated a well-defined lytic lesion in the distal tibial metaphysis. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a T1-hypointense lesion extending to the subchondral region with post‐contrast enhancement, an eccentric hypointense area, linear marrow extension, adjacent soft-tissue hyperintensity, and a thick-walled fluid collection along the medial and posterior distal tibia with cortical breach. During debridement and curettage, purulent material was obtained and sent for studies. Culture grew Streptococcus agalactiae, and appropriate intravenous antibiotics were initiated.

A 71-year-old Chinese man with no significant medical history presented with three months of watery diarrhea (six to ten episodes per day) and mild abdominal pain. He denied blood or mucus in the stool. On examination, he had one oral ulcer and abdominal tenderness without rebound tenderness or shifting dullness. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 12.5×10^9/L, hemoglobin 67 g/L, ESR 130 mm/h, CRP 117 mg/L, positive antinuclear antibody titer 1:3200, positive antiphospholipid antibodies, complement C3 50 mg/dL, C4 12 mg/dL, and positive syphilis serology (TPPA/TPHA, TRUST). Tuberculin skin test and T-spot were negative. Fecal bacterial and viral studies, including C. difficile, Salmonella, Campylobacter, and Yersinia, were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed pleural effusion, ascites, pericardial effusion, and marked thickening of the colonic mucosa. Analysis of ascitic fluid showed pale-yellow fluid, Rivalta positive, with 462×10^6 nucleated cells/L (72% monocytes, 27.7% neutrophils). Colonoscopy demonstrated multiple circular, wide, clean-based ulcers in the terminal ileum and colon without mucous or hyperplastic perianal lesions. Histopathology of intestinal biopsies showed ganglion cells and fissure-like (crack) ulcers.

A 73-year-old man was evaluated three times over three weeks for intermittent epigastric and lower thoracic pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting. On the first two visits, point-of-care abdominal ultrasonography and inspection of the PEG-J catheter were unremarkable, and ECGs and troponin levels excluded myocardial ischaemia. Gastroscopy showed candida oesophagitis, for which fluconazole was prescribed, and laxatives were started for chronic constipation. On the third visit, he reported daily, normal-formed stools.

His history was notable for myocardial infarction, chronic idiopathic constipation, Parkinson’s disease, and placement of a PEG-J tube 1.5 years earlier for levodopa/carbidopa administration.

On examination he was diaphoretic. Vital signs were normal (HR 67/min, BP 141/80 mmHg, T 36.6°C). Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed sparse, normal-sounding peristalsis and severe pressure tenderness in the upper left abdomen and epigastrium without rebound or guarding. The PEG-J insertion site appeared normal and the catheter was stable.

Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 39 mg/L, lipase 14 U/L, troponin-T 16 ng/L (unchanged), creatine kinase 366 U/L, and lactate 2.2 mmol/L; renal and liver function were normal. ECG showed sinus rhythm without ST–T changes.

To evaluate for peptic or duodenal ulcer disease, cholecystitis, perforation, constipation related to Parkinson’s disease, intestinal ischaemia, and possible PEG-J complications, an abdominal CT scan with intravenous contrast was performed.

An 84-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, mitral regurgitation, hyperlipidemia, and prior gastrointestinal bleeding on anticoagulation underwent an abdominal CT scan on February 10, 2023. The scan revealed a 39 × 20 mm lesion at the lower pole of the right kidney, characterized by heterogeneous contrast enhancement, a hypoattenuating center, and lower enhancement than the renal cortex in the portal venous phase. In the same study, the uterus appeared heterogeneously enlarged with cystic changes. Multiple pulmonary nodules, predominantly in the left lower lobe and right upper lobe, the largest measuring 9 mm, were also noted. Given the imaging findings and concern for renal cell carcinoma with possible pulmonary metastases, the case was discussed at an interdisciplinary tumor board, and a decision was made to perform a percutaneous biopsy of the renal lesion.

A 28-year-old woman was referred for evaluation after a routine Pap smear suggested cervicitis. She is para 3, with an intrauterine contraceptive device (Copper T 380A) placed 2 years ago. Her last menstrual period was 5 days ago, and she had sexual intercourse 8 days before presentation. She has no genital symptoms except a history of intermittent whitish vaginal discharge since IUCD placement. She denies intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and has no dysuria. She is married monogamously but reports that her spouse has other partners. 

On examination she appears well. External genitalia are normal with no lesions. Speculum examination reveals scanty, whitish mucopurulent discharge from the cervical os. The ectocervix is reddened, edematous, and mildly tender on swabbing, without bleeding or visible ulceration; the IUCD string is in place. 

Pap smear shows superficial, intermediate, parabasal, and endocervical cells, with frequent binucleated epithelial cells, all suggestive of herpes simplex cervicitis. 

Initial laboratory tests: HIV antibody nonreactive; serologic screening for Chlamydia trachomatis and syphilis negative; endocervical swab culture yields normal flora.

A 46-year-old woman with a 15-year history of HIV infection, on stable antiretroviral therapy, presented with a 1-week history of cough, fever, and vomiting. Four months earlier, she had an asymptomatic positive SARS-CoV-2 test; since then, she noted a 15-kg weight loss and persistent fatigue. A chest CT scan on this admission showed findings suggestive of Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, which was treated successfully with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. 

Despite clinical improvement, she developed profound hyponatremia (sodium, 118 mmol/L). Random serum cortisol levels were 21 and 29 nmol/L on two occasions. She was started on IV hydrocortisone, with normalization of sodium to 143 mmol/L and resolution of vomiting and anorexia. 

On examination, she appeared well, with central adiposity and hyperpigmentation of the gums and abdominal skin. Muscle strength was normal, heart and lung examinations were unremarkable, and her abdomen was soft and non-tender. 

Further evaluation revealed a plasma ACTH level <3 ng/L (reference, 7.2–63.3 ng/L). MRI of the pituitary gland demonstrated a normal-appearing pituitary. All anterior pituitary hormone levels, including TSH, LH, FSH, prolactin, GH, and IGF-1, were within normal ranges. Screening tests for adrenal antibodies were negative, and investigations for tuberculosis (Elispot, sputum AFB, BAL culture, and cytology) were also negative.

A 26-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 21-day history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and malaise. He had moved from northeast Nebraska to California three months earlier to work on wind farms in the Mojave Desert. Shortly after arriving, he developed intermittent low-grade fever, nausea, vomiting, malaise, and abdominal pain, which he treated with over-the-counter cold medications and ibuprofen. 

Ten days before presentation to our center, he was admitted to a local hospital in Tehachapi Valley, California, for worsening symptoms and was found to have rhabdomyolysis (creatine kinase 1451 U/L) presumed secondary to exertion and dehydration; he received intravenous fluids. Laboratory studies showed only mild elevations in liver enzymes. Abdominal ultrasound and CT scan demonstrated fatty infiltration of the liver and hepatosplenomegaly. Urine and blood cultures were negative, and he was discharged after six days.

Three days later, he returned to our emergency department with persistent and worsening symptoms. He denied consumption of unpasteurized animal products, contact with livestock or wild animals, and had no sick contacts. Vital signs were blood pressure 124/55 mm Hg, pulse 64 beats/min, temperature 98.3 °F, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Examination revealed right upper quadrant tenderness and a positive Murphy’s sign; the remainder was unremarkable. Laboratory studies again showed mild transaminase elevations. Abdominal ultrasound revealed small calcified gallstones, echogenic sludge, gallbladder wall thickening, and a positive sonographic Murphy’s sign, consistent with acute cholecystitis. He was started on ceftriaxone and intravenous hydration and underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy the next day.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of absolute constipation, non-projectile vomiting of recently eaten food, low-grade fever, progressive abdominal distension, and sharp, fixed umbilical pain worsened by feeding. She had no history of abdominal surgery, peritonitis, or trauma. On examination, she appeared dehydrated, moderately anemic, and cachectic. Vital signs were stable. The abdomen was uniformly distended, tender with guarding, and bowel sounds were reduced; other system examinations were unremarkable. A supine abdominal radiograph showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with prominent valvulae conniventes; erect films demonstrated multiple air-fluid levels. Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin level of 12.4 g/dL, leukocytosis (17.5 × 10^9/L), negative HIV and hepatitis panels, and normal renal and liver function. She was resuscitated with intravenous fluids, had nasogastric decompression and urinary catheterization, and was scheduled for an emergency laparotomy.

A 32-year-old G3P2 woman was followed antenatally after identification at 12 weeks’ gestation of a 14×12 cm intramural uterine fibroid. Pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery at 41 weeks were uncomplicated. Five weeks postpartum, she presented with a 2-day history of lower abdominal pain and malaise. Her temperature was 39.0 °C. Pelvic examination revealed foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 9 cm intramural uterine mass without retained products of conception. Blood cultures grew anaerobic organisms, and she improved with 72 hours of intravenous antibiotics followed by oral therapy.

One week later (6 weeks postpartum), she re-presented with the sensation of a mass protruding through the vagina but was afebrile on examination. A fleshy tissue was noted at the introitus. Computed tomography of the pelvis demonstrated a large fluid collection within the lower uterine segment.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 7-month history of petechiae and purpura. A skin biopsy had confirmed leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and she had been treated with anti-inflammatory agents. Over several weeks, she developed worsening fatigue, night sweats, fever, and weight loss, along with new pulmonary symptoms and declining renal function. Physical examination revealed diffuse petechiae and purpuric lesions, especially on the lower limbs.

Laboratory studies showed:
- White blood cell count 3.8 × 10^3/mL (normal 4.5–11 × 10^3)  
- Hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL (11.6–15)  
- Platelet count 73 × 10^3/mL (150–450 × 10^3)  
- Blood urea nitrogen 92 mg/dL (6–24); creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (0.6–1.1)  
- C-reactive protein 80 mg/L (<10)  
- Blood cultures (two sets) negative  
- Anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody positive; ANA and anti–double-stranded DNA negative  
- Complement levels C3 and C4 both low  
- Urinalysis with 2+ protein, 2+ blood, 10–12 RBCs/HPF  

Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly. Chest CT demonstrated consolidations in the left upper lobe. Bone marrow biopsy revealed 40% cellularity with increased erythroid precursors and megaloblastic changes in both erythroid and myeloid lineages.

Because of a childhood history of a ventricular septal defect, transthoracic echocardiography was performed. It showed multiple mobile masses in the right ventricular outflow tract and on both the tricuspid and pulmonary valves, and a turbulent flow with a peak gradient of approximately 80 mmHg across a hypertrophied muscle bundle. Transesophageal echocardiography further demonstrated a muscle bundle dividing the right ventricle into proximal and distal chambers, with multiple attached masses involving the endothelium and valves.

A 42-year-old man presented six months after distorting his right lower leg while climbing stairs. He heard a tearing sound at the time and experienced immediate pain and immobilization. Conservative treatment—including activity limitation, partial weight bearing, and compression stockings—failed to relieve his symptoms. He reported spasmodic pain and swelling of the medial right calf, with a maximal walking distance of 300–400 m. 

On examination, there was focal tenderness over the right medial gastrocnemius, muscle stiffness, swelling, and a palpable bulge in the medial calf that became more prominent on tiptoeing. When the muscle was relaxed, a soft spot was palpable in the same area. He also noted hyposensitivity and hypalgesia of the right leg in a non-dermatomal distribution. Reflexes and motor strength were normal, and there was no Tinel’s sign. Peripheral pulses were intact. Circumferential measurement of the calves showed 46 cm on the right and 45 cm on the left; exercise did not alter girth. Intracompartmental pressure in the superficial posterior compartment increased from 40 cm H2O at rest to 80 cm H2O after exercise, while remaining 40 cm H2O on the unaffected side.

Ultrasound of the medial right calf demonstrated subcutaneous adipose tissue imbibition with fluid lamellae but no abscess, seroma, or hematoma. Neurologic electrophysiologic studies showed no lesion of the sciatic nerve, no polyradicular syndrome, and no spinal canal stenosis. An MRI of the right lower leg showed a superficial hypointense lesion in the proximal third of the medial gastrocnemius muscle, which was interpreted as a superficial scar, possibly a status post muscle rupture.

A previously healthy 6-year-old boy presented with a 2-day history of progressive abdominal pain, distension, nausea, and persistent vomiting following an elective upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsies. The procedure was performed under analgosedation to evaluate for celiac disease—given intermittent dizziness, nausea, abdominal pain, elevated deamidated gliadin peptides, and HLA-DQ2 and ‑DQ8 positivity—by a senior pediatric gastroenterologist without periprocedural complications. Three duodenal biopsies were obtained; histology showed normal mucosa. His history was negative for bleeding disorders, anticoagulant use, trauma, or abuse. On examination, he appeared fatigued, diaphoretic, and pale, with tachycardia, high-pitched bowel sounds, abdominal distension, and marked upper-abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.2 mmol/L (nv 7.4–9.1), platelets 441 Gpt/L (nv 150–530), prothrombin time 94% (nv 70–130%), aPTT 24.1 s (nv 27–40 s), and INR 1.03 (nv 0.8–1.25). An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large intramural mass within the duodenal wall causing proximal small-bowel obstruction.

A 40-year-old African woman was referred with a 1-day history of slurred speech, facial asymmetry, and left-sided weakness. She had a 10-year history of hypertension (noncompliant for 2 weeks), chronic menorrhagia, two prior strokes 5 years earlier, and childhood encephalitis. On examination she was pale, had purpuric patches over elbows, knees, and lower legs, a blood pressure of 103/67 mmHg, and left-sided power of 1/5. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 4.3 g/dL, platelet count 18 × 10^9/L, white count 10.5 × 10^9/L, and normal renal function. She was transfused 1 unit of whole blood.  

On hospital day 4 she developed tonic–clonic seizures and new jaundice. Repeat labs showed hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL, white count 13.5 × 10^9/L, platelet count 22 × 10^9/L, normal coagulation studies, lactate dehydrogenase 2611 μ/L, elevated direct and indirect bilirubin, and low globulin. HIV, hepatitis B and C, ANA, AST, ALT, and malaria smear were all normal. A repeat head CT scan revealed a periventricular hemorrhage. A peripheral blood film demonstrated normocytic normochromic red cells, schistocytes ++, occasional normoblasts, polychromatic cells, neutrophilic left shift, and markedly reduced platelets.

A 14-year-old boy, previously healthy, became acutely overwhelmed, confused, depressed, and agitated in October 2015. He expressed suicidal and homicidal thoughts, was hospitalized briefly, and started aripiprazole for presumed major depressive disorder with psychotic features. His early history included a childhood depressive episode treated successfully with sertraline and placement in a gifted school; possible Asperger’s syndrome was noted. In 2014–2015, he received antibiotics for Mycoplasma pneumoniae and farm‐related bug bite infections. Family history was significant for mood disorders, autoimmune diseases, and neurologic conditions. The family kept multiple pets (including stray cats) and reported prior cat scratches and exposure to ticks and fleas.

In the weeks after initial hospitalization, his psychosis worsened with intrusive thoughts, phobias, emotional lability, rage outbursts, and multimodal hallucinations, leading to school refusal and a second psychiatric admission in December 2015. By April 2017, despite trials of antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, antidepressants, benzodiazepines, and an 11-week out-of-state psychiatric admission with normal EEG, MRI, and autoimmune encephalopathy panels, his 24-hour psychosis persisted. A positive ANA titer (1:320), rising CRP (1.03 mg/dL → 1.96 mg/dL), and elevated CSF interferon-gamma (6.0 pg/mL) prompted rituximab for presumed autoimmune encephalitis, which transiently reduced but did not eliminate psychotic episodes. In January 2017, he met criteria for pediatric acute‐onset neuropsychiatric syndrome (PANS) based on abrupt OCD-like symptoms and concurrent anxiety, emotional lability, aggression, school deterioration, and somatic signs; streptococcal, Mycoplasma, Lyme, and viral tests were negative or equivocal. When “stretch mark–like” lesions appeared on his thighs and axilla, a dermatologist noted they were not consistent with striae.

An 11-year-old boy was evaluated for generalized muscle weakness of more than six years’ duration. His parents noted poor school performance, repeated falls, difficulty keeping up in sports, progressive inability to climb stairs, and excessive fatigue. There was no muscle pain, trauma, or infection preceding the onset. Family history was notable for a maternal uncle in his late teens with similar symptoms who is now bedridden.

On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. He had slight muscle wasting, a waddling gait, lumbar hyperlordosis, toe walking, flat feet, and prominent calf enlargement. There was reduced strength of the proximal lower-limb muscles and a positive Gowers’ sign. Cranial nerves were intact, and there were no upper or lower motor neuron lesion signs. He was fully conscious but had a Montreal Cognitive Assessment score of 20, indicating cognitive impairment.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count. Serum enzymes were markedly elevated: creatine kinase 20 232.3 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 206 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 192.4 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 645 µg/dL. Muscle biopsy demonstrated extensive loss of skeletal muscle fibers replaced by fat and fibrosis. Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram were essentially normal.

An man in his 80s with diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia presented with his sixth episode of hemoptysis over 18 months. Each episode ranged from blood-tinged sputum to nearly hemorrhagic expectoration but did not cause hemodynamic instability. On this occasion he reported severe hemoptysis. Vital signs were stable. Physical examination revealed wet rales over the posterior lung fields and was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 6.2×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 0.8 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.06 µg/L, and a hemoglobin drop from 120 to 90 g/L. Chest radiograph demonstrated an infiltrative shadow in the right middle and lower lung fields. Noncontrast CT showed a consolidation in the right lower lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed two aneurysmal structures within the consolidation that were contiguous with a pulmonary artery and demonstrated outflow into a pulmonary vein.

A 62-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a progressively enlarging, painful ulcer on the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He reported an abrasion with focal skin loss after loading a package into his car at the time of onset. He was seen twice in the emergency department and treated first with dicloxacillin for 1 week and then with doxycycline for 1 additional week, without meaningful improvement. His medical history included hepatitis C, hypertension, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He denied fevers, fatigue, myalgias, arthralgias, gastrointestinal symptoms, or travel outside the United States. 

On examination, he was afebrile, with blood pressure 110/67 mm Hg and heart rate 73 bpm. On the right dorsal hand, there was a sharply demarcated, 3-cm ulcer with thick overlying crust and an adjacent 1-cm crusted ulcer, each surrounded by erythema. Finger range of motion was limited by pain. There was no lymphadenopathy. The right radial pulse was 1+, with normal capillary refill and skin warmth. Radiographs showed no osseous defect. 

Wound cultures grew coagulase-negative Staphylococcus and Candida parapsilosis. Tissue cultures for atypical mycobacteria and deep fungal organisms were negative. The patient continued doxycycline and wound care with only slight improvement. A complete blood count, metabolic panel, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were all within normal limits. 

A punch biopsy of the ulcer margin showed a sparse, superficial lymphocytic infiltrate with increased small thin-walled blood vessels, some erythrocyte extravasation, and epidermal acanthosis. There were no collections of neutrophils or granulomas and no evidence of vasculitis or vascular occlusion. 

At this point, infection, pustular dermatosis of the dorsal hands, malignancy, vasculitis, vasculopathy, and embolic disease were felt to be unlikely, and pyoderma gangrenosum was not suspected because of lack of clinically consistent features and pathology.

A 71-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of uncontrollable movements of the right hand and right leg. His medical history included coronary artery disease with prior myocardial infarctions, percutaneous coronary interventions with stents, cardiac resynchronization therapy–defibrillator placement, and chronic heart failure (NYHA class II; LVEF 30%). He had no history of stroke or other movement disorders. 

On examination, he was alert with slight dysphonia. Pupils were symmetric with normal light reaction, and ocular movements were full. His tongue was central but exhibited involuntary movements. Strength was full in all extremities. Coordination testing revealed mild inaccuracy of the right arm and leg; the left side was precise. He demonstrated choreoathetosis of the right face, arm, and leg, and a slight postural tremor, greater on the left than the right. He reported unsteadiness on Romberg’s test; sensation was intact.

Routine blood tests and urinalysis were unremarkable. Computed tomography angiography of the neck revealed subocclusion of the proximal left internal carotid artery and 30% stenosis of the proximal right internal carotid artery. Ultrasound of the thyroid and neck showed a benign left thyroid nodule (TIRADS 2). Brain MRI with MRA demonstrated diffusely expanded ventricles and cortical sulci without acute ischemic lesions, and segmental stenosis of the extracranial left internal carotid artery.

A 35-year-old woman presented with mild pain in her right leg for 4 years, which worsened with walking. She denied any history of trauma, fever, or penetrating injury. Physical examination revealed deep tenderness over the medial distal aspect of the right leg; ankle motion was full and there was no neurovascular deficit. Laboratory studies, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and complete blood count, were within normal limits. Radiographs of the right leg (anteroposterior and lateral views) showed an oval to serpentine-shaped lucent lesion with a well-circumscribed sclerotic margin in the distal tibial metaphysis. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a fluid-filled cavity surrounded by a hyperintense granulation layer (penumbra sign) on T1-weighted images.

A 28-year-old man presented with a one-year history of left testicular pain and a suspicious solid mass. He denied cryptorchidism, testicular trauma, hydrocele, infections, fever, or a family history of testicular tumors. On examination, the scrotal skin was normal, both testes were of regular size without palpable mass, and urination was normal; a left inguinal hernia was noted. Scrotal ultrasonography revealed a grade I left varicocele and a 12×18 mm hypoechoic intratesticular mass with internal calcified septa; the epididymides and remaining testicular parenchyma appeared normal. The patient’s serum α-fetoprotein, β-hCG, and lactate dehydrogenase levels were within normal limits, and routine blood, urine, and biochemical tests were unremarkable. Given the imaging characteristics and concern for malignancy, the patient was admitted for surgical management.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of odynophagia and neck pain, worsened by swallowing and neck movement. She had no history of trauma, fever, cough, or shortness of breath. Her medical and surgical history was unremarkable. On examination, she was afebrile. Neck pain increased with passive movement in all directions, and there was paracervical tenderness but no external swelling. A two-finger-breath trismus was noted. Intraoral and nasopharyngolaryngoscopic examinations revealed a bulging posterior pharyngeal wall from the nasopharynx to the oropharynx with normal overlying mucosa. Laboratory studies showed a normal leukocyte count and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/hr. A provisional diagnosis of retropharyngeal abscess was made, and a cervical radiograph demonstrated loss of cervical lordosis with prevertebral thickening at the C1–C2 levels. Subsequent CT of the neck showed focal prevertebral soft tissue thickening measuring 1 cm at C1–C2, with calcification extending into the atlantodental joint space and no rim-enhancing collection or air pockets in the prevertebral or retropharyngeal spaces.

A 3-year-old girl presented with 1 week of abdominal pain and fever to 40°C, associated with non-projectile, non-bilious vomiting and dysuria. Her parents reported worsening abdominal pain over the prior 4 days and difficulty voiding for 48 hours. She had a history of recurrent abdominal pain over several months without identified cause. On examination, she was alert with a temperature of 40°C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 120/min, and abdominal distension with a tender infra-umbilical mass. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 14,000/mm³ with neutrophils 8.6/mm³ and lymphocytes 3.48/mm³, C-reactive protein 135 mg/dL, procalcitonin 0.20 ng/mL, and normal serum creatinine. Viral serologies (EBV, CMV) and COVID PCR were negative. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 147×74×67 mm cystic mass in the infra-umbilical region. A low-dose CT scan confirmed a large fluid-filled mass posterior to the bladder displacing it anteriorly, consistent with an enlarged vagina (hydrocolpos).

A 63-year-old white woman presented with a 1-month history of asymptomatic red-brown rings on her lower extremities. Six weeks before the development of lesions, she underwent two sessions of sodium tetradecyl sulfate injections for venous reflux disease, spaced 2 weeks apart. The rings appeared 3 days after the injections and developed at all prior injection sites. She had been treated empirically with clotrimazole/betamethasone diproprionate cream for presumed tinea without improvement. On examination, there were numerous nonblanching annular to arcuate patches composed of confluent petechiae with a few telangiectasias symmetrically involving both lower extremities. A punch biopsy was obtained. The clinical differential diagnosis included pigmented purpuric dermatosis, post­sclerotherapy hyperpigmentation, porokeratosis, granuloma annulare, and vasculitis.

A 2-year-6-month-old girl presented with a 10-day history of fever, cough, and tachypnea. On admission, her temperature was 38.5 °C and SpO2 was 67% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed fine crackles in the posterior lung fields. Examination showed clubbing of the fingers, pigeon-breast deformity, and a chilblain-like rash on the face; her anterior fontanelle measured 0.3×0.3 cm. Growth parameters were below average (height 87 cm [–1.08 SD], weight 11.5 kg [–0.82 SD]). She had monthly respiratory infections since age 6 months and activity-related fatigue since age 2. Her 27-year-old father developed exertional dyspnea at age 22, has finger clubbing, facial tissue loss, and was diagnosed with CTD-associated ILD based on positive ANA and SRP autoantibody; his HRCT showed interstitial pneumonia with pulmonary cysts.  
Laboratory studies in the child showed CRP 54.2 mg/L, ESR 89 mm/H, WBC 16.3×10^3/mm^3; normal liver, renal, and thyroid function; IgG 25.3 g/L, IgA 3.26 g/L, IgM 1.69 g/L; normal complement levels; decreased CD4+ T lymphocytes; positive ANA (1:1000), ANCA, RF, and anti-CCP antibodies; IL-6 62.4 pg/mL; and negative pathology for malignancy. Chest HRCT showed diffuse ground-glass opacities; brain MRI revealed widened sulci and enlarged extra-axial spaces; echocardiogram and abdominal/vascular ultrasounds were normal.  
She was diagnosed with ILD and severe pneumonia and received IVIG, antibiotics, mechanical ventilation, and methylprednisolone pulse therapy; her respiratory symptoms improved and the ventilator was withdrawn on day 22.

A 39-year-old man from a low socioeconomic background, living in an urban area, presented with an acute disturbance of consciousness without fever. He had no significant medical or surgical history except for heavy daily smoking and excessive cannabis use (over 20 joints per day). On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 10/15, with no focal neurologic signs and no cardio-respiratory abnormalities; he was afebrile, and blood glucose was normal. Laboratory studies revealed a mild inflammatory syndrome with a white blood cell count of 17,000/mm³. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal, with no signs of meningitis or antibodies linked to autoimmune encephalitis. Toxicologic screening was positive for cannabis only. Urgent brain MRI showed bilateral and symmetric T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities in the hippocampi with restricted diffusion, absence of contrast enhancement, and slight hippocampal volume reduction.

A 28-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history of inability to achieve complete sexual intercourse because of pain. She reported regular 5-day menses every 28 days; menstrual bleeding was scarce and emerged only along the right lateral aspect of the vagina. On physical examination, the external genitalia appeared normal, and the hymenal membrane was intact except for a microperforation at the 10 o’clock position. Pelvic ultrasonography performed after catheterization of the microperforation and infusion of saline into the vaginal canal showed normal morphology of the uterus, cervix, and bladder. Transperineal ultrasonography revealed a small, incomplete vaginal septum measuring 3 mm at the right lateral vaginal wall.

A 50-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 5-month history of dyspnea on exertion (Modified Medical Research Council grade 1), low-grade fever, nonproductive cough, and pain in the small joints of his hand. He denied hemoptysis, palpitations, visual disturbances, and significant weight loss. Vital signs were within normal limits, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests revealed a normal complete blood count, biochemistry panel, and serum calcium; negative rheumatoid factor, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody; an elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level of 88.8 U/L; and a negative Mantoux test (2 × 2 mm induration). Chest radiography showed bilateral hilar prominence. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and perilymphatic nodules. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly. Spirometry showed a forced vital capacity of 3.02 L (63% of predicted). Flexible bronchoscopy revealed a polypoid, ball-like mass occluding the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid analysis showed lymphocytosis and was negative for malignant cells, acid-fast bacilli, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis by GeneXpert.

A 36-year-old woman presented at 12 weeks of gestation by her last menstrual period with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain. Her obstetric history was significant for one cesarean delivery four years earlier. She was hemodynamically stable. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a gestational sac in the anterior myometrium at the level of the previous uterine scar. The uterine cavity and cervical canal were empty, and there was thin or absent myometrium between the gestational sac and the bladder.

A 68-year-old man presented with sudden onset of pain in the left lower chest and upper abdomen, persisting at rest and worsened by coughing or rolling over. His history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, chronic renal insufficiency, renal stones, obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP, peripheral arterial disease, diverticulosis, colon polyps, and benign prostatic hypertrophy. He smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years and consumed about 21 beers per week. Medications included metformin, enalapril, amlodipine, simvastatin, and aspirin. He had childhood asbestos exposure and worked repairing telephone equipment. He denied fevers, sweats, or weight loss. Examination showed tenderness over the left lower ribs but clear lung fields and no lymphadenopathy.

An ECG was normal. Chest radiograph revealed a loculated mass in the right upper lobe. Chest CT showed a 6-cm apical mass with central cystic areas, adjacent ground-glass opacities, and a 0.2-cm noncalcified nodule; there was no mediastinal lymphadenopathy. PET-CT demonstrated moderate uptake in the mass. Over the next month, his chest pain resolved but he developed a productive whitish cough and mild exertional dyspnea. On follow-up, breath sounds were diffusely diminished without crackles or wheezes. A percutaneous needle biopsy of the lung mass was planned under CT guidance.

A 33-year-old woman was referred for recurrent throbbing pain in the mandibular right first molar (tooth #46). She had no history of trauma, hospitalization, or endocrine or systemic disease. Hematologic tests including complete blood count, calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase were within normal limits. On head and neck examination, there was no adenopathy, paresthesia, or motor nerve deficit. Intraoral examination showed unerupted maxillary left molars and tooth #17, moderate oral hygiene, healthy gingiva, and normal tooth mobility. An orthopantomogram obtained previously demonstrated radiolucent enlargements suggestive of resorption in teeth #16, #36, #37, #46, #47 and in the unerupted #17, #26, #27, and #28. 

To better characterize these lesions, a cone-beam CT scan was performed with 0.5-mm slices and 3D rendering. CBCT images revealed uniform, well-defined radiolucent cavities within the pulp chambers of multiple teeth. In teeth #36 and #37, the resorptive defects had perforated the lingual root surfaces. Cross-sectional images of #26 showed apical periodontitis, maxillary sinus membrane thickening, and a sinus-root communication. Tooth #46 was positive to electric pulp testing, without caries or discoloration, and was slightly tender to percussion; CBCT demonstrated internal resorption in its distal root and pulp chamber with a lingual perforation.
