Additional internal resorptive cavities were identified in teeth #15, #14, #13, #33, #34, #35, #43, #44, and #45, many of which had not been apparent on the panoramic film.

A 3-year-old girl, the second child of nonconsanguineous Dominican parents, was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Around age 1 year she developed genu varum. Initial studies showed normal serum calcium, low serum phosphorus, and markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone levels. Radiographs of the knees and wrists demonstrated cupping and fraying of the metaphyses consistent with rickets. She was diagnosed with vitamin D–deficiency rickets and treated with ergocalciferol for 2 years. Although her serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level rose from 22 ng/mL to 80 ng/mL, radiographs showed progression of rachitic changes with widening of the physes. At age 3 years she began to complain of bone pain and had polyuria, polydipsia, and enuresis. Laboratory studies at that time revealed a serum bicarbonate level of 19–20 mmol/L, glycosuria (glucose >1000 mg/dL) with normal blood glucose, proteinuria (>300 mg/dL), serum phosphorus of 2.2 mg/dL, serum creatinine of 0.4 mg/dL, urinary phosphorus of 43.6 mg/dL, urinary creatinine of 18.4 mg/dL, and a tubular reabsorption of phosphate of 56.9%. These findings are consistent with a proximal tubular defect (Fanconi syndrome) leading to hypophosphatemic rickets.

A 69-year-old woman with a history of hypertensive heart disease, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, gastroesophageal reflux, renal insufficiency, former smoking, obesity (BMI 39.2), and macromastia underwent double coronary artery bypass grafting using the left internal mammary artery without perioperative complications. Shortly afterward, she developed septicemia, mechanical instability of the sternum, and mediastinitis. The sternotomy was managed with vacuum-assisted closure and re-sutured successfully five weeks after surgery.  

During this period, she complained of persistent pain in her left breast. Initial ultrasonography revealed a 2 cm hyperechoic edema of the breast fat centrally, without focal masses. Seven weeks after surgery, examination showed slight erythema over one third of the breast, most pronounced centrally and in the inner quadrants, with a palpable painful lump measuring 8 × 6 cm. Laboratory tests revealed mildly elevated C-reactive protein. Given her recent wound infection, mastitis was suspected and empirical antibiotics were started.  

Two weeks later, antibiotics had no effect, and a new 2–3 cm movable lump in the left axilla raised concern for a pathologic lymph node. Ultrasonography demonstrated edema and disruption of normal glandular architecture, without well-defined masses or fluid collections. Three weeks after that, repeat ultrasound showed a poorly defined hyperechoic mass with irregular hypoechoic zones and acoustic shadowing. Clinical findings of nipple retraction and skin thickening further suggested inflammatory carcinoma. Mammography revealed asymmetric increased density of the left breast, thickened areolar skin, nipple retraction, and diffuse glandular destruction consistent with inflammatory carcinoma.

A 35-year-old Middle Eastern woman presented with hyperpigmented lesions over her palms and soles. She first noted the lesions at age 16; they gradually increased in number but remained confined to the palmoplantar surfaces and periungual areas. She reported no symptoms, aggravating or relieving factors. Her medical, surgical, drug, family, and social histories were unremarkable. 

On examination, there were numerous, sharply demarcated, round-to-oval macules, 1–5 mm in diameter, with varying shades of brown on the palms, soles, and periungual regions. Dermoscopic evaluation revealed a parallel furrow and lattice-like pattern. The mucous membranes, hair, and nails were normal, and there were no neurological, cardiac, or gastrointestinal abnormalities on examination.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count with differential, liver and renal function tests, cortisol, adrenocorticotropic hormone, vitamin B12, thyroid-stimulating hormone, anti–nuclear antibody, lactate dehydrogenase, and immunoglobulin levels, were all within normal limits. Whole-genome sequencing did not reveal any pathogenic variants. The patient was reassured and offered a trial of laser therapy.

A 51-year-old woman presented with two years of right superior eyelid discomfort, progressive blurred vision in the right eye, and diplopia on upgaze. Best-corrected visual acuity was 1.2 OD and 1.5 OS. Both upper eyelids were swollen, and eye movement was bilaterally restricted on upgaze; hard masses were palpable under the temporal upper lids. Intraocular pressures were 17 mmHg in both eyes. Funduscopic examination and OCT of the right eye revealed chorioretinal folds involving the macula; the left fundus appeared normal. Goldmann perimetry of the right eye showed decreased sensitivity in the lower field. Orbital MRI demonstrated enlargement of bilateral lacrimal glands—more pronounced on the right—without abnormalities of extraocular muscles or infraorbital nerves; the right globe was deformed by the enlarged gland. Laboratory studies showed a normal blood cell count, negative C-reactive protein, elevated total IgG (1916 mg/dL) and IgG4 (450 mg/dL), normal interleukin-6 and angiotensin-converting enzyme, normal thyroid hormones, negative thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibody, and negative ANA, PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA, and anti-SSA/SSB antibodies. Whole-body CT revealed enlargement of bilateral lacrimal and submandibular glands and segmental enlargement of the pancreatic tail. FDG-PET/CT showed increased uptake in the lacrimal and submandibular glands.

A 27-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of afebrile seizures. MRI of the brain showed symmetric T2 hyperintensity in the medial globus pallidus without remarkable signal changes on T2* GRE sequences. Karyotyping revealed mosaic trisomy 21 (47, XX, +21 in 8 of 20 cells).  
Developmental history disclosed mild psychomotor delay: she began walking at age 2 years, had delayed speech and regression of previously acquired words. At age 4 years, dystonic contractions of both hands and early swallowing difficulty were noted.  
Repeat MRI at age 5 years demonstrated persistent bilateral hyperintense signal in the medial globus pallidus on FLAIR and new surrounding hypointense signal on T2* GRE, creating the combined appearance known as the “eye-of-the-tiger” sign. Neither diffusion restriction nor contrast enhancement was observed.

A 12-year-old girl presented with “periodic abdominal pain for six months and acute difficulty in urination with lower abdominal pain for 1 day.” She had intermittent cramping and voiding problems over six months, which resolved spontaneously, but 1 day before admission she became unable to void and developed suprapubic distension and discomfort.  
On examination, the abdomen was soft and non-tender, with dullness to percussion over the suprapubic region consistent with bladder distension. There was no urethral discharge. A non-tender, well-circumscribed mass measuring about 3 × 2 cm was palpable between the anterior vaginal wall and the urethral meatus. Digital rectal examination was normal.  
Pelvic MRI revealed an inhomogeneous signal shadow in the cervical canal and vagina suggestive of blood accumulation, raising concern for vaginal or hymenal atresia. Transperineal ultrasound confirmed a cystic mass in the cervical canal and vagina consistent with hematocolpos in the setting of possible vaginal atresia.

A 29-year-old woman was referred in March 2021 for evaluation of right clavicle pain that had persisted intermittently for at least 3 years. In 2018, she first noted medial right clavicle pain with palpable enlargement but denied any history of trauma, osteomyelitis, or autoimmune disease. A noncontrast chest CT in 2018 showed an expanded right medial clavicle with increased sclerosis, cortical breakthrough, scalloping, erosions, and hook-like inferior medial osteophytes; there was no soft-tissue mass or pathologic fracture. A core-needle biopsy at that time yielded only lamellar trabecular bone and was nondiagnostic.

Since 2018, she experienced monthly throbbing pain episodes—often at night or during menses—radiating to the right shoulder and neck, causing postural compensation. On examination, there was mild tenderness and a bony irregularity over the right mid-clavicle without lymphadenopathy. Radiographs in March 2021 demonstrated interval worsening of cortical irregularity, erosions, and scalloping at the right mid-clavicle. A whole-body Tc-99 bone scan in April 2021 revealed intense uptake confined to the right medial clavicle.

At this time, the differential diagnosis included both benign and malignant neoplasms, as well as nonneoplastic processes such as chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO), SAPHO syndrome, osteomyelitis, Paget’s disease, and fibrous dysplasia. Given the previous nondiagnostic core biopsy, an open biopsy of the right medial clavicle was recommended.

A 70‐year‐old man was admitted for evaluation of new‐onset nephrotic syndrome. He had routine health checks with normal labs until 6 months earlier, when serum albumin fell from 4.3 to 3.2 g/dL. One month before admission he noted lower‐extremity edema. His family doctor found massive proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, 12.5 g/g) and hypoalbuminemia (1.7 g/dL). On admission, blood pressure was 148/97 mmHg and pulse 82/min. 

Laboratory data: WBC 7600/µL; Hb 12.9 g/dL; platelets 401,000/µL; BUN 22.0 mg/dL; creatinine 1.39 mg/dL; albumin 2.0 g/dL; total cholesterol 363 mg/dL; ANA <1/40; anti–DNA antibody <2.0 IU/mL; HBs-Ag and HCV-Ab negative; C3 96 mg/dL; C4 35 mg/dL; IgG 1157 mg/dL; IgG4 225 mg/dL (normal 11–121); urine RBCs 20–29/HPF; N-acetyl-β-D-glucosaminidase 96.8 IU/L; β2-microglobulin 2816 µg/L; selectivity index 0.29.

Renal biopsy: Light microscopy showed diffuse thickening of glomerular capillary walls with spike formation and interstitial lymphoplasmacytic infiltration; 40% of the interstitium exhibited fibrosis without storiform pattern. Immunofluorescence revealed granular deposits along the GBM positive for IgG (3+), C4 (1+), C1q (1+), and trace C3, but negative for IgA and IgM. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated >10 IgG4-positive plasma cells per high-power field in the interstitium and diffuse granular IgG4 positivity along the GBM.

A 20-year-old nulliparous woman presented with 1 month of lower abdominal pain and tenderness. She denied dysuria, urinary symptoms, bowel changes, fever, vaginal discharge, chronic illness, cough, or weight loss. Menstrual cycles were regular. Physical examination revealed only abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies, including hematologic and biochemical panels, were unremarkable.  
Ultrasonography demonstrated free fluid with septations and multiple peritoneal surface implants. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed multiple subcentimeter mesenteric and omental nodules and a 4.0 × 2.0 cm nodular lesion in the left adnexa. Serum CA-125 was elevated at 91 IU/mL (normal < 35 IU/mL).  
Fluorine-18 FDG PET/CT revealed metabolically active lower cervical and mediastinal lymph nodes (largest 1.1 × 1.9 cm; SUVmax 8.9), metabolically quiescent gross ascites, and multiple FDG-avid peritoneal deposits with nodularity (SUVmax 12.2).

A 75-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history of asymptomatic skin redness that she had not sought treatment for. She had no significant past medical history. On examination, there were reticulated, erythematous macules and patches crossing the midline of the anterior neck, upper chest, and upper back. Dermoscopic evaluation revealed dotted vessels and numerous uniform, structureless yellowish‐white spots and patches of irregular shapes and varying sizes diffusely distributed over a reddish background.

A 52-year-old African woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a 2-month history of intermittent periumbilical abdominal pain and progressive generalized weakness. The pain was piercing, radiated to the upper and left lower quadrants, and was not associated with umbilical discharge. Over the week before presentation, she experienced low-grade fevers, abdominal discomfort, painful urination, constipation, and anorexia. She denied early satiety, diarrhea, gross hematuria, or other lower urinary–tract symptoms. She also reported a 3-kg weight loss over the past month. Her medical history was notable only for well-controlled diabetes; she had no prior surgeries and no history of smoking or alcohol use. On examination, she appeared mildly pale and dehydrated; vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination revealed an obese but soft abdomen with a fixed, tender mass in the hypogastric region. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 7.75 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL with microcytic hypochromic indices, platelets 471 × 10^9/L, and mild hyponatremia (131 mmol/L); renal and hepatic panels were otherwise unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a heterogeneous, nonvascularized intra-abdominal mass measuring 11 × 8.8 cm and an enlarged liver (17.7 cm). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a multilobulated, thick-walled mass measuring 7.4 × 5.6 × 8.7 cm with multiple air locules along the midline anterior abdominal wall indenting the superior dome of the bladder.

A 58-year-old right-handed man presented with recurrent left forearm and hand weakness. In July 2020, he developed sudden severe left shoulder pain followed by left finger-extension weakness and was diagnosed with posterior interosseous nerve syndrome elsewhere; the pain partially improved, but weakness persisted. In January 2021, his shoulder pain recurred and shortly thereafter he noted left finger-flexion weakness. Ten days later he was admitted. 

On examination, he had no weight loss or muscle weakness except in the left forearm. He had persistent shoulder-girdle pain without a clear dermatomal pattern. Neurologic examination showed severe weakness of muscles innervated by the left posterior interosseous nerve and mild to moderate weakness in muscles innervated by the median nerve (including the anterior interosseous branch) and ulnar nerve. There was atrophy of these muscles on the dorsal and palmar surfaces of the left forearm and hand. Deep tendon reflexes were normal and there were no sensory deficits or pathologic reflexes.

Laboratory tests, including antinuclear, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, antiganglioside, and antiviral antibodies, were normal. Cervical spine MRI and brachial-plexus MR neurography were nondiagnostic. Nerve conduction studies on the left showed reduced compound muscle action potential amplitudes in the median, anterior interosseous, ulnar, radial, and posterior interosseous nerves, with no conduction block in the median, ulnar, or radial nerves. Sensory nerve conduction studies were normal. Lower-extremity studies were normal.

Needle electromyography of forearm muscles innervated by the median, anterior interosseous, ulnar, and posterior interosseous nerves revealed abnormal spontaneous activity in all these distributions; recruitment and interference patterns were delayed and poor for muscles innervated by the ulnar and posterior interosseous nerves, but were normal for muscles innervated by the median and anterior interosseous nerves. EMG of proximal muscles (serratus anterior, deltoid, biceps, triceps, vastus medialis) was normal.

A 32-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 1-month history of sudden onset, activity-related pain in his left groin. He worked a sedentary job, denied recent trauma or high-energy sports, and had no other health issues except heterozygous beta thalassemia (confirmed by elevated HbA2). He did not smoke, drank socially, and had a BMI of 27. On examination, there was severe pain with flexion, internal rotation, and adduction of the left hip, with restricted range of motion compared to the right. The Trendelenburg sign was negative, and he had an antalgic gait on the left. Plain radiographs showed a small osteopenic lesion around the fovea capitis. MRI of the left hip demonstrated low signal intensity on T1-weighted images of the femoral head and T2-weighted images showed bone marrow edema of the femoral head and neck. Imaging differential considerations included transient osteoporosis and avascular necrosis.  
The patient was advised to remain non–weight bearing and to follow up in 4 weeks.

A 17-year-old previously healthy female presented with a 3-day history of tender, red nodules on both lower legs that had enlarged and become increasingly painful. She denied trauma, fevers, recent infections, ill contacts, or similar lesions in others. Three weeks earlier, she had received her second dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine and experienced only one day of malaise afterward. She had no side effects after the first dose. She denied recent streptococcal pharyngitis or new medications. Her medical history was negative for systemic infections or inflammatory conditions, including tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and inflammatory bowel disease. 

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Multiple tender, warm, erythematous nodules measuring 2–3 cm were noted on the anterior tibial surfaces bilaterally, and a single similar lesion was present on her left forearm. No other abnormalities were found.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 37 mm/hr (normal <25 mm/hr) and a C-reactive protein level of 1.7 mg/dL (normal <0.8 mg/dL). Complete blood count with differential was within normal limits. Antistreptolysin-O titers were not elevated, and an interferon-gamma release assay was negative. Given the clinical appearance, a biopsy was deferred.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of recurrent abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She reported intermittent periods of bowel obstruction lasting several days without flatus, which resolved spontaneously, accompanied by a 4-kg unintentional weight loss and anorexia. Her vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination revealed a lower midline laparotomy scar, no distension or palpable masses, and subjective tenderness in the right upper and lower quadrants without peritoneal signs. Her past history included miliary tuberculosis treated after exploratory laparotomy for a pelvic abscess at age 19. Laboratory studies showed a neutrophilia of 8.38 ×10^9/L (reference 2–7.5), white-cell count 10.7 ×10^9/L, CRP 2.6 mg/L, and lymphocytes 1.53 ×10^9/L. A CT scan from 2019 demonstrated swirling and stranding of omental and mesenteric fat inferior to the hepatic flexure, raising suspicion for internal herniation of omental fat. A repeat CT in the current presentation showed interval enlargement of this swirling fat mass (from 1.8 × 2.6 cm to 5.5 × 7.6 cm) with associated small-bowel dilatation and wall thickening, but no clear transition point. Given the recurrent pain, imaging suggestive of partial small-bowel obstruction, and her history of abdominal tuberculosis, the decision was made to proceed with diagnostic laparoscopy.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of fever, conjunctivitis, and generalized tender erythematous, edematous papules and plaques on the trunk and extremities.  
Her medical history was significant for rectal cancer treated 6 months earlier with mitomycin C, 5-fluorouracil, and radiation, with no evidence of recurrence. She denied upper respiratory symptoms, arthritis, connective tissue disease, recent travel, and had no history of keloids or hypertrophic scarring. She took sertraline and had been on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection, which resolved and was discontinued 3 days after presentation.  
On examination she was febrile. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 10.7 K/mm3 with 71% neutrophils and 17% bands. A skin biopsy from her back revealed leukocytoclastic neutrophilic and mononuclear infiltrates in the dermis without vasculitis. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy was positive for CD43, CD68, and myeloperoxidase.

A 40-year-old Ethiopian man presented with a 6-month history of painless subcutaneous swellings under the chin and at the back of the neck. Three months after the initial swellings appeared, he developed pruritic, raised lesions over his forearms, thighs, legs, and face that worsened in size and itchiness during the day and with sunlight exposure. Two months before presentation he noted new painless swellings in his axillary and inguinal regions. Treatment with oral loratadine and topical steroids for presumed nodular urticaria produced no significant improvement.  

Two weeks before admission he experienced worsening fatigue, anorexia, and epigastric pain. Three days before presentation he developed high-grade fever, headache, chills, rigors, and worsened epigastric discomfort. On examination, temperature was 36.0 °C, pulse 95/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. He had conjunctival injection, facial puffiness, and multiple firm, non-tender lymph nodes (2–4 cm) in the submandibular, anterior and posterior cervical, axillary, posterior auricular, and inguinal regions bilaterally. No hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Skin examination revealed generalized urticarial papules on the face, neck, and upper extremities; a macular erythematous rash on the trunk; and eczematous plaques with excoriations on the extremities.  

Laboratory studies showed normal liver, renal, coagulation, and lipid panels. Viral hepatitis and HIV tests were negative. VDRL was positive but TPHA was negative. Complete blood count revealed WBC 4500/mm3 (eosinophils 9%), hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, and platelets 284,000/mm3. Fasting glucose levels were 86 mg/dL and 98 mg/dL on two occasions.  

Excisional lymph node biopsy demonstrated florid hyperplasia and vascularization of germinal centers and parafollicular areas, marked eosinophilic infiltration, vascular proliferation, and background fibrosis.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of recurrent diarrhea, postprandial bloating, anorexia, and weight loss. There was no fever, night sweats, vomiting, or melena. Physical examination and routine laboratory studies were unremarkable. Serum chromogranin A was marginally elevated at 169 ng/mL (normal range not specified), and 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid was 3.6 mg (normal). CT enterography demonstrated a single 5 × 4 cm spiculated mesenteric mass encasing the ileocolic artery; it was hypoenhancing compared with skeletal muscle and did not show necrosis or calcification. There was contiguous thickening of the duodenum (D2/D3) and proximal transverse colon. No other lymphadenopathy, liver lesions, or ascites were seen. The lesion showed intense uptake on 68 Ga-DOTANOC PET/CT and on 18F-FDG PET/CT.

A 72-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of dyspnea on exertion and at rest following a recent PCR-confirmed COVID-19 infection. He denied fevers, chills, night sweats, chest pain, palpitations, cough, hemoptysis, nausea, or vomiting but reported one week of fatigue and weakness. On admission, his temperature was 39.2 °C, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed diminished breath sounds over the right lung fields; heart sounds were normal. His medical history included hypertension and insulin-dependent diabetes.  
A chest radiograph showed a large right-sided pleural effusion, and CT imaging demonstrated the same effusion with ground-glass opacities in the left lung consistent with prior COVID-19 changes. A right-sided chest tube was placed, yielding approximately 500 mL of milky fluid.

A 42-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of intermittent palpitations and a newly detected cardiac murmur. She had no history of hypertension, diabetes, or connective-tissue disorders, and no family history of congenital heart disease. Vital signs were: blood pressure 109/64 mm Hg, pulse 77 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, temperature 36.5 °C. Cardiac auscultation revealed a continuous grade 3/6 murmur best heard at the right second and third intercostal spaces. A chest radiograph showed normal heart size, and electrocardiography showed no ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests—including NT-proBNP, coagulation profile, anti-nuclear antibody, complete blood count, cardiac enzymes, and lipid panel—were all within normal limits. 

Transthoracic echocardiography with Doppler imaging revealed a tunnel-like structure with continuous flow signals originating from the left coronary sinus and draining into the right atrium. The pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio was 1.3 : 1. The left ventricle was of normal size, with a calculated ejection fraction of 64%, and all valves appeared normal. An exercise treadmill test produced no ischemic changes.

A 74-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, and a history of Hurthle cell thyroid carcinoma status post thyroidectomy presented with several months of unintentional weight loss and a painful right lower quadrant abdominal mass. She denied fevers, chills, vomiting, diarrhea, or obstipation. On examination, she had diffuse abdominal tenderness and an indurated, erythematous, and warm mass in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16.2 × 10^9/L with 92% neutrophils; blood and urine cultures were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 7.8 × 4.3 cm mass abutting the right pelvic sidewall and a superficial fluid collection in the anterior abdominal wall with a cutaneous fistula.

A 67-year-old normoweight man presented with several years of gradually enlarging, tumor-like masses of the neck and upper back. He had a history of poorly controlled hypertension and moderate alcohol consumption. He denied dyspnea or dysphagia but reported discomfort lying supine and cosmetic concerns. On physical examination, four soft, painless, poorly defined masses were noted: one in the anterior neck; two firm-elastic masses in the occipito-cervical region extending laterally over the sternocleidomastoid muscles down to the level of C3; and a firm-elastic “buffalo hump” spanning C3 to T5. Symmetric lipomatous enlargement of the trunk conferred a pseudo-athletic appearance. Neurologic examination was normal, and cardiovascular evaluation revealed only essential hypertension. Routine laboratory studies were unremarkable. MRI of the head and neck with and without contrast showed bilateral, symmetric, non-encapsulated subcutaneous fat deposits that were hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted sequences, without evidence of invasive or malignant features.

A previously healthy 19‐year‐old man was brought after a motor vehicle crash with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6 and a closed fracture of the humerus. A head CT scan showed a subdural hematoma, and he underwent emergency craniotomy and hematoma evacuation. In the surgical ICU, his neurologic status improved and he was extubated on hospital day 5; he was restless but obeyed commands. He was transferred to the ward on day 7, and received intravenous haloperidol (total dose, 20 mg over 24 hours) for agitation. On day 10, he became febrile to 39.0°C, developed increased spasticity, and his GCS score decreased to 10; laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (23×10^3/mm^3). A repeat CT of the brain showed no new findings. He was treated empirically for meningitis with antibiotics and returned to the ICU. He remained febrile to 40.0°C, with a central venous pressure of 1 cm H₂O, labile blood pressure, and tachycardia. On day 11, his spasticity worsened, his temperature rose to 40.5°C, and his GCS score fell to 8, necessitating reintubation. Serum creatine kinase was elevated at 7481 U/L; septic workup was negative, and repeat head CT was unchanged.

A 41‐year‐old man was evaluated for a 4-month history of progressive abdominal distension, diffuse abdominal pain, and marked weight loss from 62 to 47 kg. He had no history of smoking, immunodeficiency, or family history of cancer. Initial treatment by traditional healers for suspected poisoning yielded no improvement. On examination, there was generalized abdominal distension, diffuse tenderness, and bilateral lower-limb edema; there was no palpable lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, or abnormality on chest auscultation. Laboratory tests showed a normal white-cell count, C-reactive protein 82 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 70 mm/h, albumin 2.6 g/dL, total protein 7.8 g/dL, gamma-glutamyl transferase 266 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 268 IU/L, and negative serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C. Abdominal ultrasonography and CT imaging revealed a roughly oval intraperitoneal cystic mass measuring 203×266×248 mm with a 3 mm-thick wall, extending from the right hypochondrium to the pelvis and displacing bowel and viscera; multiple intra-abdominal lymphadenopathies and bilateral pleural effusions (right greater than left) were also noted. Initial differential diagnoses included lymphoma and dysembryoma.

A 33‐year‐old previously healthy man presented with 2 days of fever, sore throat, irritability, and an inability to drink water because of severe anxiety when he saw or thought about water. One month earlier, he had traveled to join a new job. He recalled being bitten on his right ear by an unknown animal three months before presentation; the wound had healed without medical care. On examination, he was agitated and febrile (38.3°C) with stable other vital signs. There was no nuchal rigidity or focal neurologic deficits. A healed scar was noted on the right pinna. Complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and C‐reactive protein were within normal limits. Computed tomography of the head showed no abnormalities. Lumbar puncture revealed a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid, and bacterial cultures were negative. Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and acyclovir were initiated but were discontinued when CSF bacterial cultures and a viral PCR panel returned negative. Real‐time PCR for rabies virus on CSF and on a nuchal‐skin biopsy specimen was negative, and no rabies virus neutralizing antibodies were detectable in CSF or plasma.

A 40-year-old woman with a history of estrogen-receptor–positive, progesterone-receptor–negative, HER2-positive breast cancer treated 5 years earlier presented with 1 year of worsening rectal bleeding. She had been in remission on tamoxifen. She reported red blood in her stools, mostly coinciding with menses, along with dyschezia, abdominal pain, occasional loose stools, and dysmenorrhea. Menstrual cycles were regular. Physical examination revealed a normal digital rectal examination without palpable mass. Hemoglobin was normal. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed a focal area of sigmoid wall thickening and a 3.2 × 4.0 cm luminal filling defect with narrowing, without surrounding inflammatory changes. Pelvic ultrasound was unremarkable. On colonoscopy, the sigmoid colon was markedly tortuous and could not be traversed; multiple 5- to 15-mm hypervascular, friable, oval lesions embedded in the proximal sigmoid colon wall were noted at the site of narrowing.

A 43-year-old previously healthy man of Sephardic-Jewish descent presented with sudden-onset chest pain and exertional dyspnea that began that morning, following a week of anorexia and diarrhea which had resolved one day earlier. In the emergency department, he was diagnosed with acute pulmonary embolism with a saddle embolus, large bilateral thrombotic burden, right ventricular (RV) systolic dysfunction, and mildly elevated serum troponin levels. He was admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit and started on therapeutic unfractionated heparin. Over the next several days, serial echocardiograms showed further deterioration of RV function, and he was transferred to a tertiary center. On arrival, he was asymptomatic with stable vital signs. Laboratory tests showed normal renal function, normal high-sensitivity troponin I, and normal lactate. Physical examination was notable only for jugular venous distention. Electrocardiography demonstrated normal sinus rhythm, a normal QRS axis, and T-wave inversion in leads V1–V4. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated RV with moderately reduced systolic function and an estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 50 mmHg. The following day, bilateral catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) was performed using the EkoSonic Endovascular System, infusing 19 mg of alteplase over 9.5 hours. During CDT, the D-dimer rose from 7000 ng/mL to 121 000 ng/mL and fibrinogen fell from 560 mg/dL to 398 mg/dL. A follow-up echocardiogram the next day showed no significant improvement. On Day 2 after CDT, he experienced an episode of exertional syncope without arrhythmia or injury. On Day 3 after CDT, computed tomographic angiography showed both worsening central thrombus burden and partial improvement in bilateral segmental and subsegmental vessels. Compression ultrasound revealed a small right popliteal vein thrombus. Brain-natriuretic peptide was 244 pg/mL, and troponin peaked at 88 ng/L. Antiphospholipid antibody testing was negative; further hypercoagulability workup was pending.

A 57-year-old man with morbid obesity (BMI, 44), hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, and a history of laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 2 years earlier presented with a 1-day history of periumbilical, colicky abdominal pain rated 7/10, nausea, and multiple episodes of bilious vomiting. One year after his bypass, he had laparoscopic enterolysis for small-bowel obstruction and two subsequent incisional hernia repairs. On examination, his abdomen was soft and nondistended, with epigastric and periumbilical tenderness and high-pitched bowel sounds. A CT scan of the abdomen showed dilatation of the gastric pouch and remnant stomach, multiple dilated jejunal loops with air–fluid levels, and a mottled intraluminal mass in the ileal lumen; the distal ileum and colon were decompressed.

A 40-year-old woman (BMI 21 kg/m^2) presented with a two-year history of gradually progressive lower back pain radiating to the right thigh, accompanied by numbness and tingling in the right lower limb. Her past medical, family, and social histories were unremarkable. On general and neurological examination, findings were intact. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine showed a well-defined T2 hyperintense lesion measuring approximately 0.9 × 1.2 × 2.0 cm extending from the lower level of L5 to the mid–S1 vertebral body, predominantly within the right L5–S1 lateral recess, causing lateral recess stenosis and compressing the right S1 traversing nerve root. Two additional small well-defined T2 hyperintense foci were noted at the S1 level, measuring 0.4 × 0.7 cm and 0.6 × 0.5 cm. Other investigations, including routine laboratory tests, revealed no abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid and serological studies were not performed.

A 24-year-old Caucasian man presented to the emergency department with painless cervical subcutaneous emphysema noted 2 hours earlier. He denied dyspnea. He reported a nonspecific cough 2 weeks prior. He had no past medical history, no medications, and no history of trauma or instrumental procedures.

On examination, vital signs were notable for a heart rate of 87 beats/min and blood pressure of 97/61 mmHg; respiratory rate and temperature were normal. Physical examination confirmed subcutaneous crepitus in the neck without chest wall tenderness or other abnormalities.

Laboratory tests showed leukocytes 13,000 cells/mm3, hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL, hematocrit 38.0%, sodium 141 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein 46 mg/dL. Electrocardiography demonstrated a normal sinus rhythm without abnormalities.

A chest radiograph confirmed cervical subcutaneous emphysema. To evaluate for pneumothorax, a thoracic CT scan was obtained, revealing extensive subcutaneous emphysema and air within the mediastinum but no pneumothorax.

A 14-year-old female student (height 179 cm, weight 110 kg; BMI 34.3 kg/m2) presented with significant infrapatellar pain when kneeling and recurrent external patellar dislocations. She had a prior diagnosis of Osgood–Schlatter disease treated conservatively and a history of irritable bowel syndrome. There was no pain with simple knee flexion or extension. Preoperative knee scores were low (Kujala 32, Lysholm 19, KOOS pain 21.4, KOOS symptoms 58.3, KOOS ADL 41.2, KOOS sports 10, KOOS QOL 25). On examination of the left knee, there was no focal tenderness, but patellar tracking and apprehension tests were positive; rotational stress, drawer, and grinding tests were negative. Range of motion was full. Laboratory tests, including inflammatory markers, were all within normal limits. Lateral radiographs at 20° of flexion showed patellar height ratios: Caton–Deschamps 1.7, Insall–Salvati 0.8, modified Insall–Salvati 2.3, Blackburne–Peel 1.6. CT measurements revealed a TT–TG distance of 21.1 mm, patellar tilt 36.5°, femoral torsion 13.6°, tibial torsion 30.2°. MRI demonstrated a sulcus angle of 129.3° and trochlear depth of 6.4 mm without meniscal or ligament injury. The patellar morphology ratio (length of patella to articular facet) was 2.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of painful swelling of the lower jaw that was gradually increasing in size. She had no history of dental intervention, trauma, weight loss, tobacco use, or smoking. Examination revealed a firm-to-hard midline mandibular swelling without tenderness or erythema. Mouth opening was normal, the oral mucosa was intact, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy.  
Computed tomography of the mandible showed an expansile lytic lesion in the midline with cortical erosion and extension into the gingivobuccal soft tissue.  
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology of the jaw lesion yielded hemorrhagic, moderately cellular smears containing numerous multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells and few spindle cells; there were no epithelial cells and no plasma cells.  
Given the presence of giant cells, the differential diagnosis included giant cell tumor and brown tumor of bone.  
What is your working differential diagnosis and what would be your next diagnostic step?

A 68-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 2-year history of a 30-lb unintentional weight loss, chronic diarrhea with abdominal pain and occasional blood, and diminished sense of taste. She also noted hyperpigmentation of her skin, loss of her nails, and a gradual onset of peripheral neuropathy in her toes progressing to lower-extremity weakness. Family history was notable only for maternal liver cancer. Initial laboratory tests showed a normal complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, folate, vitamin B12, and thyroid function; HIV was negative. Anti-nuclear antibodies were positive, but complement levels were normal, and serum protein electrophoresis showed elevated alpha-2 globulins. Ten months after symptom onset, colonoscopy revealed two colonic polyps (tubular and inflammatory), and upper endoscopy revealed one fundic gland polyp; otherwise both examinations were unremarkable. Twenty months after onset, computed tomography showed prominent gastric folds and a small-bowel filling defect, but magnetic resonance enterography showed no small-bowel lesion. She was evaluated by hematology, endocrinology, rheumatology, and neurology without a diagnosis.  
On examination at a gastrointestinal referral center, she had onychodystrophy of the fingers and toes and hyperpigmentation of the palms and soles. Repeat laboratory testing showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin decreased from 13.7 g/dL to 9.3 g/dL over 6 months), hypoalbuminemia (2.6 g/dL), low total protein (5.5 g/dL), hypocalcemia, and low vitamin B12. Celiac serologies and repeat urine and serum protein electrophoresis were normal. Because of previously noted gastric fold thickening, an upper endoscopy was performed and revealed polypoid mucosal changes in the gastric antrum, body, and duodenum. Cold-forceps biopsies of the distal stomach demonstrated tortuous foveolae and lamina propria edema. Congo red staining was negative. Based on the initial histology, the leading differential diagnosis included Menetrier disease.

A 2-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a neck radiographic abnormality discovered during routine tuberculosis screening (positive family exposure). She had no symptoms of neck pain, radiculopathy, weakness, sensory changes, or bladder/bowel dysfunction, and no history of falls, ingestion, or neck trauma. On examination, she was alert and playful, with normal gait; cranial nerve, motor strength, tone, and reflexes were all normal; meningeal signs were absent. There were no skin abrasions, punctures, scars, or erythema on the anterior or posterior neck. The hospital’s child protection team found no evidence of abuse or neglect. Laboratory evaluation was unremarkable. A cervical spine CT with angiography revealed a 4 cm needle-shaped metallic object entering between the C7–T1 interspinous space and terminating at C5–C6, passing medial to but not violating the right vertebral artery. Chest and abdominal radiographs showed no additional foreign bodies, and a skeletal survey was negative for fractures.

An 89-year-old woman presented with a 24-hour history of severe, sharp, intermittent lower abdominal pain radiating to her back. She had vomited once (non-bilious, no blood) and had not opened her bowels for 24 hours. There was no fever or dysuria. Her medical history included an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and rheumatoid arthritis. On examination, her abdomen was soft but tender in the left iliac fossa without guarding or palpable masses. Glasgow Coma Score was 15/15. Vital signs were: respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, blood pressure 117/64 mm Hg, heart rate 75 beats/min, temperature 36.8 °C. Pain was scored at 9/10. Routine blood tests were unremarkable, with no evidence of infection. Because of concern for a worsening AAA, a CT angiogram was obtained. Overnight, the scan was reported as a stable AAA without rupture and an incomplete small bowel obstruction, possibly due to faecal loading of the caecum. The patient was treated with laxatives and an enema, but she did not improve, and clinically her symptoms did not correlate with the CT findings.

A 53-year-old man with a 20-pack-year smoking history and occasional alcohol use presented with an initial episode of 400 mL of blood expectoration, followed by 100–150 mL daily for 2–3 days. Over the past 9 months, he had three similar episodes requiring hospitalization. He denied fever, chest pain, or weight loss. He had undergone cholecystectomy 3 years earlier and had no history of diabetes or other immunosuppressive conditions. He received multiple courses of antibiotics for presumed lower respiratory infection without improvement. 

On examination, his vital signs were normal and he was not in respiratory distress. Oral hygiene was poor with dental caries. Chest auscultation revealed scattered crackles over the left lower lobe. 

Chest radiograph showed an inhomogeneous opacity in the left lower zone with elevation of the left hemidiaphragm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a hypodense lesion with irregular margins in the anterior segment of the left lower lobe adjacent to the descending aorta, along with subcarinal lymphadenopathy. 

An image-guided transthoracic lung biopsy revealed type 2 alveolar cell hyperplasia with negative immunohistochemical markers for malignancy. Flexible bronchoscopy confirmed bleeding from the left lower lobe but showed no endobronchial lesion. Bronchial washings were negative for acid-fast bacilli, GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, fungi, and pyogenic bacteria. 

A CT angiogram disclosed dilated vascular channels within the lesion without evidence of contrast extravasation or aortic abnormality.

A 55-year-old man was referred for cardiology assessment after developing atrial fibrillation, presenting with palpitations and exertional dyspnea. He was on anticoagulation with well-controlled rate. His past history was notable only for erectile dysfunction. Kidney function was normal, but there was proteinuria (albumin/creatinine ratio 33.4 mg/mmol; protein/creatinine ratio 43 mg/mmol). There was no family history of cardiac disease, and he had no children.

Electrocardiogram showed rate-controlled atrial fibrillation with prominent T-wave inversion in leads V3–V5. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated moderate, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy; strain analysis was not performed due to poor image quality.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with increased LV mass, preserved global systolic function but reduced long-axis function, no regional wall motion abnormalities in the inferolateral wall, and no systolic anterior motion or LV outflow tract obstruction. The right ventricle appeared normal. Native T1 mapping values ranged from 798 to 859 ms, with elevated values in the basal-mid inferolateral segments and low values in the remaining segments. Late gadolinium enhancement showed a non-ischaemic pattern of fibrosis in the inferolateral wall. T2 STIR sequences showed no edema.

A 45-year-old woman with no cardiovascular risk factors underwent mechanical mitral valve replacement (bi-leaflet prosthesis) three years earlier for severe rheumatic mitral stenosis. She presented with resting dyspnea and asthenia. On examination, she was in sinus tachycardia with a blood pressure of 91/60 mmHg, and the closing click of the prosthetic valve was diminished. She was taking acenocoumarol, and the admission international normalized ratio was 7.2. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography showed a completely immobile leaflet and a small, dense, hyperechogenic mass tightly attached to the disk plane with centripetal growth. The mean gradient across the mitral prosthesis was 27 mmHg, and the pressure half-time was 200 ms. At this stage, obstruction of the mitral prosthesis due to thrombosis, pannus formation, or a combination of both was considered.

A 9-day-old boy was referred for a 5 cm soft swelling of the left side of the neck and inspiratory stridor. The perinatal period was uneventful; he was born at 39 weeks 4 days by vaginal delivery with Apgar scores of 10 and weighed 3024 g at presentation (76 g weight loss since birth). Arterial oxygen saturation was 95–99% supine but fell to 85–90% in the right lateral decubitus position. Examination revealed a posterior pharyngeal wall swelling causing extrinsic airway compression; there was no vocal cord paralysis. Laboratory studies showed no evidence of infection. Neck CT and MRI demonstrated a 60 × 50 mm cystic lesion with an air–fluid level on the left side of the neck, extending from the epipharynx to the superior mediastinum. For urgent relief of respiratory distress, 20 mL of exudate was aspirated under ultrasound guidance, resulting in improved respiratory status and feeding; bacteriology of the aspirate showed no bacterial growth. A few days later, the neck swelling and stridor recurred.

A 25-year-old man from southern Mexico presented with a 1-year history of persistent nonproductive cough and more than 10% unintentional weight loss. He denied fever or dyspnea initially. Over time he developed whitish sputum, mild hemoptysis, fevers to >102.2°F, and resting dyspnea, prompting transfer to a referral center. He reported MSM exposures, no animal contacts, and no tobacco, alcohol, or illicit-drug use. He was unvaccinated as an adult.

On examination, temperature was 102.7°F, heart rate 120/min, and respiratory rate 30/min. Findings included oral candidiasis; multiple purple skin and palatal lesions with elevated borders; bilateral, nontender, indurated cervical lymphadenopathy; a hyperdynamic precordium; asymmetric chest expansion; diminished breath sounds and fremitus; and a flat percussion note over the left hemithorax.

Laboratory studies showed normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, MCV 80.9 fL, RDW 17.3%), leukocytes 6500/µL with lymphocytes 300/µL, platelets 183 000/µL; normal renal and liver tests; procalcitonin 0.84 µg/L; and arterial blood gas with pH 7.45, PCO2 26.4 mm Hg, PO2 51.6 mm Hg on FiO2 27%. He tested positive for HIV (confirmed by p24 antigen, antibody, and Western blot) and HHV-8, with a CD4 count of 7 cells/µL and viral load 126 916 copies/mL; hepatitis B and C tests were negative.

Chest imaging revealed bilateral pleural effusions, a consolidation with air bronchograms in the left lower lobe, and an endobronchial lesion obstructing the left main bronchial lumen. Bronchoscopy showed an exophytic mass occluding 80% of the left main bronchus, with chronic inflammatory changes.

A 69-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with sudden severe retrosternal pain radiating to the left hemithorax, vomiting, and dyspnea that began after food intake three days before presentation. On transfer, she was conscious and oriented. Vital signs were: heart rate 117 bpm, blood pressure 91/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, temperature 37.5 °C, and oxygen saturation 85% on FIO2 50%. Physical examination revealed subcutaneous emphysema in the right lateral neck region and decreased breath sounds with bibasal rales. Arterial blood gases showed pH 7.29, pO2 52 mmHg, pCO2 42 mmHg, HCO3– 20 mEq/L, and lactate 4.22 mmol/L. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilia and elevated acute-phase reactants. A chest radiograph demonstrated a massive left hydropneumothorax, which was treated with closed thoracostomy. Due to persistent symptoms, computed tomography angiography of the chest was performed, revealing pneumomediastinum and a large pleural effusion, findings suggestive of an esophageal perforation.

A 71‐year‐old man with a history of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (usual interstitial pneumonia pattern) and heavy smoking was referred for evaluation of a left upper lobe pulmonary nodule found on routine CT surveillance. He was asymptomatic. CT of the chest demonstrated a 1.2×1.0 cm irregular, lobulated solid nodule in the left upper lobe in a background of peripheral reticulation consistent with stable usual interstitial pneumonia. One month later, PET/CT confirmed the nodule with indeterminate FDG uptake and findings of active fibrosis but no other abnormal uptake. Physical examination was unremarkable, and laboratory assessments were within normal limits. Given his age, ILD history, and nodule growth, concern was raised for pulmonary malignancy and a CT‐guided percutaneous biopsy was performed.

An 82-year-old man presented with a right lower quadrant mass noted one year earlier during a routine physical examination. He reported no abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, nausea, or vomiting, and denied any history of trauma or prior abdominal surgery. His medical history included diverticulosis of the descending and sigmoid colon; he was taking atorvastatin. A prior colonoscopy had been unremarkable. On examination, his abdomen was soft, non-tender, and non-distended, with normal bowel sounds and no palpable mass. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen performed 10 months earlier demonstrated a 4.5 cm right lower quadrant mass with a densely calcified rim and mixed-density internal components, including calcifications; the lesion was described as nonspecific but was interpreted as a possible cecal tumor or liposarcoma. In view of these findings, the patient was referred for laparoscopic exploration with possible cecectomy.

A 17-year-old male with a history of asthma presented with 24 hours of progressive shortness of breath and chest tightness at rest that did not respond to bronchodilators. He denied recent illness; he had a dental cleaning 3 days earlier and no family history of cardiac disease or coagulopathy. On presentation, he was well appearing. Vital signs were blood pressure 107/56 mm Hg, heart rate 97 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 99.4 °F, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Cardiac examination was unremarkable. Lungs were clear without wheezing, rhonchi, or crackles. There was no jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, or edema. Extremities were well perfused with symmetric pulses.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete metabolic panel and blood count. A urine toxicology screen for nine substances, including cocaine and amphetamines, was negative. Electrocardiography revealed ST-segment elevations in leads I and aVL and T-wave inversions in the inferior and lateral leads. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated regional wall motion abnormalities of the inferior left ventricular segments with preserved global systolic function. Two hours after presentation, his oxygen saturation fell to 91% on room air; he was placed on 4 L nasal cannula with improvement to 96%. Chest radiography showed scattered bilateral hazy opacities. A computed tomographic angiogram of the chest excluded pulmonary embolism but demonstrated multifocal ground-glass opacities in both lungs. 

He was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit for further evaluation. The working differential diagnosis included COVID-19–related myocarditis, non–COVID-19 myocarditis, and multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children.

A 26-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 2, presented for prenatal care at 7 weeks’ gestation. Her history was notable for prior methamphetamine and cannabis use but was otherwise unremarkable, including a nonreactive syphilis antibody at that time. At 23 weeks’ gestation, she reported a one-month history of a worsening headache, which she attributed to a minor head injury, as well as a persistent auricular aura characterized by muffled hearing and intermittent blurred vision. A noncontrast head CT demonstrated numerous ill-defined lytic lesions throughout the calvarium. Laboratory studies revealed a rapid plasma reagin titer of 1:32; HIV testing was negative.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of fever and rapidly progressive fullness in the throat, pain on swallowing, dysphagia, and dyspnea. On examination, there was local redness at the root of the tongue but no other mucosal inflammation. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with a left shift and elevated C-reactive protein; thyroid-stimulating hormone, triiodothyronine, and thyroxine levels were normal. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a non-homogeneous, mass-like prominence at the base of the tongue compressing the epiglottis and narrowing the pharynx. Neck ultrasound failed to identify the thyroid gland in its normal pretracheal location. Contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated a 1.7 cm non-homogeneous, contrast-enhancing area at the tongue base with peripheral calcifications; several adjacent 1 cm nodular structures enhanced similarly to thyroid tissue, and no thyroid gland was seen in the usual neck location.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a 20-year history of persistent, sometimes ulcerating, swollen masses in her oral mucosa. She denied fever, fatigue, weight loss, or gastrointestinal symptoms and had not undergone prior investigations beyond intermittent topical corticosteroids and mouthwashes.  

On examination:  
• Firm, nontender, infiltrating mass on the right lateral tongue (3×2 cm) with a granular surface  
• Firm, nontender, infiltrating mass in the right retromolar trigone (2×2 cm) with a granular surface  
• Cobblestone-like swelling of the lower lip mucosa  
• Multiple palpable, nontender, firm, mobile cervical lymph nodes bilaterally  

Laboratory tests:  
• Complete blood count and serum biochemistry normal except fasting glucose 143 mg/dL  
• ESR 41 mm/h; C-reactive protein, calcium, vitamin B12, folate, and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme normal  

Imaging and pathology:  
• Chest radiograph normal with no hilar lymphadenopathy  
• Mantoux and pathergy tests negative  
• Neck ultrasonography showed lymphadenitis  
• Incisional biopsy of a retromolar lesion and biopsy of a cervical lymph node showed well-demarcated noncaseating granulomas of epithelioid cells and lymphocytes in edematous stroma  
• E Ziehl-Neelsen and PAS stains showed no organisms  
• Mycobacterial culture of the oral lesion had no growth

A 32-year-old man was admitted for evaluation of an intense, right-sided hemicranial headache that worsened with coughing. Three weeks earlier, he developed a dry cough followed by a brief febrile upper respiratory infection treated with antibiotics; the fever resolved but the cough persisted. Two weeks before admission, he noted pulsating pain behind the right eye associated with nausea and vomiting; there were no visual changes, diplopia, or other neurologic symptoms.  
His past medical history was negative; he denied trauma, surgery, or previous headaches. He played recreational football.  
On examination, temperature was normal, other vital signs were stable. Neurologic examination was normal except for a slightly wider right rima oculi and mild neck stiffness on forward flexion; there was no conjunctival injection or proptosis.  
Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance; other inflammatory markers were normal. Noncontrast head CT was normal. Lumbar puncture yielded clear cerebrospinal fluid with normal cytobiochemical results.  
Because his cough-induced hemicranial headache did not fit criteria for a primary headache disorder and was considered a “red flag,” further evaluation was pursued.  
The patient’s examination remained otherwise unremarkable.

A 42-year-old man living in the Southwestern United States presented in November with fever, body aches, and chills without cough or sore throat. He was tachycardic, and chest radiography showed bilateral patchy consolidations. Rapid influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and Streptococcus A tests were negative. A complete blood count showed a normal white-cell count, neutrophils 79% (reference 44–72%), and lymphocytes 6.2% (reference 22–41%). He was treated with azithromycin, cefdinir, and antiviral therapy.

In December, he returned with left-sided back pain and subjective fevers. Urinalysis and abdominal radiograph were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13.1 K/µL (reference 4.8–10.8), eosinophils 3.54 K/µL (reference 0.00–0.51), basophils 0.26 K/µL (reference 0.00–0.12), and lymphocytes 9.7% (reference 22–41%).

In February, lumbar spine MRI suggested a bone lesion of uncertain behavior. CT of the lumbar spine revealed a 10 mm lytic defect in the posterior L5 vertebral body with an associated soft-tissue component extending into the right ventral epidural space. No other bony lesions were seen, and no primary malignancy was identified. A pulmonary reticulonodular opacity in the left upper lobe/lingula was noted to be “more suggestive of an infectious or inflammatory process.” Mediastinal nodes were nonspecific.

In March, repeat MRI showed marrow infiltration of the dorsal L5, erosion of the posterior cortex, and extension into the epidural space encasing the right L5 root. The radiologist’s differential included lymphoma, myeloma/plasmacytoma, and metastatic disease. Later that month, he presented with right-sided rib pain; CT angiography revealed a new lytic lesion in the posterior right 11th rib and slight enlargement of the left upper lobe pulmonary nodule. With a presumptive diagnosis of malignancy, the patient was taken for surgical biopsy of the L5 lesion and the right rib mass.

A 36-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B on antiviral therapy and a history of obesity presented with an unintentional weight loss of approximately 50 kg over 8 months. He had chronic dysphagia with documented esophageal candidiasis. Family members reported long-standing cognitive deficits since childhood. On neurologic examination, he had involuntary choreic movements, orofacial dyskinesia, and an ataxic gait.

Initial cranial CT showed marked diffuse accentuation of cortical sulci and cisterns for his age, caudate nucleus atrophy predominantly in the head, and ex-vacuo dilation of the anterior horns of the lateral ventricles. Brain MRI confirmed these findings and additionally demonstrated putaminal atrophy and hypointensity of the basal nuclei on susceptibility-weighted sequences.

To evaluate for abetalipoproteinemia, fundoscopy, serum vitamin E, VLDL, and LDL levels were obtained and were within normal limits. Serum creatine kinase was elevated. A peripheral blood smear revealed numerous acanthocytes.

A 69-year-old Hispanic man with no significant medical history presented with a 3-week history of fever and confusion that began 4 days after his first dose of the mRNA-1273 SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. He initially saw his primary physician and was treated with acetaminophen and NSAIDs, but intermittently continued to spike fevers associated with confusion that resolved with acetaminophen. On the day of hospital presentation, he awoke febrile (maximum temperature 102.6°F) with diaphoresis and an inability to answer questions appropriately. His family noted similar episodes of fever and confusion over the preceding weeks. He had no personal or family history of autoimmune disease.

On examination, he was alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Vital signs were notable for fever of 102.6°F, heart rate 115 beats/min, and blood pressure 157/67 mm Hg. There was no neck stiffness or focal neurologic deficit; motor and sensory examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 44 mm/hr (reference 0–20), C-reactive protein 0.5 mg/L (reference <3), and normal results for antinuclear antibodies, myeloperoxidase and proteinase-3 ANCA, and complement levels. Complete blood count, liver function tests, and metabolic panel were unremarkable. 

A lumbar puncture revealed a normal opening pressure and clear fluid. CSF analysis demonstrated protein 119 mg/dL (reference 25–55), glucose 52 mg/dL (reference 45–75), leukocyte count 300/mm³ (reference 0–8) with 72% neutrophils. CSF VDRL was nonreactive, oligoclonal bands were negative, and JC virus PCR was negative. Serum protein electrophoresis was unremarkable.

Brain MRI showed increased FLAIR signal in the bilateral mesial temporal and anterior inferior frontal lobes with small scattered, ill-defined faint foci of enhancement. Gram stain and fungal culture of the CSF were negative, and CSF cultures (bacterial, fungal) and a viral panel were all negative. Other tests, including urinalysis, parvovirus serology, and SARS-CoV-2 testing, were unremarkable.

A 62-year-old man presented with increased frequency of ear infections and recurrent impaction of cerumen. On otoscopic examination, there was significant bilateral narrowing of the external auditory canals, impairing visualization of the tympanic membranes, more pronounced on the right. The patient described previous cerumen removals as so uncomfortable that anesthesia was required. He reported awareness of bony outgrowths in both ear canals for the past 30 years and had declined surgical treatment when first offered. Further history revealed that he was an avid free-diver daily during summer months from early teens to late adulthood without any ear protection; he ceased diving 15 years ago. High-resolution CT of the temporal bones demonstrated bilateral dense, sessile osseous outgrowths arising from the osseous portion of the external auditory canals, causing near-occlusion of the canals with residual luminal diameters of 1–2 mm; no soft tissue densities or bone erosions were observed.

A 35-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 4, presented 5 days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with a 3-week history of severe headache, recurrent sinusitis symptoms, and progressive blurring of vision followed by complete vision loss one week earlier. During pregnancy she developed gestational diabetes, managed as an inpatient with fluids and insulin. While hospitalized, she developed periorbital edema and purulent orbital discharge, and later became confused with uncontrolled blood sugar levels. On examination she was alert but confused, afebrile, and had normal peripheral findings. Neurologic examination revealed increased tone, brisk reflexes, and unsustained clonus, with preserved power. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (17.8 × 10^9/L), neutrophilia (14.36 × 10^9/L), severe anemia (hemoglobin 5.9 g/dL), hyponatremia (125 mmol/L), and hypokalemia (3.0 mmol/L); HIV test and cultures were negative. A head CT scan demonstrated an ill-defined peripheral enhancing midline lesion involving both frontal lobes, compressing the hypothalamus, abutting the optic chiasm and cribriform plates, with focal bone erosion. Brain MRI revealed a peripheral enhancing collection centered in the paranasal sinuses, extending into the retroorbital spaces bilaterally and the anterior cranial fossa, with restricted diffusion and adjacent bifrontal and left basal gangliocapsular high signal intensity.

A 60-year-old woman with a 10-year history of systemic sclerosis (SSc), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, managed intermittently with prednisone, hydroxychloroquine, and bosentan, presented with progressive skin lesions. She first noted thickening of the backs of her hands and forearms, sclerodactyly, Raynaud’s phenomenon, perioral radiating striae, and tight facial skin. Over several weeks, she developed necrosis and ulcers on the fingertips of her third fingers, which then extended to multiple ulcers on her upper and lower limbs and trunk.

On examination, there were deep ulcers with irregular, undermined edges on all four limbs. Lower limb ulcers showed dark red granulation tissue, copious purulent discharge, and bloody exudate. She reported severe pain (visual analog scale score 5) requiring continuous oxycodone. Her modified Rodnan skin score was 24.

Initial studies revealed: C-reactive protein 65.5 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 66 mm/h, positive anti–Scl-70 antibodies, CD4+ T-cell count 359/µL. Echocardiography confirmed pulmonary hypertension; chest CT showed interstitial fibrosis and esophageal dilation. Secretion cultures grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

The working diagnosis was SSc-related vasculitis complicated by infection. She received methylprednisolone (20 mg daily for 10 days, then taper to 8 mg daily), intravenous immunoglobulin (10 g daily for 3 days), targeted antibiotics (amikacin, imipenem, linezolid), bosentan 62.5 mg twice daily, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Despite these interventions, there was no significant improvement in her ulcers or systemic inflammation.

A 23-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with nine days of high-grade fevers and chills in a diurnal pattern, associated with fatigue. Four days before admission she was treated with amoxicillin–clavulanate for presumed tonsillopharyngitis. Three days into her illness she developed nausea and multiple episodes of bilious vomiting, followed by severe, colicky right upper quadrant abdominal pain without clear aggravating or relieving factors. She had traveled from her home island to the capital two days before symptom onset.

On examination, she appeared dehydrated, jaundiced, and toxic. Temperature was 39 °C, heart rate 110 beats/min, and mean arterial pressure 73 mmHg. She had pharyngitis and palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed a positive Murphy’s sign and guarding in the right upper quadrant.

Laboratory studies showed lymphocytosis and monocytosis with normal total leukocytes and platelets, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminases, marked hyperferritinemia, and an elevated C-reactive protein level. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated gallbladder wall edema with a positive sonographic Murphy’s sign. CT of the abdomen revealed hepatosplenomegaly, and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography confirmed acute acalculous cholecystitis.

The patient was admitted and treated with intravenous fluids, cefotaxime, metronidazole, and analgesics.

A 59-year-old man, previously healthy, presented with progressive ascending paresthesia and weakness beginning 10 days after a flu-like illness. Within 24 hours he developed paresthesia in his upper limbs, and by day 2 he had weakness of the lower and then upper limbs, along with discrete dysphagia and frequent choking on liquids. He was admitted on day 8 of symptoms. Three days into hospitalization he developed respiratory weakness and worsening dysphagia; by day 14 he had facial diplegia. No autonomic dysfunction was noted. 

On examination, he had flaccid tetraplegia (MRC grade 3/5 in the upper limbs and 2/5 in the lower limbs), absent reflexes, glove-and-stocking hypoesthesia, a positive Romberg sign, and facial diplegia. Nerve conduction studies showed sensory and motor demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with decreased motor conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies in the ulnar, median, tibial, and peroneal nerves, prolonged F-wave latencies in all four limbs, and decreased sensory conduction velocities in the right musculocutaneous and left ulnar nerves. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed albumino-cytologic dissociation with 0 white cells and protein 0.7 mg/dL.

He was diagnosed with Guillain-Barré syndrome and received a single course of IV immunoglobulin, with progressive improvement; at discharge his strength was MRC 4+ and respiratory and bulbar signs had resolved. Two weeks later, he returned with worsening dysphagia and new sensory ataxia. Examination showed positive Romberg sign, loss of deep sensation on the right, absent reflexes, MRC grade 4+ strength, a weak gag reflex, and mild facial diplegia. He was treated with a second course of IV immunoglobulin, resulting in complete resolution of dysphagia and ataxia. After discharge he continued to improve, recovering all reflexes, with only mild proximal weakness and paresthesia treated with pregabalin.

A 45-year-old woman, previously healthy, reported an eight-year history of bilateral foot swelling and pain and seven years of recurrent nodules on her legs and feet that burst to form ulcers. She denied medication use, systemic symptoms, or a family history of similar illness. 

On examination, there was pitting edema of both feet and lower legs and multiple irregular, slightly tender ulcers (1–2 cm) with sloping edges and slough-covered floors over the medial malleolus of the right foot and the lateral aspect of the left foot. The surrounding skin showed erythema, hyperpigmentation, and multiple scars of healed lesions. No thrills, bruits, or varicose veins were present; all peripheral pulses were palpable. Systemic examination was unremarkable.

Routine laboratory studies (complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, urinalysis) and chest radiographs were within normal limits. HIV-1 and HIV-2 ELISA were nonreactive, and the Mantoux test was negative. Bleeding time, clotting time, and prothrombin time were normal. Color Doppler ultrasonography of both lower limbs was unremarkable.

Based on the history and investigations, differential diagnoses included chromoblastomycosis, mycetoma, vasculitis, and erythema induratum.

A 7‐day‐old boy, born at 39 weeks’ gestation (birth weight 2.45 kg), was brought for evaluation of failure to pass urine via the penis since birth. On day 5, after separation of the umbilical cord stump, the mother noted soakage of clothes and an intermittent stream of fluid from the inferior margin of the umbilicus. The infant was afebrile; abdomen was soft and non‐distended. Genital examination revealed a normally formed penis with two urethral openings: one at the glans tip and a second at the penoscrotal junction, without chordee. A 3‐French ureteric catheter could be passed 5 cm into the dorsal (glanular) meatus, whereas a size 6 infant‐feeding tube passed freely from the ventral (penoscrotal) meatus into the bladder. Following calibration, urinary flow improved from the ventral meatus and decreased at the umbilicus.  
An abdominal ultrasound showed a patent urachal tract from the bladder dome to the umbilicus; the kidneys and ureters were normal. A retrograde urethrogram, with contrast instilled separately into each meatus, demonstrated two distinct urethral channels, each originating from the bladder. The dorsal urethra was narrow, irregular, and stenotic in segments; the ventral urethra was of good caliber and smooth.

A 71-year-old woman presented in March with sharp right orbital pain, ptosis, and headache. Ten days earlier she had experienced self-limited right otalgia without fever. Her history included paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on rivaroxaban, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and prior bacterial pneumonia; there was no recent dental intervention.  
CT angiography showed thrombosis of the right superior ophthalmic vein. Four-day follow-up MRI with contrast revealed thrombi in the left transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, and internal jugular vein, along with phlebitis of both superior ophthalmic veins and mild left meningeal enhancement. Empiric treatment with linezolid and ceftriaxone was given for suspected meningitis, together with heparin and corticosteroids for possible vasculitis; no lumbar puncture or blood cultures were performed. A thrombophilia screen was negative. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no endocarditis. Two-week MRI showed partial recanalization of ophthalmic veins but persistent other thrombi. The patient improved and was discharged on acenocoumarin.  

In April, she was readmitted after a fall; head CT showed new cerebellar and periventricular ischemic lesions. She developed fever, psychomotor slowing, disorientation, and bilateral visual loss. Empiric linezolid, acyclovir, meropenem, and dexamethasone were started for suspected meningoencephalitis. MRI revealed bilateral occipital infarcts, a left cerebellar lesion, and multifocal meningeal enhancement. No lumbar puncture or cultures were obtained; total-body CT was negative for malignancy.  

In May, after partial recovery, she returned with headache and rigors. Chest CT showed a 4-cm nodular lesion with a 2.5-cm cavitation in the left upper lobe and bilateral pleural effusions. Brain MRI demonstrated worsening thromboses in the transverse sinuses, sigmoid sinuses, and internal jugular veins. Blood tests showed elevated C-reactive protein and leukocytosis. Three sets of blood cultures grew Streptococcus constellatus.

A 59-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia in remission, receiving chemotherapy in preparation for stem-cell transplant, presented with fever. On arrival he was febrile, tachypneic, and hypoxic on room air. Laboratory studies showed neutropenia for at least 23 days, a normal coagulation profile, and mild thrombocytopenia (56 000/µL). A chest radiograph revealed a left lung–base infiltrate. He was admitted and started on broad-spectrum antibiotics for health-care–associated pneumonia and fluconazole for possible fungal infection. 

Within 36 hours he was transferred to the ICU for frank hemoptysis, respiratory failure, and refractory shock. Repeat chest radiography showed progression of infiltrates in the left upper and middle lobes. Bronchoscopy revealed no endobronchial lesions but profuse hemorrhage from the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe; instillation of epinephrine, cold saline, and thrombin failed to control the bleeding. His respiratory status worsened, requiring PEEP of 15 cm H2O and 100% FiO2, later on APRV mode, yet he could not tolerate FiO2 less than 100%. Arterial blood gases showed pH 7.27, PaCO2 42 mm Hg, PaO2 63 mm Hg on 100% FiO2.

A 78‐year‐old man was referred with a 2-month history of left‐sided otalgia and ipsilateral hearing loss that began after an episode of otorrhea and progressively worsened. His medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, stage III chronic renal failure, a recent diagnosis of type II diabetes, and functional endoscopic sinonasal surgery 3 years earlier for chronic rhinosinusitis. His daily medications included subcutaneous insulin, oral dexamethasone, simvastatin, amlodipine, and proton-pump inhibitor therapy, among others.

Two months prior, nasal endoscopy revealed a hyperemic lesion almost totally obstructing the nasopharynx and bilaterally extending to the tubal ostia. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the head showed a large bilateral median-paramedian nasopharyngeal lesion occupying the left parapharyngeal space, with invasion and erosion of the left clivus and possible hypoglossal canal involvement. Subsequent CT imaging demonstrated bilateral partial erosion of the middle skull base and clival bone with moderate soft-tissue contrast enhancement, and PET scan showed increased 18-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake along the middle skull base.

Given these findings, a neoplastic lesion of the skull base was suspected. The patient underwent three endoscopic biopsies of the nasopharyngeal lesion, all of which returned negative histopathological results. He was then referred for a neuronavigation-guided biopsy under general anesthesia. On endoscopic examination immediately before biopsy, the nasopharynx appeared free of disease, with intact mucosa and no visible anomaly.

A 38-year-old man presented with a 24-hour history of severe right lower-quadrant abdominal pain associated with anorexia, nausea, and vomiting. On examination, he had local rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant. His temperature was 38.4 °C, pulse 115 beats/min, blood pressure 120/60 mmHg, and respiratory rate 30 breaths/min. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 19,000 per μL with 87% band forms; other results were within normal limits. His medical history was unremarkable. Because of the clinical presentation, a presumptive diagnosis of acute appendicitis was made, and the patient was taken to the operating room for an emergency appendectomy.

A 25-year-old previously healthy male agricultural worker lost consciousness while cleaning inside an empty manure pit. After approximately 15 minutes inside the pit, he was rescued by a colleague, who also collapsed shortly after exit. On initial on‐site assessment, the patient was unresponsive and hyperventilating. His blood pressure was 200/110 mm Hg, heart rate 140 beats/min, and peripheral oxygen saturation 90%. He developed a generalized seizure, was treated with midazolam, and was intubated. Point-of-care ultrasound demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 20%. During transport to the emergency department, he became hypotensive and required high-dose vasopressors.

On arrival, he developed acute pulmonary edema and reactive pneumonitis on chest CT. Despite mechanical ventilation with high PEEP and 100% FiO₂, SpO₂ remained 91%. Arterial blood gas analysis showed metabolic acidosis with a lactate level of 8.0 mmol/L; there was no methemoglobinemia. Hypotension persisted from combined vasodilatation and biventricular failure. ECG revealed sinus tachycardia at 130 beats/min with diffuse ST-segment elevations. Bronchoscopy was unremarkable. His body temperature was 34.7 °C.
