The rescuing colleague had bilateral conjunctivitis but rapidly recovered without cardiopulmonary symptoms.

A 62-year-old woman with stage IIIC ovarian carcinoma, initially treated with six cycles of neoadjuvant paclitaxel, carboplatin, and bevacizumab followed by debulking surgery and maintenance bevacizumab, presented two months after her last oncologic follow-up with a 2-week history of dysarthria, dizziness, rightward lateropulsion, tinnitus, and gait instability leading to several falls. On examination, she had dysarthric speech, truncal and appendicular ataxia with rightward drift, and persistent tinnitus. A PET-CT scan showed partial response of her ovarian carcinoma with stable residual disease, and a brain MRI demonstrated cortico-subcortical atrophy without focal lesions. Given stable oncologic imaging and no structural explanation for her acute cerebellar syndrome, a paraneoplastic neurological syndrome was suspected.

A 26‐year‐old woman, gravida 2 para 1 at 31 weeks of gestation, developed sudden, severe abdominal pain just before boarding a three‐hour flight. She reported a similar brief episode of pain that morning, localized to the left upper quadrant. On arrival at the emergency department, she appeared pale. Vital signs were: respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 100% on room air, blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, and pulse 93 beats per minute. She had diffuse abdominal pain, but palpation of the uterus did not elicit additional tenderness.  
Obstetrical ultrasound showed a fetal heart rate of 115 BPM and no sonographic evidence of placental abruption. Cardiotocography revealed no tachycardia, normal beat‐to‐beat variability, and accelerations without decelerations.  
A bedside ultrasound of the maternal abdomen demonstrated free intra‐abdominal fluid. Laboratory testing revealed a plasma hemoglobin level of 6.4 mmol/L. Ultrasound‐guided aspiration of the fluid yielded blood. At that moment, the differential diagnosis included rupture of a splenic artery aneurysm, rupture of a uterine artery, uterine rupture, or partial placental abruption.

A 78-year-old woman with reported seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, maintained on prednisone (10 mg daily) and methotrexate, presented with acute onset of shortness of breath. She was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and hypoxic to 87% on room air. Admission laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9770 cells/mcL, procalcitonin 0.23 ng/mL (low likelihood for bacterial etiology), normal cardiac biomarkers, lymphocyte count 480 cells/mcL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 98 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein 24.6 mg/dL. On examination, there were bilateral rhonchi and fine basilar crackles; an erythematous rash was noted on her chest, with oral and nasal mucositis and epistaxis. She had no history of lung disease and no smoking or occupational exposures. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest showed diffuse bilateral consolidations and ground-glass opacities with subpleural sparing. Echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 75% with no other abnormalities. Blood and sputum cultures, including Legionella, were negative, and the serum methotrexate level was normal at 0.13 mcmol/L. Methotrexate was discontinued, and she was started on empiric antibiotics, diuretics, and leucovorin; subsequently, she became neutropenic and encephalopathic.

A 57-year-old man with seronegative inflammatory bowel disease–associated arthritis and stage IV urothelial carcinoma was evaluated for painful necrosis of the distal fingers and toes. Six months earlier, after disease progression on avelumab, he began erdafitinib. Three months into treatment, he developed dystrophic nails with onycholysis, periungual erythema, and purulent infections of both feet, which were treated with nail avulsion and debridement. Although the infections resolved, he continued to have peeling and bleeding of the hands and feet. Two months later, imaging showed decreased metastatic disease, and erdafitinib was discontinued because of worsening digital erosions and ulcerations that impaired his activities of daily living. Within two weeks, he developed necrosis of multiple distal digits, prompting hospital admission for pain control and further evaluation.

On examination, there was necrosis of all ten distal fingertips and the first and second toes of the left foot and first through third toes of the right foot, with surrounding scale, erythema, and hyperkeratotic subungual debris; mucous membranes were spared. He denied Raynaud phenomenon but noted exacerbation of pain in cold temperatures. Laboratory studies showed chronic normocytic anemia without other abnormalities. Vascular workup, including coagulation studies, computed tomography angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, upper-extremity ultrasound, and transthoracic echocardiography, excluded a thromboembolic process. Rheumatologic studies (antinuclear antibody; anti–double-stranded DNA; anti-ribonucleoprotein; anti-histone; anti-Ro; anti-La; rheumatoid factor; anticardiolipin; β2-glycoprotein I; lupus anticoagulant; antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies; myeloperoxidase antibodies), cryocrit, serum protein electrophoresis, and urine protein electrophoresis were all negative.

A 14-year-old boy presented with a 10-month history of a painful mass in his left knee. The mass began the size of a marble and gradually enlarged to the size of a tennis ball. There was no redness or fever. On examination, the range of motion in the left knee was 0°–20°. A complete blood count showed a leukocyte count of 7.7 × 10^3 per mm^3. Plain radiographs of the knee revealed soft-tissue swelling without bony abnormality. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated intermediate signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images in the Hoffa pad region, suprapatellar bursa, and popliteal bursa, with areas of low signal intensity suggestive of hemosiderin deposits.

A 13-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of loose upper front teeth and bleeding gums of two years’ duration.  
Her medical history was notable for recurrent skin rashes and keratotic patches on the elbows, knees, and soles since age 4, worsening in winter.  Dental history included premature exfoliation of a primary tooth.  Family history revealed consanguineous parents and an elder sibling with similar but milder skin lesions; pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable.

On examination, there were well-demarcated yellowish hyperkeratotic plaques on the palms and soles extending onto the dorsal surfaces, with peeling skin and underlying erythema; similar lesions were present on both knees.  Intraoral examination showed 28 teeth with proclination and spacing of the upper incisors, rotations of premolars, a diffuse gingival swelling around the lower left molars, and increased mobility with apical migration of the gingival margin around the upper and lower incisors.  

Periodontal assessment revealed generalized bleeding on probing and deep pockets particularly around teeth 11, 21, 36, 37, 41, and 46.  Orthopantomograph and full-mouth intraoral periapical radiographs demonstrated vertical bone loss in those same regions.

A 32-year-old man presented three months after sustaining a laceration to the volar aspect of the left index finger at the proximal interphalangeal crease, which had been sutured in an emergency department. He subsequently underwent an operation for suspected infectious tenosynovitis of the flexor tendon sheath. On examination, the patient had diffuse pain on palpation of the volar surface of the digit and pain with flexion, but there was no redness and he maintained full finger motion. Two-point discrimination was 6 mm on both sides of the digit. Clicking with flexion was noted over the middle phalanx. Scars were present at the fingertip and in the palm, but the original laceration site was not explored during the prior surgery. Differential diagnosis included subacute infectious tenosynovitis and triggering due to a partial flexor tendon laceration. An MRI of the finger was obtained to clarify the diagnosis.

A 19-year-old male presented with pain in the upper right first molar. He was short in stature and had drooping, hypermobile shoulders. Facial features included frontal bossing, mild hypertelorism, mid-face deficiency, and relative mandibular prognathism; intelligence was normal. Family history was notable for similar findings in his father. Intraoral examination revealed a high-arched palate, a unilaterally constricted maxillary arch, multiple over-retained deciduous teeth, and few erupted permanent teeth.  
Chest radiography demonstrated hypoplasia of the lateral aspects of both clavicles and upper thoracic scoliosis. Skull radiographs showed widened cranial sutures with multiple wormian bones, frontal and parietal bossing, hypoplastic mid-facial bones, and loss of pneumatisation of the sphenoid sinus. A panoramic dental view revealed multiple impacted teeth, over-retained deciduous teeth, a hypoplastic maxillary sinus, and slender coronoid processes. Pelvic imaging showed an abnormally shaped pelvis with coxa vara. Hand and wrist radiographs demonstrated slender, elongated metacarpals and phalanges with tapering distal phalanges.

A 40-hour-old male African neonate was brought to the hospital for persistent high fever, poor feeding, irritability, and episodic jerky movements since day 1 of life. He was born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery after prolonged rupture of membranes (>48 hours) and 18 hours of labor. Amniotic fluid was foul-smelling. At birth he had an Apgar score of 3 at 1 minute and 7 at 10 minutes after resuscitation. He initially breastfed weakly and was discharged home <24 hours after delivery.

On examination, temperature was 39.1 °C, respiratory rate 65/min, oxygen saturation 80% on room air, heart rate 153/min, weight 3 kg. He was irritable, responsive only to pain, had poor suck and Moro reflexes, normal tone and fontanelles, and ongoing seizures. Chest examination showed no retractions, normal percussion, and broncho-vesicular breath sounds. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Random blood sugar was 5.1 mmol/L.

Laboratory studies: blood culture and sensitivity and chest radiograph were ordered. The father declined lumbar puncture. A diagnosis of early-onset neonatal sepsis, with differential of neonatal meningitis and perinatal asphyxia, was made. Empirical treatment with IV ampicillin and gentamicin, maintenance fluids, phenobarbitone, and humidified oxygen was started. Chest radiograph was reported as essentially normal. After 48 hours, fever subsided but one convulsion occurred; otherwise the infant began improving.

Blood culture grew glucose non-fermenting colonies; Gram stain revealed Gram-negative rods.

A 52-year-old Hispanic man with hypertension and GERD presented with a 3-week history of severe, constant left flank pain that worsened with fasting or after meals. He also had 2 weeks of progressive weakness, fatigue, and a 10-lb weight loss. He denied bleeding, changes in bowel habits, alcohol or tobacco use, and had no personal or family history of malignancy or thrombotic events. He was on omeprazole and iron supplements. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. He had conjunctival pallor, scleral icterus, and mild to moderate left flank and epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Admission labs showed:  
• Hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL; hematocrit 17.9%; MCV 96.2 fL; RDW 23.4%  
• WBC 4,100/μL; platelets 88,000/μL; reticulocyte count 0.86%  
• LDH 6,235 IU/L; haptoglobin < 8.0 mg/dL; total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL (direct 0.5 mg/dL); ALT 67 IU/L; AST 165 IU/L  
• INR 1.2; PTT 25.4 s; direct antiglobulin test negative  
Abdominal CT showed acute mesenteric inflammation of the central small-bowel mesentery compatible with mesenteric panniculitis. Peripheral blood smear revealed numerous schistocytes and occasional hypersegmented neutrophils. This constellation of findings was concerning for an atypical presentation of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), and urgent plasmapheresis was planned.

A 41-year-old man presented with 10 days of fever, shortness of breath, bilateral parotid swelling, and cough. He had been treated with azithromycin as an outpatient with only partial response. On examination, there was bilateral parotid gland enlargement and tenderness without palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm/h, a C-reactive protein level of 189 mg/L, and positive antinuclear antibodies; infectious serologies were negative. A chest radiograph revealed airspace shadowing in the left upper zone with infiltrative markings and an obscured left cardiophrenic angle.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a left apicoposterior pulmonary mass with collapse consolidation, small left pleural and pericardial effusions, and a left lower lobe nodule with mildly enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. Head and neck CT showed markedly enlarged parotid glands, enlarged right submandibular and bilateral lacrimal glands, multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes, and extensive paranasal sinus disease. Abdominal CT revealed bilateral renal masses and a left adrenal adenoma.

Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT showed intense FDG uptake in the bilateral parotid and right submandibular glands (SUVmax, 7.6 in the left parotid), multiple small cervical lymph nodes (SUVmax, 3.5), nasal mucosa and maxillary sinuses, left apicoposterior lung opacity (SUVmax, 7.7), mediastinal lymph nodes (SUVmax, 3.0), left lower lobe nodule (SUVmax, 3.6), diffuse splenic uptake (SUVmax, 4.9) without focal lesions, multiple bilateral renal cortical lesions (highest SUVmax, 8.7), mild FDG-avid pericardial effusion (SUVmax, 1.7), intense diffuse prostatic uptake (SUVmax, 12.8), and heterogeneous bone marrow uptake.

A CT-guided biopsy of the left upper lobe pulmonary mass was performed.
Biopsy demonstrated granulomatous noncaseating inflammation with small foci of necrosis and no evidence of malignancy.

A 31-year-old multigravida Hispanic woman at 33 weeks of gestation presented after a syncopal episode at a homeless shelter. She complained of headache but denied nausea, vomiting, neck pain, fever, chills, visual changes, or weight loss. She emigrated from Guatemala 2 years earlier and had a history of epilepsy controlled with levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. She reported similar syncopal episodes after her first child’s birth 10 years ago.  
On examination, her vital signs were normal. She was alert and oriented with no focal neurologic deficits. Cardiac, pulmonary, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable except for the gravid uterus. Peripheral pulses were intact without edema.  
During hospitalization, she developed recurrent hypotension (systolic blood pressure down to 72 mm Hg, mean arterial pressure as low as 52 mm Hg) that responded to intravenous fluid boluses.  
A noncontrast head CT showed multiple small cerebral calcifications without enhancement or edema. MRI with SWAN sequence confirmed multiple rounded hypointense areas corresponding to these calcifications throughout the white matter, thalamus, and basal ganglia.  
A cysticercosis IgG assay was negative. She was also tested for SARS-CoV-2, syphilis IgG, hepatitis B surface antibody, hepatitis C antibody, HIV antigen/antibody, tuberculosis (QuantiFERON-TB), respiratory syncytial virus, influenza, and rubella antibodies, all of which were nonreactive. Obstetrical evaluation was unremarkable, and syncope secondary to obstetrical complications was ruled out.

A 79-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a conjunctival “salmon-patch” lesion concerning for lymphoma. Three years earlier, her left eye underwent pars plana vitrectomy with 1,000 cSt silicone oil placement for a retinal detachment; the oil was removed three months later. One year after oil removal, a pinkish-orange mass was noted at the temporal bulbar conjunctiva of the left eye, and it had been gradually enlarging. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye. Pupils, extraocular movements, and intraocular pressures were normal. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye revealed an ill-defined salmon-patch lesion on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva, with multiple small cysts within the lesion, more prominent superiorly. Fundus examination of the left eye showed an attached retina with multiple peripheral laser scars; the right eye was unremarkable.

A 36-year-old man who works as a rice-field farmer presented with a 1-year history of right-eye proptosis and a 2-month history of foul-smelling nasal discharge accompanied by episodes of nasal itching. He denied constitutional symptoms, and there was no relevant family history. 

On examination, there was proptosis of the lower right eyelid and a firm, round swelling near the medial canthus of the right eye. Nasal endoscopy revealed a friable, polypoidal reddish mass on the inferior turbinate extending into the opening of the nasolacrimal duct, and multiple friable, polypoidal reddish masses in the nasopharynx that bled on contact. Routine biochemical and hematological tests were normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses and orbits showed an intensely enhancing extraconal mass lesion in the inferior right orbit, with rarefaction of the inferior orbital wall and bony nasolacrimal duct. The nasolacrimal duct was enlarged, and similar enhancing masses were seen in the inferior turbinate and nasopharynx, containing small areas of air and calcification. A leash of blood vessels originating from the nasopharyngeal wall was seen supplying the lesion.

MRI demonstrated on T2-weighted imaging a heterogeneously hyperintense, multilobulated mass originating in the nasal cavity and nasopharynx, extending into the oropharynx, with a few flow voids. On postcontrast T1-weighted images, there was an intensely enhancing multilobulated mass in the inferior right orbit and nasal cavity, with nonenhancing foci and a cerebriform appearance as well as extension via the nasolacrimal duct causing proptosis.

A healthy 17-year-old female presented with blurred vision in her left eye. Visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. Funduscopic examination of the left eye revealed intraretinal hemorrhages, lipid exudation, and central macular edema. Wide-field fluorescein angiography of the left eye demonstrated microaneurysms in the central macula with leakage and areas of peripheral capillary nonperfusion. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography confirmed macular edema and subretinal fluid. A laboratory work-up showed normal complete blood count, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and international normalized ratio. Tests for lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin antibody, homocysteine, Protein C, and Protein S were normal; an incidental Factor V Leiden mutation was identified.

An 18-year-old woman with relapsed high-risk acute myeloid leukemia, on azacitidine, venetoclax and gemtuzumab therapy, presented to the hospital in early July with multiple new skin lesions. In late June, she noted a “red spot” on her left hip that became swollen and turned black over several days. One week later, she developed several “boils” around her intergluteal cleft. She denied fevers, chills or systemic symptoms. Her only relevant exposures were swimming in freshwater rivers and lakes in May and June. She had been on prophylaxis with levofloxacin, acyclovir, pentamidine and micafungin and had remained on clindamycin, cefepime was added given her immunocompromised status. On examination, the left hip lesion was necrotic with surrounding edema; the intergluteal lesions were indurated, discolored and draining fluid without tenderness. A punch biopsy of the hip lesion was performed, and bacterial cultures were negative. A fungal culture grew hyphae, and two days later histopathology with Gomori methenamine silver stain showed broad, aseptate “sausage-like” hyphae branching at 90° angles amidst dermal and subcutaneous acute and chronic inflammation with extensive necrosis but no angioinvasion.

A 66‐year‐old man with a history of acne vulgaris and rosacea treated with doxycycline presented with a 2‐year history of facial erythema and progressive swelling of the eyelids and forehead. He reported intermittent watery eyes and a sensation of heaviness in the eyelids but denied pruritus or pain. He was otherwise healthy, with no personal or family history of thrombosis, and his malignancy screenings were up-to-date. His acne and rosacea had been resistant to courses of prednisone and doxycycline.

On examination, there was symmetric nonpitting edema with overlying macular erythema of the bilateral eyelids, forehead, cheeks, nose, and ears. There was no alopecia of the eyebrows and no rash elsewhere on the hands, neck, trunk, or back.

Initial laboratory studies, including complete blood cell count, thyroid‐stimulating hormone level, antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody, antinuclear antibody, serum and urine protein electrophoresis, and immunoglobulin G level, were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography did not show cavernous sinus thrombi. Endoscopy and patch testing were unremarkable. An outside biopsy review did not show mucin deposition.

An 8-year-old boy presented with a 2-day history of fever, vomiting, and severe headache. His past medical history was notable for two concussions and a recent upper respiratory infection. On initial examination he was afebrile, alert, and without focal neurologic deficits. Given his history of head trauma, a noncontrast head CT was obtained and revealed asymmetrical white matter hypodensity and edema in the right frontal and temporal lobes without hemorrhage or midline shift, “of concern in cases of meningoencephalitis.” Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed marked leukocytosis (1660 cells/L) and elevated protein (250 mg/dL); bacterial cultures and viral PCRs were pending. He was started on ceftriaxone and vancomycin. Within hours, he developed left-sided hemiparesis and altered mental status, requiring intubation. Brain MRI on day 1 demonstrated patchy areas of enhancement throughout the right cerebral white matter, midbrain, and pons with significant FLAIR hyperintensity and minimal right-to-left midline shift, which was described as “highly suggestive of ADEM.” High intracranial pressure (ICP) management was initiated, and pulse-dose methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/d) was started. On hospital day 2, he exhibited decerebrate posturing, and a repeat MRI showed marked progression of diffuse cerebral edema involving both hemispheres with worsening midline shift and a new hemorrhage in the right cerebral hemisphere.

A 74-year-old woman with longstanding vitreomacular traction (VMT) in the right eye was initially observed given 20/20 vision. Nine months later, she noted decreased vision to 20/50, and spectral-domain OCT confirmed persistent VMT. Baseline fundus examination, including binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy, biomicroscopy, and OCT, showed no retinal breaks or detachment. She underwent pneumatic vitreolysis with intravitreal perfluoropropane (C3F8) gas. Seven days later, VMT release was achieved and visual acuity improved to 20/40.

One month after the gas injection, examination revealed a shallow pocket of localized subretinal fluid inferior and temporal to the fovea, with subtle adjacent outer retinal changes. Fluorescein angiography showed non-fluorescence corresponding to the loculated subretinal fluid and a darker background fluorescence in that zone compared with the superior fundus.

A 27-year-old white woman with congenital septo-optic dysplasia presented with acute, recurrent, painless, bilateral, simultaneous, intermittent, stereotyped tonic conjugate upward deviation of her eyes. The episodes began after a stressful social encounter and increased in frequency and duration over months, occurring 2–3 times per week and lasting minutes to hours. She remained fully conscious with intact sphincter function and had no observed seizure activity. Occasionally the eye deviations were accompanied by dystonic body posturing. She denied bradykinesia, autonomic symptoms, or orolingual dyskinesias.

Her past history was significant for intrauterine brain hypoxia secondary to maternal diabetes and cocaine use, and she had stable hypopituitarism managed with hormone replacement. She also had migraine without aura. Current medications included levothyroxine, clonazepam, estradiol, hydrocortisone, metoprolol, nitroglycerin, and progesterone.

Brain MRI demonstrated a stable middle cranial fossa arachnoid cyst without hydrocephalus, pituitary hypoplasia, absence of the olfactory bulb, tuber cinereum, and anterior commissure, and optic nerve hypoplasia. EEG was normal. Endocrinologic studies showed a TSH of 0.01 mIU/L (consistent with levothyroxine therapy) and normal cortisol and estrogen levels on replacement.

On neuro-ophthalmologic examination, visual acuity was count-fingers at 3 ft in the right eye and 20/400 in the left eye, unchanged from baseline. She had pendular congenital nystagmus with roving eye movements, mild impairment of abduction and adduction in both eyes, and constricted visual fields (10° right, 30° left). Pupils were isochoric and poorly reactive. Anterior segments were unremarkable. Dilated fundus examination showed small optic nerves bilaterally with a cup-to-disk ratio of 0.7 and a flat hyperpigmented lesion on the left optic disc.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 3-hour history of sudden, severe abdominal pain that began in the right hypochondrium and migrated to the epigastrium, associated with nausea and vomiting. He had no history of gallstone disease or prior abdominal surgery. On arrival, blood pressure was 120/77 mmHg, pulse 77 beats/min, temperature 36.7 °C, respiratory rate 17 breaths/min, and SpO₂ 97 % on 3 L oxygen. Examination revealed epigastric tenderness and guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16.7×10⁹/L, CRP 5 mg/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, bilirubin 13 μmol/L, AST 32 U/L, ALT 44 U/L, GGT 36 U/L, and amylase 15 U/L. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed pH 7.30, pCO₂ 5.5 kPa, pO₂ 11.7 kPa, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, base excess –3.7 mmol/L, and lactate 4 mmol/L.  
Because of the sudden onset, a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm was suspected, and CT angiography of the chest and abdomen was performed. The study showed no aneurysm, no free fluid or gas, no bowel obstruction, gallstones without signs of acute cholecystitis or biliary dilation, and extensive colonic diverticula without diverticulitis. Due to the extensive diverticula and now more diffuse pain, a tentative diagnosis of diverticulitis was made; intravenous antibiotics were started, and the patient was admitted for close observation.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a painful, slowly enlarging mass in the right thigh extending to the perineal area, associated with paresthesia in the right thigh and shin. She denied fever, abdominal pain, digestive symptoms, chest pain, cough, hemoptysis, or urticaria. She appeared ill but afebrile and non-toxic. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, the overlying skin was normal in color; there was a firm, ~5.7 cm long mass in the right groin/femoral region without erythema or warmth. Complete blood count and serum chemistries were normal, with no eosinophilia. Ultrasonography revealed a cystic mass initially thought to be a femoral hernia. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the pelvis demonstrated a well-defined, multiloculated cystic mass in the right femoral/perineal region with no communication with the peritoneal cavity.

A 60-year-old man presented with 3 months of progressive pain in the right axilla and posteromedial right upper extremity, rated 10/10. He had undergone C5–6 anterior fusion for cervical spondylosis 5 years earlier and had no intervening trauma. He worked as a taxi driver. On examination, there was no sensory disturbance, no abnormal tendon-jerk reflexes, and no muscle weakness. He had known cervicothoracic scoliosis diagnosed before his cervical fusion. Frontal cervical radiographs showed a right cervicothoracic curvature with a Cobb angle of 17° before fusion and 19° at presentation. CT of the cervical spine revealed bone spurs on the C6–7 facets, and MRI showed decreased intervertebral height but preserved C6–7 nerve root canals. Further CT imaging demonstrated osteophytes of the superior costal facet and articular process at the right T2–3 level, and MRI showed a protruded disc at T2–3. Measurements on CT revealed that the right T2 nerve root canal width and height were reduced compared to the left side and to normal ranges. Blood tests, electrocardiogram, electromyogram, somatosensory evoked potentials, and head MRI were all normal.

A female infant was born at 33 weeks’ gestation (birth weight 1,055 g) via cesarean section for fetal distress. The delivery was uncomplicated, and the infant was never intubated. On day 1 of life, laboratory studies showed a platelet count of 34 × 10^9/L, and the patient received a platelet transfusion. Hemoglobin was 17.4 g/dL and hematocrit 51.1%; there was no anemia or polycythemia. A septic work up, including blood cultures, was negative. On ophthalmic examination with pharmacologic dilation, the anterior segments were normal bilaterally with no external ecchymoses. In the right eye, the optic nerve appeared normal and the retina was fully vascularized. In the left eye, the optic nerve and macula were normal, but there was a large nasal subretinal hemorrhage measuring approximately 10–12 disc diameters and an intraretinal white-centered hemorrhage. The retina was attached, fully vascularized, and there was no active retinopathy of prematurity or vitreous hemorrhage.

A 63-year-old man presented with a 10-minute episode of painless loss of vision in his right eye. He had had a similar 30-minute episode the night before that resolved spontaneously. An ophthalmologic evaluation was reportedly unremarkable. He was admitted with a provisional diagnosis of amaurosis fugax versus nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. His history was notable for a chronic nonproductive cough, recurrent fevers, and a 10-kg weight loss over 1 month. He had type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia and was a non-smoker.

On examination, direct and indirect pupillary reflexes were normal, both eyes were pseudophakic, and there was no afferent pupillary defect. The right optic disc appeared pale, and funduscopic examination revealed a cherry-red spot on the right macula. Temporal arteries were non-tender and non-pulsatile. Motor and sensory exams of the limbs were normal.

Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.6 g/dL), an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 117 mm/h, C-reactive protein of 111 mg/L, and an HbA1c of 7.2%. Autoimmune serologies (cANCA, pANCA, ANA) were negative. Brain MRI demonstrated a small right occipital ischemic infarct. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed moderately diffuse mural thickening and mild enhancement of the aortic arch and its major branches.

A 34-year-old woman with a history of vitiligo presented with six months of episodic speech and language impairment. Her family history was notable for a sister with Sydenham chorea. Neurologic examination revealed brisk reflexes on the left side only. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral frontal subcortical T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions with a micronodular, curvilinear perivascular pattern of gadolinium enhancement. CSF analysis showed a lymphocytic pleocytosis (9 cells/mm3), normal protein and glucose levels, increased CSF IgG, and absent oligoclonal bands. Chest and abdominal CT scans were unremarkable. Serum testing, including ANA, rheumatoid factor, anti-Ro, anti-La, anti-RNP, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, ANCA, ASCA, complement levels (C3, C4), ACE, viral serologies (HBsAg, HCV, HIV, HTLV), and syphilis testing, was within normal limits. The patient received methylprednisolone, 1 g/day for 5 days, with complete clinical and radiological resolution at three months. She had no relapses during a six-month follow-up and underwent an uncomplicated pregnancy two years after onset. Six years after initial presentation, she developed new cognitive impairment and headaches. Repeat MRI revealed new nodular and linear perivascular T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the frontal subcortical and deep white matter with corresponding contrast enhancement. Considering a disease relapse, a brain biopsy was performed.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fevers and night sweats beginning four months after ascending aortic and arch grafting for a type A aortic dissection. He reported a 10-kg weight loss and high-grade fevers (up to 39 °C). On initial emergency evaluation, C-reactive protein was mildly elevated; no source of fever was identified, and blood cultures were obtained. When all four bottles grew gram-positive cocci, he was admitted. 

On examination, temperature was 39.3 °C, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, pulse 96/min, and respiratory rate 21/min. Cardiac and pulmonary exams were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed splenomegaly without tenderness or hepatomegaly. There were no petechiae, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, or lymphadenopathy. 

Laboratory results showed WBC 7,700/µL (neutrophils 81%), CRP 7.9 mg/dL, ferritin 353 ng/mL, rheumatoid factor 19 IU/mL, complement C3 83 mg/dL, C4 28 mg/dL, ANA < 1:40, PR3-ANCA 2.7 IU/mL, MPO-ANCA 1.4 IU/mL, sIL-2R 1130 U/mL, and a negative T-SPOT.TB. Urinalysis revealed protein 3+ and blood 1+. 

Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated fluid collection around the aortic graft, splenomegaly (spleen index 720) with multiple splenic thrombi, and hepatomegaly.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of difficulty eating and speaking. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. Two months earlier he noted mobility of upper left posterior teeth and, 15 days before presentation, underwent extraction under local anesthesia. Injections had been administered into the palatal mucosa and buccal vestibule on the left side. Three days after the extraction, he developed a painless ulcer at the anesthetic infiltration site that did not respond to local treatment. One week later he felt a mobile bone fragment on the palate, detached it himself, and subsequently experienced nasal regurgitation of food and impaired speech.

On examination, there was no facial asymmetry or lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, teeth 25–27 were absent, and an oval palatal perforation approximately 1 cm × 1 cm was present on the left hard palate. The site showed no sinus opening, suppuration, tenderness, or erythema.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/h. Results of a complete blood count, blood sugar level, liver and renal function tests, serology for syphilis, bacteriologic culture including fungal stains, and acid-fast bacilli staining for tuberculosis were all unremarkable.

Cone-beam computed tomography of the palate revealed a well-defined radiolucent defect measuring about 11.9 mm × 10.3 mm in the left hard palate, an intact maxillary sinus, and discontinuity of the nasal floor.

A 62-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy underwent orthotopic heart transplantation 5 months earlier. His post-transplant immunosuppressive regimen included mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone, and tacrolimus, along with prophylactic trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, fluconazole, and valganciclovir. He presented to the emergency department with 2 days of fever, vomiting, and diarrhea. He denied respiratory symptoms.

On examination, he appeared fatigued but was in no acute distress. Temperature was 96.5°F (35.8°C), blood pressure 158/89 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. The only notable finding was sinus tachycardia. There was no jugular venous distension, and the chest was clear to auscultation without crackles or wheezes.

Laboratory studies showed sodium 119 mmol/L, potassium 6.5 mmol/L, creatinine 2.7 mg/dL, and a white-blood-cell count of 5.56 K/μL with a normal differential. A chest radiograph demonstrated patchy opacification in the posterior left upper lobe and the lingula, with a small left pleural effusion. Abdominal computed tomography revealed splenomegaly. A chest CT scan confirmed a possible loculated effusion in the anterior segment of the left upper lobe and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy.

Initial blood cultures grew gram-negative rods, and empirical therapy for a presumed intraabdominal source was started. Two days later, a blood culture grew gram-positive rods.

A 6-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of recurrent episodes of cough and fever over 6 months. During the most recent episode, he had fever and right-sided chest pain for 7 days that did not improve with oral antibiotics. On examination, his temperature was 102.4°F, and he was in moderate respiratory distress. Laboratory studies showed marked leukocytosis. A chest radiograph revealed consolidation of the right lower lobe with areas suggestive of cystic bronchiectasis. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest demonstrated a multiseptated, air-filled cystic mass localized to the postero-basal and medio-basal segments of the right lower lobe. There was no apparent communication with segmental bronchi, no aberrant systemic arterial supply, and no surrounding consolidation or ground-glass opacities.

A 66-year-old Japanese man with hyperuricemia and bronchitis presented with sudden urinary retention and fever. Three days after symptom onset, he was treated with levofloxacin and silodosin without improvement, and a urethral catheter was placed. He was admitted for persistent symptoms. 

Medications: febuxostat, theophylline, ambroxol, long-acting β-agonist/inhaled corticosteroid. No prior urinary symptoms.  
On examination: blood pressure 139/75 mmHg, pulse 85 bpm, temperature 37.5 °C. Skin: erythematous nodules on face and extremities. Eyes: misty vision; diagnosed with uveitis. 

Laboratory studies: 
• Serum creatinine 1.09 mg/dL (eGFR 51 mL/min/1.73 m²).  
• C-reactive protein 14.0 mg/dL; calcium 9.4 mEq/L; PSA 16.3 ng/mL.  
• Urinalysis: dipstick proteinuria (1+), no pyuria or casts; transient microscopic hematuria.  
• Blood and urine cultures: negative.  
• Urinary β2-microglobulin 38,952 µg/L; proteinuria 0.45 g/gCr; no hematuria on repeat.  
• Serum soluble IL-2 receptor 3010 U/mL; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D 85 pg/mL; PTH 47.0 pg/mL; ACE 10.1 U/L.  
• MPO-ANCA, PR3-ANCA, and anti-GBM antibodies: negative.  
• Workup negative for neoplasia; autoimmune disorders; eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; Behçet’s disease; cryoglobulinemic vasculitis; fungal and Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.

Imaging:  
• Contrast CT: lymphadenopathy in hilar, mediastinal, inguinal, and other nodes.  
• FDG-PET/CT: uptake in those lymph nodes, subcutaneous tissue, spleen, mild diffuse renal uptake, and prostate.

Procedures:  
• Skin biopsy of nodules: erythema nodosum.  
• Transbronchoscopic lymph node biopsy: epithelioid cell granulomas; diagnosed as systemic sarcoidosis.  

During hospitalization, renal function worsened (SCr 2.2 mg/dL, eGFR 22.4 mL/min/1.73 m²) despite catheter drainage. After nephrology consultation, kidney and prostate biopsies were performed to clarify the cause of acute kidney injury and urinary retention.

A 34-month-old boy was evaluated for a 2-year history of intermittent, bilateral, intense pain, warmth, and redness of his feet. Each episode lasted minutes to hours and was precipitated by exercise or warmth (for example, covering his legs with blankets) and relieved by cooling (cold water). The attacks were symmetrical and confined to the feet without proximal extension. There was no history of similar family symptoms, medication use, or blood transfusions. 

On multiple visits, he appeared well with normal vital signs. There was no pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, organomegaly, or lymphadenopathy. During an episode, both feet were visibly red and warm; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Complete blood count with differential: normal  
• Serum immunoglobulin E: 11 IU/mL (normal)  
• Cholesterol: 146 mg/dL; triglycerides: 49 mg/dL  
• Blood urea nitrogen: 16 mg/dL; creatinine: 0.7 mg/dL  
• Liver enzymes: ALT 22 U/L; AST 34 U/L  
• Uric acid: 3.7 mg/dL  
• Antistreptolysin O titer: negative  
• Urinalysis and stool studies: normal  
• Fasting glucose: 89 mg/dL; 2-hour postprandial glucose: 122 mg/dL  

Imaging and other studies were unremarkable:  
• X-rays of feet and legs: normal  
• Doppler ultrasound of lower-limb arteries: normal blood flow  
• Nerve conduction studies of both peroneal nerves: normal  
• Pelvic and abdominal sonography: normal  
• Brain CT scan: normal

A 41-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a splenic mass discovered two months earlier after a fall associated with persistent abdominal pain. He reported a long history of diffuse abdominal discomfort, nausea, vomiting—worse when supine or after eating— and unintentional weight loss, the bulk of which occurred 8–9 months before presentation. He denied fevers, night sweats, changes in appetite, or changes in bowel habits. His medical history included arthritis, back pain, and a remote motor vehicle accident with rib fractures. He smoked two to three packs of cigarettes daily (45 pack-year history) and consumed about seven standard alcoholic drinks per week.  
On examination, his blood pressure was 149/87 mm Hg, pulse 60 beats/min, temperature 97.3°F, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air; BMI was 30.3 kg/m^2. Laboratory evaluation revealed chloride 111 mmol/L (98–109), ALT 65 U/L (16–61), and RDW-CV 15.9% (11.5–15.3%). Carcinoembryonic antigen, lactate dehydrogenase, and ECG were normal.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a large (9.5 × 10.3 × 11.7 cm) heterogeneously enhancing splenic lesion (average 132.9 HU; normal spleen 40–60 HU) without calcifications. No other intraabdominal abnormalities were noted, although the splenic vein was markedly dilated. Given the concern for neoplasm versus hemorrhagic lesion, percutaneous biopsy was deferred and a laparoscopic splenectomy was planned.

A 79-year-old man with a history of stage IIa left maxillary superficial melanoma, treated with surgical resection and local radiation, began pembrolizumab (200 mg IV every 3 weeks) after recurrent disease. One week after the first dose, he developed loss of appetite and episodic, twice‐daily watery, nonbloody diarrhea. Over the subsequent 4 months, his symptoms persisted and he had laboratory abnormalities: hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, albumin 2.4 g/dL, vitamin D 25-OH 16 ng/mL, and zinc 54 µg/dL.

Stool studies, including fecal leukocytes, lactoferrin, stool cultures, and Clostridium difficile toxin assay, were normal. Colonoscopy showed normal-appearing colonic mucosa with unremarkable random biopsies. Upper endoscopy to the second part of the duodenum revealed a small gastric antral erosion but normal duodenal mucosa. Wireless capsule endoscopy demonstrated villous blunting in the second part of the duodenum with intact distal small-bowel mucosa.

A 47-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol use and alcoholic chronic pancreatitis was referred for 2 days of upper abdominal pain and vomiting. On admission, his temperature was 37.8 °C. Laboratory tests showed an amylase of 245 IU/L, a C-reactive protein of 14.99 mg/dL, and a white blood cell count of 14 900/μL. Plain abdominal CT revealed a 7 cm cystic lesion within the lumen adjacent to the second portion of the duodenum that contained high-density material; the pancreas was slightly enlarged, the main pancreatic duct was dilated, and there were calcifications in the uncus. Upper endoscopy showed duodenal deformation by a submucosal tumor-like mass; there was no active bleeding and the scope could not be advanced. On hospital day 4, his hemoglobin fell from 14.0 to 11.1 g/dL. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a high-density spot on the cyst wall. Angiography identified a pseudoaneurysm in a branch of the anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, which was successfully embolized. Anemia stabilized thereafter. An upper gastrointestinal series showed a filling defect in the duodenum without contrast entering the cyst. MRCP did not demonstrate communication between the cyst and the biliary or pancreatic ducts. Follow-up CT on day 27 after embolization showed shrinkage of the cyst to 2 cm and improvement of duodenal obstruction. The patient declined surgery and was discharged on hospital day 34.

A 41-year-old man was admitted with unconsciousness 4 days after surgery for intracerebral hemorrhage. Four days earlier, he had presented with acute headache and a cranial CT scan that showed an intracerebral bleed; he then underwent bilateral external ventricular drainage and placement of an Ommaya reservoir. He was transferred to the rehabilitation high-dependency unit. A follow-up CT scan of the head demonstrated bilateral frontal lobe hemorrhage with scalp swelling, pneumoperitoneum in the anterior thorax and neck, and small bilateral pleural effusions.

On admission, the Glasgow Coma Scale score was 2-T-1. Gastrointestinal decompression returned dark-red fluid, and tracheostomy suction yielded dark tea–colored urine. Physical examination revealed a soft neck without meningeal signs, bilateral pupils 3.5 mm in diameter with sluggish light reflexes, thick breath sounds bilaterally, flaccid limbs without voluntary movement, negative pathologic reflexes, a modified Rankin Scale score of 5, a Fugl-Meyer Assessment score of 0, and an Activity of Daily Living score of 0. His history included untreated hypertension and an appendectomy 20 years earlier. Admission diagnoses were postoperative intracerebral hemorrhage, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, pulmonary infection, and hypertension.

A 50-year-old woman was referred with a 14-year history of gradually progressive, mildly pruritic skin lesions, first noted in the groin. She had a history of Hashimoto’s hypothyroidism managed with levothyroxine and no other significant medical or drug history.

On examination, violaceous-brown macules and patches with fine peripheral scale involved approximately 90% of her body surface, prominently affecting the face and other sun-exposed areas. Exfoliation within violaceous lesions was noted on the palms. Telangiectasia was seen at the centers of lesions on the face. There was no mucosal involvement.

She underwent two skin biopsies that showed atypical features suggestive of LPP. Treatment with oral prednisolone (20 mg daily) for 6 months produced no improvement. A third skin biopsy was performed, and microscopic examination revealed acanthosis, mild superficial perivascular inflammation, a lichenoid interface reaction with some Civatte bodies in the basal layer, upper dermal melanin incontinence, and vascular ectasia. PAS staining showed mild basement-membrane thickening. Alcian blue staining revealed no mucin deposition. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrated multiple granular deposits of IgG and IgM at the epidermis and dermoepidermal junction.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal liver enzymes, borderline lipid profile, normal fasting blood sugar, normal myoglobin, and elevated LDH (515 U/L). Serologic tests for anti-SCL-70, anti-SSA, anti-SSB, anti-Jo-1, anti-Smith, and anti-RNP/Sm IgG were all negative. A chest CT showed no interstitial lung disease.

A 60-year-old Ethiopian man presented with worsening periumbilical, colicky abdominal pain of 6 days’ duration, associated with multiple episodes of vomiting of ingested matter, failure to pass feces or flatus, and abdominal distension for 2 days. He reported intermittent similar pain over the past 6 months managed with over-the-counter analgesics. He denied abdominal trauma, rectal bleeding, weight loss, tuberculosis exposure, or prior abdominal surgery. His medical history was significant only for hypertension treated with amlodipine.  

On examination, he appeared acutely ill. Vital signs: pulse 112/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 150/80 mmHg. He had dry mucous membranes. The abdomen was mildly distended with visible peristalsis, hyperactive bowel sounds, and hyper-tympanic percussion. A soft, non-tender, 20×10-cm mass was palpable in the periumbilical region. Digital rectal examination revealed stool without blood.  

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and serum chemistry, were normal. An erect abdominal radiograph demonstrated centrally located distended small-bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels.  

Preoperative differential diagnoses included small-bowel volvulus (supported by clinical exam and x-ray), postoperative adhesions (unlikely given no surgery history), underlying malignancy (no weight loss or bleeding), and incarcerated hernia (no abdominal defect).

A 79-year-old woman with hypertension and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presented with fatigue, pleuritic chest pain worsened by inspiration, dyspnea at rest, nonproductive cough, and low-grade fever for several days. She had undergone an uncomplicated transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) 6 months earlier. 

On examination: temperature 38.0 °C, heart rate 112 bpm, blood pressure 140/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Heart and lung sounds were normal; jugular venous pressure was not elevated.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 14.4 × 10^9/L (3.6–10.5), ESR 86 mm/h (<30), procalcitonin 0.05 ng/mL (<0.5), and CRP 177 mg/L (0–5). Electrocardiogram demonstrated a new left bundle branch block and PR-segment elevation in aVR. Cardiac enzymes were within normal limits: CK 45 U/L (0–170), CK-MB 13 U/L (0–24), troponin-T 15 pg/mL (<14).

Chest X-ray and CT scan revealed only a minimal left pleural effusion. Transesophageal echocardiography showed the TAVI bioprosthesis in normal position and function with mild paravalvular regurgitation (grade 1), left ventricular EF 65%, and no signs of endocarditis. 

Empirical treatment with clarithromycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and ibuprofen was initiated for presumed acute bronchitis. After 7 days, the patient remained symptomatic and inflammatory markers rose, leading to broad-spectrum antibiotic changes. Blood cultures and comprehensive microbiology and virology studies remained negative.

On hospital day 11, she developed a high fever of 38.5 °C, worsening pleuritic chest pain, and malaise; WBC peaked at 19.9 × 10^9/L and CRP at 274.6 mg/L. Antibiotics were again escalated. 

On day 12, repeat transthoracic echocardiography revealed a new small pericardial effusion (3 mm) extending toward the right ventricular apex without signs of tamponade.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of right-sided lower abdominal pain. The pain began suddenly in the periumbilical region, migrated to the right lower quadrant, worsened with movement, and was associated with nausea and anorexia. She denied vomiting, diarrhea, rectal bleeding, urinary symptoms, or gynecological symptoms. She had normal bowel movements and no prior similar episodes. Her medical history was notable for sarcoidosis and recurrent respiratory infections.

On examination, she appeared unwell but was afebrile. Vital signs were: pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute. Abdominal examination revealed marked tenderness in the right iliac fossa with rebound tenderness and localized guarding; the rest of the abdomen was soft and nontender with normal bowel sounds.

Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 7.1 × 10^9 cells/L and a C-reactive protein level of 16.6 mg/L. Renal and liver function tests, urinalysis, and a pregnancy test were all within normal limits. Based on the presentation, a presumptive diagnosis of acute appendicitis was made, and the patient was admitted for observation.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressively worsening right foot pain described as “crushing and burning” radiating into the posterior calf but sparing the heel. Her history was notable for immune dysregulation due to an actin-related protein complex subunit 1B gene mutation, with recurrent infections and skin ulcers. Neuropathic pain medications and opioids provided inadequate relief. She also reported numbness over the plantar aspect of the foot, again sparing the heel. Two weeks before presentation, she noted weakness of right ankle plantarflexion and toe flexion. She denied trauma to the leg or lumbar spine symptoms.

On examination, there was no muscle atrophy. Multiple well-healed ulcers were present over the anterior tibial regions. Left lower-limb strength was normal. On the right, toe flexion was weak, and ankle plantarflexion could be easily overcome on supine testing. Light-touch sensation was diminished over the plantar surface of the right foot, sparing the heel. The patient perceived a 128 Hz tuning fork for more than 10 seconds at the first metatarsophalangeal joints bilaterally. Reflexes were 2+ at both patellae and the left Achilles tendon, but the right Achilles reflex was absent.

MRI of the right foot without contrast showed nonspecific muscular edema suggestive of myositis or acute denervation, without other abnormalities. Neurology and Pain Medicine initially diagnosed complex regional pain syndrome. Rheumatology recommended electrodiagnostic studies.

Nerve conduction studies showed borderline normal sural amplitudes, low-normal superficial peroneal sensory amplitudes, absent bilateral medial plantar mixed-nerve responses, low-normal peroneal motor amplitudes, and mildly to markedly decreased tibial motor amplitudes (left vs right). Needle electromyography revealed abnormal spontaneous activity most marked in distal tibial-innervated muscles, with no axonal continuity to intrinsic forefoot muscles. These findings indicated a generalized length-dependent sensorimotor polyneuropathy that was predominantly axonal, with a superimposed right tibial mononeuropathy localizing proximal to the soleus branches. The findings were consistent with the patient’s severe right foot pain and ankle plantarflexion and toe flexion weakness. She was subsequently referred for a right sural nerve biopsy.

A 9-year-old spayed female German Shepherd dog was evaluated for a two-week history of progressive nonambulatory tetraparesis. The dog initially improved on prednisone (1.1 mg/kg/day) and omeprazole but then deteriorated despite an increased prednisone dose; appetite and water intake remained normal. Medical history included prior urinary tract infections, a right tarsal fracture, and a left cranial cruciate ligament repair.

On admission, the dog was bright and responsive, panting with a rectal temperature of 39.4 °C, heart rate 120 bpm, and systolic blood pressure 160 mmHg. Physical examination revealed a firm movable mass on the left tarsus, marked hind-limb muscle atrophy, and a right tarsal surgical scar. Neurologic examination showed nonambulatory tetraparesis worse on the right, absent general proprioception in the pelvic limbs and left thoracic limb, delayed proprioception in the right thoracic limb, and decreased spinal reflexes in all four limbs (front limbs more severely affected); there was no spinal hyperesthesia. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Initial differential diagnoses included multifocal neoplasia, infectious or inflammatory disease, paraneoplastic syndrome, and degenerative intervertebral disc disease or spinal canal stenosis; ischemic insult, trauma, and intoxication were considered less likely. 

CBC revealed leukocytosis (20.7×10^3 cells/μL) with neutrophilia. Serum biochemistry showed elevated alkaline phosphatase (614 U/L) and alanine aminotransferase (242 U/L); other values were within normal limits. Urinalysis obtained by cystocentesis indicated specific gravity >1.035, 3+ blood, >75 RBC/HPF, 6–15 WBC/HPF, and cocci in aggregates consistent with bacterial cystitis.

Cervical radiographs demonstrated mild C4–C5 intervertebral disc narrowing and moderate proliferation of the C3–C4 and C4–C5 articular facets. Abdominal and thoracic imaging was unremarkable. The dog was hospitalized with IV fluids and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, after which temperature normalized and ambulatory status returned on three limbs except the right thoracic limb.

On day 3, localization was refined to the C6–T2 spinal segments. MRI of the cervical spine revealed heterogeneously contrast-enhancing soft tissue in the right ventrolateral spinal canal from C6 to T1 that was T2 hyperintense and T1 isointense, contiguous with the right ventral C8 and, to a lesser degree, C7 nerve roots, both of which were enlarged and extended into the intervertebral foramina. Adjacent C6–C7 articular facet tissue was T2 hyperintense, contrast-enhancing, and mildly compressive. A small focal T2 hyperintense, contrast-enhancing lesion was also noted in the left ventral C8 nerve root. The spinal cord signal remained normal. These findings were considered possibly compatible with infiltrative neoplasia, although inflammatory and infectious causes were also considered.

A 42-year-old woman in otherwise good health with no personal or family history of psoriasis or systemic disease first noted nontender circinate erosions and vesicles on her soft and hard palate approximately 10 years ago. Over the next several months, similar lesions developed on the tongue, buccal mucosa, gingiva, vermilion border, and oropharynx. Five years ago, an oral surgeon documented erosive loss of lingual papillae; the lesions then became painful, causing ageusia and preventing her from eating most foods. Three years ago, she developed severely painful sterile pustules on the distal fingertips, accompanied by edema, erythema, calor, pain, erosions, and paresthesia, as well as separation and pitting of nail plates. She sought care from emergency departments, infectious-disease specialists, surgeons, and dermatologists in three states. Initial differential diagnoses included bacterial and fungal paronychia, pyoderma, herpetic whitlow, and cellulitis. Lesional swabs and blood cultures confirmed lack of pathologic organisms. She then underwent multiple failed topical and systemic therapies, including clobetasol, calcipotriol, tazarotene, tacrolimus, mupirocin, clotrimazole, terbinafine, intralesional triamcinolone, cephalexin, doxycycline, linezolid, prednisone, valacyclovir, and apremilast, and no sulfa-based agents were given because of anaphylaxis. Treatments for her oral lesions—including dexamethasone oral solution, chlorhexidine, tacrolimus, fluconazole lozenges, and valacyclovir—also failed. Interim palliative care consisted of incision and drainage of pustules and petrolatum with occlusion. Her body-mass index fell below 18, and during apremilast therapy she had prolonged nausea, vomiting, and anorexia requiring sublingual ondansetron and liquid nutritional supplements.

A woman in her early thirties with a history of ankylosing spondylitis, obstructive sleep apnea, and recently diagnosed hypertension (2‐month history) presented after an optometry appointment at which her blood pressure was 230/155 mmHg. She denied fever, headache, dizziness, chest pain, visual changes, or shortness of breath. Home medications included hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, sulfasalazine 1000 mg twice daily, and adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 14 days.

On admission, her blood pressure was 201/133 mmHg, heart rate was 107 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation was 99% on room air. Physical examination revealed 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities; cardiopulmonary and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Chest radiography and electrocardiography showed no acute pathology beyond sinus tachycardia, and head CT was negative.

Laboratory studies revealed a serum creatinine of 1.47 mg/dL (baseline, 0.7 mg/dL) and serum albumin of 1.8 g/dL. Urinalysis demonstrated a specific gravity of 1.028, heavy proteinuria (>500 mg/dL), glucosuria, and 5 red blood cells per high‐power field. A urine protein:creatinine ratio exceeded 6 g/g. A 24‐hour urine collection confirmed protein excretion of 11.3 g. Renal ultrasound showed symmetric kidneys of normal size with preserved cortical thickness and no hydronephrosis. An extensive workup including ANA, anti‐scleroderma antibody, paraproteinemia studies, C3, and C4 was non‐revealing. Her blood pressure was controlled with intravenous antihypertensives and transitioned to oral labetalol, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide, but serum creatinine did not return to baseline.

Due to lack of improvement in serum creatinine levels, she underwent a kidney biopsy.

A 52-year-old housewife reports a 12-year history of recurrent cystitis for which she has taken a different antibiotic each month, together with repeated bladder flushes, without lasting relief. She describes episodes of urinary frequency (pollakiuria), a terminal burning sensation when voiding, recurrent gross hematuria, constant bladder pressure, and dysuria. On some occasions, midstream urine and vaginal swabs grew Escherichia coli and Enterococci.

Her medical history is notable for episodes of depression since puberty, first diagnosed at age 48; she completed 50 hours of behavioral therapy and currently takes antidepressants. Her mother also had a history of depression.

Urological evaluation included urine cultures from a catheter, which were sometimes sterile and sometimes positive for E. coli. Renal and bladder sonography showed no abnormalities and no postvoid residual. Transvaginal urethrocystoscopy revealed a normal urethral meatus, bladder mucosa, and ureteral orifices, with no cystocele. Micturating cystourethrography demonstrated a normally configured bladder without vesicoureteral reflux. An excretory urogram was normal, and abdominal and pelvic CT showed only uterine fibroids, with no evidence of fistula.

Psychological assessment noted inhibited gestures and facial expressions, a depressive affect, high motivation, an insecure personality structure, and compulsive defense mechanisms, with a high level of personality organization.

A 70-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea and fatigue over several weeks. He had chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukemia diagnosed in 1996, initially treated with hydroxyurea and interferon α, then imatinib through 2005, and on dasatinib 70 mg twice daily for the past 32 months. He developed tachypnea (respiratory rate 25/min), fatigue, and bilateral pleural effusions. Analysis of the effusions showed transudative, nonmalignant fluid (effusion glucose 116 mg/dL; effusion LDH 188 IU/L, serum LDH 1073 IU/L; effusion protein 31 g/L, serum protein 67 g/L). Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a right ventricular systolic pressure of 73 mm Hg. Right heart catheterization confirmed severe pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular failure and a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. He was classified as WHO functional class IV. Serologic tests, chest CT, ventilation–perfusion scan, and abdominal ultrasonography did not identify alternative causes of pulmonary hypertension.

A 47-year-old man was referred by a rheumatologist to the Oral Medicine Department because of recurrent, painful oral lesions present since his youth that impaired daily functioning. His past history included extensive iliac-vein and inferior-vena-cava thrombosis, recurrent pseudofolliculitis, and episodes of genital ulcers. Laboratory evaluation revealed persistently elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. On intraoral examination, multiple shallow, painful ulcers with erythematous halos and yellowish-white pseudomembranes (largest ~0.7 cm) were noted on the right and left buccal mucosa and the right lateral tongue. No new cutaneous lesions were observed. Given this presentation, initial differential diagnoses included recurrent aphthous stomatitis, medication-induced oral lesions, Crohn’s disease, Sweet syndrome, cyclic neutropenia, herpes infections, erythema multiforme, HIV infection, and various autoimmune diseases. Further investigations were undertaken.

A 44-year-old man presented with severe headaches, bilateral hearing loss, and gait instability of several weeks’ duration. On examination, Rinne and Weber tests were consistent with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss; tandem gait was intact, and cranial nerves were otherwise normal. Routine hematologic and biochemical studies were within normal limits. Audiometry confirmed a bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, worse on the left than on the right. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with intravenous contrast revealed an enhancing mass in the anterior horn of the right lateral ventricle; no susceptibility-weighted or T2*gradient-echo sequences were obtained. Neurosurgical resection was performed without complication, and histopathological analysis confirmed a pilocytic astrocytoma. Postoperatively, the patient’s hearing loss and gait instability persisted unchanged.

A 40-year-old man presented with a three-month history of a left flank mass. The mass was initially non-painful but had become mildly painful over the preceding weeks. He denied fever, chills, trauma, or dermatologic conditions. On examination, there was a palpable, non-erythematous, non-warm, subcutaneous mass in the left flank. Vital signs were within normal limits.

An abdominal and pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a 7-cm subcutaneous cystic lesion on the left flank with an estimated volume of 70 cc; no other intra-abdominal cysts were identified. A chest radiograph and chest CT scan were unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and liver function tests, were normal. An ELISA for echinococcal antigens was negative. Abdominal CT scan oriented to the viscera showed no additional abnormalities, though the superficial cyst was not well visualized on this study.

A 72-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an incidentally detected murmur. He had a history of well-controlled hypertension and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. He denied chest pain, dyspnoea, constitutional symptoms, or any history of infections, including tuberculosis or syphilis. He had no family history of aortic disease or autoimmune disorders and reported no systemic symptoms suggestive of vasculitis or connective tissue disease.

On examination, blood pressure was 160/59 mm Hg and heart rate 59 beats per minute. There was prominent head-nodding (De Musset’s sign), a grade IV/VI diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, and bounding carotid pulsations. Lung and other cardiovascular findings were unremarkable.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a tricuspid aortic valve with severe aortic insufficiency and an enlarged ascending aorta; left ventricular ejection fraction was 60%. Contrast CT angiography confirmed a fusiform aneurysm of the ascending thoracic aorta measuring 5.7 × 6.5 cm. Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a central aortic regurgitant jet occupying 60% of the left ventricular outflow tract. Laboratory tests revealed a normal complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein. Preoperative coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries.

The patient underwent aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthesis and supracoronary replacement of the ascending aorta. Intraoperative histopathologic examination of the aortic wall demonstrated lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with some fibrosis, consistent with non-infectious ascending aortitis.

A 60-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and an appendectomy 35 years earlier presented with colicky abdominal pain radiating across the abdomen. He denied nausea or vomiting. He had chronic constipation, with his last bowel movement 10 days earlier but continued to pass flatus. His medications included levothyroxine, metformin, and prazosin. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. The abdomen was distended, soft, non-tender, with decreased bowel sounds. Rectal examination revealed an empty ampulla. Laboratory tests were unremarkable except for hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL and platelet count 80 000/mm3. Abdominal radiographs showed multiple air-fluid levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a sac-like clustering of jejunal and ileal loops in the central abdominal cavity with twisting and engorgement of the superior mesenteric vessels just left of the midline in the epigastric region.

A 29‐year‐old man with DiGeorge syndrome and a history of repaired omphalocele presented with worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting one week after lifting a heavy wagon and falling to the ground. On admission, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed a 3/6 holosystolic murmur, tenderness in the left upper quadrant with palpable fullness and mild guarding, and a midline surgical scar superior to the umbilicus. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, hematocrit 37.2%, white-cell count 13.38×10^3/mcL, platelet count 119×10^3/mcL, INR 1.2, alanine aminotransferase 999 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 275 U/L, total bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL, and lipase 12 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a heterogeneously hypoechoic, avascular mass in the left upper quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a large heterogeneous, low-attenuation collection in the left abdomen just inferior to the left hepatic lobe. CT angiography showed a non-enhancing, smoothly contoured mass without active extravasation; axial images suggested non-enhancing vascular structures, and coronal images raised the possibility of torsion of a hepatic lobe.

A 40-year-old woman presented with nontraumatic umbilical bleeding that began 2 days earlier. She noted her shirt soaked in blood over her umbilicus on awakening and had intermittent bleeding since, accompanied by nonradiating periumbilical pain worsened by movement, nausea, and emesis. She reported a similar but painless umbilical bleeding episode 5 years earlier that resolved without imaging. Her medical history included hypertension, GERD, class III obesity (BMI 45), depression, and anxiety; she had a single cesarean delivery 12 years earlier. Current medications included losartan, propranolol, escitalopram, bupropion, gabapentin, oral contraceptives, trazodone, and topical diclofenac. She denied tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use. On exam, blood pressure was 125/81 mmHg, pulse 65/min, afebrile. The abdomen was nondistended with normal overlying skin except for dried blood at the umbilicus; deep palpation elicited mild periumbilical tenderness and produced a thin, serosanguinous fluid from the umbilicus. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. A same-day CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a small fat-containing umbilical hernia with a likely small area of fat necrosis just superior to the hernia. Laboratory studies revealed a mildly elevated high-sensitivity CRP of 13.8 mg/L; CBC, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests were normal.

An 18-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 12-month history of right-sided nasal obstruction, intermittent nasal discharge, and occasional epistaxis. On anterior rhinoscopy, a yellow-colored, hard, irregular mass was seen occupying the right nasal cavity. She denied any history of intranasal foreign-body insertion. A noncontrast CT scan of the paranasal sinuses revealed a well-defined calcified mass situated between the nasal septum and the inferior turbinate on the right side.

A 71-year-old woman was admitted to a local hospital in Oslo hours after returning from a four-week holiday in Thailand. She had a two-day history of fatigue and developed rapid onset of nausea, vomiting, fever, and exhaustion. On examination, she was febrile (39.5 °C) with a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 12×10^9 cells/L and a C-reactive protein level of 9 mg/L. Intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin were started for presumed urosepsis, but later that day she became confused, developed speech disturbances, and was noted to have nuchal rigidity.

She was transferred to the tertiary care center and received 4 g of ceftriaxone. On arrival, she had obvious nuchal rigidity, incoherent speech, motor agitation, and confusion. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score was initially 12, dropping to 9, at which point she was intubated. A cerebral CT scan with angiography showed no acute ischemia, hemorrhage, or vascular occlusion. 

A lumbar puncture yielded cloudy cerebrospinal fluid under increased pressure. CSF analysis revealed a glucose concentration of 0.1 mmol/L (serum glucose 11.1 mmol/L), a protein level of 6.9 g/L, and 2115 leukocytes/mm^3 with 87.3% neutrophils. An acridine orange stain of the CSF showed no microbes. A nigrosin stain did not reveal cryptococci, although the examiner noted the presence of unidentified elements.

A 28-year-old unmarried man with a known history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency since childhood presented with a 13-year history of insidious onset psychiatric illness characterized by a continuous course with multiple exacerbations. The most recent exacerbation lasted six weeks prior to admission. His symptoms included:  
• Muttering to himself and unprovoked aggression toward family members.  
• Irritability and over-talkativeness with pressured speech.  
• Delusional beliefs that rays from the sun and moon were entering his brain, causing him to become violent.  
• Beliefs that planets Mars and Saturn were inserting and removing thoughts against his will, causing transient blanking of his mind.  
• Auditory hallucinations: hearing voices of Pakistani troops threatening to kill him and destroy his nation.  
• Grandiose delusions of possessing special healing powers.  
• Behavior changes during exacerbations: unplanned charitable donations of shop inventory and income, excessive smoking, decreased sleep (by ~3 hours), and increased appetite.  

He had never been asymptomatic, though symptom severity fluctuated with treatment trials. He had three prior psychiatric admissions and trials of three classes of antipsychotics and mood stabilizers with only partial improvement. There was a family history of psychotic illness in his mother and two elder sisters. Developmental history and premorbid temperament were unremarkable.  

On examination, there was black discoloration of the upper and lower gingiva; all other physical findings were normal. Mental status examination revealed increased psychomotor activity, decreased reaction time, pressured speech, euphoric affect, delusions of persecution, control, grandiosity, thought insertion and withdrawal, second- and third-person auditory hallucinations, impaired judgment, and poor insight.  

Laboratory studies were within normal limits: hemoglobin 14 g/dL, hematocrit 40.6%, MCV 98.6 fl, MCH 32.4 pg, MCHC 32.9 g/dL, serum bilirubin 0.88 mg/dL, and no red blood cells detected on urinalysis.

A 10-year-old girl was referred for a recurrent left mandibular abscess. This was her third presentation in the past year. She reported left mandibular pain, swelling, and trismus. Vital-tooth tests were positive; percussion tests were negative. She was in good general health. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of >30 g/L; complete blood count was normal.  
An orthopantomogram revealed mixed dentition with no apparent lesions of the mandible or maxilla. The patient had no history of trauma, previous medications, gingival bleeding, or dental caries.  
Empiric intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone and metronidazole) were started, but the abscess recurred. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the maxillofacial region showed diffuse swelling and oedematous imbibition of the left masseter muscle and surrounding soft tissues, interruption of the cortical bone of the left mandibular ramus (maximum 1 cm), inhomogeneous cancellous bone with multiple areas of osteolysis (2 cm craniocaudal), and a small soft hypodense component adjacent to the cortical defect.  
Two days later, contrast-enhanced MRI of the left mandible demonstrated diffuse structural alteration of the vertical and horizontal mandibular rami, irregular cortical discontinuity, widespread intermediate T2 signal in cancellous bone with moderate enhancement, focal cortical interruption near the unerupted second molar, and significant volume increase of the masseter muscle.  
These findings, even considering the clinical evolution, supported the initial hypothesis of osteomyelitis. The next step was to biopsy the lesion.

A 69-year-old woman presented one month after bilateral lower-limb amputations (right supracondylar, left transtibial) for peripheral arterial occlusive disease, now admitted for a surgical-site infection. She reported new-onset, medium-intensity, biparietal throbbing headache and focal neurologic signs including dysarthria, right facial palsy, and left hemiparesis (predominantly of the left upper limb). Her medical history included end-stage renal disease on thrice-weekly dialysis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, prior myocardial infarction without coronary disease, and cor pulmonale. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Temporal pulses were mildly diminished with bilateral tenderness over the temporal regions. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. The left and right lower limbs showed healing amputation stumps. Neurologically, she was alert and oriented with mild dysarthria, intact comprehension and memory, normal cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in the right upper limb, 2/5 strength in the left upper limb, brisk symmetric reflexes, and no cerebellar or meningeal signs.

Initial laboratory tests showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 65 mm/h. A plain cranial CT scan revealed an ischemic infarct in the right posterior cerebral artery territory in the occipital region and additional cortical-subcortical hypodensities in the middle cerebral artery distribution. Notably, there were multiple bilateral calcifications of the superficial temporal arteries, involvement and calcification of the ophthalmic arteries, and calcification of the vertebral arteries (critical grade on the left).

A 57-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of persistent nausea and vomiting, anorexia, constipation, and a 30-kg weight loss. Two months earlier, esophagogastroduodenoscopy had shown tiny erosions of the distal esophagus with a sliding hiatal hernia; diluted bile and retained food in the stomach; erythema, edema, and erosions in the gastric corpus and antrum; one small smooth protrusion along the greater curvature; and erythematous changes in the duodenum. His medical history was notable only for well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral agents; he had no prior surgeries, allergies, transfusions, or other medications.
