On examination, his pulse was 103 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/90 mm Hg, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, non-tender, and otherwise normal. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 9.2×10^3/mm^3, hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, an elevated amylase level (140 U/L), electrolyte abnormalities consistent with acute kidney injury, and normal tumor markers. After intravenous fluids, his creatinine normalized, and he underwent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT, which showed marked gastric and duodenal distention (up to 6 cm) with a transition point at the duodenojejunal junction; the more distal small-bowel loops were collapsed and appeared encapsulated anterior to the colon, findings “suggestive of internal hernia with possible adhesive band at the DJ junction.” No masses or significant bowel-wall thickening were identified; CT of the chest showed no intrathoracic malignancy.

Two days after admission and correction of electrolytes, he underwent diagnostic laparoscopy. The entire abdominal viscera were enveloped by a dense fibrocollagenous membrane, with the liver plastered to the abdominal wall, the stomach fused to the transverse colon by a thick membrane, and the small bowel completely encapsulated. Multiple tissue specimens were obtained and sent for culture, histopathology, and acid-fast bacilli staining.

A 4-year-old girl was referred on January 20, 2022, for evaluation of generalized erythematous macular lesions. She had a history of a febrile seizure but was not receiving phenobarbital. Initial assessment led to a presumed drug reaction; she was treated with diazepam and methylprednisolone, improved over 3 days, and was discharged without new medications. One week later, she was readmitted with recurrence of skin findings—erythematous papules on the arms, legs, and abdomen—and involvement of the eyes and oral mucosa. On examination, her heart and lung sounds were normal, and there were no neurological or abdominal abnormalities. Laboratory studies were obtained: a white blood cell count of 3,500/μl, hemoglobin of 10.1 g/dl, platelets 327,000/μl, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 89 mm/hr, C‐reactive protein negative, and normal renal function and electrolytes. Intravenous fluids were administered. Given the concern for Stevens–Johnson syndrome and the possibility of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, a nasopharyngeal RT-PCR test and serologic assays for SARS-CoV-2 (IgM and IgG) were requested.

A male newborn, the third child of healthy nonconsanguineous parents and a twin pregnancy, was referred at 5 days of life for persistent axial hypotonia and poor feeding. He was born at 38+1 weeks by vaginal delivery; birth weight was 2560 g (10th percentile), length 49 cm (25–50th percentile), and head circumference 35 cm (50–75th percentile). Apgar scores were 9 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes due to hypotonia. 

On examination, the infant was alert but hypotonic with poor head control and weak sucking. Notable findings included joint hypermobility, arachnodactyly, finger joint contractures, and transient right genu recurvatum. He had a “senile” facial appearance with hypertelorism, down-slanting palpebral fissures, ocular exotropia, arched nose with bulbous tip, high-arched palate, short philtrum, down-turned mouth, thin upper lip, micrognathia, low-set ears, and translucent, lax skin. Cardiac auscultation was normal; peripheral pulses were symmetric.

Ophthalmologic and abdominal ultrasound examinations were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed dilation of the aortic root at the sinuses of Valsalva (13 mm; Z score +3) without insufficiency; the remainder of the aorta was within normal limits. A small patent foramen ovale and patent ductus arteriosus with a hemodynamically insignificant left-to-right shunt were noted.

A 32‐year‐old man with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department after coughing up approximately 300 mL of bright‐red blood over 3 hours, which began immediately after a sneezing episode. He was a taxi driver, did not smoke or drink alcohol, and denied any history of chest trauma, use of aspirin or NSAIDs, prior hemoptysis, pulmonary or infectious symptoms, or relevant family history. On examination, his temperature was 36.8 °C, pulse 88/min, respirations 18/min, blood pressure 128/88 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver biochemistry, coagulation profile, and urinalysis, were all normal. A posterior–anterior chest radiograph showed an ill‐defined opacity around the left hilum. Chest CT demonstrated soft‐tissue opacity within the left mainstem bronchus with a needle‐shaped material protruding from it.

An 83-year-old Hispanic man with end-stage renal disease on thrice-weekly hemodialysis, hypertension, coronary artery disease with prior myocardial infarction and stent, seizure disorder, and remote colectomy with colostomy presented with bilateral lower-extremity weakness. He first noticed weakness around the knees after an early dinner at 3 PM, progressed to difficulty rising from a chair and walking, and persisted for several hours, prompting hospital presentation. Three days earlier, he had a similar episode that resolved after dialysis. Between episodes he ambulated normally. He denied fever, cough, diarrhea, trauma, or changes in bowel or bladder function. His medications included aspirin, clopidogrel, simvastatin, metoprolol, multivitamin, folic acid, calcium acetate, phenytoin, and omeprazole. He had a recent seizure requiring intubation and was discharged on phenytoin; prior potassium levels had reached 8.3 mEq/L. On examination, hip flexor strength was 2/5 bilaterally, cogwheel rigidity was noted at both knees, and sensory testing and reflexes were normal. Cranial nerves and upper extremity strength were intact. ECG showed peaked T waves, and serum potassium was 7.8 mEq/L. Chest radiograph revealed no acute infiltrates or fluid overload. His diet included rice, beans, pork chops, beef, chicken, and salad.

A 66-year-old Japanese man presented with a gradually enlarging, painful mass on the plantar aspect of his right foot. He first noticed the lesion approximately 20 years ago. On examination, the mass measured about 30 mm in diameter at the level of the fourth metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint; there was no overlying redness or warmth. Routine hematological investigations were unremarkable, including a serum uric acid concentration of 6.5 mg/dL (reference range 3.0–7.0 mg/dL). Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a soft tissue mass extending from just below the fourth MTP joint. On T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and short tau inversion recovery sequences, the lesion exhibited heterogeneous low signal intensity with internal septations and evidence of bone erosion around the second, third, and fourth MTP joints. Given these findings, the leading diagnostic considerations were amyloidosis, gouty tophus, and fibromatosis.

A 45-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and end-stage renal disease presented with acute left eye vision loss and fever. On examination, he was tachycardic at 120 beats per minute. Laboratory evaluation revealed a troponin level of 5.64 ng/mL and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 80 mm/hour.  
   
A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed no acute infarction, and CT angiography of the head revealed no significant vascular stenosis. Ophthalmologic evaluation demonstrated a central retinal artery occlusion. Subsequently, he developed altered mental status and hypotension. MRI of the brain showed multiple infarcts in different vascular territories. Blood cultures were persistently positive for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus.  
   
Transthoracic echocardiography was unremarkable. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed large, mobile vegetations on the mitral valve. Coronary angiography demonstrated multivessel occlusions in the ostial and mid segments of the left anterior descending artery and in the distal right coronary artery. In the right coronary artery, there was a tubular, snake-shaped filling defect.

A female infant was noted on prenatal ultrasonography to have a markedly dilated esophagus and a prominent gastric bubble in the setting of polyhydramnios. She was delivered vaginally at 38 weeks and 0 days of gestation with a birth weight of 1740 g. Shortly after birth, tense blisters and areas of epidermal detachment were observed on the face and extremities. Abdominal radiography demonstrated a grossly distended stomach with no gas visible in the intestinal tract beyond the pyloric region. Targeted abdominal ultrasonography revealed an echogenic pylorus with no passage of gastric contents into the duodenum.

A 38-year-old nondiabetic white woman presented with intermittent numbness and tingling in all extremities. Four months earlier in Puerto Rico, she had confirmed Zika virus infection (IgM ELISA and plaque-reduction neutralization test positive; RT-PCR negative) with a generalized maculopapular rash, fever, headache, conjunctivitis, arthralgia, and myalgia. Tests for Dengue and Chikungunya viruses were negative, and she had evidence of prior West Nile virus exposure (IgG elevated, IgM negative). Her history included a remote episode of painful genital and oral ulceration of unknown etiology; tests for herpes, syphilis, HIV, tuberculosis, and toxoplasmosis were negative.

She denied visual symptoms. Uncorrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left. Confrontation visual fields, pupillary responses, anterior segment examination, and intraocular pressures were normal bilaterally. Slit-lamp ophthalmoscopy of the right eye revealed microaneurysms in the macula. Infrared reflectance imaging demonstrated a hyporeflective lesion in the macula. Fundus fluorescein angiography showed perifoveal microaneurysms in the inner retinal circulation. Optical coherence tomography revealed a focal detachment of the retinal pigment epithelium adjacent to outer retinal and RPE irregularity underlying the region of inner retinal change, without macular edema. Fundus-controlled microperimetry showed preserved retinal sensitivity. These imaging findings remained stable over six weeks of follow-up.

A 5-year-old girl was referred for failure to thrive. She was the fifth child of unrelated parents from the same village in southern Lebanon. Born at term via vaginal delivery, her birth weight was 2200 g; the pregnancy was uneventful, and there was no maternal medication use, smoking, or alcohol intake. Her perinatal course was notable for neonatal jaundice requiring phototherapy. Family history included mental retardation in a maternal uncle and a congenital heart defect in an older brother.

In early infancy, she had feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, recurrent respiratory infections, and eczematous skin lesions. Since birth, her urine had a musty odor, although repeated urine analyses were normal. Developmentally, she was hyperactive with significant speech delay (vocabulary of 10–15 words; few two-word sentences); gross and fine motor skills were age-appropriate, and she understood simple commands but had a short attention span and impulsive behavior.

On examination, her height was 84 cm, weight 10 kg, and head circumference 44 cm (all <3rd percentile). She had fair, dry skin and sparse fine blond hair. Facial features included an elongated face with a high sloping forehead, sparse lateral eyebrows, long eyelashes, telecanthus with hypertelorism, low-set ears, a broad nasal bridge with prominent tip, micrognathia, a thin upper lip, a high-arched palate, dental caries, and a sacral dimple. Eczematous changes were present mainly in the flexural areas of the extremities. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

Laboratory studies revealed normal results for: complete blood count; blood urea nitrogen; creatinine; electrolytes; total serum protein; liver function tests; lipid profile; thyroid hormones; urine organic acids; plasma acylcarnitine and free carnitine; plasma amino acids; serum lactate and pyruvate; plasma zinc; immunoglobulins (including IgE); urinalysis and cultures; stool studies; insulin-like growth factor 1; anti-endomysial antibodies; sweat chloride; and a 46,XX karyotype. MRI of the brain, spinal radiographs, voiding cystourethrogram, and upper gastrointestinal series were all normal. Echocardiography showed only trace mitral regurgitation. Bone-age assessment was delayed by two years.

A 65-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department as a full trauma alert after a single-vehicle accident. She was a restrained driver, found ambulatory next to her crashed vehicle. Medical history included juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, intraductal carcinoma and lobular carcinoma in situ of the left breast, and major depressive disorder. On arrival, her airway was intact; breath sounds were slightly diminished over the right anterior chest; radial pulses were strong; extremities were warm and well perfused; and Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15. E-FAST examination showed no free fluid in the abdominal quadrants or pelvis, though cardiac views were unobtainable. Secondary survey revealed a large hematoma and tenderness over the right superolateral chest wall and shoulder; the abdomen and spine were nontender. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with intravenous contrast demonstrated a large right breast hematoma with contrast blush, indicating active hemorrhage, and no acute abnormalities of the lungs, mediastinum, abdomen, or pelvis. She received fentanyl for pain and was initially stable, but immediately after the CT scan she became hypotensive with altered mental status, required transfusion of 1 unit of whole blood, and was intubated for a decreased Glasgow Coma Scale score.

A 41-year-old primigravida at 22 weeks’ gestation (conceived via IVF for endometriosis) presented with sudden-onset severe left-sided abdominal pain of 90 minutes’ duration while sitting, associated with nausea and dizziness but no urinary or gastrointestinal symptoms. She reported normal fetal movements. She had hypermobile wrists but no other signs of connective tissue disorder and no relevant personal or family history.

On examination she was afebrile and tachycardic, with local peritonism in the left renal angle and left iliac fossa despite opioid analgesia. Her body habitus was slim. The uterus was soft and non-tender. Vaginal examination showed a closed os without discharge or bleeding, with extreme tenderness on left adnexal palpation. There were no palpable abdominal masses and bowel sounds were normal.

Arterial blood gas analysis revealed a deep metabolic and lactic acidosis with respiratory compensation, which partially responded to fluid resuscitation. Urinalysis showed no haematuria. Bedside transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated no signs of fetal distress or intrauterine growth retardation and normal kidneys and ovaries. Initial haemoglobin and renal function were within normal limits.

Despite fluid resuscitation, she became hemodynamically unstable, with evidence of fetal distress. A midline laparotomy was performed, which revealed a large left retroperitoneal haematoma displacing the uterus to the right; the haematoma was left undisturbed. A cesarean section delivered a non-viable fetus.

A 77‐year‐old trans man presented with a painless perineal swelling located dorsal and right to his urethral perineal fistula (“Boutonnière”). He had undergone phalloplasty with a radial forearm free‐flap and construction of a Boutonnière in 1984, during which labia minora tissue was used to extend the urethra. His history included recurrent Escherichia coli urinary tract infections and treated vesicoureteral reflux in 1995. He also reported lifelong difficulty emptying his bladder, requiring a pelvic tilt to void. 

He first noticed the asymptomatic swelling in 2014. In 2015, examination revealed a soft, non‐tender mass that enlarged on Valsalva but showed no inflammation. CT imaging demonstrated a fluid collection extending from the perineum to the retrovesical space without connection to adjacent organs. Voiding cystourethrography showed no diverticula or fistula. Because he had no increase in UTIs or voiding difficulty, no intervention was undertaken.

Over the next four years, the mass grew from 2×2 cm to approximately 5×10 cm, and the patient developed more frequent UTIs and worsening obstructive voiding. In 2019, a perineal incision yielded a large amount of non‐odorous, viscous, turbid fluid. The cavity was irrigated, a Penrose drain placed, and cultures were negative for bacterial growth. One‐month follow‐up sonography showed a residual fluid volume of 6 mL. The patient’s voiding technique remained unchanged, and he has experienced no UTIs since the procedure.

A 16-year-old athletic white male with no significant medical history first presented in September 2017 with left foot and ankle pain after an eversion injury from a fall down a flight of stairs. Radiographs at an outside facility were unremarkable; he was splinted and discharged without planned follow-up.

In September 2018, he was referred for persistent left foot arch pain that interfered with his athletic performance. Physical examination localized tenderness to the medial midfoot. Radiographs showed an accessory navicular bone and signs of insertional tendonitis. Magnetic resonance imaging was ordered, and he was placed in a below-knee cast for 3 weeks, non–weight bearing. Serial radiographs over the following weeks showed no change in navicular appearance. He was then transitioned to a UCBL custom orthotic, later to stability shoes, and was asymptomatic for two months.

In February 2019, he experienced a sudden relapse of pain. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels were within normal limits. In March 2019, diagnostic ultrasound suggested mild posterior tibialis tenosynovitis. Because his symptoms persisted, a follow-up MRI with contrast was obtained, which demonstrated bone marrow edema of the navicular bone.

A male infant born at 31+5 weeks’ gestation weighing 1275 g had persistent respiratory distress and remained on CPAP since birth. Attempts to place a nasogastric tube failed at 10 cm. He was diagnosed with type C oesophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) and a ventricular septal defect. On day 5 of life, thoracoscopic repair of the oesophageal atresia was performed; intraoperative laryngeal inspection noted a possible mild type I laryngeal cleft without laryngomalacia. Postoperatively, he no longer required CPAP but remained oxygen-dependent. Under speech-language supervision, bottle feeding with thickened liquids was initiated and supplemented by nasoduodenal feeds; nonetheless, he developed aspiration pneumonia. 

At 7 weeks of age, a Videofluoroscopic Swallowing Study showed penetration on slightly thick liquids (IDDSI level 1) but no aspiration, and no penetration or aspiration with moderately thick liquids (IDDSI level 2). 

At 8 weeks, a diagnostic laryngotracheobronchoscopy (dLTB) was performed. TEF recurrence could not be assessed due to respiratory distress during the procedure. Endoscopy revealed severe obstructing tracheobronchomalacia with CO₂ accumulation, oesophageal stenosis, and palpation of the interarytenoid area suggested either a type I laryngeal cleft or a deep interarytenoid notch.

A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with a worsening facial rash that began 6 days earlier. It initially appeared as red papules over the left cheek; her pediatrician prescribed acyclovir for presumed eczema herpeticum and instructed her to discontinue all topical products. Over the next 3 days, the rash progressed markedly, and she was brought to the hospital. 

Her medical history was notable only for a nonspecific facial rash of 2 years’ duration on both cheeks, diagnosed as atopic dermatitis and treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily. She had been applying this ointment to her face at least daily for 2 years, pausing for no more than 1–2 days at a time because the rash promptly returned. She stopped the ointment completely 3 days before presentation. She denied fever, systemic symptoms, or personal or family history of atopy.

On examination, she was afebrile and appeared well. There were confluent erythematous, edematous plaques in the bilateral periorbital areas (left more than right), studded with numerous 2– to 3-mm pustules, some coalescing into “lakes of pus.” A few pustules were also noted in the perioral area. There were no signs of steroid-induced atrophy, such as skin thinning or increased vascular prominence.

An 11-day-old male newborn, birth weight 2.4 kg, was referred for evaluation of progressive abdominal distension and reluctance to feed for 8 days. He was delivered at term by cesarean section after an uncomplicated pregnancy. A few hours after birth, he developed respiratory distress and was admitted to a local NICU. He passed urine and meconium normally and received expressed breast milk via a nasogastric tube. Initial laboratory studies demonstrated a leukocyte count of 14 400/mm3 with 76% neutrophils; other values were within normal limits. A plain abdominal radiograph was unremarkable. He received intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics without fever or vomiting.

Despite therapy, his abdomen became progressively distended. On transfer, the leukocyte count was 7900/mm3 and the platelet count was 31 000/mm3. Abdominal radiographs showed free intraperitoneal air; ultrasound was inconclusive. He was then referred to our facility.

On arrival, the heart rate was 126 beats/min, respiratory rate 38 breaths/min, and he had mild dehydration. The abdomen was distended and tense. A repeat radiograph confirmed pneumoperitoneum. Tube laparostomy released free air and a small amount of turbid fluid.

A 54-year-old woman with no significant medical history and a remote nine-year smoking history (quit 30 years ago) was transferred for evaluation of sudden discoloration and numbness of her left fourth finger. The evening before presentation, she felt a sharp pinch in the middle phalanx and noted a blue circular spot. On awakening, the entire middle phalanx appeared bruised, was tender to palpation, and she experienced numbness. She denied trauma, coagulopathy, drug use, or similar prior episodes. 

On examination, the volar aspect of the middle phalanx of the left fourth digit was bluish, warm, slightly tender, and had decreased sensation. The distal phalanx had normal color with brisk capillary refill. All fingers had full range of motion. Radial pulses were equal and strong bilaterally, and the remainder of the hand was normal.

An ultrasound arterial duplex of the left upper extremity was performed and was normal.

A 27-year-old previously healthy Malay man presented with a 1-week history of acute, severe blurring of vision in the right eye, associated with frontal headache and vomiting. There was no pain on eye movement and no history suggestive of infection or connective-tissue disease. On examination, visual acuity was counting fingers at 2 feet in the right eye and 6/18 in the left eye (improving to 6/12 with a pinhole). A relative afferent pupillary defect was present in the right eye. Red saturation and light brightness were reduced, and color vision was absent in the right eye. Confrontation testing revealed a central scotoma in the right eye extending superiorly to the paracentral area. Two days later, color vision deteriorated in the left eye. The anterior segments were normal bilaterally. Fundoscopic examination showed bilateral generalized optic disc swelling with tortuous vessels and splinter hemorrhages, more pronounced on the right; the maculae were normal. The remainder of the neurologic examination was normal. Differential diagnoses included raised intracranial pressure, bilateral optic neuritis, and meningeal infiltration. An urgent computed tomography scan showed bilateral enhancement of the optic nerves suggestive of optic neuritis, with normal brain parenchyma.

A 34-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, with no significant medical history, was admitted at 36 weeks of gestation for severe preeclampsia and rapidly progressive vulvar swelling. She was apyretic, and there was no history of trauma, infection, or topical medication use. Blood pressure was 170/110 mm Hg, and urine dipstick showed 3+ proteinuria. Examination of the external genitalia revealed massive edema of the labia minora and majora, predominantly on the left side, with fissuring of the inner aspect of the right labia majora and a serous discharge. Obstetrical examination showed a tense uterus, a closed cervix, intact membranes, and cephalic presentation. Continuous fetal monitoring demonstrated a flat heart-rate pattern without accelerations. There were no signs of lower-limb thrombosis or regional lymphadenopathy, and only mild pedal edema. Because of suspected retroplacental hematoma, a cesarean delivery was performed, yielding a female infant weighing 2500 g with Apgar scores of 10 and 10. Initial laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, a normal platelet count, normal prothrombin level and liver transaminases, a negative infectious workup, serum protein of 21 g/L, and 24-hour proteinuria of 4 g.

A 66-year-old Japanese woman who had immigrated from Okinawa, the only subtropical region of Japan, had been diagnosed six months earlier with systemic lupus erythematosus after presenting with bleeding tendency, pancytopenia, serositis, positive anti–double-stranded DNA antibody, proteinuria, and renal biopsy showing class IV lupus nephritis. She was also HTLV-1 positive without evidence of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. She received immunosuppression with high-dose intravenous steroids, prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus, with improvement in nephritis, hypocomplementemia, and pancytopenia.

Two months after starting immunosuppression, she developed nausea and abdominal pain; one month later she was admitted with severe leg edema and diffuse abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed thrombocytopenia, elevated C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, and alkaline phosphatase, and no eosinophilia. Cytomegalovirus pp65 antigen was markedly elevated; multiple stool cultures were negative. Her nephritis was stable and pancytopenia had not recurred. CT of the abdomen showed circumferential thickening of the walls of the ascending colon, colon, and small intestine with increased surrounding fat density, and a small pulmonary nodule in the right middle lobe. Lower endoscopy revealed redness, edema, and erosion from the cecum to the descending colon, but stool studies by direct smear and filter‐paper culture remained negative. On the basis of these findings, she was diagnosed with cytomegalovirus enteritis; mycophenolate mofetil and tacrolimus were discontinued, ganciclovir was administered, and she was managed by fasting.

After a transient improvement, her abdominal symptoms recurred and, eight days after admission, her respiratory status worsened, necessitating intubation. Because bacterial pneumonia and pneumocystis pneumonia were considered as differential diagnoses, broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungals were administered, but her respiratory status did not improve, and CT demonstrated diffuse infiltrative shadows and progression of pulmonary infiltrates.

A 73-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with six weeks of diarrhea, hematochezia, left lower-quadrant abdominal pain, and a 25-lb weight loss. She denies vomiting, diet changes, sick contacts, or travel.  
On examination, her mucous membranes are dry; abdominal tenderness is diffuse but most pronounced in the left lower quadrant; bowel sounds are sluggish.  
Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 10 g/dL, white blood cell count 15 × 10^3/μL, sodium 131 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20.2 mmol/L (normal anion gap), albumin 2.1 g/dL, globulin 3.9 g/dL.  
Stool studies are negative for Clostridium difficile PCR and Giardia lamblia antigen.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrates wall thickening of the distal descending and sigmoid colon concerning for colitis.  
Colonoscopy reveals ulcerated mucosa and multiple punched-out ulcers throughout the colon.

A 22-year-old Caucasian woman presented to the emergency department with a 4-week history of amenorrhea and lower abdominal pain. She had been treated for primary hypothyroidism with levothyroxine 200 mcg daily but had discontinued the medication one month earlier. Menarche occurred at age 11; her menstrual cycles were irregular. She denied use of any contraception, had no history of in vitro fertilization or known gynecologic pathology, and reported one prior spontaneous pregnancy complicated by severe sepsis at age 18.

On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal palpation revealed bilateral, mobile adnexal masses. Laboratory evaluation showed:
- Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH): 515 IU/mL (reference 0.4–4)  
- Free thyroxine (fT4): undetectable (reference 0.7–1.8 ng/dL)  
- Cancer antigen-125 (CA-125): 1,045 U/mL (reference 0–10)  
- Elevated hematocrit and hypoproteinemia  
- Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia  
- Mildly elevated liver enzymes and creatinine  

Transvaginal ultrasound identified a single intrauterine fetus with regular cardiac activity, consistent with 9 weeks 2 days of gestation; both ovaries were massively enlarged (right 15 × 14 × 16.6 cm; left 15 × 8.2 × 18.3 cm) with extensive multilocular cysts and moderate ascites. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated mild mitral valve prolapse and a circumferential pericardial effusion without hemodynamic compromise.

A 67-year-old man fell approximately 1 m from the cargo bed of a truck and was transported with quadriplegia and neurogenic shock, managed with an adrenergic vasopressor. He was alert on arrival (GCS score 14 [E3,V5,M6]) with a respiratory rate of 23 breaths/min, blood pressure 106/69 mmHg while receiving dopamine (5.5 μg/kg/min), heart rate 70 bpm (sinus), and SpO₂ 99% on 1 L O₂. Head CT showed a small epidural hematoma over the frontal bone. His history included a bifrontal craniotomy for aneurysm clipping 3 years earlier. He also had fractures of the C4–6 spinous processes, T2–3 vertebral bodies, bilateral first ribs, and the sternum. T2-weighted MRI demonstrated high-intensity signals in the spinal cord at C3–4 and T2 levels. Whole-body 3D-CT angiography revealed occlusion of the basilar artery trunk and poor visualization of the left vertebral artery distal to the posterior inferior cerebellar artery; there were no abnormal findings such as arterial dissection in the vertebral artery near the cervical fracture, and no obvious clivus fracture was identified on multiplanar CT images. Neurologically, he exhibited only quadriplegia. Antithrombotic therapy was withheld due to his ongoing surgical management for multiple injuries.

A 22‐year‐old man with extensive steroid‐dependent and azathioprine‐refractory ulcerative colitis (UC) presented in February 2014 with a clinically moderate relapse. One year earlier, he had 6–7 bloody bowel movements per day and diffuse abdominal pain; colonoscopy had shown multiple ulcerations from the rectum to the ascending colon (Mayo subscore 3). He improved with high‐dose methylprednisolone (60 mg daily) and mesalamine but relapsed during steroid tapering and was started on azathioprine (2.5 mg/kg/day).

He also had a preexisting, severe, inflammatory skin eruption on his chest and back, characterized by comedones, papules, and pustules. This eruption had preceded the UC diagnosis, was unresponsive to tetracyclines, clindamycin, isotretinoin, and sulfur derivatives, and worsened when he received prednisone (10–15 mg daily). It had caused significant anxiety and social withdrawal.

On examination in February 2014, clustered papules and pustules were noted on the thorax and back. Laboratory tests showed a mild increase in fibrinogen and CRP levels. In March 2014, colonoscopy demonstrated mucosal edema, erythema, and diffuse erosions (Mayo subscore 2).

A dermatologist was consulted, and the differential diagnosis included rosacea, other dermatitis, and flat warts.

A 48-year-old man with a 35-year history of tobacco and alcohol use presented with a 3-month history of progressive nonproductive cough, oropharyngeal pain, intermittent hoarseness, and a 6-kg weight loss. Initial outpatient treatment with amoxicillin and ibuprofen yielded no improvement. He reported dyspnea on minimal exertion and odynophagia. 

On examination, he was afebrile, eupneic at rest, noncyanotic, and well hydrated. No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy was noted. Two nonbleeding lesions with a moriform appearance and poorly defined borders were seen on the hard palate. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. Pulmonary auscultation revealed bilaterally decreased vesicular breath sounds with inspiratory crackles; respiratory rate was 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 60% on room air. Examination of the extremities showed digital clubbing and cyanosis without edema.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, hematocrit 40.6%, leukocyte count 23 630/mm³ with 15% band forms, and neutrophils with toxic granulations. Three sputum samples were negative for acid-fast bacilli. 

Chest radiographs demonstrated bilateral, symmetrical perihilar infiltrates with a “butterfly-wing” pattern. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed marked thickening of the interlobular septa, numerous bronchiectases, and bilateral reticular interstitial infiltrates. Cervical CT showed a vegetative lesion with irregular borders in the right nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal regions.

A 76-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of left palatal swelling. She had self-extracted her upper left second molar 3 years earlier and underwent extraction of the first molar 5 months before presentation; the latter was reportedly traumatic, with possible involvement of the maxillary sinus floor. Her medical history included uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and anticoagulant therapy; she denied prior facial trauma, sinusitis, or maxillary surgery.

On examination, there was mild swelling of the left cheek, paresthesia of the left infraorbital region, and left nasal obstruction for 1 month. Intraorally, a 2.5×3.0-cm palatal swelling was present in the left premolar–molar area, with obliteration of the buccal vestibule and expansion of the alveolar segment; the overlying mucosa was normal and all teeth were vital.

Computed tomography revealed a unilocular, radiolucent, expansile lesion measuring 35×31×34 mm in the left maxillary sinus, with resorption of the anterior and posterior sinus walls, obliteration of the osteomeatal complex, and cortical expansion of the palatal and buccal walls. Aspiration yielded straw-colored fluid and temporarily reduced the lesion’s size. An incisional biopsy via the buccal vestibule disclosed an unspecified odontogenic cyst, and a provisional diagnosis of odontogenic keratocyst was rendered.

A 49-year-old man presented with acute chest pain and palpitations. He had a history of congenital aortic stenosis but no prior records, and no family history of sudden death or syncope. On examination he was diaphoretic, with a radial pulse of 240 beats per minute, blood pressure 80/— mm Hg, and a mild systolic murmur at the left second intercostal space; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

A 12-lead ECG showed a broad-complex tachycardia with right bundle branch block morphology, a right superior (“north-west”) axis, and negative QRS complexes in leads V2 through V6. Intravenous adenosine was administered three times without change in the rhythm. Multiple attempts at electrical cardioversion restored sinus rhythm transiently, but the tachycardia reinitiated within a few beats; between attempts, the ECG demonstrated diffuse ST-segment depressions and ST elevations in leads V1 and aVR. Intravenous amiodarone (600 mg) followed by two 200-mg oral doses successfully suppressed the tachycardia, and the ST-segment changes normalized.

Laboratory studies revealed a markedly elevated troponin level; other values were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, a bicuspid aortic valve with mild-to-moderate stenosis and regurgitation, and an ascending aortic aneurysm measuring 47 mm. Coronary angiography revealed no obstructive disease.

An electrophysiology study was performed after a 24-hour washout of amiodarone. In sinus rhythm, the PR interval was 192 ms, there was no preexcitation, and the resting HV interval was prolonged at 77 ms with no bundle branch block. Ventriculoatrial conduction during ventricular pacing was absent. Atrial pacing at the clinical tachycardia cycle length revealed both suprahisian and pronounced infrahisian Wenckebach conduction. Programmed atrial stimulation produced an antegrade jump with typical AV nodal echo beats, inducing a complete phase-3 right bundle branch block.

After intravenous orciprenaline and atropine, stable 1:1 AV conduction at the tachycardia cycle length was achieved—presumably over a slow pathway—and the ECG exhibited the same phase-3 right bundle block as seen clinically. Eventually, rapid atrial stimulation induced a sustained tachycardia: there was AV dissociation, every QRS complex was preceded by a His potential with an HV interval similar to that in sinus rhythm, and changes in V–V cycle length were preceded by changes in H–H intervals. A brief run of three ventricular beats with left bundle branch block morphology also showed His potentials preceding each QRS complex, albeit with a longer HV interval.

A 32-year-old G5T2P1A1L2 at 21 weeks and 3 days of gestation presented to labor and delivery triage with acute lower abdominal pain and a presyncopal episode. She denied fever, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel habits, vaginal bleeding, contractions, or membrane rupture. Her obstetrical history included one classical cesarean for stillbirth, two elective cesareans, and a prior uterine dehiscence noted at surgery, as well as referral for a suspected abnormally adherent placenta after an anatomy scan showed a complete anterior placenta previa with loss of the placental-myometrial interface, multiple large irregular lacunae, and marked vascularity abutting the bladder.

On arrival, she was awake and oriented but hypotensive (80/40 mmHg) with a heart rate of 71 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Fetal heart rate was 145 beats/min. She received a fluid bolus, after which blood pressure improved to 92/51 mmHg. The abdomen was soft with tenderness and rebound in the right lower quadrant; the uterus itself was nontender. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 87 g/L, leukocytes 12.0×10^9/L, platelets 154×10^9/L, AST 13 U/L, ALT 7 U/L, and negative Kleihauer-Betke. A month earlier, her hemoglobin had been 92 g/L.

An emergent abdominal ultrasound showed a normal liver, biliary tree, common bile duct, spleen, aorta, kidneys, and gallbladder, with no hydronephrosis or renal stones. The appendix was not visualized, and there was no evidence of ovarian torsion. However, there was free fluid with low-level echoes throughout the abdomen, and in the left flank a large 14×10 cm heterogeneous echogenic area without internal vascularity concerning for an intra-abdominal hematoma. Obstetrical ultrasound again confirmed a single live fetus, a heterogeneous anterior placenta with multiple lacunae, and difficulty delineating the placental-myometrial border, with increased vascularity at the placental base and along the bladder interface.

A 67-year-old woman noted a slowly enlarging swelling beneath her left mandible over 12 months, associated with mild pain but no fever, weight loss, dysphonia or cough. On examination, there was a firm, well-circumscribed mass adjacent to the left submandibular gland. Laboratory studies, including thyroid function tests, were normal. Neck ultrasonography showed a normally located thyroid gland with two small nodules in the right lobe and, separately, a 28.7 × 26.8 mm vascularized, iso- to hypoechoic solid lesion with anechoic areas behind the left submandibular gland. Because of its location and sonographic appearance, an MRI of the neck was obtained, which demonstrated a 25 × 19 × 23 mm ovular prestyloid mass with irregular T1 signal, a slightly hyperintense central area on T2, and a peripheral component not clearly separable from the submandibular gland. These findings were thought to represent a prestyloid space lesion—exophytic pleomorphic adenoma, neurogenic tumor, or lymphadenopathy—and FNAC was planned.

A 45-year-old woman presented with an 8-day history of binocular vertical diplopia and a subjective restriction in elevation. Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism and polycystic ovarian syndrome; she had no prior ocular surgery or trauma. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 6/4.5 bilaterally, intraocular pressures were normal, and pupils were equal and reactive. Extraocular motility testing showed mild (–1) limitation of elevation in adduction of the left eye with pain on right gaze, and cover testing revealed a left hypotropia of 4 prism diopters. Anterior and posterior segment exams were unremarkable.

A contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and orbits demonstrated normal superior oblique muscles and trochlear tendon complexes. Given suspicion for acquired Brown syndrome of inflammatory origin, she was started on ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily. Five days later, she returned with increased trochlear-region pain and worsening diplopia. Examination revealed moderate (–2) limitation of elevation in adduction of the left eye; other findings were stable. Oral prednisolone 25 mg daily was initiated, with subjective pain relief but persistent motility deficit.

One month after presentation, her motility deficit progressed to bilateral moderate (–2) elevation limitation in adduction. A repeat orbit MRI again showed no superior oblique hypertrophy, tendon inflammation, or trochlear attachment abnormalities. Rheumatology evaluation and serologic testing for mixed connective tissue disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis were negative. She remained symptomatic over the next 11 months while receiving up to 50 mg daily of oral prednisolone, which was tapered and replaced with methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine.

A 51-year-old man presented with severe neck pain and massive swelling. Fourteen days earlier, a furuncle-like lesion had appeared on the nape of his neck and had since rapidly enlarged. He had declined medical evaluation because of concern about COVID-19. He denied any history of diabetes mellitus, trauma, or insect bites to the area but had a long history of occipital folliculitis; his medical history also included hyperlipidemia and coronary artery bypass grafting one year ago. 

On examination, there was a large purplish inflammatory mass on the nape of the neck with multiple purulent sinus tracts discharging a thin, dishwater-like fluid. Neck motion was severely limited by pain. Patches of cicatricial alopecia and tufted folliculitis were noted on the occiput. 

Laboratory studies showed a blood glucose level of 537 mg/dL, an HbA1c of 13%, a leukocyte count of 14.6 × 10^3/μL (normal, 4.0–11.0), an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 67 mm/hour, and a C-reactive protein level of 37.1 mg/L.

An 86-year-old woman presented with right thigh pain and a swelling that she first noted one year earlier, with progressive enlargement over the past three months. She denied fever, erythema, or tenderness at the site. On examination, there was a tense, non-pulsatile, non-tender swelling on the medial aspect of the right thigh; distal pulses were intact, and there was no neurological deficit. Seventeen months earlier, she had sustained a right femoral shaft fracture after a fall and underwent dynamic compression plate fixation two days later without immediate complications. She did not attend subsequent follow-up visits.  
Plain radiographs of the femur showed a healed lateral cortex fracture with cortical erosion on the medial side and protrusion of screws through the medial cortex. A duplex ultrasound scan of the thigh revealed a cystic lesion with a “yin-yang” colour-flow pattern and a to-and-fro Doppler waveform at its neck, as well as a large internal thrombus.

A 17-year-old male presented with an asymptomatic patch of hair loss on his right frontal scalp. He reported that the patch had been present since birth without any change in size. There was no history of scalp trauma, traction, or perinatal scalp injury. On dermatologic examination, a well-defined, triangular alopecic patch measuring 2.5 × 3.5 cm was observed in the right frontal area; there was no erythema, atrophy, or inflammation. Trichoscopy revealed predominantly vellus hairs interspersed with fine white hairs and white dots. A skin biopsy from the lesion demonstrated multiple miniaturized hair follicles with mild perifollicular inflammatory-cell infiltration and intact epidermis and dermis.

A 43-year-old man presented with intermittent fevers occurring once or twice monthly for 5 months. He was a current smoker and occasional alcohol drinker who had emigrated from mainland China 7 months earlier; language barriers limited the history obtained at presentation. He had a history of animal husbandry in Heilongjiang Province, where two cows in his herd had spontaneous abortions 10 months prior, but this was not recognized initially. Two months after arriving in Japan, he developed sudden fevers with chills, malaise, bitter taste, mild constipation, and myalgia that resolved spontaneously over 2 to 3 days. At presentation, his vital signs were normal except for a temperature of 37.3°C. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 4400/μL, alkaline phosphatase 389 IU/L, and C-reactive protein 4.56 mg/dL. Abdominal computed tomography revealed mild splenomegaly. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained, and he was managed as an outpatient in good general condition.
Three days later, blood cultures grew nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli. On hospital day 8, using an automated Phoenix system, the organism was identified as Ochrobactrum anthropi. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no evidence of endocarditis. Under the provisional diagnosis of bacteremia of unknown origin, he was started on ciprofloxacin 400 mg twice daily, with symptomatic relief.

A 45-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of intense frontal headache, nausea, and temporal and spatial disorientation. Over the same period, he developed inappropriate behavior. On arrival he was afebrile, with a blood pressure of 170/100 mm Hg. Neurologic examination showed spontaneous eye opening but reduced blink rate; lack of spontaneous movements; mutism; waxy flexibility; negativism; and catalepsy. There was no cranial-nerve palsy, and deep tendon reflexes were normal. He manifested repetitive stereotypic perioral movements and clonic jerks of the right upper limb lasting for more than five minutes, interpreted as continuous partial motor status with impaired consciousness. After intravenous phenytoin (20 mg/kg), he had improvement in interaction and complete remission of the abnormal movements but remained mute and unable to speak, though he could follow commands (motor aphasia). Laboratory studies revealed no signs of infection or metabolic disturbance. A lumbar puncture showed six cells/mL, glucose 56 mg/dL, total protein 27 mg/dL, and negative bacterial and fungal cultures. Noncontrast head CT disclosed a hypodense area in the left temporal region with small hyperdense spots. On hospital day 2, EEG revealed diffuse disorganization of cerebral activity with predominantly slow delta waves in the left posterior–medial temporal region and no epileptiform discharges.

A 91-year-old man with a history of right middle cerebral artery stroke 5 years earlier, resulting in left hemiparesis, presented with a choking episode while being fed a samosa with pea curry in a recumbent position. He immediately developed tachypnea, dry cough, tachycardia, and aphonia, and arrived in the emergency department 30 minutes later. 

On examination, his respiratory rate was 35 breaths/min, pulse 140 beats/min, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, temperature 97.9 °F, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. His buccal mucosa was mildly dry. Auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds over the left supramammary and suprascapular regions; the remainder of the respiratory and cardiovascular examinations was unremarkable. Neurologic examination was notable only for chronic left-sided weakness.

Arterial blood gas analysis was normal, and routine blood tests were within normal limits. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. A chest radiograph demonstrated mild haziness in the left upper zone. 

Given the clinical suspicion of foreign body aspiration, a high-resolution computed tomography scan of the chest was obtained, revealing an 8 × 7 mm oval, hyperdense object partially obstructing the left upper lobe bronchus, associated with partial atelectasis of the left upper lobe and mild emphysematous changes in the left lower lobe.

A 23-year-old Pakistani woman presented with a 2-month history of recurrent blackouts, blurring of vision, and moderate frontal headaches radiating to the whole head, associated with vertigo, dizziness, palpitations, and postural weakness. She had been diagnosed with epilepsy 2 months earlier and was taking antiepileptic medication.  

On examination, pulses in both upper limbs were deficient and blood pressure could not be measured. She was anemic, and a bruit was audible over the left subclavian fossa. Fundoscopy showed optic-disk cupping with irregular margins in the right eye; the left eye was normal. Respiratory, neurologic, and psychiatric evaluations were unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, platelet count 494 000/mL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 35 mm/hr. Red-cell indices showed microcytosis (MCV 58.7 fL) and hypochromasia (MCH 19.2 pg). Serum ferritin was elevated at 315.5 ng/mL. Hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrated hemoglobin A₂ 4.7%. Liver tests were abnormal (direct bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL; ALT 152 U/L; ALP 317 U/L), and C-reactive protein was positive. Serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, transferrin, antinuclear antibodies, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and electroencephalogram were normal.  

A computed tomography angiogram of the chest showed a normal ascending and descending aorta and aortic arch, but diffuse intimal thickening with narrowing at the origins of the brachiocephalic, right common carotid, and left subclavian arteries, with extensive collateral circulation in the neck, chest, and axillae.

An 81-year-old man presented with progressive exertional dyspnea, abdominal distension, and vomiting for 3 days. He had a history of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction for 2 years and an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm identified on CT screening. He denied hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and smoking. One week before presentation, furosemide, bisoprolol, and amiodarone were initiated.

On examination, temperature was normal; blood pressure 104/68 mmHg; heart rate 85 beats/min (irregular); respiratory rate 20 breaths/min; SpO₂ 96% on 3 L/min O₂. Cardiac auscultation revealed an irregularly irregular rhythm and a grade III/VI systolic murmur at the apex. ECG showed atrial fibrillation. Chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly and mild pulmonary edema. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a severely dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 20.8% and moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation. Laboratory tests showed creatinine 2.6 mg/dL (eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73 m²), NT-proBNP 28 007 pg/mL, and troponin T 86.6 ng/L.

He was admitted with acute decompensated heart failure and treated with intravenous diuretics and amiodarone. On hospital day 2, he developed intermittent dull chest and back pain. Vital signs were stable (BP 107/77 mmHg; HR 85 bpm; SpO₂ 96% on 3 L/min O₂). ECG showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and T-wave inversions in V5–V6. Serial cardiac enzymes showed no dynamic change.

On hospital day 3, he developed worsening dyspnea, cold extremities, hypotension (BP ~99/67 mmHg), and lactic acidosis. He was intubated for hypoxic respiratory failure and underwent synchronized cardioversion for atrial fibrillation, which restored sinus rhythm. Dopamine infusion was started for blood pressure support. Given a high surgical risk (STS score 35.7%), mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair was planned, and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) was requested to assess valve anatomy.

During TEE, difficulty in probe insertion necessitated sedation with midazolam, ketamine, and cisatracurium. After successful insertion, heart rate was 111 bpm and blood pressure 99/67 mmHg on dopamine. The initial mid-esophageal long-axis view at approximately 120° demonstrated an ascending aorta measuring 41 mm in diameter with no evidence of dissection.

A 47-year-old man fell from a 6-foot ladder and sustained an open left ankle injury. Examination revealed a 4×2 cm anteromedial wound with venous bleeding, mild numbness of the great toe, and a well-perfused foot. A positive saline load test indicated joint involvement. Initial radiographs showed a comminuted distal tibial plafond fracture with valgus angulation and shortening, plus a transverse distal third fibular shaft fracture. He tested negative for COVID-19. 

Three hours after presentation, he underwent irrigation and debridement with an ankle-spanning external fixator. Three weeks later, definitive ORIF of the tibia and fibula was performed. At two-week follow-up, incisions were well-healed; he remained non-weight-bearing and began passive stretching exercises. 

At three months post-operation, radiographs demonstrated complete fibular union but minimal healing of the tibial metaphysis despite maintained alignment, and he was instructed to begin intermittent weight-bearing. 

At four months, he was fully weight-bearing in a cam boot; radiographs showed no further tibial healing. On his first unprotected attempt at ambulation, he heard a “pop” and had immediate ankle pain. Imaging revealed acute displacement of the tibial fracture with apex anterior angulation; hardware remained intact. He resumed toe-touch weight-bearing. 

Laboratory studies showed normal thyroid-stimulating hormone and vitamin D levels, slightly elevated liver enzymes and glucose, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/hr, and a C-reactive protein level of 21 mg/L. He reported symptoms consistent with COVID-19 and tested positive.

A 32-year-old Caucasian transgender man presented with acute phallic swelling and pain of 2 days’ duration that began suddenly. He had been on intramuscular testosterone for 5 years with satisfactory virilization. Seven days earlier, he underwent an uncomplicated robotic laparoscopic total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and diagnostic cystoscopy under general anesthesia; sequential compression devices were used, and he was discharged on acetaminophen with codeine. He denied recent trauma, dysuria, or use of antidepressants or other psychotropic medications; he smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily. On examination, the clitoris measured approximately 4.0×2.0 cm, with modest tenderness to palpation and no visible edema; the glans clitoris appeared unaffected. He was afebrile. Two days later, he returned with worsening clitoral pain described as “searing” and difficulty walking. Examination showed more substantial engorgement and significant tenderness; abdominal, vulvar, and bimanual examinations remained unremarkable, and he remained afebrile. Laboratory studies revealed a normal serum chemistry panel, white-cell count 6900/mL with a normal differential, hemoglobin 14.4 g/dL, hematocrit 45%, peripheral oxygen saturation 98% on room air, negative sickle-cell screen, and negative serum d-dimer. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis and perineum showed mild tissue edema at the vaginal cuff, no pelvic abscess or hematoma, and enlargement of the clitoral corpus cavernosa.

A 32-year-old Qatari man with a 2-year history of hypertension, type 1 diabetes since age 9, and end-stage renal disease on peritoneal dialysis presented after a witnessed generalized tonic–clonic seizure lasting 2–3 minutes, associated with loss of consciousness and tongue biting. The day before, he experienced headache and dizziness without fever. On arrival, he was confused and irritable; blood pressure was 220/140 mm Hg, heart rate 100 beats/min, and temperature 37.1 °C. Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, liver function tests, serologic vasculitis screen, and serum thiamine level. Because of agitation and loss of airway protection the patient was intubated and started on an intravenous infusion of labetalol. 

Four hours after admission, noncontrast CT of the brain showed diffuse hypodensity of the brainstem. Phenytoin 300 mg was administered via nasogastric tube. An electroencephalogram revealed diffuse bilateral slowing in the theta and delta range without epileptiform discharges. 

Magnetic resonance imaging 48 hours after admission demonstrated a swollen brainstem with central and peripheral high signal in the pons, midbrain, and middle cerebellar peduncles on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery and T2-weighted images; normal signal intensity on diffusion-weighted images; increased apparent diffusion coefficient values; isointense signal on T1-weighted images without contrast enhancement; and normal intracranial MR angiography. The basal cisterns and posterior fossa cerebrospinal fluid spaces were tight, but there was no tonsillar herniation.

A 39-year-old man with a 15-year history of daily heavy alcohol use presented with 1 day of epigastric pain associated with nausea and vomiting. He had a similar but milder episode 3 months earlier that improved with oral medication. He had no other known medical conditions.  
On examination, vital signs were normal. He had icteric sclera and tenderness in the right upper quadrant and epigastrium.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 19,500/mm3 (90% neutrophils) and total and direct bilirubin levels of 7.1 and 5.3 mg/dL, respectively.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple echogenic gallstones with posterior acoustic shadowing, a thickened gallbladder wall (5.4 mm), and dilation of the intrahepatic biliary ducts. The sonographic impression was acute calculous cholecystitis.  
He was treated empirically for acute cholecystitis with acute cholangitis with ceftriaxone, metronidazole, diclofenac, and intravenous fluids. After 36 hours of initial stability, he developed sudden worsening of abdominal pain, dyspnea, high-grade fever, and diaphoresis over 6 hours, along with two episodes of bilious vomiting.  
On re-examination, he was tachycardic (132 bpm), tachypneic (36/min), hypotensive (85/60 mmHg), febrile (38.7°C), and hypoxemic (SpO2 88% on 5 L nasal oxygen). He had diffuse abdominal tenderness and distention.  
An erect chest radiograph demonstrated free intraperitoneal air beneath the diaphragm.

A 64-year-old woman presented with several years of painful, non-itchy swelling of the vulva, which became more pronounced over the past year. She denied fever, cough, shortness of breath, weight loss, changes in bowel movements, oral ulcers, or joint pain. Ten years earlier, she underwent hysterectomy complicated by lower-leg deep vein thrombosis and a normal colonoscopy. 

On examination, both labia majora had indurated, verrucous, skin-colored plaques with overlying intact vesicles, and the mons pubis was erythematous and indurated. There were also bilateral brown, non-scaly indurated plaques over the lower legs, consistent with lipodermatosclerosis.

The initial differential diagnosis included cutaneous Crohn’s disease, tuberculosis, and acquired lymphangioma circumscriptum. A punch biopsy of a labial vesicle showed dilated lymphatic channels, and an ellipse biopsy of the mons pubis revealed non-caseating epithelioid granulomas. Ziehl–Neelsen, Periodic Acid–Schiff, and Grocott’s Methenamine Silver stains were negative for mycobacterial and fungal elements.

Laboratory tests showed a normal blood count and normal kidney and liver function. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and a quantiferon test for tuberculosis were negative. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated normal lung parenchyma, skin thickening with abdominal wall fat stranding, normal bowel loops, and an absent prehepatic inferior vena cava.

A 31‐year‐old man was referred for evaluation of a swelling in the buccal region of the maxillary left central and lateral incisors. Five years earlier, he had sustained trauma to the upper anterior teeth after being struck by a hard object. Until recently, the teeth had been asymptomatic, but over the past few weeks he noted a painless swelling that gradually enlarged and caused discomfort. He had no systemic illnesses and reported an allergy to penicillin.

On intraoral examination, there was a 2 × 2 cm fluctuant swelling of the labial mucosa extending from the left central to the left lateral incisor. The swelling was soft, nonmobile, nontender, and the overlying gingiva appeared normal. The affected teeth were slightly tender to percussion but showed no mobility. Thermal and electronic pulp tests elicited no response in the right central incisor, left central incisor, and left lateral incisor; all other anterior teeth responded normally.

A periapical radiograph demonstrated a well‐defined, unilocular, rounded radiolucency at the apices of the left central and left lateral incisors. Cone‐beam computed tomography confirmed extensive bone destruction measuring approximately 552 mm3, with loss of both buccal and palatal cortical plates, producing a through‐and‐through (“tunnel”) appearance. 

The differential diagnosis was (a) periapical granuloma (b) radicular cyst and (c) chronic apical periodontitis.

A 69-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of lower abdominal discomfort and difficulty passing urine, including poor stream, dysuria, and difficulty voiding. He was hemodynamically stable. Examination was unremarkable except for a tense, distended bladder extending to the umbilicus. A bladder scan showed a volume >999 mL. Digital rectal examination revealed a large prostate without suspicious features. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 95 g/L, white-cell count 21.5×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 265 mg/L, potassium 5.0 mmol/L, creatinine 699 μmol/L (baseline eGFR 28 mL/min), current eGFR 19 mL/min, and INR 7.2. His history included chronic renal failure, past renal stones, hypertension, left ventricular failure, atrial fibrillation on warfarin, hyperlipidemia, myocardial infarction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and ex-smoking. A noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a dilated right renal pelvis and proximal ureter with extravasation of urine into the retroperitoneum anterior to the psoas and perinephric fat stranding, consistent with ureteric perforation. There was no evidence of urolithiasis, and the left urinary tract appeared normal.

A 74-year-old man with a history of remote myocardial infarction presented to the emergency department with dizziness and palpitations. He denied chest pain. One week earlier, he had outpatient Holter monitoring for syncopal palpitations without a diagnosis. On arrival, his heart rate was 180 bpm and blood pressure 102/78 mmHg. Physical examination, including cardiovascular and respiratory systems, was unremarkable.

A 12-lead ECG showed a broad complex tachycardia with features suggestive of ventricular tachycardia. Intravenous adenosine (6 mg, 6 mg, 12 mg) via a large antecubital cannula produced no change in rate, and transient side effects confirmed successful administration. Intravenous amiodarone was started, but the patient’s blood pressure fell to 80/60 mmHg, necessitating synchronized DC cardioversion to sinus rhythm.

Two hours later, telemetry documented a recurrent broad complex tachycardia at similar rate but with a different QRS morphology. While he remained hemodynamically stable, a Valsalva manoeuvre was attempted and immediately terminated the tachycardia. Over the next 12 hours, multiple episodes of this second tachycardia occurred, each consistently terminated by Valsalva manoeuvre. Subsequent routine blood tests, including calcium, magnesium, and potassium, were within normal limits.

A 49-year-old Japanese man presented with a 2-year history of hoarseness without fever, odynophagia, weight loss, or dysphagia. He had no history of head and neck surgery but had diabetes mellitus (HbA1c, 6.1%) and untreated dental caries. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a surface-irregular mass on the anterior one-third of the left vocal cord; the remainder of the larynx and hypopharynx appeared normal. Neck examination showed no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, renal and liver function tests, were within normal limits. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C RNA were negative. Chest radiography was unremarkable. The patient subsequently underwent direct laryngoscopy and excision of the vocal cord mass.

A 25-year-old woman presented with acute pain in the right temporomandibular joint (TMJ) and severe restriction of mouth opening. She had no systemic illnesses or allergies and was taking oral contraceptives. Over the prior 5 years, she had undergone orthodontic treatment with removable and fixed appliances; bruxism had been managed with a night splint.

Three months before referral, she awoke with severe right TMJ pain and inability to close her mouth; self-repositioning produced a loud crack. Pain was 7/10 on a numeric scale. Methocarbamol and a night splint provided minimal relief, and physiotherapy worsened her symptoms. Active mouth opening was limited to 20 mm (passive, 30 mm) with intense pain.

On re-evaluation, pain worsened to 8/10; active opening remained 20 mm with a habitual deviation of the mandible to the left and protective abduction posture on the left. Lateral and protrusive movements of the mandible were severely painful and restricted; there was no crepitus. A panoramic radiograph had shown flattened condyles and slightly widened TMJ spaces bilaterally.

MRI of the TMJs revealed discrete erosion of the right mandibular condyle with bone marrow oedema, minor joint effusion, and anterior displacement of the right articular disc with suspected ligament tear; the left TMJ was unremarkable. The findings were interpreted as osteoarthritic changes of the right TMJ corresponding with constant pain.

Treatment with ibuprofen, a full-time lower-jaw splint, soft diet, and repeated splint adjustments failed. A switch to diclofenac provoked an allergic reaction. CBCT confirmed right condylar bone erosion. Mandibulo-maxillary fixation with elastic loops and later wire ligatures produced transient improvement. 

Rheumatologic evaluation showed a CRP of 0.60 mg/L, negative rheumatoid serology, and negative HLA-B27; estrogen levels were low and contraceptives were discontinued. An intra-articular cortisone injection into the right TMJ yielded modest improvement, with active opening increasing to 23 mm but persistent pain at maximal opening.

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 3-week history of gait disturbance, generalized weakness, blurred vision, and generalized tonic–clonic seizures. These symptoms were preceded by headaches for 6 months, treated symptomatically. She reported no fever, weight loss, night sweats, vomiting, trauma, or known tuberculosis exposure.

On examination, she appeared ill but was afebrile. Vital signs were: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 115/75 mmHg, pulse 99 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There was no lymphadenopathy. Neurologic examination showed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, intact speech, no meningism, increased tone in all extremities, and an ataxic gait.

Brain MRI revealed an irregular ring-enhancing lesion in the left cerebellum measuring 2.9 × 3.0 cm, with extensive surrounding vasogenic edema, mass effect on the brainstem, compression of the fourth ventricle, dilatation of the lateral and third ventricles, periventricular CSF extravasation, and restricted diffusion of the rim. These features were described as suggestive of pilocytic astrocytoma versus hemangioblastoma with moderate obstructive hydrocephalus.

The patient was treated with anticonvulsants, dexamethasone, and analgesics. She underwent ventriculoperitoneal shunting, which revealed clear CSF under high pressure. One week later, she underwent a suboccipital craniotomy and en bloc resection of the deep-seated left cerebellar lesion, which was sent for histopathological analysis.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of intermittent claudication that had worsened suddenly over the days before admission, accompanied by bilateral cyanosis of the toes. She rated her lower extremity pain as 10 out of 10. Her medical history was notable only for long-standing cigarette smoking; she denied diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and other comorbidities. On examination, both femoral and distal pulses were absent bilaterally, and a trophic ulcer with partial necrosis of the right hallux was present. Laboratory tests, including renal function, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the abdomen revealed an irregular, extensive, subtotal occlusive lesion of the infrarenal aorta.

A 77-year-old man was referred to dermatology for evaluation of right leg skin lesions 2 weeks after treatment for presumed lower-extremity cellulitis with oral cephalexin. He reported persistent right leg tenderness and generalized malaise. His medical history included progressive bilateral ulnar and median nerve neuropathy over several months and seropositive rheumatoid arthritis of 13 years’ duration, managed with hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and prednisone. 

On examination, the right lower leg had scattered inflamed, tender nodules; the left medial calf showed a well-demarcated indurated inflammatory plaque with desquamation. Additionally, there were faintly erythematous, ill-defined macules and papules on the flanks and abdomen. 

Skin biopsies of the lower-extremity lesions were stained with hematoxylin–eosin, Brown–Hopps, Fite, and Gomori methenamine silver. Results demonstrated lymphohistiocytic and granulomatous inflammation with areas of neutrophils and numerous acid-fast bacilli, suggesting a mycobacterial infection with a type 2 reaction. Tissue PCR testing was negative for tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium complex. 

When the patient returned after completing 14 days of cephalexin, the leg lesions had improved, but violaceous papules on the back persisted. He also reported worsening fatigue, weight loss, progressive peripheral neuropathy, and flares of his arthritis. A repeat skin biopsy from the low back again showed findings consistent with a mycobacterial infection.

A 54-year-old man presented with two months of gradually progressive left hip pain, worse with prolonged walking and stair climbing and relieved by rest. He had no history of trauma, alcohol use, steroid intake, systemic illness, or prior hip pathology. On examination, flexion and internal rotation of the left hip were restricted at end range by pain, and there was tenderness over the anterior joint line. Plain radiographs of the pelvis and hips were unremarkable. His Harris hip score was 48, with pain as the predominant limiting factor. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left hip revealed a subchondral, discontinuous, serpiginous radiolucent line parallel to the articular surface that was hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, with adjacent T2 hyperintensity due to marrow edema. Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry showed osteopenia (average T score –1.4), and serum vitamin D₃ was 8 ng/mL.

A 32-year-old man with a history of neurofibromatosis type 2 presented with a painless swelling on the left side of his neck that had been gradually increasing in size over one year. On examination, there was a soft, spherical, nonpulsatile, nontransilluminant, nontender mass in the left anterior triangle, freely mobile relative to overlying skin and underlying structures.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a well-defined isodense, nonenhancing mass in the left lateral neck, abutting the left lateral wall of the trachea and oesophagus medially, the carotid sheath laterally, and the vertebral body posteriorly, with no vertebral bony defects.  

MRI of the neck revealed the lesion to be hyperintense on T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and fat-saturated sequences, suggesting a proteinaceous or hemorrhagic component. On axial T2-weighted images, the mass exhibited a small beak-like extension toward the esophagus, leading to a radiologic impression of an esophageal duplication cyst.

A 27-year-old man with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia presented with acute worsening of low back pain. While traveling abroad, he had been hospitalized for severe anemia and managed with subcutaneous morphine and two units of packed red cells. After discharge, he experienced recurrence of back pain but denied similar prior episodes, personal or family bleeding disorders, falls or trauma, fever, abdominal pain, and motor or sensory deficits; bowel and bladder function remained intact. Two days after symptom onset, examination revealed a positive straight-leg–raising test on the right and hepatosplenomegaly. He was referred for an MRI of the spine as an outpatient but returned a few hours later with severe pain radiating to the right groin and thigh. 

On admission, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable but lay in bed with the right leg flexed. There was tender fullness over the right iliac crest region and right upper gluteal area; passive motion of the hip aggravated the pain, and no focal neurologic deficits were noted.

Initial laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 2.4×10^3/μL, a platelet count of 110×10^3/μL, and a hemoglobin concentration of 6.5 g/dL. The INR was 1.5, the aPTT 41 seconds, the D-dimer 0.98 mg/L FEU, and the fibrinogen concentration 5.3 g/L. A clotting-factor assay revealed a factor VII level of 25%. Biochemical studies showed indirect hyperbilirubinemia and an AST level of 45 U/L. He was receiving regular red-cell transfusions and deferasirox; his most recent serum ferritin level was 3247 ng/mL, and an MRI-based liver-iron concentration, measured five months earlier, was 39.9 mg/g of dry liver.

An MRI of the pelvis was obtained.

A 37-year-old woman with a history of hypothyroidism and class III obesity (BMI 42.2 kg/m2) underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy under standard thromboprophylaxis (compression stockings, 5000 IU heparin preoperatively and enoxaparin 60 mg subcutaneously 6 h after surgery). She ambulated on postoperative day 1. That morning, shortly after standing, she fainted and was found to be tachycardic (140 bpm) and hypotensive (systolic pressure 80 mmHg). The Jackson-Pratt drain showed no blood. After initial resuscitation, the leading diagnostic considerations were myocardial infarction, anastomotic leakage, and pulmonary embolism. 
Abdominopelvic ultrasonography showed minimal free fluid in the abdominal cavity. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a dilated right ventricle and atrium with a pulmonary acceleration time of 60 msec.

A 75-year-old Japanese woman presented with progressive dyspnea and back pain after eating for 2 months. Her past surgical history included an open appendectomy at age 17 and a laparotomy for adhesive small-bowel obstruction at age 69; there was no history of upper abdominal surgery or trauma. On examination, she was 155.2 cm tall, weighed 53.0 kg (BMI 22.0), and had lower abdominal surgical scars. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. A chest radiograph revealed gas-filled loops of bowel in the left hemithorax. Computed tomography showed prolapse of the stomach, small intestine, colon, pancreas, and spleen into the left thoracic cavity above the diaphragm, with marked compression of the left lung, leading to the diagnosis of a diaphragmatic hernia such as a para-esophageal hiatal hernia or Bochdalek hernia.

An 8-month-old boy was brought for evaluation of his right eye, which had never opened since birth. Three months earlier the parents noted a gradually enlarging swelling beneath the right lower lid that protruded more with coughing. On examination, the right lower lid was everted with exposure keratinization of the palpebral conjunctiva, mild redness, and occasional discharge. The left eye was normal on external inspection but showed an inferior key-hole iris coloboma and chorioretinal coloboma on indirect ophthalmoscopy. An orbital ultrasound A+B-scan of the right eye revealed no identifiable intraocular structures but demonstrated a cystic (hyperechoic) space in the orbit. The left eye ultrasound confirmed the known coloboma. Multidetector CT of the orbits showed a small right globe, a dysplastic right optic nerve, and a nonenhancing intraorbital cyst; there was no intracranial communication or extension.

A 37-year-old Ethiopian woman presented with 4 hours of severe colicky abdominal pain, frequent bilious vomiting, and abdominal distention. She is HIV-positive on HAART for 6 years, with no known baseline CD4 count or viral load. She denied prior surgery, trauma, or tuberculosis treatment.  
On examination, she appeared acutely ill and intermittently distressed by pain. Vital signs were: temperature 36.5 °C, pulse 100 beats/minute, blood pressure 90/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths/minute. She had dry mucous membranes. The abdomen was slightly distended, with generalized tenderness, guarding, and rigidity; bowel sounds were hypoactive. Digital rectal examination revealed stool on the examining finger; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 18,400 per microliter (87.7% neutrophils), hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, and platelet count 329,000 per microliter; electrolytes and organ function tests were normal.  
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple dilated small-bowel loops and free fluid in the pouch of Morrison and the vesical spaces. A plain abdominal radiograph showed dilated small-bowel loops with a few centrally located air-fluid levels.  
She was diagnosed with acute small-bowel obstruction with peritonitis, presumed secondary to gangrenous small-bowel volvulus. After fluid resuscitation and nasogastric decompression, surgery was offered; however, it was delayed by 13 hours due to the patient’s initial refusal. When she later consented, she was taken for emergency laparotomy.

A 59-year-old Caucasian man with a 2-year history of genetically confirmed HFE C282Y homozygous hereditary hemochromatosis presented for clinical and therapeutic evaluation.
