His past medical history was notable for metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, autoimmune hypothyroidism, and severe chondrocalcinosis. He reported recurrent headaches but denied neurological symptoms and had no family history of neurological disease.

On examination, he was overweight (BMI 27) with mild hepatomegaly; a neurological examination disclosed only a mild right-sided hypokinetic-rigid syndrome. Laboratory studies showed: 
• Complete blood count normal except platelets 144,000/mm3 (reference 150–450,000/mm3)  
• Ferritin 4728 ng/ml (25–300), serum iron 282 μg/dl (50–150), transferrin saturation 90%  
• AST 55 U/L, ALT 103 U/L; normal bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, GGT  
• Negative markers of inflammation and hemolysis; normal renal function; normal vitamin D-PTH axis  
• Ceruloplasmin 21 mg/dl (20–60) with normal plasma and urine copper; no Kayser-Fleischer rings  

Abdominal ultrasound and elastography showed diffuse steatosis and severe fibrosis (F4). Liver MRI revealed severe siderosis; biopsy confirmed hepatocellular iron overload and NASH. Heart MRI documented mild iron overload. Genetic testing for other HH genes (TFR2, SLC40A1, HJV, HAMP) was negative.

A prior brain MRI performed for headache demonstrated bilateral hypointensities on T2* gradient-echo and T2-weighted images within the globus pallidus, substantia nigra, dentate nuclei, and left pulvinar, which were interpreted as cerebral siderosis. To further characterize these findings, a noncontrast brain CT was obtained.

A 4.5-month-old Caucasian boy was admitted with a 2-week history of fever following vaccination and 5 days of jaundice and drowsiness. Parents noted abdominal distension since birth. He was the only child of first cousins and had normal growth parameters at birth; weight at 4 months was 8500 g, dropping to 8000 g at admission. There was no history of vomiting, diarrhea, or neurologic symptoms. On examination, he was pale, icteric, and mildly tachypneic, with severe abdominal distension and palpable hepatomegaly and splenomegaly; there was no rash or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests on admission revealed: hemoglobin 7.6 g/dl, platelets 65 × 10^9/l, white cells 7050/µl, neutrophils 3730/µl; total bilirubin 7.2 mg/dl (direct 5.8 mg/dl); AST 2930 U/l, ALT 603 U/l; PT 35 s, PTT 100 s; albumin 2.8 g/dl; triglycerides 1110 mg/dl; ferritin 5370 ng/ml. Peripheral blood smear demonstrated a lymphocyte with cytoplasmic vacuolation. Testing for Epstein–Barr virus and cytomegalovirus by PCR and blood cultures were negative. Echocardiography and renal artery sonography were normal. Bone marrow aspiration was nonspecific.

A 12-year-old girl presented with 3 days of high spiking fevers (103°F), headache, body aches, and 1 day of an itchy rash. She had no bleeding, urinary, or respiratory symptoms and no known allergen exposures. Her past history was notable only for simple febrile convulsions. On examination, she was febrile, with cervical lymphadenopathy and an urticarial rash over her trunk and limbs that shifted distribution with each fever spike. Her pulse was 92/min, BP 100/70 mmHg, and extremities were warm. Respiratory, neurological, and abdominal examinations were normal.

Initial laboratory studies showed WBC 5,580/mm3 (85% neutrophils), platelets 116,000/mm3, CRP 161 mg/L, and ESR 40 mm in the first hour. She was treated empirically for viral fever and possible dengue, and she received IV cefotaxime when high fevers persisted. 

On illness Day 4, she developed nonpurulent conjunctivitis, periorbital edema, hypotension, and tachycardia, necessitating ICU admission and two inotropes for 3 days; urine output remained normal. Abdominal ultrasound revealed bilateral pleural effusions and moderate ascites without hepatosplenomegaly. Liver enzymes were elevated (ALT 86 U/L, AST 115 U/L) and bilirubin was 12 mg/dL; hypoalbuminemia was noted. Blood cultures were sterile. Serologic tests for measles, leptospirosis, rubella, dengue, Epstein–Barr virus, influenza PCR, and ANA were all negative. CRP peaked at 289 mg/L on Day 5 and fell to 9.2 mg/L by Day 16; ferritin on Day 10 was 694.5 ng/mL.

Initial differential diagnoses included viral myocarditis, systemic lupus erythematosus, toxic shock syndrome, Scarlet fever, systemic onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, and atypical Kawasaki disease.

A 70-year-old nonsmoking woman with hypertension and parkinsonism was struck by a taxi, sustaining a left tibial plateau fracture (AO/OTA type 41B2, Schatzker type III). Preoperative echocardiography showed normal ventricular function without a septal defect. Two days later, she underwent open reduction and internal fixation with an allograft and locking plate under epidural anesthesia. The postoperative course was uneventful, and she was discharged with a long leg splint. On the 10th postoperative day, turbid discharge from a reddened surgical wound prompted initiation of intravenous antibiotics for wound infection. Shortly thereafter, her consciousness acutely changed from clear to unresponsive (GCS E4V1M1), with dullness, muteness, and nearly quadriplegia. Her respiratory rate was 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, blood pressure 195/110 mmHg, and heart rate 115 bpm; she was initially afebrile. Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein, anemia, mild renal impairment, low fibrinogen, and elevated fibrin degradation products and D-dimer. Chest radiography and brain computed tomography were unremarkable. Brain magnetic resonance imaging performed three hours after loss of consciousness revealed multiple tiny foci of high signal intensity on diffusion-weighted imaging at the cortex of the bilateral frontal and right parietal lobes. Based on the images, which involved the bilateral hemispheres, septic emboli or cerebral fat embolism were considered.

A 73-year-old man was referred for surgical consultation regarding progressive erectile dysfunction. His history was notable for type 2 diabetes and Peyronie’s disease treated 32 years earlier with plaque excision and a dermal penile skin graft. He reported a non-tender, rapidly growing mass in the distal penile shaft that prevented use of a vacuum erection device. He denied pain, erythema, drainage, or ulceration.

On examination, there was a well-healed scar and a 3 cm firm nodule on the left lateral distal shaft, with moderate corporal fibrosis. No signs of infection were present. 

Pelvic MRI without contrast revealed a 2.4 × 2.8 × 4.1 cm rim-enhancing, hemorrhagic-appearing mass without internal solid components, abutting and mildly compressing the left corpus cavernosum; the tunica albuginea was intact but thickened, and the right corpus cavernosum and corpus spongiosum were normal. 

Penile duplex ultrasound after intracavernosal alprostadil injection demonstrated a 4 cm mass with complex internal echoes and no Doppler flow, causing compression of the adjacent corpora and mild leftward deviation. Mid-shaft plaque without calcification was also noted. 

Given the persistent curvature, erectile dysfunction refractory to medical therapy, and the penile mass, the patient elected excision of the mass.

A 43-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 20-day history of insidious onset of progressive numbness of the left lower extremity and weakness of the right lower extremity. He had two episodes of urinary incontinence and at the time of evaluation he could not walk without assistance. He denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, or trauma.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. Mental status, cranial nerves, and upper extremities were normal. In the right lower extremity, there was hyperreflexia, 2/5 strength in all muscle groups, decreased sensation to mild palpation, vibration, and position, and a positive Babinski sign. On the left, motor strength was full, but sensation to noxious stimulation was decreased from the T4 dermatome to the plantar surface of the foot.

A non-contrasted CT scan of the brain was normal. MRI of the thoracic spine revealed a contrast-enhancing intramedullary mass extending from C7 to T1, measuring 33 × 12 mm.

The initial differential diagnosis included astrocytoma and ependymoma.

A 33-year-old man was referred urgently with severe retrosternal chest pressure and dyspnea that began two hours earlier, on a background of intermittent chest pain over two weeks. He has no history of hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, smoking, recreational drug use, or family history of cardiac disease. Physical examination: BMI 27, afebrile, blood pressure 141/81 mmHg (equal in both arms), heart rate 62 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Chest clear, no jugular venous distention, heart sounds normal without murmurs. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V6 consistent with an anterolateral STEMI. Initial labs: creatinine 74 μg/mL, normal CBC and coagulation studies, alkaline phosphatase 154 U/L, ALT 39 U/L, AST 72 U/L, CK-MB mass 13 ng/mL, troponin 0.1 ng/mL, normal lipid panel, urinalysis with proteinuria. Hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. HIV antibody test was positive; CD4+ count was 643 cells/μL.

A previously healthy full-term 6-month-old male infant was brought to the Emergency Department with an 8-hour history of not moving his right arm and marked fussiness. He had been behaving normally until a brief unsupervised period when the babysitter discovered he would not move his right arm. On arrival, his heart rate was 169 beats per minute; other vital signs were normal. He could move all extremities except the right upper extremity, which had a visible deformity; the neurologic examination was otherwise normal. Radiographs of the right arm showed an acute spiral right humeral fracture and healed fractures of the right mid-radius and ulna. This prompted a comprehensive child abuse workup. A skeletal survey demonstrated thickened cortices in the midshafts of the left humerus, radius, and ulna with subtle cortical irregularity, suggestive of healed fractures. Computed tomography of the head was negative, and dilated funduscopic examination showed no retinal hemorrhages. Four days before presentation, the infant had fallen from his bed onto carpeted flooring, cried briefly, and returned to baseline; a similar fall months earlier had caused no injury. Development was appropriate. There was no family history of fractures, bone or connective tissue disorders, bleeding disorders, or domestic violence. Laboratory studies revealed normal serum calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, copper, ceruloplasmin, parathyroid hormone, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, free thyroxine, and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels; a urine drug screen was negative. Genetic testing for osteogenesis imperfecta (COL1A1 and COL1A2) was performed and returned negative.

A 66-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presented with chronic epigastric abdominal pain, subjective fever, nausea, and vomiting over the last several months. The patient, who speaks only Haitian Creole, was taking amlodipine. An abdominal ultrasound showed no intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilatation but revealed a dilated common bile duct measuring 8 mm at the porta hepatis and a calcified mass in the gallbladder fossa. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 10 cm lesion with both cystic and solid components arising in the gallbladder fossa, with possible invasion of the gastric antrum. Laboratory testing showed a white-cell count of 12.85 × 10^3/μL (neutrophils 8.69 × 10^3/μL), alkaline phosphatase 127 U/L, AST 45 U/L, ALT 31 U/L, glucose 431 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1c 14.5%. HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis A tests were negative. Tumor markers including CEA, AFB, and CA19-9 were within normal limits. Blood cultures at 72 hours were negative for bacteria and fungus. Hematology-oncology, surgery, and infectious disease teams were consulted. Surgery was deferred due to extension of the mass into the duodenum and stomach. The patient was started on piperacillin–tazobactam, hydralazine, insulin, ketorolac, morphine, and acetaminophen.

A 36-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented to the psychiatry emergency room accompanied by his wife for psychiatric evaluation. He was disoriented, agitated, restless, and unable to participate in the interview. Vital signs revealed a pulse rate of 104 bpm; oxygen saturation was normal on admission. Examination showed a flushed face, runny nose, goose flesh, pinpoint pupils, mild hand tremors, joint rubbing, and incessant yawning. He denied gastrointestinal symptoms and substance use. His wife reported he had been taking unspecified shoulder pain medications and noted “weird” behavior over the past six months, including falling asleep unexpectedly. Collateral from his PCP revealed a history of heroin addiction, initiation of methadone maintenance (40 mg daily) five months prior, and ongoing heroin use despite methadone noncompliance. Urine toxicology was positive for opiates and negative for methadone. His Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale score was 19/47, consistent with moderate opioid withdrawal. He was admitted to the medical floor for methadone tapering. The neurology team was consulted for persistent altered mentation, with consideration of blood–brain barrier damage from chronic heroin use versus hypoxic encephalopathy; over the first three days he had three episodes of hypoxia (lowest saturation, 92%). A head CT without contrast showed physiologic calcifications in the pineal and choroid plexus and marked diffuse white matter abnormalities in both cerebral hemispheres and the cerebellum. Five days later, brain MRI revealed a constellation of findings highly suggestive of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

A 37-year-old woman presented with severe bilateral flank pain for 2 weeks. Her history was notable for systemic lupus erythematosus, hypertension, and membranous nephropathy complicated by left and right renal vein thromboses 9 and 5 months earlier. On arrival she was hemodynamically stable but hypertensive (167/85 mm Hg). Physical examination revealed left costovertebral-angle tenderness without other abnormalities. Laboratory evaluation showed a serum creatinine of 0.48 mg/dL, proteinuria, and an otherwise unremarkable renal panel. A comprehensive autoimmune workup (anti-dsDNA, ANCA, antihistone, antiphospholipid antibodies, CRP, ESR, complement) was negative.

An outside single-venous-phase contrast-enhanced CT scan was interpreted as right hydronephrosis. A multiphasic CT performed on admission demonstrated a fluid-density structure encasing the calyces on the excretory (delayed) phase, with normal-caliber calyces containing excreted contrast. Comparison with imaging one month earlier showed no interval change. A MAG3 renal function study revealed symmetric normal flow and function without evidence of obstruction. MRI of the right kidney showed a T2-hyperintense peripelvic and perinephric fluid signal encasing the calyces, with no arterial enhancement on postcontrast T1 and minimal delayed enhancement at 10 minutes.

A 28-year-old man from Bangladesh, previously healthy, presented with a 7-day history of right knee pain unresponsive to NSAIDs and without fever. On day 3, he developed swelling and difficulty walking due to restricted knee motion. He denied animal contact, unpasteurized‐milk consumption, trauma, or rash, and no other joints were affected. 

On examination, he was afebrile and normotensive. His right knee was tender, warm, and swollen with a reduced range of motion; other joints were normal. 

Laboratory studies on admission showed: WBC 7.8×10^3/µL; hemoglobin 14.4 g/dL; platelets 189×10^3/µL; neutrophils 72.1%; lymphocytes 15.1%; ESR 24 mm/h; CRP 175.6 mg/dL. Blood tests for autoimmune markers, including rheumatoid factor, were negative; serologic tests for Treponema pallidum and Neisseria species were also negative.

Imaging of the right knee included a normal AP radiograph and ultrasound revealing a large joint effusion with internal septations. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no vegetations and an ejection fraction of 57%, to exclude infective endocarditis.

Arthrocentesis yielded turbid, light-yellow fluid. Analysis revealed lactate 12.8 mmol/L, total nucleated cell count 18 500/µL (55% neutrophils), and 2250 RBC/µL.

A 42-year-old man with 30 pack-years of smoking, cannabis use, alcohol dependence, and the use of herbal products for addiction cessation presented with a 3-day history of acute urinary retention, hematemesis, and progressive neurological deficits. On day 3, he developed marked paraparesis of the lower limbs (muscle strength 2/5), was unable to stand or walk, and had hyperreflexia with sustained clonus in the lower extremities. Sensory function—including proprioception, light touch, and vibration—was normal. He also had hypertonic sphincters and hyperalgesia. Cranial nerve and upper limb examinations were normal. He was febrile, and his condition deteriorated into respiratory distress requiring intubation and sedation.

Lumbar puncture revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid without albuminocytologic dissociation: glucose 0.49 g/L, protein 0.20 g/L, chloride 121 mmol/L, 14 white blood cells (70% lymphocytes), and 14 red blood cells per mm³; cultures were sterile. Blood tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL falling to 8.2 g/dL), leukocytosis (18 350 cells/μL), platelet counts fluctuating between 98 000 and 136 000 cells/μL, hyponatremia corrected from 117.5 mEq/L to 146 mEq/L over 8 days, potassium levels between 5.5 and 4.6 mEq/L, elevated AST (134 U/L) and ALT (65.9 U/L), and CRP 128.8–131.2 mg/L. Renal function remained normal.

Initial brain MRI showed multiple bilateral, symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the periventricular and periaqueductal regions, dorsomedial thalami, medial temporal lobes, caudate nuclei, and brainstem, with diffusion restriction and low ADC values. Spinal MRI demonstrated diffuse T2 hyperintensities throughout the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar cord. A follow-up MRI a few days later revealed worsening of these lesions, new involvement of the lenticular nuclei, and patchy contrast enhancement in the cerebral peduncles, superior cerebellar peduncles, superior colliculi, right pons, and bilateral medulla. There was more extensive bilateral FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes and periventricular white matter and progression of the spinal cord lesions.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed lymphadenopathy in the bilateral cervical and axillary regions, left inguinal lymphadenopathy, and marked peri- and pararenal soft-tissue infiltration.

A 28‐year‐old man (ASA physical status 1) underwent elective laparoscopic right inguinal hernia repair under general anesthesia. He had no significant medical history. Preoperative vital signs were normal. After induction with propofol, fentanyl, and cisatracurium, and antibiotic prophylaxis with cefazolin, two ultrasound‐guided nerve blocks were performed. Thirty minutes later, pneumoperitoneum was established with CO2 at an intra‐abdominal pressure of 18–20 mmHg. Ventilation was set to a tidal volume of 400 mL at 14 breaths per minute, and initial EtCO2 was 32 mmHg.

Over the next hour, EtCO2 rose gradually to 60 mmHg despite increasing the respiratory rate to 25 bpm, raising fresh‐gas flow to 15 L/min, and delivering 100% FiO2. The anesthesia circuit, CO2 absorber, water trap, and filter were changed. Core temperature remained normal, and there was no masseter rigidity. After surgical desufflation, palpation revealed subcutaneous crepitus extending to the neck. An arterial blood gas sample showed pH 7.23, PaCO2 56.1 mmHg, HCO3– 23.2 mmol/L, and PaO2 524 mmHg.

Fifteen minutes later, EtCO2 decreased to 45 mmHg. At the end of the 4‐hour procedure, the patient was awake, hemodynamically stable, and EtCO2 was below 45 mmHg. A bedside lung ultrasound was performed, and then a chest radiograph showed gas in the subcutaneous tissues of the chest wall and root of the neck but no evidence of pneumothorax or gas in the mediastinum.

A 43-year-old man with a history of migraine (untreated) presented 2 hours after the sudden onset of diplopia, speech alteration, and decreased level of consciousness with marked fluctuations. He denied exposure to toxins. On examination, he had right-sided hemiparesis, binocular strabismus with impaired convergence and vertical eye movements, nonreactive miotic pupils, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score that fluctuated between 8 and 10. Routine laboratory studies, including toxicology and drug screens, were normal. A noncontrast head CT showed no hemorrhage or early ischemic changes.

A 35-year-old man was referred for painful, firm, immobile nodules with low-volume pus discharge along a surgical scar on the dorsum of his left hand. He reported a tumoral swelling in the second metacarpal area of the same hand for 12 months, which had gradually enlarged and restricted index-finger movement. Six months earlier, an orthopedic surgeon had excised the lesion, after which he felt completely improved and did not pursue follow-up. Four months postoperatively, small painful, immobile ulcerated nodules with minimal discharge developed along the surgical scar. He works as an electrical technician, with no obvious history of trauma or other medical problems. On examination, the dorsum of the left hand was swollen, and tender immobile nodules with crusted ulcerations and scant discharge were palpable along the scar. Hematological and biochemical tests were normal, and hand radiographs showed no abnormalities. An incisional biopsy of the nodules was performed.

An 8-year-old boy presented with a 2-year history of intermittent swelling on the right side of his neck. The swelling had an insidious onset and gradually increased, becoming more prominent during prolonged speaking, crying, or straining. He denied voice changes, chronic cough, difficulty breathing or swallowing, trauma, or prior surgery.

On examination at rest, there was a small, soft tissue swelling in the lower third of the right neck, anteromedial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. With the Valsalva maneuver, the swelling became markedly larger and fusiform in shape. The mass was soft, compressible, non-tender, non-pulsatile, and non-transilluminant. Fibreoptic laryngoscopy showed no abnormalities in the larynx or hypopharynx.

A neck radiograph demonstrated a well-defined soft tissue swelling on the right side without air, calcification, or phlebolith. Ultrasonography revealed mild prominence of the right internal jugular vein at rest, which increased markedly during Valsalva, with turbulence on color and spectral Doppler. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck confirmed mild dilation of the right internal jugular vein at rest and fusiform dilatation measuring 24 by 35 mm during Valsalva, extending from the C4 level to the clavicle (approximately 7 cm). On Valsalva, the entire right internal jugular vein and ipsilateral sigmoid and transverse sinuses were markedly prominent compared to the left. Screening CT of the brain was otherwise normal.

A 61-year-old man with atrial fibrillation and stented ischemic heart disease, treated with rivaroxaban, clopidogrel, metoprolol, candesartan, and atorvastatin/ezetimibe, presented with sudden intense cervico-thoracic pain and intermittent paresthesia of both hands. The pain began at rest and worsened with neck extension; he denied thoracic or abdominal pain. Vital signs were blood pressure 143/100 mmHg bilaterally, heart rate 103 bpm, respiratory rate 15/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and temperature 36.8°C. Neurologic examination showed lower-limb weakness (right M2 proximal, M1 distal; left M4 proximal, M2 distal), right-greater-than-left lower-limb hypoesthesia, left upper-limb hypoesthesia, and bilateral Babinski signs. ECG showed sinus rhythm without signs of acute ischemia. Laboratory tests revealed normal leukocytes, platelets, hemoglobin, electrolytes, and CRP; creatinine was 121 µmol/L. Coagulation studies showed PT 61% (INR 1.2) and PTT 41 seconds. Contrast-enhanced cervico-thoraco-abdominal CT angiography demonstrated a posterior cervical epidural mass from C5 to T1 measuring 7.5 cm by 7 mm with a “spot sign,” indicating focal contrast extravasation. MRI of the cervical and upper thoracic spine revealed a posterior epidural lesion from C2 to T5 compressing the spinal cord at C6–C7, isointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense with hypointense foci on T2-weighted images, and showing a blooming artifact on GRE sequences.

A 4-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of microcephaly and visual impairment. Prenatal ultrasound in the third trimester documented microcephaly, confirmed at birth with a head circumference of 29.5 cm (39 weeks + 5 days). Birth weight and length were normal. Amniocentesis results included negative CMV DNA, normal aneuploidy screening, and normal comparative genomic hybridization array. Brain MRI demonstrated a reduced skull-to-face ratio and simplified gyral pattern consistent with microcephaly.
At 3 months of age, ophthalmologic examination revealed a superotemporal lens opacity outside the visual axis, nystagmus, and large-angle alternating esotropia with cross-fixation; ocular motility was otherwise normal. Funduscopic examination showed a pale optic disc and retinal pigmentary changes. On subsequent examinations, the fundus exhibited a “salt and pepper” appearance with well-demarcated, rounded atrophic areas resembling retinal lacunae.

A 32-year-old woman presented with an isolated swelling in the right thigh that had grown gradually over 3 years. She reported mild right leg pain worsened by movement. She had close contact with dogs and cats and lived in a low–socioeconomic‐status area of northern Afghanistan. There was no history of surgery or trauma to the legs. She was afebrile and in good general health. On examination, a 10 cm × 6 cm mass was palpable on the anterolateral right upper thigh; it was superficial, soft in nature, immobile, non-tender, and had well-defined margins. There were no overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory findings were normal. Thigh ultrasonography revealed a well-defined cystic lesion in the anterolateral upper thigh with internal daughter cysts, measuring 8.5 cm × 4.1 cm. The sonographic features were suggestive of an intramuscular hydatid cyst.

A 57-year-old man was admitted after sustaining blunt abdominal trauma when his right flank struck a motorcycle in two separate incidents. On arrival, his blood pressure was 95/60 mm Hg, heart rate 90 beats per minute, and he was afebrile. He reported right flank pain and had minor abrasions over that area; he had no significant past medical history. Laboratory studies revealed a red blood cell count of 4 100 000 /µL, hemoglobin 10 g/dL, platelet count 160 000 /µL, blood urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed >150 red blood cells and 1 to 2 white blood cells per high-power field. Other laboratory values were within normal limits. Renal ultrasonography demonstrated disruption of the lower pole of the right kidney with a surrounding hematoma but no detectable abnormal shunt flow. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a grade IV right renal injury with a deep laceration extending to the hilum and a large perirenal hematoma. Additionally, there was a mass-like structure in the renal hilum region that showed avid enhancement in the arterial phase with washout in the venous and delayed phases, raising suspicion for a renal tumor.

A 53-year-old African-American woman with no prior medical history presented with progressive nausea and vomiting. Over the preceding month, she had experienced fatigue, headaches, intermittent vertigo, tinnitus, and ataxia, and she reported an unintentional 30-pound weight loss over 4 months. On neurologic examination, she had right gaze-evoked nystagmus, postural instability, and an unsteady shuffling gait. Fundoscopic, respiratory, and other systemic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal biochemistry, normal C-reactive protein, normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and a serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level of 51 U/L (reference range 12–60 U/L). 

Noncontrast brain CT revealed marked dilation of all four ventricles. Brain MRI demonstrated patency of the cerebral aqueduct and ruled out cerebral or subarachnoid mass lesions, consistent with communicating hydrocephalus. Lumbar puncture yielded clear cerebrospinal fluid with lymphodominant pleocytosis, an elevated protein concentration of 104 mg/dL, markedly decreased glucose of 21 mg/dL, and a normal opening pressure. Chest CT showed bilateral thoracic lymphadenopathy.

A 64-year-old man with no notable medical history was referred for fever and visual disturbances. Six days before admission, he developed fever and a nonproductive cough. Four days later, he noticed a central black spot in both visual fields. An ophthalmic evaluation revealed bilateral central scotomata and exudative retinal detachment on optical coherence tomography, with a normal fundus examination.

On admission, his temperature was 38.7 °C, blood pressure 108/78 mmHg, pulse 100 /min, respiratory rate 30 /min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. He reported mild headache, confusion, diarrhoea, urinary incontinence, and a persistent round yellowish lesion in his central vision. Breath sounds were diminished over the right lower lung field. He was disoriented to place; other neurologic findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (12.8 × 10^9/L) with 93.8% neutrophils, elevated C-reactive protein (31.91 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (1.30 ng/mL), hyponatremia (131 mmol/L), mildly elevated creatinine (1.12 mg/dL), elevated AST (152 U/L), ALT (222 U/L), and LDH (479 U/L). Urinalysis demonstrated microscopic haematuria and proteinuria without leukocyturia.

Given the fever, headache, confusion, and visual symptoms, a lumbar puncture and neuroimaging were performed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed protein 55.7 mg/dL, normal cell count, and glucose 92 mg/dL. Brain MRI revealed no mass lesions, inflammatory changes, or acute ischemia. Chest radiography showed right lower lung–field infiltrates, and chest CT demonstrated consolidation in the right lower lobe.

A 33-year-old woman presented with fever, chills, and a persistent mass in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. Twenty days earlier, she had undergone incision and drainage for presumed mastitis; the wound failed to heal and discharged pus. She had no history of tuberculosis, diabetes, or breast cancer. She was married, had a 3-year-old child, and was breastfeeding. Vital signs: temperature 38°C, pulse 89/min, blood pressure 126/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 19/min. Examination revealed a 5×6 cm firm mass with an erythematous open 1.5×1.5 cm wound discharging brownish fluid in the left upper outer quadrant. Dark reddish plaques were noted over both lower legs and the dorsum of the feet. Laboratory tests: WBC 11.8×10^3/µL (77.3% neutrophils), platelets 418×10^3/µL, CRP 4.9 mg/dL, ESR 56 mm/h; blood cultures were negative. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Breast ultrasound showed a 5×5 cm irregular, hypoechoic heterogeneous mass with an ipsilateral axillary lymph node. Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy demonstrated chronic mastitis with granulation tissue and numerous foreign-body giant cells but no evidence of malignancy.

An 11-year-old boy was evaluated for a 6-week history of right cheek pain. His past medical history included allergic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis, treated until 3 months earlier. Six weeks ago, he had high fever, sore throat, and right cheek pain with mild swelling; a rapid strep test was positive, and amoxicillin led to initial improvement. Four weeks later, the cheek pain recurred with mild tenderness and swelling. Head CT revealed mild mucosal thickening and effusion in both sinuses, and a course of cefditoren was given without relief. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was tenderness over the right cheek in the distribution of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve without hyperalgesia. Neurologic and oral examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Empiric clarithromycin for presumed sinusitis did not alleviate the pain. Brain MRI showed no evidence of neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve.

An 82-year-old man (BMI 20.3 kg/m2) being treated for Mycobacterium avium complex since 2018 presented with rapidly progressive vision loss in his right eye over one week. His regimen included amikacin liposomal nebulizer 590 mg/day, azithromycin 250 mg/day, rifampin 300 mg twice daily, and ethambutol 900 mg/day (started June 2018 with no dose adjustments). His medical history included hypertension, bilateral age-related macular degeneration, and prior retinal detachment; he had no tobacco or recreational drug use and drank one alcoholic beverage per week.

On initial examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye (previously 20/25 OU). Pupils were equal and reactive; intraocular pressure was normal OU. Four days later, visual acuity was counting fingers at 6 ft OD and 20/40 OS; confrontational visual fields and extraocular movements were full OU. He was referred to neuro-ophthalmology.

One week later, visual acuity had worsened to counting fingers at 1 ft OD and 20/50 OS, with a right relative afferent pupillary defect. Color vision was 2/14 OD and 1/14 OS, and funduscopic exam showed trace nerve pallor OD > OS. Humphrey visual field testing showed borderline‐reliability defects in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated borderline optic nerve thickness in the right eye (79 µm) and full thickness in the left eye (95 µm), with baseline macular ganglion cell layer measurements obtained. Brain MRI showed no evidence of intracranial infection.

A 15-year-old Caucasian female was admitted with a 6-month history of progressive postprandial epigastric discomfort, nausea, vomiting (relieved by emesis), and weight loss. She appeared pale, dehydrated, and at the lower limit of her growth curve (weight 46 kg, height 150 cm). Vital signs were temperature 36.9 °C, heart rate 83 bpm, respiratory rate 21 breaths/min, and blood pressure 98/59 mm Hg. She had no prior surgeries, no medications, and no known medical or intellectual disabilities.

On examination, she had halitosis and a mobile palpable mass measuring approximately 25 × 9 cm between the xiphoid and umbilicus. Bowel sounds were normal, with no guarding or peritonitis. Digital rectal examination was normal. Cardiopulmonary and urogenital exams were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed anemia (hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL, hematocrit 25.1%); all other values including white cells, platelets, electrolytes, renal and liver tests, and C-reactive protein were within normal limits.

An abdominal X-ray was non-diagnostic. Ultrasound showed a well-defined 26 × 9 × 9 cm mass in the epigastric region. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed, non-homogeneous intragastric mass measuring 26.6 × 9.7 × 9.8 cm, lacking vascular supply, containing air bubbles, and exhibiting a characteristic mottled appearance.

A 40-year-old man with no prior medical history except postbulbar ulceration presented with 3 days of absolute constipation, acute abdominal pain, and nausea. On examination, he was tachycardic (heart rate, 106 beats/min), with abdominal distension and diffuse tenderness. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 15,320/mm³ and a C-reactive protein level of 33.5 mg/dL. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed mildly distended and thickened ileal loops clustered in the hypogastric quadrant and enclosed within a sac formed by a thickened peritoneal membrane with contrast uptake and a “cocoon-like appearance,” causing upstream small-bowel dilatation with air–fluid levels. Peritoneal fluid was noted within the sac, and perihepatic calcifications were seen in the thickened peritoneal membrane. Although an internal hernia was initially considered, it was ruled out based on the finding of a distinct peritoneal membrane encasing the ileal loops.

A 47-year-old woman was referred after an abdominal ultrasound performed for routine evaluation revealed multiple hyperechoic liver lesions. She was asymptomatic, with a body-mass index of 24 kg/m2, and had no history of malignancy. Both she and her mother are homozygous for the HFE H63D mutation but had not required treatment for hemochromatosis. On examination, vital signs and the physical examination were normal. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and liver-function tests. Homeostatic Model Assessment for Insulin Resistance was elevated at 3.2, but fasting glucose and an oral glucose-tolerance test were within normal limits. Serum ferritin was 309 ng/mL, with normal transferrin concentration and saturation. Upper endoscopy, colonoscopy, and gynecologic examination were unrevealing. Tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and alpha-fetoprotein, were within normal limits. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan demonstrated multiple focal hypodense liver nodules that, after intravenous contrast administration, showed similar enhancement to normal liver parenchyma. An abdominal MRI revealed multiple pseudonodular lesions in both lobes, without displacement or invasion of hepatic vascular structures, diffusion restriction, or enhancement after contrast. A signal drop on out-of-phase compared with in-phase sequences confirmed intracellular lipid content within the lesions. T2 relaxometry MRI of the liver and myocardium showed normal iron concentrations.

An 81-year-old man with a history of rheumatoid arthritis on prednisone and no history of alcohol abuse presented in spring 2018 to the emergency department with severe lethargy and was intubated for airway protection. He was hypotensive, requiring norepinephrine support. On examination, his abdomen was soft but distended. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 10.8×10^9/L with a neutrophil shift, a creatinine level of 2.1 mg/dL (baseline unknown), and metabolic acidosis (arterial pH 7.29, PCO2 39 mm Hg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, base deficit 7 mmol/L). The serum lactate concentration was 6.8 mmol/L. Liver function tests were within normal limits, and the serum albumin level was 2.3 g/dL. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no thrombus and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45%. Ammonia levels, acetaminophen values, and a comprehensive toxin panel were unremarkable.  
Because of worsening lactic acidosis and concern for mesenteric ischemia, he underwent exploratory laparotomy, which was unrevealing. Postoperatively, he was admitted to the surgical intensive care unit for mechanical ventilation and continued hemodynamic support. His lactate rose to 14.4 mmol/L, pH fell to 7.21, bicarbonate to 13 mmol/L, and base deficit increased to 14 mmol/L. Central venous oxygen saturation remained around 50%. Point-of-care echocardiography revealed global hypokinesis and ventricular dilatation. He required escalating vasoactive support, including epinephrine and vasopressin. Approximately 20 hours after surgery, a nephrology consultation was requested for possible dialysis in the setting of refractory lactic acidosis.

An 11-year-old boy was admitted for treatment of pressure ulcers in the buttock and sacrum. In 2016, he had sudden lower‐limb weakness and paresthesia, from which he recovered with treatment. Since 2020, he noted progressive weakness of the left lower limb, and by 2022 he developed loss of touch, pain, and temperature sensation in that limb. Superficial sensation on the left declined, muscle strength worsened to grade 0, and the left lower limb hypertrophied rapidly, while the right lower limb underwent atrophy.

Family history was negative for hereditary disorders; parents were healthy and non-consanguineous; a brother has lymphocytic leukemia.

On examination, he appeared malnourished, with a long face and mildly downslanting palpebral fissures. Multiple soft, mobile, non-tender, adipose-like masses were present on the right chest wall, back, and left lower abdomen (largest 14×8 cm). He had thoracic scoliosis; the right lower-limb muscle was atrophic (strength grade 2) with intact sensation; the left lower limb was markedly enlarged (strength grade 0) with loss of all sensation. No pathological reflexes were elicited.

Laboratory tests: hemoglobin 103 g/L, hematocrit 32.4%, mean corpuscular volume 79 fL, platelets 408×10^9/L; normal liver and kidney function, blood glucose, electrolytes, and coagulation; negative serologic tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and syphilis.

Imaging:
- X-rays of lower limbs and pelvis showed asymmetry: right femur, foot, and pelvic bones smaller than left; left acetabular dysplasia with femoral-head dislocation; abnormal development of the left proximal fibula.
- Chest X-ray showed right-sided rib enlargement, thoracic scoliosis, and a 65×161 mm soft-tissue density under the right chest wall.
- Head CT was normal.
- Chest CT revealed irregular thickening of subcutaneous fat in the right chest wall, multiple nodular soft tissue lesions, rib changes, and irregular thickening of the right pleura with a mass.
- Thoracic MRI showed abnormal signals from C3 to T6 in the spinal canal and cord suggestive of a vascular malformation, a right thoracic cavity mass with large vascular malformation, and a subcutaneous mass under the right back chest wall with adjacent rib enlargement.
- Lumbar MRI was unremarkable.
- Echocardiography was within normal limits except for mild valvular regurgitation.
- Color Doppler ultrasound of the lower limbs showed no abnormal arterial or venous flow.

A 16-year-old North African female with known type 1 diabetes mellitus presented with dyspnea and palpitations. She reported a fever of 38.5 °C the day before, one week of loose stools, reduced oral intake, and had stopped insulin. On arrival: blood pressure 125/85 mmHg, heart rate 117/min, respiratory rate 39/min; finger-stick glucose 655 mg/dL; urinary ketones positive. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.09, lactate 2.9 mmol/L (reference 0.5–2.2), anion gap 44. Laboratory studies showed CRP 25 mg/L, sodium 130 mEq/L, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, and mild transaminase elevation. Chest radiograph and urinalysis were unremarkable. Physical examination was notable only for mild abdominal tenderness.

She was admitted to the ICU for diabetic ketoacidosis management with intravenous fluids, continuous insulin infusion, and potassium replacement. After 24 hours, ketonemia resolved and glucose normalized; a 10% dextrose infusion was added to prevent hypoglycemia. Despite this, lactate rose to 5 mmol/L with persistent acidemia and hyperventilation. Escalation of insulin and dextrose infusions led to a peak lactate of 12 mmol/L, yet she remained hemodynamically stable without hypotension or tachycardia. Echocardiography showed hyperdynamic left ventricular function without shock. Transition to subcutaneous insulin and continued hydration resulted in a decline in lactate, resolution of hyperventilation, and glucose around 150 mg/dL.

During her ICU stay, she was noted to have significant growth delay, hepatomegaly, and a Cushingoid appearance. Glycated hemoglobin was 12%. Liver tests remained abnormal (AST 180 U/L, ALT 82 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 135 U/L, GGT 58 U/L). Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated homogeneous hepatomegaly.

A 5-year-old boy presented with a 3-week history of mouth ulcers on both cheeks. He had been treated with systemic antibiotics for 1 week at another clinic without improvement and was referred for consideration of biopsy. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. His face was mildly swollen with slight deformity. Intraoral inspection revealed ulcers on the mucous membranes of both cheeks, each bearing a white deposit approximately 3×2 mm in size; the lesions were firm, nonadherent, and tender to palpation. Saliva and salivary glands appeared normal. Bilateral submandibular lymph nodes were palpable, mobile, tender, and about 5 mm in diameter. The patient had normal occlusion without dental crowding. Behavioral observation revealed that he repeatedly sucked his cheeks while playing and continued to do so despite reminders.

A 52-year-old woman who works as a microbiologist presented with a subacute, gradually progressive headache, dizziness, and partial seizures. She had no past medical or surgical history and denied raw milk ingestion, tick bites, or illicit drug use. On examination, higher mental functions and speech were intact; there was mild papilledema but otherwise normal cranial nerves, motor strength, sensation, and reflexes. Vital signs were stable. 

Basic laboratory tests—including complete blood count, liver-function tests, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and connective-tissue screening—were unremarkable. Serologic tests for syphilis, HIV, mammography, and tumor markers were negative. 

Serum Brucella melitensis immunoglobulins were elevated (IgM 12.2 U/ml and IgG 127.4 U/ml; normal <12 U/ml). In cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), ELISA revealed a Brucella titer of 1 : 40 (normal <1 : 20). CSF analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (63 cells, 88% lymphocytes), mildly elevated protein, and normal glucose. Bacterial cultures were negative for aerobic and anaerobic organisms. CSF PCR for tuberculosis, herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus was negative. Both CSF Brucella total antibodies and oligoclonal bands were positive; the corresponding serum sample lacked these bands. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated a 2.6 × 3.5 cm deep white-matter mass in the peritrigonal temporal lobe with surrounding vasogenic edema, no restricted diffusion, slightly increased flow, and normal cerebral blood volume. Postgadolinium T1 sequences showed minimal enhancement. Diffusion tensor imaging indicated slight reduction in anisotropy with preserved fiber-tract organization. MR spectroscopy was suggestive of an inflammatory rather than neoplastic process. Radiological differential diagnoses included neurosarcoidosis, lymphoma, and low-grade glioma. CSF cytology and flow cytometry were normal.

Three term infants, aged 5 to 9 weeks, were referred to neurosurgery for scalp swelling. One had a vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery after failure to progress; two were delivered via uncomplicated cesarean section. All had fetal scalp electrodes placed during labor. They were otherwise healthy and reaching developmental milestones appropriately.

On examination, each infant was awake and alert. Scalp masses were non-tender, soft, compressible, fluctuant, and crossed suture lines; palpation of the skull was normal. No other abnormalities were noted.

Skull radiographs in two patients demonstrated well-circumscribed smooth masses overlying the skull without fractures, lucency, or sclerosis; in the third patient, radiographs showed no soft-tissue abnormality despite the physical findings. Noncontrast CT scans in two patients confirmed soft-tissue swellings with Hounsfield units similar to water, normal ventricles, cisterns, and cerebrospinal fluid spaces, and no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage, fracture, or mass effect.

A 35-year-old woman (G2P1) at 38 weeks’ gestation was admitted for a repeat elective cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia. Her past medical and obstetrical history were unremarkable; preoperative electrocardiography was normal. Initial vital signs after spinal anesthesia (0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine 11 mg with fentanyl 10 µg intrathecally plus prophylactic phenylephrine infusion) were stable: BP 120/70 mmHg, HR 60 beats/min, SpO2 99%. Twelve minutes into the operation, during placental removal, she suddenly lost consciousness with up-rolling of the eyes, developed apnea, and her SpO2 fell to 88%. Mask ventilation with 100% oxygen was initiated, and spontaneous respiration returned after 2 minutes, with BP 105/67 mmHg and HR 89 beats/min. On recovery, she was asymptomatic, pupils were equal and reactive, and there were no focal neurologic deficits. Estimated blood loss was 740 mL, and arterial blood gases remained normal. Given concerns for pulmonary or amniotic fluid embolism and cerebral ischemia, a whole-body contrast-enhanced CT scan was performed, revealing a hypoattenuating region near the right coronary cusp of the aortic valve. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a mean and peak aortic valve gradient of 25 mmHg and 44 mmHg (peak velocity 3.3 m/s; valve area 1.7 cm2). Subsequent transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated what was thought to be a bicuspid aortic valve and a 1.0 × 1.7 cm mobile echogenic mass near the base of the right coronary cusp.

A 14-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of an incidental finding of asymptomatic hyperCKemia (26,372 IU/L). He had no family history of neuromuscular disease, no parental consanguinity, and no exposure to myotoxic medications. He had been active in high-performance sports (3 h daily) without myalgia, cramps, or pigmenturia, but CK levels remained above 20,000 IU/L after cessation of exercise. Neuromuscular and systemic examinations were normal. Initial electromyography and nerve conduction studies were normal. Cardiac and respiratory assessments were unremarkable. Myositis-specific (Mi2, TIF1γ, MDA5, NXP2, SAE1, Jo1, SRP, PL7, PL12, EJ, OJ), myositis-associated (Ku, PM-Scl75/100, Ro52), and antinuclear antibodies were negative, and thyroid-stimulating hormone was normal. Given his sex and CK elevation, an X-linked dystrophinopathy was considered, but multiplex polymerase chain reaction and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification analyses detected no DMD deletions. Six months later, a right quadriceps muscle biopsy showed muscle fiber necrosis with endomysial and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, without fibrosis or fatty infiltration. A repeat electromyography revealed a myopathic pattern. These findings were felt to be consistent with polymyositis.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a six-month history of persistent scalp rashes accompanied by generalized skin lesions, severe pruritus, and malaise. She had been treated for presumed seborrhoeic dermatitis and psoriasis with topical econazole nitrate and triamcinolone acetonide for months without improvement. Her medical history was notable for well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus on insulin and untreated onychomycosis of the toenails for two years.

On examination, there were multiple scaly erythematous patches on the scalp with thick grayish-yellow crusts, areas of alopecia, and broken hairs. Under Wood’s lamp illumination, broken hairs showed bright-green fluorescence. Dermoscopic evaluation of scalp hairs revealed Morse code–like hairs, white sheath-surrounded hairs, and short broken hairs. Widespread large erythematous patches with elevated, well-demarcated borders and white superficial scales involved the face, neck, ears, trunk, extremities, and skin folds (perineum, groin, and axillae). All toenails showed discoloration and subungual hyperkeratosis. No lymphadenopathy was present.

Direct microscopic examination (10% KOH smear and fluorescence stain) of the broken scalp hairs demonstrated ectothrix hyphae and spores. KOH examination of skin scrapings from the trunk and subungual debris was also positive for fungal hyphae. Further history revealed recent contact with a stray cat.

A 54-year-old woman with a 15-pack-year smoking history presented with 7 months of NYHA class III exertional dyspnea without cough, wheezing, chest tightness, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or peripheral edema. She had no rashes, arthralgias, myalgias, travel, or exposure history. Oxygen saturation was 91% on 3 L/min oxygen; blood pressure 115/76 mm Hg; heart rate 82 beats/min. Pulmonary examination revealed normal breath sounds without wheezes, crackles, or pleural rubs. Cardiac examination showed normal S1 and S2 and an early-peaking grade II/VI crescendo–decrescendo murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids. No stigmata of chronic liver disease were present. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction > 60% and mild to moderate subaortic stenosis without other valvular abnormalities or shunts on color Doppler. Transesophageal echocardiography with agitated saline injection revealed more than 20 bubbles in the left atrium after the fourth cardiac cycle, consistent with an extracardiac right-to-left shunt. Computed tomography of the chest showed no interstitial lung disease or large pulmonary arteriovenous malformations.

A 37-year-old man from an under-resourced area presents with a lifelong history of recurrent skin and pulmonary infections. Since age 2, he has experienced multiple “cold” abscesses on the back, groin, and buttocks caused by Staphylococcus aureus, three of which required incision and drainage. He also has a history of atopic dermatitis with early-onset rash, weight loss, and hyperpigmented skin lesions. He has no history of parental consanguinity, and prenatal exposures were denied.

Medications include ascorbic acid, ferrous sulfate, megestrol acetate for appetite stimulation, and acetaminophen. He experienced abscess recurrences in 2012, 2013, 2014, and 2016, and beginning in 2017 developed bowel and bladder incontinence. In 2018 and 2019 he had fevers, chills, rhinitis, and a dry cough treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungals. In 2021, hydrocortisone was gradually tapered to 5 mg daily. In 2022, he presented with a large 5×7 cm axillary abscess and stage II pressure ulcers on the buttocks, all draining foul-smelling discharge.

Laboratory studies show:  
• Serum IgE 10 000 IU/ml (normal <100) with eosinophilia  
• Mild anemia, elevated ESR, low iron indices  
• Normal total white-cell count with neutrophilia  

Chest radiograph reveals peribronchial thickening, multiple small nodules in the right lung, hyperinflation, and mild scoliosis; no consolidation or effusion. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55–60% and mild thickening of the mitral valve leaflets.

An 85-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of decreased vision in both eyes and headache. She had undergone uncomplicated bilateral cataract surgery 13 years earlier and had been previously diagnosed with Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease at another clinic. On examination, the best-corrected visual acuity was 0.8 in the right eye and 1.0 in the left eye; intraocular pressures were normal bilaterally. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy revealed pseudoexfoliation deposits, pseudophakia with posterior capsulotomy, and cells in the vitreous cavity of both eyes. Funduscopic examination showed choroidal detachments in both eyes. Indocyanine green angiography demonstrated obscuration of the choroidal veins at the posterior poles. Optical coherence tomography revealed retinal pigment epithelium undulations and choroidal thickening in both eyes. The axial length measured 22.85 mm in each eye. Laboratory studies were notable only for a triglyceride level of 148 mg/dl and a leukocyte count of 8.8 × 10^9 cells/l; the hemoglobin A1c was 5.7%.

A 73-year-old man was admitted with progressively worsening shortness of breath (NYHA class IV) and fatigue two months after surgical mitral valve repair. His postoperative course had been complicated by haemothorax requiring re-thoracotomy, severe enterococcal sepsis treated with vancomycin, and a right frontal watershed stroke with residual left arm paresis. His history also included hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and coronary artery disease treated with bypass grafting at the time of his mitral repair.

On examination, he appeared pale, had pale conjunctivae, and a holosystolic 3/6 apical murmur radiating to the axilla. Mild bibasilar crackles and bilateral lower extremity edema were present. Blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, heart rate 80 bpm, and temperature 36.6 °C. Chest radiography showed a small left pleural effusion without infiltrates.

Laboratory studies revealed haemoglobin 6.6 g/dL (13.6–17.2 g/dL), haematocrit 0.20 (0.39–0.49), reticulocytes 5% (0.5–2%), haptoglobin 0.01 g/dL (0.5–2.4 g/dL), total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL (0.3–1.2 mg/dL) with indirect bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL (<0.2 mg/dL), and lactate dehydrogenase 1382 U/L (100–247 U/L). Brain natriuretic peptide was 374.2 pg/mL (<100 pg/mL). Creatinine and cardiac enzymes were normal. C-reactive protein was <0.05 mg/dL. A direct Coombs test, a specific Coombs test, and cold agglutination testing were all negative.

An 83-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer (inguinal lymph nodes and bone), a seizure disorder, and a prior right thalamic infarct with residual left-sided weakness was being transported home after an oncologist visit when he was noted to be unresponsive with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6. He arrived in the emergency department mildly confused but alert and oriented. He recalled feeling extremely warm before losing consciousness and upon awakening felt very confused. He also described several falls over the past 6 months while walking to his mailbox, which he had attributed to leg weakness. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, or speech difficulties but endorsed generalized weakness, abdominal distention, constipation, and bilateral leg swelling.  
Vital signs: blood pressure 156/76 mm Hg, heart rate 45–52 bpm, temperature 98.7 °F, respiratory rate 13/min, oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Examination revealed moderate abdominal distention, bilateral lower extremity edema, and unchanged chronic left-sided weakness. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL (baseline), normal electrolytes, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, glucose 118 mg/dL, normal cardiac enzymes, and a negative urine drug screen. Mental status and bradycardia improved after a 500 mL intravenous fluid bolus.  
The patient underwent a comprehensive syncope evaluation—including ECG, transthoracic echocardiogram, orthostatic vital signs, electroencephalogram, head CT, basic laboratories, and medication review—which did not identify a clear etiology.

A 79-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, psoriasis (on ustekinumab), and rheumatoid arthritis (on methotrexate) presented with severe pain (10/10) and a unilateral vesicular rash distributed along the left C5–T2 dermatomes. On initial examination her temperature was 37.2 °C and other vital signs were stable. She was diagnosed clinically with herpes zoster and treated with intravenous acyclovir for 9 days, oral analgesics, and multiple neuraxial nerve blocks for pain control. Fourteen days after rash onset, she noted new weakness of the left upper extremity without sensory loss and denied any trauma. On neurologic examination, strength was 2+/5 for shoulder abduction and adduction and 3+/5 for elbow flexion and extension on the left. Initial laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and renal and hepatic panels, were within normal limits. Electromyography of the left arm demonstrated denervation potentials in the brachioradialis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, deltoid, extensor indicis, and C6 paraspinal muscles. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left brachial plexus showed hyperintense signals on T2-weighted images and isointense signals on T1-weighted images in the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and subscapularis muscles, without definite contrast enhancement.

A 71-year-old Japanese man presented with right facial numbness and itching, cervical pain, and right arm numbness with spasms. His medical history included hypertension managed with amlodipine for 10 years. In 2016, he developed numbness and hypoesthesia in the right trigeminal distribution and was diagnosed with idiopathic trigeminal nerve palsy; treatment with gabapentin, amitriptyline, pregabalin, and clonazepam provided no relief. In 2019, he noted cervical pain and right arm numbness but had no objective neurologic findings.

On examination in 2020, he had mild right facial palsy with numbness confined to the right cheek and involuntary twitching at the right labial commissure. His speech was slightly slurred, and the right side of his mouth fatigued with continued chewing. Bilateral trapezius muscle tenderness (right-dominant) elicited a pain score of 62 mm on a visual analog scale. Right arm numbness was rated 9/10, and triceps spasm corresponded to C6 involvement. Manual muscle testing was not performed.

Blood biochemistry was within normal limits. Cervical radiographs showed straightening of the C2–C7 lordosis and possible right C6 neuroforaminal narrowing on oblique views. Cervical MRI revealed disc protrusions at C5/6 and C6/7 without spinal cord compression or neuroforaminal stenosis.

These findings suggested cervical discogenic pain or facet arthritis, and his facial symptoms suggested oral dyskinesia or another neurological disorder, but not trigeminal nerve palsy. He was started on mirogabalin 5 mg/day, extended-release paroxetine 12.5 mg/day, clonazepam 0.5 mg/day, and biperiden 2 mg/day at bedtime, with no improvement after one week. A stellate ganglion block was then performed, which also failed to improve his symptoms.

A 68-year-old man was brought with a 1-day history of acute severe agitation, extreme fearfulness on seeing his reflection, and refusal of food and water, preceded by 5 days of untreated low-grade fever and headache. Six months earlier he had an unprovoked stray dog bite (Class I) with no post-exposure antirabies vaccination. His hypertension was treated irregularly; there was no history of head injury, other medical or psychiatric illness, or substance use. On examination, he was afebrile, alert, and oriented; pulse 110/min, blood pressure 160/110 mm Hg. Plantar responses were bilaterally extensor and optic fundi were normal. Mental status examination showed increased psychomotor activity, ideas of reference, and visual hallucinations; primary cognition was intact, but judgment and insight were impaired. Biochemical tests, chest radiograph, electrocardiogram, and electroencephalogram were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed multiple vascular infarcts and demyelinating patches secondary to vascular, toxic, or inflammatory etiologies, suggesting multiple vascular infarcts in different stages of evolution or rabies encephalitis. A contrast-enhanced MRI after 48 hours showed the same findings.

A 34-year-old non-Turkish Caucasian woman with a history of Behcet’s disease refractory to multiple immunosuppressive regimens presented with severe diffuse abdominal pain and reported a recent exacerbation of skin ulcerations and orogenital aphthae. Her medical history included chronic sinusitis, migraines, and Crohn’s disease; she smoked one pack of cigarettes daily. Her medications included mycophenolate mofetil, methotrexate (self-discontinued 2 weeks earlier), azathioprine, infliximab, and prednisone (recently increased to 80 mg daily then tapered to 50 mg).

On hospital day 2, she developed rapidly progressive shortness of breath and hypoxemia, necessitating intubation and mechanical ventilation. She was febrile to 102.7°F. Examination showed a cushingoid appearance, a healing left mandibular ulcer, multiple punched-out mucocutaneous ulcerations, and diffuse bilateral wheezes. The PaO2/FiO2 ratio was 132, and echocardiography was normal. Chest radiography revealed extensive bilateral alveolar infiltrates; chest CT demonstrated numerous small nodules and patchy ground-glass opacities. Bronchoscopy showed multiple upper airway aphthous ulcers, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained a predominance of neutrophils.

Empiric broad-spectrum antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral therapy was started along with intravenous methylprednisolone (60 mg every 6 h). Bacterial, fungal, and viral cultures, including studies for Aspergillus and Pneumocystis jirovecii, were unremarkable. Serologic and immunologic tests — PCR for cytomegalovirus, influenza A and B antigens, HIV antibody, Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgG and IgM, Legionella, and Cryptococcal antigens — were negative. The CD4 count was 96 cells/mm3. A vasculitis panel (c-ANCA, p-ANCA, rheumatoid factor, ANA titers, creatine kinase, aldolase) was unremarkable. Urinalysis and renal function were normal. Antibiotics were subsequently discontinued.

A 20-month-old boy presented with acute left lower extremity pain and refusal to bear weight. He was uncooperative, and no history of trauma was elicited. He held his left hip in flexion and external rotation. There was no swelling or overt signs of inflammation. On passive rotation of the left hip, he exhibited generalized discomfort referred to the entire leg. He had a low-grade fever of 37.2 °C, and his erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 12 mm/hour. Anteroposterior and frog-leg radiographs of the pelvis were normal, and a probability of transient synovitis was suspected. He was treated with ibuprofen and discharged with plans for follow-up.

A 21-year-old man presented with 2 h of constant substernal chest tightness radiating to the left shoulder, unrelated to respiration. He denied dyspnea. His heart rate was 67 bpm, blood pressure 130/75 mmHg, jugular venous pressure was normal, and there was no peripheral edema. Cardiac auscultation was unremarkable, and lung fields were clear. ECG showed sinus rhythm with ST-segment elevation in the precordial leads and leads II, III, and aVF. Initial troponin was 0.239 ng/mL (normal <0.1 ng/mL) and creatine kinase 469 U/L (peak 1563 U/L; normal <169 U/L). He received aspirin, heparin, and a ticagrelor loading dose. 

Coronary angiography revealed a thrombotic subtotal occlusion of the left anterior descending artery at the first diagonal branch take-off, with no other lesions or atherosclerotic changes in the remaining vessels. Thrombus aspiration and glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor infusion failed to restore full flow, so a 4.0 × 18 mm drug-eluting stent was implanted with FilterWire protection, resulting in TIMI III flow. Transthoracic echocardiography showed anterior wall hypokinesia with mildly reduced ejection fraction. 

To exclude an embolic source, transesophageal echocardiography with contrast was negative for intracardiac shunt or other embolic sources. Laboratory tests for thrombophilia and autoimmune disease were normal, and lipid and glucose levels were within reference ranges. The patient denied cigarette smoking but reported frequent cannabis use. Urine toxicology was positive for delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol only. He was discharged on dual antiplatelet therapy, a beta-blocker, and a statin with advice to avoid cannabis.

A 52-year-old man presented with a one-year history of progressive, painful swelling of the right parotid gland. He denied facial weakness, recent travel, pet exposure, or high-risk activities. He was a physician living in a semi-rural area of North-Rhine Westphalia, Germany. Examination revealed a firm, tender mass in the right parotid region without overlying erythema or facial nerve palsy. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. MRI of the neck showed a 2.7 × 1.6 × 1.6 cm cystic lesion in the deep lobe of the right parotid gland with extension toward the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Empiric therapy with cefuroxime and metronidazole produced no improvement. Surgical exploration revealed a cystic, inflammatory mass adherent to the main trunk of the facial nerve and adjacent muscle; grossly, the lesion appeared necrotic and infiltrative. Histopathological examination of the resected tissue demonstrated chronic granulating and necrotizing inflammation, and periodic acid–Schiff staining revealed deeply blue-stained slender structures surrounded by necrotic debris.

A 19-year-old man presented with a lifelong history of constipation and tenesmus, with recent onset of rectal bleeding. He had no abdominal pain, weight loss, or significant past medical or surgical history. Family history was negative for bowel disease or colorectal cancer. On examination he was pale; digital rectal examination was not possible because of partial rectal obstruction. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 7600/µL, hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, hematocrit 38.8%, mean corpuscular volume 65 fL, ferritin 6.3 ng/mL, platelet count 361 000/µL, and ESR 5 mm/h; coagulation and liver tests were normal. Stool studies were negative. Colonoscopy revealed a large semi-circumferential infiltrative mass with a polypoid appearance in the rectum, 5 cm from the anal verge, raising concern for malignancy. A biopsy of the lesion was obtained, and the remainder of the colon appeared normal.

A 38-year-old obese woman (BMI 30), on postpartum day 18 after a cesarean delivery at 30 weeks for severe preeclampsia, presented with a 2-day history of severe (8/10) headache and acute moderate right‐sided weakness. Several hours before presentation she developed difficulty speaking and understanding, although she was able to repeat words and sentences. She denied fever or trauma.  
On examination, temperature was 36.8 °C, blood pressure 150/100 mm Hg, heart rate 94 bpm. Ophthalmologic exam showed papilledema. Neurologic examination revealed an alert but agitated patient, right hemiparesis (MRC 4/5), right central facial paresis, and no meningeal signs. Language assessment demonstrated initial mutism followed by nonfluent speech with echolalia, absent spontaneous output, good articulation, preserved repetition, severe anomia, and markedly impaired auditory and reading comprehension (alexia and agraphia), consistent with mixed transcortical aphasia.  
Noncontrast head CT in the ED showed hyperdense straight sinus, vein of Galen, and left lateral mesencephalic vein; venous infarction of the left thalamus, basal ganglia, external and internal capsules, and corona radiata with hemorrhagic transformation in the head and corpus of the left caudate nucleus. MRI of the brain revealed left hydrocephalus, rightward ventricular compression, and slight hemorrhagic transformation in the left basal nuclei and thalamus. MR venography demonstrated near-complete occlusion of the superior sagittal sinus, straight sinus, vein of Galen, and the left deep venous system, with partial occlusion of the left transverse and sigmoid sinuses and left internal jugular vein.

A 15-year-old Indo-Aryan male presented with a sudden, painless decrease in vision in his right eye for 4 days. He had no significant ocular or family history, and review of systems was unremarkable. Best corrected visual acuity was 6/60 in the right eye and 6/6 unaided in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 15 mmHg in the right eye and 16 mmHg in the left eye. There was an afferent pupillary defect in the right eye. Slit-lamp examination of both anterior segments was normal. Dilated fundus examination showed a normal left eye. In the right eye, there was telangiectasia of the retinal vessels with subretinal lipid exudation in the superotemporal and superonasal quadrants, subretinal fluid extending into the fovea, and a single flap horseshoe tear at the 10 o’clock equatorial region without secondary changes. Complete blood counts, viral serology, chest radiograph, and Mantoux test were all normal. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the right macula demonstrated a hyporeflective space between the retinal pigment epithelium and neurosensory retina, consistent with subretinal fluid.

A 24-year-old woman with no history of trauma or systemic symptoms noted a nodule in her right zygomatic region that had grown progressively over 3 months. On examination, there was a 1.0-cm, firm, well-circumscribed, freely mobile subcutaneous nodule without overlying skin changes or regional lymphadenopathy. The patient was otherwise healthy. Initial clinical hypotheses included an epidermoid cyst, a trichilemmal cyst, and a pilomatrixoma. 

An excisional biopsy yielded an irregularly shaped, white-yellow mass measuring 1.0 × 0.6 cm. Histopathological examination demonstrated a non-encapsulated proliferation of mesenchymal tissue extending from the dermis into the hypodermis. The lesion was composed of thin spindle cells arranged in interlacing bundles amid thick, hyaline collagen fibers, with focal myxoid areas, extravasated erythrocytes, and a sparse lymphoid infiltrate, without cytologic atypia. 

Immunohistochemical studies showed diffuse positivity for muscle-specific actin (HHF35) and smooth muscle actin (SMA), slight positivity for Ki-67 in a small number of nuclei, and negativity for CD34 and desmin.

A 73-year-old man with HPV-negative stage IVA oropharyngeal cancer (cT4N2bM0) underwent induction chemotherapy with docetaxel (75 mg/m2), cisplatin (75 mg/m2) on day 1, and fluorouracil (750 mg/m2/day) on days 1–5, along with nasogastric‐tube feeding. His history was notable for a distal subtotal gastrectomy with Billroth I reconstruction for duodenal ulcer at age 33. Two weeks after starting chemotherapy, he developed progressive upper abdominal distention that interrupted enteral nutrition. He was alert, afebrile, and had no signs of neurologic, psychiatric, endocrine, or collagen-vascular disorders. His only prior medication with motility effects, short-acting opioid, had been discontinued more than two weeks earlier. Laboratory studies were within normal limits, without acute kidney injury, liver injury, electrolyte disturbances, endocrinopathies, or hyperglycemia. Contrast‐enhanced abdominal CT showed an abnormally dilated stomach without intestinal dilation. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy performed after three days off enteral feeding revealed a large amount of retained gastric content but no evidence of gastric outlet obstruction or mucosal damage.

A 34-year-old G5P3 woman was referred at 33 + 0 weeks of gestation for evaluation of a suspected fetal liver anomaly. Ultrasound showed an isolated, fluid-filled lesion measuring 67.9 × 61.6 × 53.3 mm in the left hepatic lobe without soft-tissue components. Color and pulsed Doppler revealed massive blood flow within the lesion. The left hepatic artery was the main feeding vessel, with peak systolic velocity of 159.6 cm/s, end-diastolic velocity of 90.2 cm/s, and pulsatility index of 0.69; the resistance index in the hepatic artery was 0.49. Left and middle hepatic veins served as draining vessels.  

Fetal biometry demonstrated macrosomia (estimated weight 2976 g, >97th percentile), mainly due to increased abdominal circumference. There was polyhydramnios (AFI 26 cm), placentomegaly, cardiomegaly (CTAR 0.569), and bilateral atrioventricular valvular regurgitation, but no hydrops fetalis. Umbilical artery Doppler was normal. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity was 68.1 cm/s (MoM 1.46) with a pulsatility index of 2.81. Antenatal corticosteroids were given, and follow-up was stable. A primary cesarean section was performed at 37 + 0 weeks, yielding a 3330 g male infant (Apgar 7, 8, 9).  

Postnatally, the infant developed persistent pulmonary hypertension requiring CPAP, inhaled nitric oxide, sildenafil, and bosentan. Congestive heart failure was treated with dobutamine and milrinone; propranolol was started for emerging hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Abdominal ultrasonography and MRI on day 1 showed a complex intrahepatic mass measuring 45.2 × 51.4 × 73.5 mm with multiple arterial branches from the left hepatic artery, celiac trunk, phrenic arteries, left internal mammary artery, and intercostal arteries, draining into the middle and left hepatic veins.  

Laboratory studies revealed microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (55 G/L), and consumptive coagulopathy (fibrinogen 68 mg/dL).

A 33-year-old man presented with a 9-month history of intermittent epigastric and right upper-quadrant pain described as burning and a pressure sensation. His medical history included recurrent spontaneous pneumothoraces treated with pleurodesis, resulting in chronic chest-wall pain and narcotic requirements. Physical examination showed mild to moderate tenderness of the deep epigastrium without palpable masses. Laboratory values, including liver chemistries, were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a 4.3 cm × 1.7 cm echogenic lesion in the caudate lobe of the liver, thought to represent either a hemorrhagic cyst or a thrombosed vascular structure. Magnetic resonance imaging identified a 4.5 cm × 1.7 cm ovoid, well-circumscribed lesion abutting the caudate lobe of the liver and the proximal stomach near the gastroesophageal junction, without an air-fluid level. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a large cystic structure without internal nodules or masses in the lesser sac adjacent to the liver and proximal stomach. Fine-needle aspiration yielded a thick, turbid, mucus-like fluid.

A 22-year-old gravida 2, para 1, living 1 woman presented at 18 weeks of gestation for her first obstetric visit. She had no history of folic acid supplementation. Routine blood and biochemical tests were within normal limits. On abdominal examination, the uterus measured approximately 16 weeks in size. Serum α-fetoprotein was markedly elevated. Ultrasound imaging demonstrated a single live fetus with severe dorsal hyperextension of the head, a markedly shortened vertebral column, and no visible fetal neck.

A 67-year-old man presented with progressive tingling and paresthesia in both lower extremities. Seven days before symptom onset, he had received a third dose of the BBIBP-CorV (Sinopharm) COVID-19 vaccine. His medical history included diabetes mellitus treated with metformin and knee arthrosis. He denied recent infections. Over two months, the sensory symptoms ascended, and weakness in the lower extremities progressed to the point of difficulty initiating ambulation. Lumbosacral MRI showed mild bulging of the L5–S1 intervertebral disc. Treatment with gabapentin and physical therapy yielded no improvement, and over the next two months the paresthesia and weakness extended to the upper extremities. 

On neurological examination, cranial nerves were intact. Motor strength (MRC scale) was 5/5 in cervical muscles, 4/5 in deltoids, 4/5 in wrist and finger movements, 3/5 proximal in the lower extremities, and 2/5 distally, with ankle dorsiflexion graded 2/5. Sensory testing revealed impaired position and vibration sense and reduced pin-prick sensation in the upper and distal lower extremities. The patient had action and postural tremor in the arms, gait ataxia, and generalized areflexia. There was no autonomic dysfunction, dysphagia, or incontinence. 

EMG and nerve conduction studies revealed absent compound muscle action potentials in the lower limbs; in the median, ulnar, and radial nerves there was increased distal latency, marked amplitude reduction, slowed conduction velocity, and conduction block, consistent with a demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy.

A 67-year-old man with a history of generalized pruritic violaceous papules diagnosed as lichen planus one year earlier presented with a 20-day history of mild bilateral ptosis, progressive dysphagia, and dysarthria. Dysphagia initially affected solids and progressed to liquids over 3 days; dysarthria was nasal and worsened with prolonged talking.
