He noted that symptoms were milder in the morning and exacerbated in the afternoon. He denied dyspnea, diplopia, headaches, vertigo, ataxia, or other systemic symptoms. His medical history included hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He had no recent infections, travel, or relevant family history.

On examination, he was afebrile, with normal blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation. Dermatologic examination revealed flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules and hyperpigmented macules on the flexural surfaces of the lower extremities. Neurologic examination showed asymmetric bilateral fatigable ptosis without ophthalmoplegia; severe reduction of the gag reflex; symmetric palate elevation; no tongue deviation or fasciculations; proximal muscle strength of 5/5 with clear fatigability, normal tone, and intact deep tendon reflexes; sensory, cerebellar, and gait examinations were normal.

Routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. Chest radiograph and noncontrast chest CT scan were normal. MRI of the brain and orbits showed no abnormalities. Motor and sensory nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography of distal and proximal muscles were normal. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz demonstrated a decremental response in the anconeus, trapezius, and orbicularis oculi muscles.

A 50-year-old woman from a rural area, with no significant medical or surgical history, presented with a painless left breast lump that had gradually increased in size over several years. She denied fever, nipple discharge, and a family history of breast cancer. On examination, a 7-cm firm, non-mobile mass with well-defined margins was palpated in the lower quadrants of the left breast, fixed to the deep tissue, without overlying skin changes or axillary lymphadenopathy. The right breast and the remainder of the systemic examination were normal.

Bilateral mammography (CC and MLO views) showed a well-circumscribed homogeneous-density mass in the inframammary fold and lower quadrants of the left breast, with no calcifications, architectural distortion, or skin thickening.

Ultrasound of the left breast revealed a thick-walled, unilocular anechoic cystic lesion containing an internal detached membrane and echogenic sediment, with no internal vascularity and no enlarged axillary lymph nodes.

Breast MRI demonstrated a cystic lesion that was hyperintense on T2-weighted and STIR sequences and hypointense on T1-weighted images; the capsular wall was smooth, moderately thickened, and showed low signal intensity on T2/STIR with regular enhancement on dynamic T1; the detached membrane was low signal on all sequences; and there was T1-isointense sedimentary material within the cyst.

A 35-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 0 with one prior miscarriage (G2A1P0), at 37 weeks’ gestation presented to the emergency department with headache, blurred vision, severe epigastric pain, and vomiting. She had a history of chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura diagnosed 1 year earlier, treated with methylprednisolone for 6 months, and in remission during pregnancy with platelet counts of 100–150 × 10^9/L. At her last antenatal visit 5 days earlier, her blood pressure was 130/80 mm Hg and platelet count was normal.

On admission, her blood pressure was 210/110 mm Hg. She received sublingual nifedipine, magnesium sulfate (loading dose followed by IM maintenance), and IV dexamethasone. Laboratory studies showed:
- Hemoglobin 9 g/dL
- Platelet count 60 × 10^9/L
- AST 765 IU/L, ALT 422 IU/L
- Total bilirubin 3.6 mg/dL (direct 2.4, indirect 1.2)
- LDH 958 IU/L
- Normal serum creatinine, electrolytes, and INR

Given the hypertension, elevated liver enzymes, hyperbilirubinemia, hemolysis (LDH elevation), and thrombocytopenia, HELLP syndrome was suspected. Blood products, including platelet concentrates, were arranged.

A 13-year-old girl presented with 5 days of generalized weakness and pain and swelling of the left lower limb. One month earlier, celiac disease had been diagnosed by duodenal biopsy and tissue transglutaminase IgA. On examination, she was thin and emaciated (height 144 cm, weight 22 kg), with pallor and enlarged cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes. The left lower limb was swollen with dilated tortuous veins; vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7 g/dL; white cells 4,000/mm3 (80% neutrophils); AST 157 IU, ALT 160 IU; total protein 4.9 g/dL; prothrombin time 23.7 s, PTTK 69.5 s, INR 2.03; vitamin D3 12 ng/dL. Doppler ultrasound revealed an echogenic thrombus in the left common femoral and deep femoral veins. She was started on intravenous antibiotics and fluids for high-grade fever and early shock. Despite therapy, fever persisted. Chest radiograph showed multiple nodular opacities. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple enlarged paraaortic, pre-aortic, peripancreatic, and inguinal lymph nodes. The Mantoux test was negative; blood cultures were sterile; sputum AFB smear was negative.

A 69-year-old woman with a history of asthma (treated with formoterol and budesonide) and multiparity presented with a 7-year history of an intensely painful bulge in her left iliac fossa. The 15 cm elongated protrusion increased with exertion and Valsalva maneuvers (eg, evacuation, urination). Over time, a smaller, less painful bulge appeared on the right side. She denied weight loss, changes in appetite, or bowel habits.

On examination, her abdomen was globose without scars. There were bilateral bulges along the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, more prominent on the left. Peristalsis was normal. Both bulges were asymmetrically distended, mobile on Valsalva, and manually reducible, with no signs of entrapment or strangulation.

An abdominal CT scan demonstrated herniation of intestinal loops in the anterior lower abdominal wall to the left of the umbilical scar, containing adipose tissue, and no signs of bowel compromise. A right inguinal hernia was also noted.

A 37-year-old Caucasian man presented with multiple chronic granulomatous skin lesions. His past medical history was notable for childhood asthma and pneumonia, and recurrent sinus infections requiring adult sinus surgery. A maternal male cousin had recently been hospitalized for disseminated Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare infection of the liver. The patient denied recent travel.

Seven years earlier, he had noted a nonpainful, nonpruritic plaque on his right shoulder that persisted and slowly spread to all four extremities. He was initially diagnosed with sarcoidosis and treated with corticosteroids and hydroxychloroquine. Although there was an initial response, the lesions persisted. Subsequent skin biopsies demonstrated numerous acid-fast bacilli within granulomas, leading to a tentative diagnosis of leprosy; he was treated with rifampin, clarithromycin, and minocycline without significant improvement. Attempts to taper steroids precipitated worsening skin lesions and high-grade fevers to 105 °F, prompting hospitalization. 

Because of pancytopenia and persistent fevers, a bone marrow biopsy was performed; it showed granulomas with acid-fast bacilli, and cultures grew Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare. Therapy was changed to clarithromycin, ethambutol, and rifampin, and corticosteroids (16 mg daily) were continued. After six months, fevers persisted, skin lesions advanced with new nodular masses and ulcerations, and CT imaging revealed enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes. Repeat skin biopsy again showed persistent MAI infection resistant to clarithromycin, ethambutol, and moxifloxacin, and described an atypical T-cell infiltrate with positive T-cell–receptor gene rearrangement, raising concern for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. 

On referral, his lesions were 3–4 inches in diameter, diffuse, raised, well-circumscribed erythematous scaly plaques without active ulceration. New skin biopsies showed a histiocytic infiltrate with few small atypical lymphocytes and long beaded bacilli in the dermis. Cultures grew Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare and Mycobacterium simiae. Bone marrow core biopsy showed normocellular marrow with foamy histiocytes in loosely formed granulomas; admixed T cells were clonal, lacked CD7, and were CD3+, CD4+, CD26+. However, the absence of epidermotropism, a lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with acid-fast mycobacteria, and the marked paucity of T cells rendered a clonal lymphoproliferative disorder involving the skin exceedingly unlikely. With cutaneous T-cell lymphoma effectively ruled out and compelling evidence of disseminated MAI infection, investigation into an underlying immune defect was performed.

A 30-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with chronic neck pain. She had two prior uncomplicated pregnancies and was taking no medications. Physical examination was unremarkable.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine was obtained and incidentally revealed a soft-tissue mass at the base of the tongue. On both T1- and T2-weighted sequences, the mass showed heterogeneous signal intensity, and multiple cystic areas were present centrally. There was no significant mass effect on surrounding structures or airway compression.  
Subsequent MRI of the neck with gadolinium demonstrated an encapsulated midline mass with small internal cysts, localized at the upper edge of the epiglottis. The lesion was isointense relative to adjacent muscle on T1-weighted images and showed early enhancement that persisted into the delayed phase.  
Laboratory testing revealed a free triiodothyronine level of 3.3 pg/mL (reference range 2.0–4.2), a free thyroxine level of 10.5 pg/dL (reference range 9.3–16.0), and a thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 17.848 IU/mL (reference range 0.37–4.2).  
Ultrasound of the neck showed absence of the thyroid gland in the pretracheal region and no cervical lymphadenopathy.

A 63‐year‐old man presented with a 5-month history of insidious onset headaches that began while typing at a computer. He described a diffuse, dull ache originating near the medial aspect of the superior angle of both scapulae, progressively radiating upward toward the occiput. The pain gradually increased during the workday, peaking in the afternoon (up to 6/10 on the Numeric Pain Rating Scale) and improving in the evening after hot showers, heating pad use, or self-massage. He reported chronic neck and shoulder tightness but otherwise led an active lifestyle outside of computer work. His medical history included a remote concussion and an acute bout of neck pain after a biking accident 5 years earlier, when imaging had ruled out red flags, and he made a full recovery apart from intermittent stiffness. 

On examination by an experienced physical therapist, cervical rotation was 55° bilaterally, side bending 10° bilaterally, and flexion/extension 50°/60°. Muscle strength was 3+/5 for middle trapezius, rhomboids, and external rotators. Deep neck flexor endurance was 45 seconds. Cervical and thoracic central posterior-to-anterior mobilizations were hypomobile from C1–7 and T1–5. Neurologic screening was normal: “Screen (−) cranial nerve, upper motor neuron, myotomes, dermatomes, deep tendon reflex tests.” The patient demonstrated pronounced thoracic kyphosis and forward head posture at his workstation. Palpation with a pincer grasp to the distal levator scapulae muscle belly (one thumb width superior and medial to the superior angle of the scapula) bilaterally reproduced his posterior neck and suboccipital pain. Tenderness with referred pain was also elicited at the levator scapulae enthesis over the medial aspect of the superior angle of the scapula, bilaterally.

A 64-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a pruritic truncal rash in the setting of systemic immunotherapy and for numerous eruptive lower‐extremity lesions. His medical history was notable for hypertension, coronary artery disease, and a 4-mm well‐differentiated cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) treated with Mohs surgery 6 years earlier. Ten months prior, he had an SCC excised from his right lower leg; subsequently, he developed multiple exophytic papules and plaques on both lower extremities, six of which were biopsied and read as well-differentiated SCC.

An initial positron-emission tomography (PET) scan showed multifocal cutaneous lesions and nonspecific pelvic lymphadenopathy suspicious for metastatic disease, and he was started on cemiplimab. Three months later, repeat PET demonstrated progression of the skin lesions and new bilateral inguinal and external iliac hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy. He then entered a clinical trial of an LILRB2 antagonist plus a PD-1 inhibitor, received four cycles of therapy, and underwent palliative radiation to the affected extremities.

He subsequently presented with diffuse pruritus and a minimally scaly red papular rash on the trunk, which was refractory to hydroxyzine and topical triamcinolone. Biopsy of the truncal rash showed spongiotic dermatitis with eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence was negative, and an immunobullous disease antibody panel was unremarkable. The differential diagnosis included an id reaction, medication hypersensitivity, and contact dermatitis. Given the multifocal eruption on both legs, consistently well‐differentiated histology, and no other high‐risk factors for aggressive SCC, the diagnosis of unresectable metastatic cutaneous SCC was questioned. An inguinal lymph node biopsy was performed and showed a benign reactive lymph node.

A 42-year-old woman with no significant medical history was admitted 7 days after known exposure to SARS-CoV-2 with nausea, relentless vomiting, headache, and a predominantly right-sided rash of 3 days’ duration. A nasopharyngeal swab for SARS-CoV-2 was positive. She was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and denied respiratory symptoms but reported ageusia and anosmia. On examination, she had mild abdominal tenderness and a cutaneous eruption consisting of dozens of thin pink papules coalescing into thin pink plaques on the posterior lateral trunk near the axillae bilaterally, with the right side more affected than the left. The rash extended to the upper lateral right thigh and right lateral lower leg but spared the palms, soles, and mucous membranes; there were no bullae, vesicles, or purpura, and she reported only mild pruritus. She denied use of any new prescription medications or skin products and had taken acetaminophen prior to rash onset. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 3.5×10^3/μL with an absolute lymphocyte count of 0.3×10^3/μL and eosinophils 0.6%, C-reactive protein 91.9 mg/L, ferritin 317 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 285 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 30 U/L, and aspartate aminotransferase 39 U/L. A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral multifocal hazy opacities.

A 28-year-old primigravida was referred at 31 weeks and 2 days of gestation after an abnormal fetal echocardiogram. At 29 weeks, “blindly ended vessels originating from the heart or transposition of the great arteries was first noticed,” but no lung abnormalities were reported. Her medical and obstetric history was unremarkable. On ultrasound at our institution, the diaphragm was elevated bilaterally, and the thoracic cavities—especially the right—were reduced in size. The heart occupied much of the left thorax with a markedly left-deviated axis due to cephalad displacement of the diaphragm. It was “not evident whether any lung tissue was present, or whether there were any lung abnormalities or pulmonary veins connecting to the left atrium as well as the right and left branches of the main pulmonary artery,” although no specific structural cardiac defects were identified. A fetal MRI confirmed a significantly decreased thoracic volume with bilaterally elevated hemidiaphragms, resulting in upward migration of the heart and rotation of the cardiac axis. Moreover, “no definite lung was identified and the trachea ended blindly near the level of the cricoid cartilage without bronchial branching.”

A 9.4-year-old US-born Hispanic boy was evaluated for recurrent, slow‐to‐resolve episodes of pneumonia since age 3. He has had five chest‐radiograph–confirmed pneumonias, most requiring hospitalization and intravenous antibiotics for persistent cough and fever. He is otherwise active with normal growth and development. He has no history of recurrent sinusitis, otitis, cellulitis, lymphadenitis, osteomyelitis, sepsis, meningitis, deep organ abscesses, or poor healing. There is no family history of recurrent infections.

Previous evaluations included two bronchoscopies with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) revealing no pathogens or anatomic abnormalities. Immunologic testing showed elevated IgG (1728 mg/dL) and IgA (408 mg/dL), protective tetanus titers, and normal pneumococcal antibody response. Tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, HIV infection, Wegener’s granulomatosis, sarcoidosis, and cystic fibrosis had all been excluded.

On admission he was well developed, febrile to 40 °C, and tachypneic but not hypoxemic. Lung exam revealed crackles and tubular sounds over the right hemithorax. Chest radiography showed right‐sided pulmonary infiltrates. The white‐cell count was 14,000/mm3 with 74% neutrophils. Empiric antibiotics were switched to vancomycin and ceftriaxone after limited response to ampicillin‐sulbactam.

Bronchoscopy showed positive Aspergillus antigen (titer 1.5) in BAL fluid and growth of >100,000 cfu/mL Streptococcus viridans. Pneumocystis, Nocardia, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fungal, and viral studies were negative. Review of serial chest imaging demonstrated variable focal opacities: diffuse nodularity in some areas and large focal consolidations in others, with no hyperinflation or small‐airway changes.

Dihydrorhodamine‐123 testing revealed 34% of neutrophils negative for fluorescence and 66% dimly positive after PMA stimulation.

A 69-year-old woman presented with dyspnea and persistent low-grade fever several weeks after a tooth extraction. Her medical history included Sjögren syndrome treated with steroids. On examination, she had a pansystolic murmur at the mitral area and multiple splinter hemorrhages. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, and CT imaging revealed multiple cerebral and renal emboli. Transesophageal echocardiography showed vegetations and perforation of the posterior leaflet (P1–P2 scallop) of the mitral valve, a perivalvular abscess cavity in the posterior annulus at P1, and severe mitral regurgitation. She was treated with intravenous antibiotics, developed pulmonary edema requiring diuretics and inotropes, and underwent mechanical mitral valve replacement; intraoperative cultures confirmed MSSA, and antibiotics continued for 6 weeks. Several weeks later, she remained febrile despite negative blood cultures. Repeat transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated complete detachment of the prosthetic valve’s posterior segment and a pseudoaneurysm arising from the anterolateral commissure of the mitral annulus. A cardiac CT angiogram confirmed a pseudoaneurysm at the anterolateral commissure communicating with the left ventricle.

A 30-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a three-week history of influenza-like symptoms, including joint and muscle aches, fatigue, fever, rigors, and tachycardia. She denied breathlessness or productive cough. She had received a course of antibiotics from her general practitioner, and although her symptoms gradually resolved, serial chest radiographs showed persistent bilateral patchy areas of consolidation.

Six weeks after the initial presentation, she was referred to the respiratory clinic. She reported feeling well apart from a dry cough and tiredness. Her medical history included childhood asthma, chronic idiopathic urticaria, irritable bowel syndrome, and multiple sclerosis treated with interferon-β (44 μg subcutaneously three times weekly) for the previous five months; the interferon-β had been discontinued because of systemic side effects. Other medications were omeprazole, mebeverine, and amitriptyline. She smoked 10–15 cigarettes per day, and her family history was notable for multiple sclerosis in her sister.

On examination, her vital signs were normal. There was no lymphadenopathy or skin lesions. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. Respiratory examination revealed bronchial breathing over the left lung, without wheeze or crepitations.

Laboratory studies at initial presentation had shown a normal full blood count, renal and liver function, calcium, and glucose levels, with a C-reactive protein level of 11 mg/L (normal <5 mg/L). At the clinic, thyroid function tests and an autoimmune screen (antinuclear antibodies, extractable nuclear antigen, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies) were normal, and 24-hour urinary calcium was normal.

A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral patchy air-space consolidation and prominent hilar shadows. Computed tomography of the thorax revealed extensive mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and multifocal patchy air-space consolidation in both lungs.

Pulmonary-function testing showed an FEV₁ of 2.8 L (95% of predicted), an FVC of 3.56 L (105% of predicted), an FEV₁/FVC ratio of 94%, a transfer factor for carbon monoxide of 74% of predicted, and a carbon monoxide transfer coefficient of 85% of predicted.

Bronchoscopy revealed fragile, hyperemic mucosa. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was negative for malignancy and infection, and acid-fast bacilli were not detected on microscopy or culture.

A 44-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive bilateral tingling and muscle weakness in his hands and feet. The paresthesias worsened until he became unable to move his extremities and was almost totally bedridden with irritating distal sensations. He denied any history of head or back trauma.

On examination, he was fully alert, with normal vital signs. He appeared slightly anemic and mildly icteric. Neurologic examination showed hyporeflexia in all four limbs, Medical Research Council muscle power grade 3/5 in the upper limbs and 1/5 in the lower limbs, and hypesthesia in all extremities without pathological reflexes.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, platelets 116 000/mm3, aspartate aminotransferase 51 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 56 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, prothrombin time 14.3 s (INR 1.3), albumin 2.6 g/dL, total protein 7.0 g/dL, creatinine 0.59 mg/dL, and normal electrolytes. Viral tests were positive for HBsAg and HBeAg, with an HBV DNA load of 1.65 × 105 IU/mL, and negative for HCV and HIV. Abdominal ultrasound showed minimal ascites.

Nerve conduction studies demonstrated prolongation of motor distal latency and F-wave latency and reduced motor conduction velocity in both sensory and motor nerves, consistent with axonal demyelination. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 7 lymphocytes/mm3 and a protein concentration of 135 mg/dL. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed polyclonal gamma-globulinemia. Brain MRI identified a lacunar infarction. The patient declined biopsy.

A 22-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of generalized painful fluid‐filled skin lesions, 7 days of yellow scleral discoloration, and 1 month of fever following removal of a tibial implant. Two years earlier, he had sustained a tibial fracture treated with internal fixation. After implant removal, he developed a surgical-site infection and persistent fever; he initially took paracetamol without relief, then obtained ciprofloxacin over the counter. Two days after starting ciprofloxacin, he developed generalized pruritus that progressed to fluid-filled rashes. He denied angioedema, dyspnea, abdominal distention, lower-limb swelling, hematemesis, melena, altered sensorium, alcohol use, or immunocompromise.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. He had icterus but no pallor, clubbing, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed multiple generalized vesicles and bullae with non-hemorrhagic crusts over the trunk and extremities (palms and soles spared). Lesions were tender, with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Mucosal findings included hemorrhagic lip crusts and penile erosion.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Leukocyte count 18,520/mm3 (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 22%, eosinophils 12%)  
• Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 423,000/mm3  
• AST 283 U/L, ALT 246 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1390 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 14 mg/dL (conjugated 13.7 mg/dL)  
• Albumin 2.4 g/dL, INR 2.7  
• Renal function and electrolytes were within normal limits.

A male infant (Twin A of dizygotic twins) was delivered at 37 weeks’ gestation by cesarean section for footling breech presentation. Prenatal ultrasound had shown intermittent hydronephrosis and incomplete bladder emptying in this fetus. The infant’s Apgar scores were 4 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. On examination, the newborn had marked abdominal distension; external genitalia appeared normal.

A postnatal renal ultrasound demonstrated bilateral hydronephrosis, hydroureter, and a markedly distended urinary bladder. Urinary catheterization yielded 75 mL of urine, decompressing the bladder. Voiding cystourethrography revealed a severely distended bladder filling most of the abdomen without vesicoureteral reflux. There was no spontaneous voiding even after 500 mL of contrast; contrast emptied only with manual Crede maneuver, showing a normal urethra and no posterior urethral valves.

Concern for intestinal function led to an upper gastrointestinal series via nasogastric tube, which showed a normal-sized duodenum, a low duodenojejunal junction, and absent peristalsis. A water-soluble contrast enema demonstrated a meconium-filled microcolon predominantly in the left hemiabdomen, with contrast reflux limited to the distal ileum.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 22-year history of left shoulder pain following a motor vehicle accident in which she sustained a splenic laceration, pneumothorax, a two-part upper humerus fracture, and fractures of ribs six through eleven. Initial management included chest-tube placement, percutaneous pinning of the humerus, and nonoperative splenic management; she was hospitalized for 10 days. Although all apparent injuries healed, she continued to experience dull left shoulder pain radiating to the left mandible, typically 2/10 but up to 8/10 in cold weather or after large meals. Physical therapy and subacromial and glenohumeral corticosteroid injections in the first year provided no relief. Ten years post-accident, orthopaedic evaluation included serial examinations, provocative tests that failed to reproduce the pain, magnetic resonance imaging showing no significant neck or shoulder pathology, and cardiac evaluation, all of which were unremarkable. Arthroscopic surgery to remove the buried humeral pins did not relieve her symptoms. Nearly 20 years after the accident, she developed episodic sharp left-sided “gassy” abdominal pain and nausea occurring two to three times weekly, lasting 3–24 hours, and resolving only after vomiting or dry heaving. She denied fevers, chills, or diarrhea. A work-up for gallbladder and hepatobiliary problems was negative.

A 66-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and a history of generalized myasthenia gravis (MG) treated with methylprednisolone (tapered to 20 mg daily) and azathioprine (100 mg daily) presented with fever, cough, dyspnea, and lumbodynia after a fall. On examination, his temperature was 38 °C, with normal other vital signs. Auscultation revealed multiple rales in both lungs. Multiple irregular, tender, warm, erythematous subcutaneous masses were noted on the chest, back, neck, and right limbs, and there was an infectious ulcerative lesion on the right lower limb. Neurologic examination showed mild weakness of the right lower limb (5–/5), otherwise normal.

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, liver and renal function, electrolytes, and coagulation. Antinuclear and extractable nuclear antibodies and tumour markers were negative. IgG, IgA, C3, and C4 were normal; IgM was low at 25 mg/dL twice (normal, 40–230). Lymphocyte subsets were normal. Respiratory virus panel, tuberculosis T-cell and antibody tests, and serologies for HBV, HCV, HIV, and syphilis were negative. CRP was 37 mg/L (normal < 5 mg/L). 

Spine X-ray showed compression fractures of L1 and L2. Neck CT revealed a mass on the left side suggesting a swollen lymph node, abscess, or tumour. Chest CT showed multiple nodular and patchy shadows in both lungs with pleural and pericardial effusions. Abdominal CT revealed gallstones and a small right renal cyst.

He was treated for presumed pneumonia with moxifloxacin, and his fever and respiratory symptoms improved. After 20 days, he developed fever with chills, worsened dyspnea, headache, right leg pain, and severe left eye pain with rapid progression to blindness. Brain CT showed multiple hypodense lesions. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the cerebral hemispheres and cerebellum on contrast T1-weighted images. Orbital MRI revealed an enhancing lesion behind the left globe and retinal detachment.

A 51-year-old man presented with dyspnea of New York Heart Association class IV and chest pain of Canadian Cardiovascular Society class III for 2 days. He reported 2 weeks of progressive fatigue, headache, sore throat, malaise, weight loss, and intermittent sweats. His medical history included arterial hypertension and a remote mild traumatic brain injury with lung contusion in 2010. On examination, he was tachycardic (103 bpm) and hypotensive (90/60 mmHg). ECG showed ST-segment elevations in leads II, III, and aVF and low-voltage QRS complexes in V1–V3. Laboratory tests revealed a C-reactive protein level of 135 mg/L (normal <5), leukocytosis (21 G/L), high-sensitivity troponin I of 0.05 µg/L (normal <0.03), and procalcitonin of 0.13 µg/L (normal <0.05). Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly with central and peripheral pulmonary venous congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a non-dilated, hypertrophied left ventricle with normal ejection fraction, mild atrioventricular regurgitation, and a large circumferential pericardial effusion measuring up to 23 mm, with diastolic right ventricular collapse, systolic right atrial collapse, and a dilated inferior vena cava consistent with tamponade physiology. Urgent pericardiocentesis drained 800 mL of bloody-tinged fluid, after which his chest pain and dyspnea resolved and troponin levels declined. The fluid was exudative with elevated protein, leukocytes, cholesterol, glucose, and amylase. Aerobic and anaerobic bacterial cultures, Ziehl–Neelsen staining, interferon-γ release assay, and long-term cultures for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were all negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed residual pericardial effusion and a modest left lower lobe infiltrate. Empiric intravenous piperacillin and ibuprofen were initiated.

A 51-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus and recent chemotherapy for uterine cancer presented to the emergency department with acute confusion. On examination she was confused but hemodynamically stable and polypneic; her blood glucose level was elevated. Laboratory evaluation confirmed diabetic ketoacidosis, which was treated promptly. To exclude cerebral metastases, noncontrast and contrast-enhanced head CT scans were obtained. On the brain windows, there was no parenchymal lesion to explain her altered mental status. On the bone windows, the left frontal sinus and left ethmoidal cells were enlarged and communicated with each other, showing endocranial expansion and a midline shift of intracranial structures toward the right side. The bony walls remained intact without thinning. On re-examination, she was found to have frontal bossing. Her mental status normalized after treatment of the ketoacidosis.

A 14-year-old boy with Beckwith-Wiedemann spectrum (mosaic paternal isodisomy of 11p15) was followed for right-sided body overgrowth, leg-length discrepancy, and prior neonatal macrosomia, transient hypoglycemia, and an umbilical wall defect. Puberty began at 11 years. At 14 years, he was noted to have right testicular enlargement: right testis 18 ml versus left 12 ml by clinical exam. Both testes were of normal consistency without palpable nodules; scrotal transillumination was opaque. The patient was asymptomatic, with a normal pubertal growth spurt and no history of trauma.  
Scrotal ultrasound showed right testis 46 × 31 × 24 mm (18 ml) and left testis 35 × 23 × 14 mm (12 ml), both with regular homogeneous echotexture and no focal lesions. Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. Complete blood count, LDH, β-hCG, α-FP, CEA, and testicular, adrenal, and thyroid hormone levels were all within normal limits. In the absence of concerning findings, a watchful-waiting approach was adopted.  
At 15 years, ultrasound confirmed persistent asymmetry (right 54.5 × 20.2 × 34.3 mm [19.7 ml]; left 46.2 × 18.6 × 29.1 mm [13.3 ml]) with unchanged homogeneous echotexture. Tumor markers and laboratory studies remained normal.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of left hip pain without trauma. She had no prior medical history. On presentation, her temperature was 37.7 °C; other vital signs were normal. She described focal tenderness in the left inguinal region, and pain was elicited with hip motion. There was no muscle weakness on examination. Initial laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, white-cell count 7,600/µL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 6 mm/hr, C-reactive protein 0.7 mg/dL, and creatine kinase 100 IU/L. On the following day, her C-reactive protein rose to 4.7 mg/dL. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis revealed increased T2 signal intensity and contrast enhancement in the left iliopsoas (iliacus) muscle, without evidence of abscess. Despite normalization of her temperature by hospital day 2, her hip pain persisted despite nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory therapy.

A 64-year-old African-American man with a history of prostate cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and chronic hepatitis C virus infection presented with four weeks of bilateral knee, hand, and neck polyarthralgias. Two weeks before presentation he noted a 5-cm annular lesion with central clearing on his abdomen. Lyme IgM antibody testing was positive, IgG bands were nonreactive, and Western blot confirmed 25- and 41-kD IgM bands, consistent with acute Borrelia burgdorferi infection. Initial laboratory studies showed normal C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, uric acid, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear and anti-citrulline antibodies, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and HIV antibody.

After two weeks of doxycycline and corticosteroids, he was admitted with progressive proximal muscle weakness, worsening dyspnea, facial and palmar dermatitis, and a 10-lb weight loss. On examination, he was afebrile with a respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute and a heart rate of 130 beats per minute. He had bibasilar crackles, violaceous eruptions over the forehead, periorbital, and nasolabial folds, hyperpigmented papular changes on the palms with ulcerated fingertips, and motor strength of 3/5 in the lower extremities and 4/5 in the upper extremities.

Laboratory evaluation showed normal chemistry and blood counts, mildly elevated transaminases, an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:40, positive anti–Jo-1 antibody, and negative cryoglobulins. Creatine phosphokinase and aldolase levels were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, spine, and extremities was unremarkable. Skin biopsies of the facial and finger lesions demonstrated superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, pigmented macrophages, vacuolar degeneration, and dermal mucin—findings interpreted as most consistent with dermatomyositis by dermatopathology. Evaluation for dyspnea revealed a normal chest radiograph, normal nuclear stress test, and normal echocardiogram.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of a swelling at the left angle of her mandible. There was no history of trauma, pain, or other precipitating event. The swelling was 2 cm in diameter, well‐circumscribed, and soft, without adherence to deeper structures. On examination, the swelling was clearly visible when she clenched her jaws and disappeared when she opened her mouth; facial nerve function and sensation were intact. Palpation during clenching made the swelling slightly larger and firmer. Intraoral examination was unremarkable, and salivary flow from the parotid and submandibular glands was normal bilaterally. Dynamic ultrasonography during contraction demonstrated a focal protrusion of the masseter muscle through a defect in the parotidomasseteric fascia, with an 8 mm collar, consistent with a fascial tear.

A 39-year-old African American man presented with a 1-week history of gnawing, constant epigastric pain that began after dining out. He denied fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. His medical history was notable for a 7-year history of chronic arthritis affecting the hands, feet, and back, for which he took naproxen as needed. He reported poor appetite and a 30-lb weight loss over the past 3 months. He emigrated from Cape Verde 20 years earlier, did not smoke or use illicit drugs, rarely drank alcohol, and had no relevant family history. 

On examination, temperature was normal, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg, pulse 111 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Abdominal examination revealed a soft, flat abdomen with normoactive bowel sounds and tenderness localized to the epigastrium without rebound or guarding. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or palpable masses.

Laboratory studies showed microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 78 fL), mild leukocytosis (11.7 × 10^3/mm^3), and iron studies consistent with iron deficiency. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated extensive mesenteric lymphadenopathy.

A 68-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of periodic, moderate epigastric pain radiating to the mesogastrium, associated with vomiting and weight loss. His medical history was notable only for hypertension; he denied alcohol use.  
On examination, he was hemodynamically stable, with epigastric tenderness, normal bowel sounds, no organomegaly, and a normal rectal examination.  
Laboratory studies showed normal liver enzymes, negative viral hepatitis markers, a negative autoimmune hepatitis panel, and normal carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed a normal liver parenchyma, a portal vein diameter of 15 mm, transient elastography stage F0, and a 15 mm submucosal lesion along the greater curvature with a “double-wall” sign (hyperechoic mucosa and hypoechoic muscular layer). The lesion had well-defined margins, no neovascularization, and no invasion of adjacent structures.  
Upper endoscopy demonstrated grade 1/2 esophageal varices in the upper third, a compressing mass on the greater curvature, portal gastropathy, and otherwise normal gastric mucosa.  
Contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-delineated, hypoattenuating, polylobate peri-gastric lesion adjacent to the greater curvature measuring approximately 102 × 80 × 60 mm, with a thin wall and homogeneous content (22–24 HU), contact but no invasion of the spleen, pancreatic tail, or left renal vessels, and no secondary collateral vessels described.

A 42-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of progressively worsening productive cough, fatigue, shortness of breath, and palpitations. She noted that she became dyspneic and fatigued when walking more than one block, which was new for her. She denied chest pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. She had no past medical history, did not smoke or use illicit drugs, and had no known occupational dust exposures. She had immigrated from Sierra Leone 10 years earlier and worked as a nursing aide, with close contact with patients who had respiratory illnesses. She reported five years of significant second-hand smoke exposure in her apartment complex. She had received two doses of the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine.

On examination, she was fatigued and in mild respiratory distress with increased work of breathing. Auscultation revealed diffuse rales and rhonchi bilaterally. Her oxygen saturation was 98% on room air at rest, which dropped to 69% after ambulation; supplemental oxygen at 3 L/min by nasal cannula improved her saturation to 99%. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

A chest CT scan demonstrated extensive bilateral emphysematous changes with multiple prominent pulmonary bullae—largest in the anterior left upper lobe and posterior right lower lobe—associated regions of bronchiectasis and bronchial wall thickening, and dilatation of the pulmonary vasculature.  
Alpha-1 antitrypsin levels were within normal limits.  
A SARS-CoV-2 test was negative.

A 22-year-old woman, gravida 1 at 22 weeks’ gestation, was admitted for decreased fetal movement and transvaginal bleeding. Two weeks earlier she had intermittent spotting; over days, fetal mobility decreased. She had no significant medical history and denied smoking, alcohol, or drug use. On admission, the fetal heart rate was 130 beats per minute; uterine contractions and fetal movements were absent; speculum examination revealed bloody discharge. Transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated absence of amniotic fluid. Empiric antibiotics (ampicillin and azithromycin) were initiated, and benzathine penicillin was given for a positive serum VDRL at 1:64. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, leukocyte count 7710/mm³, platelet count 217 000/mm³, C-reactive protein 31 mg/dL, and negative HIV tests. Three days later, she developed fever, abdominal pain, leukocytosis, and further elevation of C-reactive protein; chorioamnionitis was suspected, and labor was induced with misoprostol. Two days after induction, she reported mild headache, neck stiffness, and fever; retained products of conception were suspected, and sharp curettage was performed with initiation of piperacillin–tazobactam and vancomycin. Head CT showed diffuse cerebral edema and hydrocephalus. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed protein 49 mg/dL, glucose 56 mg/dL, five lymphocytes/mm³, adenosine deaminase 4.6 U/L; CSF VDRL and cryptococcal antigen were negative.

A 74-year-old woman with controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a remote history of marginal zone B-cell lymphoma presented in summer with 1–2 days of abdominal pain and watery diarrhea, body aches, and 2–3 weeks of progressive dyspnea and dry cough. She reported a 20-pound unintentional weight loss. She denied travel, sick contacts, or recent hospitalization. She smoked 3–5 cigarettes per day.  

On examination, temperature was 38.9 °C, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, heart rate 110 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air; lung auscultation revealed diffuse crackles and end-expiratory wheezes. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  

Laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, hematocrit 28.9%, white blood cell count 5.5 × 10^3/μL, platelet count 311 × 10^3/μL, blood urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, and urinalysis with hyaline casts and epithelial cells. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus arrhythmia with a new first-degree atrioventricular block.  

Chest radiograph and computed tomography revealed pulmonary infiltrates with hyperinflated lungs, centrilobular emphysema, scattered blebs and bullae, consolidation with air bronchograms in the right upper and lower lobes, and a small right pleural effusion. She was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia and given bronchodilators.  

Despite treatment, she developed hypoxic respiratory failure, hemoptysis, and worsening infiltrates, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. Bronchoscopic bronchoalveolar lavage yielded progressively hemorrhagic fluid consistent with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.

A 41-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a four-day history of intermittent non-specific chest pain, on a background of progressive exertional dyspnea over several months and recent loss of appetite. She denied fever, cough, hemoptysis, pleuritic pain, or upper respiratory symptoms. She had no significant past medical history, was not diabetic, and took no medications. She smoked 30 pack‐years. She lived in Darwin, Northern Territory, and was an avid gardener who often walked barefoot and used large amounts of potting mix. She had no known tuberculosis exposures, no relevant travel or occupational history, and no alcohol or drug misuse.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable; there was no clubbing, edema, cyanosis, or lymphadenopathy. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 11.5×10^9/L with neutrophilia of 7.9×10^9/L and a C-reactive protein of 15 mg/L. Serial troponins, liver and renal function, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Quantiferon Gold testing was negative. Pulmonary function tests were near normal (FVC 97% predicted, FEV1 92% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.787, DLCO 77%, TLC 89% predicted).

Chest radiography demonstrated an opacity in the right mid-zone. Contrast CT of the chest showed a 36×22 mm mass in the right lower lobe without endoluminal bronchial lesions or mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. PET-CT revealed mild to moderate FDG uptake in the right lower lobe mass and no FDG-avid nodal or distant lesions. Flexible bronchoscopy showed no endobronchial abnormality. Using radial EBUS with a guide sheath, a heterogeneous peripheral lesion was localized in the posterior segment of the right lower lobe. Brushings, biopsies, washings, and a transbronchial cryobiopsy were obtained from the targeted site.

A 38-year-old woman presents for follow-up of multiple cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) treated over the past decade, including one that metastasized to her orbit and neck. She was born in El Salvador and reports a rash beginning at age three, with gradual development of numerous asymptomatic, tan-pink macules and flat-topped papules on the face, trunk, and extremities. Eight months ago, she was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung and treated with carboplatin, pembrolizumab, and paclitaxel, with initial tumor response.

On examination, there are numerous 3–8 mm light tan-pink, round-to-oval papules coalescing into plaques, some with fine scale, distributed on the trunk and extremities. A shave biopsy of a right shoulder lesion shows multiple large keratinocytes with blue-gray cytoplasm and varying-sized keratohyalin granules within the upper spinous and granular layers.

A 68-year-old Japanese woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease was brought to the emergency department after fainting preceded by dizziness. She reported one month of anorexia. On admission her Glasgow Coma Scale was 15 (E4V5M6), and vital signs were: temperature 36.8°C, blood pressure 128/75 mmHg, heart rate 152 irregular beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable, including normal conjunctivae, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and normal chest, cardiac, and abdominal findings. 

Initial laboratory studies showed: WBC 10 300/µL, BUN 34 mg/dL, creatinine 4.09 mg/dL, sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 2.6 mEq/L, chloride 87 mEq/L, glucose 262 mg/dL, β-glycated hemoglobin 5.9%, CRP 0.07 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed 1+ protein, 4+ glucose, and + ketones with no blood cells or casts. Electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation. Chest radiograph and CT scans of the brain, chest, abdomen, and pelvis were normal. 

She was admitted for intravenous fluids, electrolyte repletion, and insulin. Over the next two days, her electrolytes, glucose, and renal function improved, but her mental status declined to a Glasgow Coma Scale of 11 (E4V3M4), and she developed fever to 37.8°C with periods of apnea and tachypnea. Glossoptosis was noted, and an oropharyngeal airway and bite block were placed. Painful dental caries were observed, but the oropharynx otherwise appeared normal. 

On hospital day 3, laboratory studies revealed WBC 14 800/µL (94.1% neutrophils) and CRP 0.08 mg/dL. Repeat chest radiograph, brain CT, brain MRI, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed no abnormalities.

A 10-year-old girl with no previous medical history presented with a 2-day history of lower extremity pain and limping. Five days before admission, she had experienced fever up to 39.1°C twice daily and headache, both of which resolved within 3 days. She subsequently developed mild diarrhea but denied cough, dyspnea, vomiting, change in smell or taste, or dark urine. She participates in sports without recent trauma or changes in her training schedule. On examination, she was afebrile, with normal vital signs; the respiratory examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph was normal. Initial laboratory studies showed an absolute lymphocyte count of 1 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein of 1.4 mg/L (normal 0–3 mg/L), and creatine kinase of 13 147 U/L (normal < 140 U/L). Lactate dehydrogenase was 631 U/L (normal 120–300 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase 288 U/L (normal < 60 U/L), and alanine aminotransferase 67 U/L (normal < 45 U/L). Renal function was normal; urine testing showed no red blood cells or hemoglobin. Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram were normal. A nasopharyngeal PCR test for SARS-CoV-2 was positive with a low cycle threshold; respiratory viral panel, Epstein–Barr virus serology, and cytomegalovirus serology were negative.

A man in his 60s presented with 3 days of weakness in both lower limbs. He had visited a hot spring 5 days before presentation. His medical history included spontaneous pneumothoraces and untreated hypertension. He was a 40 pack-year smoker, drank alcohol daily, and took no regular medications. On examination, his temperature was 39.1°C, blood pressure 198/94 mm Hg, heart rate 115 bpm (irregular, atrial fibrillation), respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Neurologically, he had mild disturbance of consciousness (Japan Coma Scale I-1, Glasgow Coma Scale E4V4M6), dysarthria, kinetic tremor in both hands, and an unsteady gait. He was inattentive, mildly hyperactive, and occasionally removed his oxygen mask.  
Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (WBC 13.7×10^9/L, neutrophils 91.4%), CRP 33.83 mg/dL, elevated liver enzymes (AST 91 U/L, ALT 63 U/L), hyponatraemia (Na 131 mmol/L), and CK 1551 U/L. Legionella pneumophila urinary antigen was positive; sputum culture was negative. Chest X-ray and CT revealed consolidation in the right lower lobe and bilateral emphysema. Head CT was normal. Brain MRI on admission showed a focal hyperintense lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum on diffusion-weighted imaging, with corresponding mild T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity; MR angiography was unremarkable. No cerebrospinal fluid examination or EEG was performed.

A 41-year-old man of Portuguese ancestry presented with cosmetically distressing nodules on both hands and on his right elbow that had been slowly increasing in size over several years. He reported no tenderness, joint stiffness, or history of trauma. He recalled that his maternal uncle had similar nodules. He was otherwise healthy, with no comorbidities, smoking, or drug use. His sister had suffered a myocardial infarction at age 45 and was on multiple lipid-lowering medications.

On examination, his blood pressure was normal and his body mass index was 32 kg/m2. Inspection and palpation revealed multiple tendon xanthomas over the extensor tendons of the hands and a prominent xanthoma at the elbow. He also had a corneal arcus and thickened Achilles tendons on both sides.  

Laboratory testing showed a fasting total cholesterol level of 403 mg/dL, an LDL-C level of 347 mg/dL, an HDL-C level of 35 mg/dL, and a normal triglyceride level. An electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, and echocardiogram were all unremarkable.

A 36-year-old Sri Lankan Sinhalese man working as a paddy farmer presented with a 3-day history of high-spiking fever, chills, severe arthralgia and myalgia, and lower-limb muscle cramps. One day before admission he developed resting dyspnea with a nonproductive cough and was anuric for 12 hours. He had no significant past medical history, occasional alcohol use, and no tobacco use. 

On examination he was febrile (39.5 °C), hypotensive (80/40 mm Hg), tachycardic (140/min), tachypneic (32/min), and dehydrated, with warm peripheries and marked orthostatic changes. He had mild icterus, injected conjunctivae, bilateral coarse pulmonary crepitations, and tender hepatomegaly without splenomegaly. He was alert and oriented.

Laboratory studies on admission showed: leukocyte count 24.6 × 10^9/L (90% neutrophils), platelet count 86 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL; peripheral smear with neutrophil leukocytosis, toxic neutrophils, myelocytes, atypical lymphocytes, and thrombocytopenia. Liver enzymes were elevated (AST 924 U/L, ALT 331 U/L), total bilirubin 55 mmol/L (direct 55%), alkaline phosphatase 459 U/L; serum creatinine 217 µmol/L, BUN 40 mg/dL, potassium 2.9 mmol/L; CRP 379 mg/dL; CK 440 µg/L; lactate 5 mmol/L; arterial blood gas pH 7.26, HCO3– 14.5 mmol/L, PaCO2 20 mm Hg.

A chest radiograph showed bilateral air-space opacifications. ECG demonstrated T-wave inversions in leads V1–V6 with troponin I 0.16 ng/mL. Echocardiography revealed global hypokinesia with an LVEF of 40%.  

A working diagnosis of severe leptospirosis with multiorgan dysfunction was made in the setting of significant mud exposure. He was admitted to a high-dependency unit, given oxygen, aggressive fluid resuscitation, inotropic support, intravenous cefotaxime, oral doxycycline, methylprednisolone, N-acetylcysteine, and electrolyte correction.

A 12-year-old girl presented with 5 days of fever, right lateral-cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy, and frontoparietal headache. Her medical history was unremarkable; she had no pets and no recent travel. On examination, she had a 3 cm tender right lateral-cervical swelling with overlying erythema. Laboratory evaluation showed a white blood cell count of 16.2×10^3/µL (12.8×10^3/µL neutrophils) with normal C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; an oropharyngeal swab was negative. Ultrasound of the neck demonstrated multiple reactive lymph nodes without central necrosis and additional reactive nodes in the left cervical and bilateral inguinal regions. She was discharged on a 14-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate, with initial improvement in lymphadenopathy and fever. Two days after completing antibiotics, she returned with recurrent severe headache and cervical swelling and was admitted. Physical examination again revealed right cervical swelling and noted a new 2 cm left parietal-occipital scalp swelling. Repeat blood counts and inflammatory markers were normal. Because of the scalp lesion, contrast-enhanced cranial magnetic resonance imaging was performed, revealing a 10 mm area of skull erosion in the left temporoparietal region. A whole-body bone scan excluded additional sites of osteomyelitis. Abdominal ultrasound showed a 1 cm round hypoechoic lesion in the spleen consistent with a granuloma.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of fever, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, mild right upper–quadrant abdominal pain, and jaundice. One week earlier, she had experienced coryza and malaise lasting 4 days that resolved without treatment. She denied drug or alcohol use and had no recent travel. 

On examination, her temperature was 38.5 °C and heart rate was 110 beats/min. She had scleral and cutaneous icterus and mild right upper–quadrant tenderness without Murphy’s sign. Liver span on the midclavicular line was 110 mm, and the spleen measured 170 mm. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy, tonsillar exudate, mucosal rash, or skin rash.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a liver of normal size with increased echogenicity (grade 2 fatty change), splenomegaly (175 mm), normal portal-vein diameter and flow, a normal suprahepatic inferior vena cava, a normal gallbladder and biliary tree without evidence of cholestasis, and mild ascites.

Laboratory results were notable for WBC 16,300/μL (57% lymphocytes, 20% variant), hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, platelets 74,000/μL, AST 239 IU/L, ALT 219 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 1294 IU/L, total bilirubin 15.9 mg/dL (direct 8.9 mg/dL), albumin 2.4 g/dL, ESR 21 mm/h, CRP 39 mg/L, and negative blood cultures (two sets). Amylase, creatinine, coagulation studies, and other chemistry values were within normal limits.

Serologic and molecular tests for hepatotropic viruses and related infections showed:  
- HBsAg negative, anti-HBs 1 mIU/mL, anti-HBc total and anti-HBc IgM nonreactive, HBV PCR negative  
- Anti-HCV reactive, HCV RNA negative  
- Anti–HAV total within normal range  
- Anti–HEV nonreactive  
- Anti–HIV (1,2) nonreactive  
- CMV PCR negative

A 50-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis treated with infliximab for over 10 years and no personal or family history of psoriasis presented with a 1-year history of an erythematous, scaly rash with deep fissures and crusting involving the nasal vestibule, ears, and scalp. She denied any preceding viral illness or streptococcal infection. Empiric treatments over the preceding 6+ months—including mid- to high-potency topical corticosteroids, antifungal creams, oral antibiotics, and oral antiviral medications—resulted in minimal to no improvement. An incisional biopsy of the left nasal vestibular mucosa revealed squamous epithelium with acanthosis, parakeratosis with scale crust, and a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the subepithelial stroma. Dermatopathology review showed psoriasiform dermatitis with subcorneal pustules and Gram-positive cocci in the scale crust, reflecting possible concomitant impetigo.

A 10-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of occipital headache and a 2-year history of growth arrest. He had grown only 1 cm over that period, dropping from the 75th–90th to the 25th percentile for height, while his weight increased from the 50th to the 75th percentile. He denied vomiting, excessive tiredness, or other symptoms. His past medical and family history were unremarkable, and his development had been normal.

On examination, his height was 136 cm (25th percentile) and weight was 42 kg (75th percentile). He was prepubertal; blood pressure was 120/67 mmHg and pulse 72 beats per minute. The thyroid gland was not palpable. Neurologic examination, fundoscopy, and visual fields were all normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed an intrasellar and suprasellar mass that was isointense to gray matter, mildly compressing the optic chiasm and displacing the pituitary stalk and posterior pituitary. After gadolinium administration, the lesion enhanced homogeneously.

Laboratory studies including a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, renal and liver function tests, and anti–coeliac screening were normal. Thyroid ultrasonography showed a normal‐sized gland with markedly heterogeneous echotexture, hypoechoic areas, and diffuse hypervascularization. Endocrine testing demonstrated:
• TSH 589 mU/L  
• Free T4 1.5 pmol/L  
• Free T3 2.2 pmol/L  
• IGF-I 8.6 nmol/L  
• Prolactin 1.23 nmol/L

A 17-year-old schoolgirl presented with a 6-month history of a progressively enlarging swelling over the right frontoparietal region and a localized headache. She denied fevers, weight loss, night sweats, seizures, or focal weakness. She had no personal or family history of tuberculosis but reported a fall 18 months earlier that resulted in a right frontal scalp bruise and a depressed skull fracture managed nonoperatively.

On examination, there was a fluctuant, nonerythematous swelling measuring 10 × 7 cm over the right frontoparietal scalp with palpable bony defects and mild tenderness but no overlying skin changes. Neurologic examination was normal. Routine hematologic and biochemical tests, including complete blood count and inflammatory markers, were within normal limits.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed an extensive bony defect of both inner and outer tables in the right frontal region, with a slightly hyperdense epidural and subgaleal collection containing mixed hypodense areas and adjacent brain parenchymal hypodensity; the lesion enhanced after contrast administration. MRI of the brain demonstrated an epidural and subgaleal lesion that was isointense to hyperintense on T1-weighted images and isointense to hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with intervening hypointense areas; there was hyperintense signal change in the adjacent brain with mass effect and midline shift. The lesion enhanced homogeneously, with nonenhancing hypodense regions centrally on contrast sequences.

A 54-year-old man with a history of psoriasis, previously managed with topical corticosteroids and emollients, presented for new fingernail changes. He had no significant past medical history. Laboratory studies, including renal function, liver function, and serum albumin, were all within normal limits. He was started on acitretin, 25 mg daily, for nail involvement unresponsive to topical therapy. Five months after initiating acitretin, paired transverse white lines were noted on all fingernails. On each nail, there were two pale lines approximately 1 mm wide, running parallel to the lunula with regular borders. The lines disappeared when pressure was applied to the nail plate and did not migrate distally as the nails grew.

A 51-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of loud snoring, voice change, and witnessed obstructive sleep apnea with excessive daytime somnolence (Epworth Sleepiness Scale score 13). He denied dyspnea. His medical history was notable for mild hypertension and diabetes. Height was 160 cm, weight 62 kg (BMI 24.2 kg/m2). On examination, his Friedman tongue position was grade III (only the soft palate visible) and the tonsils were hidden in the tonsillar fossa. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a 20×20 mm round cystic mass at the base of the tongue that displaced the epiglottis posteriorly and narrowed the airway; the vocal cords could not be seen. No other lesions were identified.  

Laboratory polysomnography showed a respiratory disturbance index of 32.2 events/h overall and 105.8 events/h in the supine position, a longest apnea of 39.7 s, a lowest SaO2 of 89%, and an average SaO2 of 97.2%.  

Contrast CT of the neck demonstrated a 33×31×27 mm well-defined cystic lesion in the midline of the tongue base, compressing the oropharyngeal airway and displacing the epiglottis posteriorly.  

Sleep videofluoroscopy under midazolam sedation showed complete pharyngeal airway obstruction during both inspiration and expiration as the mass pulled the epiglottis down and backward, with the epiglottic tip in contact with the posterior pharyngeal wall throughout the respiratory cycle.

A 21-year-old man presented with 3 months of fever, a 6-kg weight loss, myalgia, and polyarthralgia unresponsive to anti-inflammatory drugs. He experienced marked relief with oral steroids, but one month after stopping them he developed cramp-like pain in both feet while walking, relieved by rest. Over the next month, he reported burning pain in the forefeet that worsened with leg elevation and improved on dangling, disturbing sleep. Ten days before presentation, the pain became continuous, associated with coldness of both feet and inability to walk.

He denied smoking, oral or genital ulcers, and had no family history of premature atherosclerosis or hyperlipidemia. Twenty days earlier, he had transient left testicular pain lasting 2 days, with minimal tunica vaginalis fluid on ultrasound that resolved spontaneously.

On examination, blood pressure was 150/100 mmHg. Both feet were cold and pale, with absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. There were a few skin infarcts on the left sole, but no toe gangrene. Ankle–brachial indices were not recorded.

Doppler ultrasound of lower-limb arteries showed complete occlusion of the anterior tibial, posterior tibial, and peroneal arteries in both legs with multiple collateral channels. Digital subtraction angiography revealed symmetric narrowing and irregularity of the mid and distal superficial femoral and popliteal arteries, and occlusion of the infrapopliteal vessels bilaterally; there were no aneurysms or stenoses in the visceral arteries.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 61 mm/hr, C-reactive protein of 21.4 mg/dL, and platelet count of 419,000/mm3. Urinalysis was normal. Antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, antiproteinase-3, and antimyeloperoxidase antibodies were negative. Serum complements were normal. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, anti–hepatitis C antibody, and HIV were negative.

A 73-year-old man presented with a one-week history of constipation and left-sided abdominal pain radiating diffusely across the lower abdomen. He denied nausea, vomiting, or other infective symptoms. He had been passing flatus but had not opened his bowels for 3–4 days. His medical history included bronchiectasis, ischaemic heart disease, aortic valve repair, and coronary artery bypass grafting; he was taking aspirin. On examination, he was febrile (38.5 °C) but haemodynamically stable, with a heart rate of 92 beats/min, blood pressure of 152/89 mmHg, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation of 99%. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 10.2×10^9 per L with neutrophils of 7.5×10^9 per L, a C-reactive protein of 91 mmol/L, and a bilirubin of 27 U/L; other results were within normal limits. At this time, the provisional diagnosis was diverticulitis, with differentials including appendicitis, pyelonephritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and, less likely, ischaemic bowel.

A 4½-year-old girl of Asian descent was evaluated for an abnormal gait. She was born at 37 weeks in a non-consanguineous family, with age-appropriate early milestones until a viral illness at 10 months after which her motor progress slowed. She began walking at 16 months but exhibited an unsteady, wide-based, steppage gait with occasional falls. Toe walking was noted at age 2, and a second viral illness at age 3 worsened her instability, resulting in at least two falls per week. Speech and language were normal until 3.5 years, when she stopped responding to her name, and speech began to regress.

On examination, her weight and height were at the 43rd and 29th percentiles. She was cooperative but with limited verbal output, inconsistently following commands. Hearing was inconsistent. Cranial nerves were otherwise normal; extraocular movements were full without nystagmus; fundus was normal. Muscle bulk was preserved, tone was normal except for mild bilateral heel-cord tightness, and strength was 4-/5 for bilateral foot eversion, good elsewhere. Deep tendon reflexes were absent at ankles and knees, 1+ elsewhere. Coordination in the upper extremities was normal; gait was wide-based, unstable, with a steppage quality. Romberg test was negative.

Nerve conduction studies showed absent sensory responses in upper and lower limbs except the sural nerve, severely decreased lower extremity CMAP amplitudes, mildly decreased upper-extremity CMAP amplitudes, normal latencies and velocities, and absent tibial F-waves. EMG showed chronic neurogenic changes in tibialis anterior and gastrocnemius muscles, consistent with a chronic axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Auditory brainstem response testing revealed bilateral auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder with profound hearing loss. Spine MRI showed subtle cauda equina enhancement; brain and internal auditory canal MRIs were unremarkable. CK, lactate, and CSF studies were normal. A comprehensive neuropathy panel and frataxin‐repeat testing were normal. Based on the clinical picture and imaging, she was started on IVIG for presumed CIDP, receiving multiple doses over two months without further improvement.

A 33-year-old man presented to the emergency department six days after the onset of fever, fatigue, and a vesiculopustular rash. Swabs of skin lesions were positive for Mpox virus by PCR. He reported multiple recent anonymous male sexual partners and denied travel outside the province.

On day 14 after symptom onset, he developed 10–15 loose brown-green liquid bowel movements per day and a 15-pound weight loss. Stool studies were negative for ova and parasites; bacteria including Yersinia enterocolitica; and viruses (noroviridae, astroviridae, adenoviridae, rotaviridae, sapoviridae). His skin lesions subsequently healed, and he was released from isolation.

On day 26, he was evaluated for ongoing nausea, cramping, and diarrhea. His medical history included mixed-type irritable bowel syndrome and gastroesophageal reflux disease; a 2021 colonoscopy had shown normal colonic and ileal biopsies. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no active skin lesions.

On day 44, a stool PCR for Mpox virus (validated only for skin lesions) was negative. Gastroscopy and colonoscopy with pansegmental biopsies demonstrated normal colonic mucosa, but ileal biopsies showed neutrophilic infiltration within the surface epithelium and lamina propria, consistent with active ileitis. HIV testing, fecal elastase, and quantitative immunoglobulins were normal.

A 46-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 10-month history of right upper quadrant pain. The pain was sharp, intermittent, radiated to the back, and was associated with nausea and vomiting. She noted that the pain was exacerbated by fatty meals; there was no change in bowel habits or urinary symptoms. She denied other medical conditions or a family history of gastrointestinal problems. 

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the upper abdomen without guarding or rebound. Routine laboratory studies, including a metabolic profile and liver function tests, were within normal limits.

An abdominal ultrasound of the right upper quadrant was performed. It demonstrated a contracted, shrunken gallbladder that was not visualized on imaging; the biliary tree appeared normal. There was no sonographic Murphy’s sign, gallbladder wall thickening was 2 mm, no pericholecystic fluid was present, and there was no intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile duct dilatation.

Based on the clinical presentation and ultrasound findings, a laparoscopic cholecystectomy was planned.

An 18‐year‐old man was brought to the emergency department after loss of consciousness in a high‐speed motor‐vehicle accident. On arrival his respiratory rate was 20 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 99% on a nonrebreather mask, blood pressure 210/130 mm Hg, pulse 107 beats/min, and Glasgow Coma Scale score 6 (E1V1M4). Physical examination revealed a bruise over the occiput, a white area in the left eye, and anisocoria with a right pupil diameter of 7 mm and a left pupil diameter of 2.5 mm. A noncontrast head CT showed a hyperdense, homogeneous, well‐defined mass in the posterior portion of the left globe and a low‐density, band‐like structure encircling the equator of the left eye. Additional findings included a fracture of the left orbital wall with opacification of adjacent ethmoid air cells, pneumocephalus, a left acute subdural hematoma, and subarachnoid hemorrhage. He underwent emergency craniotomy for the subdural hematoma and was admitted to the intensive care unit.

A 20-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of frequent hospitalizations for refractory periodic vomiting and new-onset hypertension. He was born at 34 weeks’ gestation as one of dichorionic diamniotic twins; antenatal ultrasound had shown a left multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK), and postnatal ultrasound confirmed multicystic change in the left kidney and a hyperechogenic right kidney of normal size. At 9 months old, he was diagnosed with stage 3a chronic kidney disease (CKD) on the basis of elevated serum creatinine. Beginning at 6 months of age, he developed sudden-onset, recurrent episodes of vomiting requiring intravenous fluids; during these episodes, blood urea nitrogen was 41.9–62.8 mg/dL and creatinine was 0.55–0.71 mg/dL. At 14 months, renal scintigraphy demonstrated 0% uptake in the left kidney and 23.4% uptake in the right kidney. Upper gastrointestinal series and endoscopy were normal. Metabolic and immunologic evaluations were unremarkable, and electroencephalography showed no neurologic abnormalities. At 20 months, his blood pressure was 116/86 mmHg (stage 2). Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging showed no adrenal enlargement, and brain magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable.

A 68-year-old man with no prior medical history experienced retrosternal chest pain and presyncope. Emergency medical services arrived after he collapsed and documented a pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest. Spontaneous circulation was restored, and a 12-lead ECG demonstrated ST elevations in leads V1–V3, Q waves in lead V2, and reciprocal ST depressions in lateral and inferior leads. During a second PEA arrest, he received CPR and thrombolytic therapy for a presumptive ST-elevation myocardial infarction. After return of spontaneous circulation, he was taken for emergent coronary angiography, which showed no hemodynamically significant stenosis or evidence of disrupted plaque in any arteries. A left ventriculogram revealed normal contraction of all segments with no dissection, left ventricular aneurysm, or mitral regurgitation. An intra-aortic balloon pump was placed for hypotension support. Despite adequate cardiac output, he remained acidotic and dependent on the balloon pump.

A 78-year-old underweight Hispanic woman with mitral stenosis and hypertension presented with 2 days of diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, dehydration, and frequent nonbloody diarrhea. She had similar untreated episodes in the past, most recently 4 years earlier. Four weeks before presentation, she had traveled to El Salvador; her travel companion was asymptomatic. She took no medications and received no travel vaccinations beyond her annual influenza shot. She denied hematochezia, urinary or respiratory symptoms, fever aside from current complaint, headache, illicit drugs, herbal remedies, and exotic foods, though she consumed local food and water while abroad.

On examination she was febrile (39.1 °C), blood pressure 116/64 mm Hg, pulse 96 beats/min, respirations 19 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on ambient air. She appeared anorexic. Abdominal palpation showed generalized tenderness without guarding or rigidity; bowel sounds were normal. Cardiac exam revealed a murmur. There were no dermatologic lesions (no larva currens or petechiae). Chest radiography suggested possible pneumonia, but respiratory examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies included stool cultures and ova-and-parasite examinations; tests for Helicobacter pylori toxin, sepsis markers, urine toxicology, hepatitis panel, and liver function were negative. On admission she received metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, and intravenous fluids. On hospital day 2 she continued to have more than six bowel movements per day. Because of her poor nutritional status and persistent diarrhea, a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen was obtained, which showed mild circumferential enhancement and wall haziness of the sigmoid colon and rectum; radiologic interpretation was that this finding was non-specific and usually seen in proctocolitis.

A 16-year-old nulliparous woman presented after obtaining a positive urine pregnancy test. She reported 6 weeks of amenorrhea and had used a barrier contraceptive method irregularly. She denied pain or bleeding. Vital signs were normal. On pelvic examination there was no tenderness. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a trilaminar endometrium without an intrauterine gestational sac; in the left adnexal region there was a 25 mm heterogeneous, vascularized mass contiguous with the left ovary. Laboratory evaluation revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 13.1 g/dL and a serum β-hCG level of 4555 IU/L.

A 32‐year‐old man presented with two asymptomatic facial lesions present unchanged in size for 12 months. He denied other skin eruptions, mucosal involvement, photosensitivity, and there was no relevant past medical, occupational, or family history. On examination, there were two erythematous macules, each about 5 mm in diameter, on the right cheek and forehead. Initial clinical differential diagnoses included discoid lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, granuloma annulare, and seborrheic dermatitis. A skin biopsy of the cheek lesion revealed prominent changes in the superficial epidermis with acantholysis primarily within the stratum granulosum, and in the dermis a predominantly superficial lymphocytic infiltrate with scattered scarce eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin showed intercellular deposits of IgG and C3 within the epidermis.

A 55-year-old white man with severe alcohol use disorder presented repeatedly over 2 years for inpatient detoxification. Upon each admission he had symmetric purpuric rashes on his lower extremities, appearing during periods of excessive ethanol intake (>300 g/day) and beginning to resolve within one week of abstinence. He denied itching, pain, fever, arthralgias, gastrointestinal symptoms, or other systemic complaints. Examination also revealed cerebellar ataxia, affective lability, mild sensorimotor polyneuropathy of the lower limbs, and hepatomegaly.

Routine blood tests over multiple admissions showed normal platelet counts and coagulation parameters, moderately elevated transaminases, and mildly increased C-reactive protein. Abdominal ultrasound showed fatty liver without cirrhosis. Serologic tests for hepatitis, HIV, and syphilis were negative. Neuroimaging, echocardiography, angiology, and capillary microscopy revealed no evidence of vasculitis or thrombosis. 

A skin biopsy of a fresh purpuric lesion demonstrated a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with reactive endothelial changes and extravasated red blood cells; vessel walls were intact without fibrin or thrombi. Immunodiagnostic studies showed markedly increased serum IgE and IgA levels, decreased B-lymphocytes and CD4 T-cells, and an elevated ratio of activated T-lymphocytes; no circulating immune complexes or autoantibodies were detected. A provocation test with vinegar (50 ml four times daily) reproduced fresh “cayenne pepper” purpura on the lower legs 24 hours after ingestion.

A 14-month-old, previously well boy presented to a district hospital in the Western Cape in December 2016 with respiratory distress related to upper airway obstruction. He was moderately acutely malnourished and newly diagnosed with HIV on admission. The child had a short history of fever, dysphagia, and lethargy. There was a household contact with pulmonary tuberculosis, but no chemoprophylaxis had been given. He had no travel history. His vaccination status was incomplete, with only birth vaccinations (BCG and oral polio vaccine) administered.
On examination, he was in shock and had respiratory distress with drooling, forward posturing, grunting, and pulsus paradoxus.
