Oropharyngeal examination revealed an inflamed and oedematous uvula and tonsils with a thick, white, friable membrane adherent to the oropharynx that bled on touch. There was no neck swelling, cervical lymphadenopathy, cranial nerve palsies, or muscle weakness. Chest examination was unremarkable.
Initial management included fluid resuscitation, supplemental oxygen, adrenaline nebulizations, and intravenous ceftriaxone. The patient was intubated because of worsening respiratory distress. Infection control precautions were implemented as for diphtheria while awaiting confirmatory results.
Laboratory investigations showed a white cell count of 1.4 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, platelet count 54 × 10^9/L, and C-reactive protein 258 mg/L. An HIV-1 antibody test and PCR were positive, with an absolute CD4 count of 356 cells/µL (29%). Epstein–Barr virus serology showed EBV nuclear antigen IgG positive and viral capsid antigen IgM negative. Herpes simplex virus 1/2 and adenovirus PCR were negative. Blood cultures yielded no growth.
Microbiological studies included a tracheal aspirate showing occasional non-branching small Gram-positive bacilli in Chinese letter formation with no neutrophils and no growth after 48 h in 5% CO_2. A nasal swab grew a pure culture of Corynebacterium colonies; auramine O smear and Xpert MTB/Rif testing for tuberculosis were negative. Two throat swabs taken in the first 24 h (one prior to antibiotics) showed no pathogens after 72 h of incubation. No membrane tissue samples were collected.

A 55-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute dyspnea, nausea, and vomiting. She reported chronic abdominal pain of 15 days’ duration, with marked exacerbation over the past hours. Her medical history included arterial hypertension, clipping of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm, and esophageal adenocarcinoma treated with chemoradiotherapy followed by surgical resection and gastric pull-up. She was awaiting elective repair of a known hiatal hernia when symptoms began.

On examination, vital signs were stable and within normal limits. Abdominal palpation elicited diffuse tenderness, most pronounced in the epigastrium, without peritoneal signs; Murphy’s sign was negative. Cardiopulmonary auscultation was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 77 mg/L, a normal white-cell count, and normal renal function and electrolyte levels. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest and abdomen demonstrated postoperative changes of esophagectomy with gastric pull-up, a large type IV hiatal hernia, and herniation of the transverse colon into the posterior mediastinum. The herniated colon was distended, contained fecal material, and showed imaging features suggestive of volvulus; no free intraperitoneal fluid was seen.

A 59-year-old man was referred for evaluation of right groin bulging. He had hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and chronic pruritus; his child had atopic dermatitis. One week earlier, after heavy drinking, he developed upper abdominal pain and nausea and was diagnosed with acute pancreatitis; he also noted a mildly painful right groin mass that did not change in size. On examination the patient was afebrile. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended. The right groin mass measured approximately 4 cm, was elastic-hard, mildly tender, nonwarm, and irreducible. Laboratory tests showed slight elevations of lactate dehydrogenase (317 IU/L), C-reactive protein (1.0 mg/dL), creatine kinase (372 IU/L), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (45 mm/h); white-cell, neutrophil, and eosinophil counts were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a right groin mass appearing to connect the peritoneal cavity to the scrotum, suggestive of an inguinal hernia; the presumed hernial contents were fatty tissue without signs of ischemia, but there was inflammatory change in the inguinal canal. Scrotal ultrasonography excluded testicular torsion. CT also showed lymphadenopathy around the stomach, para-aortic region, and mesentery; prior gastroscopy had shown no gastric malignancy. On the basis of these findings, the mass was diagnosed as an irreducible but nonincarcerated right inguinal hernia, and elective surgical repair was planned.

A 38‐year‐old Hispanic man with a 10‐year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and alcohol‐induced cirrhosis (Child‐Pugh C, MELD 45) presented with progressive encephalopathy. One month earlier, he had developed sudden, severe, localized pain in his left thigh at rest, without fever, chills, trauma, or skin lesions. Pain was only partially relieved by oral analgesics, and he became unable to walk. On admission, his temperature was 37°C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 112/min, and respiratory rate 24/min. He was conscious, oriented, and exhibited grade II hepatic encephalopathy. Examination of the left thigh revealed a poorly defined 10×10 cm tender mass with tense, erythematous, ecchymotic skin and increased warmth; pain worsened with limb movement, but there was no peripheral edema or joint signs. Neurologic examination showed decreased vibratory and pain sensation in the legs. Laboratory studies demonstrated macrocytic normochromic anemia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and PTT, elevated glucose, elevated liver enzymes, hypoalbuminemia, and normal creatine phosphokinase. Blood cultures and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative.  
Plain radiography of the thigh showed only soft‐tissue edema. Doppler ultrasound excluded deep vein thrombosis. MRI of the left thigh revealed edema and inflammatory changes in the quadriceps muscle with hyperintense signal on T2‐weighted images and a subacute hematoma.

A 59-year-old woman with recently diagnosed ulcerative colitis presented with 3 days of bloody diarrhea, diffuse abdominal pain, anorexia, and weight loss. She was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and on examination was cachectic with diffuse abdominal tenderness but no peritoneal signs. Initial laboratories showed: WBC 15.9 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, platelets 128 × 10^3/µL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, INR 1.3, PT 16.6 s, PTT 42.8 s, lactate 2.11 mmol/L, ESR 20 mm/h, CRP 6.37 mg/dL, ferritin 93 ng/mL. She was treated for an ulcerative colitis flare with IV methylprednisolone and oral mesalamine.  
Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed a new occlusive main portal vein thrombosis extending into right and left branches with hepatic hypoperfusion and moderate-to-severe pancolitis. Unfractionated heparin was initiated. Shortly thereafter, she developed large-volume hematochezia, hypotension, and was transferred to the ICU. Repeat labs showed WBC 51 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, PTT >150 s, lactate 7.4 mmol/L. CT imaging demonstrated ischemic enterocolitis. Heparin was held, she received red blood cells, and underwent successful TIPS placement. Her pain, leukocytosis, and lactic acidosis improved; hemoglobin and vital signs stabilized.  
Heparin was restarted days later. A hypercoagulable panel showed a positive lupus anticoagulant; anti-beta2-glycoprotein, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, FLAER for PNH, and JAK2 mutation were negative. She had a history of miscarriage. Hematochezia abated on corticosteroids, mesalamine, and heparin, and she was transitioned from IV methylprednisolone to oral prednisone.  
Shortly afterward she developed worsening abdominal pain and hematochezia, prompting a return to IV methylprednisolone and increased mesalamine. Over 24 h she became lethargic and platelet count fell from 152 × 10^3/µL to 50 × 10^3/µL; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia was confirmed and anticoagulation was switched to argatroban. While on argatroban she had another large-volume bleed and became obtunded; head CT was negative for hemorrhage. Blood cultures grew Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus species, and Candida tropicalis, and she was started on broad antimicrobials while steroids were tapered.  
Serial CT venography then showed an expanding superior sagittal sinus thrombus and new cerebral venous thromboses despite therapeutic anticoagulation. She was transitioned to bivalirudin but progressed to disseminated intravascular coagulation and septic shock, and ultimately died under comfort measures.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressively worsening pelvic pain, dysuria, asthenia, anorexia, and weight loss without fever. His history was notable for acute myeloid leukemia in remission for 3 years; he had no diabetes or known immunosuppression. On admission, temperature was 37.2 °C, heart rate 95/min, blood pressure 98/65 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Abdominal examination revealed hypogastric and perineal tenderness. Digital rectal examination was very painful and limited. Laboratory tests showed C-reactive protein 100 mg/L, white blood cell count 5830/μL with neutrophil predominance, sterile urine on culture, prostate-specific antigen 0.3 ng/mL, and a negative Xpert MTB/RIF test. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a large, well-defined, heterogeneous, hypodense pelvic mass with thick internal septa. Pelvic MRI revealed a 600 mL septated collection in the prostatic cavity that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2, showed diffusion restriction on DWI with low ADC, and had a thickened, enhancing wall on T1 FatSat post-gadolinium sequences.

A 41-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 2-week history of progressive gait unsteadiness, low back pain, and weakness of the lower limbs. On examination, she had mild bilateral proximal lower-limb weakness, hyperreflexia, and severe loss of vibration and position sense in the feet. Somatosensory evoked potentials showed markedly reduced amplitude on the left and absent cortical potentials on the right. Spinal cord MRI (3.0 T) revealed a thin, longitudinally extensive T2-hyperintense signal involving the posterior columns from C2 to C6 without contrast enhancement.  
   
She underwent extensive laboratory testing, including routine blood tests; thyroid function; serum electrophoresis; serum cobalamin, folate, and urinary methylmalonate; cerebrospinal fluid analysis (cell counts, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands); serum antibodies against aquaporin-4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein; rheumatological screening (ANA, ANCA, cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factor, lupus anticoagulant, antiphospholipid antibodies, complement levels, celiac and thyroid antibodies); serology for neurotropic viruses (HSV, CMV, EBV, HBV, HCV, HIV, HTLV I-II), Borrelia burgdorferi, and Treponema pallidum; and brain MRI. All results were normal. Serum copper was low (26 µg/mL; normal 65–165), ceruloplasmin was normal, and serum zinc was mildly elevated (1093 µg/L; normal 600–1080). The patient denied any history of zinc supplementation or abuse.

A 28-year-old man came to the emergency department with sudden weakness of all four limbs that began 3 hours earlier. He denied facial or respiratory weakness, sensory changes, or autonomic symptoms. He recalled mild muscle soreness after exercising the previous day and a heavy intake of bread at dinner. His weakness began in the hands and feet and progressed proximally to involve the arms and legs. He had no paresthesia, breathlessness, dysphagia, or medications (including herbal supplements). He had no known thyroid disease, no family history of similar episodes, and no other chronic illnesses. He did report occasional, transient leg weakness after exercise since his early twenties.

On examination, blood pressure was 134/78 mm Hg, heart rate 84 beats/min, and body mass index 19.9 kg/m2. There was no goiter, lymphadenopathy, or jugular venous distension. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams were unremarkable. Neurologically, he had flaccid paralysis (motor grade 1/5) in all extremities with intact sensation.

An ECG showed a heart rate of 78 beats/min, flat T waves, and prolonged QT/QTc of 542/621 ms. Initial blood tests (available 1.5 hours after arrival) revealed a serum potassium level of 1.50 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0) and arterial blood gas showing metabolic acidosis. Intravenous potassium infusion was started, during which his blood pressure briefly dropped to 80/50 mm Hg and ECG showed bradycardia, ST-segment depression, and U waves; cardiac enzymes were normal, and repeat potassium was 1.35 mmol/L. The infusion rate was increased, and oxygen was administered. After 20 minutes, his blood pressure rose to 110/60 mm Hg, heart rate to 67/min, but chest discomfort persisted. He was admitted to the intensive care unit. Twelve hours later, ECG normalized and QRS duration returned to normal. Muscle strength began to improve four hours after presentation and fully recovered by 24 hours, by which time potassium was 3.4 mmol/L without further infusion.

To evaluate the cause of hypokalemia, urine sodium and potassium and serum aldosterone and renin levels were measured and were within normal limits. Thyroid function tests were normal. After potassium normalized, levels remained stable off infusion. A long exercise test to assess for inherited neuromuscular disease showed no abnormalities.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of visual disturbances in her left eye, beginning as photophobia from bright objects in the central field. She denied trauma, infection, or recent vaccination. She had no history of diabetes or hypertension but had undergone mitral valve surgery 5 years earlier. 

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/500 OS. She had no headache, retrobulbar pain, or orbital pain. Automated perimetry showed a temporal hemianopic defect in the left eye and a normal right visual field. Funduscopic examination revealed no optic disc abnormalities bilaterally. A left relative afferent pupillary defect was present, and intraocular pressures were 16 mm Hg OU. 

She was admitted and received intravenous corticosteroid pulse therapy. On the following day, her left eye vision deteriorated to no light perception. Two days after admission, MRI of the brain with gadolinium contrast demonstrated a round, 11.5 mm space-occupying lesion in the suprasellar cistern compressing the left optic nerve near the chiasm. On T1-weighted images, the lesion contained areas of high and iso- to low-intensity signal; on T2-weighted images it was iso- to low-intensity. Postcontrast T1-weighted images showed patchy enhancement within the lesion.

An 8-year-old girl was brought to clinic for progressive deformity of the right fifth finger over 3 to 4 months. There was no history of trauma, laceration, or injury, and she had no fever or erythema. On examination, there was an extensor lag of the distal interphalangeal joint and volar curvature of the distal phalanx of the right fifth digit. Radiographs of the right hand showed abnormal volar and radial curvature of the distal phalanx of the fifth finger with widening of the epiphyseal plate.

A 9-year-old immunized girl with a history of migraines and anxiety presented with 2–3 weeks of right flank and right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. Over the previous 3 months she had unintentional weight loss from the mid-70th percentile to the 14th percentile. She denied fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, or hematochezia. Initial laboratory evaluation showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 41 mm/hr; complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver panel, antitissue transglutaminase IgA, total IgA, and urinalysis were otherwise unremarkable.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed two ill-defined, hypoechoic lesions in the right hepatic lobe. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated five T1-hypointense, T2-hyperintense lesions in the posterior right hepatic lobe, each measuring 1.0–2.6 cm in diameter. An ultrasound-guided needle biopsy of a hepatic lesion showed necrotizing granulomata with chronic periportal and lobular inflammation.  
Acid-fast bacillus and Grocott methenamine silver stains were negative for mycobacterial and fungal organisms. Biopsy findings showed no steatosis, cholestasis, or features of focal nodular hyperplasia or hepatic adenoma. The patient’s only medication, topiramate, was weaned. Further evaluation revealed normal C-reactive protein, angiotensin-converting enzyme level, total immunoglobulins, and neutrophil oxidative burst. Testing for tuberculosis, Bartonella, and HIV was negative, and Epstein-Barr virus serologies indicated past but not acute infection. Chest radiographs showed no evidence of sarcoidosis. No clear etiology for the hepatic granulomata was identified.

A 39-year-old man presented with right flank pain that progressed over two days to severe back pain, bilateral flank pain, scrotal pain, and bilateral thigh pain. He had no significant medical history. Analgesics administered at a local health center relieved his back pain, but his testicular and thigh pain worsened.  
On examination, blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg, pulse 130 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and temperature 37°C. The leg-raising test was negative, and the neurovascular status of both legs was intact. Scrotal examination was unremarkable; both the cremasteric reflex and Prehn's sign were negative. There was no edema or swelling of the lower limbs.  
Laboratory studies showed a D-dimer level of 17 mg/L (normal, 0–0.49 mg/L), creatinine 124 µmol/L (normal, 64–110 µmol/L), white blood cell count 10×10^3/L (normal, 4–10×10^3/L), and C-reactive protein 5 mg/L (normal, 0–5 mg/L). Prothrombin time was 13.8 seconds (normal, 9.4–12.5 seconds), with normal APTT (28.4 seconds) and INR (1.1). Urinalysis was positive for blood.  
Bedside abdominal ultrasound showed no significant abnormalities. Doppler ultrasound of both legs revealed deep vein thrombosis extending from the external iliac veins to the distal veins of both legs. Computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a large thrombus in the distal inferior vena cava extending to the renal artery and both external and internal iliac veins, with no evidence of renal calculi or other abdominal pathology.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of sudden-onset headache, weakness, visual disturbance, and a 3-month history of unintentional 15 kg weight loss. He experienced gait disturbance, word-finding difficulty, left-sided visual impairment, nausea, and vomiting. His wife noted confusion and muddled speech. He had no history of head trauma. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, a left cataract, and right wet macular degeneration. 

On examination, heart rate was 69 bpm, blood pressure 177/95 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C. He was euvolemic with no peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis. Cardiovascular examination revealed a new ejection systolic murmur loudest at the aortic area, radiating to the carotids. Neurologically, he had a left homonymous hemianopia, left visual inattention, an upgoing left plantar reflex, and impaired left-sided coordination; tone, power, and sensation were otherwise normal.

Initial laboratory results showed creatinine 120 µmol/L (eGFR 54 mL/min/1.73 m2), white cell count 8.8×10^9/L, C-reactive protein <5 mg/L, blood glucose 9.7 mmol/L, serum ketones 0.8 mmol/L, and negative procalcitonin. ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 105 bpm. Chest radiograph and non-contrast head CT were unremarkable. Brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging revealed a small right occipital focus of restricted diffusion consistent with embolic infarction; MR angiography was normal.

On hospital day 4, his Glasgow Coma Scale decreased to 3, requiring intubation. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed protein 1.35 g/L, glucose 6.9 mmol/L, and negative NMDA receptor antibodies. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated suspicious lesions on the aortic and mitral valves. Transoesophageal echocardiography confirmed vegetations on the pulmonary, mitral, and aortic valves. Intravenous amoxicillin and acyclovir were initiated, and ceftriaxone was added while awaiting blood cultures. Multiple blood cultures returned negative. A panel of blood tests including antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, rheumatoid factor, HIV, carcinoembryonic antigen, CA19-9, and anti-neuronal paraneoplastic antibodies were all negative.

A 61-year-old woman with cervical cancer metastatic to paraaortic and left supraclavicular lymph nodes was treated with systemic chemotherapy: paclitaxel and bevacizumab administered for 63 and 36 days before presentation, respectively, each followed the next day by cisplatin. On day 0, she was admitted for marked elevation of liver enzymes: AST 173 U/L, ALT 221 U/L, γ-GTP 2553 U/L, and ALP 5188 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography showed wall thickening of the extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts and of the gallbladder, with bile-duct strictures and dilatations. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed wall thickening of both extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts with luminal narrowing and dilation, and gallbladder wall thickening. On day 2, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy and nasobiliary drainage was performed. Biopsy of the common bile duct showed no malignant cells and only modest infiltration of neutrophils; bile cytology was also negative for malignancy. Ursodeoxycholic acid was started on day 6. On day 9, cholangiography via the drainage tube revealed strictures and dilatations with irregular wall contours in the intrahepatic bile ducts of both lobes, whereas extrahepatic bile-duct changes were modest.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of numerous asymptomatic raised skin lesions and a 2-week history of hoarseness of voice. He was otherwise healthy; no family members had similar skin lesions. 

On examination, there were multiple discrete skin-colored to yellow, dome-shaped, firm papulonodules symmetrically distributed over the face, trunk, and extremities, with a predilection for flexural and intertriginous areas. An extensive Koebner response was noted on the chest and shoulders at sites of contact with the straps of an insecticide sprayer. Indirect laryngoscopy revealed numerous yellow papulonodules in the larynx. Systemic examination was otherwise normal.

Laboratory studies showed: complete blood count, ESR, fasting blood sugar, renal, liver, and thyroid function tests within normal limits. Lipid profile: total cholesterol 138 mg/dL (normal <200), triglycerides 205 mg/dL (normal <150), VLDL 41 mg/dL (normal <30), LDL 80 mg/dL (normal <100), HDL 17 mg/dL (normal >40). Serum osmolarity and electrolytes were normal. MRI of the brain showed no abnormalities. Serum protein electrophoresis showed no M-band. Urine was negative for Bence Jones proteins. Skeletal survey was normal. Fasting lipid profile of his father showed elevated triglycerides (348 mg/dL), high VLDL (69 mg/dL), low HDL (32 mg/dL), with normal total cholesterol and LDL levels.

A punch biopsy of a nodule on the back revealed histopathologic features consistent with xanthoma. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD68 but negative for S100 and CD1a.

A 35-year-old man with a 20-year history of tachycardia and palpitations presented with worsening symptoms despite daily sotalol therapy. On admission, his pulse rate was 110–160 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, and temperature normal. Electrocardiography showed a short PR interval and a delta wave, consistent with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. He received sotalol and underwent direct-current cardioversion, but recurrent tachyarrhythmia prompted further evaluation.

Chest radiography showed an elevated cardiothoracic ratio due to marked right atrial enlargement. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a normal left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 50%, normal right ventricular size but severe right ventricular systolic dysfunction, and a markedly enlarged right atrium compressing both ventricles; there was no significant valvular disease except a mildly increased tricuspid valve gradient (mean 3 mmHg, peak 8 mmHg) and a localized pericardial effusion posterior to the left ventricle measuring 21 mm. 

Spiral CT angiography demonstrated a large blood-containing structure measuring approximately 127 × 122 × 72 mm anterior to the right atrium and right ventricle without thrombus. The lesion caused displacement and compression of the right atrium, right ventricle, and tricuspid valve, and displaced the right coronary artery and its branches leftward. Both the superior and inferior vena cavae drained normally into the right atrium. Given the adjacency of the lesion to the right coronary artery and its broad muscular connection to the right atrial free wall, surgical resection was planned over catheter ablation.

An 82-year-old woman with coronary artery disease (status post stenting) and known gallstones presented with two weeks of postprandial abdominal pain, persistent nausea, and vomiting. On examination she was tachycardic (pulse 102 beats/min), hypotensive (blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg), and showed signs of extracellular dehydration (clammy skin, decreased skin turgor, sunken eyes). Laboratory evaluation revealed hypokalemia and hypochloremia. A urinary catheter showed reduced urine output. Following fluid resuscitation and placement of a nasogastric tube, 400 cc of gastric fluid was drained. After hemodynamic stabilization, esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated normal mucosa up to the second part of the duodenum, no dilatation, and retained bile. To investigate the cause of gastric outlet obstruction, an abdominal CT scan was performed, which revealed a cholecystoduodenal fistula, marked gastric distention with pneumobilia, and a 4 cm calcified stone impacted at the duodenojejunal junction.

A 23-year-old white woman from a rural area of Espírito Santo, Brazil, presented with a 4-year history of slowly progressive erythematous lesions on her forehead. She was otherwise healthy and a non-smoker. Initially diagnosed with leprosy at another center, she received rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine for 2 years without improvement. Subsequently, she was treated for rosacea with topical metronidazole gel and oral doxycycline for 1 year, also without response. A skin biopsy had shown a diffuse lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with granulomas. Tuberculin skin test and sputum bacilloscopy were negative.

On admission, multiple erythematous infiltrated plaques were noted on the forehead, cheeks, chin, and left earlobe, and a 3-mm ulcer was observed near the right labial commissure. Oral examination revealed multiple mulberry-like gingival ulcers with hemorrhagic dots. Posterior cervical and submandibular lymph nodes were enlarged (1.5–2 cm). There was no fever, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or respiratory symptoms. Chest CT showed residual calcified granulomas in the right middle lobe. Cervical CT revealed enlarged lymph nodes in the jugular, submandibular, intraparotid, and posterior cervical chains.

A 74-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with transient loss of consciousness after three days of vomiting, diarrhea, and anorexia. She had undergone abdominal adhesiolysis 12 days earlier. Her history included type 2 diabetes managed with metformin, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and hyperuricemia. On arrival, she was conscious but mildly disoriented, dehydrated, and anuric. The abdomen was soft without tenderness or distension. Vital signs were: blood pressure 70/40 mmHg, heart rate 104 bpm, respiratory rate 30/min, temperature 34 °C, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Point-of-care ultrasound and subsequent abdominal CT scan showed no obstruction, free fluid, or intra-abdominal infection. Echocardiography and ECG excluded cardiac injury. Laboratory studies revealed serum creatinine 11.2 mg/dL (baseline eGFR 3 mL/min/1.73 m2), BUN 56 mg/dL; arterial blood gas: pH 7.07, PCO2 22.3 mmHg, HCO3– 6.4 mmol/L, base excess –21.3 mmol/L; lactate 8.1 mmol/L; anion gap 24 mEq/L.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of nausea, vomiting, headache, photophobia, fever, anorexia, abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. He is a gardener living in a rodent-infested informal settlement. He has a history of weekend binge ethanol use. There was no recent travel. On examination, he was tachycardic (128 bpm), hypotensive (69/35 mmHg), febrile (38.1 °C) and profoundly jaundiced with prominent conjunctival suffusion. Lung auscultation revealed left lower–zone crackles; the abdomen was generally tender with guarding. He received fluid resuscitation, vasopressors and empiric ceftriaxone. 
Laboratory studies showed CRP 349 mg/L, leukocytes 20.21×10^9/L, blood urea nitrogen 20.8 mmol/L, creatinine 331 μmol/L, total bilirubin 126 μmol/L (conjugated 109 μmol/L), ALT 35 U/L, AST 98 U/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, albumin 28 g/L, platelets 38×10^9/L; INR 1.23, fibrinogen 9.0 g/L, D-dimer 1.05 mg/L. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis: protein 0.41 g/L, glucose 3.7 mmol/L, 2 lymphocytes, 40 erythrocytes, no polymorphs, negative Gram stain and culture. HIV serology was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Abdominal CT revealed peri-appendiceal fluid but, on surgical review, findings were inconsistent with appendicitis.

A 72-year-old man presented with two days of worsening dyspnea and seven days of chest pain. Seven days earlier, he had an episode of severe substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm with profuse sweating. His medical history included type II diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and chronic smoking.  
On examination, blood pressure was 80/60 mmHg, pulse 120 beats per minute (regular, low volume), and oxygen saturation 88% on room air.  
Electrocardiography showed ST-segment elevations in leads V1 through V4. Serum troponin T was 12 ng/mL.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed:  
• Left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% with extensive apical, anterolateral, and anteroseptal wall hypokinesia.  
• A pulsatile left ventricular cavity bounded by a thin endomyocardial border with dyskinetic motion.  
• Color Doppler demonstrated no flow between the left ventricular cavity and myocardial layers.  
• No pericardial effusion or epicardial disruption was seen.

A 57-year-old previously healthy man was transferred with sudden loss of consciousness and vomiting. Four days earlier, he developed fever up to 39°C of unknown origin and was diagnosed locally with dengue fever based on a weakly positive IgM. He had no history of trauma, antiplatelet or anticoagulant use, or other significant medical problems. He reported no recent travel.  

On arrival, blood pressure was 161/82 mmHg, heart rate 97/min, respiratory rate 25/min, and temperature 37.8°C. He was comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6; pupils measured 3.0 mm (left) and 4.0 mm (right) with slow light reflexes. Chest, cardiac, and abdominal examinations were normal, and there were no rashes, petechiae, or ecchymoses.  

Laboratory tests from the day before transfer showed WBC 8.32×10^9/L, hemoglobin 171 g/L, hematocrit 52.5%, platelets 31×10^9/L, AST 272 IU/L, ALT 225 IU/L, BUN 6.47 mmol/L, and creatinine 83.4 µmol/L.  

Head CT revealed a left subdural hemorrhage with subfalcine herniation and brain infarction; CT angiography showed no vascular abnormality. Abdominal CT suggested perirenal inflammation, and chest CT showed slight bilateral lower lobe inflammation.  

Despite thrombocytopenia (platelets 20×10^9/L), he underwent evacuation of the subdural hematoma and decompressive craniectomy, then was transferred to the ICU. He received platelet transfusion, fluids, and norepinephrine for hypotension and elevated lactate (8 mmol/L).  

On ICU admission, WBC was 23.55×10^9/L, hemoglobin 85 g/L, hematocrit 24.5%, platelets 42×10^9/L; urinalysis was normal. Peak AST reached 3320 IU/L and ALT 1780 IU/L. Coagulation showed PT 13.7 s, APTT 49 s, and fibrinogen 2.89 g/L. CRP was 8.14 mg/L, procalcitonin 1.49 ng/mL, and BNP 215.54 pg/mL.  

Serologic tests were negative for hepatitis A, B, C, and E; HIV; syphilis; CMV; and EBV. Dengue antigen, IgM, IgG, and RNA were negative. Triglycerides were normal, and ferritin was 3021.7 ng/mL. Upon further questioning, his son reported a rat bite one month earlier.

A 27-year-old nulliparous Japanese woman with a history of infantile epilepsy presented at 13 weeks of gestation. She resumed antiepileptic therapy at age 17 and, without preconception counseling, continued her pregnancy while taking valproate 1400 mg/day, phenobarbital 140 mg/day, and carbamazepine 1200 mg/day. Drug levels at 13 weeks were within therapeutic ranges: valproate 80 μg/ml, phenobarbital 26.1 μg/ml, and carbamazepine 10.5 μg/ml. Despite therapy, she experienced three convulsions per week. She took folic acid 5 mg/day.  
Second-trimester ultrasound at 20 weeks was limited by maternal obesity (BMI 30 kg/m2) and showed no anomalies. At 25 weeks, transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated contracture of the fetal right wrist joint suggesting a radial ray defect. From 32 weeks onward, the fetus exhibited growth retardation.  
At 34 weeks, estimated fetal weight was 1660 g (−2.5 SD), biparietal diameter 74.9 mm (−2.8 SD), abdominal circumference 261.7 mm (−1.5 SD), femur length 58 mm (−1.3 SD), right ulna 35 mm (−8.4 SD) versus left ulna 53 mm (−1.1 SD), and no right radial ray was detected.  
At 37 weeks, three-dimensional ultrasonography revealed a saddle nose deformity.  
On the basis of the right radial ray defect and saddle nose, a syndromic diagnosis was suspected.

A 58-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 2-week history of severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits. He reported a few days of decreased appetite and food intolerance. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 65 mm/h, C-reactive protein 5.24 mg/dL, procalcitonin 0.2 mg/dL, a leukocyte count of 13.34×10^3/μL (71% neutrophils), and normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, hematocrit 28.2%). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an infiltrative, tumor-like mass involving the right colon and adjacent mesentery with luminal narrowing, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, and thickening of the anterior pararenal peritoneum with enlarged retroperitoneal nodes. Colonoscopy showed obstructing edema at the right colon without an intraluminal mass, and biopsies demonstrated inflammatory infiltrates of leukocytes, plasmacytes, and eosinophils. Gastroscopy was performed to exclude a duodenal origin. MRI of the abdomen reported a right colon mass with features suggestive of neoplasm. Based on these findings, an exploratory laparotomy was planned.

A 66-year-old Japanese man was referred with a complaint of food impaction in the left buccal region. He denied any oral injury, tumor, or cyst. His medical history included hypertension, gastric ulcer, gout, nephrolithiasis, and alcohol dependence; he smoked 10–15 cigarettes per day for 45 years and had no known allergies. On intraoral examination, an orifice containing inspissated food debris was noted posterior to the papilla of the parotid duct in the left buccal mucosa. After removal of the debris, a pouch measuring 14 mm in diameter and 8 mm in depth was observed. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a discontinuity of the buccal mucosa with a cavity containing fluid and air, and radiopaque contrast–soaked gauze placed in the cavity delineated the extent of the pouch. T2-weighted magnetic resonance images revealed a pouch with an opening, a slightly thickened wall, and a partial defect in the left buccinator muscle. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images demonstrated enhancement of the pouch wall extending over the surrounding tissues anteroposteriorly in the buccal region and superiorly in the left maxilla, suggestive of an inflammatory reaction.

A 35-year-old gravida 1, para 1 woman was referred at 28 weeks’ gestation. Prenatal ultrasonography showed:  
• Moderate fetal ascites without cutaneous edema, pleural or pericardial effusion, or polyhydramnios  
• Bilateral scrotal hydrocele  
• Peritesticular calcification  
There was no evidence of abdominal calcification, dilated bowel loops, or intra-abdominal cystic masses.

An 82-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia presented with an 8-day history of oral pain and burning that made eating difficult. Eight days earlier, he had begun topical imiquimod therapy for a basal cell carcinoma on his left shoulder. He had used imiquimod in the past without incident and had no new medications or known drug allergies.

On examination, there were hemorrhagic crusts on the vermillion border, erosive gingivitis, stomatitis, and ulcers on the palate. The skin showed erosions at the application site and discrete erosions on the back involving approximately 5% of the body surface area, along with atypical target lesions on the left arm and a positive Nikolsky sign. There was no ocular, genital, or anal mucosal involvement.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, a normal chest radiograph, and a C-reactive protein level of 17.8 mg/L. The initial differential diagnosis included erythema multiforme major versus Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Empiric oral prednisone and valacyclovir were initiated but were rapidly discontinued after negative herpes simplex virus and varicella–zoster virus PCR from mucosal lesions, and negative Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae serologies.

A 72‐year‐old man who underwent a mobile‐bearing posterior‐stabilized total knee arthroplasty (PS‐TKA) 12 years earlier for osteoarthritis presented with recurrent right knee instability and pain on weight‐bearing. He denied any trauma. His medical history included atrial fibrillation and angina. He was independent in activities of daily living, ambulating with a walker. His body mass index was 36.7 kg/m2. On examination, the right knee had a range of motion from –15° of extension to 80° of flexion. There was no tenderness at rest, no heat, redness, or swelling, and no medial or lateral ligament dysfunction. Radiographs showed narrowing of the medial joint space suggestive of polyethylene (PE) insert wear. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated osteolysis and an intraosseous cyst on the lateral proximal tibia. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 4920 cells/μL and a C‐reactive protein level of 0.04 mg/dL. Radiographic criteria for aseptic loosening were not met, and osteolysis associated with increased PE wear particles was diagnosed. Revision of both femoral and tibial components was planned.

A 64-year-old Vietnamese man with no prior medical history presented in April 2020 with daily fevers, night sweats, and an unintentional 4-kg weight loss over several weeks. He is a former smoker and a shrimper (off season since November 2019). Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed mild transaminase elevations and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate; viral hepatitis serologies were negative. Right upper-quadrant ultrasound revealed multiple hypoechoic lesions in both lobes of the liver. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 6-cm multicystic, partially enhancing mass in the right hepatic lobe. The patient underwent percutaneous drainage; purulent fluid grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Tests for tuberculosis and malaria were negative.

A 78-year-old man with a 4-year history of JAK2-positive primary myelofibrosis presented for pretrial imaging after developing hyperleukocytosis (WBC 85 000/µL), progressive splenomegaly (18 cm), and constitutional symptoms (nocturnal sweating, fatigue). Prior bone marrow biopsy had shown grade 3 reticulin fibrosis with 100% cellularity and no blasts. Before initiation of a JAK inhibitor trial, he underwent abdominal ultrasound and MRI. Ultrasound revealed splenomegaly (18 cm longitudinal) and bilateral hyperechoic soft tissue masses around the renal hilum and pelvic regions extending to the proximal ureters without mass effect; Doppler imaging demonstrated internal vascularity. MRI confirmed marked splenomegaly, ascites, and signs of hepatic and marrow iron overload. Both kidneys were enlarged, with parapyelic and perihilar solid lesions showing markedly low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images, an infiltrative pattern extending along the proximal ureters, and no restricted diffusion. The patient had no urinary tract symptoms, and urinalysis was normal.

A 27-year-old Emirati man presented with severe episodic crampy abdominal pain of 4 years’ duration, occurring approximately twice weekly and significantly impairing his life. He had seen multiple specialists and undergone extensive work-ups—including CBC, liver and renal profiles, CRP, gastroscopies, colonoscopies, abdominal CT, and laparoscopy—all reported as normal. On acute admission, further history revealed he also experienced spontaneous, non-pitting swellings of the face, hands, feet, or scrotum twice weekly, often accompanied by a non-pruritic, reticular rash. These episodes developed over 36 hours and resolved over 5–7 days without treatment. He denied fevers, weight loss, bowel-habit changes, or respiratory symptoms. Treatments with analgesics, high-dose antihistamines, antibiotics, corticosteroids, and omalizumab had no effect.

On examination during a pain episode, he was tender over the abdomen with guarding and decreased bowel sounds; there was no distension, rigidity, or peripheral swelling. Complement studies obtained one month earlier (but not previously followed up) showed low C4 and absent C1-INH function. Abdominal CT demonstrated diffuse mucosal thickening of the proximal jejunum and gastric mucosa with minimal free fluid. Colonoscopy revealed severe mucosal edema in the transverse colon with luminal narrowing.

A 15-year-old Omani girl presented with episodic palpitations since birth and mild dizziness. She had no significant past medical history and no family history of similar symptoms. On examination, her blood pressure was 124/59 mmHg and pulse 108/min; she appeared well, with no goiter or other thyroid stigmata. Cardiac evaluation showed sinus tachycardia with occasional ventricular ectopy on ECG and a normal echocardiogram. Laboratory studies revealed a normal hemoglobin level, C-reactive protein of 97 mg/L (0–8), and normal electrolytes. Thyroid tests showed free T4 30.7 pmol/L (8.7–13.6), free T3 9.0 pmol/L (3.8–6.0), and TSH 1.56 mIU/L (0.60–3.70). Thyroid autoantibodies were negative. Prolactin was 727 mIU/L (71–566). Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated altered echotexture with tiny cystic areas (2–4 mm) in both lobes, normal vascular flow, no nodules, and no lymphadenopathy. A technetium-99m thyroid scan showed 3.2% uptake (1–4%) without cold nodules. MRI of the pituitary gland and brain was normal in size and morphology.

A 38-year-old woman from Rasht in northern Iran presented with a 2-month history of gradually increasing epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. The pain was nonpositional, non–food-related, and nonradiating. She also reported intermittent afternoon fevers with chills occurring every 1–3 days (5 to 7 cycles), occasional arthralgias during febrile episodes, anorexia, nausea, and a 7 kg weight loss. She denied travel, herbal medications, pet exposure, or family history of liver disease.

On examination, her blood pressure was 115/75 mm Hg, heart rate 86 beats/min, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. She was alert and oriented. Pulmonary auscultation revealed diffuse wheezing, and abdominal examination showed tenderness in the right upper quadrant without hepatosplenomegaly.

Right upper quadrant ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass with a lobulated border containing cystic areas, measuring 90 × 62 mm in liver segments 6 and 8. She was treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole, but her pain worsened and a nonproductive cough developed.

Abdominal CT demonstrated a large, ill-defined multiloculated hypodense lesion (90 × 80 mm) with central cystic areas in segments 5 and 6, hypodense from arterial through equilibrium phases without hemangioma features. Multiple lymph nodes up to 11 mm were noted in the porta hepatis, paracaval, and para-aortic regions. A small 2 × 3 mm hypodense lesion was also seen in segment 6; postcontrast images showed centripetal enhancement in the porto-venous phase.

Chest HRCT and PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 were negative. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy showed no evidence of malignancy. A complete blood count revealed 32 percent eosinophils. Serologic tests for amoebae and Echinococcus granulosus were negative.

A 65-year-old woman presented for evaluation of longstanding subtle yellowish papules coalescing into plaques on the lateral aspects of her neck and redundant, lax skin in flexural areas including the axillae, face, neck, and groin. Her noncutaneous history was notable for angioid streaks with an atrophic retinal break in the right eye, angina pectoris, a prior myocardial infarction, peripheral artery disease, coronary artery disease, vitreous degeneration, and bilateral posterior vitreous detachment. On examination, the papules on the neck were small, yellow-cream in color, and plucked-chicken skin–like; the axillary skin was lax and redundant. No other skin lesions were noted. To further characterize possible alterations in dermal elastic tissue and calcium deposition, noninvasive imaging with multiphoton microscopy (MPM) tomography and dynamic optical coherence tomography (OCT) was performed on an area of lax skin in the right axilla.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 1-day history of acute, sharp left iliac fossa pain rated 7/10 on a visual analogue scale, associated with fever and nausea. He denied vomiting, urinary symptoms, changes in bowel habits, weight loss, or recent trauma. His medical and surgical histories were unremarkable, and he had no chronic illnesses.

On examination, he was febrile and had focal tenderness with guarding in the left iliac fossa; there was no palpable mass or costovertebral angle tenderness. Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 12.1×10^3/µL with 87.3% neutrophils and a fibrinogen level of 839 mg/dL. A chest radiograph was normal. An abdominal radiograph showed diffuse bowel gas without air-fluid levels, consistent with a reflex ileus.

Because of the clinical suspicion of diverticulitis, a high-frequency linear‐probe ultrasound of the left iliac fossa was performed, revealing moderate reactive thickening of the descending and sigmoid colon wall with an adjacent oval, noncompressible, hyperechoic mass lacking internal vascularity and surrounded by a subtle hypoechoic line.

A 40-year-old Chinese woman presented with a 2-week history of nonproductive cough and a history of recurrent, self-resolving rashes on her wrists and knees. She had no significant personal or family medical history. Review of systems was otherwise unremarkable.  
On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Lung fields were clear bilaterally, and there was no palpable lymphadenopathy.  
Laboratory studies including a complete blood count, serum biochemistry, and tumor markers (CEA, NSE, CA125, CA199, AFP) were all within normal limits. HIV testing was negative. A purified protein derivative skin test (5 IU) was negative.  
Arterial blood gas analysis on room air showed pH 7.432, PaO₂ 77.1 mm Hg, PaCO₂ 38.8 mm Hg, and an A–a gradient of 26.6 mm Hg. Pulmonary function tests revealed a vital capacity of 87% predicted, an FEV₁/FVC ratio of 100% predicted, and a DLCO of 86% predicted.  
High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated diffuse fine nodular lesions, ground-glass opacity, and minor mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

A 37-year-old man was admitted with a 3-day history of left upper-quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and marked fatigue. His only surgical history was a sleeve gastrectomy 10 years earlier without complications. He denied substance use and any abdominal trauma. On examination, his temperature was 39 °C, and he had tenderness in the left upper quadrant without guarding. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level above 300 mg/L and a leukocyte count of 12 750/mm3; other blood tests were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a 70-mm mass adjacent to the left colic flexure with contrast-enhanced walls and heterogeneous contents, with a suspicion of invasion into the adjacent pancreatic fatty tissue and spleen. Colonoscopy was deferred because of concern for colonic perforation and localized peritonitis.

A 76-year-old woman, previously independent, was referred during the COVID-19 pandemic with a 6-week history of cognitive decline. Her daughter reported difficulty navigating her own home and impairment in familiar tasks such as using cutlery. Over this period, she became mood-labile and developed psychotic features, including delusions that her family was poisoning her and visual hallucinations of the room expanding and contracting. 

Her medical history included rheumatic heart disease with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on warfarin, stage 3B chronic kidney disease, and depression for which sertraline had been started 3 weeks earlier. 

On neurological examination, she was unsteady on her feet and had visual and tactile neglect on the left side. Reflexes were brisk throughout, and she exhibited startle myoclonus. She had an inappropriate affect, giggling in response to questions, and scored 5/10 on the Abbreviated Mental Test. 

Routine blood tests were within normal limits except for an elevated INR of 9.9. She was apyrexial and had no respiratory symptoms. An urgent noncontrast CT scan of the head was performed to exclude subdural haematoma and was unremarkable.

An 81-year-old woman presented with subjective neck pain one month after a minor vehicular incident. As a back-seat passenger on a rough road, she struck her head on the car’s ceiling without loss of consciousness and was able to walk afterward. She initially visited an orthopedic clinic, where cervical spine radiographs were interpreted as showing no fracture. Over the subsequent weeks, her neck pain gradually worsened. On presentation, vital signs were stable. On physical examination, there was no midline cervical tenderness. She could flex her neck forward without difficulty, but backward extension caused severe pain. She had full strength in all extremities, normal sensation, and no neurological deficits. Clinically, a cervical sprain was suspected.

A 21-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 31 weeks of gestation was admitted with confusion and a history of a generalized tonic-clonic seizure one hour earlier. On arrival her blood pressure was 210/130 mmHg. Bedside ultrasound showed a single viable fetus appropriate for 29 weeks and normal amniotic fluid volume. Urinalysis revealed 4+ proteinuria. She was diagnosed with eclampsia and given a 4 g loading dose of magnesium sulfate. Three minutes later she had another generalized seizure and received diazepam (10 mg IV). Because of respiratory distress she was intubated and taken for an emergency cesarean section. Anesthesia was induced with thiopental sodium and cisatracurium and maintained with isoflurane in 50% oxygen / nitrous oxide. A female infant weighing 1100 g was delivered with a 1-minute Apgar score of 7. 

Postoperatively she remained intubated and was transferred to the ICU for mechanical ventilation. Antihypertensive therapy included a nitroglycerin infusion and oral amlodipine; magnesium sulfate infusion and dexamethasone were continued. After she regained consciousness and was extubated, she had a third generalized seizure 15 minutes later and was re-intubated. Laboratory studies showed Hb 13.5 g/dL, Hct 37%, WBC 16 590/mm³, platelets 50 000/mm³, AST 375 U/L, ALT 183 U/L, LDH 1213 U/L, PT 52.1 s, aPTT 25.2 s, and INR 1.44, consistent with HELLP syndrome. Thiopental sodium infusion was administered, seizures abated, and she was extubated approximately 6 hours later.

On postoperative day 1, MRI of the brain demonstrated increased-intensity lesions on T2, FLAIR, diffusion‐weighted, and ADC sequences in the bilateral basal ganglia, frontal centrum semiovale, bilateral parietotemporal and occipital regions, and the left cerebellum.

A 36-year-old hirsute man presented with a recurrent discharging sinus over the right cheek, first noted 2 years earlier and previously operated on twice. He denied toothache, pain on jaw movement, history of tuberculosis, insect bites, or trauma to the area. On examination, the preauricular region of the right cheek showed a small opening surrounded by mild inflammation; the hair density on the cheek appeared normal. The discharge was turbid, slightly foul-smelling, non-bloody, and did not contain hair, sebum, or yellow granules. Radiologic evaluation ruled out involvement of the temporomandibular joint, gums, teeth, parotid gland, and maxilla or mandible as a source of infection. A provisional diagnosis of an infected dermoid cyst was made, and the patient was treated with anti-inflammatory drugs and a 7-day course of oral flucloxacillin and metronidazole, with excisional biopsy planned after local infection control.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a painless swelling in the left lower lip. He recalled trauma to that area about 1 year earlier. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, single, oval, sessile swelling measuring approximately 2 cm on the labial mucosa of the lower lip. The mass was soft to firm, non-tender, and the overlying mucosa was of normal color without ulceration or bluish discoloration. There was no associated pain or paresthesia. The clinical impression was a mucocele, and an excisional biopsy was planned.

A 66-year-old Japanese woman presented with low back and right buttock pain since November 2019 that progressed to bilateral leg pain and intermittent claudication. In June 2020, she underwent elective L2–S1 decompression and interbody fusion for lumbar spinal stenosis. Her medical history included right distal radius fracture repair, carpal tunnel release, dyslipidemia treated with rosuvastatin, and pregabalin for numbness; she smoked 20 cigarettes per day.  

Preoperative radiographs showed spondylotic changes with L2–L3 instability and disc narrowing at L3–L4 and L4–L5; MRI confirmed L2–S1 spinal canal stenosis. Myelography revealed dural canal narrowing at L2–S1. Pulmonary function tests showed mild obstruction; baseline blood counts, serum biochemistry, chest radiograph, ECG, and echocardiography were normal.  

General anesthesia was induced with propofol, fentanyl, and rocuronium and maintained with sevoflurane, fentanyl, oxygen, and air. Tranexamic acid 1000 mg was given intravenously at surgery start and 2000 mg immediately postoperatively. The 291-minute surgery had 850 mL blood loss, 250 mL urine output, and 400 mL autologous blood returned.  

Upon awakening in the supine position, she experienced a 1-minute generalized tonic–clonic seizure; seizures briefly abated after propofol but then recurred multiple times. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.10, PaCO2 15.3 mmHg, and HCO3– 13.9 mEq/L. Serum glucose was 105 mg/dL; sodium 142 mmol/L; potassium 4.0 mmol/L; chloride 110 mmol/L; calcium 8.9 mg/dL. Head CT showed no hemorrhage or intracranial lesion. By ICU transfer, she had a total of 10 seizures treated with diazepam.

A 67-year-old man was referred by a neurosurgeon to our physiotherapy clinic for bilateral sciatica. His history included:
• Four years earlier: left medullary stroke (Wallenberg syndrome) with right-sided pain and temperature sensory loss; on aspirin, antihypertensive, statin, and antidiabetic medications.  
• One year later: coronary artery bypass surgery followed by abdominal aortic aneurysm repair.  
• Risk factors: diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, smoking, sedentary lifestyle, high–red meat diet, and alcohol use.  

Symptom history:
• One year before physiotherapy: right knee pain with low back pain evolving into burning pain posteriorly in the knee, then anterior tibia and toe; fluctuating in location and intensity.  
• Orthopedic evaluation: knee MRI and thigh ultrasound were normal.  
• Subsequent left posterior thigh–knee pain prompted spine MRI and CT, which showed L4–5 and L5–S1 disc bulging with L5 root impingement.  
• Neurosurgeon diagnosed bilateral lumbosacral radiculopathy and administered epidural corticosteroids, local anesthetic, and ozone therapy; left-leg symptoms improved, right-leg pain persisted.  
• Recently underwent endoprosthetic repair of right popliteal artery thrombosis and aneurysm; Doppler ultrasound still showed thrombosis but “good vascular compensation” via recanalization; vascular surgeon prescribed anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy and deferred further revascularization.  

At physiotherapy evaluation:
• Resting right-leg pain 6/10, worsened by walking and daily activities, limited to ~1000 steps/day.  
• Neurologic exam: reduced right-sided pain and temperature sensation; normal muscle strength and reflexes.  
• SLUMP and straight-leg–raise tests reproduced left thigh–knee pain; sustained on right, they increased pain and paresthesia.  
• Bilateral erector spinae muscle spasm; painful, limited lumbar flexion/extension.  
• Skin over right tibia and foot appeared thin, brittle, pale, and cooler than left.  
• Vital signs: pulse 55 bpm regular; brachial BP 120/80 mm Hg.  
• Popliteal and posterior tibial pulses and pressures were normal on left but weak/undetectable on right. Inguinal compression reproduced anterior thigh tingling; no vascular bruits.  
• Plantar flexion test and 6-minute walk (stopped at 67 m) reproduced familiar burning pain.  
• Ankle–brachial index on right was 0 (undetectable ankle systolic pressure) and normal on left.

A 28-year-old nonsmoking male prisoner presented with several weeks of fresh hemoptysis, fever, anorexia, and weight loss. He had known exposure to pulmonary tuberculosis but no risk factors for pulmonary embolism or bronchiectasis. On examination, he was tachycardic, ill-appearing, and underweight. Chest auscultation revealed bronchial breathing in both upper lobes and diffuse inspiratory and expiratory crackles. Chest radiography showed bilateral diffuse reticulonodular opacities with fibrotic changes in the apices. Sputum AFB and nucleic acid amplification confirmed pan-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and standard first-line therapy was started. Despite treatment, he continued to have significant hemoptysis and required three units of packed red blood cells to maintain a hemoglobin around 9 g/dL. Fibreoptic bronchoscopy showed normal airways without an endobronchial mass or obvious bleeding source; bronchoalveolar lavage and biopsies revealed acute inflammation and AFB. A CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrated a thick-walled cavitary lesion filled with blood, surrounded by fibrotic and bronchiectatic changes.

A 22-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left cervical mass noted on routine examination. She reported no symptoms of chest pain, dyspnea, cough, fever, or weight loss. Her medical history was unremarkable. On physical examination, vital signs were normal. A soft, non-tender mass was palpable in the left supraclavicular area; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, electrolytes, and thyroid function tests, were within normal limits. Cervical ultrasound demonstrated a 2.4×3.8 cm hypoechoic lesion in the left supraclavicular region. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed two adjacent cystic lesions: one measuring 3.8×2.3×5.1 cm in the lower anterior neck and another measuring 2.7×2.2×1.8 cm in the anterior mediastinum abutting the left common carotid artery; both had smooth, mildly enhancing walls and a small calcification at the rim. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded inflammatory cells without malignant features or a specific diagnosis.

A 79-year-old man presented with acute dyspnea. His history was notable for three years of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (GOLD group B), mild pulmonary hypertension, depression, multinodular goitre, and prior colon polypectomy. One month earlier, he developed palpitations and progressive dyspnea due to atrial fibrillation treated with bisoprolol, digoxin, and apixaban without clinical improvement. He then underwent biphasic external electrical cardioversion (120 J, anterior–posterior), which restored sinus rhythm and relieved his symptoms. Eleven days later, he underwent a second identical cardioversion for recurrent atrial fibrillation. Five days after the second procedure, he returned with acute dyspnea. Bedside ultrasound revealed a large right pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yielded 2 L of milky fluid. Laboratory analysis showed a transudative effusion with triglycerides 6.11 mmol/L and cholesterol 1.3 mmol/L.

A 3-month-old Chinese girl was referred for evaluation of a one-week history of diarrhoea followed by a single afebrile seizure. She had been previously healthy, born at term with unremarkable perinatal history, and had transitioned from exclusive breastfeeding to various cow’s-milk formulas because of recurrent loose stools and excessive flatulence. On examination, she was moderately dehydrated and tachycardic; her weight was 6.2 kg and length 61 cm. Abdominal exam revealed a ballotable right kidney. Initial laboratory studies showed sodium 117 mmol/L, chloride 90 mmol/L, potassium 9 mmol/L, and metabolic acidosis. She received IV normal saline bolus and controlled fluid correction, plus calcium resonium to lower the potassium; her electrolytes normalized over four days. Stool studies for rotavirus and reducing substances were negative. Cow’s-milk protein allergy was suspected; she was switched to extensively hydrolysed formula with resolution of diarrhoea. Neurologic exam and brain ultrasound were normal. Urine culture grew Enterobacter, and she completed a 7-day course of cefuroxime. Renal ultrasound showed a right duplex kidney with gross hydronephrosis and hydroureter, and a voiding cystourethrogram demonstrated grade 5 vesicoureteric reflux on the right side.

A 19-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 13-day history of high-grade fever, headache, retroorbital pain, and myalgias. One day before admission he became restless and irritable. On examination, his temperature was 101°F, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. He was drowsy and disoriented (Glasgow Coma Scale score 12/15), with no focal neurological deficit or meningeal signs. He was jaundiced. Abdominal examination revealed tender hepatomegaly (liver span 18 cm). Chest examination showed mild to moderate right-sided pleural effusion. 

Laboratory evaluation on admission revealed respiratory alkalosis on arterial blood gas analysis. Ultrasonography demonstrated gallbladder wall thickening, hepatomegaly (17 cm), splenomegaly (13.6 cm), mild to moderate ascites, and pleural effusion. Initial management for suspected dengue hemorrhagic fever with fulminant hepatic involvement was instituted, including intravenous artesunate, broad-spectrum antibiotics, acyclovir, and dexamethasone.

On Day 2, serologic tests for dengue were positive (NS1, IgM, and IgG), and a peripheral smear showed gametocytes and schizonts of Plasmodium vivax. Tests for hepatitis A, B, C, and E were negative. Serum ferritin was 40 000 ng/mL (normal 12–300), triglycerides 292 mg/dL (normal < 140), and fibrinogen was low.

A 38-year-old G2P4 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries presented after 37 days of amenorrhea with vaginal spotting and lower abdominal discomfort. Her serum β-hCG level was 22 200 mIU/ml. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a gestational sac at the anterior uterine isthmus within the prior hysterotomy site, consistent with a cesarean scar pregnancy. She underwent hysteroscopic resection without complications; her β-hCG level fell to 17 965 mIU/ml on postoperative day 2. At 24 days postoperatively, she was asymptomatic but had a β-hCG level of 76 196 mIU/ml; transvaginal ultrasound showed widening of the lower uterine segment by 6 mm but no discrete mass. She was observed closely. Twenty-seven days later (51 days postoperatively), she experienced three days of vaginal bleeding. Her β-hCG level was 2799 mIU/ml. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a 5.8×2.7 cm hypoechoic, poorly marginated lesion in the myometrium of the lower uterine segment at the prior scar, with abundant Doppler flow. MRI revealed a 4.0×4.4×4.0 cm heterogeneous mass at the cesarean scar surrounded by prominent vascularity. Based on these findings, a gestational trophoblastic tumor was suspected, and the patient was diagnosed with low-risk stage I gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

A 72-year-old man with a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a one-week history of difficulty urinating, characterized by incomplete emptying, dribbling, and increased urinary frequency. He denied lower back pain, chills, fever, weight loss, rash, fatigue, or dry mouth. He was taking metformin 1 g twice daily and glipizide 10 mg once daily; fasting blood glucose on admission was 8.43 mmol/L.

On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Digital rectal examination revealed a smooth, soft, nontender prostate without palpable nodules and a shallow central sulcus.

Laboratory studies showed elevated inflammatory markers on complete blood count, procalcitonin 0.080 ng/mL, and prostate-specific antigen 1.66 μg/L. Urinalysis revealed glucose 1+, occult blood 3+, protein trace, and leukocytes 2+. Quantitative urine sediment analysis showed 115 red blood cells/μL, 118 white blood cells/μL, and 7 white blood cell clumps/μL; urine culture showed no growth. Bladder ultrasound demonstrated a postvoid residual volume of approximately 655 mL. Transabdominal ultrasound of the urinary tract showed prostate enlargement with calcifications measuring 5.0 × 3.6 × 3.8 cm. Abdominal CT scan indicated prostate hyperplasia, with prostate MRI recommended if deemed necessary. In the emergency department, he had undergone urinary catheterization for acute urinary retention. Given the presumed diagnosis of benign prostatic hyperplasia causing urinary retention, he was scheduled for transurethral resection of the prostate.

A 22-year-old woman, 5 months postpartum, presented with a 3-month history of a left breast lump associated with pain and tenderness. Fifteen days before presentation, she noted nipple retraction and thick nipple discharge from the affected side. She was unable to breast-feed from the left breast. She denied fever or trauma. On examination, the left breast was enlarged with erythematous and inflamed overlying skin. The nipple–areola complex was enlarged and hyperpigmented, and thick discharge was expressed. In the upper outer quadrant, there was a large (6.0 × 5.0 × 2.4 cm), multinodular, tender, firm-to-hard mass that was free from the chest wall and skin. The right breast was normal. Inflammatory carcinoma was suspected clinically. Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded a benign inflammatory lesion. The patient received a 2-week course of antibiotics, but the lump persisted.

A 26-year-old uncircumcised Caucasian man presented with a 3-month history of an ulcerated lesion on the dorsal aspect of the penis, located between the coronal sulcus and the prepuce. The lesion was not associated with pain or discharge. Two years earlier, he had noticed a tiny cyst in his dorsal foreskin. On examination, the foreskin was swollen and somewhat difficult to retract. At the dorsal coronal sulcus–prepuce junction, there was a 1.5 cm whitish ulcer overlying a hard nodule that appeared fixed to the corpora cavernosa. Inguinal lymph nodes were not enlarged. The patient was admitted for surgical excision.

A 59-year-old woman was referred after a pancreatic-tail lesion was detected on CT during preoperative evaluation for small-bowel obstruction. She was asymptomatic. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including CA19-9 (34.6 U/mL; normal < 37 U/mL) and CEA (0.8 ng/mL; normal < 5.0 ng/mL), were within normal limits.  
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 16 mm unilocular cystic lesion in the pancreatic tail with enhancement of the cyst wall. MRI demonstrated low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images in the lesion. Endoscopic ultrasonography showed a unilocular cyst with a focally thickened wall; contrast-enhanced harmonic EUS confirmed enhancement of the thickened wall. The cyst did not communicate with the main pancreatic duct.  
Given the concern for cystic neoplasms, including mucinous cystic neoplasm, robot-assisted distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy was planned for both diagnosis and treatment.

A 17-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of asymptomatic, persistent, slowly progressive brownish skin lesions on the trunk. He was otherwise healthy, with no relevant medical history, medication use, or family history. On examination, there were hyperpigmented, hyperkeratotic confluent macules and papules coalescing into reticulated plaques over the upper trunk. Wood’s light examination showed no fluorescence. Rubbing the lesions with 70% isopropyl alcohol did not remove them. Oral and nail examinations were unremarkable.

A 51-year-old man presented to the neurology clinic with a one-week history of right-sided retrobulbar pain unrelieved by over-the-counter analgesics. One week later he awoke with constant binocular vertical diplopia that worsened on downgaze but denied changes in visual acuity, photopsias, or trauma. His medical history was negative for hypertension, diabetes, or other vascular risk factors. Examination showed mild depression and intorsion of the right eye on downward gaze consistent with isolated right fourth cranial nerve palsy; the remainder of the neurologic and ophthalmologic examination was unremarkable. Ophthalmology testing for thyroid eye disease and acetylcholine-receptor autoantibodies to evaluate for Myasthenia Gravis were negative. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits was inconclusive. Computed tomographic angiography of the head demonstrated an enlarged vein in the anterior interhemispheric fissure draining into a prominent inferior sagittal sinus but did not suggest a specific vascular abnormality.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of nausea, vomiting, and epigastric discomfort. She denied weight loss, additional gastrointestinal symptoms, fevers, or night sweats. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Physical examination was normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a normal-sized spleen with heterogeneous parenchyma and multiple hypoechoic nodules up to 1.0 cm in diameter. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI confirmed multiple splenic nodules with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and homogeneous enhancement; the largest lesion measured 1.0 cm.  
PET-CT demonstrated no fluorodeoxyglucose uptake. An extensive work-up for occult malignancy and infectious disease was negative.

A term newborn girl was noted at birth to have a swelling in the sacrococcygeal region. There were no other congenital anomalies or neurologic deficits. On examination, the mass was soft to firm, oval, and mobile, measuring approximately 15 × 10 cm, occupying the coccygeal area and bilateral gluteal folds. The overlying skin exhibited slight bosselation without ulceration and showed a bluish-red discoloration posteriorly. On rectal examination, the mass did not extend into the pelvis. Pelvic CT and MRI demonstrated a 14.5 × 9.5 cm cystic to solid mass with areas of hemorrhage confined to the coccygeal, buttock, and intergluteal regions, with no invasion into adjacent structures. Echocardiography revealed a patent ductus arteriosus with a small left-to-right shunt, mild pulmonary arterial hypertension, and a patent foramen ovale, findings deemed physiological. Serum α-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin levels were within normal limits. No preoperative biopsy was performed, and a complete surgical excision with coccygectomy was planned.

A 48-day-old boy was brought to the emergency department after an afebrile tonic–clonic seizure. He was born at 37 weeks 4 days by cesarean delivery with a birth weight of 1830 g and required neonatal intensive care for low birth weight; he was fed regular formula and discharged at 24 days with normal serum calcium (9.2 mg/dl), ionized calcium (2.57 mEq/l), and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 78%. Over the following weeks, he remained exclusively formula-fed but had limited sunlight exposure at home. On presentation, he was intermittently convulsing and irritable. His temperature was 36.5°C, blood pressure 98/64 mmHg, heart rate 156/min, respiratory rate 40/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination was notable only for irritability; there were no dysmorphic features or rashes. Laboratory studies showed:  
  • Serum calcium 6.13 mg/dl (normal 8.5–10.5)  
  • Alkaline phosphatase 2137 IU/l (normal 45–450)  
  • Intact parathyroid hormone 306 pg/ml (normal 10–65)  
  • Serum phosphorus 7.2 mg/dl (normal 4.5–6.5)  
Chest radiography demonstrated no cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion (cardiothoracic ratio 52%). A wrist radiograph showed no radiographic signs of rickets.

A 58-year-old woman presented to the rheumatology clinic with a 2-month history of fatigue, weakness, polyarthritis, and joint swelling. Nine months earlier, she had been diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary hypertension after a 3-year history of progressive dyspnea (now NYHA class IV) and orthopnea, without cough or sputum, accompanied by low-grade fever and night sweats. Echocardiography at that time showed a pulmonary arterial systolic pressure (PASP) of 80 mm Hg, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, mild mitral regurgitation, and moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation. Chest CT revealed alveolar infiltrates in the posterior segment of the left basal lobe and multiple 6–8 mm peripheral lung nodules. Vital signs were normal, and pulmonary function testing was within normal limits.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 45 mm/h, an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:320, and an anti-centromere antibody level of 94.8 AU/ml. Tests for anti–Scl-70, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and rheumatoid arthritis were negative.

On examination, there was effusion of the right second, third, and fourth metacarpophalangeal joints; right second and third proximal interphalangeal joints; left second, third, and fourth metacarpophalangeal joints; and left fourth and fifth proximal interphalangeal joints. Raynaud’s phenomenon was elicited by cold‐water immersion of the hands. Chest auscultation revealed coarse crackles. Repeat echocardiography showed a PASP of 55 mm Hg after treatment, and ECG demonstrated sinus bradycardia with P pulmonale and biphasic P waves.

A 36-year-old man was referred with a 6-month history of painful, progressive vision loss in his right eye. He had known HIV infection for 15 years, with a most recent CD4 count of 105 cells/μL; he had previously received antiretroviral therapy for 4 years but had discontinued treatment. He had no systemic symptoms or involvement of the left eye.

On examination, visual acuity in the right eye was no light perception; intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg in the right eye and 15 mm Hg in the left eye. Conjunctival injection was present. The right pupil was mid-dilated, reactive, and showed a grade-2 relative afferent pupillary defect. Funduscopic examination of the right eye revealed hazily seen patches of retinal whitening, an attached retina, and a pale optic disc.

A presumptive diagnosis of acute retinal necrosis or endogenous endophthalmitis of possible viral etiology with subretinal abscess was made. The patient underwent a core vitrectomy with intravitreal ganciclovir (2 mg/0.1 mL) and received oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily for 3 days). A vitreous biopsy specimen was sent for microbiological studies. Routine blood tests, including hemoglobin, blood glucose, blood urea, and serum creatinine, were normal. A postoperative B-scan ultrasound of the right eye showed moderate-intensity echoes throughout the vitreous cavity with localized elevations in all quadrants and submembranous opacities suggestive of exudates.

A 4-year-old boy, born at term and previously healthy, was brought by his mother for evaluation of an opening on the right side of his neck. The opening was noted at birth and intermittently discharged a thick, mucoid fluid, especially after upper respiratory infections. His mother also observed recurrent, painless swelling on the same side of the neck, which gradually increased in size but without overlying skin changes. There was no history of trauma, surgery, or family history of similar problems. Immunizations were up to date.

On examination, he was afebrile, with normal vital signs. A small pinhead-sized opening was seen on the anterior border of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle, in the lower third of the neck, approximately 3 cm above the medial end of the clavicle. There was no active discharge, tenderness, erythema, or palpable mass at the time of examination.

Laboratory testing, including renal function prior to contrast administration, was normal. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck showed an approximately 5 cm well-defined tubular tract extending from the right anterolateral neck (anteromedial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, anterior to the carotid vessels, and lateral to the thyrohyoid cartilage) and terminating posterior to the right tonsillar pillar.

A 28-year-old primigravida was referred at 36 weeks of gestation for suspected fetal ventriculomegaly. Her obstetric, medical, and family histories were unremarkable; serologic testing for TORCH infections was negative, and a mid-trimester anatomic survey was normal. 

At 34 weeks, ultrasound showed a male fetus with dilation of the bilateral lateral ventricles (18 mm and 10 mm), as well as the third and fourth ventricles. Adjacent to the left lateral ventricle was a well-circumscribed, round anechoic cyst measuring 13 × 10 mm; Doppler assessment was not performed at that time. Fetal biometry was appropriate for gestational age.

At 36 weeks and 5 days, ventricular measurements were unchanged, but the left parieto-occipital cyst had enlarged to 32 × 27 × 25 mm, with surrounding hyperechoic areas consistent with pericystic hemorrhage; the left lateral ventricle contained an irregular hyperechoic collection suggesting intraventricular hemorrhage. Color and spectral Doppler ultrasound demonstrated turbulent flow within the cyst, with an arterial jet arising from a vessel at the left parieto-temporal junction. The feeding artery could be traced from the circle of Willis, and three-dimensional color-flow imaging confirmed the course of the posterior cerebral artery to the lesion.
