Fetal ultrasound also showed cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly, and the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity was 103.5 cm/s (> 1.5 MoM).

A 56-year-old man presented with mild intermittent diplopia and a 2-year history of bilateral eyelid swelling and proptosis, for which he had received no treatment. He denied symptoms of dry eyes or dry mouth. Exophthalmometric measurements were 21 mm on the right and 19 mm on the left. Ocular motility was full, and visual acuity, intraocular pressure, and funduscopic examination were normal.

Five years earlier, both submandibular glands were noted to be enlarged, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy showed atypical lymphoid hyperplasia and periductal fibrosis, suggestive of sclerosing sialadenitis but insufficient for a definitive diagnosis.

Laboratory studies revealed normal thyroid function and antinuclear antibody titers. Serum IgG was elevated at 2770 mg/dL; IgA and IgM were within normal limits.

Orbital computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement and homogeneous enhancement, with thickening of the right inferior rectus and both lateral rectus muscles.

Given the imaging findings, orbital lymphoma was highly suspected, and an incisional biopsy of the right lacrimal mass was performed.

A 63‐year‐old woman with no prior medical history was diagnosed with COVID-19 and treated with azithromycin, zinc, and vitamin C. On day 15 after symptom onset, she developed painless, mildly pruritic, erythematous maculopapular lesions with atypical targetoid morphology on the trunk and lower limbs. There was no mucosal involvement. She denied any recent herpes infection, had no similar eruptions in her past, and no family history of similar lesions. Complete blood count, biochemical parameters, and serological tests—including Herpes simplex virus IgM and IgG, Epstein–Barr virus IgM and IgG, Cytomegalovirus IgM and IgG, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti–hepatitis C virus—were within normal limits.

A 59-year-old Caucasian man was evaluated for generalized chorea of 1.5 years’ duration. He had no relevant family history. As a child, he was diagnosed with celiac disease, adhered to a gluten-free diet with resolution of gastrointestinal symptoms, but as an adult returned to a normal diet without issues until recent months, when he reported recurrence of abdominal pain and diarrhea. His psychiatric history included possible schizotypal personality disorder, depression, anxiety, and past alcohol dependence. His medications for the past three years were trazodone 100 mg/day, venlafaxine 375 mg/day, and mirtazapine 15 mg/day; quetiapine 100 mg/day had been added six months earlier for paranoid ideation without change in his movements. On examination, he had moderate generalized chorea with dystonic facial movements and right-hand posturing. His motor score on the United Huntington’s Disease Rating Scale was 9. Laboratory evaluations including blood chemistry, peripheral blood smear, creatine kinase, liver enzymes, thyroid function tests, ceruloplasmin, and Huntington’s disease gene were unremarkable. He had a mild microcytic anemia with low ferritin but no ferritin mutations. Anti-gliadin antibodies were markedly elevated (IgG 139 U [normal 0–20 U], IgA 72 U [normal 0–20 U]). Non-contrast brain MRI showed mild–moderate cerebral atrophy, periventricular and pontine microvascular changes, an old right subinsular hemorrhage, and a chronic left frontoparietal infarct.

A 53-year-old right-handed woman underwent craniotomy for gross total resection of a 5.7-cm right frontoparietal meningioma after a 3-day history of headache and mild dysarthria. She had no prior neurologic disease. Postoperatively, she was unable to produce speech except for occasional unintelligible sounds but could understand spoken language and communicate by writing. Examination revealed left central-type facial palsy with slight peri-oral weakness on spontaneous movement, mild deviation of the tongue to the left on protrusion, and no limb motor or sensory deficits. Video-fluoroscopic swallowing study showed no impairment. On postoperative day 2, brain MRI showed an acute diffusion-weighted imaging lesion at the medial margin of the resection cavity corresponding to the right primary motor cortex face area, with surrounding peritumoral cerebral edema.

A 9-year-old girl with no significant past medical or family history presented with a 6-month history of intermittent, irregular, sudden jerky movements involving all four limbs and the head. The movements began in the right lower limb and over one month spread to the right upper limb, head, left lower limb, and then left upper limb. The jerks occurred asynchronously, lasted less than a second, were not associated with loss of consciousness, showed no diurnal variation or clustering, and never occurred during sleep. She experienced occasional falls, slippage of objects from her hands, and spillage of food.

Three months after onset, she developed drooling of saliva, progressive swallowing difficulty, and speech problems; at presentation she was limited to semisolid foods, had severe dysarthria, and could only utter a few words. Inappropriate laughter accompanied onset of bulbar symptoms. Concurrently, she developed abnormal posturing of the limbs—first on the right, then on the left—with stiffness that resolved completely in sleep. In addition, she had poor attention and declining school performance. There was no history of convulsions, fever, headache, vomiting, visual complaints, motor weakness, sensory impairment, bowel or bladder dysfunction, jaundice, gastric complaints, bleeding tendency, or measles. She was fully vaccinated.

On examination, she was alert, conscious, and inappropriately smiling with drooling of saliva and a persistently open mouth. Cognitive function was severely impaired. Ophthalmologic examination revealed a Kayser–Fleischer ring in both eyes. There were repeated dystonic, synchronous uprolling movements of both eyes without impairment of sensorium. She had severe dysarthria, dysphagia, and tongue dystonia, but gag reflex and palatal movements were normal. The motor exam showed generalized rigidity with normal muscle strength, normal deep-tendon reflexes, and flexor plantar responses. Multifocal myoclonus involved the head and all four limbs, more prominent on the right. Dystonic posturing of all limbs was also present. Sensory and cerebellar examinations were normal. Gait was short-shuffling with festination. Other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, renal function, and liver function. Serum copper was elevated, serum ceruloplasmin was reduced, and 24-hour urinary copper excretion was increased. Slit-lamp examination confirmed bilateral Kayser–Fleischer rings. Electroencephalogram (EEG) was normal despite the multifocal myoclonus, and ultrasonography of the abdomen was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated bilateral hyperintensities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, midbrain, and pons on T2 and FLAIR sequences.

A 77-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of an enlarging, erythematous-to-brownish indurated lesion on the left thigh. The lesion was mildly tender and had expanded centrifugally without any preceding trauma or infection. Her medical history included hip replacement surgery, cataracts, and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine; thyroid-stimulating hormone levels were normal. On examination, there was a large annular plaque with an erythematous mildly tender border on the medial left thigh and no ulceration. Initial differential diagnoses included eosinophilic cellulitis, necrobiosis lipoidica, and morphea. A punch biopsy was inconclusive. At follow-up, the lesion had migrated distally to the left lower limb. A second punch biopsy from the new tender area revealed a mild lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with vascular proliferation in the superficial and deep dermis, and septal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with slight thickening in the subcutaneous tissue; no neutrophilic infiltrate or well-formed granulomas were seen, consistent with septal panniculitis with vascular proliferation. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 25 mm/h (normal, 2–30 mm/h) and a neutrophil count of 8.5 × 10^9/L (normal, 2.0–7.5 × 10^9/L); all other tests, including antinuclear antibody, α-1 antitrypsin, serum amylase, and serum lipase, were within the normal range.

A 60-year-old woman presented with exertional dyspnea, with mild limitation during ordinary physical activities. Electrocardiography showed a complete left bundle branch block and sinus tachycardia. Doppler echocardiography revealed a severely dilated left ventricle (61 mm in systole and 71 mm in diastole), a mildly dilated left atrium (40 mm), and an ejection fraction of 30%. Cardiac catheterization confirmed left ventricular dilatation and normal coronary arteries. Chagas disease serology was negative. She was started on carvedilol, losartan, and furosemide, with clinical improvement.  

Her history was notable for cholecystectomy for biliary lithiasis complicated by pancreatitis, hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine, and no smoking or alcohol use. Two siblings had dilated cardiomyopathy, and a brother died suddenly in adolescence.  

One year after symptom onset, she was admitted to the ICU with cardiogenic shock and treated with dobutamine. Following discharge, she underwent cardiac resynchronization therapy for refractory heart failure but continued to have episodes of cardiogenic shock requiring dobutamine dependence.  

Two years after symptom onset, she was referred for cardiac transplantation. On examination, she had cold extremities, slow capillary refill, hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, tachycardia, a third heart sound, and hepatomegaly without peripheral edema. Echocardiography showed a left ventricle measuring 68 mm in systole and 74 mm in diastole, a left atrium of 44 mm, and an ejection fraction of 18%. Routine biochemical and hematological tests were normal.  

Under the presumed clinical diagnosis of idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, she underwent orthotopic cardiac transplantation and received prednisone, cyclosporine, and mycophenolate mofetil. Her post-transplant course was uneventful with good graft function. Two and a half years later, she died of acute heart failure.

An 82-year-old Japanese man with prostate cancer on darolutamide presented in winter with a 5-day history of appetite loss, fatigue, and dry cough, followed by difficulty mobilizing. He had hypertension and osteoporosis, no smoking history. On admission he was afebrile; pulse 96 beats/min; SpO₂ 92% on room air. Inspiratory crackles were heard at both lung bases. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 17,400/µL (82.7% neutrophils) and a C-reactive protein level of 16.88 mg/dL. Chest radiography revealed bilateral infiltrative shadows and ground-glass opacities. High-resolution CT of the chest showed bilateral extensive nonsegmental peripheral ground-glass opacities and areas of ground-glass opacity surrounded by a ring of consolidation (reversed halo sign).

Darolutamide was discontinued because drug-induced organizing pneumonitis was suspected, and ampicillin/sulbactam was started for presumed bacterial pneumonia. After 9 days, his appetite, fatigue, and radiographic findings improved, and he was discharged. Three days later he developed fever, cough, and dyspnea; CT again showed bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities and reversed halo signs. He was readmitted, treated with tazobactam/piperacillin, improved, and discharged. One day later he again experienced fever and dyspnea with SpO₂ 89% on room air, and CT demonstrated recurrent bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities and reversed halo signs. He was readmitted for further evaluation.

An 11.5-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of facial and dental abnormalities. She was born at term (3500 g) to a first pregnancy with an unremarkable perinatal course. In the neonatal period, she was noted to have an extra digit on the left hand, torticollis, flexion contractures of digits in the right hand, and a malformed right thumb. Psychomotor development was mildly delayed in infancy. 

Her history included multiple osteoarticular abnormalities, structural inner ear anomalies, facial dysmorphism, frontal bone thinning, lumbar vertebral deformities, and underweight status. She required ongoing care by pediatricians, audiologists, pulmonologists, and rehabilitation specialists.

On orthodontic examination, she had bilateral Angle class II malocclusion, an overjet of 7.7 mm, and an overbite of 12.7 mm. Facial features included exophthalmos, hypertelorism, full cheeks, and prominent superciliary ridges. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated absence of the right second molar tooth germs (upper and lower), the right second lower premolar, and all third molars, with a retained deciduous tooth in the position of the right lower second premolar. 

Cephalometric analysis revealed a reduced mentolabialis sulcus angle, skeletal class II with upper incisor proclination (WITS index 8.6 mm), a retrognathic facial type, and mandibular hypoplasia resulting in an oblique retrognathic profile.

A 25-year-old multiparous woman presented with an 8-month history of bilateral breast enlargement. She reported painful, swollen breasts with multiple palpable nodules and erythema. She had used a levonorgestrel implant for two years. On examination, there was bilateral, symmetrical breast enlargement, erythematous skin with peau d’orange changes, and edema. A 4-cm mass was palpable in the lower inner quadrant of the right breast; no mass was felt on the left. A right axillary lymph node was palpable. She denied any personal or family history of breast cancer.

Bilateral mammography was nondiagnostic due to extremely dense breast tissue. Breast ultrasound revealed heterogeneous echotexture with multiple circumscribed solid, hypoechoic masses in both breasts, measuring 3–8 cm in diameter, and two right axillary lymph nodes with cortical thickening. The lesions were categorized as BI-RADS 4A.

Percutaneous core needle biopsy of the right breast mass showed breast parenchyma composed of ductal–lobular units and stromal tissue containing a complex pattern of linear spaces lined by spindle cells. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong positivity for CD34, actin, and calponin, and negativity for estrogen and progesterone receptors. Fine-needle aspiration of the right axillary lymph node revealed lymphoid hyperplasia.

A 16-year-old Caucasian male presented with one week of daily fever, headache, sore throat, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, diffuse joint pain, and rash. About one month earlier he had mild cold-like symptoms; his mother tested positive for COVID-19. Two weeks before presentation he received the first dose of the Pfizer/BioNTech SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. His symptoms began with fevers, headache, and sore throat; gastrointestinal symptoms resolved after three days. He tested negative on rapid strep and Monospot, and received amoxicillin and ondansetron. Four days into illness his oral intake fell, and he developed bilateral edema, erythema, heat, and pain in the metacarpophalangeal joints, elbows, knees, and ankles, which impaired ambulation. He also developed a rash. Pediatric evaluation showed ESR and CRP four times normal; amoxicillin was stopped, and he was referred for higher-level care. 

On presentation to our emergency department his joint findings had partially improved but persistent erythema over the metacarpophalangeal joints and 1+ nonpitting ankle edema remained. His primary complaint was sore throat (7/10), relieved by ketorolac. Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C; heart rate 87 bpm; respiratory rate 18/min; blood pressure 113/73 mm Hg; SpO2 100% on room air. Examination revealed bilateral conjunctival injection, pharyngeal erythema without exudate, erythematous skin over the metacarpophalangeal joints, nonpitting ankle edema, and a blanching salmon-pink maculopapular rash from the suprapubic area to both ankles. Abdominal exam showed no hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory studies: WBC 8.9 × 10^3/mm^3, neutrophils 84% (high), lymphocytes 5% (low), eosinophils 7% (high), platelets 207 × 10^3/mm^3, ESR 60 mm/h (high), CRP 21.7 mg/dL (high), D-dimer 311 ng/mL (high), fibrinogen 777 mg/dL (high), ALT 115 U/L (high), aldolase 15.1 U/L (high), CK 29 U/L (low), troponin < 0.010 ng/mL. Non-glycosylated ferritin was normal. A respiratory viral panel and SARS-CoV-2 PCR were negative. He was admitted for further evaluation.

A 61-year-old man presented with melena, left upper abdominal pain, pallor, and lightheadedness. His hemoglobin was 4.9 g/dL, with RBC count 2.25 million/µL, elevated RDW, and low MCH and MCV. He received packed red-cell transfusions. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed hyperemia and violaceous spots in the distal duodenum but no active bleeding. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a markedly dilated superior mesenteric vein with a pre-occlusive focal stenosis at its distal portion, bypassed by multiple varicoid venous plexuses around the pancreatic head, duodenum, and proximal jejunum. The portal vein measured 17 mm and showed no CT signs of cirrhosis, ascites, or pancreatic abnormalities. The patient had no history or CT evidence of major abdominal surgery, pancreatitis, chronic hepatopathy, or cancer.

A previously healthy 7-month-old male infant was referred for a 2-week history of intermittent fever up to 39 °C. He had received a 2-week course of oral cefotaxime-clavulanic acid for acute otitis media. Three days before presentation, he became continuously irritable and cried persistently.  
On examination, he was normoxic and breathing comfortably. A tender, mildly erythematous swelling (4 × 3 cm) was noted on the left anterior chest wall without any history of trauma.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 22,000/mm3 (neutrophils 15,000/mm3) and a C-reactive protein level of 240 mg/L.  
A chest radiograph demonstrated soft-tissue thickening over the lower left chest wall.  
Ultrasound of the mass revealed a heterogeneous fluid collection (3 cm) surrounding the middle arch of the left seventh rib, with irregular cortical lysis of the rib.

A 45-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 3-month history of right-sided hip pain. On examination, she had discomfort with right hip movement and an antalgic gait. Initial pelvic MRI showed multiple solid lesions with intermediate signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences, marked contrast enhancement, restricted diffusion, and a fluid-fluid level within a lesion at the left anterosuperior iliac crest. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed lytic lesions in the iliac bones, ilio-pubic rami, left scapula, and right glenoid without any identifiable primary neoplasm. FDG PET-CT demonstrated hypermetabolic activity in these lytic bone lesions and in a thyroid isthmic nodule. Neck ultrasound confirmed a Bethesda VI papillary thyroid nodule and incidentally detected a vascularized mass posterior to the left thyroid lobe consistent with a parathyroid adenoma. Sestamibi scintigraphy corroborated the presence of a left parathyroid adenoma. Laboratory evaluation showed a calcium level of 12.6 mg/dL and a parathyroid hormone level of 1385 pg/mL.

A 35-year-old Hispanic man presented with 1 week of generalized malaise, abdominal pain, fatigue, subjective fever, sore throat, joint pain, watery diarrhea, oral-intake intolerance, and a petechial skin rash. The rash began as blisters on his palms and soles, progressing to non-confluent erythematous macules with burning and itching that spread to his arms, chest, and trunk. He had 2–3 episodes of diarrhea daily, which had resolved by presentation. His only medication was diclofenac potassium, 100 mg twice daily for back pain over the past week; he denied other medications, tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use. Family and psychosocial histories were unremarkable.

On examination, temperature was 39.6 °C, pulse 132 beats/min, blood pressure 132/77 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18/min. He appeared well groomed. Skin showed non-confluent, non-blanching erythematous macules. Head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat examination was normal. Lungs were clear, heart sounds were normal without murmurs, and abdomen was soft and non-tender. Neurologically, he was alert and oriented with intact cranial nerves, reflexes, and 5/5 strength in all extremities.

Initial laboratory studies showed anemia, thrombocytopenia, C-reactive protein 21.9 mg/L, mild transaminitis (ALT 55 U/L, AST 35 U/L), and normal bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. He was treated supportively for presumed viral gastroenteritis. 

Persistent fever prompted ICU transfer and empiric vancomycin, aztreonam, azithromycin, and oseltamivir; cultures remained negative, and vancomycin was discontinued. Vasculitis and autoimmune panels were unremarkable. He then developed encephalopathy and had a seizure, requiring intubation; head CT showed no acute intracranial process.

Repeat studies revealed platelet count 10 ×10^3/µL, hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL, reticulocyte count 10%, prothrombin time 11.3 s, PTT 27.1 s, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, LDH 1172 U/L, haptoglobin 0 mg/dL, schistocytes on peripheral smear, total hemolytic complement < 14 U/mL, and a positive direct Coombs test. High-dose intravenous steroids and IV immunoglobulin were initiated for suspected immune-mediated hemolysis versus acute vasculitis. 

Skin biopsy demonstrated patchy granular C5b-9 deposition along superficial dermal vessels and the dermo–epidermal junction.

A 16-year-old previously healthy girl presented three months after a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection with frontal headaches, decreased visual acuity, and new-onset polyuria and polydipsia. Her COVID-19 had been confirmed by nasopharyngeal RT-PCR, with initial symptoms of chills, fever, fatigue, anosmia, ageusia, and mild nasal congestion; she was unvaccinated. Family history was notable for maternal Graves’ disease. On examination, temperature was 36.5 °C, pulse 70 beats/min, and blood pressure 110/80 mmHg. Neurologic examination showed no meningeal signs. Twenty-four–hour urine volume was 10 000 ml with 9800 ml of fluid intake. Visual acuity was 1/10 bilaterally; funduscopic and visual-field examinations were normal. MRI of the hypothalamic–pituitary region demonstrated convex enlargement of the pituitary gland (height, 9 mm) with intense homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium. Systemic inflammatory markers, complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, and calcium were normal. An extensive hormonal evaluation was unremarkable. Further testing showed a normal serum angiotensin-converting enzyme, normal tumor markers, a negative tuberculin skin test, and an unremarkable chest radiograph. Dermatologic examination revealed no skin lesions, and bone radiographs showed no lytic lesions.

A 38-year-old patient presented with progressive bilateral visual loss over four months, accompanied by throbbing temporal headache. There was no eye redness, vomiting, or neck stiffness. On ophthalmologic examination, the patient could count fingers at three meters, and fundoscopic examination showed pale optic discs bilaterally, consistent with optic atrophy. Brain MRI was normal. Topical betaxolol was administered without visual improvement.

One month later, the patient was evaluated by neurology for persistent headache and bilateral visual loss of five months' duration. Repeat fundoscopic examination confirmed bilateral optic atrophy. There was no memory deficit, other cranial nerve palsies, sensory or motor deficits, or bladder/bowel dysfunction. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed normal chemistry and cellularity, and repeat brain MRI remained normal. A diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension was made; the patient was treated with acetazolamide and serial lumbar punctures, reporting slight visual improvement.

Three months later, the patient was admitted with one week of lower-extremity weakness, numbness, and tingling, along with bladder and bowel dysfunction. Vision had deteriorated further during this period. On examination, blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg, pulse 90/min, respirations 24/min, and temperature 37.2°C. The patient was alert and oriented. Visual acuity was counting fingers at two meters. There was flaccid paraplegia and sensory loss below the T4 dermatome. No meningeal signs were present.

Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, liver and renal function, and urinalysis. Serologies for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and VDRL were negative. CSF protein was elevated at 145 mg/dL; glucose was 55 mg/dL; no cells or organisms were seen; CSF VDRL was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. T2-weighted spine MRI demonstrated a long, central T3–T6 hyperintense lesion with mild cord expansion and proximal central canal dilation.

A 3-month-old female infant was admitted with recurrent vomiting, respiratory problems, and progressive abdominal distension. She was born at home via spontaneous vaginal delivery to a mother without prenatal care; no birth records are available. The infant had no previous clinical visits. On examination, the abdomen was markedly distended and tense; she had repeated vomiting for 3 days, no stool output, and decreased urine output. Laboratory studies showed: sodium 128 mEq/L; potassium 4.15 mEq/L; calcium 8.1 mg/dL; albumin 2.8 g/dL; WBC 21 300/mL; C-reactive protein 11.97 mg/L; platelets 353 000/mcL; hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL; hematocrit 30.7%. A standing abdominal X-ray revealed absence of intestinal gas and leftward displacement of the intestines consistent with complete obstruction. Ultrasound demonstrated a solitary 10 × 10 × 14 cm cystic lesion extending from the liver or right kidney to the pelvis, displacing the liver, right kidney, and intestines. MRI confirmed a solitary 10 × 10 × 14 cm cystic structure in the right abdomen extending to the pelvis, possibly originating from the liver.

A 42-year-old man was referred for sudden onset of severe back and chest pain. He had a history of dyslipidemia but no history of traumatic injury; he had received acupuncture on his back several weeks earlier. On admission, his blood pressure was 125/69 mmHg, pulse 91 bpm, and temperature was normal. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 15,400 cells/μL, hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, and C-reactive protein 0.05 mg/dL. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a post-mediastinal hematoma and an unusual vascular structure branching from the abdominal aorta at the level of the superior mesenteric artery. This vessel formed an aneurysm from which unidentifiable channels extended both cranially and caudally alongside the aorta; the cranial channel appeared to track toward the left subclavian circulation.

A 25-year-old married woman presented with a history of primary amenorrhea and painful sexual intercourse. She reported normal breast development and pubic hair. At age 14, ultrasonography suggested absence of uterus and vagina. There was no family history of amenorrhea, and no maternal exposures during pregnancy. She was a non-smoker, non-alcoholic, with no prior surgeries or medical illnesses.

On examination, vital signs were stable. She weighed 74 kg and was 162 cm tall. Breast development was Tanner stage V. External genitalia showed normal labia majora, labia minora, pubic hair, and an external urethral meatus. There was no palpable vaginal pouch or bulging hymen.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, WBC 14,400/mm3, platelets 60,000/mm3. Hormonal levels, including LH, FSH, prolactin, progesterone, and testosterone, were within normal limits. Peripheral blood karyotype was 46,XX.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated absence of the uterus, cervix, and proximal two-thirds of the vagina, as well as absence of the left kidney.

A 40-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of hypercalcemia. She had a history of recurrent right kidney stones treated with lithotripsy. There was no family history of hypercalcemia or stones. Her BMI was 23.2 kg/m^2. On examination, a 2 cm solid mass was palpable in the left thyroid lobe.

Laboratory tests:
• Serum calcium 14.2 mg/dL (normal 8.4–10.2)  
• PTH 380 pg/mL (normal 10–65)  
• Creatinine 0.6 mg/dL; eGFR 114 mL/min/1.73 m^2  

Neck ultrasound showed a 24×21×17 mm highly vascularized mixed cystic and solid nodule in the left thyroid lobe. After intravenous hydration, calcium decreased to 12.8 mg/dL.

One month later:
• Calcium 12.3 mg/dL  
• PTH 310 pg/mL  
99mTc sestamibi scintigraphy demonstrated focal uptake in the left posterior thyroid region.

Ultrasound-guided FNAB (20-gauge needle, five passes) yielded two cytologic slides and washout fluid for PTH measurement. Cytology revealed oncocytic cells with large hyperdense nuclei, and immunostains were negative for PTH, PAX8, CD10, and thyroglobulin. The washout fluid PTH was 181 pg/mL. Six days after FNAB, calcium was 8.1 mg/dL.

An 18F-choline PET scan showed a metabolically active hypodense nodule measuring 23×16×18 mm below the left thyroid lobe, “consistent with a diagnosis of hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue.”

A 73-year-old man was transferred from a hospital in Bangkok after a 3-week ICU stay for fulminant multiorgan dysfunction that began with nausea, vomiting, diplopia, dizziness, and weakness during travel in Thailand. His past medical history included hypertension, two-vessel coronary artery disease, a known monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, and an episode of non-oliguric acute renal failure nine years earlier.

During his ICU course, he experienced acute kidney injury requiring intermittent hemodialysis, upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, a non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction, hemodynamic instability managed with vasopressors, respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, and a generalized maculopapular rash treated with colchicine and topical glucocorticoids. He received multiple antibiotics and antifungals without identification of a clear sepsis focus beyond the lungs.

On repatriation, he was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, nonoliguric, awake but disoriented, with a 3/6 holosystolic murmur and a nonpetechial maculopapular rash on his lower legs. Laboratory studies on arrival included:

  • Serum creatinine ~1.5 mg/dL (eGFR ~30 mL/min/1.73 m2) off dialysis  
  • Urinalysis: specific gravity 1.020, pH 5.0, 3+ heme, 4+ protein, trace leukocyte esterase  
  • Urine sediment: multiple well-formed erythrocyte casts, granular casts, a few broad waxy casts, 10–20 erythrocytes/hpf, 3–5 leukocytes/hpf, no bacteria or crystals  
  • Proteinuria quantified at 5 g per gram of creatinine  

Given the erythrocyte casts and heavy proteinuria, a pulse of corticosteroids was administered, and a CT-guided renal biopsy was performed. Autoantibody serology including ANA, ANCA, and anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies was negative. Complement levels (C3, C4) were normal. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation revealed an M band of IgG λ-light chains; serum κ- and λ-light chains were 13 mg/L and 130 mg/L (ratio 0.1), consistent with his known monoclonal gammopathy.

A 15-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of dizziness, nausea, and progressive weakness. She denied smoking, alcohol, diuretic use, vomiting, or diarrhea, and her family history was unremarkable. She exercises daily. On examination, blood pressure was 135/80 mm Hg, heart rate 75 beats/min, with normal heart and abdominal examinations. ECG showed sinus rhythm with a QT interval of 600 ms. Laboratory tests revealed serum potassium 1.8 mmol/L, pH 7.6, pCO2 48 mm Hg, HCO3– 47 mmol/L, and mild creatine kinase elevation (321 U/L). Serum creatinine, sodium, calcium, phosphate, magnesium, and uric acid were normal. A spot urine sample showed sodium 50 mmol/L, potassium 65 mmol/L, and a transtubular potassium gradient of 16. Over the next six days, she received high-dose potassium chloride with gradual correction. Further evaluation showed plasma renin <0.3 ng/mL/h (normal 0.3–7), plasma aldosterone 3.4 ng/dL (normal 5–40), cortisol 10.5 μg/dL (normal 3–20), and ACTH 15 pg/mL (normal 5–45). Abdominal CT was unremarkable.

A 20-year-old previously healthy white woman presented with acute onset of substernal chest pain that began after a psychosocial stressor. An electrocardiogram showed anterolateral ST-segment elevation. Serum troponin I was 276 ng/mL (normal < 0.034 ng/mL). Emergent coronary angiography demonstrated normal coronary arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed anterolateral left ventricular hypokinesis and an ejection fraction of 35%. The patient was started on beta-blocker therapy for presumed cardiomyopathy.

A 51-year-old woman presented with progressive exertional dyspnoea and a 3-year history of intermittent exertional chest pain that had never been evaluated. Her medical history included hyperthyroidism and an old lacunar infarction. Initial laboratory tests showed a normal N-terminal prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide (99.3 pg/mL) and normal cardiac enzymes (TnT <3.0 pg/mL; CK-MB 0.61 ng/mL). Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 64% with no wall motion abnormalities. During a treadmill exercise test, 1.4 mm of horizontal ST-segment depression developed in leads II, III, aVF, V5, and V6 at peak exercise. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing demonstrated reduced exercise capacity (VO2 65%, VO2/kg 18.67 mL/kg/min, VE/VCO2 40, 5.3 METs). Contrast-enhanced cardiac CT angiography showed no significant coronary stenosis. However, there was a tortuous coronary vessel in the pre-pulmonic space with multiple dilated aneurysmal sacs, the largest measuring 10.5 × 6.0 mm, and a fistulous drainage diameter of 2.5–3.1 mm. The differential diagnosis of her exertional dyspnoea and chest pain included coronary steal syndrome as a major concern, while variant angina and microvascular disease were less concerning.

A 29‐year‐old woman with a history of biopsy-proven celiac disease diagnosed at age 20 and previously stable on a gluten-free diet presents with progressive dyspnea, pleuritic chest and abdominal pain, and recurrent large-volume hemoptysis. Over the past year, after reintroducing gluten, she had two similar hemoptysis episodes treated with 8-week courses of oral corticosteroids; her diet was not altered. Between episodes, flexible bronchoscopy and bacterial and fungal cultures were unremarkable. She underwent a right video-assisted thoracic surgery upper-lobe wedge biopsy, which demonstrated haemosiderin-laden macrophages and lymphocytic bronchiolitis.

On presentation, she was tachycardic (heart rate 130/min), hypertensive (160/95 mm Hg), tachypneic (24 breaths/min), and hypoxemic (SpO₂ 88% on room air). Lung examination revealed diffuse crepitations. A CT pulmonary angiogram showed bilateral ground-glass infiltrates with mild interlobular septal thickening and no pulmonary embolus. Nasopharyngeal aspirate was negative for viruses. Autoimmune serologies revealed negative ANA and anti-GBM antibodies; c-ANCA was weakly positive but MPO and PR3 antibodies were negative. Complement levels, rheumatoid factor, CRP, and CK were within normal limits. Renal function was normal (eGFR > 90 mL/min, Cr 60 µmol/L), with 11 × 10⁶/L erythrocytes in urine but no active sediment. She was anemic (Hb 80 g/L), with platelets of 296 × 10⁹/L and normal coagulation studies.

A 12-year-old Turkish girl was born at 38 weeks’ gestation to unrelated healthy parents. She was asymptomatic until 1 year of age, when she developed recurrent pustular skin lesions that responded transiently to corticosteroids and antibiotics, leaving hyperpigmented scars. Between ages 1 and 12 years, she required four hospitalizations for these lesions. No family history of similar skin disease was noted.

At age 12, she was hospitalized for arthralgias of the knees, elbows, and ankles and arthritis of the left knee, with concomitant pustular skin lesions. During that admission, she developed septicemia and respiratory insufficiency requiring intensive care. After recovery, she was referred for further evaluation.

On examination, she had hyperpigmented scar lesions on the right face, bilateral inguinal and paraumbilical regions, and paronychia of the thumbnails. She had a left-knee contracture limiting motion, episcleritis, and failure to thrive (weight and height below the third percentile).

Laboratory studies showed iron-deficiency anemia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and elevated acute-phase reactants: hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, C-reactive protein 6.5 mg/dL (reference 0–0.1), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 100 mm/hr (0–20), and serum amyloid A 123 mg/L (0–8). Total IgE, eosinophil count, lymphocyte subsets, and oxidative burst activity of granulocytes were normal. Autoantibodies (ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor) were negative. She had two BCG scars, a 12 mm tuberculin response, and a negative QuantiFERON assay. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography showed splenomegaly. Skin biopsy of hyperpigmented lesions demonstrated neutrophil infiltration in the epidermis and subepidermal pustular dermatosis. Chest radiography and skeletal surveys were normal.

A 42-year-old man with no significant medical history was evaluated for abdominal pain and mild elevations in liver enzymes. Initial ultrasonography revealed multiple hypoechoic lesions in the liver. CT of the abdomen showed multiple low-attenuation areas within the hepatic parenchyma. Following CT-guided liver biopsy, the patient’s hemoglobin dropped from 14 to 10.2 g/dL, and he received packed red-cell transfusions. He was transferred for further management.

On arrival, he complained of right upper quadrant discomfort without nausea, vomiting, fever, or chills. Vital signs: blood pressure 80/30 mm Hg, pulse 110 beats/min; respiratory and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable. The abdomen was soft, with tenderness in the right upper quadrant but no guarding or rigidity.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL (13–18)  
• Hematocrit 28% (40–53)  
• Platelets 139 × 10^9/L (150–400)  
• AST 30 IU/L (5–30), ALT 19 IU/L (5–30)  
• GGT 153 U/L (6–50), ALP 195 U/L (50–100)  
• Total bilirubin 5 mg/dL, ammonia 60 µg/dL  
• PT 12.5 s (11–14), INR 1.14, aPTT 44.3 s (20–40), fibrinogen 420 mg/dL (180–400)

He was managed conservatively in the ICU with stable hemoglobin and no further transfusions. After transfer to the surgical ward, contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a heterogeneous 10.6 × 11.4 cm mass in hepatic segments VI and VII, with high-density fluid in the right paracolic gutter suggestive of hemoperitoneum. MRI of the liver showed innumerable T2-hyperintense nodules throughout the liver with delayed enhancement and a large T2-hyperintense lesion in segments VI and VII containing multiple smaller lesions with delayed enhancement.

A 27-year-old gravida 1 woman underwent a routine second‐trimester obstetrical ultrasound at 24 weeks of gestation. Her first‐trimester scan at 6 weeks and all routine antenatal laboratory tests, including a normal fetal karyotype, were unremarkable, and there was no family or personal history of genetic or congenital disorders.

Ultrasound findings were as follows:
• Midsagittal view of the chest demonstrated dilatation of the trachea and main bronchi distal to an obstructive level.  
• Sectional imaging of the thorax showed bilaterally enlarged, uniformly hyperechoic lungs.  
• Parasagittal imaging of the thoracoabdominal region revealed inversion of the diaphragm.  
• A moderate volume of fetal ascites was also present.

A 21-year-old woman presented with 12 hours of sudden-onset right lower quadrant abdominal pain and nausea. On examination, she had tenderness in the right lower quadrant without rebound or guarding and no focal point tenderness at McBurney’s point or the umbilicus. Laboratory tests were notable only for a mild leukocytosis. Pelvic and abdominal ultrasound showed a 3 cm right ovarian cyst with low-level internal echoes, suggestive of an endometrioma, but was otherwise unremarkable. 

Because of persistent pain, a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained. An axial image demonstrated mesenteric fat telescoping into a bowel segment in the right lower quadrant, with the specific structures involved not clearly identified. Diagnostic laparoscopy was then performed and was unrevealing. The patient’s symptoms improved, and she was discharged.

Over the next month, she had further episodes of acute abdominal pain and underwent outpatient CT enterography. Coronal and axial images revealed a tubular structure within the cecum; the small-bowel loops appeared normal. The structure was dilated, with mural thickening and hyperenhancement. No distinct “lead point” was identified on CT.

A 54-year-old man is evaluated for worsening low back pain and bilateral lower‐extremity symptoms.  

History of Present Illness  
• Eight years earlier, he had low back pain, bilateral leg numbness, and intermittent claudication to 10 m. Conservative measures failed and he underwent L4–L5 decompression and fusion with symptom relief.  
• Seven months ago, he developed insidious low back pain with bilateral leg pain and fatigue; intermittent claudication now limited to ~50 m requiring a walking stick; saddle numbness and urinary and fecal dysfunction without clear triggers.  

Past Medical History  
• Lumbar spine surgery 8 years ago; otherwise unremarkable.  

Physical Examination (second admission)  
• Sensation: numbness bilaterally below the groin.  
• Motor: Iliopsoas, quadriceps, and tibialis anterior muscles 4/5 bilaterally; extensor hallucis longus and gastrocnemius 3/5 bilaterally.  
• Reflexes: Knee and Achilles reflexes reduced; negative straight‐leg–raise and no pathological reflexes.  

Laboratory Studies  
• No laboratory abnormalities reported.  

Imaging Studies  
• CT (sagittal and axial): forward displacement of the L4 vertebral body post-fusion; lumbar degenerative changes with multilevel disc herniations at L2–S1.  
• MRI T2‐weighted (sagittal and axial): forward displacement and irregular margins of L4; multilevel intervertebral disc protrusions; high T2 signal within the spinal cord extending over multiple segments.

An 18-year-old Caucasian male collapsed during football practice with full‐body convulsions, breathlessness, and gasping. Emergency medical services found him in ventricular fibrillation and delivered a single 200 J biphasic shock, restoring sinus rhythm, circulation, and consciousness. He remained agitated, and telemetry showed recurrent ventricular tachycardia at 180 bpm; blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg, oxygen saturation 92%, and respiratory rate 20 bpm. He was intubated and transferred to the hospital.

After 24 hours, he was extubated without neurologic deficits. He was previously healthy, took no medications, and had no family history of cardiovascular disease. Initial laboratory studies were unremarkable except for a high‐sensitivity troponin I concentration of 230 ng/L (normal, 0–53.5). Qualitative toxicology was positive for plasma kratom and caffeine, with a mitragynine level of 98 ng/mL. The patient confirmed that he consumed 250 mL of an energy drink with 2 g of kratom powder just before practice.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left and right ventricular size and function with no valvular abnormalities. Coronary computed tomography angiography revealed normal coronary arteries with no atherosclerosis or anomalies. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging did not detect any structural cardiac involvement.

A 34-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus for 1 year, managed with metformin and gliclazide, presented with 3 months of unintentional 26 kg weight loss and bilateral burning thigh pain (VAS 5–6) worse at night, preceded by 5 months of anorexia and fatigue. Despite the pain, she could still ambulate slowly but was unable to work or perform household chores. She denied weakness, numbness, fever, or trauma. Screening for respiratory, gastrointestinal, hyperthyroid, and connective tissue disease, as well as depression, an eating disorder, and psychosocial stressors, was negative. Her HbA1c at presentation was 6.9%; there was no retinopathy or nephropathy.

On examination, she appeared cachectic (BMI 15.5) with marked subcutaneous fat loss and muscle atrophy. Random blood glucose was 7.0 mmol/L. Both quadriceps were tender without signs of inflammation. Neurologic exam showed lower-limb muscle wasting, hypotonia, hyporeflexia at knees and ankles, and grade 4/5 power in both quadriceps (other lower-limb muscles 5/5); sensation was intact. Basic hematology, biochemistry, autoimmune screening, inflammatory markers, serum CK, thyroid tests, tuberculosis workup, chest and femoral radiographs, and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Repeat HbA1c was 6.2% and fasting glucose 5.0 mmol/L, so antidiabetic agents were withheld. She was admitted for further evaluation.

Nerve conduction studies demonstrated mild slowing of motor and sensory conduction velocities, mildly reduced peroneal CMAP amplitudes, and mild conduction block in both peroneal nerves, interpreted as possible mild or early patchy demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy, probably CIDP. She declined CSF examination, and although the NCS features did not fulfil diagnostic criteria, she was treated as having CIDP.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of arm and leg cramps, fatigue, and carpal spasms, with similar intermittent episodes over the past 2 years. She denied diuretic or laxative use, vomiting, diarrhea, polyuria, or polydipsia. There was no family history of similar symptoms. On examination, her blood pressure was 98/66 mm Hg without orthostatic changes; she appeared euvolemic. Chvostek’s sign and Trousseau’s sign were both positive. Laboratory tests showed hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypokalemia. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed pH 7.51 (7.35–7.45), bicarbonate 33.5 mmol/L (22–30), PCO2 42 mm Hg (32–45), and chloride 86 mEq/L (102–109). Complete blood count, fasting glucose, creatinine, liver function tests, thyroid profile, rheumatoid factor, and antinuclear antibodies were normal. Renal ultrasonography showed no nephrocalcinosis. Urinalysis demonstrated a pH of 6.7 and a specific gravity of 1.018. Genetic studies were not available.

A 33-year-old gravida 1 woman conceived with letrozole ovulation induction and intrauterine insemination. Her medical history was notable for migraines; she had undergone laparoscopic right salpingo-oophorectomy and appendectomy for chronic right-sided pelvic pain. 

At 5 weeks 2 days’ gestation, transvaginal ultrasound showed three gestational sacs, only two of which contained yolk sacs. At 6 weeks 2 days, ultrasound confirmed a viable dichorionic twin pregnancy with two gestational sacs, two yolk sacs, and two fetal poles. 

At 9 weeks 2 days, she experienced vaginal bleeding and again 4 days later. In both emergency evaluations, ultrasound confirmed a viable twin pregnancy with a normal dividing membrane and no subchorionic hemorrhage; no intertwin hemorrhage was seen. She continued to have intermittent bleeding but remained hemodynamically stable. 

At 11 weeks, her vaginal bleeding had ceased; she denied contractions, cramping, and discharge. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a 15.0 mm thickness of the intertwin dividing membrane, consistent with an intertwin membrane hemorrhage. Baby aspirin was held, and she was counseled on bleeding and preterm labor precautions.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a tumor of her lower left ankle and reported hypesthesia of the second through fourth digits of her left foot, along with episodes of lower back pain. On examination, decreased sensation was confirmed in digits two to four of the left foot. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine revealed a long-segment, intraspinal, extradural soft-tissue mass in the left L4–S1 paravertebral region. The lesion showed homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration, compressed the L4 and L5 nerve roots, and caused destruction of the fifth lumbar vertebral body. A neurinoma was diagnosed. Further MRI of the left ankle showed a space-occupying lesion with similar homogeneous contrast enhancement. In addition, there was a cutaneous lesion suspicious for a neurofibroma. A systemic disorder such as neurofibromatosis was considered.

A 30-year-old Ethiopian gravida 3, para 2 woman at 40 weeks + 1 day of gestation presented with 12 hours of labor pains and grade-2 meconium-stained amniotic fluid. She denied dyspnea, cough, headache, or visual changes, and her past medical and family history was unremarkable. On admission, her blood pressure was 140/85 mmHg, heart rate 88–92 beats/min, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. A preeclampsia work-up showed a hematocrit of 42%, normal liver enzymes, and negative urine protein. In the second stage, cesarean section was performed for fetal bradycardia, delivering a 3200 g male infant with Apgar scores of 7 and 8. Postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony and incision extension was managed medically and surgically, and she received two units of blood. Four hours postpartum, she developed dyspnea with oxygen saturation 85% on room air, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, heart rate 115 beats/min, and bilateral basal crackles. A diagnosis of pulmonary edema, presumed secondary to preeclampsia, was treated with 80 mg of IV furosemide, resulting in rapid improvement and discontinuation of oxygen the next day. Five days later, she acutely developed severe dyspnea and hypoxia (oxygen saturation 70% on room air), and pulmonary thromboembolism was suspected. While awaiting CT imaging and empirical anticoagulation, she progressed to respiratory failure despite 15 L of 100% oxygen via face mask. Laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 26% and a WBC count of 14 400/mm³; liver and renal function were normal. She was admitted to the ICU and intubated. Given the clinical course, heart failure was also considered, and 40 mg of IV furosemide was administered with adequate diuresis (hematocrit 26.3%). Bedside chest ultrasound revealed bilateral pleural effusions with unremarkable fluid analysis.

A 32-year-old woman with a 17-year history of ovarian dysfunction treated cyclically with conjugated estrogens and medroxyprogesterone presented after a 3-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure. For 3 months she had experienced photophobia and nausea, and she had episodic focal seizures every 3 months over the preceding 3 years, managed as an outpatient with levetiracetam 1000 mg/day. Her blood pressure on presentation was 124/77 mmHg, and routine laboratory tests were normal. 

Head CT on day 1 revealed a low-density area in the left occipital lobe. MRI showed a corresponding high-intensity area on diffusion-weighted and T2-weighted images and increased cerebral blood flow in the same region on arterial spin labeling. She was treated with nicardipine (target systolic pressure ≈110 mmHg), levetiracetam increased to 3000 mg/day, and edaravone 60 mg/day. 

By day 12 she developed motor aphasia and apraxia. T2-weighted imaging demonstrated enlargement of the left parieto-occipital high-intensity area and further increased perfusion on arterial spin labeling. Glycerol and magnesium sulfate were administered. 

On day 26 her aphasia and apraxia worsened, prompting addition of perampanel and a course of steroid pulses. By day 29 CT and MRI showed further spread of the T2 hyperintensity from the left parieto-occipital region into the temporal lobe, with persistent hyperperfusion on arterial spin labeling. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI showed no contrast enhancement.

A male infant was born at 37 +4 weeks’ gestation to a 37-year-old woman after an otherwise uneventful pregnancy, during which the mother was diagnosed with granulomatous mastitis. Maternal rheumatologic studies, including ANA, anti–CCP, RF, and other autoantibodies, were normal.  
At birth, his weight was 2810 g, length 48 cm, and head circumference 33.5 cm; Apgar scores were 8 and 10. On routine examination, he had generalized, persistent net-like, marbled erythema that blanched under pressure; no asymmetry or other anomalies were noted.  
Initial laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 6.12×10^3/μL, hemoglobin of 17.1 g/dL, platelet count of 213×10^3/μL, normal coagulation parameters, and normal thyroid function. Evaluation for neonatal lupus (ANA, anti–SS-A, anti–SS-B, anti–dsDNA) was negative.  
At 3 months of age, he was admitted with poor feeding, lethargy, and a fever of 38°C. Vital signs included a pulse of 120/min, respiratory rate of 40/min, and blood pressure of 85/40 mm Hg. The purple, mottled skin pattern was more pronounced with fever. Growth parameters remained at the 50th–75th percentiles.  
He underwent a sepsis workup, including blood cultures, lumbar puncture, abdominal and brain ultrasound, and echocardiography, all of which were unremarkable. He was also referred to a pediatric rheumatologist to investigate vasculitis and neonatal lupus; rheumatologic tests were inconclusive.

A 54-year-old woman presented with what was described as a common toothache. She had recently undergone a neurological examination with brain MRI and was referred for evaluation of a possible dentally originating lesion. On intraoral examination, there was a palpable, fluctuant swelling in the upper labial sulcus beneath the right nasolabial fold. Orthopantomography and occlusal radiographs showed no bony changes, and electrical pulp testing demonstrated vitality of all associated teeth. Ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, ovoid, approximately 2-cm anechoic cystic lesion in the nasolabial sulcus. MRI of the face demonstrated a well-defined, round mass in the right nasal alar region that was homogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images and homogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images.

A 52-year-old African American woman with untreated HIV infection (CD4 396 cells/μL) and a history of discoid lupus, hepatitis C, active tobacco, alcohol, and intravenous drug use presented with three months of progressive abdominal pain, distension, and fever. She had not been hospitalized or on antiretroviral therapy, and denied sick contacts. On examination, her temperature was 39.6 °C; she had a distended abdomen with right costo-vertebral angle tenderness and track marks on the right lower extremity. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 9240/μL (71% neutrophils), hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, albumin 1.9 g/dL; chemistry, amylase, and lipase were normal. Urinalysis revealed 5–10 RBCs/hpf without WBCs; pregnancy test was negative. A urine drug screen was positive for cocaine and opiates.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 17.5 cm × 12.8 cm multicystic mass arising from the right kidney, containing multiple septations but no evidence of local invasion.

A 13-year-old girl was evaluated for intermittent fevers (up to 39°C) of one month’s duration, night sweats, weight loss, and no pruritus. On examination she appeared pale and had a faint rash over her upper body. Hemoglobin was 10.4 g/dL; white-cell count, 8.2×10^9/L; platelet count, 511×10^9/L; lactate dehydrogenase, 582 U/L; C-reactive protein, 5 mg/dL. A chest radiograph showed right-sided mediastinal enlargement and left parahilar bulging. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT scan revealed a bulky conglomerate of lymph nodes involving all mediastinal compartments, extending to the left hilum and displacing mediastinal vessels without invasion. Abdominal CT showed an increased number of normal-sized lymph nodes at the mesenteric root. Serologic tests for cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, toxoplasmosis, aspergillosis, histoplasmosis, brucellosis, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, rickettsiosis, and paracoccidioidomycosis were negative. Three sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative, but a tuberculin skin test had 15 mm of induration at 72 hours. PET scan demonstrated multiple areas of intense 18F-FDG uptake (SUV, 5.6–6.3) in coalescent right anterior and posterior mediastinal lymph nodes and left peribronchial nodes, findings reported as highly suspicious for neoplastic disease.

A 50-year-old man with longstanding schizophrenia was transferred for evaluation of persistent postprandial fatigue. He had been treated with clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, with the dose increased to 500 mg daily over 4 months. In January, he reported marked fatigue after meals, and a postprandial finger‐stick blood glucose measurement was approximately 40 mg/dL. Despite the addition of 20 g of glucose to each meal, postprandial levels remained low. On transfer, his BMI was 26.5, and vital signs and neurologic examination were normal. Current medications included clozapine 500 mg daily, metoclopramide, and lemborexant. Laboratory testing showed a blood glucose level of 165 mg/dL, insulin 54.3 μU/mL, and C-peptide 7.9 ng/mL. Insulin antibodies were negative, and levels of growth hormone, somatomedin C, and cortisol were within normal limits. Abdominal imaging studies showed no mass lesions. A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test demonstrated a rise in blood glucose from 104 mg/dL to 289 mg/dL at 60 minutes, followed by a decline to 52 mg/dL at 120 minutes; insulin levels peaked above 309 μU/mL at 60 minutes.

A 26‐year‐old woman from Huancayo in the Peruvian Highlands, with lifelong close contact with dogs known to consume animal entrails, presented with intermittent thoracic spine pain rated 8–9/10, lasting up to 1½ hours, over the prior two months. She denied fever, cough, night sweats, hemoptysis, or fatigue but reported a 5-lb unintentional weight loss and decreased appetite during that time. On routine chest radiography, a right middle lobe (RML) lesion was seen. Chest CT revealed a 4.5 cm × 3.7 cm low‐attenuation, pleural‐based lobulated mass in the right lateral lung field. CT‐guided percutaneous aspiration yielded 20 mL of clear fluid without immediate complication, apart from a small pleural effusion. Five hours later, she developed pleuritic chest pain at the biopsy site, weakness, near‐syncope, and dizziness. Vital signs: T 98.8 °F, HR 76, RR 18, orthostatic BP 90/51 → 106/51 mm Hg, SpO₂ 97% on room air. Examination showed decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the RML, with egophony at the right base; a grade III/VI systolic ejection murmur was heard at the pulmonic area; no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi. Laboratory tests: WBC 11.5 × 10^3/µL. Post‐biopsy chest X-ray showed an ill‐defined RML opacity with a small pleural effusion. Repeat CT chest showed a 3.5 cm × 3.2 cm septated, air‐filled juxta‐pleural RML lesion with new small right pleural effusion and no pneumothorax; fluid density made blood unlikely. Pleural fluid analysis: pale red, exudative (protein 4.4 g/dL; LDH 255 U/L), 5,500 WBCs (18% eosinophils), 2,280 RBCs; cytopathology: “No WBCs, malignant cells, fungus or organisms.” Echinococcal antibody EIA was  <0.80 (negative); pleural fluid AFB stain was negative.

A 29-year-old man with a history of asthma, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and stage IIIa chronic kidney disease was found unresponsive at home. He received intranasal naloxone, after which he had witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity. On arrival to the emergency department, his pupils were pinpoint. Laboratory studies revealed a troponin level of 837 ng/L (reference 0–22 ng/L), arterial blood gas with pH 7.15 (7.32–7.43) and pCO2 85 mmHg (41–54 mmHg), lactate 5.3 mmol/L (0.6–1.4 mmol/L), and a urine toxicology screen positive for opiates. Initial noncontrast head CT demonstrated ill-defined hypodensities in the subcortical white matter, bilateral basal ganglia, and cerebellar hemispheres. A repeat CT 12 hours later showed diffuse cerebral edema with partial effacement of the fourth ventricle and basilar cisterns, as well as mild tonsillar and uncal herniation. Brain MRI revealed restricted diffusion involving the cerebral white matter, caudate nuclei, internal capsules, lentiform nuclei, hippocampi, vermis, and cerebellar hemispheres, with relative sparing of the subcortical U-fibers. Gradient-echo sequences showed petechial hemorrhages within the basal ganglia and cerebellum. MR angiography was normal. The patient was admitted to the ICU for supportive care.

A 63‐year‐old man presented with progressive dyspnea, fatigue, and decreased exercise tolerance over several months. Four years earlier, he had undergone orthotopic heart transplantation with an uneventful postoperative course. He denied chest pain, palpitations, or syncope. Recent coronary angiography showed no graft vasculopathy and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. He had never experienced cellular or humoral rejection.

Resting ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm at 87 beats/min without abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal ventricular sizes and systolic function with biatrial enlargement. Pharmacological stress cardiac MRI excluded ischemia but incidentally revealed a foreign body in the epicardial adipose tissue. A noncontrast chest CT confirmed a tubular epicardial structure, identified as a retained inflow pump connection of a left ventricular assist device left in situ at transplantation.

On examination, cardiac auscultation disclosed a pericardial friction rub at the left sternal border. Pulmonary exam showed bilateral basal crackles and left‐sided dullness to percussion with decreased breath sounds. Jugular venous pressure was elevated on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign). There was pitting edema of the legs and a distended abdomen. Repeat echocardiography showed pericardial thickening (≥ 3 mm), a septal “bounce” with interventricular dependence, paradoxical diastolic ventricular filling with respiration, and a dilated inferior vena cava with diminished respiratory variation.

A 59-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of a persistent dry cough of one year’s duration. He first noted upper airway irritation and cough after drinking homemade wine; the cough persisted throughout the day without sputum production, dyspnea, chest pain, fevers, or weight loss. His medical history included hyperlipidemia and prostatitis; he was a former smoker (5 pack-years, quit 30 years ago). Physical examination was unremarkable.

Two-view chest radiography was normal. Pulmonary function tests showed a forced vital capacity of 3.65 L (76% predicted), FEV1 of 3.16 L (86% predicted), FEV1/FVC of 0.86, total lung capacity 5.81 L (87% predicted), residual volume 2.16 L (92% predicted), and diffusion capacity 89% predicted. Methacholine challenge was negative. Chest CT showed only small nonspecific mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes and minimal lingular atelectasis.

In November and December 2015, two sputum cultures grew Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Specific antibody testing demonstrated elevated S. cerevisiae IgA of 22.2 U (normal <20 U) and IgG of 48.8 U (normal <20 U, positive >35 U). Tests for other fungal antibodies were negative. He received a 30-day prednisone taper (starting 60 mg daily) and a bronchodilator with near resolution of cough that recurred after stopping steroids. Antihistamines and a proton-pump inhibitor yielded no improvement. Repeat chest CT in May 2016 was unchanged.

Bronchoscopy with BAL in May 2016 showed a tiny polypoid lesion; cultures and cytology of BAL were negative, and no cell count was obtained. In June 2016, S. cerevisiae IgA and IgG remained elevated; total IgE was normal at 5.9 kU/L, and peripheral eosinophils were 0.9%. In September 2016, repeat bronchoscopy revealed diffuse airway erythema and the same polypoid lesion. Biopsies showed acute and chronic inflammation without eosinophils; PAS stain was negative. BAL cell differential showed 32% lymphocytes and 68% macrophages; cultures and stains for bacteria, mycobacteria, Pneumocystis jirovecii, and fungus were negative.

A 21-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of her right maxillary lateral incisor. She had undergone root canal treatment of that tooth 5 years earlier and had recently undergone post preparation during which her dentist noted a perforation. Her medical history was noncontributory. 

On examination, the tooth was tender to percussion and palpation, and there was slight intraoral swelling adjacent to the gingival margin. 

A periapical radiograph showed enlargement of the root canal at the middle third, consistent with post preparation adjacent to the existing obturation material, and revealed a large, well-defined periapical radiolucency with a corticalized margin. 

Cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a 1.3 × 1.5 × 1.3 cm periapical lesion that had eroded both the buccal and palatal cortical plates and confirmed a root perforation extending from the middle third toward the apical third of the root.

The preoperative working diagnosis was a previously treated tooth with symptomatic apical periodontitis, and acute apical abscess was also considered. Surgical retreatment, including sealing of the perforation, was planned with the patient’s consent.

A 35-year-old woman (gravida 2, para 1, abortion 1) underwent dilation and curettage at 9 weeks’ gestation for a missed abortion two weeks earlier. One week later, she returned for repeat D/C because of a suspected hematoma, but the procedure was halted due to hemorrhage. On admission to our hospital, her hemoglobin was 11.2 g/dL, hematocrit 35.1%, and β-hCG 3518 mIU/mL. There was no active vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a 60 × 60 × 56 mm hyperechogenic, heterogeneous mass in the anterior uterine wall extending to the left, with minimal fluid in the endometrial cavity and normal adnexa. Color Doppler imaging demonstrated prominent venous vascular signals within the lesion.

A 43-year-old woman presented with acute intestinal obstruction and hemodynamic instability. She had a lifelong history of severe chronic constipation and recurrent episodes of functional bowel obstruction. In 2007, she underwent a subtotal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis for presumed colonic inertia; histologic examination of the colon was normal, but her obstructive symptoms persisted. In 2012, she had a small-bowel volvulus treated by surgical detorsion without noted cause. Superficial ileal and rectal biopsies at that time showed only nonspecific inflammation.

On current admission, she was tachycardic (148 beats/min), hypotensive (systolic 75 mmHg), and had marbled lower limbs; temperature was 37.9 °C. Abdominal CT revealed marked hydroaeric distention and pneumatosis of the small-bowel loops. Emergent laparotomy disclosed an ileal volvulus on a markedly dilated small intestine and a mesentery that was long and detached from the posterior abdominal wall, suggesting an incomplete common mesentery; no adhesions were seen. The volvulus was detorsed without resection.

Postoperatively, the patient had persistent abdominal pain, distention, and no return of bowel function; repeat CT confirmed recurrent small-bowel dilation. On day 13, she underwent re-exploration: again, no adhesions were found, and there was marked dilation proximal to the ileorectal anastomosis. The anastomosis appeared widely patent on palpation. A lateral ileostomy was performed, after which bowel function promptly returned and her condition improved.

A 25-year-old Somalian primigravida at 33 weeks’ gestation presented with 16 hours of acute-onset abdominal pain and distension, four episodes of nonprojectile vomiting, and lightheadedness. She denied trauma or significant medical history. On admission, blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg, pulse 110/min, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 36.5°C, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, and Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Abdominal examination revealed marked distension with direct and rebound tenderness and no detectable fetal heartbeat.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 30 900/µL with 80% granulocytes, platelet count 351 000/µL, normal liver and renal function tests, and urinalysis with +2 ketones and +1 protein. After initial resuscitation with two liters of intravenous normal saline, an obstetric ultrasound demonstrated a nonviable singleton fetus at 33 weeks (estimated weight 2200 g) and substantial free fluid with echogenic debris in the peritoneal cavity (cul-de-sac, paracolic gutters, and hepatorenal recess); solid organs and bowel loops appeared unremarkable. 

Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT revealed large-volume intraperitoneal fluid (average density 33 HU), uninterrupted uterine wall enhancement, a well-formed nonenhancing fetus, a laterally located placenta with contrast blush, and no abnormalities of the solid abdominal organs or bowel wall.

A 63-year-old Japanese man presented with a 2-month history of progressive fatigue and a 5-kg weight loss. His past medical history included cerebral infarction, aortic stenosis, carotid stenosis, overactive bladder, and hyperlipidemia, all well controlled on lansoprazole, carvedilol, mirabegron, and cilostazol. He smoked 14 cigarettes daily until age 45 and drank alcohol daily.  

On examination he appeared pale without rash or lymphadenopathy. Temperature was 37.5 °C, blood pressure 92/59 mmHg, heart rate 78 bpm. Cardiopulmonary exam was normal, with no rales or abnormal heart sounds; no clubbing or edema.  

Laboratory studies showed:  
- Hematology: leukocytes 1 530/µL, hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, platelets 75 000/µL  
- Chemistry: albumin 2.8 g/dL, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, AST 65 IU/L, ALT 57 IU/L, ALP 1673 IU/L, GGT 106 IU/L, LDH 517 IU/L, CRP 1.97 mg/dL  
- Sarcoid markers: ACE 34.1 U/L (8.3–21.4), lysozyme 29.8 µg/mL (5–10.2), soluble IL-2 receptor 7835 U/mL (145–519)  
- Serologies: ANA negative, ANCA negative, RF negative, interferon-γ release assay negative, viral hepatitis serologies negative, beta-glucan 0.8 pg/mL  

Chest radiograph and CT showed no lung or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Abdominal CT demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly and bilateral renal enlargement.  

A bone marrow biopsy revealed numerous non-caseating epithelioid granulomas within hematopoietic tissue.

A 44-year-old woman (weight 103 kg; BMI 41.8) with hypothyroidism, borderline type II diabetes mellitus, gastroesophageal reflux disease, hypertriglyceridemia, and prior vertical banded gastroplasty 10 years earlier (initial weight 140 kg, nadir 80 kg) underwent laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. She was discharged uneventfully. On postoperative day 5, she reported epigastric discomfort and underwent an abdominal CT scan, which was reported as normal by the radiologist. On day 10, she presented with sudden massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding. In the emergency department she was hemodynamically stable (hemoglobin, 12 g/dL) and was intubated for endoscopy to prevent aspiration. A review of the CT images noted that the remnant stomach was fluid-filled. During endoscopy, a large clot was seen in the gastric pouch, but no bleeding source was identified; two clips were placed on a suspicious area, and hemostasis was managed endoscopically. She received 2 L of normal saline and was admitted to the ICU. Four hours later, she had recurrent oral bleeding, hypotension (blood pressure 80 mm Hg systolic, pulse 125 beats/min), abdominal distention with dull percussion, and a nasogastric tube returned 500 mL of bright blood. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.5 g/dL, white blood cells 1.5 × 10^9/L, platelets 180 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 46 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 20 mm/h, and normal PT, PTT, and INR. Given ongoing hemorrhagic shock, surgical exploration was undertaken.

A 42-year-old woman was evaluated for right-sided maxillary pain and purulent nasal drainage. She reported that the pain began 2 years earlier and intensified over the past 2 months, accompanied by foul-smelling pus. Twenty-three years ago she had multiple dental extractions in the same area that were complicated by an untreated maxillary sinus issue. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, gastric ulcers, dizziness, and fainting, all well controlled with medication. On extraoral examination, there were no abnormalities. Intraorally, her maxilla was edentulous, and there was a fistula in the right molar region with purulent foul-smelling drainage; palpation elicited pain despite no denture use. A panoramic radiograph showed a homogeneous, slightly circular radiopaque mass about 2.0 × 2.5 cm in the right maxillary sinus with ill-defined borders and disruption of the lower cortical layer.  
The initial clinical–radiographic differential diagnosis included inflammatory or infectious processes (such as chronic sinusitis from an oroantral perforation), fungus balls (mycetoma or aspergillosis), a retained foreign body, or large antroliths; less likely considerations were cementoblastoma, complex odontoma, calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumors, fibrous dysplasia, calcifying cystic odontogenic tumors, and osteosarcoma.  
Surgical exploration was performed.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of holocranial, throbbing headache that was nearly continuous and worsened with coughing, disturbing his sleep. Over the preceding month, he noted progressive unsteadiness of gait without falls, and during the week before presentation he had recurrent vomiting. He denied visual obscurations or diplopia and had no upper-limb incoordination. He had a remote history of childhood febrile seizures without recurrence and no other medical history of note.

On examination, he was afebrile. Fundoscopic evaluation revealed early papilledema. Extraocular movements were full. Coordination testing showed bilateral finger–nose and heel–knee incoordination with dysdiadochokinesia. His gait was spastic–ataxic. Strength, sensation, and reflexes were otherwise normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver and renal function tests, serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, chest radiography, and abdominal ultrasound, were all within normal limits. HIV-1 and HIV-2 serological tests were negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated multiple bilateral cerebral cystic lesions and a large right cerebellar cyst exerting mass effect on the fourth ventricle and brainstem. Diffuse T2-weighted hyperintense lesions were present in the subcortical and cerebellar white matter. The cystic lesions showed contrast enhancement without evidence of hemorrhage.

Lumbar puncture yielded slightly xanthochromic cerebrospinal fluid containing 26 leukocytes (45% polymorphonuclear, 55% lymphocytes), protein of 106 mg/dL, and glucose of 149 mg/dL. CSF cryptococcal antigen was negative.

A 94-year-old man with hypertension and bullous pemphigoid presented with a new, intensely pruritic papule at the site of his first mRNA-1723 (Moderna) COVID-19 vaccination, received 2 days earlier. An adhesive bandage had been applied over the injection site and remained in place for 24 hours. Two days after vaccination, severe pruritus prompted vigorous scratching. On examination, there was a 5-mm erythematous papule overlying the right deltoid. The initial differential diagnosis included a lesion of bullous pemphigoid, bullous impetigo, and allergic or irritant contact dermatitis to the adhesive bandage. A 4-mm punch biopsy was performed. Histopathologic examination revealed suppurative and granulomatous dermatitis surrounding a neutrophilic microabscess in the reticular dermis. Within the infiltrate and inside multinucleated giant cells, thick-walled, nonseptate, bifurcated hyphae were identified. Periodic acid–Schiff stain confirmed the presence of fungal hyphae.

A 76-year-old man with a history of distal gastrectomy with D1+ lymphadenectomy and Billroth-I reconstruction for early gastric cancer 13 years earlier underwent surveillance endoscopy, which revealed an ulcerative lesion on the lesser curvature of the remnant stomach. Biopsy showed well-differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma. Hematologic studies, including carcinoembryonic antigen, α-fetoprotein, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and carbohydrate antigen 125, were within normal limits; total protein was slightly low at 6.5 g/dL. An upper gastrointestinal series demonstrated a 12-mm type 0-IIc lesion confined to the mucosa. Endoscopy confirmed an 18-mm type 0-IIc mucosal lesion. Abdominal contrast-enhanced CT revealed a slightly enhanced 13 × 10 mm nodule near the lesser curvature of the remnant stomach. Endoscopic ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion without vascular flow and a slightly indistinct margin. Endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the nodule yielded no cancer cells. The gastric lesion was removed by endoscopic submucosal dissection, and pathology showed submucosal invasion (625 μm), ulceration, and negative margins. Three months later, repeat contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated enlargement of the perigastric nodule to 16 × 12 mm.

A 6-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of intensely pruritic pustular lesions on the trunk and extremities. One month earlier, he had been diagnosed with generalized pustular psoriasis and treated with oral corticosteroids and topical calcipotriol without improvement. He denied fever or constitutional symptoms. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and there was no family history of dermatologic or rheumatologic disease. On examination, there were multiple scaly pustular eruptions forming annular or serpiginous patterns distributed across the face, neck, trunk, and extremities; the palms, soles, and mucous membranes were spared. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, normal serum biochemistry, and normal serum protein electrophoresis.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of nonbilious vomiting and features of gastric outlet obstruction. He had undergone excision of a type I choledochal cyst with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy at 4 months of age. Preoperative MRCP at that time showed pancreaticobiliary malunion, a type I choledochal cyst, and a dilated pancreatic duct suggestive of chronic pancreatitis; no annular pancreas or pancreatic rests were noted. On examination, the abdomen was soft, with epigastric fullness and visible reverse gastric peristalsis. An upper gastrointestinal contrast study demonstrated near-total obstruction of the first part of the duodenum. Upper endoscopy revealed a large polypoidal mass completely obliterating the lumen of the first duodenal segment, and the endoscope could not be passed beyond this point.

A 58-year-old postmenopausal, lifelong nonsmoking woman was evaluated for a 13-month history of dry cough that caused gagging and occasional emesis. She reported frequent nocturnal awakenings. Past medical history included hyperlipidemia and obstructive sleep apnea. She denied rhinorrhea, sneezing, wheezing, dyspnea, postnasal drip, heartburn, chest pain, fever, sputum production, hemoptysis, weight loss, or night sweats. There was no history of ACE-inhibitor use. She worked handling Christmas trees and had a dog at home. She had no history of asthma, sinusitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, allergies, or tuberculosis.
