Physical examination revealed normal vital signs, a perforated right tympanic membrane, clear oropharynx, normal nasal mucosa, and no polyps. Lung auscultation was unremarkable with no wheezes or crackles. Cardiac exam was normal. There was no clubbing, cyanosis, rash, or peripheral edema.

Spirometry showed FEV₁ 112% of predicted, FVC 111% of predicted, FEV₁/FVC 81%, and normal flow–volume loops. DLCO was 97% of predicted. A methacholine challenge test demonstrated a PC₂₀ >16 mg/dL. Chest CT showed no infiltrates, effusions, or lymphadenopathy. Sinus CT was normal. A 24-hour esophageal pH probe on proton-pump inhibitor therapy was negative for reflux. CBC showed WBC 9.2×10⁹/L with 1% eosinophils. Electrolytes and renal function were normal. Serologies for Bordetella pertussis and RSV were negative. Exhaled nitric oxide was elevated at 158 ppb (normal <30 ppb). Flexible bronchoscopy with biopsy of the left main bronchus revealed peribronchiolar chronic inflammation with eosinophils and thickened basement membrane. Sputum eosinophils were not assessed.

A 40-year-old woman presented with gradual vision loss in both eyes over 2 years. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/400 in each eye. Medical and medication histories were unremarkable, and she had no history of hypertension, diabetes, hematologic abnormalities, or other systemic disease. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable. 
Color fundus photography showed loss of the normal foveal reflex with macular edema bilaterally and hard exudates in the inferotemporal retina of the right eye. Early- and late-phase fluorescein angiography demonstrated perifoveal telangiectasia and microaneurysms predominantly in the superior and nasal macula of both eyes, with late staining and leakage. Blue-wavelength autofluorescence revealed hyperautofluorescent areas corresponding to cystoid macular edema in both eyes. 
Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography revealed significant intraretinal fluid in both eyes and subretinal fluid in the left eye, with central macular thicknesses of 721 µm (right) and 673 µm (left). Optical coherence tomography angiography showed saccular parafoveal capillary telangiectasia, capillary dropout, and decreased vascular density in both superficial and deep capillary plexuses; deep plexus involvement exceeded superficial plexus, and both crossed the horizontal meridian in each eye.

A previously healthy 3-year-old girl was brought in with a 5-day history of fever (up to 40.5 °C), anorexia, and weakness. She had no cough, vomiting, diarrhea, myalgias, or altered consciousness. She had played in grass near her grandmother’s house during a festival in Lu’an City, Anhui Province—an area known for tick-borne illness—and her grandfather had died of a tick-borne hemorrhagic fever in 2017. Initial treatment with acetaminophen and oseltamivir at a community hospital failed to resolve her fever.

On admission (July 5), temperature was 39.4 °C, pulse 100 bpm, respiratory rate 14/min, and blood pressure 110/90 mmHg. Examination revealed petechiae and ecchymoses on the trunk; neurologic exam was normal.

Laboratory studies showed leukopenia (1.91 × 10^9/L), thrombocytopenia (78 × 10^9/L), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (1620 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase (81 U/L), and alkaline phosphatase (160 U/L). Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. Chest CT demonstrated increased lung markings. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia. Empiric cefoperazone–sulbactam and ganciclovir were initiated.

A 42-year-old white man was transferred for evaluation of a 6-month history of worsening headache and new-onset left facial and tongue numbness accompanied by dizziness. His medical history was notable for acute sinusitis and recent-onset hypertension. On presentation, his blood pressure was 161/98 mmHg. Neurologic examination revealed ataxia, dysmetria, vertigo, and a positive Romberg’s test. Noncontrast head CT showed two areas suspicious for acute hemorrhage: one within the fourth ventricle and the other adjacent to the right cerebellum. MRI with and without contrast revealed two additional lesions—one in the left lateral cerebellar hemisphere and another in the medial posterior left temporal lobe; all lesions exhibited significant signal dropout on gradient echo sequences, and the right cerebellar mass demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement. The initial differential diagnosis included multiple cavernous malformations versus hemorrhagic metastatic lesions. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen, and a chest X-ray were ordered and were within normal limits.

A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and a history of left liver lobectomy for living-donor liver transplantation 27 years earlier presented with sudden hematemesis. She had no personal or family history of autoimmune disease, denied changes in medications (antihypertensives and glucose-lowering drugs), alcohol use, or illicit drug use. On examination, she was pale, with a heart rate of 115 bpm; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory results were: hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, platelets 105 000/µL, INR 1.4, total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, albumin 3.2 g/dL, AST 205 U/L, ALT 260 U/L, GGT 106 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 50 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a dysmorphic right liver lobe with morphologic features suggestive of cirrhosis. After hemodynamic resuscitation with crystalloid fluids, urgent upper endoscopy revealed four large esophageal varices with multiple red spots and active bleeding on one varix, which was successfully treated with variceal band ligation; terlipressin and ceftriaxone were administered. Viral hepatitis was excluded, and laboratory testing showed an elevated immunoglobulin G level (24.45 g/L) and positive antinuclear antibodies at a titer of 1:160.

A 41-year-old man presented with a swelling of the chest wall. The mass had been present since birth, had grown later in life until it burst 15 years ago, and then, three months after the rupture, had gradually enlarged to its current size. He reported no pain or overlying skin changes. His medical history included asthma and a percutaneous coronary intervention in 2019; medications were aspirin, clopidogrel, and an inhaled short-acting beta-agonist as needed. He was a non smoker. On examination, there was a 7 cm × 7 cm soft, round, slightly mobile, non-fluctuant, non-pulsatile, non-tender subcutaneous mass over the sternum. The overlying skin was of normal color and temperature. The provisional diagnosis was lipoma. No investigations were performed, and surgical excision was planned at the patient’s request.

A 48-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department for recurring crampy, generalized abdominal pain of one month’s duration, refractory to evaluation at another hospital. He was a farmer by occupation. On presentation, he was afebrile, blood pressure was 144/80 mmHg, and pulse was 88 beats per minute. He reported associated poor appetite, nausea, abdominal distention, cold sweating, and general weakness, but denied fever, diarrhea, or other symptoms. 

On examination, there was hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse tenderness to deep palpation of the entire abdomen without rebound tenderness or guarding. Results of other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hypochromic microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, hematocrit 27.9%) with basophilic stippling of erythrocytes and mildly abnormal liver function tests. The white blood cell count and levels of creatinine, glucose, total bilirubin, lipase, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Abdominal radiographs and CT scans showed no abnormalities. Liver ultrasonography, tumor markers, and viral hepatitis screening tests were negative.

He was admitted with a provisional diagnosis of nonspecific abdominal pain. A urine porphyrin test was positive, leading to a diagnosis of acute intermittent porphyria and initiation of hemin therapy. However, in spite of the hemin therapy, the pain did not improve.

A 34-year-old woman presented with weight gain, dry skin, hair loss, cold intolerance, extreme fatigue, and a progressively enlarging neck mass. On examination, the goiter was very firm and nontender. Laboratory testing revealed an elevated TSH (>8 mIU/L), anti–thyroglobulin antibody (2873 IU/mL), anti–thyroid peroxidase antibody (218 IU/mL), and elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. She was treated with L-thyroxine (100–150 µg daily) for two years without improvement; the goiter continued to enlarge, and she developed dyspnea, dysphagia, and progressive hoarseness. Thyroid ultrasound and CT imaging showed hyperplasia of both lobes with marked retrotracheal extension, deformation of the larynx, and compression and displacement of the trachea. Flexible laryngoscopy confirmed bilateral paramedian vocal-cord position and bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy. Shortly thereafter, she presented with respiratory distress.

A 21-year-old man was evaluated for longstanding, hardened subcutaneous “tumor” growths and spinal deformities. He had noted these lesions since birth, with marked progression after age 8. He complained of pain, difficulty moving, and short thumbs.

On examination, he had multiple contractures of the upper and lower limbs and spine. His posture revealed scoliosis, marked thoracic lordosis, dorsolumbar and cervical stiffness, and a protruding left scapula. Palpation showed ectopic ossifications in the paravertebral musculature. He had difficulty opening his mouth, swallowing, and performing full thoracic inspiration. Both hips and shoulders were stiff, with atrophy of the deltoid, trapezius, biceps, triceps, gluteus medius, and quadriceps muscles. Elbow and ankle flexion-extension were severely limited. His gait was equine, with the right knee fixed in flexion and the left in extension.

Laboratory tests revealed normal serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, urea, creatinine, and parathyroid hormone levels. Radiographs demonstrated multiple calcified lesions, heterotopic bone formation, and bone bridges involving the lumbar, cervical, and thoracic spine, as well as the pelvis and both knees.

A 9-year-old previously healthy girl presents with a 2-year history of intermittent, colicky right upper-quadrant abdominal pain that occurs after meals—especially fatty foods—and is sometimes accompanied by bloating and infrequent vomiting. She has a normal appetite, no weight loss, no jaundice, and no pruritus. There is no family history of biliary disease. Physical examination is unremarkable: normal vital signs, no scleral icterus, and a soft, non-tender abdomen without masses. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver-function tests, and coagulation profile, are within normal limits.  
Abdominal ultrasonography shows a focal 1.9 × 1.5 cm dilatation of the biliary duct at the hepatic hilum with internal low-level echoes; the gallbladder is moderately distended and stone-free. The impression is a choledochal cyst, and an abdominopelvic CT scan is recommended.  
CT imaging reveals a well-defined, round, 3 × 2.7 cm hypodense mass at the porta hepatis with a smooth, thin wall that appears to communicate with the biliary tree. The common bile duct is normal in caliber, and there is no evidence of biliary obstruction. The radiology report suggests a type II choledochal cyst.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A woman in her early twenties, at 6 months’ gestation, presented with a 3-week history of a painful, bleeding swelling of the gingiva that interfered with eating and toothbrushing. She had a history of chronic microcytic hypochromic anemia and was undergoing fixed orthodontic treatment, which limited her oral hygiene. Examination revealed generalized gingivitis with heavy plaque accumulation and mouth breathing. Between the first and second upper right molars, there was a 1.5 × 1.0 × 0.4 cm pedunculated, non-tender, lobulated gingival mass that bled easily on touch. 

Oral hygiene instruction and complete surgical excision of the lesion were performed. One week later, the lesion recurred and required a second excision. Seven days thereafter, gingival inflammation had reduced.

Eighteen months later, during her second pregnancy (5th month), she returned with similar symptoms. Two discrete nodular overgrowths measuring 1 × 0.5 × 0.5 cm and 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 cm were noted between the upper right premolars and molars. Dental hygiene reinforcement and a third excision were undertaken. One month postpartum, a smaller overgrowth persisted despite improved hygiene and scaling.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of a progressive, painful skin eruption that began on her torso and spread to her extremities. She reported anorexia, fatigue, and one episode of fever the day before presentation, but denied night sweats, chills, weight loss, recent infections, Raynaud’s phenomenon, oral ulcers, photosensitivity, or serositis. Her medications included amiloride for hypertension, used for 10 years, with no recent new drugs.

On examination, she was afebrile, non-toxic-appearing, and hemodynamically stable. Skin examination showed widespread erythematous papules coalescing into dusky, annular plaques with central erosions, distributed over the trunk and extremities; the face, palms, and soles were spared. There was no mucosal involvement, joint findings, or lymphadenopathy.

On hospital day 2, despite remaining afebrile and stable, she developed peripheral sheet-like detachment and desquamation over 30% of her body surface area, with a positive Nikolsky sign.

A punch biopsy of affected skin showed prominent epidermal necrosis with minimal superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates and no eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence studies were unremarkable.

A 52-year-old man with a 3-day history of left scrotal pain and swelling presented to the emergency department with fever. He had type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral hypoglycemic agents and no history of obstructive voiding or trauma. On examination, his temperature was 100°F, heart rate was elevated, and blood pressure was normal. The left scrotum was erythematous and tender, and the left testis and epididymis were enlarged. Digital rectal examination revealed a normal prostate. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis; urinalysis demonstrated numerous pus cells. His random blood glucose was 154 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1c was 7.8%. He reported a prior urinary tract infection with Escherichia coli. Scrotal ultrasonography revealed multiple gas shadows within the left epididymis and testis, scrotal wall inflammation, and fluid in the tunical sacs. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed pockets of gas in the scrotum and testis, with preserved fat planes around normal-appearing seminal vesicles and sigmoid colon. The kidneys and ureters were unremarkable.

A 9-year-old boy presented with on-and-off high-grade fever for 1 week, associated with loss of appetite, joint pain, and myalgia. He was tachypneic (respiratory rate, 32/min), tachycardic (heart rate, 143/min), and had an oxygen saturation of 93% on room air. The child was underweight (BMI, 13 kg/m2) with mild pallor. Chest auscultation revealed decreased air entry in the left lung fields with a few crepitations and a grade 3/6 continuous murmur at the left second intercostal space. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed anemia (hemoglobin, 8.8 mg/dl) and an elevated C-reactive protein level (96 mg/dl). A chest radiograph demonstrated a wedge-shaped homogeneous opacity in the left middle zone and multiple small-to-medium opacities in both lung fields, with borderline cardiomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus (pulmonary end, 3.0 mm) with multiple vegetations in the main pulmonary artery, the largest measuring approximately 9 × 6 mm; pulmonary artery pressure was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed multiple septic emboli with pulmonary infarction.

A 66-year-old woman was brought to the toxicology unit unconscious by ambulance. She had five prior suicide attempts but had not seen a psychiatrist in 10 years. Her medical history included well-controlled rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and folic acid, hypertension on enalapril, osteoarthritis on diclofenac, and occasional alprazolam use. She reported rare alcohol consumption and was in her usual state of good health.

On arrival, she was comatose (Glasgow Coma Scale score 3) with blood pressure 115/70 mm Hg, heart rate 85 beats/min, respiratory rate 25–30 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, temperature 36.0 °C, bilateral miosis, absent pupillary reflexes, absent deep tendon reflexes, and fine pulmonary crackles. No nuchal rigidity or focal neurologic deficits were noted.

Laboratory tests showed blood glucose 12.2 mmol/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 3.76 mmol/L, urine ketones positive, and proteins 30 mg/dL. Renal and hepatic chemistries were within reference ranges. D-dimer was elevated at 3254 ng/mL. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed pH 7.26, pCO2 3.5 kPa, HCO3– 14 mmol/L, base excess –15.4 mmol/L, and anion gap 21.7 mmol/L.

She was treated supportively with intravenous fluids, oxygen by nasal cannula, and furosemide, achieving transient hemodynamic stabilization but remained comatose without reflexes. Semi-quantitative urine toxicology screening detected low levels of benzodiazepines (477 ng/mL) and excluded opiates, tramadol, methadone, and cannabis. Testing for 5-hydroxytryptophan and its metabolites was not possible. A PCR test for SARS-CoV-2 was negative.

A female term neonate, born at 39 weeks after an uneventful pregnancy, was admitted on day 2 of life with progressive respiratory distress. She developed tachypnea and required supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula, initially at 2 L/min (21 % FIO₂) and increasing to 4 L/min (28 % FIO₂) with episodes of oxygen desaturation to 40 %. Physical examination revealed severe bilateral nasal obstruction without other anomalies. After topical oxymetazoline decongestion, nasal endoscopy demonstrated bilateral intranasal masses immediately below the inferior turbinates. Facial computed tomography showed bilateral cystic dilation of the nasolacrimal ducts with extension of cystic masses into and nearly occluding the anterior nasal cavity.

An 80-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a right upper abdominal encapsulated fluid collection. Two weeks earlier, he presented with abdominal pain and nausea. Abdominal ultrasonography and computed tomography in the emergency department showed a large fluid collection in the right upper abdominal cavity and gallbladder stones. He had no past history of abdominal surgery or trauma. On admission, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed slight tenderness and a palpable mass in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory tests showed albumin 2.3 g/dL (3.5–5.0), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 82 mm/h, C-reactive protein 5.2 mg/dL (0.00–0.80), and calcium 7.7 mg/dL (8.6–10.2); viral hepatitis markers were negative. A repeat CT scan demonstrated an 18.9-cm right hepatic subcapsular fluid collection. Abdominal MRI revealed multiple common bile duct stones with biliary dilatation and a large subcapsular fluid collection along the lower margin of the right hepatic lobe without any direct communication with the biliary system.

A 60-year-old woman presented with several months of constipation and mild intermittent abdominal pain. She was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and laboratory tests were within normal limits. She had no prior abdominal surgeries. An abdominal radiograph was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 5.6×7.2 cm mass in the right colon consistent with colon cancer and showed that all small-bowel loops were displaced to the left hypochondrium. Colonoscopy could not be completed because the right colon formed a 180° angle with the cecum. The patient was taken for right hemicolectomy. At laparotomy, there was no ascites. A thin, translucent membrane was found encasing the entire small intestine and extending between the parietal peritoneum and the posterior abdominal wall. Through the membrane, the small bowel appeared viable, peristaltic, and freely mobile.

A 19-year-old woman from Bangladesh presented with a painful lump in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. The lesion had been present for months but had not been examined previously. On examination, there was a 2-cm ulcerated mass leaking pus-like material and ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy without evidence of cutaneous fistula. She denied fever, breastfeeding, use of hormonal contraception, trauma, or prior breast irradiation. A needle aspiration of the pus-like discharge was sent for microbiological and molecular analysis. Breast ultrasonography revealed a well-defined cystic lesion measuring 35 × 19 mm with posterior wall acoustic enhancement, peripheral hypervascularization, and reactive axillary lymph nodes. A chest radiograph showed no pulmonary abnormalities. Mammography was deferred because of her young age. To exclude breast cancer, a core‐needle (tru-cut) biopsy was performed.

A 19-year-old woman presented with two weeks of progressive dyspnea on exertion and cough productive of blood-tinged sputum. She reported a 30-lb weight loss, drenching night sweats, and a history of menorrhagia. Six months prior, she had been incarcerated for one year. She denied smoking, multiple sexual partners, or drug use.

On transfer to our hospital, her temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 126/84 mm Hg, pulse 115 beats/min, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air (improving to 96% on 2 L nasal cannula). Examination revealed an anxious young woman with coarse crackles bilaterally, regular tachycardia, and 1+ pitting edema of the lower extremities.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, hematocrit 28.6%, MCV 91 fL, platelets 198 × 10^3/µL, electrolytes within normal limits, creatinine 0.66 mg/dL, BUN 5 mg/dL, PT 14.2 s, PTT 24 s, INR 1.1, and a negative respiratory viral panel. Urinalysis revealed 176 RBCs/HPF without casts, 7 WBCs/HPF, and 100 mg/dL proteinuria.

Chest radiography demonstrated patchy bilateral infiltrates. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. She was admitted with a presumed diagnosis of pneumonia and started on IV azithromycin and ceftriaxone. Over the next 12 hours, her oxygen requirement increased to 5 L nasal cannula, prompting ICU transfer and cessation of her heparin drip for suspected alveolar hemorrhage. She subsequently required endotracheal intubation for worsening hypoxemia.

A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 32 weeks + 3 days of gestation was admitted for acute respiratory distress and suspected metabolic acidosis. Her history included congenital muscular dystrophy (Ullrich’s disease) and familial renal glucosuria due to SGLT2 mutations. Antenatal course had been uneventful until she sustained right malleolar fractures 3 days earlier, for which she received up to 4 g/day of paracetamol. Over the 24 hours before admission she experienced nausea, two episodes of vomiting, and markedly reduced oral intake. 

On examination she was fully conscious but agitated, with a respiratory rate >50 breaths per minute. Temperature was 36.4 °C, blood pressure 130/70 mm Hg, heart rate normal, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. 

Arterial blood gas analysis revealed pH 7.06, PCO₂ 9 mm Hg, bicarbonate 2 mmol/L, lactate 0.9 mmol/L, and an anion gap of 28 mmol/L. Serum glucose was 112 mg/dL, creatinine 0.36 mg/dL, and acetone 0.26 g/L. Urinalysis showed 4+ glucose and 4+ acetone. Blood assays for paracetamol and salicylates were negative.

A 50-year-old Caucasian man presented with a six-month history of an enlarging mass in his left popliteal fossa and calf, accompanied by intermittent popliteal pain. He noted cosmetic concern but denied systemic symptoms. 

On examination, there was a non-tender, well-defined, cystic swelling extending from the superior popliteal fossa to the junction of the middle and distal third of the calf; the mass transilluminated. Knee flexion was restricted by the size of the swelling; ankle range of motion was full. 

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and inflammatory markers, were normal. Plain radiographs of the knee and tibia showed no abnormalities. 

Ultrasound confirmed a cystic lesion. A provisional diagnosis of a Baker’s cyst was made. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the knee and leg demonstrated a large, multiloculated cystic lesion measuring 24 × 10 × 12 cm in the posteromedial aspect of the knee and calf, closely related to the semimembranosus muscle.

A 50-year-old woman was referred in 2013 after an incidental systolic murmur was detected on open-access echocardiography. She was asymptomatic and had no significant medical history. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a dilated vessel arising from the right coronary cusp with turbulent colour flow into the right atrium. Cardiac CT confirmed a giant right coronary artery with a fistulous connection into the right atrium. A myocardial perfusion scan showed no ischaemia, and because of her asymptomatic status, normal biventricular function, and absence of inducible ischaemia, she was managed conservatively with routine follow-up.

Two years later, between scheduled visits, she developed several months of dyspnoea, low-grade fevers, weight loss, and lower back discomfort. On examination she was febrile and tachycardic. Laboratory tests revealed haemoglobin 64 g/L (115–165), mean corpuscular volume 78.9 fL (83–101), and C-reactive protein 142 mg/L (0–5). A chest radiograph was clear and ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis did not show malignancy or spinal lesions but identified an occlusive pulmonary filling defect in the left lower lobe consistent with pulmonary embolism. Transthoracic echocardiography then revealed new left ventricular dilatation with mildly impaired systolic function, echobright masses on the right and non-coronary cusps of the aortic valve with moderate aortic regurgitation, and a large, highly mobile structure in the right atrium arising from the distal communication of the right coronary artery fistula.

An 84-year-old Asian woman was admitted for evaluation of a 6-month history of liver function test abnormalities, intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort, fatigue, and an unintentional 4-kg weight loss. She has a 50-year history of Raynaud phenomenon and a confirmed diagnosis of CREST syndrome complicated by pulmonary hypertension, for which she had received bosentan for 7 years. Initial esophageal dysmotility–associated pain had improved with pantoprazole. 

Laboratory studies revealed an alkaline phosphatase level of 953 U/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase level of 1164 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 81 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 89 U/L, total bilirubin 13 μmol/L, and albumin 33 g/L. Bosentan was first reduced and then switched to macitentan without improvement in her biochemical cholestasis. There were no new medications. Hepatitis serologies were negative. Autoimmune testing showed a positive antinuclear antibody (consistent with CREST), negative antimitochondrial antibody, and negative other liver autoantibodies. Serum immunoglobulins, including IgG4, were within normal limits. Tumor markers (CA 19-9 and CEA) were normal.

Abdominal ultrasound showed no cholecystitis, cholelithiasis, or biliary duct dilatation. Computed tomography of the abdomen was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a prominent common bile duct and prominent, irregular central hepatic ducts with areas of beading and narrowing in both lobes.

A 60-year-old Chinese woman presented with a two-month history of blurred vision and distortion. She had hypertension for eight years and diabetes for two years, without limb or heart abnormalities, and no history of ocular trauma or surgery. The best-corrected visual acuity was 0.02 in the right eye and 0.6 in the left eye; intraocular pressures were 23 mmHg OD and 21 mmHg OS. Slit-lamp examination showed a mildly shallow anterior chamber in the right eye and a normal depth in the left eye. Bilateral cortical and nuclear cataracts were present. Numerous pigmented, radially oriented lines were seen on the anterior capsule of both eyes, more pronounced in the right eye. Fundus examination revealed a right macular hole at one-quarter pupillary distance and a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.4 in both eyes without glaucomatous damage; the retinal vessels followed a normal course. Optical coherence tomography of the right eye confirmed loss of the neuroepithelial reflex in the fovea. Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the right eye showed anterior lens position, anterior rotation of the ciliary body, a shallow anterior chamber, and peripheral iris bombe.

A 53-year-old man with stage V chronic kidney disease on hemodialysis presented with acute respiratory failure, chest pain, and a one-week history of worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. His medical history included coronary artery disease with two prior stent placements, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hypercholesterolemia, and gout. One month earlier, he had undergone creation of a left upper extremity arteriovenous fistula.

On admission, he was intubated. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis, elevated liver enzymes with a negative hepatitis panel, and increased myoglobin, lipase, and creatinine. He also had azotemia, metabolic disturbance, and mild coagulopathy. A chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly. Despite treatment with vancomycin, imipenem–cilastatin, doxycycline, and micafungin, his white-cell count rose to 61,000/mm3, and he developed persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support. He had diarrhea, but colonoscopy findings were unremarkable. Blood and sputum cultures were negative, and serologic tests for CMV, Brucella, Rickettsia rickettsii, alpha-fetoprotein, smooth muscle and mitochondrial antibodies, antinuclear antibody, and direct Coombs test were all negative.

During his hospitalization, he developed atrial fibrillation and altered mental status. Brain CT demonstrated multiple areas of decreased attenuation with focal mass effect and a subacute intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the left frontal lobe; the differential diagnosis included subacute infarcts and metastases. He died 20 days after admission without a definitive premortem diagnosis.

At autopsy, there were multiple small hemorrhagic papules on the chest; severe atherosclerotic coronary artery disease; and multiple necrotic nodular lesions in the heart, thyroid, lung, and hemorrhagic lesions in the brain. Microscopic examination of lesions in the heart, thyroid, and lung showed acute inflammation and septate fungal hyphae branching at approximately 45°. In the brain, fungal balls composed of similar branching hyphae were identified. Blood and lung cultures obtained at autopsy were negative.

A male neonate was delivered at 38 weeks’ gestation by uncomplicated cesarean section. Birth weight was 3240 g, and Apgar scores were 9 and 10 at 1 and 10 minutes, respectively. One hour after birth, he developed respiratory distress characterized by grunting and tachypnea. On examination in the neonatal unit, breath sounds were diminished over the left hemithorax, and an anterior bulge was noted on the left side of the chest. 

Three hours after birth, a chest radiograph demonstrated a hyperlucent left hemithorax with a median lobular air collection that displaced and distorted the mediastinum. A solid density at the left apex with a convex inferior border suggested a displaced thymus or an apical cap. Two thin, short radiopaque vertical lines were visible over the sternum, reminiscent of anterior junction lines or septa. There were indirect signs of increased left thoracic volume, including ipsilateral rib splaying.

A 14-year-old girl with a history of biopsy-proven lupus nephropathy maintained on mycophenolic acid (500 mg/day) and prednisolone (40 mg/day) presented with a 3-day history of headache and her first generalized seizure. She had also received two doses of an mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 12/15. Her blood pressure was 190/117 mm Hg, heart rate 150 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She had generalized edema and a urinary tract infection but no meningeal signs. Metabolic causes were eliminated.

Laboratory studies revealed:
  • Creatinine 18.47 mg/L  
  • Potassium 5.6 mmol/L  
  • ESR 116 mm/h  
  • Hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL  
  • WBC count 28.12 × 10^3/mm^3  
  • CRP 58 mg/L  
  • Procalcitonin 5.9 ng/mL  
  • ANA positive  

A noncontrast CT scan of the brain demonstrated subtle bilateral, grossly symmetrical cortical and subcortical hypodensities in the posterior parietal lobes, which remained unchanged after contrast administration.

A 38-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B carrier status and a remote history of colonic interposition for childhood esophageal atresia presented with a 1-day history of dysphagia and abdominal pain. Two weeks earlier, he had been hospitalized for abdominal pain and nonbloody diarrhea; colonoscopy at that time showed linear, noncircumferential ulcerations of the right colon with moderate wall edema and loss of vascular pattern, normal transverse and descending colon, and a few sigmoid diverticuli. He received empiric antibiotics then mesalamine and was discharged.

On return, he had progressive dysphagia for solids and liquids and mild epigastric tenderness. Vital signs were normal, and laboratory studies, including electrolytes, blood counts, and liver chemistries, were within normal limits. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed only mild colonic wall thickening. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a normal native esophagus; at the esophagocolonic anastomosis 25 cm from the incisors there was circumferential ulceration and severe stricture, and the colonic conduit was diffusely erythematous with overlying exudate, mucus, and areas of ulceration; the cologastric anastomosis and stomach appeared normal. The esophagocolonic stricture was dilated to 10 mm. Biopsies from the colonic conduit showed architectural disarray with crypt distortion, Paneth cell metaplasia, acute and chronic inflammatory exudate, and granulation tissue. Infectious studies on conduit aspirate and biopsy were negative, and CT angiography showed no vascular stenosis or signs of ischemia in the conduit.

A 21-day-old female newborn was admitted with a one-week history of progressive, painful swelling of the right hypochondrium. The child was born at 39 weeks’ gestation by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, with an APGAR score of 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes and a birth weight of 4800 g. The umbilical cord was ligated at home, and parents reported suppuration of the umbilical stump on day 5 of life. On admission, the infant was irritable, pale, and febrile, with an inflammatory mass extending from the epigastrium to the right hypochondrium. Vital signs showed fever; the remainder of the abdomen and systemic examinations were normal. Laboratory tests revealed a C-reactive protein level of 64 mg/dL, leukocytosis of 20,800/mm3 with neutrophil predominance, and hemoglobin of 8.2 g/dL. Blood cultures were obtained. The first abdominal ultrasound was interpreted as a choledochal cyst. Empirical therapy with a cephalosporin, ampicillin, and gentamicin was initiated. On day 21, surgical consultation prompted a repeat abdominal ultrasound by a pediatric sonographer, which demonstrated a 17 mL, oval, hypoechoic lesion with fine mobile echoes, thick regular walls, and peripheral vascularization in segment VIII of the liver, without intra- or extrahepatic bile duct dilatation.

An 18-year-old man presented with a six-month history of swelling and a discharging sinus over the anterolateral aspect of his right chest wall. Nine months earlier, he had sustained a bamboo stick injury to that region, managed conservatively. Since then, he experienced intermittent chest pain followed by wound discharge but denied fevers, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms.

On examination, there was localized swelling, erythema, and a sinus tract with granulation tissue over the right 6th rib. No regional lymphadenopathy was noted, and respiratory and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 11,020 per cubic millimeter, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 2 mm per hour, and a C-reactive protein level of 2.24 mg per liter.

Chest radiographs (posteroanterior and oblique views) demonstrated a lytic lesion of the right 6th rib with surrounding sclerosis and a radiolucent rim. A computed tomography scan of the chest revealed sclerosis and erosion of the anterior end of the right 6th rib with minimal adjacent pleural thickening.

A 20-year-old man from an endemic region in Uttar Pradesh, India, presented with a 2-month history of a small swelling near the medial aspect of his left cubital fossa. He denied pain, trauma, discharge or rapid growth. Examination revealed a 2×1 cm subcutaneous, slightly elongated, soft, non-tender, cystic swelling not fixed to deeper tissue. He was referred for fine-needle aspiration with a clinical diagnosis of a benign soft-tissue neoplasm. Aspiration yielded 1 mL of clear fluid; wet-mount preparation revealed numerous motile microfilariae. Cytology smears showed sheathed microfilariae with a cephalic space length-to-breadth ratio of 1 : 1, spherical nuclei in a single regular row, absence of nuclei at the tail tip, and minimal inflammatory cells.

A 63-year-old male underwent evaluation for acute bronchitis. He was healthy with a body-mass index of 24.7 kg/m2. Chest radiography identified a retrocardiac mass, and CT imaging demonstrated a 10 × 4.4 × 10.6 cm lipomatous mass in the posterior mediastinum with a vascular pedicle into the abdomen, suggestive of paraesophageal herniation of greater omentum. He complained of a retrosternal pressure sensation aggravated in the supine position, without gastroesophageal reflux symptoms. Clinical examination was unremarkable. Preoperative gastroscopy showed a 4 cm axial hernia with orthotopic positioning of the esophagogastric junction, normal mucosa, and physiological passage. The patient underwent laparoscopic omental repositioning, dorsal crurorhaphy reinforced with biosynthetic mesh, and fundophrenicopexy; fundoplication was not performed. The first three postoperative days were uneventful, and the patient tolerated a puréed diet. On postoperative day four, after initiation of solid food, he experienced multiple daily regurgitations and a persistent globus sensation. A contrast-enhanced oesophagogram revealed near-complete stenosis of the esophagogastric junction.

A 26-year-old primigravida was referred at 26 weeks of gestation for suspected fetal intrauterine growth restriction discovered on routine ultrasound. The ultrasound at 26+4 weeks showed:

• Asymmetric intrauterine growth restriction (<3rd percentile)  
• Normal amniotic fluid volume  
• Deformed skull and shortened, bowed long bones  
• Compressed chest cavity with broken ribs and a fractured humerus  

Both parents had normal phenotypes, no family history of genetic or skeletal disorders, and no pregnancy risk factors. An amniocentesis was performed, revealing a fetus karyotype of 46,XY and a normal SNP comparative genomic hybridization assay. Sequencing of the FGFR3 gene from amniocytes showed no clinically significant variants.

Because of multiple anomalies, breech presentation, and an unfavorable prognosis, a planned Cesarean section was performed at 39 weeks. The male newborn weighed 2490 g (<3rd percentile) and measured 44 cm in length. Apgar scores were 6 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Severe respiratory failure required endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. 

Postnatal management included ventilation support, antimicrobial and infusion therapies, parenteral nutrition, and analgesia. Radiographs of the head, chest, abdomen, and extremities confirmed multiple bone deformities and fractures present before birth. A right ulnar fracture was initially immobilized in a cast but the cast was removed the next day because of impaired microcirculation and signs of epidermal necrosis. 

Over the first year of life, the infant required two additional hospitalizations for pneumonia and COVID-19 and prolonged high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy. Growth and motor development were delayed; at one year, height and weight remained below the third percentile, the limbs were deformed, and muscle tone was reduced. Nutritional support by nasogastric tube was ongoing.

A 30-year-old woman who had undergone bilateral aesthetic breast augmentation with Poly Implant Prothèse (PIP) implants in 2007 presented electively in January 2015 for removal and replacement of her implants. She was otherwise healthy, with a body-mass index of 20 kg/m2, a non-smoker, and had no clinical signs of capsular contracture; inframammary scars were inconspicuous. Under general anesthesia, both implants were removed via previous inframammary incisions. On the right, the implant was intact, with no paraprosthetic fluid and a normal capsule. On the left, approximately 50 mL of milky seroma fluid was encountered; air bubbles were visible within the shell, and "fatty" smears appeared on the gloves. Manual compression of the explanted device caused rupture of the shell. Further exploration of the left implant pocket revealed a well-demarcated yellowish mass measuring 4 × 5 cm in the central lower quadrant of the breast, overlying the fascia of the pectoralis major muscle. A malignant neoplasm was suspected, and an excisional biopsy with histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses was performed.

A 72-year-old woman with bilateral Crowe type IV developmental dysplasia of the hip and a history of mitral valve replacement on warfarin (1 mg daily) and aspirin (100 mg daily) presented with progressive enlargement and severe pain of her left buttock over several weeks without trauma. She had no relevant family history. Initial presentation to an emergency hospital occurred after self-injury in the setting of severe pain; she was found to be in hemorrhagic shock and had a hemoglobin level of 5.1 g/dL. After transfer for workup of anemia, including colonoscopy without a source of bleeding, she was referred for evaluation of a suspected hip-joint hematoma versus suppurative arthritis. On admission, her blood pressure was 93/58 mmHg, pulse 62/min, and temperature 35.9 °C. She had severe left hip motion pain with flexion contracture; the left buttock, groin, and proximal thigh were markedly enlarged with tense overlying skin. Laboratory studies showed WBC 10 700/µL, CRP 10.8 mg/dL, RBC 1.71 × 10^6/µL, Hb 5.5 g/dL, Ht 18%, platelets 285 000/µL, and PT-INR 1.34. Ultrasonography revealed a cystic lesion in the left buttock, and echo-guided paracentesis yielded blood-like fluid. A pelvic radiograph confirmed Crowe type IV dysplasia bilaterally. A noncontrast CT scan demonstrated a large cavity extending from the left hip joint into the buttock and proximal thigh.

A 23‐year‐old man presented with a 2‐day history of severe left lower–quadrant abdominal pain, accompanied by progressive nausea, anorexia, and a mild fever of 38 °C. He reported no urinary symptoms or diarrhea. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, his abdomen was soft and flat, with severe rebound tenderness in the left lower quadrant; the traditional McBurney sign on the right was negative. Laboratory tests showed a white‐cell count of 14.5 × 10^3 per μL with 75% neutrophils. An abdominal CT scan was obtained and revealed situs viscerum inversus totalis and a dilated appendix in the left iliac fossa containing calcific coproliths, with a small pelvic effusion.

A 60-year-old Indian man presented with a 2-day history of altered sensorium and abdominal distension. Over the preceding 3 months he had slow mentation, inattention, word‐finding difficulty, agitation, persecutory delusions, visual hallucinations, and constipation. He denied any medication use.

On examination he was drowsy with a hoarse voice, dry skin, puffy face, madarosis, cold extremities, and slowed reflexes. His abdomen was distended with absent bowel sounds. Chest and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed macrocytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, MCV 100 fL), leukopenia (3,900/mm3), and normal glucose, liver and kidney function, arterial blood gases, and electrolytes. Septic workup was sterile. Chest radiograph and ECG were normal. Abdominal ultrasound and plain radiographs demonstrated diffuse gaseous distension with dilated loops and air-fluid levels. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed dilated small-bowel loops; whole‐body CT was otherwise unremarkable.

Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), ANA, and HIV serologies were normal. Thyroid examination was non-tender and without goiter. Neck CT showed a diffusely atrophic thyroid with low attenuation. Thyroid studies revealed TSH 76.5 µIU/mL (normal 0.39–3.55), FT4 0.1 ng/dL (0.75–1.54), and FT3 0.42 pg/mL (2.0–4.9). Serum anti-TPO antibodies were 581 U/mL (normal <60).

Brain MRI showed mild diffuse atrophy with prominent sulci, periventricular ooze on FLAIR, and T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in periventricular and subcortical white matter. EEG was normal. CSF examination revealed elevated protein, normal glucose, and was positive for anti-TPO antibodies. Gut manometry demonstrated features of intestinal dysmotility.

A 37-year-old woman with a history of hypothyroidism, remote amphetamine use, and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 10 years earlier (initial 120-lb weight loss) presented with a 4-month history of recurrent syncope, diaphoresis, and an unintentional 60-lb weight loss. She reported multiple episodes of neuroglycopenic symptoms and self-measured blood glucose levels below 50 mg/dL despite taking up to six over-the-counter glucose tablets daily.

On admission, her plasma glucose was 43 mg/dL, with non–anion gap metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia (2.8 mmol/L). She required ICU-level care with hourly glucose monitoring. A 72-hour fast was attempted but halted after severe hypoglycemia necessitated intravenous dextrose. Diazoxide and continuous D5W infusions were administered with persistent hypoglycemia.

An endocrinology evaluation at glucose levels <50 mg/dL showed fasting insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin levels that were within normal limits but not suppressed. Sulfonylurea use, exogenous insulin administration, autoimmune diabetes, cortisol deficiency, and celiac disease were biochemically excluded. On hospital day 10, her glucose remained at 47 mg/dL, with a C-peptide of 3.1 ng/mL (0.8–3.5) and insulin of 3.6 µIU/mL (2.0–19.6), again not suppressed. Total parenteral nutrition was initiated.

Cross-sectional imaging with CT and MRI revealed a subtle contour abnormality near the pancreatic tail. Endoscopic ultrasound was unremarkable. A gallium-68 dotatate PET scan demonstrated a focal area of radiotracer uptake in the distal pancreas.

A 58-year-old man presented in mid-summer after being found unconscious at home. He had one week of progressive gait instability but no other preceding neurologic or infectious symptoms.

His history was notable for poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma of the parotid gland diagnosed 7 months earlier, treated with seven cycles of chemotherapy (last dose 2 weeks earlier), and asymptomatic brain metastases identified 2 months before. He declined whole-brain radiation therapy. Other conditions included prostate cancer in remission, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and visual seizures on antiepileptic medication.

On examination he was somnolent but arousable, febrile (102.4°F), and tachycardic, with normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation on 2 L/min nasal cannula. Neurologically, he was disoriented to time and place, dysarthric, amnestic, and had a new resting tremor in both upper extremities; there was no nuchal rigidity, focal weakness, or sensory deficits.

Laboratory tests showed mild hyponatremia and elevated creatine kinase, with normal liver function, blood count, and urinalysis. Urine drug screen was positive only for cannabinoids. Blood and urine cultures, chest radiography, and noncontrast head CT were unremarkable.

He was started on empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and systemic glucocorticoids for possible infection or vasogenic edema, and his antiseizure medication was continued. After 24 hours his mental status partially improved, prompting suspicion of a seizure, but EEG revealed generalized background slowing without epileptogenic foci. Two days after presentation he remained febrile with persistent tremors but improved cognition. A lumbar puncture showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (95 cells/mm3, 8% neutrophils, 53% lymphocytes, 25% plasma cells, 14% monocytes), elevated glucose and protein; CSF Gram stain and cytology were negative, as were HSV-1/2 RT-PCR and Cryptococcus antigen. CSF and serum testing for West Nile virus IgM, IgG, and PCR were ordered.

An 80-year-old man with terminal, poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the base of the tongue (cT2N2b), status post tracheostomy, gastrostomy, and arterial embolization of multiple branches of the bilateral external carotid arteries 2 weeks earlier for hemoptysis, presented with 3 days of left upper- and lower-extremity weakness. He denied sensory changes, headache, fever, or other neurologic symptoms. He took only acetaminophen. Vital signs were within normal limits. Neurologic examination showed 4/5 strength in the left upper and lower extremities; NIH Stroke Scale score was 2. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. No blood cultures were obtained.

Noncontrast CT of the brain revealed a hypodense region at the right parietal vertex with a 15 mm focal circular lesion surrounded by edema, plus a smaller adjacent focus; there was no hemorrhage or acute infarct. CT angiography of the head and neck showed a newly developed large, eccentric, saccular aneurysm of the distal right common carotid artery with surrounding soft tissue asymmetry, gas, and bony displacement; these findings had enlarged since the embolization procedure two weeks prior. MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium demonstrated a 2 cm right parietal lesion with peripheral ring enhancement and avid central restricted diffusion, a medially adjacent 1 cm lesion, and an anterior subcentimeter lesion, all with extensive vasogenic edema. MRI of the neck confirmed an irregular aneurysm at the right carotid bulb with diffuse soft tissue enhancement.

A 70-year-old man with a 30–pack-year smoking history presented with worsening right-sided ear pain and purulent ear discharge. The pain began 3 months earlier after a dental procedure and transiently improved with intermittent antibiotics, but then worsened. Over the preceding 3 weeks, he developed frontal and right temporal headaches and progressive dysphagia, initially to solids and then to liquids, resulting in a 20-pound weight loss and malnutrition. He denied changes in hearing or vision.

On examination, the patient was afebrile. He had a hoarse voice, right palatal weakness, and tenderness over the right lateral neck and peri-auricular area. The right external auditory canal was mildly edematous with scant otorrhea, and the tympanic membrane was intact. There was no facial nerve weakness and the tongue was midline.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13.5 × 10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 15.3 mg/L. A head and neck CT without contrast revealed an infiltrative process in the right upper neck and skull base with bony destruction involving the occipital bone and extension to the hypoglossal canal, jugular bulb, and stylomastoid foramen. MRI with a T1 Dixon sequence demonstrated hyperintense soft-tissue infiltration of the right skull base and occipital bone with mild meningeal enhancement but no abscess. A barium swallow study showed persistent laryngeal penetration and aspiration. 

Imaging findings were concerning for a skull base infectious process or an invading malignancy.

A 56-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with 3 weeks of progressive, localized right posterior chest wall pain and swelling. He denied fevers, chills, cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, or recent travel. He had a 25-pack-year smoking history and occasional alcohol use. 

On examination, he was afebrile and had a hard, fixed 7 × 10 cm mass over the right posterior chest wall at the level of the 11th rib, with minimal tenderness and no overlying erythema or drainage. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 17,000 cells/mm^3. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 3 × 2.5 cm right posterior chest wall mass at the 11th rib with minimal right lower lobe parenchymal changes and no pleural effusion. Ultrasound-guided needle biopsy revealed an inflammatory process; stains for bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, and fungi were negative. 

Three weeks after CT, MRI showed interval growth to a 9 × 9 × 5 cm centrally necrotic mass infiltrating the right hemidiaphragm, with only minimal right lower-lobe involvement. 

The patient was taken to surgery, at which time he had a 10 × 12 cm erythematous, fluctuant mass with a 5 × 5 cm area of central skin necrosis. A wide local excision with debridement of the abscess cavity and a portion of latissimus dorsi was performed. The mass extended through the 10th interspace into the pleural cavity, prompting tube thoracostomy drainage. Purple-tinged purulent material was evacuated, and surrounding erythema improved by the end of the procedure. 

He was discharged on postoperative day 5 with a wound VAC and an 8-week course of ampicillin–sulbactam. Imaging at 6 weeks postoperatively showed adequate healing of the chest wall and complete resolution of the mass.

A 23-year-old G1P0 woman was referred at 24 weeks 6 days’ gestation for concern about fetal microcephaly. On ultrasound, the biparietal diameter and head circumference were below the third percentile for gestational age. A midline calvarial defect was noted in the posterior fontanelle region, with herniation of meninges and dysmorphic brain tissue. Normal cerebral landmarks were absent, and the supratentorial ventricular system could not be identified. The posterior fossa appeared small, and the transcerebellar diameter was difficult to measure. The nuchal fold thickness was normal, the face was unremarkable, the amniotic fluid volume was normal, and no extracranial anomalies were detected.

Fetal MRI confirmed a high parietal midline calvarial defect at the posterior fontanelle, with herniation of small disorganized brain and meninges without a defined sac or skin covering. The supratentorial brain was small, lacking normal anatomy, including lateral ventricles, germinal matrix, lamination patterns, and midline structures. The posterior fossa was small, with cerebellum and brainstem distorted toward the defect. The family was counseled that the prognosis was poor.

The infant was delivered at 39 weeks 6 days by cesarean section and was alive at birth. On day 9 of life, examination revealed a 3-cm midline defect in the posterior fontanelle with no skin or meningeal covering and exposed malformed brain protruding approximately 2 cm. The head circumference was below the first percentile. Prophylactic antibiotics were initiated, and postnatal MRI and CT venography were performed.

A 39-year-old G3P3 woman presented with a 1-month history of relatively abrupt onset of shortness of breath that worsened toward the end of the day. She also reported marked orthopnoea when supine that was relieved by sleeping prone. She denied cough, chest tightness, palpitations, or other medical problems; her three pregnancies and deliveries had been uncomplicated. There was no family history of premature cardiac death or cardiovascular disease.

On examination, blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air in all positions. A single-breath count was 7. Cardiovascular examination revealed a pulmonary-area ejection murmur; lung fields were clear.

Laboratory studies, including a basic metabolic panel, haemoglobin, and renal function tests, were normal. Lactate dehydrogenase was mildly elevated at 289 U/L. An electrocardiogram was unremarkable. Chest radiography showed mild cardiomegaly with obliteration of the pulmonary-artery bay. Transthoracic echocardiography performed twice showed normal right and left heart size and function. The patient could not complete pulmonary function tests. High-resolution CT of the chest and noncontrast CT were normal. CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated a dilated main pulmonary artery (31 mm; normal ≤29 mm) and no filling defects in the pulmonary vasculature.

A 78-year-old woman underwent left total knee arthroplasty via a lateral parapatellar approach for Kellgren–Lawrence grade III osteoarthritis with valgus deformity. Her medical history included bronchial asthma on long-term inhaled steroids, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and well-controlled type 2 diabetes (preoperative HbA1c 6.3 %, fasting glucose 110 mg/dL). The surgery was completed without intraoperative complications.

On postoperative day 2, she noted swelling and pain of the left thigh. Examination revealed a firm, tender thigh with palpable subcutaneous crepitus; the surgical wound bled slightly but was not erythematous. She was afebrile and fully alert.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the left thigh showed extensive emphysema in the subcutaneous and intermuscular planes extending toward the hip. Given the concern for possible gas-forming infection, arthrocentesis was performed; Gram stain and culture of the aspirate were pending. Blood cultures were also obtained. The LRINEC score was calculated as 1.

A 67-year-old woman with no prior medical history experienced emotional stress at a family funeral. Four days later, she developed sudden-onset chest pain and shortness of breath. In the local health centre, her blood pressure fell to 60/30 mmHg, and troponin-T was elevated. The ECG demonstrated widespread ST-elevations in the anterior and inferior leads consistent with Grade 3 ischaemia. Lung auscultation revealed fine crepitant rales; cardiac examination was otherwise unremarkable. She received ticagrelor, enoxaparin, and aspirin and was transferred for primary percutaneous coronary intervention.  

On arrival at the hospital, she remained hypotensive (60/30 mmHg) with an oxygen saturation of 75% and continued to report intense chest pain. The ECG showed extensive ST-elevations in all precordial leads and the inferior leads, with a triangular (lambda-shaped) appearance of the QRS-ST-T waveform in leads II, III, aVF, and V3–V6. Telemetry revealed repeated episodes of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia at 165 b.p.m., during which she transiently lost consciousness. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 20%.

A 12-year-old boy was referred with a four-month history of episodic, progressively severe, atypical left-sided chest pain causing significant functional disturbance. Pain occurred at rest and with exertion; he adopted back-arching postures for relief. He had no other cardiac symptoms and no family history of cardiac disease. Initial echocardiography at the referring centre showed a dysplastic aortic valve with mild aortic regurgitation and left ventricular hypertrophy. Serial troponin-I measurements in the week before referral revealed one mildly elevated value (32 ng/L; upper limit 26 ng/L). Prior local presentations were managed as presumed pericarditis without improvement on anti-inflammatory therapy. Differential diagnoses considered included musculoskeletal pain, gastro-oesophageal reflux (treated with a proton-pump inhibitor), and non-organic pain; these interventions led to only mild symptom improvement.

On assessment: heart rate 80/min, blood pressure 115/60 mmHg, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, afebrile. Cardiac exam revealed a 2/4 early diastolic murmur; there were no signs of heart failure or endocarditis. Laboratory tests showed normal blood count, renal/liver function, and inflammatory markers. Chest radiograph was normal. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy; no arrhythmias were recorded on monitoring.

Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a dysplastic, functionally bicuspid aortic valve with a hypoplastic left coronary cusp, mild-to-moderate aortic regurgitation, no aortic stenosis, and apparent normal origins of the coronary arteries with antegrade flow. Left ventricular systolic function was preserved.

During a standard Bruce-protocol treadmill exercise test, the patient experienced worsening chest pain at rest and exercise, leading to early termination. ECG immediately post-exercise showed mild infero-lateral ST-segment depression. No regional wall-motion abnormalities were noted on stress echocardiography.

A 57-year-old woman with poorly controlled type I diabetes mellitus and tardive dyskinesia was transferred for management of right‐eye angle closure with persistently elevated intraocular pressures despite two laser peripheral iridotomies, an anterior chamber paracentesis, and maximal medical therapy. On presentation, vision in the right eye was no light perception and intraocular pressure ranged from 47 to 53 mm Hg. Examination showed periorbital edema, 360° chemosis with mucoid discharge, microcystic corneal edema, and a flat anterior chamber with central lenticulocorneal touch. The iris was mid-dilated and constricted peripherally against the cornea. A posterior-push mechanism was suspected.

Because of the poor view, orbital ultrasonography (B-scan) was performed, demonstrating profound thickening of the posterior sclera and sub-Tenon’s fluid forming a clear T-sign. Computed tomography of the orbits showed wall thickening of the globe consistent with scleritis and retrobulbar fat stranding without an abscess or mass.

Initial laboratory evaluation revealed a white blood cell count of 18.0 K/µL with neutrophil predominance, C-reactive protein of 2.7 mg/dL, and a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Aerobic, anaerobic, and fungal blood cultures were drawn. Intravenous vancomycin, aztreonam, and metronidazole were started. Posterior scleritis treatment was begun with intravenous indomethacin, and systemic corticosteroids were withheld pending culture results. Ocular pain management and measures to deepen the anterior chamber and lower intraocular pressure were initiated.

A 4-month-old female infant was admitted for mild neonatal jaundice, cough, and rhinorrhea. On examination, she was afebrile with stable vital signs and a normal physical exam without hepatosplenomegaly. Abdominal ultrasonography showed slight thickening of the gallbladder wall. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) was normal, effectively excluding biliary atresia.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Total bilirubin 156.6 μmol/L (normal 3.4–20.5) with direct bilirubin 121.6 μmol/L (normal 0–10).  
• AST 160 U/L (4–32), ALT 65 U/L (4–33).  
• Lactic acid 5.25 mmol/L (0.5–2.2).  
• Total bile acids 210.6 μmol/L (1.0–10).  
• Alpha-fetoprotein 47 328 ng/mL (< 25).  

Infectious workup including CMV serology and TORCH panel was negative. No kaolin stools were observed.

An 18-year-old man presented with 6 months of right medial ankle pain and swelling after a twisting injury while playing football. He was initially treated as a sprain with ice, anti-inflammatories, and a 3-week below-knee cast without radiographic evaluation. After cast removal, he continued to have pain on walking. On examination, there was localized swelling over the distal medial malleolus and tenderness along the deltoid ligament; there was no distal tibial bone–tenderness, and ankle range of motion was normal. Standard ankle radiographs and 3-dimensional CT revealed a small bone fragment attached to the anterior and distal aspect of the medial malleolus of the right tibia. The fragment appeared smooth and rounded with well-formed cortices. The left ankle was normal.

A 76-year-old man presented with abdominal pain and constipation. His history included osteoporosis, Parkinsonism, prior L2–L3 arthrodesis for spondylodiscitis, chronic lumbar pain, and bent spine syndrome. Home medications were pantoprazole, aspirin (CardioASA), bromazepam, transdermal fentanyl, and bisoprolol.

On examination he was oriented, malnourished with muscle atrophy and hypotonia. Vital signs: HR 68 bpm, BP 120/70 mmHg, T 36°C. Abdominal exam showed diffuse tenderness without peritoneal signs.

Labs: Hb 11.2 g/dL; WBC 10.8×10^3/µL; total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL; AST 40 U/L; ALT 28 U/L; ALP 115 U/L; amylase 406 U/L; CRP 150 mg/L.

Abdominal ultrasound for suspected chronic pancreatitis showed multiple pancreatic calcifications and an irregular aortic caliber. CT angiography revealed dissection of the right common iliac artery with an ulcerated plaque, dilation of the gallbladder and extrahepatic biliary tract, and small (≤3 mm) hypodense lesions in the pancreatic head. Fondaparinux was started.

Ten days later he developed sudden anemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and worsening cholestasis; the abdomen was now painless and there was no gastrointestinal bleeding. Bedside ultrasound showed a distended gallbladder with non-homogeneous hyperechoic material and mild intrahepatic biliary dilation; the common bile duct was obscured. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a markedly distended gallbladder filled with hyperdense, non-homogeneous content, regular wall thickness, and a focal area of suspected active bleeding along the anterior wall, with increased dilation of the intra- and extrahepatic ducts.

A 12-year-old boy with a history of an unrepaired patent ductus arteriosus presented with 3 months of progressive fatigue. He had been followed symptomatically without routine imaging. He had no other medical or family history of note.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Inspection revealed anterior chest wall bulging. Cardiac auscultation disclosed rumbling diastolic and systolic murmurs along the right parasternal border radiating toward the subxiphoid and apical regions. No stigmata of connective-tissue disease were present.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, organ function tests, and D-dimer level, were all normal. Screenings for HIV, tuberculosis, and syphilis were negative.

A frontal chest radiograph showed a smooth, well-defined left hilar opacity closely abutting the left cardiac border. The initial differential diagnoses included aneurysmal dilation of the left atrium and a pericardial cyst.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large patent ductus arteriosus and evidence of pulmonary arterial hypertension, with otherwise limited additional information.

A 33-year-old man was referred for evaluation of recurrent sino-pulmonary infections and a presumed diagnosis of sarcoidosis. At age 27, he first noted exertional dyspnea while playing basketball. Initial pulmonary function tests showed a preserved FEV1/FVC ratio of 95% and a DLCO of 59%. CT of the chest demonstrated mediastinal and axillary lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and reticulonodular infiltrates in the mid and lower lung zones. A transbronchial lung biopsy revealed scattered, poorly formed granulomas and mild chronic interstitial inflammation. Bone marrow aspiration and trephine were unremarkable.

He was treated with a tapering course of prednisolone beginning in July 2021 with minimal clinical benefit. His history was notable for chronic rhinosinusitis requiring septoplasty and endoscopic sinus surgery in March 2023. In April 2023, he was hospitalized for infective sinusitis and multilobar pneumonia. Ear swabs grew Staphylococcus and Haemophilus species, but sputum cultures were negative. Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics, there was no significant clinical improvement on repeat chest CT, which showed dense consolidation in the left lower lobe and right upper lobe.

FDG-PET in September 2023 revealed increased uptake in the sinuses, mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes, and spleen. Azathioprine was started as a steroid-sparing agent but was discontinued after 2 weeks due to persistently low total protein and globulin levels. Due to low globulin measurements, immunoglobulin levels were assessed.

A 52‐year‐old overweight woman with hypertension and stage II chronic kidney disease was referred for worsening renal function and resistant hypertension. On admission, she had mild asymptomatic anemia (hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL), serum creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (eGFR 30 mL/min/1.73 m2), nonselective nephrotic‐range proteinuria (6.58 g/24 h), Bence‐Jones proteinuria (1.71 g/24 h), and markedly elevated serum kappa free light chains (96 000 mg/L) with normal total calcium and no bone lesions or full‐blown nephrotic syndrome. The coagulation profile was uninterpretable (likely due to monoclonal protein), but bleeding time was normal.

Bone marrow biopsy showed > 90% clonal plasma cells; FISH confirmed micromolecular kappa multiple myeloma with t(14;16) translocation and R-ISS stage 3, complete immunoparesis, and absent CRAB criteria.

Cardiac evaluation revealed NT-proBNP 1242 pg/mL and high-sensitivity troponin T 2298 pg/mL. ECG showed sinus tachycardia, first-degree AV block, right‐axis deviation, and right conduction delay. Abdominal fat pad Congo red stain was negative.

Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated a 4.4 × 2.8 cm right atrial mass projecting through the tricuspid valve and a 1.5 cm mass at the right ventricular apex; biventricular function was preserved, and there was no left ventricular hypertrophy or significant valvular regurgitation.

CT pulmonary angiogram revealed right ventricular thrombi, a large thrombus in the pulmonary trunk and main branches, segmental pulmonary emboli, partial thrombosis of the inferior vena cava extending to the renal veins, and complete left renal vein thrombosis. The patient was hemodynamically stable, with mild asthenia, normal blood pressure, no dyspnea, and 99% oxygen saturation on room air. Unfractionated heparin was initiated, and she was referred for cardiac surgery.

A 7-week-old male Golden Retriever was evaluated for failure to thrive and stunted growth despite adequate nutrition. Two days earlier he had been dewormed for hookworms and found to have a grade 4/6 systolic heart murmur with increased respiratory effort. On presentation, he was dull, panting, febrile (101.8°F), heart rate 100 bpm, with bounding femoral pulses, bruising in axillae and inguinal areas, and a grade 4/6 bilateral apical systolic murmur.  

CBC revealed severe normocytic, normochromic anemia (Hct 0.118 L/L [RI 0.27–0.37]) and extreme leukocytosis (165.37 × 10^9/L [RI 8.8–22.4]). A blood film manual differential showed extreme neutrophilia (segmented 110.8 × 10^9/L; bands 31.4 × 10^9/L; metamyelocytes 5.0 × 10^9/L; myelocytes 1.7 × 10^9/L), moderate monocytosis (8.3 × 10^9/L [RI 0.5–1.6]), prominent toxic changes, and very rare intracellular and extracellular rod-shaped bacterial structures.  

Serum biochemistry showed moderately increased alanine phosphatase (388 U/L [RI 93–221]) and γ-glutamyl transferase (16 U/L [RI 0–2]), with mild decreases in BUN, creatinine, and albumin. Urinalysis revealed isosthenuria (USG 1.012) and 2+ bilirubinuria. PCV/TS were 17%/60 g/L, blood glucose 137 mg/dL, and blood pressure 160 mm Hg.  

Echocardiography showed trace to mild mitral and tricuspid regurgitation with mild left heart enlargement. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated numerous hepatic nodules (some cavitated), mottled/micronodular splenomegaly, renal perihilar steatitis, diffuse gastrointestinal fluid, scant echogenic peritoneal effusion, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy.  

The dog was hospitalized, received a packed red blood cell transfusion and IV ampicillin/sulbactam. Abdominal effusion was submitted for culture. On hospital day 2, enrofloxacin was added to antimicrobial therapy.

A 59-year-old man presented with a painless but bothersome bulging perianal “tumor.” He denied prior surgeries or a family history of colorectal cancer. He was a smoker with a history of thrombophlebitis. On examination in the lithotomy position, there was a 3-cm soft mass at the posterior anal margin. On palpation, hemorrhoidal disease was excluded. Vital signs were normal, and there was no overlying erythema or warmth. A pelvic MRI showed a large ovoid lesion arising from the posterior wall of the anal canal, situated between the external sphincters and prolapsing into the intergluteal cleft; the lesion had homogeneous fluid content and showed no tissue contrast enhancement. The radiologist noted no apparent signs of malignancy but could not determine the precise nature of the mass.

A 4-year-old girl with cerebral palsy, psychomotor delay, and severe spastic paraplegia was admitted with a 3-day history of fever and bilateral knee pain. She was born preterm at 1600 g after fetal distress. Her feeding history initially consisted solely of milk products. On examination, she was pale, anxious with strangers, febrile (38.8 °C), pulse 124 bpm, blood pressure 100/64 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22/min. Oral hygiene was poor; skin was normal. One day after admission, she developed tense bruising and swelling around both knees with pain on palpation of the distal femoral metaphyses; passive motion was nearly complete. 

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 9220/μL, hemoglobin 5 g/dL (microcytic hypochromic anemia), platelets 440,000/μL, ESR >140 mm/h, CRP 90 mg/L, and iron 7 μmol/L; alkaline phosphatase, calcium, and phosphate were normal. 

Knee radiographs demonstrated osteopenia, a dense “white line” at the tibial metaphyses, metaphyseal rarefaction, periosteal reaction, and bilateral distal femoral epiphyseal displacement. Ultrasound revealed periosteal detachment with soft-tissue infiltration. MRI of the knees was interpreted as osteomyelitis of the left distal femur with a subperiosteal abscess and joint effusion. 

An orthopedic consultation listed trivial trauma, septic arthritis, and osteomyelitis as leading considerations. Urgent needle aspiration yielded a gelatinous red fluid, and empirical intravenous oxacillin and gentamicin were initiated. Bacterial cultures of the aspirate returned negative, and antibiotics were discontinued.

A 63-year-old man presented with a several-month history of nonproductive cough and dyspnea on exertion. Six months after symptom onset he noted low-grade fever and erythematous rash on the face, anterior chest, and back. His respiratory symptoms progressed, and chest radiography and CT revealed mediastinal lymphadenopathy, emphysematous changes, and diffuse fine nodular and reticular shadows in both lung fields consistent with interstitial lung disease.

On examination, he had facial and truncal erythema and fine crackles in both lung fields but no muscle weakness or myalgia. Vital signs were notable for room-air SpO₂ of 92%. Laboratory studies showed normal creatine kinase and aldolase levels, mild elevations of AST, ALT, and LDH, and elevated C-reactive protein, KL-6, and SP-D. Rheumatoid factor, ANA, and anti–Jo-1 antibodies were negative, as were sputum bacterial cultures and a tuberculin skin test. Electromyography revealed no myogenic changes, and pulmonary function testing demonstrated a restrictive pattern.

Given the suspicion for clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease, testing for anti–CADM-140/MDA5 antibody was performed and returned negative. Additional studies revealed an elevated serum ACE level of 51.8 IU/L and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid containing 3.28×10⁵ cells/mL with 49% lymphocytes and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 8.40.

A 12-year-old right-handed Hispanic boy presented with chronic intermittent pain on the ulnar side of his left wrist three months after injuring it during baseball practice. Immediately after hitting the ball, he noted diffuse swelling over the ulnar border and limited range of motion due to pain. Initial anteroposterior, lateral, and oblique wrist radiographs were reported as negative, and he was diagnosed with a wrist sprain and immobilized in a brace. After one week, a general orthopaedic surgeon confirmed no evident fractures on repeat radiographs and recommended continued conservative treatment; four additional weeks of splinting provided minimal relief. Referral to physical medicine and rehabilitation led to physical therapy, but the patient continued to experience mild discomfort. New wrist radiographs remained negative. Subsequent MRI demonstrated bone edema and a disruptive linear signal in the hook of the hamate. Upon evaluation in the hand clinic, he reported weakness when gripping a bat and intermittent pain but denied numbness or tingling. Examination revealed tenderness at the ulnar aspect of the wrist, grip strength of 3/5 on the affected side, preserved range of motion without erythema or atrophy, and intact sensation. Hook of hamate pull test elicited moderate pain. Tinel’s sign and Phalen’s test were negative, and the Allen test ruled out ulnar artery compromise.

A 47-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of jaundice, weight loss, and intermittent low-grade fever. On examination, there was a tender mass in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (12,800 cells/mm3) and an elevated C-reactive protein level (5.2 mg/dL); serologic tests for hepatitis B and C were negative, and the α-fetoprotein concentration was 2.3 ng/dL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 9.0-cm mass in liver segments VI and VII, with arterial-phase enhancement and washout on equilibrium-phase images. Colonoscopy and upper endoscopy were unremarkable. Percutaneous ultrasound-guided needle biopsy of the lesion demonstrated proliferation of spindle-shaped cells mixed with inflammatory myofibrohistiocytes, suggesting the diagnosis.

A 62-year-old woman with a history of lupus anticoagulant on warfarin and grade II obesity (BMI 38.5) status post laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding in 2003 presented with a 3-day history of bright red blood with clots per rectum. She also reported left-lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, emesis, lightheadedness, weakness, and exertional dyspnea. On arrival, she was afebrile, and her vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed a hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL and an INR of 2.1. 

Because of the rectal bleeding, colonoscopy was performed and revealed diverticulosis and a foreign body eroding through the transverse colon. A CT scan of the abdomen with oral contrast was then obtained. The CT images demonstrated erosion of the lateral portion of the gastric band into the gastric wall and erosion of the distal tip of the band tubing into the transverse colon, with surrounding inflammatory changes but no fistulas or abscesses.
