A 12-year-old boy with no prior medical history noted lower-abdominal bloating and began restricting his food intake 3 months earlier. He exercised obsessively to match his reduced intake, had a distorted body image (“my belly is fat”), and was anxious about weight gain. On initial evaluation, his BMI was 11.5 kg/m2 and his heart rate was 40 beats/min. He was started on enteral nutritional supplements and underwent head MRI and abdominal ultrasound to identify underlying disease.

Seven days later, he became disoriented and was admitted. He was 145 cm tall, weighed 20.9 kg (BMI 9.9 kg/m2), and had impaired consciousness (GCS E3V4M6), bradycardia (≈ 40 beats/min), and slow breathing (≈ 10 breaths/min). Blood tests revealed hypercapnia, hypoglycemia, elevated creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and transaminases. Hypoglycemia and dehydration were corrected slowly to avoid refeeding syndrome. On hospital day 2, he had further impaired consciousness (GCS E1V1M1) and hypotension attributed to marked hypoglycemia and dehydration; his condition improved with continued correction. On day 4, his AST peaked at 4,782 U/L, ALT at 2,265 U/L, and prothrombin time was 28%, consistent with an acute liver-failure–like state. He received glucose infusions, enteral nutrition, and supportive care, after which his liver enzymes gradually improved.

A 43-year-old obese Caucasian man with a history of insomnia, bipolar disorder, and chronic headache presented with multiple episodes of brief seizures, all induced by laughter when he watched comedy shows. He had experienced several mild episodes over the past month, each lasting approximately 5–10 seconds, characterized by the onset of laughter followed by arm shaking and a sensation that “his consciousness was being vacuumed away.” He denied tongue biting or incontinence. He averaged five episodes per day. There was no family history of seizure disorder.

On examination, he was alert and hemodynamically stable. Neurologic examination was normal. Serum electrolytes and glucose were within normal limits. A sleep-deprived electroencephalogram (EEG) was normal. Brain MRI revealed an arachnoid cyst measuring 4.2 × 2.1 cm in the right anterior middle cranial fossa. He underwent two days of video EEG monitoring, which showed several bursts of generalized high-amplitude spike-and-wave activity with frontotemporal predominance, associated with staring, eye rolling, unresponsiveness, and tonic-clonic movements for 5–10 seconds, all provoked by deep, belly laughter; he reported complete lack of awareness during these episodes.

A male infant was delivered at 35 2/7 weeks’ gestation via cesarean section for recurrent fetal heart rate decelerations. The pregnancy was notable for first-trimester cystic hygroma and persistent intrauterine growth restriction. Prenatal ultrasound revealed absence of the corpus callosum, high-riding third ventricle, absent cavum septum pellucidum, indented occiput, and an absent ductus venosus draining directly to the hepatic vasculature. Noninvasive prenatal testing was low risk for trisomies 13, 18, 21, and monosomy X; amniocentesis was declined.

At birth, Apgar scores were 9 and 9. Birth weight was 1510 g (1st percentile), length 38.5 cm (1st percentile), and head circumference 30 cm (8th percentile). On examination, he had short palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, low-set ears, micrognathia, flat nasal bridge, elongated philtrum, thin upper lip, anteverted nares, hirsutism, and single palmar creases. Neurologically, he was centrally hypotonic with bilateral upper-limb hyperreflexia and a sacral dimple with a hair tuft.

He remained in the NICU for 70 days. Brain MRI confirmed agenesis of the corpus callosum and septum pellucidum with parallel colpocephalic ventricles; EEG showed poorly differentiated low-voltage background and temporal sharp transients. He required prolonged noninvasive respiratory support without parenchymal lung disease. Echocardiography demonstrated a small apical VSD, moderate PDA, small secundum ASD, and left superior vena cava to coronary sinus; the PDA later closed spontaneously. He had severe feeding intolerance despite negative GI imaging and required continuous enteral feeds and total parenteral nutrition.

Genitourinary examination revealed an underdeveloped scrotum with bilateral undescended testes, incomplete foreskin, and distal penile shaft enlargement. A pinpoint coronal hypospadic meatus could not be catheterized despite multiple attempts, and manual expression of the distal penis was required for voiding. Voiding cystourethrogram showed pooling of contrast in a urethral diverticulum. The initial differential diagnosis for the genitourinary abnormality included anterior urethral valves, megalourethra, or a urethral diverticulum secondary to distal urethral atresia; the working diagnosis was a coronal hypospadias with anterior urethral valves leading to a urethral diverticulum.

A 30-year-old man with a history of substance use disorder presented after an accidental gunshot wound to the suprapubic abdomen. CT imaging showed intraperitoneal air and blood, suggesting bowel perforation; the bullet rested in the subcutaneous tissues posterior to the sacrococcygeal junction. He underwent laparotomy, during which a sigmoidectomy, small-bowel resection, and end colostomy were performed. 

He initially recovered without complication, but on postoperative day 5 he developed fever and an exquisitely painful ulcer at the midline laparotomy incision near the entry site. Superficial and dermal sutures were removed, a short-term wound VAC was placed, and he was started on IV levofloxacin. Within 24 hours the ulcer dramatically enlarged; blood cultures were drawn, antibiotics were escalated to IV ertapenem and vancomycin, and wound care was changed to wet-to-dry dressings. Despite these interventions, the ulcer continued to expand.

An extensive infectious workup—including bacterial and fungal blood cultures, MRSA nucleic acid assay, and bacterial and fungal wound-tissue cultures—returned negative. On examination the ulcer was rapidly expanding, exquisitely tender, and had heaped-up, undermined, violaceous borders with copious purulent exudate; it surrounded but did not involve the umbilicus or stoma, and the deep fascial closure remained intact. 

On postoperative day 13, the patient was taken to the operating room for conservative surgical debridement of one quadrant of the ulcer and biopsy for histopathologic evaluation.

A male infant was delivered at 34 weeks’ gestation by cesarean section for fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios. His mother had systemic lupus erythematosus treated with hydroxychloroquine and low-dose prednisolone and was positive for anti-SSa/Ro and anti-SSb/La antibodies. The Apgar scores were 9, 9, and 9 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes. His heart rate remained between 60 and 100 bpm; physical examination was unremarkable. He was admitted to the NICU, where echocardiography showed a restrictive ventricular septal defect, a wide patent foramen ovale, and a small secundum atrial septal defect with left-to-right shunt. On day 14, antibody testing confirmed high-titer antinuclear antibodies (>1:1000) and 52-kD anti-SSa/Ro and anti-SSb/La positivity. Beginning on day 11, he developed progressive respiratory failure requiring supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators, and diuretics. A chest CT on day 36 showed bilateral areas of diffuse ground-glass opacity and air bronchograms. On day 39, invasive mechanical ventilation was initiated for presumed acute pulmonary edema; he had fever, elevated C-reactive protein, and blood and urine cultures positive for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, and he received 14 days of antibiotics. A permanent pacemaker was placed on day 50, with transient clinical improvement. Two days later, he again developed fever and elevated C-reactive protein but had negative cultures and completed another week of antibiotics. He was weaned to high-flow nasal cannula by day 64 but required reintubation within 24 hours of weaning. Inflammatory markers remained normal, cultures were repeatedly negative, and a follow-up chest CT demonstrated progression of the bilateral ground-glass opacities.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 1-day history of left groin pain that was gradually improving. He had a remote motor vehicle accident 1.5 years earlier complicated by urinary frequency and occasional incontinence. On examination, the left testicle and epididymis were tender without significant swelling or systemic signs of inflammation. High-frequency color-Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum revealed a heterogeneous, hypoechoic, avascular lesion in the superior left testis and bilateral microlithiasis. He was started on antibiotics for possible epididymoorchitis. Serum alfa-1 fetoprotein and β-HCG levels were within normal limits. A repeat ultrasound 6 days later showed interval enlargement of the hypoechoic center of the lesion.

A 3-year-old Karan boy from a Myanmar border village was referred for evaluation of nonproductive cough of 1 month and progressive abdominal distension with low-grade fever of 2 weeks. His weight (10 kg) was below the third percentile, and he appeared severely malnourished and pale. He had no history of contact with tuberculosis. He regularly consumed undercooked mountain crabs.

On examination, he was mildly tachycardic and tachypneic, with an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed fine crepitations in the right upper lobe and decreased breath sounds in the right lower lobe. Heart sounds were distant. He had pale conjunctiva, hepatosplenomegaly, and multiple cervical lymphadenopathies.

Laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 27%, a white-cell count of 22 510 cells/mm3 with 14% eosinophils, and platelets of 917 000 cells/mm3. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated, albumin was 3.3 g/dL, and globulin was 8.5 g/dL. A sputum acid-fast–bacilli smear was negative, and a tuberculin skin test was negative.

A chest radiograph demonstrated haziness in the right middle lobe and minimal reticulonodular infiltration in both upper lung fields. Abdominal ultrasound revealed marked ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, and a small pericardial effusion (0.68 cm).

A 6-year-old girl was brought to a rural primary-care emergency center in Bangladesh with vaginal bleeding of 2 hours’ duration. The child’s mother reported that the bleeding began mildly but increased over time; there were no other bleeding sites, and no history of trauma or sexual abuse. The girl had no significant past medical history and was fully immunized. On arrival she was pale and anxious. Vital signs: blood pressure 95/65 mm Hg, pulse 118 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min. Her weight and height were age-appropriate. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Perineal packing revealed active bleeding from the external genitalia; the hymen was intact and there were no signs of injury to external structures. After fluid resuscitation, she was taken to the operating room and placed under deep sedation. A thorough perineal inspection again showed no lacerations or trauma. Bright red blood and clots were noted at the vaginal introitus. Clots were removed, and bleeding from within the vagina was confirmed. Further history elicited that she had swum in a nearby pond just before the onset of bleeding.

A 21-year-old man was referred for numerous asymptomatic hypopigmented skin lesions that had appeared 10 years earlier. The lesions persisted and gradually increased in number, becoming widely disseminated. He had no history of systemic disease, phototherapy, or UV exposure; family history was unremarkable. On examination, there were numerous 2–5 mm hypopigmented, nonfollicular, keratotic lichenoid papules symmetrically distributed over the entire body, some coalescing into larger linear plaques on the extensor surfaces of the upper arms. Multiple direct mycological examinations and fungal cultures of scale were negative. Histopathologic examination showed orthohyperkeratosis, irregular acanthosis, and sporadic papillomatosis. Routine laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and chest radiography, were all normal.

A 24-year-old previously healthy man presented with a one-week history of gradual onset of right-sided body weakness associated with fever, headache, and vomiting. He denied trauma, seizures, bleeding diathesis, or recent dental procedures. On examination, he was alert and oriented. Vital signs were within normal limits. Notable findings included bilateral digital clubbing and a pulmonary bruit heard over the left lung base accentuated by inspiration. He was neither cyanotic nor hypoxic. Neurologic examination showed Medical Research Council grade 4/5 weakness of the right upper and lower limbs, brisk reflexes, decreased tone on the right, and a positive right Babinski reflex; cranial nerves were intact. Oral examination revealed poor hygiene and dental caries; there were no mucocutaneous telangiectasias. Laboratory studies, including differential white blood cell count and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits. Urgent contrast-enhanced CT of the brain demonstrated a rim-enhancing lesion with perilesional edema in the left parietal lobe consistent with an abscess. A chest radiograph obtained because of the pulmonary bruit showed a well-demarcated, lobulated radio-opaque nodule in the left lower lung zone.

A 55-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for evaluation of a 1-year history of progressive peripheral visual field loss, nyctalopia, and dyschromatopsia. She noted onset of symptoms shortly after beginning ezetimibe, 10 mg daily, for hypercholesterolaemia. Her medical history was notable for statin intolerance, asthma, and rosacea; there was no family history of retinal dystrophy, and prior ocular examinations had been normal.

On examination, visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and 6/7.5 in the left eye with her usual multifocal correction. Pupils were equal and reactive without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Humphrey 30-2 perimetry confirmed repeatable concentric constriction bilaterally. Colour vision testing with Ishihara plates showed 1/17 correct plates in each eye. 

Within four weeks of stopping ezetimibe, full-field and multifocal ERG, pattern ERG, and multifocal VEP were reported as unremarkable. Funduscopic examination revealed normal optic nerves with no retinal lesions or intraocular inflammation. Optical coherence tomography of the maculae and retinal nerve fibre layers was normal. MRI of the brain, optic apparatus, and orbits showed no abnormalities. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, pituitary profile, inflammatory markers, an autoantibody panel (anti-retinal antibodies, anti-nuclear antibody, anti-dsDNA, extractable nuclear antigens, complement studies, lupus anticoagulant), serum electrophoresis, and thrombophilia screening—were all within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound and chest radiography were unremarkable. This workup for carcinoma-associated retinopathy was negative.

A 60-year-old immunocompetent Japanese man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented in December 2021 with fever, headache, sore throat, and lumbar pain. His medications included vildagliptin, metformin, and luseogliflozin. He had received his second dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine 10 days before presentation. The day after vaccination, he developed fatigue, lumbar pain, and a severe headache. Two days later, he noted a temperature of 38 °C and sore throat. Seven days after vaccination, he experienced numbness and tingling pain in the right forehead. A noncontrast head CT was normal.

On day 10 after vaccination, he presented to the emergency department. He reported that his worst symptom was a tightening headache across the entire head, predominantly in the right frontal and temporal regions; the pain was intermittent and worsened even with light touch of the hair. His temperature was 36.4 °C and other vital signs were normal. Examination revealed no skin lesions, no nuchal rigidity, and a negative jolt accentuation test. Laboratory tests were unremarkable except for a mildly elevated C-reactive protein level of 0.27 mg/dL (reference, 0–0.14). He received oral acetaminophen and was discharged.

Two days later, he was seen in general medicine. He was afebrile and his fatigue, lumbar pain, and sore throat had nearly resolved, but headache and right forehead numbness persisted. He was thought to have vaccine side effects complicated by trigeminal neuralgia and was started on carbamazepine 400 mg/day. After two weeks, his symptoms had only slightly improved, with persistent severe pain. He was then switched to amitriptyline 10 mg daily, after which his pain dramatically improved within a few days.

A 73-year-old man presented with 3 days of lethargy and anorexia. His history was notable for metastatic melanoma treated with 7 cycles of pembrolizumab, discontinued 9 weeks earlier because of immune-related retinopathy, for which he was on prednisolone 25 mg daily and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis prophylaxis. On examination, he was jaundiced but alert, without asterixis; the abdomen was soft and non-tender. Laboratory studies on admission showed: alkaline phosphatase 354 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 839 U/L, alanine transaminase 1341 U/L, total bilirubin 60 μmol/L, and preserved synthetic function. Viral hepatitis serologies were negative. Autoimmune testing revealed an antinuclear antibody titer >1:1280, with other autoimmune hepatitis markers negative. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated no biliary tract obstruction, no hepatic metastases, and no portal vein thrombosis.

A 63-year-old Indonesian man presented with 1 week of sudden-onset binocular horizontal diplopia, constant and worse on left gaze, and left facial muscle weakness. He denied changes in visual acuity, trauma, or prior similar episodes. His history included 10 years of hypertension on treatment and left-eye anisometropic amblyopia; he had no smoking or drug use. Vital signs were normal. Visual acuity was 0.8 in the right eye and 0.08 in the left. Primary gaze was orthotropic; red glass testing showed uncrossed diplopia. On left gaze, the right eye failed to adduct and the left eye failed to abduct; there was no nystagmus. Eyelid position, pupillary reactions, color vision, and visual fields were intact. Anterior segment was unremarkable; fundus exam showed myopic changes with sharp optic disc margins bilaterally. Neurologic exam revealed left facial nerve palsy with incomplete eyelid closure, inability to raise the left eyebrow, and forehead involvement; the remainder of the exam was normal. Blood glucose and lipid profile were within normal limits. Brain MRI (T2W FLAIR) showed hyperintense periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles (“Dawson’s fingers”), multiple small round hyperintense lesions in the cortex and juxtacortical cerebellar hemispheres with post-contrast enhancement, and a small hyperintense lesion in the left paramedian pontine reticular formation in the dorsal pons with post-contrast enhancement. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated hyperintensity attributable to T2 shine through, with normal apparent diffusion coefficient maps, effectively excluding acute ischemia.

A previously healthy 5-year-old girl presented to the pediatric emergency department in generalized tonic-clonic status epilepticus and fever. Two months earlier, she had been treated for right medial clavicular sterile osteomyelitis with intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin. On arrival, she was febrile (39 °C), tachycardic (142 beats/min), tachypneic (36 breaths/min), and ill-appearing; blood pressure was 131/94 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% on a non-rebreather mask. After seizure termination with lorazepam and phenytoin, she exhibited hypoventilation requiring intubation. Neurologic examination showed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9, bilaterally reactive pupils, strong gag and cough reflexes, and no focal deficits. 

Initial investigations, including CSF studies (protein 0.28 g/L, glucose 4.1 mmol/L, 1 WBC/µL, 1 RBC/µL with rare lymphocytes), extensive infectious serologies (including tuberculosis and brucellosis), metabolic, hematologic, immunodeficiency, and genetic testing (primary immunodeficiency panel, whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing) were unrevealing. Inflammatory markers were elevated (CRP 106 mg/L, ESR 47 mm/hr, von Willebrand factor >199.5%). Brain CT was normal; EEG showed diffuse nonspecific slowing without epileptiform discharges.

On hospital day 1, she developed signs of raised intracranial pressure—fixed dilated pupils, bradycardia, hypertension—and bilateral papilledema. CT angiography revealed multiple hypodensities, diffuse cerebral edema with a 5 mm midline shift, and impending right uncal herniation. First-tier intracranial pressure–lowering measures were instituted: head elevation to 30°, sedation, hyperventilation targeting PaCO₂ 35–40 mmHg, osmotherapy with 3% NaCl and mannitol, maintenance of MAP >60 mmHg, and normothermia. Concurrently, vasculitis–directed therapy was begun with IVIG (1 g/kg) and methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day for 5 days), followed by maintenance steroids and monthly cyclophosphamide. 

Brain MRI/MRA demonstrated diffuse T2 hyperintensity and swelling of the right cortex, vessel-wall enhancement of the middle cerebral arteries, and irregularity of the M1 and M2 segments bilaterally. Despite these therapies, she continued to show clinical and radiologic signs of refractory elevated intracranial pressure.

A 30‐year‐old woman presented with a 4-month history of intermittent, colicky abdominal pain localized to the epigastrium and left hypochondrium. The pain was mild, non-radiating, and exacerbated by fatty meals. She reported occasional nausea without vomiting, and denied fever, jaundice, changes in bowel habits, or weight loss. Her medical and surgical history was notable only for a cesarean section three years earlier, and she had been diagnosed incidentally with situs inversus totalis during a routine medical examination. 

On examination, she was afebrile and in no acute distress. Cardiac auscultation revealed normal heart sounds on the right side of the chest. Abdominal examination showed mild tenderness in the left upper quadrant without guarding. Laboratory tests demonstrated a white-cell count of 9800/mm^3 and normal liver-function tests. 

Chest radiography confirmed dextrocardia with a right-sided gastric bubble and a left-sided liver shadow. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple echogenic foci, 3–7 mm in size, within the gallbladder and a common bile duct diameter of 6 mm.

A 13-year-old Syrian female was evaluated for severe cutaneous ulceration and scarring of the face and hands, accompanied by dyspigmentation. Her parents reported that symptoms began in her first year of life with skin redness and blistering in sun-exposed areas, progressing to ulcers, scarring, and deformity of the nose, hands, and fingers. There was also a history of urine discoloration in early childhood. There was no family history of similar symptoms or consanguinity. 

On physical examination, the face showed areas of dyspigmentation and hypertrichosis on the cheeks and forehead, crusted old ulcers, and a sclerodermatous appearance with linear and spotted atrophic lesions; the nose was severely deformed and scarred. The teeth exhibited reddish-brown discoloration under visible light. Eye examination revealed conjunctivitis, scleromalacia, and mild blepharitis without corneal injury. The dorsum of the hands had extensive ulcerations with sclerodermatous changes and acrolysis of the distal phalanges. The liver was palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin; the spleen was not palpable. Under Wood’s lamp, there was bright red fluorescence of the teeth and bright green fluorescence in the interdigital spaces of the hands.

A 24-hour urine porphyrin profile showed markedly elevated uroporphyrins (9820 nmol/24 h; reference ≤30) and coproporphyrin I (2514 nmol/24 h; reference ≤168).

A previously healthy 23-year-old man presented with general malaise and a one-week history of progressively worsening sore throat. He reported low-grade fever, dyspnea, and inspiratory chest pain but denied gastrointestinal symptoms, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or hemoptysis and had no history of smoking, alcohol use, illicit drugs, or recent travel. On examination, he was tachycardic (150 beats/min), hypotensive (97/50 mmHg), tachypneic (28 breaths/min), febrile (39.0 °C), and required 4 L/min of oxygen to maintain a saturation of 95%. He had pharyngeal erythema, cervical lymphadenopathy, and tenderness over the anterior neck without restriction of movement. Lung auscultation revealed reduced air entry and inspiratory crackles at both bases; the cardiovascular, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory findings included leukocytosis (26.4 × 10^9 cells/L) with neutrophilia, thrombocytopenia (28 × 10^9 cells/L), C-reactive protein 250 mg/L, urea 14.8 mmol/L, creatinine 180 µmol/L, bilirubin 21 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 196 IU/L, and a positive D-dimer. Chest radiography showed multiple pulmonary opacities, a cavitating lesion in the left upper lobe, and bilateral pleural effusions. Urinary Legionella and pneumococcal antigen tests, throat culture, HIV, and mononucleosis screens were negative; cerebrospinal fluid analysis and echocardiography were normal. Despite fluid resuscitation, hypotension persisted, and he was transferred to the intensive care unit for inotropic support and treated with intravenous benzylpenicillin and clarithromycin. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed numerous bilateral pulmonary nodules with varying degrees of cavitation and necrosis, along with bilateral pleural effusions.

A 51-year-old woman presents with a painless lump in her left breast that she first noticed 12 years ago. Two weeks after a motor vehicle collision with a seatbelt injury to her chest, she detected an inner-quadrant breast mass. The lesion remained stable, with only slight firmness in recent years, until it began to enlarge over the past 4 months. She reports no pain, skin changes, nipple discharge, fever, or systemic symptoms.

On examination, there is mild asymmetry of the left breast and a firm, non-tender mass in the inner quadrant. The overlying skin is intact without erythema or warmth, and there is no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. The patient is otherwise clinically stable.

Breast ultrasound demonstrates a large, complex, partially visualized avascular mass composed of two interconnected components: one isoechoic to hypoechoic circumscribed mass with a thick calcified wall and posterior acoustic shadowing, which transitions into a hypoechoic region with partially circumscribed and partially indistinct margins.

A 39-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder, epilepsy, and asthma was admitted for an acute psychotic episode. During evaluation she was noted to be cachectic, reporting intermittent non-bilious vomiting, anorexia, and a 51-kg weight loss over 3 years; she denied abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, or fevers. Her last menstrual period was over 6 months ago. She had no history of tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drug use.  
On examination, her temperature was 36.9 °C, pulse 85 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, blood pressure 121/67 mm Hg, and BMI 17. She appeared cachectic with marked muscle wasting. Abdominal examination revealed a firm, non-tender, partly mobile mass in the upper abdomen; bowel sounds were normoactive. Rectal exam was normal.  
Laboratory studies showed a microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL, hematocrit 18.9%); she received transfusion. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a normal esophagus but, on advancement, the scope appeared to pass directly into the small intestine with no visible stomach; retroflexion showed the gastroesophageal junction with only a remnant of the gastric cardia.  
A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated a 23.7 × 12 × 7.5 cm mass extending from the left upper to the right lower quadrant, representing invagination of the stomach into the duodenum consistent with gastroduodenal intussusception; there was secondary dilation of the distal esophagus to 5.8 cm and compression of the pancreas and hepatic flexure of the colon.

A 35‐year‐old Japanese woman was referred to the Marfan syndrome center for follow‐up care. She had been suspected to have Marfan syndrome in childhood because of spider‐like fingers, a left inguinal hernia, scoliosis, and mitral valve prolapse. She underwent posterior spinal fusion for scoliosis at age 13 and was advised to limit athletic activities. 

On examination at age 29, her height was 167 cm, weight 50 kg, and arm span 173 cm (arm span/height = 1.04). She had arachnodactyly with mild camptodactyly, a positive thumb sign, pectus excavatum, left hindfoot deformity, reduced elbow extension, and dural ectasia. Cardiac auscultation revealed a midsystolic click consistent with mild mitral valve prolapse. The external ears appeared normal. Her systemic score for Marfan syndrome was ≥7 points.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed no dilatation of the sinuses of Valsalva (30 mm; Z-score 1.23). Ophthalmologic examination revealed no lens dislocation. She did not meet the revised Ghent criteria for Marfan syndrome.

At age 35, hybridization capture–based next‐generation sequencing of a hereditary thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection panel (including FBN1, FBN2, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3, TGFB2, TGFB3, ACTA2, MYH11, MYLK, COL3A1, EFEMP2, FLNA, and SLC2A10) was performed.

A 35-year-old woman with right breast cancer status post lumpectomy and chemotherapy in July 2020 presented in December 2020 with progressive shortness of breath, cough, and systemic “intoxication” symptoms. Bacterial cultures and bacilloscopy of bronchoalveolar lavage, bronchial aspirate, and biopsy specimens were all negative. Initially, COVID-19 was suspected, and despite a negative SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR result, she was treated for COVID-19 without improvement; her serological reactions to SARS-CoV-2 were also negative. Laboratory testing revealed marked eosinophilia (2640 mm3) and mild elevations in ferritin, interleukin-6, and C-reactive protein, with otherwise normal routine blood tests. Serial measurements from August to December showed a linear increase in the eosinophil percentage, reaching 28.78% when her respiratory failure began. Chest CT initially showed normal pulmonary parenchyma but later revealed unilateral inflammatory foci localized to the upper and middle lobes of the right lung, with lobar-segmental distribution. After eosinophils reached their maximum value and correlation with clinical and CT findings, a decision was made to initiate glucocorticoid therapy.

An 80-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 3-week history of intermittent fevers up to 101.4°F with chills, occipital headache, and recurrent falls. He denied neck pain, rash, visual changes, photophobia, phonophobia, chest pain apart from stable angina managed with sublingual nitroglycerin, palpitations, cough, or weight loss. His medical history included coronary artery disease, prior stroke, patent foramen ovale repair, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and gout. Medications were aspirin, atorvastatin, finasteride, and tamsulosin.

On examination he was febrile (101.4°F), blood pressure 162/80 mm Hg, pulse 110/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiovascular exam showed sinus tachycardia and a grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur; the thyroid was not enlarged or tender and there was no lymphadenopathy or rash. Neurologic and other system examinations were unremarkable.

Initial investigations included a normal white-cell count, negative chest radiograph, and negative blood and urine cultures. A head CT showed only old infarcts. Four days later, persistent fever prompted re-admission: ESR was 86 mm/hr and CRP 192 mg/L. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiograms showed no vegetations. A contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a heterogeneous thyroid gland with surrounding hazy changes. Thyroid function tests showed total T3 6 ng/dL, free T4 2.55 ng/dL, and TSH 0.01 mIU/mL. Thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase antibodies were undetectable. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated an enlarged, heterogeneous right lobe (6.5 × 3.1 × 2.7 cm) and isthmus (1.4 cm AP) without discrete nodules and with mildly increased intrinsic vascularity.

A male infant (birth weight 3450 g) was born at 39 weeks’ gestation by uncomplicated vaginal delivery in cephalic presentation. There was no history of birth trauma. Apgar scores were 9 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. On day 1 of life, left scrotal swelling and bluish discoloration were noted. Physical examination showed a tender, swollen left scrotum without abdominal distention.

Scrotal ultrasonography with power Doppler demonstrated a normally echogenic left testis with preserved vascular flow and a collection of hematic fluid in the left scrotum. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous fluid collection beneath the right lobe of the liver.

An abdominal CT scan was performed and identified a right adrenal hematoma without evidence of hemoperitoneum.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 234 000/mm^3, normal coagulation tests, total bilirubin 5.4 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL.

A 42-year-old athletic woman presented with right groin pain of 2 years’ duration, initially associated with jogging and progressively limiting her daily and sporting activities. On examination, she had a positive impingement test and internal rotation limited to 20° at 90° of hip flexion. Plain anteroposterior and lateral radiographs showed a normal alpha angle and a 12×14 mm calcified irregular lesion at the superolateral acetabular rim. Excluding the lesion, the center-edge angle was 15° (25° on the contralateral side), and the Tönnis angle was 24°. A CT scan confirmed a 12×14 mm bony fragment adjacent to the joint surface at the superolateral rim, and the anteroinferior iliac spine was intact.

A 48-year-old Japanese woman with high myopia presented with decreased vision in her left eye. Axial lengths were 29.0 mm (right) and 28.7 mm (left), with refractive errors of –11.5 and –10.5 diopters; best-corrected visual acuity was 20/28 and 20/16. Mild cataract was noted in both eyes. Fundoscopy and optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the left eye showed an epiretinal membrane and a parafoveal yellow-grayish spot. 

Three years later, she reported blurred vision in the left eye; BCVA fell to 20/33 and OCT revealed thickening of the epiretinal membrane. She underwent pars plana vitrectomy with epiretinal membrane and internal limiting membrane peeling in the left eye. Six months postoperatively, BCVA was 20/28; fundoscopy demonstrated chorioretinal atrophy in the parafovea and OCT showed irregularities of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) with increased transmission signal from the sclera, suggesting RPE atrophy.

Three weeks thereafter, BCVA decreased acutely to 20/100. OCT revealed elevation of the RPE with disruption of the ellipsoid and interdigitation zones and an increase in choroidal thickness at that site from 134 µm to 151 µm. Fluorescein angiography showed early hyperfluorescence without leakage at the corresponding site, and no evidence of choroidal neovascularization (CNV) or lacquer crack. Indocyanine green angiography did not detect abnormal vessels suggestive of CNV. Because myopic CNV could not be excluded, intravitreal ranibizumab was administered. Two days after injection, vision declined further to 20/222; fundus examination remained unchanged, but OCT revealed a nodule-like outer retinal lesion with RPE disruption and a decrease in choroidal thickness to 142 µm, suggesting punctate inner choroiditis. Careful observation was recommended.

An 84-year-old woman with a history of lacunar infarction managed with antiplatelet therapy sustained an occipital head injury. Initial head CT showed a thin acute subdural hematoma over the left frontal convexity without fractures, and she was neurologically intact. Three weeks later, she presented with new-onset left ptosis, diplopia, and vomiting. Repeat head CT demonstrated bilateral chronic subdural hematomas, larger on the right side. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed a complete left oculomotor nerve palsy with ptosis, diplopia, and a dilated pupil.

A 13-year-old girl with no medical history was referred for orthodontic assessment, during which a panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined radiolucent lesion in the anterior mandible extending from the distal aspect of the left canine to the mesial aspect of the right first premolar. Cone beam CT revealed a 19 × 10.6 mm unilocular radiolucency in the anterior mandible with intact buccal and lingual cortices, slight swelling of the lingual cortex, and no root resorption or displacement. Pulp vitality testing of the left mandibular canine through the right first premolar was positive. Initial differential diagnoses included traumatic bone cyst and odontogenic keratocyst.

A 28-year-old man presented with severe pain in his upper front teeth. On examination, he had a full complement of permanent teeth. The maxillary central incisors appeared broader mesiodistally than usual. The right maxillary lateral incisor was positioned palatally between the central incisor and canine; the left lateral incisor occupied its normal position. A labial groove extended from the middle third to the incisal edge of tooth 11, with extensive discoloration around the groove. Tooth 21 had a large mesiodistal crown dimension without indentations, and a deep carious pit with discoloration on its lingual aspect.  
An intraoral periapical radiograph showed for tooth 11 a single large crown with two roots and two root canals, and for tooth 21 a single wide crown with a fused, mesiodistally broad single root containing two root canals that joined apically (Vertucci type II). In both teeth, caries extended to the pulp. Thermal and electrical pulp testing elicited no response in teeth 11 and 21.

A 52-year-old woman farmer from a rural area was referred for evaluation of a chronic granulomatous lesion of the palate and persistent hoarseness. Three months earlier she had a flu-like illness, but hoarseness persisted. She denied systemic disease and chronic medications. She worked for many years in sugarcane fields and had a 4-year history of nasal crusting and occasional bleeding. She had smoked for 6 months and wore upper and lower complete dentures continuously. 

On examination, she was mouth-breathing, with nasal obstruction and a nasal voice. Extrabuccally, there was drooping of the right nasal ala and a perforated nasal septum. Intrabuccally, there was a granulomatous lesion covering the hard palate, soft palate, uvula, and extending into the oropharynx, with an erythematous surface and several scratchable white plaques.

Initial diagnostic hypotheses included mucosal leishmaniasis, paracoccidioidomycosis, and candidosis. A nystatin oral rinse was prescribed, and hemogram, chest radiograph, and nasal bone radiograph were obtained. The hemogram showed microcytosis, moderate hypochromia, basophilic stippling, and mild polychromasia. Chest imaging revealed increased pulmonary markings. Nasal bone radiograph showed an intact bony septum. Direct mycological examination of the lesion was negative, and there was no clinical improvement after antifungal therapy.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a one-year history of gradually increasing abdominal swelling. Over the past few months she had experienced urinary urgency and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. She reported intermittent cyclic lower abdominal cramps and denied any episodes of menses. She had no fever, diarrhea, constipation, vomiting, or weight loss. Her medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, there was a large, non-tender, non-pulsatile abdominal mass extending from the pelvis to the xiphisternum, predominantly on the right side but crossing the midline. Secondary sexual characteristics were appropriate for her age (Tanner stage IV). Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, urinalysis, and pregnancy test, were all within normal limits. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a large cystic lesion with a thick echoic collection extending from the epigastric region to the pelvis, posterior to the urinary bladder, filling nearly the entire abdominal cavity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a hypodense, non-enhancing, fluid-filled mass within the vaginal canal measuring 28.5 × 11.3 × 12.0 cm, with a small fluid collection in the uterine cavity, and compression of the urinary bladder and distal ureters resulting in moderate bilateral hydroureteronephrosis.

A 6‐year‐old, 31.7-kg spayed female mixed-breed dog was evaluated for a firm subcutaneous mass adjacent to the right mandible. Three months earlier, the dog had a 3-cm mass near the right mandibular lymph node, associated with hyporexia and lethargy. Initial hematology, serum biochemistry, urinalysis, thoracic radiographs, and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Fine-needle aspirates showed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilic infiltrates. The dog was treated empirically with tramadol, ciprofloxacin, and clindamycin.

One week later, mandibular swelling worsened. CT revealed a 3.5-cm, right-sided, soft-tissue-attenuating, mildly contrast-enhancing retrobulbar mass extending cranially to the caudal maxilla and medially to the nasopharynx, with severe enlargement of the retropharyngeal and mandibular lymph nodes. An incisional biopsy showed marked granulomatous and eosinophilic inflammation with fibrosis; periodic acid–Schiff and Grocott’s methenamine silver stains were negative, and aerobic, anaerobic, and fungal cultures were negative. Prednisone was instituted, and the mass transiently decreased.

Six weeks later, follow-up CT showed progression of the lesion from the tympanic bulla to the pterygoid bone and ventrally to the mandibular lymph node. An en bloc removal of the right mandibular lymph node and adjacent tissue was performed. Histopathology revealed pyogranulomatous lymphadenitis with irregular, nonseptate, PAS- and GMS-positive bulbous hyphal organisms and vascular encroachment. A presumptive diagnosis of mucormycosis was made, and itraconazole was initiated.

Two weeks later, the dog was referred for hyperbaric oxygen therapy. On presentation, vital signs were normal. A 6-cm fluctuant mass was palpable caudoventral to the right mandibular ramus and a firm mass over the right caudal maxilla extending into the ventral orbit. Fine-needle aspiration yielded 125 mL of serous fluid. The lesions and signalment were considered most consistent with an oomycete or zygomycete infection. Punch biopsies were submitted for fungal and oomycete culture and susceptibility testing. Prednisone and hyperbaric oxygen therapy were started.

Three weeks later, the dog acutely became blind in both eyes. Neurologic examination revealed absent menace responses bilaterally, decreased conscious proprioception in the left pelvic limb, and preservation of direct and consensual pupillary light reflexes OD (right eye) but an inconsistent consensual response OS (left eye). The remainder of the neurologic and ophthalmologic examination was unremarkable. Lesion localization was multifocal, with evidence for both cortical and spinal cord involvement. Laboratory testing showed mild hypoalbuminemia (2.5 g/dL), mild blood urea nitrogen elevation (36 mg/dL), and moderate hypoglycemia (55 mg/dL). Mean systolic blood pressure was 110 mm Hg. Magnetic resonance imaging was declined by the owner.

A 60-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation and prior cerebral infarction presented with 38 hours of progressive left testicular pain without trauma. Physical examination findings were not detailed in the report. Emergency scrotal ultrasound was performed:

• 2D gray-scale ultrasonography showed a well-defined, heterogeneous hypoechoic area measuring approximately 16 × 11 × 10 mm within the left testis; the surrounding parenchyma appeared homogeneous.  
• Color Doppler flow imaging and color Doppler energy detected no blood flow or energy signal within the lesion, with normal signals in the remainder of the testis.  
• Contrast-enhanced ultrasound revealed a 20 × 15 mm patchy area of no enhancement in the left testicular parenchyma during the arterial, venous, and delayed phases; contrast filled the surrounding tissue starting at 45 seconds, peaked at 60 seconds, and faded by 80 seconds.  
• Quantitative CEUS parameters comparing the lesion to adjacent normal tissue showed delayed time to peak (29.32 s vs. 18.42 s), shorter rise time (5.67 s vs. 11.67 s), and reduced maximum intensity (61.9% vs. 100%), consistent with hypoperfusion.  
• Laboratory studies revealed mildly elevated C-reactive protein and leukocyte count; testicular tumor markers were negative.

A 65-year-old man presented with a one-month history of cough, sputum production, and chest pain. He was a 40 pack-year current smoker with no significant medical history. On admission, his temperature was 36.5 °C, respiratory rate 18/min, and moist rales were heard over the left lung. Arterial blood gas on room air showed PaO2 69 mmHg, PaCO2 36 mmHg, and pH 7.43. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 7.99 × 10^9 cells/l, 69% neutrophils, and a C-reactive protein level of 36.38 mg/l. Electrolytes, renal and liver function tests were normal. Serologic tests for tumor markers, Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Coxiella psittaci, hepatitis B and C viruses, and HIV were negative. Tests for antinuclear antibodies, P-ANCA, c-ANCA, and cyclic citrullinated protein antibodies were negative.

High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated extensive high-density shadows in the left lung with air bronchograms, pleural thickening, and enlargement of hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes without abnormal enhancement. Bronchoscopic examination showed mucosal thickening and tracheobronchial stenosis in the left lung; transbronchial biopsy revealed interstitial fibrous tissue hyperplasia and chronic inflammatory cell infiltration. After a 10-day course of amoxicillin–clavulanic acid and roxithromycin, his symptoms improved but the CT findings remained unchanged. Percutaneous lung biopsy from the left lower lobe again showed nonspecific interstitial fibrosis and chronic inflammation. One month later, PET-CT demonstrated persistent left-lung high-density opacities with increased uptake, favoring inflammation but “without the exception of adenocarcinoma.” A second percutaneous biopsy and EBUS-TBNA both yielded only chronic inflammatory changes with no tumor cells. No definitive diagnosis was established, and the patient declined open lung biopsy.

A woman in her seventies presented with altered bowel habit, anorexia, and abdominal discomfort. She had a history of diverticulosis and no intrauterine device use. On examination, her abdomen was distended with left iliac fossa tenderness. Laboratory studies showed elevated inflammatory markers and normal tumor markers (CA 125, 10 U/mL; CEA, 1 ng/mL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a heterogeneous mass causing large-bowel obstruction at the sigmoid colon with internal calcifications. She underwent a laparoscopic defunctioning sigmoid loop colostomy. One month later, follow-up CT demonstrated progression of the ill-defined pelvic mass directly involving the uterine fundus with associated hydronephroureter. Sigmoidoscopy revealed sigmoid diverticula and a benign-appearing stricture; biopsies showed mild inflammation without features of malignancy. MRI demonstrated involvement of the uterus, left adnexa, and mesenteric root, broadening the differential diagnosis.

A 39-year-old previously healthy Hispanic woman presents with a 4-year history of right knee pain and intermittent purulent drainage. The symptoms began days after she felt a “prick” while kneeling; no obvious wound was noted. She developed warmth, progressive swelling, and pustules with purulent oozing.  
 
Initial management by her primary care physician included a 10-day course of ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin-clavulanate for presumed cellulitis, but the findings persisted. She was referred for an arthrotomy and debridement for suspected septic prepatellar bursitis; intraoperative cultures showed no growth, and she received 6 weeks of high-dose IV penicillin G with temporary improvement. Over the next three years, she had recurrent pustules and drainage managed with multiple antibiotic regimens.  

An MRI of the knee revealed an extensive phlegmon with inflammatory changes, synovitis in Hoffa’s fat pad, and irregularity of the inferior joint capsule. She was referred to the Musculoskeletal Oncology Clinic due to concerns for malignancy in the setting of a suspected recurrent infectious process.  

On examination she was afebrile without systemic symptoms. The right knee was warm and tender, with multiple anterior-inferior sinus tracts draining serosanguineous fluid. Range of motion and neurovascular status were preserved. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 5.8 × 10^3/ml, an ESR of 63 mm/h, and a CRP of 19.8 mg/l. Imaging review supported a persistent right knee infection, and she was scheduled for excisional debridement of the suspected phlegmon.

A 74-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of low back pain and right-sided sciatica. The pain began after lifting, causing back strain, and initially resolved in 4 days. One week before admission, he experienced a severe recurrence of backache; three days later the pain radiated to his right buttock, posterior thigh, ankle, and big toe. The pain was nearly constant and worsened with strenuous activity. He denied paresthesia, contralateral symptoms, or bladder dysfunction. His medical history was unremarkable, and he was not taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications. Neurological examination showed a right steppage gait, normal spinal range of motion, a negative straight leg raising test, sensory depression in the right L4 and L5 dermatomes, and weakness of right foot dorsiflexion. Routine laboratory tests were normal. MRI of the lumbar spine revealed a well-defined dorsal extradural lesion at the L3–L4 levels, posterior to the L4 vertebral body, associated with an L3–L4 disc protrusion and apparent connection to that level. T1-weighted images showed heterogeneous intermediate to high signal intensity; T2-weighted images showed high signal intensity; and gadolinium-enhanced images demonstrated rim enhancement of the lesion. Based on these findings, the differential diagnosis included disc herniation, tumor, and hematoma. Due to the severity of his pain, surgical intervention was planned.

A 19-year-old woman presented with missing teeth for the past 15 years and heat intolerance with reduced perspiration. She reported delayed eruption of permanent teeth that became carious and exfoliated. Her parents were first cousins but asymptomatic; one elder sister had milder similar features. Antenatal and birth history were unremarkable.

On examination, she was calm and of normal intelligence but of shorter stature than her siblings. Facial features included a concave profile with prognathic mandible, reduced anterior facial height, and mild periorbital hyperpigmentation with wrinkling. Scalp hair was thin, lustreless, with a receding hairline and premature graying. There was a crusted lesion below the right nostril. Hand and finger morphology was normal; toes were broad, short, and widely spaced; nails appeared normal. Body temperature was 99°F.

Intraoral examination showed 16 missing teeth, multiple root stumps, and erupted teeth that were small, hypoplastic, and microdontic. Both arches were underdeveloped with decreased vertical bone height and shallow sulci. Radiographs confirmed multiple missing and submerged teeth, periradicular radiolucencies, maxillary hypoplasia, prognathic mandible, and reduced facial height.

A sweat pore count test with 2% iodine in alcohol showed markedly decreased visible sweat pores, indicating hypohidrosis.

A 62-year-old woman was admitted with six months of progressive, confluent red scaly plaques that began on the scalp and eventually involved 100% of her body surface area. Initial scalp lesions were diagnosed as psoriasis and treated with topical corticosteroids without benefit. Two months later she developed widespread plaques accompanied by hair loss and nail plate thickening; a skin biopsy at that time was nondiagnostic. Oral methotrexate 10 mg weekly was given for 6 weeks, but her rash and overall condition worsened, with new lesions on the torso and thighs. She also had a COVID-19 infection two weeks before admission. 

On examination, she was afebrile (37.3 °C) and had diffuse erythroderma with extensive scaling, punched-out erosions on the torso and thighs, lower eyelid ectropion, scalp alopecia, and yellow thickened nail plates. Movement was painful due to inflammation. Her history was notable for depression and a nodular goiter.

Laboratory studies showed a high-normal leukocyte count (9.85 × 10^9/L) with mild neutrophilia (7.90 × 10^9/L), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (30 mm/h), normal C-reactive protein, normal liver and kidney function, mild proteinuria (0.2 g/L), glucosuria (2.8 mmol/L), and hypoproteinemia (80.2 g/L, decreasing to 63.8 g/L). PCR testing of skin lesions was positive for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, and cultures grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. 

Given the possibilities of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and paraneoplastic or hematologic causes of erythroderma, the patient underwent chest radiography, abdominal ultrasound, transvaginal ultrasound, colonoscopy, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, peripheral blood microscopy, T-cell receptor gene clonality testing, and flow cytometry; all studies were unremarkable.

An 81-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, prior cerebrovascular accident, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a 60 pack-year smoking history presented after a witnessed non-mechanical fall “several hours” earlier. She had new left facial droop and slurred speech without head trauma. Home medications included atorvastatin, ticagrelor, and metformin. 

On arrival, she was asymptomatic but hypotensive and tachycardic: temperature 98.5°F, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, heart rate 110/min, oxygen saturation 93% on room air. She was confused (GCS 14, best verbal response). Initial laboratory tests showed troponin 2.60 ng/ml (≤0.05) and creatinine 2.19 mg/dl (0.60–1.20). Other admission labs included mild leukocytosis and elevated BUN. 

ECG showed minimal ST-segment elevation and T-wave inversion in leads V2–V3. Non-contrast head CT revealed only chronic microvascular changes without acute pathology. She received aspirin and heparin. Repeat troponin fell to 1.98 ng/ml after 1 hour. Serial ECGs showed transient resolution of ST elevation with subsequent biphasic T-wave inversions in leads V1–V6. Brain MRI and MR angiography of head and neck were unremarkable.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated mid-anteroseptal and apical akinesis with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40–45%.

A 55-year-old man originally from Eritrea, living in the Netherlands for over 20 years, underwent a Bentall procedure with a mechanical aortic valve in 2015 for aortic-root dilatation and valve insufficiency. In July 2018, he was referred for evaluation of progressive fatigue and unintentional weight loss. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 111 mm/h, serum creatinine of 161 µmol/L, and hemoglobin of 4.8 mmol/L (MCV 85 fL). Iron studies revealed mild iron deficiency (ferritin 233 µg/L, transferrin-iron saturation 42 µmol/L). Urinalysis demonstrated mild proteinuria (albumin-to-creatinine ratio 24 mg/mmol) and microscopic hematuria (3–10 erythrocytes per high-power field) without overt signs of glomerulonephritis. The patient initially declined further workup. 

Over the following months, his condition worsened with marked weight loss and pallor. The ESR was 95 mm/h, hemoglobin stabilized at 6.7 mmol/L, hematuria increased, and renal function deteriorated further. The differential diagnosis at this point included a vasculitis or a paraneoplastic condition. Further testing revealed an elevated anti–glomerular basement membrane antibody level (40 U/mL). A PET-CT scan demonstrated high F-FDG uptake around the prosthetic aortic valve and aortic graft, suggesting infection of the Bentall prosthesis.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of persistent left iliac fossa pain, suprapubic discomfort during micturition, nausea, and vomiting. Her surgical history included splenectomy at age 6 for hereditary spherocytosis and cholecystectomy at age 22. Examination revealed normal vital signs, abdominal distension, and direct and rebound tenderness in the pelvis. Laboratory tests showed metabolic acidosis, elevated serum lactate and amylase, neutrophilic leukocytosis (13.6 × 10^9 cells/L), elevated C-reactive protein (10.6 mg/dL), and thrombocytosis (409 × 10^9 cells/L); renal function and β-hCG were normal. Plain abdominal radiographs were unremarkable. A dual-phase contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated several enhancing masses up to 5 cm in the abdomen and pelvis, a pelvic mass with poor enhancement and surrounding fat stranding, a small amount of fluid in the recto-uterine pouch, and an enhancing lesion in segment 1 of the liver; no other abnormalities were noted.

A 45-year-old woman presents with intermittent right posterolateral knee pain. The pain began after increasing her walking exercise over the past few weeks. She describes sharp pain localized to the back and outer aspect of the knee, especially during end-range knee flexion and extension. 

On examination, there is no joint swelling. Range of motion is full and smooth without crepitus. Ligament testing including anterior and posterior drawer, valgus–varus stress, Lachman’s, pivot-shift, and Apley’s tests are all normal. Manual muscle testing of the knee and ankle muscle groups is normal. Palpation reveals tenderness maximally over a small bony structure posterior to the lateral femoral condyle.

Weight-bearing radiography shows a small ossified sesamoid bone in the lateral head of the gastrocnemius tendon and minimal degenerative changes (Kellgren–Lawrence grade 1). Ultrasound examination shows no joint effusion, synovial thickening, intra-articular loose body, tendon or ligament tear, bursal fluid collection, ganglion cyst, or occult fracture; compression with the probe over the sesamoid reproduces the patient’s pain.

A 24-year-old Yemeni woman presented in April 2017 with a 4-year history of progressive weakness, bone pain, and inability to walk. She reported delayed ambulation, not walking until age 2½, and lifelong difficulty running or climbing stairs. In adolescence she received calcium and vitamin D supplements without improvement. At age 16, during her first pregnancy, she experienced leg pain, difficulty rising from a seated position, and sustained a pelvic fracture during vaginal delivery. Over subsequent years she became bedridden due to severe weakness and generalized bone pain. A neurologic evaluation, including nerve conduction studies, was normal.

There was no family history of similar disease. On examination, her height was 144 cm and weight 49 kg. She had normal dentition and hair. She exhibited generalized muscle weakness and tenderness, bilateral bowing of the femurs, and genu valgus deformities.

Laboratory studies over several years demonstrated persistent hypophosphatemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase activity, low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels, normal serum calcium concentrations, and negative anti-transglutaminase IgA antibodies. In April 2017, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry revealed severe osteoporosis (hip T score −5.0; spine T score −6.0). Radiographs showed osteopenia around hip joints, abnormal pelvic shape, bowing of both femurs, and bilateral genu valgus deformity.

A 46-year-old man presented with palpitations and dyspnea on mild exertion. He had been noted to have an asymptomatic systolic murmur at age 17 but was lost to follow-up. On admission, he had dyspnea with minimal exertion and mild ankle swelling. Cardiac examination revealed an apical systolic murmur (grade 4/6) and a continuous murmur (grade 3/6) at the right parasternal border. Vital signs were: heart rate 85 bpm, blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Lung fields were clear, and the chest radiograph was unremarkable. Routine blood tests were normal except for an elevated NT-proBNP of 700 pg/mL. ECG showed sinus rhythm with premature supraventricular beats, left atrial enlargement, and right ventricular hypertrophy.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated continuous turbulent flow on color Doppler from the right coronary sinus to the roof of the right atrium and severe mitral valve prolapse with flail of the P1 scallop and prolapse of P2 and P3, resulting in severe regurgitation. The left ventricle was dilated (LVEDV 172 mL, LVESV 73 mL) with preserved ejection fraction (58%), and the left atrium was severely dilated (LAVi 85.9 mL/m^2). The right atrium and right ventricle were dilated with mild RV systolic dysfunction (fractional area change 35%), moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary hypertension (systolic PAP 51 mmHg). Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a flow velocity of 5.2 m/s at the right atrial drainage orifice.

Cardiac catheterization revealed a left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs 1.8), mean pulmonary artery pressure 25 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 15 mmHg, and PVR 1.03 Wood units. Coronary angiography showed a large tunnel originating from the right coronary sinus and draining into the right atrium; the origin of the right coronary artery was not identified. Computed tomography angiography revealed an extracardiac, anterior-type tunnel arising from the ascending aorta at the right coronary sinus, coursing anteroinferiorly, making a sharp U-turn toward the roof of the right atrium along the posterior interatrial septum, and draining into the right atrium through a restrictive opening. The distal tunnel was narrower, and the right coronary artery originated from the tunnel near its U-turn.

A 59-year-old man was evaluated for a 1-year history of recurrent palpitations consisting of sudden-onset, regular tachycardia episodes lasting approximately 5 minutes, which had increased in frequency over the past few weeks. He had no prior cardiac disease, took no medications, and had no exercise limitation or cardiovascular risk factors. Vital signs and a general physical examination were unremarkable.  
Baseline ECG showed sinus rhythm at 75 bpm, a PQ interval of 160 ms, QRS duration 107 ms with an incomplete right bundle branch block, no signs of ventricular pre-excitation, and a QTc of 441 ms. Transthoracic echocardiography and stress echocardiography were normal. A 48-hour Holter recording captured one non-sustained atrial tachycardia at 147 bpm without symptoms; clinical tachycardia remained undocumented. In the absence of malignant arrhythmia, supraventricular re-entrant tachycardia was suspected, and the patient was taught vagal maneuvers and instructed on using a wearable smart device to record single-lead ECG tracings during palpitations.  
Subsequently, the patient recorded episodes of regular wide QRS complex tachycardia at 145–160 bpm with a left bundle branch block morphology. On one occasion, he traced a wide LBBB tachycardia at 160 bpm (CL 375 ms) and, during the same symptomatic period, a narrow-complex tachycardia at 200 bpm (CL 300 ms).

A 55-year-old man presented with one month of constant, severe right upper-quadrant and periumbilical abdominal pain lasting 1–2 hours, postprandial nausea, vomiting, and eight days without defecation but with flatus passage. He had a 20-year history of raw opium use and had undergone cholecystectomy three weeks earlier for gallstones without relief of his pain. He reported chronic constipation for one year. He denied pruritus or changes in urine or stool color.

On examination he was hemodynamically stable. His sclerae were mildly icteric, and there was bluish discoloration of the periodontal tissues (Burton’s sign). The abdomen was distended with diminished bowel sounds and mild tenderness in the periumbilical and right upper-quadrant regions without rebound or guarding.

Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, MCV 82 fL), normal leukocyte count, AST 100 IU/L, ALT 76 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 3100 IU/L, GGT 1057 IU/L, total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, ESR 31 mm/hr, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. Serum electrolytes and urinalysis were normal.

Plain abdominal radiograph demonstrated generalized ileus with fecal impaction. Hepatic ultrasound revealed mild fatty infiltration with normal intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. Viral serologies for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative. ANA, ASMA, AMA, LKM1, and P-ANCA were within normal limits. MRCP showed no biliary strictures or obstruction.

To investigate the cause of intrahepatic cholestasis, a liver biopsy was planned.

A 40‐year‐old Hispanic woman with bronchial asthma and depression presented with several months of pruritic blistering lesions on her face and trunk, a photosensitivity rash on her face and neck, right‐sided cervical lymphadenopathy, nonerosive joint pain in her elbows and wrists, hair loss, and painful swallowing of solids and liquids. She denied Raynaud’s phenomenon, dyspnea, hematuria, and proximal muscle weakness. On examination, she had pink conjunctivae, an erythematous malar rash, painless superficial oral ulcers, a solitary nontender right cervical lymph node, and vesicular lesions over her face and trunk with excoriations. Her elbows and wrists were tender without swelling; neurologic examination was unremarkable. 

Initial differential diagnoses included bullous systemic lupus erythematosus, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, dermatitis herpetiformis, and bullous pemphigoid. Laboratory studies showed a normal CBC and metabolic panel; ANA titer 279 IU/mL (normal <7.5), anti–double‐stranded DNA 119 IU/mL (normal <9), anti‐Smith >8 AI (normal <0.9); anti‐RNP, anti‐centromere, anti–topoisomerase‐1, anti–Jo‐1, anti‐SSA, and anti‐SSB antibodies were negative. ESR was 18 mm/hr, CRP 1.8 mg/L (normal 0–4.8), complement levels were normal, and ANCA was negative. 

Cervical lymph node biopsy showed follicular hyperplasia. Skin biopsy revealed subepidermal vesicular dermatitis with overlying epidermal necrosis, a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate, and focal interface changes. Direct immunofluorescence showed no epidermal or vascular deposits of immunoglobulins or fibrin but linear C3 and IgG and weak linear IgM at the basement membrane. Salt‐split skin immunofluorescence demonstrated linear C3 and IgG and weak IgM on the dermal (floor) side of the split skin. 

Because of her odynophagia, mixed connective tissue disease with dysphagia from systemic sclerosis was considered; anti‐RNP, anti‐centromere, anti–topoisomerase‐1, and anti–Jo‐1 antibodies were negative. Polymyositis was deemed unlikely as she had no muscle weakness and her creatine kinase and aldolase levels were normal.

A 43-year-old woman with no significant medical history underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic umbilical hernia repair. Preoperative CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV and oral contrast showed normal bilateral kidneys and ureters. A 16 Fr Foley catheter was placed preoperatively and removed on postoperative day 1, when she voided spontaneously. On postoperative day 2, she developed an ileus, managed conservatively. On postoperative day 4, she reported dysuria, urinary hesitancy, and right flank pain. Her temperature was 38.2 °C, heart rate 93 bpm, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, and respiratory rate 22 breaths/minute. On examination, the abdomen was soft but distended with right costovertebral angle tenderness. Her white blood cell count was 17,000 cells/mm³, and serum creatinine rose from 0.7 mg/dL preoperatively to 5.5 mg/dL. A bladder scan estimated a volume of 600 mL, and catheterization yielded a postvoid residual of 800 mL. Renal ultrasound showed moderate right hydroureteronephrosis with a complex perinephric fluid collection. CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast demonstrated severe right-sided hydronephrosis, a perinephric fluid collection, and a dilated ureter down to the level of the bladder. At this time, the differential diagnosis included acute pyelonephritis, obstructive nephrolithiasis, and iatrogenic injury.

A 74-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, and pollen allergy presented with persistent fever of 2 weeks’ duration. He reported a yearlong history of right inguinal swelling and scrotal discomfort but had not sought care because symptoms were mild. On admission he was alert; blood pressure 178/81 mm Hg; pulse 115 beats/min; temperature 36.9 °C; SpO₂ 100% on room air. Breath and heart sounds were normal. His abdomen was flat and soft. The right scrotum measured approximately 20 × 10 cm, was firm, and showed erythema and warmth extending from the right inguinal region, without pain. Laboratory testing showed a white-cell count of 18.5 × 10³/μL and a C-reactive protein level of 16.85 mg/dL; other values were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a right inguinal hernia containing the appendix, an enlarged appendix with unclear wall continuity at its tip, surrounding adipose-tissue haziness, and a multilocular fluid collection with a capsule-like appearance indicating an abscess extending from the right inguinal canal into the scrotum.

An 18-year-old healthy Japanese man presented after being struck in the left eye by a handball. His best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU, and intraocular pressure was 15 mmHg OU. Wide-field fundus photography of the left eye demonstrated a peripheral retinal tear extending from the 1 to 3 o’clock position, associated macula-on rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, and a whitish lesion in the superotemporal periphery. The right eye was unremarkable. Fluorescein angiography of the left eye revealed capillary stasis and perivascular leakage in the whitish area, with more peripheral nonperfusion; the hyperperfused region corresponded to the area of the retinal tear.

A 71-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with acute upper abdominal pain, fever, and vomiting. On examination, he had a soft epigastric mass with moderate tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 6.2 g/dl, a white-cell count of 13 000/μl, and a C-reactive protein level of 42 mg/l. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest and abdomen revealed a cystic lesion in the left hypochondrium with a thickened wall, focal peripheral calcification, and internal air bubbles. A fistulous tract was seen connecting the lesion to the stomach, and no liver or lung lesions were identified.

A 36-year-old previously healthy Indonesian man presented with sudden onset of left-sided weakness while working. He denied any prior medical or neurologic disorders and had no family history of cognitive impairment, movement disorders, or early stroke. On examination in the emergency department, his blood pressure was 156/95 mmHg, pulse 91 beats/min, respirations 16 breaths/min, and temperature 36 °C. General examination was unremarkable. Neurologic examination showed left hemiparesis (muscle power grade 4), mild dysarthria, and left central facial palsy; there were no cognitive deficits, extrapyramidal signs, or ataxia. NIH Stroke Scale score was 4.

Noncontrast head CT revealed extensive, symmetric calcifications in the bilateral basal ganglia, internal capsules, thalami, cerebral subcortical white matter, and cerebellar dentate nuclei. Initial laboratory studies including blood count, coagulation profile, and chemistry were normal. Serum calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, alkaline phosphatase, calcitonin, thyroid hormone, and parathyroid hormone levels were all within normal limits, and HIV serology was negative.

Brain MRI demonstrated an acute infarct in the right posterior limb of the internal capsule and an old lacunar infarct in the left internal capsule; T2-weighted images showed hypointense signals, and T1-weighted images showed slight hyperintense signals in the calcified regions. MRA and MRV showed no intracranial large-vessel stenosis, aneurysm, vascular malformation, or dural sinus thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed no abnormal parenchymal or leptomeningeal enhancement. Perfusion SPECT showed hypoperfusion in the bilateral basal ganglia and thalamic regions and heterogeneous uptake in both cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres.

Further evaluation including carotid duplex ultrasonography, transthoracic echocardiography, 24-hour Holter monitoring, D-dimer, hematologic tests, coagulation profiles, autoimmune panels, and inflammatory markers were all unremarkable.

A 75-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history of progressive, diffuse telangiectasia affecting her face, trunk, upper extremities, and oral mucosa. Dermoscopic evaluation showed dilated vessels and red lacunae. Nailfold capillary examination was unremarkable. Over the past 2 years, she noted exertional dyspnea (on climbing stairs) and fatigue but denied diarrhea, weight loss, myalgia, or cold intolerance. Four years earlier, she had been diagnosed elsewhere with polycythemia vera and treated with hydroxyurea. 

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits, and the physical exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed a red blood cell count of 5.52 × 10^12/L and a hemoglobin concentration of 156 g/L. Erythropoietin was elevated at >750 mIU/mL. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated bilateral perinephric fluid collections. Chest computed tomography was normal. 

Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation identified an IgA-lambda monoclonal protein. A ventilation/perfusion scan of the lungs showed evidence of intrapulmonary shunting. Bone marrow biopsy revealed less than 10% plasma cells with lambda light-chain restriction. Abdominal computed tomography showed no organomegaly. Nerve conduction studies were normal. Assessment of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis and thyroid function yielded results within normal limits.

A 31-year-old man presented with a chief complaint of a “forwardly placed lower jaw.” He had undergone cleft lip and palate repair at 6 months and again at 1½ years of age.  
On frontal examination, there was nasal columellar distortion, a left-sided cleft lip scar, increased lower facial height, competent lips, and a nonconsonant smile. At rest, there was no maxillary incisal show; on smiling, 50% of the maxillary incisors were visible, and the lower incisors were visible at rest.  
Profile examination revealed a concave profile, midface deficiency with a flat cheekbone contour, sub–pupil region deficiency, an acute nasolabial angle, a hypotonic upper lip, retrusive lips, a positive lip step, a prominent chin, an average mandibular plane angle, and increased throat length.  
Intraoral examination showed a repaired left cleft palate, supernumerary teeth, a missing maxillary left lateral incisor, a malformed and tipped maxillary left central incisor, palatally displaced maxillary lateral incisors, mild lower incisor crowding due to retroclination, anterior and posterior crossbites, a reverse overjet of 6 mm, a reverse overbite of 10 mm, and bilateral Class III molar relationships. There was no TMJ pain or centric relation–centric occlusion discrepancy.  
Bolton analysis demonstrated a 7.21-mm overall mandibular tooth-size excess and a 5.31-mm mandibular anterior excess.  
Cephalometric analysis revealed SNA 69.5°, SNB 79°, ANB –9.5°, consistent with a Class III skeletal pattern. The maxillary and mandibular incisors were retroclined. Lateral cephalometry confirmed no TMJ pathology on the orthopantomogram.

A 31-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of a palpable, firm, nontender mass in the left side of her neck. She had no history of thyroid dysfunction, constitutional symptoms, or prior radiation exposure, and her family history was noncontributory. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, there was a firm mass in the left thyroid lobe without cervical lymphadenopathy or bruit. Thyroid function tests and a complete blood count, metabolic panel, and liver function tests were all normal. Ultrasonography of the thyroid revealed a 2.98 × 3.45 × 3.88 cm hypo- to isoechoic nodule in the lower pole of the left lobe with internal linear striations and cystic areas (occupying < 50% of the lesion), without calcifications or surrounding lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration of the nodule yielded many lymphoid cells of variable size and some atypical large lymphoid cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and prominent nucleoli, and the cytopathology report described the specimen as suspicious for a lymphoproliferative disorder. Excisional biopsy was recommended.

A 14-year-old female with obesity and a recent diagnosis of confluent and reticulated papillomatosis was started on minocycline 100 mg daily. Two weeks after beginning therapy, she developed fever, facial edema, cervical lymphadenopathy, and a diffuse rash. Despite discontinuation of minocycline and administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics at a local hospital, her symptoms progressed over the next 10 days, prompting transfer to the intensive care unit.

On examination, there was a diffuse exanthematous eruption on the trunk; pseudovesicular erythematous papules on the face, chest, and intertriginous areas; marked facial edema; and hyperpigmented, reticulated plaques on the chest against a Fitzpatrick skin type V–VI background. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (65.0 × 10^9/L) with 17% eosinophils, creatinine 1.85 mg/dL, AST 2650 U/L, ALT 767 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 181 U/L, prothrombin time 25.1 s, partial thromboplastin time 62.1 s, ferritin 9259.2 ng/mL, LDH 7326 U/L, procalcitonin 82.18 ng/mL, fibrinogen 90 mg/dL, and an ESR of 26 mm/h. Multiple cytokines were elevated, including IL-2, IL-2R, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-13, IL-17, and IFN-γ. An extensive infectious-disease evaluation for bacterial, viral, fungal, and tick-borne pathogens was notable only for human herpesvirus 6 by PCR. Hematology–oncology ruled out occult malignancy with flow cytometry, bone marrow biopsy, and comprehensive imaging. Rheumatology evaluated and excluded lupus, macrophage activation syndrome, IgG4-related disease, and other autoimmune/autoinflammatory conditions. Genetics performed whole-genome sequencing, which returned negative for all tested conditions.
