An 81-year-old Japanese man presented with severe upper abdominal pain. On admission, he was diagnosed with acute cholecystitis and gallstones and underwent percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage (PTGBD). He then developed severe pancreatitis attributed to a biliary stone and was managed conservatively; his course was complicated by a paralytic ileus requiring decompression. Four months later he was transferred for further evaluation.

Cholangiography via the PTGBD tube demonstrated a filling defect consistent with a stone, drainage of the cystic duct into the right hepatic duct, and an early junction of the right and left hepatic ducts, indicating duplication of the extrahepatic bile duct. Contrast medium flowed from the terminal bile duct into a papillary outpouching, and the main pancreatic duct joined at the same site.

Duodenoscopy revealed a swollen papilla of Vater with a single orifice exuding biliary fluid. Abdominal CT showed a small intraduodenal cystic lesion adjacent to the head of the pancreas with wall characteristics similar to the duodenum.

A 19-year-old Chinese man presented with recurrent limb convulsions and numbness over the past year, without joint pain, edema, gastrointestinal symptoms, or other triggers, and had lost 5 kg. One week before referral, his convulsions worsened. Initial laboratory tests showed blood calcium 1.50 mmol/L (corrected 1.95; normal 2.08–2.6), magnesium 0.49 mmol/L, potassium 3.38 mmol/L, albumin 17.3 g/L, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) 113 pg/mL (normal 15–65), with phosphorus 1.12 mmol/L and a positive fecal occult blood test. He received albumin, calcium gluconate, and potassium-magnesium supplements, with symptomatic relief.

On examination, his BMI was 17.2 kg/m2; vital signs were normal. There was no peripheral edema, and abdominal and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

Repeat laboratory studies revealed calcium 2.37 mmol/L, magnesium 0.73 mmol/L, potassium 4.19 mmol/L, phosphorus 1.19 mmol/L, PTH 16.7 pg/mL, albumin 25.2 g/L, and persistent positive fecal occult blood. White-cell count was 3.8×10^9/L with lymphopenia. Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, and K were low. Immunoglobulins A, G, and M and complement C3 and C4 were decreased. Lymphocyte subsets (CD4+, CD8+, CD19+) were below normal. HIV, RPR, and IBD screening were negative; liver, renal, thyroid, endocrine, and tumor marker panels were unremarkable; 24-hour urine protein was normal.

Parathyroid ultrasound showed small hypoechoic nodules bilaterally. Abdominal MRI revealed an enlarged lymph node anterior to the right psoas and minimal pelvic fluid. Capsule endoscopy was normal. Gastroscopy showed white spots in the duodenum, and biopsy of the descending duodenum demonstrated mucosal and submucosal lymphatic dilation.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of progressive weakness of both lower limbs and a 6-month history of an unhealed painless oral ulcer and hair loss. The weakness began in the right leg, gradually involved the left, and progressed to inability to walk; upper limbs were unaffected. She developed urinary and fecal incontinence over the past month and had lost orientation of time and place, with insidious forgetfulness and social withdrawal. She denied fever, joint pain, photosensitivity, rash, Raynaud’s phenomenon, gastrointestinal symptoms, visual changes, or sensory symptoms. She had a history of three units of blood transfusion at a cesarean section 12 years ago; no diabetes, hypertension, or known autoimmune disease. On exam, she was cachectic and anemic; vital signs were normal. Oral thrush and glossitis were present; alopecia was noted. Neurologic exam showed hypertonia and 2/5 strength in both lower limbs, brisk reflexes with clonus, extensor plantar responses; upper extremities, cranial nerves, cerebellar function, and funduscopic exam were unremarkable. Higher cerebral function testing revealed a total score of 2 on the International HIV Dementia Scale, consistent with dementia. Initial labs showed pancytopenia with normocytic anemia, mild elevation of liver enzymes, normal vitamin B12 level (669 pg/ml), normal thyroid function, and negative serologies for syphilis and toxoplasmosis. CSF analysis revealed pleocytosis and elevated protein. Brain MRI demonstrated generalized atrophy; spinal MRI showed no lesions or contrast enhancement.

An 11-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes since age 8, from a low socioeconomic background, presented after severe diabetic ketoacidosis treated with standard insulin, fluid and electrolyte protocols. His glycaemic control was poor with two subsequent moderate DKA admissions. On transfer to our paediatric diabetes clinic, he was noted to have:  
• Height 127.5 cm and weight 25 kg (< 3rd centile for age and sex), Tanner stage 1  
• Liver palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin; no jaundice, splenomegaly or ascites  
• Serum glucose 238 mg/dl; glycated haemoglobin 114 mmol/l  
• Total cholesterol 271 mg/dl; triglycerides 175 mg/dl  
• Normal acid–base status (pH 7.39, bicarbonate 24 mmol/l); lactate 1.1 mmol/l  
• Normal transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin and prothrombin time  
Further evaluation for hepatomegaly showed:  
• Negative antinuclear, anti–smooth muscle, antimitochondrial and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies  
• Negative serologies for Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis A, B, C and HIV  
• Normal serum iron studies, ceruloplasmin and copper levels  
Endocrine and growth evaluation revealed:  
• Normal thyroid function; negative coeliac serology  
• Insulin-like growth factor 1 at lower limit of normal  
• Bone age 9.9 years (Greulich–Pyle)  
• Subnormal peak on clonidine growth-hormone stimulation test (6.9 ng/dl)  
Abdominal ultrasound confirmed marked hepatomegaly with regular echo texture and a normal portal vein. His insulin dose was increased to 2.3 IU/kg daily with renewed diabetes education. Based on hepatomegaly, short stature, dyslipidaemia and a history of poor control, Mauriac’s syndrome was hypothesized and a liver biopsy was planned.

A 54-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidemia, and gout presented with recurrent episodes of burning chest discomfort, profuse diaphoresis, and a syncopal event occurring in the mornings before restroom use. He denied exertional triggers and walked 10 miles daily without limitation. Since 2015, his evaluation had included a normal 24-hour Holter monitor, exercise stress test, tilt-table test, and transthoracic echocardiography. Because of continued palpitations and sweating during symptomatic episodes, a mobile cardiac outpatient telemetry device was placed. While wearing the device, he experienced chest burning and diaphoresis coinciding with marked ST-segment elevations. He was brought emergently to the hospital. On admission, an ECG showed sinus rhythm without ST-segment deviation. High-sensitivity troponin I was 3.5 pg/mL (reference 0–14.4 pg/mL). Echocardiography revealed normal left ventricular function without wall-motion or structural abnormalities. Coronary angiography demonstrated patent epicardial vessels without obstructive lesions but sluggish flow in the left anterior descending artery.

A 69-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an abnormal chest shadow. She reported a chronic cough but had never smoked and had no history of trauma or thoracic surgery. Laboratory studies showed no evidence of organ dysfunction or active inflammation. Chest computed tomography revealed a 30 mm well-circumscribed mass in the right hilar region, which had increased in size compared with imaging from three years earlier. On 18F-fluoro-deoxy-glucose positron emission tomography, the lesion demonstrated avid uptake (maximum SUV, 6.5). Bronchoscopic examination showed slight narrowing of the superior bronchial ostia from extrinsic compression, while the mucosa appeared normal. Bronchial mucosal and transbronchial lung biopsies yielded only normal tissue. Given concern for primary lung cancer, a video-assisted thoracic surgical right upper lobectomy was performed. Grossly, the tumor was firm, pale gray, and well circumscribed, with no invasion of the pulmonary artery or bronchus. Intraoperative frozen-section analysis indicated a benign process.

A 7‐year‐old boy with anuric end‐stage renal disease from bilateral congenital renal dysplasia, on chronic hemodialysis (days 1, 3, 5, and 8), was admitted with Enterobacter cloacae bacteremia. His history included pulmonary hypoplasia with chronic lung disease and developmental delay. He received intravenous ceftriaxone for 3 days, then was switched to cefepime 50 mg/kg every 24 hours, administered immediately after each dialysis session.

On day 3 of cefepime therapy, his mother noticed leg weakness and intermittent loss of balance. On day 5, he fell from a seated position in the dialysis chair without any changes in volume status or electrolytes. On day 7, he fell while walking; staff noted a “drunken” gait with slight sway on toe standing and limited eccentric control. By day 8, he was disoriented to person and place and had severe truncal ataxia, requiring assistance to stand. Fifteen minutes into dialysis he displayed ratcheting flexion movements of head and trunk and a brief unilateral hand tremor. He was normotensive and not tachycardic.

Laboratory studies showed: sodium 141 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, chloride 100 mEq/L, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, creatinine 6.7 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 134 mg/dL, total calcium 9.8 mg/dL, albumin 3.4 g/dL, and phosphorus 4.5 mg/dL. Plasma cefepime levels were not obtained. A head CT and lumbar puncture were scheduled under anesthesia but canceled when his symptoms resolved before the procedures. Electroencephalography demonstrated generalized spike‐and‐wave bursts up to 7 seconds, interpreted as consistent with his underlying renal disease. His neurologic signs were most pronounced immediately before dialysis sessions, peaking on the morning after the longest dialysis gap (day 8).

A 29-year-old man with no past medical history presented with chest pain worsened by deep breathing and movement, hemoptysis, and intermittent palpitations ongoing for 3 hours. He recalled a headache, fatigue, and fever that resolved about 1 month earlier. He was a lifelong nonsmoker, denied alcohol or drug use, and worked as a truck driver. He had completed a two-dose COVID-19 vaccination series 5 months before presentation.

On examination, vital signs were normal except for a heart rate fluctuating between 160 and 220 beats per minute. Heart sounds were normal without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; there was no arthritis, lymphadenopathy, or rash. An electrocardiogram showed atrial flutter at 220 bpm without ST-segment changes. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed significant biventricular enlargement, diffuse hypokinesis, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 23%, a small pericardial effusion, and thrombi in both ventricles; valvular function was normal.

Laboratory studies demonstrated a high-sensitivity troponin level >13,000 ng/L (normal <4), brain natriuretic peptide 1294 pg/mL, ferritin 460 µg/mL, C-reactive protein 127 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.92 ng/mL, aspartate aminotransferase 5813 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 4295 U/L, prothrombin activity 38%, and factor V activity 58%. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography showed bilateral ground-glass opacities and consolidations, bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli, and thrombi in the left and right ventricles, the left superior pulmonary vein, and the right internal jugular vein. Brain CT angiography revealed right transverse sinus thrombosis. Doppler ultrasonography of the lower extremities identified left popliteal vein thrombosis.

A 29-year-old woman with Down syndrome presented for evaluation of refractory forearm lesions in the setting of psoriasis and hidradenitis suppurativa. She had been treated with clobetasol ointment once daily, which improved psoriatic plaques on her trunk and extremities, but lesions on the ventral forearms remained unchanged. Examination showed numerous asymptomatic, erythematous, keratotic papules in annular and arcuate patterns on the ventral forearms. A potassium hydroxide preparation from the forearm lesions was negative. She also had erythematous papulonodules, scars, sinus tracts, and double-headed open comedones in the axillae and groin consistent with hidradenitis suppurativa, for which she was receiving benzoyl peroxide wash, clindamycin lotion, and oral doxycycline. The clobetasol dose was increased to twice daily, but at follow-up, psoriasis and hidradenitis suppurativa were minimally improved and the forearm lesions were unchanged. Adherence to the topical regimen was challenging. The clinical differential diagnosis of the forearm lesions included elastosis perforans serpiginosa versus partially treated psoriasis.

A 34-year-old unbooked G4P3 Nigerian woman presented with a 6-week history of moderate, constant, generalized, non-colicky abdominal pain and progressive swelling. Her last menstrual period was 19 September 2020, and a serum pregnancy test was positive. She had no early ultrasound. On examination, she appeared chronically ill and pale but afebrile; pulse 135 beats/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg. The abdomen was non-uniformly distended, moved with respiration, and had mild generalized tenderness; there was right iliac fossa tenderness and a non-tender right iliac fossa mass with a smooth outline that was non-mobile, above but not below. Pelvic examination showed a gaping introitus with anterior vaginal wall bulge; the cervix was displaced anterolaterally toward 10 o’clock and the os was closed. Hematocrit was 14%; full blood count, electrolytes, urea, and creatinine were normal. Four units of blood were cross-matched and intravenous antibiotics started. Initial transabdominal ultrasound showed a viable intrauterine pregnancy with the placenta on the right lateral uterine wall, no adnexal mass, and echo-rich fluid in all quadrants; an abdominal tap yielded 10 mL of non-clotting blood. A repeat ultrasound revealed a left adnexal ectopic gestation and persistent echo-rich intraperitoneal fluid collection.

A 43-year-old man with an 8-year history of type II diabetes mellitus managed with metformin (500 mg three times daily) and a history of oral opium addiction was brought to the emergency department on January 8, 2023, after ingesting approximately 90 g of metformin in a suicide attempt. He reported 2 hours of dizziness, anorexia, weakness, lethargy, drowsiness, nausea, and vomiting. He was alert and communicative. His temperature was 37 °C, blood pressure 115/75 mmHg, pulse 90 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. He received intravenous normal saline, 60 g of activated charcoal via a nasogastric tube, sodium bicarbonate 44 mEq, ondansetron 8 mg, and pantoprazole 80 mg. Initial laboratory findings included:  
• Sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 5 mEq/L  
• BUN 14 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL  
• Blood glucose 180 mg/dL  
• Arterial pH 7.26, PCO2 57.2 mmHg, HCO3– 25.9 mEq/L, base excess –2.4 mEq/L  
• Lactate 15 mmol/L (reference 0.5–2.2 mmol/L)

A 26-year-old woman at 11 weeks of gestation presented with severe nausea, dizziness, and 4 days of continuous double vision. She had hyperemesis gravidarum since 6 weeks’ gestation. Her gait difficulty from dizziness had worsened slightly each day. She denied weakness, paresthesias, or sensory loss. She was alert, with normal cognition.  
On neurologic examination, she had dysconjugate gaze, marked left-eye abduction restriction, and modest restriction of both eyes in other directions without nystagmus or ptosis; pupils were equal and reactive. Ocular misalignment was nonfluctuating. Facial strength, sensation, palate elevation, tongue, and hearing were normal. Limb tone, bulk, and strength were normal. Rapid alternating movements were slow, and the knee–heel–shin test was imprecise. Vibratory and temperature sensation were intact, but proprioception was impaired. She was unable to stand or walk without assistance despite full strength.  
Brain MRI revealed no areas of restricted diffusion or other signal abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable. Needle electromyography of the left upper and lower extremities was normal. Brainstem stroke was excluded by MRI. Myasthenia gravis was denied by lacking diurnal fluctuation of symptoms and easy fatigability.

A 38-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 7-month history of a gradually enlarging, non-tender, firm, mobile mass in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. There were no skin changes or palpable ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes. Routine laboratory tests were normal.

Mammography (craniocaudal, mediolateral oblique, and spot compression views) revealed an oval, circumscribed, isodense mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, measuring 3.5 × 2.5 × 3 cm (BI-RADS 4a), without suspicious calcifications.

Breast ultrasound showed an oval, circumscribed, complex solid-and-cystic heterogeneous mass at 2 o’clock in the left breast with posterior acoustic enhancement. The lesion contained floating curvilinear structures (“serpent sign”).

A complementary liver ultrasound demonstrated multiple, variably sized, anechoic lesions throughout the liver, suggestive of cysts. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen confirmed multiple nonenhancing, fluid-density liver cysts; the lungs were clear.

A 59-year-old woman without previous psychiatric or neurological disease presented to the emergency department with pervasive existential anxieties and delusional beliefs of thought insertion and external control, accompanied by audible thoughts. Examination required lorazepam for severe anxiety.  
Laboratory studies revealed mild hypothyroidism (status post–hemithyroidectomy) treated with levothyroxine and hyponatremia from excessive water intake treated with sodium supplementation. Complete blood count, folic acid, vitamin B12, ceruloplasmin, and serologies for HIV, Borrelia burgdorferi, and Treponema pallidum were unremarkable.  
Antipsychotic treatment with risperidone, later switched to chlorprothixene, failed to relieve her delusional ideas.  
Neurological examination showed dysdiadochokinesis (left hand), mild hyperkinetic movements, bradykinesia on finger tapping, and a broad-based gait without rigidity, tremor, or postural instability. She became disoriented to time and place and exhibited long-term memory deficits with episodes of fear, agitation, and perseveration.  
Neuropsychological testing (CERAD+ battery) demonstrated impaired verbal recognition, severe visuospatial dysfunction, reduced semantic and phonemic fluency, and decreased cognitive flexibility; the MMSE score was 22/30 and the FAB score was 10/18. SCID-II showed no personality disorder.  
EEG demonstrated a normal alpha rhythm without epileptiform potentials. Brain MRI revealed generalized cerebral atrophy with putaminal rim sign, a hyperintensity at the lateral margin of the putamen, and ventriculomegaly.  
CSF analysis showed normal tau and beta-amyloid levels, no intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis, negative autoimmune encephalitis antibodies, and absence of protein 14-3-3.  
These findings raised suspicion for an underlying neurodegenerative process.

A 37‐year‐old Caucasian woman, gravida 1 para 1 with no significant medical history, presented with a 10‐day history of a painful ulcer on the left breast and intermittent afternoon fevers up to 38.5 °C. Three days before presentation, she noted an edematous pustule in the lower outer quadrant of the left breast that evolved into a 1 cm ulcer. She was treated empirically with oral cefuroxime. Seven days later her ulcer had rapidly enlarged to 10 × 5 cm, involving the inferior half of the breast but sparing the areola and nipple. On admission her temperature was 36.6 °C, blood pressure 112/69 mm Hg, and heart rate 90 bpm. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (23 000 neutrophils/mm^3) and a C‐reactive protein level of 144 μg/ml. Despite intravenous ampicillin–sulbactam and metronidazole, she continued to have afternoon fevers and the ulcer expanded by 1–2 cm per day. Blood and wound cultures were repeatedly negative. Given the lack of improvement, she underwent surgical debridement and tissue biopsy; the fascia appeared macroscopically uninvolved.

A 40-year-old man with a history only of tobacco use presented with two days of right arm paresthesia and worsening pain. He reported months of lethargy and night chills without measured fevers and a self-limited diarrheal episode weeks earlier. On arrival he was afebrile, tachycardic (heart rate 135 beats/min), and had a grade VI systolic murmur. The right radial pulse was absent. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 18,200 /mm3 with normal metabolic and liver panels. CT angiography revealed an occlusive thrombus in the right brachial artery. He was started on unfractionated heparin and transferred for vascular surgery, where thrombectomy of the axillary, brachial, radial, and ulnar arteries yielded inflamed arterial tissue and white embolic debris; Gram stain demonstrated many neutrophils without organisms. Postoperatively, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography showed a severely regurgitant bicuspid aortic valve with a multilobar, mobile 2.5 cm mass. He subsequently developed a fever to 101.7 °F. Empiric vancomycin and ceftriaxone were initiated after multiple blood cultures were drawn. On hospital day 1 he underwent aortic valve replacement; valvular tissue was submitted for aerobic, anaerobic, and fungal culture. Histologic examination revealed extensive necrosis and fibrin-rich vegetations with bacterial forms present. All blood and tissue cultures remained negative, and the formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded valve tissue was sent for broad-range bacterial nucleic acid amplification testing.

A 76-year-old woman with Stage IIA (pT2aN1M0) poorly differentiated lung adenocarcinoma initially presented with hemoptysis and shoulder pain. She underwent left upper lobectomy, which revealed a KRAS-mutant, ALK-negative, EGFR/BRAF wild-type tumor with one metastatic hilar lymph node and prominent anthracosilicosis with non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation in lymph nodes. After four cycles of adjuvant cisplatin and vinorelbine, she began adjuvant durvalumab (20 mg/kg every 4 weeks).

Three months after initiation of durvalumab, routine non-contrast chest CT showed new mediastinal lymphadenopathy. PET–CT demonstrated highly FDG-avid bilateral mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes, areas of increased uptake in the right scapula, left iliac crest, posterior ilium, and a 4 mm right upper lobe nodule. She was asymptomatic. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of stations 7, 4R, and 11R nodes was performed, revealing epithelioid histiocytes arranged in non-caseating granulomas with anthracotic pigment and polarizable silicotic material. No malignant cells or fungi were identified, and smear and culture for acid-fast bacilli were negative.

A 77-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia, coronary artery disease with prior stent placement, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and Parkinson’s disease presented with fever, altered mentation, and a right gluteal wound extending into the perineum. His family reported that he had applied a heating pad to the area 24 hours before the wound appeared because of pain. On arrival he was diaphoretic. Vital signs were: temperature 100.1 °F, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 91% on room air, which improved to 99% on 4 L/min of nasal oxygen. Examination of the perineum and right gluteal folds showed erythema with desquamation and blisters but no fluctuance or purulence; “this was consistent with a second-degree burn.” Laboratory studies revealed a white-blood-cell count of 29.1 K/μL, a lactate of 2.15 mmol/L, and a C-reactive protein level of 13.0 mg/dL. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) score was 3. He received an intravenous fluid bolus and empiric vancomycin plus piperacillin–tazobactam, with arrangements for transfer to a burn facility. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was ordered and was pending at the time of transfer.

A 68-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of recurrent right-upper-quadrant pain, loss of appetite, and dyspepsia. He denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, jaundice, or a history of tuberculosis or hepatitis. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including liver function tests and complete blood count, were within normal limits; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 30 mm/h. Chest radiography was normal. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a distended gallbladder with multiple gallstones, associated cholecystitis, and a gallbladder mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 5 mm thickened gallbladder wall, and the interface between the liver and gallbladder was obscured, possibly indicating infiltration into the liver parenchyma.

A 62-year-old man from a rural town in Western Australia presented with a 6-month history of myalgia, lower back pain, and progressive muscle weakness (lower > upper limbs), leading to reduced exercise tolerance (50 m), frequent falls, and use of a walking aid. He had been referred for suspected neurogenic claudication; lumbar MRI showed heterogeneous bone marrow signal in the lumbar spine and pelvis and an L5/S1 disc protrusion causing mild canal narrowing, but no indication for surgery. He also reported 2 years of myalgia involving shoulders, upper arms, forearms, back, and thighs, progressive grip weakness of the left hand, and “shooting pains” down the left forearm. He denied morning stiffness, rash, chest pain, dyspnea, weight loss, anorexia, or night sweats.

His medical history included type 2 diabetes (metformin, gliclazide, sitagliptin), hypertension (olmesartan/amlodipine), and gastroesophageal reflux (omeprazole). He did not smoke and drank 5–6 mid-strength beers daily. There was no history of congenital weakness, hypotonia, bulbar or respiratory involvement, or high-arched palate.

On examination, he appeared well. Blood pressure was 130/80 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats/min, afebrile. No lymphadenopathy, rash, or arthritis. Muscle strength was 4/5 in shoulder abduction, 3/5 in hip flexion, with reduced grip strength and left wrist‐extension weakness; distal lower-limb strength was preserved. Reflexes were normal; plantars were downgoing. Neck‐extension strength was 4/5 without fatigability. There was mild proximal lower-limb muscle atrophy.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 11.7×10^9/L (eosinophils 1.79×10^9/L), hemoglobin and platelets normal, CK 523 U/L. Thyroid, renal, parathyroid hormone, vitamin B_12, and folate levels were normal. Serum protein electrophoresis showed no paraproteins; kappa/lambda ratio 1.69. IgG1 12.20 g/L, IgG4 17.3 g/L, IgA 6.16 g/L; IgM and renal proteinuria were unremarkable. HIV, hepatitis B and C, ANCA, ANA, and ENA antibodies were negative; myositis panel was positive for PL-12 antibody. Stool examination showed Entamoeba coli cysts and Strongyloides IgG 1.54. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis revealed no interstitial lung disease or masses. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated moderate left ulnar compression at the elbow and mild left carpal tunnel syndrome without radiculopathy. Electromyography of multiple muscles showed no evidence of myopathic or inflammatory changes. Spirometry showed a restrictive pattern. Bone marrow biopsy revealed reactive marrow with eosinophilia but no plasmacytosis or clonal B-lymphocyte population.

A 31-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus (hemoglobin A1c 12.8%), depression, and a 17 pack-year smoking history presented with 1 day of rhinorrhea and 5 hours of fever (38.4°C) and dyspnea. He noted fatigue, postnasal drip, nausea, and mild, sharp left-sided pleuritic chest pain. On exam, he was mildly distressed; blood pressure was 124/74 mmHg, heart rate 127/min, respirations 24/min. Lungs were clear, heart was regular without murmurs, and abdominal and oropharyngeal exams were unremarkable. Initial labs showed leukocyte count 12.4×10^3/µL (89.3% neutrophils), glucose 367 mg/dL, anion gap 18 mEq/L, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. Chest radiograph was normal; CT pulmonary angiogram showed only central airway thickening. He received IV fluids, morphine, and ondansetron and was diagnosed with an upper respiratory tract infection. He declined admission, was prescribed amoxicillin–clavulanate (not filled), and discharged.

He returned the next day with worsening fatigue, subjective fever, arthralgias, and a diffuse rash. Vital signs were normal. Examination revealed multiple erythematous, tender macules on his trunk and extremities and erythema of the right tonsillar pillar. He again declined admission.

Two days later, blood cultures from his first visit grew long, thin, Gram-negative rods. He was admitted; he reported persistent rash but otherwise felt well. He recalled preceding watery eyes and oropharyngeal lesions that had resolved. On admission, vital signs were normal. Labs showed leukocyte count 12.9×10^3/µL (74.2% neutrophils), glucose 398 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein 59.2 mg/L. Skin exam disclosed multiple 2–3 cm, erythematous, irregular, minimally indurated, mildly tender patches on the chest, and three 7–8 cm targetoid lesions with central clearing on his back. He also had tender gums and poor dentition. The patient was started on IV piperacillin–tazobactam.

The following morning, infectious diseases consultation elicited recent exposures: several school contacts with international travel, two ticks crawling on him about one week before initial presentation, and a dog bite to his ear three weeks earlier without local infection. He also had contact with a pet cat and dog that had fleas. He denied allergies, new sexual partners, or prior STIs. The patient was continued on piperacillin–tazobactam and started empirically on doxycycline for possible tick-related illnesses.

A 14-year-old boy with an 8-year history of asthma, managed intermittently with inhaled salbutamol, budesonide and montelukast, presented with two weeks of progressive dyspnea, chest tightness, nocturnal and morning cough productive of whitish sputum, and a whistling sound during breathing. He denied fever, night sweats or weight loss. He had received multiple courses of oxygen therapy and nebulized bronchodilators at other facilities without relief and was referred for further management. His past history included treated pulmonary tuberculosis, tonsillectomy, recurrent upper respiratory infections and NSAID allergy. 

On admission: temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure elevated, respiratory rate 23 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He weighed 26 kg (BMI 15.4 kg/m2). Exam showed a barrel-shaped chest with scoliosis, hyperresonance to percussion, centrally placed trachea, and reduced breath sounds with scattered wheezes, more prominent on the right.

Initial chest radiograph showed bilateral areas of lucency with reduced lung volumes, clear costophrenic and cardiophrenic angles, and no mediastinal shift. Spirometry revealed a 20% improvement in peak expiratory flow after bronchodilator. A provisional diagnosis of bilateral pneumothorax versus giant bullae was made. 

High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated multiple thin-walled cystic lesions of varying sizes in both lungs, the largest measuring 10.9 by 9.8 by 7.5 cm in the right upper lobe, with associated collapse in the right middle lobe. The trachea, main bronchi, and mediastinal structures were normal in caliber and position.

A 45‐year‐old woman with lupus nephritis complicated by end‐stage renal disease on peritoneal dialysis for 12 years presented with confusion and was admitted for hypertensive encephalopathy. Dermatology was consulted for lower‐extremity skin findings first noticed years earlier and worsening over the past several months. She denied triggers, color change, or drainage, and reported pain only with pressure. 

Physical examination showed stocking‐like hyperpigmented macules and patches with overlying firm papules, nodules, and plaques in a subtle reticular pattern on both lower extremities and upper arms. She also had firm, yellow‐to‐orange, well‐circumscribed nodules overlying the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints of both hands. 

Laboratory testing revealed a serum uric acid level of 7.7 mg/dL. 

Plain radiographs of the hands and legs demonstrated diffuse tumoral “calcification” throughout the soft tissues of both hands, multiarthrodial degeneration in the distal interphalangeal joints, ill‐defined calcifications of the distal left thigh and calf, and a left knee effusion with synovitis, erosive changes, and marrow edema.

A 79‐year‐old man with a 10‐year history of seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis treated with prednisolone, chloroquine, sulfasalazine, and leflunomide presented with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, abdominal distension, lower‐extremity edema, and weight gain. He had a history of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction managed with furosemide, spironolactone, and digitalis, and was on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism and metformin for diabetes. He was a heavy smoker.

On examination, he appeared chronically ill and pale. Heart rate was 76 bpm, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and no respiratory distress. Jugular venous pressure was elevated to 45°. Cardiac auscultation was normal; pulmonary auscultation showed bi-basal hypoventilation. Abdominal examination revealed ascites, hepatomegaly, and collateral venous circulation. There was Grade III pitting edema of both legs. Multiple firm, painless, mobile nodules were present on the hands, elbows, knees, lower back, and buttocks. His hands, wrists, shoulders, and elbows were tender with limited passive movement.

Intravenous diuretics produced a positive clinical response. Chest radiography showed pleural thickening and fibrotic tracts at the left lung base. A thoracic CT performed 10 months earlier (when he was lost to follow-up) revealed a 10×11 mm right upper‐lobe pulmonary nodule, pleural thickening with fibrotic tracts, and an 8×6 cm low-density lesion abutting the right heart chambers. 

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 50–55% without significant valvular disease and an estimated pulmonary systolic arterial pressure of 30 mmHg. A large hyperechoic mass overlying the right heart chambers severely restricted diastolic filling; the inferior vena cava was dilated and noncollapsible.

N-terminal pro–brain natriuretic peptide was 347 pg/mL (normal ≤125 pg/mL). Cardiac MRI revealed a well-defined, multiloculated intra-pericardial mass (10×9×6 cm) anterior to the right atrium and ventricle. The lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on native T1-weighted images, and surrounded by a thick, hyperenhancing capsule without any intralesional solid or nodular components. There was global pericardial enhancement with mild pericardial thickening of 4 mm. The mass caused severe restriction of right ventricular diastolic filling.

A 7-year-old boy presented with a 3-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless mass in his left upper abdominal wall, accompanied by weight loss and drenching night sweats. He had no history of trauma, allergies, or developmental abnormalities. On examination, he appeared ill, with mild pallor but was afebrile and not jaundiced. In the left hypochondriac region there was an irregular, hard, non-tender mass measuring 13 × 14 cm; the mass was mobile and adhered only to the overlying skin. There was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 10 g/dL and a white-cell count of 9000/mm³; other routine biochemical and hematological tests were normal.  
Ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, predominantly hypoechoic subcutaneous mass measuring 7 × 4 cm with areas of acoustic shadowing and increased vascular flow on color Doppler. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a micro-lobulated, hyperdense, calcified mass measuring 8 × 7 × 4 cm centered in the left external oblique muscle, abutting but not infiltrating the underlying internal oblique muscle. There were no enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes and no other abdominal abnormalities.

A 27‐year‐old man was referred for evaluation of left scrotal swelling and erythema. He reported recurrent episodes of left‐sided epididymitis over the past 6 months and had received three courses of ceftriaxone and doxycycline without improvement. Three days before presentation, he noted undocumented fever with diffuse swelling and redness of the left scrotum. He denied urinary urgency, frequency, dysuria, perineal or abdominal pain, and had no fertility concerns; he fathered a child 2 years earlier. 

On examination, the left testicle was tender and erythematous, improving with elevation (positive Prehn’s sign). The right testicular and digital rectal examinations were unremarkable, and no lymphadenopathy was present.

Laboratory studies including complete blood count, C‐reactive protein, nucleic acid amplification tests for chlamydia and gonorrhea, serum prolactin, testosterone, luteinizing hormone, and follicle‐stimulating hormone were all within normal limits. Urinalysis showed true hematuria.

Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated a thickened, hypoechoic left epididymis with normal vascularity and no hydrocele or varicocele. Pelvic ultrasound revealed a 3.0 × 1.4 cm cystic structure adjacent to the left side of the prostate and a 0.5 cm calcified focus at the terminal segment of the left seminal vesicle, obstructing the left ejaculatory duct.

Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed left seminal vesicle dilation and an impacted stone in the left ejaculatory duct, and additionally showed absence of the left kidney with compensatory hypertrophy of the right kidney.

A 69-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of sharp pain localized to the right lumbar area. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 45–pack-year smoking history. On examination, pulses were intact and symmetric in both upper and lower extremities, and there was no palpable abdominal mass. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 11,500/μL (normal range, 5,000–10,000/μL), a C-reactive protein level of 3.0 mg/dL (normal <0.5 mg/dL), and a hemoglobin level of 13 g/dL (normal range, 13.8–17.2 g/dL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated a saccular aneurysmal outpouching in the infrarenal abdominal aorta resembling a “windsock,” along with a large intramural hematoma, localized aortic wall thickening, and calcification.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of headache, initially described as sinus and facial discomfort that later extended to the occiput, accompanied by shortness of breath and chest pain. She denied polydipsia or polyuria. Multiple evaluations by ear, nose, and throat specialists excluded a sinus infection. On hospital admission, cardiac troponin was elevated (initially 0.109 ng/mL and 0.111 ng/mL; normal <0.01 ng/mL) without ischemic changes on electrocardiography. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiogram of the chest demonstrated multiple pulmonary nodules and mass lesions bilaterally. Renal function was normal. A pituitary-dedicated magnetic resonance imaging study revealed an enlarged heterogeneous pituitary gland measuring 1.7 × 1.2 × 1.3 cm with infundibular thickening without cavernous sinus invasion or optic chiasm compression. She received symptomatic headache treatment including topiramate, nortriptyline, and a short course of dexamethasone, with slight improvement, and was discharged after 3 days.

A 79-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis had undergone TAVI with a self-expanding valve seven months earlier and was discharged on dual antiplatelet therapy. Pre-TAVI coronary angiography had shown no coronary artery disease. He awoke suddenly with intense angina at rest, which resolved after about 2 hours, and presented the next morning to the chest pain unit. He was asymptomatic on arrival; vital signs were stable and the cardiac, pulmonary, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. The 12-lead ECG showed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests revealed a high-sensitivity troponin T of 386 ng/L, rising to 590 ng/L after 3 hours (normal < 14 ng/L), and a D-dimer of 1.42 mg/L (normal < 1.28; age-adjusted cut-off 0.79); white blood cell count and C-reactive protein were within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no regional wall motion abnormalities. He received intravenous unfractionated heparin and aspirin. Early invasive coronary angiography revealed no coronary occlusion. Pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection were considered and were ruled out by multidetector CT, which incidentally indicated thrombosis of the prosthetic aortic valve.

A 53-year-old woman was admitted with a 4-day history of worsening lower-limb pain, fever, lower-limb weakness, and a rash. She had tested positive for COVID-19 by PCR 4 days before admission; her last vaccination (Pfizer booster) was 6 months earlier. Her past medical history was unremarkable; she took no regular medications and had a 10 pack-year smoking history. On examination, there was livedo reticularis of both lower limbs, non-palpable peripheral pulses, and profound, proximal, symmetric weakness of the lower limbs. Initial laboratory tests showed: D-dimer 444 mg/l (80–500), CRP 8.9 mg/l (<5), ESR 24 mm/hr (0–20), CK 524 U/L (25–200), WCC 14.9 ×10^9/l (4–10), neutrophils 10.6 ×10^9/l (2–7.5), creatinine 56 μmol/l (45–84), urea 5.7 mmol/l (2.5–7.8), eGFR >90 ml/min. A CT angiogram of the legs excluded acute arterial occlusion. Three days later, the CK had risen to 24 250 U/L. MRI of the lower legs showed diffuse, symmetrical muscle edema in all compartments with perifascial fluid and subcutaneous edema.

A 59-year-old man presented to the emergency department with left-sided abdominal pain that worsened with deep breathing and palpation. He denied any recent trauma, fever, or cough. His history was significant for hereditary spherocytosis treated with splenectomy, hypertension, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and right meniscectomy. Medications included ramipril and allopurinol; he was allergic to penicillins. 

On examination, he was alert and comfortable, with a blood pressure of 160/100 mm Hg, heart rate 80 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and temperature 36.4 °C. The abdomen was distended and tender to palpation on the left, without guarding or peritoneal signs; bowel sounds were present. Capillary refill was under 2 seconds.

Point-of-care abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a rounded, hypertrophic accessory splenic tissue with inhomogeneous parenchyma and a peripheral hyperechoic semilunar area measuring up to 18 mm in thickness, consistent with a subcapsular hematoma, along with free fluid in the peritoneal cavity.

A man in his 50s with end-stage kidney disease due to hypertension and a prior right nephrectomy underwent deceased-donor kidney transplantation 3 years before without rejection. He received induction immunosuppression with alemtuzumab and solumedrol and was maintained on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. Prophylaxis with sulfamethoxazole–trimethoprim and valganciclovir was discontinued 2 months earlier because of recurrent leukopenia.

He presented with a 10-day history of right shoulder pain and swelling and a fever of 100.6°F. Examination revealed a soft-tissue mass over the right scapula; he was hemodynamically stable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a right upper lobe pulmonary nodule with satellite lesions. PET/CT demonstrated a large, partially necrotic, intensely FDG-avid mass inferior to the right scapula and multiple FDG-avid masses in the lungs, brain, and cecum. Tumor markers were negative.

A 24-year-old Indian man with no significant past medical history first presented in 2017 with a 2-month history of intermittent hematuria without dysuria, stone passage, flank pain, fever, or urethral discharge. He was a nonsmoker, social drinker, and lived mostly in Hong Kong with occasional travel to India, where he recalled mosquito bites. On examination he was afebrile. Midstream urine microscopy showed 10–100 white blood cells/µL, <10 red blood cells/µL, and culture was negative. A KUB radiograph showed no radiopaque stones. He was referred to urology; eosinophils were elevated at 2.4×10^9/L (0–0.5) and 21% of differential (<6%), with otherwise normal liver, renal, clotting, and prostate-specific antigen tests. Flexible cystoscopy and urinary system ultrasound were unremarkable, urine cytology was negative, and repeat urine studies were unchanged. He was managed conservatively.

In 2024 he re-presented with hematuria and new-onset milky urine. Physical examination revealed a left scrotal swelling; urethral milking produced no discharge. Midstream urine showed 51–100 RBCs/µL, no WBCs, and negative culture. Early morning urine culture for acid-fast bacilli was negative. Spot urine protein/creatinine ratio was 109 mg/mmol (<23), and chyle was detected in the urine. Contrast-enhanced CT urogram demonstrated prominent para-aortic and para-caval lymph nodes up to 0.9 cm, with otherwise unremarkable kidneys, ureters, and bladder. Scrotal ultrasound revealed a large left hydrocele with floating echogenic debris. Serum immunoglobulin E was elevated at 138 IU/mL (<100). Blood tests for microfilaria, filarial PCR, and filaria IgG4 antibody were negative; urine was negative for parasites.

Intranodal lymphangiography was performed by ultrasound-guided injection of lipiodol into bilateral inguinal lymph nodes. Fluoroscopy showed antegrade lipiodol flow through iliac and lumbar lymphatics; lipiodol opacification of the right renal pelvis, ureter, and urinary bladder confirming a right lymphorenal fistula; markedly tortuous lymphatic vessels in the left retroperitoneum and pelvis; and pooling of lipiodol in dependent parts of the bladder. A delayed KUB radiograph showed lipiodol outlining the left scrotal sac.

A 33-year-old man with no cardiovascular risk factors was admitted for acute, resting, “infarct-type” chest pain of 1-day duration. One week earlier he had a febrile, flu-like illness treated with antipyretics. He is BMI 22, normotensive (120/70 mm Hg), heart rate 60 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, O₂ saturation 90% on room air, and has no signs of heart failure. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable.  
Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm, PR interval 160 ms, QRS 84 ms, and ST-segment elevations of 1.5 mm in inferior and apical-low lateral leads, 1 mm in basal leads, with reciprocal changes.  
Chest radiograph suggests COVID-19 lung involvement. Non-contrast chest CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities occupying approximately 40–50% of lung fields.  
Transthoracic echocardiography reveals a non-dilated left ventricle, normal wall thickness, global LVEF 61%, and normal global longitudinal strain (–18.6%).  
Laboratory studies show ultra-sensitive troponin 21 888 ng/L (≈1200× upper limit), leukocytes 12 000/µL, CRP 80 mg/L, normal lipase, and normal renal function.  
Given the presentation and ST elevations, an emergency coronary angiogram was performed and showed entirely normal coronary arteries.

A 23-year-old man with a history of chronic suppurative otitis media and right ear conductive hearing loss underwent cholesteatoma resection in 2006, with two subsequent radical resections for recurrent cholesteatoma in 2009 and 2012. In March 2016, a routine MRI revealed a 30 mm hyperintense, non–contrast-enhancing mass in the right parotid gland. By July 2016, the mass had become painful, and in September 2016 the patient noted right-sided facial droop corresponding to grade 2 facial nerve dysfunction on the House–Brackmann scale. In October 2016, otoscopic and tympanoscopic examination showed typical postoperative changes but was negative for recurrent cholesteatoma. MRI sequences demonstrated a lesion with low to intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images and hyperintensity on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images.

A 74-year-old man with coronary artery disease, hypertension, and hypothyroidism presented for a planned coronary artery bypass graft. He experienced mild abdominal pain and nausea after the procedure, which resolved within 48 hours and he was discharged. Two weeks later, he returned with fevers, chills, and dyspnea. Laboratory evaluation revealed a leukocyte count of 22.3 k/μL (normal 3.2–10.6) and lactic acidosis. Abdominal computed tomography showed an acute necrotic collection in the head of the pancreas. Serum lipase was not elevated. He was started on piperacillin–tazobactam and bowel rest. Blood cultures grew Escherichia coli, and he completed 14 days of cefazolin followed by cefuroxime. He was advanced to nasojejunal tube feeding for nutritional support. Four weeks later, he developed recurrent abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting; repeat imaging demonstrated improvement of the head inflammation but persistent inflammation in the tail of the pancreas with a new pseudocyst in the lesser sac abutting the stomach. Nine weeks later, imaging showed resolution of the pseudocyst but a new infiltrating, hyperenhancing soft-tissue mass at the pancreatic tail extending to the greater curvature of the stomach and the splenic hilum. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed a cystic lesion in the pancreatic head and an infiltrating mass-like lesion in the perigastric and peripancreatic region, as well as multiple small perigastric lymph nodes. Fine-needle aspiration of the mass lesion was performed.

A 15-year-old male presented with a 4-week history of watery diarrhea (20 episodes per day), vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain aggravated by spicy foods. He reported an 8-kg weight loss (≈15% of body weight). Physical examination revealed brownish macules on the hands and feet, hyperchromic punctate lesions on the trunk, and onychodystrophy. His medical history was notable for cleft lip and palate repair and recurrent diarrheal episodes since childhood.

Laboratory studies demonstrated mild hypoproteinemia and hypoalbuminemia (total protein 3.52 g/dL [normal 6.6–8.3], albumin 2.09 g/dL [3.5–5.2]), zinc deficiency (51 µg/dL [70–120]), low vitamin B12 (<150 pg/mL [300–900]), and otherwise unremarkable blood counts and metabolic panel.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed multiple type II and III Yamada polyps on atrophic gastric mucosa and nodular lymphoid lesions in the duodenum. Colonoscopy revealed numerous sessile and subpedunculated polyps throughout the colon and rectum.

A 62‐year‐old man was referred for evaluation of progressive respiratory failure attributed to bilateral diaphragmatic dysfunction. Over several months he had experienced low‐grade fever, neck and shoulder arthralgias, nocturnal hypoventilation, fatigue, and a ring‐shaped rash on the back of his right leg that expanded to 10 cm in diameter. He also noted transient numbness of the left side of his face. He reported dyspnea that worsened in the supine position but denied limb weakness, sensory changes in his extremities, or headache.

He was otherwise healthy. He had stopped smoking decades earlier, drank two units of alcohol daily, and took no medications.

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Upright respiratory rate was 24 breaths per minute, SpO₂ 97%. When supine for 45 seconds, his respiratory rate rose to 40 breaths per minute, paradoxical respiratory movements appeared, and SpO₂ fell to 91%. Percussion revealed an elevated left lung base. Chest radiographs showed elevation of the left hemidiaphragm. Fluoroscopic sniff testing demonstrated paradoxical motion of both hemidiaphragms. Pulmonary function testing revealed a supine vital capacity decrease of over 20% of predicted. Arterial blood gases showed pH 7.40, PaCO₂ 4.9 kPa, PaO₂ 7.8 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 24.6 mmol/L, base excess –0.2 mmol/L.

Antibodies to extractable nuclear antigens (SSA, SSB, RNP, Sm, SCL‐70, Jo‐1) and serology for Q fever were negative. Diaphragmatic ultrasonography revealed no inspiratory thickening. Polysomnography off ventilatory support showed out‐of‐phase thoracoabdominal movements and intermittent desaturation. Phrenic‐nerve conduction studies demonstrated normal distal motor latency and CMAP amplitude bilaterally; needle EMG of the right hemidiaphragm showed good recruitment without spontaneous activity, leading to the conclusion that there was no evidence of traumatic phrenic‐nerve palsy.

A 21-year-old man with no history of alcohol, tobacco, or drug use presented with persistent jaundice since early childhood, noted first at age 5, and worsening over the past 6 months with occasional non-projectile vomiting. There was no fever, pruritus, abdominal pain, or pale stools; dark urine was reported. Birth history was unremarkable without neonatal jaundice or transfusions, and development was normal. He had tried various undocumented alternative therapies without benefit. On examination, he had visible jaundice without hepatosplenomegaly; the remainder of the physical exam was normal. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 7.5 mg/dL (direct 0.6 mg/dL), normal liver enzymes (AST, ALT, ALP, GGT), and normal synthetic function. A comprehensive hemolytic workup (reticulocyte count, LDH, peripheral smear, antiglobulin tests) was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography was normal.

A 16-year-old male was referred for evaluation and endodontic treatment of the maxillary left lateral incisor because of aesthetic and functional impairment. He reported a history of dental trauma at age 5, when a fall caused intrusion and subsequent exfoliation of the primary maxillary left lateral incisor; orthodontic traction of the impacted permanent successor was required. On examination, the permanent tooth exhibited an amorphous, small, darkened crown; the adjacent gingiva was normal. There was no spontaneous pain, but the tooth was tender to vertical percussion and nonresponsive to pulp-vitality testing. Panoramic and periapical radiographs suggested a developmental dental anomaly, with more than one root canal, an area of apical rarefaction, and a pronounced crown-root dilaceration.

A 57-year-old Japanese man with stage IVB ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma had initially received cisplatin plus pemetrexed followed by pemetrexed maintenance. Upon progression after nine months, he was started on alectinib (300 mg daily) as second-line therapy. Three months into alectinib treatment, he developed dyspnea on exertion. On room air, his oxygen saturation was 82%; arterial blood gas measurement showed a PaO2 of 58.2 torr. Pulmonary function testing revealed a restrictive ventilatory defect (vital capacity 2.11 L, 57.1% predicted) and a diffusion impairment (DLCO 4.84 mL/min/mmHg, 22.8% predicted). Chest CT demonstrated shrinkage of the left upper lobe primary lesion but new bilateral ground-glass opacities and areas of consolidation. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid analysis showed a lymphocyte proportion of 34.4%, and cultures were negative. Transbronchial lung biopsy revealed an organizing pneumonia/nonspecific interstitial pneumonia overlapping pattern without evidence of malignant infiltration. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 9300/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 1.41 mg/dL.

A 60-year-old man presented for an annual skin examination. Two large, well-delineated patches on the dorsal forearms showed a mixture of hyperpigmented, hypopigmented, telangiectatic, and slightly atrophic macules. Similar superficial telangiectasias were noted on the neck and anterior chest. The patient was unaware of the precise onset but reported gradual progression over several years without symptoms. He has a 25-year history of chronic occupational sun exposure and never used regular photoprotection. His Fitzpatrick skin type is III.  

Medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, asthma, and basal cell carcinoma. Current medications are amlodipine/benazepril (for 6 years), chlorthalidone, rosuvastatin, metformin, and inhaled mometasone.  

Potassium hydroxide preparation of lesion scrapings was negative. A punch biopsy of a forearm lesion showed epidermal atrophy with blunting of rete ridges, increased basal-layer pigmentation without melanin incontinence, and prominent superficial blood vessels.

A 26-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of cystic fibrosis (CF) and CF-related diabetes presented at 29 weeks of gestation with increasing nausea and worsening respiratory symptoms. She had mild CF lung disease (pre-pregnancy FEV1 2.62 L [87% predicted]; current FEV1 2.09 L [69% predicted]), pancreatic insufficiency, chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, and CF-related diabetes managed with insulin (hemoglobin A1c, 6.1%). She had no microalbuminuria. Her first pregnancy, eight years earlier, was uncomplicated and resulted in a healthy child at 36 weeks. 

Her second pregnancy was unplanned; she was followed in a high-risk clinic by obstetrics, respiratory medicine, and endocrinology. At 26 weeks, she had an outpatient pulmonary exacerbation (FEV1 2.13 L [71% predicted], blood pressure 118/87 mm Hg) treated with oral ciprofloxacin. At 28 weeks, she developed worsening nausea, increased respiratory symptoms, and left upper quadrant discomfort; blood pressure was 123/90 mm Hg, and urine dipstick was negative for protein. She continued outpatient ciprofloxacin and metoclopramide. 

One week later, she was admitted with persistent respiratory symptoms and nausea. On admission, blood pressure was 153/89 mm Hg. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, platelet count 101 × 10^9/L, alanine transaminase 179 mmol/L (reference <65), lactate dehydrogenase 279 mmol/L (reference <240), and urate 523 mmol/L (reference 150–400). Urine protein/creatinine ratio was normal, and coagulation and renal function were within normal limits. A fetal ultrasound was unremarkable.

A 67-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of hypercholesterolaemia, depression, fibromyalgia, and migraine (on propranolol) was referred for evaluation of drop attacks over the past 8 years. These episodes occurred monthly within minutes of standing or during early walking, sometimes with transient loss of consciousness lasting seconds, and were accompanied by headaches, light-headedness, dyspnoea, and chest pain. She sustained multiple fractures from the attacks. Between episodes, she experienced daily orthostatic symptoms. 

Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including thyroid and adrenal function, were normal. Neurological evaluation (EEG, CT, MRI) was normal. ECG, echocardiography, and 72-hour ambulatory rhythm monitoring showed no abnormalities. Exercise testing to 80 W reproduced her dyspnoea, chest pain, and light-headedness with a modest hypertensive response (peak BP 197/67 mmHg) but no ischaemia. An implanted loop recorder documented normal sinus rhythm during eight consecutive syncope episodes.

Supraventricular tachycardias up to 180 bpm were observed and treated with metoprolol, which temporarily reduced symptoms. When the dose was reduced due to dyspnoea, her original complaints returned. Repeat echocardiography, ambulatory rhythm monitoring, exercise testing, and coronary CT angiography were unremarkable.

Supine BP was 130/85 mmHg and rose to 180/90 mmHg within 30 seconds of standing, reproducing her symptoms. On 70° head-up tilt testing, systolic BP increased from 135/85 to 200/105 mmHg within 90 seconds, and nitroglycerine also provoked a hypertensive response. Heart rate remained stable and she did not lose consciousness.

A 36-year-old man with a 3-year history of paranoid schizophrenia presented for routine follow-up. He had been treated with oral risperidone (6 mg daily) and trihexyphenidyl (4 mg daily) but demonstrated poor adherence. To improve compliance, intramuscular long-acting fluphenazine decanoate (25 mg) was added to his regimen every 2 weeks. 

At his one-month follow-up, he reported dull pain and mild swelling at the right gluteal injection site, for which he received diclofenac 50 mg twice daily for 5 days. At the next appointment (2 weeks later), he described worsening pain with marked discomfort on movement. On examination, there was a 4 cm × 4 cm deep-seated necrotic ulcer at the injection site and two firm subcutaneous nodules in the surrounding area.

A 78-year-old man, hospitalized for craniopharyngioma resection with a prolonged postoperative course complicated by infections, noted a 7-day history of a nonpruritic, nontender eruption localized to the right inguinal fold, which did not improve with miconazole powder. He denied a history of similar eruptions or any family history of skin disease.

On examination, 15 to 20 pink-white verrucous papules were arranged in a linear, non-Blaschkoid distribution in the right inguinal fold. The left crural fold, genitalia, and other skin areas were unaffected. Hands and feet were free of papules, and nail examination was unremarkable.

A 3-mm punch biopsy of a representative papule was performed. Histopathologic evaluation revealed suprabasal acantholysis and dyskeratosis, including corps ronds and grains, with parakeratosis and hyperkeratosis. There was no evidence of herpetic infection.

A 2-month-old male was brought with 2 days of feeding weakness, frequent convulsions, and increased cyanosis. There was no relevant family or medical history. Examination revealed low-set ears with adhesion of the left ear to the head, micrognathia, bilateral talipes equinovarus, and a distinctive facial appearance. Respiratory exam showed subcostal, substernal, and intercostal retractions with fine rales bilaterally. The abdomen was soft; all four extremities were cold. A bilateral direct inguinal hernia was present, and both testicles were palpable. Neurologic examination noted a tendency to limb spasms, with normal sensation, tone, and reflexes. The patient had documented intrauterine growth restriction.

Vital signs: heart rate 140–150/min, respiratory rate 40–50/min, afebrile.  
Laboratory studies: HCO3 24 meq/l; calcium 7.5 mg/dl; WBC 7900/mm3; PO2 72 kPa; PCO2 23 kPa; pH 7.63; platelets 279×10^9/l; MCV 94 fl; hemoglobin 11.4 g/dl; urea 1.6 mg/dl; creatinine 0.6 mg/dl.

Transthoracic echocardiogram showed left ventricular atrophy, mitral atresia, an 8 mm secundum atrial septal defect with left-to-right flow, a 7 mm ventricular septal defect with right chamber dilation, tricuspid regurgitation, right ventricular systolic pressure of 65 mm Hg, the aorta arising from the right ventricle, and pulmonary valve stenosis pressure of 30 mm Hg. Abdominal ultrasound revealed irregular thickening of the inferior posterior bladder wall. A bone radiograph was normal. Scrotal ultrasound was obscured by intestinal gas. Cranial ultrasound raised suspicion for intraventricular hemorrhage. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a widened left frontal-parietal subdural space with cortical atrophy, enlargement of the Sylvian fissure, and focal cortical thickening in the right parietal lobe suggestive of a neuronal migration defect.

A 54-year-old man was admitted with sudden onset of speech impairment and right-sided weakness.  
Medical history: arterial hypertension, dyslipidemia, and lumbar–sacral spondylosis; no prior ischemic events.  
Family history: sibling with hypertension and intracerebral hemorrhage at age 54.  
On examination: mild central facial paresis on the right, mild right hemiparesis, right hemihypesthesia, motor aphasia; NIHSS score 10; mRS 4.  
Initial noncontrast head CT showed no acute ischemia or hemorrhage.  
CT angiography revealed occlusion of the left MCA M2 segment with leptomeningeal collaterals (Tan score 3).  
CT perfusion demonstrated a large penumbra without hemorrhage.  
Thrombolysis was deferred due to concern for an underlying neoplasm or basal ganglia calcification.  
One-day follow-up CT showed an ischemic lesion in the left insula, parietal lobe, and superior temporal gyrus, a hyperdense artery sign, and unilateral hyperdensity in the left basal ganglia.  
Brain MRI confirmed ischemic changes and showed unilateral basal ganglia calcification.

An 80-year-old man with hypertension and coronary artery disease presented with a three-day history of emesis and diarrhea diagnosed as gastroenteritis. He reported dizziness and weakness but denied headache, blurry vision, paresthesias, or syncope. He also described a three-day history of complex visualizations of a moving car that was colorful, life-like, and drove realistically in front of him. These visualizations occurred exclusively when his eyes were closed and resolved immediately upon opening his eyes. They were present for most of the time his eyes were closed, making sleep difficult. He had insight that the car was not real. He denied any other sensory hallucinations or illusions.

He had no history of head trauma, cerebrovascular disease, psychosis, or dementia. His ophthalmologic history was unremarkable; he used glasses only for reading. He was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Physical examination was significant only for mild abdominal tenderness; there were no signs of cognitive impairment. Fundoscopic examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 4.6 billion cells/L, sodium 119 mEq/L, potassium 3.2 mEq/L, carbon dioxide 24.6 mEq/L, anion gap 10, glucose 186 mg/dL, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. A urine drug screen was negative. A chest radiograph was normal, and electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm.

A 53-year-old previously healthy man who worked as a tree cutter in the hilly central province of Sri Lanka presented on the sixth day of illness with fever, myalgia, and headache. He had developed a generalized erythematous macular rash on the fourth day, involving the trunk, limbs, palms, and soles. He was transferred for persistent hypotension despite fluid resuscitation.

On arrival, temperature was 102 °F, blood pressure 80/50 mmHg, pulse 100 bpm (thready). Examination showed discrete macular erythema over most of the body including palms and soles, mild ankle edema and ankle joint swelling, without eschar, lymphadenopathy, or splenomegaly; the liver edge was palpable 2 cm below the costal margin; lungs were clear.

He received intravenous normal saline, empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline, a norepinephrine infusion (0.4 μg/kg/min), and hydrocortisone (50 mg every 6 h) for presumed septic shock. Initial electrocardiogram was normal; chest radiograph was clear. Laboratory results demonstrated leukocytosis with neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, elevated transaminases, C-reactive protein 139 mg/dL, and procalcitonin 5.78 ng/mL. Arterial blood gas on FiO₂ 0.6 showed PaO₂ 75 mmHg (PaO₂/FiO₂ 125). Blood and urine cultures and HIV test were negative.

Approximately 36 h later, he developed worsening dyspnea and hypotension. Repeat arterial blood gas revealed type 1 respiratory failure with PaO₂/FiO₂ 136; chest radiograph now showed bilateral alveolar and interstitial infiltrates. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia without ST–T changes. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated an ejection fraction of 40–45% with global hypokinesia. Serum troponin I was 4.9 ng/mL (normal < 0.12) and NT-proBNP was 11 954 pg/mL. He was electively intubated and transferred to the intensive care unit for ventilatory and inotropic support.

A 16-year-old, 48-kg male with idiopathic scoliosis was scheduled for posterior spinal osteotomy. He had no notable medical or family history; first- and second-degree relatives had undergone anesthesia without adverse events. Physical examination showed spinal and thoracic deformities with normal lower-limb muscle strength. Radiographs confirmed scoliosis. Preoperative serum creatine kinase was elevated at 1158.3 U/L (normal 24–195); electrocardiogram, blood counts, renal function, and coagulation studies were normal. He was classified as ASA physical status 1.

On the morning of surgery, he received penehyclidine hydrochloride and dexamethasone 30 minutes before induction. General anesthesia was induced with midazolam 3 mg, sufentanil 20 μg, cis-atracurium 10 mg, and propofol 60 mg. After endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation was set with a tidal volume of 8 mL/kg, respiratory rate 16/min, and I:E ratio of 1:2. The end-tidal CO2 (PetCO2) immediately after induction was 38 mmHg. Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane, propofol, and remifentanil. Surgery began at 9:45 am.

At 9:50 am, the PetCO2 rose abruptly to 59 mmHg, heart rate increased to 100 bpm, and the surgeon noted increased muscle tension. The anesthesiologist deepened anesthesia, administered additional cis-atracurium, replaced the soda lime, and increased minute ventilation. By 10:00 am, the PetCO2 had climbed to 144 mmHg, heart rate to 135 bpm, and nasopharyngeal temperature to 38.3°C. Arterial blood gas at that time showed pH 6.748, PCO2 > 130 mmHg, K+ 6.4 mmol/L, and ionized Ca2+ 1.46 mmol/L.

A 10-year-old girl, previously healthy, presented with a 1-day history of diffuse abdominal pain, watery diarrhea, and a temperature of 37.6 °C. She reported no rash or pruritus. On initial evaluation at a local clinic, she was hypotensive and tachycardic (heart rate 156 beats/min), with a tendency toward somnolence. Rapid infusion of crystalloid restored her blood pressure to 120/68 mmHg within 15 minutes, but within hours her systolic pressure again dropped to 40 mmHg, prompting transfer to our hospital.

On arrival, she remained somnolent and pale. Vital signs were: blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, heart rate 180 beats/min, temperature 38.1 °C. Her weight was 34.3 kg (baseline 34.0 kg). Initial laboratory studies revealed:
- WBC 41.0 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 23.3 g/dL, hematocrit 64.4%
- Albumin 2.3 g/dL, BUN 42 mg/dL, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, CRP 3.24 mg/dL
- Arterial blood gas consistent with metabolic acidosis
- Urinalysis on admission: protein 100 mg/dL, blood 3+, RBC >100/HPF (subsequent urinalysis showed no proteinuria)

Chest radiograph showed a cardiothoracic ratio of 45% without pleural effusion. Echocardiography demonstrated a small pericardial effusion and an ejection fraction of 50%. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed massive ascites and mild small-bowel dilatation. Despite continued aggressive fluid resuscitation (normal saline, albumin, fresh frozen plasma) and vasopressor support with dopamine, her systolic blood pressure remained between 70 and 90 mmHg on day 1. A repeat CT scan showed new bilateral pleural effusions and persistent ascites. She was intubated for respiratory support. 

On day 2, her serum albumin fell to 1.8 g/dL and her body weight rose to 40.7 kg. She developed oliguria (300 mL/day) and hyperkalemia (6.6 mEq/L) in the setting of acute renal failure.

A 23-year-old man with no significant past medical history was referred for evaluation of unexplained dyspnea. He had been in his usual state of health until 2 weeks before admission, when he developed fever, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea. Three days later, he experienced vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. After admission for these symptoms, he developed marked palpitations, dyspnea, and orthopnea.

His parents both have diabetes, his grandfather died of myocardial infarction at age 74, and his maternal uncle has acromegaly. He had no known connective tissue disorder or previous cardiovascular disease.

On examination, temperature was 37.9 °C, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, heart rate 110 beats/min, and respiratory rate 22 breaths/min. Lung auscultation revealed fine basal crepitations and mild expiratory rhonchi bilaterally. Cardiac examination disclosed an early diastolic murmur; neck veins were distended without visible pulsations. There was no peripheral edema or ascites.

Laboratory studies showed a brain natriuretic peptide level of 340 pg/mL. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly and bilateral mild pleural effusions. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with T-wave inversions in leads V3 and V4.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a mildly dilated, hypertrophied left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 48%, impaired diastolic function, moderate mitral regurgitation, and severe aortic regurgitation. The aortic root measurements were: annulus 3.2 cm, sinus of Valsalva 4.9 cm, and sinotubular junction 7.5 cm.

CT aortography confirmed marked dilation of the aortic root and ascending aorta (maximum diameter 10 cm) and a descending aortic diameter of 2.5 cm.

A 59-year-old man underwent a 10-hour, 55-minute pancreaticoduodenectomy complicated by 1500 mL blood loss and large-volume resuscitation. Intubation required both direct and video laryngoscopy with additional anterocaudal force and external laryngeal manipulation; a 7.5 mm endotracheal tube was ultimately placed without obvious mucosal trauma and secured at 22 cm. The intraoperative course was otherwise uneventful, and the trachea was extubated at the end of surgery.

On postoperative day 1, he noted slurred speech and a swollen tongue. Examination by nursing staff revealed dysarthria and deviation of the tongue to the left; there were no other cranial nerve deficits, no limb weakness, no sensory loss, and he was alert and oriented. A neurologic consultation confirmed isolated dysarthria and leftward tongue deviation without other focal findings. An MRI of the brain without contrast was performed and showed no acute infarction or other intracranial abnormalities.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of narrowing of her vaginal and urethral orifices, accompanied by moderate itching and erythema of the genital region and chronic constipation. Over the past year, she developed anal pain and difficulty passing stools, dyspareunia, and episodes of urinary retention. For 6 years, she had recurrent oral erosions on the gums with a burning sensation when eating spicy foods. She underwent multiple cystoscopies and proctoscopies during the last 3 years for urethral and anal dilatation, which provided only short-term relief. She denied vaginal discharge. Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine; she had a dental filling placed 18 years ago. There was no relevant family history.

On mucocutaneous examination, there was intense erythema of the vulva and vestibule, partial fusion of the labia minora and majora, and burying of the clitoris. Old hypo- and hyperpigmented patches were present on the labia and clitoral region. Introital stenosis (Grade 2+) prevented speculum examination. The anal mucosa showed hyperpigmentation, fissuring, scaling, and marked stenosis. Oral examination revealed violaceous plaques on the labial and lingual aspects of the maxillary and mandibular gingiva. Skin, hair, and nails were normal. Routine laboratory investigations were unremarkable.

An 18-year-old man with no medical, ocular, or trauma history presented with a 4-day history of blurred vision in his left eye. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in the right eye and 0.9 in the left eye; refractive error was –5.0 diopters bilaterally. The anterior segment was normal. Fundus examination of the left eye revealed a single gray-white lesion in the superior juxtafoveal region. Automated visual field testing (10-2 SITA-Standard) showed decreased threshold sensitivity corresponding to the lesion. Spectral-domain OCT demonstrated disruption of the photoreceptor inner and outer segment junction and undulation of the retinal pigment epithelium with backscattering.

A 28-year-old man with hypertension and obesity presented with a 1-day history of binocular horizontal diplopia, most prominent on left gaze, which resolved when either eye was covered. He also reported a 1–2-week history of paresthesia in the distal right hand and forearm and in the fifth toe of the right foot. On examination, all cranial nerves and neurologic findings were normal except for a left lateral rectus palsy. Laboratory studies showed a mild leukocytosis (11.3×10^9 cells/L) without other hematologic or electrolyte abnormalities. A noncontrast CT scan of the head was unremarkable. MRI of the brain and spinal cord with and without gadolinium revealed T2 hyperintense lesions in the periventricular white matter of the frontal and parietal lobes, in the subcortical white matter of the left temporal lobe, and in the left pons (the pontine lesion showed contrast enhancement). In the cervical spinal cord, a T2 hyperintense lesion was noted on the left side of the C5–C6 segment.

A 6-month-old female infant of Iranian descent, born to consanguineous parents, was delivered by cesarean section at 32 weeks of gestation for breech presentation. Her birth weight was 2.5 kg and length was 43 cm. Since 3 months of age, she had persistent, treatment-resistant diarrhea and concerns about failure to thrive. At 6 months, her weight was 8.0 kg and her length was 68 cm. The parents also noted congenital flexion deformities of both knees and mild inversion of the feet. An initial orthopedic evaluation attributed these deformities to intrauterine growth retardation and breech delivery. On referral to pediatric rheumatology, examination revealed hyperpigmented diffuse nodules on the proximal interphalangeal joints, with stiffness, restricted mobility, and pain on movement, as well as erythematous, hyaline-appearing plaques in the perianal region. No other abnormalities were noted on physical examination. The patient was scheduled for standard radiographic imaging, echocardiography, abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography, a metabolic panel (including serum cobalamin), an iron profile (including ferritin), electromyography, genetic testing, and a bone survey.

A 38-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of recurrent, non-radiating epigastric pain associated with nausea, mild fever, and occasional vomiting. He reports no change in bowel habits or weight loss. His medical and surgical histories are unremarkable. On examination, vital signs are notable only for low-grade fever; abdominal examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness without masses or organomegaly. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and basic metabolic profile, are within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT shows a thick-walled cystic lesion along the greater curvature of the stomach with enhancement of the inner lining and focal calcification. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrates a cystic formation adjacent to the gastric wall with an echogenic internal mucosal layer and a hypoechoic intermediate muscular layer. A barium-meal examination reveals an intramural filling defect indenting the gastric contour consistent with a cystic structure.

A 3-year-old girl with no medical or family history presented with dyspnea of 3 days’ duration. On examination, she was tachypneic with retractive breathing and low oxygen saturation; she was afebrile and fully alert. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13,600/mm3, hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL, platelets 268,000/mm3, C-reactive protein 0.01 mg/dL, procalcitonin 0.05 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 311 U/L (reference <245 U/L), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 1080 U/mL (reference <496 U/mL). Urinary vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid levels were normal. A chest radiograph revealed a large mediastinal mass.
