Unenhanced CT of the chest showed a large anterior mediastinal mass with linear and punctate calcifications. Contrast-enhanced CT performed 11 days later demonstrated a bilobed mass in the anterior mediastinum with linear and punctate calcifications arranged in curvilinear septa.

A 33-year-old Han man presented with 2 days of neck pain and right-sided numbness in both the upper and lower limbs. Two days before admission, after a prodromal cold, he noted neck pain worsened by turning his head, followed by progressive numbness on the right. One day later, he developed mild weakness of the left arm and leg without interference with daily activities. He denied fever, headache, visual changes, bowel or bladder symptoms. His medical history was unremarkable.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Cranial nerves were intact. Strength was 4/5 in the left arm and leg; tone and deep tendon reflexes were normal in all limbs. Pain sensation was diminished below the right clavicle. Proprioception and vibration were reduced on the left side. The left Babinski sign was present.

Laboratory studies: complete blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, and antinuclear antibody panel were normal; cancer markers were negative; serum HSV, CMV, and EBV DNA were undetectable. CSF analysis showed 24 × 10^6 cells/L and protein 185 mg/L; Gram stain, acid-fast stain, culture, oligoclonal bands, and AQP4 antibody were negative. Visual evoked potentials were normal.

Brain MRI was unremarkable. Cervical MRI demonstrated a long-segment T2 hyperintensity extending from the medulla through the cervical cord with focal enhancement at C2–C3.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a hyperkeratotic plaque on the left forehead. Two years earlier, 3 months after a roadside fall, a small papule appeared and over time expanded peripherally into an annular plaque with a warty surface; ulceration developed over the past 3 months. She denied sensory changes, tingling, or numbness in the area and had no hypopigmented lesions or nerve enlargement elsewhere. There was no lymphadenopathy. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests and a chest radiograph were normal. A tuberculin skin test showed 20 mm of induration.

A 40-year-old man with HIV infection, on antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, lamivudine, efavirenz) for 2 years, presented with an 8-month history of generalized, asymptomatic skin lesions. The lesions began on an elbow and then appeared on the extremities, buttocks, ears, and face but spared the trunk. He denied fever, nasal stuffiness, or sensory changes. On examination, there were multiple discrete, nontender, erythematous to skin-colored papules and nodules, 5 mm to 2 cm in diameter, symmetrically distributed on the elbows, knees, buttocks, ears, eyebrows, palms, and soles; some lesions around the elbows had crusted plaques, and palmar lesions showed umbilication and verrucosity. Peripheral nerves were not thickened, and systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests including complete blood count, urinalysis, liver and renal function tests, chest radiograph, and abdominal ultrasound were normal. His CD4 count had risen from 16 cells/mm3 at baseline to 104 cells/mm3 at the onset of the skin lesions. Differential diagnoses considered included histoid Hansen’s disease, histoplasmosis, post–kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, and diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis.

A 28-year-old man presented with a bleeding ulcer on his right dorsal foot. The lesion measured 1.5 cm in diameter, had raised edges, and was bordered laterally by a 1 × 2 cm dark subcutaneous blanchable area. The foot was erythematous, swollen, and painful. He reported that the lesion started 5 months earlier as a purple papule that enlarged slowly. He denied fever or systemic symptoms. His weight was normal, and he was a smoker. His history included a pilonidal sinus excision 3 years earlier, acne conglobata, and a surgically deroofed axillary lesion. At presentation, he was receiving clindamycin (300 mg twice daily) and rifampicin (300 mg twice daily) for active lesions in the femoral and perianal regions. On occupational review, he noted kneeling on his right leg to pave streets and had recently started wearing a new, rigid, tight pair of work shoes. Rifampicin was stopped, clindamycin was increased to 300 mg three times daily, and ciprofloxacin (500 mg twice daily) was added. Despite this regimen, over the following weeks the lesion progressed, forming small ulcers with brown-yellow discharge and sinus tracts, evolving into a dark erythematous plaque. Further testing showed a normal blood glucose level and a negative bacterial culture of the wound exudate.

A 19-year-old man with no past medical history presented with several weeks of dull, heavy pain in the right costovertebral region. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory investigations, including complete blood count and liver function tests, were within normal ranges. The patient lived in a region where hydatid disease is endemic. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed a 45 mm oval cystic lesion in the retrohepatic space, closely attached to the lateral aspect of the right hemidiaphragm and the right hepatic lobe; the lesion had regular contours, contained both liquid and fatty components, and demonstrated peripheral calcification. The radiological appearance was suggestive of a hydatid cyst; however, hydatid serology was negative, and the patient reported no exposure to livestock or dogs.

A 68-year-old man with a history of hypertension treated with amlodipine 5 mg and azilsartan 20 mg each morning was scheduled for transurethral resection of a bladder tumor under general anesthesia using 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) for fluorescence guidance. His blood pressure was typically around 130/70 mmHg. Preoperative chest radiograph, electrocardiogram, and laboratory tests were normal. On the morning of surgery, he took only amlodipine. Three hours before anesthesia induction, he ingested 5-ALA at 20 mg/kg orally. Just before induction, his blood pressure was 98/61 mmHg and heart rate 82 beats/min. Anesthesia was induced with propofol 100 mg, rocuronium 50 mg, fentanyl 100 μg, and remifentanil infusion. Five minutes later, just before tracheal intubation, his blood pressure suddenly fell to 47/32 mmHg without any ST-T changes or arrhythmia on ECG.  

Despite administration of phenylephrine totaling 0.2 mg and ephedrine totaling 10 mg over the next 10 minutes, his blood pressure remained at approximately 50/33 mmHg. There was no wheezing or erythema. A 100 mL bolus of hydroxyethyl starch failed to raise his blood pressure. Transthoracic cardiac ultrasonography showed normal systolic function, no wall-motion abnormalities, and a normal-size inferior vena cava.

A 72-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of a lesion in the macula of his right eye. He was asymptomatic, and visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. The left eye examination was unremarkable. In the right eye, funduscopic examination revealed an orange-red, serpentine, track-like lesion inferior to the fovea extending temporally to the equator, with overlying retinal pigment epithelium changes. Near-infrared imaging showed alternating hyper- and hyporeflective spots along the lesion. Indocyanine green angiography demonstrated early filling of the large branching lesion and no leakage in the late phase. Enhanced depth imaging optical coherence tomography through the lesion showed a hyporeflective structure originating at the choroid–scleral junction, elevating the overlying retina, with focal disruption of the Bruch’s–retinal pigment epithelium complex and a few hyperreflective foci in the outer retina. En face swept-source OCT angiography with a custom slab through the full choroidal thickness revealed a large, tortuous vessel-like lesion with a signal similar to that of adjacent physiological choroidal vessels.

A 40‐year‐old man presented with a 1‐month history of swelling of the lower lip, similar to an episode 8 months earlier that had been biopsied elsewhere (report unavailable). His medical history was noncontributory. On examination, there was diffuse, nodular swelling of the lower lip, soft to firm in consistency. A provisional diagnosis of mucocele was made. Routine hematologic tests, including RBC count, differential count, platelet count, hemoglobin, and ESR, were within normal limits. Incisional biopsy of the lip lesion revealed circumscribed aggregates of noncaseating granulomatous inflammation composed of lymphocytes and epithelioid histiocytes with multinucleated giant cells, with a peripheral rim of lymphocytes in a vascular fibrous stroma. Subsequent investigations included serum angiotensin-converting enzyme levels (normal), Mantoux test (negative), chest radiograph (normal), periodic acid–Schiff stain for fungi (negative), acid-fast bacilli stain for mycobacteria (negative), and evaluation for foreign material and allergy (none detected; no history of allergy). The patient denied gastrointestinal symptoms, and no further gastrointestinal evaluation was performed.

A 71-year-old man with metastatic renal cell carcinoma presented with a highly pruritic rash over his chest, arms, and back causing sleep disturbance that began 2 months after receiving four doses of ipilimumab and nivolumab. He initially used topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines without relief, followed by an eight-day taper of oral prednisone (60 mg), also without improvement. On dermatologic evaluation, scattered eroded, erythematous macules and papules were observed on the trunk and arms. A punch biopsy of the left arm demonstrated suprabasal acantholysis with occasional dyskeratotic cells and perivascular lymphocytic inflammation with eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence studies were negative.

A 70-year-old man presented with 5 days of painless bleeding, initially from the right nostril, followed by black stools and cola-colored urine. His history included hypertension and type II diabetes; medications were daily aspirin, metformin, and a recent short course of azithromycin. He denied bleeding disorders, anticoagulant use, smoking, alcohol, or illicit drugs. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable but had active right-sided epistaxis; lungs were clear and the abdomen was soft without bruising.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, hematocrit 32.4%, lactate dehydrogenase 662 IU/L, prothrombin time > 120 s, activated partial thromboplastin time > 240 s, and INR > 10. Urinalysis revealed 4+ blood and > 50 RBCs per high-power field. CT of the head and sinuses demonstrated mucosal thickening in the right maxillary sinus. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed bilateral multilobar airspace infiltrates (most prominent in the left lower lobe) and a 2-cm right adrenal mass. Immediate PT and aPTT mixing studies fully corrected the coagulopathy, suggesting factor deficiency. He received four units of fresh frozen plasma over the first 5 days and was started on 10 mg of vitamin K₁ daily, which controlled his bleeding and normalized his INR. HIV and hepatitis panels were negative. Further history disclosed marital discord and an extramarital affair; despite no anticoagulant use, rodenticide or superwarfarin exposure was suspected. Although malignancy was considered, it was deemed unlikely and not pursued.

A 74-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease was admitted for urinary retention. He reported no chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or family history of sudden cardiac death and denied substance or alcohol use. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable and asymptomatic. Laboratory tests, including serum electrolytes and cardiac biomarkers, were within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal systolic function and no wall motion abnormalities or left ventricular hypertrophy. The initial 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated runs of non–sustained ventricular tachycardia and subtle ST-segment elevation in lead V1.

A 46-year-old woman with longstanding active rheumatoid arthritis and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis presented with dysphagia and neck fullness. Her history included pulmonary nodules, a right nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma, and a total thyroidectomy performed three months earlier for an enlarging goiter with mild tracheal compression. Preoperatively, TSH was 4.22 μU/mL, free T4 0.96 ng/dL, free T3 3.5 pg/mL, calcitonin 7.1 pg/mL, and antithyroid microsomal antibody levels >1000 IU/mL. Thyroid ultrasound had shown a solitary 1.0×0.6×0.8 cm nodule; fine-needle aspiration revealed nodular goiter with lymphocytic thyroiditis. Postoperatively, she received suppressive levothyroxine and low-dose radioactive iodine.

Four months after thyroidectomy, she noted neck fullness again. On examination, a palpable mass was present. Ultrasound revealed a large solid nodule of mixed echogenicity in the right anterior neck compartment measuring 5.6×3.3×2.3 cm, and another in the left anterior compartment measuring 2.9×2.3×1.7 cm; residual tissue was also seen at the original isthmus plane. Given the rapid growth and concern for malignancy, fine-needle aspiration was deferred and surgical excision was planned.

A 41-year-old man with Child-Pugh B liver cirrhosis and chronic pancreatitis presented with 3 days of progressive dyspnea, retrosternal pain radiating to the back, repeated vomiting, and fever. On arrival, he was confused and agitated. Vital signs: temperature 38.5 °C; heart rate 150 beats/min; respiratory rate 40 breaths/min. Physical examination revealed a supple but tender abdomen with normal bowel sounds and muffled breath sounds over the right lung. Laboratory studies showed macrocytic anemia, leukocytes 18 500 /mm3, normal serum enzymes, C-reactive protein 303 mg/L, and lactate 7.4 mmol/L. Chest radiograph demonstrated a right-sided silhouette sign and small mediastinal radiolucent streaks. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax confirmed pneumomediastinum and revealed a dilated esophagus with a distal tear, bilateral pleural effusions, and heterogeneous retro- and paracardiac collections.

A 51-year-old man with end-stage renal failure from biopsy-proven IgA nephritis began hemodialysis in 1977. He received cadaveric kidney transplants in 1980, 1985, and 1997 and underwent parathyroidectomy in 1998. He remained dialysis-free until December 2003 when graft function declined; immunosuppression was tapered to prednisone alone by October 2004 and withdrawn completely at the end of June 2005 after removal of the graft for presumed rejection.

In June 2005 he developed an inflammatory syndrome with low-grade fever (up to 37.5 °C) and general weakness. A transplant biopsy showed tubulointerstitial nephritis, interpreted as rejection, and the graft was removed. Days later fever recurred and he reported testicular pain; ultrasound suggested epididymitis, but ciprofloxacin did not relieve symptoms. Over the next 12 weeks he experienced insomnia, severe pruritus, a 4-kg weight loss, and migratory arthralgias; joint imaging was unrevealing.

Laboratory testing revealed rising serum calcium at 2.84 mmol/L (normal 2.2–2.65) with normal to moderately elevated intact PTH, alkaline phosphatase of 173 U/L (normal 35–104), and moderately elevated C-reactive protein. Vitamin D had been discontinued more than three months earlier. He was switched to low-calcium dialysate and to sevelamer for phosphate control, but hypercalcemia and symptoms persisted.

A 32-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 2-week history of epileptic seizures. Initially, he had two episodes of focal aware seizures manifesting as left-arm convulsions lasting 2–3 seconds without altered sensorium. The next day, he had two similar focal aware seizures. On day 3, he experienced a generalized tonic–clonic seizure with eye deviation, limb jerking, tongue biting, and loss of consciousness lasting 1–2 minutes, followed by a 20-minute postictal state. He then noted paresthesia in the left extremities, and 1 week after onset he had a 2-minute episode of transient sensory loss in the left limbs. There was no history of trauma, infection, or febrile illness, and family history was unremarkable. Neurological examination was normal.

Electroencephalography showed sharp waves, sharp–slow complexes, and irregular δ waves originating from the bilateral temporal lobes, predominantly on the left. One week before admission, conventional MRI with spectroscopy and angiography was normal. Laboratory studies—including blood and urine cell counts, chemistry, coagulation profile, thyroid function, CSF routine and immuno-antibodies, tumor biomarkers, and screening for NMDA-R, CASPR2, AMPAR1, AMPAR2, LGI1, and GABAR-B2 antibodies—were all normal. On hospital day 2, repeat brain MRI revealed poorly defined bilateral frontoparietal lesions that were hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted, FLAIR, and STIR images. Antiepileptic therapy with oxcarbazepine was initiated, and the patient remained seizure-free thereafter.

A 52-year-old man presented with 5 days of severe hematemesis and melena. He reported bright-red emesis, dizziness, and cold, clammy skin. A similar episode occurred one month earlier without further evaluation. He denied alcohol use, smoking, antiplatelet or NSAID use, and had no family history of GI disease.

On examination, blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 120 beats/min and weak, respiratory rate 22/min, and temperature 37 °C. There were no stigmata of chronic liver disease or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies were within normal limits, including hemoglobin 11 mg/dl, leukocyte count 10 000/mm³, platelets 400 000/mm³, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dl, ALT 40 U/l, AST 38 U/l, albumin 4.0 g/dl, and prothrombin time 12 s.

Despite fluid resuscitation, tranexamic acid, and pantoprazole, hematemesis persisted. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed multiple dilated vascular channels in the fundic part of the stomach with normal liver parenchyma and portal vasculature. Upper GI endoscopy revealed an angiomatous nodular lesion in the fundus without ulceration, which was inadvertently disrupted during the procedure, leading to further bleeding.

A 24-year-old man was referred for evaluation of decreased visual acuity, described as transient with little impact on his daily life over the past few months. He had no prior systemic or ocular history and was not taking any medications. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye; intraocular pressure was 13 mmHg bilaterally. Pupils were normal with no relative afferent defect, color vision was 10/10 in both eyes, and extraocular movements were full. The anterior segments and lenses were unremarkable. Funduscopic examination revealed multiple small yellow dots confined to the macula in both eyes, with a normal retinal periphery. A 30-2 Humphrey visual field and fluorescein angiography were normal. Optical coherence tomography of both eyes showed no retinal layer irregularities. Blood tests, including complete blood count, blood chemistry, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, lipid profile, coagulation tests, and a complete collagenogram, were all within normal limits. Electrophysiological testing was also normal bilaterally. Because of a suspected inherited condition, his parents were examined: his father had normal findings and visual acuity of 20/20 in each eye; his mother had visual acuity of 20/20 bilaterally and exhibited similar bilateral macular yellow dots on fundus examination. Neither parent had any systemic or ocular complaints. Over 6 years of follow-up, the patient and his mother showed no progression of the macular findings and no change in visual acuity.

A 21-year-old phenotypic female presented with primary amenorrhea and a desire for fertility. She was 146 cm tall, weighed 67 kg (BMI 31.3 kg/m2), and had cubitus valgus and a webbed neck; external genitalia were unambiguously female. Her medical history was notable only for multiple childhood tympanoplasties. There was no family history of gynecologic disease or short stature. Transabdominal ultrasound showed uterine hypoplasia. Contrast-enhanced pelvic MRI demonstrated a 30 mm-long uterus with vaginal thinning and no identifiable gonads. CT of the chest and abdomen was normal. Serum studies revealed estradiol ≤ 5.0 pg/ml, luteinizing hormone 25.5 mIU/ml, and follicle-stimulating hormone 98.4 mIU/ml. Peripheral-blood karyotyping showed 45,X/46,XY mosaicism (8 of 30 cells 45,X; 22 of 30 cells 46,XY).

An 87-year-old man was referred for hiccups that persisted for a full day despite prior symptomatic treatments (esomeprazole, metoclopramide, dimethicone, prokinetic and antispasmodic herbal medicines). Over the previous 2 years, he had two similar 3-day episodes with intervening 4–7 days of relief; this was his third episode, and it had not abated with shakuyakukanzoto. He denied dysphagia, chest pain, chest discomfort, nausea, or headache. His medications included frequent esomeprazole for hiccups and chronic amlodipine and bisoprolol for hypertension; he had never used corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable; there was no nuchal rigidity or cranial-nerve deficit. Laboratory studies were within normal limits, without evidence of diabetes mellitus or immunosuppression. Cranial MRI showed only chronic lacunar infarcts; no tumors or ventricular enlargement were seen. Chest CT revealed a midesophageal diverticulum projecting rightward at the level of the tracheal bifurcation; there was no lymphadenopathy or other thoracoabdominal abnormality. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated several white deposits throughout the esophagus. A midesophageal diverticulum was noted on the right wall approximately 30 cm from the incisors, with white residue at its margin that was readily flushed away; inside the diverticulum, extensive white deposits were present.

A 31-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a one-hour history of sudden onset left-sided weakness of both upper and lower extremities following a fall while seated. He also reported a frontal headache, slurred speech, and nonradiating, burning epigastric pain. His past medical history was notable only for recurrent left flank pain previously treated as renal colic with NSAIDs. He smoked 18 pack-years and denied alcohol or drug use.  

On examination, he was alert and oriented; blood pressure and heart rate were normal and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Neurologic examination revealed nonfluent speech with intact comprehension and repetition, preserved sensation, and marked left-sided weakness (1/5 strength in both upper and lower limbs) with a muted left Babinski sign. Cranial nerves were intact.  

Initial laboratory tests showed elevated cardiac enzymes, normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 7 g/dl), reticulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, prolonged aPTT, normal PT/INR, and evidence of intra-renal injury (BUN-to-creatinine ratio 17:1). Indirect hyperbilirubinemia and elevated inflammatory markers were present; electrolytes and haptoglobin were normal. Urinalysis revealed 2+ proteinuria and 3+ hematuria.  

An ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm, a prolonged PR interval, and diffuse ST-segment elevation. Echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% with bi-atrial dilation. Cardiac catheterization revealed nonobstructive coronary arteries consistent with microvascular thrombosis.  

Brain CT scan revealed a large acute nonhemorrhagic infarction in the right fronto-parietal–temporal lobes and multiple lacunar infarctions, which were confirmed by MRI. Magnetic resonance angiography showed total occlusion of the right middle cerebral artery.

A 63‐year‐old man with a history of achalasia and dyspepsia presented with sudden onset of severe right chest pain, epigastric pain, retrosternal chest pain, and respiratory distress. He was tachycardic (130 beats/min), normotensive, afebrile, and had an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. Physical examination revealed diminished breath sounds on the right side and epigastric tenderness. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Chest computed tomography showed pneumomediastinum, right pleural effusion, and collapse of the right lung lobe. Analysis of the pleural fluid grew Candida albicans, raising suspicion for esophageal rupture.

A 27-year-old man from central Iran noted a small pimple on his right upper eyelid 4 months before presentation. Over time, it slowly enlarged into a well-defined, firm, nontender, subcutaneous, skin-colored nodule measuring 1 cm × 1 cm, with slightly erythematous raised borders, crusting, and no pain or systemic symptoms.  
On examination, vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including CBC, ESR, CRP, and blood chemistries, were within normal limits. A culture of lesion fluid grew Staphylococcus aureus. The patient underwent sequential courses of cephalexin, cloxacillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and a brief course of systemic steroids—each for 10 days—with no improvement.  
Given his residence in an area endemic for cutaneous leishmaniasis and the lesion’s lack of response to therapy, cutaneous leishmaniasis versus basal cell carcinoma was proposed as the leading diagnostic considerations.

A 16-year-old girl presented with epigastric pain of several days’ duration associated with hiccups, nausea, and vomiting but without fever or other abdominal pain. She had no significant medical or family history. On examination, she was afebrile, and there was no abdominal tenderness or other remarkable findings. Laboratory studies showed an elevated serum IgG4 concentration of 244 mg/dL (normal range, 3–201 mg/dL). Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a submucosal mass with intact overlying mucosa at the gastric fundus. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a calcifying submucosal lesion measuring 7.1 × 3.1 cm extending from the gastric fundus to the greater curvature of the upper body and suggested a hypodense focus in liver segment IV. Abdominal ultrasound showed a 2.72-cm poorly defined hyperechoic lesion in segment IV of the liver. A repeat MRI confirmed the gastric mass but no liver lesion. According to the imaging report, the differential diagnosis of the gastric submucosal mass included gastrointestinal stromal tumor, leiomyoma, lipoma, schwannoma, and other submucosal tumors.

A 65-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral valve disease had undergone placement of a 25-mm bileaflet mechanical mitral valve 18 months earlier. She is on warfarin (no aspirin due to hypersensitivity). She presents with a 2-week history of worsening dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea.  
On examination, temperature 98.1°F, blood pressure 92/61 mm Hg, heart rate 120 bpm, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, and SpO2 92% on room air. Jugular venous pressure was 10–12 cm; basal crackles were heard bilaterally; trace lower-extremity edema was present.  
An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia and nonspecific ST-T changes. Chest radiography revealed bilateral interstitial prominence and small pleural effusions. The INR was 3.8; other laboratories were unremarkable.  
Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 60–65%, a poorly visualized prosthetic mitral valve, a mean transmitral gradient of 20 mm Hg, a peak E-wave velocity of 2.9 m/s, a Doppler velocity index of 3.85, and a pressure half-time of 254 ms, with no visible mass.  
Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a fixed posterior prosthetic leaflet and a partially restricted anterior leaflet, with a mean gradient of 42 mm Hg at a heart rate of 87 bpm and no visible mass.  
Cardiac CT showed severely restricted motion of both prosthetic leaflets; evaluation for pannus was limited by streak artifact near the valve ring.

A 47-year-old woman with well-controlled diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, anemia, hypothyroidism, and myopia presented with right ocular pain and erythema after a knitting-needle injury. On initial examination, right-eye visual acuity was hand motion and left eye was 8/10. Pupils were equal and reactive bilaterally, with a 1+ relative afferent pupillary defect on the right. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed a partial-thickness scleral laceration, conjunctival laceration, and hyphema; the left anterior chamber was deep and clear. Intraocular pressure was 10 mm Hg in both eyes, extraocular movements were normal, and fundus examination of the right eye was obscured by hyphema. The lacerations were repaired, and on the following day the patient reported new-onset blurred vision. Examination then revealed hyperemic conjunctiva, subconjunctival hemorrhage, visible suture tracks, 4+ red blood cells in the anterior chamber, early cataract changes, and intraocular pressure of 14 mm Hg in both eyes. Posterior-segment examination of the right eye showed a diminished foveal reflex, retinal edema at the posterior pole, and a cherry-red spot; visual acuity remained hand motion at 1 m with a 1+ relative afferent pupillary defect. Optical coherence tomography of the right eye revealed marked hyperreflectivity and thickening of the inner retinal layers, with loss of their normal stratification.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of burning on urination, urinary frequency, nocturia, and constant 5/10 suprapubic pain that did not radiate. She denied fever, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, weight change, palpitations, heat or cold intolerance, peripheral edema, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was one week earlier. Physical examination revealed lower abdominal tenderness, most pronounced in the para-umbilical area, without costovertebral angle tenderness.

Laboratory tests showed a negative serum β-hCG, normal CBC and BMP, and a urinalysis with 10–25 WBCs per high-power field, moderate bacteria, moderate mucus, moderate yeast, and positive nitrites; cervical NAAT was negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. A diagnosis of lower urinary tract infection was made, and she received a 10-day course of antibiotics as an outpatient.

Despite treatment, her dysuria, frequency, and burning worsened. She reported chronic constipation, with two hard, non-bloody stools per week managed intermittently with stool softeners. There was no history of abdominal trauma or family gastrointestinal disease. 

Because of persistent symptoms, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. It demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.3 × 6.8 cm multiloculated, enhancing hypodense and isodense mass extending superiorly from the dome of the bladder to the posterior surface of the umbilicus, with surrounding acute inflammatory stranding and minimal fluid. There was possible invasion into the bladder dome, secondary thickening of an adjacent distal small-bowel loop, and perivesical stranding around a thick-walled, collapsed bladder.

Given these findings, differential diagnoses included patent urachus, urachal sinus, urachal diverticulum, and malignant transformation of a urachal remnant, and diagnostic laparoscopy was planned.

A 55-year-old mentally impaired man was admitted with a 2-day history of progressive dysphagia and odynophagia after an alleged ingestion of a foreign body. He was breathing spontaneously in a reduced but stable general condition, with a heart rate of 115 bpm, blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg, and no fever. Laboratory studies, including leukocyte count and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. For further evaluation, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck and chest was performed, revealing a mass-forming, circular lesion of predominantly fluid density in the cervical esophagus just below the upper esophageal sphincter; the esophageal wall could not be clearly delineated. There was no evidence of a radiopaque foreign body and no pneumomediastinum. In addition, there were pulmonary infiltrates in the left upper and lower lobes. Radiological differential diagnoses included periesophageal fluid collection as a result of esophageal perforation or distention of the esophageal lumen by a large non-radiopaque foreign body.

A 66-year-old white man presented to the Emergency Department with abrupt onset of dyspnea, palpitations, and lightheadedness. In the ED, he was found to be in monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and was electrically cardioverted into normal sinus rhythm. His medical history included a cerebrovascular accident, Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations, hypertension, incidentally noted pulmonary nodules, and chronic kidney disease (baseline GFR 40–45 mL/min/1.73 m2). He was taking losartan and warfarin and had no family history of sudden cardiac death.

Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits, and coronary angiography ruled out ischemia. His electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, but an epsilon wave in V1, a QRS duration of 140 ms, and T-wave inversions in leads V1–V5. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved left ventricular function and no valvular disease, but a markedly dilated right ventricle with severely reduced systolic function. Based on an epsilon wave in V1–V3, T-wave inversions in V1–V3 with QRS >110 ms, an RV outflow tract dimension >32 mm, and severe RV dilation and hypokinesia, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia was highly suspected. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was indicated but not performed because of chronic kidney disease and patient preference. A septal endomyocardial biopsy was considered but deferred due to its low yield. Given the patient’s pulmonary nodules, cardiac sarcoidosis remained in the differential diagnosis.

A 61-year-old woman was referred to the otolaryngology clinic by a maxillofacial surgeon after a presurgical dental‐implantation plain radiograph reportedly showed a lytic lesion destroying the wall of the right maxillary sinus. The patient denied facial pain, rhinorrhea, recurrent sinusitis, nasal congestion, and had no history of sinonasal surgery or trauma. Anterior rhinoscopy revealed no mass or lesion. Diagnostic nasal endoscopy demonstrated a hypoplastic inferior concha on the right side and absence of the infundibulum and uncinate process; the left side was normal. A paranasal CT scan with 2-mm coronal and axial slices showed an aplastic right maxillary sinus with complete opacification, absence of the right uncinate process and infundibulum, and slight enlargement of the right nasal fossa. The remaining paranasal sinuses appeared normal.

A 24-year-old woman was referred for a 2-month history of joint pain, fever, abdominal pain, and five episodes of diarrhea per day. The symptoms would resolve after several days, only to recur every few weeks. She had no family history of inflammatory bowel disease or familial Mediterranean fever. 

On admission, she had elevated C-reactive protein (6.44 mg/dL) and serum amyloid A protein (400.2 µg/mL), hypoalbuminemia (albumin 2.9 g/dL), slight anemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL), and thrombocytosis (platelets 542,000/µL). Stool and blood cultures were negative for pathogens.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed hyperenhancement of the bowel wall in the lower ileum and colon. Colonoscopy revealed multiple round ulcers throughout the colon, longitudinal ulcers with a cobblestone appearance in the descending and sigmoid colon, and a perianal abscess; the terminal ileum appeared normal. Biopsies from ulcer margins showed mucosal inflammatory cell infiltration without epithelioid granulomas or amyloid deposits. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy with biopsies showed no lesions of Crohn’s disease, and infectious etiologies including tuberculosis and cytomegalovirus were excluded. 

A working diagnosis of Crohn’s disease was made, and the patient was started on intravenous infliximab, high-dose 5-aminosalicylic acid, and azathioprine. Over the next 40 weeks, she had recurrent fevers, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and persistently elevated CRP. After intensifying infliximab dosing without improvement, a follow-up colonoscopy 5 months later showed diffusely granular, friable mucosa with loss of vascular pattern throughout the colon, including the rectum. Biopsy specimens now demonstrated crypt distortion, crypt abscesses, and dense inflammatory infiltrates, suggesting ulcerative colitis.

A previously healthy 5-year-old boy presented with a 2-week history of fever, cough, and progressive shortness of breath. On examination, he was tachypneic and hypoxic, with bilateral diffuse wheezes and crepitations. His past history included occasional ER visits for wheezing responsive to albuterol; there was no personal or family history of asthma or atopy, and he was on no regular medications.

Initial laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 194,000 cells/mm3 with 50% eosinophils, rising to 224,000 cells/mm3 over 24 hours; there was concomitant anemia and thrombocytopenia. A peripheral smear revealed marked eosinophilia with reactive lymphocytes and no blast cells. Lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 785 U/L. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities progressing rapidly to a “white-out” consistent with early acute respiratory distress syndrome; echocardiography showed normal cardiac function. Urgent leukopheresis was performed.

Despite this intervention, his respiratory status worsened, necessitating mechanical ventilation. Repeat chest imaging after leukopheresis showed significant clearing of infiltrates, and he was extubated one week later. Chest CT revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities, and CT of the paranasal sinuses was normal. After extubation, neurological examination showed hyperreflexia, asymmetrical quadriparesis, spasticity, and encephalopathy. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple confluent white-matter lesions in the bilateral centrum semiovale with post-gadolinium enhancement and microhemorrhages, suggestive of ischemic insults and possible vasculitic changes.

A 76‐year‐old woman was referred for repeat catheter ablation because of highly symptomatic recurrence of atrial fibrillation. She had undergone pulmonary vein isolation, cavotricuspid isthmus ablation, and complex fractionated atrial electrogram ablation in 2018. Her medical history included surgical closure of a sinus venosus atrial septal defect and redirection of an anomalous right upper pulmonary vein at age 65. On admission, blood pressure was 130/64 mm Hg, heart rate 70 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. 

A 7‐day Holter recording documented atrial fibrillation with a mean heart rate of 86 beats/min. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal biventricular size and function, mild left ventricular diastolic dysfunction, and moderate left atrial enlargement (indexed volume 44 mL/m2). Preprocedural computed tomography demonstrated patent pulmonary veins draining normally to the left atrium.

A zero‐fluoroscopy procedure was performed under general anesthesia. After two transseptal punctures guided by 3D electroanatomic mapping and intracardiac echocardiography, voltage mapping confirmed isolation of the left ipsilateral pulmonary veins but reconnection of the right ipsilateral veins; re‐isolation was performed. Posterior‐wall (“box”) and mitral‐isthmus ablation lines were then deployed without terminating atrial fibrillation. A synchronized 360‐J cardioversion restored sinus rhythm and re‐confirmed pulmonary‐vein isolation.

During remapping of the mitral isthmus, the patient developed a persistent atrial tachycardia with a cycle length of 280 ms. Activation mapping of the left atrium failed to cover the full tachycardia cycle length, whereas mapping within the distal coronary sinus unfolded the entire cycle length.

A 57-year-old man presented with 1 week of colicky then dull moderate abdominal pain, abdominal distension, obstipation, and vomiting. He had a similar transient episode 2 weeks earlier that resolved with conservative management. He denied diarrhea, weight loss, or chronic cough. His past history was notable for pulmonary tuberculosis treated 1 year ago; he had no prior abdominal surgery. On examination, the abdomen was soft, distended, with visible peristalsis and hyperactive bowel sounds; there were no surgical scars or hernias. Rectal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a normal hemoglobin and leukocyte count and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. An erect chest radiograph showed multiple bilateral pulmonary opacities with emphysematous changes. Abdominal plain films demonstrated dilated small-bowel loops with multiple air–fluid levels and a radio-opaque shadow in the right lower abdomen of unclear significance. Abdominal ultrasonography was reported as suggestive of intussusception of bowel loops in the right lower abdomen causing intestinal obstruction. A diagnosis of small-bowel obstruction was made. He initially refused surgery, improved with conservative management, and was discharged. Three days later, he was readmitted with recurrent obstructive symptoms. Abdominal radiography again showed multiple air–fluid levels and the radio-opaque shadow now located in the pelvis. Exploratory laparotomy was planned.

A 47-year-old man was referred to the outpatient clinic with persistent ocular redness unresponsive to topical chloramphenicol. One month earlier, he had been diagnosed with uveitis by an ophthalmologist and treated with topical prednisolone and atropine, resulting in resolution of inflammation except for residual synechiae. His medical history included miliary pulmonary tuberculosis diagnosed 18 months earlier, which had been treated with a six‐month regimen of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol; sputum conversion was documented after 14 days and radiologic abnormalities resolved.

At presentation he reported no respiratory symptoms or constitutional complaints. Vital signs were within normal limits, and physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal serum calcium, creatinine, and electrolytes; erythrocyte sedimentation rate 5 mm/h; C-reactive protein <6.0 mmol/L; and angiotensin-converting enzyme 86 U/L (reference range 12–82 U/L). A chest radiograph demonstrated mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy with right-sided interstitial densities. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax confirmed bilateral mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy and patchy interstitial opacities in the right upper lobe.

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial needle aspiration of a paratracheal lymph node revealed no acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl–Neelsen stain, negative cultures, and negative PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex DNA. Despite these findings, empirical antituberculous therapy was initiated. Two months later, follow-up CT of the chest showed persistent mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy with unchanged interstitial opacities and new multiple small nodules along the right major fissure.

One year after her first delivery, during an unplanned second pregnancy, a 25-year-old woman was first seen at 34 weeks’ gestation. She reported three generalized tonic–clonic seizures in the preceding 24 hours and intermittent myalgias, arthralgias, and low-grade fevers throughout pregnancy despite continued low-dose prednisolone. On examination, her blood pressure was 200/110 mm Hg in the ankle and her pulse rate was 100 beats per minute; there was no albuminuria. Abdominal examination revealed a fundal height corresponding to 26 weeks and a faintly audible fetal heart sound. Laboratory studies including INR, PT, and APTT were within normal limits; C-reactive protein was 3 mg/dL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 33 mm in the first hour. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, moderate aortic regurgitation with mildly thickened valve leaflets, and an ejection fraction of 63%. Carotid and vertebral Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated mild stenosis of a post-stent segment and 65–70% stenosis of the left common carotid and internal carotid arteries; renal Doppler was unremarkable. Obstetric ultrasonography with Doppler velocimetry revealed a single live fetus with severe growth restriction, oligohydramnios (amniotic fluid index, 5 cm), and severely deranged end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery.

A 33-year-old Asian man with chronic schizophrenia presented with a six-month history of progressive dyspnea and dry cough. He was in severe respiratory failure on room air (PaO2 7.74 kPa, PaCO2 4.17 kPa). His medications included risperidone 2 mg daily and sertraline 50 mg daily for three years. He smoked five pack-years, with no travel history, illicit drug use, or occupational exposures.

On examination, he had fine bibasal crackles and digital clubbing. Laboratory studies showed an elevated ESR (43 mm/h) and a rheumatoid factor of 1:40; ANA, ANCA, dsDNA antibodies, and extractable nuclear antigens were all negative. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated diffuse ground-glass attenuation, marked reticular change most prominent in the lower lobes, and multiple discrete areas of consolidation. Bronchoscopy was unremarkable. Bronchoalveolar lavage revealed 26% neutrophils (normal < 7%) and 7.7% eosinophils (normal < 3%); bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial studies were negative.

A seven-month-old male infant was brought to the emergency department with persistent vomiting and delayed developmental milestones. He was unable to lift his head, roll over, or sit unsupported. He was born at term (38 weeks’ gestation) via uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery; birth weight was 2630 g. On examination, he had dysmorphic facial features, bilateral esotropia, a head circumference of 50 cm, scoliosis, high muscle tone with clasp-knife spasticity, and brisk deep tendon reflexes in all limbs. Brain MRI showed absence of the septum pellucidum, dilatation of the lateral and third ventricles with a box-like configuration of the frontal horns, colpocephaly, a stretched and thinned corpus callosum with an absent or hypoplastic splenium, and hypoplastic optic nerves and chiasma. There was no evidence of increased intracranial pressure or transependymal CSF seepage. The pituitary gland, pituitary infundibulum, and olfactory nerves were within normal limits.

A 74-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 2-week history of jaundice and fatigue. She had no risk factors for viral hepatitis, did not consume alcohol, and denied herbal or dietary supplement use. Her only medication was irbesartan for well-controlled hypertension. On examination, she was jaundiced with hepatomegaly and had no other stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory studies showed: normal full blood count; serum bilirubin 3.6 mg/dL; alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 1011 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 168 IU/L; albumin 37 g/L; globulin 51 g/L; IgG 31.1 g/L (normal <16 g/L); and prothrombin time 16 s. Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:5120; smooth muscle, liver-kidney microsomal, and mitochondrial antibodies were absent. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative. A liver ultrasound showed normal-sized bile ducts with no features of chronic liver disease. A liver biopsy on day 6 demonstrated severe interface hepatitis with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate consistent with severe AIH. She scored 7 on the simplified diagnostic criteria for AIH, consistent with “definite autoimmune hepatitis.” Budesonide 9 mg daily was commenced. She began to improve both clinically and biochemically, with her ALT dropping to 85 IU/L within 10 days. After this initial response, her ALT rose again to 421 U/L despite remaining on budesonide.

A 21-year-old, 69-kg primigravida at 38 weeks’ gestation underwent an elective cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia for fetal anomalies. In the sitting position, she received 10.5 mg of 0.75% hyperbaric bupivacaine, 10 μg of fentanyl, and 200 μg of morphine intrathecally. She was then placed supine with left uterine displacement. A bilateral sensory block to T3 was confirmed, and the operation was uneventful.

Approximately 40 minutes after the intrathecal injection, during uterine exteriorization, she reported right-sided perioral numbness, dysphagia, and dysarthria. Five minutes later, she developed right horizontal nystagmus, right-sided ptosis with facial droop, and right upper-extremity weakness with a “claw hand” (strength 2/5). Vital signs and mentation remained normal, and she denied shortness of breath or chest pain.

At the conclusion of surgery, her neurologic deficits were unchanged. A noncontrast head CT showed no intracranial pathology. Ninety minutes after the injection, her facial droop and ptosis began to resolve, but her right upper-extremity weakness persisted. All neurologic signs resolved by 120 minutes. Subsequent brain MRI, neck-vessel MRA, and an echocardiogram with agitated-saline bubble study were all normal.

A 58-year-old Hispanic man with hypertension and diabetes presented with acute onset of mucosal bleeding, diffuse petechiae, and easy bruising. He denied any prior history of bleeding. On examination, he had widespread petechiae on the arms, legs, and abdomen, numerous oral lesions, and gingival bleeding. Laboratory studies showed a platelet count of 3 × 10^9/L; white cells and hemoglobin were normal. Coagulation tests including prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, fibrinogen level, and D-dimer were within normal limits. Hemolysis markers—bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, and haptoglobin—were normal, and a direct Coombs test was negative. Peripheral blood smear demonstrated sparse platelets without clumping and normal morphology of other cell lines. Platelet-specific antibody testing was negative. Viral serologies for HIV and hepatitis A, B, and C were nonreactive. An antinuclear antibody screen was negative. A platelet factor 4 antibody ELISA was weakly positive, but a confirmatory serotonin-release assay was negative. Abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatic steatosis and mild splenomegaly (spleen length 12.6 cm). Further history revealed no recent infections; a COVID-19 test was negative. He had received his first dose of the Moderna SARS-CoV-2 vaccine three weeks before the onset of bleeding.

A 57-year-old woman, a high-risk BRCA gene carrier with a history of left breast cancer treated 5 years ago (wide local excision and radiotherapy), underwent her annual screening MRI. On MRI, there was a 12 × 7 mm lesion in the lower central aspect of the right breast with Type 3 enhancement, classified as MRI 4 (BI-RADS 4B). No abnormal axillary lymph nodes were seen.

She was recalled for further assessment. A screening mammogram revealed a new 14 mm asymmetric density in the lower central right breast that persisted on tomosynthesis (M4, BI-RADS 4B). 

Ultrasound of the right breast showed an 8 × 7 mm necrotic hypoechoic lesion with irregular contours in the 6A position (U5, BI-RADS 5) and an unchanged benign fibroadenoma at 3 o’clock. Ultrasound also identified right axillary lymph nodes with eccentrically thickened cortices up to 5 mm (above the institution’s normal of 2.3 mm), measuring 9 × 19 mm; the fatty hilum was preserved and there was no increased cortical vascularity.

On directed questioning, she reported receipt of her first dose of the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine in her right arm 3 days before this assessment (after the MRI).

A 14-year-old Chinese girl was evaluated for abnormal liver-function test results. Her history was notable for preterm birth at 34 weeks, repaired cleft palate, bilateral conductive hearing loss, spina bifida occulta (treated with laminectomy), perimembranous ventricular septal defect (surgically closed), treated right cataract with prior retinal detachment, and cerebral atrophy. She took no medications and denied alcohol or tobacco use.

On examination, she was afebrile, with normal vital signs, and had hepatomegaly without tenderness or guarding. Laboratory tests showed an alanine aminotransferase level of 85 U/L (reference 7–40), total bilirubin 22 µmol/L (reference 5–21), alkaline phosphatase 206 U/L (reference 44–147), γ-glutamyltransferase 284 IU/L (reference 9–48), and ammonia 87.3 µmol/L (reference 11–35). Serum α-fetoprotein was normal at 2 µg/L. Electrolytes, creatinine, and glucose were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed hepatomegaly and absence of intrahepatic portal veins. The splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein joined to form a common vein that drained directly into the intrahepatic inferior vena cava at the level of the hepatic venous confluence. Hypertrophic hepatic arteries arising from the celiac axis were noted, supplying the liver as the sole vascular inflow.

Primovist-enhanced MRI of the liver showed multiple focal hepatic lesions. Most lesions were hyperintense on T1-weighted images, hypointense with a central scar on T2-weighted images, displayed mild homogeneous arterial hyperenhancement, and remained hyperintense in the hepatobiliary phase. No washout or capsule was identified; some lesions exhibited a central feeding vessel and central scar.

A female infant was born at 41 weeks’ gestation weighing 3.6 kg after an uncomplicated pregnancy. On day of life 3, she developed left-sided wheezing and respiratory difficulty while receiving phototherapy for hyperbilirubinemia in the NICU. Her respiratory rate intermittently rose to 57 breaths per minute with mild subcostal retractions. Pulse oximetry was 92% with intermittent desaturations. Auscultation revealed inspiratory wheezing localized to the left hemithorax. A chest radiograph demonstrated a focal opacity near the medial aspect of the left upper lobe. No other remarkable findings were noted on initial laboratory tests.

A 41-year-old woman presented with acute abdominal and back pain. Two days earlier, she had been treated at an outside hospital for a presumed urinary tract infection with systemic antibiotics, but her abdominal pain worsened and she developed high fever. She had no significant past medical history. On examination, her temperature was 40.0 °C; she had mild abdominal tenderness with rebound and marked pallor of the conjunctiva. Laboratory studies showed: Hb 7.3 g/dL, WBC 16,500/μL, platelets 18,000/μL, CRP 18.0 mg/dL, AST 146 IU/L, ALT 79 IU/L, LDH 899 IU/L, total protein 4.6 g/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL, creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, prothrombin time 44.1 %, fibrin/fibrinogen degradation products 239.4 μg/mL, D-dimer 75.1 μg/mL, antithrombin III activity 53 %, base excess −13.0 mmol/L, and lactate 12.9 mmol/L. Tumor markers and viral hepatitis serologies were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed thick-walled multilocular cystic lesions of both ovaries without pelvic ascites. Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated an 11.1 × 7.9-cm left ovarian cystic mass and a 6.3 × 4.4-cm right ovarian cystic mass, both with low echogenicity and septations. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of one of the cystic masses yielded purulent fluid.

A 59-year-old woman with a history of glaucoma and bilateral congenital cataract surgery was referred for evaluation of a right laterotracheal mediastinal mass. She had experienced progressive respiratory symptoms over four months. On examination, she was in good condition with normal vital signs; oral examination revealed poor dentition. 

Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a left lower-lung opacity and a 57 × 45 mm right laterotracheal mass in the upper right mediastinum, displacing the superior vena cava anteriorly and compressing the contralateral trachea, with well-defined margins and no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. 

Flexible bronchoscopy revealed a yellowish, granular appearance; biopsy showed pulmonary actinomycosis. She received intravenous penicillin G (20 million U/day for 6 weeks) followed by oral penicillin (3 g/day for 3 months). On follow-up CT, the left basal opacity had resolved but the right mediastinal mass persisted unchanged.

A 48-year-old man with Down syndrome and gout presented with a 2-day history of a new, pruritic, nontender rash that began on his buttocks and spread to his thighs. He denied new exposures, travel, or contactants; indomethacin had been started 3 weeks earlier. One week before the rash, he had a productive cough; a chest radiograph was normal. 

On examination, there were symmetric, well-demarcated, erythematous plaques on the buttocks and bilateral thighs without pain or rubor. Drug reaction was less likely given the lack of truncal involvement, and contact dermatitis was initially favored; he was treated with emollients, triamcinolone 0.1% ointment, and hydroxyzine. 

Punch biopsy of a thigh lesion showed dermal edema and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate extending to the mid-dermis, composed of lymphocytes, neutrophils, and rare eosinophils, interpreted as most consistent with a hypersensitivity reaction. 

Two days later, he returned to the emergency department with worsening rash, fever, chills, tachycardia, and a temperature of 101°F. The eruption was now diffuse on the trunk and legs. Laboratory studies showed a leukocytosis of 17.3×10^3 cells/µL with 91% neutrophils, an AST of 58 U/L, ALT of 75 U/L, and an alkaline phosphatase of 310 U/L. He was admitted for presumed sepsis and started on intravenous vancomycin. For the rash, diagnostic consideration was given to cellulitis, Sweet syndrome, and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis.

A 36-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of progressively heavy menstrual bleeding and new-onset dysmenorrhea. Over the past 7 months, her menstrual duration increased from 4 to 6 days, and her menstrual blood loss became three times her usual volume. Two months before presentation, she developed crampy hypogastric pain during menses. Her obstetric history was notable for a cesarean delivery 15 years earlier and three induced abortions. 

On examination, the uterus was anteverted, 7.0 × 6.0 × 6.0 cm, firm but nontender, with no adnexal masses. A routine blood count showed hemoglobin 125 g/L and a normal white-cell and platelet count. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed an endometrial thickness of 20 mm and a 31 × 24 × 24 mm mixed echogenic lesion within the uterine cavity. Color Doppler demonstrated internal blood flow. Repeat ultrasound at our institution showed a 61 × 55 × 54 mm anteverted uterus with two low-echo areas in the myometrium; the larger was 11 × 8 mm in the posterior wall. The uterine cavity line was indistinct. Within the mixed echogenic lesion (31 × 24 × 24 mm) was an irregular anechoic area measuring 20 × 18 × 16 mm. Ovaries appeared normal.

A 41-year-old gravida 4 para 2 woman at 15 weeks 5 days of gestation presented with decreased appetite and severe vomiting. Her BMI was 45.1 kg/m2; she had no other medical history. Initial laboratory tests revealed WBC 14 k/µL, Hgb 13.7 g/dL, PLT 354 k/µL, AST 354 IU/L, ALT 574 IU/L, ALP 125 IU/L, and total bilirubin 4.8 mg/dL. Abdominal ultrasound and MRCP showed hepatic steatosis, pericholecystic fluid, and gallbladder wall thickening. Serologic testing was notable for a positive ANA at 1:640; infectious, metabolic, and other serologic studies were negative. She was treated with methylprednisolone and antibiotics, and by hospital day 5 her AST had decreased to 91 IU/L, ALT 185 IU/L, ALP 127 IU/L, and total bilirubin 7.3 mg/dL; she was discharged on a steroid taper and antiemetics. Three days later, she returned with vomiting, pruritus, and jaundice. Labs showed WBC 18.4 k/µL, Hgb 12.1 g/dL, PLT 166 k/µL, AST 51 IU/L, ALT 88 IU/L, ALP 191 IU/L, total bilirubin 15 mg/dL, total protein 6.8 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and INR 2.2. Repeat ANA was >1:1280; viral and bacterial tests were negative. She denied fever, sick contacts, or hepatotoxic drug use. A repeat abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatic steatosis and an absent fetal heart rate, confirmed by fetal ultrasound on hospital day 2. Dilation and evacuation were performed on day 3.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of lower abdominal pain and periumbilical erythema. Over the past 8 days, he also experienced nausea, vomiting, fever, and umbilical discharge. On examination, his temperature was 38.7 °C. His abdomen was soft, and there was erythema and a tender mass at the umbilicus with purulent discharge. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 22,000 mm–3; urinalysis was normal. 

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous 7.2 × 3.2 cm midline mass extending from the anterior and superior wall of the urinary bladder to the umbilicus, containing gas. Colour power Doppler revealed increased vascularity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a tubular hypodense mass extending from the dome of the bladder to the umbilicus, with rim enhancement of the fluid collection and surrounding fat stranding. 

Cystoscopy demonstrated an inflamed area at the bladder dome with poor purulent drainage.

A 25-year-old G1P0 woman was referred at 26 weeks of gestation after routine ultrasound showed an isolated hyperperistaltic fetal colon with multiple hyperechoic, ball-like structures rolling within the bowel. The female fetus had normal biometry and amniotic fluid volume. The intestinal wall was unremarkable, with no ascites, bowel dilatation, or extraluminal calcified meconium. Initial differential diagnoses included anorectal malformation with urodigestive fistula, cystic fibrosis, cystinuria, and fetal infection. Follow-up ultrasound demonstrated persistent echogenic foci. The parents declined amniocentesis. Maternal serologic tests showed no recent seroconversion for CMV, EBV, parvovirus, or herpes simplex virus. Parental screening for 35 common CFTR mutations was negative. At 31 weeks, fetal MRI showed a normal upper gastrointestinal tract. The colon and rectum were not dilated, exhibited intermediate signal on T2-weighted images and high signal on T1-weighted images (consistent with meconium), and the rectum terminated at a normally positioned anal line beneath the bladder neck, excluding a high anorectal malformation.

A 6-year-old castrated male Golden Retriever was evaluated for decreased activity and loss of appetite. Two years earlier, the dog had undergone jejunojejunostomy for foreign body ingestion. The dog spent time both indoors and outdoors and had a habit of eating soil and grass. On presentation, temperature was 39.4 °C, heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 42 breaths/min. Complete blood count showed mild leukocytosis (21 120/μL). Serum biochemistry revealed elevated total protein (8.5 g/dL; reference 5.0–7.2) and C-reactive protein (>17 mg/dL; reference <1.0). Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple well-circumscribed spherical masses (30–65 mm) with heterogeneously mixed echogenicity throughout the peritoneal cavity. Fine-needle aspiration of the masses yielded numerous neutrophils, macrophages, and septate hyphae; no bacteria were detected. Samples were submitted for fungal culture and susceptibility testing.

A 26-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (stage V lupus nephritis in remission, Raynaud-like discoloration, malar rash) presented with 5–6 months of slowly progressive, painless swelling of the left labium minus. She denied pain, pruritus, gastrointestinal symptoms, or related family history and had trialed clobetasol cream, oral fluconazole, and a 28-day prednisone taper with minimal improvement. Current medications included an oral contraceptive, loratadine, hydroxychloroquine, and low-dose prednisone. Examination showed firm induration and enlargement of the left labium minus without extension to the labia majora or perianal region; no palpable lymphadenopathy was noted. A previous biopsy revealed reactive squamous epithelium with submucosal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. A repeat punch biopsy showed collections of multinucleated giant cells surrounded by lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, focal polarizable crystalline-like material within giant cells, and dermal edema. Periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott’s Methenamine Silver, Acid-Fast Bacilli, and Fite’s acid-fast stains were negative for microorganisms, and an immunostain for spirochetes was negative. Pathology was consistent with a granulomatous process.

A female neonate was born at 38 + 6 weeks’ gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 23-year-old primigravida. Her birth weight was 2250 g (<3rd percentile), Apgar scores 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. The mother had regular prenatal care; first-trimester serologies including hepatitis B, HIV, and syphilis were negative. Two days before labor she experienced a flu-like syndrome with fever (38.5 °C); on admission she was afebrile, COVID-19 rapid test negative, and dengue serology was negative. She was treated with ampicillin for presumed intrapartum sepsis. Maternal blood cultures were negative and CRP was elevated at 130 mg/L.  

At admission to the special care nursery, the infant was active, pink, and feeding well. Initial labs showed a white-cell count of 11.4 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 7.2 × 10^9/L, I/T ratio 0.01, hemoglobin 173 g/L, platelets 169 × 10^9/L, CRP 34.6 mg/L, and procalcitonin 1.48 μg/L. Blood and gastric-aspirate cultures were drawn, and empiric ampicillin plus cefotaxime was started.  

On day 3 of life the infant developed a morbilliform rash with petechiae over the back and intermittent fever to 38 °C. Vital signs remained stable; examination showed no hepatosplenomegaly or neurologic signs. Repeat labs revealed leukocytes 16.4 × 10^9/L, platelets 78 × 10^9/L, and CRP 43 mg/L. Blood and gastric-aspirate cultures remained negative. Brain and cardiac ultrasounds were unremarkable; lumbar puncture showed 0 cells/mm^3, normal protein and glucose. Antibiotics were escalated to meropenem and amikacin.  

When fever persisted and platelets continued to fall, a detailed maternal history by phone revealed that, two days postpartum, the mother had developed rash, low-grade fever, and persistent arthralgia. Based on this information, clinicians considered mosquito-borne congenital infections before further testing.

A 31-year-old man with type 1 diabetes presented with an 8-month history of beard hair breakage, uneven hair length, and “white dots” limited to his beard. He had no hair changes elsewhere and no family history of hair disorders. An initial diagnosis of seborrheic dermatitis treated with triamcinolone lotion yielded no improvement. On examination, white nodes were observed on hair shafts throughout the beard with relative sparing of the mustache. Beard hair density was normal; scalp and eyebrow hair were normal. The surrounding skin was normal without erythema or scale. Trichoscopy revealed widened nodes in the hair shaft with splaying and fraying resembling paint brushes thrust together. No lice, nits, peripilar scale, or casts were identified on trichoscopy. A bacterial swab grew normal skin flora, and hair-pull fungal culture was negative. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, triiodothyronine, thyroxine, and hemoglobin levels were within the normal range. The patient, employed as a barber, began wearing a facial covering to work about 9 months before presentation. He denied excessive grooming or chemical treatments but was observed frequently adjusting his mask and grasping at his beard.

A 17-year-old boy with cerebral palsy and a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placed at age four for hydrocephalus presented with a two-month history of intermittent fever, abdominal pain, and constipation. He lived in a care home and had refractory seizures. His symptoms transiently improved with antipyretics and laxatives. Several courses of empiric parenteral ceftriaxone produced no lasting benefit. 

On examination, blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg, pulse 100 beats/min, and temperature 38.5 °C. Abdominal palpation revealed generalized tenderness without guarding or rebound. Laboratory studies showed elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein, and mild leukocytosis. An abdominal X-ray was unremarkable. Ultrasonography demonstrated a fluid collection (pseudocyst) at the distal tip of the VP shunt. 

A noncontrast brain CT scan showed no acute intracranial process. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was obtained via both lumbar puncture and shunt reservoir puncture. CSF analysis from both sites revealed pleocytosis with neutrophil predominance, elevated protein, and low-normal glucose, consistent with bacterial shunt infection. Empiric intravenous meropenem and vancomycin were initiated.

A 32-year-old woman (G2P2) presented with a 6-month history of cyclic pain and swelling in the lower abdominal region. She had two prior cesarean sections, the most recent 2 years earlier. She reported that the pain began a few days before menstruation and resolved afterward, with increasing intensity over time. On examination, a 2-cm, well-defined, tender mass was palpated within the lower-segment cesarean scar. The lesion was superficial, tender on deep palpation, and without erythema or discharge. Ultrasonography of the scarred area revealed a heterogeneous mass with increased vascularity and no evidence of associated herniation or other pathologies.

A 52-year-old right-handed woman with a history of alcohol abuse, liver cirrhosis, and epilepsy (on phenytoin) presented after 48 hours of nausea and vomiting and two witnessed generalized tonic–clonic seizures. Nine months earlier, she had been treated for herpes simplex virus encephalitis. Her medications included aspirin, hydrocodone-acetaminophen, folic acid, thiamine, pyridoxine, and phenytoin 100 mg daily. She drank 2–6 beers per day.

On arrival, vital signs were blood pressure 113/72 mm Hg, heart rate 106 beats/min, temperature 102.0 °F, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, BMI 23.8 kg/m2. In the emergency department, she received lorazepam, diazepam, fosphenytoin, lacosamide, and one dose of IV acyclovir. Initially unresponsive, she gradually began following commands but then developed fluent aphasia.

Laboratory studies showed negative cerebrospinal fluid PCR, platelets 101 K/mL, potassium 2.8 mM/L, anion gap 25, glucose 228 mg/dL, AST 125 IU/L, lactate 3.4 mM/L, subtherapeutic phenytoin level 4.2 μg/mL; urine drug screen and blood alcohol were negative. Chest X-ray and head CT were unremarkable. Brain MRI showed no definite asymmetric FLAIR abnormality in the left medial temporal lobe compared with prior imaging.

Video EEG monitoring revealed no epileptiform activity but focal slowing over the left temporoparietal region while she remained fluently aphasic.

A 71-year-old woman with a 3-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus and autoimmune hepatitis in the context of antiphospholipid syndrome presented with an asymptomatic rash on the central chest, slowly expanding over 8 months. Her obstetric history was notable for four spontaneous miscarriages, and she had a deep venous thrombosis 6 years earlier. Current medications included prednisone 12.5 mg daily, mycophenolate mofetil 1.5 g daily, and hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily. 

On examination, there were erythematous macules merging into a reticulate pattern with a slightly purpuric hue on the mid-chest and base of the neck. 

Laboratory studies showed thrombocytopenia (70,000 cells/μL), a homogeneous antinuclear antibody pattern at 1:320, positive anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, and anti–β2-glycoprotein I antibodies (IgM 36 IU/mL; IgG 24 IU/mL; reference <20 IU/mL). Tests for anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, rheumatoid factor, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, cryoglobulins, and proteins C and S were negative. Complement levels (C3, C4), prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and D-dimer were within normal limits.

An incisional skin biopsy showed expansion of the superficial and mid-dermal vasculature by intravascular proliferation of small-to-enlarged endothelial cells forming closely spaced capillaries that filled and occluded vascular lumina in a glomeruloid pattern. Intravascular thrombi containing erythrocytes and a scant lymphocytic infiltrate were present, and no significant cellular atypia was noted.

A 74-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with a one-day history of abdominal distension, repeated vomiting, and pain. He had not passed stool or flatus for two days and noted mild, vague abdominal discomfort for several weeks. He also reported urinary frequency and nocturia for months but denied fever, chills, hematuria, trauma, or prior abdominal or urologic procedures.

On examination, he appeared toxic. Vital signs were blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, temperature 99.6 °F, pulse 105 bpm, respiratory rate 23/min. Abdominal examination revealed distension, absent bowel sounds, and mild epigastric tenderness. Other systems were unremarkable.

Initial management included IV fluids, Foley catheter placement, and nasogastric decompression. Baseline labs showed leukocytosis, elevated serum creatinine, and pyuria on urine microscopy. Two weeks earlier, a CT scan had shown left nephrolithiasis with mild bilateral perinephric stranding; he did not follow up.

Ultrasound now demonstrated a large septated cystic lesion in the liver and an enlarged prostate (38 g) with 5 mm intravesical protrusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed:
- An irregular, lobulated cystic lesion with enhancing walls, measuring ~7.3 × 7.5 × 5.5 cm, posterior to the pancreatic head and uncinate process, resembling a pancreatic pseudocyst.
- Serum amylase and lipase were within normal limits.
- A subcapsular hepatic cystic collection (15 × 11 × 10 cm) indenting the stomach and duodenum.
- A 13 × 7 mm calculus in the left renal pelvis.
- Bilateral perinephric soft-tissue stranding and moderate free fluid in the abdomen and pelvis.

A 57-year-old woman presented with two months of mild right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain without episodes of severe pain. She had a long history of headache managed without prescription medications. On examination, she was afebrile, and there was no Murphy’s sign or other acute findings. Laboratory tests revealed normal complete blood count, coagulation studies, and liver function. Tumor markers were within normal limits: CA19-9 21.83 U/mL (reference <27 U/mL), CA125 9.11 U/mL (reference <35 U/mL), and CEA 1.28 ng/mL (reference <5 ng/mL).  
Ultrasound showed a thickened gallbladder wall and a hyperechoic intraluminal structure. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an enlarged gallbladder (10.0×4.6×4.3 cm) with a rough, thickened wall and multiple medium-density lesions fused into a thick, high-density layer attached to the inner wall. MRI revealed a smooth-edged intraluminal signal that was high on T1-weighted images and low on T2-weighted images. A flocculent lesion with mixed-density signal was seen. Gadolinium-enhanced sequences showed gallbladder wall enhancement, and diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated a markedly high signal with a smooth edge inside the lumen. The patient declined PET–CT.

A 2-month-old male infant, first of dichorionic diamniotic twins, was admitted for persistent anaemia and HIV exposure. He was born at 34 weeks’ gestation by cesarean section (birth weight 2.080 kg) to a 30-year-old Nigerian mother who arrived in Italy at 27 weeks and tested positive for HIV and CMV; antiretroviral therapy was started. At birth, the male twin’s HIV-RNA PCR was negative, and he received zidovudine prophylaxis for 6 weeks. TORCH screening and abdominal and cerebral ultrasonography were negative. One week before transfer, he was hospitalized elsewhere for severe anaemia (Hb 5.1 g/dL) and received a blood transfusion. On presentation, he was afebrile (36.5 °C), pulse 135 bpm, respirations 35/min, weight 3.910 kg. Examination was normal except for hepatomegaly (4 cm below right costal margin). Laboratory tests (one week after transfusion) showed WBC 12 000/mm3, Hb 9.1 g/dL, platelets 198 000/mm3, reticulocytes 169 000/mm3, total bilirubin 1.31 mg/dL (direct 0.64 mg/dL), LDH 945 U/L, and normal renal and hepatic function. Zidovudine‐induced myelosuppression was suspected, and folic acid and oral iron were started. Over the next days, hemoglobin fell to 6.8 g/dL despite supportive care, requiring additional transfusions. Causes of blood loss and hemolysis were investigated: direct and indirect Coombs tests and fecal occult blood were negative; hemoglobin electrophoresis was unremarkable. On repeat examination, splenomegaly was noted and confirmed by ultrasound. Malaria was then considered.

A 76-year-old white woman was referred for evaluation of an intraoral nodule of 2 weeks’ duration. She had a history of rheumatoid arthritis and hypercholesterolemia, and varices were noted on her feet and legs. On examination, there was a painless, firm, bluish nodule on the lower labial mucosa, measuring 10 × 5 × 5 mm and covered by normal-appearing mucosa. The lesion was biopsied, and during the procedure an encapsulated, dark red nodular proliferation was visualized.

A 33-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of the absence of menstruation. She weighed 66.8 kg and was 1.58 m tall. Physical examination showed normal breast development and normal axillary and pubic hair. Gynecologic examination revealed normal external genitalia with an intact hymen. On rectal examination, no uterus was palpable. Vaginometry with a cotton swab demonstrated a vaginal depth of approximately 8 cm.  
Segmental skeletal examination and radiographs of the hands and feet showed bilateral shortening of the fourth metacarpals, a small hallux, short and pointed distal phalanges, and clinodactyly. Pelvic ultrasound revealed a short-sized, solid-appearing uterus (14 cm3) without a visible uterine cavity; the right ovary measured 1.7 cm, and the left ovary was not visualized. Renal ultrasound showed a hypotrophic right kidney and a normal left kidney.  
Chromosomal analysis demonstrated a normal 46,XX karyotype. Plasma levels of follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, prolactin, and thyroid-stimulating hormone were within normal limits.

A 44-year-old previously healthy woman was referred for evaluation of bilateral hand weakness. Five weeks earlier, she had a motorcycle accident with transient loss of consciousness. Initial head CT was unremarkable, and she underwent internal fixation of a right medial malleolar fracture under spinal anesthesia. On the first postoperative day, she received 5% dextrose in 0.9% saline, and on hospital day six she experienced headache and vomiting managed with 5% dextrose in 0.45% saline and antiemetics. Repeat head CT on hospital day seven was normal. One week after discharge, her family noticed episodes of uncontrollable laughter and crying without context, associated with generalized weakness and fatigue. On exam, she had a pseudobulbar affect, normal strength (grade V) in all muscle groups, and hyperreflexia. Her serum sodium was 140 mmol/L. Brain MRI showed symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the bilateral caudate and putamen with corresponding diffusion-weighted imaging hyperintensity. Cerebrospinal fluid studies, including meningitis/encephalitis and autoimmune encephalitis panels, anti–aquaporin-4, anti-MOG, and antinuclear antibodies, were negative. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography of the upper extremities were unremarkable except for poor activation on maximal effort.
