A cervical spine MRI showed mild spinal canal stenosis, which was insufficient to explain her bilateral hand weakness.

A 7-year-old Persian boy presented with a 2-day history of right lower quadrant abdominal pain that gradually increased in intensity and was accompanied by nausea and vomiting. He had no prior medical or surgical history and was fully vaccinated. On examination, he was afebrile (temperature 37 °C) with a blood pressure of 111/72 mmHg, pulse 75 beats/min, and respiratory rate 17 breaths/min. Abdominal palpation revealed focal tenderness and rebound in the right lower quadrant; the remainder of the abdominal and neurologic examinations was normal. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6.7 × 10^3/µL (neutrophils 58%, lymphocytes 31%), hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, hematocrit 33%, mean corpuscular volume 69.2 fL, red-cell distribution width 17%, platelets 294 × 10^3/µL, aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 27 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated enhanced pericecal fat echogenicity with mild free fluid in the interloop spaces.

A 28-year-old woman was followed by breast surgeons since age 22 for abnormal breast lesions. Her medical history included autism, developmental delay, seizure disorders, and encephalitis in infancy. She had used oral contraceptive pills for contraception for 10 years and was taking risperidone, topiramate, clonazepam, and oxcarbazepine. There was no family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

At age 22, she underwent excision of a left breast fibroadenoma. At 24, bilateral excisional breast biopsy showed benign lobular hyperplasia and adenosis; follow-up was by regular ultrasonography (US).

At 25, she noted palpable lumps in both breasts. US revealed a 1.0 cm hypoechoic right breast lesion at 4 o’clock with ill-defined margins (BI-RADS 3). Conservative management with serial US was chosen. Six months later, multiple lesions were seen; the left breast lesion had enlarged and was BI-RADS 4. Oral contraceptives were stopped, and observation continued. Three months later, the left lesion decreased in size (BI-RADS 3). One year later, new palpable masses were present; US showed the left lesion had grown from 5.8 cm to 8.6 cm and there was an additional right-breast lesion (both BI-RADS 4). Given the size and imaging findings, the patient was scheduled for excision of two lesions in each breast.

A 70-year-old man with a history of colorectal cancer complicated by intestinal ischaemia underwent haemicolectomy with resection of the ileum and jejunum, resulting in a terminal jejunostomy and complete dependence on parenteral nutrition via a long-standing vena saphena magna arteriovenous shunt. He also had hypertension, chronic hepatitis B infection, and microcytic anaemia. Over the past 6 weeks, he experienced progressive dyspnoea and fatigue. On examination, he had rales bilaterally and peripheral oedema; blood pressure was 130/70 mmHg and heart rate 76 b.p.m. Repeated ECGs showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 70–100 b.p.m. NT-proBNP was 315 pmol/L. He was admitted for intravenous loop diuretics. 

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% with dilated atria and a left ventricular end-diastolic diameter of 5.6 cm. Coronary angiography revealed no significant coronary artery disease. After decongestion, right-heart catheterization demonstrated a resting cardiac output of 7.2 L/min (cardiac index 3.63 L/min/m2), mean pulmonary arterial pressure 15 mmHg, mean pulmonary-capillary wedge pressure 8 mmHg, mean right atrial pressure 4 mmHg, and systemic vascular resistance 856 dyn·s/cm5; NT-proBNP had fallen to 25 pmol/L. Endomyocardial biopsy showed subendocardial fibrosis without evidence of myocarditis, storage disease, or metabolic disease. Blood tests excluded autoimmune disorders and deficiencies in micronutrients or vitamins. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated reduced left ventricular systolic function and eccentric hypertrophy without focal fibrosis.

A 73-year-old woman, with a history of acute pancreatitis treated 2 months earlier, was found incidentally to have a hepatic mass on contrast-enhanced abdominal CT. She reported daily alcohol intake (>60 g/day for >20 years) but had no known chronic liver disease. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory results, including liver enzymes, inflammatory markers, viral hepatitis serologies, and serum tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, AFP, AFP-L3, PIVKA-II), were all within normal limits.

Ultrasound could not visualize the lesion because it lay just beneath the diaphragm. Noncontrast CT showed an ill-defined, 15 mm hypodense nodule in segment 8. On dynamic contrast-enhanced CT, the nodule exhibited early arterial enhancement with gradual and prolonged enhancement in the portal and equilibrium phases. MRI performed 2 months later showed no change in size. The lesion was hypointense on in-phase and out-of-phase T1-weighted images without focal fat, moderately hyperintense on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, and slightly hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 800). Precontrast fat-suppressed T1-weighted imaging revealed hypointensity.

Dynamic MRI with gadoxetic acid demonstrated early arterial enhancement and persistent portal and transitional phase enhancement. On the hepatobiliary phase, the nodule was inhomogeneously hypointense with scattered slightly isointense foci relative to background liver. Angiography-assisted CT showed portal perfusion defects of the nodule and surrounding parenchyma on CT during arterial portography. CT during hepatic arteriography revealed inhomogeneous arterial supply in the early phase and reduced enhancement in the delayed phase; the surrounding liver exhibited irregular perfusion defects and differing arterial blood supply patterns. Five minutes post–contrast injection, neither the nodule nor the surrounding parenchyma showed prolonged enhancement. No central stellate scar, fibrous capsule, or evidence of chronic liver deformity was seen on any imaging.

A 31-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of high-grade fevers (daily maximum, 38.3 °C) accompanied by chills. She had travelled to Malaysia 6 weeks earlier. She reported a brief episode of watery, nonbloody diarrhea and an occasional cough but denied dyspnea, chest pain, or chronic medical conditions. 

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. She had prominent bilateral parotid swelling (approximately 5 × 4 cm), which was soft, tender, and nonfluctuant, and she had mild right inguinal lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed leukopenia, and viral serologies (including Cytomegalovirus IgM and Epstein–Barr virus IgM) and multiple blood cultures were negative. The patient was started on amoxicillin–clavulanate and supportive care. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed multiple mildly enlarged, nonenhancing, nonnecrotic lymph nodes in the submental, bilateral deep cervical, and upper abdominal regions, findings described as suggestive of a granulomatous process.

A 20-year-old previously healthy, unvaccinated man presented with a two-week history of fever, malaise, and bilateral painful parotid swelling. One week into his illness, he developed nausea, anorexia, and mild right upper quadrant discomfort but denied dark urine or pruritus. He reported no recent medication use. He had no history of liver disease, alcohol consumption, travel, autoimmune disorders, or chronic illness.

On examination, he was febrile (38.5 °C) with tender bilateral parotid enlargement. He had scleral icterus and mild hepatomegaly without splenomegaly. Moderate bilateral testicular tenderness was noted without swelling. There were no signs of meningeal irritation or focal neurologic deficits.

Laboratory tests on presentation showed:  
• AST 792 U/L, ALT 680 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL  
• Alkaline phosphatase 89 U/L, GGT 32 U/L  
• Amylase 45 U/L; lipase within normal limits  

Serologic studies revealed:  
• Mumps IgM: Positive  
• Hepatitis A, B, C, and E serologies: Negative  
• EBV IgM and CMV IgM: Negative  
• HIV rapid test: Negative  
• ANA and anti–smooth muscle antibodies: Negative  

Liver ultrasound demonstrated normal hepatic size and echotexture, no biliary ductal dilatation, and no hepatosplenomegaly.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of chronic abdominal pain accompanied by diarrhea and generalized weakness. An abdominal ultrasonogram showed an inflamed appendix. On examination, there was localized tenderness and rebound in the right iliac fossa at McBurney’s point. The total leukocyte count was elevated at 16,000/mm^3, and other routine biochemical and hematological tests were within normal limits. A clinical diagnosis of chronic appendicitis was made, and the patient underwent an appendectomy. Intraoperatively, the appendix appeared inflamed and was studded with several small tubercles on the serosal surface and adjacent periappendiceal fat. The appendix and a mesenteric lymph node were submitted for histopathological examination.

A 6-year-old boy from rural south-central Missouri was seen for 3 weeks of intermittent, colicky abdominal pain rated 6/10, vomiting after meals, and constipation with soft, jelly-like stools. He denied new foods or rash. On exam, his abdomen was soft, non-tender, non-distended, with normal bowel sounds and no masses or organomegaly. An abdominal ultrasound was normal, and stool cultures showed no pathogens or toxins. His symptoms improved over several days with dietary modification (bananas, rice, crackers, yogurt) and hydration.

Eleven months later, now age 7, he developed an intensely pruritic rash. He had played in nearby woods and that evening ate a hamburger and salad. Overnight, he noted itchy, asymmetric, oval erythematous maculopapules on his extremities, chest, and back; his face was spared. He had no new soaps or detergents. His mother also recalled that, since the hamburger meal, he had experienced abdominal pain and diarrhea—symptoms that, in retrospect, had recurred over the past 11 months. The family lives in an area where tick bites are common.

A 16-year-old male presented with a 4-month history of a progressively enlarging mass in the anterior aspect of the superotemporal left orbit. He denied any history of trauma, surgery, or prior periorbital disease, and his past medical history was unremarkable. On external examination, there was a subtle, firm, non-tender enlargement over the left superotemporal orbital rim; the mass was adherent to the underlying bone but the overlying skin was mobile.  
  
Computerized tomography (CT) of the orbits with and without contrast showed a 15 mm nodular lesion in the superotemporal periorbita abutting the lateral rim of the left orbit. The mass was hyperdense, contrast-enhancing, and without osseous erosive changes or intraorbital extension.  

Given the location and imaging characteristics, a dermoid cyst was considered first, and an epidermoid inclusion cyst was also in the differential. To exclude other benign and malignant mesenchymal tumors, an orbitotomy with excisional biopsy was planned.

A 26-year-old man presented with a five-month history of vague lower abdominal pain, bloating, dysuria, and changes in bowel habits. There was no weight loss, night sweats, or appetite change. His medical, surgical, and social histories were unremarkable. On examination, the abdomen was soft and non-tender without palpable masses. Complete blood count, metabolic panel, and tumor markers were within normal limits. Colonoscopy and upper endoscopy showed no abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated multiple loculated cystic masses throughout the abdomen and pelvis, with a dominant multicystic lesion in the pelvis. A provisional diagnosis of pseudomyxoma peritonei was made based on the imaging findings, and the patient was referred for diagnostic laparoscopy and biopsy.

A 42-year-old man with an 11-year history of Crohn’s disease treated chronically with prednisolone (20 mg/day) presented with a 3-month history of mild dyspnea, cough, asthenia, and weight loss. He smoked 6 pack-years. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a peripheral lymphocyte count of 890/μL (CD4 lymphocytes 374/μL, 42%) and a serum angiotensin-converting–enzyme level of 118 U/L (elevated). 

Chest CT revealed bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, a left apical irregular nodule, bilateral perihilar infiltrates, upper lobe micronodules, and proximal bronchial thickening. Abdominal CT demonstrated multiple hepatic and splenic nodules and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. PET scanning showed metabolic activity in all these lesions and in osteolytic lesions of the spine, ribs, clavicle, and humerus.

Bronchoscopy revealed diffuse inflammatory changes. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 77% neutrophils and 8% lymphocytes (CD4/CD8 ratio 1.9), with no viral, bacterial, or fungal organisms identified. Cultures were negative for Mycobacterium species. Bronchial biopsies demonstrated noncaseating granulomas composed of epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells.

A 63-year-old woman presented with 2 days of left eye pain, photophobia, conjunctival injection, and progressive visual acuity loss. The pain started suddenly, was constant, and had worsened. She denied trauma or systemic symptoms. Six weeks earlier she had undergone tube-shunt surgery for left-eye glaucoma; preoperative intraocular pressure (IOP) was around 40 mm Hg, and at a routine postoperative visit hours before symptom onset, left-eye IOP was 8 mm Hg. Her medications included oral acetazolamide and topical brimonidine/timolol and dorzolamide. Medical history was notable for hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, bilateral cataract extraction, and aortic valve replacement managed with warfarin and aspirin. On examination, she was afebrile with blood pressure 148/79 mm Hg. Both eyelids were normal, and extraocular movements were intact. Visual fields in the right eye were normal. The left eye had conjunctival injection, an unreactive pupil, photophobia, and impaired color vision; IOP was 7 mm Hg. Point-of-care ocular ultrasound showed bilateral convex layers protruding into the vitreous that did not extend to the optic nerve head.

A 14‐year‐old girl with a history of spina bifida at the L3 level and lifelong urinary and fecal incontinence presented with multiple asymptomatic, whitish‐raised lesions on the inner aspects of both thighs and on the labia majora that had been present since infancy. Because of her incontinence, she had used diapers continuously since early childhood. She denied any rash beyond these lesions, constitutional symptoms, or sexual activity. Previous treatments, including topical antifungals, topical corticosteroids, and systemic antibiotics, produced no improvement. On examination, the perineal and perianal skin showed multiple, moist, flat‐topped papules (3–12 mm in diameter) and a few verrucous nodules, some coalescing into plaques, with soiling by fecal material. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Routine blood counts and biochemistry were within normal limits. Enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay for HIV, VDRL, and TPHA were non-reactive. Polymerase chain reaction for human papillomavirus was negative.

A 45-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 5-day history of intractable vomiting, epigastric pain, and lumbar pain radiating toward the thoracic base. Within this period, he developed muscle pain and a gradual decrease in strength in both upper and lower limbs. He is a former coal miner (retired 5 years ago) and a 14-pack-year smoker.

On examination, he had pale skin, no organomegaly, no bleeding, and normal cardiovascular and respiratory findings. Neurologic examination revealed a peripheral proximal tetraparesis predominantly affecting the upper limbs, with preserved sensory function.

Initial laboratory evaluation showed severe microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 5.52 g/dL, MCV 67.8 fL), elevated serum iron (199.7 µg/dL), ferritin (883.7 ng/mL), and transferrin saturation (57%), with a normal corrected reticulocyte count. White blood cell and platelet counts were within normal limits.

Peripheral blood smear demonstrated anisocytosis, hypochromic red cells with basophilic granules, occasional ovalocytes, and “droplet” cells. Direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative. Bone marrow aspirate showed erythroid hyperplasia with 46% sideroblasts and 42% ringed sideroblasts.

Additional chemistry tests revealed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (50 mm/1 h), indirect hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 1.47 mg/dL), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 150 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 117 U/L, and normal renal function and electrolytes.

A 67-year-old Caucasian man with non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and ocular rosacea presented with a 4-year history of slowly progressive facial swelling and redness. He denied any history of acne vulgaris or new exposures to medications or cosmetics. On examination, there was symmetric, nonpitting edema with erythema over the periorbital and malar regions. A 4-mm punch biopsy of the affected skin showed mild spongiosis, peri-adnexal mixed inflammatory infiltrate, dermal edema, perivascular and perifollicular lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, prominent solar elastosis, and ectatic superficial dermal blood vessels. No granulomata were observed, and both colloidal iron and periodic acid–Schiff stains were negative.

A 47-year-old woman with a history of essential hypertension managed with valsartan presented with acute left leg pain and discoloration of the forefoot. Two weeks earlier, she had received a leuprolide acetate injection for uterine fibroids. The pain began as mild but progressed to severe rest pain in the calf and distal foot, accompanied by mottling of the toes. On examination, pulses were absent in the left lower extremity, and the forefoot appeared mottled, suggesting ischemia. CT angiography of the lower limbs showed monophasic flow in the proximal left leg. The images revealed bilateral persistent sciatic arteries, aneurysmal dilatation of the left sciatic artery, hypoplastic femoral arteries, and complete thrombosis of the proximal left sciatic artery with collateral vessel filling distally.

A 37-year-old woman with no prior medical or surgical history presented with a 2-month history of progressive abdominal pain and distension, worsening fatigue, and an 8-kg weight loss. She denied fever or night sweats. On examination, she appeared cachectic; abdominal examination revealed dullness to percussion without tenderness or palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed a leukocytosis, normal creatinine, and an elevated serum CA 125 level of 414.6 U/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated mild ascites of slightly high attenuation (38 HU) causing scalloping of the liver margins, omental fat stranding with nodular peritoneal thickening, and multiple mesenteric lymphadenopathies associated with diffuse thickening and enhancement of the small-bowel wall.

A 92-year-old woman from Kosovo (formerly Yugoslavia) presented with chest pain, dyspnea, and bilateral lower-extremity edema. Her medical history included stage 4 chronic kidney disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus on insulin, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease status post two coronary bypass grafts and seven stents, myelodysplastic syndrome with anemia, and osteoporosis complicated by multiple rib fractures. Home medications comprised clonidine, doxazosin, hydralazine, isosorbide mononitrate, nifedipine, aspirin, furosemide, carvedilol, empagliflozin, and denosumab.

On examination she was tachypneic and hypoxemic (SpO2 in the low 90% range). Initial laboratory studies showed: sodium 121 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.4 mg/dL two days earlier), hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL (12.1 g/dL two days earlier), troponin 14 pg/mL (decreasing to 13 pg/mL at four hours), and B-type natriuretic peptide 393 pg/mL. Urinalysis revealed glucosuria (1000 mg/dL), hematuria (52 red cells per high-power field), leukocytes >900 per high-power field, leukocyte esterase 500, and proteinuria 70 mg/dL.

Noncontrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a dense opacity in the right lower lobe, small bilateral pleural effusions, moderate atrophy of the left kidney compared with the right, moderate left hydronephrosis, and mild bladder wall thickening. Renal ultrasonography confirmed mild to moderate left-sided hydronephrosis without detectable masses.

On hospital day 2, cystoscopy revealed a mass at the left ureteropelvic junction and a posterior bladder wall mass, the latter of which was resected. Further history disclosed that the patient was born and had lived for several decades in the Balkan Peninsula.

A 35-year-old Indian woman presented with a 4-month history of generalized lymphadenopathy. She denied fever, cough, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, lymph nodes were multiple, discrete, firm, and measured 3–4 cm in diameter; there was no hepatosplenomegaly or cutaneous lesions. Routine biochemical tests were within normal limits. Serologic tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and HIV were negative. A chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities. She had no history of diabetes, hypertension, tuberculosis, immunosuppressive therapy, or travel abroad. Clinically, a diagnosis of lymphoma was made and fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the lymph nodes was advised.

A 69-year-old woman with monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and a 5-year history of dermatomyositis (previously treated with azathioprine and low-dose methylprednisolone) presented with acute weakness, muscle pain, and joint pain. Azathioprine had been discontinued months earlier. On arrival, she was tachycardic (140/min), tachypneic (30/min), hypotensive (75/55 mmHg, mean 55 mmHg), oliguric, and had extensive skin mottling and absent venous filling. Arterial lactate was 3.7 mmol/L with a base deficit of –8.9 mmol/L. Mixed venous oxygen saturation was 35–45%, and cardiac index was 0.9–1.2 L/min/m2. Laboratory studies showed hematocrit 69%, serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, colloid osmotic pressure 4.6 mmHg, serum myoglobin 336 µg/L, and creatine kinase 173 IU/L. Intravenous fluids and a 500 mg bolus of prednisolone were administered. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an underfilled, diffusely hypokinetic left ventricle (ejection fraction 35%), diastolic dysfunction, and a small pericardial effusion without tamponade. Dobutamine and epinephrine infusions were started, and aggressive fluid resuscitation continued, resulting only in transient hemodynamic improvement. Despite ongoing therapy, hematocrit remained elevated (62%), lactate rose to 9.5 mmol/L (base deficit –16.7 mmol/L), and signs of hypovolemia persisted. The patient subsequently developed anasarca and acute respiratory distress requiring difficult intubation. She died of refractory shock 12 hours after ICU admission. Complement studies drawn on admission and analyzed postmortem showed C3 14 mg/dL (normal 86–184), C4 <6 mg/dL (normal 10–40), C1 inhibitor 14 mg/dL (normal 18–32), and C1 inhibitor activity 34% (normal 70–130%). Autoantibody panels were negative, and no infectious or malignant focus was identified.

A 19‐month‐old boy was referred for chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, vomiting, and abdominal distension. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; newborn screening was normal. Since infancy he had five daily episodes of oily, bulky, foul‐smelling stools without bilious vomiting. By 6 months of age, failure to gain weight prompted evaluation that excluded cystic fibrosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, disorders of lipid metabolism, thyroid disease, adrenal insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, and celiac disease. He received multivitamins with no improvement. From 10 months, a high-calorie formula provided partial symptom relief and weight gain. Developmental milestones were appropriate, vaccinations were up to date, and family history was unremarkable.

On examination, weight was 9 kg (−3 SD), length was 75 cm (−3 SD), vital signs were stable, and the abdomen was distended but soft without organomegaly. Neurologic and other system examinations were normal. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, inflammatory markers, hepatic and renal function, electrolytes, glucose, bilirubin, ammonia, pancreatic enzymes, and urine studies, were within normal limits. Stool microscopy revealed fat globules. Abdominal ultrasonography showed mild intestinal wall thickening; the liver was normal. Funduscopic examination and echocardiography were normal.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a milky‐white “snow‐storm” appearance of the duodenal mucosa. Duodenal biopsies showed fat‐laden vacuolization of enterocytes without villous atrophy, suggesting a lipid‐trafficking disorder.

A 71-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of right lower quadrant abdominal pain. Twelve hours before presentation, she experienced an acute, sharp pain that evolved into a constant ache. She had no nausea, vomiting, melena, hematochezia, or hematemesis. Her past history included colonoscopic findings of diverticulosis and possible irritable bowel syndrome; she had never had diverticulitis or abdominal surgery. There was no family history of inflammatory bowel disease or gastrointestinal malignancy.

On examination, her heart rate was 99 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 143/76 mmHg, temperature 97.9 °F, and pain score 6/10. Abdominal examination revealed diffuse tenderness in the right lower quadrant without rigidity, guarding, or rebound. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 12,900/µL with 77% neutrophils; electrolytes and lipase were normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated extension of contrast from the right posterior colon, cranial to a normal-appearing appendix. The appendix showed no wall thickening, inflammation, or dilation. Multiple diverticula were noted throughout the colon. The radiologic impression was a perforated diverticulum or small contained rupture.

A 66-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of gradually enlarging soft-tissue masses in the cervico-occipital region. He reported no pain or systemic symptoms. His past medical history was unremarkable aside from heavy chronic alcohol use. On examination, there was diffuse enlargement of the anterior neck, described as a “horse collar,” and three large, symmetric humps at the posterior neck. Vital signs were within normal limits. Endocrine studies, including cortisol and thyroid function tests, were normal, and routine laboratory tests, including a lipid panel, revealed no abnormalities. To evaluate the neck masses and distinguish among potential causes—including morbid obesity, neurofibromatosis, Cushing syndrome, and lymphoma—magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck was obtained.

A 65-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of a painful, progressively enlarging swelling of the tongue. He denied cough, fever, dysphagia, or weight loss. He was a nonsmoker, chewed tobacco for 15 years, consumed alcohol daily for 15 years, had hypertension on treatment, and no history of diabetes. On examination, he was well nourished and in good general condition. Intraoral examination revealed an 8 × 6 cm firm swelling of the left anterior two-thirds of the tongue that crossed the midline; the surface was smooth, margins were well defined, and tongue movements were normal without deviation. No cervical lymphadenopathy was present, and systemic examination was unremarkable. Clinically, a submucosal carcinoma of the tongue was suspected. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm in the first hour. A deep punch biopsy from the lateral aspect of the lesion was performed.

A 17-year-old white female presented with a seven-week history of a painless swelling on the apical aspect of the upper left buccal sulcus that had gradually increased in size. She had no significant medical history. On examination, there was facial asymmetry without palpable lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, a well-defined, rubbery, nonulcerated, painless mass was palpated at the upper left buccal sulcus. Ultrasonography showed a rounded, hypoechoic soft-tissue mass. An excisional biopsy was performed, and the lesion was completely removed.

A 38-year-old man with congenital hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine was evaluated for blurred vision after a transient ischemic attack. CT angiography of the head was unremarkable. Extracranial CT angiography showed no atherosclerotic disease or vascular stenosis but revealed incidentally a 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.2 cm homogeneously enhancing mass at the base of the tongue on arterial-phase images. No thyroid tissue was visible at the level of the thyroid cartilage. Laboratory testing showed a TSH level of 0.312 mIU/L (reference range, 0.350–5.000 mIU/L) and a free T4 level of 1.11 ng/dL (reference range, 0.70–1.25 ng/dL).

A 28-year-old African American woman was hospitalized with a 2-month history of asymmetrically distributed polyarthralgias of the wrists, ankles, and knees, daily fevers up to 103 °F, tachycardia, headaches, and a pruritic dermatitis. She had been recently treated for presumed pyelonephritis with levofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole without improvement. Her past medical history included hypertension and childhood atopic dermatitis. She was unemployed due to symptom burden.  

On examination, she was febrile and tachycardic. Dermatologic findings included hyperpigmented plaques with a symmetric distribution on the lateral face, neck, arms, hands, upper back, buttocks, and legs, many of which exhibited linear and flagellate morphology with occasional scale and erythema. Musculoskeletal examination showed diffuse joint tenderness without synovitis; muscle strength was 5/5 throughout.  

Initial laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (WBC 16.5 × 10^9/L) with eosinophilia (absolute eosinophils 2.26 × 10^9/L), anemia (hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL), normal platelets, elevated inflammatory markers (ESR > 130 mm/hr; CRP 23.7 mg/L), hyperferritinemia (13 660 mcg/L), and mild transaminase elevation (AST/ALT in the 150s U/L). Creatine kinase was 77 U/L and aldolase was 14.3 U/L. An extensive infectious and autoimmune work-up (including ANA, ENA, ANCA, RF, viral panels, blood and urine cultures, hepatitis, HIV, RPR, gonorrhea, chlamydia, monospot, respiratory viral panel, and SARS-CoV-2) was negative. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Pelvic and lumbar spine radiographs showed mild sclerosis of the sacroiliac joints and lower lumbar spine. Her fever and systemic symptoms did not improve with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.

A healthy 23-year-old woman (secunda gravida) was referred at 20 3/7 weeks’ gestation for evaluation of fetal tachycardia and hydrops fetalis. Ultrasound showed a fetal heart rate of 175–180 bpm, a structurally normal heart, normal systolic function, and a regular rhythm with 1:1 atrioventricular conduction but minimal heart-rate variability. Spectral Doppler demonstrated increased retrograde flow during atrial systole in the ductus venosus and hepatic and pulmonary veins, and monophasic ventricular filling. Ascites and a small pericardial effusion were present. Maternal antithyroglobulin and anti-SSA/SSB antibodies were negative; fetal anemia and infection were excluded. A fetal magnetocardiogram at 21 5/7 weeks’ gestation demonstrated an incessant narrow QRS tachycardia with a cycle length of 333 ms (181 bpm), predominantly 1:1 retrograde ventriculoatrial conduction (VA = 77 ms), and brief episodes of VA dissociation with sinus capture beats.

A 15-year-old teenager with complex congenital heart disease presented to the emergency department with incessant palpitations and dizziness. On arrival, a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 125 beats per minute was observed, with a long RP′ interval and negative P waves in the inferior leads. The tachycardia was briefly terminated by intravenous adenosine but immediately recurred. In sinus rhythm, the QRS-axis remained unchanged, and P waves became positive in the inferior leads, indicating atrial activation from the sinus node.

The patient was born with situs solitus congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries, mild sub-pulmonary stenosis, and a perimembranous ventricular septal defect. He underwent pulmonary artery banding at 3 months and surgical closure of the VSD at age 3. He continued to have residual pulmonary arterial hypertension and hypoxia (85–90%) from a residual right-to-left shunt. Apart from the arrhythmia episodes, he was New York Heart Association Class II with a Grade 5/6 systolic murmur. Transthoracic echocardiography estimated the systemic right ventricular ejection fraction at 45%. He was not on antiarrhythmic medications.

Integrating the congenital heart defect and ECG findings, the differential diagnoses included twin atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia, atrial tachycardia, and atypical (fast–slow) atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia.

A 68-year-old man with metastatic melanoma involving an axillary lymph node and mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy was treated with two cycles of ipilimumab and nivolumab but discontinued due to immune-related colitis and other toxicities. Four months later, a PET-CT showed progression of mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes and hypercalcemia; mediastinal lymph node biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas. He remained off ICPI therapy.

Ten months after ICPI initiation, he developed a two-week history of progressive headaches, visual changes, and word-finding difficulty. On neurologic examination, he had a right incongruent homonymous hemianopia, finger agnosia, acalculia, left-right disorientation, and alexia. Brain MRI showed subtle leptomeningeal enhancement and T2 FLAIR signal abnormality in the left occipital pole and overlying left parietal lobe. 

Lumbar puncture revealed a protein level of 75 mg/dL (reference 15–50 mg/dL), 13 white blood cells, and normal glucose; CSF cytologic examination was negative. During hospitalization, he experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure and was started on levetiracetam.

A 15-year-old girl with a history of allergic rhinitis and mild intermittent asthma was referred after a chest CT showed diffuse bilateral cavitary lung lesions. Six months earlier, she had developed congestion and epistaxis treated as sinusitis. Over 8 weeks, she worsened with cough, dyspnea, intermittent fevers, migratory arthralgias, right otitis media, night sweats, weight loss, and small-volume hemoptysis despite multiple courses of antibiotics. On arrival, she was febrile (38.6 °C), tachycardic (122 bpm), tachypneic (26 breaths/min), and required 2 L/min of oxygen to maintain normal saturation. Examination revealed boggy nasal turbinates, dried blood in the nares, cobblestoning of the oropharynx, diffuse coarse breath sounds without egophony, and tenderness of the hips and knees without synovitis. 

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (17.3 k/mm3), thrombocytosis (698 k/mm3), anemia (hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL), elevated ESR (119 mm/hr), CRP (197 mg/L), ferritin (687 ng/mL), D-dimer (2184 ng/mL), and urinalysis with proteinuria, hematuria, and an elevated microalbumin/creatinine ratio. A respiratory viral PCR panel including SARS-CoV-2 was negative. Sinus CT revealed marked sinusitis with partial absence of the medial walls of both maxillary sinuses. Chest radiograph confirmed bilateral cavitary lesions with perihilar fullness.

Rheumatology and infectious diseases specialists recommended testing for ANCAs, cardiac enzymes, and sputum cultures. Troponin T and BNP were elevated, and echocardiography showed right coronary artery dilation (3.9 mm). The ANCA panel was positive at 1:80, but both c-ANCA and p-ANCA were negative. Sputum, fungal, and mycobacterial studies were uniformly negative, and bronchoalveolar lavage cultures grew only a small Acremonium colony. Sinus biopsy demonstrated no vasculitis or fungal elements but grew Pseudomonas. The patient was treated with antibiotics and antifungals without complete resolution, and repeat echocardiography showed progressive coronary dilation to 4.4 mm.

A 78-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia was brought to the emergency department for right-sided arm weakness after a fall from bed. He could not recall whether weakness preceded the fall. He was last known normal about 94 minutes earlier. On examination, he had right facial weakness, right upper extremity drift, and right lower extremity drift (NIHSS score of 5). A noncontrast CT head showed no hemorrhage; CT cervical spine showed chronic degenerative changes without acute injury. CT angiography demonstrated severe proximal right vertebral artery stenosis with occlusion at V2 and retrograde filling at V4. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. He received intravenous tPA approximately three hours after last known normal, with improvement to an NIHSS score of 1. 

Three hours later, he developed difficulty breathing. He was seated in a tripod position with labored respirations, stridor, tachycardia, and oxygen saturation of 70% on room air (improving to 80% on a nonrebreather mask). His neck circumference was visibly expanding. The team’s initial concern was tPA-induced angioedema, and he was given methylprednisolone, diphenhydramine, and famotidine. On examination of the upper oropharynx, there was no visible mucosal swelling. He was unable to protect his airway, and an emergency physician performed orotracheal intubation. During laryngoscopy, there was marked narrowing of the posterior oropharynx and larynx.

A 64-year-old man presented with palpitations, sweating, weight loss, nausea, and vague abdominal pain. His history included toxic multinodular goiter and well-controlled hypertension. On exam, blood pressure was 150/90 mmHg, pulse 100 /min, with tachycardia, tremor, and mild exophthalmos. A prior evaluation noted a right adrenal mass and negative pheochromocytoma studies. Laboratory tests showed TSH 0.005 μIU/mL (0.27–4.2), free T4 0.68 ng/dL (0.93–1.7), free T3 2.36 pg/mL (2–4.4), sodium 145 mmol/L (136–145), and potassium 4.7 mmol/L (3.5–5.5). Thyroid ultrasound revealed multiple heterogeneous solid-cystic nodules up to 25×18 mm, and thyroid scintigraphy demonstrated hyperactive nodules. Abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass measuring 170×120 mm adjacent to the right kidney with cystic areas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen identified a 150×120 mm mass arising from the right adrenal gland, with peripheral calcification and multicentric hypodense cystic necrotic regions, causing minimal compression of the inferior vena cava and biliary structures. PET/CT after 6.8 mCi F18-FDG showed no abnormal uptake in the 142×121 mm calcified multilocular solid-cystic mass extending from the upper pole of the right kidney.

A 25-year-old Japanese woman was referred for evaluation of a 4-week history of a painless nodule in her lower lip thought to be malignant. She was in good health until she noted the lesion and had no history of tobacco or alcohol use. Three weeks before the lesion appeared, she had unprotected orogenital contact with her steady partner. Physical examination revealed a 2.0-cm nodule of the lower lip with a central ulcer and a slightly elevated, indurated, erythematous margin. There was no fever or cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel except for a C-reactive protein level of 6.48 mg/dL (reference < 0.30 mg/dL). Serum squamous cell carcinoma antigen and carcinoembryonic antigen were within normal limits. Tests for HIV I/II, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody were negative. Ultrasonography of the lesion demonstrated an oval 17 × 11 × 12 mm mass in the left lower lip with heterogeneous internal echoes, an indistinct border, and very abundant blood flow on color Doppler except at the center. Probe‐pressure testing revealed that the tumor was soft. Magnetic resonance imaging could not be performed because of a metal crown on a front tooth.

A 36-year-old Asian woman presented with an eight-week history of progressive abdominal distention, decreased appetite, and nausea. She denied fever, vomiting, or menstrual irregularities but reported a 4-kg weight loss over three months. Initial treatment with antiemetics by an internist provided no relief. A subsequent abdominal CT scan showed thickening of the gastric wall, widely loculated ascites throughout all quadrants, and multiple intra-abdominal lymphadenopathies. Chest CT demonstrated a “tree in bud” sign with a solid nodule and bilateral pleural effusions predominant on the left. An initial pelvic ultrasound suggested ascites, pleural effusion, and a left ovarian mass. On referral to our service, physical examination confirmed non-tender abdominal distention. Repeat transabdominal ultrasound revealed normal uterus, ovaries, and endometrium, with no fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Laboratory data showed a hemoglobin level of 13.0 g/dL and a CA 125 level of 1200 U/mL (reference <35 U/mL); liver and renal function tests were normal. We considered peritoneal tuberculosis, peritoneal carcinomatosis, and advanced ovarian cancer as possible causes of her presentation. Given that histopathology is the diagnostic gold standard, we recommended diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal biopsy, and the patient consented.

A 12-year-old boy was evaluated for recurrent upper-eyelid swelling. Since age 7, he has had four to five sudden episodes annually, each lasting 4–7 days. Episodes feature eyelid erythema without pain, fever, or prodromal symptoms, and resolve spontaneously. There is no family history of similar symptoms or any history of trauma.

On examination, there is bilateral mild ptosis (~2 mm) with marked laxity and thinning of the eyelid skin. Extraocular movements are full, and the corneas are clear. There is no lacrimation, hyperemia, or conjunctival injection.

Laboratory studies, including serum protein and albumin, liver and thyroid function tests, renal function tests, and urinalysis, are all within normal limits. C1-esterase-inhibitor levels are normal, and there are no systemic signs of angioedema. Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder is unremarkable.

A 23-year-old otherwise healthy man from Morocco presented with a 3-year history of an abnormal atrophic skin texture on the lower back. The lesion expanded slowly over several months, then stabilized 2 months before evaluation. He denied pain, pruritus, or paresthesia. He had not used any topical or systemic treatments, took no medications, and had no history of allergies or similar family lesions. Review of systems was unremarkable.

On examination, there was a 4 × 11 cm well-demarcated, hyperpigmented atrophic plaque with a “cliff-drop” border on the lower back; the surrounding skin was normal. A 4-mm punch biopsy showed dermal edema with a mild perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate including plasma cells and normal collagen architecture. Laboratory studies, including Lyme screening serology (IgG antibody), antinuclear antibody, and rheumatoid factor, were all negative.

A 50-year-old woman, previously well, presented initially with a week of flu-like symptoms and three days of purulent ear discharge, followed by vomiting, collapse, and reduced consciousness. She was diagnosed with Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis secondary to otitis media, treated with antibiotics and supportive care, and discharged 11 days later. Three days after discharge, she was readmitted after a fall with gradually increasing lower‐limb weakness and painless urinary retention. On examination, she was afebrile and fully conscious. Cranial nerves and upper limbs were normal. Lower limbs showed slightly reduced tone, pyramidal‐pattern weakness, brisk reflexes, bilateral extensor plantar responses, and a sensory level at T10. Initial blood tests showed mild neutrophilic leukocytosis; other routine results were normal. An urgent MRI of the spinal cord showed no epidural collection, no discitis, and no intrinsic cord signal abnormality. MR venography of the cerebral veins was normal. Brain MRI revealed several ill-defined high T2 signal foci in the corona radiata bilaterally. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (12 polymorphs, 96 lymphocytes per mm3), elevated protein (1.84 g/L), normal glucose, no oligoclonal bands, negative virology, and no organisms cultured.

A 29-year-old man was seen in September 2009 seeking extraction of his lower right lateral incisor (tooth 42) by his own choice. He reported having been in a motor-vehicle collision 16 months earlier. On intraoral examination, tooth 42 was of normal color, exhibited no mobility, and responded positively to cold sensibility testing (EndoFrost®). In contrast, the adjacent lower right central incisor (tooth 41) appeared slightly grayish and had a negative response to sensibility testing. 

A panoramic radiograph obtained at the time of the accident showed a two-fragment, middle-third horizontal root fracture of tooth 42. A current periapical radiograph demonstrated a radiolucent lesion at the apex of tooth 41 and a thin radiolucent line in the middle third of the root of tooth 42. Cone beam computed tomography confirmed an oblique fracture line in the middle third of tooth 42 without evidence of a hypodense lesion in the surrounding periodontium. The CBCT also showed external dentinal root resorption and apex remodeling with calcification in tooth 44 and obliteration of the apical third of the root canal in tooth 43.

An 18-year-old female student presented with a 6-month history of intermittent abdominal pain and constipation. There was no pain during defecation, rectal bleeding, or urinary symptoms, and her menstrual cycles were normal. Vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination revealed no organomegaly or palpable masses. On digital rectal examination, the anal sphincter tone and rectal mucosa were normal, but a firm, tender extraluminal mass was palpable posterior to the rectal wall; its lower border was felt but the upper border could not be reached. Proctoscopy was unremarkable.  
Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging showed a large, rounded, thick-walled, multiloculated cystic mass measuring 72 × 50 × 45 mm in the presacral (precoccygeal) space posterior to the rectum, displacing the rectum to the right. The lesion was hyperintense on T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and short tau inversion recovery sequences, with internal septations and a small soft-tissue component. The uterus and ovaries appeared normal.

A 28-year-old woman presented with 40 days of intermittent low-grade fever, cough, hemoptysis, and dyspnea. She had no systemic symptoms, no smoking or alcohol history, and no significant past illnesses. Initial chest radiographs and CT scans showed diffuse bilateral thick-walled cavitating nodules of varying sizes, consolidation in the right lower lobe, and a small right pleural effusion; mediastinal lymph nodes and vasculature appeared normal. Echocardiography demonstrated trivial tricuspid regurgitation without vegetations and normal left ventricular function. 

On examination she was pale and tachycardic (pulse 160/min), hypotensive (90/60 mm Hg), tachypneic (30/min), and afebrile. Respiratory auscultation revealed diffuse crackles and occasional rhonchi in the right mid and lower lung fields. Other systems were unremarkable. 

Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 11 370/mm3 (90% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, and platelets 248 000/mm3. Sputum cultures were negative for pyogenic bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, and fungi. She received broad-spectrum antibiotics without improvement; hemoglobin later fell to 7.1 g/dL despite transfusion, and she continued to have cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss. Repeat workup included negative blood cultures and Mantoux skin test, normal abdominal ultrasound, and serologies negative for ACE, ANA, RF, C-ANCA, anti-GBM, and anti-aspergillus antibodies, but positive CRP and intermittent P-ANCA by indirect immunofluorescence. 

Bronchoscopy revealed normal airway architecture but active bleeding from the right lower lobe bronchus that could not be controlled endoscopically.

A previously healthy 5-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of cough and fever. On examination, he was tachypneic and had crackles over the right hemithorax. Laboratory tests revealed hemolytic anemia (hemoglobin, 10.9 g/dL; normal range, 11.5–14.0), a normal white-cell count (6.8×10^9/L) without eosinophilia, and an elevated C-reactive protein level (22.0 mg/L; normal <10.0 mg/L). Chest radiography showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates with small pleural effusions. Mycoplasma pneumoniae was detected by PCR of a pharyngeal swab, and serum M pneumoniae–specific IgM and IgG antibody levels were strongly positive. A diagnosis of M pneumoniae community-acquired pneumonia was made, and oral clarithromycin (15 mg/kg per day in two doses) was started.

After the third dose, the next morning he awoke with massive swelling of the lower lip. He had no dyspnea, pruritus, tongue swelling, mucosal erosions, wheals, or target-like lesions, and he had not received any other medications. He was given a single dose of oral levocetirizine and betamethasone, and the lip swelling resolved slowly over 24 hours. A clinical diagnosis of angioedema was made.

A 69-year-old Caucasian man with a history of a precancerous supraglottic mass treated with resection and radiation, compensated alcoholic cirrhosis, and a right hemicolectomy presented with a 4-month history of daily melena. He denied nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hematemesis, hematochezia, reflux symptoms, changes in bowel habits, weight loss, and the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Over the preceding 3 years he had intermittent melena requiring blood transfusions; it progressed to daily melena in the past 4 months despite two prior EGDs, two colonoscopies, and one video capsule endoscopy that identified no bleeding source. In the last 2 months his hemoglobin ranged from 6.2 to 7.4 g/dL, necessitating 2 units of packed red blood cells weekly and biweekly intravenous iron infusions; he had not received oral iron in the 6 months before admission. 

On presentation he was asymptomatic and hemodynamically stable. Rectal examination revealed black, tarry stool. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 4.4 g/dL and an acute kidney injury; he received two units of packed red blood cells. Iron studies were consistent with iron deficiency (ferritin 109 ng/mL; transferrin 194 mg/dL; TIBC 225 µg/dL; serum iron 38 µg/dL; iron saturation 16.9%). CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated cirrhosis. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a nonbleeding, clean-based ulcer in the gastric body and nonbleeding gastric varices.

A 44-year-old Black African woman presented with a 6-week history of progressive, persistent, painless left-sided facial and scalp ulcerations that began as small areas of skin erosion. Two weeks after onset, she was diagnosed elsewhere with septic and allergic dermatitis because of persistent itching of the area. She admitted to frequent manipulation of the lesion because of tingling and a crawling sensation, followed by loss of sensation. 

Her past medical history was negative for brain surgery, hypertension, stroke, diabetes, herpes or syphilis infections, and head trauma. She reported social withdrawal and low mood due to stigma from her facial ulcer.

On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure 110/80 mm Hg, temperature 36.0 °C, weight 75 kg. Dermatologic exam showed a deep, left-sided ulcer involving the upper eyebrow, bridge of the nose, ala nasi, upper lip, forehead, and scalp in the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. Neurologic exam revealed decreased pain sensation and loss of sensation over the ulcerated area. Other system examinations were normal.

Laboratory investigations, including full blood count, blood glucose, and syphilis serology, were all normal. HIV serology was reactive. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. The patient declined a referral for cranial CT imaging due to travel and resource constraints.

A 37-year-old man presented with sudden onset of chest tightness and pain 1 hour after his evening meal. He had no history of vomiting, trauma, or prior chest pain. Initial management at a local clinic with analgesics, antibiotics, aminophylline, and oxygen provided no relief, and his symptoms progressed over 5 hours. On arrival, he was critically ill and dyspnoeic, with an SaO2 of 60% on room air and 90% on 4 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula.  
Physical examination revealed signs of respiratory distress.  
A chest radiograph showed a right hydropneumothorax, a collapsed right lung, air in the pleural cavity, a mediastinal shift to the left, and infiltrates in the left lung.  
Surgeons inserted a water-seal chest tube, yielding air and 1200 mL of food material.  
Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics were initiated within the first 8 hours.

A 29-year-old G2P1 woman was referred for evaluation of secondary infertility and a presumed left hydrosalpinx. She had no significant medical history, took no regular medications, and reported regular menstrual cycles. Her obstetric history was notable for a prior right tubal ectopic pregnancy treated via laparoscopic salpingotomy.

Preoperative transvaginal ultrasound showed:
• A 64 × 26 mm echo-poor, elongated cystic structure in the left adnexa with dorsal sound enhancement, suggestive of hydrosalpinx  
• A simple-appearing left ovarian cyst  
• Otherwise normal uterus and adnexa; no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas  

The patient underwent hysteroscopy, chromopertubation, and laparoscopy. Intraoperative findings:
• Normal cervical canal and uterine cavity; both tubal ostia patent  
• Anteverted, anteflexed uterus with a hyperemic, irregular surface consistent with adenomyosis  
• Right adnexa with post-salpingotomy changes; left adnexa entirely unremarkable without hydrosalpinx or ovarian cyst  
• No endometriotic lesions or pelvic adhesions  

An ovarian cystectomy on the left and salpingectomy were deferred given the normal appearance. Chromopertubation confirmed bilateral tubal patency. Postoperative recovery was uneventful.

As part of the routine postoperative assessment to exclude ureteral injury, the bladder and kidneys were scanned:
• An intravesical 51 × 43 mm smooth-walled cystic mass without internal vascularity in the left bladder wall  
• Right kidney normal; left kidney showed second-degree pelvicalyceal dilatation  
• Sonographic evidence of a duplicated collecting system on the left, with a cystic structure at the upper pole and prominent calyces

A 33-year-old man presented with fatigue and cold sweats during housework. Two days earlier he had experienced a retrosternal burning sensation when lifting a 30-lb weight as he began light bodybuilding. One week before admission he had an upper respiratory tract infection. He had no cardiac risk factors, did not smoke or use drugs, and had no past medical history.

On examination his vital signs were stable and findings were unremarkable. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, normal axis, and no ST–T changes except a tall R wave in V1; right and posterior leads were normal. High-sensitivity troponin T was 87 ng/dL at presentation and 84 ng/dL at 2 hours (upper limit of normal, 24 ng/dL). D-dimer, ESR, and CRP were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal biventricular size and function with an ejection fraction of 55%, no wall motion abnormalities, and no significant valvular disease.

He was treated for presumed acute coronary syndrome with aspirin, clopidogrel, beta-blocker, statin, and low-molecular-weight heparin. Coronary multislice CT angiography demonstrated a zero calcium score, mild mid-LAD stenosis, and otherwise normal coronary arteries. On day 3, while holding his 2-year-old child, he had a similar retrosternal pain. Repeat ECGs and troponin levels were unchanged. After re-evaluation, invasive coronary angiography was scheduled.

A 57-year-old man was brought by ambulance after sudden-onset crushing chest pain radiating to his jaw and left arm. A prehospital electrocardiogram showed anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, which degenerated into ventricular fibrillation, prompting defibrillation and cardiopulmonary resuscitation. On arrival, he was diaphoretic and in acute distress. His temperature was 36.1 °C, blood pressure 97/61 mm Hg, heart rate 112 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Lung fields were clear, and cardiovascular examination revealed a regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, strong peripheral pulses, and no jugular venous distention. 

His history was notable for hyperlipidemia, anxiety, depression, and α-1 antitrypsin deficiency; he had no known cardiac disease but reported significant emotional stress related to his mother’s recent enrollment in hospice care. Laboratory studies showed a high-sensitivity troponin level of 12 ng/L at presentation and 55 ng/L one hour later (upper reference limit, 51 ng/L). Complete blood count and renal function were normal. Chest radiography revealed low lung volumes and patchy opacities suggestive of atelectasis. Point-of-care cardiac ultrasound demonstrated anterior apical wall motion abnormalities. A repeat ECG in the emergency department confirmed ST-segment elevations in the anterior leads. 

He received thrombolytic therapy and a loading dose of clopidogrel before transfer to a percutaneous coronary intervention–capable facility, where he underwent urgent coronary angiography.

A 64-year-old woman was evaluated for new-onset left eyelid drooping and facial weakness. Twelve days earlier, she had sustained an abrasion to her left forehead in a motor-vehicle accident. Nine days after the injury, she noted left ptosis; three days later, she developed left facial paralysis without other symptoms. On transfer to our hospital, she was alert, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable. Neurologic examination confirmed left ptosis and a peripheral pattern of left facial palsy; there was no trismus, dysphagia, or limb weakness. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, serum chemistry, urinalysis, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis—were unremarkable. Chest radiograph, noncontrast brain computed tomography, and brain magnetic resonance imaging showed no abnormalities. She had no history of tetanus vaccination or prior tetanus infection.

A man in his 60s (weight 61 kg) presented to the emergency department after a common krait bite to the right gluteal region sustained at midnight while walking near his farm. He arrived at 5 AM with dysphagia, bilateral ptosis, and shortness of breath. His blood pressure was 80/45 mm Hg, heart rate 130 beats/min, and respiratory rate 28–30 breaths/min. In view of cardiorespiratory failure, he was intubated and started on vasopressor support. Twenty vials of polyvalent anti-snake venom were administered intravenously over 3 hours. A complete blood count was normal, a 20-minute whole blood clotting test was normal, the prothrombin time was 13.5 sec (INR 1.2), and liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. He remained mechanically ventilated for 36 hours, was extubated with restored muscle strength, and was discharged on day 3 with persisting body aches. Six days after discharge (nine days after the bite), he returned with arthralgia of all major joints. He had no history of fever or exanthem.

A 46-year-old man was referred with a 5-day history of nausea, anorexia, slight fever, and bilateral thigh pain. His temperature was 37.0°C; blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation were normal. He was muscular with a BMI of 26.8 kg/m2. He had undergone cholecystectomy 4 years earlier, at which time preoperative labs showed a white blood cell count of 13,700/μL with 22.4% eosinophils; testing for the FIP1L1-PDGFRα fusion gene was negative and he received no treatment. He had drug allergies to bepotastine and mequitazine but no history of asthma, dermatitis, or recent new medications, and no family history of liver or blood disorders.

On admission, the white blood cell count was 31,700/μL with 72.3% eosinophils; platelet count was 6.7×10^4/μL; prothrombin time was 53%; activated partial thromboplastin time was 47.4 seconds; fibrinogen was 90 mg/dL; fibrin degradation products were 25.3 μg/mL; D-dimer was 8.6 μg/mL. Liver enzymes were elevated (AST 146 U/L, ALT 181 U/L, ALP 538 U/L, γ-GTP 381 U/L), total bilirubin was 2.7 mg/dL, albumin 2.9 g/dL, and C-reactive protein 11.7 mg/dL. Immunoglobulin E was 8,857 IU/mL; soluble IL-2 receptor was 2,999 U/mL. Tests for hepatitis B and C, antinuclear and antimitochondrial antibodies, and parasitic eggs and antibodies were negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed atrophy of the left hepatic lobe, enlargement of the right lobe, and an irregular contrast-enhanced area in segments 4/8 without bile duct obstruction or periportal collar sign. High-density thrombi (~8 cm) were seen in both femoral veins, and lymphadenopathy was noted from the periportal region to the groin. The lungs were unremarkable.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed no esophagitis but diffuse gastric mucosal erythema and erosion; biopsy showed few eosinophils. Bone marrow aspiration demonstrated slight hypercellularity, normal eosinophil morphology, no blasts, normal megakaryocytes, and no chromosomal abnormalities.

A 64-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF <25%) and NYHA class III–IV heart failure underwent implantation of a biventricular ICD (CRT-D) in a left pectoral submuscular pocket. He had first- to second-degree AV block, broad LBBB (QRS 168 ms), and echocardiographic dyssynchrony. He reported marked symptomatic improvement to NYHA I.

Four weeks later, he developed minimal redness at the implantation site without systemic signs. Eight weeks after implantation, the system was explanted, and he received a second-generation cephalosporin. Preoperative CRP was mildly elevated (28 mg/L), procalcitonin and leukocyte count were normal. An intraoperative swab grew Staphylococcus capitis, but its clinical significance was deemed questionable.

After healing, a new CRT-D was implanted in a right pectoral submuscular pocket; the generator was wrapped in an antibiotic envelope, the pocket was irrigated with vancomycin and gentamicin, and he received 3 days of IV cefazolin. The postoperative course was unremarkable until 8 weeks later, when discrete local reddening recurred. In November 2018, PET-CT showed periodontitis and increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the ICD pocket and around a 2014 knee endoprosthesis.

The ICD was explanted. Blood cultures, pocket swabs, and knee-aspirate cultures were sterile. Inflammatory markers remained minimally altered (mildly elevated CRP, normal procalcitonin and leukocyte count) and mild hypereosinophilia was noted. Arthroscopic synovial biopsy of the knee prosthesis was sterile, and the dental focus was extracted. A dermatology consult excluded pyoderma gangrenosum. A 72-hour skin patch test for titanium allergy was negative but limited by short exposure.

A 59-year-old man was referred for endodontic retreatment of the right mandibular first molar. Initial examination revealed extensive crown destruction; the tooth was tender to occlusal percussion and vestibular palpation. Preoperative periapical radiography showed short canal fillings in the mesial and distal roots. Retreatment was completed with removal of gutta-percha, mechanical preparation, irrigation with NaOCl and EDTA, and obturation using thermoplasticized gutta-percha and a fiber-reinforced post, followed by a temporary resin crown. 

One year later, the patient returned without the temporary crown. He reported pain on percussion, palpation, and mastication. On examination, there was a 7 mm buccal probing defect on the mesial root and a visible buccal fracture line. Periapical radiography of the mesial root showed widening of the coronal canal space consistent with a fracture and a small periapical radiolucency.

A 27-year-old woman, 24 weeks pregnant, presented with 3 months of progressive shortness of breath and a productive cough that had prompted multiple outpatient visits. She had no recent travel and lived in Chicago. On examination, she was afebrile, with stable vital signs, and had crackles at the right lung base; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory testing revealed a leukocyte count of 11.4 × 10^3/μl. A chest radiograph was unremarkable, and she declined a chest CT scan due to concerns about radiation; she was discharged on oral antibiotics. Three weeks later, her respiratory symptoms worsened; her leukocyte count was 12 × 10^3/μl, and she again declined CT imaging and received another course of oral antibiotics. One month later, she was admitted with hemoptysis and severe dyspnea. A chest radiograph showed a large airspace opacity in the right upper lobe. Chest CT revealed a mass-like consolidation in the right upper lobe measuring up to 9 cm in diameter and an additional 2.2 cm mass in the left lower lobe.

A 21-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with repeated vomiting, anuria, and abdominal and paracardiac pain since the morning after smoking more than 20 homemade cannabis joints the previous night. He had no fever. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative, and he had received a COVID-19 booster one week earlier without incident. On admission, blood pressure was 152/70 mm Hg; other vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed acute renal failure and an inflammatory syndrome; there was no peripheral eosinophilia. An abdominal and pelvic CT scan showed no acute pathology or urinary tract obstruction. A few hours after admission, his condition deteriorated with respiratory failure and hypoxemia accompanied by worsening abdominal pain, prompting transfer to the intensive care unit. A chest CT scan revealed bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities with ground-glass patches, regular septal thickenings, and bilateral pleural effusions; the cardiothoracic index was normal. Bronchoalveolar lavage demonstrated hypereosinophilia.

A 20-month-old boy with global developmental delay was transferred for worsening failure to thrive after inadequate caloric intake during a 3-day admission at an outside hospital. He was born at 39 weeks’ gestation, small for gestational age (birth weight 2.33 kg, second percentile), and had an unremarkable newborn screen. He sat at 6 months, cruised at 12 months, and at 20 months was unable to walk independently or speak. There was no history of diarrhea, constipation, recurrent vomiting, or seizures. Physical examination showed weight 7.4 kg (<third percentile), height 66 cm (<third percentile), head circumference 45 cm (<third percentile), and no dysmorphic features. Renal ultrasound and echocardiogram were normal; bone age was delayed by ~6 months. At 18 months, thyroid-stimulating hormone, free T4, random cortisol, insulin-like growth factor 1, and lead level were all within normal limits. Previous genetic tests included a normal karyotype and chromosomal microarray. On admission, a comprehensive metabolic panel was normal except for a persistently low serum creatinine (<0.06 mg/dL) and an elevated blood urea nitrogen (26 mg/dL). A nasogastric tube was placed for nutritional support. Medical Genetics was consulted, and a three-generation pedigree suggested maternal inheritance consistent with an X-linked or mitochondrial disorder. A urine creatine disorder panel was ordered.

A 67-year-old man presented after several recent falls and episodes of decreased consciousness. He was found to be profoundly hypoglycemic without prior history of such episodes. His medical history included hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, transient complete heart block, alcohol abuse, and Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome; he had no history of bariatric or other gastric surgery. Physical examination was unremarkable. He required a continuous intravenous infusion of 40% dextrose, subcutaneous octreotide, and oral dextrose tablets to maintain euglycemia. Laboratory studies during hypoglycemia revealed inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide levels and a negative plasma sulfonylurea screen. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a 2.2-cm arterially enhancing lesion in the tail of the pancreas, with no evidence of multifocal or metastatic disease on further imaging. On the basis of sustained hypoglycemia, inappropriate endogenous hyperinsulinemia, and a focal pancreatic lesion, a decision was made to proceed with distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy.

A 17-year-old nulliparous girl presented with disabling dysmenorrhea and cramping since age 16, refractory to analgesics and NSAIDs. Menarche occurred at 12 years; menstrual cycles are regular. She reports no dyspareunia or dyschezia. Physical examination revealed a painful mass in the left pelvic cavity. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, urinalysis, ESR, CEA, CA 15-3, and β-hCG, were normal; CA 125 was slightly elevated at 40 U/mL. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a well‐circumscribed mass in the outer left myometrium with a heterogeneous hypoechoic center and an annular vascular rim. Pelvic MRI on a 3T unit demonstrated a 30 mm intramyometrial lesion in the left uterine horn, separate from the endometrial cavity. The lesion had central heterogeneous hyperintensity on T1‐weighted images (suggesting hemorrhagic content) and was surrounded by a thick hypointense rim on T2‐weighted sequences. No other pelvic endometriotic lesions were identified. An incidental duplication of the right urinary system was noted on MR urography.

A 71-year-old man with hypertension underwent implantation of a 25-mm Carpentier-Edwards Perimount bovine pericardial aortic bioprosthesis in 2008 for aortic stenosis. At a routine evaluation in May 2020, the transvalvular velocity was 3.3 m/s, there was no aortic regurgitation, left ventricular ejection fraction was 57%, and diastolic diameter was 50 mm. In September 2020, he presented with several days of progressive dyspnea, fever, cough, and chest pain. On examination, temperature was 39.0 °C, blood pressure 145/60 mmHg, pulmonary rhonchi were present, and no cardiac murmur was heard. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 9.4 × 10^9/L (reference < 8.3), a procalcitonin level of 0.33 µg/L (reference < 0.5), and an N-terminal pro–brain natriuretic peptide level of 7220 ng/L (reference < 194). Chest CT demonstrated ground-glass opacities and consolidation in the right lung, with no pulmonary emboli. Multislice CT coronary angiography showed no coronary obstructions. SARS-CoV-2 RNA testing was negative, and blood cultures were negative. Antibiotic therapy was initiated for presumed pneumonia.

A 39-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 6-month history of gradual worsening of visual acuity in her left eye. Her medical history included thyroid hypoplasia treated with levothyroxine; she was a smoker and modestly overweight. Laboratory studies showed hypercholesterolemia (251 mg/dl) and positive CMV IgG, with normal C-reactive protein and thyroid function. Three years earlier, refraction was plano in the right eye and +0.25 sph + 0.25 cyl × 85° in the left. At presentation, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye (+0.50 sph) and 20/25 in the left eye (+2.50 sph). Anterior segments, pupillary reactions, extraocular movements, intraocular pressures, and exophthalmometry were normal bilaterally. Funduscopic examination revealed prominent choroidal folds in the left macular and perioptic region without papilledema; the right fundus was unremarkable. Structural OCT confirmed the folds, and B-scan ultrasonography excluded retrobulbar masses and showed no T-sign. Axial length was 23.91 mm in the right eye and 22.74 mm in the left; keratometry values were similar between eyes. Ishihara testing disclosed mild dyschromatopsia in the left eye. Humphrey visual field testing showed a modest peripapillary sensitivity reduction in the left eye. Orbital MRI demonstrated posterior flattening of the left globe, an enlarged perioptic subarachnoid space (optic nerve sheath diameter, 0.67 cm vs. 0.60 cm in the right), and a “V” sign at the base of the posterior flattening. Enhanced-depth OCT revealed similar subfoveal choroidal thickness bilaterally (218 μm right, 214 μm left) but increased peripapillary choroidal thickness in the left eye (138 μm vs. 91 μm). A neurologic evaluation was unremarkable.

A 58-year-old man was brought to the trauma center after a high-speed motor-vehicle collision. He was intubated at the scene following a prolonged extrication and arrived unresponsive with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3 T. On admission he was hypotensive. A focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) was negative for intra-abdominal blood, but the left upper quadrant view showed a large left hemothorax. A left-sided chest tube was placed, yielding 900 mL of blood initially and an additional 200 mL per hour over the next 2 hours. Given the ongoing hemorrhage and resuscitation requirements, the patient was taken emergently to the operating room for exploration.

A 28-year-old man with no past medical or family history presented for elective enucleation of a mandibular cyst. Preoperative laboratory tests, including an electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, and serum biochemistry, were within normal limits. General anesthesia was induced with propofol (2 mg/kg) and fentanyl (2 μg/kg), and rocuronium (0.5 mg/kg) facilitated intubation. Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane in an oxygen/air mixture, and the patient was mechanically ventilated to maintain an end-tidal CO2 of 35–40 mmHg. Intraoperative medications included cefazolin, granisetron, dexamethasone, morphine, paracetamol, and lornoxicam. At the end of surgery, neuromuscular blockade was reversed with sugammadex, and the trachea was extubated. 

In the postanesthesia care unit (PACU), his vital signs remained stable, and oxygen was delivered via facemask at 6 L/min. Ten minutes after arrival, he became alert and then experienced a myoclonic jerk lasting 45 minutes, involving the upper trunk and left arm, with intact orientation and ability to follow commands. Fifteen minutes later, a similar episode recurred and ceased after administration of intravenous propofol (40 mg). A third episode occurred 30 minutes after arrival. Forty-five minutes after arrival, a neurologist found no abnormalities other than involuntary movements of the left shoulder and upper arm and considered a partial seizure. Electroencephalography (EEG) and laboratory studies, including electrolytes and biochemistry, were normal. The patient was transferred to the ward; the myoclonus did not recur, and he was discharged on postoperative day 2 without sequelae.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of fever, chills, night sweats, diarrhea, and painful oral lesions. She underwent liver transplantation 8 years earlier for biliary cirrhosis and has been maintained on prednisone 5 mg/day and mycophenolate sodium 360 mg/day. Three months after transplantation she had a cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection treated successfully with ganciclovir. 

Oral examination revealed three well-defined shallow ulcerative lesions covered by fibrin with regular erythematous borders: one 1 cm lesion on the hard palate; a 0.5 cm lesion on the vestibular and palatal gingiva between teeth 16 and 17; and a 1.0 cm lesion on the left soft palate near the uvula. 

Given her immunosuppression and history of CMV, the leading diagnoses were CMV reactivation or herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. Exfoliative cytology of the lesions and an anti-CMV immunoglobulin G test were performed, and she was started on ganciclovir 300 mg three times daily. After 7 days there was no clinical improvement, and both cytology and serology results were negative. A chest radiograph was normal.

Because of persistent oral lesions and ongoing diarrhea, two incisional biopsies of the oral ulcers (gingiva and palate) were obtained, and a colonoscopy with biopsy of a rectal lesion was performed. Colonoscopy showed areas of inflammatory change with mucosal erosion and an extensive 2 cm ulcer on the descending colon extending to the rectum.

A 29-year-old nulliparous woman with a consanguineous partner was referred at 21 weeks’ gestation for evaluation of fetal renal anomalies. Detailed obstetrical ultrasound showed placenta praevia, bilaterally large undifferentiated hyperechoic kidneys with multiple corticomedullary micrometric cysts, and a markedly hyperechoic liver with tiny bile-containing cystic structures. Fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume were normal. The patient declined amniocentesis; carrier testing for PKHD1 was negative.

At 25 weeks, ultrasound demonstrated a narrow fetal thorax, and oligohydramnios developed by 27 weeks. At 29 weeks, imaging revealed an enlarged cavum vergae and an unusually trabeculated subarachnoid space. A cesarean delivery was performed at 36 weeks for placenta praevia; the male infant weighed 3050 g and had Apgar scores of 7, 7, and 7.

The infant developed respiratory distress with respiratory acidosis and was transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit. Cerebral sonography suggested abnormal gyration, and echocardiography showed a large secundum atrial septal defect with bidirectional shunting and an atrial septal aneurysm. Postnatal renal ultrasonography confirmed numerous predominantly cortical and subcortical microcysts. The infant experienced seizures and both pulmonary and intracranial hemorrhages. Over the next two days, he had persistent primary metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia and hyperlactatemia in the absence of hypoglycemia.

An 11-year-old girl was admitted with a one-week history of redness and photophobia in the left eye, which progressed to pain on eye movement, periorbital swelling, and erythema. She had normal vital signs. On examination, there was erythema and swelling around the left eye, painful and limited globe movements, and visual acuity of 5/10 in the left eye versus 10/10 in the right; the remainder of the cranial-nerve and systemic examination was normal. She was diagnosed with preseptal cellulitis and treated with intravenous clindamycin. A computed tomography scan of the orbits showed no evidence of orbital cellulitis. After 3 days without clinical improvement, ophthalmology consultation was obtained. Slit-lamp and fundus examination revealed diffuse choroiditis (posterior uveitis) in the left eye. Ocular ultrasonography demonstrated increased posterior scleral wall thickness (2.4 mm) and a classic T-sign, confirming episcleritis. A rheumatology consultation was recommended.
