A 47-year-old man with no prior medical or surgical history and no tobacco, alcohol, or drug use presented with a 4-month history of a slowly enlarging abdominal mass in the epigastrium. He denied weight loss, fever, night sweats, changes in bowel habits, anorexia, or vomiting. He appeared well; vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, there was a firm, immobile, tender mass measuring approximately 10 cm × 5 cm in the epigastric region. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 000/µL (normal range 4000–11 000/µL) and a C-reactive protein level of 220 mg/L (normal range 0–3 mg/L). Colonoscopy revealed no abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated a large heterogeneous mass within the anterior abdominal wall, measuring 10 cm in greatest diameter, with extensive inflammatory changes in the surrounding fat and regular thickening of the transverse colon. MRI of the abdomen confirmed an infiltrative mass adherent to the posterior rectus sheath, the transverse colon, and the stomach, with no evidence of a colonic fistula. A multidisciplinary team decided to proceed with surgical resection of the mass.

A 7-day-old girl was admitted with moaning and fever. She was born at 42 + 1 weeks’ gestation, with an uneventful perinatal course and an Apgar score of 9/10. On admission, her only abnormal finding was tachypnoea. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 95 mg/l (normal, 0–10 mg/l), a white-blood-cell count of 15,800/μl (normal, 5,000–21,000/μl) with 11% banded neutrophils (normal, 0–4%), and a platelet count of 21,000/μl (normal, 150,000–450,000/μl). Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (gentamicin and amoxicillin/clavulanic acid) were initiated. Blood cultures grew Escherichia coli; antibiotics were narrowed to amoxicillin alone. Clinical and laboratory parameters normalized, and she was discharged after 17 days on oral antibiotics for two more weeks.

Seventeen days after discharge, routine follow-up showed a rise in inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 194 mg/l; white-blood-cell count, 29,800/μl with 4% banded neutrophils), but she had no clinical symptoms and her examination was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 4.0 cm hypoechoic mass in the left upper quadrant between the upper pole of the left kidney and the stomach. Antigranulocyte antibody scintigraphy with 99mTc-sulesomab demonstrated a photopenic area surrounded by a rim of increased uptake in the same location, suggesting an abscess.

A two‐month‐old boy presented with chronic vomiting and up to 20 watery diarrheal stools per day since the second week of life, associated with fever, failure to thrive, and sepsis. He was born at term to non‐consanguineous parents; family history was non‐contributory. Mixed breast and formula feeding was tolerated until onset of symptoms. Initial treatment with broad‐spectrum antibiotics and transition to amino acid–based formula yielded no improvement. Diarrhea progressed to mucoid stools, and severe eczema developed on the perioral region, palms, and back. He required parenteral nutrition for malnutrition and underwent treatment for central‐line Staphylococcus aureus sepsis.

Laboratory evaluation revealed moderate anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia (1.73 g/dL), normal enzymatic liver and kidney function tests, normal serum IgG, IgA, and IgM, and markedly elevated total IgE (>2000 g/L) with specific IgE for cow’s milk (18.2 KUI/L, class IV) and multiple food allergens. Hormonal studies showed normal pancreatic function, low TSH, elevated anti‐thyroid peroxidase antibody, and low C4 complement. Repeated stool bacterial, viral, and parasitic studies were negative. Flow cytometry demonstrated low CD19+ B cells with normal numbers of CD3+ T cells and CD56+CD16+ NK cells.

At four months of age, combined upper and lower endoscopy showed:  
• Duodenal mucosa with severe villous architectural alteration, mild‐to‐moderate lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, mild cryptitis, intraepithelial lymphocytes, 100 eosinophils per high‐power field (HPF), and lamina propria fibrosis.  
• Gastric mucosa with mild chronic gastritis, up to 5 eosinophils per HPF, and lymphoid aggregates.  
• Colonic mucosa with architectural distortion, mucinous damage, glandular atrophy, chronic inflammation with fibrosis, and 10–30 eosinophils per HPF.  

Immunohistochemistry revealed a predominantly CD3+ T‐cell infiltrate with similar distribution of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and scattered CD38+ plasma cells. Given early‐onset refractory diarrhea, eczema, autoimmunity, and abnormal immunologic findings, a primary immunodeficiency was suspected, and a blood sample was sent for detailed T-cell subset phenotyping.

A 36-year-old man with stage IV poorly differentiated lung adenocarcinoma and known brain metastases was admitted after a fall and progressive lethargy. On admission, his serum calcium was 21.3 mg/dL (reference 8.9–10.3), ionized calcium 2.72 mmol/L (1.0–1.25), serum phosphorus 1.3 mg/dL (2.4–4.7), and creatinine 1.30 mg/dL (0.64–1.27). Electrocardiogram showed a shortened QT interval. Three weeks prior, his calcium levels were normal; ten days prior, his renal function was normal, and he received his first chemotherapy. 

Initial management included aggressive IV fluids, calcitonin, and zoledronic acid (4 mg IV on hospital days 1 and 9). After the first dose of zoledronic acid, calcium nadired at 11.0 mg/dL on day 7 but rebounded to 12.8 mg/dL by day 9. Further evaluation revealed PTH levels of 33.2, 55.4, and 133.0 pmol/L (reference 1.3–6.8) on hospital days 2, 6, and 9, respectively. On day 4, 25-hydroxyvitamin D was 7 ng/mL (25–80) and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D was 14 pg/mL (15–75); PTHrP was 8.2 pmol/mL (0–2.3). 

Neck MRI, 99mTc-sestamibi scan, and ultrasound showed no parathyroid adenoma. Imaging demonstrated widespread abdominal metastases with small lytic bone lesions. Pathology from a resected brain metastasis stained negative for PTH but positive for PTHrP. On hospital day 12, a single dose of denosumab (120 mg) normalized his serum calcium.

A 23-year-old man presented with sudden onset of severe frontal headache of 2 hours’ duration associated with nausea, vomiting, and chest heaviness. He had no significant past medical history, denied illicit drug use, but reported a 23–pack-year history of smoking. On examination, he was distressed but alert and oriented. Neck stiffness and dilated reactive pupils were noted; there were no focal neurologic deficits. His blood pressure was 178/103 mmHg, heart rate 87 bpm, respiratory rate 26/min, temperature 38.9 °C, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. An ECG showed >2 mm of ST-segment elevation in leads V2 through V5. Initial high-sensitivity troponin was 1.48 mg/dL (normal <0.16 mg/dL). He was taken for percutaneous coronary intervention, which revealed normal coronary arteries with TIMI flow grade 3. A post-angiography ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal ventricular function without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 17.9×10^3/µL with lymphocytosis, platelets of 123×10^3/µL, and a C-reactive protein level of 12 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L).

A 47-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a left-sided neck mass and ipsilateral headache. She denied fever, myalgia, sore throat, or head and neck trauma. Neurological and general physical examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 18 mm/h and a C-reactive protein level of 0.2 mg/dL (both within normal limits). Carotid ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic soft‐tissue mass encircling the upper half of the left common carotid artery, with mild luminal narrowing but without accelerated blood flow. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck demonstrated a circumferential soft‐tissue halo around the left common carotid artery and bulb from D1 to just below the bifurcation at C5, measuring up to 12 mm in thickness anteriorly, without luminal distortion or an intimal flap. The perivascular tissue was hypointense on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and showed homogeneous enhancement on fat-saturated postcontrast T1-weighted images; there was no intramural hemorrhage, and fast spin-echo T2-weighted images were otherwise unremarkable. A small right‐sided level II lymph node was also noted.

An 80-year-old woman presented with 2 weeks of worsening back pain, 5 days of dyspnea on exertion, and fever. Two days before admission, she had transient unconsciousness and a temperature of 40°C. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes; she was a passive smoker on oral antidiabetic therapy and had no prior autoimmune or hematologic disorders.

On examination, she was alert but dyspneic without chest pain. Temperature was 38.2°C; blood pressure, 106/72 mmHg; pulse, 110 bpm; oxygen saturation, 90% on room air. Findings included bilateral pulmonary crackles, a II/VI systolic apical murmur, jugular venous distension, jaundice, and petechiae and purpura on the toes. Neurologic exam was nonfocal.

Laboratory studies showed platelet count 13 × 10^3/μL, estimated glomerular filtration rate 22 mL/min/1.73 m^2, total bilirubin 7.3 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 812 IU/L, brain natriuretic peptide 1306 pg/mL, creatine kinase 411 IU/L, CK-MB 40 IU/L, and troponin I 19 966 pg/mL. Haptoglobin was undetectable; D-dimer was 33.9 μg/mL; coagulation studies were near normal.

Chest radiograph revealed bilateral congestion. ECG showed ST-segment depression in leads V5 and V6 with sinus tachycardia at 105 bpm. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 50% with inferior-posterior wall hypokinesis. Chest CT demonstrated pulmonary congestion without focal infection. Brain CT and MRI showed no intracranial hemorrhage or infarction.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 10-year history of daily headaches. Her past medical history was notable for migraine. She reported that her headaches worsened upon standing and improved when she lay down. An MRI of the head demonstrated downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils more than 3 mm below the foramen magnum.

A 25-year-old man presented with painful sores on the upper and lower lips, worsened by eating and talking. Four days earlier, he noted “canker sores” in the oral cavity, and two days later similar lesions appeared on the lips. He had had a fever about one week before the onset of the oral lesions. He initially applied petroleum jelly without relief, then used triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% in orabase once daily, with partial improvement of the intraoral ulcers but persistence of the lip lesions. He denied use of other medications, allergies, systemic disease, alcohol use, or smoking, but reported frequent lip licking and poor nutrition. No lesions were present on other parts of the body.

On examination, vital signs were normal and no lymphadenopathy was noted. The lips bore serosanguineous crusts that were tender and bled easily. Intraoral examination showed erythematous, irregular lesions with diffuse borders on the upper and lower labial mucosa. A white hyperkeratotic plaque that could not be scraped off was present on the left buccal mucosa. A removable yellowish-white plaque was seen on the dorsal tongue without underlying erythema, and there were scalloped lateral tongue margins. A painless 2×1×0.5 cm hard nodule lay midline on the hard palate. Oral hygiene was poor with multiple carious, endodontic, and edentulous sites.

Psychological assessment (DASS-21) was normal. Based on history and clinical examination, the working diagnosis was suspected herpes-associated erythema multiforme (HAEM). The differential diagnosis for the lip lesions included exfoliative cheilitis, which lacks herpes virus involvement. Serological testing for anti–HSV-1 IgG was indicated to confirm the diagnosis.

A 59-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder, hepatitis C, prior substance use disorder, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus, residing in a tertiary mental health facility, underwent evaluation for asymptomatic hyponatremia. A CT scan of the chest and head demonstrated a small pericardial effusion. No further investigations were documented at that time.

Seven months later, she developed a fever. Chest radiography revealed enlargement of the pericardial silhouette, and transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a small-to-moderate pericardial effusion without an apparent cause. She denied chest or abdominal pain, dyspnea, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, appetite changes, recent illness, or infectious contacts. Her medications included antihypertensive, antihyperglycemic, and antipsychotic agents. She was a current smoker and had a remote history of cocaine, amphetamine, marijuana, and opioid use.

On examination, she was afebrile, normotensive, and not jaundiced. The abdomen was soft and non-tender without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 71.1 mg/L (normal <7.5), white blood cell count 12.6 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0), hemoglobin 92 g/L (115–160), and sodium 133 mmol/L (135–145). Other electrolytes, renal function, and liver function tests were unremarkable. The patient denied any recent foreign-body ingestion; however, records indicated that two years earlier she had undergone esophagogastroduodenoscopy for removal of a 10 cm felt pen from the stomach fundus to antrum.

One week after the echocardiogram, a CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed interval enlargement of the pericardial effusion. Incidentally, there were lobulated complex fluid collections with peripheral enhancement in the left lobe of the liver, consistent with a hepatic abscess.

A 51-year-old woman with fibromyalgia, right-sided sciatica, DVT, asthma, nephrolithiasis, vertigo, and oral/genital herpes returned from the Dominican Republic with a 10-day history of progressive lower extremity sensory changes and weakness. She had transient bilateral arm pain with neck and head pressure before onset of leg symptoms. She reported one day of urinary hesitancy and described “leg heaviness,” worse on the right, causing a fall without loss of consciousness. Vital signs were normal. Examination showed bilateral knee flexor/extensor strength 3/5, dysesthesia to touch and pinprick from mid-thigh distally, absent knee reflexes, and bilateral Babinski signs without clonus. A bladder scan excluded significant retention. MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine was performed. Laboratory studies showed WBC 5.1×10^3 cells/mL, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 371×10^3 cells/mL, eosinophils 5.7%, normal metabolic panel, vitamin B12 290 pg/mL, ESR 30.9 mm/h, CRP 5.9 mg/L; CPK, aldolase, methylmalonic acid, Lyme titers, copper level, and SSA/SSB were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture yielded CSF with WBC 360 cells/mL (100% lymphocytes), protein 182 mg/dL, and no albumin-cytologic dissociation. An initial EMG study during the first week was unremarkable.

A 70-year-old woman was referred after her optometrist noted left optic disc edema on routine examination. Her history included metastatic small-cell lung cancer diagnosed 1 year earlier, treated with six cycles of carboplatin and etoposide 6 months prior, chest radiation, and maintenance atezolizumab. Other medical conditions included idiopathic thrombocytopenia, asthma, Crohn’s disease, gastroesophageal reflux, restless leg syndrome, and dyslipidemia; medications included gabapentin, pantoprazole, ferrous fumarate, rosuvastatin, and pramipexole.

At neuro-ophthalmology consultation she denied blurred vision, eye pain, or headache. Visual acuity was 20/25 in both eyes, pupils were equally reactive with no relative afferent pupillary defect, and Humphrey 24-2 visual fields were normal bilaterally. Dilated fundus examination showed a normal right optic nerve and left optic disc edema. OCT of the retinal nerve fiber layer revealed thickness of 107 μm in the right eye and 356 μm in the left eye. High-definition OCT over the optic nerve showed no signs of vitreopapillary traction.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 43 mm/h and a normal C-reactive protein level of 4.5 mg/L. The patient had no symptoms suggestive of giant cell arteritis. To exclude other causes of optic disc edema, she underwent MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast and MR venography of the head, which showed no orbital masses, no leptomeningeal disease, no dural venous sinus thrombosis, and no signs of raised intracranial pressure such as an empty sella or transverse sinus stenosis. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 14 cm H2O, one nucleated cell, and normal protein and glucose.

A 62-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B and treated hepatocellular carcinoma (segment VIII) underwent microwave ablation. Six months later, he presented with a 2-week history of shortness of breath, productive cough, and right-sided chest pain. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 37 mm/h (reference 0–10 mm/h), AST 30 U/L, ALT 33 U/L, and negative tuberculosis, fungal, and sputum cultures. Bronchoscopy was performed and was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated a fluid attenuation biloma at the prior ablation site with a tract extending cranially through the diaphragm into the right lower pleural space, accompanied by a right anterior basal mass-like consolidation. This imaging raised concern for a thoracobiliary fistula.

A 57-year-old woman reported a year-long history of progressive fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, and declining concentration attributed to work stress. Over the past four weeks, she developed apathy, mutism, fluctuating confusion, amnesia, disorganization, and urinary incontinence, prompting hospital admission.

On examination she was bradycardic and hypothermic, with dry skin, delayed relaxation of tendon reflexes, myalgias, and a small pericardial effusion. Laboratory tests revealed severe hypothyroidism (high TSH, low free T4), elevated AST and creatine kinase, hypercholesterolemia, and macrocytic anemia despite normal serum vitamins B1, B6, B9, B12, methylmalonic acid, and holotranscobalamin; homocysteine was mildly elevated. Serum anti–thyroid peroxidase antibodies were markedly elevated and anti–TSH receptor antibodies were also elevated; thyroid ultrasound showed gland atrophy.

Brain MRI demonstrated scattered T2-hyperintense white-matter lesions in the temporal lobes and the EEG showed diffuse slowing. CSF analysis revealed elevated protein, S-100 protein, and neuron-specific enolase without pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands; anti–thyroid peroxidase antibodies were detected in CSF. Infectious studies (viral, bacterial, and spirochetal serologies), paraneoplastic and autoimmune synaptic antibody panels, toxicology screens, and systemic immunologic studies were unremarkable. Other limbic encephalopathies, paraneoplastic, infectious, metabolic, or toxic causes were excluded.

A 79-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation (on aspirin), type 2 diabetes mellitus, well-controlled asthma, and hypertension, who tested positive for COVID-19 one month earlier, presented with progressive bilateral lower-extremity edema and dyspnea over one month. He reported two-pillow orthopnea but denied chest pain, fever, cough, or gastrointestinal symptoms. On examination, vital signs were normal; there were bibasilar crackles, jugular venous distention to 9 cm, and 2+ pitting edema of the legs. Laboratory evaluation showed a pro–B-type natriuretic peptide level of 8458 pg/mL (previously 3301 pg/mL) and an unremarkable D-dimer. A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities, pulmonary congestion, and interposition of the right hepatic flexure of the colon between the subdiaphragmatic space and the right dome of the liver (Chilaiditi’s sign), which was not present on a radiograph one month earlier. Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation without ischemic changes. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 40% (down from 70% one year prior), normal right ventricular size, reduced right ventricular contractility, and a dilated right atrium. A CT scan of the chest without contrast, performed to exclude pulmonary embolism, showed no embolus. 

He was admitted for presumed decompensated heart failure and received IV furosemide, with a net negative fluid balance of 6.8 L over 48 hours. Home medications were resumed. After three days, he achieved euvolemia, with resolution of edema and improvement in jugular venous pressure. However, he continued to experience dyspnea and developed mild pleuritic chest pain in the right subcostal region, without hypoxemia or fever.

A 30-year-old woman presented with 1-month history of gradually progressive dull aching pain and swelling of the left knee and calf, aggravated by rest and activity, associated with night pain and low-grade evening fever. Over the past week, she developed difficulty walking, particularly tiptoe stand, and inability to squat. She reported anorexia and unquantified weight loss but denied small or large joint pain elsewhere, low back pain, morning stiffness, urinary symptoms, trauma, respiratory symptoms, or known tuberculosis exposure. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, she appeared ill and anemic. Vital signs were normal. The left calf was markedly swollen, firm, erythematous, and tender; the left knee had global swelling, mild erythema, warmth, a tender Baker's cyst on the posteromedial aspect, painful and restricted range of motion, and weak left plantar flexion (MRC grade 3/5). Peripheral pulses were intact; no lymphadenopathy. Initial blood tests showed anemia, elevated ESR and CRP, and neutrophilic leukocytosis. Ultrasound demonstrated a large hypoechoic fluid collection in the calf extending from a suprapatellar effusion. Under ultrasound guidance, 60 mL of serosanguinous fluid was aspirated from the calf and 20 mL from the knee. Synovial fluid analysis revealed: WBC 13,650 /mm3 (92% neutrophils), protein 4.2 g/dL, glucose 41 mg/dL, adenosine deaminase 96 U/L; Gram stain showed no organisms, cultures were negative, AFB smear was negative.
